simple_explanation: To know the meaning of something clearly. When information makes sense to you and you can explain it back, you understand it.
example_2: Please explain it again — I don't understand.
example_3: She understands three languages fluently.
collocations: understand clearly, fully understand, hard to understand, understand the point
related_phrasal_verbs: get across, figure out, catch on
action_sequence: Before: hear something confusing → During: think and ask a question → After: the idea makes sense: 'Now I understand.'
grammar_pattern: understand + noun/clause (I understand the rule / I understand why you left.)
common_mistake: I am understanding the problem.
correct_version: I understand the problem.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Understand' is a state verb (a state of mind, not an action), so it normally isn't used in the -ing form.
pronunciation_tip: The middle "der" is a quick, unstressed schwa — don't linger on it.
spelling_tip: "Under" + "stand" — two words you already know, joined.
etymology: Old English "understandan" (under + standan, literally "to stand among/near" → to grasp mentally).
prefix_root_suffix: under- = beneath/among + stand = to be positioned
mnemonic: To UNDERSTAND something, you mentally STAND UNDER it and see how it's built.
memory_trick: When something finally makes sense, say 'Got it, I understand' out loud — it ties the word to the feeling of clarity.
visual_association: A lightbulb switching on above someone's head.
emotion_feel: Neutral (relief when it happens, frustration when it doesn't)
difference_explained: Know = you have the information. Understand = you see how or why it works. You can know a rule without understanding it.
mini_conversation:
A: Can you repeat that, please?
B: Sure — do you understand it better now?
everyday_scene: Everyday: A teacher pauses and asks the class, “Does everyone understand so far?”
news_style_line: News-style: “Researchers still don't fully understand how the virus spreads indoors.”
casual_conversation: Casual: “Wait, I don't understand — can you explain that part again?”
mcq_options: A) To ignore  B) To grasp the meaning of  C) To forget  D) To argue
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: I didn't ______ the instructions, so I asked again. → understand
find_and_fix_to_correct: She don't understand the joke. → She doesn't understand the joke.
translate: मुझे यह बात समझ नहीं आई। → I didn't understand this.
write_your_own_sentence: Write one sentence about a subject you understand well now but found hard before.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to know the meaning of something clearly'?
usage_tip: 'Sorry, I didn't understand — could you repeat that?' is polite and natural in class or at work.

simple_explanation: To fail to remember something. When a memory slips away and you can't bring it back to mind, you forget it.
example_2: I always forget people's names right after meeting them.
example_3: He forgot to call his mother back.
collocations: forget completely, easily forget, forget on purpose, never forget
action_sequence: Before: plan to call a friend → During: get busy with other work → After: realise: 'I forgot to call!'
grammar_pattern: forget + to-infinitive (a future action) vs. forget + -ing (a past action): "I forgot to lock it" vs "I'll never forget locking myself out."
common_mistake: I forgot to locked the door.
correct_version: I forgot to lock the door.
why_it_s_wrong: After 'forgot to', use the base verb (lock), not the past form (locked).
pronunciation_tip: The first syllable reduces to "fer", not a full "for".
spelling_tip: Double the T before -ting/-ten: forgetting, forgotten.
etymology: Old English "forgietan" (for- = away/completely + gietan = to grasp) — to lose one's grasp of something.
prefix_root_suffix: for- = away/completely + get = to obtain, grasp
mnemonic: FOR-GET = you reach FOR something to GET it back, but it's gone from memory.
memory_trick: Every night, say one thing you almost forgot today: 'I almost forgot to…'.
visual_association: A thought bubble popping like a soap bubble.
difference_explained: With a place, use leave: 'I left my phone at home.' Forget is for the thing or the action: 'I forgot my phone.'
mini_conversation:
A: Where's your umbrella?
B: Oh no, I forgot it at home again.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character pats their pockets and says, “Wait — I think I forgot my phone!”
news_style_line: News-style: “Many commuters forget to renew their transit passes before the deadline.”
casual_conversation: Casual: “Sorry I'm late — I completely forgot about the meeting.”
mcq_options: A) Remember  B) Forgive  C) Forbid  D) Forge
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Please don't ______ to bring your ID card tomorrow. → forget
find_and_fix_to_correct: I am forgetting my password every week. → I forget my password every week.
translate: मैं अक्सर उसका नाम भूल जाता हूँ। → I often forget his/her name.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something you once forgot to take to school or work.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to fail to remember something'?
usage_tip: 'Forget to do' = you didn't do it. 'Forget doing' = you did it but have no memory of it.

simple_explanation: To choose something firmly after thinking about it. When you weigh your options and finally pick one, you decide.
example_2: They decided to move to a new city.
example_3: I can't decide which shirt to buy.
collocations: decide quickly, hard to decide, decide against, finally decide
related_phrasal_verbs: settle on, make up one's mind
action_sequence: Before: look at two options → During: compare and think → After: choose one: 'I decided to take the job.'
grammar_pattern: decide + to-infinitive (I decided to leave) or decide + wh-clause (I decided what to wear).
common_mistake: I decided going to the party.
correct_version: I decided to go to the party.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Decide' is followed by 'to + base verb', not the -ing form.
etymology: Latin "decidere" (de- = off + caedere = to cut) — literally "to cut off" other options.
mnemonic: To DECIDE is to "cut off" every other option, like cutting a path with a knife (Latin caedere = to cut).
memory_trick: DE-CIDE sounds like 'the side' — you pick one side.
visual_association: A fork in the road with a signpost.
emotion_feel: Neutral (can carry tension before, relief after)
difference_explained: Choose = pick from options (choose a shirt). Decide = make up your mind, often about an action (decide to leave).
mini_conversation:
A: Have you decided on a restaurant?
B: Yes, let's decide on the Italian place.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character stares at two doors and finally says, “Okay, I've decided — I'm going through this one.”
news_style_line: News-style: “The committee is expected to decide on the new policy by Friday.”
casual_conversation: Casual: “I still haven't decided what to order.”
mcq_options: A) Delay  B) Choose  C) Deny  D) Divide
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: We haven't ______ where to go for vacation yet. → decided
find_and_fix_to_correct: She decide to leave early. → She decided to leave early.
translate: हमने कल जाने का फैसला किया। → We decided to go tomorrow.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a decision you made this year using 'decided to'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to choose something firmly after thinking about it'?
usage_tip: 'I've decided to…' announces a firm plan. 'I can't decide' is common when choosing.

simple_explanation: To make something clear or easy to understand. When you describe something step by step so another person understands it, you explain it.
example_2: The teacher explained the rule with an example.
example_3: I can't explain why I feel this way.
collocations: explain clearly, explain in detail, fully explain, hard to explain
related_phrasal_verbs: spell out, break down, walk through
action_sequence: Before: someone is confused → During: break the idea into simple steps → After: they understand
grammar_pattern: explain + noun (explain the rule) / explain + that-clause / explain + to + person (explain it to me).
common_mistake: Explain me the rule.
correct_version: Explain the rule to me.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Explain' does not take the person straight after it. Say: explain something TO someone.
pronunciation_tip: The "x" sounds like "ks", blending into the following "pl".
spelling_tip: Ends in -ain, like "plain" and "main" (all from the same Latin root, planus).
etymology: Latin "explanare" (ex- = out + planus = flat/plain) — to make something flat/clear.
mnemonic: To EXplain is to lay something out flat and PLAIN so everyone can see it clearly.
memory_trick: EX-PLAIN: make it 'plain' — simple and clear.
visual_association: A hand pointing at a whiteboard diagram.
difference_explained: Tell takes a person directly: 'Tell me the rule.' Explain needs 'to': 'Explain the rule to me.'
mini_conversation:
A: I'm confused about this step.
B: Let me explain it again, slowly.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A detective gathers everyone and says, “Let me explain exactly what happened.”
news_style_line: News-style: “Officials explained the new traffic rules at a press briefing today.”
casual_conversation: Casual: “I don't get it — can you explain that one more time?”
mcq_options: A) Hide information  B) Make something clear  C) Argue loudly  D) Ask a question
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Could you ______ how this machine works? → explain
find_and_fix_to_correct: He explained me the situation. → He explained the situation to me.
translate: कृपया मुझे यह नियम समझाइए। → Please explain this rule to me.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence asking a teacher or senior to explain something to you.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to make something clear or easy to understand'?
usage_tip: 'Could you explain what this means?' is a polite way to ask for help.

simple_explanation: To reach a place after traveling. The moment your journey ends and you get to your destination, you arrive.
example_2: We arrived at the airport two hours early.
example_3: What time does your flight arrive?
collocations: arrive on time, arrive late, newly arrived, arrive safely
related_phrasal_verbs: show up, turn up, get in
action_sequence: Before: travel on the bus → During: reach the stop → After: walk in: 'I arrived at 9.'
grammar_pattern: arrive at (a small/specific place) vs. arrive in (a city/country): "arrive at the station", "arrive in Delhi."
common_mistake: I arrived to the hotel at noon.
correct_version: I arrived at the hotel at noon.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'arrive at' for a building or small place and 'arrive in' for a city or country — never 'arrive to'.
pronunciation_tip: The first syllable is a light schwa — almost swallowed.
etymology: Old French "ariver", from Latin "ad ripam" (to the shore) — originally "to reach the shore."
mnemonic: Long ago, to ARRIVE meant to reach the RIVer's shore — both words share that Latin "riv" root.
memory_trick: You arrive AT the station and IN the city: small place AT, big place IN.
visual_association: A suitcase being set down at a front door.
difference_explained: Reach takes a direct object: 'I reached the office.' Arrive needs at/in: 'I arrived at the office.' Never 'reached to'.
mini_conversation:
A: Has the bus arrived yet?
B: Not yet, it should arrive in five minutes.
everyday_scene: Everyday: An announcer's voice echoes, “Flight 204 has now arrived at gate 12.”
news_style_line: News-style: “Relief supplies finally arrived in the flood-hit village this morning.”
casual_conversation: Casual: “Text me the moment you arrive, okay?”
mcq_options: A) Depart  B) Arrange  C) Approve  D) Argue
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Our guests will ______ around 7 p.m. tonight. → arrive
find_and_fix_to_correct: They arrived to school late. → They arrived at school late.
translate: हम शाम को स्टेशन पहुँचे। → We arrived at the station in the evening.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about when you arrived at school, college or office today.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to reach a place after traveling'?
usage_tip: 'Arrive home' needs no preposition: 'I arrived home late.'

simple_explanation: To pick one thing out of several options. When you're given options and you select the one you want, you choose.
example_2: You may choose one dessert from the menu.
example_3: It's hard to choose between the two jobs.
collocations: choose wisely, choose between, free to choose, carefully choose
related_phrasal_verbs: pick out, go with, opt for
action_sequence: Before: see several options → During: compare them → After: pick one: 'I chose the blue one.'
grammar_pattern: Irregular verb: choose – chose – chosen. choose + to-infinitive (chose to stay) or choose + between/among.
common_mistake: I choosed the blue one.
correct_version: I chose the blue one.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Choose' is irregular: the past is 'chose', not 'choosed'.
pronunciation_tip: Long "oo" sound, soft "ch" at the start.
spelling_tip: Past tense changes the spelling entirely: choose → chose → chosen.
etymology: Old English "ceosan" — a very old Germanic word for selecting.
word_family: choice (n.), choosy (adj., informal), chosen (adj., as in "the chosen path")
mnemonic: CHOOSE rhymes with SHOES — imagine standing in a shoe shop, having to CHOOSE one pair.
memory_trick: Double O = two options to look at: chOOse. One O in the past: chOse.
visual_association: A hand hovering between two doors, about to pick one.
emotion_feel: Neutral (can carry pressure when the choice is hard)
difference_explained: Choose (/tʃuːz/, rhymes with 'news') is present. Chose (/tʃəʊz/, rhymes with 'rose') is past.
mini_conversation:
A: Which flavor do you want?
B: I'll choose chocolate, please.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character faces two paths and says, “I have to choose — there's no going back now.”
news_style_line: News-style: “Voters will choose their next representative on election day.”
casual_conversation: Casual: “Just choose whichever one you like — I'm easy either way.”
mcq_options: A) Choosed  B) Chose  C) Choosen  D) Chosen
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Please ______ a seat near the window. → choose
find_and_fix_to_correct: She choose the red dress yesterday. → She chose the red dress yesterday.
translate: आप कोई भी रंग चुन सकते हैं। → You can choose any color.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something you chose recently (a phone, a course, a dish).
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to pick one thing out of several options'?
usage_tip: 'You can choose any one' is common in shops and forms. Also: 'choose between A and B'.

simple_explanation: To keep something in your mind, or bring it back to mind. When a memory stays with you, or comes back to you when needed, you remember it.
example_2: Do you remember our first meeting?
example_3: I can't remember where I put my glasses.
collocations: vaguely remember, remember clearly, hard to remember, remember fondly
related_phrasal_verbs: bring to mind, look back on
action_sequence: Before: something happens → During: time passes → After: it comes back to mind: 'I remember that day.'
grammar_pattern: remember + to-infinitive (a future task) vs. remember + -ing (a past event): "remember to call" vs "remember calling."
common_mistake: I remember to meet him last year.
correct_version: I remember meeting him last year.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Remember + -ing' is for a past memory. 'Remember + to' is for a task you still have to do.
pronunciation_tip: Three clear syllables — don't drop the middle "mem".
spelling_tip: "Re" + "member" — think of remembering as calling a MEMBER of your memory back.
etymology: Latin "re-" (again) + "memor" (mindful) — to be mindful again of something.
mnemonic: RE-MEMBER = to put a MEMBER (a piece) of the past back together in your mind again.
memory_trick: RE-MEMBER: bring a 'member' of your past back into your thoughts.
visual_association: An old photograph being pulled out of a drawer.
difference_explained: You remember something yourself. Someone or something reminds you: 'Remind me to call him.'
mini_conversation:
A: Do you remember her name?
B: Yes, I remember — it's Priya.
everyday_scene: Everyday: An elderly character smiles and says, “I remember it like it was yesterday.”
news_style_line: News-style: “The city held a ceremony to remember those lost in the disaster.”
casual_conversation: Casual: “Remember to lock the car before you leave.”
mcq_options: A) Forget  B) Recall  C) Remind  D) Repeat
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: I ______ meeting her at a wedding years ago. → remember
find_and_fix_to_correct: I don't remember to lock the door this morning. → I don't remember locking the door this morning.
translate: क्या तुम्हें मेरा नाम याद है? → Do you remember my name?
write_your_own_sentence: Write one sentence with 'remember + -ing' about a childhood memory.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to keep something in your mind, or bring it back to mind'?
usage_tip: 'Remember to…' is a friendly reminder: 'Remember to bring your ID.'

simple_explanation: To help someone learn something. When you show or explain a skill or subject so someone else learns it, you teach.
example_2: My father taught me how to ride a bike.
example_3: She teaches English at a local school.
collocations: teach a lesson, teach yourself, teach by example, teach effectively
action_sequence: Before: a student can't do something → During: the teacher shows and explains → After: the student can do it
grammar_pattern: Irregular verb: teach – taught – taught. teach + someone + something (teach me Spanish) or teach + someone + to-infinitive.
common_mistake: She teached me how to swim.
correct_version: She taught me how to swim.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Teach' is irregular: the past is 'taught', not 'teached'.
etymology: Old English "tæcan" — to show, point out, or demonstrate.
prefix_root_suffix: no prefix — native Old English root "tæcan"
mnemonic: TEACH rhymes with REACH — a good teacher REACHes out to help students TEACH themselves.
memory_trick: TAUGHT rhymes with CAUGHT: what you are taught gets caught in your head.
visual_association: A hand guiding another hand across a chalkboard.
difference_explained: The teacher teaches; the student learns. 'He taught me English' / 'I learned English from him.' Never 'He learned me.'
mini_conversation:
A: Can you teach me chess?
B: Sure, I'll teach you the basics tonight.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A wise mentor says, “I can't do this for you — but I can teach you how.”
news_style_line: News-style: “The program teaches basic digital skills to first-time smartphone users.”
casual_conversation: Casual: “Could you teach me how you made this recipe?”
mcq_options: A) Teached  B) Taught  C) Teaches  D) Teaching
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: My grandmother ______ me this recipe when I was young. → taught
find_and_fix_to_correct: He teach yoga every morning. → He teaches yoga every morning.
translate: मेरे पिता ने मुझे साइकिल चलाना सिखाया। → My father taught me how to ride a bicycle.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a person who taught you something useful.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to help someone learn something'?
usage_tip: 'Can you teach me how to…?' is a natural way to ask someone to show you a skill.

simple_explanation: To hold and move something from one place to another. When you support the weight of something and move it with you, you carry it.
example_2: He carried the boxes upstairs by himself.
example_3: She always carries an umbrella in the monsoon.
collocations: carry heavy, carry along, carry safely, carry on your back
related_phrasal_verbs: carry on, carry out, carry through
action_sequence: Before: pick up the bag → During: walk with it → After: put it down at home
grammar_pattern: carry + object (+ place): "carry the bag to the car." Phrasal: "carry on" = continue; "carry out" = perform a task.
common_mistake: I am carrying always my phone.
correct_version: I always carry my phone.
why_it_s_wrong: A habit uses the simple present, not -ing, and 'always' goes before the main verb.
pronunciation_tip: Short "a" like in "cat", rolled straight into "ree".
spelling_tip: Change y to i before -ed/-ies: carried, carries.
etymology: Old French "carier", from Latin "carrus" (a wheeled cart) — originally "to transport by cart."
mnemonic: CARRY comes from CAR ("carrus" = cart) — a car CARRIES things, just like you carry a bag.
memory_trick: A CART CARRIES things: carry = move something while holding it.
visual_association: Someone balancing grocery bags in both arms.
difference_explained: Carry is about holding something while moving. Bring is about coming towards the speaker with it: 'Bring your notebook tomorrow.'
mini_conversation:
A: This is heavy — can you help?
B: Sure, I'll carry the other end.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A hero scoops someone up and says, “Hold on — I've got you, I'll carry you out of here.”
news_style_line: News-style: “Volunteers carried supplies to families cut off by the floods.”
casual_conversation: Casual: “Let me carry that for you, it looks heavy.”
mcq_options: A) To transport by holding  B) To throw away  C) To repair  D) To buy
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: She can't ______ all those bags alone — help her. → carry
find_and_fix_to_correct: He carry the bag every day to school. → He carries the bag every day to school.
translate: क्या तुम यह थैला उठा सकते हो? → Can you carry this bag?
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about what you always carry in your bag.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to hold and move something from one place to another'?
usage_tip: Carry often means 'have with you': 'Do you carry cash?'

simple_explanation: To stay in one place until something happens. When you pause and let time pass before doing the next thing, you wait.
example_2: We waited an hour for the bus.
example_3: Can you wait here while I park the car?
collocations: wait patiently, wait in line, worth the wait, wait a moment
related_phrasal_verbs: wait for, wait up, wait around
action_sequence: Before: arrive at the bus stop → During: stand and watch the road → After: the bus comes
grammar_pattern: wait for + noun (wait for the bus) / wait + to-infinitive (can't wait to go).
common_mistake: Please wait me at the gate.
correct_version: Please wait for me at the gate.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Wait' needs 'for' before the person or thing: wait FOR someone.
spelling_tip: "Wait" (verb, to pause) vs. "weight" (noun, heaviness) — easy to mix up in spelling.
etymology: Old North French "waitier" — to watch, guard, or be on the lookout.
prefix_root_suffix: no prefix — root from Old French "waitier" (to watch)
mnemonic: WAIT sounds like "WEIGHT" — imagine time feeling heavy (like a WEIGHT) while you WAIT.
memory_trick: Picture a bus-stop sign: 'WAIT FOR BUS HERE' — wait and for always travel together.
visual_association: Someone tapping their foot while checking a clock.
difference_explained: Wait = spend time until something happens. Expect = think something will happen. 'I'm waiting for the bus; I expect it at 9.'
tone: Neutral (can be impatient or hopeful depending on context)
mini_conversation:
A: How much longer?
B: Just wait a few more minutes, please.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character checks their watch and mutters, “We can't wait much longer — we have to go now.”
news_style_line: News-style: “Patients are waiting months for routine medical appointments, the report found.”
casual_conversation: Casual: “Wait, don't leave yet — I'm almost ready!”
mcq_options: A) Hurry up  B) Stay until something happens  C) Leave quickly  D) Forget something
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: I'll ______ outside until you're done. → wait
find_and_fix_to_correct: She is waiting the bus since morning. → She has been waiting for the bus since morning.
translate: कृपया यहाँ मेरा इंतज़ार करो। → Please wait for me here.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about how long you waited for something recently.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to stay in one place until something happens'?
usage_tip: 'Wait a minute' and 'Can you wait for me?' are very common in daily speech.

simple_explanation: To feel sure that something is true. When you believe something, you accept it as true in your mind, even if you can't fully prove it.
example_1: I believe you are telling the truth.
example_2: I don't believe in ghosts.
example_3: She believes he will keep his promise.
collocations: believe in, hard to believe, firmly believe, believe it or not
action_sequence: Before: hear a claim → During: think about it → After: accept it: 'I believe you.'
grammar_pattern: believe + (that) clause / believe in + noun (I believe (that) she's right. / I believe in hard work.)
common_mistake: I am believing you.
correct_version: I believe you.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Believe' describes a state of mind, so it doesn't normally take -ing.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: bi-LEEV; the "ie" makes a long "ee" sound.
spelling_tip: Remember "i before e except after c" -- believe, not "beleive."
etymology: Old English "belyfan"/"geliefan," related to "lief" (dear) -- literally "to hold dear/to trust."
prefix_root_suffix: be- (intensive prefix) + lieve/lief (dear, trusted) = to hold as true/dear
mnemonic: BELIEVE has "LIE" hidden in it -- but to believe someone, you trust they're NOT telling a lie.
memory_trick: Never beLIEve a LIE — the word 'lie' is hidden inside.
visual_association: A hand resting over a heart while nodding firmly.
emotion_feel: Trust and certainty (or its absence, when in doubt)
difference_explained: Believe is the verb (I believe). Belief is the noun (my belief). Spelling: -ve for the verb, -f for the noun.
mini_conversation:
A: He says he found the money on the street.
B: I don't believe him -- that story sounds fake.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A detective leans forward and says, "I don't believe in coincidences."
news_style_line: News-style: "Officials say they believe the situation is now under control."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Honestly, I can't believe how fast this year has gone."
mcq_options: A) To feel sure something is true  B) To forget completely  C) To argue loudly  D) To ask a question
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: I ______ that things will get better soon. → believe
find_and_fix_to_correct: She don't believe his excuse. → She doesn't believe his excuse.
translate: मुझे लगता है कि वह सच बोल रहा है। → I believe he is telling the truth.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something you believe is important in life.

usage_tip: 'I believe so' is a polite yes when you are fairly sure.

simple_explanation: To form a picture or idea of something in your mind. When you imagine something, you create it in your thoughts even though it isn't really there in front of you.
example_1: Close your eyes and imagine a quiet beach.
example_2: I can't imagine living without my phone.
example_3: Imagine winning the lottery -- what would you do?
collocations: imagine that, hard to imagine, just imagine, imagine yourself
action_sequence: Before: close your eyes → During: picture a place → After: describe what you saw
grammar_pattern: imagine + noun / imagine + -ing (Imagine the possibilities. / Imagine living on the moon.)
common_mistake: I imagine to travel around the world someday.
correct_version: I imagine traveling around the world someday.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Imagine' is followed by the -ing form, not 'to + verb'.
pronunciation_tip: Four syllables, stress on the second: i-MA-jin; the "g" is soft like in "gem."
spelling_tip: Notice the ending "-ine" pronounced like "in," not "eye-n."
etymology: From Latin "imaginari" (to picture to oneself), from "imago" (image, likeness).
prefix_root_suffix: imagin(e) = root (from Latin imago, "image") + no separate suffix in base form
mnemonic: IMAGE is hidden inside IMAGINE -- you create a mental IMAGE when you imagine.
memory_trick: IMAGinE has an IMAGE inside: you make a picture in your mind.
visual_association: A thought bubble filled with colorful, floating pictures.
difference_explained: Imagine is the verb. Imagination is the noun (the ability): 'Use your imagination.'
mini_conversation:
A: What would you do if you won a million dollars?
B: I can't even imagine -- maybe travel the world!
everyday_scene: Everyday: A child stares at the sky and whispers, "Just imagine what's out there."
news_style_line: News-style: "Experts imagine a future where most homes generate their own power."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I can't imagine how tired you must be after that flight."
mcq_options: A) To picture something in your mind  B) To measure something exactly  C) To argue about something  D) To forget something

find_and_fix_to_correct: I imagine to be a doctor one day. → I imagine being a doctor one day.
translate: जरा कल्पना करो कि तुम चाँद पर हो। → Just imagine that you are on the moon.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence imagining your life five years from now.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to form a picture or idea of something in your mind'?
usage_tip: 'I can't imagine…' shows surprise or sympathy: 'I can't imagine how hard that was.'

simple_explanation: To suddenly understand or become aware of something. You realize something when a fact becomes clear to you, often quite suddenly, like a small "aha" moment.
example_1: I realized I left my keys at home.
example_2: She realized her mistake too late.
example_3: I didn't realize how late it was.
collocations: realize your mistake, suddenly realize, fail to realize, realize the importance
related_phrasal_verbs: catch on, wake up to, dawn on
where_it_s_used: Personal reflection, mistakes, sudden understanding, storytelling
action_sequence: Before: don't notice something → During: a clue appears → After: 'Oh! Now I realize.'
grammar_pattern: realize + (that) clause (I realized (that) I was wrong.)
common_mistake: I am realizing my mistake now.
correct_version: I realize my mistake now.
why_it_s_wrong: Here 'realize' means becoming aware, a state, so the simple present sounds natural, not -ing.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the first syllable: REE-uh-lyze; the "s"/"z" spelling varies by British vs. American English.
spelling_tip: British English often spells it "realise" (with an s); American English uses "realize" (with a z).
etymology: From French "réaliser," from Latin "realis" (real, actual) -- literally "to make real" (in the mind).
mnemonic: REAL is inside REALIZE -- you suddenly see what's REALly true.
memory_trick: REAL-ize: something suddenly becomes REAL in your mind.
visual_association: A lightbulb flickering on suddenly in a dark room.
emotion_feel: Sudden clarity, sometimes mixed with surprise or regret
difference_explained: Recognize = identify someone or something you know (I recognized her voice). Realize = understand a fact (I realized she was upset). British spelling 'realise' is also correct.
mini_conversation:
A: Why did you turn back?
B: I realized I forgot my wallet.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character freezes mid-step and says, "Wait... I just realized something."
news_style_line: News-style: "Residents realized the danger only after the water levels rose sharply."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I just realized I never replied to your message, sorry!"
mcq_options: A) To suddenly become aware of something  B) To build something  C) To forget something on purpose  D) To argue with someone
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: He didn't ______ his phone was missing until he got home. → realize
find_and_fix_to_correct: She don't realize how late it is. → She doesn't realize how late it is.
translate: मुझे अचानक एहसास हुआ कि मैं अपना पासवर्ड भूल गया हूँ। → I suddenly realized that I had forgotten my password.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a time you suddenly realized you had made a mistake.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to suddenly understand or become aware of something'?
usage_tip: 'I didn't realize…' is a soft way to apologise: 'Sorry, I didn't realize you were busy.'

simple_explanation: To offer an idea or plan for someone to consider. When you suggest something, you put an idea forward politely, leaving the other person free to accept or reject it.
example_1: I suggest we leave early to avoid traffic.
example_2: The doctor suggested more rest and water.
example_3: Can you suggest a good restaurant nearby?
collocations: suggest an idea, strongly suggest, suggest a solution, suggest a time
action_sequence: Before: a problem comes up → During: think of an idea → After: 'I suggest we leave early.'
grammar_pattern: suggest + (that) clause / suggest + -ing (I suggest (that) you rest. / I suggest resting.)
common_mistake: I suggest you to see a doctor.
correct_version: I suggest you see a doctor.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Suggest' can't take object + 'to' verb. Use 'suggest (that) you + base verb' or 'suggest + -ing'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: suh-JEST; the "gg" sounds like a single "j" sound.
spelling_tip: Double "g" in the middle -- su-GG-est, not "sugest."
etymology: From Latin "suggerere" (to bring up from below, suggest), from "sub-" (under) + "gerere" (to carry).
prefix_root_suffix: sug- (under, variant of sub-) + gest (to carry) = to "carry" an idea forward gently
mnemonic: SUGGEST sounds like "suggest a GUEST" -- you politely offer an idea, like inviting someone in.
memory_trick: Suggest = Soft advice. Both start with S.
visual_association: A hand gently placing a small idea card on a table.
difference_explained: Advise can take person + to: 'I advise you to rest.' Suggest cannot: 'I suggest (that) you rest.'
mini_conversation:
A: I don't know what to cook tonight.
B: I suggest trying that new pasta recipe.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A detective taps the map and says, "I suggest we start our search here."
news_style_line: News-style: "Analysts suggest the market will recover within a few months."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Can I suggest something? Maybe try a different route home."
mcq_options: A) To order someone firmly  B) To offer an idea for consideration  C) To refuse politely  D) To forget a plan
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: I ______ we take a short break before continuing. → suggest
find_and_fix_to_correct: He suggested to open a new store. → He suggested opening a new store.
translate: मैं सुझाव देता हूँ कि हम जल्दी निकलें। → I suggest that we leave early.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence suggesting a weekend plan to a friend.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to offer an idea or plan for someone to consider'?
usage_tip: 'I suggest we…' and 'May I suggest…?' are polite ways to give ideas in meetings.

simple_explanation: To say what someone or something is like, using words. When you describe something, you use words to paint a picture of it so someone else can imagine it too.
example_1: Can you describe the man you saw?
example_2: She described her trip in great detail.
example_3: Please describe how the accident happened.
collocations: describe in detail, briefly describe, best describe, describe someone as
related_phrasal_verbs: sum up, lay out, spell out
where_it_s_used: Storytelling, reports, exams, police statements, reviews
action_sequence: Before: look at something → During: notice colour, size and shape → After: put it into words
grammar_pattern: describe + noun (+ as + adjective) (Describe the house. / She described him as kind.)
common_mistake: Describe me about your day.
correct_version: Describe your day to me.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Describe' takes a direct object. Don't add 'about', and don't put the person straight after it.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: dih-SKRYBE; the "c" sounds like "s" here.
spelling_tip: Remember the pattern: de-SCRIBE, related to "scribe" (a writer).
etymology: From Latin "describere" (to write down, copy), from "de-" (down) + "scribere" (to write).
prefix_root_suffix: de- (down, fully) + scrib(e) (to write) = to "write out" fully in words
mnemonic: DESCRIBE contains SCRIBE (a writer) -- to describe is to "write down" a picture in words.
memory_trick: DE-SCRIBE: a scribe writes down every detail — describe = give the details.
visual_association: An artist sketching a portrait from someone's spoken words.
difference_explained: Describe = say what something is like (looks, details). Explain = say why or how it works.
mini_conversation:
A: What was the hotel like?
B: Let me describe it -- small but really cozy.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A witness leans toward the officer and says, "Let me describe exactly what I saw."
news_style_line: News-style: "Survivors described the scene as chaotic but calm under the circumstances."
casual_conversation: Casual: "How would you describe your new roommate?"
mcq_options: A) To hide details about something  B) To give a detailed account in words  C) To argue against something  D) To measure something exactly
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Can you ______ your ideal vacation? → describe
find_and_fix_to_correct: She described about her weekend to us. → She described her weekend to us.
translate: कृपया अपने घर का वर्णन करें। → Please describe your house.
write_your_own_sentence: Write two sentences describing your house or room.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to say what someone or something is like, using words'?
usage_tip: Interviews often start with 'Describe yourself in three words.'

simple_explanation: To talk about something briefly or refer to it. When you mention something, you say it quickly in passing, without explaining it fully.
example_1: She mentioned your name in the meeting.
example_2: He mentioned that he might be late.
example_3: Don't mention this to anyone else, please.
collocations: mention briefly, not to mention, worth mentioning, mention something in passing
related_phrasal_verbs: bring up, touch on, refer to
action_sequence: Before: talk about many things → During: say one thing quickly → After: move on to the next topic
grammar_pattern: mention + noun/that-clause (He mentioned the problem. / He mentioned that he was tired.)
common_mistake: She mentioned about her new job.
correct_version: She mentioned her new job.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Mention' already includes the idea of 'about', so it takes a direct object.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the first syllable: MEN-shun; the "-tion" ending is pronounced "shun."
etymology: From Latin "mentio" (a calling to mind, a reminding), related to "mens" (mind).
word_family: mention (n. -- "a mention"), mentioned (adj., as in "the above-mentioned")
mnemonic: MENTION is a quick MENtal note -- you bring something up briefly, not in full detail.
memory_trick: MENTION = say it for a moMENT only.
visual_association: A small sticky note passed quickly across a desk.
difference_explained: Mention = say briefly. Discuss = talk in detail. Neither takes 'about'.
mini_conversation:
A: Did Raj say anything about the party?
B: He mentioned it briefly, but no details yet.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A spy leans in and whispers, "You never mentioned there'd be guards."
news_style_line: News-style: "The report briefly mentioned rising costs without going into further detail."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Oh, by the way, I forgot to mention -- dinner's at seven."
mcq_options: A) To explain in full detail  B) To refer to something briefly  C) To completely ignore  D) To shout angrily
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: He didn't ______ the price when we spoke. → mention
find_and_fix_to_correct: I want to mention about the schedule change. → I want to mention the schedule change.
translate: उसने बैठक में इस समस्या का ज़िक्र किया। → He mentioned this problem in the meeting.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something a friend mentioned to you recently.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to talk about something briefly or refer to it'?
usage_tip: 'Don't mention it' is a polite reply to 'thank you'.

simple_explanation: To agree, often reluctantly, that something is true. When you admit something, you finally say it's true, even though you may have hidden it or felt embarrassed before.
example_1: He admitted that he was wrong.
example_2: I have to admit, the plan worked better than expected.
example_3: She admitted breaking the vase.
collocations: admit a mistake, admit defeat, reluctantly admit, freely admit
related_phrasal_verbs: own up (to), come clean, fess up
where_it_s_used: Confessions, arguments, apologies, courtroom, personal reflection
action_sequence: Before: hide a mistake → During: feel guilty → After: say: 'I admit it was me.'
grammar_pattern: admit + -ing / admit + (that) clause (He admitted stealing it. / He admitted that he stole it.)
common_mistake: He admitted to steal the money.
correct_version: He admitted to stealing the money.
why_it_s_wrong: In 'admit to', 'to' is a preposition, so it takes -ing: 'admitted to stealing'. You can also drop 'to': 'admitted stealing'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: ad-MIT; double the "t" before adding endings (admitted, admitting).
spelling_tip: Double the final "t" when adding "-ed" or "-ing" -- admitted, admitting.
etymology: From Latin "admittere" (to let in, allow), from "ad-" (to) + "mittere" (to send).
prefix_root_suffix: ad- (to, toward) + mit (to send) = literally "to send toward" -> to let a truth in
mnemonic: ADMIT sounds like "add MIT" -- you finally let a truth "in," admitting it exists.
memory_trick: AD-MIT: you let the truth in, like a hospital admits a patient.
visual_association: A locked door slowly creaking open to let the truth out.
emotion_feel: Reluctance mixed with relief once said
difference_explained: Confess is stronger and often about a crime or sin. Admit is everyday: 'I admit I'm tired.'
mini_conversation:
A: Did you eat the last slice of cake?
B: Okay, I admit it -- it was me.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A suspect finally lowers his head and says, "Fine, I admit it -- I was there."
news_style_line: News-style: "The company admitted to delays in shipping caused by supply issues."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I have to admit, that movie was better than I expected."
mcq_options: A) To deny something completely  B) To confess that something is true  C) To forget about something  D) To celebrate an achievement
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: She finally ______ that she had made a mistake. → admitted
find_and_fix_to_correct: He admit that he was late. → He admitted that he was late.
translate: उसने स्वीकार किया कि वह गलत था। → He admitted that he was wrong.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence admitting a small mistake you made.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to agree, often reluctantly, that something is true'?
usage_tip: 'I admit I was wrong' is a strong, honest way to take responsibility.

simple_explanation: To disagree with someone, often loudly, or to give reasons for an opinion. You argue when you exchange strong opinions with someone who disagrees, or when you explain reasons to support your point of view.
example_2: My brother and I argue over silly things.
example_3: She argued that the plan was too risky.
collocations: argue about, argue with someone, argue that, argue over
related_phrasal_verbs: argue back, fight over, quarrel with
action_sequence: Before: two people disagree → During: raise voices and give reasons → After: stop and calm down
grammar_pattern: argue with + person + about/over + noun (They argued with each other about the bill.)
common_mistake: We argued about that he was late.
correct_version: We argued about the fact that he was late.
why_it_s_wrong: After a preposition like 'about', use a noun or -ing, not a 'that' clause.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the first syllable: AR-gyoo; the "gue" ending is a hard "g" + "oo" sound.
spelling_tip: Ends in "-gue," not "-g" -- argue, arguing, argued.
etymology: From Latin "arguere" (to make clear, prove, accuse), via Old French "arguer."
prefix_root_suffix: argu(e) = root (from Latin arguere, to prove/accuse) + no prefix/suffix in base form
mnemonic: ARGUE rhymes with "AR-you-going-to-fight" -- picture two people raising their voices.
memory_trick: ARGUE starts with 'ARG' — the sound of an angry person: 'Arrgh!'
visual_association: Two speech bubbles colliding with jagged edges.
difference_explained: Argue is with words. Fight can be with words or physical. 'They argued' is milder than 'they fought'.
mini_conversation:
A: Why are you two arguing again?
B: We're just arguing about whose turn it is to cook.
everyday_scene: Everyday: Two characters stand nose to nose as one shouts, "We are not arguing about this again!"
news_style_line: News-style: "Lawmakers argued for hours over the new budget proposal."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Stop arguing, you two -- let's just split the bill evenly."
mcq_options: A) To agree quietly  B) To disagree or debate, often with strong feeling  C) To sleep peacefully  D) To celebrate together
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: They ______ about who should pay the bill. → argued
find_and_fix_to_correct: She argue with her sister every day. → She argues with her sister every day.
translate: वे अक्सर पैसों को लेकर बहस करते हैं। → They often argue about money.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something you and a sibling or friend argued about.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to disagree with someone, often loudly, or to give reasons for an opinion'?
usage_tip: Argue WITH someone ABOUT something — both prepositions are needed.

simple_explanation: To have the same opinion as someone else, or to say yes to something. When you agree, you accept an idea, plan, or opinion as correct or acceptable -- you're on the same page as someone else.
example_2: We finally agreed on a restaurant for dinner.
example_3: She agreed to help with the project.
collocations: agree with, agree to, totally agree, mutually agreed
related_phrasal_verbs: go along with, come round to, see eye to eye
action_sequence: Before: listen to an opinion → During: think it's right → After: nod: 'I agree.'
grammar_pattern: agree with + person / agree to + noun/verb (I agree with you. / I agree to help.)
common_mistake: I am agree with you.
correct_version: I agree with you.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Agree' is a full verb, so it doesn't need 'am/is/are' before it.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: uh-GREE; the "ee" is a long, clear vowel sound.
etymology: From Old French "agreer" (to please, consent to), from Latin "ad-" (to) + "gratus" (pleasing).
prefix_root_suffix: a- (to, variant of ad-) + gree (pleasing, from Latin gratus) = to come "toward" a pleasing view
mnemonic: AGREE ends in "-GREE," which sounds like "GREEN light" -- agreeing gives the go-ahead.
memory_trick: Hindi says 'main sehmat hoon' (I am agreed). In English the verb works alone: 'I agree.'
visual_association: Two puzzle pieces clicking neatly together.
difference_explained: Agree WITH a person or opinion. Agree TO a plan or request. Agree ON a decision a group shares.
mini_conversation:
A: I think we should leave earlier tomorrow.
B: I agree, let's aim for 7 AM.
everyday_scene: Everyday: Two rivals finally shake hands as one says, "Fine, I agree -- truce."
news_style_line: News-style: "Both nations agreed to resume trade talks next month."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Honestly, I completely agree with what you just said."
mcq_options: A) To have the same opinion or say yes  B) To argue strongly  C) To completely ignore someone  D) To feel confused
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: I ______ with your decision to postpone the trip. → agree
find_and_fix_to_correct: I don't agree with, but I'll go along. → I don't agree, but I'll go along with it.
translate: मैं तुम्हारी बात से सहमत हूँ। → I agree with what you said.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something you agree with your parents about.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to have the same opinion as someone else, or to say yes to something'?
usage_tip: 'I agree with you', 'I agree to the terms', 'We agree on the price'.

simple_explanation: To have a different opinion from someone else. When you disagree, you think differently from someone else about an idea, plan, or fact, and you say so.
example_2: We disagreed on where to go for vacation.
example_3: I politely disagreed with my manager.
collocations: disagree with, strongly disagree, respectfully disagree, agree to disagree
action_sequence: Before: hear an idea → During: think it's wrong → After: say: 'I respectfully disagree.'
grammar_pattern: disagree with + person/idea (I disagree with your opinion.)
common_mistake: I disagree about your opinion.
correct_version: I disagree with your opinion.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'disagree with' for a person or opinion. 'Disagree about/on' is for the topic: 'We disagree about politics.'
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the third syllable: dis-uh-GREE; the "dis-" is short and unstressed.
spelling_tip: "Dis-" + "agree" -- just add the prefix, no spelling change needed.
etymology: From "dis-" (not, opposite of) + "agree" -- literally "to not agree."
mnemonic: DISAGREE = DIS (not) + AGREE -- the opposite of saying yes.
memory_trick: DIS + AGREE = not agree.
visual_association: Two arrows pointing away from each other.
emotion_feel: Tension, but can also be calm and respectful
difference_explained: Disagree = have a different opinion. Refuse = say no to doing something.
mini_conversation:
A: I think the new policy is a good idea.
B: I have to disagree -- I think it will cause problems.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A board member stands and says calmly, "I'm afraid I have to disagree with that plan."
news_style_line: News-style: "Economists disagree on how quickly prices will fall."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I see your point, but I still disagree a little."
mcq_options: A) To have a different opinion  B) To fully accept an idea  C) To stay silent  D) To celebrate a decision
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: I ______ with the idea of working on weekends. → disagree
find_and_fix_to_correct: She disagree with the new rule. → She disagrees with the new rule.
translate: मैं इस फैसले से असहमत हूँ। → I disagree with this decision.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a polite sentence disagreeing with an idea at work or college.

reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to have a different opinion from someone else'?
usage_tip: 'I'm afraid I disagree' is a polite way to disagree in meetings.

hindi_meaning: सोचना, जानने की इच्छा होना, आश्चर्य करना
simple_explanation: To feel curious and want to know something. When you wonder about something, you think about it because you're curious, often without knowing the answer.
example_1: I wonder what time the store closes.
example_2: She wondered why he never called back.
example_3: I often wonder about life on other planets.
collocations: wonder about, wonder whether, wonder why, make someone wonder
action_sequence: Before: notice something strange → During: think 'why?' → After: ask someone
grammar_pattern: wonder + if/whether/wh- clause (I wonder if he's coming. / I wonder why she left.)
common_mistake: I wonder that he will come.
correct_version: I wonder if he will come.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Wonder' holds a question in your mind, so it takes if/whether or a wh-word, not 'that'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the first syllable: WUN-der; the "o" sounds like "uh."
spelling_tip: "Won-der" -- don't confuse with "wander" (to walk without direction), a common spelling mix-up.
etymology: From Old English "wundor" (a marvel, miracle), related to "wonderful."
prefix_root_suffix: wonder = root (from Old English wundor, marvel) -- no prefix/suffix breakdown
word_family: wonderful (adj.), wonderfully (adv.), wonder (n. -- "a sense of wonder")
mnemonic: WONDER sounds like "WANDER" in your mind -- your thoughts wander around a question.
memory_trick: WONDER = WHO? WHAT? WHEN? — a mind full of questions.
visual_association: A question mark floating above someone's head as they gaze into the distance.
difference_explained: Wonder (/ˈwʌndə/, 'wun') = think curiously. Wander (/ˈwɒndə/, 'won') = walk around without a plan.
mini_conversation:
A: I wonder if it will rain tomorrow.
B: The forecast says it might, so bring an umbrella.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character stares out the window and murmurs, "I wonder where he went."
news_style_line: News-style: "Scientists wonder whether the discovery could change future treatments."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I wonder if the bus is running late again."
mcq_options: A) To know something for certain  B) To feel curious about something  C) To argue about a topic  D) To ignore a question
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: I ______ what she's doing right now. → wonder
find_and_fix_to_correct: I wonder that she likes the gift. → I wonder whether she likes the gift.
translate: मुझे आश्चर्य है कि वह अभी तक क्यों नहीं आया। → I wonder why he hasn't arrived yet.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a polite request starting with 'I was wondering if…'.
