usage_tip: 'I was wondering if you could…' is a very polite way to ask a favour.

simple_explanation: To give an answer without being completely sure. When you guess, you try to give an answer even though you don't know for certain -- it's an informal estimate.
example_1: I guess it's going to rain today.
example_2: Can you guess how old I am?
example_3: I guessed the answer and got it right.
collocations: guess right, guess wrong, take a guess, best guess
where_it_s_used: Casual conversation, games, quizzes, informal opinions
action_sequence: Before: face a question → During: think but don't know for sure → After: give an answer anyway
grammar_pattern: guess + noun/clause (Guess my age. / I guess she's not coming.)
common_mistake: I am guessing that he is at home, as a casual opinion.
correct_version: I guess he's at home.
why_it_s_wrong: When 'guess' means 'I think', use the simple present: 'I guess he's at home.'
pronunciation_tip: Rhymes with "less" -- GES, with a hard "g" and short "e."
spelling_tip: Double "s" at the end -- guess, guessed, guessing.
etymology: From Middle English "gessen," likely related to Old Norse or Middle Low German roots meaning "to get" or "to try to hit upon."
prefix_root_suffix: guess = root (Middle English gessen) -- no prefix/suffix breakdown
mnemonic: GUESS looks like "GUEST" with an S -- an uninvited GUEST idea just pops into your head.
memory_trick: GUESS has a silent U — you just have to guess it's there.
visual_association: A dice being rolled, landing on an unknown number.
difference_explained: A guess admits you might be wrong. Assume means you act as if it's true.
mini_conversation:
A: Guess who I saw at the mall today!
B: I have no idea -- tell me!
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character shrugs and says, "I guess we'll find out soon enough."
news_style_line: News-style: "Officials say the final cost is anyone's guess at this stage."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I guess I'll just order the usual again."
mcq_options: A) To state a fact with full certainty  B) To give an answer without being sure  C) To refuse to answer  D) To write something down formally
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: I ______ we should just wait and see what happens. → guess
find_and_fix_to_correct: I guessing it will be sunny tomorrow. → I guess it will be sunny tomorrow.
translate: मुझे लगता है कि वह देर से आएगा। → I guess he will come late.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence guessing the answer to a question you don't know.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to give an answer without being completely sure'?
usage_tip: 'I guess so' = a soft yes. 'Guess what!' introduces news.

simple_explanation: To feel unsure that something is true or will happen. When you doubt something, you don't fully believe it -- you have questions or worries about whether it's true.
example_1: I doubt he will finish on time.
example_2: She doubted her own decision at first.
example_3: I doubt it will rain today.
collocations: doubt it, no doubt, seriously doubt, have doubts about
action_sequence: Before: hear a promise → During: feel unsure → After: say: 'I doubt it.'
grammar_pattern: doubt + (that) clause / doubt + if/whether (I doubt (that) he'll come. / I doubt if it's true.)
common_mistake: I doubt that he will not come.
correct_version: I doubt that he will come.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Doubt' already carries a negative meaning, so adding 'not' says the opposite of what you mean.
spelling_tip: Remember the silent "b" -- doubt, doubtful, doubtless -- it stays even though you don't hear it.
etymology: From Latin "dubitare" (to hesitate, waver), via Old French "douter."
prefix_root_suffix: doubt = root (from Latin dubitare, to hesitate) -- no separate prefix/suffix
mnemonic: DOUBT has a silent B, just like your doubt is a silent, unspoken worry inside your head.
memory_trick: DOUBT has a silent B — you doubt it's even there.
visual_association: A cloudy question mark hovering over someone's shoulder.
difference_explained: 'I doubt he's honest' = I think he is NOT honest. 'I suspect he's lying' = I think he IS lying. They point in opposite directions.
mini_conversation:
A: Do you think he'll pass the exam?
B: Honestly, I doubt it -- he hasn't studied much.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A detective narrows her eyes and mutters, "I doubt that's the whole story."
news_style_line: News-style: "Analysts doubt the new policy will take effect before next year."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I doubt we'll finish this project by Friday."
mcq_options: A) To feel completely sure  B) To feel unsure that something is true  C) To celebrate a success  D) To explain clearly
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: I ______ she'll agree to the plan. → doubt
find_and_fix_to_correct: I doubt about his honesty. → I doubt his honesty.
translate: मुझे शक है कि वह समय पर पहुंचेगा। → I doubt that he will arrive on time.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something you doubt will happen this year.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to feel unsure that something is true or will happen'?
usage_tip: 'No doubt' = certainly. 'I doubt it' = probably not.

simple_explanation: To think something is true without proof. When you assume something, you accept it as probably true based on little or no evidence, sometimes without realizing you might be wrong.
example_2: Don't assume he's angry just because he's quiet.
example_3: I assumed the meeting was cancelled.
collocations: assume responsibility, safely assume, wrongly assume, let's assume
related_phrasal_verbs: take for granted, jump to conclusions
action_sequence: Before: see a clue → During: fill the gap in your mind → After: act as if it's true
grammar_pattern: assume + (that) clause (I assumed (that) you were coming.)
common_mistake: I assume that he is agree with us.
correct_version: I assume that he agrees with us.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Agree' is a verb, so it takes -s after he/she/it. It never follows 'is'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: uh-SOOM; the "su" sounds like "soo."
spelling_tip: Double "s" together in the middle -- a-s-s-u-m-e.
etymology: From Latin "assumere" (to take up, adopt), from "ad-" (to) + "sumere" (to take).
prefix_root_suffix: as- (to, variant of ad-) + sume (to take) = to "take up" as true
mnemonic: ASSUME contains "SUM" -- you quickly "sum up" a guess without checking the full facts.
memory_trick: AS-SUME: act AS if it's SURE, without proof.
visual_association: Someone building a house on a foundation they never checked.
emotion_feel: Overconfidence, sometimes followed by embarrassment if wrong
difference_explained: Both mean 'think without proof'. Presume sounds more formal and suggests a stronger reason.
mini_conversation:
A: Why didn't you bring an umbrella?
B: I assumed it wouldn't rain today.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character raises an eyebrow and says, "Never assume -- always check first."
news_style_line: News-style: "Officials had assumed the bridge could handle the extra weight."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I just assumed you'd already eaten, sorry!"
mcq_options: A) To prove something with evidence  B) To think something is true without checking  C) To completely deny something  D) To celebrate an outcome
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: I ______ you had already left, so I locked the door. → assumed
find_and_fix_to_correct: I assume he is knowing the answer. → I assume he knows the answer.
translate: मैंने मान लिया कि तुम पहले से जानते थे। → I assumed that you already knew.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something you assumed that turned out wrong.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to think something is true without proof'?
usage_tip: 'I assume you've had lunch?' is a friendly way to check.

simple_explanation: To decide something after considering all the facts, or to end something. You conclude something when you finish thinking about the facts and reach a final decision, or when you formally end a speech, meeting, or report.
example_1: We concluded that the plan was too risky.
example_2: The report concludes with three key recommendations.
example_3: After the trial, the jury concluded he was innocent.
collocations: conclude that, safely conclude, conclude a deal, conclude a speech
related_phrasal_verbs: wrap up, wind down, sum up
action_sequence: Before: collect the facts → During: think them through → After: reach a decision: 'We concluded that…'
grammar_pattern: conclude + (that) clause / conclude + with + noun (We concluded that it was safe. / She concluded with a joke.)
common_mistake: We concluded to the meeting.
correct_version: We concluded the meeting.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Conclude' takes its object directly; no 'to' before it.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: kun-KLOOD; the "u" is a long "oo" sound.
spelling_tip: Ends in "-clude," related to "include" and "exclude" -- all share the same root.
etymology: From Latin "concludere" (to shut up, finish), from "com-" (together) + "claudere" (to close).
prefix_root_suffix: con- (together) + clud(e) (to close) = to "close together" -> finish/decide
mnemonic: CONCLUDE has "CLOSE" hidden in meaning -- you CLOSE a discussion by reaching a conclusion.
memory_trick: CON-CLUDE sounds like CLOSE: the end of a speech, book or meeting.
visual_association: A book closing gently after the final page.
difference_explained: Include = put something inside a group. Conclude = end, or decide after thinking.
mini_conversation:
A: So, what did the doctors conclude?
B: They concluded it was just stress, nothing serious.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A lawyer closes her folder and says, "In conclusion, the evidence speaks for itself."
news_style_line: News-style: "Investigators concluded the fire was caused by an electrical fault."
casual_conversation: Casual: "So, to conclude, I think we should just go with plan B."
mcq_options: A) To start something new  B) To decide or finish something after considering facts  C) To argue without a reason  D) To copy someone else's idea
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The judge ______ that there was not enough evidence. → concluded
find_and_fix_to_correct: We concluded with that he was right. → We concluded that he was right.
translate: हमने निष्कर्ष निकाला कि योजना सही नहीं थी। → We concluded that the plan was not correct.
write_your_own_sentence: Write the last sentence of a short speech, starting with 'To conclude,'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to decide something after considering all the facts, or to end something'?
usage_tip: 'To conclude, …' is a clean way to end a presentation or essay.

simple_explanation: To talk about a topic with someone in detail. When you discuss something, you talk it over with other people, sharing opinions and ideas to understand it better or make a decision.
example_2: We discussed the project for over an hour.
example_3: The teacher asked us to discuss the topic in pairs.
collocations: discuss in detail, discuss with, briefly discuss, discuss options
related_phrasal_verbs: talk over, go over, hash out
action_sequence: Before: set a topic → During: share views and listen → After: agree on a plan
grammar_pattern: discuss + noun -- never "discuss about" (We discussed the issue, not "discussed about the issue.")
common_mistake: Let's discuss about the plan.
correct_version: Let's discuss the plan.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Discuss' already means 'talk about', so 'discuss about' repeats the idea.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: dis-KUSS; the double "s" gives a strong final hiss.
spelling_tip: Double "s" at the end -- discuss, discussed, discussion.
etymology: From Latin "discutere" (to shake apart, examine), from "dis-" (apart) + "quatere" (to shake).
prefix_root_suffix: dis- (apart) + cuss (to shake, from Latin quatere) = to "shake apart" and examine
mnemonic: DISCUSS sounds like "this CUSS" -- people once "discussed" loudly, almost arguing, to shake out the truth.
memory_trick: Discuss = talk about. The 'about' is already inside the word.
visual_association: Several people sitting around a round table, all speaking in turn.
difference_explained: Same meaning, different grammar: discuss the plan / talk about the plan.
mini_conversation:
A: Can we discuss the schedule for next week?
B: Sure, let's talk about it after lunch.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A CEO gestures to the chairs and says, "Sit down -- we need to discuss the numbers."
news_style_line: News-style: "Ministers will discuss the new trade agreement later this week."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Can we discuss dinner plans after work?"
mcq_options: A) To argue angrily  B) To talk about something in detail  C) To ignore a topic  D) To write a report silently
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: We need to ______ this issue before making a decision. → discuss
find_and_fix_to_correct: They discussed about the new policy. → They discussed the new policy.
translate: आइए हम इस मुद्दे पर चर्चा करें। → Let's discuss this issue.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a topic you discussed with your family this week.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to talk about a topic with someone in detail'?
usage_tip: 'Can we discuss this later?' is a polite way to delay a topic at work.

simple_explanation: To make someone believe that something is true. When you convince someone, you use reasons or evidence until they start to believe what you're saying is true.
example_1: I convinced her to try the new restaurant.
example_2: He convinced me that the plan would work.
example_3: It took a while to convince my parents.
collocations: convince someone of, easily convinced, hard to convince, convince someone to do
related_phrasal_verbs: talk into, win over, bring around
action_sequence: Before: someone is unsure → During: give reasons and proof → After: they believe you
grammar_pattern: convince + person + to + verb / convince + person + that clause (I convinced him to stay. / I convinced him that it was safe.)
common_mistake: I convinced him for staying.
correct_version: I convinced him to stay.
why_it_s_wrong: The pattern is 'convince someone to do something' or 'convince someone that…', never 'for'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: kun-VINS; the final "ce" sounds like "s."
spelling_tip: Ends in "-vince," not "-vense" -- convince, convinced, convincing.
etymology: From Latin "convincere" (to overcome, prove wrong), from "con-" (thoroughly) + "vincere" (to conquer).
prefix_root_suffix: con- (thoroughly, together) + vince (to conquer, from Latin vincere) = to fully "conquer" someone's doubts
mnemonic: CONVINCE contains VINCE -- imagine friend "Vince" is so persuasive he can CONVINCE anyone.
memory_trick: CONVINCE shares a root with 'victory' (Latin vincere, to win): you win their mind.
visual_association: A scale slowly tipping toward one side as reasons pile up.
difference_explained: Convince is often about belief (convince him that it's true). Persuade is often about action (persuade him to come). Everyday English uses both for action.
mini_conversation:
A: I really don't want to go to the party.
B: Come on, let me convince you -- it'll be fun!
everyday_scene: Everyday: A salesman leans in with a grin and says, "Let me convince you -- you won't regret this."
news_style_line: News-style: "The evidence convinced the jury within just two hours."
casual_conversation: Casual: "You don't have to convince me -- I'm already in!"
mcq_options: A) To make someone doubt something  B) To make someone believe something is true  C) To ignore someone's opinion  D) To argue without any reason
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: It took a lot of effort to ______ him to change his mind. → convince
find_and_fix_to_correct: She convinced to him that it was true. → She convinced him that it was true.
translate: मैंने उसे यात्रा पर चलने के लिए मना लिया। → I convinced him to come on the trip.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about how you convinced someone to try something new.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to make someone believe that something is true'?
usage_tip: 'I'm convinced (that)…' = I'm fully sure.

simple_explanation: To make someone decide to do something by giving good reasons. When you persuade someone, you convince them to take action -- not just believe something, but actually do it.
example_2: She persuaded her boss to give her more time.
example_3: We couldn't persuade him to change his mind.
collocations: persuade someone to, try to persuade, hard to persuade, persuade successfully
related_phrasal_verbs: talk into, win over, bring round
action_sequence: Before: a friend says no → During: give good reasons → After: they say yes
grammar_pattern: persuade + person + to + verb (She persuaded him to stay longer.)
common_mistake: He persuaded that I should come.
correct_version: He persuaded me to come.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'persuade someone to do something'. The 'that' pattern also needs the person: 'He persuaded me that…'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: per-SWAYD; the "sua" sounds like "sway."
spelling_tip: Watch the "-suade" ending, related to "persuasion" and "dissuade."
etymology: From Latin "persuadere," from "per-" (thoroughly) + "suadere" (to urge, advise).
prefix_root_suffix: per- (thoroughly) + suade (to urge, from Latin suadere) = to thoroughly urge someone
mnemonic: PERSUADE sounds like "per-SWAY-d" -- a good argument can SWAY someone's decision.
memory_trick: PERSUADE sounds like 'per sweet': you use sweet, good reasons.
visual_association: Someone gently pushing a door that's slightly stuck, until it finally opens.
difference_explained: Persuade uses reasons, and the other person still chooses. Force leaves no choice.
mini_conversation:
A: I don't think I can afford the trip.
B: Let me try to persuade you -- we found a cheaper flight!
everyday_scene: Everyday: A friend nudges another and says, "Come on, let me persuade you -- one more round won't hurt."
news_style_line: News-style: "Campaigners are trying to persuade the government to change the law."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I finally persuaded my parents to let me travel alone."
mcq_options: A) To force someone against their will  B) To convince someone to take action through reasons  C) To ignore someone's request  D) To confuse someone
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: She tried to ______ her friend to join the gym with her. → persuade
find_and_fix_to_correct: I persuaded that she should stay. → I persuaded her to stay.
translate: मैंने उसे परीक्षा के लिए पढ़ाई करने के लिए मना लिया। → I persuaded him to study for the exam.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about how you persuaded a friend to come with you somewhere.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to make someone decide to do something by giving good reasons'?
usage_tip: Sales and interviews: 'How would you persuade a customer to buy…?'

simple_explanation: To say you are unhappy or unsatisfied about something. When you complain, you express that something is wrong or unfair, often to get it fixed or just to let off frustration.
example_2: He always complains about the weather.
example_3: I want to complain to the manager about the service.
collocations: complain about, complain to, constantly complain, file a complaint
related_phrasal_verbs: moan about, grumble about, speak up
where_it_s_used: Customer service, workplace, daily annoyances, relationships
action_sequence: Before: get cold food → During: call the waiter → After: tell them the problem
grammar_pattern: complain about + noun / complain to + person (He complained about the delay to the staff.)
common_mistake: She complained the food was cold to the waiter.
correct_version: She complained to the waiter that the food was cold.
why_it_s_wrong: The order is: complain TO a person, ABOUT a thing, or THAT + clause. Don't split the clause with 'to the waiter'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: kum-PLAYN; the "ai" makes a long "ay" sound.
spelling_tip: Ends in "-plain," related to "complaint" -- remember the connection.
etymology: From Old French "complaindre," from Latin "complangere" (to bewail), from "com-" (intensive) + "plangere" (to beat the breast, lament).
prefix_root_suffix: com- (intensive) + plain (to lament, from Latin plangere) = to strongly express unhappiness
mnemonic: COMPLAIN contains PLAIN -- when something isn't fine, you make it very PLAIN that you're unhappy.
memory_trick: COMPLAIN has 'PLAIN' inside: you say plainly that something is wrong.
visual_association: A speech bubble filled with small storm clouds.
difference_explained: Complain is the verb. Complaint is the noun. 'I want to complain' / 'I want to make a complaint.'
mini_conversation:
A: This Wi-Fi is so slow again.
B: Why don't you complain to the internet company?
everyday_scene: Everyday: A customer slams a receipt on the counter and says, "I want to complain about this order."
news_style_line: News-style: "Residents have complained repeatedly about noise from the construction site."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I'm not trying to complain, but this soup is really cold."
mcq_options: A) To express happiness about something  B) To express dissatisfaction about something  C) To explain a topic clearly  D) To agree with a decision
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: He ______ about his neighbor's loud music every week. → complains
find_and_fix_to_correct: She complained about that the room was dirty. → She complained that the room was dirty.
translate: उसने खाने की गुणवत्ता के बारे में शिकायत की। → He complained about the quality of the food.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a polite sentence complaining about a late delivery.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to say you are unhappy or unsatisfied about something'?
usage_tip: At a shop or hotel, 'I'd like to complain about…' is firm but polite.

simple_explanation: To say sorry for something you did wrong. When you apologize, you tell someone you're sorry for a mistake or for hurting them, often explaining briefly why.
example_2: He apologized to his sister for yelling.
example_3: She never apologized for the mistake.
collocations: apologize for, apologize to, sincerely apologize, publicly apologize
where_it_s_used: Conflict resolution, customer service, relationships, formal letters
action_sequence: Before: make a mistake → During: feel sorry → After: say: 'I apologize for…'
grammar_pattern: apologize to + person + for + noun/-ing (He apologized to me for being rude.)
common_mistake: I apologize you for the mistake.
correct_version: I apologize to you for the mistake.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Apologize' can't take the person directly. Use 'apologize TO someone FOR something'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: uh-PAH-luh-jyze; four syllables total.
spelling_tip: American English: "apologize" (-ize); British English often uses "apologise" (-ise).
etymology: From Greek "apologia" (a speech in defense), via Latin, later shifting to mean "expressing regret."
prefix_root_suffix: apo- (away, from Greek) + log(y) (speech) + -ize (verb suffix) = literally "to speak away/in defense," now meaning "to say sorry"
mnemonic: APOLOGIZE contains "LOGI" -- you give a logical, sincere reason when you say sorry.
memory_trick: Apologize = say sorry: sorry TO you, FOR the mistake — the same prepositions.
visual_association: An outstretched hand offering a small folded note that says "sorry."
difference_explained: Apologize is the verb. Apology is the noun: 'I apologize' = 'Please accept my apology.' British spelling: apologise.
mini_conversation:
A: You really hurt my feelings yesterday.
B: I know, and I want to apologize for that.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character kneels beside a friend and says quietly, "I owe you an apology -- I was wrong."
news_style_line: News-style: "The company issued a public apology after the data breach."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I want to apologize for missing your call earlier."
mcq_options: A) To celebrate a success  B) To say sorry for a mistake  C) To argue about a decision  D) To ignore a problem
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: He ______ for forgetting her birthday. → apologized
find_and_fix_to_correct: She apologized me for the delay. → She apologized to me for the delay.
translate: उसने देर से आने के लिए माफी माँगी। → He apologized for arriving late.
write_your_own_sentence: Write an email line apologizing for a late reply.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to say sorry for something you did wrong'?
usage_tip: 'I apologize for the delay' is standard in emails and customer service.

simple_explanation: To say you will definitely do something. When you promise, you give your word that you will do something, and the other person trusts you to keep it.
example_1: I promise to call you tonight.
example_2: She promised to help him move next week.
example_3: He broke his promise and didn't show up.
collocations: keep a promise, break a promise, promise to, make a promise
action_sequence: Before: someone needs help → During: give your word → After: keep it
grammar_pattern: promise + to + verb / promise + (that) clause (I promise to try. / I promise (that) I'll try.)
common_mistake: I promise you that I will trying my best.
correct_version: I promise you that I will try my best.
why_it_s_wrong: After 'will', always use the base verb.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the first syllable: PRAH-mis; the "-ise" ending sounds like "iss," not "eyes."
spelling_tip: Ends in "-mise," not "-mice" -- promise, promised, promising.
etymology: From Latin "promissum," past participle of "promittere" (to send forth, assure), from "pro-" (forward) + "mittere" (to send).
prefix_root_suffix: pro- (forward) + mise (sent, from Latin mittere) = literally "sent forward" -> a pledge for the future
word_family: promising (adj., as in "a promising future"), promised (adj.)
mnemonic: PROMISE has "MISS" hidden in it -- if you break a promise, you MISS what you said you'd do.
memory_trick: Pinky promise: hook your little finger and say 'I promise'.
visual_association: Two little fingers linking together in a pinky promise.
difference_explained: A promise is personal. A guarantee is formal, often backed in writing or with money: 'a one-year guarantee'.
mini_conversation:
A: Will you really come to my show?
B: I promise -- I wouldn't miss it.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A parent kneels down and says softly, "I promise, I'll always be here for you."
news_style_line: News-style: "The mayor promised to fix the roads before the end of the year."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I promise I'll text you as soon as I land."
mcq_options: A) To refuse to do something  B) To give your word that you will do something  C) To forget an obligation  D) To argue about a plan
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: She ______ to finish the report by Friday. → promised
