usage_tip: Both work: 'I promise to…' and 'I promise (that) I will…'.

simple_explanation: To tell someone about a possible danger or problem in advance. When you warn someone, you let them know something bad might happen, so they can be careful or avoid it.
example_1: I warned him about the icy road.
example_2: She warned us not to be late.
example_3: The sign warns visitors about the deep water.
collocations: warn against, warn someone about, give a warning, without warning
action_sequence: Before: see danger ahead → During: tell people quickly → After: they get ready
grammar_pattern: warn + person + about/of + noun / warn + person + not to + verb (She warned him about the danger. / She warned him not to go.)
common_mistake: He warned about the danger to us.
correct_version: He warned us about the danger.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Warn' puts the person straight after it: warn someone ABOUT or OF something.
pronunciation_tip: Rhymes with "born" -- WORN; the "a" sounds like "or" in this word.
spelling_tip: Just four letters -- warn, warned, warning; don't confuse with "worn" (past participle of "wear").
etymology: From Old English "warnian" (to take heed, caution), related to "ware" (aware, wary).
prefix_root_suffix: warn = root (from Old English warnian, to take heed) -- no separate prefix/suffix
mnemonic: WARN sounds like "WARM" -- a warning is like a warm siren going off before danger arrives.
memory_trick: WARN sounds like 'war': warn people before danger comes.
visual_association: A bright yellow triangle sign flashing before a sharp turn.
difference_explained: Warn = tell someone about danger to protect them. Threaten = say you will cause harm.
mini_conversation:
A: I'm going to try that shortcut through the forest.
B: I'd warn you against it -- people get lost there.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A guard raises a hand and says firmly, "I'm warning you -- don't go any further."
news_style_line: News-style: "Officials warned residents to prepare for heavy flooding this weekend."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Just a heads-up, I want to warn you the traffic is really bad today."
mcq_options: A) To praise someone  B) To alert someone about possible danger  C) To ignore a problem  D) To celebrate good news
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The doctor ______ him about the risks of smoking. → warned
find_and_fix_to_correct: She warned to him about the storm. → She warned him about the storm.
translate: उसने मुझे सड़क की स्थिति के बारे में चेतावनी दी। → He warned me about the road conditions.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence warning a friend about heavy traffic.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to tell someone about a possible danger or problem in advance'?
usage_tip: 'I'm warning you' sounds strong. 'Just a warning:' is softer.

simple_explanation: To tell someone what you think they should do. When you advise someone, you give your opinion about what they should do, usually because you know more about the situation.
example_1: I advise you to see a doctor.
example_2: The lawyer advised her to sign the contract.
example_3: I would advise against traveling this week.
collocations: advise against, strongly advise, advise someone to, seek advice
where_it_s_used: Professional advice, healthcare, legal matters, mentoring
action_sequence: Before: someone has a problem → During: listen → After: advise them what to do
grammar_pattern: advise + person + to + verb (I advise you to rest. / I advise against it.)
common_mistake: Can you give me an advise?
correct_version: Can you give me some advice?
why_it_s_wrong: Advise (with S, /z/ sound) is the verb. Advice (with C, /s/ sound) is an uncountable noun, so no 'an'.
pronunciation_tip: The final "s" sounds like a "z": ad-VYZE, unlike "advice" (ad-VYCE).
spelling_tip: Verb = advise (with an "s"); noun = advice (with a "c") -- a very common learner mix-up.
etymology: From Old French "aviser," from Latin "ad-" (to) + "visere" (to look at, consider).
prefix_root_suffix: ad- (to) + vise (to look, from Latin visere) = to "look toward" and guide someone
mnemonic: ADVISE has an S like "verbS do thingS" -- remember "S" for the verb, "C" for the noun (advice).
memory_trick: ICE is a thing, so the noun is advICE.
visual_association: A signpost gently pointing someone in a wiser direction.
difference_explained: Advise (/ədˈvaɪz/) = verb. Advice (/ədˈvaɪs/) = uncountable noun: 'some advice', never 'an advice'.
mini_conversation:
A: I'm not sure whether to take the job.
B: I'd advise you to think it over for a few days.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A mentor places a hand on a student's shoulder and says, "I'd advise you to trust your instincts."
news_style_line: News-style: "Health officials advised the public to stay indoors during the heatwave."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I'd advise booking your tickets early -- they sell out fast."
mcq_options: A) To ignore someone's problem  B) To recommend what someone should do  C) To argue with someone  D) To forget an instruction
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The teacher ______ students to review their notes before the test. → advised
find_and_fix_to_correct: She gave me a good advise about the interview. → She gave me good advice about the interview.
translate: डॉक्टर ने उसे आराम करने की सलाह दी। → The doctor advised him to rest.
write_your_own_sentence: Write one sentence using both 'advise' and 'advice'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to tell someone what you think they should do'?
usage_tip: 'I'd advise you to…' is polite and professional.

simple_explanation: To firmly say that something must happen, even if others disagree. When you insist, you stand your ground and keep saying something must be done or is true, refusing to change your mind easily.
example_1: She insisted on paying the bill.
example_2: He insisted that he was right.
example_3: My mother insisted we visit her every Sunday.
collocations: insist on, insist that, politely insist, insist firmly
action_sequence: Before: someone says no → During: repeat firmly → After: they accept
grammar_pattern: insist on + -ing / insist that + clause (She insisted on going. / She insisted that she go/goes.)
common_mistake: He insisted to pay for dinner.
correct_version: He insisted on paying for dinner.
why_it_s_wrong: The pattern is 'insist ON + -ing' or 'insist (that) + clause', not 'insist to'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: in-SIST; the "s" sounds are both clear and sharp.
spelling_tip: One "n," double "s" at the end -- insist, insisted, insisting.
etymology: From Latin "insistere" (to stand upon, persist), from "in-" (upon) + "sistere" (to stand).
prefix_root_suffix: in- (upon) + sist (to stand, from Latin sistere) = to "stand upon" one's point firmly
mnemonic: INSIST sounds like "IN-SIST-ent" -- you stand firm and won't back down.
memory_trick: IN-SIST: you stand firm, IN your position.
visual_association: Someone planting their feet firmly on the ground, refusing to move.
difference_explained: Insist = demand firmly. Persist = keep going for a long time despite problems.
mini_conversation:
A: Please, let me pay for the coffee.
B: No, I insist -- you got it last time.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A grandmother pushes a plate closer and says, "Eat more -- I insist!"
news_style_line: News-style: "The company insists its products meet all required safety standards."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Really, I insist -- take the last piece of cake."
mcq_options: A) To quietly agree with someone  B) To firmly demand or maintain something  C) To forget a request  D) To politely decline
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: He ______ on driving us to the airport himself. → insisted
find_and_fix_to_correct: She insisted to help with the cooking. → She insisted on helping with the cooking.
translate: उसने जिद करके मुझे अपने साथ चलने के लिए कहा। → He insisted that I come with him.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a time someone insisted on paying for you.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to firmly say that something must happen, even if others disagree'?
usage_tip: 'I insist!' is common when you offer to pay or help.

simple_explanation: To say something is true, even though it hasn't been proven. When you claim something, you state it firmly as fact, but other people might still need proof before fully believing you.
example_1: He claims to be an expert.
example_2: The company claims its product is 100% natural.
example_3: She claimed she had never met him before.
collocations: claim responsibility, falsely claim, claim to be, make a claim
where_it_s_used: Insurance, news reporting, legal disputes, advertising
action_sequence: Before: have an opinion → During: say it strongly as fact → After: others ask for proof
grammar_pattern: claim + to + verb / claim + (that) clause (He claims to know her. / He claims that he knows her.)
common_mistake: He claimed that he is the winner.
correct_version: He claimed that he was the winner.
why_it_s_wrong: In reported speech about the past, the verb in the that-clause usually moves back a tense.
pronunciation_tip: Rhymes with "game" -- KLAYM; the "ai" makes a long "ay" sound.
etymology: From Old French "clamer," from Latin "clamare" (to shout, call out).
prefix_root_suffix: claim = root (from Latin clamare, to shout/call) -- no separate prefix/suffix
mnemonic: CLAIM sounds like "CLAY-M" -- you shape a statement out of "clay," presenting it as true.
memory_trick: CLAIM rhymes with NAME: you put your name on something as yours or as true.
visual_association: A hand raised confidently while others look on with raised eyebrows.
difference_explained: Claim = say something is true. Prove = show evidence that it is true.
mini_conversation:
A: He says he can run a marathon in under three hours.
B: That's what he claims, but I've never seen proof.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A reporter holds up a microphone and asks, "What do you say to those who claim you're guilty?"
news_style_line: News-style: "The company claims its new device can last a full week on one charge."
casual_conversation: Casual: "He claims he fixed it himself, but I have my doubts."
mcq_options: A) To prove something with full certainty  B) To state something as true, without full proof  C) To completely deny a fact  D) To ask a question
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: She ______ that she never received the email. → claims
find_and_fix_to_correct: He claim to know the answer. → He claims to know the answer.
translate: उसने दावा किया कि उसने कभी झूठ नहीं बोला। → He claimed that he had never lied.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about an advert that claims something you don't believe.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to say something is true, even though it hasn't been proven'?
usage_tip: Also used for money or items: 'claim insurance', 'baggage claim'.

simple_explanation: To say that something is not true. When you deny something, you refuse to admit it's true, even if other people believe it or have evidence.
example_2: She denied any involvement in the plan.
example_3: He denies that he was even there.
collocations: flatly deny, deny responsibility, deny an accusation, categorically deny
action_sequence: Before: someone accuses you → During: hear the claim → After: say: 'No, that's not true.'
grammar_pattern: deny + -ing / deny + (that) clause (He denied taking it. / He denied that he took it.)
common_mistake: He denied to take the money.
correct_version: He denied taking the money.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Deny' is followed by -ing or a that-clause, not 'to + verb'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: dih-NYE; rhymes with "sky."
spelling_tip: "Y" changes to "ie" before adding "-s" or "-ed" -- denies, denied, but keep "y" before "-ing" -- denying.
etymology: From Old French "denier," from Latin "denegare" (to deny utterly), from "de-" (away) + "negare" (to say no).
prefix_root_suffix: de- (away, negation) + ny (to say, from Latin negare) = to firmly "say away" -> refuse
mnemonic: DENY sounds like "die-NO" -- you firmly say "no" to a claim.
memory_trick: DENY = say 'nay' (no).
visual_association: A hand held up firmly, palm out, blocking an accusation.
difference_explained: Deny = say something is not true. Refuse = say no to doing something.
mini_conversation:
A: Did you eat my sandwich?
B: No, I deny it completely -- wasn't me!
everyday_scene: Everyday: A suspect crosses his arms and says, "I deny everything -- you have no proof."
news_style_line: News-style: "The official denied any wrongdoing during the press conference."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I know it was you -- don't even try to deny it!"
mcq_options: A) To admit something is true  B) To say that something is not true  C) To celebrate an achievement  D) To ask a question
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: She ______ knowing anything about the surprise party. → denied
find_and_fix_to_correct: He deny that he broke the vase. → He denies that he broke the vase.
translate: उसने पैसे चुराने से इनकार किया। → He denied stealing the money.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about someone who denied breaking something.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to say that something is not true'?
usage_tip: 'He denied the charges' is common in news.

simple_explanation: To say that something is definitely true or will definitely happen. When you confirm something, you make it certain -- either by proving it's true or by agreeing that a plan will definitely go ahead.
example_2: The doctor confirmed that it was just a cold.
example_3: Can you confirm the meeting time?
collocations: confirm a booking, confirm a reservation, please confirm, confirm receipt
where_it_s_used: Bookings, appointments, official emails, test results
action_sequence: Before: a plan is unsure → During: check the details → After: 'Yes, confirmed for 5 pm.'
grammar_pattern: confirm + noun / confirm + (that) clause (Please confirm your seat. / She confirmed that she'd come.)
common_mistake: Please confirm me the details.
correct_version: Please confirm the details for me.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Confirm' takes the thing as its object. The person comes after 'for' or 'to'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: kun-FURM; the "ir" sounds like "ur."
spelling_tip: Related to "firm" -- con-FIRM, easy to remember by the root word "firm" (solid, certain).
etymology: From Latin "confirmare" (to strengthen, establish), from "com-" (intensive) + "firmare" (to make firm).
prefix_root_suffix: con- (intensive, together) + firm (steady, from Latin firmus) = to make thoroughly firm/certain
mnemonic: CONFIRM has FIRM inside it -- you make something solid and FIRM by confirming it.
memory_trick: CON-FIRM: make it FIRM, with no more doubt.
visual_association: A green checkmark stamping firmly onto a document.
difference_explained: Confirm = make certain. Conform = follow rules or behave like others.
mini_conversation:
A: Is the flight still leaving at 6?
B: Yes, I just confirmed it with the airline.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A pilot's voice crackles over the radio, "Control, please confirm runway is clear."
news_style_line: News-style: "Officials confirmed that the missing hikers had been found safe."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Can you confirm you got my email from yesterday?"
mcq_options: A) To make something uncertain  B) To make something definitely certain  C) To completely ignore a fact  D) To argue about a plan
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Please ______ your attendance by Friday. → confirm
find_and_fix_to_correct: She confirmed to us that the meeting is happen. → She confirmed to us that the meeting is happening.
translate: कृपया अपनी बुकिंग की पुष्टि करें। → Please confirm your booking.
write_your_own_sentence: Write an email line confirming a meeting time.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to say that something is definitely true or will definitely happen'?
usage_tip: 'Could you please confirm the time?' is standard in emails.

simple_explanation: To say what you think will happen in the future. When you predict something, you make a statement about the future, often based on evidence, experience, or patterns you've noticed.
example_1: I predict it will rain later.
example_2: Experts predict a rise in prices next year.
example_3: No one could predict how the game would end.
collocations: predict the future, accurately predict, hard to predict, predict a result
action_sequence: Before: study the signs → During: think about what comes next → After: say it before it happens
grammar_pattern: predict + (that) clause / predict + noun (Scientists predict (that) sea levels will rise. / They predicted a win.)
common_mistake: I predict that it will rains tomorrow.
correct_version: I predict that it will rain tomorrow.
why_it_s_wrong: After 'will', always use the base verb, with no -s.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: pri-DIKT; the first syllable is a quick, unstressed "pri."
spelling_tip: Related to "dictionary" and "dictate" -- all share the root "dict" (to say).
etymology: From Latin "praedicere" (to say beforehand), from "prae-" (before) + "dicere" (to say).
prefix_root_suffix: pre- (before) + dict (to say, from Latin dicere) = literally "to say beforehand"
mnemonic: PREDICT has "DICT" (say) + "PRE" (before) -- you SAY something BEFORE it happens.
memory_trick: PRE-DICT: 'pre' = before, 'dict' = say. Say it before it happens.
visual_association: A weather map with arrows showing where a storm will move next.
difference_explained: A prediction usually has reasons or data behind it. A guess may have none.
mini_conversation:
A: Who do you think will win the match?
B: I predict our team will win by two goals.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A fortune teller waves a hand over a crystal ball and says, "I predict great changes ahead."
news_style_line: News-style: "Meteorologists predict heavy rainfall across the region this weekend."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I predict we'll be stuck in traffic for at least an hour."
mcq_options: A) To describe something from the past  B) To say what will happen in the future  C) To argue about a decision  D) To completely ignore facts
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Analysts ______ that sales will increase next quarter. → predict
find_and_fix_to_correct: She predicted that he will won the race. → She predicted that he would win the race.
translate: वैज्ञानिकों ने भविष्यवाणी की कि तापमान बढ़ेगा। → Scientists predicted that the temperature would rise.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence predicting the result of a match or exam.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to say what you think will happen in the future'?
usage_tip: Weather and sport: 'Experts predict heavy rain this week.'

simple_explanation: To remember something from the past. When you recall something, you bring a memory back to mind, often something specific like a name, date, or event.
example_2: He recalled the exact date of the accident.
example_3: Can you recall where you left your keys?
collocations: recall clearly, vaguely recall, fail to recall, recall a memory
related_phrasal_verbs: bring to mind, look back on
action_sequence: Before: an event happens → During: years pass → After: bring it back to mind
grammar_pattern: recall + noun / recall + -ing (I recall the day clearly. / I recall meeting him once.)
common_mistake: I don't recall to meet him before.
correct_version: I don't recall meeting him before.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Recall' is followed by -ing for a past memory, like 'remember + -ing'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: ri-KAWL; rhymes with "small."
spelling_tip: "Re-" + "call" -- a straightforward combination, no spelling tricks.
etymology: From "re-" (again, back) + "call" -- literally "to call back" to mind.
prefix_root_suffix: re- (again, back) + call (from Old Norse kalla, to summon) = to "call back" a memory
mnemonic: RECALL = RE (again) + CALL -- you "call" a memory back again into your mind.
memory_trick: RE-CALL: call a memory back again.
visual_association: A filing cabinet drawer sliding open to reveal an old photograph.
difference_explained: You recall something yourself. Something reminds you. Companies also 'recall' faulty products (call them back).
mini_conversation:
A: Do you recall what time the train left?
B: I think it was around 9, but I'm not totally sure.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A witness pauses and says, "Let me recall exactly what happened that night."
news_style_line: News-style: "The manufacturer issued a recall after safety concerns were raised."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I vaguely recall mentioning that to you last week."
mcq_options: A) To forget something completely  B) To remember something from the past  C) To predict a future event  D) To argue about a fact
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: I can't ______ where I put my glasses. → recall
find_and_fix_to_correct: She don't recall his name. → She doesn't recall his name.
translate: मुझे याद नहीं कि मैंने अपनी चाबी कहाँ रखी। → I can't recall where I put my keys.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence starting 'I clearly recall…'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to remember something from the past'?
usage_tip: 'Do you recall…?' sounds formal. In daily talk, 'Do you remember…?' is more common.

simple_explanation: To know someone or something because you've seen them before. When you recognize someone or something, your brain matches it to something you already know from before -- you know who or what it is.
example_1: I recognized her from the photo.
example_2: I barely recognized him with the new haircut.
example_3: The teacher recognized the student's hard work.
collocations: instantly recognize, hardly recognize, recognize an achievement, widely recognized
action_sequence: Before: see a face → During: search your memory → After: 'Oh, it's Rahul!'
grammar_pattern: recognize + noun (I recognize that man from somewhere.)
common_mistake: I recognize him from the photo yesterday.
correct_version: I recognized him from the photo yesterday.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Yesterday' fixes the action in the past, so the verb must be past tense.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the first syllable: REK-ug-nyze; four syllables total.
spelling_tip: Watch the "-gn-" spelling -- recognize, recognition (the "g" stays even though it's barely pronounced in some forms).
etymology: From Latin "recognoscere" (to know again, examine), from "re-" (again) + "cognoscere" (to know).
prefix_root_suffix: re- (again) + cogn(ize) (to know, from Latin cognoscere) = to "know again"
mnemonic: RECOGNIZE = RE (again) + COGNIZE (to know, related to "cognitive") -- to KNOW something AGAIN.
memory_trick: RE-COGNIZE: 're' = again, 'cognize' = know. Know again.
visual_association: A puzzle piece clicking into place as a face becomes familiar.
difference_explained: Recognize = identify someone or something known. Realize = understand a fact. British spelling: recognise.
mini_conversation:
A: Do you recognize that man over there?
B: Yes, he was my classmate years ago!
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character squints across the room and says, "Wait... do I recognize you from somewhere?"
news_style_line: News-style: "The award recognizes outstanding contributions to local communities."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I didn't even recognize you with your new glasses!"
mcq_options: A) To completely forget someone  B) To identify someone or something known before  C) To argue with someone  D) To predict a future event
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: I almost didn't ______ her with her short hair. → recognize
find_and_fix_to_correct: She don't recognize me anymore. → She doesn't recognize me anymore.
translate: मैंने उसे भीड़ में तुरंत पहचान लिया। → I recognized him in the crowd immediately.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about someone you didn't recognize at first.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to know someone or something because you've seen them before'?
usage_tip: 'I didn't recognize you!' is a friendly greeting when someone has changed.

simple_explanation: To think carefully about something, or to show an image like a mirror does. "Reflect" has two everyday uses: to think deeply about something (reflect on your day), or to bounce back light or an image, like a mirror.
example_1: I like to reflect on my day before sleeping.
example_2: The lake reflected the mountains perfectly.
example_3: She took a moment to reflect on her choices.
collocations: reflect on, reflect a change, quietly reflect, reflect light
action_sequence: Before: finish a task → During: think back over what went well or badly → After: plan to do better
grammar_pattern: reflect on + noun (Take time to reflect on what happened.)
common_mistake: I reflected about my mistakes.
correct_version: I reflected on my mistakes.
why_it_s_wrong: When it means 'think deeply', use 'reflect on' (or 'upon'), not 'about'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: ri-FLEKT; the "fl" blend is pronounced clearly.
spelling_tip: Related to "reflection" and "reflex" -- all share the root "flect" (to bend).
etymology: From Latin "reflectere" (to bend back), from "re-" (back) + "flectere" (to bend).
prefix_root_suffix: re- (back) + flect (to bend, from Latin flectere) = to "bend back" (light or thought)
mnemonic: REFLECT = RE (back) + FLECT (bend) -- light bends BACK off a mirror, and your mind bends BACK over a memory.
memory_trick: A mirror reflects your face; when you reflect, your mind looks back at itself.
visual_association: A calm lake perfectly mirroring the mountains and sky above it.
difference_explained: Reflect = think deeply, or bounce back light. Reflex = an automatic body reaction.
mini_conversation:
A: How was your first year at university?
B: Looking back, I reflect on it as a year full of lessons.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character stares into a still lake and says softly, "Sometimes I just need to reflect."
news_style_line: News-style: "The report reflects growing concerns about job security."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Take a minute to reflect before you answer that question."
mcq_options: A) To think carefully about something, or mirror it  B) To argue loudly  C) To completely forget something  D) To predict the future
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: She paused to ______ on the lessons she'd learned that year. → reflect
find_and_fix_to_correct: He reflected about his career choices. → He reflected on his career choices.
translate: पानी में पहाड़ों की छवि प्रतिबिंबित हो रही थी। → The image of the mountains was reflected in the water.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence reflecting on what you learned this month.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to think carefully about something, or to show an image like a mirror does'?
usage_tip: 'Take some time to reflect' is common in teaching and coaching.

simple_explanation: To think carefully about something before deciding. When you consider something, you think about it seriously, weighing the pros and cons, before making a decision.
example_2: We're considering moving to a new city.
example_3: Have you considered all the risks?
collocations: seriously consider, take into consideration, consider carefully, consider an option
related_phrasal_verbs: think over, weigh up, mull over
action_sequence: Before: get an offer → During: weigh pros and cons → After: decide
grammar_pattern: consider + noun/-ing -- never "consider to" (Consider taking the earlier train, not "consider to take.")
common_mistake: I'm considering to change my job.
correct_version: I'm considering changing my job.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Consider' is always followed by -ing, not 'to + verb'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: kun-SID-er; four syllables total.
etymology: From Latin "considerare" (to observe closely, contemplate), possibly from "com-" (with) + "sidus" (star) -- originally an astrological term.
prefix_root_suffix: con- (with, together) + sider (star, from Latin sidus) = originally "to observe the stars closely," now "to think carefully"
mnemonic: CONSIDER sounds like "con-SIDE-er" -- you look at both SIDEs of a decision before choosing.
memory_trick: CON-SIDER: look at all SIDEs before you decide.
visual_association: A person standing at a fork in the road, weighing both paths.
difference_explained: Consider = think about options. Decide = make the final choice. Considering comes first.
mini_conversation:
A: Are you thinking about studying abroad?
B: Yes, I'm seriously considering it for next year.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A CEO taps the table and says, "Let's take a moment to consider all our options."
news_style_line: News-style: "The council is considering new measures to reduce traffic in the city center."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Have you considered just renting instead of buying?"
mcq_options: A) To completely ignore an option  B) To think carefully about something  C) To argue about a plan  D) To immediately decide without thought
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: We are ______ several candidates for the position. → considering
find_and_fix_to_correct: She is considering to buy a new car. → She is considering buying a new car.
translate: कृपया मेरे सुझाव पर विचार करें। → Please consider my suggestion.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a change you are considering making.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to think carefully about something before deciding'?
usage_tip: 'Please consider…' is a polite request in formal letters.

simple_explanation: To explain exactly what a word or idea means. When you define something, you state its exact meaning clearly, often the way a dictionary would.
example_1: Can you define this word for me?
example_2: The dictionary defines 'happy' as feeling pleasure or contentment.
example_3: It's hard to define true success.
collocations: clearly define, define a term, define a boundary, loosely defined
related_phrasal_verbs: spell out, lay down, pin down
action_sequence: Before: see an unclear word → During: find its exact meaning → After: state it clearly
grammar_pattern: define + noun + as + description (Define success as reaching your own goals.)
common_mistake: Please define about this word.
correct_version: Please define this word.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Define' takes a direct object; don't add 'about'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: dih-FYNE; rhymes with "fine."
spelling_tip: One "f" -- de-FINE, related to "final" and "finish" (same root, "fin").
etymology: From Latin "definire" (to set limits, determine), from "de-" (completely) + "finire" (to bound, finish).
prefix_root_suffix: de- (completely) + fine (to bound/limit, from Latin finire) = to completely set the limits/meaning of something
mnemonic: DEFINE has "FINE" inside -- you draw a clear, FINE line around a word's exact meaning.
memory_trick: DE-FINE comes from Latin finis, 'boundary': draw a boundary around a meaning.
visual_association: A magnifying glass held over one object, holding it sharp while everything around it stays blurred.
difference_explained: Define = give the exact meaning. Describe = give details of what something is like.
mini_conversation:
A: How would you define a 'good friend'?
B: Someone who's honest and always there for you.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A professor writes on the board and says, "Let's define this term before we go further."
news_style_line: News-style: "The new law clearly defines what counts as a safety violation."
casual_conversation: Casual: "How would you even define 'success' these days?"
mcq_options: A) To completely ignore a topic  B) To explain the exact meaning of something  C) To argue about a definition  D) To predict future events
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The teacher asked us to ______ the word in our own words. → define
find_and_fix_to_correct: Can you define me this term? → Can you define this term for me?
translate: इस शब्द को परिभाषित करना कठिन है। → It is hard to define this word.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence defining the word 'friend' in your own way.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to explain exactly what a word or idea means'?
usage_tip: Exam questions often say 'Define the term…'.

simple_explanation: To make something easier to understand by explaining it more clearly. When you clarify something, you remove confusion by explaining a point again, often in simpler or more detailed terms.
example_1: Let me clarify what I meant.
example_2: Could you clarify the instructions, please?
example_3: She clarified her position during the interview.
collocations: clarify a point, clarify further, need to clarify, clarify a misunderstanding
related_phrasal_verbs: explain further, spell out, make clear
action_sequence: Before: people are confused → During: explain more simply → After: it becomes clear
grammar_pattern: clarify + noun (Let's clarify the details.)
common_mistake: Can you clarify about your answer?
correct_version: Can you clarify your answer?
why_it_s_wrong: 'Clarify' takes a direct object; don't add 'about'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the first syllable: KLA-ruh-fye; four syllables total.
spelling_tip: Related to "clear" and "clarity" -- all share the root "clar" (clear/bright).
etymology: From Latin "clarificare," from "clarus" (clear, bright) + "-ficare" (to make).
prefix_root_suffix: clar(i) (clear, from Latin clarus) + -fy (to make) = "to make clear"
mnemonic: CLARIFY has CLEAR inside its meaning -- you make something CLEAR by clarifying it.
memory_trick: CLAR-ify: make it CLEAR (same root).
visual_association: Foggy glass being wiped clean to reveal a clear view.
difference_explained: Explain = make something understood. Clarify = make something that was confusing clearer, often after a first explanation.
mini_conversation:
A: Wait, are we meeting at 3 or 4?
B: Let me clarify -- it's 4 PM, not 3.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A lawyer raises a hand and says, "Just to clarify, my client was not present that night."
news_style_line: News-style: "The spokesperson clarified that the new rule applies only to new employees."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Sorry, can you clarify what you mean by 'soon'?"
mcq_options: A) To make something more confusing  B) To make something easier to understand  C) To completely ignore a question  D) To argue about a point
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Could you ______ what you meant by that comment? → clarify
find_and_fix_to_correct: He clarified about the rules to us. → He clarified the rules for us.
translate: कृपया अपनी बात को स्पष्ट करें। → Please clarify your point.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence starting 'Just to clarify,'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to make something easier to understand by explaining it more clearly'?
usage_tip: 'Just to clarify, …' is a polite way to check facts in a meeting.

hindi_meaning: व्याख्या करना, अर्थ निकालना, अनुवाद करना
simple_explanation: To explain the meaning of something, especially something unclear. When you interpret something, you explain what it means, often based on your own understanding -- this can be a text, a dream, an event, or spoken words in another language.
example_1: I interpreted her silence as agreement.
example_2: Different readers interpret the poem differently.
example_3: He works as someone who interprets sign language.
collocations: interpret data, interpret a dream, widely interpreted, misinterpret
related_phrasal_verbs: read into, make sense of, translate
where_it_s_used: Language translation, literature, data analysis, art, dreams
action_sequence: Before: see a sign or hear words → During: think what they mean → After: decide the meaning
grammar_pattern: interpret + noun + as + noun/adjective (She interpreted his silence as anger.)
common_mistake: I interpreted that he was angry from his silence.
correct_version: I interpreted his silence as anger.
why_it_s_wrong: The pattern is 'interpret something AS something', not 'interpret that'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: in-TUR-prit; four syllables total.
spelling_tip: Related to "interpreter" (a person who translates spoken language) -- remember the connection.
etymology: From Latin "interpretari" (to explain, expound), from "interpres" (an agent, negotiator, translator).
prefix_root_suffix: inter- (between) + pret (agent/negotiator, from Latin interpres) = literally "one who stands between" and explains
mnemonic: INTERPRET sounds like "enter-PRINT" -- you "print" your own understanding onto someone else's words.
memory_trick: INTER-PRET: go between ('inter') two people and give the meaning.
visual_association: A pair of glasses held up, turning a blurred shape behind them into a clear one.
difference_explained: Translate = change words into another language. Interpret = explain the meaning (also used for live spoken translation).
mini_conversation:
A: What do you think this painting means?
B: I interpret it as a symbol of hope.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A detective studies the note and says, "I interpret this as a warning, not a threat."
news_style_line: News-style: "Analysts interpret the latest figures as a sign of slowing growth."
casual_conversation: Casual: "How did you interpret what she said at the meeting?"
mcq_options: A) To completely ignore something  B) To explain or understand the meaning of something  C) To argue about a fact  D) To predict a future event
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: It's easy to ______ his quietness as rudeness, but he's just shy. → interpret
find_and_fix_to_correct: She interpreted that his smile as friendliness. → She interpreted his smile as friendliness.
translate: हर कोई इस कविता की अलग-अलग व्याख्या करता है। → Everyone interprets this poem differently.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about how you interpreted a friend's silence.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to explain the meaning of something, especially something unclear'?
usage_tip: An interpreter translates speech live; a translator works with written text.

simple_explanation: To stop sleeping and become conscious. When you wake, you come out of sleep and become alert -- you can wake yourself up or wake someone else up.
example_1: I wake up at 6 every morning.
example_2: The baby woke up crying in the night.
example_3: Please wake me up before 7 AM.
collocations: wake up, wake someone up, wide awake, wake up early
related_phrasal_verbs: wake up, get up, rise and shine
action_sequence: Before: sleep → During: the alarm rings → After: open your eyes: 'I woke up at 6.'
grammar_pattern: wake (up) + (person) (I woke up early. / She woke him up gently.)
common_mistake: I waked up early today.
correct_version: I woke up early today.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Wake' is irregular: the past is 'woke', not 'waked'.
pronunciation_tip: Rhymes with "cake" -- WAYK; a clear, single-syllable word.
spelling_tip: Irregular past tense: wake, woke, woken -- not "waked."
etymology: From Old English "wacan" (to become awake, arise), related to "watch" and "waken."
prefix_root_suffix: wake = root (from Old English wacan) -- no separate prefix/suffix
mnemonic: WAKE rhymes with "CAKE" -- imagine waking up to the smell of fresh cake in the morning.
memory_trick: WAKE → WOKE → WOKEN, like BREAK → BROKE → BROKEN.
visual_association: An alarm clock ringing loudly beside a sleepy face slowly opening its eyes.
difference_explained: Wake (up) is the action. Awake is the state: 'I woke up at 6 and I'm still awake.'
mini_conversation:
A: What time did you wake up today?
B: I woke up really early, around 5:30.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character jolts upright in bed and gasps, "I just woke up from the strangest dream."
news_style_line: News-style: "Residents woke up to heavy snowfall covering the entire city."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Ugh, I woke up late and missed the bus."
mcq_options: A) To fall asleep  B) To stop sleeping and become alert  C) To get dressed  D) To eat breakfast
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: I usually ______ up before my alarm goes off. → wake
find_and_fix_to_correct: She waked up at seven this morning. → She woke up at seven this morning.
translate: मैं हर सुबह छह बजे जाग जाता हूँ। → I wake up at six every morning.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about what time you woke up today.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to stop sleeping and become conscious'?
usage_tip: 'Wake up' is more common than 'wake' alone: 'Wake me up at 6.'

simple_explanation: To rest with your eyes closed and mind unconscious. When you sleep, your body and mind rest, usually at night, and you're not aware of what's happening around you.
example_1: I sleep for eight hours every night.
example_2: The cat slept on the sofa all afternoon.
example_3: I couldn't sleep because of the noise.
collocations: sleep well, sleep late, go to sleep, sleep soundly
related_phrasal_verbs: sleep in, sleep over, doze off
action_sequence: Before: lie down → During: close your eyes and rest → After: wake up fresh
grammar_pattern: sleep + (time expression) (I sleep for seven hours. / I slept until noon.)
common_mistake: I sleeped very well last night.
correct_version: I slept very well last night.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Sleep' is irregular: the past is 'slept', not 'sleeped'.
spelling_tip: Double "e" in the middle -- sleep, sleeping, but irregular past tense "slept" (no double e).
etymology: From Old English "slæp" (sleep, rest), a common Germanic word.
prefix_root_suffix: sleep = root (from Old English slæp) -- no separate prefix/suffix
mnemonic: SLEEP has two E's like two closed EYES resting side by side.
memory_trick: SLEEP → SLEPT, like KEEP → KEPT and SWEEP → SWEPT.
visual_association: A person curled up under a blanket with a small "Z" floating above their head.
difference_explained: Sleep is the verb. Asleep is the state: 'The baby is asleep.' Fall asleep = start sleeping.
mini_conversation:
A: You look tired today.
B: Yeah, I didn't sleep well last night.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A tired traveler collapses onto the bed and mutters, "I could sleep for a whole week."
news_style_line: News-style: "Doctors recommend adults sleep at least seven hours a night."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I really need to sleep earlier this week."
mcq_options: A) To rest with your eyes closed and mind unconscious  B) To eat a large meal  C) To exercise vigorously  D) To travel somewhere new
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: I didn't ______ well because of the storm last night. → sleep
find_and_fix_to_correct: He sleeped for ten hours yesterday. → He slept for ten hours yesterday.
translate: मैं रोज़ रात को आठ घंटे सोता हूँ। → I sleep eight hours every night.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about how many hours you slept last night.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to rest with your eyes closed and mind unconscious'?
usage_tip: 'Sleep well!' and 'Did you sleep well?' are everyday greetings.

simple_explanation: To clean something with water, often with soap. When you wash something, you use water (and usually soap) to remove dirt from it, like your hands, clothes, or dishes.
example_1: Please wash your hands before eating.
example_2: She washed the dishes after dinner.
example_3: I need to wash my car this weekend.
collocations: wash your hands, wash the dishes, wash clothes, wash up
related_phrasal_verbs: wash up, wash away, wash out
action_sequence: Before: hands are dirty → During: use soap and water → After: they are clean
grammar_pattern: wash + noun (Wash your hands. / Wash the car.)
common_mistake: I washing my hands right now.
correct_version: I am washing my hands right now.
why_it_s_wrong: The present continuous needs am/is/are + -ing.
pronunciation_tip: Rhymes with "gosh" -- WAHSH; the "a" sounds like "ah."
spelling_tip: "Wa-sh" -- no extra letters needed; wash, washed, washing.
etymology: From Old English "wascan" (to wash), a common Germanic word related to "water."
prefix_root_suffix: wash = root (from Old English wascan) -- no separate prefix/suffix
word_family: washing (n., as in "washing machine"), washer (n.), unwashed (adj.)
mnemonic: WASH sounds like the "swoosh" of water rinsing something clean.
memory_trick: WASH = Water And Soap Help.
visual_association: Soapy bubbles rinsing off a pair of hands under running water.
difference_explained: Wash = clean with water. Wipe = clean by rubbing, often with a cloth.
mini_conversation:
A: Have you washed your hands yet?
B: Yes, I just washed them before dinner.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A mother calls from the kitchen, "Go wash your hands before you touch anything!"
news_style_line: News-style: "Health experts remind the public to wash hands regularly to prevent illness."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Can you wash the dishes tonight? I did them yesterday."
mcq_options: A) To make something dirty  B) To clean something with water  C) To cook a meal  D) To fold clothes
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Don't forget to ______ your hands before dinner. → wash
find_and_fix_to_correct: She wash her car every Sunday. → She washes her car every Sunday.
translate: खाने से पहले अपने हाथ धो लो। → Wash your hands before eating.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about when you wash your clothes.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to clean something with water, often with soap'?
usage_tip: 'Wash up' means wash the dishes in British English, wash hands and face in American English.

simple_explanation: To clean or smooth something using a brush, often your teeth or hair. When you brush something, you use a brush to clean it or make it neat, most commonly your teeth or your hair.
example_1: I brush my teeth twice a day.
example_2: She brushed her hair before leaving the house.
example_3: Don't forget to brush your teeth after lunch.
collocations: brush your teeth, brush your hair, brush aside, brush up on
related_phrasal_verbs: brush up on, brush aside, brush off
action_sequence: Before: put toothpaste on the brush → During: brush for two minutes → After: rinse your mouth
grammar_pattern: brush + noun (Brush your teeth. / Brush your hair.)
common_mistake: I brush my teeth in the morning yesterday.
correct_version: I brushed my teeth in the morning yesterday.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Yesterday' needs the past tense 'brushed'.
pronunciation_tip: Rhymes with "rush" -- BRUSH; the "u" is a short, quick sound.
spelling_tip: Ends in "-ush," like "rush" and "push" -- brush, brushed, brushing.
etymology: From Old French "broisse" (a bundle of twigs used for sweeping), related to Latin "bruscia."
prefix_root_suffix: brush = root (from Old French broisse) -- no separate prefix/suffix
word_family: brush (n., the object itself), toothbrush (n.), hairbrush (n.)
mnemonic: BRUSH rhymes with "RUSH" -- you quickly RUSH the BRUSH through your hair or teeth each morning.
memory_trick: BRUSH sounds like the 'brrsh' of a toothbrush.
visual_association: A toothbrush moving in small circles across a bright, clean smile.
difference_explained: A comb has one row of teeth; a brush has many bristles. You can brush or comb your hair, but only brush your teeth.
mini_conversation:
A: Did you brush your teeth already?
B: Yes, right after breakfast.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A child grumbles while holding a toothbrush, "Do I really have to brush my teeth again?"
news_style_line: News-style: "Dentists recommend brushing your teeth twice a day for at least two minutes."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Hurry up and brush your hair, we're leaving in five minutes!"
mcq_options: A) To clean or smooth something with a brush  B) To eat quickly  C) To fall asleep  D) To argue with someone
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: She always ______ her teeth right before bed. → brushes
find_and_fix_to_correct: He brush his hair every morning. → He brushes his hair every morning.
translate: मैं रोज़ सुबह अपने दाँत ब्रश करता हूँ। → I brush my teeth every morning.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about how many times a day you brush your teeth.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to clean or smooth something using a brush, often your teeth or hair'?
usage_tip: 'Brush your teeth', 'brush your hair' — no 'the' before teeth or hair.

simple_explanation: To put on clothes. When you dress, you put clothes on your body, often getting ready for the day, an event, or a specific occasion.
example_1: I dress quickly in the morning.
example_2: She dressed the children for school.
example_3: He always dresses smartly for work.
collocations: get dressed, dress up, dress warmly, dress smartly
related_phrasal_verbs: dress up, dress down, get dressed
where_it_s_used: Morning routine, fashion, formal events, weather
action_sequence: Before: take clothes out → During: put them on → After: ready: 'I'm dressed.'
grammar_pattern: dress (up/down) + (adverb) (Dress warmly for the trip. / Dress up for the party.)
common_mistake: I am dress every morning at seven.
correct_version: I dress every morning at seven.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Dress' is the main verb here, so the simple present needs no 'am'.
pronunciation_tip: Rhymes with "less" -- DRESS; a short, single-syllable word.
spelling_tip: Double "s" at the end -- dress, dressed, dressing.
etymology: From Old French "dresser" (to arrange, prepare), from Latin "directus" (straight, direct).
prefix_root_suffix: dress = root (from Old French dresser, to arrange) -- no separate prefix/suffix
word_family: dress (n., a piece of clothing), dressed (adj.), undress (v.)
mnemonic: DRESS sounds like "press" your clothes flat -- you DRESS neatly after ironing.
memory_trick: Dress as a verb = put on your dress (clothes).
visual_association: A closet door opening to reveal a neatly hung row of outfits.
emotion_feel: Neutral, sometimes excited before an occasion
difference_explained: Dress / get dressed = the action of putting clothes on. Wear = have clothes on: 'I'm wearing a blue shirt.'
mini_conversation:
A: What should I wear to the interview?
B: Dress smartly -- maybe a shirt and trousers.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character checks the mirror and says, "I need five more minutes to dress properly."
news_style_line: News-style: "Forecasters advise residents to dress warmly ahead of the cold snap."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Should we dress up for the party or keep it casual?"
mcq_options: A) To take off clothes  B) To put on clothes  C) To wash clothes  D) To fold clothes
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: You should ______ warmly -- it's freezing outside today. → dress
find_and_fix_to_correct: She dress very nicely for the wedding. → She dressed very nicely for the wedding.
translate: बाहर बहुत ठंड है, इसलिए गर्म कपड़े पहनो। → It's very cold outside, so dress warmly.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about how long it takes you to get dressed in the morning.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to put on clothes'?
usage_tip: 'Get dressed' is more common than 'dress': 'Get dressed, we're late!'

simple_explanation: To prepare food by heating it. When you cook, you prepare food using heat -- boiling, frying, baking, or grilling -- to make it ready to eat.
example_2: My father cooks amazing curry.
example_3: She's cooking pasta for tonight's dinner.
collocations: cook dinner, cook a meal, home-cooked, cook from scratch
related_phrasal_verbs: cook up, whip up, prepare a meal
action_sequence: Before: cut the vegetables → During: heat them in a pan → After: serve the food
grammar_pattern: cook + noun (for + person) (Cook dinner for the family.)
common_mistake: I cook the dinner yesterday.
correct_version: I cooked the dinner yesterday.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Yesterday' puts the action in the past, so the verb needs -ed.
pronunciation_tip: Rhymes with "book" -- KOOK (short "oo" sound), not a long "oo" like in "food."
spelling_tip: Double "o" -- cook, cooked, cooking; don't confuse with "cock" or "coke."
etymology: From Old English "coc" (a cook, person who prepares food), from Latin "coquus," related to "coquere" (to cook).
prefix_root_suffix: cook = root (from Old English coc, from Latin coquus) -- no separate prefix/suffix
word_family: cooking (n.), cooked (adj.), cooker (n., British English), cookery (n.)
mnemonic: COOK rhymes with "BOOK" -- imagine following a recipe BOOK while you COOK.
memory_trick: A COOK COOKS in the kitchen: the person and the action share one word.
visual_association: Steam rising from a bubbling pot on a stove.
difference_explained: A cook is a person. A cooker is the stove or pressure pot. 'My mother is a good cook', not 'a good cooker'.
mini_conversation:
A: What are you cooking tonight?
B: I'm cooking rice and chicken curry.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A chef wipes their hands on an apron and says, "Tonight, we cook something special."
news_style_line: News-style: "The charity cooks free meals for over 200 families every week."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I don't feel like cooking tonight -- let's just order pizza."
mcq_options: A) To wash dishes  B) To prepare food using heat  C) To eat quickly  D) To buy groceries
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: My mother always ______ dinner for the whole family. → cooks
find_and_fix_to_correct: He cook dinner every night. → He cooks dinner every night.
