simple_explanation: To clean or dry a surface by rubbing it with a cloth. When you wipe something, you use a cloth or your hand to quickly rub away dirt, dust, or liquid from a surface.
example_1: I wipe the table after every meal.
example_2: She wiped the counter clean before cooking.
example_3: He wiped his hands on a towel.
collocations: wipe clean, wipe down, wipe away, wipe your feet
related_phrasal_verbs: wipe down, wipe away, wipe out
action_sequence: Before: see a spill → During: rub it with a cloth → After: the table is clean and dry
grammar_pattern: wipe + noun (+ down/clean) (Wipe the table down. / Wipe the mirror clean.)
common_mistake: I wipe the table yesterday morning.
correct_version: I wiped the table yesterday morning.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Yesterday morning' is finished time, so use the past tense 'wiped'.
pronunciation_tip: Rhymes with "ripe" -- WYPE; the "i" is a long sound.
spelling_tip: Silent "e" at the end changes the vowel sound -- wipe (long i), not "wip."
etymology: From Old English "wipian" (to wipe, rub clean), a common Germanic word.
prefix_root_suffix: wipe = root (from Old English wipian) -- no separate prefix/suffix
word_family: wiper (n., as in "windshield wiper"), wipeout (n., informal)
mnemonic: WIPE rhymes with "SWIPE" -- you swipe a cloth across a surface to wipe it clean.
memory_trick: WIPE rhymes with SWIPE: a quick sideways stroke with a cloth.
visual_association: A cloth gliding smoothly across a shiny, dust-free table.
difference_explained: Wipe = clean by rubbing, usually with a cloth. Wash = clean with water.
mini_conversation:
A: The table's still sticky.
B: Sorry, let me wipe it down again.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character grabs a cloth and mutters, "Let me just wipe this mess up before anyone notices."
news_style_line: News-style: "Volunteers wiped down surfaces at the shelter as part of the cleanup effort."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Can you wipe the counter before we start cooking?"
mcq_options: A) To clean a surface by rubbing it  B) To cook a meal  C) To fold clothes neatly  D) To water plants
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Please ______ your shoes before stepping inside. → wipe
find_and_fix_to_correct: She wipe the table every morning. → She wipes the table every morning.
translate: कृपया खाने के बाद मेज़ को पोंछ दो। → Please wipe the table after eating.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about what you wipe after eating.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to clean or dry a surface by rubbing it with a cloth'?
usage_tip: 'Wipe your feet' is said at the door before entering a house.

simple_explanation: To go somewhere to buy things. When you shop, you visit a store (or a website) to look at and buy items like food, clothes, or gifts.
example_1: I shop for groceries every weekend.
example_2: We shopped for hours before finding the perfect dress.
example_3: She likes to shop online rather than in stores.
collocations: shop online, shop around, go shopping, window shop
where_it_s_used: Groceries, malls, online stores, gifts, weekends
action_sequence: Before: make a list → During: walk around the market and choose things → After: pay and carry the bags home
grammar_pattern: shop for + noun (I shop for clothes on weekends.)
common_mistake: I shopping every Saturday.
correct_version: I go shopping every Saturday.
why_it_s_wrong: For a habit, use 'go shopping' or 'shop'. '-ing' alone can't be the main verb.
pronunciation_tip: Rhymes with "top" -- SHAHP; short and sharp.
spelling_tip: Double the "p" before adding "-ing" or "-ed" -- shopping, shopped.
etymology: From Middle English "shoppe" (a booth or stall), related to Old High German "scopf" (a shed).
prefix_root_suffix: shop = root (from Middle English shoppe) -- no separate prefix/suffix
mnemonic: SHOP rhymes with "STOP" -- you STOP at a SHOP to buy something.
memory_trick: SHOP is both the place and the action: you shop at a shop.
visual_association: A shopping cart slowly filling up with colorful items.
difference_explained: Shop = the whole activity of looking and buying. Buy = pay for one thing. You can shop without buying.
mini_conversation:
A: What are you doing this weekend?
B: I'm going to shop for some new shoes.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character glances at a long receipt and jokes, "I think I shopped a little too much today."
news_style_line: News-style: "More consumers are choosing to shop online rather than visit physical stores."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Do you want to shop for groceries together this evening?"
mcq_options: A) To sell items in a store  B) To go somewhere to buy things  C) To cook a meal  D) To clean a house
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: We usually ______ for groceries on Sunday mornings. → shop
find_and_fix_to_correct: She shop at the mall every week. → She shops at the mall every week.
translate: मैं हर हफ्ते बाजार में खरीदारी करता हूँ। → I shop at the market every week.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about where you usually go shopping.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to go somewhere to buy things'?
usage_tip: 'I'm just looking' is what you say when a shopkeeper offers help and you're only browsing.

simple_explanation: To relax or stop working for a while to recover energy. When you rest, you stop doing an activity so your body or mind can recover and feel refreshed again.
example_1: I need to rest after work.
example_2: She rested for an hour after the long hike.
example_3: The doctor told him to rest his injured leg.
collocations: rest well, get some rest, rest assured, take a rest
related_phrasal_verbs: rest up, take a break, lie down
action_sequence: Before: feel tired → During: sit or lie down quietly → After: feel fresh again
grammar_pattern: rest + (for + time expression) (I rested for two hours.)
common_mistake: I am resting every Sunday.
correct_version: I rest every Sunday.
why_it_s_wrong: A regular habit uses the simple present, not the continuous form.
pronunciation_tip: Rhymes with "best" -- REST; short and clear.
spelling_tip: Simple spelling -- rest, rested, resting; no double letters needed.
etymology: From Old English "ræst" (rest, sleep, repose), a common Germanic word.
prefix_root_suffix: rest = root (from Old English ræst) -- no separate prefix/suffix
mnemonic: REST rhymes with "BEST" -- resting is the BEST way to recover your energy.
memory_trick: REST is what you do in a REST room: stop and recover.
visual_association: Someone lying back in a hammock under a shady tree.
difference_explained: Rest = stop activity to recover energy. Relax = let go of stress. You can relax while doing something, but resting means stopping.
mini_conversation:
A: You look exhausted.
B: I know, I really need to rest this weekend.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A coach tells an exhausted player, "Take a seat and rest -- you've earned it."
news_style_line: News-style: "Doctors advise patients to rest fully before returning to work."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I just want to rest on the couch all afternoon."
mcq_options: A) To work harder  B) To relax and stop activity to recover  C) To argue with someone  D) To travel somewhere
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: After the long trip, we finally sat down to ______. → rest
find_and_fix_to_correct: He rest a lot after the surgery. → He rested a lot after the surgery.
translate: लंबी यात्रा के बाद, हमें आराम करने की जरूरत थी। → After the long trip, we needed to rest.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about how you rest after a long day.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to relax or stop working for a while to recover energy'?
usage_tip: 'Get some rest' is a caring thing to say to someone who is tired or ill.

simple_explanation: To become calm and free from stress or tension. When you relax, your body and mind become calm -- your muscles loosen and your worries fade for a while.
example_1: I like to relax with music.
example_2: She relaxed on the beach for hours.
example_3: Try to relax before the interview.
collocations: relax completely, just relax, relax your muscles, time to relax
action_sequence: Before: feel stressed → During: breathe slowly or listen to music → After: feel calm
grammar_pattern: relax + (adverb/prepositional phrase) (Relax for a while. / Relax at home.)
common_mistake: Please relax yourself before the exam.
correct_version: Please relax before the exam.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Relax' is complete by itself, so 'yourself' isn't needed.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: ri-LAKS; the "x" sounds like "ks."
spelling_tip: One "l," ends in "-ax" -- relax, relaxed, relaxing.
etymology: From Latin "relaxare" (to loosen, ease), from "re-" (again) + "laxare" (to loosen).
prefix_root_suffix: re- (again) + lax (loose, from Latin laxus) = to become "loose" again
mnemonic: RELAX sounds like "re-LAX(ative)" -- loosen up, let your muscles LAX (loose) and easy.
memory_trick: RELAX = RE + LAX: let your body become loose ('lax') again.
visual_association: A person floating peacefully on calm, still water.
difference_explained: Relaxed = how a person feels ('I feel relaxed'). Relaxing = what causes it ('a relaxing holiday').
mini_conversation:
A: You seem really tense today.
B: I know, I just need to relax for a bit.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character sinks into a chair and sighs, "Finally -- time to just relax."
news_style_line: News-style: "Experts recommend simple breathing exercises to help people relax under stress."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Just relax, everything's going to be fine."
mcq_options: A) To become tense and anxious  B) To become calm and free from stress  C) To argue about a plan  D) To work harder than usual
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: After a long week, I just want to ______ at home. → relax
find_and_fix_to_correct: She relax every evening after work. → She relaxes every evening after work.
translate: छुट्टी के दिन मुझे घर पर आराम करना पसंद है। → I like to relax at home on holidays.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about what helps you relax.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to become calm and free from stress or tension'?
usage_tip: 'Relax, it's fine' calms someone down. 'Relaxed' describes a person; 'relaxing' describes a thing.

simple_explanation: To move your body to stay healthy and fit. When you exercise, you do physical activity -- like running, stretching, or lifting weights -- to keep your body strong and healthy.
example_2: She exercises at the gym three times a week.
example_3: Doctors recommend regular exercise for a healthy heart.
collocations: exercise regularly, get exercise, physical exercise, exercise routine
related_phrasal_verbs: work out, keep fit, warm up
action_sequence: Before: put on sports shoes → During: move your body for 30 minutes → After: feel fit
grammar_pattern: exercise + (frequency/time expression) (I exercise three times a week.)
common_mistake: I do exercise every day.
correct_version: I exercise every day.
why_it_s_wrong: As a verb, 'exercise' works alone. 'Do exercise' sounds less natural than 'exercise' or 'do exercises'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the first syllable: EK-ser-syze; three syllables total.
spelling_tip: Watch the "-cise" ending, pronounced like "size" -- exercise, exercised, exercising.
etymology: From Latin "exercitium," from "exercere" (to keep busy, train), from "ex-" (thoroughly) + "arcere" (to keep off/restrain).
prefix_root_suffix: ex- (out, thoroughly) + ercise (to keep busy/train, from Latin arcere) = to thoroughly "work" the body
mnemonic: EXERCISE contains "EX" (out) + "ERCISE" (energy released outward) -- you push your energy out through movement.
memory_trick: EX-ER-CISE: three syllables, like three sets at the gym.
visual_association: Someone jogging briskly through a park at sunrise.
difference_explained: Exercise = move your body for health. Practise = repeat a skill to get better at it.
mini_conversation:
A: How do you stay so fit?
B: I exercise every morning before work.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A trainer claps and shouts, "Alright, everyone -- let's exercise like we mean it!"
news_style_line: News-style: "Health officials recommend at least 30 minutes of exercise most days of the week."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I've been trying to exercise more since the new year started."
mcq_options: A) To rest completely  B) To move your body to stay healthy  C) To eat a large meal  D) To sleep for a long time
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: He tries to ______ for at least 30 minutes every day. → exercise
find_and_fix_to_correct: She exercise every morning before school. → She exercises every morning before school.
translate: मैं हर सुबह व्यायाम करता हूँ। → I exercise every morning.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about how often you exercise.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to move your body to stay healthy and fit'?
usage_tip: 'Exercise' is also a noun: 'Walking is good exercise.'

simple_explanation: To run slowly and steadily, usually for exercise. When you jog, you run at an easy, relaxed pace -- faster than walking but slower than sprinting -- often to stay fit.
example_1: I jog in the park every morning.
example_2: He jogs five kilometers every day.
example_3: We jogged along the river at sunrise.
collocations: go jogging, jog regularly, morning jog, jog around the park
action_sequence: Before: warm up → During: run slowly and steadily → After: cool down and stretch
grammar_pattern: jog + (frequency/place) (I jog every morning. / I jog in the park.)
common_mistake: I jog to the gym yesterday.
correct_version: I jogged to the gym yesterday.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Yesterday' needs the past tense, and 'jog' doubles the g: jogged.
pronunciation_tip: Rhymes with "dog" -- JAHG; short and clear.
spelling_tip: Double the "g" before adding "-ing" or "-ed" -- jogging, jogged.
etymology: From Middle English "joggen" (to shake, jolt), possibly imitative in origin.
prefix_root_suffix: jog = root (from Middle English joggen) -- no separate prefix/suffix
mnemonic: JOG rhymes with "LOG" -- imagine jogging steadily past a fallen log in the park.
memory_trick: JOG = Just Going slowly, running.
visual_association: A pair of running shoes hitting a path at a steady, even pace.
difference_explained: Jog = run slowly for exercise. Run = move fast on foot, for any reason.
mini_conversation:
A: Where were you this morning?
B: I went for a jog around the lake.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character laces up their shoes and says, "Let's jog before it gets too hot."
news_style_line: News-style: "More people have taken up jogging as a simple way to stay active."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Want to jog together this weekend? It's more fun with company."
mcq_options: A) To walk very slowly  B) To run at a slow, steady pace  C) To swim across a lake  D) To rest on a bench
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: She likes to ______ around the park before breakfast. → jog
find_and_fix_to_correct: He jog every morning before work. → He jogs every morning before work.
translate: मैं हर सुबह पार्क में टहलता (हल्की दौड़) हूँ। → I jog in the park every morning.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about where you like to jog.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to run slowly and steadily, usually for exercise'?
usage_tip: 'Jog someone's memory' means help them remember.

simple_explanation: To extend your body or muscles to become longer or looser. When you stretch, you extend your arms, legs, or whole body to loosen tight muscles, often before or after exercise.
example_2: She stretched her legs after the long flight.
example_3: Remember to stretch your muscles before the workout.
collocations: stretch your muscles, stretch out, warm up and stretch, stretch your legs
related_phrasal_verbs: stretch out, warm up, loosen up
action_sequence: Before: feel stiff → During: pull your arms and legs long → After: feel loose
grammar_pattern: stretch + noun (Stretch your arms. / Stretch your legs.)
common_mistake: I stretch my muscles yesterday before the run.
correct_version: I stretched my muscles yesterday before the run.
why_it_s_wrong: A finished past action needs the past tense 'stretched'.
pronunciation_tip: Rhymes with "fetch" -- STRETCH; the "tch" makes a sharp "ch" sound.
spelling_tip: Ends in "-tch," not just "-ch" -- stretch, stretched, stretching.
etymology: From Old English "streccan" (to stretch out, extend), a common Germanic word.
prefix_root_suffix: stretch = root (from Old English streccan) -- no separate prefix/suffix
mnemonic: STRETCH sounds like a long, drawn-out "STRRR-ETCH" -- imagine your arms slowly extending as you say it.
memory_trick: STRETCH sounds long, like a stretched rubber band.
visual_association: Someone reaching their arms up high, standing on their toes at sunrise.
difference_explained: Stretch = pull your body or a material longer. Extend = make something longer in time or size (extend a deadline).
mini_conversation:
A: My back feels so stiff.
B: Try to stretch a little before you sit down again.
everyday_scene: Everyday: An athlete bends forward slowly and says, "Never skip your stretch before a big race."
news_style_line: News-style: "Physiotherapists recommend a short stretch routine before any workout."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Let's stretch for five minutes before we start the run."
mcq_options: A) To extend your muscles or body  B) To sit quietly  C) To eat a large meal  D) To fall asleep quickly
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Always ______ before you begin any exercise routine. → stretch
find_and_fix_to_correct: She stretch her arms every morning. → She stretches her arms every morning.
translate: दौड़ने से पहले मैं अपनी मांसपेशियों को स्ट्रेच करता हूँ। → I stretch my muscles before running.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about when you stretch during the day.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to extend your body or muscles to become longer or looser'?
usage_tip: 'Stretch your legs' can also mean go for a short walk.

simple_explanation: To remove hair closely from your skin using a razor. When you shave, you use a razor to cut hair very close to the skin, usually on your face, legs, or underarms.
example_2: My dad shaves before work every day.
example_3: She shaved her legs before the beach trip.
collocations: shave your face, shave every day, close shave, shave off
action_sequence: Before: put on shaving cream → During: move the razor over the skin → After: wash the face
grammar_pattern: shave + (noun, optional) (He shaves every morning. / He shaved his beard off.)
common_mistake: He shave his beard yesterday.
correct_version: He shaved his beard yesterday.
why_it_s_wrong: A finished past action needs the past tense 'shaved'.
pronunciation_tip: Rhymes with "wave" -- SHAYV; a clear, long "a" sound.
spelling_tip: Silent "e" at the end -- shave, shaved, shaving.
etymology: From Old English "sceafan" (to scrape, shave), related to "shape" and "scrape."
prefix_root_suffix: shave = root (from Old English sceafan, to scrape) -- no separate prefix/suffix
word_family: shaving (n., as in "shaving cream"), shaver (n.), clean-shaven (adj.), unshaven (adj.)
mnemonic: SHAVE rhymes with "WAVE" -- a razor glides in smooth WAVE-like strokes as you shave.
memory_trick: SHAVE rhymes with WAVE: move the razor in smooth waves.
visual_association: A razor gliding smoothly across a lathered chin in the mirror.
difference_explained: Shave = remove hair close to the skin with a razor. Cut = make hair shorter with scissors.
mini_conversation:
A: You look different today.
B: Yeah, I finally shaved off my beard.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character looks in the mirror and sighs, "I really need to shave before the interview."
news_style_line: News-style: "The barber shop has seen a rise in customers wanting a classic straight-razor shave."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I didn't have time to shave this morning, sorry for the stubble."
mcq_options: A) To grow hair longer  B) To remove hair closely with a razor  C) To wash your face with soap  D) To comb your hair neatly
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: He usually ______ before leaving for the office. → shaves
find_and_fix_to_correct: He shave every morning before breakfast. → He shaves every morning before breakfast.
translate: वह हर सुबह दफ्तर जाने से पहले शेव करता है। → He shaves every morning before going to the office.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about how often a man in your family shaves.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to remove hair closely from your skin using a razor'?
usage_tip: 'A close shave' means a narrow escape from danger.

simple_explanation: To arrange your hair neatly using a comb. When you comb your hair, you use a comb to make it smooth, neat, and tangle-free.
example_1: I comb my hair before school.
example_2: She combed her daughter's hair gently.
example_3: He combed his hair back neatly for the interview.
collocations: comb your hair, comb through, fine-tooth comb, comb back
where_it_s_used: Grooming, morning routine, personal care, appearance
action_sequence: Before: hair is messy → During: run the comb through it → After: hair is neat
grammar_pattern: comb + noun (Comb your hair. / Comb the tangles out.)
common_mistake: I combing my hair every morning.
correct_version: I comb my hair every morning.
why_it_s_wrong: A daily habit needs the simple present. '-ing' needs am/is/are before it.
spelling_tip: Remember the silent "b" at the end -- comb, combed, combing.
etymology: From Old English "camb" (a comb, crest), a common Germanic word.
prefix_root_suffix: comb = root (from Old English camb) -- no separate prefix/suffix
mnemonic: COMB has a silent B, just like a COMB silently glides through your hair without a sound.
memory_trick: COMB has a silent B, like a tooth hiding in the comb.
visual_association: A comb gliding smoothly through neatly parted hair.
difference_explained: A comb has one row of teeth; a brush has many bristles. You can comb or brush hair, but only brush your teeth.
mini_conversation:
A: Your hair looks great today!
B: Thanks, I actually combed it properly for once.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character stands before a mirror and mutters, "Let me just comb this mess before we go."
news_style_line: News-style: "The salon offers a full styling service, from washing to combing to cutting."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Can you comb my hair? I can't reach the back."
mcq_options: A) To wash your hair with shampoo  B) To arrange hair neatly using a comb  C) To cut hair short  D) To dry hair with a towel
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: She always ______ her hair before leaving the house. → combs
find_and_fix_to_correct: He comb his hair before school every day. → He combs his hair before school every day.
translate: वह स्कूल जाने से पहले अपने बाल कंघी करता है। → He combs his hair before going to school.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about when you comb your hair.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to arrange your hair neatly using a comb'?
usage_tip: 'Comb through' means search carefully: 'Police combed through the files.'

simple_explanation: To make clothes smooth and flat using a hot iron. When your clothes are wrinkled, you use a hot iron appliance to press them flat and smooth.
example_1: I need to iron my shirt before the meeting.
example_2: My mother irons the school uniforms every Sunday.
example_3: Can you iron this dress for the party?
collocations: iron a shirt, iron clothes, iron out (wrinkles), iron board
where_it_s_used: Housework, laundry, getting ready for work/events
action_sequence: Before: the shirt is creased → During: move the hot iron over it → After: the shirt is smooth
grammar_pattern: iron + noun (iron the shirt / iron your trousers)
common_mistake: I ironing my clothes now.
correct_version: I am ironing my clothes now.
why_it_s_wrong: The present continuous needs 'am/is/are' before the -ing verb.
spelling_tip: Same spelling as the metal "iron" -- only context tells you if it's noun or verb.
etymology: From the noun "iron" (the metal, Old English "isern") -- the tool used gave its name to the action of ironing clothes, first recorded in the 19th century.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- "iron" is a simple base word
word_family: iron (n. -- the metal/the appliance), ironing (n. -- the activity), ironed (adj. -- already pressed)
mnemonic: You press an IRON (the metal appliance) to IRON (flatten) your clothes.
memory_trick: IRON is pronounced 'EYE-urn' — the R is almost silent.
visual_association: Steam rising from a hot iron gliding over a wrinkled shirt.
difference_explained: Both mean make clothes flat. 'Iron' is standard. 'Press' is common in India and in 'dry cleaning and pressing'.
mini_conversation:
A: Why does your shirt look so neat?
B: I ironed it this morning before work.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character grabs a hot iron and mutters, "I can't go to this interview looking like I slept in my suit."
news_style_line: News-style: "The factory recalled a batch of irons after reports of overheating."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Can you iron my shirt while I make breakfast?"
mcq_options: A) To wash clothes  B) To smooth clothes with heat  C) To fold clothes  D) To sew clothes
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Can you ______ my shirt before the wedding? → iron
find_and_fix_to_correct: She irons her clothes yesterday. → She ironed her clothes yesterday. (past tense needed for a completed past action)
translate: वह हर सुबह अपनी कमीज़ पर इस्तरी करता है। → He irons his shirt every morning.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about who irons clothes in your home.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to make clothes smooth and flat using a hot iron'?
usage_tip: Indians often say 'press' ('Press my shirt'). In standard English, 'iron' is more common.

simple_explanation: To clean a floor using a broom. When dust or dirt gathers on the floor, you sweep it away with a broom into a pile, then remove it.
example_1: I sweep the kitchen floor every evening.
example_2: He swept the leaves off the porch.
example_3: Please sweep the classroom before you leave.
collocations: sweep the floor, sweep up, sweep away, a clean sweep
action_sequence: Before: see dust on the floor → During: move the broom across it → After: collect the dust and throw it away
grammar_pattern: sweep + noun (sweep the floor / sweep the yard)
common_mistake: I sweep the floor already.
correct_version: I have already swept the floor.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Already' with a finished action needs the present perfect: 'have swept'.
pronunciation_tip: One syllable, long "ee" sound: SWEEP, rhymes with "sleep."
spelling_tip: Double "e" -- ee like in "sweep the street."
etymology: From Old English "swapan," meaning to move something with a sweeping motion -- the same root gave us "swoop."
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- "sweep" is a simple base word
word_family: sweep (n. -- a sweeping motion), sweeper (n. -- person/device), swept (past tense/participle)
mnemonic: SWEEP rhymes with "SLEEP" -- you SWEEP the floor before you go to SLEEP.
memory_trick: SWEEP → SWEPT, like SLEEP → SLEPT and KEEP → KEPT.
visual_association: A broom pushing a small pile of dust across a wooden floor.
difference_explained: Sweep = clean with a dry broom. Mop = clean with a wet mop.
mini_conversation:
A: The floor is so dusty.
B: I know, I'll sweep it after lunch.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A shopkeeper sweeps the doorway at dawn, muttering, "Same dust, every single day."
news_style_line: News-style: "Volunteers gathered to sweep and clean the local park over the weekend."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Can you sweep the porch before the guests arrive?"

find_and_fix_to_correct: She sweeped the floor this morning. → She swept the floor this morning. ("sweep" is irregular -- past tense is "swept," not "sweeped")
translate: उसने सुबह आँगन में झाड़ू लगाई। → She swept the courtyard in the morning.

simple_explanation: To clean a floor or carpet using a vacuum cleaner machine. Instead of a broom, you use an electric machine that sucks up dust and dirt -- that action is called vacuuming.
example_1: I vacuum the living room every Saturday.
example_2: He vacuums his car seats once a month.
example_3: Could you vacuum the stairs before guests arrive?
collocations: vacuum the carpet, vacuum cleaner, vacuum up crumbs
action_sequence: Before: plug in the machine → During: move it over the carpet → After: empty the dust bag
grammar_pattern: vacuum + noun (vacuum the carpet / vacuum the car)
common_mistake: I vacuum the carpet yesterday.
correct_version: I vacuumed the carpet yesterday.
why_it_s_wrong: A finished past action needs -ed: vacuumed.
pronunciation_tip: Two syllables, stress on the first: VAC-yoom.
etymology: From Latin "vacuus" (empty) -- the cleaning device is named after the vacuum (empty space/suction) it creates to pull in dust.
prefix_root_suffix: vacu- (from Latin vacuus, empty) + -um (noun ending) -- borrowed whole from Latin
word_family: vacuum (n. -- the machine/empty space), vacuuming (n./gerund -- the activity), vacuumed (adj./past participle)
mnemonic: A VACUUM cleaner sucks dust into empty (VACUUS) space inside it.
memory_trick: VACUUM has double U: two 'u's for the long 'yoo' sound.
visual_association: A vacuum cleaner hose pulling crumbs off a carpet.
difference_explained: Vacuum = clean with an electric machine that sucks dirt. Sweep = clean with a broom.
mini_conversation:
A: This carpet is covered in crumbs.
B: I'll vacuum it right now.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character rushes to vacuum the rug seconds before the doorbell rings, whispering, "They're early!"
news_style_line: News-style: "The company unveiled a new robot that can vacuum an entire house in twenty minutes."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I need to vacuum before my parents visit this weekend."
mcq_options: A) To clean using suction from a machine  B) To wash with soap and water  C) To fold and store  D) To paint over
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: We ______ the rugs every weekend to keep them clean. → vacuum
find_and_fix_to_correct: She vacuum the floor every day. → She vacuums the floor every day. (third person singular needs "-s": vacuums)
translate: वह हर हफ्ते अपने कमरे में वैक्यूम क्लीनर चलाती है। → She vacuums her room every week.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about which room you would vacuum first.

usage_tip: Spelling: one C, two Us — vacuum.

simple_explanation: To pour water on plants or the ground to help them grow. Plants need water to stay alive, so you regularly pour water onto the soil around them -- this action is called watering.
example_1: I water my plants every morning.
example_2: She waters the garden before the sun gets too hot.
example_3: Don't forget to water the tomatoes while I'm away.
collocations: water the plants, water the garden, water the lawn
action_sequence: Before: the soil is dry → During: pour water around the plant → After: the plant looks fresh
grammar_pattern: water + noun (water the plants / water the flowers)
common_mistake: I water the plants yesterday.
correct_version: I watered the plants yesterday.
why_it_s_wrong: A finished past action needs -ed: watered.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the first syllable: WAH-ter (the "t" often sounds like a soft "d" in casual speech).
spelling_tip: Same spelling as the noun "water" -- only the sentence position tells you it's a verb.
etymology: From Old English "waeter" (the noun) -- the verb sense, "to supply with water," developed naturally from the noun and has been in use since medieval times.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- "water" is a simple base word used as noun and verb
word_family: water (n. -- the liquid), watering can (n. -- the tool), watered (adj./past participle)
mnemonic: You WATER a plant by giving it WATER -- the noun becomes the action.
memory_trick: WATER is both the noun and the verb: you water plants with water.
visual_association: A watering can pouring a gentle stream over green leaves.
difference_explained: Water (verb) = give water to plants on purpose. Wet = make something damp, often by accident.
mini_conversation:
A: Your plants look so healthy!
B: I water them every single morning.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character kneels by a wilting plant and says softly, "I'm sorry, I forgot to water you all week."
news_style_line: News-style: "Farmers were told to water their crops early in the morning to reduce evaporation."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Can you water the plants while I'm on vacation?"
mcq_options: A) To cut plants  B) To pour water on something  C) To plant seeds  D) To remove weeds
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Please ______ the flowers before you leave for school. → water
find_and_fix_to_correct: She water the roses every day. → She waters the roses every day. (third person singular needs "-s")
translate: वह हर शाम अपने बगीचे में पानी देती है। → She waters her garden every evening.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about which plants you water at home.

usage_tip: 'My mouth is watering' means you smell or see tasty food.

simple_explanation: To give food to a person or animal. When someone or something can't get food on their own, you feed them -- you give them food to eat.
example_1: I feed my dog twice a day.
example_2: She feeds the birds in the park every morning.
example_3: Could you feed the baby while I cook dinner?
collocations: feed the dog, feed a baby, feed the animals, breast-feed
related_phrasal_verbs: feed up (fatten/tire of), feed off (rely on)
action_sequence: Before: the cat is hungry → During: put food in its bowl → After: the cat eats happily
grammar_pattern: feed + object + (with/on) food (feed the cat / feed the cat some fish)
common_mistake: I feeded my cat this morning.
correct_version: I fed my cat this morning.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Feed' is irregular: the past is 'fed', not 'feeded'.
pronunciation_tip: Long "ee" sound, one syllable: FEED, rhymes with "need."
spelling_tip: Irregular past tense "fed" -- no "-ed" ending like regular verbs.
etymology: From Old English "fedan," related to "food" -- literally "to give food to."
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- "feed" is a simple base word related to "food"
word_family: feed (n. -- animal food), feeding (n./gerund), fed (past tense/participle), feeder (n. -- device, e.g., bird feeder)
mnemonic: FEED rhymes with "NEED" -- every living thing NEEDs to be FED.
memory_trick: FEED → FED: drop one E, like BLEED → BLED.
visual_association: A hand scattering birdseed as pigeons gather around.
difference_explained: You feed someone else. You eat yourself. 'I feed the baby'; 'The baby eats.'
mini_conversation:
A: Has the cat eaten yet?
B: Not yet, I'll feed her right now.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A farmer scatters grain at dawn, saying, "Come on, come and eat, all of you."
news_style_line: News-style: "Volunteers gathered at the shelter to feed hundreds of families this holiday season."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Can you feed the fish while I'm at work today?"
mcq_options: A) To wash  B) To give food to  C) To train  D) To carry
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Don't forget to ______ the goldfish before bed. → feed
find_and_fix_to_correct: She feed the baby every three hours. → She feeds the baby every three hours. (third person singular needs "-s": feeds)
translate: वह हर सुबह पक्षियों को दाना खिलाती है। → She feeds the birds every morning.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about an animal you have fed.

reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to give food to a person or animal'?
usage_tip: 'Fed up' means bored or annoyed: 'I'm fed up with this traffic.'

simple_explanation: To close something securely so it can't be opened without a key. When you want to keep something safe or private, you lock it -- using a key, code, or latch to secure it shut.
example_1: I always lock the door before I leave.
example_2: She locked her bike outside the store.
example_3: Remember to lock your phone when you're not using it.
collocations: lock the door, lock the car, lock up, under lock and key
related_phrasal_verbs: lock up, lock in, lock out
action_sequence: Before: close the door → During: turn the key → After: the door can't open
grammar_pattern: lock + noun (lock the door / lock the drawer)
common_mistake: I forgot to locked the door.
correct_version: I forgot to lock the door.
why_it_s_wrong: After 'to', use the base verb: to lock.
pronunciation_tip: Short "o" sound, one syllable: LAHK, rhymes with "rock."
spelling_tip: Double "c" would be wrong -- just one "c": l-o-c-k.
etymology: From Old English "loc," meaning a bolt, bar, or fastening device -- the verb developed directly from the noun for the device.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- "lock" is a simple base word
word_family: lock (n. -- the device), locked (adj.), locksmith (n. -- person who makes/fixes locks), unlock (v.)
mnemonic: LOCK rhymes with "ROCK" -- a locked door feels as solid and unmovable as a rock.
memory_trick: LOCK and KEY: a lock needs a key to open.
visual_association: A key turning inside a metal lock with a satisfying click.
emotion_feel: Reassurance, sometimes mild anxiety before checking
difference_explained: Close = shut. Lock = shut so it can't be opened without a key or code.
mini_conversation:
A: Did you lock the front door?
B: Yes, I double-checked before we left.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character checks the handle twice, whispering, "Lock it. Lock it again. We can't be too careful."
news_style_line: News-style: "Residents were advised to lock their doors and windows following a series of break-ins."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Did you lock the car? I don't remember doing it."
mcq_options: A) To open something  B) To secure something shut  C) To break something  D) To paint something
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Please ______ the office before you go home tonight. → lock
find_and_fix_to_correct: She locks the door yesterday before leaving. → She locked the door yesterday before leaving. (past tense needed for a completed past action)
translate: बाहर जाने से पहले दरवाज़ा ताला लगाना मत भूलना। → Don't forget to lock the door before going out.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about what you lock before leaving home.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to close something securely so it can't be opened without a key'?
usage_tip: 'Lock yourself out' means you left the key inside and can't get in.

simple_explanation: To open something that was locked, usually with a key or code. When a door, phone, or box is locked, you unlock it by using the right key, password, or code to open it.
example_1: I unlock my phone with my fingerprint.
example_2: She unlocked the front door and stepped inside.
example_3: He couldn't unlock his car because he lost the key.
collocations: unlock the door, unlock a phone, unlock a file, unlock your potential
where_it_s_used: Doors, phones, computers, safes, figurative "unlock potential/opportunities"
action_sequence: Before: the door is locked → During: turn the key → After: the door opens
grammar_pattern: unlock + noun (unlock the gate / unlock the screen)
common_mistake: I unlock the door yesterday.
correct_version: I unlocked the door yesterday.
why_it_s_wrong: A finished past action needs -ed: unlocked.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: un-LOCK, not UN-lock.
spelling_tip: "Un-" + "lock" -- no extra letters, just the prefix attached directly.
etymology: From "un-" (reverse action) + "lock" -- formed in Middle English to describe undoing a lock.
prefix_root_suffix: un- = reverse/opposite action + lock = to fasten shut
mnemonic: UN + LOCK = undo the LOCK, just like "undo" reverses an action.
memory_trick: UN + LOCK = the opposite of lock.
visual_association: A key clicking a lock open, or a phone screen lighting up after a fingerprint scan.
emotion_feel: Relief or anticipation, sometimes mild frustration if it's difficult
difference_explained: Unlock = remove the lock. Open = move the door. You unlock first, then open.
mini_conversation:
A: The gate won't open.
B: Wait, I have the key -- let me unlock it.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character fumbles with a set of keys in the dark, muttering, "Come on, come on, unlock already."
news_style_line: News-style: "The app was updated to let users unlock their front door remotely from their phone."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Can you unlock the car? My hands are full."
mcq_options: A) To close something  B) To open something that was locked  C) To break something  D) To hide something
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: I need my code to ______ my laptop every morning. → unlock
find_and_fix_to_correct: She unlock the door with her key. → She unlocks the door with her key. (third person singular needs "-s": unlocks)
translate: उसने अपनी चाबी से दरवाज़ा खोला। → She unlocked the door with her key.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about how you unlock your phone.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to open something that was locked, usually with a key or code'?
usage_tip: Phones: 'Unlock your screen'. Games: 'unlock a new level'.

simple_explanation: To fill a battery with electrical power. When a phone or laptop battery gets low, you connect it to a power source to charge it -- to fill it back up with energy.
example_1: I charge my phone every night.
example_2: Please charge your laptop before the meeting.
example_3: My earbuds only take ten minutes to charge fully.
collocations: charge a phone, fully charged, charge overnight, charging cable
action_sequence: Before: the battery is low → During: plug in the charger → After: the battery is full
grammar_pattern: charge + noun (charge the battery / charge my phone)
common_mistake: My phone is charging since two hours.
correct_version: My phone has been charging for two hours.
why_it_s_wrong: For a length of time, use 'for' with the present perfect continuous: 'has been charging for two hours'.
pronunciation_tip: One syllable, "ch" sound like in "chair": CHAHRJ.
etymology: From Old French "charger" (to load), from Latin "carricare" (to load a cart) -- the electrical sense ("to load with energy") developed in the 18th-19th centuries.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- "charge" is a simple base word (from Old French)
word_family: charge (n. -- electrical load, or a fee), charger (n. -- the device), charged (adj.), recharge (v.)
mnemonic: You CHARGE your phone to load it with energy, just like you'd CHARGE (load) a cart with goods.
memory_trick: CHARGE: like a charging bull, full of energy.
visual_association: A phone screen glowing with a battery icon slowly filling up.
emotion_feel: Mild urgency (when battery is low), otherwise neutral
difference_explained: Charge = fill a battery. Recharge = fill it again. In India, 'recharge' also means top up your mobile balance.
mini_conversation:
A: My phone's at 2 percent!
B: Quick, charge it before we leave.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character glances at a blinking red battery icon and sighs, "Not now, please just charge already."
news_style_line: News-style: "The city installed new public stations where residents can charge electric scooters for free."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Can I borrow your charger? My phone's about to die."
mcq_options: A) To turn it off  B) To fill it with electrical power  C) To clean it  D) To repair it
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: I always ______ my phone before I go to bed. → charge
find_and_fix_to_correct: I charging my phone right now. → I am charging my phone right now. (need auxiliary "am" with the -ing form)
translate: मैं रोज़ रात को अपना फ़ोन चार्ज करता हूँ। → I charge my phone every night.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about how long your phone takes to charge.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to fill a battery with electrical power'?
usage_tip: 'Charge' also means ask for money: 'They charged me ₹200.'

simple_explanation: To disconnect a device from the electrical socket. When you're done using an appliance, or want to save electricity, you unplug it -- you pull its plug out of the wall socket.
example_1: Please unplug the toaster after breakfast.
example_2: She unplugged the iron before leaving the house.
example_3: Remember to unplug the charger when it's not in use.
collocations: unplug an appliance, unplug the charger, unplug and restart
action_sequence: Before: the device is plugged in → During: pull the plug out of the socket → After: no power flows
grammar_pattern: unplug + noun (unplug the kettle / unplug the fan)
common_mistake: I unplugged off the TV.
correct_version: I unplugged the TV.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Unplug' already means disconnect, so don't add 'off'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: un-PLUG.
etymology: From "un-" (reverse action) + "plug" -- a straightforward compound formed once electrical plugs became common household items.
prefix_root_suffix: un- = reverse/opposite action + plug = to insert into a socket
word_family: plug (n./v. -- base word), unplugged (adj., also means "without electronic instruments" in music), plugged in (opposite adj. phrase)
mnemonic: UN + PLUG = pull the PLUG UN-done, disconnecting it from power.
memory_trick: UN + PLUG = pull the plug out.
visual_association: A hand pulling a plug out of a wall socket.
difference_explained: Switch off = stop the power with the switch. Unplug = take the plug out of the socket completely.
related_words: plug, socket, electricity, appliance, switch off
mini_conversation:
A: Did you unplug the iron before we left?
B: Yes, I checked twice.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character yanks a cable out of the wall just as sparks fly, shouting, "Unplug it, now!"
news_style_line: News-style: "Officials advised residents to unplug electronics ahead of the incoming storm."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Can you unplug the fan before you leave the room?"
mcq_options: A) To turn something on  B) To disconnect from power  C) To repair a device  D) To clean a socket
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Always ______ small appliances when you're not using them. → unplug
find_and_fix_to_correct: She unplug the lamp before painting the wall. → She unplugged the lamp before painting the wall. (past tense needed for a completed past action)
translate: सोने से पहले टीवी अनप्लग करना मत भूलना। → Don't forget to unplug the TV before you sleep.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about which device you unplug at night.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to disconnect a device from the electrical socket'?
usage_tip: 'Unplug' also means take a break from phones and the internet: 'I unplug on Sundays.'

simple_explanation: To stop and leave a vehicle in a particular place. When you drive somewhere, you find a space and park your car there -- you stop it and leave it until you need it again.
example_1: I park my car in the garage every night.
example_2: He parked the car right in front of the store.
example_3: You can't park here -- it's a no-parking zone.
collocations: park the car, parking space, park illegally, double park
related_phrasal_verbs: park up (informal, to stop and park)
action_sequence: Before: find an empty space → During: drive into it slowly → After: turn off the engine and lock it
grammar_pattern: park + noun (park the car / park the bike)
common_mistake: I parked the car in the parking.
correct_version: I parked the car in the car park.
why_it_s_wrong: In standard English, 'parking' is the activity; the place is a 'car park' (UK) or 'parking lot' (US).
spelling_tip: Same spelling as the noun "park" (a green space) -- context tells you which meaning is meant.
etymology: The verb comes from the noun "park" (an enclosed piece of land) -- by the early 20th century, "to park" came to mean leaving a vehicle in a designated space, as if enclosing it.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- "park" is a simple base word
word_family: park (n. -- green space or parking spot), parking (n./gerund), parked (adj.), parking lot (n.)
mnemonic: You PARK your car near the PARK (the green space) when you go for a walk.
memory_trick: PARK your car the way you'd sit in a park: stop and stay.
visual_association: A car sliding neatly into an empty parking space between two lines.
difference_explained: Stop = come to a halt, even for a moment. Park = stop and leave the vehicle there.
mini_conversation:
A: Where did you park?
B: Just around the corner, near the bakery.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character circles the block twice, groaning, "There's never anywhere to park downtown."
news_style_line: News-style: "The city announced new fines for drivers who park in bicycle lanes."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Just park anywhere on this street, it's free after six."
mcq_options: A) To drive quickly  B) To leave a vehicle in a space  C) To wash a car  D) To sell a car
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: You can ______ your bike right next to the entrance. → park
find_and_fix_to_correct: She park the car outside the shop. → She parks the car outside the shop. (third person singular needs "-s": parks)
translate: उसने अपनी कार दुकान के सामने पार्क की। → She parked her car in front of the shop.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about where you park your bike or car.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to stop and leave a vehicle in a particular place'?
usage_tip: 'No parking' signs mean you can't leave a vehicle there.

simple_explanation: To regularly travel between home and work or school. If your job or school is far from home, you commute every day -- you travel back and forth, often by bus, train, or car.
example_1: I commute to work by train every day.
example_2: She commutes two hours each way to her job in the city.
example_3: He decided to commute by bicycle to save money.
collocations: commute to work, daily commute, long commute, commute by train
where_it_s_used: Work life, city living, transportation, daily routines
action_sequence: Before: leave home → During: travel by bus or train → After: reach the office
grammar_pattern: commute + (to/from + place) (commute to the office / commute from the suburbs)
common_mistake: I commute to office since three years.
correct_version: I have commuted to the office for three years.
why_it_s_wrong: For a length of time, use 'for' with the present perfect: 'have commuted for three years'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: kuh-MYOOT.
spelling_tip: One "m," double "u" sound but single letter -- c-o-m-m-u-t-e (double "m," not double "u").
etymology: From Latin "commutare" (to change/exchange completely) -- English first used "commute" for exchanging one thing for another, and by the late 1800s, for regularly traveling to work (originally linked to commuted/reduced train fares).
prefix_root_suffix: com- (together/thoroughly) + mute (from Latin mutare, to change) -- "to change completely," later narrowed to mean a regular trip
word_family: commute (n. -- the trip itself), commuter (n. -- person who commutes), commuting (n./gerund)
mnemonic: COMMUTE sounds like "come-and-go-MUTE" -- the same silent, repeated trip every day.
memory_trick: COMMUTE: to and from work, every day, like a loop.
visual_association: A crowded train platform full of people checking their watches.
difference_explained: Commute = the regular daily trip to work or college. Travel = any journey, often long or occasional.
mini_conversation:
A: How long is your commute?
B: About 45 minutes by bus, one way.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A tired character stares out a train window at dawn, thinking, "Same seat, same station, every single day."
news_style_line: News-style: "A new survey found that the average commute time in the city has increased by ten minutes."
casual_conversation: Casual: "How do you commute to work these days -- car or metro?"
mcq_options: A) To travel regularly between home and work  B) To take a vacation  C) To move house permanently  D) To drive for fun
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Most employees ______ to the office by bus or train. → commute
find_and_fix_to_correct: She commute to work by bus every day. → She commutes to work by bus every day. (third person singular needs "-s": commutes)
translate: वह रोज़ ट्रेन से दफ़्तर आता-जाता है। → He commutes to the office by train every day.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about how long your daily commute takes.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to regularly travel between home and work or school'?
usage_tip: A 'commuter' is a person who travels to work daily.

simple_explanation: To leave a place, especially at the start of a journey. "Depart" is a formal word for leaving -- you'll hear it most often at airports, train stations, and in written schedules.
example_1: The train will depart at 9 a.m. sharp.
example_2: Our flight departs from gate 12 in twenty minutes.
example_3: She departed for Paris early this morning.
collocations: depart from, depart on time, scheduled to depart, depart for (a destination)
where_it_s_used: Airports, train stations, travel schedules, announcements
action_sequence: Before: wait on the platform → During: the train starts moving → After: the station is left behind
grammar_pattern: depart + from/for + place (depart from the station / depart for London)
common_mistake: The train departs to Delhi.
correct_version: The train departs for Delhi.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'depart for' + destination, or 'depart from' + starting point.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: dee-PAHRT.
etymology: From Old French "departir," from Latin "dis-" (apart) + "partire" (to divide) -- literally "to divide apart," which came to mean "to leave."
prefix_root_suffix: de- (apart) + part (from Latin partire, to divide) = to divide oneself apart, i.e., to leave
mnemonic: DEPART sounds like "de-PART" -- you become a separate PART from the group when you depart.
memory_trick: DE-PART: you become apart from the place you leave.
visual_association: A departure board flipping to show a train's platform and time.
emotion_feel: Neutral, sometimes tinged with anticipation or sadness (goodbyes)
difference_explained: Same meaning. Depart is formal (signs, tickets). Leave is everyday.
mini_conversation:
A: What time does our flight depart?
B: It departs at 6:45, so we should head to the gate.
everyday_scene: Everyday: An announcer's voice echoes through a station, "The next train will depart from platform four."
news_style_line: News-style: "The flight was delayed and did not depart until three hours after its scheduled time."
casual_conversation: Casual: "We should leave for the airport now -- our flight departs in two hours."
mcq_options: A) To arrive somewhere  B) To leave a place  C) To wait for someone  D) To cancel a trip
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The ferry will ______ from the harbor at noon. → depart
find_and_fix_to_correct: The plane departs to New York at noon. → The plane departs for New York at noon. (use "for" with a destination)
translate: ट्रेन सुबह सात बजे रवाना होगी। → The train will depart at seven in the morning.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about when your train or bus departs.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to leave a place, especially at the start of a journey'?
usage_tip: 'Departures' is the airport sign for flights leaving.

simple_explanation: To put things into a bag, box, or suitcase, usually for a trip or storage. Before traveling or storing something, you pack -- you carefully put your clothes, items, or belongings into a bag or container.
example_1: I need to pack my suitcase tonight.
example_2: She packed her bags the night before the flight.
example_3: Don't forget to pack an umbrella -- it might rain.
collocations: pack a bag, pack your bags, pack up, overpack
related_phrasal_verbs: pack up (finish packing/leave), pack in (stop doing something, British informal)
where_it_s_used: Travel, moving house, shopping (packed lunch), logistics
action_sequence: Before: collect clothes → During: fold them into the bag → After: close the bag
grammar_pattern: pack + noun (pack a suitcase / pack your clothes)
common_mistake: I am packing since morning.
correct_version: I have been packing since morning.
why_it_s_wrong: With 'since', use the present perfect continuous: 'have been packing'.
pronunciation_tip: Short "a" sound, one syllable: PAK, rhymes with "back."
spelling_tip: Double "c" would be wrong -- just p-a-c-k.
etymology: From Middle Dutch "pak" (a bundle) -- the verb developed from the noun, meaning to put things together into a bundle or container.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- "pack" is a simple base word
word_family: pack (n. -- a bundle, or a group like "wolf pack"), packing (n./gerund), packed (adj.), package (n./v.), unpack (v.)
mnemonic: PACK rhymes with "BACKPACK" -- you PACK things into your BACKPACK before a trip.
memory_trick: PACK your bag like a PACKet: everything tight inside.
visual_association: An open suitcase on a bed, half-filled with neatly folded clothes.
difference_explained: Pack = put things into a bag. Unpack = take them out.
mini_conversation:
A: Are you ready for the trip?
B: Almost -- I just need to pack my shoes.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character throws clothes into a suitcase at the last minute, shouting, "I have ten minutes to pack, help me!"
news_style_line: News-style: "Airlines reminded travelers to pack liquids in containers under 100 milliliters."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Have you packed everything for the trip yet?"
mcq_options: A) To unload items  B) To put items into a bag or box  C) To wash clothes  D) To buy new luggage
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: We need to ______ our bags before the taxi arrives. → pack
find_and_fix_to_correct: She packed her bag since last night. → She packed her bag last night. (use simple past with a specific past time, not "since")
translate: उसने यात्रा से पहले अपना बैग पैक किया। → She packed her bag before the trip.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about what you always pack for a trip.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to put things into a bag, box, or suitcase, usually for a trip or storage'?
usage_tip: 'Pack up' means finish and put things away.

simple_explanation: To take things out of a bag, box, or suitcase. After you arrive somewhere or receive a delivery, you unpack -- you take everything out of the bag or box and put it away.
example_1: I need to unpack my suitcase after the trip.
example_2: She unpacked her boxes as soon as she moved into the new apartment.
example_3: We were too tired to unpack, so the bags sat by the door.
collocations: unpack a suitcase, unpack boxes, unpack groceries
where_it_s_used: Travel, moving house, deliveries, returning home
action_sequence: Before: reach home → During: open the bag and take things out → After: put everything away
grammar_pattern: unpack + noun (unpack the bag / unpack the boxes)
common_mistake: I unpack my suitcase yesterday.
correct_version: I unpacked my suitcase yesterday.
why_it_s_wrong: A finished past action needs -ed: unpacked.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: un-PAK.
etymology: From "un-" (reverse action) + "pack" -- formed to describe undoing the act of packing.
prefix_root_suffix: un- = reverse/opposite action + pack = to bundle items together
mnemonic: UN + PACK = take everything back out that you once PACKed.
memory_trick: UN + PACK = the opposite of pack.
visual_association: Clothes and shoes scattered around an open suitcase being emptied onto a bed.
emotion_feel: Relief (arriving home) mixed with mild tiredness
difference_explained: Unpack = take things out and put them away. Empty = make something have nothing inside.
mini_conversation:
A: Did you unpack yet?
B: Not yet, I just got home an hour ago.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character drops their suitcase by the door and sighs, "I'll unpack tomorrow, I promise."
news_style_line: News-style: "New residents were seen unpacking moving trucks along the street all weekend."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Can you help me unpack these boxes in the kitchen?"
mcq_options: A) To fill a bag with items  B) To take items out of a bag or box  C) To close a suitcase  D) To buy new bags
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Let's ______ the boxes before it gets dark. → unpack
find_and_fix_to_correct: She unpack her suitcase right after arriving. → She unpacked her suitcase right after arriving. (past tense needed for a completed past action)
translate: घर पहुँचते ही उसने अपना सामान खोला। → As soon as she got home, she unpacked her bags.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about how soon you unpack after a trip.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to take things out of a bag, box, or suitcase'?
usage_tip: 'Let's unpack this idea' means examine it in detail.

simple_explanation: To make a place neat and organized. When a room is messy, you tidy it -- you put things back in their place so everything looks neat.
example_1: I need to tidy my room before guests arrive.
example_2: She tidied the living room before her friends came over.
example_3: Can you tidy your desk? It's covered in papers.
collocations: tidy up, tidy a room, keep tidy, tidy away
where_it_s_used: Housework, classrooms, offices, before guests arrive
action_sequence: Before: the room is messy → During: put things back in place → After: the room looks neat
grammar_pattern: tidy (+ up) + noun (tidy your room / tidy up the kitchen)
common_mistake: I tidyed my room this morning.
correct_version: I tidied my room this morning.
why_it_s_wrong: After a consonant, final -y becomes -i before -ed: tidied.
pronunciation_tip: Two syllables, stress on the first: TY-dee.
spelling_tip: Ends in "-y," which changes to "-ied" in the past tense: tidied.
etymology: From Middle English "tidi" (timely, in good condition), related to "tide" (time) -- originally meant "in good/proper condition," later narrowed to mean neat and orderly.
prefix_root_suffix: tidy comes from "tide" (time) + -y (adjective-forming suffix), now used as both adjective and verb
word_family: tidy (adj. -- neat), tidiness (n.), untidy (adj. -- opposite), tidily (adv.)
mnemonic: TIDY sounds like "TIME-y" -- it's TIME to make things neat and TIDY.
memory_trick: TIDY and TIDIED: the Y hides as an I before -ed.
visual_association: A cluttered desk transforming into neat stacks of books and pens.
difference_explained: Tidy = put things in order. Clean = remove dirt. A room can be tidy but dusty.
mini_conversation:
A: This room is a mess!
B: I know, I'll tidy it up after lunch.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A parent stands in a doorway, arms crossed, saying, "This room needs to be tidy before dinner."
news_style_line: News-style: "Experts say a few minutes spent tidying each day can reduce household stress significantly."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Can you tidy the kitchen before Mom gets home?"
mcq_options: A) To make something messy  B) To make something neat and organized  C) To break something  D) To paint something
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Please ______ your room before we go to the park. → tidy
find_and_fix_to_correct: She tidy her desk every Friday. → She tidies her desk every Friday. (third person singular needs "-ies": tidies)
translate: उसने स्कूल जाने से पहले अपना कमरा व्यवस्थित किया। → She tidied her room before going to school.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about how often you tidy your desk.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to make a place neat and organized'?
usage_tip: 'Tidy up' is very common: 'Tidy up your room before guests come.'

simple_explanation: To wash your body by standing under running water. Instead of a bath, you shower by standing under a stream of water from a showerhead and washing yourself.
example_1: I shower every morning before work.
example_2: He showers right after his workout at the gym.
example_3: She likes to shower with cold water in summer.
collocations: shower quickly, take a shower (noun use), shower every day, cold shower
where_it_s_used: Morning routines, hygiene, after exercise, hotels
action_sequence: Before: turn on the water → During: wash under the running water → After: dry yourself with a towel
grammar_pattern: shower (+ time expression) (shower every morning / shower before bed)
common_mistake: I am showering since 10 minutes.
correct_version: I have been showering for 10 minutes.
why_it_s_wrong: For a length of time, use 'for', not 'since', with the present perfect continuous.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the first syllable: SHOW-er, rhyming with "flower," not "shore."
spelling_tip: Same spelling as the noun "shower" (both rain and bathing) -- context makes the meaning clear.
etymology: From Old English "scur" (a fall of rain/hail) -- the verb sense "to bathe under falling water" developed once indoor plumbing made showers common in the 19th-20th centuries.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- "shower" is a simple base word
word_family: shower (n. -- the act, or the appliance), showered (past tense), showering (n./gerund)
mnemonic: A SHOWER of rain outside is like the SHOWER of water you stand under to wash.
memory_trick: SHOWER sounds like 'shout-er' without the T — rhymes with 'power'.
visual_association: Steam rising as water streams down from a showerhead.
difference_explained: Shower = standing under running water. Bath = sitting in a tub of water. In India, 'take a bath' often means any wash.
mini_conversation:
A: I'm going to shower before we go out.
B: Okay, I'll wait for you downstairs.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character rushes into the bathroom, calling out, "I'll shower fast, give me five minutes!"
news_style_line: News-style: "The gym reported a rise in members who shower and change before heading straight to work."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Can I shower first? I have an early meeting."
mcq_options: A) To wash under running water  B) To sleep for a short time  C) To wash clothes  D) To cook a meal
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: I always ______ right after my morning run. → shower
find_and_fix_to_correct: She shower every morning before school. → She showers every morning before school. (third person singular needs "-s": showers)
translate: वह हर सुबह जल्दी नहाता है। → He showers early every morning.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about whether you prefer a morning or evening shower.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to wash your body by standing under running water'?
usage_tip: 'Take a shower' (US) or 'have a shower' (UK) are more common than 'shower' alone.

simple_explanation: To sleep for a short time, usually during the day. When you're tired in the afternoon, you might take a nap -- a short sleep, often 20 minutes to an hour, to recharge.
example_1: I usually nap for twenty minutes after lunch.
example_2: The baby naps twice a day.
example_3: He napped on the couch while the movie played.
collocations: take a nap, nap time, quick nap, power nap
action_sequence: Before: feel sleepy after lunch → During: sleep for 20 minutes → After: wake up fresh
grammar_pattern: nap (+ time expression) (nap for an hour / nap in the afternoon)
common_mistake: I napping in the afternoon usually.
correct_version: I usually nap in the afternoon.
why_it_s_wrong: A habit uses the simple present, and 'usually' goes before the main verb.
pronunciation_tip: Short "a" sound, one syllable: NAP, rhymes with "map."
spelling_tip: Doubles the "p" before "-ing" or "-ed": napping, napped.
etymology: From Old English "hnappian" (to doze) -- a very old Germanic word for a brief sleep.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- "nap" is a simple base word
word_family: nap (n. -- the short sleep itself), napping (n./gerund), napped (past tense)
mnemonic: NAP rhymes with "MAP" -- close your eyes and take a quick NAP, then wake up ready to MAP out your day.
memory_trick: NAP is a small word for a small sleep.
visual_association: Someone curled up on a couch with a blanket in the middle of the afternoon.
difference_explained: A nap is short, usually in the daytime. Sleep is the long rest at night.
mini_conversation:
A: You look sleepy.
B: Yeah, I think I'll nap for a bit before dinner.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character collapses onto the sofa mid-afternoon, mumbling, "Just five minutes, I promise."
news_style_line: News-style: "A new study found that a short afternoon nap can improve memory and focus."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I think I'll nap for half an hour before we head out."
mcq_options: A) To sleep for a short time during the day  B) To sleep all night  C) To exercise briefly  D) To eat a small meal
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The baby needs to ______ for at least an hour after lunch. → nap
find_and_fix_to_correct: She naps since two hours. → She has been napping for two hours. (use present perfect continuous with "for," not simple present with "since")
translate: वह हर दोपहर थोड़ी देर झपकी लेता है। → He naps for a little while every afternoon.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about when you like to take a nap.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to sleep for a short time, usually during the day'?
usage_tip: 'Power nap' = a 15–20 minute nap to feel fresh.

simple_explanation: To sleep lightly for a short time, often casually or by accident. "Snooze" is a relaxed, informal way of saying you dozed off briefly -- like falling asleep on the sofa without meaning to.
example_1: I snoozed on the couch during the movie.
example_2: Grandpa snoozed in his armchair after lunch.
example_3: I set my alarm to snooze for ten more minutes.
collocations: snooze button, snooze off, hit snooze
where_it_s_used: Weekend mornings, alarms, lazy afternoons, casual conversation
action_sequence: Before: the alarm rings → During: press snooze and close your eyes → After: the alarm rings again
grammar_pattern: snooze (+ time/place expression) (snooze for a while / snooze on the sofa)
common_mistake: I snoozed since one hour on the sofa.
correct_version: I've been snoozing on the sofa for an hour.
why_it_s_wrong: For a length of time, use 'for' with the present perfect continuous.
etymology: Origin uncertain; first recorded in English around the late 18th century as an informal word for a light sleep, likely imitative of a soft breathing/snoring sound.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- "snooze" is a simple, informal base word
word_family: snooze (n. -- the light sleep, also the alarm button), snoozing (n./gerund), snoozed (past tense)
mnemonic: SNOOZE rhymes with "SNORE" -- you SNOOZE quietly, sometimes with a little SNORE.
memory_trick: The SNOOZE button on the alarm gives you a few more minutes of sleep.
visual_association: Someone dozing off on a sunny sofa with a book open on their chest.
difference_explained: A nap is planned. Snoozing is light, often accidental sleep, or delaying an alarm.
mini_conversation:
A: Where's Dad?
B: He's snoozing in front of the TV again.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character hits the alarm clock and mumbles, "Just one more snooze," before falling back asleep.
news_style_line: News-style: "Sleep experts warn that repeatedly hitting snooze can leave you feeling more tired, not less."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I totally snoozed through the first half of the show."
mcq_options: A) To exercise  B) To doze off briefly  C) To eat quickly  D) To argue
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: I always ______ for ten more minutes before actually getting up. → snooze
find_and_fix_to_correct: He snooze on the sofa every Sunday. → He snoozes on the sofa every Sunday. (third person singular needs "-s": snoozes)
translate: वह छुट्टी वाले दिन सोफे पर ऊँघता रहता है। → He snoozes on the sofa on his day off.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about how many times you press snooze in the morning.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to sleep lightly for a short time, often casually or by accident'?
usage_tip: 'You snooze, you lose' means if you're slow, you miss the chance.

simple_explanation: To clean a floor using a mop and water. After sweeping away dry dirt, you mop the floor -- you use a wet mop to wash and clean the surface.
example_1: I mop the kitchen floor every weekend.
example_2: She mopped the floor after the party ended.
example_3: Can you mop up that spilled juice?
collocations: mop the floor, mop up, mop and bucket
related_phrasal_verbs: mop up (clean liquid, or figuratively, deal with the aftermath of something)
action_sequence: Before: the floor is dirty → During: wipe it with a wet mop → After: the floor dries clean
grammar_pattern: mop + noun (mop the floor / mop the kitchen)
common_mistake: I moped the floor yesterday.
correct_version: I mopped the floor yesterday.
why_it_s_wrong: Short words ending in one vowel + one consonant double the consonant: mop → mopped.
pronunciation_tip: Short "o" sound, one syllable: MAHP, rhymes with "top."
spelling_tip: Doubles the "p" before "-ing" or "-ed": mopping, mopped.
etymology: Origin uncertain, possibly from Latin "mappa" (napkin/cloth) via Old French -- first used for the cleaning tool, later as a verb, from the 15th-16th centuries.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- "mop" is a simple base word
word_family: mop (n. -- the cleaning tool), mopping (n./gerund), mopped (past tense)
mnemonic: MOP rhymes with "TOP" -- you MOP from TOP to bottom of a dirty floor.
memory_trick: MOP → MOPPED, like STOP → STOPPED.
visual_association: A wet mop leaving clean streaks across a tiled floor.
difference_explained: Sweep = dry broom. Mop = wet cloth on a stick. You usually sweep first, then mop.
mini_conversation:
A: Someone spilled water in the kitchen.
B: I'll grab the mop and clean it up.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A worker leans on a mop at the end of a long shift, sighing, "One more floor and I'm done."
news_style_line: News-style: "The restaurant was fined after inspectors found staff had not mopped the kitchen floor in days."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Watch out, I just mopped this part of the floor -- it's still wet."
mcq_options: A) To sweep with a broom  B) To wash a floor with a wet mop  C) To vacuum a carpet  D) To dust furniture
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Please ______ the bathroom floor after your shower. → mop
find_and_fix_to_correct: She mop the floor every Saturday. → She mops the floor every Saturday. (third person singular needs "-s": mops)
translate: उसने रसोई में पोछा लगाया। → She mopped the kitchen floor.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about which floor in your home gets mopped daily.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to clean a floor using a mop and water'?
usage_tip: 'Mop up' means clean up the last of something.

simple_explanation: To remove dust from furniture or surfaces. When shelves or tables collect a thin layer of dust, you dust them -- you wipe it away with a cloth.
example_1: I dust the shelves every Sunday.
example_2: She dusted the bookshelf before her guests arrived.
example_3: He dusts his desk every morning before starting work.
collocations: dust the shelves, dust furniture, dust off
related_phrasal_verbs: dust off (clean something rarely used, or figuratively, revive an old idea)
where_it_s_used: Housework, allergies, old furniture, spring cleaning
action_sequence: Before: see dust on the shelf → During: wipe it with a dry cloth → After: the shelf shines
grammar_pattern: dust + noun (dust the table / dust the bookshelf)
common_mistake: I dust the shelves since last week.
correct_version: I haven't dusted the shelves since last week.
why_it_s_wrong: For something not done since a time, use the negative present perfect: 'haven't dusted since'.
pronunciation_tip: One syllable, short "u" sound: DUHST, rhymes with "must."
spelling_tip: Same spelling as the noun "dust" -- context (an object like "the shelf") shows it's a verb.
etymology: From the Old English noun "dust" -- the verb sense ("to remove dust from something") developed in the 16th century.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- "dust" is a simple base word
word_family: dust (n. -- the fine particles), dusty (adj.), duster (n. -- the cleaning tool), dusting (n./gerund)
mnemonic: You DUST the shelf to remove the DUST that has settled on it.
memory_trick: DUST is both the dirt and the action of removing it.
visual_association: A cloth wiping a clean streak across a dusty wooden shelf.
difference_explained: Dust = remove dry dust with a cloth. Clean is general and can use water or soap.
mini_conversation:
A: This shelf is so dusty!
B: I know, I haven't had time to dust it this week.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character runs a finger along a shelf and frowns at the gray streak, saying, "This place needs a serious dusting."
news_style_line: News-style: "Museum staff carefully dust the historic artifacts once a month using soft brushes."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Can you dust the TV stand while I vacuum?"
mcq_options: A) To wash with soap  B) To wipe away fine particles  C) To paint a surface  D) To polish shoes
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Could you ______ the bookshelves before the guests arrive? → dust
find_and_fix_to_correct: She dust the furniture every week. → She dusts the furniture every week. (third person singular needs "-s": dusts)
translate: उसने अलमारी की धूल साफ की। → She dusted the cupboard.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about what gets dusty fastest in your room.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to remove dust from furniture or surfaces'?
usage_tip: 'Dust off' means start using something again after a long time.

simple_explanation: To move on foot at a normal speed. Walking is the most basic way humans move -- putting one foot in front of the other at a regular pace, not running.
example_1: I walk to school every day.
example_2: They walked along the beach at sunset.
example_3: She walks her dog every evening.
collocations: walk to school, walk the dog, take a walk, walk fast/slowly
related_phrasal_verbs: walk in, walk out, walk away, walk up
