action_sequence: Before: put on shoes → During: move on foot step by step → After: reach the place
grammar_pattern: walk (+ to/along/around + place) (walk to the park / walk around the block)
common_mistake: I walk to school yesterday.
correct_version: I walked to school yesterday.
why_it_s_wrong: A finished past action needs -ed: walked.
pronunciation_tip: The "l" is silent -- say WAWK, not WALK with a hard "l."
spelling_tip: Silent "l" is easy to forget -- remember w-a-l-k even though you don't pronounce the "l."
etymology: From Old English "wealcan" (to roll, toss, wander) -- the meaning narrowed over time to "move on foot."
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- "walk" is a simple base word
word_family: walk (n. -- a stroll), walker (n. -- person who walks), walking (n./gerund), walkway (n.)
mnemonic: WALK looks like "WALL-K" but sounds like "WAWK" -- the silent L just stands there, like a wall you walk past.
memory_trick: WALK has a silent L: say 'wawk'.
visual_association: Footprints leaving a trail along a quiet sidewalk.
difference_explained: Go = move to a place in any way. Walk = go on foot. 'I go to school' doesn't say how; 'I walk to school' does.
mini_conversation:
A: Do you want to walk or take the bus?
B: Let's walk, it's such a nice day.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character steps outside and takes a deep breath, saying, "I think I'll just walk home tonight."
news_style_line: News-style: "Doctors recommend walking for at least thirty minutes a day to improve heart health."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Want to walk to the cafe instead of driving?"
mcq_options: A) To move quickly by running  B) To move on foot at a normal pace  C) To travel by car  D) To stand still
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: We usually ______ to the market instead of driving. → walk
find_and_fix_to_correct: She walk to work every morning. → She walks to work every morning. (third person singular needs "-s": walks)
translate: वह हर सुबह पार्क में टहलती है। → She walks in the park every morning.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about how far you walk every day.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to move on foot at a normal speed'?
usage_tip: 'Walk someone home' means go with them for safety or company.

simple_explanation: To move quickly on foot, faster than walking. Running is moving your legs fast so both feet leave the ground briefly -- it's faster and more tiring than walking.
example_1: I run every morning before breakfast.
example_2: He ran to catch the bus before it left.
example_3: She runs five kilometers every weekend.
collocations: run fast, run a race, run late, run out of time
related_phrasal_verbs: run away, run out, run into, run over
action_sequence: Before: see the bus leaving → During: move fast on foot → After: reach it just in time
grammar_pattern: run (+ to/from/across + place) (run to the station / run across the field)
common_mistake: I runned to catch the train.
correct_version: I ran to catch the train.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Run' is irregular: past 'ran', past participle 'run'.
pronunciation_tip: Short "u" sound, one syllable: RUHN, rhymes with "sun."
spelling_tip: Doubles the "n" before "-ing": running (but past tense is irregular: ran).
etymology: From Old English "rinnan"/"iernan" -- an ancient Germanic word for fast movement on foot.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- "run" is a simple base word
word_family: run (n. -- a jog/race, or a streak), runner (n.), running (n./gerund), runway (n.)
mnemonic: RUN rhymes with "SUN" -- run fast enough and you'll feel like you're chasing the SUN.
memory_trick: RUN → RAN → RUN: the vowel changes and comes back, like a runner doing a lap.
visual_association: Someone sprinting down a track, arms pumping, feet barely touching the ground.
difference_explained: Run = move fast on foot. Jog = run slowly, usually for exercise.
mini_conversation:
A: We're going to miss the train!
B: Then let's run!
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character glances at their watch, gasps, and shouts, "We're late, run!"
news_style_line: News-style: "Thousands of runners took part in the city marathon this weekend."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I run three times a week to stay in shape."
mcq_options: A) To move quickly on foot  B) To sit and rest  C) To swim  D) To drive a car
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: He had to ______ to catch the last bus home. → run
find_and_fix_to_correct: She runned in the marathon last year. → She ran in the marathon last year. (irregular past tense of "run" is "ran")
translate: वह हर सुबह पार्क में दौड़ता है। → He runs in the park every morning.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a time you ran to catch a bus or train.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to move quickly on foot, faster than walking'?
usage_tip: 'Run' also means manage: 'She runs a small shop.'

simple_explanation: To push off the ground with your legs and briefly leave the ground. When you jump, you bend your knees and spring upward or forward, leaving the ground for a moment before landing.
example_1: The kids jump on the trampoline for hours.
example_2: She jumped over the puddle to keep her shoes dry.
example_3: He jumped for joy when he heard the good news.
collocations: jump over, jump for joy, jump up, jump rope
related_phrasal_verbs: jump in, jump out, jump up, jump at (an opportunity)
action_sequence: Before: bend your knees → During: push off the ground → After: land on your feet
grammar_pattern: jump (+ over/into/up) (jump over the fence / jump into the pool)
common_mistake: She jumped over of the fence.
correct_version: She jumped over the fence.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Over' is enough; don't add 'of' after it.
pronunciation_tip: One syllable, short "u": JUHMP, rhymes with "bump."
spelling_tip: No silent letters -- j-u-m-p, straightforward spelling.
etymology: Origin uncertain; likely imitative in origin (echoing the sound/action of a quick spring), first recorded in English in the 16th century, replacing the older word "leap" in everyday use.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- "jump" is a simple base word
word_family: jump (n. -- the action), jumpy (adj. -- nervous), jumper (n. -- one who jumps, or British word for sweater)
mnemonic: JUMP rhymes with "BUMP" -- you JUMP over a BUMP in the road.
memory_trick: JUMP sounds like the thump when you land.
visual_association: A child mid-air above a trampoline, arms outstretched.
emotion_feel: Excitement, joy, sometimes fear or surprise
difference_explained: Jump = push off with both feet. Hop = jump on one foot, or make small quick jumps.
mini_conversation:
A: Did you see her score the winning goal?
B: Yes! I jumped out of my seat cheering.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character sees the winning lottery numbers and jumps off the couch, shouting, "We won! We actually won!"
news_style_line: News-style: "Stock prices jumped sharply after the company announced record profits."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I nearly jumped out of my skin when the phone rang so loudly."
mcq_options: A) To sit down suddenly  B) To push off the ground and briefly leave it  C) To crawl slowly  D) To speak loudly
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The cat loves to ______ onto the highest shelf in the room. → jump
find_and_fix_to_correct: He jump over the wall to get his ball back. → He jumped over the wall to get his ball back. (past tense needed for a completed past action)
translate: बच्चे खुशी से उछल-कूद कर रहे थे। → The children were jumping around with joy.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about the highest thing you have jumped over.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to push off the ground with your legs and briefly leave the ground'?
usage_tip: 'Jump the queue' means go ahead of people who were waiting.

simple_explanation: To move upward, often using your hands and feet. When you climb, you go up something -- like a mountain, ladder, or tree -- often using both your hands and feet for support.
example_1: We climb the stairs to reach our apartment.
example_2: He climbed the tree to get the cat down.
example_3: They climbed the mountain in six hours.
collocations: climb a mountain, climb the stairs, climb a tree, climb up/down
related_phrasal_verbs: climb up, climb down, climb over
action_sequence: Before: stand at the bottom → During: use hands and feet to go up → After: reach the top
grammar_pattern: climb (+ up/down + noun) (climb up the ladder / climb the hill)
common_mistake: We climbed up on the mountain last week.
correct_version: We climbed the mountain last week.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Climb' already means go up, so 'climb up on' is not needed; 'climb the mountain' is enough.
pronunciation_tip: Say KLYM, not KLYMB -- the final "b" is completely silent.
spelling_tip: The silent "b" is a common spelling trap -- remember c-l-i-m-b, even though you don't say the "b."
etymology: From Old English "climban," a Germanic word meaning to move upward using the hands and feet.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- "climb" is a simple base word
word_family: climb (n. -- the ascent), climber (n. -- person who climbs), climbing (n./gerund)
mnemonic: CLIMB has a silent B, like the climber is too out of breath (B) to say it.
memory_trick: CLIMB has a silent B: say 'klime'.
visual_association: A hiker's hand reaching for the next rocky ledge on a steep trail.
emotion_feel: Determination, effort, sometimes fear (heights) or accomplishment
difference_explained: You climb (go up) yourself. You raise (lift) something else.
mini_conversation:
A: How was the hike?
B: Tough! We had to climb almost two hours to reach the top.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A climber grips the rock face and breathes hard, saying, "Almost there -- just a little further to the top."
news_style_line: News-style: "Two hikers were rescued after attempting to climb the peak in dangerous weather conditions."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I hate climbing stairs -- let's just take the elevator."
mcq_options: A) To move downward  B) To move upward using hands and/or feet  C) To sit still  D) To run quickly
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: It took us three hours to ______ to the top of the hill. → climb
find_and_fix_to_correct: She climb the ladder to fix the roof. → She climbed the ladder to fix the roof. (past tense needed for a completed past action)
translate: उसने पेड़ पर चढ़कर आम तोड़ा। → He climbed the tree and picked a mango.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a hill, tree or wall you have climbed.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to move upward, often using your hands and feet'?
usage_tip: 'Climb down' can mean admit you were wrong.

simple_explanation: To move slowly on your hands and knees, close to the ground. Crawling means moving along the ground using your hands and knees instead of standing -- babies do this before they learn to walk, and it's also used for moving slowly in general (like traffic).
example_1: The baby began to crawl at eight months old.
example_2: He crawled under the table to find his keys.
example_3: Traffic crawled along the highway during rush hour.
collocations: crawl under, crawl through, traffic crawls, crawl on all fours
where_it_s_used: Babies, traffic, tight spaces, military training
action_sequence: Before: the baby sits → During: moves on hands and knees → After: reaches the toy
grammar_pattern: crawl (+ under/through/along) (crawl under the fence / crawl through the tunnel)
common_mistake: The baby is crawling since three months.
correct_version: The baby has been crawling for three months.
why_it_s_wrong: With a length of time, use 'for' and the present perfect continuous: 'has been crawling for three months'.
spelling_tip: "-awl" ending, like "crawl," "sprawl," "shawl" -- a common English spelling pattern.
etymology: Possibly from Old Norse "krafla" (to scratch/paw) -- entered English in the medieval period, describing slow movement close to the ground.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- "crawl" is a simple base word
word_family: crawl (n. -- the slow movement, or a swimming stroke), crawling (n./gerund), crawled (past tense), crawler (n.)
mnemonic: CRAWL rhymes with "SMALL" -- babies are SMALL, so they CRAWL before they can walk.
memory_trick: CRAWL like a CRAB on the ground: low and slow.
visual_association: A baby moving on hands and knees across a soft rug toward a toy.
emotion_feel: Neutral, sometimes frustration (traffic) or delight (a baby's first crawl)
difference_explained: Crawl = move on hands and knees. Creep = move slowly and quietly so no one notices.
mini_conversation:
A: Look, she's crawling toward the toy!
B: Wow, that's her first time crawling that far.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A soldier drags himself under barbed wire, gritting his teeth, "Almost there, just keep crawling."
news_style_line: News-style: "Traffic crawled to a standstill after the accident closed two lanes of the highway."
casual_conversation: Casual: "My baby just started crawling last week -- I have to watch her every second now."
mcq_options: A) To move quickly upright  B) To move slowly on hands and knees  C) To jump repeatedly  D) To stand still
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: We had to ______ through the small gap in the fence. → crawl
find_and_fix_to_correct: The baby crawled since she was six months old. → The baby has crawled since she was six months old. (use present perfect with "since" for an action that started in the past and continues)
translate: बच्चा फर्श पर रेंग रहा है। → The baby is crawling on the floor.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something that crawls in your garden.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to move slowly on your hands and knees, close to the ground'?
usage_tip: 'Traffic was crawling' means it was moving very slowly.

simple_explanation: To move through water using your arms and legs. Swimming is moving your body through water by kicking your legs and moving your arms, usually without touching the bottom.
example_1: I swim in the pool every weekend.
example_2: She swims two kilometers every morning.
example_3: The children swam in the lake all afternoon.
collocations: swim in the pool, swim laps, learn to swim, swim across
action_sequence: Before: get into the water → During: move arms and legs → After: reach the other side
grammar_pattern: swim (+ in/across/to + place) (swim in the sea / swim across the river)
common_mistake: She swimmed across the lake last summer.
correct_version: She swam across the lake last summer.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Swim' is irregular: swim – swam – swum.
pronunciation_tip: Short "i" sound, one syllable: SWIHM, rhymes with "him."
etymology: From Old English "swimman" -- an ancient Germanic word for moving through water using the body's own motion.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- "swim" is a simple base word
word_family: swim (n. -- a session of swimming), swimmer (n.), swimming (n./gerund), swimwear (n.)
mnemonic: SWIM rhymes with "HIM" -- teach HIM how to SWIM.
memory_trick: SWIM → SWAM → SWUM, like SING → SANG → SUNG.
visual_association: Someone gliding smoothly through clear blue water, leaving a trail of small ripples.
difference_explained: Swim = move through water. Float = stay on top of the water without moving forward.
mini_conversation:
A: Do you want to go to the beach today?
B: Sure, I'd love to swim in the sea.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A coach shouts from the poolside, "Kick harder, swim like your life depends on it!"
news_style_line: News-style: "The young athlete broke the national record for swimming the 100-meter freestyle."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Let's go swimming this weekend -- it's supposed to be really hot."
mcq_options: A) To move through water using arms and legs  B) To float without moving  C) To walk on a wet surface  D) To dive from a great height
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: We ______ in the ocean every time we visit the coast. → swim
find_and_fix_to_correct: He swim in the lake every summer. → He swims in the lake every summer. (third person singular needs "-s": swims)
translate: बच्चे झील में तैर रहे हैं। → The children are swimming in the lake.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about where you learned to swim, or would like to.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to move through water using your arms and legs'?
usage_tip: 'Go swimming' is more common than 'go for swim'.

simple_explanation: To move through the air, usually with wings or in an aircraft. Flying means moving through the air -- birds fly using their wings, and people fly by traveling in an airplane.
example_1: We fly to Dubai next month.
example_2: The bird flew straight into the tree.
example_3: They flew from Delhi to London for the wedding.
collocations: fly a plane, fly abroad, time flies, fly high
related_phrasal_verbs: fly off, fly by, fly out
where_it_s_used: Travel, airports, birds, figurative speed ("time flies")
action_sequence: Before: board the plane → During: the plane goes up into the air → After: land in another city
grammar_pattern: fly (+ to/from + place) (fly to Paris / fly from Mumbai)
common_mistake: We flied to Japan last year.
correct_version: We flew to Japan last year.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Fly' is irregular: fly – flew – flown.
pronunciation_tip: Rhymes with "sky" and "try" -- one syllable: FLY.
spelling_tip: The "y" changes to "ie" before "-s": flies (but stays "y" before "-ing": flying).
etymology: From Old English "fleogan" -- an ancient Germanic word for moving through the air.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- "fly" is a simple base word
word_family: fly (n. -- the insect, unrelated meaning), flight (n. -- the journey), flyer/flier (n.), flying (n./gerund)
mnemonic: FLY rhymes with "SKY" -- birds FLY up into the SKY.
memory_trick: FLY → FLEW → FLOWN, like KNOW → KNEW → KNOWN.
visual_association: An airplane cutting through white clouds against a blue sky.
difference_explained: Fly = move through the air. Flow = move smoothly like water. Past tenses: flew / flowed.
mini_conversation:
A: When do you fly out?
B: Our flight leaves early Saturday morning.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A pilot's voice crackles over the intercom, "We are now ready to fly -- please fasten your seatbelts."
news_style_line: News-style: "The airline announced it will fly a new direct route between the two cities starting next year."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I hate flying long distances -- my legs get so stiff."
mcq_options: A) To move through the air  B) To travel by road  C) To swim underwater  D) To walk quickly
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: We ______ to visit our grandparents every summer. → fly
find_and_fix_to_correct: She flied to New York for business. → She flew to New York for business. (irregular past tense of "fly" is "flew")
translate: वे कल सुबह की फ्लाइट से मुंबई जाएंगे। → They will fly to Mumbai on tomorrow morning's flight.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a place you have flown to, or want to.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to move through the air, usually with wings or in an aircraft'?
usage_tip: 'Time flies' means time passes quickly.

simple_explanation: To operate and control a vehicle, like a car. Driving means controlling a car (or another vehicle) using the steering wheel, pedals, and gears to move from one place to another.
example_1: I drive to work every day.
example_2: She drives her kids to school every morning.
example_3: He drove all night to reach the wedding on time.
collocations: drive a car, drive safely, drive fast, learn to drive
related_phrasal_verbs: drive off, drive away, drive up
where_it_s_used: Commuting, road trips, learning to drive, errands
action_sequence: Before: start the car → During: steer on the road → After: park at the destination
grammar_pattern: drive (+ noun/to + place) (drive the car / drive to the office)
common_mistake: I drived to the market this morning.
correct_version: I drove to the market this morning.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Drive' is irregular: drive – drove – driven.
pronunciation_tip: Rhymes with "five" and "hive" -- one syllable: DRYV.
spelling_tip: Silent "e" at the end -- d-r-i-v-e, which drops before adding "-ing": driving.
etymology: From Old English "drifan" (to force to move, to push) -- the modern sense of "operating a vehicle" developed once cars became common in the early 20th century.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- "drive" is a simple base word
word_family: drive (n. -- a car trip, or motivation), driver (n.), driving (n./gerund), driveway (n.)
mnemonic: DRIVE rhymes with "FIVE" -- you need to be at least sixteen to legally DRIVE.
memory_trick: DRIVE → DROVE → DRIVEN, like RIDE → RODE → RIDDEN.
visual_association: Hands on a steering wheel, watching the road stretch ahead through the windshield.
emotion_feel: Neutral, sometimes stressful (traffic) or freeing (open road)
difference_explained: You drive a car (you control it from inside). You ride a bike, horse or bus.
related_words: car, steering wheel, license, road, traffic
mini_conversation:
A: How did you get here so fast?
B: I drove -- traffic was surprisingly light today.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character grips the wheel tightly on a rainy night, muttering, "Just drive carefully, almost home."
news_style_line: News-style: "New regulations will require all new drivers to complete an additional ten hours of practice."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I can drive you to the station if you want, it's on my way."
mcq_options: A) To walk somewhere  B) To operate and control a vehicle  C) To repair a car  D) To sell a car
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: My father taught me how to ______ when I turned eighteen. → drive
find_and_fix_to_correct: She drived her new car to work today. → She drove her new car to work today. (irregular past tense of "drive" is "drove")
translate: वह हर दिन दफ़्तर तक गाड़ी चलाकर जाती है। → She drives to the office every day.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about who drives in your family.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to operate and control a vehicle, like a car'?
usage_tip: 'Drive someone crazy' means annoy them a lot.

simple_explanation: To travel by sitting on or in something, like a bicycle, horse, or bus. Riding means being carried by a vehicle or animal -- you ride a bicycle by pedaling it, or ride a horse by sitting on its back.
example_1: I ride my bicycle to school every day.
example_2: She rides her motorcycle to work.
example_3: He rode a horse for the first time on vacation.
collocations: ride a bike, ride a horse, ride the bus, take a ride
related_phrasal_verbs: ride out (endure something difficult), ride along
where_it_s_used: Cycling, horseback riding, public transportation, theme parks
action_sequence: Before: get on the bicycle → During: pedal along the road → After: get off at the park
grammar_pattern: ride (+ noun) (ride a bike / ride the subway)
common_mistake: I rided my bicycle to the park.
correct_version: I rode my bicycle to the park.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Ride' is irregular: ride – rode – ridden.
pronunciation_tip: Rhymes with "side" and "wide" -- one syllable: RYD.
spelling_tip: Silent "e" at the end -- r-i-d-e, which drops before "-ing": riding.
etymology: From Old English "ridan" -- an ancient Germanic word originally meaning to travel on horseback, later extended to any vehicle you sit on or in.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- "ride" is a simple base word
word_family: ride (n. -- a trip, or a rollercoaster ride), rider (n.), riding (n./gerund)
mnemonic: RIDE rhymes with "SIDE" -- you sit by the SIDE of a horse or bike when you RIDE.
memory_trick: RIDE → RODE → RIDDEN, like DRIVE → DROVE → DRIVEN.
visual_association: Someone pedaling a bicycle down a tree-lined path, wind in their hair.
difference_explained: Ride = sit on or in something that moves (bike, horse, bus). Drive = control a car or truck.
mini_conversation:
A: How do you get to college?
B: I usually ride my bike, it's faster than the bus.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character hops onto an old bicycle and calls back, "Race you to the end of the street!"
news_style_line: News-style: "The city added new bike lanes to make it safer for people to ride to work."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Do you want to ride bikes to the park this afternoon?"
mcq_options: A) To walk somewhere  B) To travel on or in something like a bike or horse  C) To fly a plane  D) To swim across water
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: She loves to ______ her horse along the beach every weekend. → ride
find_and_fix_to_correct: He rided his bicycle around the block. → He rode his bicycle around the block. (irregular past tense of "ride" is "rode")
translate: वह हर सुबह अपनी साइकिल चलाकर स्कूल जाता है। → He rides his bicycle to school every morning.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about the first time you rode a bicycle.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to travel by sitting on or in something, like a bicycle, horse, or bus'?
usage_tip: 'Give someone a ride' (US) or 'a lift' (UK) means take them in your vehicle.

simple_explanation: To go from one place to another, especially a long distance. Traveling means journeying somewhere, often far away -- for a holiday, for work, or simply to see new places.
example_1: I love to travel to new countries.
example_2: They traveled across Europe by train last summer.
example_3: She travels for work almost every month.
collocations: travel abroad, travel light, travel by train, love to travel
action_sequence: Before: book tickets → During: go by train or plane → After: reach a new place
grammar_pattern: travel (+ to/by + place/method) (travel to Spain / travel by plane)
common_mistake: I travel to Goa last winter.
correct_version: I traveled to Goa last winter.
why_it_s_wrong: A finished past action needs the past tense. UK doubles the L (travelled); US doesn't (traveled).
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the first syllable: TRAV-uhl.
spelling_tip: One "l" in the base word, but American English keeps it single before "-ing"/"-ed" (traveling, traveled) while British English doubles it (travelling, travelled).
etymology: From Old French "travail" (hard work/toil) -- because journeys were once so difficult, the word for "hard labor" came to mean "to journey."
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- "travel" comes from Old French "travail" but doesn't decompose in modern English
mnemonic: TRAVEL comes from "TRAVAIL" (hard work) -- old journeys were such hard work that the words became linked.
memory_trick: TRAVEL has 'VEL' like velocity: going places.
visual_association: An open suitcase next to a passport and a boarding pass on a bed.
difference_explained: Travel is usually the verb (I travel). Journey is usually the noun (a long journey).
mini_conversation:
A: What are your plans for the holidays?
B: I want to travel somewhere I've never been before.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character stares at a world map pinned to their wall and whispers, "One day, I'll travel to every one of these places."
news_style_line: News-style: "The report found that more people are choosing to travel by train instead of flying to reduce their carbon footprint."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I really want to travel more once I save enough money."
mcq_options: A) To stay in one place  B) To go from one place to another, often far away  C) To work from home  D) To exercise daily
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: We hope to ______ around Southeast Asia next year. → travel
find_and_fix_to_correct: She travels to Europe last year for a conference. → She traveled to Europe last year for a conference. (use past tense with a specific past time expression like "last year")
translate: वे हर साल किसी नए देश की यात्रा करते हैं। → They travel to a new country every year.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about the longest journey you have travelled.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to go from one place to another, especially a long distance'?
usage_tip: 'Travel light' means carry very little luggage.

simple_explanation: To walk around slowly without a clear destination. When you wander, you walk somewhere just to explore, with no particular place you're trying to reach -- it's relaxed and unplanned.
example_1: We wandered around the old city for hours.
example_2: He likes to wander through the market on weekends.
example_3: The children wandered off and got lost in the mall.
collocations: wander around, wander off, wander aimlessly, let your mind wander
action_sequence: Before: walk into a market → During: move around with no plan → After: find something interesting
grammar_pattern: wander (+ around/through/off) (wander around the city / wander off alone)
common_mistake: Don't wander from the group, or you'll get lose.
correct_version: Don't wander from the group, or you'll get lost.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Lose' is a verb (misplace). The adjective meaning 'unable to find your way' is 'lost'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the first syllable: WAHN-der.
spelling_tip: Don't confuse with "wonder" (to feel curious) -- "wander" has an "a," "wonder" has an "o."
etymology: From Old English "wandrian," related to "wend" -- an ancient Germanic word meaning to move about without a fixed direction.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- "wander" is a simple base word
word_family: wander (n. -- a leisurely walk), wanderer (n.), wandering (n./gerund/adj.)
mnemonic: WANDER has an "A" like "Around" -- you wander AROUND with no destination.
memory_trick: WANDER has an A, like 'walking Around'.
visual_association: Someone strolling through narrow cobblestone streets with no map in hand.
difference_explained: Wander (/ˈwɒndə/) = walk around without a plan. Wonder (/ˈwʌndə/) = think curiously.
mini_conversation:
A: What did you do in the old town?
B: Nothing planned, we just wandered around and took photos.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A traveler steps off a bus in an unfamiliar city, smiling, "Let's just wander and see where we end up."
news_style_line: News-style: "Officials urged hikers not to wander off marked trails during the storm warning."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I love vacations where we can just wander around with no fixed plan."
mcq_options: A) To walk with a clear destination  B) To walk around with no fixed destination  C) To run quickly  D) To sit and rest
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: We spent the afternoon just ______ around the old town. → wandering
find_and_fix_to_correct: She wander through the museum for two hours. → She wandered through the museum for two hours. (past tense needed for a completed past action)
translate: वह पूरे दिन बाज़ार में इधर-उधर घूमता रहा। → He wandered around the market all day.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a place where you like to wander.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to walk around slowly without a clear destination'?
usage_tip: 'My mind wandered' means you stopped paying attention.

simple_explanation: To run after someone or something to try to catch them. When you chase something, you run after it because you want to catch it -- like a dog chasing a ball, or the police chasing a thief.
example_1: The dog loves to chase the ball in the park.
example_2: The police chased the car through the busy streets.
example_3: Kids love to chase each other during recess.
collocations: chase after, chase down, high-speed chase, chase a dream
where_it_s_used: Sports, movies, playgrounds, figurative goals ("chase your dreams")
action_sequence: Before: see a cat → During: run after it → After: it climbs a tree
grammar_pattern: chase (+ after) + noun (chase the thief / chase after the ball)
common_mistake: The dog chased after of the cat.
correct_version: The dog chased the cat.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Chase' takes a direct object. 'Chase after' is also fine, but never 'after of'.
etymology: From Old French "chacier," from Latin "captiare" (to try to catch) -- related to "capture" and "catch."
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- "chase" is a simple base word (from Old French)
word_family: chase (n. -- the pursuit itself), chaser (n.), chasing (n./gerund)
mnemonic: CHASE rhymes with "RACE" -- when you CHASE someone, it becomes a RACE to catch them.
memory_trick: CHASE rhymes with RACE: a chase is a race to catch someone.
visual_association: A dog sprinting across a park, ears flapping, eyes locked on a bouncing ball.
emotion_feel: Excitement, urgency, sometimes fear (if being chased)
difference_explained: Follow = go behind someone. Chase = run after them fast to catch them.
mini_conversation:
A: Where's the puppy?
B: Out in the yard, chasing butterflies again.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A detective sprints through a crowded street, shouting, "Stop! Someone chase him, he's getting away!"
news_style_line: News-style: "Police confirmed they chased the stolen vehicle for several miles before making an arrest."
casual_conversation: Casual: "My little brother loves to chase our cat around the house."
mcq_options: A) To walk slowly behind someone  B) To run after someone or something to catch it  C) To hide from someone  D) To wait patiently
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The children love to ______ each other around the playground. → chase
find_and_fix_to_correct: The cat chase the mouse under the sofa. → The cat chased the mouse under the sofa. (past tense needed for a completed past action, or "chases" for a habitual action)
translate: कुत्ता बिल्ली का पीछा कर रहा था। → The dog was chasing the cat.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something a dog or child chased.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to run after someone or something to try to catch them'?
usage_tip: 'Chase your dreams' means try hard to achieve them.

simple_explanation: To go after or behind someone or something. To follow means to move behind someone in the same direction, or to do what instructions or rules tell you to do.
example_1: Please follow me to the meeting room.
example_2: The dog followed its owner everywhere.
example_3: Please follow the instructions carefully.
collocations: follow instructions, follow the rules, follow closely, follow up
related_phrasal_verbs: follow up, follow through, follow along
action_sequence: Before: the guide walks ahead → During: walk behind the guide → After: reach the room
grammar_pattern: follow + noun (follow the path / follow the instructions)
common_mistake: Please follow me to the room, isn't it?
correct_version: Please follow me to the room.
why_it_s_wrong: A polite request doesn't take a question tag like 'isn't it'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the first syllable: FAHL-oh.
spelling_tip: Double "l" -- f-o-l-l-o-w, easy to forget the second "l."
etymology: From Old English "folgian" -- an ancient Germanic word meaning to go after or accompany someone.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- "follow" is a simple base word
mnemonic: FOLLOW has two L's -- one to LEAD, one to FOLLOW right behind.
memory_trick: FOLLOW has two Ls, like two people walking one after the other.
visual_association: Footprints in the snow, one set trailing closely behind another.
difference_explained: Follow = go behind at a normal pace. Chase = run after someone to catch them.
mini_conversation:
A: How do I get to the station from here?
B: Just follow this road until you see the sign.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A guide waves a group forward, saying, "Follow me closely, the path gets narrow ahead."
news_style_line: News-style: "Officials asked residents to follow the evacuation instructions carefully during the storm."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Just follow the signs and you'll find the parking lot easily."
mcq_options: A) To lead someone forward  B) To go behind or obey someone/something  C) To stop moving  D) To argue with someone
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Please ______ the instructions carefully to avoid mistakes. → follow
find_and_fix_to_correct: She follow the recipe exactly every time. → She follows the recipe exactly every time. (third person singular needs "-s": follows)
translate: कृपया मेरे पीछे-पीछे आइए। → Please follow me.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a rule you always follow.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to go after or behind someone or something'?
usage_tip: Social media: 'Follow me on Instagram.' Also: 'Did you follow that?' = did you understand?

simple_explanation: To go in front and guide others, or to be in charge of a group. To lead means to go first and show others the way, or to be the person in charge who guides a team or project.
example_1: She will lead the team this year.
example_2: He led the hikers safely to the summit.
example_3: She leads a team of ten engineers.
collocations: lead a team, lead the way, lead by example, take the lead
related_phrasal_verbs: lead on, lead to, lead up to
action_sequence: Before: the team needs direction → During: walk in front and guide them → After: reach the goal together
grammar_pattern: lead + noun (lead the team / lead the group)
common_mistake: She leaded the meeting yesterday.
correct_version: She led the meeting yesterday.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Lead' is irregular: the past is 'led', not 'leaded'.
pronunciation_tip: As a verb, it rhymes with "seed": LEED. The metal "lead" rhymes with "bed" instead -- same spelling, different word.
spelling_tip: Irregular past tense "led" (no double "e") -- easy to confuse with "lead" the metal.
etymology: From Old English "laedan" (to cause to go with one, to guide) -- originally meaning to guide someone on a journey.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- "lead" is a simple base word
mnemonic: LEAD (verb) rhymes with "NEED" -- a good leader knows what the team NEEDs.
memory_trick: LEAD (/liːd/) → LED (/led/), like FEED → FED.
visual_association: A person at the front of a hiking group, pointing the way up a trail.
difference_explained: Lead (/liːd/) is present. Led (/led/) is past. Lead (/led/) is also a metal, which is why people misspell the past tense.
mini_conversation:
A: Who's leading the project this time?
B: I am -- it's my first time in charge of a big team.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A captain turns to the crew and says firmly, "Follow me, I'll lead us out of here."
news_style_line: News-style: "The senator will lead a delegation to discuss trade agreements next month."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Do you want to lead this project, or should I take charge?"
mcq_options: A) To follow someone else  B) To guide or be in charge of a group  C) To hide from a group  D) To ignore instructions
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: She was chosen to ______ the new marketing team. → lead
find_and_fix_to_correct: He lead the meeting yesterday morning. → He led the meeting yesterday morning. (irregular past tense of "lead" is "led")
translate: वह इस साल पूरी टीम का नेतृत्व करेगी। → She will lead the whole team this year.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a time you led a group or team.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to go in front and guide others, or to be in charge of a group'?
usage_tip: A 'team lead' is the person in charge of a small team.

simple_explanation: To apply force to move something away from you. When you push something, you use your hands or body to move it forward or away from yourself.
example_1: Please push the door open, don't pull it.
example_2: He pushed the shopping cart down the aisle.
example_3: She pushed the door shut behind her.
collocations: push a button, push a cart, push open, push someone away
related_phrasal_verbs: push on, push through, push back
where_it_s_used: Doors, buttons, sports, figurative encouragement ("push yourself")
action_sequence: Before: put your hands on the door → During: press forward → After: the door opens
grammar_pattern: push + noun (push the door / push the button)
common_mistake: Push to the door to open it.
correct_version: Push the door to open it.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Push' takes a direct object, with no 'to'.
pronunciation_tip: Short "u" sound, one syllable: POOSH, rhymes with "bush."
etymology: From Old French "pousser," from Latin "pulsare" (to beat/push) -- related to "pulse."
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- "push" is a simple base word
word_family: push (n. -- a shove or effort), pushy (adj. -- overly forceful), pushing (n./gerund)
mnemonic: PUSH rhymes with "BUSH" -- PUSH through the BUSH to clear a path.
memory_trick: PUSH = press forward, away from you, like the door sign.
visual_association: Two hands pressing firmly against a heavy door, forcing it open.
difference_explained: Push = move away from you. Pull = move towards you. Doors often say PUSH or PULL.
mini_conversation:
A: The door won't open!
B: Try pushing it instead of pulling.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character strains against a heavy door, grunting, "Push! It's stuck, just push harder!"
news_style_line: News-style: "Officials pushed for new safety regulations following the factory incident."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Can you push the cart? My hands are full with the bags."
mcq_options: A) To pull something toward you  B) To apply force to move something away  C) To lift something up  D) To drop something
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: You need to ______ the button twice to turn on the machine. → push
find_and_fix_to_correct: She pushed to the swing to make it move. → She pushed the swing to make it move. (no "to" needed before the direct object)
translate: उसने दरवाज़ा धकेलकर खोला। → He pushed the door open.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something you pushed that was very heavy.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to apply force to move something away from you'?
usage_tip: 'Don't push me' means don't pressure me.

simple_explanation: To apply force to bring something toward you. When you pull something, you grab it and draw it closer to yourself, using your hands, arms, or a rope.
example_1: Please pull the door, don't push it.
example_2: He pulled the rope to raise the flag.
example_3: She pulled her suitcase through the airport.
collocations: pull a rope, pull a lever, pull over, pull apart
related_phrasal_verbs: pull over, pull out, pull through, pull apart
where_it_s_used: Doors, ropes, vehicles, figurative influence ("pull strings")
action_sequence: Before: hold the handle → During: move it towards you → After: the drawer opens
grammar_pattern: pull + noun (pull the rope / pull the door)
common_mistake: Pull to the handle to open it.
correct_version: Pull the handle to open it.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Pull' takes a direct object, with no 'to'.
pronunciation_tip: Short "oo" sound, one syllable: rhymes with "full" and "bull."
etymology: From Old English "pullian" -- a Germanic word meaning to tug or draw something toward oneself.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- "pull" is a simple base word
word_family: pull (n. -- a tug or influence), pulling (n./gerund), pulled (past tense)
mnemonic: PULL rhymes with "FULL" -- PULL the rope until the bucket is FULL.
memory_trick: PULL has two Ls, like two hands pulling a rope.
visual_association: A hand gripping a rope, leaning back to pull with all its strength.
difference_explained: Pull = move towards you, often easily. Drag = pull something heavy along the ground with effort.
mini_conversation:
A: This drawer won't budge!
B: You have to pull it harder, it always sticks.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character grips the rope and yells, "Pull! Everyone pull together, now!"
news_style_line: News-style: "Rescuers used ropes to pull the stranded hikers to safety."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Can you pull the curtains, the sun's too bright."
mcq_options: A) To move something away from you  B) To apply force to bring something toward you  C) To drop something  D) To lift something above your head
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: You need to ______ the lever to start the machine. → pull
find_and_fix_to_correct: He pulled to the rope with all his strength. → He pulled the rope with all his strength. (no "to" needed before the direct object)
translate: उसने रस्सी को ज़ोर से खींचा। → He pulled the rope hard.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something you pull open every day.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to apply force to bring something toward you'?
usage_tip: 'Pull someone's leg' means joke with them.

simple_explanation: To pull something heavy along the ground, often with effort. Dragging means pulling something -- usually heavy or awkward -- along a surface, using force because it resists moving easily.
example_1: He had to drag the heavy box across the room.
example_2: She dragged the suitcase up the stairs.
example_3: The cat dragged its toy across the floor.
collocations: drag a bag, drag your feet, drag along, drag and drop
related_phrasal_verbs: drag on (continue too long), drag along (bring someone reluctantly)
where_it_s_used: Moving furniture, luggage, heavy objects, computer use ("drag and drop")
action_sequence: Before: the sofa is too heavy to lift → During: pull it slowly along the floor → After: it reaches the corner
grammar_pattern: drag + noun (+ place expression) (drag the box across the room)
common_mistake: She drag the sofa to the corner.
correct_version: She dragged the sofa to the corner.
why_it_s_wrong: A finished action needs the past tense, and 'drag' doubles the g: dragged.
pronunciation_tip: Short "a" sound, one syllable: DRAG, rhymes with "bag."
spelling_tip: Doubles the "g" before "-ing" or "-ed": dragging, dragged.
etymology: Likely from Old Norse "draga" (to draw/pull), related to "draw" -- entered English describing the act of pulling something heavy along a surface.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- "drag" is a simple base word
word_family: drag (n. -- resistance or an annoying task, as in "what a drag"), dragging (n./gerund), dragged (past tense)
mnemonic: DRAG rhymes with "BAG" -- you DRAG a heavy BAG across the floor.
memory_trick: DRAG sounds heavy and slow, like the scrape on the floor.
visual_association: Deep scrape marks on the floor left behind a heavy dragged box.
difference_explained: Carry = lift and hold while moving. Drag = pull along the ground without lifting.
mini_conversation:
A: This suitcase is so heavy!
B: Just drag it, don't try to lift it.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character grunts, dragging a heavy trunk across the attic floor, muttering, "Whoever packed this thing hates me."
news_style_line: News-style: "Workers used a crane to drag the fallen tree off the highway after the storm."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Can you help me drag this couch to the other room?"
mcq_options: A) To carry something lightly  B) To pull something heavy along a surface  C) To throw something far  D) To lift something overhead
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: We had to ______ the fallen branch off the path. → drag
find_and_fix_to_correct: He dragged to the box across the yard. → He dragged the box across the yard. (no "to" needed before the direct object)
translate: उसने भारी बैग को घसीटकर कमरे में लाया। → He dragged the heavy bag into the room.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something heavy you once dragged.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to pull something heavy along the ground, often with effort'?
usage_tip: Computers: 'drag and drop' a file. 'The meeting dragged on' = it felt too long.

simple_explanation: To raise something upward using your hands or arms. Lifting means picking something up and raising it off the ground or a surface, usually using your arms or a machine.
example_1: Can you lift this box for me?
example_2: He lifted the heavy suitcase into the car.
example_3: She lifts weights at the gym three times a week.
collocations: lift weights, lift a box, lift up, lift off (rockets)
where_it_s_used: Exercise, moving furniture, weightlifting, rockets ("lift off")
action_sequence: Before: bend your knees → During: raise the box with your arms → After: put it on the table
grammar_pattern: lift + noun (+ up) (lift the box / lift the bag up)
common_mistake: I lift this heavy table alone yesterday.
correct_version: I lifted this heavy table alone yesterday.
why_it_s_wrong: A finished past action needs -ed: lifted.
pronunciation_tip: Short "i" sound, one syllable: LIHFT, rhymes with "gift."
etymology: From Old Norse "lypta," related to "loft" (air/sky) -- originally meaning to raise something up into the air.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- "lift" is a simple base word
word_family: lift (n. -- the act of lifting, or British for "elevator"), lifted (past tense), lifting (n./gerund)
mnemonic: LIFT rhymes with "GIFT" -- LIFT the GIFT box carefully so nothing breaks.
memory_trick: LIFT is also the Indian and British word for an elevator: it lifts you up.
visual_association: Someone lifting a heavy barbell overhead at the gym, muscles straining.
difference_explained: Lift = pick something up physically. Raise = move up, often more formal (raise your hand, raise a price).
mini_conversation:
A: This box is too heavy for me alone.
B: Let's lift it together, one, two, three.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A crowd counts down before a rocket launch: "Three, two, one -- lift off!"
news_style_line: News-style: "Engineers used a crane to lift the damaged bridge section for repairs."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Can you help me lift this sofa? It's heavier than it looks."
mcq_options: A) To push something forward  B) To raise something upward  C) To drag something along the floor  D) To throw something far
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: He can ______ over eighty kilograms at the gym. → lift
find_and_fix_to_correct: She lift the box onto the shelf easily. → She lifts the box onto the shelf easily. (third person singular needs "-s": lifts)
translate: उसने भारी बक्सा उठाकर मेज़ पर रखा। → He lifted the heavy box and put it on the table.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about the heaviest thing you can lift.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to raise something upward using your hands or arms'?
usage_tip: 'Give someone a lift' (UK) means give them a ride.

simple_explanation: To let something fall, or to fall accidentally. When you drop something, it falls from your hand to the ground -- either by accident, or because you deliberately let it go.
example_1: Be careful not to drop the glass.
example_2: He dropped his phone and cracked the screen.
example_3: She dropped the kids off at school on her way to work.
collocations: drop something, drop off, drop by, drop out
related_phrasal_verbs: drop off, drop by, drop out, drop in
action_sequence: Before: hold a glass → During: it slips from your hand → After: it breaks on the floor
grammar_pattern: drop + noun (drop the ball / drop the plate)
common_mistake: I dropped my keys since this morning and can't find them.
correct_version: I dropped my keys this morning and can't find them.
why_it_s_wrong: Simple past with a specific past time ('this morning') doesn't take 'since'.
pronunciation_tip: Short "o" sound, one syllable: DRAHP, rhymes with "stop."
spelling_tip: Doubles the "p" before "-ing" or "-ed": dropping, dropped.
etymology: From Old English "dropa" (a drop of liquid) -- the verb sense "to let fall" developed from the noun for a small falling bead of liquid.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- "drop" is a simple base word
word_family: drop (n. -- a small amount, or a fall), dropped (past tense), dropping (n./gerund)
mnemonic: DROP rhymes with "STOP" -- when something DROPs, it STOPs falling once it hits the ground.
memory_trick: DROP → DROPPED: double P before -ed.
visual_association: A glass slipping from a hand, shattering into pieces on the floor.
difference_explained: You drop something (you let it go). Something falls by itself. 'I dropped the cup; the cup fell.'
mini_conversation:
A: I heard a crash in the kitchen.
B: Sorry, I dropped a plate -- it's fine, nothing broke.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character fumbles with a tray, gasps, and watches it crash to the floor, saying, "Oh no, I dropped everything."
news_style_line: News-style: "Fuel prices dropped for the third week in a row, offering relief to commuters."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Careful, don't drop that -- it's my grandmother's vase."
mcq_options: A) To lift something up  B) To let something fall  C) To throw something far  D) To hold something tightly
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Please don't ______ the plates -- they're very fragile. → drop
find_and_fix_to_correct: She drop her phone and it broke. → She dropped her phone and it broke. (past tense needed for a completed past action)
translate: उसने गलती से अपना फ़ोन गिरा दिया। → He accidentally dropped his phone.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something you once dropped and broke.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to let something fall, or to fall accidentally'?
usage_tip: 'Drop someone at the station' means take them there in your vehicle. 'Drop by' = visit briefly.

simple_explanation: To send something through the air using your arm and hand. Throwing means using your hand and arm to launch something -- like a ball -- so it moves through the air toward a person or place.
example_1: Can you throw the ball to me?
example_2: He threw the ball across the yard.
example_3: She threw away the old newspapers.
collocations: throw a ball, throw away, throw a party, throw up
related_phrasal_verbs: throw away, throw up, throw out, throw in
where_it_s_used: Sports, games, cleaning ("throw away"), parties ("throw a party")
action_sequence: Before: hold the ball → During: swing your arm forward → After: the ball flies away
grammar_pattern: throw + noun (+ to/at) (throw the ball to him / throw a rock at the wall)
common_mistake: He throwed the ball very hard.
correct_version: He threw the ball very hard.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Throw' is irregular: throw – threw – thrown.
pronunciation_tip: Rhymes with "grow" and "know" -- one syllable: THROH.
spelling_tip: Silent "w" at the end, and "thr-" at the start -- t-h-r-o-w, easy to confuse with "though" or "through."
etymology: From Old English "thrawan" (to twist/turn) -- the meaning shifted over time to "to hurl something through the air with a twisting arm motion."
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- "throw" is a simple base word
word_family: throw (n. -- a toss, or a distance), thrower (n.), throwing (n./gerund), thrown (past participle)
mnemonic: THROW rhymes with "GROW" -- THROW the ball, watch your skill GROW.
memory_trick: THROW → THREW → THROWN, like GROW → GREW → GROWN.
visual_association: A hand releasing a ball mid-air, arm still extended from the throw.
difference_explained: Threw (past of throw) and through (from one side to the other) sound the same: 'He threw the ball through the window.'
mini_conversation:
A: Can you throw me that towel?
B: Sure, catch!
everyday_scene: Everyday: A player winds up on the field, and the crowd holds its breath as they shout, "Throw it now!"
news_style_line: News-style: "The athlete set a new record for the longest javelin throw at the championship."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Throw me the remote, it's right next to you."
mcq_options: A) To catch something  B) To send something through the air using your arm  C) To carry something carefully  D) To hold something still
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Can you ______ the keys down to me from the balcony? → throw
find_and_fix_to_correct: She throwed the trash in the bin. → She threw the trash in the bin. (irregular past tense of "throw" is "threw")
translate: उसने गेंद दीवार की तरफ फेंकी। → He threw the ball at the wall.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a game where you throw a ball.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to send something through the air using your arm and hand'?
usage_tip: 'Throw a party' means organise one. 'Throw away' = put in the bin.

simple_explanation: To grab hold of something that is moving through the air. Catching means using your hands to grab something that's flying or falling toward you, before it hits the ground.
example_1: I caught the ball with one hand.
example_2: She caught the frisbee just before it hit the water.
example_3: He caught the falling vase before it broke.
collocations: catch a ball, catch a cold, catch the bus, catch up
related_phrasal_verbs: catch up, catch on, catch up with
where_it_s_used: Sports, illness ("catch a cold"), transportation ("catch the bus")
action_sequence: Before: the ball comes towards you → During: open your hands → After: hold it tight
grammar_pattern: catch + noun (catch the ball / catch the bus)
common_mistake: He catched the ball perfectly.
correct_version: He caught the ball perfectly.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Catch' is irregular: the past is 'caught', not 'catched'.
spelling_tip: Double "t" is wrong here -- just c-a-t-c-h.
etymology: From Old North French "cachier," related to Latin "captiare" (to try to seize) -- the same root that gave English "chase" and "capture."
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- "catch" is a simple base word
word_family: catch (n. -- the act of catching, or a hidden problem, as in "what's the catch"), catcher (n.), catching (n./gerund/adj., as in "catching a cold")
mnemonic: CATCH rhymes with "MATCH" -- CATCH the ball, you'll be a MATCH for any player.
memory_trick: CATCH → CAUGHT, like TEACH → TAUGHT.
visual_association: A hand snapping shut around a ball just before it hits the ground.
difference_explained: Catch = take hold of something moving. Hold = keep something in your hands.
mini_conversation:
A: Ready? I'm throwing it now!
B: Go ahead, I'll catch it.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A player leaps into the air, and the commentator shouts, "What a catch, absolutely incredible!"
news_style_line: News-style: "Fishermen reported a record catch of tuna this season along the coast."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Quick, catch it before it falls!"
mcq_options: A) To throw something away  B) To grab something moving through the air  C) To drop something on purpose  D) To push something forward
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: She had to run fast to ______ the last bus home. → catch
find_and_fix_to_correct: He catched the fish with a net. → He caught the fish with a net. (irregular past tense of "catch" is "caught")
translate: उसने गेंद को हवा में ही पकड़ लिया। → He caught the ball in mid-air.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a time you caught something that was falling.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to grab hold of something that is moving through the air'?
usage_tip: 'Catch a cold', 'catch a bus', 'catch you later' — catch is used far beyond balls.

simple_explanation: To hit something with your foot. Kicking means swinging your leg and striking something -- like a ball -- with your foot.
example_1: He can kick the ball very far.
example_2: She kicked the ball into the goal.
example_3: He accidentally kicked the table and stubbed his toe.
collocations: kick a ball, kick off, kick out, free kick
related_phrasal_verbs: kick off (start something), kick out (expel), kick in (start to take effect)
where_it_s_used: Football/soccer, martial arts, accidents, figurative ("kick off a project")
action_sequence: Before: run towards the ball → During: swing your leg → After: the ball flies away
grammar_pattern: kick + noun (kick the ball / kick the door)
common_mistake: He kicked to the ball hard.
correct_version: He kicked the ball hard.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Kick' takes a direct object, with no 'to'.
pronunciation_tip: Short "i" sound, one syllable: KIHK, rhymes with "pick."
etymology: Origin uncertain, possibly related to Scandinavian languages -- entered English in the 14th century meaning to strike with the foot.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- "kick" is a simple base word
word_family: kick (n. -- the action, or a thrill), kicker (n.), kicking (n./gerund)
mnemonic: KICK rhymes with "PICK" -- PICK a spot on the ball, then KICK it there.
memory_trick: KICK sounds like the sharp sound of a foot hitting a ball.
visual_association: A foot connecting sharply with a football, sending it flying toward the goal.
difference_explained: Kick = strike with your foot. Hit = strike with your hand or an object.
mini_conversation:
A: Did you see that goal?
B: Yes! What a powerful kick.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A player lines up the ball, takes a breath, and the crowd chants, "Kick it! Kick it now!"
news_style_line: News-style: "The striker's late kick secured a dramatic win in the final minute of the match."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Careful, don't kick the ball near the window!"
mcq_options: A) To hit something with your hand  B) To hit something with your foot  C) To throw something far  D) To catch something quickly
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The player will ______ the ball to start the match. → kick
find_and_fix_to_correct: She kick the ball every time she plays. → She kicks the ball every time she plays. (third person singular needs "-s": kicks)
translate: उसने गेंद को ज़ोर से किक मारी। → He kicked the ball hard.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a game where you kick a ball.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to hit something with your foot'?
usage_tip: 'Kick off' = start (a match or a meeting). 'Kick the habit' = stop a bad habit.

simple_explanation: To move by turning over and over, like a ball or wheel. Rolling means moving in a circular, tumbling motion -- like a ball rolling down a hill, or a wheel rolling along the road.
example_1: The ball rolled down the hill.
example_2: He rolled the dice and won the game.
example_3: The baby rolled over for the first time today.
collocations: roll down, roll over, roll up, roll the dice
related_phrasal_verbs: roll over, roll up, roll out, roll in
action_sequence: Before: push the ball gently → During: it turns over and over → After: it stops at the wall
grammar_pattern: roll (+ down/over/up) (roll down the hill / roll over in bed)
common_mistake: The ball rolled since ten minutes.
correct_version: The ball has been rolling for ten minutes.
why_it_s_wrong: For a length of time, use 'for' with the present perfect continuous.
pronunciation_tip: One syllable, rhymes with "goal" and "bowl": ROHL.
spelling_tip: Double "l" -- r-o-l-l, easy to forget the second "l."
etymology: From Old French "roler," from Latin "rotulare" (to roll), related to "rota" (wheel) -- the same root that gives us "rotate."
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- "roll" is a simple base word
word_family: roll (n. -- a turn, or bread roll), rolling (n./gerund/adj.), rolled (past tense)
mnemonic: ROLL rhymes with "BOWL" -- a ball will ROLL right into the BOWL.
memory_trick: ROLL has double L, like two wheels rolling.
visual_association: A ball tumbling end over end down a grassy slope.
emotion_feel: Neutral, sometimes playful (games) or alarming (something rolling out of control)
difference_explained: Roll = move by turning. Role = a part someone plays. Same sound, different meaning.
mini_conversation:
A: Where did the ball go?
B: It rolled all the way under the car.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character watches a coin spin and finally settle, whispering, "Just roll my way, just this once."
news_style_line: News-style: "The truck's cargo rolled off the highway after the driver swerved to avoid an animal."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Watch out, the ball is rolling toward the street!"
mcq_options: A) To move by turning over and over  B) To stand completely still  C) To jump high into the air  D) To sink underwater
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The coin ______ under the sofa and we couldn't find it. → rolled
find_and_fix_to_correct: The ball roll down the hill quickly. → The ball rolled down the hill quickly. (past tense needed for a completed past action)
translate: गेंद पहाड़ी से नीचे लुढ़क गई। → The ball rolled down the hill.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something that rolled under your bed.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to move by turning over and over, like a ball or wheel'?
usage_tip: 'Roll' also means a list of names: 'the attendance roll'. 'Roti roll' is a food.

simple_explanation: To move smoothly across a surface without lifting your feet or the object. Sliding means moving smoothly over a surface, like ice or a playground slide, without bouncing or turning -- just a smooth glide.
example_1: The kids slide down the playground slide all day.
example_2: She slid across the icy pavement and nearly fell.
example_3: He slid the letter under the door.
collocations: slide down, slide across, slide into, let it slide (figurative -- to ignore something)
where_it_s_used: Playgrounds, ice, wet floors, doors ("sliding door")
action_sequence: Before: step on the wet floor → During: move smoothly without control → After: stop or fall
grammar_pattern: slide (+ down/across/into) (slide down the hill / slide across the ice)
common_mistake: She slided on the wet floor and fell.
correct_version: She slid on the wet floor and fell.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Slide' is irregular: the past is 'slid', not 'slided'.
pronunciation_tip: Rhymes with "ride" and "wide" -- one syllable: SLYD.
spelling_tip: Silent "e" at the end -- s-l-i-d-e, which drops before "-ing": sliding.
etymology: From Old English "slidan" -- a Germanic word meaning to glide smoothly over a surface.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- "slide" is a simple base word
word_family: slide (n. -- the playground equipment, or a photo slide), sliding (n./gerund/adj., as in "sliding door"), slid (past tense)
mnemonic: SLIDE rhymes with "RIDE" -- kids RIDE down a playground SLIDE.
memory_trick: SLIDE → SLID: the E slides away.
visual_association: A child zooming down a curved playground slide, arms raised.
difference_explained: Slide = move smoothly, often on purpose. Slip = slide by accident and lose balance.
mini_conversation:
A: Careful, the floor is wet!
B: Too late, I already slid halfway across it.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character grabs the railing just in time, laughing nervously, "Whoa, I nearly slid right off the deck."
news_style_line: News-style: "Officials warned drivers that icy roads could cause vehicles to slide out of control."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Watch your step, the tiles are slippery and you might slide."
mcq_options: A) To move smoothly across a surface  B) To jump repeatedly  C) To stand still  D) To climb upward
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The children love to ______ down the hill on their sleds. → slide
find_and_fix_to_correct: He slided down the banister and laughed. → He slid down the banister and laughed. (irregular past tense of "slide" is "slid")
translate: बर्फ़ पर उसका पैर फिसल गया। → His foot slid on the ice.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a time you slid on a wet floor.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to move smoothly across a surface without lifting your feet or the object'?
usage_tip: 'Slide' also means one page of a presentation: 'Next slide, please.'

simple_explanation: To make a small jump, often on one foot. Hopping means making a quick, small jump -- often on one leg, like a rabbit hopping or a child hopping on one foot.
example_1: The rabbit hopped across the garden.
example_2: The children hopped over the puddles on their way to school.
example_3: She hopped on one foot after stubbing her toe.
collocations: hop over, hop on one foot, hop in (get into a car quickly), hop around
related_phrasal_verbs: hop in, hop on, hop off
where_it_s_used: Playgrounds, animals (rabbits, frogs), quick trips ("hop on a plane")
action_sequence: Before: stand on one foot → During: push up → After: land on the same foot
grammar_pattern: hop (+ over/on/into) (hop over the fence / hop into the car)
common_mistake: The frog hop into the pond.
correct_version: The frog hopped into the pond.
why_it_s_wrong: A finished past action needs the past tense, and 'hop' doubles the p: hopped.
pronunciation_tip: Short "o" sound, one syllable: HAHP, rhymes with "stop."
spelling_tip: Doubles the "p" before "-ing" or "-ed": hopping, hopped.
etymology: From Old English "hoppian" -- a Germanic word meaning to spring or jump lightly, especially on one leg.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- "hop" is a simple base word
word_family: hop (n. -- a small jump, or a short flight/trip, e.g., "a quick hop to Paris"), hopping (n./gerund), hopped (past tense)
mnemonic: HOP rhymes with "STOP" -- HOP once, then STOP.
memory_trick: HOP → HOPPED, like STOP → STOPPED.
visual_association: A rabbit springing lightly across a grassy lawn in small bounces.
difference_explained: Hop (short o) = jump on one foot. Hope (long o, silent e) = wish for something. Hopped vs hoped.
mini_conversation:
A: How was your trip to London?
B: Quick -- just a two-day hop for a meeting.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A child hops across stepping stones in a garden, giggling, "One more hop and I win!"
news_style_line: News-style: "The airline is offering cheap fares for short hops between neighboring cities."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Just hop in the car, we're already late!"
mcq_options: A) To make a big jump with both feet  B) To make a small jump, often on one foot  C) To walk slowly  D) To fall down
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The kids ______ over the small puddles on the sidewalk. → hop
find_and_fix_to_correct: The bunny hop across the yard yesterday. → The bunny hopped across the yard yesterday. (past tense needed for a completed past action)
translate: खरगोश बगीचे में उछल-कूद कर रहा था। → The rabbit was hopping around the garden.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about an animal that hops.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to make a small jump, often on one foot'?
usage_tip: 'Hop in!' is a casual way to invite someone into your car.

simple_explanation: To move lightly with small jumps, or to deliberately miss/leave something out. "Skip" can mean happily bouncing along while walking (like a child skipping), or choosing not to do something you'd normally do, like skipping breakfast.
example_2: The children skipped happily through the park.
example_3: He skipped his usual gym class today.
collocations: skip breakfast, skip a class, skip rope, skip a step
related_phrasal_verbs: skip out (leave without permission), skip over
action_sequence: Before: see a long list → During: jump over one item → After: move to the next
grammar_pattern: skip + noun (skip breakfast / skip the chapter)
common_mistake: I skip my breakfast yesterday to save time.
correct_version: I skipped my breakfast yesterday to save time.
why_it_s_wrong: A finished past action needs the past tense, and 'skip' doubles the p: skipped.
pronunciation_tip: Short "i" sound, one syllable: SKIHP, rhymes with "trip."
spelling_tip: Doubles the "p" before "-ing" or "-ed": skipping, skipped.
etymology: Origin uncertain, likely from Scandinavian roots (compare Swedish "skutta," to skip/leap) -- entered English in the medieval period.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- "skip" is a simple base word
word_family: skip (n. -- a light jump, or an act of omission), skipping (n./gerund), skipped (past tense)
mnemonic: SKIP rhymes with "TRIP" -- SKIP happily on a TRIP to the park.
memory_trick: SKIP → SKIPPED: double P.
visual_association: A child bouncing along a sidewalk with light, happy hops.
emotion_feel: Neutral, sometimes light and joyful (skipping while walking) or guilty (skipping responsibilities)
difference_explained: Skip = leave out on purpose. Miss = fail to catch, attend or notice, often by accident.
mini_conversation:
A: Are you coming to the meeting?
B: No, I think I'll skip it this time -- I have too much work.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character glances at their calendar and sighs, "I think I'll just skip the party tonight."
news_style_line: News-style: "Health experts warn that skipping meals regularly can slow down your metabolism."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Let's skip the boring parts and just get to the good stuff."
mcq_options: A) To attend something carefully  B) To move with light jumps, or to deliberately miss something  C) To run very fast  D) To repeat something twice
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: I usually ______ lunch when I'm really busy at work. → skip
find_and_fix_to_correct: She skip class every Friday. → She skips class every Friday. (third person singular needs "-s": skips)
translate: वह कभी-कभी नाश्ता छोड़ देता है। → He sometimes skips breakfast.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a meal you sometimes skip.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to move lightly with small jumps, or to deliberately miss/leave something out'?
usage_tip: 'Skip a class' or 'skip a meal' means miss it on purpose.

hindi_meaning: गोता लगाना, छलांग लगाकर पानी में कूदना
simple_explanation: To jump head-first into water, or to go quickly downward. Diving means jumping into water headfirst with your arms out in front, or moving quickly and steeply downward, like a bird diving toward the ground.
example_1: She loves to dive into the swimming pool.
example_2: He dove off the high board without hesitating.
example_3: The eagle dived toward its prey.
collocations: dive into the pool, dive deep, scuba dive, dive off the board
where_it_s_used: Swimming pools, scuba diving, sports, birds of prey
action_sequence: Before: stand at the edge → During: jump head first → After: enter the water
grammar_pattern: dive (+ into/off) (dive into the water / dive off the cliff)
common_mistake: She dived into the pool since morning.
correct_version: She has been diving into the pool since morning.
why_it_s_wrong: A repeated action continuing from a past time to now needs the present perfect continuous with 'since'.
pronunciation_tip: Rhymes with "five" and "hive" -- one syllable: DYV.
spelling_tip: Silent "e" at the end -- d-i-v-e, which drops before "-ing": diving.
etymology: From Old English "dufan" -- a Germanic word meaning to plunge down, especially into water.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- "dive" is a simple base word
word_family: dive (n. -- the jump, or a bar/restaurant informally called a "dive"), diver (n.), diving (n./gerund)
mnemonic: DIVE rhymes with "FIVE" -- count to FIVE, then DIVE into the pool.
memory_trick: DIVE: D for Down, head first.
visual_association: A swimmer's body slicing cleanly into water, barely making a splash.
difference_explained: Jump = leave the ground with your feet. Dive = go head first, usually into water.
mini_conversation:
A: Are you scared of the high board?
B: A little, but I'm going to dive anyway.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A diver stands at the edge of a cliff, takes a breath, and whispers, "Here goes nothing," before diving.
news_style_line: News-style: "Marine biologists dive regularly to study coral reefs affected by rising ocean temperatures."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Come on, dive in, the water's actually really warm!"
mcq_options: A) To float on the surface  B) To jump headfirst, especially into water  C) To swim slowly  D) To climb out of the water
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: He decided to ______ off the highest board at the pool. → dive
find_and_fix_to_correct: He dive into the lake without checking the depth. → He dove into the lake without checking the depth. (past tense needed for a completed past action -- "dove" or "dived" both work)
translate: उसने बिना सोचे-समझे पानी में छलांग लगा दी। → He dove into the water without thinking.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a place where you would like to dive.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to jump head-first into water, or to go quickly downward'?
usage_tip: 'Dive into' also means start something with energy: 'Let's dive into the topic.'

simple_explanation: To stay on the surface of water or air without sinking. When something floats, it rests on top of the water (or rises through the air) instead of sinking or falling -- like a leaf floating on a pond.
example_1: The boat floats calmly on the lake.
example_2: Wood floats, but stones sink to the bottom.
example_3: She floated on her back and looked up at the sky.
collocations: float on water, float in the air, float away, float around
action_sequence: Before: drop a leaf in the pond → During: it stays on top → After: the wind moves it slowly
grammar_pattern: float (+ on/in/away) (float on the water / float away)
common_mistake: The leaf is floating since I saw it an hour ago.
correct_version: The leaf has been floating since I saw it an hour ago.
why_it_s_wrong: With 'since', use the present perfect continuous.
pronunciation_tip: Rhymes with "boat" and "coat" -- one syllable: FLOHT.
spelling_tip: "oa" combination makes the long "o" sound -- f-l-o-a-t, like "boat" and "coat."
etymology: From Old English "flotian," related to "fleet" (a group of ships) -- both come from the idea of staying on the surface of water.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- "float" is a simple base word
word_family: float (n. -- a device that floats, or a parade float), floating (n./gerund/adj.), floated (past tense)
mnemonic: FLOAT rhymes with "BOAT" -- a BOAT should always FLOAT, never sink.
memory_trick: FLOAT has 'OAT' — oats float on milk.
visual_association: A lily pad resting gently on the still surface of a pond.
difference_explained: Swim = move through water on purpose. Float = stay on the surface without effort.
mini_conversation:
A: I can't believe how calm the lake is.
B: Perfect day to just float and relax.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character lies back in the pool, closes their eyes, and sighs, "I could just float here forever."
