news_style_line: News-style: "Engineers explained how the massive cargo ship manages to float despite its enormous weight."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Just relax and float on your back -- you won't sink."
mcq_options: A) To sink underwater  B) To stay on the surface of water or air  C) To swim quickly  D) To dive downward
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Try to relax and just ______ on your back in the pool. → float
find_and_fix_to_correct: The boat float on the water peacefully. → The boat floats on the water peacefully. (third person singular needs "-s": floats)
translate: पत्ता पानी की सतह पर तैर रहा था। → The leaf was floating on the surface of the water.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something that floats on water.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to stay on the surface of water or air without sinking'?
usage_tip: 'Float an idea' means suggest it to see how people react.

simple_explanation: To go down below the surface of water and not come back up. When something sinks, it goes underwater and stays there, instead of floating -- like a heavy stone dropped into a lake.
example_1: The stone sank to the bottom of the lake.
example_2: The old ship sank during the storm.
example_3: Heavy objects sink, but light ones float.
collocations: sink to the bottom, sink or swim, sinking feeling, sink in (understand fully)
where_it_s_used: Boats, swimming, figurative emotions ("heart sank"), physics
action_sequence: Before: the boat fills with water → During: it goes down → After: it rests at the bottom
grammar_pattern: sink (+ to/into) (sink to the bottom / sink into the mud)
common_mistake: The ship sinked during the storm last night.
correct_version: The ship sank during the storm last night.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Sink' is irregular: sink – sank – sunk.
pronunciation_tip: Short "i" sound, one syllable: SIHNK, rhymes with "think."
etymology: From Old English "sincan" -- an ancient Germanic word meaning to go down below the surface, especially of water.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- "sink" is a simple base word
word_family: sink (n. -- the kitchen basin, unrelated meaning), sinking (n./gerund/adj.), sunk (past participle)
mnemonic: SINK rhymes with "THINK" -- THINK fast, or your boat will SINK.
memory_trick: SINK → SANK → SUNK, like DRINK → DRANK → DRUNK.
visual_association: Bubbles rising as a heavy object disappears slowly beneath dark water.
difference_explained: Things sink. Living things drown: they die from being under water.
mini_conversation:
A: Did the boat make it to shore?
B: No, unfortunately it sank halfway across the lake.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A crew member watches water rush into the hold and shouts, "We're taking on water, she's going to sink!"
news_style_line: News-style: "Rescue teams worked through the night after the fishing boat began to sink offshore."
casual_conversation: Casual: "My heart just sank when I saw the exam results."
mcq_options: A) To rise above water  B) To go down below the surface of water  C) To float calmly  D) To move sideways
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The small boat began to ______ after hitting the rock. → sink
find_and_fix_to_correct: The old boat sinked slowly into the lake. → The old boat sank slowly into the lake. (irregular past tense of "sink" is "sank")
translate: तूफ़ान में नाव डूब गई। → The boat sank in the storm.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something that sank in water.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to go down below the surface of water and not come back up'?
usage_tip: A 'sink' is also the basin in a kitchen. 'It hasn't sunk in' = I haven't fully understood it yet.

simple_explanation: To control the direction of a vehicle, like a car or boat. Steering means turning the wheel (or handlebars) of a vehicle to control which direction it moves in.
example_1: Can you steer the boat toward the shore?
example_2: He steered the car carefully around the sharp bend.
example_3: She steered the boat away from the rocks.
collocations: steer a car, steer clear of, steer away from, steering wheel
where_it_s_used: Driving, boating, cycling, figurative guidance ("steer a conversation")
action_sequence: Before: see a turn ahead → During: turn the wheel → After: the car changes direction
grammar_pattern: steer + noun (steer the car / steer the ship)
common_mistake: He steer the car around the corner too fast.
correct_version: He steered the car around the corner too fast.
why_it_s_wrong: A finished past action needs -ed: steered.
pronunciation_tip: Rhymes with "here" and "clear" -- one syllable: STEER.
spelling_tip: "ee" makes the long "e" sound -- s-t-e-e-r, like "deer" and "cheer."
etymology: From Old English "stieran," related to "stern" (the back of a ship) -- originally meant to guide a ship's direction.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- "steer" is a simple base word
word_family: steer (n. -- young cattle, unrelated meaning), steering wheel (n.), steering (n./gerund)
mnemonic: STEER rhymes with "CLEAR" -- STEER carefully to keep the road CLEAR.
memory_trick: The STEERing wheel is what you use to STEER.
visual_association: Two hands gripping a steering wheel, turning it smoothly around a curve.
difference_explained: Drive = operate the whole vehicle. Steer = control only the direction.
mini_conversation:
A: This road is really narrow.
B: I know, just steer carefully and we'll be fine.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A captain grips the wheel through rough waves, shouting over the wind, "Steer us straight, don't let her turn!"
news_style_line: News-style: "The driver managed to steer the bus safely to the shoulder after the tire blew out."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Can you steer while I change the radio station?"
mcq_options: A) To stop a vehicle completely  B) To control the direction of a vehicle  C) To repair an engine  D) To clean a car
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: You need both hands to ______ the boat in rough water. → steer
find_and_fix_to_correct: She steers the boat since an hour without stopping. → She has been steering the boat for an hour without stopping. (use "for" with a duration and present perfect continuous, not "since" with simple present)
translate: उसने सावधानी से गाड़ी मोड़ पर चलाई। → He steered the car carefully around the turn.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about how you steer a bicycle.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to control the direction of a vehicle, like a car or boat'?
usage_tip: 'Steer clear of' means avoid: 'Steer clear of junk food.'

simple_explanation: To do a job or make an effort to do something. "Work" means spending time and energy doing a task, whether it's a paid job or any effort toward a goal.
example_1: I work in an office downtown.
example_2: My father works at a hospital.
example_3: This old radio doesn't work anymore.
collocations: work hard, work overtime, work from home, work as a team
related_phrasal_verbs: work out, work on, work up to
action_sequence: Before: reach the office → During: do your tasks → After: finish for the day
grammar_pattern: work + at/in/on/for + noun (work at a bank / work on a project)
common_mistake: I am working in a hospital since five years.
correct_version: I have been working in a hospital for five years.
why_it_s_wrong: For a length of time up to now, use 'for' with the present perfect continuous.
pronunciation_tip: Short, single syllable -- rhymes with "shirk," not "walk."
etymology: Old English "weorc" (deed, action) -- one of the oldest words in the language for effort/labor.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- a simple base word
mnemonic: WORK rhymes with "lurk" -- picture someone lurking at their desk, grinding away at WORK.
memory_trick: WORK and WORD differ by one letter: your work speaks for you.
visual_association: A person typing at a desk with a cup of coffee beside them.
emotion_feel: Neutral, sometimes tiring or satisfying depending on context
difference_explained: Work = the activity (uncountable). Job = your paid position (countable). 'I have a job'; 'I have a lot of work.'
mini_conversation:
A: Where do you work?
B: I work at a small design studio downtown.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A tired employee mutters, "I can't believe I have to work this weekend too."
news_style_line: News-style: "Officials say the new bridge repairs will not begin work until next spring."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Sorry, I can't talk long -- I'm still at work."
mcq_options: A) To sleep  B) To make an effort or do a job  C) To travel  D) To celebrate
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: She has to ______ late tonight to finish the report. → work
find_and_fix_to_correct: He working at a bank for ten years. → He has worked at a bank for ten years.
translate: वह एक बैंक में काम करता है। → He works at a bank.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about where you work or want to work.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to do a job or make an effort to do something'?
usage_tip: 'Does it work?' means does it function. 'Work out' = exercise, or solve.

simple_explanation: To spend time learning about a subject. When you study, you read, practice, and think carefully about a topic so you can understand or remember it.
example_2: She is studying medicine at university.
example_3: We studied for the exam together.
collocations: study hard, study for an exam, study abroad, study a subject
related_phrasal_verbs: look into, dig into, cram for
action_sequence: Before: open your books → During: read and make notes → After: close the book, feeling ready
grammar_pattern: study + noun (study biology) or study for + noun (study for a test)
common_mistake: She studies since three hours.
correct_version: She has been studying for three hours.
why_it_s_wrong: For a length of time up to now, use 'for' with the present perfect continuous.
pronunciation_tip: Two syllables: STUD-ee, with stress on the first.
spelling_tip: Note the "-y" ending changes to "-ies" in third person: he studies (not studys).
etymology: From Old French "estudie," ultimately from Latin "studium" (zeal, application, eagerness to learn).
prefix_root_suffix: stud(y) = root (from Latin studium, "eagerness") -- no separate prefix/suffix
mnemonic: STUDY starts with "STUD" -- picture a sturdy student studying with steady focus.
memory_trick: STUDY → STUDIED: Y becomes I before -ed.
visual_association: A student at a desk surrounded by open textbooks and highlighters.
difference_explained: Study = the effort (reading, practising). Learn = the result (you now know it).
mini_conversation:
A: What are you studying tonight?
B: I'm studying for tomorrow's chemistry test.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A student surrounded by books sighs, "I still have three chapters left to study."
news_style_line: News-style: "Officials say students will study a revised curriculum starting next year."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I can't come out tonight -- I need to study for my exam."
mcq_options: A) To rest completely  B) To spend time learning a subject  C) To travel abroad  D) To ignore homework
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: He has to ______ every night to pass the final exam. → study
find_and_fix_to_correct: She study English every day. → She studies English every day.
translate: वह हर रात गणित पढ़ाई करता है। → He studies math every night.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about which subject you study most.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to spend time learning about a subject'?
usage_tip: 'Study' is also a noun for a room: 'He is in his study.'

simple_explanation: To gain new knowledge or a new skill. When you learn something, information or a skill goes from not knowing it to knowing it, often through study or practice.
example_2: I'm learning to play the guitar.
example_3: She learned a lot from that internship.
collocations: learn quickly, learn from mistakes, learn a language, learn by heart
related_phrasal_verbs: pick up, catch on, take in
action_sequence: Before: don't know a skill → During: practise it → After: can do it
grammar_pattern: learn + noun/to-infinitive (learn Spanish / learn to swim)
common_mistake: I am learning English since two years.
correct_version: I have been learning English for two years.
why_it_s_wrong: For a length of time up to now, use the present perfect continuous with 'for', not the simple continuous.
pronunciation_tip: Rhymes with "burn" and "turn" -- the "ea" makes a short "er" sound.
spelling_tip: Don't confuse with "learnt" (British past tense) vs. "learned" (American past tense) -- both are correct.
etymology: Old English "leornian" (to get knowledge, to be taught), related to the idea of following a track or trail.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- a simple base word
mnemonic: LEARN contains "EAR" -- you LEARN by using your EARS to listen and absorb new things.
memory_trick: LEARN has 'EAR' inside: you learn by listening.
visual_association: A brain slowly filling up with colorful puzzle pieces.
emotion_feel: Curiosity, sometimes pride after mastering something
difference_explained: You learn from someone. Someone teaches you. Never 'He learned me.'
mini_conversation:
A: How's your Japanese coming along?
B: Slowly -- I'm learning a few new words every day.
everyday_scene: Everyday: An old mentor smiles and says, "You never stop learning, kid -- not if you're doing it right."
news_style_line: News-style: "Researchers say children learn new words fastest between the ages of two and five."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I'm trying to learn how to cook -- wish me luck."
mcq_options: A) To forget something  B) To gain new knowledge or skill  C) To teach someone else  D) To sell something
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: It's never too late to ______ a new skill. → learn
find_and_fix_to_correct: She learn Spanish very fast. → She learns Spanish very fast.
translate: बच्चे नई भाषाएं जल्दी सीखते हैं। → Children learn new languages quickly.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a skill you learned recently.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to gain new knowledge or a new skill'?
usage_tip: 'Learnt' is British; 'learned' is used in both British and American English.

simple_explanation: To look at written words and understand their meaning. When you read, your eyes move over letters and words and your brain turns them into meaning.
example_1: I read a book every night before bed.
example_2: She reads the newspaper every morning.
example_3: He read the letter twice before replying.
collocations: read aloud, read carefully, read between the lines, avid reader
related_phrasal_verbs: read up on, read through, read into
action_sequence: Before: open the book → During: follow the words → After: understand the story
grammar_pattern: read + noun (read a book) or read + to + person (read to a child)
common_mistake: I readed the book yesterday.
correct_version: I read the book yesterday.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Read' keeps the same spelling in the past, but it is pronounced 'red'.
pronunciation_tip: Present tense rhymes with "seed"; past tense rhymes with "bed" -- same spelling, different sound.
spelling_tip: Don't add an extra "e" -- it's "read," not "reed" (that's a different word, a plant).
etymology: Old English "rædan" (to advise, interpret, guess) -- narrowed over time to mean "interpret written text."
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- a simple base word
mnemonic: READ rhymes with "seed" -- plant the SEED of knowledge by reading.
memory_trick: READ (reed) today, READ (red) yesterday — like LEAD and LED in sound.
visual_association: An open book with a pair of eyes above it, tracking steadily across the page.
difference_explained: Read = look at text and understand it. Study = read carefully in order to learn.
mini_conversation:
A: What are you reading these days?
B: I just started reading a mystery novel.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A detective flips through a file and mutters, "Let me read that report one more time."
news_style_line: News-style: "Studies show fewer teenagers read printed newspapers than a decade ago."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Have you read the message I sent you last night?"
mcq_options: A) To write new text  B) To look at and understand written words  C) To listen to music  D) To draw a picture
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: She likes to ______ before falling asleep every night. → read
find_and_fix_to_correct: He readed the newspaper this morning. → He read the newspaper this morning.
translate: मैं हर दिन अखबार पढ़ता हूँ। → I read the newspaper every day.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about the last book or article you read.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to look at written words and understand their meaning'?
usage_tip: 'Read out' means read aloud for others.

simple_explanation: To make letters or words on a surface to communicate something. When you write, you use a pen, pencil, or keyboard to put your thoughts into words that others can read.
example_1: I write in my journal every day.
example_2: She wrote a letter to her grandmother.
example_3: He writes for a local newspaper.
collocations: write a letter, write down, write clearly, write an essay
related_phrasal_verbs: write down, write up, write off
where_it_s_used: Letters, emails, essays, journals, creative work
action_sequence: Before: take a pen → During: put words on paper → After: read what you wrote
grammar_pattern: write + noun (write a letter) or write to + person (write to a friend)
common_mistake: She writed a beautiful poem.
correct_version: She wrote a beautiful poem.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Write' is irregular: write – wrote – written.
pronunciation_tip: The "w" is silent -- say it exactly like "right."
spelling_tip: Don't forget the silent "w" at the start, and the silent "e" at the end.
etymology: Old English "writan" (to scratch, draw, or incise runes/letters) -- originally referred to carving marks.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- a simple base word
mnemonic: WRITE has a silent "W" -- like a Writer's pen quietly scratching Words onto paper.
memory_trick: WRITE has a silent W, like WRONG and WRAP.
visual_association: A hand holding a pen, moving steadily across a blank page.
difference_explained: Write = make words. Right = correct, or the opposite of left. Same sound.
mini_conversation:
A: Have you written the report yet?
B: Not yet, I'll write it tonight.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A novelist stares at a blank page and whispers, "I just need to write the first line."
news_style_line: News-style: "The author says she wrote most of the novel during the winter months."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Can you write down your address for me?"
mcq_options: A) To speak loudly  B) To put words on paper or a screen  C) To listen carefully  D) To draw a map
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Please ______ your full name on the form. → write
find_and_fix_to_correct: I writed an email to my boss. → I wrote an email to my boss.
translate: कृपया अपना नाम यहाँ लिखें। → Please write your name here.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about who you last wrote a message to.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to make letters or words on a surface to communicate something'?
usage_tip: 'Write down' = note it on paper. 'Write to' someone = send them a letter or email.

simple_explanation: To write words using a keyboard. When you type, you press keys on a computer or phone to create letters and words instead of writing them by hand.
example_1: I type my reports on a laptop.
example_2: She types very fast on her phone.
example_3: He typed the whole essay in an hour.
collocations: type quickly, type an email, type a document, learn to type
where_it_s_used: Office work, emails, computers, phones, texting
action_sequence: Before: open a document → During: press the keys → After: words appear on screen
grammar_pattern: type + noun (type a message) or type on + device (type on a keyboard)
common_mistake: I am typing this report since morning.
correct_version: I have been typing this report since morning.
why_it_s_wrong: With 'since', use the present perfect continuous.
pronunciation_tip: Rhymes with "ripe" -- a long "i" sound, not a short one.
spelling_tip: Only one "p," and don't forget the silent "e" at the end.
etymology: From Greek "typos" (a mark, impression, model) via Latin and French; the verb sense (to write with a typewriter/keyboard) developed in the 19th century.
prefix_root_suffix: type = root (from Greek "typos," a mark/impression) -- no clear prefix/suffix in the verb form
mnemonic: TYPE rhymes with "wipe" -- imagine wiping your fingers before you TYPE on the keyboard.
memory_trick: TYPE: T for Tap the keys.
visual_association: Fingers moving quickly across a lit-up keyboard.
difference_explained: Write = with a pen, or in general. Type = using a keyboard.
mini_conversation:
A: Can you type faster than me?
B: Probably -- I type about seventy words a minute.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A journalist hunches over her laptop, typing furiously, "I need to type this before the deadline hits."
news_style_line: News-style: "Officials say the new software lets users type in over forty languages."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Hold on, let me type that down before I forget it."
mcq_options: A) To speak into a phone  B) To write using a keyboard  C) To draw a picture  D) To read aloud
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Could you please ______ this letter for me? → type
find_and_fix_to_correct: She typing the report right now since an hour. → She has been typing the report for an hour.
translate: वह बहुत तेज़ टाइप करती है। → She types very fast.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about how fast you can type.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to write words using a keyboard'?
usage_tip: 'Type' is also a noun meaning kind: 'What type of music do you like?'

simple_explanation: To produce text or images on paper using a machine. When you print something, a printer copies a document or photo from your computer onto paper.
example_1: I need to print these documents now.
example_2: Can you print this file in color?
example_3: The office printed a thousand flyers for the event.
collocations: print a document, print in color, print out, out of print
action_sequence: Before: click Print → During: the printer puts ink on paper → After: collect the pages
grammar_pattern: print + noun (print a report) or print out + noun (print out the tickets)
common_mistake: Please print out this file on your printer machine.
correct_version: Please print this file.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Printer' already means the machine, so 'printer machine' repeats the idea.
pronunciation_tip: One syllable, with a clear "r" sound: PRINT, not "pint."
spelling_tip: Remember the "r" after the "p" -- pr-int, not "pint."
etymology: From Old French "preinte," from Latin "premere" (to press) -- originally referred to pressing an image or mark onto a surface.
prefix_root_suffix: print = root (from Latin premere, "to press") -- no clear prefix/suffix in this form
mnemonic: PRINT contains "INT" like "ink" -- a PRINTer uses INK to put words on paper.
memory_trick: PRINT has 'PRINT' in 'PRINTER': the machine that prints.
visual_association: Sheets of paper sliding out of a humming printer tray.
difference_explained: Print = make a paper copy from a computer file. Copy (photocopy) = make a copy from paper.
mini_conversation:
A: Is the printer working today?
B: Yes, I already printed the tickets.
everyday_scene: Everyday: An assistant rushes in and says, "The contracts are printed and ready for signing."
news_style_line: News-style: "The newspaper announced it will stop printing a physical edition next year."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Can you print two copies of this for the meeting?"
mcq_options: A) To delete a file  B) To produce text or images on paper  C) To send an email  D) To save a document
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: I need to ______ these tickets before we leave. → print
find_and_fix_to_correct: She printed out the file on the computer screen. → She printed out the file from the computer.
translate: कृपया इस दस्तावेज़ को प्रिंट करें। → Please print this document.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something you printed recently.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to produce text or images on paper using a machine'?
usage_tip: 'Print out' and 'print' mean the same. A 'printout' is the printed page.

simple_explanation: To use math to find a number or answer. When you calculate something, you use numbers and math operations to work out an amount, total, or result.
example_1: I calculate my monthly budget carefully.
example_2: The accountant calculated the total profit.
example_3: Can you calculate how much we owe?
collocations: calculate the cost, calculate carefully, roughly calculate, calculate a total
related_phrasal_verbs: work out, add up, figure out
action_sequence: Before: see the numbers → During: add or multiply them → After: get the total
grammar_pattern: calculate + noun (calculate the cost) or calculate how/what (calculate how much it costs)
common_mistake: I calculated about the total bill.
correct_version: I calculated the total bill.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Calculate' takes a direct object; don't add 'about'.
pronunciation_tip: Four syllables, stress on the first: CAL-cyoo-late.
etymology: From Latin "calculare," from "calculus" (a small stone used for counting) -- ancient people literally counted with pebbles.
prefix_root_suffix: calcul(us) = root (Latin for "pebble/stone used for counting") + -ate = verb suffix
mnemonic: CALCULATE contains "CALC" like "calculator" -- you CALCULATE using a CALCulator.
memory_trick: CALCULATE and CALCULATOR: the machine that calculates.
visual_association: A calculator screen filling up with a long string of numbers.
difference_explained: Count = find how many (1, 2, 3…). Calculate = work out an answer using maths.
mini_conversation:
A: How much will the trip cost in total?
B: Give me a second, let me calculate it.
everyday_scene: Everyday: An engineer stares at a whiteboard and says, "Let me calculate the load one more time before we proceed."
news_style_line: News-style: "Economists calculated that the policy could save households hundreds of dollars a year."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Wait, let me calculate the tip before we split the bill."
mcq_options: A) To guess randomly  B) To work out a number using math  C) To forget a number  D) To write a letter
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Let's ______ the total cost before we decide. → calculate
find_and_fix_to_correct: He calculate the bill wrong yesterday. → He calculated the bill wrong yesterday.
translate: कृपया कुल खर्च की गणना करें। → Please calculate the total expense.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something you calculate every month.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to use math to find a number or answer'?
usage_tip: 'A calculated risk' is a risk you thought about carefully.

simple_explanation: To be in control of or successfully handle something. When you manage something, you organize, lead, or control it so it runs smoothly -- this could be a team, a business, or even your own time.
example_1: She can manage a large team well.
example_2: He manages the sales department.
example_3: I don't know how she manages three jobs at once.
collocations: manage a team, manage time, barely manage, manage to do something
related_phrasal_verbs: get by, cope with, pull off
where_it_s_used: Business, leadership, daily tasks, coping under pressure
action_sequence: Before: the task looks hard → During: keep trying → After: succeed: 'I managed it!'
grammar_pattern: manage + noun (manage a store) or manage + to-infinitive (manage to arrive on time)
common_mistake: I manage to finishing the report.
correct_version: I managed to finish the report.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Manage to' is followed by the base verb, not -ing. A finished past action also needs the past tense.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the first syllable: MAN-ij, not man-AGE.
spelling_tip: Watch the soft "g" sound in "-age," like in "message" or "package."
etymology: From Italian "maneggiare" (to handle, train horses), from Latin "manus" (hand) -- originally about handling something skillfully.
prefix_root_suffix: manage = root (from Latin manus, "hand") -- no separate prefix/suffix
mnemonic: MANAGE contains "MAN" -- imagine a MAN with a plan, MANaging his team well.
memory_trick: MANAGE has 'MAN' + 'AGE': it takes a grown-up to manage things.
visual_association: A person juggling several balls smoothly without dropping one.
emotion_feel: Confident, sometimes stressed if things get overwhelming
difference_explained: Manage = handle or succeed. Arrange = plan and organise details in advance.

B: Honestly, I just plan my week very carefully.

news_style_line: News-style: "The company announced a new executive to manage its overseas operations."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I don't know how you manage to stay so calm during exams."

simple_explanation: To arrange things in an orderly, planned way. When you organize something, you put things in order or plan an event so everything works smoothly, rather than being messy or chaotic.
example_1: I need to organize my desk today.
example_2: She organized a birthday party for her friend.
example_3: Please organize these files by date.
collocations: organize an event, organize files, well organized, organize a meeting
related_phrasal_verbs: sort out, set up, arrange for
action_sequence: Before: things are messy → During: put them in groups and order → After: everything is easy to find
grammar_pattern: organize + noun (organize a trip) or organize + noun + by/into (organize files by date)
common_mistake: I need to organize about my schedule.
correct_version: I need to organize my schedule.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Organize' takes a direct object; don't add 'about'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the first syllable: OR-guh-nize.
spelling_tip: Remember the "-ize" (American) or "-ise" (British) ending -- both are accepted.
etymology: From French "organiser," from Latin "organum" (tool, instrument) -- the idea of arranging parts into a working whole.
prefix_root_suffix: organ = root (Latin "organum," tool) + -ize = verb suffix (to make/do)
mnemonic: ORGANIZE sounds like "organ" -- think of a well-ORGANIZEd body where every ORGAN has its place.
memory_trick: ORGANIZE has 'ORGAN': like body organs, each part in its right place.
visual_association: A messy desk transforming into neat, labeled folders.
emotion_feel: Calm, satisfied once things are in order
difference_explained: Arrange = put things in a nice order or position. Organize = plan and manage a bigger system or event.
mini_conversation:
A: Who's organizing the office party this year?
B: I am -- I'm still working out the details.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A wedding planner checks her clipboard and says, "Everything's organized down to the last detail."
news_style_line: News-style: "Volunteers organized a cleanup drive along the riverbank this weekend."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Can you help me organize my closet this weekend?"
mcq_options: A) To make something messy  B) To arrange things in an orderly way  C) To forget an appointment  D) To delete files
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: We need to ______ the files before the audit. → organize
find_and_fix_to_correct: She organize the event very well last year. → She organized the event very well last year.
translate: कृपया इन फाइलों को व्यवस्थित करें। → Please organize these files.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about how you organize your study time.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to arrange things in an orderly, planned way'?
usage_tip: British spelling: organise. 'An organised person' plans ahead.

simple_explanation: To decide in advance what you will do. When you plan, you think ahead and prepare the steps needed to reach a goal or organize an event.
example_1: We plan to travel next summer.
example_2: They are planning a wedding for June.
example_3: I planned my whole week on Sunday.
collocations: plan ahead, plan a trip, according to plan, carefully planned
related_phrasal_verbs: plan out, plan for, plan around
where_it_s_used: Trips, events, careers, daily schedules, goals
action_sequence: Before: decide a goal → During: write the steps → After: follow the steps
grammar_pattern: plan + to-infinitive (plan to travel) or plan + noun (plan a party)
common_mistake: I am planning to going there next week.
correct_version: I am planning to go there next week.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Plan to' is followed by the base verb, not -ing.
pronunciation_tip: Short, single syllable -- rhymes with "man" and "can."
etymology: From French "plan," originally meaning a flat surface or map -- extended to mean a scheme or design for the future.
prefix_root_suffix: plan = root (from French/Latin "planum," flat surface) -- no separate prefix/suffix
mnemonic: PLAN rhymes with "MAP" in sound of purpose -- you PLAN your route like drawing a MAP.
memory_trick: PLAN → PLANNED: double N before -ed.
visual_association: A calendar with circled dates and arrows connecting them.
emotion_feel: Hopeful, sometimes anxious if plans might change
difference_explained: Decide = make a choice. Plan = work out how and when to do it.
mini_conversation:
A: What are your plans for the weekend?
B: I'm planning to visit my parents.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A general points at a map and says, "This is the plan -- we move at dawn."
news_style_line: News-style: "The city plans to build three new parks by next year."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Do you have any plans for tonight?"
mcq_options: A) To act without thinking  B) To decide in advance what to do  C) To forget an appointment  D) To cancel an event

write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about what you plan to do this weekend.

reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to decide in advance what you will do'?
usage_tip: 'Plan B' means a backup option.

simple_explanation: To get something or yourself ready for a future event. When you prepare, you take steps beforehand so you're ready when the actual moment or task arrives.
example_2: She prepared for the interview all week.
example_3: We need to prepare the room before the guests arrive.
collocations: prepare for an exam, prepare a meal, well prepared, prepare in advance
related_phrasal_verbs: gear up, get ready, brace for
action_sequence: Before: the exam is near → During: study and practise → After: feel ready
grammar_pattern: prepare + noun (prepare a report) or prepare for + noun (prepare for the exam)
common_mistake: I am preparing to the exam since Monday.
correct_version: I have been preparing for the exam since Monday.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'prepare for' + an event. With 'since', use the present perfect continuous.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the last syllable: pri-PAIR.
spelling_tip: Note the single "r" in the middle -- pre-PARE, not "preparre."
etymology: From Latin "praeparare" (prae- "before" + parare "to make ready") -- literally "to make ready beforehand."
prefix_root_suffix: pre- = before + par(e) = root (Latin parare, "to make ready")
mnemonic: PREPARE contains "PARE" like "pair" -- PREPARE two things (a PAIR) so you're ready for anything.
memory_trick: PRE-PARE: get ready BEFORE ('pre') the event.
visual_association: A chef laying out ingredients neatly before cooking begins.
difference_explained: Prepare something = make it ready (prepare dinner). Prepare for something = get ready for an event (prepare for the exam).
mini_conversation:
A: Are you ready for tomorrow's presentation?
B: Almost -- I've been preparing my slides all night.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A coach tells the team, "We've prepared for this moment all season -- go out there and play."
news_style_line: News-style: "Officials are preparing emergency shelters ahead of the coming storm."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I need to prepare a few things before the guests arrive."
mcq_options: A) To forget about something  B) To get ready for something in advance  C) To cancel an event  D) To relax completely

find_and_fix_to_correct: He prepare his speech last night. → He prepared his speech last night.

write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about how you prepare for an exam.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to get something or yourself ready for a future event'?
usage_tip: 'Prepare yourself' is used for bad news: 'Prepare yourself for a shock.'

simple_explanation: To study a subject carefully to find new information. When you research something, you investigate it in depth -- reading, testing, or gathering facts to learn something new or confirm the truth.
example_1: I need to research this topic more.
example_2: Scientists researched the effects of the new drug.
example_3: She spent hours researching flights online.
collocations: conduct research, research thoroughly, market research, research a topic
related_phrasal_verbs: look into, dig up, delve into
action_sequence: Before: have a question → During: read many sources → After: find the answer
grammar_pattern: research + noun (research a topic) or do research on + noun (do research on climate change)
common_mistake: I did a research about this topic.
correct_version: I did research on this topic.
why_it_s_wrong: As a noun, 'research' is usually uncountable, so no 'a'. Use 'research on' or 'into' a topic.
pronunciation_tip: Stress can fall on either syllable: RE-search (noun, common) or re-SEARCH (verb, common) -- both are used.
spelling_tip: Remember the "sear" in the middle, like "search" -- re + search.
etymology: From French "recercher" (re- "again" + cercher "to search") -- literally "to search again/thoroughly."
prefix_root_suffix: re- = again + search = root (to look for) -- literally "to search again/thoroughly"
mnemonic: RESEARCH contains "SEARCH" -- you RESEARCH by SEARCHing again and again for facts.
memory_trick: RE-SEARCH: search again and again.
visual_association: A magnifying glass hovering over a stack of open books.
difference_explained: Search = look for one thing. Research = study a topic deeply and carefully.
mini_conversation:
A: How's your thesis going?
B: I'm still researching sources for the second chapter.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A scientist adjusts her glasses and says, "We've researched this for years -- the results don't lie."
news_style_line: News-style: "New research suggests that regular walking can improve long-term heart health."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I researched a few hotels before booking this one."
mcq_options: A) To ignore new information  B) To investigate a topic carefully  C) To guess an answer  D) To copy someone's work
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Before buying a laptop, she likes to ______ different brands online. → research
find_and_fix_to_correct: He is doing researches on climate change. → He is doing research on climate change.
translate: वैज्ञानिकों ने इस बीमारी पर शोध किया। → Scientists researched this disease.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something you researched before buying.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to study a subject carefully to find new information'?
usage_tip: 'Do some research' is more natural than 'do a research'.

simple_explanation: To look at or examine something again carefully. When you review something, you go back over it -- like notes, a document, or a movie -- to check it, judge it, or remember it better.
example_1: I review my notes before every test.
example_2: The teacher reviewed the homework with the class.
example_3: She wrote a review of the new restaurant.
collocations: review notes, write a review, review the document, under review
related_phrasal_verbs: go over, look back on, check over
action_sequence: Before: finish a report → During: read it again carefully → After: fix any errors
grammar_pattern: review + noun (review the report) -- often used before a decision or exam
common_mistake: I reviewed about the report before the meeting.
correct_version: I reviewed the report before the meeting.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Review' takes a direct object; don't add 'about'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: ri-VYOO.
etymology: From French "revoir" (re- "again" + voir "to see") -- literally "to see again," i.e., to look back over something.
prefix_root_suffix: re- = again + view = root (to see/look) -- literally "to see again"
mnemonic: REVIEW contains "VIEW" -- you REVIEW something by taking another VIEW of it.
memory_trick: RE-VIEW: view again.
visual_association: Someone highlighting key lines in a printed document with a red pen.
difference_explained: Review = look at again. Revise (UK) = study again for an exam, or change and improve something.
mini_conversation:

B: Yes, I reviewed them this morning -- they look correct.

casual_conversation: Casual: "Can you review my essay before I submit it?"

spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to look at or examine something again carefully'?
usage_tip: A 'review' is also an opinion about a film or product: '5-star review'.

simple_explanation: To go over something again to correct or improve it. When you revise, you look back at something you've already done -- like notes or an essay -- and change or improve it.
example_1: I need to revise this essay tonight.
example_2: She revised her essay twice before submitting it.
example_3: We revise our lessons every weekend before exams.
collocations: revise for exams, revise a draft, thoroughly revise, revise and edit
related_phrasal_verbs: go over, look back on, rework
action_sequence: Before: the exam is next week → During: go over your notes again → After: feel confident
grammar_pattern: revise + noun (revise the plan) or revise for + noun (revise for exams -- British usage)
common_mistake: I revise my exam tomorrow.
correct_version: I'm going to revise for my exam tomorrow.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'revise for' an exam. You revise your notes, not the exam itself.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: ri-VYZE, rhyming with "surprise."
spelling_tip: Ends in "-ise," not "-ize," in this word -- even in American English, "revise" always uses "s."
etymology: From Latin "revisere" (re- "again" + visere "to look at, visit") -- literally "to look at again."
prefix_root_suffix: re- = again + vis(e) = root (Latin videre, "to see") -- literally "to see/look again"
mnemonic: REVISE rhymes with "advise" -- you REVISE your work after getting good ADVICE.
memory_trick: RE-VISE: look again to improve.
visual_association: A page covered in red pen corrections and crossed-out sentences.
emotion_feel: Focused, sometimes a bit tense before exams
difference_explained: Revise = go over again to learn or improve. Review = look at again to check.

B: Revising for my chemistry exam, mostly.

casual_conversation: Casual: "I'm revising my notes before tomorrow's test."
mcq_options: A) To delete something completely  B) To go over something to correct or improve it  C) To ignore mistakes  D) To write something for the first time

find_and_fix_to_correct: She revise her essay every night this week. → She revises her essay every night this week.

write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about how many days you need to revise for an exam.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to go over something again to correct or improve it'?
usage_tip: In India and the UK, 'revise' = study for an exam. In the US, 'review' is used instead.

simple_explanation: To learn something so well that you can remember it exactly. When you memorize something, you repeat or practice it until you can recall it from memory without looking, like a poem or a phone number.
example_1: I memorize new words every day.
example_2: She memorized the entire speech.
example_3: Kids often memorize songs quickly.
collocations: memorize by heart, memorize a poem, quickly memorize, hard to memorize
related_phrasal_verbs: learn by heart, commit to memory
action_sequence: Before: read the poem → During: repeat it many times → After: say it without looking
grammar_pattern: memorize + noun (memorize the list) -- often paired with "by heart"
common_mistake: I memorized about the poem for class.
correct_version: I memorized the poem for class.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Memorize' takes a direct object; don't add 'about'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the first syllable: MEM-uh-rize.
etymology: From Latin "memoria" (memory), via French "mémoriser" -- the act of committing something to memory.
prefix_root_suffix: memor(y) = root (Latin memoria) + -ize = verb suffix (to make/do)
mnemonic: MEMORIZE contains "MEMORY" -- you MEMORIZE by storing things safely in your MEMORY.
memory_trick: MEMORIZE comes from MEMORY: put it into memory.
visual_association: A stack of cards being turned one by one, with an arrow looping back to the start.
difference_explained: Memorize = learn so you can repeat it exactly. Remember = keep or bring back to mind.

B: I just memorized them with flashcards.
everyday_scene: Everyday: An actor paces backstage muttering, "I need to memorize this last scene before curtain call."
news_style_line: News-style: "Researchers found that students who memorize vocabulary in short sessions retain it longer."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I still haven't memorized my new phone number."

find_and_fix_to_correct: He memorize his speech every day this week. → He memorizes his speech every day this week.
translate: मुझे यह कविता याद करनी है। → I need to memorize this poem.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something you memorized as a child.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to learn something so well that you can remember it exactly'?
usage_tip: British spelling: memorise. 'Learn by heart' means the same.

simple_explanation: To do something repeatedly to get better at it. When you practice, you repeat an activity -- like speaking, playing an instrument, or a sport -- again and again so you improve.
example_2: She practices piano for an hour every day.
example_3: The team practiced hard before the match.
collocations: practice regularly, practice makes perfect, practice speaking, daily practice
action_sequence: Before: try a skill → During: repeat it again and again → After: get better at it
grammar_pattern: practice + gerund (practice speaking) or practice + noun (practice English)
common_mistake: I practice to speak English every day.
correct_version: I practice speaking English every day.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Practise' is followed by -ing, not 'to + verb'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the first syllable: PRAK-tis.
spelling_tip: American English: "practice" for both noun and verb. British English: "practice" (noun) vs. "practise" (verb).
etymology: From Greek "praktike" (practical action), via Latin and French -- the idea of doing something repeatedly to improve.
prefix_root_suffix: practic(e) = root (from Greek praktike, "practical") -- no clear separate prefix/suffix
mnemonic: PRACTICE contains "ACT" -- you PRACTICE by repeating an ACTion again and again.
memory_trick: UK: practiCe is the noun (like adviCe), practiSe is the verb. US uses 'practice' for both.
visual_association: A musician playing the same short passage over and over on a piano.
difference_explained: UK: practise (verb), practice (noun). US: practice for both. Indian textbooks usually follow UK spelling.

news_style_line: News-style: "Experts say daily practice, even just fifteen minutes, builds language fluency faster."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I really need to practice my Spanish more this month."

find_and_fix_to_correct: She practices to play the violin every evening. → She practices playing the violin every evening.

write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something you practise every day.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to do something repeatedly to get better at it'?
usage_tip: 'Practice makes perfect' — the famous saying.

simple_explanation: To give your full attention to one thing. When you focus, you concentrate all your attention on a single task or subject, ignoring distractions around you.
example_1: I need to focus on my homework now.
example_2: She focused on her breathing to stay calm.
example_3: Try to focus during the meeting.
collocations: focus on, stay focused, lose focus, focus attention
related_phrasal_verbs: zoom in on, hone in on, tune out
action_sequence: Before: switch off the phone → During: give all attention to one task → After: finish it quickly
grammar_pattern: focus on + noun/gerund (focus on the task / focus on studying)
common_mistake: I need to focus in my exam.
correct_version: I need to focus on my exam.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'focus on', not 'focus in'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the first syllable: FOH-kus.
etymology: From Latin "focus" (hearth, fireplace) -- originally the center of a home, later extended to mean a central point of attention.
prefix_root_suffix: focus = root (Latin for "hearth/center") -- no clear prefix/suffix
mnemonic: FOCUS sounds like "hocus" (as in hocus pocus) -- FOCUS hard, like magic, and everything else disappears.
memory_trick: FOCUS like a camera: point it at ONE thing.
visual_association: A camera lens sharpening a blurry photo into a clear image.
difference_explained: Almost the same. Focus = point attention at one thing. Concentrate = hold that attention for a long time. Both take 'on'.
mini_conversation:

B: Try to focus on one subject at a time.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A coach grabs a player's shoulders and says, "Focus. Block everything else out and just focus."
news_style_line: News-style: "Analysts say the company plans to focus more on renewable energy next year."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Sorry, can we focus on the plan for a second?"
mcq_options: A) To ignore something completely  B) To give full attention to one thing  C) To relax fully  D) To forget an important task

find_and_fix_to_correct: She focus on her studies every night. → She focuses on her studies every night.

write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about what helps you focus.

usage_tip: 'Stay focused' is common advice before an exam or task.

simple_explanation: To think very hard and pay close attention to one thing. When you concentrate, you put all your mental effort into a single task, blocking out other thoughts and distractions.
example_1: I can't concentrate with this noise.
example_2: She concentrated hard during the test.
example_3: It's difficult to concentrate when you're tired.
collocations: concentrate hard, unable to concentrate, concentrate fully, concentrate on a task
related_phrasal_verbs: zone in, buckle down, tune out
where_it_s_used: Studying, work, driving, meditation, noisy environments
action_sequence: Before: sit in a quiet place → During: think hard about one problem → After: solve it
grammar_pattern: concentrate on + noun/gerund (concentrate on the exam / concentrate on driving)
common_mistake: I can't concentrate in this problem.
correct_version: I can't concentrate on this problem.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'concentrate on', not 'concentrate in'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the first syllable: KON-sen-trate.
etymology: From Latin "concentrare" (con- "together" + centrum "center") -- literally "to bring together toward a center."
prefix_root_suffix: con- = together + centr(e) = root (center) + -ate = verb suffix
mnemonic: CONCENTRATE contains "CENTER" -- you CONCENTRATE by bringing all your thoughts to the CENTER.
memory_trick: CON-CENTRE-ATE: bring everything to the centre.
visual_association: A person closing their eyes and blocking out all background noise.
difference_explained: Both take 'on'. Concentrate suggests longer, harder mental effort.
mini_conversation:

B: Sorry, I'm trying to concentrate on this report.

find_and_fix_to_correct: He can't concentrate about his work today. → He can't concentrate on his work today.

simple_explanation: To successfully reach a goal through effort. When you achieve something, you succeed at a goal you worked hard for, like passing an exam or finishing a project.
example_1: I achieved my goal this year.
example_2: She achieved top marks in the final exam.
example_3: The team achieved great results this season.
collocations: achieve a goal, achieve success, achieve results, hard to achieve
related_phrasal_verbs: pull off, reach for, live up to
action_sequence: Before: set a goal → During: work hard for months → After: reach it
grammar_pattern: achieve + noun (achieve success/a goal/a target)
common_mistake: I achieved to become a doctor.
correct_version: I achieved my goal of becoming a doctor.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Achieve' takes a noun object (a goal, a result), not 'to + verb'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: uh-CHEEV.
spelling_tip: Remember "achi-EVE" -- like the name "Eve" at the end.
etymology: From Old French "achever" (a- "to" + chief "head/end") -- literally "to bring to a head/completion."
prefix_root_suffix: a- = to (from French) + chieve = root (French chief, "head/end") -- literally "to bring to completion"
mnemonic: ACHIEVE ends like "believe" -- if you BELIEVE in yourself, you can ACHIEVE your goals.
memory_trick: ACHIEVE: 'I before E, except after C' — achIEve.
visual_association: A runner crossing the finish line with arms raised.
difference_explained: Get = receive or obtain (easy). Achieve = reach something through effort.
mini_conversation:
A: How was your first year of business?
B: We achieved more than we expected, honestly.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A coach raises a trophy and says, "This is what we achieved together, as one team."
news_style_line: News-style: "The charity announced it had achieved its fundraising target a month early."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I'm really proud of what we achieved this year."
mcq_options: A) To fail at a task  B) To successfully reach a goal  C) To ignore a plan  D) To begin something new
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: She worked hard all year to ______ her dream of becoming a doctor. → achieve
find_and_fix_to_correct: He achieve his goal last year. → He achieved his goal last year.
translate: उसने अपने सपने को हासिल कर लिया। → He achieved his dream.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a goal you achieved this year.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to successfully reach a goal through effort'?
usage_tip: 'Achievement' is the noun: 'Getting this job is a big achievement.'

simple_explanation: To finish doing something fully. When you complete something, you finish every part of it -- nothing is left undone.
example_1: I complete my homework every night.
example_2: She completed the marathon in under four hours.
example_3: He needs to complete this form before Friday.
collocations: complete a task, complete a form, complete successfully, nearly complete
related_phrasal_verbs: wrap up, round off, finish up
action_sequence: Before: start a task → During: work step by step → After: nothing is left to do
grammar_pattern: complete + noun (complete the assignment/the course)
common_mistake: I have completed my homework yesterday.
correct_version: I completed my homework yesterday.
why_it_s_wrong: A finished past time like 'yesterday' needs the simple past, not the present perfect.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: kuhm-PLEET.
spelling_tip: Double "e" in the middle -- com-PLETE, not "complet."
etymology: From Latin "completus," past participle of "complere" (com- "together" + plere "to fill") -- literally "to fill up fully."
prefix_root_suffix: com- = together/fully + plet(e) = root (Latin plere, "to fill")
mnemonic: COMPLETE contains "PLETE" like "please" -- it PLEASES you to COMPLETE a task.
memory_trick: COMPLETE: every piece is there, nothing missing.
visual_association: A checklist with every single box ticked off.
difference_explained: Finish = reach the end. Complete = finish with every part done. Forms are completed; races are finished.
mini_conversation:
A: Have you completed the application yet?
B: Almost -- just one section left.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A pilot announces over the radio, "Mission complete -- bringing her home now."
news_style_line: News-style: "Engineers say the new highway project will be complete by the end of the year."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I need to complete this form before I can leave."
mcq_options: A) To start something new  B) To finish something fully  C) To delay a task  D) To forget a task
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Please ______ the application before submitting it. → complete
find_and_fix_to_correct: She completed to fill the form yesterday. → She completed the form yesterday.
translate: कृपया शुक्रवार से पहले यह फॉर्म पूरा करें। → Please complete this form before Friday.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a course or project you completed.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to finish doing something fully'?
usage_tip: 'Complete the form' is standard on official forms.

simple_explanation: To reach the end of an activity. When you finish something, you come to the end of it -- there's nothing more to do or add.
example_1: I will finish this book tonight.
example_2: He finished his dinner quickly.
example_3: She finished the race in second place.
collocations: finish first, finish on time, almost finished, finish a race
related_phrasal_verbs: finish up, finish off, wrap up
action_sequence: Before: start reading → During: read the last page → After: close the book
grammar_pattern: finish + gerund (finish eating) or finish + noun (finish the race)
common_mistake: I finished to read the book.
correct_version: I finished reading the book.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Finish' is followed by -ing, not 'to + verb'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the first syllable: FIN-ish.
spelling_tip: Only one "n" and one "s" -- "finish," not "finnish" (that's a nationality!).
etymology: From Old French "finir," from Latin "finis" (end, boundary) -- the same root as "final" and "finite."
prefix_root_suffix: finish = root (from Latin finis, "end") -- no clear separate prefix/suffix
mnemonic: FINISH sounds like "FIN," a fish's tail -- you see the FIN at the very end, when you FINISH.
memory_trick: FINISH has 'FIN', like the French word for 'the end'.
visual_association: A checkered flag waving at the finish line of a race.
difference_explained: You finish an activity (finish work). Something ends by itself (the film ended).
mini_conversation:
A: Are you done with the report?
B: Almost -- I'll finish it in ten minutes.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A runner collapses at the line, gasping, "I finished -- I actually finished."
news_style_line: News-style: "Construction crews expect to finish the new bridge by next spring."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Let me finish this call and I'll be right there."
mcq_options: A) To begin an activity  B) To reach the end of an activity  C) To pause temporarily  D) To repeat a task
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: I need to ______ this assignment before dinner. → finish
find_and_fix_to_correct: She finished to clean her room an hour ago. → She finished cleaning her room an hour ago.
translate: मैं आज रात यह किताब खत्म कर दूंगा। → I will finish this book tonight.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about what you finished doing last night.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to reach the end of an activity'?
usage_tip: 'Are you finished?' / 'Have you finished?' — both common.

simple_explanation: To begin doing something. When you start something, you take the first step of an activity -- the moment it begins.
example_2: The movie starts at eight.
example_3: She started her own business last year.
collocations: start early, start a business, get started, start over
related_phrasal_verbs: start off, start over, kick off
action_sequence: Before: everything is ready → During: press go → After: the activity is running
grammar_pattern: start + gerund/to-infinitive (start working / start to work) -- both are correct
common_mistake: The class start at nine every day.
correct_version: The class starts at nine every day.
why_it_s_wrong: He/she/it in the simple present needs -s: starts.
pronunciation_tip: One syllable, rhymes with "art" and "cart" -- START.
spelling_tip: Note the silent-ish "r" combo -- st-ART, not "stort."
etymology: Old English "steortian" (to kick, struggle) -- evolved through Middle English to mean "to make a sudden movement," then "to begin."
prefix_root_suffix: start = root (Old English steortian) -- no clear separate prefix/suffix
mnemonic: START sounds like a car engine "starting" -- vroom, and you're off!
memory_trick: START and STOP: the two ends of every task.
visual_association: A green traffic light switching on, signaling "go."
difference_explained: Almost the same. Start is more common in speech and is used for machines. Begin sounds slightly more formal.
related_words: begin, launch, kick off, initiate, open
mini_conversation:
A: What time does the movie start?
B: It starts at 7:30, so we should leave now.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A director shouts, "And... start! Everyone in position, action!"
news_style_line: News-style: "The company will start production of the new model next month."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Should we start without her, or wait a bit longer?"
mcq_options: A) To stop an activity  B) To begin an activity  C) To finish a task  D) To repeat something

find_and_fix_to_correct: We starts the meeting at ten o'clock. → We start the meeting at ten o'clock.

write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about what time your day starts.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to begin doing something'?
usage_tip: 'Start' also works for machines: 'The car won't start.'

simple_explanation: To start doing something. "Begin" means the same as "start," but it's used a bit more formally, often in writing or official speech.
example_2: The ceremony began with a speech from the mayor.
example_3: Let's begin the lesson with a quick review.
collocations: begin with, begin a journey, newly begun, begin again
related_phrasal_verbs: kick off, set off, embark on
action_sequence: Before: wait for the time → During: the first step happens → After: the event is underway
grammar_pattern: begin + gerund/to-infinitive (begin working / begin to work) -- both are correct
common_mistake: The meeting begin at ten sharp.
correct_version: The meeting begins at ten sharp.
why_it_s_wrong: He/she/it in the simple present needs -s: begins.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: bi-GIN, rhyming with "win."
spelling_tip: Double the "n" before "-ing" and "-ers": beginning, beginner.
etymology: Old English "beginnan" (be- + ginnan, "to open, begin") -- one of the oldest verbs in English for starting something.
prefix_root_suffix: be- = prefix (making the verb transitive/intensive) + gin = root (Old English, "open/start")
word_family: beginning (n.), beginner (n.), began (past tense), begun (past participle)
mnemonic: BEGIN sounds like "be-GIN" -- BE ready, and GIN(ger) up the courage to BEGIN.
memory_trick: BEGIN → BEGAN → BEGUN, like SWIM → SWAM → SWUM.
visual_association: Curtains slowly opening on an empty stage.
difference_explained: Begin is slightly more formal. Machines 'start', they don't 'begin'.
mini_conversation:
A: Should we begin the presentation now?
B: Yes, let's begin -- everyone's here.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A narrator's voice echoes, "Our story begins on a quiet winter morning."
news_style_line: News-style: "Construction on the new stadium is set to begin next month."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Let's begin -- everyone's already here."
mcq_options: A) To stop something  B) To start something  C) To repeat something  D) To finish something

find_and_fix_to_correct: The class begin at nine every morning. → The class begins at nine every morning.

write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about when your school or office year begins.

reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to start doing something'?
usage_tip: Spelling: beginNING has double N.

simple_explanation: To formally request something, or to use something in a practical way. "Apply" has two common uses: to officially ask for a job or place (apply for a job), or to use a rule, skill, or substance in practice (apply the cream, apply the rule).
example_1: I will apply for this job.
example_2: She applied to five different universities.
example_3: Please apply the cream twice a day.
collocations: apply for a job, apply online, apply pressure, apply a rule
related_phrasal_verbs: sign up, put in for, try out for
where_it_s_used: Jobs, university admissions, skincare, rules and laws
action_sequence: Before: see a job opening → During: send the form → After: wait for a reply
grammar_pattern: apply for + noun (apply for a job) or apply to + noun (apply to a situation)
common_mistake: I applied in this job last week.
correct_version: I applied for this job last week.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'apply for' a job and 'apply to' a company.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: uh-PLY, rhyming with "sky."
spelling_tip: Note the "-y" changes to "-ied" in past tense: applied (not applyed).
etymology: From Old French "aplier," from Latin "applicare" (ad- "to" + plicare "to fold") -- literally "to fold toward," extended to mean "to put to use."
prefix_root_suffix: ap- = to/toward (form of "ad-") + ply = root (Latin plicare, "to fold")
mnemonic: APPLY sounds like "a PLY" of wood -- you APPLY layer by layer, like putting effort into a job application.
memory_trick: APPLY → APPLIED: Y becomes I before -ed.
visual_association: A hand dropping an envelope labeled "Application" into a mailbox.
emotion_feel: Hopeful, sometimes anxious while waiting for a response
difference_explained: Apply FOR the job or visa. Apply TO the company or college.
mini_conversation:
A: Did you apply for that marketing job?
B: Yes, I applied online yesterday.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A young graduate stares at a job posting and says, "I'm going to apply -- what's the worst that can happen?"
news_style_line: News-style: "Officials say new visa rules will apply to all applicants starting next month."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Have you applied for that scholarship yet?"
mcq_options: A) To reject an offer  B) To formally request something  C) To cancel a plan  D) To ignore an opportunity
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: You should ______ for that position before the deadline. → apply
find_and_fix_to_correct: She applied in the university last month. → She applied to the university last month.
translate: मैं इस नौकरी के लिए आवेदन करूंगा। → I will apply for this job.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a job or course you applied for.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to formally request something, or to use something in a practical way'?
usage_tip: 'Apply' also means put on: 'Apply cream to the skin.'

simple_explanation: To hand in or send something for approval. When you submit something, you formally give it to someone else -- like a form, an assignment, or an application -- for them to review or approve.
example_1: I need to submit my assignment.
example_2: She submitted her resignation letter yesterday.
example_3: Please submit the form online before Friday.
collocations: submit an application, submit a form, submit by (deadline), officially submit
related_phrasal_verbs: hand in, turn in, send off
where_it_s_used: School assignments, job applications, official forms, workplace reports
action_sequence: Before: finish the form → During: click Submit → After: get a confirmation
grammar_pattern: submit + noun (submit the report) or submit to + noun (submit to review)
common_mistake: I submitted my homework in the teacher.
correct_version: I submitted my homework to the teacher.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'submit something to someone', not 'in'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: suhb-MIT.
etymology: From Latin "submittere" (sub- "under" + mittere "to send") -- literally "to send under/yield to."
prefix_root_suffix: sub- = under + mit = root (Latin mittere, "to send")
mnemonic: SUBMIT sounds like "sub" + "MIT" -- you SEND your work UNDER (sub) the deadline, MIT(ting) it in on time.
memory_trick: SUBMIT → SUBMITTED: double T before -ed.
visual_association: A hand clicking a glowing "Submit" button on a screen.
difference_explained: Send = post or email anything. Submit = hand in something formally for approval or marking.
related_words: application, form, deadline, hand in, present
mini_conversation:
A: Did you submit the report yet?
B: Yes, I submitted it online an hour ago.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A student hits enter on the keyboard and whispers, "There -- submitted, right before midnight."
news_style_line: News-style: "Officials say residents can submit complaints through the new online portal."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Have you submitted your visa application yet?"
mcq_options: A) To ignore a deadline  B) To formally hand in or send something  C) To delete a document  D) To reject a request
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Make sure to ______ your assignment before midnight. → submit
find_and_fix_to_correct: She submit her project yesterday. → She submitted her project yesterday.
translate: कृपया शुक्रवार से पहले फॉर्म जमा करें। → Please submit the form before Friday.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something you submitted online recently.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to hand in or send something for approval'?
usage_tip: 'Submit' is the button on online forms.

simple_explanation: To give someone a job. When a company hires someone, it officially employs that person to work for them, usually for pay.
example_1: We hire new employees every month.
example_2: The company hired ten new engineers this year.
example_3: She was hired as a marketing manager.
collocations: hire staff, hire an employee, newly hired, hire someone for a job
related_phrasal_verbs: take on, bring on board, sign up
action_sequence: Before: need a worker → During: interview people → After: give one of them the job
grammar_pattern: hire + person + as/for + noun (hire her as a manager)
common_mistake: The company hired to him last week.
correct_version: The company hired him last week.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Hire' takes the person directly, with no 'to'.
spelling_tip: Don't confuse with "higher" (comparative of "high") -- same sound, different spelling and meaning.
etymology: Old English "hyrian" (to hire, employ, pay for service) -- related to Germanic roots meaning "wages."
prefix_root_suffix: hire = root (Old English hyrian, "to pay for service") -- no clear separate prefix/suffix
word_family: hire (n., as in "car hire"), hiring (n./adj.), hired (adj.), rehire (v.)
mnemonic: HIRE rhymes with "FIRE" -- a company can HIRE you or FIRE you, opposite actions, same sound pattern.
memory_trick: HIRE sounds like HIGHER: a company hires people to go higher.
visual_association: A handshake sealing a new job offer across a desk.
emotion_feel: Positive, hopeful (for the hired person), decisive (for the employer)
difference_explained: Hire = give someone a job (the moment). Employ = keep someone working for you (ongoing).
mini_conversation:
A: Did they hire anyone for the sales role?
B: Yes, they hired someone last week.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A manager shakes a candidate's hand and says, "Welcome aboard -- we're glad to hire you."
news_style_line: News-style: "The company announced plans to hire five hundred new workers this quarter."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I heard they're hiring at that new cafe downtown."

find_and_fix_to_correct: They hired to three new teachers this year. → They hired three new teachers this year.

write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about who you would hire to fix your phone.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to give someone a job'?
usage_tip: In India and the UK, 'hire' also means rent: 'hire a car'.

simple_explanation: To remove someone from their job. When a company fires an employee, it ends that person's job, usually because of poor performance or misconduct.
example_1: They fired him for being late.
example_2: The manager fired two employees for stealing.
example_3: She was fired after missing several deadlines.
collocations: get fired, fire someone on the spot, unfairly fired, fire an employee
where_it_s_used: Workplace conflict, layoffs, HR decisions, job loss
action_sequence: Before: an employee breaks rules → During: the boss takes action → After: the employee loses the job
grammar_pattern: fire + person (fire the employee) or be fired (passive: get fired)
common_mistake: He was fire from his job yesterday.
correct_version: He was fired from his job yesterday.
why_it_s_wrong: The passive needs the past participle 'fired': 'was fired'.
spelling_tip: Same spelling as the noun "fire" (flames) -- context tells you the meaning.
etymology: The verb sense "to dismiss from a job" is a 19th-century American English extension of "fire" (to discharge a gun) -- the idea of "firing someone out" of a position.
prefix_root_suffix: fire = root (extended figurative use of the noun "fire") -- no clear separate prefix/suffix
word_family: fire (n., as in dismissal or flames), firing (n./adj.), fired (adj.)
mnemonic: FIRE rhymes with "HIRE" -- opposite actions: a company can HIRE you in, or FIRE you out.
memory_trick: FIRE someone: they are burnt out of the job.
visual_association: A cardboard box of belongings being carried out of an office.
emotion_feel: Negative, stressful, sometimes shame or anger
difference_explained: Fire = the employer ends your job. Resign = you choose to leave.
related_words: dismiss, sack, layoff, unemployment, job loss
mini_conversation:
A: I heard Sam got fired yesterday.
B: Really? I thought he was doing fine.

news_style_line: News-style: "The company fired its chief financial officer following the audit report."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Did you hear? He got fired from his job last week."

find_and_fix_to_correct: The company fire him last month. → The company fired him last month.

write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about why someone might be fired from a job.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to remove someone from their job'?
usage_tip: 'You're fired!' is informal. Formal: 'dismissed' or 'let go'.

simple_explanation: To teach someone a skill through practice. When you train someone, you teach and guide them through repeated practice until they can do a task or job well.
example_1: I train new staff every week.
example_2: She trains athletes for the national team.
example_3: New employees are trained for two weeks.
collocations: train staff, train hard, well trained, train for a marathon
related_phrasal_verbs: coach up, prepare for, work out
where_it_s_used: Workplace onboarding, sports, animal training, military
action_sequence: Before: new staff can't use the software → During: show and practise with them → After: they can do it alone
grammar_pattern: train + person + in/for + noun (train employees in safety procedures)
common_mistake: I am trained the new staff this week.
correct_version: I am training the new staff this week.
why_it_s_wrong: The present continuous needs -ing (training), not the past participle.
etymology: From Old French "trainer" (to drag, draw along), from Latin "trahere" (to pull) -- the sense "to instruct/prepare" developed from the idea of "drawing someone along" a course of learning.
prefix_root_suffix: train = root (Latin trahere, "to pull/draw along") -- no clear separate prefix/suffix
mnemonic: TRAIN sounds like the vehicle "train" -- think of TRAINing your brain like a TRAIN moving forward, step by step.
memory_trick: TRAIN a team like a TRAIN: one coach pulling many carriages.
visual_association: A coach demonstrating a move while a trainee repeats it step by step.
difference_explained: Teach = give knowledge (subjects). Train = build practical skills through practice.
mini_conversation:
A: How long does it take to train a new hire here?
B: Usually about two weeks of hands-on training.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A veteran soldier tells a recruit, "I trained for years before I was ready for this -- you will too."
news_style_line: News-style: "The company will train over two hundred new staff members before the store opens."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I'm training for a half-marathon next month."
mcq_options: A) To ignore a skill  B) To teach someone through practice  C) To fire an employee  D) To relax completely

find_and_fix_to_correct: She train new employees every month. → She trains new employees every month.

write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a skill someone trained you in.
