simple_explanation: To watch over and direct people's work. When you supervise, you oversee others as they work, making sure tasks are done correctly and helping when needed.
example_2: The manager supervises the entire warehouse team.
example_3: She supervised the students during the exam.
collocations: supervise closely, supervise staff, directly supervise, supervise a project
related_phrasal_verbs: oversee, keep an eye on, watch over
action_sequence: Before: staff start working → During: watch and guide them → After: the work is done correctly
grammar_pattern: supervise + noun (supervise the workers/the project)
common_mistake: She supervises about the interns this summer.
correct_version: She supervises the interns this summer.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Supervise' takes a direct object; don't add 'about'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the first syllable: SOO-per-vize.
spelling_tip: Ends in "-ise" or "-ize" (both accepted) -- remember the "super" (over) + "vise" (see) breakdown.
etymology: From Latin "super-" (over) + "videre" (to see) -- literally "to oversee, watch over."
prefix_root_suffix: super- = over + vis(e) = root (Latin videre, "to see") -- literally "to see over/watch over"
mnemonic: SUPERVISE contains "VISE" like "vision" -- you SUPERVISE by keeping your VISION on the team at all times.
memory_trick: SUPER-VISE: 'super' (above) + 'vise' (see): see from above.
visual_association: A supervisor with a clipboard, watching over a busy factory floor.
difference_explained: Supervise = watch over daily work. Manage = be responsible for people, plans and results.
mini_conversation:
A: Who supervises the new interns?
B: I do -- I check in with them twice a day.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A foreman walks the site and says, "I supervise every shift here -- nothing gets past me."
news_style_line: News-style: "The ministry appointed a new officer to supervise the region's schools."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Who's supervising the kids at the pool today?"
mcq_options: A) To ignore workers completely  B) To watch over and direct people's work  C) To fire an employee  D) To take a break from work
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: A senior nurse will ______ the new trainees during their first week. → supervise
find_and_fix_to_correct: He supervise the whole team by himself. → He supervises the whole team by himself.
translate: वह रात की शिफ्ट की निगरानी करता है। → He supervises the night shift.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about who supervises your work or studies.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to watch over and direct people's work'?
usage_tip: A 'supervisor' is a person who checks others' work.

simple_explanation: To give a task or responsibility to someone else. When you delegate, instead of doing everything yourself, you hand off part of the work to another person you trust.
example_1: I delegate tasks to my team.
example_2: A good manager knows how to delegate.
example_3: She delegated the report to her assistant.
collocations: delegate tasks, delegate authority, learn to delegate, delegate responsibility
related_phrasal_verbs: hand off, pass on, assign to
action_sequence: Before: have too many tasks → During: give one task to a colleague → After: focus on the important one
grammar_pattern: delegate + noun + to + person (delegate the task to Maria)
common_mistake: I delegate to him this task last week.
correct_version: I delegated this task to him last week.
why_it_s_wrong: The order is 'delegate + task + to + person'. 'Last week' also needs the past tense.
pronunciation_tip: The verb is stressed and pronounced DEL-uh-gate (with a long final vowel); the noun is DEL-uh-gut.
spelling_tip: Note the "-gate" ending in the verb form, and "-gate" pronounced differently in the noun.
etymology: From Latin "delegare" (de- "away" + legare "to send, appoint") -- literally "to send someone away with a task/authority."
prefix_root_suffix: de- = away + leg(ate) = root (Latin legare, "to send/appoint")
mnemonic: DELEGATE contains "GATE" -- you open the GATE and let someone else pass through with the task.
memory_trick: DELEGATE: give a LEG of the work to someone else.
visual_association: A manager handing a folder of tasks across the table to a teammate.
emotion_feel: Neutral, sometimes relief once responsibility is shared
difference_explained: Assign = give someone a task. Delegate = give away a task that was your own responsibility.
mini_conversation:
A: You look overwhelmed with all this work.
B: I know -- I really need to learn to delegate more.
everyday_scene: Everyday: An overworked manager sighs and admits, "I need to delegate more -- I can't keep doing everything myself."
news_style_line: News-style: "Experts say new leaders often struggle to delegate tasks effectively in their first year."
casual_conversation: Casual: "You should delegate some of that work -- you're doing too much."
mcq_options: A) To do all the work alone  B) To give a task to someone else  C) To refuse a task  D) To finish a project
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: A good leader knows how to ______ tasks to the right people. → delegate
find_and_fix_to_correct: She delegate the project to her team yesterday. → She delegated the project to her team yesterday.
translate: एक अच्छा प्रबंधक काम दूसरों को सौंपना जानता है। → A good manager knows how to delegate work.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a task you would delegate to a teammate.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to give a task or responsibility to someone else'?
usage_tip: A 'delegate' (noun) is a person sent to represent a group at a meeting.

simple_explanation: To discuss something to reach an agreement. When you negotiate, you talk with someone to reach a deal that both sides can accept, often about price, terms, or conditions.
example_1: I need to negotiate my salary.
example_2: They negotiated a better price for the car.
example_3: The two companies negotiated a new contract.
collocations: negotiate a deal, negotiate with, negotiate terms, successfully negotiate
related_phrasal_verbs: haggle over, work out, hammer out
action_sequence: Before: the price is high → During: offer and counter-offer → After: agree on a price
grammar_pattern: negotiate + noun (negotiate a contract) or negotiate with + person (negotiate with the seller)
common_mistake: I negotiated about a lower price with the seller.
correct_version: I negotiated a lower price with the seller.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Negotiate' takes the deal as its direct object; don't add 'about'.
pronunciation_tip: Five syllables: ni-GOH-shee-ate, with stress on the second syllable.
etymology: From Latin "negotiari" (neg- "not" + otium "leisure") -- literally "to be busy, not at leisure," originally meaning "to conduct business."
prefix_root_suffix: neg- = not + oti(um) = root (Latin, "leisure") + -ate = verb suffix -- literally "to be busy/not idle"
mnemonic: NEGOTIATE contains "GO" -- both sides GO back and forth until they NEGOTIATE a deal.
memory_trick: NEGOTIATE: 'NEGO' sounds like 'go' back and forth until you agree.
visual_association: Two people shaking hands across a table after a long discussion.
difference_explained: Bargain = argue about price, usually in a market. Negotiate = discuss formally to reach any agreement.
mini_conversation:
A: Did you get a discount on the apartment?
B: Yes, I negotiated the rent down a bit.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A businesswoman leans forward and says, "Let's negotiate -- I think we can both walk away happy."
news_style_line: News-style: "The two nations began negotiating a new trade agreement this week."
casual_conversation: Casual: "You should try to negotiate your salary before accepting the offer."
mcq_options: A) To refuse an offer completely  B) To discuss something to reach an agreement  C) To ignore a problem  D) To pay full price without question
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: You should always try to ______ the price before buying a used car. → negotiate
find_and_fix_to_correct: He negotiate a better deal last week. → He negotiated a better deal last week.
translate: मुझे अपनी तनख्वाह के बारे में बातचीत करनी है। → I need to negotiate my salary.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something you negotiated a price for.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to discuss something to reach an agreement'?
usage_tip: In markets: 'Can we negotiate the price?' is a polite way to bargain.

simple_explanation: To show or explain something formally to a group of people. When you present something, you formally show or explain it to an audience, like giving a talk or showing a report.
example_1: I will present my project tomorrow.
example_2: She presented her research at the conference.
example_3: He presents the weekly sales report to the team.
collocations: present a report, present findings, formally present, present to the board
related_phrasal_verbs: lay out, put forward, show off
where_it_s_used: Business meetings, school projects, conferences, media
action_sequence: Before: prepare slides → During: stand and explain to the group → After: answer questions
grammar_pattern: present + noun + to + audience (present the plan to the board)
common_mistake: I will presented my project next week.
correct_version: I will present my project next week.
why_it_s_wrong: After 'will', use the base verb.
pronunciation_tip: Verb: pri-ZENT (stress on second syllable). Noun/adjective: PREZ-uhnt (stress on first).
spelling_tip: Same spelling for verb, noun, and adjective -- only pronunciation and stress change.
etymology: From Old French "presenter," from Latin "praesentare" (prae- "before" + sentare "to place") -- literally "to place before someone."
prefix_root_suffix: prae- = before + sent = root (Latin sentare, "to place") -- literally "to place before"
mnemonic: PRESENT (verb) rhymes with "event" -- you PRESENT your ideas at an EVENT.
memory_trick: The verb is pre-SENT (stress on the 2nd syllable); the noun is PRE-sent.
visual_association: A person standing beside a slideshow, pointing at a chart.
difference_explained: Present is the verb (I present). Presentation is the noun (my presentation).
mini_conversation:
A: Are you nervous about presenting tomorrow?
B: A little, but I've practiced my slides a lot.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A nervous employee takes a deep breath and says, "Alright, let's present this idea to the board."
news_style_line: News-style: "The scientist will present her findings at an international conference next week."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Can you present the results at tomorrow's meeting?"
mcq_options: A) To hide information  B) To formally show or explain something  C) To ignore an audience  D) To cancel a meeting
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: She will ______ her findings at the conference next month. → present
find_and_fix_to_correct: He present his ideas at the meeting yesterday. → He presented his ideas at the meeting yesterday.
translate: वह अगले हफ्ते अपना प्रोजेक्ट प्रस्तुत करेगी। → She will present her project next week.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a topic you would like to present.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to show or explain something formally to a group of people'?
usage_tip: 'Present' also means give formally: 'present an award'.

simple_explanation: To think of many ideas quickly, often with a group. When you brainstorm, you and often others share as many ideas as possible about a topic, without judging them right away, to find good solutions.
example_1: Let's brainstorm ideas for the party.
example_2: The team brainstormed names for the new product.
example_3: We brainstormed solutions to the problem for an hour.
collocations: brainstorm ideas, brainstorm session, quickly brainstorm, brainstorm solutions
related_phrasal_verbs: bounce ideas around, think out loud, throw ideas out
action_sequence: Before: have a problem → During: share many ideas quickly → After: choose the best one
grammar_pattern: brainstorm + noun (brainstorm ideas/solutions) -- often used with "about" or no object at all
common_mistake: We brainstormed about for new ideas yesterday.
correct_version: We brainstormed new ideas yesterday.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Brainstorm' can take ideas as a direct object; 'about for' is not needed.
pronunciation_tip: Two clear syllables, both stressed evenly: BRAIN-storm.
etymology: A compound of "brain" + "storm," coined in the mid-20th century to describe a sudden burst of creative ideas, like a storm in the mind.
prefix_root_suffix: brain = root (organ of thought) + storm = root (sudden burst) -- a compound word, not a prefix/suffix structure
mnemonic: BRAINSTORM = BRAIN + STORM -- picture a STORM of ideas swirling around inside your BRAIN.
memory_trick: BRAIN + STORM: a storm of ideas in the brain.
visual_association: A whiteboard covered in colorful sticky notes and scribbled ideas.
difference_explained: Discuss = talk about a topic. Brainstorm = produce many ideas fast, without judging them.
mini_conversation:
A: We need fresh ideas for the campaign.
B: Let's brainstorm this afternoon before the deadline.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A creative director claps her hands and says, "Alright team, let's brainstorm -- no bad ideas today."
news_style_line: News-style: "The city invited residents to brainstorm ideas for the new community park."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Can we brainstorm a few options before deciding?"
mcq_options: A) To reject all ideas  B) To quickly generate many ideas  C) To finalize a single decision  D) To criticize a plan
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The team decided to ______ new ideas before starting the project. → brainstorm
find_and_fix_to_correct: They brainstorm new slogans last Friday. → They brainstormed new slogans last Friday.
translate: चलो नए प्रोजेक्ट के लिए विचार-मंथन करते हैं। → Let's brainstorm ideas for the new project.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a problem your team could brainstorm.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to think of many ideas quickly, often with a group'?
usage_tip: 'Let's brainstorm' is common in offices and classrooms.

simple_explanation: To plan a time for something to happen. When you schedule something, you fix a specific time or date for it to happen, so it's organized in advance.
example_1: I need to schedule a doctor's appointment.
example_2: She scheduled a meeting for Monday morning.
example_3: The flight is scheduled to depart at noon.
collocations: schedule a meeting, tightly scheduled, reschedule, ahead of schedule
related_phrasal_verbs: pencil in, set up, block off
action_sequence: Before: check everyone's time → During: pick a day and time → After: put it in the calendar
grammar_pattern: schedule + noun + for + time (schedule the call for 3 PM)
common_mistake: I scheduled the meeting in Monday.
correct_version: I scheduled the meeting for Monday.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'schedule something for' a day or time, not 'in'.
pronunciation_tip: American: SKEJ-ool. British: SHED-yool. Both are correct depending on the accent.
spelling_tip: Watch the silent "c" -- sch-EDULE, easy to misspell as "schedual."
etymology: From Old French "cedule" (a slip of paper, note), from Latin "schedula" -- originally a small written document, later meaning a timetable.
prefix_root_suffix: schedul(e) = root (Latin schedula, "small written note") -- no clear separate prefix/suffix
mnemonic: SCHEDULE contains "DUE" -- everything on your SCHEDULE has a time it's DUE.
memory_trick: SCHEDULE: UK says 'SHED-yool', US says 'SKED-jool'. Both are correct.
visual_association: A calendar app filling up with colored blocks of appointments.
difference_explained: Plan = decide what to do. Schedule = fix exactly when it happens.
mini_conversation:
A: When can we schedule the call?
B: How about Thursday afternoon?
everyday_scene: Everyday: An assistant checks her tablet and says, "You're scheduled for back-to-back meetings all afternoon."
news_style_line: News-style: "The airline announced its flights are now scheduled to resume next Monday."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Can we schedule a call for sometime this week?"
mcq_options: A) To cancel an event  B) To fix a time for something to happen  C) To forget an appointment  D) To delay indefinitely
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Let's ______ the meeting for next Tuesday morning. → schedule
find_and_fix_to_correct: We schedule the appointment on next Friday. → We scheduled the appointment for next Friday.
translate: मुझे डॉक्टर से मिलने का समय तय करना है। → I need to schedule a doctor's appointment.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a meeting or class you have scheduled.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to plan a time for something to happen'?
usage_tip: 'Ahead of schedule' = early. 'Behind schedule' = late.

simple_explanation: To come together with someone in the same place. When you meet someone, you and that person are in the same place at the same time, often for the first time or by plan.
example_1: I meet my friends every Friday.
example_2: Nice to meet you!
example_3: We met at a coffee shop downtown.
collocations: meet someone, meet up, pleased to meet you, meet a deadline
related_phrasal_verbs: meet up, meet with, run into
action_sequence: Before: plan a time and place → During: arrive and see each other → After: talk together
grammar_pattern: meet + person (meet a friend) or meet with + person (meet with a client)
common_mistake: I meeted her at the party last night.
correct_version: I met her at the party last night.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Meet' is irregular: the past is 'met', not 'meeted'.
spelling_tip: Double "e" -- "meet," not "meat" (that's food!) or "mete" (an old word for measure).
etymology: Old English "metan" (to meet, encounter, find) -- one of the oldest verbs for coming together with someone.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- a simple base word
mnemonic: MEET rhymes with "GREET" -- when you MEET someone, you often GREET them too.
memory_trick: MEET → MET: drop one E.
visual_association: Two people shaking hands for the first time, smiling.
difference_explained: Meet = come together, often by plan or for the first time. See = notice with your eyes, or visit someone you know.
mini_conversation:
A: Have you two met before?
B: No, nice to meet you!
everyday_scene: Everyday: Two strangers lock eyes across a crowded room, and one says, "I feel like we've met before."
news_style_line: News-style: "World leaders are set to meet next week to discuss the new trade agreement."
casual_conversation: Casual: "It's so nice to finally meet you in person!"
mcq_options: A) To avoid someone  B) To come together with someone  C) To forget someone  D) To argue with someone
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: I'd love to ______ you for coffee sometime this week. → meet
find_and_fix_to_correct: We meeted at the conference last year. → We met at the conference last year.
translate: मुझे आपसे मिलकर खुशी हुई। → I'm happy to meet you.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about where you met your best friend.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to come together with someone in the same place'?
usage_tip: 'Nice to meet you' for the first time; 'Nice to see you' after that.

simple_explanation: To welcome someone politely, often with words or a gesture. When you greet someone, you say hello or show a friendly welcome, usually the moment you see them.
example_1: I greet my neighbors every morning.
example_2: She greeted us with a warm smile.
example_3: He greets every customer at the door.
collocations: greet warmly, greet someone at the door, greet with a smile, formally greet
related_phrasal_verbs: welcome in, say hello, wave to
where_it_s_used: Meetings, hospitality, customer service, daily manners
action_sequence: Before: a guest arrives → During: say hello and smile → After: welcome them inside
grammar_pattern: greet + person (greet the guests) or greet + person + with + noun (greet her with a hug)
common_mistake: He greeted to me at the entrance.
correct_version: He greeted me at the entrance.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Greet' takes the person directly, with no 'to'.
spelling_tip: Double "e" -- "greet," easy to confuse with "great" (excellent), which sounds different.
etymology: Old English "gretan" (to approach, address, salute) -- one of the oldest words for a friendly welcome.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- a simple base word
mnemonic: GREET rhymes with "MEET" -- you GREET someone the moment you MEET them.
memory_trick: GREET with a GREAT smile.
visual_association: A host at a doorway extending a hand and smiling widely.
difference_explained: Greet = say hello. Welcome = greet warmly and make someone feel at home.
mini_conversation:
A: How does the hotel staff treat guests?
B: They greet everyone warmly at the door.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A butler opens the grand door and says, "Welcome -- allow me to greet you properly."
news_style_line: News-style: "Crowds gathered at the airport to greet the returning athletes."
casual_conversation: Casual: "She always greets me with such a big smile."
mcq_options: A) To ignore someone  B) To welcome someone politely  C) To argue with someone  D) To leave without saying goodbye
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The receptionist will ______ you when you arrive at the office. → greet
find_and_fix_to_correct: She greeted to her guests warmly. → She greeted her guests warmly.
translate: वह हर सुबह अपने पड़ोसियों का अभिवादन करता है। → He greets his neighbors every morning.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about how people greet each other in your family.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to welcome someone politely, often with words or a gesture'?
usage_tip: 'Season's greetings' is used on festival cards.

simple_explanation: To ask someone to come to an event or place. When you invite someone, you politely ask them to join you at an event, like a party, dinner, or meeting.
example_1: I will invite my friends over.
example_2: She invited us to her wedding.
example_3: We invited the whole team to the celebration.
collocations: invite someone over, invite to a party, kindly invite, formally invited
related_phrasal_verbs: ask over, have someone round, ask along
where_it_s_used: Parties, weddings, business events, social gatherings
action_sequence: Before: plan a party → During: send messages to friends → After: they come to the party
grammar_pattern: invite + person + to + noun/event (invite her to the party)
common_mistake: I invited to him for dinner.
correct_version: I invited him for dinner.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Invite' takes the person directly, with no 'to' before them. Use 'invite someone to/for' an event.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: in-VYTE.
spelling_tip: Note the silent "e" at the end -- "invite," not "invit."
etymology: From Latin "invitare" (to invite, treat kindly) -- related to the idea of welcoming someone into your company.
prefix_root_suffix: in- = intensifier (from Latin) + vit(e) = root (Latin invitare, related to "welcome")
mnemonic: INVITE contains "VITE" like "invite" someone to visit -- you INVITE guests to VISIT you.
memory_trick: INVITE: you send an INVITation.
visual_association: A colorful envelope with "You're Invited!" printed on the front.
difference_explained: Invite = ask someone to come to an event. Call = phone someone, or shout to get attention.
mini_conversation:
A: Are you inviting Sam to the party?
B: Of course, I already invited him yesterday.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A host raises a glass and says, "I'm so glad I invited all of you tonight."
news_style_line: News-style: "The mayor invited local business owners to a meeting about the new development plan."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Do you want to invite a few friends over this weekend?"
mcq_options: A) To exclude someone  B) To ask someone to an event  C) To reject an offer  D) To ignore a guest
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: We would like to ______ you to our housewarming party. → invite
find_and_fix_to_correct: She invited to her friends to the concert. → She invited her friends to the concert.
translate: मैं अपने दोस्तों को घर बुलाऊंगा। → I will invite my friends over.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about who you would invite to your birthday.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to ask someone to come to an event or place'?
usage_tip: 'Invite' as a noun ('Thanks for the invite') is informal; 'invitation' is standard.

simple_explanation: To make one person known to another for the first time. When you introduce people, you tell them each other's names so they can get to know one another.
example_2: He introduced himself to the new colleagues.
example_3: She introduced her boyfriend to her parents.
collocations: introduce yourself, formally introduce, introduce a topic, briefly introduce
related_phrasal_verbs: bring in, present to, break the ice
where_it_s_used: Social gatherings, business meetings, classrooms, presentations
action_sequence: Before: two people don't know each other → During: say each person's name to the other → After: they shake hands
grammar_pattern: introduce + person + to + person (introduce him to my mother)
common_mistake: Let me introduce you my friend.
correct_version: Let me introduce you to my friend.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Introduce' needs 'to' before the second person: introduce A to B.
pronunciation_tip: Four syllables, stress on the third: in-truh-DOOS.
etymology: From Latin "introducere" (intro- "inward" + ducere "to lead") -- literally "to lead inward/bring in."
prefix_root_suffix: intro- = inward + duc(e) = root (Latin ducere, "to lead") -- literally "to lead in"
mnemonic: INTRODUCE contains "INTRO" -- you give an INTRO when you INTRODUCE two people.
memory_trick: INTRO-DUCE: an INTRO leads people into knowing each other.
visual_association: Two people shaking hands as a third gestures between them.
difference_explained: Introduce = make people known to each other. Present = show something formally to a group.
mini_conversation:
A: Have you two met?
B: No, could you introduce us?
everyday_scene: Everyday: A host gestures toward the stage and says, "Please allow me to introduce our next speaker."
news_style_line: News-style: "The company introduced its new product line at yesterday's press event."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Let me introduce you to my roommate -- you two will get along."

simple_explanation: To greet someone warmly when they arrive. When you welcome someone, you make them feel comfortable and happy to be there, often with kind words or a friendly gesture.
example_2: They welcomed us with open arms.
example_3: The hotel staff welcomed every guest by name.
collocations: welcome warmly, feel welcome, welcome aboard, warm welcome
related_phrasal_verbs: greet warmly, take in, roll out the red carpet
where_it_s_used: Hospitality, new jobs, guests, first days, customer service
action_sequence: Before: a guest arrives at the door → During: smile and say 'Welcome!' → After: invite them in
grammar_pattern: welcome + person (welcome the guests) or welcome + person + to + place (welcome them to the team)
common_mistake: They welcomed to us at the airport.
correct_version: They welcomed us at the airport.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Welcome' takes the person directly, with no 'to' before them.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the first syllable: WEL-kuhm.
spelling_tip: Note the "-come" ending pronounced "kuhm," not like the word "come" alone.
etymology: Old English "wilcuma" (wil- "desire, pleasure" + cuma "guest/comer") -- literally "a guest whose coming pleases you."
prefix_root_suffix: wil- = pleasure/desire + come = root (a person who comes) -- literally "a pleasing guest"
mnemonic: WELCOME contains "COME" -- you WELCOME someone by inviting them to COME in.
memory_trick: WEL-COME: it's WELL that you COME.
visual_association: An open front door with a glowing "Welcome" mat outside.
difference_explained: Greet = say hello. Welcome = greet warmly and make someone feel wanted.
mini_conversation:
A: Thanks so much for having us.
B: You're very welcome -- come in!
everyday_scene: Everyday: A team leader claps a newcomer on the back and says, "Welcome aboard -- we're glad to have you."
news_style_line: News-style: "The town welcomed hundreds of visitors for the annual summer festival."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Welcome to the team -- let me show you around."
mcq_options: A) To reject someone  B) To greet someone warmly  C) To ignore a guest  D) To argue with a visitor
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The staff always ______ new customers with a friendly smile. → welcome
find_and_fix_to_correct: The hotel welcomed to us very kindly. → The hotel welcomed us very kindly.
translate: हम सभी नए छात्रों का स्वागत करते हैं। → We welcome all new students.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence welcoming a guest to your home.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to greet someone warmly when they arrive'?
usage_tip: 'You're welcome' is the polite reply to 'thank you'.

simple_explanation: To tell someone you're grateful for something they did. When you thank someone, you express gratitude, usually by saying "thank you" or explaining why you appreciate what they did.
example_1: I thank you for your help.
example_2: She thanked her teacher for the extra help.
example_3: He thanked everyone at the end of his speech.
collocations: thank someone for, sincerely thank, thank you very much, thank in advance
related_phrasal_verbs: give thanks, show gratitude, express appreciation
where_it_s_used: Gratitude, politeness, speeches, gifts, everyday manners
action_sequence: Before: someone helps you → During: feel grateful → After: say 'Thank you for your help.'
grammar_pattern: thank + person + for + noun/gerund (thank her for helping)
common_mistake: I thank to you for the gift.
correct_version: I thank you for the gift.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Thank' takes the person directly, with no 'to'.
spelling_tip: Note the "th" sound at the start -- say it softly, tongue between teeth.
etymology: Old English "thancian" (to give thanks, express gratitude), related to "think" -- originally the idea of holding someone kindly in your thoughts.
prefix_root_suffix: thank = root (Old English thancian, related to "think") -- no clear separate prefix/suffix
mnemonic: THANK sounds like "THINK" -- when you THANK someone, you're letting them know you THINK kindly of what they did.
memory_trick: THANK and THINK: when you think of someone's help, you thank them.
visual_association: A handwritten "Thank You" card being handed over with a smile.
difference_explained: Thank is the verb (I thank you). Thanks is the noun or casual form (Thanks! / Many thanks).
mini_conversation:
A: I brought you some soup since you're sick.
B: Thank you so much, that's really kind.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A tearful winner grips the trophy and says, "I just want to thank everyone who believed in me."
news_style_line: News-style: "The mayor thanked emergency workers for their quick response during the storm."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Thank you so much for picking me up today."
mcq_options: A) To blame someone  B) To express gratitude to someone  C) To ignore someone's help  D) To criticize someone
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: I want to ______ you for all your help this week. → thank
find_and_fix_to_correct: She thanked to her friends for the surprise party. → She thanked her friends for the surprise party.
translate: आपकी मदद के लिए धन्यवाद। → Thank you for your help.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence thanking a teacher for something specific.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to tell someone you're grateful for something they did'?
usage_tip: 'Thank you so much' / 'Thanks a lot' — 'Thanks' is the casual form.

simple_explanation: To tell someone you're happy about their success. When you congratulate someone, you praise them and share their happiness after something good happens to them, like passing an exam or getting married.
example_1: I congratulate you on your success.
example_2: We congratulated her on winning the award.
example_3: He congratulated the team after their victory.
collocations: congratulate someone on, warmly congratulate, congratulate the winner, sincerely congratulate
related_phrasal_verbs: give kudos, cheer on, applaud for
action_sequence: Before: hear good news → During: go to the person → After: say 'Congratulations on your success!'
grammar_pattern: congratulate + person + on + noun/gerund (congratulate him on passing the exam)
common_mistake: I congratulated to her for the wedding.
correct_version: I congratulated her on the wedding.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'congratulate someone ON something', not 'to' or 'for'.
pronunciation_tip: Five syllables, stress on the third: kuhn-GRACH-oo-late.
spelling_tip: Watch the double consonant pattern and "-ulate" ending -- congrat-ULATE.
etymology: From Latin "congratulari" (con- "together" + gratulari "to show joy") -- literally "to share joy together."
prefix_root_suffix: con- = together + gratul(ate) = root (Latin gratulari, "to show joy")
mnemonic: CONGRATULATE contains "GRAT" like "grateful/great" -- you CONGRATULATE someone for doing something GREAT.
memory_trick: CONGRATULATE has a T in the middle, not a D: congraTulate.
visual_association: Confetti falling as friends clap for someone holding a diploma.
difference_explained: Congratulate = say you're happy about someone's success or event. Praise = say someone did something well.
mini_conversation:
A: I got the job!
B: Congratulations! I'm so happy for you.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A proud father hugs his son and says, "Congratulations -- you've earned every bit of this."
news_style_line: News-style: "The president congratulated the national team on their historic victory."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Congratulations on the new job -- you deserve it!"
mcq_options: A) To criticize someone's failure  B) To praise someone for their success  C) To ignore an achievement  D) To feel jealous of someone
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: We would like to ______ you on your recent promotion. → congratulate
find_and_fix_to_correct: They congratulated to him for graduating. → They congratulated him on graduating.
translate: हम आपको आपकी सफलता पर बधाई देते हैं। → We congratulate you on your success.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence congratulating a friend on their new job.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to tell someone you're happy about their success'?
usage_tip: 'Congratulations!' (with -s) is what you say directly.

simple_explanation: To stop being angry with someone for something they did wrong. When you forgive someone, you decide to let go of your anger or hurt feelings about a mistake they made, and move past it.
example_1: I forgive you for being late.
example_2: She forgave her friend after the argument.
example_3: He found it hard to forgive himself for the mistake.
collocations: forgive and forget, forgive someone for, hard to forgive, quick to forgive
related_phrasal_verbs: let go, move on, make peace
where_it_s_used: Relationships, arguments, mistakes, religion, personal growth
action_sequence: Before: someone hurts you → During: they apologise → After: let go of the anger
grammar_pattern: forgive + person + for + noun/gerund (forgive him for lying)
common_mistake: I forgive to her for the mistake.
correct_version: I forgive her for the mistake.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Forgive' takes the person directly, with no 'to'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: fer-GIV, rhyming with "live."
etymology: Old English "forgiefan" (for- "completely" + giefan "to give") -- literally "to give completely/give up a grudge."
prefix_root_suffix: for- = completely (intensifying prefix) + give = root -- literally "to give up completely"
mnemonic: FORGIVE contains "GIVE" -- when you FORGIVE, you GIVE up your anger completely.
memory_trick: FOR-GIVE: give up your anger FOR someone.
visual_association: Two people hugging after a long, tearful apology.
difference_explained: Forgive = stop being angry. Forget = stop remembering. You can forgive without forgetting.
related_words: pardon, apologize, sorry, reconcile, let go
mini_conversation:
A: I'm really sorry for what I said.
B: It's okay, I forgive you.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character wipes away a tear and says, "I forgive you -- holding onto this anger was hurting me more."
news_style_line: News-style: "The community leader urged residents to forgive and rebuild after the conflict."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I hope you can forgive me for forgetting your birthday."
mcq_options: A) To stay angry forever  B) To stop being angry about a mistake  C) To punish someone  D) To forget someone completely
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: She decided to ______ her brother for the argument. → forgive
find_and_fix_to_correct: He forgive her for the mistake last year. → He forgave her for the mistake last year.
translate: कृपया मुझे देर होने के लिए माफ कर दो। → Please forgive me for being late.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about someone you forgave.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to stop being angry with someone for something they did wrong'?
usage_tip: 'Forgive me' is a strong apology; 'Excuse me' is for small things.

simple_explanation: To believe that someone is honest and reliable. When you trust someone, you believe they will act honestly and won't let you down, so you feel safe relying on them.
example_1: I trust my best friend completely.
example_2: She trusts her doctor's advice.
example_3: He never trusted strangers easily.
collocations: trust completely, build trust, hard to trust, trust someone's judgment
related_phrasal_verbs: rely on, believe in, count on
action_sequence: Before: get to know someone → During: see them keep promises → After: feel you can rely on them
grammar_pattern: trust + person/noun (trust her decision) or trust + person + to-infinitive (trust him to do it right)
common_mistake: I trust in my friend to keep secrets.
correct_version: I trust my friend to keep secrets.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Trust' usually takes a person directly. 'Trust in' is for big ideas like God or fate.
pronunciation_tip: One syllable, rhymes with "must" and "just" -- TRUST.
spelling_tip: Note the "-ust" ending -- tr-UST, not "trussed" (a different word entirely).
etymology: From Old Norse "traust" (confidence, firmness) -- related to the idea of something solid and dependable.
prefix_root_suffix: trust = root (Old Norse traust, "confidence") -- no clear separate prefix/suffix
mnemonic: TRUST rhymes with "MUST" -- when you TRUST someone, you feel you MUST rely on them.
memory_trick: TRUST: you can Rely Upon Someone Totally.
visual_association: Two hands clasped firmly together, steady and unshaking.
difference_explained: Believe = think something is true. Trust = be sure someone is honest and reliable over time.
mini_conversation:
A: Can I tell you something private?
B: Of course, you can trust me.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A partner squeezes another's hand and says, "I trust you with my life -- you know that."
news_style_line: News-style: "Surveys show public trust in the new policy has grown since it was introduced."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I really trust your opinion on this -- what do you think?"
mcq_options: A) To doubt someone completely  B) To believe someone is honest and reliable  C) To ignore someone's advice  D) To argue with someone
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: I really ______ you to make the right decision. → trust
find_and_fix_to_correct: She trust her sister with everything. → She trusts her sister with everything.
translate: मुझे अपने सबसे अच्छे दोस्त पर पूरा भरोसा है। → I trust my best friend completely.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a person you trust completely.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to believe that someone is honest and reliable'?
usage_tip: 'Trust me' is a common promise. A 'trust' is also a charity organisation.

simple_explanation: To have strong, warm feelings of affection for someone or something. When you love someone or something, you feel deep care, warmth, or strong liking toward them.
example_1: I love spending time with my family.
example_2: She loves her children more than anything.
example_3: He loves playing the guitar in his free time.
collocations: fall in love, love unconditionally, love dearly, love at first sight
related_phrasal_verbs: care for, be fond of, be crazy about
action_sequence: Before: meet someone → During: spend time together → After: feel strong affection
grammar_pattern: love + noun/gerund (love music / love reading)
common_mistake: I am loving you very much.
correct_version: I love you very much.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Love' is a state verb, so it's normally used in the simple form. 'I'm loving it' is informal advertising style.
pronunciation_tip: Rhymes with "dove" and "glove" -- LOVE (short "u" sound, not long).
spelling_tip: Silent "e" at the end -- "love," not "luv" (informal texting spelling only).
etymology: Old English "lufu" (love, affection), a very ancient Germanic root shared across many European languages.
prefix_root_suffix: love = root (Old English lufu) -- no clear separate prefix/suffix
mnemonic: LOVE rhymes with "DOVE," a bird often used as a symbol of LOVE and peace.
memory_trick: LOVE: the heart shape ♥ looks like a V inside the word.
visual_association: Two hands forming a heart shape against a sunset.
difference_explained: Like = find pleasant. Love = feel strong affection. 'I like tea; I love my family.'
mini_conversation:
A: Do you really love this city?
B: I do -- I could never imagine living anywhere else.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character looks into another's eyes and whispers, "I think I've loved you since the day we met."
news_style_line: News-style: "Volunteers say they simply love giving back to their community every weekend."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I love this song -- can you turn it up?"
mcq_options: A) To dislike something  B) To feel deep affection for someone or something  C) To ignore someone  D) To fear something
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: I ______ spending weekends with my grandparents. → love
find_and_fix_to_correct: She is loving her new job so much. → She loves her new job so much.
translate: मुझे अपने परिवार के साथ समय बिताना बहुत पसंद है। → I love spending time with my family.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a hobby you love.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to have strong, warm feelings of affection for someone or something'?
usage_tip: 'I'd love to' is a warm way to accept an invitation.

simple_explanation: To find someone or something pleasant or enjoyable. When you like something, you feel a positive, friendly interest in it -- less intense than love, but still a genuine preference.
example_2: She likes reading mystery novels.
example_3: He doesn't like waking up early.
collocations: really like, like a lot, would like, like the idea
related_phrasal_verbs: be fond of, take to, go for
where_it_s_used: Preferences, hobbies, food, social media, casual conversation
action_sequence: Before: try something → During: enjoy it → After: want it again
grammar_pattern: like + noun/gerund (like music / like swimming)
common_mistake: I am liking this movie so far.
correct_version: I like this movie so far.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Like' is a state verb, so it normally doesn't take -ing.
pronunciation_tip: Rhymes with "bike" and "hike" -- LIKE, with a long "i" sound.
spelling_tip: Silent "e" at the end -- "like," and remember it changes to "liking" (drop the e) with "-ing."
etymology: Old English "lician" (to please, be pleasing) -- originally the subject was the thing that pleased, not the person (a structure still visible in "methinks").
prefix_root_suffix: like = root (Old English lician, "to please") -- no clear separate prefix/suffix
mnemonic: LIKE rhymes with "hike" -- if you LIKE something, you'd happily HIKE a long way to get it.
memory_trick: LIKE on social media: one small tap = you find it pleasant.
visual_association: A thumbs-up icon glowing beside a smiling face.
difference_explained: Do you like tea? = in general. Would you like tea? = right now, an offer.
mini_conversation:
A: Do you like spicy food?
B: Yes, actually, I like it quite a lot.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character shrugs casually and says, "Honestly? I like this plan -- let's go with it."
news_style_line: News-style: "A new survey shows most people like shorter work weeks when given the choice."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I really like your new haircut!"
mcq_options: A) To strongly dislike something  B) To find something pleasant or enjoyable  C) To ignore something  D) To fear something
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: I really ______ the new restaurant that opened downtown. → like
find_and_fix_to_correct: She is liking her new job a lot. → She likes her new job a lot.
translate: मुझे चॉकलेट आइसक्रीम पसंद है। → I like chocolate ice cream.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a food you like and one you don't.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to find someone or something pleasant or enjoyable'?
usage_tip: 'Would you like…?' is a polite offer. 'Do you like…?' asks about taste.

simple_explanation: To have a very strong dislike for someone or something. When you hate something, you feel a strong, negative emotion toward it -- much stronger than simply not liking it.
example_1: I hate waiting in long lines.
example_2: She hates being late for meetings.
example_3: He hates cold weather.
collocations: absolutely hate, hate the idea of, hate to admit, can't stand/hate
related_phrasal_verbs: can't stand, be sick of, be fed up with
where_it_s_used: Strong dislikes, frustration, pet peeves, opinions
action_sequence: Before: meet something unpleasant → During: feel strong dislike → After: want to avoid it
grammar_pattern: hate + noun/gerund (hate spiders / hate waiting)
common_mistake: I am hating this traffic today.
correct_version: I hate this traffic today.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Hate' is a state verb, so it normally doesn't take -ing.
pronunciation_tip: Rhymes with "gate" and "late" -- HATE, long "a" sound.
spelling_tip: Silent "e" at the end -- "hate," and it changes to "hating" (drop the e) with "-ing."
etymology: Old English "hete" / "hatian" (strong dislike, hostility) -- an old Germanic root for intense negative feeling.
prefix_root_suffix: hate = root (Old English hatian) -- no clear separate prefix/suffix
mnemonic: HATE rhymes with "GATE" -- when you HATE something, you want to shut the GATE on it forever.
memory_trick: HATE is LOVE's opposite; both have 4 letters.
visual_association: A red "X" stamped firmly over an unwanted object.
emotion_feel: Strong negative emotion, frustration or aversion
difference_explained: Dislike = not like (mild). Hate = dislike very strongly.
mini_conversation:
A: How do you feel about Mondays?
B: Honestly, I hate them.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character slams the door and mutters, "I hate when people are late -- every single time."
news_style_line: News-style: "The survey found most commuters hate the daily traffic on that particular highway."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I hate getting up early on weekends."
mcq_options: A) To feel mild interest  B) To feel a very strong dislike  C) To love deeply  D) To feel neutral about something
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: I absolutely ______ waiting in long airport lines. → hate
find_and_fix_to_correct: She is hating her new schedule this month. → She hates her new schedule this month.
translate: मुझे लंबी लाइनों में इंतज़ार करना बिल्कुल पसंद नहीं है। → I hate waiting in long lines.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a chore you hate.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to have a very strong dislike for someone or something'?
usage_tip: 'I hate to say this, but…' softens bad news.

simple_explanation: To admire someone because of their good qualities or achievements. When you respect someone, you value their opinions, achievements, or character, and treat them politely because of that.
example_2: She respects her elders deeply.
example_3: He earned the respect of his colleagues.
collocations: earn respect, mutual respect, respect someone's decision, treat with respect
related_phrasal_verbs: look up to, hold in high regard, honor
action_sequence: Before: see someone's good actions → During: admire their qualities → After: treat them with care
grammar_pattern: respect + person/noun (respect the rules / respect her decision)
common_mistake: I respect to my parents a lot.
correct_version: I respect my parents a lot.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Respect' takes a direct object, with no 'to'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: ri-SPEKT.
spelling_tip: Watch the "sp" in the middle -- re-SPECT, not "respekt."
etymology: From Latin "respectus" (re- "back" + specere "to look") -- literally "to look back at/consider," implying regard for someone.
prefix_root_suffix: re- = back + spect = root (Latin specere, "to look") -- literally "to look back at/consider"
mnemonic: RESPECT contains "SPECT" like "inspect" -- you RESPECT someone by really looking closely (inSPECTing) at their worth.
memory_trick: RE-SPECT: 're' = back, 'spect' = look: look up to someone.
visual_association: A person bowing slightly toward an elder as a sign of regard.
difference_explained: Respect = admire and value. Obey = follow orders. You can respect someone without obeying them.
mini_conversation:
A: Why do people admire your grandfather so much?
B: Everyone respects him for his honesty and kindness.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A wise elder tells a young apprentice, "Respect is earned, not given -- remember that."
news_style_line: News-style: "The community leader was widely respected for decades of quiet service."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I really respect how hard you've worked for this."
mcq_options: A) To ignore someone's opinion  B) To admire someone for their good qualities  C) To argue with someone  D) To fear someone
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: We should always ______ other people's opinions, even if we disagree. → respect
find_and_fix_to_correct: She respect her teachers a lot. → She respects her teachers a lot.
translate: मैं अपने बड़ों का बहुत सम्मान करता हूँ। → I respect my elders a lot.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a person you respect and why.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to admire someone because of their good qualities or achievements'?
usage_tip: 'With respect, …' is a polite way to disagree.

simple_explanation: To help or encourage someone, especially during a hard time. When you support someone, you help them, encourage them, or stand by them, whether emotionally, financially, or practically.
example_2: Her family supported her through college.
example_3: He always supports his friends' dreams.
collocations: fully support, financial support, support each other, support a cause
related_phrasal_verbs: back up, stand by, root for
action_sequence: Before: a friend has a hard time → During: stay with them and help → After: they feel stronger
grammar_pattern: support + person/noun (support the team / support her choice)
common_mistake: I support to my friend's business idea.
correct_version: I support my friend's business idea.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Support' takes a direct object, with no 'to'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: suh-PORT.
spelling_tip: Watch the double "p" -- su-PP-ort, and the "-port" ending like "transport."
etymology: From Latin "supportare" (sub- "under" + portare "to carry") -- literally "to carry from underneath, hold up."
prefix_root_suffix: sub- = under + port = root (Latin portare, "to carry") -- literally "to carry from underneath"
mnemonic: SUPPORT contains "PORT" -- a PORT holds up ships, and you SUPPORT people by holding them up too.
memory_trick: SUP-PORT: a port supports ships; you support people.
visual_association: A pair of hands gently holding up a leaning structure.
difference_explained: Help = make a task easier. Support = help and encourage over time, often emotionally.
mini_conversation:
A: I'm thinking of quitting my job to study art.
B: Whatever you decide, I'll support you.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A friend places a hand on someone's shoulder and says, "Whatever happens, I've got your back -- I support you."
news_style_line: News-style: "The charity said local businesses have generously supported its winter relief program."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Thanks for supporting me through all of this."
mcq_options: A) To oppose someone's decision  B) To help or encourage someone  C) To ignore a friend's problem  D) To criticize someone harshly

simple_explanation: To make it easier for someone to do something. When you help someone, you do something to make their task or situation easier, whether it's carrying something heavy or explaining a hard problem.
example_1: I help my mother cook dinner.
example_2: Can you help me with this bag?
example_3: She helped him study for the test.
collocations: help out, ask for help, help with, need help
related_phrasal_verbs: help out, pitch in, lend a hand
where_it_s_used: Daily favors, emergencies, teamwork, chores, studying
action_sequence: Before: someone struggles → During: do part of the work → After: the task becomes easy
grammar_pattern: help + person + (to) + verb (help him (to) finish the work)
common_mistake: Can you help me for my homework?
correct_version: Can you help me with my homework?
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'help someone WITH something', not 'for'.
pronunciation_tip: One syllable, rhymes with "yelp" and "kelp" -- HELP.
spelling_tip: Simple spelling -- "help," just watch the silent nothing; it's phonetic.
etymology: Old English "helpan" (to help, assist, benefit) -- a very old and stable Germanic verb.
prefix_root_suffix: help = root (Old English helpan) -- no clear separate prefix/suffix
mnemonic: HELP sounds exactly like calling for HELP -- picture someone shouting "HELP!" and a friend rushing over.
memory_trick: HELP: four letters, the first word to shout in trouble.
visual_association: Two hands reaching toward each other to pull someone up.
difference_explained: Same meaning. Assist is more formal (a hospital, an office).
mini_conversation:
A: This box is too heavy for me.
B: Here, let me help you carry it.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A stranded driver waves down a passing car and shouts, "Please, can you help me? My car broke down."
news_style_line: News-style: "Volunteers rushed to help residents affected by the flooding this week."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Can you help me move this table to the other room?"
mcq_options: A) To make a task harder  B) To make a task easier for someone  C) To ignore a request  D) To argue with someone
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Could you please ______ me carry these boxes upstairs? → help
find_and_fix_to_correct: Can you help me for this problem? → Can you help me with this problem?
translate: मैं अपनी माँ को खाना बनाने में मदद करता हूँ। → I help my mother cook dinner.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about how you help at home.
