usage_tip: 'Can I help you?' is what shop staff say. 'Help yourself' = take what you want.

simple_explanation: To give part of something you have to someone else, or use something together. When you share, you give a portion of what you have to another person, or you both use or enjoy the same thing at the same time.
example_1: I will share my lunch with you.
example_2: They shared a taxi to save money.
example_3: Can I share this article with my classmates?
collocations: share responsibility, share a room, share an opinion, willing to share
related_phrasal_verbs: share out, go halves, split up
where_it_s_used: Friendship, family meals, social media, teamwork
action_sequence: Before: have one thing → During: give part to a friend → After: both enjoy it
grammar_pattern: share + noun + with + person (share your notes with me)
common_mistake: I shared with him my book.
correct_version: I shared my book with him.
why_it_s_wrong: The thing comes right after 'share', then 'with + person'.
pronunciation_tip: Rhymes with "care" and "chair" -- the "sh" sound is soft, not "s".
etymology: Old English "scearu" (a cutting, share, portion), related to "shear" -- originally the idea of dividing something into parts.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- "share" is a simple root word
mnemonic: SHARE has "HARE" inside it -- imagine a hare splitting a carrot with a friend.
memory_trick: SHARE: split one thing so each person has a part.
visual_association: Two hands splitting a cookie evenly.
difference_explained: Divide = split into parts. Share = divide AND give parts to others, or use together.
mini_conversation:
A: Can I share your umbrella?
B: Of course, come stand under here.
everyday_scene: Everyday: Two friends split the last slice of pizza, one saying, "Here, we'll share it."
news_style_line: News-style: "Neighbors came together to share supplies during the storm."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Do you want to share this dessert? It's huge."
mcq_options: A) To keep for yourself  B) To give part of something to others  C) To throw away  D) To hide something
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Let's ______ the cost of the gift between all of us. → share
find_and_fix_to_correct: She shares always her problems with me. → She always shares her problems with me. (adverb "always" goes before the main verb)
translate: क्या तुम मेरे साथ अपना छाता बांटोगे? → Will you share your umbrella with me?
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something you shared with a friend.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to give part of something you have to someone else, or use something together'?
usage_tip: 'Share' online = post or forward: 'Share this video.'

simple_explanation: To feel concerned about someone or something, or to look after them. When you care about someone, their happiness and well-being matter to you, and you often help or look after them.
example_1: I really care about my family.
example_2: Doctors care for patients around the clock.
example_3: He doesn't care what other people think.
collocations: care about, care for, take care, don't care
related_phrasal_verbs: care for, look after, take care of
action_sequence: Before: someone is ill → During: bring food and medicine → After: they get better
grammar_pattern: care about/for + noun (I care about my health.)
common_mistake: I care of my grandmother every weekend.
correct_version: I care for my grandmother every weekend.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Care for' = look after. 'Care about' = feel it matters. 'Take care of' also means look after.
pronunciation_tip: One syllable -- rhymes with "hair" and "share," not "car."
etymology: Old English "caru" meaning sorrow or anxiety; the meaning softened over time to mean concern or attention for someone.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- "care" is a simple root word
mnemonic: CARE rhymes with "share" -- when you CARE, you SHARE your attention with someone.
memory_trick: CARE sounds like CAR: you take care of a new car.
visual_association: A hand gently resting on someone's shoulder.
difference_explained: Care FOR = look after (care for a patient). Care ABOUT = feel something is important (care about the environment).
mini_conversation:
A: Are you okay? You seem upset.
B: Thanks for asking -- it means a lot that you care.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A nurse gently adjusts a blanket and says, "Don't worry, we're going to take good care of you."
news_style_line: News-style: "Volunteers say they simply care about helping their community recover."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Text me when you get home, okay? I just care about you."
mcq_options: A) To feel concern or look after someone  B) To completely forget about someone  C) To argue with someone  D) To avoid someone
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: My grandmother used to ______ for me when I was sick. → care
find_and_fix_to_correct: She cares about of her students a lot. → She cares about her students a lot. (no "of" needed after "about")
translate: वह अपने बच्चों की बहुत परवाह करती है। → She cares about her children a lot.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about someone you take care of.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to feel concerned about someone or something, or to look after them'?
usage_tip: 'Take care!' is a friendly goodbye.

simple_explanation: To help someone feel better when they are sad, worried, or in pain. When someone is upset, you comfort them by being kind, saying gentle words, or simply being with them so they feel less alone.
example_1: She tried to comfort her crying friend.
example_2: He comforted the child after the nightmare.
example_3: The nurse's calm voice comforted the anxious patient.
collocations: comfort someone, seek comfort, offer comfort, words of comfort
action_sequence: Before: a friend is crying → During: sit with them and speak kindly → After: they feel a little better
grammar_pattern: comfort + person (comfort your sister / comfort him)
common_mistake: I comforted to her when she was crying.
correct_version: I comforted her when she was crying.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Comfort' takes a direct object, with no 'to'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the first syllable: CUM-fert (the "o" sounds like "u" in "cup").
spelling_tip: Remember "fort" inside "comfort" -- a fort makes you feel safe and protected.
etymology: From Old French "conforter," from Latin "confortare" (com- "together, thoroughly" + fortis "strong") -- originally meant to strengthen greatly.
prefix_root_suffix: com- (together/thoroughly) + fort = strong -> to strengthen with support
mnemonic: COMFORT has FORT inside -- a fort protects you, and comfort makes you feel protected and calm.
memory_trick: COMFORT has 'FORT': a strong place where you feel safe.
visual_association: A warm cup of tea placed into cold hands.
difference_explained: Same idea. Console is more formal and used for serious loss.
mini_conversation:
A: I failed my driving test again.
B: Come here, let me comfort you -- you'll pass next time.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A friend wraps a blanket around someone's shoulders, whispering, "It's okay, I've got you."
news_style_line: News-style: "Volunteers arrived to comfort families affected by the flooding."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I just wanted to comfort you, not fix everything."
mcq_options: A) To make someone feel calmer or less upset  B) To argue with someone  C) To ignore someone's feelings  D) To make someone laugh loudly
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: He put his arm around her shoulder to ______ her. → comfort
find_and_fix_to_correct: She comforted with her son after the accident. → She comforted her son after the accident. (no preposition needed before the object)
translate: माँ ने रोते हुए बच्चे को सांत्वना दी। → The mother comforted the crying child.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about how you comfort a sad friend.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to help someone feel better when they are sad, worried, or in pain'?
usage_tip: 'Comfort food' is food that makes you feel good.

simple_explanation: To give someone support or confidence to do something. When you encourage someone, you help them feel more confident or motivated, often with kind words or support, so they keep trying.
example_1: My coach always encourages me to try harder.
example_2: Her parents encouraged her to study abroad.
example_3: The teacher encouraged quiet students to speak up.
collocations: encourage someone to, strongly encourage, encourage growth, encourage participation
related_phrasal_verbs: cheer on, urge on, root for
action_sequence: Before: someone feels unsure → During: tell them they can do it → After: they try confidently
grammar_pattern: encourage + person + to + verb (encourage him to apply)
common_mistake: She encouraged me for study harder.
correct_version: She encouraged me to study harder.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'encourage someone TO + verb', not 'for'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: en-CUR-ij.
etymology: From Old French "encoragier" (en- "make, put into" + corage "courage," from Latin "cor" meaning heart) -- literally "to put heart into."
prefix_root_suffix: en- = to put into + courage = heart/bravery
mnemonic: EN-COUR-AGE has "COURAGE" in the middle -- to encourage someone is to give them courage.
memory_trick: EN-COURAGE: put COURAGE into someone.
visual_association: A hand giving someone a gentle push forward, smiling.
difference_explained: Encourage = give confidence so someone chooses to act. Force = make them act without choice.
mini_conversation:
A: I don't think I can finish this marathon.
B: You can do it -- I'll be there to encourage you the whole way.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A coach kneels beside an exhausted runner and says, "Get up -- I know you have one more mile in you."
news_style_line: News-style: "The program aims to encourage more young people to pursue science careers."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Just wanted to encourage you -- you're doing better than you think."
mcq_options: A) To give someone confidence or support  B) To make someone afraid  C) To stop someone from acting  D) To criticize someone harshly
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Good teachers ______ their students to ask questions. → encourage
find_and_fix_to_correct: He encouraged me studying medicine. → He encouraged me to study medicine. (need "to + verb" after the person)
translate: शिक्षक ने छात्रों को कड़ी मेहनत करने के लिए प्रोत्साहित किया। → The teacher encouraged the students to work hard.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about someone who encouraged you to try something new.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to give someone support or confidence to do something'?
usage_tip: 'Keep going!' and 'You can do it!' are encouraging lines.

simple_explanation: To say good things about someone because they did something well. When you praise someone, you tell them (or others) that they did a great job, which makes them feel proud and appreciated.
example_1: The teacher praised her for the excellent essay.
example_2: The manager praised the whole team for meeting the deadline.
example_3: Parents should praise effort, not just results.
collocations: praise highly, deserve praise, praise someone for, faint praise
related_phrasal_verbs: build up, speak highly of, sing someone's praises
action_sequence: Before: someone does good work → During: notice it → After: say it was excellent
grammar_pattern: praise + person + for + noun/gerund (praise her for winning)
common_mistake: He praised to the students for their hard work.
correct_version: He praised the students for their hard work.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Praise' takes a direct object, with no 'to'.
pronunciation_tip: Rhymes with "raise" -- the "ai" makes a long "A" sound.
spelling_tip: Don't confuse with "prize" -- "praise" has an "a" before the "i."
etymology: From Old French "preisier" (to prize, value), from Latin "pretiare" (to price), related to "price" and "precious."
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- from Latin root "pretiare" (to value)
mnemonic: PRAISE sounds like "raise" -- when you praise someone, you raise them up with kind words.
memory_trick: PRAISE rhymes with RAISE: praise raises someone's confidence.
visual_association: A gold star being placed next to someone's name.
difference_explained: Praise = kind words. Prize = an award you win.
mini_conversation:
A: I finally finished my thesis!
B: That's amazing -- I have to praise you, that took real discipline.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A director looks at the final cut and says, "This is the best work you've ever done."
news_style_line: News-style: "Officials praised the volunteers for their tireless efforts during the crisis."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I have to praise you -- dinner was absolutely amazing tonight."
mcq_options: A) To criticize someone's mistakes  B) To say good things about someone's achievement  C) To ignore someone completely  D) To compare two people
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The coach ______ the young player for her incredible speed. → praised
find_and_fix_to_correct: She was praised because her good behavior. → She was praised because of her good behavior. (use "because of" before a noun, not just "because")
translate: बॉस ने उसकी मेहनत की बहुत तारीफ की। → The boss praised her hard work a lot.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a time a teacher praised you.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to say good things about someone because they did something well'?
usage_tip: 'Praise someone FOR something': 'She praised him for his honesty.'

simple_explanation: To say that someone or something caused a problem or did something wrong. When something bad happens, you blame the person or thing you believe is responsible for it.
example_1: Don't blame me for your mistake.
example_2: He blamed the traffic for being late.
example_3: She always blames herself when things go wrong.
collocations: blame someone for, put the blame on, take the blame, blame game
related_phrasal_verbs: point fingers, take the fall, own up
action_sequence: Before: something goes wrong → During: look for who caused it → After: say it's their fault
grammar_pattern: blame + person + for + noun (blame him for the delay) / blame + thing + on + person (blame the delay on him)
common_mistake: He blamed on me for the accident.
correct_version: He blamed me for the accident.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'blame someone FOR something' or 'blame something ON someone'. Not both together.
spelling_tip: B-L-A-M-E, silent "e" at the end makes the "a" long.
etymology: From Old French "blasmer," from Latin "blasphemare" (to blaspheme, revile) -- the same root as "blaspheme," softened over time to mean "hold responsible."
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- from Latin "blasphemare"
mnemonic: BLAME rhymes with "shame" -- when you blame someone, you try to give them the shame for what happened.
memory_trick: BLAME: point a finger — the B looks like a pointing hand.
visual_association: A pointing finger aimed directly at someone.
difference_explained: Blame the driver FOR the accident. Blame the accident ON the driver. Same meaning, different order.
mini_conversation:
A: The project failed -- whose fault is it?
B: Let's not blame anyone, let's just fix it.
everyday_scene: Everyday: Two characters argue over a broken vase, one shouting, "Don't you dare blame this on me!"
news_style_line: News-style: "Officials blamed the outage on outdated equipment."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I'm not trying to blame you, I just want to understand what happened."
mcq_options: A) To thank someone  B) To hold someone responsible for something bad  C) To forgive someone  D) To help someone
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: You can't ______ me for something I didn't do. → blame
find_and_fix_to_correct: She blamed to her brother for the mess. → She blamed her brother for the mess. (no "to" after "blamed")
translate: उसने अपनी गलती के लिए मुझे दोष दिया। → He blamed me for his mistake.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something people often blame on the weather.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to say that someone or something caused a problem or did something wrong'?
usage_tip: 'I don't blame you' means your reaction is understandable.

simple_explanation: To say that someone or something has faults or did something wrong. When you criticize something, you point out what is wrong with it rather than what is good about it, sometimes to help improve it and sometimes just to complain.
example_2: Critics criticized the movie for its weak plot.
example_3: He hates being criticized in front of others.
collocations: criticize harshly, heavily criticized, criticize openly, constructive criticism
related_phrasal_verbs: pick apart, put down, find fault with
action_sequence: Before: see a mistake → During: point out what's wrong → After: suggest a fix
grammar_pattern: criticize + person/thing + for + noun (criticize him for his behavior)
common_mistake: The teacher criticized about my grammar.
correct_version: The teacher criticized my grammar.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Criticize' takes a direct object; don't add 'about'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the first syllable: KRIT-uh-syze.
spelling_tip: Notice "critic" at the start of "criticize" -- remember the connection.
etymology: From Greek "kritikos" (able to judge/discern), via "critic" -- originally about careful judgment, later focused on pointing out faults.
prefix_root_suffix: critic (from Greek "kritikos," a judge) + -ize = to make/do the action of judging
mnemonic: CRITICIZE contains "CRITIC" -- a critic's job is to criticize (find faults in) things.
memory_trick: CRITIC-IZE: act like a film CRITIC.
visual_association: A red pen circling mistakes on a page.
difference_explained: Criticize = point out faults in someone or their work. Complain = say you're unhappy about something.
mini_conversation:
A: The report says our sales dropped again.
B: The board is going to criticize the whole marketing team.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A chef throws down a spoon after tasting the dish and says, "This is nowhere near good enough."
news_style_line: News-style: "The report criticized the city's handling of the water crisis."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I know you're trying to help, but please stop criticizing everything I do."
mcq_options: A) To praise someone's work  B) To point out faults or mistakes  C) To completely ignore something  D) To copy someone's idea
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: My brother always ______ my driving, even though he doesn't drive well either. → criticizes
find_and_fix_to_correct: He always criticize her cooking. → He always criticizes her cooking. (third-person singular needs "-s")
translate: आलोचकों ने उस किताब की बहुत आलोचना की। → Critics criticized the book a lot.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about how to criticize someone politely.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to say that someone or something has faults or did something wrong'?
usage_tip: 'Constructive criticism' means comments meant to help you improve.

simple_explanation: To make jokes about someone or playfully bother them, often in a friendly way. When you tease someone, you say playful or joking things about them, usually as a friend, though it can sometimes hurt their feelings if it goes too far.
example_1: My brother always teases me about my haircut.
example_2: Stop teasing your sister -- she's really upset.
example_3: They teased him gently about his new car.
collocations: tease someone about, gently tease, tease relentlessly, tease mercilessly
related_phrasal_verbs: poke fun at, wind up, make fun of
action_sequence: Before: notice a funny habit → During: joke about it playfully → After: everyone laughs
grammar_pattern: tease + person + about + noun (tease him about his shoes)
common_mistake: They teased of him for his accent.
correct_version: They teased him about his accent.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'tease someone ABOUT something', not 'of'.
etymology: From Old English "tæsan" (to pull apart, comb out fibers, as with wool) -- the modern sense of "provoke playfully" developed later, by extension.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- "tease" is a simple root word
mnemonic: TEASE sounds like "please" -- a friendly tease is meant to please, not hurt.
memory_trick: TEASE sounds like 'tees-ing': friends tee you up for a joke.
visual_association: A friend nudging another's shoulder with a mischievous grin.
difference_explained: Tease = joke in a light, friendly way. Bully = hurt or scare someone again and again.
tone: Informal, can be Positive or Negative depending on context
mini_conversation:
A: You're wearing socks with sandals again?
B: Hey, stop teasing me -- it's comfortable!
everyday_scene: Everyday: A sibling grins and nudges another, saying, "Oh come on, admit it, you're blushing."
news_style_line: News-style: "The comedian's routine gently teased public figures without ever crossing into insult."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I'm only teasing -- you know I love your cooking really."
mcq_options: A) To seriously insult someone  B) To playfully joke with or provoke someone  C) To completely ignore someone  D) To help someone with a task
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: My friends always ______ me about being afraid of spiders. → tease
find_and_fix_to_correct: She teased at him for losing the game. → She teased him for losing the game. (no "at" needed before the object)
translate: दोस्त उसे उसकी नई साइकिल के लिए छेड़ रहे थे। → Friends were teasing him about his new bicycle.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about how your siblings or friends tease you.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to make jokes about someone or playfully bother them, often in a friendly way'?
usage_tip: Teasing is usually friendly; if it hurts, it becomes bullying.

simple_explanation: To become friends again with someone after an argument or disagreement. When two people or groups reconcile, they stop being angry with each other and restore their friendship or relationship.
example_1: The two brothers finally reconciled after years apart.
example_2: It took months for the couple to reconcile after the fight.
example_3: The two countries reconciled after decades of tension.
collocations: reconcile with, try to reconcile, fully reconciled, reconcile differences
related_phrasal_verbs: make up, patch things up, bury the hatchet
where_it_s_used: Family conflict, friendships, international relations, divorce/marriage
action_sequence: Before: two friends fight → During: they talk and apologise → After: they are friends again
grammar_pattern: reconcile with + person (reconcile with her sister) / be reconciled to + situation
common_mistake: They reconciled together after the fight.
correct_version: They reconciled after the fight.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Reconcile' already means come together again, so 'together' is not needed.
pronunciation_tip: Four syllables, stress on the first: REK-uhn-syle.
spelling_tip: Remember "con" + "cile" -- don't drop the silent "e" before adding "-iation" (reconciliation).
etymology: From Latin "reconciliare" (re- "again" + conciliare "to bring together, unite") -- literally "to bring together again."
mnemonic: RE-CON-CILE = "RE" (again) + friends CONnect again after a fight -- to reconcile is to reconnect.
memory_trick: RE-CONCILE: 're' = again, 'concile' = come together (like council).
visual_association: Two hands, once pulled apart, slowly reaching toward each other again.
difference_explained: Reconcile = become friends again. Compromise = each side gives up something to agree.
mini_conversation:
A: Have you talked to your dad since the argument?
B: Yes, we finally reconciled last weekend.
everyday_scene: Everyday: Two old friends stand awkwardly at a doorway before one says, "I've missed you -- can we start over?"
news_style_line: News-style: "The two nations agreed to reconcile after years of diplomatic tension."
casual_conversation: Casual: "We finally reconciled after not speaking for almost a year."
mcq_options: A) To fight again  B) To become friends again after a disagreement  C) To ignore someone forever  D) To move to a new city
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: After the argument, it took a long time for them to ______. → reconcile
find_and_fix_to_correct: She reconciled to her sister last week. → She reconciled with her sister last week. (use "reconcile with," not "reconcile to," for people)
translate: दोनों भाइयों ने कई सालों बाद आपस में सुलह कर ली। → The two brothers reconciled after many years.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about two people who reconciled after a fight.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to become friends again with someone after an argument or disagreement'?
usage_tip: Banks: 'reconcile accounts' means make two records match.

simple_explanation: To become someone's husband or wife in an official ceremony. When two people marry, they make a legal and often religious promise to spend their lives together as husband and wife or spouses.
example_1: They plan to marry next summer.
example_2: She married her college sweetheart.
example_3: He proposed and they got married in Italy.
collocations: marry young, get married, marry someone, happily married
related_phrasal_verbs: settle down, tie the knot, get hitched
action_sequence: Before: two people decide to marry → During: the wedding ceremony happens → After: they are husband and wife
grammar_pattern: marry + person, no preposition (marry him, not marry with him)
common_mistake: She married with her boyfriend last year.
correct_version: She married her boyfriend last year.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Marry' takes the person directly, with no 'with'. 'Get married TO someone' is also correct.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the first syllable: MAR-ee, rhymes with "carry."
etymology: From Old French "marier," from Latin "maritare," related to "maritus" (husband) -- the root of "marital" and "marriage."
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- from Latin "maritus" (husband)
mnemonic: MARRY rhymes with "carry" -- when you marry someone, you carry that promise for life.
memory_trick: MARRY → MARRIED: Y becomes I before -ed.
visual_association: Two wedding rings being placed side by side.
difference_explained: She married him. / She got married to him. / They got married. Never 'married with'.
mini_conversation:
A: I heard you and Raj are engaged!
B: Yes, we're going to marry next spring.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A groom takes a deep breath at the altar and whispers, "I can't believe I finally get to marry you."
news_style_line: News-style: "The couple announced they will marry in a small ceremony next month."
casual_conversation: Casual: "We've been dating for five years -- I think it's time to get married."
mcq_options: A) To become someone's husband or wife  B) To break up with someone  C) To become friends with someone  D) To move away from someone
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: They decided to ______ after dating for three years. → marry
find_and_fix_to_correct: He wants to marry with a doctor. → He wants to marry a doctor. (no "with" needed after "marry")
translate: उन्होंने पिछले साल एक-दूसरे से शादी की। → They married each other last year.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about when someone in your family got married.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to become someone's husband or wife in an official ceremony'?
usage_tip: 'Get married' is more common in speech: 'They got married in May.'

simple_explanation: To legally end a marriage. When a married couple divorces, they officially and legally end their marriage and are no longer husband and wife.
example_1: They decided to divorce after ten years.
example_2: My parents divorced when I was seven.
example_3: She divorced him after discovering the truth.
collocations: get divorced, file for divorce, amicable divorce, divorce rate
where_it_s_used: Family law, relationships, personal life stories
action_sequence: Before: a marriage has problems → During: go to court → After: the marriage legally ends
grammar_pattern: divorce + person (divorce her) / get divorced from + person
common_mistake: She divorced from her husband last year.
correct_version: She divorced her husband last year.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Divorce' takes the person directly. 'Get divorced from' is also correct.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: dih-VORSS.
spelling_tip: Remember "vor" in the middle, similar to "divert" -- both involve "turning."
etymology: From Old French "divorce," from Latin "divortium" (di-/dis- "apart" + vertere "to turn") -- literally "to turn apart."
mnemonic: DI-VORCE has "VOR" like "divert" -- divorce means the paths of two people turn apart/divert.
memory_trick: DI-VORCE: 'di' = apart, two ways.
visual_association: A wedding ring being placed alone on a table.
difference_explained: Separate = live apart, still married. Divorce = legally end the marriage.
mini_conversation:
A: I heard Priya and Sam split up.
B: Yes, they finalized their divorce last month.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A lawyer slides papers across a table and says quietly, "This will officially end the marriage."
news_style_line: News-style: "The celebrity couple confirmed they are finalizing their divorce."
casual_conversation: Casual: "It was hard, but we both agreed the divorce was for the best."
mcq_options: A) To legally end a marriage  B) To start dating someone  C) To plan a wedding  D) To move to a new house
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: After years of arguing, they finally decided to ______. → divorce
find_and_fix_to_correct: They divorced with each other peacefully. → They divorced each other peacefully. (no "with" needed)
translate: उन्होंने पांच साल की शादी के बाद तलाक ले लिया। → They divorced after five years of marriage.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a neutral sentence explaining what 'divorce' means.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to legally end a marriage'?
usage_tip: 'Divorced' is also an adjective: 'He is divorced.'

hindi_meaning: डेट पर जाना, प्रेम-संबंध में रहना
simple_explanation: To go out with someone romantically, or to be in a romantic relationship. When you date someone, you spend time together romantically, going out to dinner, movies, or other activities, usually before deciding to become a couple or get married.
example_2: He's been dating her for six months.
example_3: They met on an app and started dating.
collocations: date someone, start dating, casually dating, dating app
related_phrasal_verbs: go out with, hang out, hook up
where_it_s_used: Relationships, apps, young adulthood, social life
action_sequence: Before: like someone → During: go out together a few times → After: become a couple
grammar_pattern: date + person, no preposition (date him, not date with him)
common_mistake: I am dating with a girl from my office.
correct_version: I am dating a girl from my office.
why_it_s_wrong: As 'go out romantically', 'date' takes the person directly, with no 'with'.
spelling_tip: Same spelling as the calendar "date" -- context tells you which meaning is used.
etymology: As in "romantic date," this sense developed in early 20th-century American English from the older meaning of "date" (a point in time) -- going out on an arranged, timed meeting.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- shares root with calendar "date" (Latin "data," given)
mnemonic: A DATE has a set TIME, just like a calendar date -- a romantic date is also a planned meeting time.
memory_trick: DATE a person = fix DATES to meet.
visual_association: Two people sharing candlelight across a small table.
difference_explained: Meet = see someone, any reason. Date = meet someone romantically.
mini_conversation:
A: So how long have you two been dating?
B: About eight months now -- it's going really well.
everyday_scene: Everyday: Two nervous people sit across a small café table, one saying, "I'm really glad we finally decided to do this."
news_style_line: News-style: "Surveys show more young adults are choosing to date less and focus on careers."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Are you seeing anyone right now, or are you not dating at the moment?"
mcq_options: A) To argue with someone  B) To go out with someone romantically  C) To write down a calendar day  D) To end a friendship
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: They've been ______ for almost a year now. → dating
find_and_fix_to_correct: She is dating with my cousin. → She is dating my cousin. (no "with" needed)
translate: वे पिछले छह महीनों से डेट कर रहे हैं। → They have been dating for the last six months.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence explaining 'date' as a calendar word.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to go out with someone romantically, or to be in a romantic relationship'?
usage_tip: 'Date' also means a calendar day or a fruit (khajoor).

simple_explanation: To put your arms around someone to show love or comfort. When you hug someone, you wrap your arms around them, usually to show affection, comfort, or to say hello or goodbye.
example_1: She hugged her father tightly at the airport.
example_2: They hugged goodbye before the long trip.
example_3: He hugged his best friend after years apart.
collocations: hug tightly, warm hug, hug goodbye, big hug
related_phrasal_verbs: embrace, wrap arms around, hold close
action_sequence: Before: see a loved one → During: put your arms around them → After: feel warm and happy
grammar_pattern: hug + person (hug your mother), no preposition needed
common_mistake: She hugged with her sister at the reunion.
correct_version: She hugged her sister at the reunion.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Hug' takes the person directly, with no 'with'.
pronunciation_tip: One syllable, short "u" sound like in "bug" or "rug."
spelling_tip: Double the "g" when adding "-ing" or "-ed": hugging, hugged.
etymology: Origin uncertain, possibly from Old Norse "hugga" (to comfort) or Germanic roots meaning "to embrace with care"; in common use in English since the 16th century.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- origin uncertain
mnemonic: HUG rhymes with "rug" -- imagine wrapping someone up like a warm rug.
memory_trick: HUG → HUGGED: double G, like two arms around someone.
visual_association: Two arms wrapped tightly around someone's shoulders.
difference_explained: Same meaning. Embrace is more formal and can also mean accept an idea: 'embrace change'.
mini_conversation:
A: I'm so nervous about the interview tomorrow.
B: Come here, let me give you a hug -- you'll be great.
everyday_scene: Everyday: Two long-lost friends run toward each other at the airport and collide into a tight hug.
news_style_line: News-style: "The rescued hikers hugged their families after being found safe."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Come here, you look like you need a hug right now."
mcq_options: A) To shake hands  B) To wrap your arms around someone affectionately  C) To wave goodbye  D) To push someone away
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: My grandmother always ______ me tightly whenever I visit. → hugs
find_and_fix_to_correct: He hug her before leaving for college. → He hugged her before leaving for college. (past tense needs "-ed")
translate: उसने हवाई अड्डे पर अपनी माँ को गले लगाया। → She hugged her mother at the airport.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about who you hug when you come home.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to put your arms around someone to show love or comfort'?
usage_tip: 'Give someone a hug' is very common.

simple_explanation: To touch someone with your lips to show love or affection. A kiss is when you touch your lips to someone (or something) as a sign of love, affection, greeting, or respect.
example_1: He kissed her on the cheek.
example_2: She kissed her baby goodnight.
example_3: They kissed under the stars.
collocations: kiss goodnight, kiss on the cheek, blow a kiss, gentle kiss
related_phrasal_verbs: blow a kiss, peck on the cheek, lock lips
where_it_s_used: Romance, family affection, greetings in some cultures, farewells
action_sequence: Before: lean close → During: touch with your lips → After: step back and smile
grammar_pattern: kiss + person + (on the + body part) (kiss her on the forehead)
common_mistake: He kissed to her on the cheek.
correct_version: He kissed her on the cheek.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Kiss' takes the person directly, with no 'to'.
etymology: From Old English "cyssan," a common Germanic word related to "coss" (a kiss) -- one of the oldest words in English for this gesture.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- from Old English "cyssan"
mnemonic: KISS rhymes with "bliss" -- a kiss often brings a feeling of bliss (happiness).
memory_trick: KISS has double S, like two lips.
visual_association: Two silhouettes leaning close together at sunset.
difference_explained: Hug = hold with arms. Kiss = touch with lips.
mini_conversation:
A: Did you tell her how you feel?
B: I didn't just tell her -- I kissed her!
everyday_scene: Everyday: Rain falls as two characters lean in slowly and finally kiss under a streetlamp.
news_style_line: News-style: "The tradition involves elders kissing the newborn's forehead as a blessing."
casual_conversation: Casual: "He kissed me goodbye before he left for the airport."
mcq_options: A) To shake someone's hand  B) To touch someone with your lips to show affection  C) To whisper into someone's ear  D) To wave at someone
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: She leaned over and ______ her son on the forehead. → kissed
find_and_fix_to_correct: They kiss each other goodbye yesterday. → They kissed each other goodbye yesterday. (past tense needed for a completed past action)
translate: उसने अपनी बेटी को सोने से पहले चूमा। → She kissed her daughter before bed.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about how people greet each other in another country you know.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to touch someone with your lips to show love or affection'?
usage_tip: In many cultures, a kiss on the cheek is a greeting.

simple_explanation: To hurt someone who trusted you by being disloyal or revealing a secret. When you betray someone, you break their trust, often by lying, being disloyal, or sharing something private that they told you in confidence.
example_1: He felt his best friend had betrayed him.
example_2: She betrayed her sister's secret to their mother.
example_3: He was betrayed by someone he trusted deeply.
collocations: betray trust, feel betrayed, betray a secret, betray a friend
related_phrasal_verbs: sell out, stab in the back, turn on
action_sequence: Before: someone trusts you → During: you break that trust → After: they feel hurt
grammar_pattern: betray + person/trust (betray her trust / betray a friend)
common_mistake: He betrayed on his friend's secret.
correct_version: He betrayed his friend's secret.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Betray' takes a direct object; don't add 'on'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: bih-TRAY.
etymology: From Old French "trair," from Latin "tradere" (to hand over, deliver) -- the same root as "traitor" and "tradition."
prefix_root_suffix: be- (intensifying prefix) + tray (from Latin "tradere," to hand over)
mnemonic: BE-TRAY sounds like "be a traitor" -- to betray is to act like a traitor toward someone who trusted you.
memory_trick: BE-TRAY: serve someone's secret on a TRAY to others.
visual_association: A hand releasing another hand it was once holding tightly.
difference_explained: Cheat = act dishonestly to gain something. Betray = break someone's trust, especially a friend's or country's.
mini_conversation:
A: I can't believe he told everyone my secret.
B: That's awful -- he really betrayed your trust.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character stares in disbelief and says quietly, "I trusted you with everything, and you betrayed me."
news_style_line: News-style: "The former employee was accused of betraying company secrets to a rival firm."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I still can't believe she betrayed me like that after all these years."
mcq_options: A) To support someone loyally  B) To break someone's trust  C) To thank someone sincerely  D) To forgive someone completely
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: She could never forgive him for the way he had ______ her. → betrayed
find_and_fix_to_correct: He betrayed to his own team. → He betrayed his own team. (no "to" needed after "betrayed")
translate: उसके सबसे अच्छे दोस्त ने उसे धोखा दिया। → His best friend betrayed him.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a character in a film who betrayed a friend.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to hurt someone who trusted you by being disloyal or revealing a secret'?
usage_tip: 'Betray' is strong: it's about broken trust.

simple_explanation: To talk about other people's private lives, often in an unkind or unconfirmed way. When you gossip, you share stories or rumors about other people, often about their private lives, and it's not always true or kind.
example_1: They love to gossip about their neighbors.
example_2: The coworkers gossiped about the new manager.
example_3: She never gossips about her friends.
collocations: gossip about, love to gossip, office gossip, juicy gossip
related_phrasal_verbs: dish the dirt, talk behind someone's back, spread rumors
where_it_s_used: Office culture, friend groups, neighborhoods, social media
action_sequence: Before: hear a rumour → During: talk about it with others → After: the story spreads
grammar_pattern: gossip + about + person/topic (gossip about the neighbors)
common_mistake: They gossiped of the new employee.
correct_version: They gossiped about the new employee.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'gossip ABOUT someone', not 'of'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the first syllable: GOSS-ip.
etymology: From Old English "godsibb" (godparent, literally "god" + "sibb," relative) -- originally meant a close friend or godparent, later shifted to mean someone who shares idle talk.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- from Old English "godsibb"
mnemonic: GOSSIP sounds like "goss" (as in "guess") -- people GUESS and whisper stories when they gossip.
memory_trick: GOSSIP has double S, like two people whispering 'sss'.
visual_association: Two people whispering behind cupped hands.
difference_explained: Discuss = talk seriously about a topic. Gossip = talk about other people's private lives, often unkindly.
mini_conversation:
A: Did you hear what happened with Maria and Tom?
B: I try not to gossip, but okay, tell me.
everyday_scene: Everyday: Two coworkers huddle by the coffee machine, whispering, "Did you hear what happened last night?"
news_style_line: News-style: "The magazine has built its entire brand around celebrity gossip."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I don't want to gossip, but you really need to hear this."
mcq_options: A) To give an official announcement  B) To talk about other people's private lives  C) To write a formal report  D) To keep a complete secret
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Please don't ______ about what I just told you. → gossip
find_and_fix_to_correct: She always gossip about her coworkers. → She always gossips about her coworkers. (third-person singular needs "-s")
translate: वे हमेशा अपने पड़ोसियों के बारे में गपशप करते हैं। → They always gossip about their neighbors.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about why gossip can be harmful.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to talk about other people's private lives, often in an unkind or unconfirmed way'?
usage_tip: 'Office gossip' is talk about colleagues' private lives.

hindi_meaning: मेलजोल बढ़ाना, सामाजिक रूप से घुलना-मिलना
simple_explanation: To spend time with other people in a friendly, casual way. When you socialize, you spend time talking and interacting with other people, usually at events, parties, or gatherings, to build friendships or connections.
example_1: I like to socialize with my coworkers after work.
example_2: She finds it hard to socialize at big parties.
example_3: The company organized an event to help new employees socialize.
collocations: socialize with, socialize easily, love to socialize, socialize online
related_phrasal_verbs: hang out, mix and mingle, network
where_it_s_used: Parties, networking events, workplaces, community gatherings
action_sequence: Before: go to an event → During: talk and laugh with people → After: make new friends
grammar_pattern: socialize + with + people (socialize with new colleagues)
common_mistake: I like to socialize to new people at parties.
correct_version: I like to socialize with new people at parties.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'socialize WITH people', not 'to'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the first syllable: SO-shuh-lyze.
spelling_tip: British English spells it "socialise"; American English spells it "socialize."
etymology: From "social" (Latin "socius," companion/ally) + "-ize" (to make/do) -- literally "to make oneself social."
mnemonic: SOCIAL-IZE = doing the action of being SOCIAL -- go out and be with people.
memory_trick: SOCIAL-IZE: be SOCIAL.
visual_association: A group of people laughing together at a small gathering.
emotion_feel: Mild anxiety for introverts, enjoyment for extroverts
difference_explained: Meet = come together with someone. Socialize = spend relaxed, friendly time with people.
mini_conversation:
A: Are you going to the office party tonight?
B: Yeah, I need to socialize a bit more with the new team.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A shy character stands alone at a party until a friend pulls them by the arm, saying, "Come on, let's go socialize a bit."
news_style_line: News-style: "Experts say socializing regularly can improve mental health, especially for older adults."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I need to get out more and socialize instead of staying home every weekend."
mcq_options: A) To avoid other people  B) To spend friendly time with others  C) To work alone quietly  D) To argue with someone
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: It's important to ______ with new people when you move to a new city. → socialize
find_and_fix_to_correct: He doesn't like socialize with strangers. → He doesn't like to socialize with strangers. (need "to" before the base verb after "like")
translate: नई नौकरी में उसे सहकर्मियों के साथ मेलजोल बढ़ाना पसंद है। → In the new job, he likes to socialize with his coworkers.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about where you like to socialize.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to spend time with other people in a friendly, casual way'?
usage_tip: British spelling: socialise.

simple_explanation: To form a close emotional connection with someone. When you bond with someone, you build a strong feeling of closeness and trust with them, often through shared experiences or time spent together.
example_1: The trip helped us bond as a family.
example_2: New puppies quickly bond with their owners.
example_3: The team bonded over long hours at work.
collocations: bond with, bond over, close bond, form a bond
related_phrasal_verbs: click with, connect with, grow close
action_sequence: Before: meet someone new → During: share experiences → After: feel close
grammar_pattern: bond + with + person (bond with your teammates) / bond + over + activity (bond over cooking)
common_mistake: They bonded together with each other quickly.
correct_version: They bonded with each other quickly.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Bond with' already means come together, so 'together' is not needed.
spelling_tip: B-O-N-D, short and simple -- not to be confused with "band."
etymology: From Old English "bond/band" (something that binds, a fastening) -- related to "bind"; the emotional sense of "close connection" developed later by extension.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- from Old English "bond," related to "bind"
mnemonic: BOND sounds like "bind" -- a bond is an emotional tie that binds two people together.
memory_trick: BOND like JAMES BOND: a strong link.
visual_association: Two puzzle pieces clicking perfectly together.
difference_explained: Connect = link or relate. Bond = form a deep, lasting emotional connection.
mini_conversation:
A: How was the camping trip with your team?
B: It was great -- we really bonded over the campfire stories.
everyday_scene: Everyday: Two rivals, stuck together during a storm, finally laugh and one says, "Maybe we're not so different after all."
news_style_line: News-style: "Researchers found that shared meals help families bond more deeply."
casual_conversation: Casual: "We really bonded during that road trip -- I feel like I know her so much better now."
mcq_options: A) To form a close emotional connection  B) To argue frequently  C) To live far apart  D) To forget about someone
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The two roommates ______ quickly over their love of cooking. → bonded
find_and_fix_to_correct: We bonded to each other during the trip. → We bonded with each other during the trip. (use "with," not "to")
translate: यात्रा के दौरान वे एक-दूसरे के साथ गहराई से जुड़ गए। → They bonded deeply with each other during the trip.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about how you bonded with a new friend.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to form a close emotional connection with someone'?
usage_tip: 'Team bonding' activities help colleagues get close.

simple_explanation: To join or link two or more things or people together. When you connect with someone, you build a relationship or understanding with them; when you connect two things, you physically or digitally link them together.
example_1: I really connect with people who love books.
example_2: Please connect the printer to your laptop.
example_3: They connected instantly during the interview.
collocations: connect with, well connected, connect to the internet, instantly connect
related_phrasal_verbs: hook up, link up, tie in
action_sequence: Before: see two wires → During: join them → After: power flows
grammar_pattern: connect + with + person / connect + noun + to + noun (connect the cable to the TV)
common_mistake: I couldn't connect with the WiFi.
correct_version: I couldn't connect to the WiFi.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'connect TO' for devices and networks, 'connect WITH' for people and feelings.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: kuh-NEKT.
etymology: From Latin "connectere" (con- "together" + nectere "to tie, bind") -- literally "to tie together."
mnemonic: CON-NECT sounds like "connect" itself -- imagine two dots being NECKED (tied) together.
memory_trick: CON-NECT: like a NECKlace that links beads.
visual_association: Two puzzle pieces or plug and socket fitting together perfectly.
difference_explained: Connect TO a network or device. Connect WITH a person or an idea.
mini_conversation:
A: How was your date last night?
B: Really good, actually -- we just connected instantly.
everyday_scene: Everyday: Two strangers on a train start talking and one says, "I don't know why, but I feel like we really connect."
news_style_line: News-style: "The new railway line will connect the two major cities within two hours."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I felt like we connected right away when we first met."
mcq_options: A) To separate two things  B) To join or link things or people together  C) To delete something  D) To forget about someone

simple_explanation: To start to be something different from before. "Become" describes a change from one state to another -- a person or thing becomes something new over time or suddenly.
example_1: She wants to become a doctor.
example_2: The sky became dark before the storm.
example_3: He became famous after his first film.
collocations: become famous, become a doctor, become clear, gradually become
related_phrasal_verbs: turn into, grow into, end up as
action_sequence: Before: be a student → During: study and work hard → After: become an engineer
grammar_pattern: become + noun/adjective (become a teacher / become tired)
common_mistake: He became to be a good friend.
correct_version: He became a good friend.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Become' is followed directly by a noun or adjective, never 'to be'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: bih-CUM.
etymology: Old English "becuman" (be- "thoroughly" + cuman "to come") -- literally "to come to be."
mnemonic: BE-COME sounds like "come to be" -- to become something is to arrive at (come to) a new state of being.
memory_trick: BE + COME: you COME to BE something.
visual_association: A caterpillar slowly transforming into a butterfly.
difference_explained: Both mean change state. Get is informal (get angry). Become is neutral or formal (become famous).
mini_conversation:
A: What do you want to become when you graduate?
B: I think I want to become an engineer.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A young athlete looks in the mirror and whispers, "One day, I'm going to become a champion."
news_style_line: News-style: "The small startup has become one of the fastest-growing companies in the country."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I never thought I'd become this confident in public speaking."
mcq_options: A) To stay exactly the same  B) To change into something new  C) To forget completely  D) To argue strongly
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: After years of hard work, she finally ______ a successful lawyer. → became
find_and_fix_to_correct: She become a teacher last year. → She became a teacher last year. (need past tense "became" for a completed past action)

write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about what you want to become in five years.
