usage_tip: 'Digital transformation' means a company moving its work online.

simple_explanation: To change something from one form, use, or belief into another. When you convert something, you change it from one type or system into a different one -- like converting money into another currency or a room into an office.
example_1: We plan to convert the garage into a gym.
example_2: She converted to a new religion after years of studying it.
example_3: You can convert dollars into euros at the bank.
collocations: convert into, convert to, easily convertible, currency converter
related_phrasal_verbs: turn into, switch over, change over
action_sequence: Before: have a Word file → During: use a converter → After: get a PDF
grammar_pattern: convert + noun + into/to + noun (convert the file to PDF)
common_mistake: I need to convert this document in PDF.
correct_version: I need to convert this document into PDF.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'convert into' or 'convert to', not 'in'.
pronunciation_tip: Verb: kuhn-VERT. Noun (a person who converted): KON-vert.
spelling_tip: Notice "vert" at the end, shared with "revert" and "divert" -- all involve "turning."
etymology: From Latin "convertere" (con- "together, thoroughly" + vertere "to turn") -- literally "to turn around completely."
mnemonic: CON-VERT sounds like "convert" itself -- to convert is to turn (vert) something completely into something else.
memory_trick: CON-VERT: turn around ('vert' = turn), like converting a file.
visual_association: A caterpillar cocoon or a machine turning raw material into a finished product.
difference_explained: Convert = change from one form or system to another. Change is the general word.
mini_conversation:
A: How much is 100 dollars in rupees?
B: Let me convert it for you using the app.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A contractor gestures around an empty attic and says, "We can convert this whole space into a bedroom."
news_style_line: News-style: "The city plans to convert the old railway station into a public library."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Can you convert this recipe from cups to grams for me?"
mcq_options: A) To destroy completely  B) To change something into a different form  C) To keep something exactly the same  D) To hide something
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: They decided to ______ the spare bedroom into a home office. → convert
find_and_fix_to_correct: She converted the file to a PDF format easily. → She converted the file to PDF format easily. (no article "a" needed before a format name like "PDF")
translate: उन्होंने पुराने खलिहान को खूबसूरत घर में बदल दिया। → They converted the old barn into a beautiful house.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a file or unit you have converted.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to change something from one form, use, or belief into another'?
usage_tip: 'Convert ₹ to $' in currency; 'convert Word to PDF' on a computer.

simple_explanation: To change your behavior or something else to fit a new situation. When you adapt, you adjust yourself or something else to work well in new or different conditions, like adapting to a new country or climate.
example_1: It took time to adapt to the new schedule.
example_2: Animals adapt to their environment over generations.
example_3: She quickly adapted to life in a new country.
collocations: adapt to, quickly adapt, adapt easily, well adapted
related_phrasal_verbs: get used to, adjust to, settle in
action_sequence: Before: move to a new place → During: change your habits → After: feel at home
grammar_pattern: adapt + to + situation (adapt to change) / adapt + noun (adapt the script)
common_mistake: It took time to adapt the new environment.
correct_version: It took time to adapt to the new environment.
why_it_s_wrong: When it means 'adjust yourself', use 'adapt TO something'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: uh-DAPT.
etymology: From Latin "adaptare" (ad- "to" + aptare "to fit"), related to "apt" -- literally "to make fit to."
mnemonic: A-DAPT sounds like "apt" -- to adapt is to become APT (suited) to a new situation.
memory_trick: ADAPT: an ADAPTER lets a plug fit a new socket.
visual_association: A chameleon slowly changing color to match its surroundings.
emotion_feel: Determination, mild stress at first, then relief
difference_explained: Adapt = change to fit. Adopt = take a child or an idea as your own.
mini_conversation:
A: How's it going living in a new country?
B: It's tough, but I'm slowly adapting to everything.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A traveler stares at an unfamiliar market and says, "I guess I just need to adapt to how things work here."
news_style_line: News-style: "Farmers are adapting their crops to survive the changing climate."
casual_conversation: Casual: "It took me a few weeks to adapt to the new work hours."
mcq_options: A) To completely ignore change  B) To adjust to a new situation  C) To copy someone else exactly  D) To refuse to change at all
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: It took her a while to ______ to the colder weather. → adapt
find_and_fix_to_correct: He adapted quickly the new rules at work. → He adapted quickly to the new rules at work. (need "to" before "the new rules")
translate: उसे नए स्कूल में ढलने में कुछ समय लगा। → It took him some time to adapt to the new school.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about how you adapted to a new city or school.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to change your behavior or something else to fit a new situation'?
usage_tip: 'Adapt' also means change a book into a film: 'adapted from a novel'.

simple_explanation: To change something slightly to make it more correct or suitable. When you adjust something, you make small changes to fix it or make it work better, and when you adjust to a situation, you get used to it gradually.
example_1: Please adjust the volume -- it's too loud.
example_2: He adjusted his tie before the interview.
example_3: It took her a few weeks to adjust to the new job.
collocations: adjust the settings, adjust to, quickly adjust, slightly adjust
action_sequence: Before: the chair is too low → During: move the lever → After: it's at the right height
grammar_pattern: adjust + noun (adjust the seat) / adjust + to + situation (adjust to a new routine)
common_mistake: I need to adjust with the new timetable.
correct_version: I need to adjust to the new timetable.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'adjust TO' when it means get used to something.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: uh-JUST.
etymology: From Old French "ajuster," from Latin "ad-" (to) + "juxta" (near, beside) -- literally "to bring near/close to a correct position."
mnemonic: AD-JUST sounds like "just right" -- to adjust something is to make it just right.
memory_trick: AD-JUST: make it JUST right.
visual_association: A hand turning a small dial to just the right position.
difference_explained: Adjust = make small changes. Adapt = make bigger changes to fit a new situation.
mini_conversation:
A: This chair feels too low.
B: Let me adjust it for you -- there's a lever underneath.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A pilot glances at the controls and mutters, "Just need to adjust our altitude slightly."
news_style_line: News-style: "The central bank adjusted interest rates for the third time this year."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Can you adjust the thermostat? It's a bit cold in here."
mcq_options: A) To completely replace something  B) To make a small change to fix or improve something  C) To destroy something  D) To ignore a problem
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Please ______ your seatbelt before the plane takes off. → adjust
find_and_fix_to_correct: She adjusted quickly at her new role. → She adjusted quickly to her new role. (use "to," not "at")
translate: कृपया अपनी सीट को थोड़ा एडजस्ट कर लीजिए। → Please adjust your seat a little.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about how you adjusted to a new timetable.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to change something slightly to make it more correct or suitable'?
usage_tip: 'Adjust' is very common in Indian English meaning 'manage with less'. Standard English prefers 'manage' or 'make do'.

hindi_meaning: विकसित होना, क्रमिक रूप से बदलना
simple_explanation: To gradually develop or change over a long period of time. When something evolves, it slowly changes and develops into a new or more advanced form, often over a long time -- species evolve, and so do ideas, technology, and relationships.
example_2: Human beings evolved over millions of years.
example_3: Her writing style has evolved a lot since her first book.
collocations: evolve over time, continue to evolve, rapidly evolving, evolve naturally
related_phrasal_verbs: develop over time, grow into, change gradually
action_sequence: Before: a simple form exists → During: it changes slowly over years → After: a new, advanced form appears
grammar_pattern: evolve + (over time/into something) (evolve into a new species)
common_mistake: Mobile phones have evolved to smartphones.
correct_version: Mobile phones have evolved into smartphones.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'evolve INTO' for the new form something becomes.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: ih-VOLV.
etymology: From Latin "evolvere" (e- "out" + volvere "to roll") -- literally "to unroll," extended to mean "to develop gradually."
mnemonic: E-VOLVE sounds like "revolve" -- things evolve slowly, revolving and turning into new forms over time.
memory_trick: E-VOLVE: slowly roll out ('volve' = roll) over time.
visual_association: A simple sketch slowly developing into a detailed, refined drawing.
difference_explained: Develop = grow or improve (can be fast). Evolve = change gradually over a long time.
mini_conversation:
A: Your music style has really changed over the years.
B: Yeah, I guess I've just evolved as an artist.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A scientist looks through a microscope and murmurs, "It's incredible how these organisms have evolved to survive."
news_style_line: News-style: "Experts say the virus continues to evolve, making new variants more resistant."
casual_conversation: Casual: "My taste in music has really evolved since high school."
mcq_options: A) To change suddenly overnight  B) To develop gradually over time  C) To stay exactly the same forever  D) To disappear completely
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Over millions of years, these creatures have ______ to survive in extreme cold. → evolved
find_and_fix_to_correct: The company has evolve a lot since it started. → The company has evolved a lot since it started. (need past participle "evolved" after "has")
translate: समय के साथ भाषाएं धीरे-धीरे विकसित होती हैं। → Languages evolve gradually over time.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about how mobile phones have evolved.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to gradually develop or change over a long period of time'?
usage_tip: 'Evolution' is the noun, used in science for slow change over generations.

simple_explanation: To become visible or to seem to be a certain way. "Appear" describes something coming into view suddenly, or it can mean something seems or looks a certain way, even if it's not confirmed.
example_1: A rainbow appeared after the rain.
example_2: He appeared at the door without warning.
example_3: She appears confident during interviews.
collocations: suddenly appear, appear confident, first appear, appear to be
related_phrasal_verbs: show up, turn up, come into view
where_it_s_used: Nature, first impressions, sudden events, formal writing
action_sequence: Before: nothing is visible → During: something comes into view → After: you can see it
grammar_pattern: appear + adjective (appear nervous) / it appears that + clause
common_mistake: He is appearing very tired today.
correct_version: He appears very tired today.
why_it_s_wrong: When it means 'seem', 'appear' is a state verb and isn't used in the -ing form.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: uh-PEER.
etymology: From Old French "aparoir," from Latin "apparere" (ad- "to" + parere "to come forth") -- literally "to come forth into view."
prefix_root_suffix: ap- (to) + pear (from Latin "parere," to come forth)
mnemonic: AP-PEAR sounds like "a peer" -- imagine a peer suddenly appearing in front of you.
memory_trick: AP-PEAR: something PEARs up — becomes visible.
visual_association: A figure slowly emerging from a fog or shadow.
difference_explained: Seem = give an impression. Appear = the same, slightly more formal, and it also means become visible.
mini_conversation:
A: What was your first impression of the new manager?
B: She appeared quite serious, but she's actually really friendly.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A figure steps out of the shadows and a character gasps, "Where did you just appear from?"
news_style_line: News-style: "New evidence has appeared that could change the outcome of the case."
casual_conversation: Casual: "He just appeared out of nowhere and scared me half to death."
mcq_options: A) To completely vanish  B) To become visible or seem a certain way  C) To hide from view  D) To argue with someone
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Dark clouds began to ______ just before the storm. → appear
find_and_fix_to_correct: She is appearing nervous during the exam. → She appears nervous during the exam. ("appear" meaning "seem" is not typically used in continuous form)
translate: बारिश के बाद आसमान में एक इंद्रधनुष दिखाई दिया। → A rainbow appeared in the sky after the rain.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence using 'appears' to describe how someone looks today.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to become visible or to seem to be a certain way'?
usage_tip: 'Appear' also means come before a court or on TV: 'appear for an exam' is Indian English for 'take an exam'.

simple_explanation: To become impossible to see or to vanish suddenly. When something disappears, it goes out of sight, often suddenly or mysteriously, so you can no longer see or find it.
example_1: The magician made the coin disappear.
example_2: My keys seem to have disappeared.
example_3: The sun disappeared behind the clouds.
collocations: suddenly disappear, completely disappear, disappear without a trace, disappear into
related_phrasal_verbs: vanish into thin air, fade away, go missing
where_it_s_used: Mystery stories, magic, environment, everyday small losses
action_sequence: Before: the object is on the table → During: you look away → After: it's gone
grammar_pattern: disappear + (from/into) + place (disappear into the crowd)
common_mistake: The thief disappeared the money from the drawer.
correct_version: The money disappeared from the drawer.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Disappear' can't take a direct object. The thing itself disappears.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the third syllable: dis-uh-PEER.
spelling_tip: Notice "appear" hidden inside "dis-APPEAR" -- just add the negative prefix "dis-."
etymology: From "dis-" (not, opposite of) + "appear" -- literally "to stop appearing," first recorded in English in the 16th century.
prefix_root_suffix: dis- (not/opposite of) + appear (from Latin "apparere," to come forth)
mnemonic: DIS-APPEAR = the opposite of APPEAR -- when something disappears, it does the opposite of appearing; it vanishes.
memory_trick: DIS + APPEAR = the opposite of appear. One S, two Ps.
visual_association: A puff of smoke where something used to be.
difference_explained: Same meaning. Vanish sounds more sudden and dramatic.
mini_conversation:
A: Where's my phone? I just had it!
B: Things always disappear right when you need them most.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A detective examines an empty room and says, "People don't just disappear without a trace."
news_style_line: News-style: "Local wildlife experts warn that the species may disappear within a decade."
casual_conversation: Casual: "My umbrella keeps disappearing every time it rains."
mcq_options: A) To suddenly become visible  B) To vanish from sight  C) To grow larger  D) To become louder
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The cat seemed to ______ the moment guests arrived. → disappear
find_and_fix_to_correct: He disappeared his wallet somewhere in the house. → His wallet disappeared somewhere in the house. ("disappear" cannot take a direct object)
translate: कोहरे में गाड़ी अचानक गायब हो गई। → The car suddenly disappeared in the fog.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something that disappeared from your room.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to become impossible to see or to vanish suddenly'?
usage_tip: 'Disappear' is often used for people who go missing.

simple_explanation: To happen, especially something that isn't planned. "Occur" is a more formal way to say something happens -- it's often used for events, accidents, or natural phenomena.
example_1: The accident occurred late at night.
example_2: Earthquakes often occur along fault lines.
example_3: It didn't occur to me that I should call first.
collocations: occur frequently, occur naturally, occur to someone, rarely occur
related_phrasal_verbs: come about, take place, crop up
where_it_s_used: Science, news reports, formal writing, accidents
action_sequence: Before: you're thinking of something else → During: an idea arrives → After: you remember it
grammar_pattern: it occurs to + person + that + clause (it occurred to me that...) / event + occurs
common_mistake: An idea occurred in my mind.
correct_version: An idea occurred to me.
why_it_s_wrong: An idea occurs TO a person, not in the mind.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: uh-KUR. Double the "r" before adding "-ed"/"-ing": occurred, occurring.
spelling_tip: Double "c" and double "r" -- "occur," and double the final "r" for "occurred."
etymology: From Latin "occurrere" (ob- "toward" + currere "to run") -- literally "to run toward, meet," later shifted to mean "to happen."
prefix_root_suffix: oc- (variant of "ob-," toward) + cur (from Latin "currere," to run)
mnemonic: OC-CUR sounds like "occur" itself -- imagine an event suddenly CURVING into existence (occurring).
memory_trick: OCCUR → OCCURRED: double R before -ed.
visual_association: A sudden ripple appearing on a still pond's surface.
emotion_feel: Neutral, sometimes surprise ("it occurred to me")
difference_explained: Same meaning. Occur is more formal. Only 'occur' is used for ideas: 'It occurred to me that…'.
mini_conversation:
A: When did the incident happen exactly?
B: It occurred sometime around midnight, according to witnesses.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A scientist studies a readout and murmurs, "This kind of reaction shouldn't occur naturally."
news_style_line: News-style: "The explosion occurred shortly after midnight, officials confirmed."
casual_conversation: Casual: "It never occurred to me that he might be lying."
mcq_options: A) To prevent something  B) To happen or take place  C) To completely disappear  D) To repeat forever
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The problem seems to ______ only when the system is under heavy load. → occur
find_and_fix_to_correct: The event occur every year in the same month. → The event occurs every year in the same month. (third-person singular needs "-s")
translate: यह घटना आधी रात के आसपास घटित हुई। → This incident occurred around midnight.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about an idea that occurred to you recently.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to happen, especially something that isn't planned'?
usage_tip: 'It never occurred to me' = I never thought of it.

simple_explanation: To take place or occur, especially without being planned. "Happen" is the everyday word for something taking place -- an event, accident, or situation that occurs, often unexpectedly.
example_1: What happened at the party last night?
example_2: Accidents can happen anywhere, anytime.
example_3: Nothing much happened while you were away.
collocations: happen suddenly, happen to be, what happened, things happen
related_phrasal_verbs: come about, take place, go on
action_sequence: Before: everything is normal → During: an event takes place → After: people talk about it
grammar_pattern: something + happens (the accident happened) / happen to + verb (I happened to see him)
common_mistake: What is happen with your new job?
correct_version: What is happening with your new job?
why_it_s_wrong: After 'is', use the -ing form: 'is happening'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the first syllable: HAP-uhn.
etymology: From Middle English "happenen," from "hap" (chance, luck), related to "happy" and "perhaps" -- originally about events occurring by chance.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- from Middle English "hap" (chance)
mnemonic: HAPPEN shares roots with "happy" and "perhaps" -- events HAPPEN by chance, just like luck (hap).
memory_trick: HAPPEN has double P, like two events in a row.
visual_association: A domino falling and setting off a chain reaction.
difference_explained: Same meaning. Happen is everyday. Occur is more formal.
mini_conversation:
A: You look upset -- what happened?
B: I don't want to talk about it right now.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character bursts through the door shouting, "You won't believe what just happened!"
news_style_line: News-style: "Investigators are still trying to determine exactly what happened before the crash."
casual_conversation: Casual: "So, what happened with your job interview yesterday?"
mcq_options: A) To take place or occur  B) To completely disappear  C) To stay hidden forever  D) To be planned in detail
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Nobody expected this to ______ so suddenly. → happen
find_and_fix_to_correct: This kind of thing happen a lot around here. → This kind of thing happens a lot around here. (third-person singular needs "-s")
translate: कल रात पार्टी में क्या हुआ था? → What happened at the party last night?
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something funny that happened this week.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to take place or occur, especially without being planned'?
usage_tip: 'What happened?' is the most common way to ask about a problem.

simple_explanation: To be real or to be present in the world. When something exists, it is real and actually present, not imaginary -- it could be a physical object, a species, or even an idea or law.
example_2: Life is believed to exist on very few other planets, if any.
example_3: This law has existed for over a century.
collocations: continue to exist, cease to exist, exist peacefully, barely exist
related_phrasal_verbs: come into being, live on, be present
action_sequence: Before: something comes into being → During: it is present in the world → After: people can see it
grammar_pattern: something/someone + exists (life exists / the problem still exists)
common_mistake: This kind of animal is not existing anymore.
correct_version: This kind of animal no longer exists.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Exist' is a state verb, so it isn't normally used in the -ing form.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: ig-ZIST.
etymology: From Latin "existere/exsistere" (ex- "out" + sistere "to stand, cause to stand") -- literally "to stand out, come into being."
mnemonic: EX-IST sounds like "exist" itself -- to EXIST is to stand out (ex) in reality, to truly be real.
memory_trick: EXIST: something that EXISTS can be pointed at, like an EXIT sign.
visual_association: A single candle flame flickering steadily in the dark, proving it's still there.
difference_explained: Live = be alive, or have your home somewhere. Exist = be real or present at all.
mini_conversation:
A: Do you think aliens really exist?
B: I honestly don't know, but I like to think they do.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A scientist stares at strange readings and whispers, "This shouldn't exist -- not according to anything we know."
news_style_line: News-style: "Researchers confirmed that the ancient species did indeed exist millions of years ago."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Sometimes I wonder if soulmates really exist."
mcq_options: A) To be real or present  B) To completely disappear  C) To pretend something is true  D) To argue about something
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Many rare species no longer ______ due to habitat loss. → exist
find_and_fix_to_correct: This problem is existing since many years. → This problem has existed for many years. (use present perfect "has existed," not present continuous)
translate: कुछ लोग मानते हैं कि भूत सच में अस्तित्व में होते हैं। → Some people believe that ghosts really exist.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about an animal that no longer exists.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to be real or to be present in the world'?
usage_tip: 'Existing customers' = customers you already have.

simple_explanation: To continue to be in the same place, condition, or state. When something remains, it stays the same or stays behind after other things have changed or left, like remaining calm during a crisis or food remaining after a party.
example_1: Please remain seated during the flight.
example_2: The situation remains unclear.
example_3: Only a few guests remained after midnight.
collocations: remain calm, remain unclear, remain silent, remain the same
related_phrasal_verbs: stay behind, hold on, keep going
where_it_s_used: News, formal instructions, emotional composure, unresolved situations
action_sequence: Before: everyone leaves → During: you stay → After: you are still there
grammar_pattern: remain + adjective (remain calm) / remain + in/at + place (remain at the office)
common_mistake: She remained silence during the whole meeting.
correct_version: She remained silent during the whole meeting.
why_it_s_wrong: After 'remain' (like 'be'), use an adjective (silent), not a noun (silence).
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: rih-MAYN.
spelling_tip: R-E-M-A-I-N -- remember "main" at the end, as if the main part stays.
etymology: From Old French "remaindre," from Latin "remanere" (re- "back" + manere "to stay") -- literally "to stay behind."
mnemonic: RE-MAIN sounds like "stay MAIN" -- what remains is the MAIN part left behind after everything else is gone.
memory_trick: RE-MAIN: stay in the MAIN place.
visual_association: A single tree still standing after a storm has passed.
difference_explained: Same meaning. Remain is more formal: 'Please remain seated.'
mini_conversation:
A: How did you stay so calm during the emergency?
B: I just told myself to remain focused and it worked.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A captain speaks calmly over the intercom, "Please remain seated -- we are experiencing some turbulence."
news_style_line: News-style: "Officials say the cause of the fire remains under investigation."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Despite everything that happened, we've remained good friends."
mcq_options: A) To leave immediately  B) To continue to stay or be in the same state  C) To completely change  D) To argue with someone
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The cause of the accident ______ unknown, according to police. → remains
find_and_fix_to_correct: The shop remain open until midnight on weekends. → The shop remains open until midnight on weekends. (third-person singular needs "-s")
translate: तूफान के बावजूद वह शांत बना रहा। → He remained calm despite the storm.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about how you remain calm under pressure.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to continue to be in the same place, condition, or state'?
usage_tip: 'Remaining' = left over: 'the remaining money'.

simple_explanation: To keep doing something without stopping. When you continue something, you keep it going instead of stopping -- this can be an action, a story, a journey, or a habit.
example_2: The rain continued all night.
example_3: She continued studying even after graduation.
collocations: continue to grow, continue working, continue reading, continue as usual
related_phrasal_verbs: carry on, keep going, go on
action_sequence: Before: start an activity → During: keep doing it without stopping → After: still doing it later
grammar_pattern: continue + to + verb / continue + verb-ing (continue to work / continue working)
common_mistake: He continued to talking for another hour.
correct_version: He continued talking for another hour.
why_it_s_wrong: Use either 'continue to + verb' or 'continue + -ing', not a mix of both.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: kuhn-TIN-yoo.
etymology: From Old French "continuer," from Latin "continuare" (from "continuus," uninterrupted, related to "continere," to hold together) -- literally "to keep going without a break."
mnemonic: CON-TIN-UE sounds like "keep going continuously" -- to continue is to keep something going without stopping.
memory_trick: CON-TINUE: keep going ('tinue' like 'tenure').
visual_association: A road stretching endlessly toward the horizon.
difference_explained: Continue = keep going without a break. Resume = start again after a break.
mini_conversation:
A: Should we take a break now?
B: Let's continue for another twenty minutes first.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A narrator's voice echoes, "And so, against all odds, their journey continued."
news_style_line: News-style: "Negotiations are expected to continue into the weekend."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Let's not stop now -- let's continue until we finish the whole chapter."
mcq_options: A) To stop completely  B) To keep doing something without stopping  C) To start something new  D) To forget about something
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Despite the rain, the players decided to ______ the match. → continue
find_and_fix_to_correct: They continue to worked on the project all week. → They continued to work on the project all week. (need past tense "continued," followed by base verb "work")
translate: बारिश पूरी रात जारी रही। → The rain continued all night.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a hobby you want to continue for years.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to keep doing something without stopping'?
usage_tip: 'To be continued…' ends a story episode.

simple_explanation: To no longer continue doing something, or to make something halt. When you stop, you end an action or movement completely -- this can be about yourself stopping an activity, or making something else halt, like traffic or a machine.
example_1: Please stop talking during the movie.
example_2: The bus stopped suddenly at the red light.
example_3: She stopped eating meat two years ago.
collocations: stop immediately, stop completely, stop by, come to a stop
related_phrasal_verbs: stop by, stop off, cut out
action_sequence: Before: an activity is going on → During: it ends → After: nothing is happening
grammar_pattern: stop + verb-ing (stop smoking) vs. stop + to + verb (stop to rest)
common_mistake: He stopped to smoke five years ago.
correct_version: He stopped smoking five years ago.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Stop + -ing' = quit the activity. 'Stop + to' = pause one thing in order to do another.
etymology: From Old English "-stoppian" (found in "forstoppian," to stop up/block), related to Latin "stuppa" (tow/fiber used for plugging) -- originally about blocking or plugging something.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- from Old English "stoppian"
mnemonic: STOP has a hard, sudden sound -- just like a car screeching to a STOP.
memory_trick: STOP → STOPPED: double P.
visual_association: A bright red stop sign at a busy intersection.
confusing_word: stop doing vs stop to do
difference_explained: Stop smoking = no more smoking. Stop to smoke = stop walking or working in order to smoke.
mini_conversation:
A: Can you stop making that noise, please?
B: Sorry, I'll stop right now.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A driver slams the brakes and the car screeches to a complete stop just in time.
news_style_line: News-style: "Officials urged residents to stop using water unnecessarily during the drought."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Can we stop for coffee on the way there?"
mcq_options: A) To begin something new  B) To end or halt an action  C) To speed up  D) To repeat something
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The music suddenly ______ in the middle of the song. → stopped
find_and_fix_to_correct: Please stop to make so much noise. → Please stop making so much noise. (use "stop + verb-ing" to mean quitting an action)
translate: कृपया यहां गाड़ी रोकिए। → Please stop the car here.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a bad habit you stopped.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to no longer continue doing something, or to make something halt'?
usage_tip: 'Stop smoking' = quit. 'Stop to smoke' = pause to have a cigarette. Very different!

hindi_meaning: रुकना, थोड़ी देर के लिए रुकना
simple_explanation: To stop for a short time before continuing. When you pause, you take a brief break from an activity, planning to continue it again soon -- like pausing a video or pausing during a conversation.
example_1: Let's pause the movie for a snack break.
example_2: She paused before answering the difficult question.
example_3: He paused the video to explain the scene.
collocations: pause briefly, pause for a moment, press pause, pause and reflect
related_phrasal_verbs: take a break, hold on, freeze frame
action_sequence: Before: speak or play → During: stop for a moment → After: continue again
grammar_pattern: pause + (before/to) + verb (pause to think) / pause + noun (pause the video)
common_mistake: She paused for think about the answer.
correct_version: She paused to think about the answer.
why_it_s_wrong: To show purpose, use 'to + verb', not 'for + verb'.
pronunciation_tip: Rhymes with "cause" -- the "au" makes a broad "aw" sound.
spelling_tip: P-A-U-S-E -- the "au" combination is key; don't write "pawse."
etymology: From Old French "pause," from Latin "pausa," from Greek "pausis" (a stopping), related to "pause" in music -- originally a brief rest or halt.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- from Greek "pausis" (a stopping)
mnemonic: PAUSE sounds like "cause" -- you PAUSE briefly, because of a good CAUSE, before continuing.
memory_trick: PAUSE has 'PAUS' like the pause button ⏸ on a video.
visual_association: A finger hovering over a pause button on a remote control.
difference_explained: Pause = stop for a short time and then continue. Stop can be permanent.
mini_conversation:
A: Can you pause the show? I need to grab some water.
B: Sure, go ahead -- I'll wait.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A storyteller pauses dramatically before saying, "And that's when everything changed."
news_style_line: News-style: "The company announced it will pause production until the investigation is complete."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Wait, pause for a second -- I didn't catch what you just said."
mcq_options: A) To stop something forever  B) To stop briefly before continuing  C) To speed something up  D) To start something for the first time
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: He ______ for a moment before answering the tricky question. → paused
find_and_fix_to_correct: Let's pause for discuss this later. → Let's pause to discuss this later. (use "to + verb," not "for + verb")
translate: वह जवाब देने से पहले थोड़ी देर रुका। → He paused for a moment before answering.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about when you pause while reading aloud.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to stop for a short time before continuing'?
usage_tip: A short pause while speaking sounds confident, not weak.

hindi_meaning: फिर से शुरू करना, पुनः आरंभ करना
simple_explanation: To start doing something again after stopping for a while. When you resume something, you begin it again after a pause or interruption, picking up exactly where you left off.
example_1: We will resume the meeting after lunch.
example_2: The match resumed after the rain stopped.
example_3: She resumed her studies after taking a year off.
collocations: resume normal, resume work, resume shortly, resume after a break
related_phrasal_verbs: pick up where you left off, carry on, start again
action_sequence: Before: stop for a break → During: the break ends → After: start again from where you stopped
grammar_pattern: resume + noun/verb-ing (resume work / resume working)
common_mistake: The class will resume to start at 9 AM.
correct_version: The class will resume at 9 AM.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Resume' already means 'start again', so 'to start' repeats the idea.
pronunciation_tip: rih-ZOOM -- don't confuse with the noun "résumé" (REZ-oo-may), which refers to a CV.
spelling_tip: R-E-S-U-M-E, no accent marks needed for this verb (unlike the noun "résumé").
etymology: From Old French "resumer," from Latin "resumere" (re- "again" + sumere "to take up") -- literally "to take up again."
prefix_root_suffix: re- (again) + sume (from Latin "sumere," to take up)
mnemonic: RE-SUME sounds like "re-assume" -- to resume is to take up (assume) an activity again.
memory_trick: RE-SUME: 're' = again, 'sume' = take up.
visual_association: A paused video suddenly playing again from the exact same spot.
difference_explained: Resume (re-ZYOOM) = start again. Résumé (REZ-yoo-may) = a CV.
mini_conversation:
A: Is the concert going to continue after this delay?
B: Yes, they said it will resume in about ten minutes.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A referee blows the whistle and shouts, "Alright everyone, let's resume the match!"
news_style_line: News-style: "Train services are expected to resume by tomorrow morning."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Let's take a five-minute break and resume the discussion after."
mcq_options: A) To stop something permanently  B) To start something again after a pause  C) To cancel an event  D) To slow something down
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Trading on the stock exchange will ______ tomorrow morning. → resume
find_and_fix_to_correct: We will resume back the lesson tomorrow. → We will resume the lesson tomorrow. ("resume" already means "start again," so "back" is unnecessary)
translate: बारिश रुकने के बाद मैच फिर से शुरू हुआ। → The match resumed after the rain stopped.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about when classes resume after a holiday.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to start doing something again after stopping for a while'?
usage_tip: Résumé (with accents) is a CV. The verb re-SUME and the noun RÉ-su-mé are said differently.

simple_explanation: To say or do something again. When you repeat something, you do or say it a second time, often to make sure it's understood or remembered.
example_2: The teacher repeated the instructions twice.
example_3: Please don't repeat this to anyone.
collocations: repeat yourself, repeat the process, constantly repeat, repeat after me
action_sequence: Before: say something → During: say it once more → After: the listener understands
grammar_pattern: repeat + noun/clause (repeat the question / repeat what you said)
common_mistake: Can you repeat again what you said?
correct_version: Can you repeat what you said?
why_it_s_wrong: 'Repeat' already means 'say again', so 'again' is extra.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: rih-PEET.
etymology: From Old French "repeter," from Latin "repetere" (re- "again" + petere "to seek, aim at") -- literally "to seek again."
mnemonic: RE-PEAT sounds like "re-beat" -- to repeat is to beat the same rhythm again and again.
memory_trick: RE-PEAT: 're' = again.
visual_association: An echo bouncing back and forth between two mountains.
difference_explained: Repeat = say or do again. Revise = study again to learn, or change to improve.
mini_conversation:
A: Sorry, I didn't hear you clearly.
B: No problem, let me repeat that for you.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A teacher raises a hand and says firmly, "I will not repeat myself again -- listen the first time."
news_style_line: News-style: "Officials warned that history could repeat itself if the warnings are ignored."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Wait, can you repeat that last part? I got a bit confused."
mcq_options: A) To say or do something again  B) To forget something completely  C) To disagree with someone  D) To finish something for the first time
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The teacher had to ______ the instructions three times. → repeat
find_and_fix_to_correct: Please repeat me the question again. → Please repeat the question for me. ("repeat" takes the thing being repeated as the object, not the person; use "for me" instead)
translate: क्या आप अपना सवाल दोबारा दोहरा सकते हैं? → Can you repeat your question again?
write_your_own_sentence: Write a polite sentence asking someone to repeat an instruction.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to say or do something again'?
usage_tip: 'Could you repeat that, please?' is the polite version of 'What?'.

simple_explanation: To stop something from happening. When you prevent something, you take action ahead of time to make sure a problem, accident, or unwanted event does not happen.
example_1: Wearing a helmet can prevent serious injury.
example_2: Regular exercise can prevent many health problems.
example_3: The fence was built to prevent accidents.
collocations: prevent from, help prevent, prevent disease, prevent accidents
related_phrasal_verbs: stop from, guard against, head off
action_sequence: Before: see a problem coming → During: take action early → After: the problem never happens
grammar_pattern: prevent + noun + from + verb-ing (prevent him from leaving)
common_mistake: The rain prevented us to go outside.
correct_version: The rain prevented us from going outside.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'prevent someone FROM + -ing', not 'to + verb'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: prih-VENT.
spelling_tip: P-R-E-V-E-N-T -- remember "vent" at the end, like preventing something from venting out.
etymology: From Latin "praevenire" (prae- "before" + venire "to come") -- literally "to come before," originally meaning "to anticipate," later shifted to "to stop something from happening."
mnemonic: PRE-VENT = to act BEFORE (pre) something can happen (vent/come out) -- stopping it in advance.
memory_trick: PRE-VENT: act BEFORE ('pre') something comes.
visual_association: A raised hand blocking a falling object before it hits the ground.
difference_explained: Prevent = stop something from happening. Avoid = keep away from it.
mini_conversation:
A: How can we prevent this problem from happening again?
B: We need better training and clearer safety rules.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A guard rushes forward, arms out, shouting, "Stop! We have to prevent this from happening!"
news_style_line: News-style: "New safety measures are being introduced to prevent further accidents at the site."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Wearing sunscreen helps prevent skin damage from the sun."
mcq_options: A) To cause something to happen  B) To stop something from happening  C) To ignore a problem  D) To repeat an action
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Washing your hands regularly can help ______ the spread of germs. → prevent
find_and_fix_to_correct: The traffic prevented her from arrive on time. → The traffic prevented her from arriving on time. (need "-ing" form after "from")
translate: नियमित व्यायाम कई बीमारियों को रोक सकता है। → Regular exercise can prevent many diseases.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about how you prevent a cold in winter.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to stop something from happening'?
usage_tip: 'Prevention is better than cure.'

simple_explanation: To make something happen, usually something bad. When something causes an event, it is the reason that event happens -- often used for problems, accidents, or effects.
example_1: Smoking can cause serious health problems.
example_2: Heavy rain caused flooding in the city.
example_3: Stress can cause headaches and sleep problems.
collocations: cause damage, cause problems, cause concern, root cause
action_sequence: Before: something happens → During: it leads to a result → After: the result is seen
grammar_pattern: cause + noun (cause a delay) / cause + person/thing + to + verb (cause it to break)
common_mistake: The accident caused for many injuries.
correct_version: The accident caused many injuries.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Cause' takes a direct object, with no 'for'.
pronunciation_tip: Rhymes with "pause" -- the "au" makes a broad "aw" sound.
etymology: From Old French "cause," from Latin "causa" (reason, motive, purpose) -- the same root as "because" and "excuse."
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- from Latin "causa" (reason)
mnemonic: CAUSE sounds like "because" -- the CAUSE is the "because" reason behind something happening.
memory_trick: CAUSE → because: the cause is the 'because'.
visual_association: A single domino tipping over and starting a chain of falling pieces.
emotion_feel: Neutral, often concern when the cause is negative
difference_explained: Cause = what makes something happen (often physical). Reason = why someone did something, or the explanation.
related_words: trigger, result in, produce, lead to
mini_conversation:
A: Do you know what caused the power outage?
B: They said a storm caused a tree to fall on the power lines.
everyday_scene: Everyday: An investigator points to burnt wires and says, "This is what caused the fire to start."
news_style_line: News-style: "Experts say pollution is a major cause of respiratory illness in the city."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I think stress at work is causing my headaches lately."
mcq_options: A) To stop something from happening  B) To make something happen  C) To completely ignore something  D) To repair a problem
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Poor sleep can ______ trouble concentrating during the day. → cause
find_and_fix_to_correct: The strong wind caused to the tree fall down. → The strong wind caused the tree to fall down. (use "cause + object + to + verb," no extra "to" before the object)
translate: तेज़ बारिश ने शहर में बाढ़ का कारण बना। → Heavy rain caused flooding in the city.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about what causes traffic jams in your city.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to make something happen, usually something bad'?
usage_tip: 'Cause' as a noun: 'the cause of the fire'. 'Cause someone to do' = make them do.

simple_explanation: To have an influence or impact on something or someone. When something affects you, it changes or influences you in some way -- your mood, health, decisions, or performance can all be affected by different things.
example_1: The bad weather affected our travel plans.
example_2: Lack of sleep can affect your concentration.
example_3: The news deeply affected the whole community.
collocations: affect negatively, greatly affect, directly affect, be affected by
action_sequence: Before: a decision is made → During: it changes things → After: people feel the results
grammar_pattern: affect + noun (affect your health) -- always a transitive verb, no preposition
common_mistake: This decision will effect our future plans.
correct_version: This decision will affect our future plans.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Affect' is the verb; 'effect' is usually the noun.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: uh-FEKT.
spelling_tip: Remember "A is for Action" -- "AFFECT" is usually the verb (an action); "EFFECT" is usually the noun (the End result).
etymology: From Latin "afficere" (ad- "to" + facere "to do, make") -- literally "to do something to," influencing a state or condition.
mnemonic: AF-FECT sounds like "affect an action" -- AFFECT is the ACTION (verb) of influencing something.
memory_trick: A for Action (verb): Affect. E for End result (noun): Effect.
visual_association: A stone dropped into water, sending ripples outward that touch everything nearby.
difference_explained: Affect = verb (to influence). Effect = noun (the result).
mini_conversation:
A: How has the move affected the kids?
B: They've adjusted well, but it did affect their sleep for a while.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A doctor explains gently, "This medication may affect your appetite for a few days."
news_style_line: News-style: "The new policy is expected to affect thousands of small businesses nationwide."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I didn't realize how much that comment would affect her."
mcq_options: A) To completely ignore something  B) To have an influence on something  C) To repeat an action  D) To end something permanently
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The loud construction noise really ______ my ability to concentrate. → affects
find_and_fix_to_correct: Her words really effect me deeply. → Her words really affect me deeply. (use "affect," the verb, not "effect," the noun)
translate: नींद की कमी आपके ध्यान केंद्रित करने की क्षमता को प्रभावित कर सकती है। → Lack of sleep can affect your ability to concentrate.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence using both 'affect' and 'effect'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to have an influence or impact on something or someone'?
usage_tip: 'The rain affected the match' / 'The rain had an effect on the match.'

simple_explanation: To have an effect on the way someone thinks, acts, or decides. When you influence someone, your words, actions, or ideas shape their opinions, choices, or behavior, often gradually rather than directly forcing them.
example_1: Good friends can influence you positively.
example_2: Her teacher influenced her decision to study medicine.
example_3: Advertising heavily influences what people buy.
collocations: heavily influence, positively influence, influence decisions, under the influence
action_sequence: Before: hear someone's opinion → During: think about it → After: change your decision
grammar_pattern: influence + person/thing (influence his decision), transitive verb, no preposition
common_mistake: My father influenced on my career choice.
correct_version: My father influenced my career choice.
why_it_s_wrong: As a verb, 'influence' takes a direct object, with no 'on'. The noun takes 'on': 'an influence on me'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the first syllable: IN-floo-uhns.
spelling_tip: Remember "fluence" is related to "fluid" -- influence "flows" from one thing to another.
etymology: From Old French "influence," from Latin "influere" (in- "into" + fluere "to flow") -- originally an astrological term meaning a fluid, invisible power flowing from the stars onto human affairs.
mnemonic: IN-FLU-ENCE sounds like "flow in" -- influence FLOWS INto someone's thinking or actions, like water shaping a riverbank.
memory_trick: IN-FLUENCE: ideas FLOW IN to change you.
visual_association: Ripples spreading outward from a single pebble dropped in water.
difference_explained: Affect = change something in any way. Influence = shape how someone thinks or acts.
mini_conversation:
A: Why did you choose engineering?
B: Honestly, my older brother really influenced that decision.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A mentor places a hand on a student's shoulder and says, "You've influenced more people than you realize."
news_style_line: News-style: "Social media continues to influence how young people form their opinions."
casual_conversation: Casual: "My grandmother really influenced the way I think about family."
mcq_options: A) To completely ignore someone  B) To shape the way someone thinks or acts  C) To forget about something  D) To argue loudly with someone
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Her music teacher greatly ______ her love for singing. → influenced
find_and_fix_to_correct: Social media influence a lot on teenagers today. → Social media influences teenagers a lot today. (need "-s" for third-person singular, and no "on" needed after "influences")
translate: उसके शिक्षक ने उसके करियर के फैसले को बहुत प्रभावित किया। → Her teacher greatly influenced her career decision.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about who influenced your career choice.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to have an effect on the way someone thinks, acts, or decides'?
usage_tip: An 'influencer' is a social media person who affects buyers.

simple_explanation: To be different or to change from one thing to another. When things vary, they are not all the same -- they differ from each other, or they change depending on the situation.
example_1: Prices vary depending on the season.
example_2: Opinions on the topic vary widely among students.
example_3: The recipe can vary based on what ingredients you have.
collocations: vary widely, vary depending on, vary in size, vary greatly
related_phrasal_verbs: differ from, change up, mix it up
action_sequence: Before: look at one shop → During: look at another → After: the prices are different
grammar_pattern: vary + (in/from/depending on) (vary in price / vary from person to person)
common_mistake: The prices vary between shop to shop.
correct_version: The prices vary from shop to shop.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'vary from X to X' or 'vary between X and Y', not 'between X to X'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the first syllable: VAIR-ee, rhymes with "carry" but with a long "A" sound.
spelling_tip: Change "y" to "i" before adding "-es" or "-ed": varies, varied.
etymology: From Old French "varier," from Latin "variare" (from "varius," diverse, changing) -- the same root as "various" and "variety."
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- from Latin "varius" (diverse)
mnemonic: VARY sounds like "various" -- things that VARY come in VARIOUS different forms.
memory_trick: VARY → VARIETY: many different kinds.
visual_association: A row of paint swatches, each a slightly different shade.
difference_explained: Vary (verb) = be different. Very (adverb) = extremely. Same sound, different spelling.
mini_conversation:
A: How much does a taxi usually cost from here?
B: It varies a lot depending on traffic and time of day.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A chef shrugs and says, "Every region cooks this dish differently -- the recipe really does vary."
news_style_line: News-style: "Prices for basic goods vary significantly from region to region."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Honestly, my mood can vary a lot depending on how much sleep I get."
mcq_options: A) To stay exactly the same  B) To be different or change  C) To completely stop  D) To copy something exactly
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The quality of the internet connection can ______ depending on your location. → vary
find_and_fix_to_correct: Her mood vary a lot during the week. → Her mood varies a lot during the week. (third-person singular needs "-s," and "y" changes to "ies")
translate: इस इलाके में मौसम साल भर बदलता रहता है। → The weather varies throughout the year in this region.

usage_tip: 'Prices may vary' is common on menus and product labels.

simple_explanation: To notice something with your eyes. "See" means your eyes catch something without you necessarily trying -- it just happens when your eyes are open.
example_1: I can see the mountains from here.
example_2: Can you see that bird on the roof?
example_3: I saw her yesterday at the market.
collocations: see clearly, see for yourself, see the point, wait and see
related_phrasal_verbs: see off, see through, see to
where_it_s_used: Everyday observation, directions, describing scenery, meetings ('see you later')
action_sequence: Before: open your eyes → During: light enters them → After: you notice the bird
grammar_pattern: see + object (I see a bird.) / see + object + verb-ing (I saw him running.)
common_mistake: I am seeing a bird on the tree right now.
correct_version: I see a bird on the tree right now.
why_it_s_wrong: 'See' is a perception (state) verb, so it doesn't usually take -ing.
spelling_tip: Double "e" at the end -- don't confuse with "sea" (the ocean), which sounds identical.
etymology: Old English "seon," from Proto-Germanic "*sehwan" -- one of the oldest words in English for visual perception.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- "see" is a simple, ancient root word
mnemonic: SEE has two E's like two EYES -- you SEE with your eyes.
memory_trick: SEE → SAW → SEEN: three shapes of one eye.
visual_association: A wide-open eye catching a distant object.
emotion_feel: Neutral, sometimes surprise when you 'see' something suddenly
difference_explained: See = notice with your eyes (no effort). Look (at) = turn your eyes on purpose. Watch = look for some time at something moving.
mini_conversation:
A: Can you see the sign from here?
B: Yes, I can see it clearly now.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A detective squints at the horizon and mutters, "I see something moving out there."
news_style_line: News-style: "Officials say residents should see improvements to the road within a month."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Oh, now I see what you mean!"
mcq_options: A) To touch something  B) To perceive with the eyes  C) To hear a sound  D) To think about something
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: I can ______ the ocean from my balcony. → see
find_and_fix_to_correct: I seeing my friend at the park yesterday. → I saw my friend at the park yesterday.
translate: मुझे यहाँ से पहाड़ दिखते हैं। → I can see the mountains from here.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about what you can see from your window.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to notice something with your eyes'?
usage_tip: 'I see' also means 'I understand'. 'See you!' = goodbye.

simple_explanation: To turn your eyes toward something on purpose. "Look" is an action you choose to do -- you point your eyes at something to see it, often followed by "at."
example_2: She looked out the window before answering.
example_3: Look both ways before crossing the street.
collocations: look at, look for, look like, look forward to
related_phrasal_verbs: look after, look up, look into, look forward to
action_sequence: Before: hear a sound → During: turn your eyes towards it → After: see what it is
grammar_pattern: look + at/for/like + noun (Look at the board. / She looks like her mother.)
common_mistake: Look the board, please.
correct_version: Look at the board, please.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Look' needs 'at' before its object.
pronunciation_tip: Short "oo" sound like in "book": /luk/, not the long "oo" in "moon."
spelling_tip: Two O's -- don't write it as "luk" or with one O.
etymology: Old English "locian" (to use the eyes, gaze), a native Germanic verb.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- a simple native root
mnemonic: LOOK has two O's like two eyes looking straight at something.
memory_trick: LOOK has two O's, like two eyes looking.
visual_association: Two eyes turning sharply toward an arrow pointing at an object.
emotion_feel: Neutral, can carry curiosity or urgency depending on tone
difference_explained: Look = choose to turn your eyes (needs 'at'). See = notice without trying.
mini_conversation:
A: Look! It's starting to snow.
B: Wow, I didn't expect that today.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A pilot points out the window and says, "Look -- there's the runway."
news_style_line: News-style: "Investigators are asking the public to look out for the missing vehicle."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Look, I really think we should leave now."
mcq_options: A) To hear something  B) To direct your eyes at something  C) To touch something gently  D) To smell something
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Please ______ at this document before you sign it. → look
find_and_fix_to_correct: She look at me strange yesterday. → She looked at me strangely yesterday.
translate: कृपया बोर्ड की ओर देखो। → Please look at the board.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence asking a class to look at something.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to turn your eyes toward something on purpose'?
usage_tip: 'Look!' alone is fine. 'Look like' = resemble: 'You look like your father.'

hindi_meaning: देखना (ध्यान से, चलती हुई चीज़ को)
simple_explanation: To look at something moving or happening for a period of time. "Watch" means you keep your eyes on something as it happens or changes, like a movie, a game, or children playing.
example_1: We watched a movie last night.
example_2: He watches the news every morning.
example_3: Watch the children while I answer the phone.
collocations: watch TV, watch a movie, watch out, watch closely
related_phrasal_verbs: watch out, watch over, watch for
action_sequence: Before: switch on the TV → During: look at the moving screen for an hour → After: turn it off
grammar_pattern: watch + object (Watch the game.) / watch + object + verb-ing (I watched him leave.)
common_mistake: I watched the radio this morning.
correct_version: I listened to the radio this morning.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Watch' is only for things you see. For sound, use 'listen to'.
pronunciation_tip: Rhymes with 'notch': /wɒtʃ/ -- the 'a' sounds like 'o,' not like in 'cat.'
spelling_tip: W-A-T-C-H -- don't drop the silent-feeling 'h' at the end.
etymology: Old English "waeccan" (to be awake, keep vigil) -- originally about staying alert, later extended to observing something over time.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- rooted in Old English 'waeccan'
mnemonic: WATCH also means the clock on your wrist -- both meanings are about paying close attention over time.
memory_trick: WATCH a match: it moves, and you follow it.
visual_association: Eyes glued to a screen showing something in motion.
difference_explained: See = notice. Watch = look at something moving for some time. 'I saw a film' (completed) / 'I'm watching a film.'
mini_conversation:
A: What are you doing tonight?
B: Just watching a movie at home.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A parent calls out, "Watch your step, the floor's still wet!"
news_style_line: News-style: "Millions tuned in to watch the historic launch live."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Do you want to watch something together tonight?"
mcq_options: A) To read silently  B) To observe something moving or happening  C) To smell something  D) To write a letter
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: I love to ______ football on weekends. → watch
find_and_fix_to_correct: She watch television every evening. → She watches television every evening.
translate: हमने कल रात एक फ़िल्म देखी। → We watched a movie last night.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a show you watch regularly.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to look at something moving or happening for a period of time'?
usage_tip: 'Watch out!' = be careful. A watch is also a wristwatch.

simple_explanation: To notice sound with your ears. "Hear" happens automatically when a sound reaches your ears -- you don't have to try, unlike "listen," which is active attention.
example_1: I can hear music next door.
example_2: Did you hear that strange noise?
example_3: She heard the phone ring from another room.
collocations: hear about, hear from, hear news, hear a sound
where_it_s_used: Phone calls, news, sounds, gossip ('I heard that...')
action_sequence: Before: a sound happens → During: it reaches your ears → After: you notice it
grammar_pattern: hear + object (I hear a noise.) / hear + object + verb-ing (I heard him singing.)
common_mistake: I am hearing you clearly now.
correct_version: I hear you clearly now.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Hear' is a perception (state) verb, so it doesn't usually take -ing.
pronunciation_tip: Sounds exactly like 'here' -- /hɪər/ -- a classic homophone pair.
spelling_tip: H-E-A-R, not 'here' (a place) -- easy to mix up since they sound identical.
etymology: Old English "hieran," from a common Germanic root meaning to perceive sound.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- a simple root word
mnemonic: HEAR contains EAR -- you HEAR with your EAR.
memory_trick: HEAR has 'EAR' inside.
visual_association: Sound waves traveling straight into an open ear.
emotion_feel: Neutral, sometimes surprise or alertness when a sudden sound is 'heard'
difference_explained: Hear = notice sound, without trying. Listen (to) = pay attention to sound on purpose.
mini_conversation:
A: Did you hear the thunder last night?
B: Yes, it woke me up!
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character freezes and whispers, "Did you hear that?"
news_style_line: News-style: "Officials say they have heard growing concerns from local residents."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I heard you got the job -- congratulations!"
mcq_options: A) To perceive sound with the ears  B) To see something clearly  C) To touch an object  D) To speak loudly
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: I couldn't ______ what she said over the noise. → hear
find_and_fix_to_correct: I hear music yesterday at the party. → I heard music yesterday at the party.
translate: मुझे पड़ोस से संगीत सुनाई दे रहा है। → I can hear music next door.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a sound you hear every morning.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to notice sound with your ears'?
usage_tip: 'I hear you' can mean 'I understand how you feel'. 'Did you hear?' introduces news.

simple_explanation: To pay attention to a sound on purpose. "Listen" means you're actively focusing your attention on a sound, like music, a person talking, or instructions.
example_2: I listen to podcasts on my way to work.
example_3: Listen carefully -- this is important.
collocations: listen to music, listen carefully, listen up, good listener
related_phrasal_verbs: listen up, listen in, listen out for
action_sequence: Before: music starts → During: pay attention to it → After: enjoy the song
grammar_pattern: listen to + noun (Listen to me. / Listen to the radio.)
common_mistake: I listen music every morning.
correct_version: I listen to music every morning.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Listen' needs 'to' before its object.
spelling_tip: Remember the silent T -- many learners mistakenly pronounce or add extra letters around it.
etymology: Old English "hlysnan" (to pay attention with the ears), related to "hlyst" (hearing).
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- rooted in Old English 'hlysnan'
mnemonic: LISTEN and SILENT share the same letters -- you have to be SILENT to truly LISTEN.
memory_trick: LISTEN has a silent T. Its letters rearrange to SILENT: you listen in silence.
visual_association: A person leaning in with a hand cupped near their ear.
emotion_feel: Neutral to caring -- often signals attentiveness or respect
difference_explained: Listen = choose to pay attention (needs 'to'). Hear = sound just reaches you.
mini_conversation:
A: Are you even listening to me?
B: Yes, sorry -- please continue.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A therapist leans forward and says softly, "I'm listening -- take your time."
news_style_line: News-style: "The mayor promised to listen to residents' concerns before the vote."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Listen, I need to tell you something important."
mcq_options: A) To speak loudly  B) To pay attention to sound on purpose  C) To read a book  D) To ignore someone
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: You need to ______ to the instructions before starting the test. → listen
find_and_fix_to_correct: Please listen my advice carefully. → Please listen to my advice carefully.
translate: कृपया शिक्षक की बात ध्यान से सुनो। → Please listen to the teacher carefully.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about the music you listen to while travelling.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to pay attention to a sound on purpose'?
usage_tip: 'Listen!' alone is fine. 'Listen up' = pay attention now.

simple_explanation: To notice something using your nose. "Smell" describes catching a scent with your nose, or describing what scent something gives off, like 'this flower smells sweet.'
example_2: I can smell something burning in the kitchen.
example_3: The flowers smell wonderful in spring.
collocations: smell good, smell bad, smell like, smell of smoke
where_it_s_used: Cooking, nature, warnings (gas leaks, smoke), describing food
action_sequence: Before: food is cooking → During: the smell reaches your nose → After: you feel hungry
grammar_pattern: smell + adjective (It smells nice.) / smell + object (I smell gas.)
common_mistake: This food is smelling delicious.
correct_version: This food smells delicious.
why_it_s_wrong: When 'smell' describes a quality, it's a state verb: 'This smells good.'
spelling_tip: Double L at the end -- 'smell,' not 'smel.'
etymology: Origin uncertain; first recorded in Middle English, possibly related to Low German/Dutch forms -- no confirmed Old English ancestor.
mnemonic: SMELL has two L's like two nostrils working together.
memory_trick: SMELL has double L, like two nostrils.
visual_association: A nose wrinkling as it catches a scent drifting through the air.
emotion_feel: Varies -- pleasant (fresh bread) or unpleasant (smoke) depending on context
difference_explained: Smell GOOD = has a nice smell (adjective after 'smell'). 'Smell well' is rare and means your nose works well.
mini_conversation:
A: What's that amazing smell?
B: I think someone's baking bread downstairs.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A chef closes her eyes over the pot and says, "Mmm, now that smells right."
news_style_line: News-style: "Residents reported an unusual smell near the factory this week."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Can you smell that? I think something's burning."
mcq_options: A) To perceive with the nose  B) To perceive with the ears  C) To perceive with the eyes  D) To perceive with the tongue
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The kitchen ______ of fresh bread this morning. → smells
find_and_fix_to_correct: This perfume is smelling really nice. → This perfume smells really nice.
translate: यह कॉफ़ी बहुत बढ़िया महक रही है। → This coffee smells amazing.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a smell that reminds you of home.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to notice something using your nose'?
usage_tip: 'Something smells fishy' = something seems suspicious.

simple_explanation: To try food or drink with your mouth to notice its flavor. "Taste" means using your tongue to check flavor, or describing how something tastes, like 'this soup tastes salty.'
example_2: She tasted the cake before serving it.
example_3: This dish tastes a bit too spicy for me.
collocations: taste good, taste bad, taste like, taste test
where_it_s_used: Cooking, restaurants, wine tasting, describing food
action_sequence: Before: put food in your mouth → During: notice its flavour → After: decide if you like it
grammar_pattern: taste + adjective (It tastes sweet.) / taste + object (I tasted the sauce.)
common_mistake: This cake is tasting really good.
correct_version: This cake tastes really good.
why_it_s_wrong: When 'taste' describes flavour, it's a state verb: 'This tastes good.'
spelling_tip: T-A-S-T-E -- silent 'e' at the end makes the 'a' say its name.
etymology: From Old French "taster" (to touch, try, taste), ultimately from Latin "taxare" (to feel, evaluate).
word_family: taste (n., flavor or preference), tasty (adj.), tasteless (adj.)
mnemonic: TASTE rhymes with WAIST -- imagine tightening your WAIST-band after TASTING too much good food.
memory_trick: TASTE has 'TA' like the tip of your tongue.
visual_association: A tongue sticking out to sample a spoonful of food.
emotion_feel: Often pleasant curiosity, sometimes disappointment if the taste is bad
difference_explained: 'It tastes good' (verb + adjective). 'It's tasty' (adjective). Both are correct.
mini_conversation:
A: Can I taste a bit of your pasta?
B: Sure, go ahead -- tell me what you think!
everyday_scene: Everyday: A judge on a cooking show closes her eyes and says, "Now that's a taste I won't forget."
news_style_line: News-style: "The new bakery is already known for bread that tastes just like homemade."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Here, taste this and tell me if it needs more salt."
mcq_options: A) To perceive flavor with the tongue  B) To perceive sound with the ears  C) To perceive light with the eyes  D) To perceive texture with the hands
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Could you ______ the soup and see if it needs more salt? → taste
find_and_fix_to_correct: I am tasting this coffee is bitter. → This coffee tastes bitter.
translate: क्या मैं सूप चख सकता हूँ? → Can I taste the soup?
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about how your favourite dish tastes.
