reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to try food or drink with your mouth to notice its flavor'?
usage_tip: 'It tastes of mango' / 'It tastes like mango' are both fine.

simple_explanation: To put your hand or fingers on something. "Touch" means making physical contact with something using your hand or skin, or, in a softer sense, moving someone emotionally.
example_2: She touched the fabric to check its quality.
example_3: His speech touched everyone in the room.
collocations: touch base, keep in touch, personal touch, don't touch
related_phrasal_verbs: touch on, touch up, touch down
where_it_s_used: Physical warnings, art/fabric, emotional reactions, staying in contact ('keep in touch')
action_sequence: Before: reach out a hand → During: put fingers on the surface → After: feel its texture
grammar_pattern: touch + object (Touch the surface gently.)
common_mistake: Please don't touching the wet paint.
correct_version: Please don't touch the wet paint.
why_it_s_wrong: After 'don't', use the base verb.
pronunciation_tip: Rhymes with 'much': /tʌtʃ/ -- the 'ou' sounds like a short 'u.'
spelling_tip: T-O-U-C-H -- the 'ou' is tricky since it doesn't sound like 'ou' in 'out.'
etymology: From Old French "tochier," possibly ultimately imitative in origin -- describing contact between surfaces.
word_family: touch (n., a light contact or feeling), touching (adj., emotional), touchy (adj., sensitive)
mnemonic: TOUCH rhymes with MUCH -- you don't need MUCH pressure to TOUCH something gently.
memory_trick: TOUCH: a soft 'ch' at the end, like fingers on a surface.
visual_association: A fingertip gently pressing onto a smooth surface.
emotion_feel: Ranges from cautious (physical warning) to warm (emotional sense)
difference_explained: Touch = put your hand on something. Feel = notice through touch, or experience an emotion.
mini_conversation:
A: Wow, that story really touched me.
B: I know -- I got emotional too.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A father gently says, "Careful, don't touch the wires."
news_style_line: News-style: "The charity's work has touched thousands of families this year."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Can I touch the fabric? It looks so soft."
mcq_options: A) To make physical contact with something  B) To listen carefully  C) To look closely at something  D) To smell something
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Please don't ______ the wet paint on the wall. → touch
find_and_fix_to_correct: She touch the baby's hand softly. → She touched the baby's hand softly.
translate: कृपया गीले पेंट को मत छुओ। → Please don't touch the wet paint.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something children shouldn't touch.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to put your hand or fingers on something'?
usage_tip: 'Keep in touch' = stay in contact. 'I'm touched' = I'm emotionally moved.

simple_explanation: To notice something through touch or to experience an emotion. "Feel" describes physical sensations (the texture of something) or emotional states (happy, tired, nervous).
example_2: She felt nervous before the interview.
example_3: Feel this blanket -- it's so soft.
collocations: feel tired, feel free, feel like, feel better
related_phrasal_verbs: feel up to, feel for, feel out
where_it_s_used: Emotions, health, texture, opinions ('I feel that...')
action_sequence: Before: something happens → During: emotion rises inside → After: you say 'I feel happy'
grammar_pattern: feel + adjective (I feel happy.) / feel like + noun/gerund (I feel like eating pizza.)
common_mistake: I am feeling happy today because of good weather.
correct_version: I feel happy today because of the good weather.
why_it_s_wrong: For emotions, the simple form is usual. 'I'm feeling' is also common in speech for temporary states.
spelling_tip: F-E-E-L -- double E, and remember its past tense is irregular: 'felt,' not 'feeled.'
etymology: Old English "felan," from a Germanic root meaning to perceive by touch or emotion.
mnemonic: FEEL rhymes with HEAL -- how you FEEL often affects how fast you HEAL.
memory_trick: FEEL → FELT, like KNEEL → KNELT.
visual_association: A hand resting over a heart, or fingers brushing a soft fabric.
emotion_feel: Varies widely -- the word itself names the emotion being described
difference_explained: Feel (long 'ee') = experience. Fill (short 'i') = make full.
mini_conversation:
A: How are you feeling today?
B: A bit better than yesterday, thanks.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character sits down heavily and admits, "Honestly, I feel exhausted."
news_style_line: News-style: "Many workers say they feel more confident about the job market this year."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I feel a little nervous about the exam tomorrow."
mcq_options: A) To experience a sensation or emotion  B) To speak clearly  C) To read quickly  D) To watch television
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: I ______ really tired after the long trip. → feel
find_and_fix_to_correct: She feels happiness yesterday about the news. → She felt happy yesterday about the news.
translate: आज मैं थका हुआ महसूस कर रहा हूँ। → I feel tired today.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about how you feel on Monday mornings.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to notice something through touch or to experience an emotion'?
usage_tip: 'How are you feeling?' is natural when someone is ill.

simple_explanation: To become aware of something, often something small. "Notice" means your attention catches something, even something subtle, like a new haircut or a small change.
example_1: I notice you got a new haircut.
example_2: Did you notice the price has gone up?
example_3: Nobody noticed the mistake in the report.
collocations: notice a change, hardly notice, notice something odd
related_phrasal_verbs: take notice of, sit up and take notice
action_sequence: Before: look around → During: see something unusual → After: it catches your attention
grammar_pattern: notice + object/clause (I noticed the door was open.)
common_mistake: I am noticing something strange about him lately.
correct_version: I've noticed something strange about him lately.
why_it_s_wrong: For an observation that continues up to now, the present perfect ('I've noticed') fits better than -ing.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the first syllable: NOH-tis, /ˈnəʊtɪs/.
etymology: From Old French "notice," from Latin "notitia" (knowledge, being known), related to "notus" (known).
prefix_root_suffix: not(e)- = root (Latin notitia, to know) + -ice = noun/verb-forming pattern
mnemonic: NOTICE contains 'NOTE' -- when you NOTICE something, you mentally make a NOTE of it.
memory_trick: NOTICE: a NOTICE board is where you notice announcements.
visual_association: A magnifying glass hovering over a small detail others walked past.
difference_explained: See = use your eyes. Notice = become aware of something, often small or new.
mini_conversation:
A: Did you notice anything different about the office?
B: Yeah, they repainted the walls!
everyday_scene: Everyday: A detective murmurs, "I noticed the footprints stopped right here."
news_style_line: News-style: "Analysts noticed a sharp change in spending patterns last quarter."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I noticed you seemed quiet today -- is everything okay?"
mcq_options: A) To ignore completely  B) To become aware of something  C) To forget something  D) To argue about something
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: I didn't ______ that the store had closed early. → notice
find_and_fix_to_correct: She notice the mistake too late. → She noticed the mistake too late.
translate: क्या तुमने ध्यान दिया कि कीमत बढ़ गई है? → Did you notice that the price has gone up?
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something small you noticed today.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to become aware of something, often something small'?
usage_tip: 'Notice period' = the time you must work after resigning.

simple_explanation: To watch something carefully and closely. "Observe" means paying close, careful attention to something, often to learn or study it -- it also can mean following a rule ('observe the law').
example_1: Scientists observe the stars every night.
example_2: The teacher observed how the students solved the problem.
example_3: We observed the birds building their nest.
collocations: observe closely, observe carefully, observe a rule, under observation
action_sequence: Before: set up the experiment → During: watch every change closely → After: write notes
grammar_pattern: observe + object (Observe the results.) / observe + object + verb-ing (She observed him working.)
common_mistake: The scientist is observing the experiment since morning.
correct_version: The scientist has been observing the experiment since morning.
why_it_s_wrong: An action continuing from a past time to now needs the present perfect continuous.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: ob-ZURV, /əbˈzɜːrv/.
spelling_tip: O-B-S-E-R-V-E -- remember the silent 'e' at the end.
etymology: From Latin "observare" (to watch, guard, pay attention to), from "ob-" (toward) + "servare" (to keep, watch).
prefix_root_suffix: ob- = toward + serv(e) = to watch/keep -- literally 'to watch toward'
mnemonic: OBSERVE has 'SERVE' inside it -- scientists SERVE the truth by carefully OBSERVING it.
memory_trick: OB-SERVE: serve the eye, watch closely.
visual_association: A researcher peering through a magnifying glass at a chart.
emotion_feel: Neutral -- suggests focus, curiosity, or professional attentiveness
difference_explained: Watch = look at for some time. Observe = watch carefully to learn something.
mini_conversation:
A: What did you observe during the experiment?
B: The liquid changed color after five minutes.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A scientist in a lab coat notes quietly, "Let's observe how it reacts overnight."
news_style_line: News-style: "Officials will observe the election process to ensure fairness."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I've been observing that he seems stressed lately."
mcq_options: A) To ignore something  B) To watch something carefully  C) To touch something gently  D) To forget something quickly
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Researchers ______ the animals' behavior for several months. → observed
find_and_fix_to_correct: Please observe to the traffic rules while driving. → Please observe the traffic rules while driving.
translate: वैज्ञानिक हर रात तारों का अवलोकन करते हैं। → Scientists observe the stars every night.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about an animal you have observed carefully.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to watch something carefully and closely'?
usage_tip: 'Observe' also means follow a rule or festival: 'observe a fast'.

simple_explanation: To look at something for a long time without looking away. "Stare" means fixing your eyes on someone or something for a long time, often without blinking -- and it can feel rude if directed at a person.
example_2: He stared at the painting for several minutes.
example_3: She caught him staring at her phone.
collocations: stare blankly, stare in disbelief, stare at, stare into space
action_sequence: Before: see something strange → During: keep looking without blinking → After: look away at last
grammar_pattern: stare at + object (She stared at the screen.)
common_mistake: He stared the painting for a long time.
correct_version: He stared at the painting for a long time.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Stare' needs 'at' before its object.
spelling_tip: S-T-A-R-E -- don't confuse with 'star' (in the sky); the silent 'e' changes the sound.
etymology: Old English "starian" (to gaze fixedly), from a Germanic root related to being rigid or fixed.
mnemonic: STARE looks like STAR -- imagine STARING up at a bright STAR without blinking.
memory_trick: STARE: like looking at a STAR for a long time.
visual_association: Wide, unblinking eyes fixed on one spot.
difference_explained: Stare = look for a long time. Glance = look very quickly.
mini_conversation:
A: Why is everyone staring at us?
B: I think you still have paint on your shirt.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character freezes mid-sentence, staring blankly at the door that just opened.
news_style_line: News-style: "Witnesses said they simply stared in shock as the events unfolded."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Stop staring at me, it's creepy!"
mcq_options: A) To glance quickly  B) To look fixedly for a long time  C) To close your eyes  D) To listen carefully
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: It's impolite to ______ at people you don't know. → stare
find_and_fix_to_correct: She was staring the stars all night. → She was staring at the stars all night.
translate: अजनबियों की तरफ़ मत घूरो। → Don't stare at strangers.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something you once stared at in surprise.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to look at something for a long time without looking away'?
usage_tip: Staring at people is considered rude in many cultures.

simple_explanation: To look at something very quickly. "Glance" means taking a fast, brief look, often to check something quickly before moving your attention elsewhere.
example_2: He glanced at the menu before ordering.
example_3: I glanced over the report but didn't read it fully.
collocations: glance at, quick glance, glance around, glance up
where_it_s_used: Checking time, quick reviews, nervousness, brief eye contact
action_sequence: Before: hold the letter → During: look at it for a second → After: put it down
grammar_pattern: glance at + object (He glanced at the clock.)
common_mistake: She glanced the letter quickly and put it down.
correct_version: She glanced at the letter quickly and put it down.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Glance' needs 'at' before its object.
spelling_tip: G-L-A-N-C-E -- don't drop the silent 'e' at the end.
etymology: From Old French "glacier" (to glide, slip), related to the idea of a quick, gliding movement of the eyes.
mnemonic: A GLANCE is as quick as a GLANCING blow -- it just touches the surface and moves on.
memory_trick: GLANCE: like a lance thrown past — quick.
visual_association: Eyes flicking briefly toward something, then away again.
difference_explained: Glance = you look quickly on purpose. Glimpse = you see something only for a moment, often by chance.
mini_conversation:
A: Can you glance at this email before I send it?
B: Sure, give me one second.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A spy glances over her shoulder before slipping into the alley.
news_style_line: News-style: "A quick glance at the numbers shows spending is up this quarter."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Just glance at this real quick -- does it look okay?"
mcq_options: A) To look for a long time  B) To take a quick look  C) To listen carefully  D) To close your eyes
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: He ______ at his phone during the meeting. → glanced
find_and_fix_to_correct: She glance at the schedule before leaving. → She glanced at the schedule before leaving.
translate: उसने अपनी घड़ी की तरफ़ सरसरी नज़र डाली। → She glanced at her watch.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about what you glance at before leaving home.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to look at something very quickly'?
usage_tip: 'At a glance' = with one quick look.

simple_explanation: To look quickly and often secretly, especially through a small gap. "Peek" means sneaking a quick look at something, often when you're curious or not really supposed to look, like peeking through a door.
example_1: The kids peeked through the curtains.
example_2: She peeked inside the box before her birthday.
example_3: He peeked around the corner to see who was there.
collocations: peek inside, peek through, sneak a peek, peek around
where_it_s_used: Surprises, curiosity, children's games, sneaking a look
action_sequence: Before: see a closed box → During: open it a little and look inside → After: close it quickly
grammar_pattern: peek at/into/through + object (She peeked through the keyhole.)
common_mistake: He peeked the box to see what's inside.
correct_version: He peeked into the box to see what was inside.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Peek' usually needs a preposition like 'into', 'at' or 'through'.
spelling_tip: P-E-E-K -- don't confuse with 'peak' (a mountain top), which sounds the same.
etymology: Origin uncertain; recorded in Middle English, possibly related to "peep" -- both describe a quick, often secretive, look.
mnemonic: PEEK sounds like PEAK -- imagine PEEKING over the PEAK of a hill to see what's on the other side.
memory_trick: PEEK: two E's, like two eyes peeking through a gap.
visual_association: One eye peering through a narrow gap in a door.
difference_explained: Peek = a quick secret look. Peak = the top of a mountain, or the highest point.
mini_conversation:
A: Can I peek at my present now?
B: No way, you have to wait until tomorrow!
everyday_scene: Everyday: A child peeks around the doorframe, giggling before darting away.
news_style_line: News-style: "Fans got a peek at the new stadium design this week."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Just let me peek at your notes for a second."
mcq_options: A) To stare openly  B) To take a quick, often secret look  C) To close your eyes tightly  D) To listen carefully
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: She couldn't resist a quick ______ inside the gift bag. → peek
find_and_fix_to_correct: He peeked in the room quickly and secretive. → He peeked into the room quickly and secretly.
translate: बच्चों ने पर्दों के पीछे से झांका। → The kids peeked through the curtains.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a time you peeked at a surprise.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to look quickly and often secretly, especially through a small gap'?
usage_tip: 'Sneak peek' = an early, short look at something.

simple_explanation: To feel or realize something without being told directly. "Sense" as a verb means picking up on something intuitively -- like feeling tension in a room without anyone saying anything.
example_2: She sensed his nervousness before he spoke.
example_3: Animals can sense danger before it happens.
collocations: sense danger, sense trouble, sense tension, sense something wrong
action_sequence: Before: someone is quiet → During: you notice small signs → After: you feel something is wrong
grammar_pattern: sense + object/clause (I sensed that something had changed.)
common_mistake: I am sensing that he is upset with me.
correct_version: I sense that he is upset with me.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Sense' is usually used in the simple form, not -ing.
spelling_tip: S-E-N-S-E -- remember it's the same word as the noun (the five senses).
etymology: From Latin "sensus" (feeling, perception), from "sentire" (to feel) -- also the source of English "sensation" and "sentiment."
prefix_root_suffix: sens(e) = root (Latin sentire, to feel) -- no separate prefix/suffix here
word_family: sense (n., a feeling or ability to perceive), sensitive (adj.), sensible (adj.)
mnemonic: SENSE sounds like CENTS -- your intuition doesn't cost CENTS, but it's still valuable when you SENSE something.
memory_trick: SENSE: your five SENSES tell you things without words.
visual_association: A hand hovering just above the skin, feeling warmth without touching.
emotion_feel: Often unease, alertness, or quiet intuition
difference_explained: Feel = experience an emotion or touch. Sense = become aware of something without being told.
mini_conversation:
A: You seem worried.
B: I don't know, I just sense something's off today.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character pauses at the door and says quietly, "I sense we're not alone."
news_style_line: News-style: "Economists sense growing caution among consumers this quarter."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I could just sense that something was different about him."
mcq_options: A) To ignore a feeling  B) To intuitively realize or feel something  C) To speak about something loudly  D) To measure something exactly
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: As soon as she walked in, she could ______ the tension in the room. → sense
find_and_fix_to_correct: She sense that something was wrong immediately. → She sensed that something was wrong immediately.
translate: मुझे कुछ गड़बड़ महसूस हो रही है। → I sense something is wrong.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a time you sensed something was wrong.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to feel or realize something without being told directly'?
usage_tip: 'It makes sense' = it's logical.

simple_explanation: To become aware of or understand something, often in a particular way. "Perceive" means noticing and interpreting something -- how you understand or see a situation, which can be different from how someone else sees it.
example_2: She perceived a hint of sarcasm in his tone.
example_3: Customers perceive the brand as reliable.
collocations: perceive as, widely perceived, perceive a threat, commonly perceived
action_sequence: Before: see how someone acts → During: form an idea → After: see them in a certain way
grammar_pattern: perceive + object + as + noun/adjective (They perceived him as arrogant.)
common_mistake: I perceived him an honest man.
correct_version: I perceived him as an honest man.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'perceive someone/something AS…', not without 'as'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: per-SEEV, /pərˈsi:v/.
spelling_tip: P-E-R-C-E-I-V-E -- remember the tricky 'ei' (like 'receive'): 'i before e except after c.'
etymology: From Old French "perceivre," from Latin "percipere" (to seize thoroughly), from "per-" (thoroughly) + "capere" (to take, seize).
prefix_root_suffix: per- = thoroughly + ceive (from Latin capere) = to take/seize -- literally 'to take in fully'
mnemonic: PERCEIVE has 'CEIVE' like RECEIVE -- when you PERCEIVE something, your mind RECEIVES an impression of it.
memory_trick: PERCEIVE: 'I before E except after C' — perCEIve.
visual_association: A pair of tinted glasses shaping how a scene is seen.
difference_explained: See = notice with your eyes. Perceive = understand or view in a particular way (formal).
mini_conversation:
A: How do people perceive the new policy?
B: Most seem to perceive it as a positive change.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A narrator explains, "How we perceive fear says more about us than the danger itself."
news_style_line: News-style: "Surveys show the public increasingly perceives the economy as unstable."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I think people perceive him as more confident than he actually feels."
mcq_options: A) To ignore completely  B) To become aware of or interpret something  C) To forget quickly  D) To touch physically
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Many customers ______ the brand as trustworthy and reliable. → perceive
find_and_fix_to_correct: He is perceive as a hard worker by his team. → He is perceived as a hard worker by his team.
translate: अलग-अलग लोग जोखिम को अलग-अलग तरह से समझते हैं। → People perceive risk differently.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about how people perceive your city.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to become aware of or understand something, often in a particular way'?
usage_tip: 'Perception' is how people see you: 'public perception'.

simple_explanation: To see something for a very short moment. "Glimpse" describes catching a brief, partial view of something -- you see it, but only for a second, not fully or clearly.
example_1: I glimpsed the celebrity's car passing by.
example_2: We glimpsed the mountains through the clouds.
example_3: She glimpsed her reflection in the shop window.
collocations: catch a glimpse of, brief glimpse, fleeting glimpse
where_it_s_used: Fleeting moments, travel, celebrity sightings, memories
action_sequence: Before: something passes by → During: see it for a second → After: it's gone
grammar_pattern: glimpse + object (I glimpsed the sea.) / catch a glimpse of + object
common_mistake: I glimpsed at the newspaper headline quickly.
correct_version: I glimpsed the newspaper headline quickly.
why_it_s_wrong: As a verb, 'glimpse' takes a direct object, with no 'at'. 'Catch a glimpse of' is also common.
pronunciation_tip: One syllable with a tricky cluster: GLIMPS, /ɡlɪmps/ -- practice the 'mps' ending slowly.
spelling_tip: G-L-I-M-P-S-E -- don't forget the silent 'e' and the 'p' before 'se.'
etymology: From Middle English "glimsen" (to shine faintly, glance), related to "glimmer" -- both about brief, partial impressions.
mnemonic: A GLIMPSE is like a GLIMMER of light -- brief and quickly gone.
memory_trick: GLIMPSE: a GLIMmer of light — seen for a moment.
visual_association: A blurry shape flashing past a train window.
emotion_feel: Often wonder, curiosity, or fleeting excitement
difference_explained: Glimpse = see briefly, often by chance. Glance = look briefly on purpose.
mini_conversation:
A: Did you see the new car outside?
B: Only a glimpse -- it drove past really fast.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A traveler presses against the train window, catching a glimpse of the coastline.
news_style_line: News-style: "The exhibit offers visitors a rare glimpse into life a century ago."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I only got a glimpse of him before he disappeared into the crowd."
mcq_options: A) To stare for a long time  B) To see something briefly  C) To listen closely  D) To completely ignore
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Through the fog, we could just ______ the outline of the mountains. → glimpse
find_and_fix_to_correct: She glimpse him at the station yesterday. → She glimpsed him at the station yesterday.
translate: मैंने उस मशहूर हस्ती की गाड़ी की एक झलक देखी। → I glimpsed the celebrity's car passing by.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a famous person you glimpsed once.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to see something for a very short moment'?
usage_tip: 'Catch a glimpse of' is the most common pattern.

simple_explanation: To notice or find something, especially something small or hidden. "Spot" means successfully noticing or identifying something, often among many other things or something that's easy to miss.
example_1: I spotted a typo in the email.
example_2: Can you spot the difference between these two pictures?
example_3: She spotted her friend in the crowded stadium.
collocations: spot a mistake, spot the difference, spot someone in a crowd
action_sequence: Before: read the page → During: see a small error → After: point it out
grammar_pattern: spot + object (Spot the mistake.) / spot + object + verb-ing (I spotted him waiting outside.)
common_mistake: I spotted on a mistake in your essay.
correct_version: I spotted a mistake in your essay.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Spot' takes a direct object, with no 'on'.
spelling_tip: S-P-O-T -- double the T when adding -ed/-ing: 'spotted,' 'spotting.'
etymology: From Middle Dutch/Middle Low German "spotte" (a stain, mark); the verb sense 'to notice/identify' developed later, as if picking out a mark among many.
word_family: spot (n., a mark or location), spotted (adj., marked with spots), spotless (adj.)
mnemonic: You SPOT something the way you'd SPOT a SPOT (stain) on a shirt -- it stands out once you notice it.
memory_trick: SPOT: a small dot you notice on a page.
visual_association: A single highlighted dot standing out in a grid of identical dots.
emotion_feel: Often satisfaction or surprise at noticing something
difference_explained: Same idea. Spot is informal and suggests finding something small or hidden.
mini_conversation:
A: I finally spotted the error in the code.
B: Great, where was it hiding?
everyday_scene: Everyday: A scout leans forward in the stands and says, "I think I just spotted our next star player."
news_style_line: News-style: "Auditors spotted several errors in the company's financial records."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I spotted your car outside -- I didn't know you were in town!"
mcq_options: A) To successfully notice or identify something  B) To completely forget something  C) To touch something carefully  D) To listen to music
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Can you ______ the mistake in this sentence? → spot
find_and_fix_to_correct: She spot her keys under the sofa this morning. → She spotted her keys under the sofa this morning.
translate: मैंने ईमेल में एक टाइपिंग गलती पकड़ी। → I spotted a typo in the email.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a mistake you spotted in a sign or menu.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to notice or find something, especially something small or hidden'?
usage_tip: 'On the spot' = immediately, right there.

simple_explanation: To discover or find something that is not easy to see. "Detect" means finding or identifying something hidden or hard to notice, often using care, instruments, or investigation.
example_1: The alarm can detect smoke instantly.
example_2: Doctors detected the illness early.
example_3: The sensor detects motion in the dark.
collocations: detect early, hard to detect, detect a problem, detect a change
action_sequence: Before: something is hidden → During: use tests or tools → After: find it
grammar_pattern: detect + object (Detect the signal.) / be detected (passive: The leak was detected quickly.)
common_mistake: The doctor detect the disease early last year.
correct_version: The doctor detected the disease early last year.
why_it_s_wrong: A finished past action needs -ed: detected.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: dee-TEKT, /dɪˈtekt/.
spelling_tip: D-E-T-E-C-T -- double check the 'ct' ending, easy to misspell as 'detact' or 'detekt.'
etymology: From Latin "detegere" (to uncover), from "de-" (un-, away) + "tegere" (to cover) -- literally 'to remove a cover.'
prefix_root_suffix: de- = away/un + tect (from Latin tegere, to cover) = to uncover
mnemonic: DETECT sounds like DETECTIVE -- a DETECTIVE's job is to DETECT clues others miss.
memory_trick: DETECT → DETECTIVE: someone who detects clues.
visual_association: A radar screen beeping as it picks up a hidden signal.
difference_explained: Detect = notice something hard to see (a disease, a signal). Discover = find something for the first time.
mini_conversation:
A: How did they find the gas leak so fast?
B: A special sensor detected it right away.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A technician stares at a blinking screen and says, "We just detected movement on the east side."
news_style_line: News-style: "Doctors say early screening helped detect the condition before symptoms appeared."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I could detect a bit of nervousness in his voice on the call."
mcq_options: A) To completely ignore  B) To discover something hidden or hard to notice  C) To forget something quickly  D) To argue about something
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: This device can ______ even the smallest gas leak. → detect
find_and_fix_to_correct: The test can detect for cancer in early stage. → The test can detect cancer at an early stage.
translate: यह अलार्म तुरंत धुआं पहचान लेता है। → The alarm can detect smoke instantly.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a machine that detects something.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to discover or find something that is not easy to see'?
usage_tip: 'Smoke detector' = a device that notices smoke.

simple_explanation: To look at or check something very carefully. "Examine" means giving something close, careful attention -- like a doctor examining a patient or a teacher examining an essay for errors.
example_1: The doctor examined the patient carefully.
example_2: She examined the contract before signing it.
example_3: Police examined the scene for clues.
collocations: examine closely, examine carefully, under examination, examine evidence
where_it_s_used: Medicine, legal cases, school, careful inspection
action_sequence: Before: see a problem → During: check every part closely → After: find the cause
grammar_pattern: examine + object (Examine the results.)
common_mistake: The doctor examine me yesterday for the fever.
correct_version: The doctor examined me yesterday for the fever.
why_it_s_wrong: A finished past action needs -ed: examined.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: eg-ZAM-in, /ɪɡˈzæmɪn/.
spelling_tip: E-X-A-M-I-N-E -- notice it contains 'exam,' which can help you remember the spelling and meaning (careful testing/checking).
etymology: From Latin "examinare" (to weigh, test, consider), from "examen" (a tongue of a balance, i.e., the needle used for weighing).
prefix_root_suffix: exam(ine) = root (Latin examinare, to weigh/test) -- no separate prefix here
mnemonic: EXAMINE contains EXAM -- just like an EXAM tests you thoroughly, to EXAMINE means to check something thoroughly.
memory_trick: EXAMINE → EXAM: both mean checking carefully.
visual_association: A magnifying glass held over a document, line by line.
difference_explained: Check = look quickly to make sure. Examine = look very carefully and in detail.
mini_conversation:
A: What did the doctor say?
B: She examined me and said it's nothing serious.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A doctor puts on gloves and says calmly, "Let's examine the wound more closely."
news_style_line: News-style: "Investigators are still examining the wreckage to determine the cause."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Can you examine this contract before I sign it?"
mcq_options: A) To ignore something completely  B) To check or study something carefully  C) To forget something quickly  D) To speak loudly about something
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The mechanic ______ the engine before giving his opinion. → examined
find_and_fix_to_correct: The teacher examine our homework every week. → The teacher examines our homework every week.
translate: डॉक्टर ने मरीज़ की ध्यान से जांच की। → The doctor examined the patient carefully.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a time a doctor examined you.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to look at or check something very carefully'?
usage_tip: A doctor 'examines' a patient; a teacher 'examines' students.

simple_explanation: To create or produce something. "Make" means to produce or create something, from physical objects to abstract things like decisions, plans, or noise.
example_1: She made a cake for the party.
example_2: They make furniture by hand.
example_3: Can you make a decision by tomorrow?
collocations: make a decision, make sense, make money, make a mistake
related_phrasal_verbs: make up, make out, make do, make for
action_sequence: Before: gather materials → During: put them together → After: something new exists
grammar_pattern: make + object (Make dinner.) / make + object + adjective (This makes me happy.)
common_mistake: I did a mistake in my homework.
correct_version: I made a mistake in my homework.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Mistake' goes with 'make', not 'do'.
spelling_tip: M-A-K-E -- silent 'e' at the end makes the 'a' say its name; irregular past tense is 'made,' not 'maked.'
etymology: Old English "macian" (to make, form, construct), a core Germanic verb.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- a simple ancient root
word_family: maker (n.), made (past tense/adj.), making (n., as in 'the making of...')
mnemonic: MAKE rhymes with CAKE -- think of a baker who MAKES a CAKE from scratch.
memory_trick: MAKE = create something new; DO = perform a task. Make a cake; do homework.
visual_association: A pair of hands shaping clay into a finished object.
emotion_feel: Neutral, often pride when something is made well
difference_explained: Make = create or produce (make tea, make a plan). Do = perform an action or task (do work, do exercise).
mini_conversation:
A: Who made this delicious cake?
B: I did -- it's my grandmother's recipe.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A chef wipes her hands and says proudly, "I made this dish myself, just for tonight."
news_style_line: News-style: "The company plans to make thousands of new jobs available next year."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Did you make this? It's really good!"
mcq_options: A) To destroy something  B) To create or produce something  C) To hide something  D) To sell something

simple_explanation: To construct something by putting parts together. "Build" means creating something, usually large or structural, by assembling materials or parts -- like a house, a bridge, or even a relationship.
example_1: They built a new house last year.
example_2: The company is building a new office tower.
example_3: It takes years to build trust in a relationship.
collocations: build a house, build trust, build a career, build up
action_sequence: Before: lay the foundation → During: add walls and a roof → After: the house stands
grammar_pattern: build + object (Build a wall.)
common_mistake: They builded a new bridge last year.
correct_version: They built a new bridge last year.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Build' is irregular: build – built – built.
pronunciation_tip: Rhymes with 'filled': /bɪld/ -- the 'ui' makes a short 'i' sound.
spelling_tip: B-U-I-L-D -- the silent 'u' after B is easy to forget; past tense is 'built,' not 'builded.'
etymology: Old English "byldan," from "bold" (a house, dwelling) -- literally, to construct a dwelling.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- from Old English 'byldan'
mnemonic: BUILD contains 'BUI' -- imagine bricklayers, brick by brick, as they BUILD a structure UP.
memory_trick: BUILD has a silent U: say 'bild'.
visual_association: A skyscraper rising floor by floor from a construction site.
emotion_feel: Often pride, ambition, or excitement about progress
difference_explained: Build = construct something large, piece by piece (house, bridge). Make = the general word.
mini_conversation:

B: About eight months from start to finish.
everyday_scene: Everyday: An architect unrolls blueprints and says, "This is what we're going to build."
news_style_line: News-style: "The city announced plans to build affordable housing downtown."
casual_conversation: Casual: "We're finally building that treehouse we talked about!"

simple_explanation: To make something new that did not exist before. "Create" means bringing something original into existence -- an idea, artwork, product, or even a problem ('create trouble').
example_2: The team created a new app in three months.
example_3: Her decision created a lot of confusion.
collocations: create a plan, create confusion, create an opportunity, create art
action_sequence: Before: have an idea → During: work on it → After: something new exists
grammar_pattern: create + object (Create a design.)
common_mistake: She creates a beautiful painting last week.
correct_version: She created a beautiful painting last week.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Last week' needs the past tense: created.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: kree-AYT, /kriˈeɪt/.
spelling_tip: C-R-E-A-T-E -- ends in '-eate,' the same pattern as 'create' related words like 'creation.'
etymology: From Latin "creare" (to make, produce, bring into being) -- also the root of "creature" and "creation."
prefix_root_suffix: creat(e) = root (Latin creare, to make) -- no separate prefix here
mnemonic: CREATE sounds like GREAT -- when you CREATE something GREAT, it's original and new.
memory_trick: CREATE → CREATIVE: using your mind to make something new.
visual_association: A blank canvas slowly filling with color under a paintbrush.
difference_explained: Make = produce anything. Create = make something new and original.
mini_conversation:
A: Who created this logo?
B: Our design team came up with it last month.
everyday_scene: Everyday: An inventor unveils a device, saying, "I created this to solve a problem no one else noticed."
news_style_line: News-style: "The new policy is expected to create thousands of jobs."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Wow, did you create this website yourself?"

simple_explanation: To plan how something will look, work, or be made. "Design" means creating a plan or drawing for how something should look or function, before it's actually built.
example_1: She designed a new logo for the company.
example_2: Engineers designed a lighter, faster engine.
example_3: He designed the layout of the new app.
collocations: design a logo, design a building, well-designed, design software
action_sequence: Before: think of the purpose → During: draw a plan → After: the plan is ready to build
grammar_pattern: design + object (Design a website.)
common_mistake: She design the poster for tomorrow's event.
correct_version: She designed the poster for tomorrow's event.
why_it_s_wrong: A finished past action needs -ed: designed.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: dih-ZAIN, /dɪˈzaɪn/ -- the 'g' is silent.
spelling_tip: D-E-S-I-G-N -- the silent 'g' before 'n' trips up many learners.
etymology: From Latin "designare" (to mark out, designate), from "de-" (out) + "signare" (to mark).
prefix_root_suffix: de- = out + sign = to mark -- literally 'to mark out a plan'
word_family: design (n., a plan or pattern), designer (n.), designed (adj.)
mnemonic: DESIGN has a SIGN inside it -- a good DESIGN SIGNals exactly how something should look or work.
memory_trick: DESIGN has a silent G: say 'di-ZINE'.
visual_association: A sketchbook filled with careful pencil drawings and measurements.
emotion_feel: Often pride, creativity, or careful thought
difference_explained: Draw = make a picture. Design = plan how something will look and work.
mini_conversation:

B: A small team of designers worked on it for months.

simple_explanation: To build something, often large, using a careful plan. "Construct" is a formal word for building something -- roads, buildings, or even ideas/arguments -- usually involving planning and multiple steps.
example_2: The government plans to construct a new hospital.
example_3: She constructed a strong argument in her essay.
collocations: construct a building, construct an argument, under construction, newly constructed
action_sequence: Before: plan the road → During: workers lay materials → After: the road is ready
grammar_pattern: construct + object (Construct a bridge.)
common_mistake: They construct the road last year.
correct_version: They constructed the road last year.
why_it_s_wrong: A finished past action needs -ed: constructed.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable when used as a verb: kuhn-STRUKT, /kənˈstrʌkt/.
spelling_tip: C-O-N-S-T-R-U-C-T -- notice 'struct' (from Latin), the same root as 'structure' and 'instruct.'
etymology: From Latin "construere" (to build, pile up together), from "con-" (together) + "struere" (to pile, build).
prefix_root_suffix: con- = together + struct (from Latin struere, to build) = to build together
mnemonic: CONSTRUCT contains STRUCT (structure) -- you CONSTRUCT a STRUCTure piece by piece.
memory_trick: CON-STRUCT → STRUCTURE: what you construct.
visual_association: Steel beams being carefully assembled into a rising framework.
difference_explained: Same meaning. Construct is more formal and technical.
mini_conversation:

B: I heard it should be done by next spring.

simple_explanation: To make or grow something, often in large amounts. "Produce" means creating something, often goods, crops, or results, especially through a process like farming, manufacturing, or effort.
example_1: This factory produces thousands of cars.
example_2: The farm produces fresh vegetables every season.
example_3: Her hard work produced excellent results.
collocations: produce results, produce goods, mass-produce, produce evidence
action_sequence: Before: raw materials go in → During: the factory works → After: finished goods come out
grammar_pattern: produce + object (Produce goods.)
common_mistake: This factory produce thousands of cars every month.
correct_version: This factory produces thousands of cars every month.
why_it_s_wrong: He/she/it in the simple present needs -s: produces.
pronunciation_tip: As a verb, stress the second syllable: pruh-DYOOS, /prəˈdju:s/ -- different from the noun 'PRO-duce' (fruit/vegetables).
spelling_tip: P-R-O-D-U-C-E -- watch the stress shift between the verb and the noun form.
etymology: From Latin "producere" (to lead forward, bring forth), from "pro-" (forward) + "ducere" (to lead).
prefix_root_suffix: pro- = forward + duce (from Latin ducere, to lead) = to lead forward, bring forth
mnemonic: PRODUCE = PRO + DUCE (lead) -- a factory PROduces goods by leading raw materials forward into finished products.
memory_trick: PRO-DUCE: verb stress on DUCE. PRO-duce (noun) = fruit and vegetables.
visual_association: A conveyor belt steadily churning out identical finished products.
emotion_feel: Neutral, sometimes pride in output or efficiency
difference_explained: Produce = verb (make). Product = noun (the thing made).

simple_explanation: To create or think of something completely new. "Invent" means being the first person to make or think of something, usually a machine, tool, or idea that never existed before.
example_1: He invented a new kind of light bulb.
example_2: Scientists invented a faster way to charge batteries.
example_3: Children often invent imaginary games.
collocations: invent a device, invent a story, newly invented, invent an excuse
action_sequence: Before: see a problem → During: think of something new → After: build a new tool
grammar_pattern: invent + object (Invent a machine.)
common_mistake: He invent a new tool last year for farmers.
correct_version: He invented a new tool last year for farmers.
why_it_s_wrong: A finished past action needs -ed: invented.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: in-VENT, /ɪnˈvent/.
spelling_tip: I-N-V-E-N-T -- contains 'vent,' as in the word 'event,' which shares the same Latin root.
etymology: From Latin "invenire" (to come upon, find), from "in-" (upon) + "venire" (to come) -- originally meant 'to discover,' later shifted to 'to create something new.'
prefix_root_suffix: in- = upon/into + vent (from Latin venire, to come) = to come upon, discover
mnemonic: INVENT contains VENT -- inventors let their imagination VENT out into something brand new.
memory_trick: INVENT → INVENTOR: someone like Edison.
visual_association: A lightbulb glowing above a workbench cluttered with new gadgets.
difference_explained: Invent = make something that didn't exist (the telephone). Discover = find something that already existed (a new planet).

B: A college student, believe it or not.

casual_conversation: Casual: "Did you really invent that excuse on the spot?"

write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about an invention that changed your life.

simple_explanation: To fix something that is broken or damaged. "Repair" means restoring something broken back to working condition -- a car, a roof, or even a damaged relationship.
example_2: The mechanic repaired the car's engine.
example_3: It will take a week to repair the road.
collocations: repair a car, repair damage, under repair, beyond repair
action_sequence: Before: something breaks → During: the mechanic fixes it → After: it works again
grammar_pattern: repair + object (Repair the roof.)
common_mistake: The mechanic repair my car yesterday.
correct_version: The mechanic repaired my car yesterday.
why_it_s_wrong: A finished past action needs -ed: repaired.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: rih-PAIR, /rɪˈpeər/.
spelling_tip: R-E-P-A-I-R -- notice the 're-' prefix meaning 'again,' as in many repair-related words.
etymology: From Old French "reparer," from Latin "reparare" (to restore), from "re-" (again) + "parare" (to prepare, make ready).
prefix_root_suffix: re- = again + pair (from Latin parare, to prepare) = to make ready again
word_family: repair (n., the act of fixing), repairable (adj.), unrepairable/irreparable (adj.)
mnemonic: REPAIR sounds like RE-PAIR -- you PAIR broken parts back together AGAIN.
memory_trick: RE-PAIR: make the PAIR (parts) fit again.
visual_association: A wrench tightening a loose bolt on a machine.
emotion_feel: Neutral, often relief once something is repaired
difference_explained: Same meaning. Fix is informal; repair is more formal and used for machines and buildings.

casual_conversation: Casual: "Can you repair my phone screen, or do I need a new one?"

simple_explanation: To repair something or make something right. "Fix" is a casual way to say you repaired something broken, solved a problem, or arranged something (like fixing a meeting time).
example_2: I need to fix this leaky faucet.
example_3: She fixed the mistake in the report quickly.
collocations: fix a problem, fix a leak, quick fix, fix a meeting
where_it_s_used: Everyday repairs, technology problems, casual arrangements
action_sequence: Before: something is broken → During: repair it → After: it works again
grammar_pattern: fix + object (Fix the printer.)
common_mistake: I fixed already the problem.
correct_version: I have already fixed the problem.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Already' goes before the main verb, usually with the present perfect.
spelling_tip: F-I-X -- short word, but remember 'fixed' and 'fixes' when conjugating.
etymology: From Latin "fixus," past participle of "figere" (to fasten) -- originally about attaching firmly, later extended to 'repair' and 'set in place.'
prefix_root_suffix: fix = root (from Latin figere, to fasten) -- no separate prefix/suffix
mnemonic: FIX rhymes with MIX -- sometimes you FIX something by MIXing the right parts back together.
memory_trick: FIX has an X — like crossing a problem off the list.
visual_association: A screwdriver tightening a loose screw on a wobbly chair.
emotion_feel: Neutral, often relief when something gets fixed
difference_explained: Fix is informal and wider (fix a problem, fix a date). Repair is for physical things.

simple_explanation: To separate something into pieces by force. "Break" means damaging or destroying something so it's no longer whole, or figuratively failing to keep a promise or rule.
example_1: He broke the window by accident.
example_2: Be careful, that vase can break easily.
example_3: She broke her promise not to tell anyone.
collocations: break a promise, break the rules, break down, break the news
related_phrasal_verbs: break down, break up, break out, break in
action_sequence: Before: drop the phone → During: the screen hits the floor → After: the screen cracks
grammar_pattern: break + object (Break the glass.)
common_mistake: I breaked my phone screen yesterday.
correct_version: I broke my phone screen yesterday.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Break' is irregular: break – broke – broken.
pronunciation_tip: Rhymes with 'cake': /breɪk/ -- note it's spelled differently from 'brake' (the car part), a common homophone confusion.
spelling_tip: B-R-E-A-K -- don't confuse with 'brake' (used to stop a car).
etymology: Old English "brecan" (to break, shatter), a common Germanic verb still central to English today.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- from Old English 'brecan'
mnemonic: BREAK rhymes with CAKE, and if you drop a CAKE, it will BREAK apart.
memory_trick: BREAK → BROKE → BROKEN, like SPEAK → SPOKE → SPOKEN.
visual_association: A glass slipping from a hand and shattering on the floor.
difference_explained: Break = separate into pieces. Brake = the part of a vehicle that stops it. Same sound.

simple_explanation: To put separate parts together to make something whole. "Assemble" means fitting individual pieces together, following a plan or instructions, to build something like furniture, a machine, or even a group of people.
example_1: It took an hour to assemble the bookshelf.
example_2: Workers assemble the cars on a factory line.
example_3: Please assemble the desk following the instructions.
collocations: assemble furniture, assemble a team, quickly assembled, assembly line
action_sequence: Before: open the box of parts → During: join them step by step → After: the shelf stands
grammar_pattern: assemble + object (Assemble the parts.)
common_mistake: We assembled together in the hall.
correct_version: We assembled in the hall.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Assemble' already means come together, so 'together' is extra.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: uh-SEM-bul, /əˈsembl/.
spelling_tip: A-S-S-E-M-B-L-E -- double 'S' at the start; the ending '-ble' is common in words like 'table' and 'assemble.'
etymology: From Old French "assembler," from Latin "assimulare" (to bring together), from "ad-" (to) + "simul" (together, at the same time).
prefix_root_suffix: as- (ad-) = to/toward + sembl(e) (from Latin simul, together) = to bring together
mnemonic: ASSEMBLE sounds like RESEMBLE -- when you ASSEMBLE the pieces correctly, the result RESEMBLEs the picture on the box.
memory_trick: AS-SEMBLE: bring things to one place, like a school ASSEMBLY.
visual_association: Scattered furniture pieces slowly forming a finished bookshelf.
emotion_feel: Neutral, sometimes mild frustration if instructions are unclear
difference_explained: Gather = collect or come together. Assemble = come together formally, or put parts together.

news_style_line: News-style: "Workers assembled the wind turbine in record time despite the storm."
casual_conversation: Casual: "This furniture was so hard to assemble -- the instructions made no sense!"

reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to put separate parts together to make something whole'?
usage_tip: 'Assembly line' = a factory line where parts are joined.

simple_explanation: To put something in place so it's ready to use. "Install" means setting up equipment, software, or a fixture so it's ready to work -- like installing a new app or a new light fixture.
example_1: I need to install this app on my phone.
example_2: The technician installed a new air conditioner.
example_3: We installed solar panels on the roof.
collocations: install software, install a program, freshly installed, install equipment
action_sequence: Before: download the file → During: follow the setup steps → After: the app is ready
grammar_pattern: install + object (Install the software.)
common_mistake: I need to installed this update tonight.
correct_version: I need to install this update tonight.
why_it_s_wrong: After 'need to', use the base verb.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: in-STAWL, /ɪnˈstɔ:l/.
spelling_tip: I-N-S-T-A-L-L -- double L at the end, a common spelling slip.
etymology: From Medieval Latin "installare" (to place in a stall/seat), from "in-" (into) + "stallum" (a stall, place) -- originally about formally placing someone in a position.
prefix_root_suffix: in- = into + stall (from Latin stallum, a place) = to put into place
mnemonic: INSTALL contains STALL -- you find the right STALL (place) and INSTALL the item there permanently.
memory_trick: IN-STALL: put a stall (a fixed place) IN.
visual_association: A progress bar filling up as new software loads onto a screen.
emotion_feel: Neutral, sometimes mild frustration with technical issues
difference_explained: Download = copy the file to your device. Install = set it up so it works.
mini_conversation:
A: Is the new printer working?
B: Almost -- I just need to install the drivers.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A technician nods and says, "All done -- I've installed the new system for you."
news_style_line: News-style: "The city plans to install new traffic cameras at busy intersections."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Can you help me install this app? I keep getting an error."
mcq_options: A) To remove something  B) To set something up so it's ready to use  C) To break something  D) To sell something
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The workers will ______ new windows in the office next week. → install
find_and_fix_to_correct: She install a new lock on the door yesterday. → She installed a new lock on the door yesterday.
translate: मुझे यह ऐप अपने फ़ोन में इंस्टॉल करना है। → I need to install this app on my phone.
