difference_explained: Wait for = spend time until something comes. Look forward to = feel happy about something coming.
mini_conversation:
A: See you at the wedding next month!
B: Yes, I'm really looking forward to it.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A soldier folds a letter and smiles, "I look forward to the day I finally come home."
news_style_line: News-style: "Organizers say residents are looking forward to the reopening of the local park."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I look forward to our coffee dates every Friday."
mcq_options: A) To dread something  B) To feel excited about a future event  C) To forget about something  D) To look behind you
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: We ______ visiting our grandparents this summer. → look forward to
find_and_fix_to_correct: I am looking forward to see the results. → I am looking forward to seeing the results. (use "seeing," the -ing form, not "to see")
translate: मुझे अगले हफ़्ते की छुट्टियों का बेसब्री से इंतज़ार है। → I'm really looking forward to next week's holidays.
write_your_own_sentence: Write an email ending using 'I look forward to…'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to feel excited about something that is going to happen'?
usage_tip: 'I look forward to hearing from you' is a standard email ending.

hindi_meaning: भरोसा करना, विश्वास करना (किसी के सहयोग पर)
simple_explanation: To rely on or trust someone or something. "Count on" means you trust that a person will help you or that something will definitely happen.
example_1: You can always count on your family.
example_2: I know I can count on you in an emergency.
example_3: Don't count on the weather being good tomorrow.
collocations: count on someone, count on it, always count on
related_phrasal_verbs: rely on, depend on, bank on
action_sequence: Before: need help → During: call a friend → After: they come
grammar_pattern: count on + noun/gerund (Count on his help / count on winning.)
word_forms: count on – counted on – counted on – counting on
common_mistake: I count on that he will come.
correct_version: I'm counting on him to come.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'count on someone to do something', not 'count on that…'.
spelling_tip: Two words; don't confuse with "account," a different word entirely.
etymology: From "count" (Latin "computare," to calculate) + "on" -- literally to calculate based on something, extended figuratively to relying on someone/something.
prefix_root_suffix: count + on (phrasal particle -- "on" adds the sense of relying/depending)
mnemonic: If you can COUNT ON someone, you can add them to your list of people who will always be there.
memory_trick: COUNT ON: they are the number you COUNT on.
visual_association: Someone leaning their full weight on a sturdy railing that doesn't budge.
difference_explained: Same meaning. Count on is slightly more informal.
mini_conversation:
A: Can I count on you tomorrow?
B: Of course, I'll be there no matter what.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A captain grips a teammate's shoulder and says, "I need to know I can count on you out there."
news_style_line: News-style: "Farmers say they can no longer count on predictable rainfall each season."
casual_conversation: Casual: "You can always count on me if you need help moving."
mcq_options: A) To doubt someone  B) To rely on or trust someone  C) To ignore someone  D) To count numbers
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: You can always ______ your best friend for honest advice. → count on
find_and_fix_to_correct: I am counting on that you will help me. → I am counting on you to help me. (use "you to help," not "that you will help")
translate: मुझे पता है कि मुश्किल समय में मैं तुम पर भरोसा कर सकता हूँ। → I know I can count on you in difficult times.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a friend you can always count on.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to rely on or trust someone or something'?
usage_tip: 'You can count on me' is a strong promise.

simple_explanation: To depend on someone or something for help or support. "Rely on" means you trust that a person or thing will support you or work correctly when you need it.
example_1: I rely on my bike to get to work.
example_2: Many families rely on this bus route every day.
example_3: You can rely on her to finish the job on time.
collocations: rely on someone, rely heavily on, rely on for
related_phrasal_verbs: depend on, count on, lean on
action_sequence: Before: have a problem → During: ask someone you trust → After: get help
grammar_pattern: rely on + noun/gerund (Rely on public transport / rely on being punctual.)
word_forms: rely on – relied on – relied on – relying on
common_mistake: I rely to my brother for advice.
correct_version: I rely on my brother for advice.
why_it_s_wrong: The preposition after 'rely' is 'on', not 'to'.
etymology: From "rely" (Old French "relier," to bind back/together) + "on" -- literally to bind oneself to something for support, extended to trusting or depending on it.
prefix_root_suffix: rely + on (phrasal particle -- "on" attaches the sense of depending/leaning)
mnemonic: To RELY ON someone is to lean back and let them carry your weight, ON their support.
memory_trick: RELY ON: you LIE back ON someone for support.
visual_association: A ladder leaning safely against a strong wall, fully supported.
difference_explained: Rely on = trust someone to help. Depend on = need something, or be decided by it.
mini_conversation:
A: How do you get to college every day?
B: I rely on the metro -- it's fast and cheap.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A pilot tells the passengers calmly, "You can rely on this crew to get you home safely."
news_style_line: News-style: "Hospitals in the region rely on generators during frequent power cuts."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I really rely on my morning coffee to wake up properly."
mcq_options: A) To avoid someone  B) To depend on someone or something  C) To compete with someone  D) To forget something
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Villagers ______ the well for their daily water supply. → rely on
find_and_fix_to_correct: She relies in her notes during the exam. → She relies on her notes during the exam. (use "on," not "in," after "rely")
translate: हम बिजली के लिए सौर ऊर्जा पर निर्भर हैं। → We rely on solar power for electricity.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about who you rely on for advice.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to depend on someone or something for help or support'?
usage_tip: 'Reliable' = someone you can rely on.

simple_explanation: To need something or someone for support, or to be decided by something. "Depend on" means one thing relies on another to happen or exist -- like a plan depending on the weather, or a child depending on parents.
example_1: It all depends on the weather.
example_2: Children depend on their parents for food and shelter.
example_3: Whether we go hiking depends on the forecast.
collocations: depend on the situation, heavily depend on, depend on whether
related_phrasal_verbs: rely on, count on, hinge on
action_sequence: Before: ask a question → During: look at the conditions → After: the answer changes with them
grammar_pattern: depend on + noun/wh-clause (Depend on luck / depend on how it goes.)
word_forms: depend on – depended on – depended on – depending on
common_mistake: The result depend on many factors.
correct_version: The result depends on many factors.
why_it_s_wrong: A singular subject in the simple present needs -s: depends.
spelling_tip: Watch the spelling of "depend" -- one "p," not "deppend."
etymology: From "depend" (Latin "de-" down + "pendere" to hang) + "on" -- literally "to hang down from," extended figuratively to relying on for support or being contingent on.
prefix_root_suffix: de- (down) + pend (to hang) + on = literally "to hang down from," now meaning "to rely on"
mnemonic: DEPEND comes from "hang down" -- imagine your plans literally hanging, DEPENDING ON one condition.
memory_trick: DEPEND: things HANG ('pend') on something else, like a pendant.
visual_association: A single string holding up a hanging lamp -- everything relies on that one thread.
difference_explained: Depend on can mean 'be decided by' (the result depends on the weather). Rely on is only about trust.
mini_conversation:
A: Are we still going to the beach tomorrow?
B: It depends on whether it rains or not.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A general studies the map and says quietly, "Everything depends on what happens at dawn."
news_style_line: News-style: "Analysts say the region's economy still depends heavily on tourism."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I don't know if I can come -- it depends on my work schedule."
mcq_options: A) To be unrelated to something  B) To rely on or be decided by something  C) To ignore a factor  D) To finish quickly
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Whether the trip happens ______ the budget. → depends on
find_and_fix_to_correct: My decision depends of your answer. → My decision depends on your answer. (the correct preposition is "on," not "of")
translate: यह पूरी तरह मौसम पर निर्भर करता है। → It completely depends on the weather.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence starting with 'It depends on…'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to need something or someone for support, or to be decided by something'?
usage_tip: 'It depends' is a useful short answer when you're not sure.

simple_explanation: To recover from an illness, disappointment, or difficult experience. "Get over" means you feel better after being sick, sad, or shocked -- the hard feeling slowly fades away.
example_1: It took him weeks to get over the flu.
example_2: She still hasn't gotten over the breakup.
example_3: It took the team a while to get over the loss.
collocations: get over a cold, get over a breakup, get over something quickly
related_phrasal_verbs: bounce back, move on, recover from
action_sequence: Before: feel ill or sad → During: time and rest help → After: feel normal again
grammar_pattern: get over + noun/gerund (Get over an illness / get over losing.)
word_forms: get over – got over – got/gotten over – getting over
common_mistake: I can't get over of my exam results.
correct_version: I can't get over my exam results.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Get over' takes its object directly, with no 'of'.
spelling_tip: Two words; don't confuse with "overcome," a more formal one-word synonym.
etymology: From "get" + "over" -- literally to cross/pass over an obstacle, extended figuratively to recovering from illness, loss, or difficulty.
prefix_root_suffix: get + over (phrasal particle -- "over" suggests moving past/beyond a difficulty)
mnemonic: To GET OVER something difficult, imagine climbing OVER a wall and leaving it behind you.
memory_trick: GET OVER: climb OVER a wall of sadness.
visual_association: A person climbing over a tall fence and looking back at it from the other side.
difference_explained: Get over = recover (informal). Overcome = defeat a difficulty (more formal).
mini_conversation:
A: How's your cold?
B: Almost gone -- I'm finally getting over it.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A friend hugs another and whispers, "It's okay to take your time -- you don't have to get over it all at once."
news_style_line: News-style: "Health officials say most patients get over the illness within a week with rest."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I still haven't fully gotten over losing that job, honestly."
mcq_options: A) To cause a problem  B) To recover from something difficult  C) To ignore a warning  D) To start an illness
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: It took her months to ______ the shock of the accident. → get over
find_and_fix_to_correct: He never get over his fear of heights. → He never got over his fear of heights. (use the past tense "got," not "get")
translate: उसे अपने दोस्त की मौत के गम से उबरने में काफी समय लगा। → It took him a long time to get over the grief of his friend's death.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about how long it took you to get over an illness.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to recover from an illness, disappointment, or difficult experience'?
usage_tip: 'I can't get over it!' can also mean 'I'm amazed'.

hindi_meaning: राज़ी हो जाना, मान जाना; होश में आना
simple_explanation: To eventually agree with something, or to wake up after being unconscious. "Come around" often describes someone changing their mind and finally agreeing, after first disagreeing or resisting.
example_1: My parents finally came around to the idea.
example_2: He was against the plan at first, but he came around eventually.
example_3: She fainted, but came around after a few minutes.
collocations: come around to the idea, eventually come around, come around slowly
related_phrasal_verbs: change one's mind, warm up to, get on board
where_it_s_used: Persuasion, family disagreements, negotiations, medical recovery
action_sequence: Before: someone says no → During: think it over → After: they agree
grammar_pattern: come around + (to) + noun/gerund (Come around to the plan / come around to agreeing.)
word_forms: come around – came around – come around – coming around
common_mistake: My boss will come around about my proposal soon.
correct_version: My boss will come around to my proposal soon.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'come around TO' an idea.
spelling_tip: Two words; British English sometimes uses "come round" instead.
etymology: From "come" + "around" -- literally to travel in a circular path back to a point, extended figuratively to changing one's opinion, regaining consciousness, or a regular event returning.
prefix_root_suffix: come + around (phrasal particle -- "around" suggests a change of direction in opinion, like circling back)
mnemonic: An opinion that seemed fixed slowly turns, COMES AROUND, like a compass needle swinging to a new direction.
memory_trick: COME AROUND: walk AROUND to the other side of the argument.
visual_association: A stubborn compass needle spinning slowly until it settles on a new direction.
difference_explained: Agree = say yes. Come around = agree slowly, after first disagreeing.
mini_conversation:
A: Your mom still doesn't like the plan.
B: Give her time -- she'll come around eventually.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A daughter smiles hopefully and says, "Give him a few days -- Dad always comes around eventually."
news_style_line: News-style: "Analysts believe public opinion will slowly come around to the new policy."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I was skeptical about the new manager, but I've come around to liking her approach."
mcq_question: "Come around" (to an idea) most nearly means:
mcq_options: A) To reject an idea permanently  B) To eventually agree after resisting  C) To forget about something  D) To argue more strongly
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: He resisted the idea for months, but he finally ______. → came around
find_and_fix_to_correct: She come around to my point of view yesterday. → She came around to my point of view yesterday. (use the past tense "came," not "come")
translate: शुरू में विरोध करने के बाद, वह आखिरकार मान गया। → After resisting at first, he finally came around.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about someone who finally came around to your idea.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to eventually agree with something, or to wake up after being unconscious'?
usage_tip: 'Come around' also means visit: 'Come around for dinner.'

hindi_meaning: पहली मुलाक़ात में ही अच्छी दोस्ती हो जाना, जल्दी घुल-मिल जाना
simple_explanation: To immediately like each other and get along well. "Hit it off" describes two people meeting and instantly enjoying each other's company, like an easy, natural friendship starting right away.
example_1: We hit it off right from the start.
example_2: My sister and her new roommate hit it off immediately.
example_3: They met at a conference and really hit it off.
collocations: hit it off immediately, really hit it off, hit it off with someone
related_phrasal_verbs: click with, get along, bond instantly
where_it_s_used: First meetings, dating, new friendships, networking
action_sequence: Before: meet someone new → During: talk easily and laugh → After: become friends quickly
grammar_pattern: hit it off + (with) + someone (They hit it off with each other.)
word_forms: hit it off – hit it off – hit it off – hitting it off
common_mistake: I hit off with him very well at the party.
correct_version: I hit it off with him very well at the party.
why_it_s_wrong: 'It' is fixed in the middle: hit IT off.
spelling_tip: Three words -- the "it" is fixed and never changes to another pronoun.
etymology: From "hit" + "it" + "off" -- an informal 19th-century idiom meaning to strike upon a good rapport immediately, likely from "hit" as "to arrive at" a good match.
prefix_root_suffix: hit + it + off (fixed idiomatic phrase -- doesn't break into a prefix/root/suffix pattern)
word_family: hit (v./n.) -- no distinct related forms for this idiom
mnemonic: When two people HIT IT OFF, their friendship starts with a spark, like hitting a match.
memory_trick: HIT IT OFF: like a ball hit perfectly on the first try.
visual_association: Two puzzle pieces clicking together perfectly on the first try.
confusing_word: hit it off vs get along
difference_explained: Hit it off = like each other immediately. Get along = have a friendly relationship over time.
mini_conversation:
A: How was the party?
B: Great -- I met someone new and we really hit it off.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A woman laughs at a party and tells her friend, "You wouldn't believe it -- we just hit it off instantly."
news_style_line: News-style: "Organizers say the mentorship program works well because pairs often hit it off within the first session."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I was so nervous meeting his parents, but we actually hit it off."
mcq_options: A) To argue immediately  B) To instantly get along well with someone  C) To end a friendship  D) To forget someone's name
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: We were strangers an hour ago, but we've really ______. → hit it off
find_and_fix_to_correct: They hit off it right away at the meeting. → They hit it off right away at the meeting. (word order is fixed: hit it off, not hit off it)
translate: हम दोनों पहली ही मुलाक़ात में अच्छे दोस्त बन गए। → The two of us hit it off from our very first meeting.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about someone you hit it off with instantly.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to immediately like each other and get along well'?
usage_tip: Common in stories: 'We hit it off immediately.'

simple_explanation: To have a serious argument that damages a friendship or relationship. "Fall out" (with someone) means you had a big disagreement, and now your relationship with that person is strained or broken.
example_1: The brothers fell out over money.
example_2: She fell out with her best friend last year and they haven't spoken since.
example_3: The two business partners fell out over the company's direction.
collocations: fall out with someone, fall out badly, fall out over money
related_phrasal_verbs: split up, have a falling-out, drift apart
action_sequence: Before: friends argue badly → During: stop talking → After: the friendship is damaged
grammar_pattern: fall out + (with) + someone (+ over + reason) (Fall out with a friend over a lie.)
word_forms: fall out – fell out – fallen out – falling out
common_mistake: My cousin fell out from me last summer.
correct_version: My cousin fell out with me last summer.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'fall out WITH' the person, not 'from'.
spelling_tip: Two words for the verb; "fallout" (one word) is the noun for radioactive debris or negative consequences.
etymology: From "fall" (Old English "feallan") + "out" -- literally to drop out of place, extended figuratively to a falling-out (an argument that damages a relationship).
prefix_root_suffix: fall + out (phrasal particle -- "out" here signals a relationship breaking apart)
word_family: fallout (n. -- consequences/radioactive debris, a related but distinct meaning)
mnemonic: Friends who FALL OUT drift apart, like leaves that FALL OUT of a tree in autumn.
memory_trick: FALL OUT: your friendship falls OUT of place.
visual_association: Two puzzle pieces that used to fit now lying apart on the table.
difference_explained: Fall out (with someone) = have a serious argument. Fall down = drop to the ground.
mini_conversation:
A: You and Priya used to be so close.
B: We fell out a while back and haven't really talked since.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A brother stares out the window and admits quietly, "We fell out years ago, and I still don't know how to fix it."
news_style_line: News-style: "The two former business partners fell out publicly over control of the company."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I hate that we fell out over something so small."
mcq_options: A) To become close friends  B) To have a serious argument that damages a relationship  C) To fall asleep suddenly  D) To move to a new house
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The sisters ______ after a huge argument at the family dinner. → fell out
find_and_fix_to_correct: They fall out last week and now they don't talk. → They fell out last week and now they don't talk. (use past tense "fell," not "fall")
translate: पैसों को लेकर दोनों भाइयों में झगड़ा हो गया। → The two brothers fell out over money.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about two friends who fell out over something small.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to have a serious argument that damages a friendship or relationship'?
usage_tip: 'Falling-out' (noun) = a serious argument.

simple_explanation: To repair a relationship or resolve a disagreement after a conflict. "Patch up" means making peace and fixing things after an argument, so the relationship can continue.
example_2: The couple patched things up after a long talk.
example_3: We patched up our friendship over coffee.
collocations: patch up a relationship, patch things up, patch up a quarrel
action_sequence: Before: friends fight → During: talk and apologise → After: the friendship is repaired
grammar_pattern: patch up + noun (Patch up a friendship / patch up a mistake.)
word_forms: patch up – patched up – patched up – patching up
common_mistake: We patched up with each other after the fight.
correct_version: We patched things up with each other after the fight.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Patch up' usually needs an object like 'things' or 'the relationship'.
spelling_tip: Two words; "patch" already has the "tch" sound spelled correctly -- don't drop the "t."
etymology: From "patch" (a small piece used to mend a hole) + "up" -- literally to mend a physical tear, extended figuratively to repairing a damaged relationship or disagreement.
prefix_root_suffix: patch + up (phrasal particle -- "up" reinforces the sense of completely mending something)
mnemonic: You sew a PATCH over a torn relationship to hold it together again, just like mending a torn shirt.
memory_trick: PATCH UP: put a PATCH on a torn friendship.
visual_association: A needle and thread sewing two torn edges of fabric back together.
difference_explained: Make up = become friends again. Patch things up = repair a relationship, often partly.
mini_conversation:
A: Are you and Sam okay now?
B: Yeah, we patched things up after a long chat.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A friend extends a hand and says, "Let's patch things up -- I don't want to lose you over this."
news_style_line: News-style: "The two neighboring countries met to patch up relations after months of tension."
casual_conversation: Casual: "We finally patched things up over dinner last night."
mcq_options: A) To end it permanently  B) To repair or resolve it after a conflict  C) To ignore the problem  D) To start a new relationship
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: After the argument, they sat down to ______ things. → patch up
find_and_fix_to_correct: They patched up they friendship after months. → They patched up their friendship after months. (use the possessive "their," not "they")
translate: लंबी बातचीत के बाद, उन्होंने अपने रिश्ते को सुधार लिया। → After a long conversation, they patched up their relationship.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about how two friends patched things up.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to repair a relationship or resolve a disagreement after a conflict'?
usage_tip: 'Patch up' also means repair something quickly: 'patch up a wall'.

simple_explanation: To join with someone to work together on something. "Team up" means two or more people or groups decide to work together, often to achieve something they couldn't easily do alone.
example_1: Let's team up for the science project.
example_2: The two companies teamed up to launch a new product.
example_3: We teamed up with our neighbors to clean the park.
collocations: team up with, team up on a project, team up to achieve
where_it_s_used: Sports, business, school projects, community work
action_sequence: Before: have a big task → During: join a partner → After: finish it together
grammar_pattern: team up + (with) + someone + (on/for) + task (Team up with a friend on a project.)
word_forms: team up – teamed up – teamed up – teaming up
common_mistake: We teamed up for solve the puzzle faster.
correct_version: We teamed up to solve the puzzle faster.
why_it_s_wrong: For purpose, use 'to + verb', not 'for + verb'.
spelling_tip: Two words; note the double "e" in "team," not "tem."
etymology: From "team" (Old English "team," offspring/group pulling together) + "up" -- literally forming a team together, extended to collaborating on a task.
prefix_root_suffix: team + up (phrasal particle -- "up" reinforces the idea of coming together as a unit)
mnemonic: Two people TEAM UP by joining forces, like puzzle pieces coming together into one TEAM.
memory_trick: TEAM UP: form a TEAM.
visual_association: Two gears interlocking and turning smoothly together.
difference_explained: Join = become part of an existing group. Team up = form a new partnership for a task.
mini_conversation:
A: How are we going to finish this presentation on time?
B: Let's team up -- you do the slides, I'll do the research.
everyday_scene: Everyday: Two rivals shake hands reluctantly and one says, "Fine, let's team up -- just this once."
news_style_line: News-style: "Two local charities have teamed up to provide meals for families in need."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Want to team up for the quiz night this Friday?"
mcq_options: A) To compete against someone  B) To join together to work on something  C) To quit a project  D) To argue with a partner
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The two artists decided to ______ on a mural for the school. → team up
find_and_fix_to_correct: They team up together to win the match. → They teamed up to win the match. (past tense "teamed," and "together" is unnecessary since "team up" already implies joining)
translate: हमने मिलकर यह प्रोजेक्ट पूरा करने का फैसला किया। → We decided to team up to finish this project.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about someone you would team up with for a project.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to join with someone to work together on something'?
usage_tip: 'Team up with' someone = join them for a task.

simple_explanation: To form a group of two people, usually for an activity. "Pair up" means people split into twos, often for a game, task, or partner exercise.
example_1: Let's pair up for this exercise.
example_2: The teacher asked the students to pair up for the debate.
example_3: We paired up with strangers during the dance class.
collocations: pair up with, pair up for an activity, pair up randomly
related_phrasal_verbs: team up, partner up, match up
action_sequence: Before: the teacher gives a task → During: find one partner → After: work in twos
grammar_pattern: pair up + (with) + someone + (for) + activity (Pair up with a classmate for the quiz.)
word_forms: pair up – paired up – paired up – pairing up
common_mistake: We paired up in groups of three.
correct_version: We split into groups of three.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Pair up' means groups of two only. For bigger groups, use 'split into groups' or 'form groups'.
spelling_tip: Note "pair" (two matching things), not "pear" (the fruit) or "pare" (to trim).
etymology: From "pair" (Latin "par," equal/a couple) + "up" -- literally forming two into a matched set, extended to partnering for an activity.
prefix_root_suffix: pair + up (phrasal particle -- "up" reinforces forming a complete matched set)
mnemonic: PAIR UP means matching UP into twos, like a PAIR of shoes always found together.
memory_trick: PAIR = two, like a pair of shoes.
visual_association: Shoes lined up neatly, always matched two by two.
difference_explained: Pair up = make groups of two. 'Group up' is rare; say 'form groups' or 'split into groups'.
mini_conversation:
A: How do we split into groups?
B: Let's just pair up with the person next to us.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A coach blows the whistle and shouts, "Alright, everybody pair up for the drill!"
news_style_line: News-style: "Volunteers were paired up with local families for the weekend mentoring program."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Do you want to pair up for the trivia night?"
mcq_options: A) To split into large groups  B) To form a group of two  C) To work completely alone  D) To disagree with a partner
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The dance instructor told everyone to ______ before the next song. → pair up
find_and_fix_to_correct: We pair up for the project last week. → We paired up for the project last week. (use past tense "paired," not "pair")
translate: शिक्षक ने हमें प्रोजेक्ट के लिए जोड़ी बनाने को कहा। → The teacher asked us to pair up for the project.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about when a teacher asked you to pair up.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to form a group of two people, usually for an activity'?
usage_tip: Teachers say 'Pair up with the person next to you.'

hindi_meaning: आदर्श मानना, सम्मान करना, प्रेरणा लेना
simple_explanation: To admire and respect someone, often wanting to be like them. "Look up to" means you see someone as an example to follow, because you admire their qualities or achievements.
example_1: I really look up to my older sister.
example_2: Young players look up to experienced athletes for inspiration.
example_3: She has always looked up to her grandmother's strength.
collocations: look up to someone, really look up to, always looked up to
where_it_s_used: Role models, mentorship, family, sports heroes
action_sequence: Before: see someone's good work → During: admire them → After: want to be like them
grammar_pattern: look up to + someone (+ for + quality) (Look up to a mentor for their patience.)
word_forms: look up to – looked up to – looked up to – looking up to
common_mistake: I look up my father for his hard work.
correct_version: I look up to my father for his hard work.
why_it_s_wrong: 'To' is needed between 'look up' and the person.
spelling_tip: Three words -- don't merge or drop the final "to."
etymology: From "look" + "up" + "to" -- literally directing one's gaze upward toward someone (as to someone taller or higher), extended figuratively to admiring or respecting them.
prefix_root_suffix: look + up + to (fixed phrasal expression -- meaning comes from the whole combination, not a prefix/root/suffix pattern)
word_family: look (v./n.) -- no distinct related word forms for this idiom
mnemonic: You LOOK UP, TO someone you admire, the way you'd look up to someone taller or on a pedestal.
memory_trick: LOOK UP TO: your eyes look UP at a tall hero.
visual_association: A child gazing upward at a tall statue of someone they admire.
confusing_word: look up to vs look up
difference_explained: Look up to = admire. Look up = search for information (look up a word).
mini_conversation:
A: Who inspired you to become a doctor?
B: My mother -- I've always looked up to her dedication.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A young athlete tells a reporter, "Ever since I was a kid, I've looked up to players who never gave up."
news_style_line: News-style: "The young volunteer said she has always looked up to community leaders who help others quietly."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I really look up to how calm you stay under pressure."
mcq_options: A) To criticize someone  B) To admire and respect someone  C) To search for someone  D) To avoid someone
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Many young readers ______ this author for her honesty. → look up to
find_and_fix_to_correct: He look up to his coach since childhood. → He has looked up to his coach since childhood. (use present perfect "has looked" with "since," not present simple "look")
translate: बच्चे अपने माता-पिता को आदर्श मानते हैं। → Children look up to their parents as role models.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a person you look up to and why.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to admire and respect someone, often wanting to be like them'?
usage_tip: Very common when talking about role models.

hindi_meaning: नीची नज़र से देखना, तुच्छ समझना
simple_explanation: To think you are better than someone else and treat them as less important. "Look down on" means unfairly judging someone as less worthy or capable, often because of pride or prejudice.
example_1: Don't look down on people who work hard.
example_2: He tends to look down on people who didn't go to college.
example_3: She never looked down on anyone, no matter their job.
collocations: look down on someone, never look down on, tend to look down on
related_phrasal_verbs: sneer at, belittle, talk down to
where_it_s_used: Prejudice, class differences, social attitudes, workplace snobbery
action_sequence: Before: meet someone different → During: think you are better → After: treat them as less important
grammar_pattern: look down on + someone (+ for + reason) (Look down on someone for their accent.)
word_forms: look down on – looked down on – looked down on – looking down on
common_mistake: She always look down at people who are different.
correct_version: She always looks down on people who are different.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Look down ON' is the phrase, and he/she needs -s: looks.
spelling_tip: Three words -- keep "down" and "on" both, don't drop either.
etymology: From "look" + "down" + "on" -- literally directing one's gaze downward at someone (as from a higher position), extended figuratively to viewing someone as inferior.
prefix_root_suffix: look + down + on (fixed phrasal expression -- meaning comes from the full combination, not a prefix/root/suffix pattern)
word_family: look (v./n.) -- no distinct related word forms for this idiom
mnemonic: LOOK DOWN ON someone as if standing above them and judging them from higher ground.
memory_trick: LOOK DOWN ON: your nose goes UP, your eyes go DOWN on others.
visual_association: Someone standing on a tall ladder, sneering down at people on the ground.
confusing_word: look down on vs look up to
difference_explained: Opposites. Look down on = think someone is worse than you. Look up to = admire.
mini_conversation:
A: He never talks to the new interns.
B: Yeah, I think he kind of looks down on them.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A worker confronts a rude customer and says firmly, "Don't look down on me just because of my job."
news_style_line: News-style: "The report criticized attitudes that look down on informal workers despite their contribution to the economy."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I hate how some people look down on those who didn't go to university."
mcq_options: A) To admire someone deeply  B) To think you are better than someone else  C) To physically look downward  D) To help someone in need
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: It's wrong to ______ someone just because they earn less than you. → look down on
find_and_fix_to_correct: He looks down to people who ask for help. → He looks down on people who ask for help. (the correct particle is "on," not "to")
translate: उसे अपने से कम पढ़े-लिखे लोगों को नीची नज़र से नहीं देखना चाहिए। → He shouldn't look down on people who are less educated than him.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about why it's wrong to look down on people.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to think you are better than someone else and treat them as less important'?
usage_tip: It describes snobbish, unkind behaviour.

simple_explanation: To meet someone by chance, without planning it. "Bump into" describes an accidental, surprise meeting with someone you know, usually in a public place.
example_1: I bumped into my teacher at the market.
example_2: I bumped into an old classmate at the airport.
example_3: You'll never guess who I bumped into today!
collocations: bump into someone, bump into each other, bump into an old friend
related_phrasal_verbs: run into, come across, cross paths with
where_it_s_used: Chance encounters, public places, catching up, small talk
action_sequence: Before: walk through the station → During: see a familiar face → After: stop and chat
grammar_pattern: bump into + someone (+ place) (Bump into a friend at the mall.)
word_forms: bump into – bumped into – bumped into – bumping into
common_mistake: I bumped with my old friend yesterday at the station.
correct_version: I bumped into my old friend yesterday at the station.
why_it_s_wrong: The particle is 'into', not 'with'.
spelling_tip: Two words; note the double "m" in "bump."
etymology: From "bump" (imitative of a dull collision sound) + "into" -- literally to physically collide with something, extended figuratively to meeting someone unexpectedly.
prefix_root_suffix: bump + into (phrasal particle -- "into" signals colliding/meeting unexpectedly)
word_family: bump (n./v. -- physical collision, related but distinct meaning)
mnemonic: You literally BUMP INTO an old friend on the street, as if you collided with them by surprise.
memory_trick: BUMP INTO: like two people bumping shoulders on a crowded street.
visual_association: Two shopping carts accidentally colliding in a crowded aisle.
difference_explained: Meet can be planned. Bump into = meet by chance.
mini_conversation:
A: You'll never guess who I saw today.
B: Who? Did you bump into someone famous?
everyday_scene: Everyday: A woman gasps at a coffee shop and says, "Oh my goodness, I can't believe I just bumped into you here!"
news_style_line: News-style: "Residents say they often bump into local celebrities who quietly shop at the neighborhood market."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Guess who I bumped into at the gym this morning -- my old roommate!"
mcq_options: A) To plan a meeting carefully  B) To meet someone by chance  C) To avoid someone on purpose  D) To argue with someone
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: I ______ my cousin while shopping for groceries yesterday. → bumped into
find_and_fix_to_correct: She bump into her friend at the mall last night. → She bumped into her friend at the mall last night. (use past tense "bumped," not "bump")
translate: बाज़ार में मेरी अचानक अपने पुराने दोस्त से मुलाकात हो गई। → I unexpectedly bumped into my old friend at the market.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about someone you bumped into unexpectedly.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to meet someone by chance, without planning it'?
usage_tip: It can also mean physically hit: 'I bumped into the door.'

hindi_meaning: पूरा करना, अंजाम देना, निष्पादित करना
simple_explanation: To do or complete a task, plan, or instruction. "Carry out" means to actually perform or finish something that was planned or ordered, like a task, experiment, or instruction.
example_1: The team will carry out the project this week.
example_2: Scientists carried out a series of experiments to test the theory.
example_3: The soldiers carried out their orders without question.
collocations: carry out a plan, carry out research, carry out instructions, carry out a task
related_phrasal_verbs: carry through, put into practice, follow through
action_sequence: Before: receive instructions → During: do each step → After: the task is complete
grammar_pattern: carry out + noun (Carry out an experiment / carry out a survey.)
word_forms: carry out – carried out – carried out – carrying out
common_mistake: The company carry out the plan next month.
correct_version: The company will carry out the plan next month.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Next month' is future, so the verb needs 'will'.
spelling_tip: Two words for the verb; "carryout" (one word) is used informally in American English as a noun for takeaway food.
etymology: From "carry" (Old French "carier," to transport) + "out" -- literally to transport something to completion/outward, extended figuratively to performing or completing a task or plan.
prefix_root_suffix: carry + out (phrasal particle -- "out" adds the sense of completing something fully)
mnemonic: You CARRY a plan all the way OUT until it's finished and done.
memory_trick: CARRY OUT: carry a plan OUT into the real world.
visual_association: A checklist with every box ticked off, one by one, until it's complete.
difference_explained: Do is general. Carry out = do a planned task, order or experiment (more formal).
mini_conversation:
A: Has the survey been done yet?
B: Not yet, but we'll carry it out next week.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A commander nods sharply and says, "Understood. We'll carry out the mission at dawn."
news_style_line: News-style: "Officials say the inspection was carried out following several safety complaints."
casual_conversation: Casual: "We finally carried out the plan we'd been talking about for months."
mcq_options: A) To cancel a task  B) To perform or complete a task  C) To ignore instructions  D) To carry something physically upstairs
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The researchers will ______ the study over six months. → carry out
find_and_fix_to_correct: They carried out with the plan successfully. → They carried out the plan successfully. (no "with" is needed after "carry out")
translate: वैज्ञानिकों ने इस विषय पर गहन शोध किया। → The scientists carried out in-depth research on this topic.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a task your team carried out successfully.

reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to do or complete a task, plan, or instruction'?
usage_tip: Formal: 'carry out research', 'carry out orders'.

hindi_meaning: पालन-पोषण करना; (बात) उठाना, चर्चा में लाना
simple_explanation: To raise a child, or to introduce a subject in a conversation. "Bring up" can mean raising and caring for a child until they grow up, or mentioning a topic during a discussion.
example_1: She was brought up in a small town.
example_2: My grandparents brought me up after my parents passed away.
example_3: He brought up an important point during the meeting.
collocations: bring up a child, bring up a topic, bring up the past
where_it_s_used: Parenting, family history, meetings, sensitive topics
action_sequence: Before: think of an idea → During: wait for the right moment → After: mention it to the group
grammar_pattern: bring up + noun (Bring up a child / bring up a subject.)
word_forms: bring up – brought up – brought up – bringing up
common_mistake: He bringed up a good idea in the meeting.
correct_version: He brought up a good idea in the meeting.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Bring' is irregular: the past is 'brought'.
spelling_tip: Two words; note "bring" changes to "brought" in the past tense: "brought up," not "bringed up."
etymology: From "bring" (Old English "bringan") + "up" -- literally to lift/carry something upward into notice, extended figuratively to raising a child or introducing a topic.
prefix_root_suffix: bring + up (phrasal particle -- "up" suggests lifting a child or topic into visibility)
mnemonic: You BRING a child UP through the years, or BRING a topic UP into the conversation.
memory_trick: BRING → BROUGHT, like THINK → THOUGHT.
visual_association: A small seedling being carefully raised upward until it becomes a strong tree.
difference_explained: Parents bring up a child. The child grows up.
mini_conversation:
A: I need to talk to you about something.
B: Sure, go ahead -- what did you want to bring up?
everyday_scene: Everyday: A grandmother smiles proudly and says, "I brought up five children in this very house."
news_style_line: News-style: "The senator brought up concerns about the new policy during the debate."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I don't want to bring up money again, but we really need to talk."
mcq_options: A) To avoid a subject completely  B) To mention or introduce a subject  C) To end a conversation  D) To physically lift something
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Please don't ______ that topic at dinner -- it's a sensitive subject. → bring up
find_and_fix_to_correct: She bring up her kids alone after the divorce. → She brought up her kids alone after the divorce. (use past tense "brought," not "bring")
translate: उसने बैठक में एक महत्वपूर्ण मुद्दा उठाया। → He brought up an important issue at the meeting.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a topic you'd like to bring up in a meeting.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to raise a child, or to introduce a subject in a conversation'?
usage_tip: 'Bring up' has two meanings: raise a child, or mention a topic.

simple_explanation: To cause something to happen. "Bring about" means to make something happen, especially an important change or result.
example_1: The new law brought about big changes.
example_2: The invention of the internet brought about a huge change in communication.
example_3: Poor management brought about the company's downfall.
collocations: bring about change, bring about a result, bring about improvement
related_phrasal_verbs: lead to, result in, give rise to
action_sequence: Before: a cause exists → During: it takes effect → After: a change happens
grammar_pattern: bring about + noun (Bring about a change / bring about progress.)
word_forms: bring about – brought about – brought about – bringing about
common_mistake: The storm bring about many damages to the crops.
correct_version: The storm brought about a lot of damage to the crops.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Brought' is the past of 'bring', and 'damage' is uncountable: 'a lot of damage'.
spelling_tip: Two words; don't confuse with "about" meaning "approximately" in other contexts.
etymology: From "bring" + "about" (Old English "onbutan," around/near) -- literally to carry something around into existence, extended figuratively to causing something to happen.
prefix_root_suffix: bring + about (phrasal particle -- "about" adds the sense of causing something into existence)
word_family: bring (v.) -- no distinct noun/adjective forms specific to this sense
mnemonic: To BRING something ABOUT is to bring a change all the way around into existence.
memory_trick: BRING ABOUT: bring a change ABOUT (around) into being.
visual_association: A single domino falling and setting off a long chain reaction.
difference_explained: Same meaning. Bring about is often used for positive or planned change.
mini_conversation:
A: What caused the change in policy?
B: Public pressure brought it about, mostly.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A historian says solemnly, "It was one decision that brought about everything that followed."
news_style_line: News-style: "Experts say the new regulations could bring about major changes to the industry."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Honestly, I don't know what brought about this sudden change in him."
mcq_options: A) To prevent something  B) To cause something to happen  C) To ignore a problem  D) To delay an event
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The reforms ______ significant improvements in education. → brought about
find_and_fix_to_correct: The new policy will bring about many benefit for workers. → The new policy will bring about many benefits for workers. ("benefit" should be plural to match "many")
translate: इस आविष्कार ने संचार के क्षेत्र में बड़ा बदलाव ला दिया। → This invention brought about a huge change in the field of communication.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a change technology has brought about.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to cause something to happen'?
usage_tip: Formal: 'bring about change', 'bring about reform'.

simple_explanation: To mention or show something to make someone notice it. "Point out" means telling someone about a fact, mistake, or detail so they become aware of it.
example_1: She pointed out a mistake in my essay.
example_2: The guide pointed out several historic buildings during the tour.
example_3: He kindly pointed out that I had the wrong date.
collocations: point out a mistake, point out that, kindly point out
related_phrasal_verbs: bring up, highlight, draw attention to
action_sequence: Before: see a problem → During: draw attention to it → After: everyone notices
grammar_pattern: point out + noun/that-clause (Point out an error / point out that something is wrong.)
word_forms: point out – pointed out – pointed out – pointing out
common_mistake: She pointed me out my mistake.
correct_version: She pointed out my mistake to me.
why_it_s_wrong: The thing comes after 'point out'; the person comes after 'to'.
spelling_tip: Two words; don't confuse with "pinpoint" (to locate exactly), a different word.
etymology: From "point" (Latin "punctum," a prick/dot) + "out" -- literally to physically point a finger outward at something, extended figuratively to drawing attention to a fact.
prefix_root_suffix: point + out (phrasal particle -- "out" reinforces the sense of bringing something into clear view)
mnemonic: You literally POINT your finger OUT toward the fact you want others to notice.
memory_trick: POINT OUT: point your finger AT something so others notice.
visual_association: A finger tapping directly on the exact spot that needs attention.
difference_explained: Show = let someone see. Point out = draw attention to something specific.
mini_conversation:
A: I think there's a mistake in the report.
B: Good catch -- can you point out exactly where?
everyday_scene: Everyday: A tour guide gestures toward the horizon and says, "If you look closely, I'll point out something most visitors miss."
news_style_line: News-style: "The report points out several weaknesses in the current safety procedures."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Thanks for pointing that out -- I completely missed it."
mcq_options: A) To hide a fact  B) To mention or show something so it's noticed  C) To argue about something  D) To forget a detail
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The teacher ______ a few grammar errors in my essay. → pointed out
find_and_fix_to_correct: He point out an error yesterday during the presentation. → He pointed out an error yesterday during the presentation. (use past tense "pointed," not "point")
translate: गाइड ने हमें शहर की कई ऐतिहासिक जगहें दिखाईं। → The guide pointed out several historic places in the city to us.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a mistake someone pointed out to you.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to mention or show something to make someone notice it'?
usage_tip: 'I'd like to point out that…' is a polite way to raise an issue.

simple_explanation: To solve a problem or understand something after thinking about it. "Figure out" means working through a confusing problem or situation until you understand it or find a solution.
example_1: I finally figured out the answer.
example_2: It took me an hour to figure out how the new phone works.
example_3: She figured out the solution to the math problem.
collocations: figure out how, figure out a solution, finally figure out
related_phrasal_verbs: work out, sort out, make out
action_sequence: Before: face a problem → During: think it through → After: find the answer
grammar_pattern: figure out + noun/wh-clause (Figure out the problem / figure out how it works.)
word_forms: figure out – figured out – figured out – figuring out
common_mistake: I can't figure out about this puzzle.
correct_version: I can't figure out this puzzle.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Figure out' takes its object directly, with no 'about'.
spelling_tip: "Figure" has a silent "u" pattern -- fi-g-u-r-e, easy to misspell as "figer."
etymology: From "figure" (Latin "figura," shape/form) + "out" -- literally to shape/work something out mentally, extended to solving or understanding something through thought.
prefix_root_suffix: figure + out (phrasal particle -- "out" suggests bringing a solution/understanding into clarity)
mnemonic: You FIGURE something OUT by shaping the confusing pieces into one clear picture.
memory_trick: FIGURE OUT: work out the FIGURES (numbers) of a problem.
visual_association: Scattered puzzle pieces slowly arranging themselves into a complete picture.
difference_explained: Figure out = solve by thinking. Find out = discover a fact, often by asking or reading.
mini_conversation:
A: This remote isn't working.
B: Give me a second, I'll figure it out.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character stares at a locked door and mutters, "There has to be a way in -- I just need to figure it out."
news_style_line: News-style: "Engineers are still working to figure out what caused the system failure."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Give me a minute -- I think I can figure this out."
mcq_options: A) To ignore a problem  B) To solve or understand something  C) To create a new problem  D) To forget a solution
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: It took the team all week to ______ the software bug. → figure out
find_and_fix_to_correct: She figure out the answer after many tries. → She figured out the answer after many tries. (use past tense "figured," not "figure")
translate: आख़िरकार मैंने इस गणित के सवाल को हल कर लिया। → I finally figured out this math problem.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a puzzle or problem you figured out.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to solve a problem or understand something after thinking about it'?
usage_tip: 'I can't figure him out' = I can't understand his behaviour.

simple_explanation: To discover a fact or piece of information. "Find out" means learning something you didn't know before, often through asking, searching, or being told.
example_1: I need to find out the train timings.
example_2: She found out the truth about the surprise party.
example_3: Can you find out what time the store closes?
collocations: find out the truth, find out about, find out why
action_sequence: Before: have a question → During: ask or read → After: learn the answer
grammar_pattern: find out + noun/wh-clause (Find out the answer / find out why it happened.)
word_forms: find out – found out – found out – finding out
common_mistake: I finded out that the shop is closed today.
correct_version: I found out that the shop is closed today.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Find' is irregular: the past is 'found'.
spelling_tip: Two words; irregular past tense "found out," not "finded out."
etymology: From "find" (Old English "findan") + "out" -- literally to discover something outward/into the open, extended to learning a fact or piece of information.
prefix_root_suffix: find + out (phrasal particle -- "out" reinforces the idea of bringing hidden information into the open)
mnemonic: You FIND the hidden truth and bring it OUT into the light.
memory_trick: FIND → FOUND, like BIND → BOUND.
visual_association: A curtain being pulled back to reveal something hidden underneath.
difference_explained: Find = locate an object. Find out = discover information.
mini_conversation:
A: Do you know why the flight got delayed?
B: Not yet, I'll find out and let you know.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A journalist leans forward and says, "I'm not stopping until I find out the truth."
news_style_line: News-style: "Investigators are still trying to find out what caused the sudden power outage."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I just found out that the concert got cancelled."
mcq_options: A) To hide information  B) To discover a fact  C) To forget something  D) To repair something
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: We only ______ about the schedule change this morning. → found out
find_and_fix_to_correct: I want to find out that why he left early. → I want to find out why he left early. (remove "that" -- unnecessary before the wh-clause)
translate: मुझे कल ही इस खबर का पता चला। → I only found out about this news yesterday.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something surprising you found out recently.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to discover a fact or piece of information'?
usage_tip: 'Find out' is used for facts, not physical objects: 'I found my keys' (not 'found out').

simple_explanation: To organize something or solve a problem. "Sort out" means fixing a messy or confusing situation, or organizing something so it works properly.
example_1: We need to sort out this misunderstanding.
example_2: I'll sort out the paperwork before Monday.
example_3: They sorted out their differences after a long talk.
collocations: sort out a problem, sort out the mess, sort things out
related_phrasal_verbs: work out, figure out, straighten out
action_sequence: Before: things are messy → During: organise them one by one → After: the problem is solved
grammar_pattern: sort out + noun (Sort out a problem / sort out the details.)
word_forms: sort out – sorted out – sorted out – sorting out
common_mistake: We need to sort out about the plan for tomorrow.
correct_version: We need to sort out the plan for tomorrow.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Sort out' takes its object directly, with no 'about'.
spelling_tip: Two words; note "sort," not "short" -- easy to misread.
etymology: From "sort" (Latin "sors," lot/category) + "out" -- literally to arrange things into categories, extended figuratively to resolving a problem or organizing something.
prefix_root_suffix: sort + out (phrasal particle -- "out" suggests arranging confusion into order)
mnemonic: You SORT confusing things OUT, like sorting a messy pile of papers into neat categories.
memory_trick: SORT OUT: sort things into order, and the problem goes OUT.
visual_association: A tangled ball of string being slowly untangled into neat, straight lines.
emotion_feel: Relief once resolved, mild stress before
difference_explained: Solve = find the answer. Sort out = organise or fix a practical problem (informal).
mini_conversation:
A: The booking system is a total mess.
B: I know, I'm trying to sort it out today.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A manager sighs and says, "Give me an hour, I'll sort this whole mess out."
news_style_line: News-style: "Officials are working to sort out the confusion caused by the new ticketing system."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Don't worry, we'll sort it out somehow."
mcq_options: A) To create more confusion  B) To organize or resolve something  C) To delay a decision  D) To argue endlessly
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: I need to ______ my finances before the trip. → sort out
find_and_fix_to_correct: She sort out the issue very quickly yesterday. → She sorted out the issue very quickly yesterday. (use past tense "sorted," not "sort")
translate: चलो, कल की योजना अभी सुलझा लेते हैं। → Let's sort out tomorrow's plan right now.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a problem you need to sort out this week.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to organize something or solve a problem'?
usage_tip: 'Sorted!' is British slang for 'done, fixed'.

hindi_meaning: हल निकालना, सफल होना; व्यायाम करना
simple_explanation: To solve a problem, to succeed in the end, or to exercise. "Work out" can mean calculating an answer, a plan succeeding despite difficulties, or physically exercising to stay fit.
example_1: I hope everything works out well.
example_2: Can you work out how much we owe each other?
example_3: I'm not sure the plan will work out.
collocations: work out fine, work out a solution, work out at the gym
related_phrasal_verbs: sort out, figure out, pan out
action_sequence: Before: have a problem → During: try different ideas → After: it ends well
grammar_pattern: work out (+ noun) (Work out a plan / everything worked out.)
word_forms: work out – worked out – worked out – working out
common_mistake: I hope the situation will work out good.
correct_version: I hope the situation will work out well.
why_it_s_wrong: After a verb like 'work out', use the adverb 'well', not the adjective 'good'.
spelling_tip: Two words for the verb; "workout" (one word) is the noun for an exercise session.
etymology: From "work" (Old English "weorc") + "out" -- literally to labor something into a finished state, extended figuratively to succeeding, calculating, or exercising physically.
prefix_root_suffix: work + out (phrasal particle -- "out" suggests reaching a final, resolved state)
mnemonic: You WORK a problem OUT until the answer comes into shape, or WORK OUT your muscles at the gym.
memory_trick: WORK OUT: problems and muscles both get worked out.
visual_association: Scattered puzzle pieces slowly falling neatly into their final place.
difference_explained: Good is an adjective (a good plan). Well is an adverb (it worked out well).
mini_conversation:
A: Are you worried about the interview?
B: A little, but I'm sure it'll work out fine.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A friend squeezes her hand and says, "I know it's scary, but I promise things will work out."
news_style_line: News-style: "Analysts say the merger deal worked out better than expected for both companies."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I go to the gym to work out three times a week."
mcq_question: "Work out" (as in "things worked out") most nearly means:
mcq_options: A) To fail completely  B) To turn out successfully  C) To argue loudly  D) To forget a plan
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Don't worry too much -- things usually ______ in the end. → work out
find_and_fix_to_correct: She works out in the gym since two years. → She has worked out at the gym for two years. (use present perfect "has worked" with "for," and the correct preposition is "at," not "in")
translate: मुझे यकीन है कि सब कुछ ठीक हो जाएगा। → I'm sure everything will work out.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a plan that worked out well.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to solve a problem, to succeed in the end, or to exercise'?
usage_tip: Three meanings: solve (work out an answer), end well (it worked out), exercise (I work out daily).

simple_explanation: To think of or produce a new idea, plan, or solution. "Come up with" means creating or thinking of something new, like an idea, excuse, or plan, usually to solve a problem.
example_1: She came up with a great idea.
example_2: The team came up with a clever solution to the problem.
example_3: He always comes up with excuses for being late.
collocations: come up with an idea, come up with a plan, come up with an excuse
related_phrasal_verbs: think up, dream up, figure out
action_sequence: Before: face a problem → During: think creatively → After: a new idea appears
grammar_pattern: come up with + noun (Come up with a solution / come up with a name.)
word_forms: come up with – came up with – come up with – coming up with
common_mistake: He come up an idea for the party.
correct_version: He came up with an idea for the party.
why_it_s_wrong: 'With' is part of the phrase, and 'came' is the past of 'come'.
spelling_tip: Three words; keep all three -- dropping "with" changes the meaning.
etymology: From "come" + "up" + "with" -- literally to arrive up alongside an idea, extended figuratively to inventing or producing an idea, plan, or solution.
prefix_root_suffix: come + up + with (fixed phrasal expression -- meaning comes from the whole combination, not a prefix/root/suffix pattern)
word_family: come (v.) -- no distinct related word forms for this idiom
mnemonic: A great idea seems to COME UP suddenly, WITH you, out of nowhere, like a lightbulb switching on.
memory_trick: COME UP WITH: an idea comes UP to the surface of your mind.
visual_association: A lightbulb suddenly glowing brightly above someone's head.
confusing_word: come up with vs think of
difference_explained: Same meaning. Come up with suggests creating something new, often under pressure.
mini_conversation:
A: We need a name for the new app.
B: Give me a minute, I'll come up with something.
everyday_scene: Everyday: An engineer scribbles on a whiteboard and shouts, "I think I finally came up with something that works!"
news_style_line: News-style: "Local students came up with an innovative design for a low-cost water filter."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I couldn't come up with a good excuse, so I just told the truth."
mcq_options: A) To forget an idea  B) To think of or produce a new idea  C) To reject a suggestion  D) To copy someone else's plan
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The chef ______ a brand-new recipe for the festival. → came up with
find_and_fix_to_correct: We are come up with a plan for next year. → We are coming up with a plan for next year. (use the present continuous form "coming," not the base "come")
translate: उसने पार्टी के लिए एक बेहतरीन विचार सोचा। → He came up with a brilliant idea for the party.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about an idea you came up with.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to think of or produce a new idea, plan, or solution'?
usage_tip: 'Can you come up with a better idea?' is common in meetings.

simple_explanation: To handle or manage a problem, task, or person. "Deal with" means taking action to manage or solve something, whether it's a difficult person, a problem, or a task.
example_1: I have to deal with this issue today.
example_2: She dealt with the angry customer calmly.
example_3: We need to deal with this problem before it gets worse.
collocations: deal with a problem, deal with stress, deal with customers
related_phrasal_verbs: handle, cope with, take care of
where_it_s_used: Problems, customer service, stress, difficult people
action_sequence: Before: a problem arrives → During: take action → After: it's handled
grammar_pattern: deal with + noun (Deal with a complaint / deal with a difficult situation.)
word_forms: deal with – dealt with – dealt with – dealing with
common_mistake: I don't know how deal with this situation.
correct_version: I don't know how to deal with this situation.
why_it_s_wrong: After 'how', use 'to + verb': 'how to deal with'.
spelling_tip: Two words; note the double "e" in "deal," not "del."
etymology: From "deal" (Old English "dælan," to divide/distribute) + "with" -- literally to handle a distribution/transaction, extended figuratively to managing or handling a situation.
prefix_root_suffix: deal + with (phrasal particle -- "with" attaches the sense of handling/managing something)
mnemonic: You DEAL WITH a problem the way a dealer handles cards -- managing it carefully, one step at a time.
memory_trick: DEAL → DEALT: one of the few verbs ending in -t, like FEEL → FELT.
visual_association: Someone calmly untangling a knot instead of panicking over it.
difference_explained: Same meaning. Handle is slightly more formal.
mini_conversation:
A: My boss keeps giving me extra work.
B: You need to deal with that directly -- talk to him.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A manager takes a deep breath and says, "Let me deal with this myself -- go take a break."
news_style_line: News-style: "The city is under pressure to deal with the growing traffic congestion."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I really don't want to deal with this drama today."
mcq_options: A) To ignore a problem completely  B) To handle or manage something  C) To create a new problem  D) To celebrate an achievement
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The manager had to ______ several complaints this morning. → deal with
find_and_fix_to_correct: She dealed with the situation very well. → She dealt with the situation very well. (the past tense of "deal" is "dealt," not "dealed")
translate: मुझे आज इस समस्या से निपटना होगा। → I have to deal with this problem today.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about how you deal with stress.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to handle or manage a problem, task, or person'?
usage_tip: 'I'll deal with it' = I'll handle it.

simple_explanation: To delay doing something, or to make someone dislike something. "Put off" usually means postponing a task to a later time, but it can also mean discouraging someone from liking or doing something.
example_2: She keeps putting off her dentist appointment.
example_3: The bad smell put me off the food completely.
collocations: put off a decision, put off until later, be put off by
action_sequence: Before: see a boring task → During: decide to do it later → After: it's still not done
grammar_pattern: put off + noun/gerund (Put off a meeting / put off doing homework.)
word_forms: put off – put off – put off – putting off
common_mistake: I always put off to do my chores.
correct_version: I always put off doing my chores.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Put off' is followed by -ing, not 'to + verb'.
spelling_tip: Two words; note "put" doesn't change in the past tense (put off stays "put off").
etymology: From "put" (Old English "putian") + "off" -- literally to place something away/apart, extended figuratively to postponing an action or discouraging someone.
prefix_root_suffix: put + off (phrasal particle -- "off" adds the sense of pushing something away in time)
word_family: put (v.) -- no distinct related word forms for this idiom
mnemonic: When you PUT something OFF, you push it further away in time, like sliding it off your to-do list for later.
memory_trick: PUT OFF: push a job OFF to later, like a snooze button.
visual_association: A task sliding further and further down a to-do list, never quite reaching the top.
difference_explained: Put off = delay to a later time. Cancel = decide it won't happen at all.
mini_conversation:
A: Have you booked the doctor's appointment yet?
B: Not yet, I keep putting it off.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A student groans over a stack of books and admits, "I've put this off for way too long."
news_style_line: News-style: "Officials confirmed the election has been put off until next spring."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I need to stop putting off my exercise routine."
mcq_options: A) To do something immediately  B) To delay or postpone something  C) To finish a task early  D) To celebrate an event
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: He kept ______ the difficult conversation with his boss. → putting off
find_and_fix_to_correct: We put off the meeting to next week already happened. → We already put off the meeting to next week. (fix the awkward word order)
translate: कृपया अपना काम कल तक के लिए मत टालो। → Please don't put off your work until tomorrow.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a task you keep putting off.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to delay doing something, or to make someone dislike something'?
usage_tip: 'Put off' also means make someone dislike something: 'The smell put me off.'

hindi_meaning: स्थापित करना, व्यवस्था करना, तैयार करना
simple_explanation: To arrange, prepare, or start something. "Set up" means putting something in place so it's ready to use, or starting something new like a business or event.
example_1: We set up the tent before dark.
example_2: They set up a new company last year.
example_3: Can you help me set up my laptop for the meeting?
collocations: set up a business, set up a meeting, set up equipment
action_sequence: Before: have an idea → During: arrange everything needed → After: it's ready to run
grammar_pattern: set up + noun (Set up a system / set up a tent.)
word_forms: set up – set up – set up – setting up
common_mistake: He setted up his own business last year.
correct_version: He set up his own business last year.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Set' has the same form in the past; 'setted' is wrong.
spelling_tip: Two words for the verb; "setup" (one word) is the noun form.
etymology: From "set" (Old English "settan," to place) + "up" -- literally to place something upright/into position, extended figuratively to establishing, arranging, or preparing something.
prefix_root_suffix: set + up (phrasal particle -- "up" adds the sense of putting something into a working/upright position)
mnemonic: You SET the pieces UP before starting -- like setting up a tent before camping.
memory_trick: SET → SET → SET, like PUT → PUT → PUT.
visual_association: Tent poles rising one by one until the whole tent stands upright.
difference_explained: Start = begin. Set up = arrange everything needed so something can start (set up a business).
mini_conversation:
A: Is the projector ready for the presentation?
B: Almost, I'm setting it up now.
everyday_scene: Everyday: An entrepreneur grins and says, "Five years ago, I set up this business with just a laptop and a dream."
news_style_line: News-style: "The government has set up a task force to investigate the flooding."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Let's set up a time to talk this week."
mcq_options: A) To destroy something  B) To arrange, prepare, or establish something  C) To ignore a task  D) To finish a meal
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: We need to ______ the sound system before the concert starts. → set up
find_and_fix_to_correct: They set up the company since 2015. → They have run the company since 2015. (rephrase, since "set up" describes a one-time founding action, not an ongoing state)
translate: उन्होंने पिछले साल अपनी नई कंपनी स्थापित की। → They set up their new company last year.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something you set up at home or work.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to arrange, prepare, or start something'?
usage_tip: 'Set up' also means trick someone: 'He was set up.' A 'setup' (noun) is an arrangement.

hindi_meaning: नियंत्रण अपने हाथ में लेना, कार्यभार लेना
simple_explanation: To take control of something, often from someone else. "Take over" means becoming responsible for or in charge of something, especially a task, role, or company that someone else had before.
example_1: She will take over as manager next month.
example_2: The new CEO took over the company after the merger.
example_3: Can you take over the driving? I'm tired.
collocations: take over a company, take over control, take over from someone
related_phrasal_verbs: hand over, step in, assume control
action_sequence: Before: someone leaves a role → During: step in → After: now you control it
grammar_pattern: take over + (as/from) + noun (Take over as captain / take over from the previous manager.)
word_forms: take over – took over – taken over – taking over
common_mistake: He take over the project from last week.
correct_version: He took over the project last week.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Last week' needs the past 'took', and 'from' isn't needed before a time.
spelling_tip: Two words for the verb; "takeover" (one word) is the noun, common in business news.
etymology: From "take" (Old Norse "taka") + "over" -- literally to take control across/beyond a boundary, extended figuratively to assuming control of something.
prefix_root_suffix: take + over (phrasal particle -- "over" signals moving control across from one person to another)
mnemonic: You TAKE control and step OVER the line where someone else left off.
memory_trick: TAKE OVER: take the steering wheel OVER from someone.
visual_association: One hand smoothly taking the steering wheel from another while driving.
difference_explained: Take over = get control from someone else. Take on = accept new work or responsibility.
mini_conversation:
A: Who's leading the project now?
B: I'm taking over from Raj starting Monday.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A young executive straightens her jacket and says, "As of today, I'm taking over this department."
news_style_line: News-style: "The larger corporation announced plans to take over its smaller competitor."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I'll take over cooking dinner if you're too tired."
mcq_options: A) To give up control  B) To assume control of something  C) To finish a task quickly  D) To ignore a responsibility
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: She's going to ______ the team once the current manager retires. → take over
find_and_fix_to_correct: They took over of the company last year. → They took over the company last year. (no "of" is needed after "take over")
translate: उसने रिटायरमेंट के बाद अपने पिता का व्यापार अपने हाथ में ले लिया। → He took over his father's business after retirement.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a job you took over from someone.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to take control of something, often from someone else'?
usage_tip: 'Takeover' (noun) = one company buying control of another.

hindi_meaning: (काम/ज़िम्मेदारी) लेना, स्वीकार करना; (कर्मचारी) रखना; चुनौती स्वीकारना
simple_explanation: To accept a responsibility, job, or challenge, or to hire someone. "Take on" means agreeing to do something difficult, hiring new staff, or accepting more work or responsibility than before.
example_1: I can't take on more work right now.
example_2: The company took on ten new employees this month.
example_3: She decided to take on the challenge of running a marathon.
collocations: take on a challenge, take on staff, take on responsibility
related_phrasal_verbs: undertake, sign up for, shoulder (a responsibility)
action_sequence: Before: see a new task → During: agree to do it → After: it's now your responsibility
grammar_pattern: take on + noun (Take on a task / take on new staff.)
word_forms: take on – took on – taken on – taking on
common_mistake: I don't want to take on with more responsibilities.
correct_version: I don't want to take on more responsibilities.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Take on' takes its object directly, with no 'with'.
spelling_tip: Two words; don't confuse with "takeaway" or "takeover," different phrasal forms.
etymology: From "take" + "on" -- literally to take something onto oneself, extended figuratively to accepting responsibility, hiring staff, or confronting a challenge.
prefix_root_suffix: take + on (phrasal particle -- "on" adds the sense of accepting something onto oneself)
