word_family: take (v.) -- no distinct related word forms for this idiom
mnemonic: You TAKE a challenge ON your own shoulders, agreeing to carry it.
memory_trick: TAKE ON: put a new load ON your shoulders.
visual_association: Someone lifting a heavy backpack onto their shoulders, ready to carry it.
difference_explained: Take on = accept extra work. Take over = take control from someone else.
mini_conversation:
A: Are you hiring right now?
B: Yes, we're planning to take on a few more people next month.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A boxer stares down his opponent and says, "I've never backed away from a challenge, and I won't take on this one lightly either."
news_style_line: News-style: "The factory plans to take on two hundred new workers next quarter."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I've decided to take on a part-time job to save some extra money."
mcq_options: A) To reject a task  B) To accept a responsibility, challenge, or new staff  C) To finish a project  D) To retire from work
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The startup is looking to ______ a few more developers this year. → take on
find_and_fix_to_correct: She take on too much work and got tired. → She took on too much work and got tired. (use past tense "took," not "take")
translate: उसने मैराथन दौड़ने की चुनौती स्वीकार की। → She took on the challenge of running a marathon.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a challenge you took on this year.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to accept a responsibility, job, or challenge, or to hire someone'?
usage_tip: 'Take on' also means compete against: 'India will take on Australia.'

simple_explanation: To give or submit something, often official or completed work. "Hand in" means submitting a completed piece of work, like homework, a form, or a resignation letter, to the right person.
example_1: I need to hand in my essay tomorrow.
example_2: Please hand in your assignments by Friday.
example_3: He handed in his resignation letter this morning.
collocations: hand in an assignment, hand in a report, hand in a resignation
action_sequence: Before: finish your homework → During: give it to the teacher → After: it's submitted
grammar_pattern: hand in + noun (Hand in homework / hand in a form.)
word_forms: hand in – handed in – handed in – handing in
common_mistake: I handed in the teacher my homework.
correct_version: I handed in my homework to the teacher.
why_it_s_wrong: The thing comes after 'hand in'; the person comes after 'to'.
spelling_tip: Two words; don't confuse with "handing," the -ing form, in casual speech.
etymology: From "hand" (Old English "hand") + "in" -- literally to pass something into someone's hands, extended figuratively to submitting work or documents.
prefix_root_suffix: hand + in (phrasal particle -- "in" signals passing something into someone's possession)
mnemonic: You physically HAND your homework IN to the teacher's desk.
memory_trick: HAND IN: your HAND puts work IN the teacher's tray.
visual_association: A stack of papers being placed neatly into a teacher's outstretched hand.
emotion_feel: Relief (once done), anxiety before a deadline
difference_explained: Same meaning. Submit is more formal and used online.
mini_conversation:
A: Did you finish the report?
B: Yes, I handed it in this morning.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A student rushes into class and gasps, "Wait, please -- I need to hand this in before the bell rings!"
news_style_line: News-style: "The minister handed in his resignation letter following the scandal."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I still haven't handed in my visa application."
mcq_options: A) To distribute something to a group  B) To submit or give something to someone in authority  C) To lose a document  D) To create a new report
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Remember to ______ your project before the deadline on Friday. → hand in
find_and_fix_to_correct: She hand in her essay late yesterday. → She handed in her essay late yesterday. (use past tense "handed," not "hand")
translate: कृपया अपना असाइनमेंट शुक्रवार तक जमा कर दें। → Please hand in your assignment by Friday.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about when you have to hand in your next assignment.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to give or submit something, often official or completed work'?
usage_tip: Schools: 'hand in homework'. Offices: 'hand in your resignation'.

simple_explanation: To give something to a group of people, one to each person. "Hand out" means distributing items -- like papers, food, or gifts -- to a group of people, usually one at a time.
example_1: The teacher will hand out the test papers.
example_2: Volunteers handed out water bottles to the runners.
example_3: She handed out flyers outside the mall.
collocations: hand out flyers, hand out food, hand out copies
where_it_s_used: Classrooms, charity events, marketing, public events
action_sequence: Before: have a stack of sheets → During: give one to each person → After: everyone has one
grammar_pattern: hand out + noun (Hand out leaflets / hand out prizes.)
word_forms: hand out – handed out – handed out – handing out
common_mistake: The teacher handed out for the students the worksheets.
correct_version: The teacher handed out the worksheets to the students.
why_it_s_wrong: Put the thing right after 'hand out', then 'to' + the people.
spelling_tip: Two words for the verb; "handout" (one word) is the noun for a printed sheet given to a group.
etymology: From "hand" + "out" -- literally to pass things outward from one's hands to many people, extended figuratively to distributing items.
prefix_root_suffix: hand + out (phrasal particle -- "out" signals distributing items outward to many people)
mnemonic: You HAND papers OUT to everyone in the room, one by one.
memory_trick: HAND OUT: hands go OUT to each person in a row.
visual_association: A line of people each receiving a leaflet, one after another, from an outstretched hand.
difference_explained: Hand out = give to many people. Hand in = give your work to one person in charge.
mini_conversation:
A: How do people know about the event?
B: We're handing out flyers all over town.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A volunteer smiles while walking through the crowd, saying, "Free water here -- I'm just handing these out to keep everyone cool!"
news_style_line: News-style: "Charity workers handed out blankets and food to families affected by the storm."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Can you help me hand out invitations at the party?"
mcq_options: A) To collect items from people  B) To distribute items to a group of people  C) To hide something  D) To submit an assignment
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The organizers ______ free samples at the entrance. → handed out
find_and_fix_to_correct: They hand out the prizes at end of the event. → They handed out the prizes at the end of the event. (use past tense "handed," and add "the" before "end")
translate: स्वयंसेवकों ने बच्चों को मुफ्त किताबें बाँटी। → The volunteers handed out free books to the children.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something that was handed out in your class.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to give something to a group of people, one to each person'?
usage_tip: A 'handout' (noun) = a printed sheet given in class.

simple_explanation: To give control, property, or an item to someone else, often formally. "Hand over" means passing something -- like power, money, or an object -- to another person, especially in a formal or serious situation.
example_1: He handed over the keys to the new owner.
example_2: The president handed over power peacefully.
example_3: She handed over the documents to the lawyer.
collocations: hand over control, hand over the keys, hand over power
action_sequence: Before: hold the keys → During: give them to someone formally → After: they are responsible now
grammar_pattern: hand over + noun + (to) + someone (Hand over the report to your manager.)
word_forms: hand over – handed over – handed over – handing over
common_mistake: He hand over the business to for his son.
correct_version: He handed over the business to his son.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Hand over' is followed directly by 'to' + person, with no 'for'.
spelling_tip: Two words for the verb; "handover" (one word) is the noun, common in business/political contexts.
etymology: From "hand" + "over" -- literally to pass something across from one person's hands to another, extended figuratively to transferring control, property, or responsibility.
prefix_root_suffix: hand + over (phrasal particle -- "over" signals a transfer of possession/control to someone else)
mnemonic: You HAND something carefully OVER to someone else's care or control.
memory_trick: HAND OVER: pass something OVER the table to someone else.
visual_association: A set of keys being placed carefully into someone else's open palm.
difference_explained: Give is general. Hand over = give control or ownership, often formally.
mini_conversation:
A: Who's running the shop now?
B: My father handed it over to me last year.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A retiring officer places his badge on the desk and says, "It's time I hand this over to someone else."
news_style_line: News-style: "The company announced plans to hand over daily operations to a new management team."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Just hand over the remote, I want to watch the news."
mcq_options: A) To keep something for yourself  B) To transfer or give something to someone else  C) To destroy something  D) To buy something
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The outgoing manager will ______ his duties to the new hire next week. → hand over
find_and_fix_to_correct: They handed over with the documents yesterday. → They handed over the documents yesterday. (no "with" is needed after "hand over")
translate: उसने अपनी दुकान अपने बेटे को सौंप दी। → He handed over his shop to his son.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something you handed over before leaving a job or class.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to give control, property, or an item to someone else, often formally'?
usage_tip: 'Handover' (noun) = the formal passing of work from one person to another.

hindi_meaning: आगे की कार्रवाई करना, दोबारा संपर्क करना, पीछा करना (काम का)
simple_explanation: To take further action or contact someone again after a first step. "Follow up" means checking back on something after it started, like sending another email or asking about progress.
example_1: I'll follow up with an email tomorrow.
example_2: The doctor asked me to follow up in two weeks.
example_3: She followed up on her job application by calling the office.
collocations: follow up on, follow up with, follow up an email
related_phrasal_verbs: check in, chase up, keep tabs on
where_it_s_used: Work emails, healthcare, customer service, job applications
action_sequence: Before: send an email → During: get no reply → After: write again to check
grammar_pattern: follow up + (on/with) + noun (Follow up on a request / follow up with a client.)
word_forms: follow up – followed up – followed up – following up
common_mistake: I will follow up about you next week regarding the offer.
correct_version: I will follow up with you next week regarding the offer.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'follow up WITH' a person and 'follow up ON' a matter.
spelling_tip: Two words for the verb; "follow-up" (hyphenated) is the noun/adjective, as in "a follow-up email."
etymology: From "follow" (Old English "folgian") + "up" -- literally to pursue something further afterward, extended figuratively to taking additional action after an initial step.
prefix_root_suffix: follow + up (phrasal particle -- "up" reinforces the sense of continuing action after an initial step)
mnemonic: After the first step, you FOLLOW UP to make sure things continue moving forward.
memory_trick: FOLLOW UP: follow the first step UP with a second one.
visual_association: A second knock on a door after the first one went unanswered.
difference_explained: Follow = go after or obey. Follow up = take the next action after a first step.
mini_conversation:
A: Did you hear back about the interview?
B: Not yet, I'm going to follow up tomorrow.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A doctor hands over a card and says, "Call this number in a week -- we'll follow up on your results then."
news_style_line: News-style: "Health officials plan to follow up with residents who reported symptoms last week."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I sent the email, but I should probably follow up if I don't hear back soon."
mcq_options: A) To ignore a previous request  B) To take further action or contact someone again  C) To cancel a plan  D) To start a new project
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The nurse said she would ______ with us after the test results arrive. → follow up
find_and_fix_to_correct: He will follow up the client tomorrow morning. → He will follow up with the client tomorrow morning. ("with" is required before the person)
translate: मैं इस सप्ताह के अंत तक इस मामले पर फिर से संपर्क करूँगा। → I will follow up on this matter by the end of the week.
write_your_own_sentence: Write an email line following up on a job application.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to take further action or contact someone again after a first step'?
usage_tip: 'Just following up on my last email' is a standard work email line.

hindi_meaning: (वादा/योजना को) पूरी तरह निभाना, अंत तक पूरा करना
simple_explanation: To complete an action or promise you started. "Follow through" means actually finishing what you said you would do, instead of stopping partway or forgetting about it.
example_1: He always follows through on his promises.
example_2: She said she would help, and she followed through.
example_3: It's easy to make plans, but hard to follow through on them.
collocations: follow through on a promise, follow through with a plan, fail to follow through
related_phrasal_verbs: carry out, keep one's word, see through
action_sequence: Before: make a promise → During: keep working at it → After: finish it completely
grammar_pattern: follow through + (on/with) + noun (Follow through on a commitment.)
word_forms: follow through – followed through – followed through – following through
common_mistake: He never follows through his promises.
correct_version: He never follows through on his promises.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'follow through ON' something.
spelling_tip: Two words; "through" is often misspelled -- remember the silent "gh."
etymology: From "follow" + "through" -- literally to continue moving completely across/past a point (as in sports, following the swing through), extended figuratively to completing what one starts or promises.
prefix_root_suffix: follow + through (phrasal particle -- "through" reinforces completing an action all the way to the end)
word_family: follow (v.) -- no distinct related word forms for this idiom
mnemonic: In sports, you FOLLOW THROUGH your swing to the very end -- don't stop halfway.
memory_trick: FOLLOW THROUGH: go all the way THROUGH to the end.
visual_association: A golfer's swing continuing smoothly past the ball instead of stopping short.
emotion_feel: Pride when done, guilt when not
difference_explained: Follow up = take the next step. Follow through = finish what you started.
mini_conversation:
A: You said you'd call the plumber, did you?
B: Yes, I followed through this morning.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A mentor pats a student on the back and says, "Great plan -- now the real test is whether you follow through."
news_style_line: News-style: "Critics say the government has failed to follow through on its promised reforms."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I always plan to exercise more, but I never actually follow through."
mcq_options: A) To start a plan without finishing it  B) To complete an action or promise you started  C) To forget about a commitment  D) To cancel an appointment
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: She promised to help and actually ______ this time. → followed through
find_and_fix_to_correct: They did not follow through with they promise. → They did not follow through with their promise. (use the possessive "their," not "they")
translate: उसने अपने वादे को आखिरी तक निभाया। → He followed through on his promise until the end.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a promise you followed through on.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to complete an action or promise you started'?
usage_tip: In sport, 'follow-through' is completing the swing of a bat or racket.

hindi_meaning: समर्थन करना, पुष्टि करना; (डेटा की) प्रतिलिपि बनाना
simple_explanation: To support someone or something, or to make a copy of information. "Back up" can mean supporting what someone says with evidence, or saving an extra copy of files in case the original is lost.
example_1: My friend backed me up during the argument.
example_2: Please back up your computer files regularly.
example_3: Her colleagues backed her up when she reported the issue.
collocations: back up a claim, back up data, back someone up
action_sequence: Before: have important files → During: copy them to another place → After: they're safe if the phone breaks
grammar_pattern: back up + noun / back + someone + up (Back up a statement / back him up.)
word_forms: back up – backed up – backed up – backing up
common_mistake: I need to back up with my files before the update.
correct_version: I need to back up my files before the update.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Back up' takes its object directly, with no 'with'.
spelling_tip: Two words for the verb; "backup" (one word) is the noun, as in "a backup file."
etymology: From "back" (Old English "bæc") + "up" -- literally to move backward for support or to save a copy behind the original, extended figuratively to supporting a claim or a person.
prefix_root_suffix: back + up (phrasal particle -- "up" reinforces the sense of standing behind and supporting something)
mnemonic: You BACK a friend UP by standing behind them, supporting what they say.
memory_trick: BACK UP: keep a copy at the BACK in case the front fails.
visual_association: A second, identical folder sitting safely behind the original, just in case.
difference_explained: Support = help in general. Back up = support someone's words or claim; or copy data.
mini_conversation:
A: They didn't believe my version of events.
B: I'll back you up -- I saw everything happen.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A partner steps forward beside her colleague and says firmly, "Whatever you tell them, I'll back you up completely."
news_style_line: News-style: "Experts urged users to back up important files after the recent wave of cyberattacks."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Make sure you back up your photos before you lose your phone data."
mcq_options: A) To delete information permanently  B) To support someone, or save a copy of something  C) To argue with someone  D) To move forward quickly
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Always ______ your important documents before formatting the computer. → back up
find_and_fix_to_correct: She back up his statement during the meeting. → She backed up his statement during the meeting. (use past tense "backed," not "back")
translate: कृपया अपडेट से पहले अपनी फाइलों का बैकअप बना लें। → Please back up your files before the update.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about how often you back up your phone photos.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to support someone or something, or to make a copy of information'?
usage_tip: 'Back me up' = support what I say. 'Backup' (noun) = a copy.

simple_explanation: To stop working suddenly, or to lose emotional control and cry. A machine or vehicle "breaks down" when it suddenly stops working properly. A person can also "break down" when they become so upset that they start crying.
example_1: The car broke down on the highway.
example_2: Our washing machine broke down again this week.
example_3: She broke down in tears during the interview.
collocations: break down completely, car breaks down, break down in tears, talks break down
related_phrasal_verbs: give out, conk out, fall apart
where_it_s_used: Cars, machines, technology, emotional stress, negotiations
action_sequence: Before: the car is running → During: the engine stops suddenly → After: it won't move
grammar_pattern: subject + break down (The printer broke down / She broke down crying.)
word_forms: break down – broke down – broken down – breaking down
common_mistake: My car broked down yesterday.
correct_version: My car broke down yesterday.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Break' is irregular: the past is 'broke', not 'broked'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress both words evenly: BREAK DOWN; the noun form "breakdown" stresses the first syllable.
spelling_tip: Two words as a verb ("the car broke down"), one word as a noun ("a breakdown").
etymology: From "break" + "down" -- literally to break into a lowered/collapsed state, extended to machines failing or emotions collapsing.
prefix_root_suffix: break + down (particle "down" adds the idea of collapsing/failing)
mnemonic: When something BREAKS, it falls DOWN and stops working.
memory_trick: BREAK DOWN: the machine breaks and falls DOWN.
visual_association: A car stopped on the roadside with its hood up, smoke rising.
difference_explained: Break down = stop working, or cry. Break up = end a relationship.
mini_conversation:
A: Why are you late?
B: Sorry, my bike broke down on the way.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A stranded driver kicks the tire and mutters, "Of course it breaks down now, of all days."
news_style_line: News-style: "Officials say the region's power grid broke down during the storm."
casual_conversation: Casual: "My laptop broke down right before the deadline."
mcq_question: "Break down" (for a machine) most nearly means:
mcq_options: A) To work perfectly  B) To stop working suddenly  C) To become faster  D) To get repaired automatically
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The old elevator tends to ______ in cold weather. → break down
find_and_fix_to_correct: The copier is breaking down, but nobody call the technician. → The copier is breaking down, but nobody has called the technician.
translate: बीच रास्ते में मेरी कार खराब हो गई। → My car broke down in the middle of the road.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a time a vehicle broke down.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to stop working suddenly, or to lose emotional control and cry'?
usage_tip: 'Break down' also means cry, or explain step by step: 'break down the problem'.

simple_explanation: To reduce the amount of something you do or use. When you "cut down" on something, like sugar, spending, or smoking, you reduce how much of it you do -- usually because it's unhealthy or too much.
example_1: I need to cut down on sugar.
example_2: The doctor told him to cut down on salt.
example_3: We're trying to cut down our monthly expenses.
collocations: cut down on, cut down expenses, cut down smoking
related_phrasal_verbs: cut back, cut out, scale down
action_sequence: Before: use too much sugar → During: use less each week → After: use much less
grammar_pattern: cut down (on) + noun (cut down on sugar / cut expenses down)
word_forms: cut down – cut down – cut down – cutting down
common_mistake: I want to cut down my phone.
correct_version: I want to cut down on my phone use.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'cut down ON' + the thing you are reducing.
pronunciation_tip: Equal stress on both words: CUT DOWN; add "on" before the thing being reduced.
spelling_tip: Always two separate words -- never "cutdown" as a verb.
etymology: From "cut" + "down" -- literally to cut something so it becomes smaller/lower, extended to reducing an amount or quantity.
prefix_root_suffix: cut + down (particle "down" shows a decrease in amount)
mnemonic: When you CUT something DOWN, you make it smaller -- cut down your sugar, and your sugar amount goes down.
memory_trick: CUT DOWN: cut the amount DOWN.
visual_association: A hand pushing a sugar bowl slowly away.
confusing_word: cut down on vs cut out
difference_explained: Cut down on = reduce. Cut out = stop completely.
mini_conversation:
A: You look healthier lately.
B: Thanks, I cut down on junk food.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A doctor taps a chart and says calmly, "You really need to cut down on the salt."
news_style_line: News-style: "The report urges households to cut down on energy use this winter."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I'm trying to cut down on how much time I spend online."
mcq_options: A) To increase something  B) To reduce the amount of something  C) To repair something  D) To advertise something
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The company asked employees to ______ on unnecessary travel. → cut down
find_and_fix_to_correct: He cut down of eating meat. → He cut down on eating meat. (the correct preposition is "on," not "of")
translate: उसने मिठाई खाना कम कर दिया। → He cut down on eating sweets.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something you want to cut down on.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to reduce the amount of something you do or use'?
usage_tip: 'Cut down' also means cut a tree to the ground.

hindi_meaning: काट देना, बीच में रोक देना
simple_explanation: To stop something suddenly and completely, or to interrupt someone. "Cut off" means to suddenly stop a supply, a connection, or a conversation -- like when a phone call ends unexpectedly or someone interrupts you mid-sentence.
example_1: The call got cut off suddenly.
example_2: Sorry, you cut me off -- please continue.
example_3: The village was cut off by the flood.
collocations: cut off the power, cut someone off, cut off from the world
related_phrasal_verbs: cut short, break off, cut in
action_sequence: Before: talk on the phone → During: the signal drops → After: the call ends
grammar_pattern: cut + object + off (cut the power off / cut her off mid-sentence)
word_forms: cut off – cut off – cut off – cutting off
common_mistake: The line was cutting off while I was talking.
correct_version: The line cut off while I was talking.
why_it_s_wrong: A sudden finished event uses the simple past.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on "off": cut-OFF when used as a verb.
spelling_tip: Two words as a verb; "cutoff" is one word only as a noun/adjective (a cutoff date).
etymology: From "cut" + "off" -- literally to sever something completely, extended to interrupting communication or supply.
mnemonic: If you CUT something, then it's OFF completely -- no more connection.
memory_trick: CUT OFF: like scissors cutting a line.
visual_association: A pair of scissors snipping a wire in half.
difference_explained: Cut off = stop suddenly (a call, supply). Cut out = remove, or stop eating something.
mini_conversation:
A: Why did you stop talking?
B: Sorry, you cut me off -- I wasn't finished!
everyday_scene: Everyday: Mid-sentence, the screen glitches and a character shouts, "Hello? We just got cut off!"
news_style_line: News-style: "Thousands of homes were cut off from water supply after the pipeline burst."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Ugh, my call got cut off right in the middle of the conversation."
mcq_options: A) To slowly reduce something  B) To stop or interrupt something suddenly  C) To repair a connection  D) To celebrate an event
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Please don't ______ me -- let me finish my point. → cut off
find_and_fix_to_correct: The company cut off the internet from us since two days. → The company has cut off our internet for two days. (use present perfect with "for" + duration)
translate: तूफान के कारण गाँव का बिजली कनेक्शन कट गया। → The village's electricity was cut off because of the storm.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a time your call got cut off.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to stop something suddenly and completely, or to interrupt someone'?
usage_tip: 'I got cut off' = my phone call ended suddenly.

simple_explanation: To officially register your arrival at a hotel, airport, or event. "Check in" means telling the front desk or counter that you've arrived, so they can give you your room key, boarding pass, or entry.
example_1: We checked in at the hotel around noon.
example_2: Passengers must check in two hours before the flight.
example_3: I'll check in with you once I land.
collocations: check in early, online check-in, check in at the counter
related_phrasal_verbs: check out, sign in, log in
action_sequence: Before: arrive at the hotel → During: show ID at reception → After: get your room key
grammar_pattern: check in (at/to) + place (check in at the hotel / check in to the flight)
word_forms: check in – checked in – checked in – checking in
common_mistake: We checked in the hotel yesterday.
correct_version: We checked in at the hotel yesterday.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'check in AT' the place, or 'check in to/into' a hotel.
pronunciation_tip: Stress both words evenly: CHECK IN; the noun "check-in" stresses the first syllable.
spelling_tip: Two words as a verb, hyphenated as a noun ("check-in time").
etymology: From "check" (to verify/register) + "in" -- literally to register your entry/arrival at a place.
mnemonic: When you CHECK IN, staff CHECK your name and let you IN.
memory_trick: CHECK IN: your name goes IN the hotel's list.
visual_association: A receptionist handing over a room key at a hotel desk.
emotion_feel: Neutral, sometimes mild relief after a long journey
difference_explained: Check in = register when you arrive. Check out = pay and leave.
mini_conversation:
A: What time can we check in?
B: Check-in starts at 2 PM.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A tired traveler drops their bag at the counter and says, "Hi, I'd like to check in, please."
news_style_line: News-style: "Airlines recommend passengers check in online to avoid long queues."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Can you check in for both of us? I'm still parking the car."
mcq_options: A) To leave a hotel and pay the bill  B) To register your arrival somewhere  C) To cancel a reservation  D) To repair something
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Guests can ______ any time after 2 PM. → check in
find_and_fix_to_correct: I checked in to the hotel since three hours. → I checked in to the hotel three hours ago. (use "ago" with simple past, not "since")
translate: हमने दोपहर को होटल में चेक-इन किया। → We checked in at the hotel at noon.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about when you checked in at an airport or hotel.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to officially register your arrival at a hotel, airport, or event'?
usage_tip: 'Check in' also means contact someone to see how they are.

simple_explanation: To pay your bill and leave a hotel, or informally, to look at or examine something. "Check out" of a hotel means settling your bill and leaving. Informally, "check this out" means "take a look at this" -- often about something interesting or new.
example_1: We checked out of the hotel at 11 AM.
example_2: Please check out by noon to avoid extra charges.
example_3: Check out this new restaurant downtown.
collocations: check out early, check out time, check out a new place
related_phrasal_verbs: check in, look into, try out
action_sequence: Before: finish your stay → During: pay the bill → After: leave the hotel
grammar_pattern: check out (of) + place / check out + noun (check out of the hotel / check out this app)
word_forms: check out – checked out – checked out – checking out
common_mistake: We check out from hotel yesterday.
correct_version: We checked out of the hotel yesterday.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'check out OF' a hotel, not 'from', and the past tense 'checked'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress both words evenly: CHECK OUT; the noun "checkout" stresses the first syllable.
spelling_tip: Two words as a verb, one word as a noun ("the checkout counter").
etymology: From "check" + "out" -- literally to register your exit, extended informally to mean "look at/investigate."
mnemonic: When you CHECK OUT, you're checking that everything's fine before going OUT the door.
memory_trick: CHECK OUT: your name comes OUT of the hotel's list.
visual_association: A hotel guest wheeling a suitcase past the front desk toward the exit.
emotion_feel: Neutral, sometimes curiosity when exploring something new
difference_explained: Leave = go away. Check out = formally finish your stay and pay.
mini_conversation:
A: What time is checkout?
B: You need to check out by 11 AM.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A guest slides a key card across the counter and says, "We're ready to check out now."
news_style_line: News-style: "Shoppers are encouraged to check out early sales before items sell out."
casual_conversation: Casual: "You should check out that new café near the station."
mcq_options: A) To ignore something  B) To look at or try something  C) To pay a fine  D) To cancel a plan
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Could you tell me what time we need to ______? → check out
find_and_fix_to_correct: I am checking out this book from library since yesterday. → I checked out this book from the library yesterday. (use simple past, and include the article "the")
translate: कृपया इस नई दुकान को ज़रूर देखिए। → Please check out this new shop.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something online you want to check out.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to pay your bill and leave a hotel, or informally, to look at or examine something'?
usage_tip: Informal: 'Check this out!' = look at this.

simple_explanation: To cancel something that was planned. When you "call off" an event, meeting, or plan, you decide it will not happen after all, usually because of a problem or change.
example_2: The match was called off due to heavy rain.
example_3: She called off the meeting at the last minute.
collocations: call off the search, call off a strike, call off an engagement
action_sequence: Before: plan a trip → During: something goes wrong → After: announce it won't happen
grammar_pattern: call off + noun (call off the game / call the game off)
word_forms: call off – called off – called off – calling off
common_mistake: They called off of the trip.
correct_version: They called off the trip.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Call off' takes its object directly; no 'of' after 'off'.
spelling_tip: Two words as a verb -- don't merge into "calloff."
etymology: From "call" + "off" -- literally to call/announce that something is turned off or stopped.
mnemonic: You CALL someone to say the event is OFF -- that's "call off."
memory_trick: CALL OFF: call out 'It's OFF!'.
visual_association: A red "CANCELLED" stamp pressed over an event poster.
difference_explained: Call off = cancel. Postpone = move to a later date.
mini_conversation:
A: Is the picnic still happening?
B: No, they called it off because of the storm.
everyday_scene: Everyday: An organizer grabs the microphone and announces, "Due to the storm, tonight's event is called off."
news_style_line: News-style: "Organizers called off the outdoor concert because of the extreme heat warning."
casual_conversation: Casual: "They called off the trip at the last minute -- such a shame."
mcq_options: A) To confirm a plan  B) To cancel a plan  C) To phone someone  D) To delay by a few minutes
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The football match was ______ because of the storm. → called off
find_and_fix_to_correct: The boss call off the meeting yesterday. → The boss called off the meeting yesterday. (use the past tense "called")
translate: बारिश की वजह से मैच रद्द कर दिया गया। → The match was called off because of the rain.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about an event that was called off.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to cancel something that was planned'?
usage_tip: 'The match was called off due to rain.'

simple_explanation: To return a phone call to someone who called you earlier. When you're busy and can't answer, or need more time to reply, you tell someone you'll "call back" -- meaning you'll phone them again later.
example_1: I'll call you back in ten minutes.
example_2: She promised to call back after checking the schedule.
example_3: He never called me back about the job.
collocations: call back later, call someone back, promise to call back
related_phrasal_verbs: ring back, get back to, phone back
where_it_s_used: Work, customer service, missed calls, phone etiquette
action_sequence: Before: miss a call → During: see the number → After: phone them
grammar_pattern: call + object + back (call him back / call back your client)
word_forms: call back – called back – called back – calling back
common_mistake: I will call back to you tomorrow.
correct_version: I will call you back tomorrow.
why_it_s_wrong: The person goes between 'call' and 'back', with no 'to'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on "back": call-BACK when used as a verb; "callback" as a noun stresses the first syllable.
spelling_tip: Two words as a verb; one word as a noun ("I'll wait for a callback").
etymology: From "call" + "back" -- literally to call again in return, i.e., to return someone's call.
prefix_root_suffix: call + back (particle "back" shows returning an action)
mnemonic: If someone calls you, you CALL them BACK -- sending the call back to them.
memory_trick: CALL BACK: the call comes BACK to the person who called first.
visual_association: A phone buzzing on a desk with a missed-call notification.
difference_explained: Call back = return a call someone made to you. Call again = phone once more.
mini_conversation:
A: You have three missed calls from your dad.
B: Oh no, let me call him back right now.
everyday_scene: Everyday: An assistant covers the phone and whispers, "He's in a meeting -- can he call you back?"
news_style_line: News-style: "The company said it would call back all customers affected by the outage."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Sorry I missed your call -- I'll call you back in five minutes."
mcq_options: A) To cancel a phone call  B) To return someone's phone call  C) To block a number  D) To send a text message
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: I'm driving right now -- can I ______ in an hour? → call you back
find_and_fix_to_correct: Please call back to me when you are free. → Please call me back when you are free. (put the object "me" between "call" and "back")
translate: कृपया थोड़ी देर बाद मुझे वापस कॉल करें। → Please call me back in a little while.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence promising to call someone back.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to return a phone call to someone who called you earlier'?
usage_tip: 'Can I call you back?' is polite when you're busy.

simple_explanation: To accept or tolerate something unpleasant without complaining. When you "put up with" something -- noise, bad behavior, a difficult situation -- you continue to accept it even though you don't like it.
example_1: I can't put up with this noise anymore.
example_2: She had to put up with her noisy neighbors for years.
example_3: I won't put up with being spoken to like that.
collocations: put up with noise, put up with behavior, can't put up with
action_sequence: Before: something annoys you → During: stay patient → After: accept it without complaining
grammar_pattern: put up with + noun/gerund (put up with the delay / put up with waiting)
word_forms: put up with – put up with – put up with – putting up with
common_mistake: I can't put up with to wait so long.
correct_version: I can't put up with waiting so long.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Put up with' is followed by a noun or -ing, not 'to + verb'.
pronunciation_tip: The stress falls on "up": put-UP-with, said quickly as one chunk.
spelling_tip: Three separate words -- never combine them; keep "with" at the end.
etymology: From "put" + "up" + "with" -- an old idiom literally meaning to "put yourself up" (endure) alongside something unpleasant.
prefix_root_suffix: put + up + with (a three-word phrasal verb -- meaning comes from the whole combination)
word_family: put (v.) -- closest related form, no separate noun form
mnemonic: When you PUT UP WITH something, you carry its weight WITH you without complaining.
memory_trick: PUT UP WITH: carry a heavy load UP the hill WITH patience.
visual_association: Someone holding a heavy bag with a strained but calm expression.
difference_explained: Same meaning. Tolerate is more formal.
mini_conversation:
A: How do you put up with that loud music every night?
B: Honestly, I just wear earplugs now.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A roommate throws up their hands and says, "I can't put up with this mess anymore!"
news_style_line: News-style: "Residents say they've had to put up with construction noise for over a year."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Honestly, I don't know how she puts up with him."
mcq_options: A) To enjoy something fully  B) To tolerate something unpleasant  C) To fix a problem  D) To avoid someone completely
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: I don't know how you ______ that terrible traffic every day. → put up with
find_and_fix_to_correct: She put up with he shouting all the time. → She put up with his shouting all the time. (use possessive "his," not "he," before the gerund)
translate: मैं अब यह शोर बर्दाश्त नहीं कर सकता। → I can't put up with this noise anymore.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something you have to put up with daily.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to accept or tolerate something unpleasant without complaining'?
usage_tip: It shows annoyance: 'I can't put up with this noise any more.'

simple_explanation: To have none of something left because it has all been used. When you "run out" of something -- milk, time, patience -- it means the supply is completely finished and there's none remaining.
example_1: We ran out of milk this morning.
example_2: The printer ran out of ink halfway through.
example_3: Time is running out to submit the form.
collocations: run out of time, run out of money, run out of patience
related_phrasal_verbs: use up, dry up, run low
action_sequence: Before: have some milk → During: use it all → After: none is left
grammar_pattern: run out of + noun (run out of sugar / running out of time)
word_forms: run out – ran out – run out – running out
common_mistake: We run out the coffee yesterday.
correct_version: We ran out of coffee yesterday.
why_it_s_wrong: Use the past 'ran', and 'run out OF' + the thing.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on "out": run-OUT when used as a verb.
spelling_tip: Two words as a verb; remember the preposition "of" before the missing item.
etymology: From "run" + "out" -- literally to run to the outside/end, extended to a supply being completely used up.
prefix_root_suffix: run + out (particle "out" shows something reaching its end/exhaustion)
mnemonic: When supplies RUN OUT, imagine them literally running away until none are left.
memory_trick: RUN OUT: the supply RUNS until it's OUT.
visual_association: An hourglass with the last few grains of sand falling.
difference_explained: Finish = complete something on purpose. Run out (of) = have nothing left, often by surprise.
mini_conversation:
A: Can I borrow a pen?
B: Sorry, I've run out of pens too.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character checks their watch nervously and says, "We're running out of time -- we have to go now!"
news_style_line: News-style: "Hospitals in the region are running out of essential medical supplies."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Ugh, we've run out of shampoo again."
mcq_options: A) To have plenty of something  B) To have none of something left  C) To buy more of something  D) To run quickly outside
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Hurry up, we're ______ of time! → running out
find_and_fix_to_correct: I have run out money for this month. → I have run out of money for this month. (don't forget the preposition "of")
translate: हमारा दूध ख़त्म हो गया। → We ran out of milk.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something that ran out at home this week.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to have none of something left because it has all been used'?
usage_tip: 'Time is running out' = there's little time left.

simple_explanation: To meet someone unexpectedly, or to unexpectedly experience a problem. When you "run into" a person, you meet them by chance, without planning it. You can also "run into" trouble, meaning a problem suddenly appears.
example_1: I ran into my old teacher today.
example_2: We ran into each other at the supermarket.
example_3: The project ran into some unexpected delays.
collocations: run into trouble, run into an old friend, run into difficulties
related_phrasal_verbs: bump into, come across, run across
action_sequence: Before: walk in the mall → During: see a familiar face → After: stop and chat
grammar_pattern: run into + noun (run into a friend / run into problems)
word_forms: run into – ran into – run into – running into
common_mistake: I run into her yesterday at the mall.
correct_version: I ran into her yesterday at the mall.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Yesterday' needs the past 'ran'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on "into": run-IN-to, said as one smooth phrase.
spelling_tip: Two words -- don't confuse with "run in to" (enter quickly).
etymology: From "run" + "into" -- literally to physically collide with something, extended to unexpectedly meeting someone or a problem.
mnemonic: If you RUN and INTO someone by accident, that's an unplanned meeting.
memory_trick: RUN INTO: run around a corner and INTO a friend.
visual_association: Two people bumping shoulders accidentally on a busy street and both smiling in surprise.
difference_explained: Same meaning for people. 'Run into' is also used for problems and costs.
mini_conversation:
A: Guess who I ran into today!
B: Who? Tell me everything!
everyday_scene: Everyday: Two old friends freeze mid-step and one laughs, "Wow, I can't believe we just ran into each other!"
news_style_line: News-style: "Engineers ran into unexpected technical issues during the bridge repair."
casual_conversation: Casual: "You'll never guess who I ran into at the gym today."
mcq_options: A) To plan a meeting carefully  B) To meet someone unexpectedly  C) To avoid a person  D) To finish a task quickly
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: I ______ my cousin at the train station yesterday. → ran into
find_and_fix_to_correct: She ran into with her boss at the mall. → She ran into her boss at the mall. (no "with" needed -- the object follows "into" directly)
translate: कल बाज़ार में मेरी अचानक अपने पुराने दोस्त से मुलाक़ात हो गई। → I ran into my old friend at the market yesterday.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about someone you ran into by chance.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to meet someone unexpectedly, or to unexpectedly experience a problem'?
usage_tip: 'Run into problems' = meet unexpected problems.

hindi_meaning: पार करना, संपर्क कर पाना, निभा लेना
simple_explanation: To succeed in reaching someone, finishing something, or surviving a difficult time. "Get through" can mean finally connecting on the phone ("I finally got through to him"), finishing a task, or managing to survive something hard, like an illness or a busy week.
example_1: I finally got through to customer service.
example_2: It took ten calls before I got through to the office.
example_3: She got through the exam despite feeling nervous.
collocations: get through to someone, get through a difficult time, get through the day
related_phrasal_verbs: get by, pull through, come through
action_sequence: Before: face a hard time → During: keep going → After: reach the other side
grammar_pattern: get through (to) + noun (get through to the manager / get through the exam)
word_forms: get through – got through – got/gotten through – getting through
common_mistake: I could not get through with him on the phone.
correct_version: I could not get through to him on the phone.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'get through TO' a person on the phone.
spelling_tip: Two words -- remember "through" has a silent "gh."
etymology: From "get" + "through" -- literally to pass through a physical barrier, extended to succeeding in communication or enduring a hard time.
prefix_root_suffix: get + through (particle "through" shows moving past an obstacle to the other side)
mnemonic: To GET THROUGH a wall of difficulty, you push past it to the other side.
memory_trick: GET THROUGH: go THROUGH a difficult tunnel to the other end.
visual_association: A hand finally pushing through a thick curtain into the light.
difference_explained: Pass = succeed in an exam. Get through = finish or survive something difficult.
mini_conversation:
A: Did you finally reach the hospital?
B: Yes, I got through after waiting twenty minutes.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A rescuer radios back through static, "We finally got through -- help is on the way!"
news_style_line: News-style: "Volunteers helped the flood victims get through the toughest weeks after the disaster."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I've been trying to get through to the bank all morning."
mcq_options: A) To ignore someone  B) To successfully contact someone  C) To argue with someone  D) To forget someone's number
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: It took me an hour to ______ to the airline's helpline. → get through
find_and_fix_to_correct: She get through the difficult year with her family's help. → She got through the difficult year with her family's help. (use past tense "got")
translate: कई कोशिशों के बाद आख़िरकार मेरी बात उससे फ़ोन पर हो गई। → After many tries, I finally got through to him on the phone.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about how you got through a hard exam.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to succeed in reaching someone, finishing something, or surviving a difficult time'?
usage_tip: Three meanings: reach by phone, finish something, survive a hard time.

simple_explanation: To successfully make someone understand your idea or message. When you "get" your point "across," you manage to explain it clearly enough that other people understand exactly what you mean.
example_1: The teacher got her point across clearly.
example_2: He struggled to get his idea across in the meeting.
example_3: Good diagrams help get complex information across.
collocations: get the message across, get a point across, get an idea across
action_sequence: Before: have an idea → During: explain it clearly → After: the listener understands
grammar_pattern: get + idea/point + across (get your point across / get across your idea)
word_forms: get across – got across – got/gotten across – getting across
common_mistake: She couldn't get across her idea to team.
correct_version: She couldn't get her idea across to the team.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Team' needs 'the'. With a noun object, 'get the idea across' is most natural.
spelling_tip: Two words -- note the double "s" in "across."
etymology: From "get" + "across" -- literally to move to the other side, extended to successfully conveying a message to someone else's understanding.
prefix_root_suffix: get + across (particle "across" shows an idea successfully crossing to another person)
mnemonic: To GET your idea ACROSS, imagine tossing it across a gap so it lands safely in the listener's mind.
memory_trick: GET ACROSS: carry your idea ACROSS a bridge to the listener.
visual_association: A message in a bottle successfully reaching the opposite shore.
emotion_feel: Effort mixed with hope for understanding
difference_explained: Explain = say how or why. Get across = succeed in making someone understand.
mini_conversation:
A: Did the audience understand your presentation?
B: I think so -- I really tried to get my point across clearly.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A director leans toward the actor and says, "Just get the emotion across -- the words don't matter as much."
news_style_line: News-style: "The campaign used simple graphics to get its safety message across to the public."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I tried three different ways to get my point across, but he still didn't get it."
mcq_options: A) To hide your true opinion  B) To make an idea understood  C) To cross a road  D) To disagree with someone
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The coach used a diagram to ______ his strategy to the players. → get across
find_and_fix_to_correct: He get his message across very well during speech. → He got his message across very well during the speech. (use past tense "got" and add "the" before "speech")
translate: शिक्षक अपनी बात छात्रों को अच्छी तरह समझा पाए। → The teacher got her point across well to the students.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about how you get an idea across in a meeting.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to successfully make someone understand your idea or message'?
usage_tip: 'I'm trying to get my point across' is common in debates.

hindi_meaning: गुज़रना (कठिन समय से), ध्यान से जाँचना
simple_explanation: To experience something difficult, or to examine something carefully step by step. "Go through" a hard time means you experience and endure it, like a loss or a struggle. "Go through" a document means you check it in detail, one part at a time.
example_1: She went through a difficult divorce.
example_2: The company went through major changes last year.
example_3: Let's go through the contract before signing.
collocations: go through a phase, go through a divorce, go through the details
related_phrasal_verbs: go over, live through, get through
where_it_s_used: Emotional struggles, paperwork, reviews, life changes
action_sequence: Before: a hard time starts → During: live through it → After: it ends
grammar_pattern: go through + noun (go through hardship / go through the report)
word_forms: go through – went through – gone through – going through
common_mistake: She is going through a lot problems recently.
correct_version: She is going through a lot of problems recently.
why_it_s_wrong: 'A lot' needs 'of' before a noun: 'a lot of problems'.
spelling_tip: Two words -- remember the silent "gh" in "through."
etymology: From "go" + "through" -- literally to pass from one side to the other, extended to enduring an experience or reviewing something item by item.
prefix_root_suffix: go + through (particle "through" shows passing from start to end of an experience or process)
mnemonic: When you GO THROUGH something hard, imagine walking THROUGH a long, dark tunnel until you come out the other side.
memory_trick: GO THROUGH: walk THROUGH a difficult forest.
visual_association: A person walking through a long, winding tunnel toward a light at the end.
difference_explained: Go through = experience, or examine in detail. Go over = review quickly.
mini_conversation:
A: She seems really stressed lately.
B: Yeah, she's going through a lot at home right now.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A friend places a hand on someone's shoulder and says softly, "I know you're going through a lot right now."
news_style_line: News-style: "The company is going through a major restructuring this quarter."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Can we go through the numbers again before the meeting?"
mcq_question: "Go through" (a difficult time) most nearly means:
mcq_options: A) To celebrate a success  B) To experience or endure something hard  C) To ignore a problem  D) To finish quickly
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: We need to ______ the report before submitting it. → go through
find_and_fix_to_correct: He is go through a hard time since last month. → He has been going through a hard time since last month. (use present perfect continuous with "since")
translate: वह पिछले साल एक कठिन दौर से गुज़री। → She went through a difficult time last year.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a difficult time someone you know went through.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to experience something difficult, or to examine something carefully step by step'?
usage_tip: 'Go through the document' = read it carefully.

simple_explanation: To review or check something carefully, often before finishing or presenting it. When you "go over" your notes, homework, or a plan, you look at it again carefully to make sure everything is correct.
example_1: Let's go over the answers together.
example_2: The teacher went over the homework before the test.
example_3: Can we go over the budget one more time?
collocations: go over the details, go over notes, go over a plan
related_phrasal_verbs: go through, look over, run through
action_sequence: Before: finish a report → During: read it once more → After: fix any mistakes
grammar_pattern: go over + noun (go over the notes / go over the agenda)
word_forms: go over – went over – gone over – going over
common_mistake: Let's go over on the report together.
correct_version: Let's go over the report together.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Go over' takes its object directly, with no 'on'.
spelling_tip: Two words -- don't confuse with "moreover" or "overgo" (not real words).
etymology: From "go" + "over" -- literally to move across the top of something, extended to reviewing or examining it point by point.
prefix_root_suffix: go + over (particle "over" shows moving across/reviewing something thoroughly)
mnemonic: When you GO OVER something, imagine your eyes moving OVER every line, checking it carefully.
memory_trick: GO OVER: your eyes go OVER the page again.
visual_association: A pen underlining each line of a checklist one by one.
difference_explained: Go over = review or check. Go through = examine every detail, or experience something hard.
mini_conversation:
A: Are you ready for the presentation?
B: Almost -- I just want to go over my slides once more.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A pilot flips through a checklist and says, "Let's go over the safety procedures one more time."
news_style_line: News-style: "Officials will go over the new regulations with local businesses next week."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Can you go over this email before I send it?"
mcq_options: A) To ignore something completely  B) To review or check something  C) To delete something  D) To argue about something
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Please ______ your answers before submitting the test. → go over
find_and_fix_to_correct: We going over the plan tomorrow morning. → We are going over the plan tomorrow morning. (add the auxiliary verb "are" for present continuous)
translate: कृपया प्रस्तुति देने से पहले एक बार स्लाइड्स को फिर से देख लें। → Please go over the slides once more before presenting.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about what you go over before a test.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to review or check something carefully, often before finishing or presenting it'?
usage_tip: 'Let's go over it once more' is common before exams.

simple_explanation: Used to give permission for someone to do something, or to proceed with a plan. "Go ahead" is often used as a friendly way to say "yes, you can do that" or to announce that you're going to proceed with something.
example_2: Go ahead and ask your question.
example_3: She decided to go ahead with the wedding despite the weather.
collocations: go ahead with, go ahead and, please go ahead
where_it_s_used: Giving permission, meetings, decisions, everyday requests
action_sequence: Before: someone asks permission → During: say 'Go ahead' → After: they start
grammar_pattern: go ahead (and) + verb / go ahead with + noun (go ahead and start / go ahead with the plan)
word_forms: go ahead – went ahead – gone ahead – going ahead
common_mistake: Go ahead to eat your food.
correct_version: Go ahead and eat your food.
why_it_s_wrong: Before a second verb, use 'go ahead AND + verb', not 'to'.
spelling_tip: Two words -- "ahead" has one word, don't split it as "a head."
etymology: From "go" + "ahead" -- literally to move forward/to the front, extended to giving or taking permission to proceed.
mnemonic: When someone says "GO AHEAD," they're waving you forward, straight ahead, with no obstacles.
memory_trick: GO AHEAD: move AHEAD — the traffic light is green.
visual_association: A green traffic light signaling cars to move forward.
difference_explained: Go ahead = start, with permission. Continue = keep doing something already started.
mini_conversation:
A: Can I start eating?
B: Go ahead, don't wait for me.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A director waves a hand and shouts, "Go ahead, action!"
news_style_line: News-style: "The council gave the go-ahead for the new community center project."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Go ahead and take the last slice, I'm full."
mcq_options: A) To stop immediately  B) To proceed or have permission to do something  C) To go back to the start  D) To refuse a request
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: "Can I ask a question?" "Sure, ______." → go ahead
find_and_fix_to_correct: He said me go ahead with the plan. → He told me to go ahead with the plan. (use "told me to," not "said me")
translate: "क्या मैं शुरू कर सकता हूँ?" "हाँ, आगे बढ़ो।" → "Can I start?" "Yes, go ahead."
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence giving someone permission with 'Go ahead'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'used to give permission for someone to do something, or to proceed with a plan'?
usage_tip: 'Go ahead' alone is a polite 'yes, please do'.

hindi_meaning: जारी रहना, चलते रहना, हो रहा होना
simple_explanation: To continue doing something, or to happen/take place. "Go on" can mean to keep doing an action without stopping ("go on with your work"), or to ask what's happening ("What's going on?").
example_1: Please go on with your story.
example_2: The meeting went on for three hours.
example_3: What's going on in here?
collocations: go on and on, what's going on, go on with your work
where_it_s_used: Meetings, stories, daily events, curiosity about situations
action_sequence: Before: someone starts talking → During: they don't stop → After: they talk for an hour
grammar_pattern: go on (with/+ -ing) (go on with the meeting / go on talking)
word_forms: go on – went on – gone on – going on
common_mistake: She go on to talk for an hour.
correct_version: She went on talking for an hour.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Go on + -ing' = continue. The past is 'went'.
spelling_tip: Two words -- simple, but don't confuse with "gone" (past participle of "go").
etymology: From "go" + "on" -- literally to keep moving forward, extended to continuing an action or something taking place.
mnemonic: When something GOES ON, it keeps moving forward without stopping.
memory_trick: GO ON: the show goes ON.
visual_association: A conveyor belt that keeps moving steadily without stopping.
confusing_word: go on doing vs go on to do
difference_explained: Go on talking = continue the same thing. Go on to talk about X = move to a new topic next.
mini_conversation:
A: What's going on out there?
B: Just some kids playing football in the street.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A detective steps into a noisy room and demands, "What is going on here?"
news_style_line: News-style: "Talks between the two sides went on late into the night."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Sorry, go on -- I didn't mean to interrupt."
mcq_options: A) What happened yesterday?  B) What is happening right now?  C) What will happen tomorrow?  D) Who is responsible?
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The concert ______ for almost three hours. → went on
find_and_fix_to_correct: The rain go on all night long. → The rain went on all night long. (use the past tense "went")
translate: बैठक तीन घंटे तक चलती रही। → The meeting went on for three hours.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence asking a friend what's going on.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to continue doing something, or to happen/take place'?
usage_tip: 'What's going on?' = what's happening? 'Go on!' = encouragement.

hindi_meaning: बराबरी बनाए रखना, गति बनाए रखना
simple_explanation: To move or progress at the same speed or level as someone or something else. "Keep up" means not falling behind -- whether it's walking at the same pace as friends, keeping up with schoolwork, or staying updated with the news.
example_1: I can't keep up with you!
example_2: He struggled to keep up with the class.
example_3: She reads the news daily to keep up with current events.
collocations: keep up with the news, keep up the pace, keep up appearances
related_phrasal_verbs: catch up, keep pace, stay on top of
where_it_s_used: Studies, fitness, news, technology, work pace
action_sequence: Before: the class moves fast → During: work hard → After: stay at the same level
grammar_pattern: keep up (with) + noun (keep up with the trends / keep up the good work)
word_forms: keep up – kept up – kept up – keeping up
common_mistake: I can't keep up the class discussion.
correct_version: I can't keep up with the class discussion.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'keep up WITH' + what you're matching.
etymology: From "keep" + "up" -- literally to hold something at a raised level, extended to maintaining the same speed or standard as others.
prefix_root_suffix: keep + up (particle "up" shows maintaining a level/standard)
mnemonic: To KEEP UP with the group, you must keep your energy UP so you don't fall behind.
memory_trick: KEEP UP: keep UP with the runner beside you.
visual_association: Two runners on a track, one slightly behind but pushing to stay level.
confusing_word: keep up with vs catch up with
difference_explained: Keep up = stay level. Catch up = reach the level after falling behind.
mini_conversation:
A: Slow down a little, please!
B: Sorry, I forget not everyone can keep up with my pace.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A runner gasps to their coach, "I'm trying, but I can't keep up with him!"
news_style_line: News-style: "Small businesses are struggling to keep up with rising costs this year."
casual_conversation: Casual: "It's hard to keep up with all these new phone apps."
mcq_options: A) To fall behind someone  B) To match someone's pace or progress  C) To stop trying  D) To ignore new information
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: It's hard to ______ with all the homework this semester. → keep up
find_and_fix_to_correct: She always keep up with fashion trends. → She always keeps up with fashion trends. (add "-s" for third-person singular present tense)
translate: मुझे तकनीक के नए बदलावों के साथ तालमेल बिठाना मुश्किल लगता है। → I find it hard to keep up with new changes in technology.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a subject you find hard to keep up with.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to move or progress at the same speed or level as someone or something else'?
usage_tip: 'Keep it up!' = continue doing well.

simple_explanation: To continue doing something without stopping, often repeatedly. "Keep on" doing something means you don't stop -- you continue the action again and again, sometimes even when it's annoying or difficult.
example_1: He kept on asking the same question.
example_2: She kept on working despite feeling tired.
example_3: The baby kept on crying all night.
collocations: keep on going, keep on trying, keep on doing
related_phrasal_verbs: go on, carry on, keep at
action_sequence: Before: start an action → During: repeat it → After: still doing it
grammar_pattern: keep on + verb-ing (keep on trying / keep on working)
word_forms: keep on – kept on – kept on – keeping on
common_mistake: He keep on to ask me for money.
correct_version: He keeps on asking me for money.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Keep on' takes -ing, and he/she needs -s: keeps.
spelling_tip: Two words -- followed by a verb-ing form, not "to + verb."
etymology: From "keep" + "on" -- literally to hold an action going forward, extended to persistent, repeated continuation.
prefix_root_suffix: keep + on (particle "on" shows continuous, repeated action)
mnemonic: KEEP ON doing something means you KEEP the action turned ON, without switching it off.
memory_trick: KEEP ON: keep ON going, like a switch that stays on.
visual_association: A wind-up toy that keeps walking forward without stopping.
difference_explained: Same meaning with -ing. Keep on often suggests the action is annoying or determined.
tone: Neutral (can sound mildly annoyed depending on context)
mini_conversation:
A: He keeps on interrupting the meeting.
B: I know, someone should say something.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A coach yells across the field, "Keep on pushing, you're almost there!"
news_style_line: News-style: "Despite the setbacks, the team kept on working toward the launch date."
casual_conversation: Casual: "My neighbor's dog just keeps on barking at night."
mcq_options: A) To stop an action suddenly  B) To continue doing something repeatedly  C) To forget about something  D) To start something new
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: If you ______ practicing, you'll get better at it. → keep on
find_and_fix_to_correct: She kept on to complain about the weather. → She kept on complaining about the weather. (use the "-ing" form, not "to + verb")
translate: वह लगातार वही सवाल पूछता रहा। → He kept on asking the same question.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something someone keeps on doing that annoys you.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to continue doing something without stopping, often repeatedly'?
usage_tip: 'Keep on trying' is encouragement.

hindi_meaning: लोकप्रिय हो जाना, समझ में आ जाना
simple_explanation: To become popular, or to finally understand something. When a trend, idea, or product "catches on," it becomes popular quickly. When a person "catches on," they finally understand something they were confused about before.
example_1: The new trend caught on fast.
example_2: The idea didn't catch on until years later.
example_3: It took him a while to catch on to the joke.
collocations: catch on quickly, catch on fast, slowly catch on
action_sequence: Before: hear a joke → During: think for a moment → After: finally understand it
grammar_pattern: catch on (to something) (catch on to the trick / the idea caught on quickly)
word_forms: catch on – caught on – caught on – catching on
common_mistake: He catch on the joke after a minute.
correct_version: He caught on to the joke after a minute.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Catch' is irregular (caught), and use 'catch on TO' something.
spelling_tip: Two words -- don't confuse with "catch up" (reach the same level).
etymology: From "catch" + "on" -- literally to grab hold of something moving, extended to an idea "catching" in people's minds (becoming popular) or a person finally "catching" the meaning (understanding).
prefix_root_suffix: catch + on (particle "on" shows something taking hold/spreading)
mnemonic: When a trend CATCHES ON, it's like fire catching on dry wood -- spreading quickly.
memory_trick: CATCH ON: an idea catches ON like fire.
visual_association: A spark jumping from one dry leaf to the next, spreading quickly.
difference_explained: Understand is general. Catch on = understand after a delay, or become popular.
mini_conversation:
A: He didn't laugh at the joke at first.
B: Yeah, it took him a second to catch on.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A shop owner watches a new gadget fly off the shelves and says, "This is really catching on fast!"
news_style_line: News-style: "The recycling initiative has slowly caught on across the city."
casual_conversation: Casual: "It took me a minute, but I finally caught on to what she meant."
mcq_options: A) To fail completely  B) To become popular or start to understand  C) To physically catch a ball  D) To forget something
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The new app took a few months to ______ with users. → catch on
find_and_fix_to_correct: This style is catch on very quickly nowadays. → This style is catching on very quickly nowadays. (use the present continuous form "is catching on")
translate: यह चलन जल्दी ही लोकप्रिय हो गया। → This trend caught on quickly.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a trend that caught on in your city.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to become popular, or to finally understand something'?
usage_tip: 'Catch on' also means become popular: 'The trend caught on fast.'

simple_explanation: To lift something, to collect someone or something, or to learn a skill casually. "Pick up" has several everyday uses: lifting an object off the ground, going to collect someone (like picking up a friend from the airport), or learning something naturally, without formal study, like picking up a new language.
example_1: Can you pick up the kids from school?
example_2: She picked up the fallen books from the floor.
example_3: He picked up some Spanish while traveling.
collocations: pick up the phone, pick up speed, pick up a language
related_phrasal_verbs: pick out, take up, catch on
where_it_s_used: Transportation, learning, tidying up, phone calls
action_sequence: Before: wait at the station → During: a car arrives → After: get in
grammar_pattern: pick up + object (pick up the pen / pick the kids up)
word_forms: pick up – picked up – picked up – picking up
common_mistake: I will pick up you at the station.
correct_version: I will pick you up at the station.
why_it_s_wrong: With a pronoun, it goes in the middle: 'pick you up'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on "up": pick-UP; the noun "pickup" stresses the first syllable.
spelling_tip: Two words as a verb; one word as a noun/adjective ("a pickup truck").
etymology: From "pick" + "up" -- literally to lift something from a lower position, extended to collecting people/things or acquiring skills informally.
mnemonic: When you PICK something UP, you lift it from down below to a higher place.
memory_trick: PICK UP: your hand picks something UP.
visual_association: A hand reaching down and lifting a dropped object off the floor.
emotion_feel: Neutral, sometimes a sense of helpfulness
difference_explained: Same meaning for people and things. Collect is slightly more formal.
mini_conversation:
A: Can you pick me up after work?
B: Sure, I'll be there by six.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A parent leans out of the car window and calls, "Hop in, I'm here to pick you up!"
news_style_line: News-style: "Sales have started to pick up after a slow first quarter."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I picked up a bit of French during my trip to Paris."
mcq_options: A) To study it in a formal class  B) To learn it naturally without formal study  C) To forget it completely  D) To translate it professionally

find_and_fix_to_correct: Please pick up the phone quick, is ringing. → Please pick up the phone quickly, it's ringing. (use the adverb "quickly," not "quick," and add the subject "it")
