usage_tip: Many meanings: collect someone, learn casually ('pick up Hindi'), answer a phone.

simple_explanation: To put something back in its proper storage place. "Put away" means tidying up by returning objects to where they normally belong, like putting toys away in a box or clothes away in a closet.
example_2: She put away the dishes after washing them.
example_3: He put his phone away during the meeting.
collocations: put away toys, put away dishes, put away laundry
related_phrasal_verbs: tidy up, clear away, store away
action_sequence: Before: finish using things → During: take them to their places → After: the room is tidy
grammar_pattern: put + object + away (put the toys away / put away the toys)
word_forms: put away – put away – put away – putting away
common_mistake: Please put your books to away.
correct_version: Please put your books away.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Put away' needs no 'to'.
spelling_tip: Two words -- "away" is one word, not "a way."
etymology: From "put" + "away" -- literally to place something at a distance/out of sight, extended to storing it properly.
prefix_root_suffix: put + away (particle "away" shows moving something out of sight/into storage)
mnemonic: When you PUT something AWAY, you send it far AWAY from the mess, into its proper spot.
memory_trick: PUT AWAY: put it AWAY from sight, in its place.
visual_association: A neatly organized shelf with everything in its labeled place.
difference_explained: Put away = store in its proper place. Put back = return to exactly where it was.
mini_conversation:
A: Mom, can I go outside now?
B: Sure, just put away your toys first.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A parent points at the floor and says gently, "Time to put away your toys before dinner."
news_style_line: News-style: "Schools are asking students to put away their phones during class hours."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Can you put away the groceries while I start cooking?"
mcq_options: A) To throw something in the trash  B) To store something in its proper place  C) To buy something new  D) To break something
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Please ______ your shoes instead of leaving them by the door. → put away
find_and_fix_to_correct: She putted away the plates after dinner. → She put away the plates after dinner. ("put" is irregular -- same form in past tense, not "putted")
translate: कृपया अपने खिलौने उनकी जगह पर रख दो। → Please put your toys away.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about what you put away after dinner.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to put something back in its proper storage place'?
usage_tip: 'Put away money' = save it.

simple_explanation: To return something to the exact place it was before. "Put back" means returning an object to its original position after you've used or moved it, like putting a book back on the shelf.
example_1: Please put back the scissors when done.
example_2: He put the book back on the shelf.
example_3: Can you put the milk back in the fridge?
collocations: put back on the shelf, put back in place, put something back
where_it_s_used: Household, libraries, shared spaces, borrowing items
action_sequence: Before: take a book from the shelf → During: use it → After: return it to the same spot
grammar_pattern: put + object + back (put the tool back / put back the tool)
word_forms: put back – put back – put back – putting back
common_mistake: Put back it on the table, please.
correct_version: Put it back on the table, please.
why_it_s_wrong: With a pronoun like 'it', it goes between 'put' and 'back'.
spelling_tip: Two words -- used with an object between or after "put back."
etymology: From "put" + "back" -- literally to place something in the direction it came from, extended to restoring it to its original position.
prefix_root_suffix: put + back (particle "back" shows returning something to its original spot)
mnemonic: If you take something, remember to PUT it BACK exactly where it came from.
memory_trick: PUT BACK: return it BACK to its spot.
visual_association: A hand sliding a book back into its exact spot on a shelf.
difference_explained: Put back = return to where it was. Put away = store tidily.
mini_conversation:
A: Where's the stapler?
B: I used it -- let me put it back on your desk.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A librarian gently reminds a visitor, "Please put the book back exactly where you found it."
news_style_line: News-style: "Volunteers helped put back the fallen street signs after the storm."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Don't forget to put the ketchup back in the fridge."
mcq_options: A) To throw something away  B) To return something to its original place  C) To buy a replacement  D) To hide something
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Please ______ the remote control on the table when you're done. → put back
find_and_fix_to_correct: I put back the book to the shelf. → I put the book back on the shelf. (word order: object comes between "put" and "back"; use "on," not "to")
translate: कृपया चाबी वापस उसकी जगह पर रख दो। → Please put the key back in its place.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something you forgot to put back.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to return something to the exact place it was before'?
usage_tip: 'Put back' also means delay: 'The meeting was put back a week.'

hindi_meaning: नीचे रखना, अपमानित करना (किसी की आलोचना करना)
simple_explanation: To place something on a surface, or to unkindly criticize someone. "Put down" most often means placing an object somewhere, like putting down a bag. It can also mean to criticize or make someone feel bad about themselves, which is a more negative, informal use.
example_1: She put down her bag on the chair.
example_2: He put down his pen and looked up.
example_3: Please put your phone down during dinner.
collocations: put down your bag, put down roots, put someone down
action_sequence: Before: hold a heavy bag → During: lower it → After: it rests on the floor
grammar_pattern: put + object + down (put the book down / put down the book)
word_forms: put down – put down – put down – putting down
common_mistake: He put down himself in front of everyone.
correct_version: He put himself down in front of everyone.
why_it_s_wrong: A reflexive pronoun goes between 'put' and 'down': 'put himself down'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on "down": put-DOWN; the noun "put-down" stresses the first syllable.
spelling_tip: Two words as a verb; hyphenated as a noun ("a put-down").
etymology: From "put" + "down" -- literally to place something at a lower position, extended informally to criticizing or belittling someone.
prefix_root_suffix: put + down (particle "down" shows lowering something physically or emotionally)
mnemonic: When you PUT something DOWN, gravity pulls it toward the ground.
memory_trick: PUT DOWN: move something DOWN onto a surface — or push a person's confidence down.
visual_association: A hand gently setting a heavy bag onto a table.
difference_explained: Put down = place on a surface, or criticise. Put off = delay.
mini_conversation:
A: Can you put that box down for a second?
B: Sure, where do you want it?
everyday_scene: Everyday: A teacher raises a hand and says firmly, "Phones down, please -- eyes on the board."
news_style_line: News-style: "The mediator asked both sides to put down their differences and negotiate."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Please put your phone down, I'm trying to talk to you."
mcq_options: A) To help someone stand up  B) To criticize or insult someone  C) To physically lower someone  D) To praise someone highly
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: He ______ his coffee cup and started the meeting. → put down
find_and_fix_to_correct: Don't put down her all the time, it's mean. → Don't put her down all the time, it's mean. (pronoun object goes between "put" and "down")
translate: उसने अपना बैग मेज़ पर रख दिया। → She put her bag down on the table.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about why we shouldn't put others down.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to place something on a surface, or to unkindly criticize someone'?
usage_tip: 'Put down' also means kill a sick animal kindly (vet).

hindi_meaning: वापस लेना, अपनी बात वापस लेना
simple_explanation: To return something you bought or borrowed, or to say that something you said earlier isn't true. "Take back" an item means returning it, often to a shop. "Take back" words means admitting you were wrong and withdrawing what you said.
example_1: I want to take back what I said.
example_2: She took the shirt back to the store for a refund.
example_3: He took back his harsh comment after apologizing.
collocations: take back a statement, take back an item, take back your words
action_sequence: Before: say something unkind → During: feel sorry → After: say 'I take it back'
grammar_pattern: take + object + back (take the shoes back / take back the shoes)
word_forms: take back – took back – taken back – taking back
common_mistake: I want to take back to you what I said.
correct_version: I want to take back what I said.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Take back' already means withdraw your words, so 'to you' isn't needed.
spelling_tip: Two words -- the object often goes between "take" and "back" with pronouns.
etymology: From "take" + "back" -- literally to physically take something in the return direction, extended to withdrawing a statement or returning an item.
prefix_root_suffix: take + back (particle "back" shows reversing an action or returning something)
mnemonic: If you TAKE something BACK, you carry it back to where it came from -- a shop, or an unkind sentence you regret.
memory_trick: TAKE BACK: pull your words BACK into your mouth.
visual_association: A hand pulling a spoken word bubble back into the mouth.
difference_explained: Return = give back or go back. Take back = return an item to a shop, or withdraw words.
mini_conversation:
A: I'm sorry, I didn't mean what I said.
B: It's okay, I know you didn't -- but thanks for taking it back.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character pauses, then says quietly, "I take it back -- I didn't mean to hurt you."
news_style_line: News-style: "The politician was pressed to take back his controversial remarks."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I'm going to take this jacket back -- it doesn't fit right."
mcq_options: A) To repeat something loudly  B) To withdraw or admit something you said was wrong  C) To write something down  D) To agree strongly with someone
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: I'm sorry, I didn't mean it -- I ______ what I said. → take back
find_and_fix_to_correct: She take back the gift because it was wrong size. → She took the gift back because it was the wrong size. (use past tense "took," and add "the" before "wrong size")
translate: मुझे माफ़ करना, मैं अपनी बात वापस लेता हूँ। → I'm sorry, I take back what I said.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something you said that you wanted to take back.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to return something you bought or borrowed, or to say that something you said earlier isn't true'?
usage_tip: Shops: 'Can I take this back?' = return it.

simple_explanation: To leave the ground and start flying, or to remove clothing/an accessory. A plane "takes off" when it lifts off the runway into the air. A person can also "take off" their shoes, coat, or glasses -- meaning to remove them.
example_1: The plane will take off soon.
example_2: The flight took off twenty minutes late.
example_3: Please take off your shoes before entering.
collocations: take off shoes, plane takes off, business takes off
related_phrasal_verbs: put on, lift off, set off
action_sequence: Before: the plane runs down the runway → During: its wheels leave the ground → After: it climbs into the sky
grammar_pattern: take off + object / subject + take off (take off your jacket / the plane took off)
word_forms: take off – took off – taken off – taking off
common_mistake: The plane take off on time yesterday.
correct_version: The plane took off on time yesterday.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Yesterday' needs the past 'took'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on "off": take-OFF; the noun "takeoff" stresses the first syllable.
spelling_tip: Two words as a verb; one word as a noun ("the takeoff was smooth").
etymology: From "take" + "off" -- literally to lift something off a surface, extended to a plane leaving the ground or removing clothing.
prefix_root_suffix: take + off (particle "off" shows separation/lifting away from a surface)
mnemonic: A plane TAKES OFF the ground and lifts into the sky.
memory_trick: TAKE OFF: the plane lifts OFF the ground.
visual_association: An airplane lifting steeply off a runway into the clouds.
difference_explained: Opposites for clothes: put on = wear; take off = remove.
mini_conversation:
A: What time does our flight take off?
B: It takes off at 6 AM sharp.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A pilot's voice crackles over the speaker, "Cabin crew, prepare for takeoff."
news_style_line: News-style: "The airline reported dozens of flights delayed before takeoff due to fog."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Take off your shoes before you come inside, please."
mcq_question: "Take off" (for a plane) most nearly means:
mcq_options: A) To land safely  B) To leave the ground and begin flying  C) To refuel  D) To change direction

find_and_fix_to_correct: He taked off his jacket because it was hot. → He took off his jacket because it was hot. (irregular past tense is "took," not "taked")

write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about what you take off when you get home.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to leave the ground and start flying, or to remove clothing/an accessory'?
usage_tip: 'Take off' also means remove clothes, or a sudden success: 'Her career took off.'

simple_explanation: To remove something, or to subtract a number. "Take away" means to remove something from a place or a person, or in math, to subtract one number from another.
example_1: They took away her old car.
example_2: The waiter took away our empty plates.
example_3: If you take away five from ten, you get five.
collocations: take away food, take away rights, take away the pain
action_sequence: Before: the plate is on the table → During: the waiter picks it up → After: the table is clear
grammar_pattern: take + object + away (take the toy away / take away the toy)
word_forms: take away – took away – taken away – taking away
common_mistake: The waiter take away my plate before I finished.
correct_version: The waiter took away my plate before I finished.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Before I finished' shows the past, so use 'took'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on "away": take-uh-WAY; noun "takeaway" stresses the first syllable.
spelling_tip: Two words as a verb; one word as a noun/adjective ("a takeaway meal").
etymology: From "take" + "away" -- literally to carry something to a distance, extended to removing or subtracting something.
prefix_root_suffix: take + away (particle "away" shows removing to a distance)
mnemonic: When you TAKE something AWAY, you carry it far AWAY from where it was.
memory_trick: TAKE AWAY: take it AWAY from here.
visual_association: A tray being carried away from an empty table.
emotion_feel: Neutral, sometimes loss or relief depending on what's removed
difference_explained: Same meaning. Take away is everyday; remove is more formal.
mini_conversation:
A: Can you take away these dishes?
B: Of course, I'll clear the table now.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A waiter gestures to the table and asks politely, "Shall I take these plates away for you?"
news_style_line: News-style: "The new policy could take away benefits from thousands of workers."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Can you take away my plate? I'm finished."
mcq_options: A) To add something new  B) To remove or subtract something  C) To repair something  D) To celebrate something
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The waiter will ______ your plates once you're finished. → take away
find_and_fix_to_correct: They take away his license last year for speeding. → They took away his license last year for speeding. (use past tense "took")
translate: वेटर ने खाली प्लेटें उठा लीं। → The waiter took away the empty plates.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something a teacher took away from a student.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to remove something, or to subtract a number'?
usage_tip: In Indian and British English, 'takeaway' = food you carry home.

simple_explanation: To get rid of something you don't want, usually by putting it in the trash. "Throw away" means discarding something because it's broken, useless, or no longer needed -- putting it in the bin.
example_2: She threw away the old newspapers.
example_3: He never throws anything away.
collocations: throw away trash, throw away an opportunity, throw away old clothes
related_phrasal_verbs: throw out, get rid of, dispose of
action_sequence: Before: find old shoes → During: put them in the bin → After: they're gone
grammar_pattern: throw + object + away (throw the trash away / throw away the trash)
word_forms: throw away – threw away – thrown away – throwing away
common_mistake: She throwed away her old shoes yesterday.
correct_version: She threw away her old shoes yesterday.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Throw' is irregular: the past is 'threw'.
spelling_tip: Two words -- remember "throw," not "through," which sounds similar but is unrelated.
etymology: From "throw" + "away" -- literally to toss something to a distance, extended to discarding it as unwanted.
prefix_root_suffix: throw + away (particle "away" shows discarding something to a distance)
mnemonic: When you THROW something AWAY, you toss it far AWAY into the trash.
memory_trick: THROW AWAY: throw it far AWAY into the bin.
visual_association: A crumpled piece of paper landing in a wastebasket.
emotion_feel: Neutral, sometimes regret if throwing away something valuable
difference_explained: Same meaning for rubbish. Throw out also means force someone to leave.
mini_conversation:
A: Should I keep these old magazines?
B: No, just throw them away.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character tosses a crumpled letter into the bin and mutters, "I should've thrown that away years ago."
news_style_line: News-style: "The city urged residents not to throw away recyclable materials with regular trash."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Can you throw away this empty bottle for me?"
mcq_options: A) To keep something safe  B) To discard something as unwanted  C) To sell something  D) To repair something
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Please ______ these old newspapers, we don't need them anymore. → throw away
find_and_fix_to_correct: He throw away his ticket by mistake. → He threw away his ticket by mistake. (use the irregular past tense "threw")
translate: कृपया इन पुराने अख़बारों को फेंक दो। → Please throw away these old newspapers.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something you threw away recently.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to get rid of something you don't want, usually by putting it in the trash'?
usage_tip: 'Throw away a chance' = waste an opportunity.

hindi_meaning: फेंक देना, निकाल देना (किसी व्यक्ति को)
simple_explanation: To discard something, or to force someone to leave a place. "Throw out" often means the same as "throw away" (discarding trash), but it can also mean removing a person from somewhere, like being thrown out of a club for bad behavior.
example_1: He got thrown out of the bar.
example_2: We threw out the broken chair.
example_3: The bouncer threw him out for fighting.
collocations: throw out garbage, get thrown out, throw out a proposal
related_phrasal_verbs: throw away, kick out, chuck out
action_sequence: Before: someone behaves badly → During: the manager asks them to leave → After: they're outside
grammar_pattern: throw + object + out (throw the trash out / throw out the trash)
word_forms: throw out – threw out – thrown out – throwing out
common_mistake: The manager throw out him from the restaurant.
correct_version: The manager threw him out of the restaurant.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'threw', and the pronoun goes in the middle: 'threw him out OF'.
spelling_tip: Two words -- don't confuse with "throughout," a completely different word.
etymology: From "throw" + "out" -- literally to toss something outside, extended to discarding items or forcibly removing a person.
prefix_root_suffix: throw + out (particle "out" shows removal to the outside)
mnemonic: If you THROW something OUT, it leaves through the door -- gone for good.
memory_trick: THROW OUT: throw someone OUT of the door.
visual_association: A bouncer pointing firmly toward the exit door.
emotion_feel: Negative when about people (anger, shame); neutral when about objects
difference_explained: Both mean discard things. Only throw out is used for forcing a person to leave.
tone: Negative (in the expel sense), Neutral (discard sense)
mini_conversation:
A: What happened to him?
B: He got thrown out for causing trouble.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A security guard grabs someone's arm and says firmly, "You're being thrown out -- let's go."
news_style_line: News-style: "The court threw out the case due to lack of evidence."
casual_conversation: Casual: "We finally threw out that old broken couch."
mcq_options: A) To welcome someone warmly  B) To force someone to leave  C) To promote someone  D) To ignore someone
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The judge decided to ______ the case due to insufficient evidence. → throw out
find_and_fix_to_correct: They throw out from the club last night for no reason. → They were thrown out of the club last night for no reason. (use passive voice "were thrown out of")
translate: उसे झगड़ा करने के कारण क्लब से निकाल दिया गया। → He was thrown out of the club for fighting.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a rule for when someone gets thrown out of a class.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to discard something, or to force someone to leave a place'?
usage_tip: 'Throw out an idea' = reject it.

simple_explanation: To return something to the person it belongs to. "Give back" means returning something -- money, a borrowed item, or even a favor -- to the person it originally came from.
example_2: He gave back the money he borrowed.
example_3: Can you give me back my umbrella?
collocations: give back the money, give something back, give back to society
action_sequence: Before: borrow a book → During: finish it → After: return it to the owner
grammar_pattern: give + object + back (give the book back / give back the book)
word_forms: give back – gave back – given back – giving back
common_mistake: Please give back to me my keys.
correct_version: Please give me back my keys.
why_it_s_wrong: With a pronoun person, put it after 'give': 'give me back my keys'.
spelling_tip: Two words -- the object often goes between "give" and "back" with pronouns.
etymology: From "give" + "back" -- literally to hand something back in the direction it came from, extended to returning borrowed or taken items.
prefix_root_suffix: give + back (particle "back" shows returning something to its origin)
word_family: give (v.), giving (n., unrelated common noun "giving back")
mnemonic: If you GIVE something BACK, it travels back into the hands of its original owner.
memory_trick: GIVE BACK: give it BACK to where it came from.
visual_association: A hand returning a borrowed umbrella to its owner at the door.
difference_explained: Same meaning. Return is more formal.
mini_conversation:
A: Can I have my notebook back?
B: Oh sorry, here -- let me give it back right now.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character holds out a wallet and says, "I found this -- let's give it back to its owner."
news_style_line: News-style: "The charity aims to give back to communities affected by the disaster."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Don't forget to give me back my charger before you leave."
mcq_options: A) To keep something forever  B) To return something to its owner  C) To buy something new  D) To throw something away
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Can you please ______ my laptop by tomorrow? → give back
find_and_fix_to_correct: He give back the book to library late. → He gave the book back to the library late. (use past tense "gave," and put the object before "back")
translate: कृपया मेरी किताब वापस कर दो। → Please give my book back.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something you borrowed and gave back.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to return something to the person it belongs to'?
usage_tip: 'Give back to society' = help your community.

hindi_meaning: मुफ़्त में दे देना, राज़ खोल देना
simple_explanation: To give something to someone for free, or to accidentally reveal a secret. "Give away" means donating or giving something without charging money. It can also mean accidentally revealing information you were supposed to keep secret.
example_2: She gave away her old clothes to charity.
example_3: His smile gave away that he was lying.
collocations: give away for free, give away a secret, give away tickets
action_sequence: Before: have old clothes → During: give them free to others → After: they're gone
grammar_pattern: give + object + away (give the toys away / give away the toys)
word_forms: give away – gave away – given away – giving away
common_mistake: Don't give away to anyone this secret.
correct_version: Don't give this secret away to anyone.
why_it_s_wrong: Put the object before 'away', then 'to + person'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on "away": give-uh-WAY; noun "giveaway" stresses the first syllable.
spelling_tip: Two words as a verb; one word as a noun ("a free giveaway").
etymology: From "give" + "away" -- literally to hand something off to a distance, extended to giving something for free or unintentionally revealing information.
prefix_root_suffix: give + away (particle "away" shows something leaving your possession)
mnemonic: When you GIVE something AWAY, it leaves your hands for good, going far AWAY to someone else.
memory_trick: GIVE AWAY: give it AWAY for free.
visual_association: A hand opening to release a balloon, letting it drift far away.
difference_explained: Give away = give for free, or reveal. Give up = stop trying.
mini_conversation:
A: How did you know I was nervous?
B: Your shaky hands gave it away.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A magician winks and says, "I can't give away my secrets -- that would ruin the trick."
news_style_line: News-style: "The store is giving away free meals to families in need this week."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Careful, your face is giving away that you're excited."
mcq_options: A) To keep it hidden successfully  B) To accidentally reveal it  C) To write it down formally  D) To forget about it
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: His nervous laugh ______ that he was hiding something. → gave away
find_and_fix_to_correct: She give away all her old books last week. → She gave away all her old books last week. (use past tense "gave")
translate: उसकी हँसी ने उसका राज़ खोल दिया। → Her laugh gave away her secret.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something you gave away to someone in need.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to give something to someone for free, or to accidentally reveal a secret'?
usage_tip: 'Giveaway' (noun) = a free gift or contest. 'Give away a secret' = reveal it.

simple_explanation: To finally agree to something you were resisting, or to stop fighting/arguing. "Give in" means you stop resisting and accept something, often after pressure, arguing, or persuasion -- like a parent finally giving in to a child's request.
example_1: She finally gave in to his request.
example_2: The teacher gave in and extended the deadline.
example_3: After hours of pleading, his mom gave in.
collocations: give in to pressure, give in to temptation, finally give in
action_sequence: Before: refuse again and again → During: feel pressure → After: finally agree
grammar_pattern: give in (to) + noun (give in to pressure / give in to demands)
word_forms: give in – gave in – given in – giving in
common_mistake: He gave in the pressure after two hours.
correct_version: He gave in to the pressure after two hours.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'give in TO' + the pressure or person.
spelling_tip: Two words -- followed by "to" before the thing you're yielding to.
etymology: From "give" + "in" -- literally to hand something inward, i.e., to yield your resistance and let something in.
prefix_root_suffix: give + in (particle "in" shows yielding/letting pressure take over)
mnemonic: When you GIVE IN, you let the pressure come IN and stop resisting.
memory_trick: GIVE IN: let the other side come IN — you stop resisting.
visual_association: A rope in a tug-of-war finally being let go by one side.
difference_explained: Give in = stop resisting and agree. Give up = stop trying.
mini_conversation:
A: Did your parents let you go to the party?
B: Yeah, after a lot of begging, they finally gave in.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A parent sighs and says, "Fine, fine -- I give in, you can have the ice cream."
news_style_line: News-style: "After weeks of protest, the company gave in and reversed its decision."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I tried to resist the cake, but I gave in eventually."
mcq_options: A) To resist strongly  B) To reluctantly agree or yield  C) To offer a gift  D) To ignore a request
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: After hours of arguing, she finally ______ and agreed to go. → gave in
find_and_fix_to_correct: He never gives in for pressure from his friends. → He never gives in to pressure from his friends. (use "to," not "for," after "give in")
translate: काफ़ी मनाने के बाद आख़िरकार वह मान गया। → After a lot of persuading, he finally gave in.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a time you gave in to a temptation.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to finally agree to something you were resisting, or to stop fighting/arguing'?
usage_tip: Parents often 'give in' to children who cry for sweets.

simple_explanation: To distribute something to a number of people, or to stop working (for a machine or your body). "Give out" often means handing something to many people, like give out free samples. It can also mean something suddenly stops working, like an engine giving out, or someone's strength giving out from exhaustion.
example_2: Volunteers gave out water at the marathon.
example_3: His knees finally gave out after the long hike.
collocations: give out information, give out prizes, energy gives out
action_sequence: Before: hold a box of prizes → During: hand one to each winner → After: everyone has a prize
grammar_pattern: give out + object (give out flyers / give out awards)
word_forms: give out – gave out – given out – giving out
common_mistake: They give out the prizes before the ceremony start.
correct_version: They gave out the prizes before the ceremony started.
why_it_s_wrong: Both verbs need the past: 'gave' and 'started'.
spelling_tip: Two words -- don't confuse with "giveaway" (a noun for a free item).
etymology: From "give" + "out" -- literally to hand something outward to many people, extended to distributing items or a machine "giving out" (failing).
prefix_root_suffix: give + out (particle "out" shows distributing widely or a system failing outward)
mnemonic: When you GIVE OUT flyers, you hand them OUT to everyone around you.
memory_trick: GIVE OUT: hand things OUT to many people.
visual_association: A row of hands stretching out to receive leaflets from a volunteer.
difference_explained: Same meaning for distributing. Give out also means stop working (a machine or body).
mini_conversation:
A: Are they still giving out free coffee?
B: Yes, but only until 10 AM.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A volunteer hands over a cup and says, "Here, we're giving out free water for the runners."
news_style_line: News-style: "The charity gave out thousands of meals to families this holiday season."
casual_conversation: Casual: "My phone battery gives out so fast these days."
mcq_options: A) To improve suddenly  B) To stop working or fail  C) To multiply quickly  D) To become brand new
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The organizers ______ free water bottles to all runners. → gave out
find_and_fix_to_correct: The old machine give out after many years of use. → The old machine gave out after many years of use. (use past tense "gave")
translate: कार्यक्रम में स्वयंसेवकों ने मुफ़्त पानी बाँटा। → Volunteers gave out free water at the event.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about who gives out prizes at your school.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to distribute something to a number of people, or to stop working (for a machine or your body)'?
usage_tip: 'My legs gave out' = they stopped working from tiredness.

simple_explanation: A polite way of saying that someone has died. "Pass away" is a gentle, respectful way to talk about someone's death, often used to soften the sad news out of kindness or respect.
example_1: Her grandmother passed away last year.
example_2: He passed away peacefully in his sleep.
example_3: The actor passed away at the age of 90.
collocations: pass away peacefully, sadly passed away, pass away suddenly
action_sequence: Before: someone is very ill → During: their life ends peacefully → After: family remembers them
grammar_pattern: subject + pass away (My grandfather passed away in 2020.)
word_forms: pass away – passed away – passed away – passing away
common_mistake: My uncle passed away since two years.
correct_version: My uncle passed away two years ago.
why_it_s_wrong: With a finished past time, use 'ago', not 'since'.
spelling_tip: Two words -- always used for people, not objects.
etymology: From "pass" + "away" -- a gentle, euphemistic extension of "pass" (to move on) meaning to leave this life.
prefix_root_suffix: pass + away (particle "away" softens the meaning of death as a gentle departure)
mnemonic: When someone PASSES AWAY, we imagine them gently passing on to somewhere else, far AWAY.
memory_trick: PASS AWAY: gently PASS from this world.
visual_association: A single candle being gently blown out.
difference_explained: Same meaning. Pass away is gentler and more polite.
mini_conversation:
A: I heard your grandmother passed away. I'm so sorry.
B: Thank you, it means a lot.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character holds a photo frame and says softly, "It's been a year since she passed away."
news_style_line: News-style: "The community mourned after the beloved local teacher passed away this week."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I'm so sorry to hear that your dog passed away."
mcq_options: A) To move to a new house  B) To die  C) To fall asleep briefly  D) To recover from illness
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: We were all very sad when our neighbor ______ last month. → passed away
find_and_fix_to_correct: His father passed away since three days. → His father passed away three days ago. (use "ago," not "since," with a specific past time)
translate: पिछले साल उनकी दादी का देहांत हो गया। → Her grandmother passed away last year.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a respectful sentence using 'passed away'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'a polite way of saying that someone has died'?
usage_tip: It's the polite, respectful way to say 'die'.

simple_explanation: To suddenly lose consciousness, or faint. "Pass out" means fainting -- your body suddenly loses consciousness, often because of heat, shock, low blood sugar, or extreme tiredness.
example_1: He passed out from the heat.
example_2: She passed out during the long ceremony.
example_3: He nearly passed out after donating blood.
collocations: pass out from heat, nearly pass out, pass out cold
action_sequence: Before: feel dizzy → During: fall to the floor → After: wake up after a moment
grammar_pattern: subject + pass out (He passed out on the train.)
word_forms: pass out – passed out – passed out – passing out
common_mistake: She passed out because she is very tired.
correct_version: She passed out because she was very tired.
why_it_s_wrong: Keep both parts of the sentence in the past: 'was tired'.
spelling_tip: Two words -- don't confuse with "passed" (simple past of "pass") used alone.
etymology: From "pass" + "out" -- literally to move out of consciousness, extended to fainting.
prefix_root_suffix: pass + out (particle "out" shows consciousness slipping away)
mnemonic: When you PASS OUT, your mind seems to "pass" right OUT of awareness for a moment.
memory_trick: PASS OUT: your mind goes OUT for a moment.
visual_association: Someone's knees buckling as the room seems to spin.
difference_explained: Same meaning. Faint is more formal.
mini_conversation:
A: What happened to him?
B: He passed out from the heat -- someone call for help!
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character sways on their feet before a friend shouts, "She's about to pass out -- grab a chair!"
news_style_line: News-style: "Several spectators passed out in the extreme heat during the outdoor event."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I almost passed out standing in that long line in the sun."
mcq_options: A) To fall asleep on purpose  B) To suddenly lose consciousness  C) To leave a room quietly  D) To finish a race
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: He felt dizzy and nearly ______ in the crowded room. → passed out
find_and_fix_to_correct: She pass out yesterday because of the heat. → She passed out yesterday because of the heat. (use past tense "passed")
translate: गर्मी की वजह से वह बेहोश हो गया। → He passed out because of the heat.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about what to do if someone passes out.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to suddenly lose consciousness, or faint'?
usage_tip: 'Pass out' also means graduate (Indian English: 'passed out of college in 2020').

simple_explanation: To give information or something you received to another person. "Pass on" means forwarding a message, item, or piece of advice to someone else -- like telling your friend something you were told.
example_1: Please pass on my thanks to her.
example_2: Can you pass on this message to the manager?
example_3: He passed on his knowledge to his students.
collocations: pass on information, pass on a message, pass on advice
action_sequence: Before: get a message → During: tell the next person → After: they know it too
grammar_pattern: pass on + object (to someone) (pass on the message / pass the message on to him)
word_forms: pass on – passed on – passed on – passing on
common_mistake: Please pass on to him this letter.
correct_version: Please pass this letter on to him.
why_it_s_wrong: Put the object before 'on', then 'to + person'.
spelling_tip: Two words -- don't confuse with "passion," which is unrelated despite looking similar.
etymology: From "pass" + "on" -- literally to hand something forward to the next person, extended to transmitting information or, euphemistically, dying.
prefix_root_suffix: pass + on (particle "on" shows forwarding something to continue onward)
mnemonic: When you PASS ON a message, imagine handing it ON to the next person in a chain.
memory_trick: PASS ON: pass the ball ON to the next player.
visual_association: A relay baton being handed from one runner to the next.
difference_explained: Pass on = give to someone else. 'Pass on' can also politely mean die, like 'pass away'.
mini_conversation:
A: Can you pass on my regards to your parents?
B: Of course, I'll tell them today.
everyday_scene: Everyday: An elder places a hand on a young apprentice's shoulder and says, "It's time I pass on what I know."
news_style_line: News-style: "The mentor program helps retiring employees pass on their expertise to newcomers."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Please pass on my congratulations to the whole team."
mcq_options: A) To ignore a message  B) To forward it to someone else  C) To delete a message  D) To translate a message
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Could you ______ this message to your sister for me? → pass on
find_and_fix_to_correct: She pass on the news to everyone yesterday. → She passed on the news to everyone yesterday. (use past tense "passed")
translate: कृपया मेरी शुभकामनाएँ उन्हें पहुँचा देना। → Please pass on my best wishes to them.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence asking someone to pass on a message.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to give information or something you received to another person'?
usage_tip: 'Pass on a message' = tell it to someone else.

hindi_meaning: फल मिलना, पूरा भुगतान कर देना
simple_explanation: To be worthwhile after effort, or to completely repay a debt. "Pay off" means the effort you put in finally brings good results, like hard work paying off with a promotion. It can also mean completely finishing paying back a loan.
example_1: Her hard work finally paid off.
example_2: All those late nights of studying paid off.
example_3: They finally paid off their car loan.
collocations: hard work pays off, pay off a loan, pay off debt
related_phrasal_verbs: work out, bear fruit, settle up
action_sequence: Before: work hard for months → During: see results slowly → After: succeed
grammar_pattern: subject + pay off (Her effort paid off. / They paid off the loan.)
word_forms: pay off – paid off – paid off – paying off
common_mistake: I hope my hard work will pay off good.
correct_version: I hope my hard work will pay off well.
why_it_s_wrong: After a verb, use the adverb 'well', not the adjective 'good'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on "off": pay-OFF; the noun "payoff" stresses the first syllable.
spelling_tip: Two words as a verb; one word as a noun ("a big payoff").
etymology: From "pay" + "off" -- literally to fully settle a payment, extended to effort or investment "paying off" (proving worthwhile).
prefix_root_suffix: pay + off (particle "off" shows a debt or effort being fully settled/resolved)
mnemonic: When your effort finally PAYS OFF, imagine cashing in a reward you've earned.
memory_trick: PAY OFF: the effort PAYS you back in the end.
visual_association: A tree finally bearing fruit after being watered for a long time.
difference_explained: Pay off = repay a whole debt, or be worth it. Pay back = return borrowed money.
mini_conversation:
A: Did all that studying help?
B: Yes, it really paid off -- I passed with top marks!
everyday_scene: Everyday: A coach pats an athlete on the back and says, "All those early mornings finally paid off."
news_style_line: News-style: "Years of research paid off with a major medical breakthrough this year."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I finally paid off my student loan last month!"
mcq_options: A) To waste time and money  B) To be worthwhile in the end  C) To fail completely  D) To borrow more money
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: All the extra practice really ______ during the final match. → paid off
find_and_fix_to_correct: Her efforts pay off finally last year. → Her efforts paid off finally last year. (use past tense "paid," not present "pay")
translate: आख़िरकार उसकी मेहनत रंग लाई। → Her hard work finally paid off.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about hard work that paid off for you.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to be worthwhile after effort, or to completely repay a debt'?
usage_tip: 'Pay off a loan' = repay it completely.

simple_explanation: To return money you borrowed, or informally, to get revenge on someone. "Pay back" usually means returning money you owe someone. Informally, it can also mean getting even with someone who did something bad to you.
example_1: I'll pay back the loan next month.
example_2: He paid back his friend within a week.
example_3: She promised to pay him back for lunch.
collocations: pay back a loan, pay back a favor, pay back in full
where_it_s_used: Borrowing money, favors, debts, informal revenge
action_sequence: Before: borrow money → During: save it up → After: return it
grammar_pattern: pay + object + back (pay the money back / pay back the money)
word_forms: pay back – paid back – paid back – paying back
common_mistake: I will pay back to you tomorrow.
correct_version: I will pay you back tomorrow.
why_it_s_wrong: No 'to': put the person between 'pay' and 'back'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on "back": pay-BACK; the noun "payback" stresses the first syllable.
spelling_tip: Two words as a verb; one word as a noun ("that was payback").
etymology: From "pay" + "back" -- literally to return payment, extended informally to getting revenge ("pay someone back" for a wrong).
prefix_root_suffix: pay + back (particle "back" shows returning money to its source)
mnemonic: If you borrow money, you must PAY it BACK to the person who gave it.
memory_trick: PAY BACK: the money goes BACK to where it came from.
visual_association: A hand placing coins back into another person's open palm.
difference_explained: Pay back = return money to a person. Pay off = clear a debt completely.
mini_conversation:
A: Thanks for lending me the money.
B: No problem, just pay me back whenever you can.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character hands over cash and says, "Here, finally paying you back for last month."
news_style_line: News-style: "The government announced a plan to pay back international loans over ten years."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Don't worry about the coffee, you can pay me back next time."
mcq_options: A) To borrow more money  B) To return money you owe  C) To donate money to charity  D) To invest money
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: I need to ______ the money I borrowed from my sister. → pay back
find_and_fix_to_correct: She pay back her brother the money last week. → She paid her brother back the money last week. (use past tense "paid," and standard word order for two objects)
translate: मुझे अगले हफ़्ते अपना उधार चुकाना है। → I need to pay back my loan next week.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about when you will pay back a loan.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to return money you borrowed, or informally, to get revenge on someone'?
usage_tip: 'Payback' (noun) informally means revenge.

simple_explanation: To reject an offer or request, or to lower the volume/level of something. "Turn down" often means saying no to an offer, invitation, or request. It can also literally mean lowering the volume of music or the heat on a stove.
example_1: She turned down the job offer.
example_2: He turned down an invitation to the party.
example_3: Can you turn down the music a bit?
collocations: turn down an offer, turn down the volume, turn down a request
action_sequence: Before: receive an offer → During: think about it → After: say no politely
grammar_pattern: turn down + noun (turn down the offer / turn the volume down)
word_forms: turn down – turned down – turned down – turning down
common_mistake: He turn down my invitation without any reason.
correct_version: He turned down my invitation without any reason.
why_it_s_wrong: A finished past action needs 'turned'.
spelling_tip: Two words -- don't confuse with "downturn" (a noun meaning decline).
etymology: From "turn" + "down" -- literally to rotate a dial to a lower setting, extended to rejecting an offer.
mnemonic: When you TURN DOWN an offer, imagine turning a volume knob DOWN to "no."
memory_trick: TURN DOWN: turn your thumb DOWN = no.
visual_association: A hand slowly twisting a volume knob to the left.
difference_explained: Same meaning. Turn down is softer and common for offers and invitations.
mini_conversation:
A: Did she accept the offer?
B: No, she turned it down -- she found a better one.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character shakes their head and says calmly, "I'm sorry, but I have to turn down this offer."
news_style_line: News-style: "The city council turned down the proposal for the new shopping mall."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Can you turn down the TV? I'm on the phone."
mcq_options: A) To accept enthusiastically  B) To reject or refuse it  C) To think about it later  D) To ask for more details
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: I had to ______ the job because of the low salary. → turn down
find_and_fix_to_correct: She turn down for the promotion last month. → She turned down the promotion last month. (use past tense "turned," and remove the unnecessary "for")
translate: उसने नौकरी का प्रस्ताव अस्वीकार कर दिया। → She turned down the job offer.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about an offer you turned down.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to reject an offer or request, or to lower the volume/level of something'?
usage_tip: 'Turn down' also means lower volume: 'Turn down the music.'

simple_explanation: To switch off a device, light, or machine. "Turn off" means stopping the power or operation of something, like a light, TV, or engine, usually by using a switch or button.
example_2: Don't forget to turn off the stove.
example_3: He turned off his phone during the movie.
collocations: turn off the lights, turn off the engine, turn off the TV
related_phrasal_verbs: switch off, shut down, power off
where_it_s_used: Electronics, safety, energy saving, daily routines
action_sequence: Before: the light is on → During: press the switch → After: the room is dark
grammar_pattern: turn off + object (turn off the light / turn the light off)
word_forms: turn off – turned off – turned off – turning off
common_mistake: Please turn off it before you leave.
correct_version: Please turn it off before you leave.
why_it_s_wrong: With a pronoun like 'it', it goes between 'turn' and 'off'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on "off": turn-OFF; the noun/adjective "turnoff" stresses the first syllable.
spelling_tip: Two words as a verb; one word as a noun ("that's a turnoff").
etymology: From "turn" + "off" -- literally to rotate a switch to the "off" position, extended to stopping any device or system.
mnemonic: TURN the switch OFF, and the power stops.
memory_trick: TURN OFF: the switch goes to OFF.
visual_association: A finger flicking a light switch downward into darkness.
difference_explained: Same meaning. Switch off is more common in Indian and British English.
mini_conversation:
A: Did you turn off the oven?
B: Yes, I checked it twice before leaving.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A parent flicks a light switch and calls out, "Turn off the TV, it's bedtime!"
news_style_line: News-style: "Officials asked residents to turn off nonessential lights to save energy."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Can you turn off the fan before you go to sleep?"
mcq_options: A) To switch something on  B) To switch something off  C) To increase the volume  D) To repair a device
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Remember to ______ the lights before leaving the room. → turn off
find_and_fix_to_correct: She turn off the computer before she left home. → She turned off the computer before she left home. (use past tense "turned")
translate: कृपया जाने से पहले लाइट बंद कर दो। → Please turn off the lights before you leave.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about what you turn off before sleeping.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to switch off a device, light, or machine'?
usage_tip: 'That's a turn-off' = something that makes you lose interest.

simple_explanation: To switch on a device, light, or machine. "Turn on" means activating power or operation, like switching on a TV, light, or computer.
example_1: Can you turn on the fan?
example_2: She turned on the lights when she entered the room.
example_3: He forgot to turn on his alarm.
collocations: turn on the lights, turn on the TV, turn on the engine
related_phrasal_verbs: switch on, power up, boot up
action_sequence: Before: the room is dark → During: press the switch → After: the light comes on
grammar_pattern: turn on + object (turn on the light / turn the light on)
word_forms: turn on – turned on – turned on – turning on
common_mistake: Please turn on it, I can't see anything.
correct_version: Please turn it on, I can't see anything.
why_it_s_wrong: With a pronoun like 'it', it goes between 'turn' and 'on'.
etymology: From "turn" + "on" -- literally to rotate a switch to the "on" position, extended to activating any device.
mnemonic: TURN the switch, and the power comes ON.
memory_trick: TURN ON: the switch goes to ON.
visual_association: A hand flicking a switch upward as a bulb lights up.
difference_explained: Same meaning. Switch on is more common in Indian and British English.
mini_conversation:
A: It's dark in here.
B: Let me turn on the lights for you.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character fumbles in the dark and says, "Hang on, let me turn on the light."
news_style_line: News-style: "The mayor turned on the city's holiday lights at the ceremony last night."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Can you turn on the AC? It's really hot in here."
mcq_options: A) To switch something off  B) To switch something on  C) To fix something broken  D) To sell something
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: It's getting dark -- can you ______ the lights? → turn on
find_and_fix_to_correct: He turn on the TV before eating breakfast. → He turned on the TV before eating breakfast. (use past tense "turned")
translate: कृपया पंखा चालू कर दो, बहुत गर्मी है। → Please turn on the fan, it's very hot.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about the first thing you turn on in the morning.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to switch on a device, light, or machine'?
usage_tip: Careful: 'turned on' can also mean sexually excited in informal English.

simple_explanation: To change or transform from one thing into something else. "Turn into" describes a change from one state or form to a completely different one, like water turning into ice, or a small problem turning into a big one.
example_1: The caterpillar turned into a butterfly.
example_2: The rain turned into snow overnight.
example_3: Their friendship turned into love.
collocations: turn into a nightmare, turn into a habit, turn into reality
action_sequence: Before: water is in the freezer → During: it gets colder and colder → After: it becomes ice
grammar_pattern: subject + turn into + noun (The dream turned into reality.)
word_forms: turn into – turned into – turned into – turning into
common_mistake: The weather turn into cold suddenly.
correct_version: The weather turned cold suddenly.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Turn into' + noun (turn into ice). For an adjective, use 'turn' alone (turned cold).
spelling_tip: Two words -- note double "n" isn't there; it's "turn," not "turrn."
etymology: From "turn" + "into" -- literally to rotate or change direction into a new form, extended to transformation from one state to another.
prefix_root_suffix: turn + into (particle "into" shows movement/change from one state to another)
mnemonic: When a caterpillar TURNS INTO a butterfly, it completely changes form.
memory_trick: TURN INTO: turn around and you're INTO a new shape.
visual_association: A caterpillar wrapped in a cocoon, emerging as a butterfly.
difference_explained: Same meaning with nouns. Turn into suggests a complete or surprising change.
mini_conversation:
A: How's the renovation going?
B: It's turning into a bigger project than we expected.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A narrator's voice echoes, "In an instant, the quiet town turned into chaos."
news_style_line: News-style: "Experts warn the mild storm could turn into a major hurricane by the weekend."
casual_conversation: Casual: "This simple project is turning into a huge headache."
mcq_options: A) To stay exactly the same  B) To change or become something else  C) To return to normal  D) To disappear completely
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Their small disagreement ______ a big argument. → turned into
find_and_fix_to_correct: The ice cream turn into liquid in the sun. → The ice cream turned into liquid in the sun. (use past tense "turned")
translate: उनकी दोस्ती धीरे-धीरे प्यार में बदल गई। → Their friendship slowly turned into love.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something that turned into something else.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to change or transform from one thing into something else'?
usage_tip: 'The frog turned into a prince' — a classic fairy-tale use.

simple_explanation: To happen or end in a particular way, often unexpectedly. "Turn out" describes the final result of a situation -- how things ended up, especially when it's different from what you expected.
example_2: The party turned out to be a lot of fun.
example_3: It turned out that he was right all along.
collocations: turn out well, turn out to be, large turnout
related_phrasal_verbs: end up, come out, work out
action_sequence: Before: make a plan → During: things happen → After: see the final result
grammar_pattern: subject + turn out (to be) + adjective/noun (It turned out to be a great day.)
word_forms: turn out – turned out – turned out – turning out
common_mistake: The trip turn out great despite the rain.
correct_version: The trip turned out great despite the rain.
why_it_s_wrong: A finished event needs the past 'turned'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on "out": turn-OUT; the noun "turnout" stresses the first syllable.
spelling_tip: Two words as a verb; one word as a noun ("a large turnout").
etymology: From "turn" + "out" -- literally to rotate outward/reveal, extended to how a situation ultimately results or how many people attend.
prefix_root_suffix: turn + out (particle "out" shows the eventual/final result becoming visible)
mnemonic: When a story finally TURNS OUT well, imagine the hidden ending finally turning OUT into view.
memory_trick: TURN OUT: the result TURNS OUT from behind a curtain.
visual_association: A curtain slowly opening to reveal the final scene.
emotion_feel: Relief or surprise, depending on outcome
difference_explained: Turn out = the result is (often surprising). End up = finally be in a place or situation.
mini_conversation:
A: How was the interview?
B: It turned out really well -- I got the job!
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character exhales in relief and says, "Well, that turned out better than I expected."
news_style_line: News-style: "Voter turnout was higher than expected in this year's election."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I was nervous about the exam, but it turned out fine."
mcq_options: A) To plan something carefully  B) To end up being something, often unexpectedly  C) To cancel an event  D) To repeat an action
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: I was worried about the trip, but it ______ to be amazing. → turned out
find_and_fix_to_correct: The show turn out to be very boring for me. → The show turned out to be very boring for me. (use past tense "turned")
translate: मुझे चिंता थी, लेकिन सब कुछ ठीक निकला। → I was worried, but everything turned out fine.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something that turned out better than expected.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to happen or end in a particular way, often unexpectedly'?
usage_tip: 'It turns out (that)…' = we discovered that…

simple_explanation: To physically face the opposite direction, or for a bad situation to improve. "Turn around" can mean literally spinning to face the other way, or figuratively, when a difficult or failing situation starts improving.
example_1: She turned around to see who called her.
example_2: He turned around and walked back home.
example_3: The struggling company managed to turn around its business.
collocations: turn around slowly, turn the business around, turn your life around
action_sequence: Before: face forward → During: spin your body → After: face the other way
grammar_pattern: subject + turn around (She turned around quickly. / They turned the company around.)
word_forms: turn around – turned around – turned around – turning around
common_mistake: He turn around and see his friend behind him.
correct_version: He turned around and saw his friend behind him.
why_it_s_wrong: Both actions are in the past: 'turned' and 'saw'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on "around": turn-uh-ROUND; the noun "turnaround" stresses the first syllable.
spelling_tip: Two words as a verb; one word as a noun ("a business turnaround").
etymology: From "turn" + "around" -- literally to physically rotate to face the opposite direction, extended to a situation improving after being bad.
prefix_root_suffix: turn + around (particle "around" shows a full change of direction or situation)
mnemonic: When you TURN AROUND, imagine spinning a full circle to face the opposite way.
memory_trick: TURN AROUND: spin AROUND to face the other way.
visual_association: A ship slowly rotating to sail in the opposite direction.
difference_explained: Turn around = face the other way. Return = go back to a place.
mini_conversation:
A: How's the new manager doing?
B: Great -- she really turned the team around.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character hears their name called and slowly turns around to reveal a shocked expression.
news_style_line: News-style: "The new coach helped turn the losing team around this season."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Turn around, you have something on your shirt!"
mcq_options: A) To make it worse  B) To improve it after a difficult period  C) To close it permanently  D) To sell it to someone else
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The new manager helped ______ the failing store within a year. → turn around
find_and_fix_to_correct: She turn around quickly when she heard the noise. → She turned around quickly when she heard the noise. (use past tense "turned")
translate: आवाज़ सुनकर वह अचानक मुड़ गई। → She turned around suddenly when she heard the noise.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a time you turned around and saw a surprise.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to physically face the opposite direction, or for a bad situation to improve'?
usage_tip: 'Turn around a business' = make a failing business succeed.

simple_explanation: To become damaged or unusable from continued use, or to become extremely tired. "Wear out" means something (like shoes or tires) becomes damaged or useless after a lot of use. People can also "wear out," meaning they become exhausted.
example_2: These tires wore out faster than expected.
example_3: The kids wore out their parents with all the questions.
collocations: wear out quickly, worn out shoes, wear someone out
related_phrasal_verbs: use up, tire out, break down
action_sequence: Before: use shoes every day → During: the soles get thin → After: they have holes
grammar_pattern: subject + wear out (The carpet wore out. / The kids wore me out.)
word_forms: wear out – wore out – worn out – wearing out
common_mistake: My shoes weared out after one month.
correct_version: My shoes wore out after one month.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Wear' is irregular: wear – wore – worn.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on "out": wear-OUT; the adjective "worn out" stresses "worn."
spelling_tip: Two words as a verb; "worn out" is the adjective form (irregular past participle "worn," not "weared").
etymology: From "wear" + "out" -- literally to erode something through use until nothing is left, extended to items breaking down or people becoming exhausted.
prefix_root_suffix: wear + out (particle "out" shows something eroding completely through use)
mnemonic: The more you WEAR shoes, the more they WEAR OUT and fall apart.
memory_trick: WEAR → WORE → WORN, like TEAR → TORE → TORN.
visual_association: A pair of shoes with holes worn through the soles.
difference_explained: Wear out = become damaged or very tired. Wear off = an effect slowly disappears.
mini_conversation:
A: Why are you getting new shoes?
B: These ones finally wore out after two years.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A parent collapses onto the sofa and sighs, "These kids have completely worn me out today."
news_style_line: News-style: "Officials say the old bridge's cables have worn out and need urgent replacement."
casual_conversation: Casual: "My phone charger keeps wearing out every few months."
mcq_options: A) To become brand new  B) To become damaged or exhausted from use  C) To grow larger  D) To become more valuable
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: These old tires will ______ soon if we don't replace them. → wear out
find_and_fix_to_correct: The batteries wear out very quick in this toy. → The batteries wear out very quickly in this toy. (use the adverb "quickly," not the adjective "quick")
translate: लगातार इस्तेमाल से जूते जल्दी घिस जाते हैं। → Shoes wear out quickly with constant use.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something you used until it wore out.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to become damaged or unusable from continued use, or to become extremely tired'?
usage_tip: 'I'm worn out' = I'm extremely tired.

simple_explanation: For an effect or feeling to gradually disappear over time. "Wear off" describes something like pain, medicine, or excitement slowly fading away until it's completely gone.
example_1: The painkiller will wear off soon.
example_2: The numbness from the injection wore off after an hour.
example_3: Her excitement about the new job slowly wore off.
collocations: effect wears off, excitement wears off, wear off gradually
action_sequence: Before: take a painkiller → During: the pain goes away → After: after hours, the pain returns
grammar_pattern: subject + wear off (The anesthesia wore off after two hours.)
word_forms: wear off – wore off – worn off – wearing off
common_mistake: The medicine effect is wear off now.
correct_version: The medicine's effect is wearing off now.
why_it_s_wrong: The present continuous needs -ing (wearing off), and 'medicine's' shows possession.
spelling_tip: Two words -- don't confuse with "wear out" (used for physical damage/exhaustion, not fading feelings).
etymology: From "wear" + "off" -- literally to erode away a surface layer, extended to a feeling or effect gradually fading.
prefix_root_suffix: wear + off (particle "off" shows an effect gradually leaving/disappearing)
mnemonic: Just as paint slowly WEARS OFF a wall, a feeling slowly fades and wears OFF over time.
memory_trick: WEAR OFF: the effect is slowly rubbed OFF.
visual_association: Bright paint slowly fading and peeling off an old wall.
emotion_feel: Gradual return to normal, sometimes disappointment
difference_explained: Wear off = an effect fades. Wear out = be used until damaged, or become exhausted.
mini_conversation:
A: Does your arm still hurt?
B: A little, but the numbness is finally wearing off.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A patient blinks slowly and murmurs, "I think the anesthesia is finally wearing off."
news_style_line: News-style: "Experts say the initial excitement around the new policy has started to wear off."
casual_conversation: Casual: "The coffee's effect is wearing off -- I need another cup."
mcq_options: A) To suddenly appear  B) To gradually disappear  C) To become stronger  D) To repair itself
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The pain medicine will ______ in a few hours. → wear off
find_and_fix_to_correct: The effect of the coffee wear off after few hours. → The effect of the coffee wears off after a few hours. (add "-s" for present tense, and "a" before "few")
translate: दर्द की दवा का असर कुछ घंटों में ख़त्म हो जाएगा। → The effect of the painkiller will wear off in a few hours.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about how long a painkiller takes to wear off.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'for an effect or feeling to gradually disappear over time'?
usage_tip: Common with medicine, anaesthesia, excitement and paint.

hindi_meaning: पूरी तरह इस्तेमाल कर लेना, ख़त्म कर देना
simple_explanation: To completely finish or consume a supply of something. "Use up" means using something completely until none of it is left, like using up all your data or all the paper in the printer.
example_1: We used up all the flour.
example_2: He used up all his savings on the trip.
example_3: The printer used up the last of the ink.
collocations: use up energy, use up resources, use up all the time
action_sequence: Before: have a full pack → During: keep using it → After: nothing is left
grammar_pattern: use + object + up (use the paint up / use up the paint)
word_forms: use up – used up – used up – using up
common_mistake: We use up all our data before month end.
correct_version: We used up all our data before the month ended.
why_it_s_wrong: Use the past 'used' and 'ended', and add 'the' before 'month'.
spelling_tip: Two words -- the "s" in "use" sounds like a "z" when pronounced.
etymology: From "use" + "up" -- literally to use something until it reaches its upper limit of consumption, meaning nothing is left.
prefix_root_suffix: use + up (particle "up" shows consuming something entirely, to its limit)
mnemonic: When you USE something UP, you use it until there's nothing left -- all used UP.
memory_trick: USE UP: use it until it's all gone — the level goes UP to empty.
visual_association: An empty tube of toothpaste squeezed flat.
emotion_feel: Neutral, sometimes mild worry about scarcity
difference_explained: Use up = you finish it by using. Run out = you find there's none left.
mini_conversation:
A: Can I borrow your charger?
B: Sorry, I used up all my battery already.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character shakes an empty paint can and sighs, "We've used up the last of it."
news_style_line: News-style: "The city has nearly used up its emergency water reserves this summer."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I already used up my data for this month."
mcq_options: A) To save something for later  B) To completely consume something  C) To buy something new  D) To repair something
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: We ______ all the paint before finishing the last wall. → used up
find_and_fix_to_correct: She use up all her energy on the first day of the trip. → She used up all her energy on the first day of the trip. (use past tense "used")
translate: हमने यात्रा के पहले दिन ही सारा पैसा ख़र्च कर दिया। → We used up all our money on the first day of the trip.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something you used up quickly this month.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to completely finish or consume a supply of something'?
usage_tip: 'Use up leftovers' = finish old food so nothing is wasted.

simple_explanation: To find something by chance, or to appear to others in a certain way. "Come across" something means finding it unexpectedly, without looking for it. "Come across as" describes the impression you give other people, like coming across as confident or rude.
example_1: I came across an old photo.
example_2: She came across an interesting article online.
example_3: He comes across as very confident.
collocations: come across as, come across an article, come across a problem
related_phrasal_verbs: run into, stumble upon, bump into
action_sequence: Before: look through old boxes → During: find something by chance → After: feel surprised
grammar_pattern: come across + noun (come across a photo) / come across as + adjective (come across as rude)
word_forms: come across – came across – come across – coming across
common_mistake: I come across this book last week at the library.
correct_version: I came across this book last week at the library.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Last week' needs the past 'came'.
spelling_tip: Two words -- remember the double "s" in "across."
etymology: From "come" + "across" -- literally to move across a space and encounter something, extended to finding something by chance or how one appears to others.
prefix_root_suffix: come + across (particle "across" shows crossing paths with something unexpectedly)
mnemonic: If you walk ACROSS a room and something unexpected COMES into view, you've "come across" it.
memory_trick: COME ACROSS: walk ACROSS a room and find something by chance.
visual_association: A hand brushing dust off a forgotten box to reveal something hidden inside.
difference_explained: Find = discover, often by looking. Come across = find by chance, without looking.
mini_conversation:
A: Where did you find this old letter?
B: I came across it while cleaning the attic.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character pauses while sorting boxes and says, "Look what I just came across -- our old family photos!"
news_style_line: News-style: "Archaeologists came across ancient pottery during the excavation."
casual_conversation: Casual: "He can come across as shy, but he's actually really funny once you know him."
mcq_options: A) To search for something on purpose  B) To find something unexpectedly  C) To buy something expensive  D) To lose something important
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: While cleaning the garage, I ______ my old bicycle. → came across
find_and_fix_to_correct: I come across her at the party last night, it was surprise. → I came across her at the party last night -- it was a surprise. (use past tense "came," and add "a" before "surprise")
translate: सफ़ाई करते समय मुझे अपनी पुरानी डायरी मिल गई। → While cleaning, I came across my old diary.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something interesting you came across online.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to find something by chance, or to appear to others in a certain way'?
usage_tip: 'He comes across as rude' = he seems rude to others.

simple_explanation: To return to a place after being away. "Come back" means returning to a place -- home, work, a country -- after being somewhere else for a while.
example_2: She came back from her trip last night.
example_3: I hope you come back to visit us soon.
collocations: come back home, come back soon, come back from vacation
action_sequence: Before: leave home in the morning → During: finish work → After: arrive home again
grammar_pattern: subject + come back (from) + place (She came back from Japan last week.)
word_forms: come back – came back – come back – coming back
common_mistake: He come back from work at 6 PM every day.
correct_version: He comes back from work at 6 PM every day.
why_it_s_wrong: He/she in the simple present needs -s: comes back.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on "back": come-BACK; the noun "comeback" stresses the first syllable.
spelling_tip: Two words as a verb; one word as a noun ("a big comeback").
etymology: From "come" + "back" -- literally to move in the return direction, meaning to return to a place.
prefix_root_suffix: come + back (particle "back" shows returning to the original place)
mnemonic: When you COME BACK, you retrace your steps BACK to where you started.
memory_trick: COME BACK: come BACK the way you went.
visual_association: A traveler stepping off a plane and being welcomed home with open arms.
difference_explained: Come back = return to where the speaker is. Go back = return to another place.
mini_conversation:
A: When are you coming back from your trip?
B: I'll be back next Monday.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character stands at the doorway and says softly, "I promise I'll come back for you."
news_style_line: News-style: "The champion athlete made a stunning comeback after a year of injury."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I can't wait for you to come back from your trip!"
mcq_options: A) To leave a place permanently  B) To return to a place  C) To start a new job  D) To forget something
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Don't worry, I'll ______ before it gets dark. → come back
find_and_fix_to_correct: She come back yesterday from her business trip. → She came back yesterday from her business trip. (use past tense "came")
translate: कृपया जल्दी वापस आ जाना। → Please come back soon.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about what time you come back home every day.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to return to a place after being away'?
usage_tip: 'Come back soon!' is a warm goodbye.

hindi_meaning: सामने आना, जारी होना, बाहर निकलना
simple_explanation: To become publicly known, to be released, or to emerge from somewhere. "Come out" can mean the truth becoming known, a new movie or product being released, or the sun literally coming out from behind clouds.
example_2: Her new book comes out next month.
example_3: The sun came out after the rain stopped.
collocations: come out with, come out true, come out of hiding
related_phrasal_verbs: turn out, get out, be released
action_sequence: Before: keep news secret → During: announce it → After: everyone knows
grammar_pattern: subject + come out (The results will come out on Friday.)
word_forms: come out – came out – come out – coming out
common_mistake: The news come out yesterday about the merger.
correct_version: The news came out yesterday about the merger.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Yesterday' needs the past 'came'.
spelling_tip: Two words -- don't confuse with "outcome" (a noun meaning result).
etymology: From "come" + "out" -- literally to move from inside to outside, extended to information becoming public or a product being released.
prefix_root_suffix: come + out (particle "out" shows something emerging or becoming visible/public)
mnemonic: When the truth COMES OUT, imagine it stepping OUT from hiding into the light.
memory_trick: COME OUT: step OUT into public view.
visual_association: The sun breaking through gray clouds after a storm.
difference_explained: A company releases a product. The product comes out.
mini_conversation:
A: When does the new album come out?
B: It comes out next Friday, I can't wait!
everyday_scene: Everyday: A reporter looks up from a phone and says urgently, "It's just come out -- the story's true."
news_style_line: News-style: "New details have come out regarding the company's financial troubles."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I heard the truth finally came out about what happened."
mcq_options: A) To be kept secret forever  B) To become known or be released  C) To be cancelled  D) To be delayed indefinitely
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The results of the exam will ______ next week. → come out
find_and_fix_to_correct: The movie come out last Friday in theaters. → The movie came out last Friday in theaters. (use past tense "came")
translate: अगले हफ़्ते परीक्षा का परिणाम आएगा। → The exam results will come out next week.
