write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a film or song that came out recently.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to become publicly known, to be released, or to emerge from somewhere'?
usage_tip: A film or book 'comes out' = is released. 'Come out' also means reveal one's sexuality.

simple_explanation: To accompany someone somewhere, or to make progress on something. "Come along" can mean joining someone on a trip or activity, or (used as a question) checking how well a task or project is developing.
example_1: Do you want to come along?
example_2: She invited her sister to come along on the trip.
example_3: How is the project coming along?
collocations: come along with, come along nicely, invite someone to come along
action_sequence: Before: start a project → During: make steady progress → After: it's taking shape
grammar_pattern: come along (with) + noun (come along with us) / How is X coming along?
word_forms: come along – came along – come along – coming along
common_mistake: How is your project come along these days?
correct_version: How is your project coming along these days?
why_it_s_wrong: The present continuous needs 'is coming along'.
spelling_tip: Two words -- "along" is one word, not "a long."
etymology: From "come" + "along" -- literally to move alongside someone, extended to accompanying them or a task making progress.
prefix_root_suffix: come + along (particle "along" shows moving together with someone or steady progress)
mnemonic: When you COME ALONG with friends, you travel ALONG beside them on their journey.
memory_trick: COME ALONG: walk ALONG with someone, or move ahead.
visual_association: A group of friends walking together down a sunny path.
difference_explained: Come along = accompany (no object needed), or make progress. Come with = accompany + person: 'Come with me.'
mini_conversation:
A: We're going to the market, want to come along?
B: Sure, let me grab my jacket!
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character waves someone over and says, "Come on, come along -- we don't want to be late!"
news_style_line: News-style: "The renovation project is coming along well, with completion expected next spring."
casual_conversation: Casual: "How's your new job coming along?"
mcq_question: "How is it coming along?" most nearly means:
mcq_options: A) How is it being destroyed?  B) How is it progressing?  C) How is it being sold?  D) How is it being ignored?
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: We're heading to the beach -- do you want to ______? → come along
find_and_fix_to_correct: She ask him to come along with she to the party. → She asked him to come along with her to the party. (use past tense "asked" and object pronoun "her")
translate: क्या तुम हमारे साथ चलना चाहोगे? → Would you like to come along with us?
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence asking a friend how their project is coming along.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to accompany someone somewhere, or to make progress on something'?
usage_tip: 'Come along!' = come with me. 'How's it coming along?' = how's progress?

simple_explanation: To take someone or something to a place and leave them there. When you "drop someone off," you drive or walk them to a place, let them out, and then continue on your own way.
example_1: I drop off my son at school every morning.
example_2: Can you drop me off at the station?
example_3: She dropped the package off at the post office.
collocations: drop off the kids, drop off a package, drop someone off at
related_phrasal_verbs: pick up, drop by, drop in
action_sequence: Before: drive to the station → During: stop and let someone out → After: drive away
grammar_pattern: drop + object + off + at/place (Drop me off at the corner.)
word_forms: drop off – dropped off – dropped off – dropping off
common_mistake: I dropped off my sister to the airport.
correct_version: I dropped my sister off at the airport.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'at' with 'drop off', and the person can go in the middle: 'dropped my sister off at'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress falls on "off": drop OFF, with a crisp "p" sound before it.
spelling_tip: Two words, no hyphen -- not "dropoff" (that's the noun form, one word).
etymology: "Drop" (let fall) + "off" (away from) -- literally to let something fall away from you, extended to leaving someone/something at a place.
prefix_root_suffix: drop + off (phrasal particle -- no prefix/suffix breakdown)
word_family: drop (v.), drop-off (n., a decline or a delivery point)
mnemonic: You DROP someone OFF the way you'd drop a passenger off a bus -- quick and on your way.
memory_trick: DROP OFF: the car stops, and someone drops OFF.
visual_association: A car pulling up to a curb and a passenger stepping out with a bag.
difference_explained: Opposites: drop off = leave someone at a place. Pick up = collect them.
mini_conversation:
A: Can you drop me off near the mall?
B: Sure, hop in -- I'll drop you off in ten minutes.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A driver pulls up to the curb and says, "This is your stop -- I'll drop you off right here."
news_style_line: News-style: "Parents were asked to drop off donations at the community center before Friday."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Text me when you're ready, and I'll drop you off on my way to work."
mcq_options: A) To pick someone up  B) To take someone/something somewhere and leave them  C) To argue with someone  D) To forget something
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Could you ______ these books at the library on your way home? → drop off
find_and_fix_to_correct: He dropped off his laptop at repair shop yesterday. → He dropped his laptop off at the repair shop yesterday. (add "the" before "repair shop")
translate: कृपया मुझे अगले चौराहे पर छोड़ दीजिए। → Please drop me off at the next intersection.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about who drops you off at school or work.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to take someone or something to a place and leave them there'?
usage_tip: 'I dropped off' can also mean I fell asleep.

simple_explanation: To choose one thing from a group of things. When you "pick out" something, you look at several options and select the one you like best.
example_1: She picked out a red dress for the party.
example_2: He picked out a gift for his mother's birthday.
example_3: Can you help me pick out a good laptop?
collocations: pick out a gift, pick out an outfit, pick out the best one
where_it_s_used: Shopping, choosing gifts, selecting from a group, identifying someone in a crowd
action_sequence: Before: see many options → During: compare them → After: choose one
grammar_pattern: pick out + noun (pick out a shirt / pick a shirt out)
word_forms: pick out – picked out – picked out – picking out
common_mistake: I picked out from three options.
correct_version: I picked one out from three options.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Pick out' needs an object: pick one out, pick out a shirt.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on "out": pick OUT, with a clear "k" sound before it.
etymology: "Pick" (choose, select) + "out" (from among others) -- literally to physically pick something out of a group.
prefix_root_suffix: pick + out (phrasal particle -- no prefix/suffix breakdown)
word_family: pick (v./n.), pick-out (not standard as noun, use "selection")
mnemonic: When you PICK something OUT, you take it OUT from a pile of choices.
memory_trick: PICK OUT: pick one OUT of the crowd.
visual_association: A hand reaching into a row of options and lifting one out.
difference_explained: Pick out = choose. Pick up = lift, or collect.
mini_conversation:
A: Which cake should we get?
B: I already picked out the chocolate one.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A shopper holds up two shirts and says, "Help me pick one out -- I can never decide."
news_style_line: News-style: "Volunteers helped families pick out warm coats before winter arrived."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I picked out a few movies for us to watch tonight."
mcq_options: A) To ignore something  B) To choose something from a group  C) To throw something away  D) To repair something
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Please ______ the book you want to read first. → pick out
find_and_fix_to_correct: She picked out three shirt at the store. → She picked out three shirts at the store. (plural noun needed)
translate: उसने दुकान से एक अच्छी किताब चुनी। → She picked out a good book from the shop.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something you picked out at a shop.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to choose one thing from a group of things'?
usage_tip: 'Can you pick me out in this photo?' = can you find me?

simple_explanation: To make a place neat and clean by removing mess. "Clean up" means to tidy an area thoroughly, often after it has become messy or dirty.
example_1: Please clean up your room before dinner.
example_2: The kids cleaned up the mess they made in the kitchen.
example_3: Volunteers cleaned up the beach after the storm.
collocations: clean up the mess, clean up after yourself, clean up the kitchen
related_phrasal_verbs: tidy up, straighten up, pick up
where_it_s_used: Household chores, community service, workplace tidiness, parenting
action_sequence: Before: the room is messy → During: remove the rubbish → After: the room is clean
grammar_pattern: clean up + noun/place (clean up the room / clean the room up)
word_forms: clean up – cleaned up – cleaned up – cleaning up
common_mistake: Please clean up after you.
correct_version: Please clean up after yourself.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Clean up after yourself' uses a reflexive pronoun, because the mess is your own.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on both words fairly evenly: CLEAN UP.
spelling_tip: Two words as a verb; "cleanup" is one word only as a noun ("the cleanup took hours").
etymology: "Clean" (free from dirt, Old English "claene") + "up" (completely) -- "up" here intensifies the action, meaning to clean thoroughly.
prefix_root_suffix: clean + up (phrasal particle -- no prefix/suffix breakdown)
mnemonic: When you CLEAN UP, you clean everything UP from the floor to the shelves.
memory_trick: CLEAN UP: pick the mess UP off the floor.
visual_association: A messy room transforming into a spotless one after sweeping and organizing.
emotion_feel: Neutral, sometimes a mild sense of duty or relief afterward
difference_explained: Clean = remove dirt. Clean up = remove mess and make the whole place tidy.
mini_conversation:
A: This kitchen is a disaster.
B: I know, let's clean up before Mom gets home.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A parent stands in a messy room and says firmly, "You're not leaving until this is all cleaned up."
news_style_line: News-style: "Hundreds of volunteers gathered to clean up the riverbank this weekend."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Can you clean up the living room before our guests arrive?"
mcq_options: A) To make something dirty  B) To tidy and remove mess from a place  C) To buy new furniture  D) To lock a door
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: We all need to ______ after the party tonight. → clean up
find_and_fix_to_correct: She clean up her desk every Friday. → She cleans up her desk every Friday. (needs -s for third-person singular present)
translate: कृपया खाने से पहले अपना कमरा साफ़ करो। → Please clean up your room before dinner.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about how you clean up after a party.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to make a place neat and clean by removing mess'?
usage_tip: 'Clean up your act' = start behaving better.

simple_explanation: To arrange things neatly and put them in order. "Tidy up" means to put things back in their place and make a space look neat and organized.
example_1: Let's tidy up the living room before guests arrive.
example_2: She tidied up her desk before leaving the office.
example_3: Can you tidy up the toys before bedtime?
collocations: tidy up the room, tidy up your desk, tidy up before guests arrive
related_phrasal_verbs: clean up, straighten up, put away
where_it_s_used: Housework, offices, classrooms, before guests arrive
action_sequence: Before: things are scattered → During: put each thing in place → After: the room is neat
grammar_pattern: tidy up + noun (tidy up the shelf / tidy the shelf up)
word_forms: tidy up – tidied up – tidied up – tidying up
common_mistake: I need tidy up my desk.
correct_version: I need to tidy up my desk.
why_it_s_wrong: After 'need', use 'to' + base verb.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on "TI-dy," with a soft "y" sound at the end: TIE-dee up.
etymology: "Tidy" (neat, orderly -- from Middle English "tidi," related to "tide," meaning timely/seasonable) + "up" (completely, intensifier).
prefix_root_suffix: tidy + up (phrasal particle -- no prefix/suffix breakdown)
mnemonic: TIDY UP rhymes a bit with "wide-y up" -- picture spreading things out neatly, not piling them.
memory_trick: TIDY UP: put everything UP in its place.
visual_association: Scattered books and clothes being neatly stacked and folded.
emotion_feel: Neutral, sometimes calming or satisfying once finished
difference_explained: Tidy up = put in order. Clean up = remove dirt and mess.
mini_conversation:
A: Guests are coming in an hour!
B: Okay, let's tidy up quickly.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character glances at a cluttered room and sighs, "Fine, I'll tidy up before you get here."
news_style_line: News-style: "Residents were encouraged to tidy up their yards ahead of the neighborhood inspection."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I always tidy up my room on Sunday nights."
mcq_options: A) To make a mess  B) To arrange things neatly  C) To break something  D) To sell something
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: I always ______ my desk before I go home. → tidy up
find_and_fix_to_correct: She tidy up the shelves every morning. → She tidies up the shelves every morning. (needs -s for third-person singular)
translate: चलो मेहमानों के आने से पहले कमरा व्यवस्थित कर लें। → Let's tidy up the room before the guests arrive.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about when you tidy up your room.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to arrange things neatly and put them in order'?
usage_tip: 'Tidy up' is more British; 'clean up' is common in both US and UK.

simple_explanation: To make something completely full. "Fill up" means to add something (like water, gas, or food) until there's no more space left.
example_1: Let's fill up the car before the trip.
example_2: He filled up his water bottle before the hike.
example_3: The stadium filled up quickly before the game started.
collocations: fill up the tank, fill up a glass, fill up with people
related_phrasal_verbs: top up, fill out, top off
action_sequence: Before: the tank is empty → During: pour in fuel → After: it's full
grammar_pattern: fill up + noun (fill up the tank / fill the tank up)
word_forms: fill up – filled up – filled up – filling up
common_mistake: Please fill up this form.
correct_version: Please fill out this form.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'fill out' or 'fill in' for forms. 'Fill up' is for containers.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on "up": fill UP, with a short, crisp "i" in "fill."
etymology: "Fill" (make full, Old English "fyllan") + "up" (to the top, intensifier) -- literally to fill something all the way to the top.
prefix_root_suffix: fill + up (phrasal particle -- no prefix/suffix breakdown)
word_family: fill (v.), filling (n./adj.), full (adj.), fulfil (v., different meaning)
mnemonic: FILL UP means fill all the way UP to the top -- like a glass with no room left.
memory_trick: FILL UP: the level goes UP to the top.
visual_association: A glass of water being poured until it reaches the very top.
emotion_feel: Neutral, sometimes satisfaction (a full stomach) or urgency (a full tank before a trip)
difference_explained: Fill up = make a container full. Fill out = complete a form. (Indian English often says 'fill up a form'.)
mini_conversation:
A: The tank is almost empty.
B: Let's stop and fill up before the highway.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A driver pulls into a station and tells the attendant, "Fill it up, please -- all the way."
news_style_line: News-style: "Gas stations reported long lines as drivers rushed to fill up before the holiday weekend."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Can you fill up my glass with some more water?"
mcq_options: A) To empty something completely  B) To make something completely full  C) To break something  D) To clean something
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: We stopped at the gas station to ______ the car. → fill up
find_and_fix_to_correct: I filled up the application form yesterday. → I filled out the application form yesterday. (use "fill out" for forms)
translate: कृपया गाड़ी में पेट्रोल भर दीजिए। → Please fill up the car with petrol.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about what you fill up before a long drive.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to make something completely full'?
usage_tip: 'Fill her up' at a petrol pump = fill the tank.

simple_explanation: To write the requested information on a form or document. "Fill out" means to complete a document -- like an application or survey -- by writing your details in the blank spaces.
example_1: Please fill out this application form.
example_2: She filled out the visa application carefully.
example_3: You need to fill out this survey before you leave.
collocations: fill out a form, fill out an application, fill out paperwork
related_phrasal_verbs: fill in, sign up, check off
where_it_s_used: Applications, government forms, surveys, medical intake forms
action_sequence: Before: get a blank form → During: write your details → After: hand it in
grammar_pattern: fill out + noun (fill out the form / fill the form out)
word_forms: fill out – filled out – filled out – filling out
common_mistake: Please fill this form.
correct_version: Please fill out (or fill in) this form.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Fill' alone means make a container full. Forms need 'fill out' or 'fill in'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on "out": fill OUT, with a clear diphthong sound in "out."
spelling_tip: Two words; commonly confused with "fill up" -- remember "out" pairs with forms.
etymology: "Fill" (make full/complete) + "out" (fully, to completion) -- to complete every blank space in a document.
prefix_root_suffix: fill + out (phrasal particle -- no prefix/suffix breakdown)
mnemonic: You FILL OUT a form by writing information all the way OUT to the edges of every blank.
memory_trick: FILL OUT: fill OUT every blank line on the form.
visual_association: A hand holding a pen above a clipboard of empty ruled lines.
difference_explained: Same meaning for forms. Fill in is more British; fill out is more American.
mini_conversation:
A: What do I do at the reception desk?
B: Just fill out this form and hand it back to them.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A receptionist slides a clipboard across the counter and says, "Just fill this out and take a seat."
news_style_line: News-style: "Applicants must fill out the online form before the midnight deadline."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Can you help me fill out this rental application?"
mcq_options: A) To throw away a document  B) To complete a form with information  C) To sign a contract without reading it  D) To copy someone else's answers
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: You must ______ this form before your appointment. → fill out
find_and_fix_to_correct: She filled up the job application yesterday. → She filled out the job application yesterday. (use "fill out" for applications/forms)
translate: कृपया यह फॉर्म भर दीजिए। → Please fill out this form.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a form you filled out recently.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to write the requested information on a form or document'?
usage_tip: 'Fill in' (UK) and 'fill out' (US) both work for forms.

simple_explanation: To stop a business or organization from operating. "Close down" means a shop, factory, or company stops running -- sometimes for good, sometimes for a while.
example_1: The old bookstore closed down last month.
example_2: The factory closed down after 40 years in business.
example_3: Many restaurants closed down during the economic crisis.
collocations: close down a business, close down permanently, forced to close down
related_phrasal_verbs: shut down, wind up, go under
where_it_s_used: Business news, factories, shops, economic hardship
action_sequence: Before: a business struggles → During: it stops trading → After: it shuts forever
grammar_pattern: close down (intransitive) or close + noun + down (The factory closed down / They closed the factory down.)
word_forms: close down – closed down – closed down – closing down
common_mistake: The shop was close down last year.
correct_version: The shop closed down last year.
why_it_s_wrong: A finished past event needs the simple past 'closed down'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress falls evenly, but "down" is slightly longer: close DOWN.
spelling_tip: Two words; the noun form is "closure," not "close-down" (though "shutdown" is used for that sense too).
etymology: "Close" (shut, from Latin "claudere") + "down" (completely, to a stop) -- "down" here signals the business coming to a complete stop.
prefix_root_suffix: close + down (phrasal particle -- no prefix/suffix breakdown)
mnemonic: When a shop CLOSES DOWN, its lights go DOWN for good.
memory_trick: CLOSE DOWN: the shutters come DOWN for good.
visual_association: A "Closed" sign hanging permanently in a dusty shop window.
difference_explained: Close = shut (for the night). Close down = stop operating permanently.
mini_conversation:
A: Did you hear about the mall?
B: Yeah, half the stores are closing down.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A worker stares at a locked storefront and mutters, "Twenty years, and now they're closing it down."
news_style_line: News-style: "The company announced it will close down three factories by the end of the year."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I heard our favorite coffee shop is closing down next week."
mcq_options: A) To open a new branch  B) To stop a business from operating  C) To hire more staff  D) To raise prices
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The local cinema had to ______ after losing too many customers. → close down
find_and_fix_to_correct: The store close down two years ago. → The store closed down two years ago. (past tense needed)
translate: पुरानी फैक्ट्री पिछले साल बंद हो गई। → The old factory closed down last year.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a shop in your area that closed down.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to stop a business or organization from operating'?
usage_tip: 'Closing-down sale' = a final sale before a shop shuts forever.

simple_explanation: To stop a machine, system, or business from working. "Shut down" means to turn something off completely, whether it's a computer, a factory, or an entire operation.
example_1: Please shut down the computer before you leave.
example_2: The power plant shut down due to a technical failure.
example_3: She shut down her laptop and went home.
collocations: shut down the computer, shut down operations, government shutdown
related_phrasal_verbs: close down, power off, turn off
action_sequence: Before: the computer is running → During: close programs and power off → After: the screen is black
grammar_pattern: shut down + noun (shut down the system / shut the system down)
word_forms: shut down – shut down – shut down – shutting down
common_mistake: I shut down the light before sleeping.
correct_version: I turned off the light before sleeping.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'turn off' for lights and switches; 'shut down' is for systems, machines and businesses.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on "down": shut DOWN, with a short, clipped "u" in "shut."
spelling_tip: Two words as a verb; "shutdown" is one word as a noun ("a computer shutdown").
etymology: "Shut" (close firmly, Old English "scyttan") + "down" (to a stop) -- originally about physically closing a door or gate, extended to stopping systems and machines.
prefix_root_suffix: shut + down (phrasal particle -- no prefix/suffix breakdown)
mnemonic: When you SHUT DOWN a computer, you shut its power all the way DOWN to zero.
memory_trick: SHUT DOWN: a computer's power goes DOWN.
visual_association: A screen going black as a computer powers off.
difference_explained: Turn off = switch off (lights, TV). Shut down = stop a system properly (computer, factory).
mini_conversation:
A: My laptop is running so slow.
B: Try shutting it down and turning it back on.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A technician flips a switch and announces, "System's shutting down -- everyone clear the room."
news_style_line: News-style: "Officials shut down the highway after reports of a gas leak nearby."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Don't forget to shut down your computer before you leave the office."
mcq_options: A) To start a new project  B) To stop a machine, system, or business from operating  C) To repair something  D) To increase speed
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The technician had to ______ the server for maintenance. → shut down
find_and_fix_to_correct: Please shut down light when you leave. → Please shut off the light when you leave. (use "shut off" or "turn off" for lights, not "shut down")
translate: कृपया जाने से पहले कंप्यूटर बंद कर दीजिए। → Please shut down the computer before you leave.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about how you shut down your computer.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to stop a machine, system, or business from working'?
usage_tip: 'Shut down' also means stop someone rudely: 'He shut me down.'

simple_explanation: To start suddenly, especially something unpleasant like a fire or a fight. "Break out" describes something bad -- like a fire, a war, or an argument -- starting suddenly and spreading quickly.
example_1: A fire broke out in the kitchen.
example_2: A fight broke out between the two fans.
example_3: War broke out between the two countries in 1990.
collocations: break out in a fire, break out in a fight, break out in a rash
related_phrasal_verbs: break down, break up, break away
action_sequence: Before: everything is calm → During: trouble starts suddenly → After: people react
grammar_pattern: [event] + break out (A fire broke out. / War broke out.)
word_forms: break out – broke out – broken out – breaking out
common_mistake: The fire broke out from the building.
correct_version: The fire broke out in the building.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'in' to show where something broke out.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on "out": break OUT, with a strong diphthong in "break."
spelling_tip: Two words; don't confuse with "breakout" (one word, used as a noun/adjective, e.g., "a breakout star").
etymology: "Break" (Old English "brecan," to shatter or force apart) + "out" (outward, into the open) -- literally to break outward from confinement, extended to something suddenly starting or spreading.
prefix_root_suffix: break + out (phrasal particle -- no prefix/suffix breakdown)
mnemonic: When a fire BREAKS OUT, it suddenly bursts OUT of control.
memory_trick: BREAK OUT: something BREAKS OUT suddenly, like a fire from a closed box.
visual_association: Flames suddenly bursting from a small spark.
difference_explained: Start is neutral. Break out = start suddenly, usually something bad (war, fire, disease).
mini_conversation:
A: Did you hear the news?
B: Yes, a fire broke out near the market last night.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A reporter speaks urgently into a camera, "A fire has broken out downtown, and firefighters are rushing to the scene."
news_style_line: News-style: "Violence broke out at the rally after tensions escalated between the two groups."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I heard a fight broke out at the party last night."
mcq_options: A) To end slowly  B) To start suddenly, often something bad  C) To repair something  D) To celebrate quietly
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: A serious argument ______ between the two neighbors. → broke out
find_and_fix_to_correct: The disease is break out in many countries. → The disease has broken out in many countries. (needs correct verb form -- present perfect)
translate: बाज़ार के पास अचानक आग लग गई। → A fire broke out near the market.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a fire or fight that broke out in a news story.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to start suddenly, especially something unpleasant like a fire or a fight'?
usage_tip: 'Break out of prison' = escape. 'Break out in a rash' = skin reaction.

simple_explanation: To enter a place illegally, usually by force. "Break into" means to force your way into a building or car, usually to steal something -- like a burglar breaking into a house.
example_1: Someone broke into our car last night.
example_2: Thieves broke into the museum and stole two paintings.
example_3: The burglar broke into the house through a back window.
collocations: break into a house, break into a car, break into a system
related_phrasal_verbs: break in, break out, break down
action_sequence: Before: thieves reach the house → During: force the door → After: enter illegally
grammar_pattern: break into + place (break into a house / break into a car)
word_forms: break into – broke into – broken into – breaking into
common_mistake: Someone broke in my house.
correct_version: Someone broke into my house.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Break into' + place; 'break in' has no object after it.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on "in-": break IN-to, said quickly as almost one word.
spelling_tip: Three words; always "into," never "in to" in this phrasal verb.
etymology: "Break" (force apart) + "into" (entering) -- literally to force your way into a place by breaking something (like a lock or window).
prefix_root_suffix: break + into (phrasal particle -- no prefix/suffix breakdown)
mnemonic: A thief BREAKS a window to get INTO a house.
memory_trick: BREAK INTO: BREAK the lock and go INTO the house.
visual_association: A broken window with a shadowy figure climbing through it.
difference_explained: Break into a house (object). Thieves broke in (no object).
mini_conversation:
A: What happened to your window?
B: Someone tried to break into our apartment last night.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A detective examines a shattered window and says, "Whoever broke in knew exactly what they were looking for."
news_style_line: News-style: "Police are investigating after thieves broke into three homes in the same neighborhood."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Our neighbor's garage was broken into last week -- so scary."
mcq_options: A) To knock politely on a door  B) To enter a place illegally by force  C) To repair a broken window  D) To sell a house
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Someone tried to ______ the office last night, but the alarm scared them off. → break into
find_and_fix_to_correct: The thief break into the shop last night. → The thief broke into the shop last night. (past tense needed)
translate: कल रात चोर हमारे घर में घुस आया। → A thief broke into our house last night.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about how to protect a house from being broken into.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to enter a place illegally, usually by force'?
usage_tip: 'Break into a smile' = suddenly smile.

simple_explanation: To gradually reduce pressure, effort, or intensity. "Ease off" means to slow down or reduce something -- like pressure, speed, or effort -- little by little instead of stopping suddenly.
example_1: The rain finally eased off in the afternoon.
example_2: He eased off the gas as he approached the turn.
example_3: My boss told me to ease off and take a break.
collocations: ease off the pressure, ease off the accelerator, ease off a bit
related_phrasal_verbs: ease up, let up, calm down
action_sequence: Before: press hard → During: slowly reduce the pressure → After: things feel lighter
grammar_pattern: ease off (+ on + noun) (ease off on the criticism / the rain eased off)
word_forms: ease off – eased off – eased off – easing off
common_mistake: Please ease off to me about the deadline.
correct_version: Please ease off on me about the deadline.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'ease off ON' a person or topic, not 'to'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on "ease": EASE off, with a long "ee" sound.
spelling_tip: Two words; note the "s" in "ease" sounds like "z."
etymology: "Ease" (comfort, freedom from difficulty, from Old French "aise") + "off" (away, reducing) -- to gradually take pressure away.
prefix_root_suffix: ease + off (phrasal particle -- no prefix/suffix breakdown)
mnemonic: When you EASE OFF the gas pedal, you take your foot OFF slowly, not suddenly.
memory_trick: EASE OFF: take your foot OFF the pressure pedal.
visual_association: A tightly gripped hand slowly loosening its grip.
difference_explained: Stop = end completely. Ease off = reduce gradually.
mini_conversation:
A: You've been working nonstop.
B: I know, I need to ease off a little.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A coach calls out, "Ease off, you're pushing too hard -- save some energy for later."
news_style_line: News-style: "Forecasters say the storm will ease off by early morning."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Can you ease off the criticism? I'm doing my best."
mcq_options: A) To increase suddenly  B) To gradually reduce pressure or intensity  C) To stop completely and instantly  D) To start something new
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The doctor told him to ______ the heavy exercise for a week. → ease off
find_and_fix_to_correct: The traffic eased off since an hour. → The traffic has eased off for an hour. (needs "for," not "since," with a duration)
translate: दोपहर तक बारिश कम हो गई। → The rain eased off by the afternoon.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence asking someone to ease off on the pressure.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to gradually reduce pressure, effort, or intensity'?
usage_tip: 'The rain eased off' = it became lighter.

simple_explanation: To go faster or make something happen more quickly. "Speed up" means to increase the pace of something, whether it's a car, a process, or a person's work.
example_1: Please speed up -- we're going to be late.
example_2: The driver sped up to pass the truck.
example_3: We need to speed up the delivery process.
collocations: speed up the process, speed up a little, speed up production
related_phrasal_verbs: slow down, hurry up, pick up the pace
action_sequence: Before: move slowly → During: press the accelerator → After: move faster
grammar_pattern: speed up (+ noun) (speed up the car / speed the process up)
word_forms: speed up – sped up – sped up – speeding up
common_mistake: The car speeded up quickly.
correct_version: The car sped up quickly.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Speed' is irregular: the past is 'sped'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on "speed": SPEED up, with a long "ee" sound.
spelling_tip: Two words; "speedup" is one word only as a rare technical noun.
etymology: "Speed" (swiftness, Old English "sped," success/swiftness) + "up" (increase) -- to increase speed.
prefix_root_suffix: speed + up (phrasal particle -- no prefix/suffix breakdown)
mnemonic: SPEED UP means your SPEED goes UP.
memory_trick: SPEED → SPED, like FEED → FED.
visual_association: A speedometer needle climbing quickly to the right.
difference_explained: Speed up = go faster (vehicles, processes). Hurry up = move faster because you're late (people).
mini_conversation:
A: We're falling behind schedule.
B: Let's speed up and finish the last section today.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A pilot announces over the radio, "We're speeding up to make up for lost time."
news_style_line: News-style: "Officials promised to speed up vaccine distribution across rural areas."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Can you speed up a little? The movie starts in ten minutes."
mcq_options: A) To slow down  B) To go faster or make something happen more quickly  C) To stop completely  D) To repeat something
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The company plans to ______ production to meet demand. → speed up
find_and_fix_to_correct: Please speed up your work more slow. → Please speed up your work. (remove "more slow" -- it contradicts "speed up")
translate: कृपया थोड़ा तेज़ करो, हमें देर हो रही है। → Please speed up a little, we're getting late.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something you would like to speed up.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to go faster or make something happen more quickly'?
usage_tip: 'Can we speed things up?' = can we go faster?

simple_explanation: To reduce speed or go at a slower pace. "Slow down" means to do something less quickly, whether driving, talking, or working, often to be safer or calmer.
example_1: Please slow down -- you're driving too fast.
example_2: The doctor told him to slow down and rest more.
example_3: Traffic slowed down near the construction site.
collocations: slow down traffic, slow down a bit, economy slows down
related_phrasal_verbs: speed up, calm down, take it easy
where_it_s_used: Driving, health advice, speaking pace, economy
action_sequence: Before: drive fast → During: press the brake gently → After: move slowly
grammar_pattern: slow down (+ noun) (slow down the car / slow the car down)
word_forms: slow down – slowed down – slowed down – slowing down
common_mistake: He slow downs when he sees the police.
correct_version: He slows down when he sees the police.
why_it_s_wrong: The -s goes on the verb: 'slows down'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on "down": slow DOWN, with a falling, calming tone.
spelling_tip: Two words; "slowdown" is one word only as a noun ("an economic slowdown").
etymology: "Slow" (Old English "slaw," sluggish) + "down" (a decrease) -- to decrease pace or speed.
prefix_root_suffix: slow + down (phrasal particle -- no prefix/suffix breakdown)
mnemonic: SLOW DOWN means your speed goes DOWN and becomes SLOW.
memory_trick: SLOW DOWN: the speed number goes DOWN.
visual_association: A speeding car gradually braking to a gentle stop.
difference_explained: Slow down = reduce speed. Stop = reach zero speed.
mini_conversation:
A: I have so much to do today!
B: Slow down, you'll get it all done.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A worried friend grabs someone's arm and says, "Slow down, you're going to hurt yourself."
news_style_line: News-style: "Economists warn the housing market is beginning to slow down."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Slow down when you talk -- I can't keep up!"
mcq_options: A) To go faster  B) To reduce speed or pace  C) To stop permanently  D) To repeat an action
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: You should ______ before the sharp turn ahead. → slow down
find_and_fix_to_correct: Slow down your car, it's too fasting. → Slow down your car, it's going too fast. (fix "fasting" to "going too fast")
translate: कृपया धीमे चलो, सड़क गीली है। → Please slow down, the road is wet.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about when drivers should slow down.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to reduce speed or go at a slower pace'?
usage_tip: 'Slow down!' is also advice to relax and not rush life.

simple_explanation: To calculate the total of several numbers. "Add up" means to combine numbers to find their sum; it can also mean that facts make logical sense together.
example_1: Let's add up the total cost.
example_2: He added up all the receipts before the meeting.
example_3: The numbers just don't add up.
collocations: add up the numbers, add up the cost, the story doesn't add up
related_phrasal_verbs: total up, work out, make sense
where_it_s_used: Shopping, budgeting, math, suspicion/logic (things not adding up)
action_sequence: Before: have a list of numbers → During: add them one by one → After: get the total
grammar_pattern: add up + noun (add up the bill) / things + add up (his excuse doesn't add up)
word_forms: add up – added up – added up – adding up
common_mistake: I added up to buy the tickets.
correct_version: I added up the cost of the tickets.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Add up' needs numbers or amounts as the object.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on "add": ADD up, with a short, clear "a" sound.
spelling_tip: Two words; the noun "add-up" is not standard -- use "total" or "sum" instead.
etymology: "Add" (join together, from Latin "addere") + "up" (to a total/completion) -- to combine numbers into a complete sum.
prefix_root_suffix: add + up (phrasal particle -- no prefix/suffix breakdown)
mnemonic: When you ADD UP numbers, they build UP into one total.
memory_trick: ADD UP: stack the numbers UP into a total.
visual_association: A calculator screen showing numbers stacking into a final total.
emotion_feel: Neutral, sometimes suspicion (when things don't add up)
difference_explained: Add = put one thing to another. Add up = find the total of several numbers.
mini_conversation:
A: How much do we owe in total?
B: Wait, let me add up all the receipts.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A detective frowns at the paperwork and mutters, "Something about this story just doesn't add up."
news_style_line: News-style: "Analysts say the government's spending figures simply don't add up."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Can you add up how much we spent on groceries this month?"
mcq_options: A) To subtract numbers  B) To calculate a total, or to make sense  C) To forget something  D) To divide into parts
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Please ______ these expenses before we submit the report. → add up
find_and_fix_to_correct: The bill add up to fifty dollars. → The bill adds up to fifty dollars. (needs -s for third-person singular present)
translate: कृपया इन सभी खर्चों को जोड़ो। → Please add up all these expenses.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about adding up your monthly expenses.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to calculate the total of several numbers'?
usage_tip: 'It doesn't add up' = something seems wrong or illogical.

hindi_meaning: बदतमीज़ी करना, ख़राब व्यवहार करना (या मशीन का गड़बड़ करना)
simple_explanation: To behave badly, or for a machine to stop working properly. "Act up" is used informally when a child, pet, or machine starts causing trouble -- misbehaving or malfunctioning.
example_1: My computer keeps acting up today.
example_2: The kids started acting up during the long car ride.
example_3: My knee has been acting up since the cold weather started.
collocations: kids acting up, the computer is acting up, my back is acting up
related_phrasal_verbs: act out, play up, mess up
action_sequence: Before: the phone works fine → During: it starts freezing → After: it doesn't work properly
grammar_pattern: subject + act up (The car is acting up. / He always acts up in class.)
word_forms: act up – acted up – acted up – acting up
common_mistake: My computer act up since yesterday.
correct_version: My computer has been acting up since yesterday.
why_it_s_wrong: With 'since', use the present perfect continuous.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on "up": act UP, with a short, sharp "a" in "act."
spelling_tip: Two words; don't confuse with "act out" (which involves performing or expressing feelings dramatically).
etymology: "Act" (behave, from Latin "agere," to do) + "up" (intensifier indicating disruption) -- to behave in an unusually troublesome way.
prefix_root_suffix: act + up (phrasal particle -- no prefix/suffix breakdown)
mnemonic: When a child ACTS UP, their bad behavior flares UP suddenly.
memory_trick: ACT UP: a machine ACTS badly, UP to mischief.
visual_association: A toy robot suddenly moving erratically and sparking.
difference_explained: Act up = not work properly, on and off. Break down = stop working completely.
mini_conversation:
A: Why is the printer so slow?
B: It's been acting up all week -- I think it needs repairs.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A frustrated parent sighs, "The kids have been acting up all day -- I need a coffee."
news_style_line: News-style: "Passengers reported delays after the airline's booking system started acting up."
casual_conversation: Casual: "My old car's been acting up lately -- I think it needs a mechanic."
mcq_options: A) To behave perfectly  B) To behave badly or malfunction  C) To perform in a play  D) To repair something
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The washing machine has been ______ since last week. → acting up
find_and_fix_to_correct: The children was acting up in class. → The children were acting up in class. ("were," not "was," with the plural subject "children")
translate: मेरा कंप्यूटर आजकल गड़बड़ कर रहा है। → My computer has been acting up these days.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a device that has been acting up.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to behave badly, or for a machine to stop working properly'?
usage_tip: Used for children behaving badly and machines not working well.

hindi_meaning: अभिनय करके दिखाना, या भावनाओं को व्यवहार से जताना
simple_explanation: To show a story through actions, or to express feelings through behavior. "Act out" can mean performing a scene physically, like in a play, or -- especially for children -- showing difficult emotions through bad behavior instead of words.
example_1: The children acted out their favorite story.
example_2: The students acted out a scene from the play.
example_3: He tends to act out when he's stressed at work.
collocations: act out a scene, act out feelings, act out in class
related_phrasal_verbs: act up, play out, express oneself
action_sequence: Before: read a story → During: play the characters → After: the audience watches
grammar_pattern: act out + noun (act out a story) / act out (used alone for behavior: The kids acted out.)
word_forms: act out – acted out – acted out – acting out
common_mistake: He acts out his anger by shout loudly.
correct_version: He acts out his anger by shouting loudly.
why_it_s_wrong: After 'by', use the -ing form.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on "out": act OUT, with a clear diphthong sound.
spelling_tip: Two words; "acting-out" (with hyphen) is sometimes used as a noun/adjective in psychology.
etymology: "Act" (perform, behave) + "out" (outwardly, visibly) -- to physically show or perform something outwardly, or let inner feelings show through behavior.
prefix_root_suffix: act + out (phrasal particle -- no prefix/suffix breakdown)
mnemonic: When feelings can't come out in words, they ACT themselves OUT in behavior.
memory_trick: ACT OUT: ACT the story OUT in front of people.
visual_association: A child stomping their feet, unable to explain in words how they feel.
difference_explained: Act = perform, or behave. Act out = perform a story, or show feelings through behaviour.
mini_conversation:
A: Why is she acting out so much lately?
B: I think she's just struggling with the move to a new school.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A drama teacher claps and says, "Great, now let's act out the final scene together."
news_style_line: News-style: "Experts say children often act out when they're struggling to express difficult emotions."
casual_conversation: Casual: "He's been acting out a lot since his parents' divorce."
mcq_options: A) To stay completely silent  B) To perform or express something through behavior  C) To calculate a total  D) To repair a machine
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The students were asked to ______ a famous scene from history. → act out
find_and_fix_to_correct: The kid act out because he was tired. → The kid acted out because he was tired. (past tense needed)
translate: बच्चे थके होने पर अक्सर व्यवहार से गुस्सा दिखाते हैं। → Children often act out when they are tired.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a story your class acted out.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to show a story through actions, or to express feelings through behavior'?
usage_tip: 'Act out' also means show bad feelings through bad behaviour.

hindi_meaning: विस्फोट होना, फुलाना, या अचानक भड़क उठना (गुस्सा)
simple_explanation: To explode, or to suddenly become very angry. "Blow up" most often means something explodes with force, but it's also used informally when someone suddenly loses their temper.
example_1: The old building blew up in a controlled demolition.
example_2: The bomb blew up before the police could stop it.
example_3: He blew up at his coworker over a small mistake.
collocations: blow up a balloon, blow up at someone, blow up a building
action_sequence: Before: feel angry inside → During: the anger builds → After: shout suddenly
grammar_pattern: blow up (+ at + person) (The bomb blew up. / She blew up at him.)
word_forms: blow up – blew up – blown up – blowing up
common_mistake: He blow up when he heard the news.
correct_version: He blew up when he heard the news.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Blow' is irregular: blow – blew – blown.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on "up": blow UP, with a long "oh" sound in "blow."
spelling_tip: Two words as a verb; "blowup" is one word as a noun (a photo blowup, or an argument).
etymology: "Blow" (Old English "blawan," to expel air forcefully) + "up" (outward/upward burst) -- literally air or force bursting upward and outward.
prefix_root_suffix: blow + up (phrasal particle -- no prefix/suffix breakdown)
mnemonic: When something BLOWS UP, it bursts UP and outward with force.
memory_trick: BLOW → BLEW → BLOWN, like GROW → GREW → GROWN.
visual_association: A balloon suddenly popping with a loud bang.
difference_explained: Explode = burst violently. Blow up = explode, or become very angry, or fill with air.
mini_conversation:
A: Why did he leave the meeting so upset?
B: He blew up when they questioned his numbers.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character storms out shouting, "I can't believe you did this -- I'm about to blow up!"
news_style_line: News-style: "Officials confirmed the old bridge was safely blown up as part of the demolition project."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Don't tell him yet -- he'll totally blow up if he finds out."
mcq_options: A) To calm down slowly  B) To explode, or to suddenly get very angry  C) To fall asleep  D) To clean something
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: He tends to ______ whenever someone criticizes his work. → blow up
find_and_fix_to_correct: The balloon is blow up already. → The balloon is already blown up. (needs the past participle "blown," not the base form)
translate: वह छोटी सी बात पर अचानक भड़क उठा। → He blew up over a small thing.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a time someone blew up in anger.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to explode, or to suddenly become very angry'?
usage_tip: 'Blow up a balloon' = fill it with air. 'Blow up a photo' = enlarge it.

hindi_meaning: थककर चूर हो जाना, जल कर बुझ जाना
simple_explanation: To become extremely tired and stressed from working too hard. "Burn out" describes feeling completely exhausted -- physically and mentally -- usually from working too much for too long without rest.
example_1: She burned out after months of overtime.
example_2: Many nurses burned out during the busy winter season.
example_3: The light bulb burned out and needs replacing.
collocations: burn out from work, feel burned out, risk of burnout
related_phrasal_verbs: wear out, wind down, run down
action_sequence: Before: work too many hours → During: feel more tired each day → After: have no energy left
grammar_pattern: subject + burn out (She burned out. / The candle burned out.)
word_forms: burn out – burned/burnt out – burned/burnt out – burning out
common_mistake: I am burn out from working too much.
correct_version: I am burned out from working too much.
why_it_s_wrong: After 'am', use the adjective form 'burned out' / 'burnt out'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on "out": burn OUT, with a clear diphthong sound.
spelling_tip: Two words as a verb; "burnout" is one word as a noun ("she's suffering from burnout").
etymology: "Burn" (Old English "byrnan") + "out" (to the end, extinguished) -- literally a fire consuming all its fuel and going out, extended to a person exhausting all their energy.
prefix_root_suffix: burn + out (phrasal particle -- no prefix/suffix breakdown)
mnemonic: A candle BURNS OUT when it runs OUT of wax -- a person burns out when they run out of energy.
memory_trick: BURN OUT: a candle burns until it goes OUT.
visual_association: A candle flame flickering and finally going dark.
difference_explained: Tired = needs rest. Burned out = exhausted for a long time from stress and overwork.
mini_conversation:
A: You seem really tired lately.
B: I think I'm starting to burn out from all these late nights.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A tired employee slumps at their desk, whispering, "I can't keep going like this -- I'm completely burned out."
news_style_line: News-style: "A new study warns that teacher burnout is at an all-time high this year."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I need a real vacation -- I'm totally burned out."
mcq_options: A) To feel full of energy  B) To become extremely tired from too much work or stress  C) To finish a task quickly  D) To start a fire
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: After working three jobs, she finally ______ and had to take a break. → burned out
find_and_fix_to_correct: He is burn out because of stress. → He is burned out because of stress. (needs the past participle "burned")
translate: लगातार काम करने से वह पूरी तरह थक गई। → She completely burned out from working continuously.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about how to avoid burning out at work.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to become extremely tired and stressed from working too hard'?
usage_tip: 'Burnout' (noun) = exhaustion from overwork.

hindi_meaning: जलकर पूरी तरह नष्ट हो जाना
simple_explanation: For a building to be completely destroyed by fire. "Burn down" describes a fire destroying an entire building or structure, leaving nothing standing.
example_1: The old barn burned down last night.
example_2: The factory burned down after an electrical fault.
example_3: Firefighters couldn't stop the house from burning down.
collocations: burn down the house, burn down to the ground, completely burned down
related_phrasal_verbs: burn out, go up in flames, raze
where_it_s_used: Wildfires, accidents, historical disasters, insurance claims
action_sequence: Before: a fire starts → During: it spreads through the house → After: only ashes remain
grammar_pattern: subject + burn down (The house burned down.) / burn + object + down (Fire burned the house down.)
word_forms: burn down – burned/burnt down – burned/burnt down – burning down
common_mistake: The house was burn down by the fire.
correct_version: The house was burned down by the fire.
why_it_s_wrong: After 'was', use the past participle 'burned'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on "down": burn DOWN, with emphasis showing total destruction.
spelling_tip: Two words; not to be confused with "burn out" (exhaustion or a fire going out).
etymology: "Burn" (consume by fire) + "down" (to the ground, completely) -- literally a structure collapsing into ashes from fire.
prefix_root_suffix: burn + down (phrasal particle -- no prefix/suffix breakdown)
mnemonic: A house BURNS DOWN when the fire brings it all the way DOWN to the ground.
memory_trick: BURN DOWN: the building falls DOWN in fire.
visual_association: A wooden house collapsing into glowing embers and ash.
difference_explained: Burn = be on fire, or damage by fire. Burn down = destroy a whole building by fire.
mini_conversation:
A: What happened to the old mill?
B: It burned down years ago -- lightning strike, I heard.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A firefighter looks at the smoking ruins and says quietly, "There was nothing we could do -- it burned down too fast."
news_style_line: News-style: "Officials say the warehouse burned down within hours due to strong winds."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Did you hear the old restaurant on Main Street burned down?"
mcq_options: A) To repaint a building  B) For a building to be destroyed completely by fire  C) To feel exhausted  D) To turn off a light
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The entire village nearly ______ during the wildfire. → burned down
find_and_fix_to_correct: The building is burn down completely. → The building has burned down completely. (needs present perfect with the past participle)
