usage_tip: Used for whole buildings, not small objects.

simple_explanation: To become completely dry after being wet. "Dry out" means something that was wet -- like clothes, soil, or wood -- loses all its moisture and becomes fully dry.
example_1: Hang your shoes up to dry out.
example_2: The clothes dried out quickly in the sun.
example_3: The soil dried out during the long summer.
collocations: dry out in the sun, dry out completely, let it dry out
related_phrasal_verbs: dry up, dry off, air out
where_it_s_used: Laundry, weather, gardening, recovery from addiction (informal)
action_sequence: Before: clothes are wet → During: hang them in the sun → After: they are completely dry
grammar_pattern: subject + dry out (The towel dried out. / Let the paint dry out.)
word_forms: dry out – dried out – dried out – drying out
common_mistake: The clothes dry out on the sun.
correct_version: The clothes dry out in the sun.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'in the sun', not 'on the sun'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on "out": dry OUT, with a clear diphthong.
spelling_tip: Two words; note the "y" changes to "i" in some related forms (dries, dried) but stays "y" here.
etymology: "Dry" (Old English "dryge") + "out" (to completion) -- to lose all moisture completely.
prefix_root_suffix: dry + out (phrasal particle -- no prefix/suffix breakdown)
mnemonic: When wet clothes DRY OUT, all the water goes OUT of them.
memory_trick: DRY OUT: the water goes OUT of the cloth.
visual_association: A wet towel on a clothesline slowly turning stiff and dry in the sun.
difference_explained: Dry out = become completely dry (clothes, skin). Dry up = a source runs out (a river, money).
mini_conversation:
A: Is the paint ready yet?
B: Not yet, it needs another hour to dry out completely.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A hiker spreads out a soaked jacket and says, "It'll dry out by morning if the wind keeps up."
news_style_line: News-style: "Farmers are worried as fields continue to dry out under the ongoing drought."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Leave the umbrella open so it can dry out before we put it away."
mcq_options: A) To become completely wet  B) To become completely dry  C) To break apart  D) To grow bigger
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Hang the wet towels outside so they can ______. → dry out
find_and_fix_to_correct: The paint will dry out in few minute. → The paint will dry out in a few minutes. (needs "a" before "few" and plural "minutes")
translate: बारिश के बाद कपड़े धूप में सूख गए। → The clothes dried out in the sun after the rain.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about how clothes dry out in the monsoon.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to become completely dry after being wet'?
usage_tip: Also used for skin, bread and soil: 'Don't let the soil dry out.'

hindi_meaning: पूरी तरह सूख जाना (नदी, स्रोत आदि का)
simple_explanation: For a source of water or resources to run out completely. "Dry up" means a river, well, or supply of something (like money or jobs) gradually disappears until there's nothing left.
example_1: The river dried up during the drought.
example_2: The well dried up after years of little rainfall.
example_3: Funding for the project dried up last year.
collocations: the river dried up, funding dried up, the well dried up
action_sequence: Before: a river flows → During: no rain for months → After: the riverbed is empty
grammar_pattern: subject + dry up (The lake dried up. / Sales dried up.)
word_forms: dry up – dried up – dried up – drying up
common_mistake: The funding is dry up since last year.
correct_version: The funding dried up last year.
why_it_s_wrong: A finished past event needs the simple past: 'dried up'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on "up": dry UP, with a short, clipped "u" sound.
spelling_tip: Two words; don't confuse with "dry out" (losing surface moisture, not a total source disappearing).
etymology: "Dry" (without moisture) + "up" (completely, to the end) -- to gradually lose all liquid until nothing remains.
prefix_root_suffix: dry + up (phrasal particle -- no prefix/suffix breakdown)
mnemonic: A river DRIES UP when its water disappears, UP and gone for good.
memory_trick: DRY UP: a river's water goes UP into the sky.
visual_association: A once-flowing riverbed now cracked and completely empty.
difference_explained: Dry up = a supply disappears. Dry out = something wet becomes dry.
mini_conversation:
A: Why did the company stop hiring?
B: I heard their funding dried up completely.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A farmer stares at the cracked earth and says, "The well's dried up -- we need rain, and soon."
news_style_line: News-style: "Several rivers in the region have dried up completely after months without rain."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Freelance work has really dried up for me this quarter."
mcq_options: A) To overflow with water  B) For a source of water or resources to run out completely  C) To become wetter  D) To grow larger
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The small pond ______ completely during the hot summer. → dried up
find_and_fix_to_correct: The lake has dry up this year. → The lake has dried up this year. (needs the past participle "dried" after "has")
translate: सूखे की वजह से कुआँ पूरी तरह सूख गया। → The well completely dried up because of the drought.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a river or pond that dried up.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'for a source of water or resources to run out completely'?
usage_tip: 'My ideas dried up' = I had no more ideas.

hindi_meaning: जम जाना, या डर से जड़ हो जाना, या रुक जाना (मशीन का)
simple_explanation: To become completely frozen, or to be unable to act because of fear or shock. "Freeze up" can mean water turning solid in the cold, but it's also used when a person is so nervous or scared that they can't move, speak, or think, or when a computer suddenly stops responding.
example_1: The pipes froze up in the cold weather.
example_2: The water pipes froze up overnight and burst.
example_3: She froze up during her speech and forgot her lines.
collocations: freeze up on stage, pipes freeze up, the screen froze up
related_phrasal_verbs: freeze over, seize up, lock up
where_it_s_used: Weather, public speaking, technology problems, fear responses
action_sequence: Before: stand in front of people → During: feel nervous → After: can't speak or move
grammar_pattern: subject + freeze up (The pipes froze up. / He froze up.)
word_forms: freeze up – froze up – frozen up – freezing up
common_mistake: My computer freeze up every day.
correct_version: My computer freezes up every day.
why_it_s_wrong: He/she/it in the simple present needs -s: freezes up.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on "freeze": FREEZE up, with a long "ee" sound.
spelling_tip: Two words; note the double "e" in "freeze," different from "frozen" (past participle).
etymology: "Freeze" (Old English "freosan," to turn to ice) + "up" (completely) -- literally to turn completely solid with cold, extended figuratively to becoming mentally or mechanically stuck.
prefix_root_suffix: freeze + up (phrasal particle -- no prefix/suffix breakdown)
mnemonic: When you FREEZE UP on stage, your whole body feels like it's turned to ice, UP and stuck.
memory_trick: FREEZE → FROZE → FROZEN, like CHOOSE → CHOSE → CHOSEN.
visual_association: A person standing perfectly still, wide-eyed, like a statue made of ice.
difference_explained: Both describe a computer that stops. Freeze up is also used for people too nervous to act.
mini_conversation:
A: How did the interview go?
B: Honestly, I froze up when they asked about my weaknesses.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A nervous actor stands under the bright lights and completely freezes up, unable to say a single word.
news_style_line: News-style: "Several homes reported burst pipes after they froze up during the cold snap."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I totally froze up when she asked me that question in front of everyone."
mcq_options: A) To relax completely  B) To become unable to move, speak, or act, often from fear  C) To celebrate loudly  D) To finish quickly
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: He completely ______ when the teacher called on him unexpectedly. → froze up
find_and_fix_to_correct: The pipe was freeze up last winter. → The pipe froze up last winter. (needs simple past "froze," not "was freeze")
translate: सर्दी में पाइप जम गया। → The pipe froze up in the cold weather.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a time you froze up in front of people.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to become completely frozen, or to be unable to act because of fear or shock'?
usage_tip: 'I froze up in the interview' = I couldn't speak from nerves.

simple_explanation: To make something warmer or hotter, or to become more intense. "Heat up" usually means warming food or a place, but it can also describe a situation, competition, or argument becoming more intense.
example_1: Let me heat up the soup for you.
example_2: She heated up leftovers for dinner.
example_3: The competition really heated up in the final round.
collocations: heat up leftovers, heat up the oven, the debate heats up
related_phrasal_verbs: warm up, cool down, boil over
action_sequence: Before: the food is cold → During: put it in the microwave → After: it's hot
grammar_pattern: heat up + noun (heat up the food) / subject + heat up (The debate heated up.)
word_forms: heat up – heated up – heated up – heating up
common_mistake: I heat up the food in five minutes ago.
correct_version: I heated up the food five minutes ago.
why_it_s_wrong: A past time needs 'heated', and 'ago' doesn't take 'in'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on "heat": HEAT up, with a long "ee" sound.
spelling_tip: Two words; "heat-up" is not commonly used as a noun.
etymology: "Heat" (Old English "haetu," warmth) + "up" (increase) -- to increase temperature.
prefix_root_suffix: heat + up (phrasal particle -- no prefix/suffix breakdown)
mnemonic: When you HEAT something UP, its temperature goes UP.
memory_trick: HEAT UP: the temperature goes UP.
visual_association: A pot on a stove slowly starting to bubble and steam.
difference_explained: Heat up = make hot. Warm up = make a little warm, or prepare for exercise.
mini_conversation:
A: Are you hungry?
B: Yeah, let me heat up some leftovers.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A commentator shouts excitedly, "This match is really heating up in the final minutes!"
news_style_line: News-style: "Tensions have heated up between the two nations following the latest trade dispute."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Can you heat up the pizza from last night?"
mcq_options: A) To make something colder  B) To make something warmer, or become more intense  C) To repair something  D) To finish eating
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Can you ______ the leftover rice for lunch? → heat up
find_and_fix_to_correct: She heat up the milk for baby. → She heated up the milk for the baby. (past tense needed, plus "the" before "baby")
translate: कृपया रात के बचे हुए खाने को गर्म कर दो। → Please heat up the leftover food from last night.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about how you heat up leftover food.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to make something warmer or hotter, or to become more intense'?
usage_tip: 'The debate heated up' = it became more intense.

simple_explanation: To become less hot, or to become calmer after being upset. "Cool down" means something becomes less hot in temperature, or a person becomes calmer after being angry or excited.
example_1: Let the tea cool down before you drink it.
example_2: The engine needs time to cool down after the race.
example_3: Take a walk to cool down after the argument.
collocations: cool down after exercise, let it cool down, cool down a bit
related_phrasal_verbs: calm down, chill out, heat up
action_sequence: Before: feel hot or angry → During: rest and breathe → After: feel calm
grammar_pattern: subject + cool down (The soup cooled down. / He cooled down after a walk.)
word_forms: cool down – cooled down – cooled down – cooling down
common_mistake: I need to cool down of my anger.
correct_version: I need to cool down.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Cool down' needs no object here, and 'of' is wrong.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on "cool": COOL down, with a long "oo" sound.
spelling_tip: Two words; "cooldown" is one word only as a noun (a post-exercise cooldown).
etymology: "Cool" (Old English "col," moderately cold) + "down" (decrease) -- to decrease in temperature or intensity.
prefix_root_suffix: cool + down (phrasal particle -- no prefix/suffix breakdown)
mnemonic: When you COOL DOWN after exercise, your body temperature comes back DOWN.
memory_trick: COOL DOWN: the temperature — or temper — goes DOWN.
visual_association: Steam rising from a hot cup of tea, slowly fading as it cools.
difference_explained: Calm down = stop being upset. Cool down = become less hot, or less angry.
mini_conversation:
A: You seem really upset.
B: I am, but I just need a few minutes to cool down.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A coach tells the angry player, "Take a seat and cool down before you say something you regret."
news_style_line: News-style: "Temperatures are expected to cool down significantly by the weekend."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Let's just cool down and talk about this calmly."
mcq_options: A) To become hotter  B) To become less hot, or calmer  C) To start an argument  D) To speed up
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Let the engine ______ before you check the oil. → cool down
find_and_fix_to_correct: Please cool down you before talking. → Please cool down before talking. (remove "you" -- cool down doesn't take an object here)
translate: बहस के बाद उसे शांत होने में समय लगा। → It took him time to cool down after the argument.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about what you do to cool down after an argument.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to become less hot, or to become calmer after being upset'?
usage_tip: After exercise, 'cool down' = stretch slowly to relax your muscles.

simple_explanation: To relax and stop worrying (informal). "Chill out" is a casual way of telling someone to relax, calm down, or stop stressing about something.
example_1: Just chill out, everything will be fine.
example_2: We chilled out at home all weekend.
example_3: Chill out, it's not a big deal.
collocations: chill out at home, just chill out, chill out for a while
where_it_s_used: Casual conversation, friends, weekends, calming someone down
action_sequence: Before: feel stressed → During: relax with friends or music → After: feel easy
grammar_pattern: chill out (intransitive, informal) (Let's chill out this weekend.)
word_forms: chill out – chilled out – chilled out – chilling out
common_mistake: Please chill out yourself before the interview.
correct_version: Please chill out before the interview.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Chill out' needs no 'yourself'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on "chill": CHILL out, with a short, crisp "i" sound.
spelling_tip: Two words; very informal -- avoid in essays or professional emails.
etymology: "Chill" (cold, informally extended to "relaxed") + "out" (intensifier) -- slang originating in relaxed, casual American English, likening a calm mood to a cool temperature.
prefix_root_suffix: chill + out (phrasal particle -- no prefix/suffix breakdown)
mnemonic: CHILL OUT means cool your mood OUT, like chilling a drink.
memory_trick: CHILL OUT: let the heat of stress OUT and feel chilled.
visual_association: Someone lying back in a hammock with sunglasses on, completely relaxed.
difference_explained: Same meaning. Chill out is informal slang.
mini_conversation:
A: I'm so stressed about the exam!
B: Chill out, you've studied so much already.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A friend flops onto the couch and says, "Let's just chill out and watch a movie tonight."
news_style_line: News-style: "Wellness experts recommend that people chill out and reduce screen time to lower stress levels."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Chill out, dude, we still have plenty of time before the flight."
mcq_options: A) To get angry  B) To relax and calm down (informal)  C) To work harder  D) To argue loudly
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: After a long week, all I want to do is ______ at home. → chill out
find_and_fix_to_correct: She needs to chill out from the stress herself. → She needs to chill out because of the stress. (remove "herself," fix preposition to "because of")
translate: चिंता मत करो, थोड़ा आराम करो। → Don't worry, just chill out for a bit.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a casual sentence about how you chill out on Sundays.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to relax and stop worrying (informal)'?
usage_tip: Informal only — avoid it in formal emails.

hindi_meaning: लॉग इन करना, खाते में प्रवेश करना
simple_explanation: To enter your username and password to access an account or system. "Log in" means typing your details to open an app, website, or computer account so you can use it.
example_1: Please log in to check your messages.
example_2: I forgot my password and couldn't log in.
example_3: You need to log in before you can post a comment.
collocations: log in to an account, log in with a password, forget to log in
related_phrasal_verbs: log out, sign in, sign up
action_sequence: Before: open the website → During: type your username and password → After: your account opens
grammar_pattern: log in (+ to + noun) (Log in to your account.)
word_forms: log in – logged in – logged in – logging in
common_mistake: I logged in my account this morning.
correct_version: I logged in to my account this morning.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'log in TO' + the account or site. 'Log into' is also used.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on "log": LOG in, with a short "o" sound.
spelling_tip: Two words as a verb ("log in to your account"); one word "login" only as a noun/adjective.
etymology: "Log" (a record, from ships' logbooks) + "in" (entering) -- originally naval/technical jargon for recording entry into a system, now standard in computing.
prefix_root_suffix: log + in (phrasal particle -- no prefix/suffix breakdown)
mnemonic: You LOG IN the way a sailor logs entries IN a logbook -- recording your entry into the system.
memory_trick: LOG IN: your name goes IN to the system's log book.
visual_association: A finger typing a password into a glowing login screen.
difference_explained: Same meaning. Sign in is often used on consumer apps.
mini_conversation:
A: I can't see my emails.
B: Did you log in with the right password?
everyday_scene: Everyday: A hacker types quickly and mutters, "I just need to log in before the system locks me out."
news_style_line: News-style: "Users were unable to log in to the app for several hours during the outage."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Can you log in and check if the payment went through?"
mcq_options: A) To leave a website  B) To enter an account using a username and password  C) To delete a file  D) To create a new password
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: You need to ______ before you can view your account details. → log in
find_and_fix_to_correct: Please log in on your account to continue. → Please log in to your account to continue. (needs "to," not "on")
translate: कृपया जारी रखने के लिए अपने खाते में लॉग इन करें। → Please log in to your account to continue.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about which app you log in to every day.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to enter your username and password to access an account or system'?
usage_tip: 'Login' (one word) is the noun: 'your login details'.

hindi_meaning: लॉग आउट करना, खाते से बाहर निकलना
simple_explanation: To exit or leave a computer account or system safely. "Log out" means closing your session in an app or website so no one else can use your account after you.
example_1: Don't forget to log out when you're done.
example_2: He logged out before leaving the library computer.
example_3: Remember to log out of your email on shared devices.
collocations: log out of an account, forget to log out, automatically log out
related_phrasal_verbs: log in, sign out, sign off
action_sequence: Before: finish your work → During: click Log out → After: the account closes
grammar_pattern: log out (+ of + noun) (Log out of your account before leaving.)
word_forms: log out – logged out – logged out – logging out
common_mistake: I forgot log out from my email.
correct_version: I forgot to log out of my email.
why_it_s_wrong: After 'forgot', use 'to' + verb; and 'log out OF', not 'from'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on "log": LOG out, with a clear diphthong in "out."
spelling_tip: Two words as a verb; "logout" is one word as a noun/adjective (a logout button).
etymology: "Log" (record) + "out" (exiting) -- the counterpart to "log in," recording your exit from a system.
prefix_root_suffix: log + out (phrasal particle -- no prefix/suffix breakdown)
mnemonic: LOG OUT is the opposite of LOG IN -- you record your exit OUT of the system.
memory_trick: LOG OUT: your name goes OUT of the system.
visual_association: A cursor clicking a red "Log Out" button on a screen.
difference_explained: Same meaning. Log off is slightly older.
mini_conversation:
A: I'm leaving the library now.
B: Wait, did you log out of the computer?
everyday_scene: Everyday: An IT worker warns, "Always log out when you leave -- we don't want anyone accessing your files."
news_style_line: News-style: "The bank advised customers to log out after every session to prevent unauthorized access."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Did you log out of the shared computer before you left?"
mcq_options: A) To create a new account  B) To exit a computer account or system  C) To change your password  D) To restart a device
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Always ______ of your account when using a public computer. → log out
find_and_fix_to_correct: She log out from the system before lunch. → She logs out of the system before lunch. (needs -s for present tense, and "of," not "from")
translate: कृपया काम खत्म होने के बाद लॉग आउट करना न भूलें। → Please don't forget to log out after you finish work.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence reminding someone to log out of a shared computer.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to exit or leave a computer account or system safely'?
usage_tip: Always log out on shared computers to keep accounts safe.

simple_explanation: To register or enroll for a class, service, or event. "Sign up" means officially registering to join something -- a course, a gym, a newsletter, or an event.
example_1: I signed up for a yoga class.
example_2: She signed up for the marathon last week.
example_3: You can sign up online in just a few minutes.
collocations: sign up for a class, sign up online, sign up early
related_phrasal_verbs: enroll in, register for, join up
action_sequence: Before: see a new course → During: fill in your details → After: you are registered
grammar_pattern: sign up + for + noun (sign up for a course)
word_forms: sign up – signed up – signed up – signing up
common_mistake: I signed up to the gym membership.
correct_version: I signed up for the gym membership.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'sign up FOR' something, not 'to'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on "up": sign UP, with a long "i" sound in "sign."
spelling_tip: Two words as a verb; "sign-up" (with hyphen) is the noun/adjective form (a sign-up sheet).
etymology: "Sign" (to write one's name, from Latin "signum," mark) + "up" (completion of registration) -- literally to write your name to formally join something.
prefix_root_suffix: sign + up (phrasal particle -- no prefix/suffix breakdown)
mnemonic: You SIGN your name to move UP onto the list of participants.
memory_trick: SIGN UP: put your SIGNature UP on the list.
visual_association: A hand holding a pen above a clipboard, adding one more tick to a short list.
difference_explained: Sign up = create a new account or register. Sign in = enter an account you already have.
mini_conversation:
A: Have you signed up for the workshop yet?
B: Not yet, but I plan to sign up today.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A volunteer coordinator announces, "If you'd like to help, just sign up at the table by the door."
news_style_line: News-style: "Thousands of people signed up for the free vaccination program within the first week."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I just signed up for a cooking class starting next month."
mcq_options: A) To cancel a membership  B) To register or enroll for something  C) To log out of an account  D) To write a letter
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: You can ______ for the newsletter on our website. → sign up
find_and_fix_to_correct: She sign up for the course last week. → She signed up for the course last week. (past tense needed)
translate: मैंने पिछले हफ्ते डांस क्लास के लिए पंजीकरण कराया। → I signed up for a dance class last week.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a course or service you signed up for.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to register or enroll for a class, service, or event'?
usage_tip: 'Sign up' (register) vs 'sign in' (enter an account you already have).

hindi_meaning: भाग न लेने का विकल्प चुनना, अलग हट जाना
simple_explanation: To choose not to take part in something. "Opt out" means actively deciding not to participate in a program, service, or agreement that you could have joined.
example_1: You can opt out of the newsletter anytime.
example_2: She opted out of the company's retirement plan.
example_3: You can opt out of data sharing in the settings.
collocations: opt out of a program, opt out of emails, opt-out option
related_phrasal_verbs: drop out, back out, pull out
where_it_s_used: Privacy settings, subscriptions, insurance, school programs
action_sequence: Before: get added to a list → During: click Unsubscribe → After: you're no longer included
grammar_pattern: opt out + of + noun (opt out of the survey)
word_forms: opt out – opted out – opted out – opting out
common_mistake: I want to opt out from this service.
correct_version: I want to opt out of this service.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'opt out OF', not 'from'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on "opt": OPT out, with a short "o" sound.
spelling_tip: Two words; "opt-out" (hyphenated) is the noun/adjective form (an opt-out option).
etymology: "Opt" (choose, from Latin "optare," to wish/choose) + "out" (away from participation) -- to actively choose to remove yourself from something.
prefix_root_suffix: opt + out (phrasal particle -- no prefix/suffix breakdown)
mnemonic: To OPT OUT, you make a choice (OPT) to step OUT of something.
memory_trick: OPT OUT: choose ('opt') to stay OUT.
visual_association: A checkbox being unchecked to remove oneself from a list.
difference_explained: Opt in = choose to join. Opt out = choose not to join, or to leave.
mini_conversation:
A: Are you doing the extra training session?
B: No, I decided to opt out this time.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character reviews a contract and says, "I'd like to opt out of this clause before I sign."
news_style_line: News-style: "New privacy laws let users opt out of having their data sold to advertisers."
casual_conversation: Casual: "You can opt out of the group chat anytime if it's too much."
mcq_options: A) To agree to join something  B) To choose not to participate in something  C) To finish an activity early  D) To repeat a task
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Employees can ______ of the optional overtime shifts. → opt out
find_and_fix_to_correct: She opt out the meeting yesterday. → She opted out of the meeting yesterday. (needs past tense "opted" and "of" before the noun)
translate: आप कभी भी न्यूज़लेटर से अलग हट सकते हैं। → You can opt out of the newsletter anytime.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a service or email list you opted out of.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to choose not to take part in something'?
usage_tip: Emails and apps: 'You can opt out at any time.'

hindi_meaning: पढ़ाई या कार्यक्रम बीच में छोड़ देना
simple_explanation: To leave school, a course, or an activity before finishing. "Drop out" means to stop attending or participating in something -- like school or a race -- before it's completed.
example_1: He dropped out of college in his second year.
example_2: She dropped out of the marathon due to an injury.
example_3: Many students drop out because of financial problems.
collocations: drop out of school, drop out of college, drop out of a race
related_phrasal_verbs: opt out, back out, give up
action_sequence: Before: join a course → During: stop attending → After: leave without finishing
grammar_pattern: drop out + of + noun (drop out of school)
word_forms: drop out – dropped out – dropped out – dropping out
common_mistake: He drop out from school last year.
correct_version: He dropped out of school last year.
why_it_s_wrong: Use the past 'dropped' and 'drop out OF', not 'from'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on "out": drop OUT, with a clear diphthong.
spelling_tip: Two words as a verb; "dropout" is one word as a noun (a high school dropout).
etymology: "Drop" (fall, let go) + "out" (away from, exiting) -- literally to fall away from a group or activity before completion.
prefix_root_suffix: drop + out (phrasal particle -- no prefix/suffix breakdown)
mnemonic: When you DROP OUT, you fall OUT of the race before the finish line.
memory_trick: DROP OUT: fall OUT of the race before the finish line.
visual_association: A runner stepping off the track mid-race while others continue on.
emotion_feel: Disappointment, sometimes determination (if it leads to something new)
difference_explained: Quit = stop doing anything. Drop out = leave school or a course before finishing.
mini_conversation:
A: Is your brother still in university?
B: No, he dropped out last semester to start a business.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A young entrepreneur explains, "I dropped out of college to chase this idea, and I've never looked back."
news_style_line: News-style: "The report found that dropout rates increased sharply during the economic downturn."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I almost dropped out of the course, but my friends convinced me to stay."
mcq_options: A) To finish something successfully  B) To leave school, a course, or activity before finishing  C) To win a competition  D) To join a new group
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Financial trouble forced him to ______ of school early. → drop out
find_and_fix_to_correct: She dropped out school because of illness. → She dropped out of school because of illness. (needs "of" before "school")
translate: उसने पैसों की तंगी के कारण कॉलेज बीच में छोड़ दिया। → He dropped out of college because of money problems.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a neutral sentence about why some students drop out of school.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to leave school, a course, or an activity before finishing'?
usage_tip: 'Dropout' (noun) = a student who left before finishing.

hindi_meaning: रुको, थोड़ा इंतज़ार करो, या मज़बूती से पकड़े रहना
simple_explanation: To wait for a short time, or to grip something firmly. "Hold on" is often used to ask someone to wait a moment, but it can also mean physically gripping something tightly or continuing to persevere through a hard situation.
example_1: Hold on, I'll be right there.
example_2: Hold on a second, let me grab my keys.
example_3: She held on tightly to the railing during the storm.
collocations: hold on a second, hold on tight, hold on to hope
related_phrasal_verbs: hold up, hang on, wait up
where_it_s_used: Phone calls, waiting, safety instructions, perseverance
action_sequence: Before: someone calls you → During: ask them to wait → After: come back to the call
grammar_pattern: hold on (+ to + noun) (Hold on a moment. / Hold on to the rail.)
word_forms: hold on – held on – held on – holding on
common_mistake: Hold on, I am coming after five minute.
correct_version: Hold on, I'll be there in five minutes.
why_it_s_wrong: 'In five minutes' = after five minutes from now; 'minute' needs -s.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on "hold": HOLD on, often said quickly in casual speech.
spelling_tip: Two words; often used as a short command -- "Hold on!"
etymology: "Hold" (Old English "healdan," to grasp) + "on" (continuing) -- literally to keep gripping something, extended to waiting or persisting.
prefix_root_suffix: hold + on (phrasal particle -- no prefix/suffix breakdown)
mnemonic: When someone says HOLD ON, they want you to hold your position and wait ON the spot.
memory_trick: HOLD ON: HOLD the phone line ON — don't hang up.
visual_association: A hand gripping tightly onto a rope during a storm.
difference_explained: Same meaning. Hold on is informal and common on the phone.
mini_conversation:
A: Can I talk to you for a second?
B: Hold on, I'm just finishing this email.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character grips the rope tightly, shouting, "Hold on! Don't let go, no matter what!"
news_style_line: News-style: "Rescuers urged the stranded hikers to hold on as help was on the way."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Hold on a second, I need to grab my jacket before we leave."
mcq_options: A) To let go immediately  B) To wait a moment, or grip something firmly  C) To finish quickly  D) To argue with someone
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: ______ a moment, I'll check if he's available. → Hold on
find_and_fix_to_correct: Hold on please, I calling you back. → Hold on please, I'll call you back. (needs "I'll" before the verb)
translate: कृपया थोड़ा रुको, मैं अभी आता हूँ। → Please hold on, I'm coming right now.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence asking someone to hold on while you check something.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to wait for a short time, or to grip something firmly'?
usage_tip: 'Hold on tight!' = grip firmly.

simple_explanation: To delay someone or something, or to physically support something. "Hold up" usually means causing a delay -- traffic, a meeting, or a person can hold you up and make you late.
example_1: Sorry I'm late, traffic held me up.
example_2: The meeting was held up by a technical problem.
example_3: Sorry, I got held up at work.
collocations: hold up traffic, get held up, hold up the roof
action_sequence: Before: leave on time → During: get stuck in traffic → After: arrive late
grammar_pattern: hold + object + up (Traffic held me up.) / be held up (I was held up at the airport.)
word_forms: hold up – held up – held up – holding up
common_mistake: I was hold up by the traffic.
correct_version: I was held up by the traffic.
why_it_s_wrong: After 'was', use the past participle 'held'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on "up": hold UP, with clear emphasis on completion of the delay.
spelling_tip: Two words as a verb; "hold-up" (hyphenated) is the noun form (a traffic hold-up, or a robbery).
etymology: "Hold" (grasp, keep) + "up" (in place, preventing progress) -- literally to hold something in a raised or stopped position, extended to causing delay.
prefix_root_suffix: hold + up (phrasal particle -- no prefix/suffix breakdown)
mnemonic: When traffic HOLDS you UP, it keeps you stuck, unable to move forward.
memory_trick: HOLD → HELD, like the traffic HELD you UP.
visual_association: A long line of cars stuck behind a stalled truck on the highway.
difference_explained: Same meaning. Hold up is informal; delay is neutral.
mini_conversation:
A: Why are you so late?
B: Sorry, I got held up in a really long meeting.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A witness tells the police, "I don't know what happened -- I just saw them hold up the store and run."
news_style_line: News-style: "Flights were held up for hours due to the severe storm."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Sorry I'm late, I got held up on a call with a client."
mcq_options: A) To finish something early  B) To delay someone or something  C) To celebrate an achievement  D) To agree with someone
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: We got ______ at the airport because of extra security checks. → held up
find_and_fix_to_correct: The traffic hold up us for two hours. → The traffic held us up for two hours. (needs past tense "held" and correct word order)
translate: ट्रैफ़िक की वजह से मुझे देर हो गई। → I was held up because of the traffic.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something that held you up this morning.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to delay someone or something, or to physically support something'?
usage_tip: 'Hold up' also means rob with a weapon: 'a bank hold-up'.

simple_explanation: To stop yourself, someone, or something from moving forward or being expressed. "Hold back" means restraining something -- like your emotions, a crowd, or your own opinion -- instead of letting it out freely.
example_1: She tried to hold back her tears.
example_2: Police held back the crowd during the protest.
example_3: He held back his true feelings during the meeting.
collocations: hold back tears, hold back the crowd, hold back feelings
related_phrasal_verbs: hold on, hold up, keep in
where_it_s_used: Emotions, crowd control, personal growth, hesitation
action_sequence: Before: feel strong emotion → During: stop yourself from showing it → After: stay calm outside
grammar_pattern: hold back + noun (hold back tears) / hold + person + back (Fear held her back.)
word_forms: hold back – held back – held back – holding back
common_mistake: She hold back her tears during the speech.
correct_version: She held back her tears during the speech.
why_it_s_wrong: 'During the speech' is past, so use 'held'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on "back": hold BACK, with a strong "a" sound.
spelling_tip: Two words; note "holdback" (one word) exists as a rare financial/technical noun.
etymology: "Hold" (grasp, restrain) + "back" (in a restrained position, not forward) -- literally to physically keep something from moving forward.
prefix_root_suffix: hold + back (phrasal particle -- no prefix/suffix breakdown)
mnemonic: When you HOLD BACK your tears, you pull your emotions BACK instead of letting them out.
memory_trick: HOLD BACK: HOLD your tears BACK inside.
visual_association: A dam straining to hold back a rush of water.
difference_explained: Hide = keep out of sight. Hold back = stop yourself from showing or doing something.
mini_conversation:
A: You seem upset -- what's wrong?
B: Nothing, I'm just trying to hold back my emotions right now.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A soldier grips the barrier, shouting to the crowd, "Hold back! It's not safe to go any closer!"
news_style_line: News-style: "Officials say outdated regulations are holding back innovation in the industry."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I could barely hold back my laughter during the meeting."
mcq_options: A) To freely express something  B) To restrain or prevent something from moving forward  C) To celebrate loudly  D) To finish a task
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: He struggled to ______ his anger during the argument. → hold back
find_and_fix_to_correct: Don't hold back your opinion, tell it me. → Don't hold back your opinion, tell me. (fix word order: "tell me," not "tell it me")
translate: उसने अपने आंसुओं को रोकने की कोशिश की। → She tried to hold back her tears.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a time you held back your feelings.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to stop yourself, someone, or something from moving forward or being expressed'?
usage_tip: 'Don't hold back' = say or do everything; don't be shy.

simple_explanation: Needing a lot of effort or skill; not easy. When a task takes real effort, patience, or skill to complete, it's difficult.
example_2: Learning a new language can be difficult at first.
example_3: It was a difficult decision to make.
collocations: extremely difficult, difficult situation, find it difficult, difficult to explain
grammar_pattern: difficult + to-infinitive (difficult to understand) / find + something + difficult (I find math difficult).
common_mistake: This is a difficult for me.
correct_version: This is difficult for me.
why_it_s_wrong: 'A' needs a noun after it. With only an adjective, drop 'a': 'This is difficult.'
pronunciation_tip: Four syllables, but the middle two are quick and light.
spelling_tip: "Dif-fi-cult" — only one F pair, in the middle.
etymology: Latin "difficilis" (dis- = not + facilis = easy) — literally "not easy."
mnemonic: DIFFICULT starts with "DIF-" like "DIFFERENT" — a difficult task is different from an easy one.
memory_trick: DIF-FI-CULT: three hard syllables for a hard word.
visual_association: A steep, rocky mountain trail.
difference_explained: Same meaning for tasks. Hard is more common in speech; hard also means firm to touch.
mini_conversation:
A: How was the test?
B: Honestly, it was really difficult.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A coach tells the team, “This next match is going to be difficult — give it everything.”
news_style_line: News-style: “Economists warn the coming months will be difficult for small businesses.”
casual_conversation: Casual: “Honestly, this project has been more difficult than I expected.”
mcq_options: A) Easy  B) Different  C) Distant  D) Diligent
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Finding a job right now is quite ______. → difficult
find_and_fix_to_correct: This is very difficult exam. → This is a very difficult exam.
translate: यह सवाल बहुत मुश्किल है। → This question is very difficult.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about the most difficult subject for you.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'needing a lot of effort or skill; not easy'?
usage_tip: 'Difficult' is more formal than 'hard'. 'A difficult person' = someone hard to deal with.

simple_explanation: Giving a pleasant feeling of physical ease, or feeling relaxed. When something feels physically pleasant, or you feel relaxed and at ease, it's comfortable.
example_2: These shoes are so comfortable I could wear them all day.
example_3: I feel comfortable talking to her about anything.
collocations: comfortable with, comfortable silence, feel comfortable, comfortable temperature
grammar_pattern: comfortable + with + noun (comfortable with the plan) / feel comfortable + -ing (feel comfortable speaking up).
common_mistake: I am comfortable to talk about it.
correct_version: I am comfortable talking about it.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Comfortable' is followed by -ing or 'with', not 'to + verb'.
pronunciation_tip: Many speakers blend "for" and "ta" into one quick sound: "KUMF-ter-bul".
spelling_tip: "Comfort" + "able" — the base word "comfort" is hidden inside.
etymology: Latin "confortare" (com- = together/thoroughly + fortis = strong) — originally "to strengthen greatly."
prefix_root_suffix: com- = together/thoroughly + fort = strong + -able = capable of
mnemonic: COMFORT + ABLE = ABLE to feel COMFORT. A comfortable chair is one that's able to give you comfort.
memory_trick: COMFORT-ABLE: ABLE to give comfort. Say it 'KUMF-tuh-bul' (3 syllables).
visual_association: Someone sinking into a soft armchair with a blanket.
difference_explained: Comfortable = adjective (a comfortable chair). Comfort = noun or verb (the comfort of home).
mini_conversation:
A: How's the new mattress?
B: Really comfortable — best sleep I've had in weeks.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A host gestures to the sofa and says, “Please, get comfortable — make yourself at home.”
news_style_line: News-style: “The airline unveiled new, more comfortable seating for economy passengers.”
casual_conversation: Casual: “Are you comfortable, or do you want another pillow?”
mcq_options: A) Painful  B) Relaxed and at ease  C) Expensive  D) Loud
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: These new shoes are surprisingly ______. → comfortable
find_and_fix_to_correct: I feel comfortable to sit here. → I feel comfortable sitting here.
translate: यह सोफ़ा बहुत आरामदायक है। → This sofa is very comfortable.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a place where you feel comfortable.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'giving a pleasant feeling of physical ease, or feeling relaxed'?
usage_tip: 'Make yourself comfortable' = relax, feel at home.

simple_explanation: Able to cause harm or injury. If something could hurt you or put you at risk, it's dangerous.
example_2: Driving in heavy fog is dangerous.
example_3: The chemical is dangerous if not handled properly.
collocations: extremely dangerous, potentially dangerous, dangerous situation, dangerous for
related_phrasal_verbs: put at risk, watch out for
grammar_pattern: dangerous + to-infinitive (dangerous to touch) / it's dangerous + to-infinitive (it's dangerous to run here).
common_mistake: This place is dangerous for swim.
correct_version: This place is dangerous to swim in.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'dangerous to + verb' (+ preposition if needed): 'dangerous to swim in'.
pronunciation_tip: "Danger" + "ous" — pronounce the base word first, then add "-uhs".
etymology: Old French "dangeros", from Latin "dominium" (power/lordship) — originally meant "under someone's power," later "risky."
mnemonic: DANGER + OUS = full OF danger. Anything DANGEROUS is overflowing with DANGER.
memory_trick: DANGER-OUS: full of DANGER.
visual_association: A yellow warning sign with an exclamation mark.
difference_explained: Dangerous = likely to cause harm. Risky = has a chance of loss or failure (a risky plan).
mini_conversation:
A: Can we cross here?
B: No, it's too dangerous — let's use the bridge.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A guide warns the group, “Stay on the path — the cliffs beyond it are dangerous.”
news_style_line: News-style: “Authorities closed the beach after warning of dangerous rip currents.”
casual_conversation: Casual: “Be careful, that wire looks dangerous — don't touch it.”
mcq_options: A) Safe  B) Difficult  C) Distant  D) Dirty
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Texting while driving is extremely ______. → dangerous
find_and_fix_to_correct: That is a very dangerous for children. → That is very dangerous for children.
translate: यह सड़क बहुत खतरनाक है। → This road is very dangerous.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a dangerous road near your home.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'able to cause harm or injury'?
usage_tip: 'Dangerous' warns people: 'It's dangerous to cross here.'

simple_explanation: Liked or supported by many people. When a large number of people like, use, or approve of something, it's popular.
example_2: Cricket is the most popular sport in India.
example_3: She's popular among her classmates.
collocations: hugely popular, popular choice, become popular, popular opinion
grammar_pattern: popular + with/among + people (popular with teenagers) / popular + for + reason (popular for its beaches).
common_mistake: This place is popular by tourists.
correct_version: This place is popular with tourists.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'popular WITH' people, not 'by'.
pronunciation_tip: The middle syllable is a quick "pyuh", not a full "pop-u".
etymology: Latin "popularis" (of the people), from "populus" (people).
mnemonic: POPULAR shares its root with POPULATION — something popular is liked by a large POPULATION of people.
memory_trick: POP-ULAR: POPS up everywhere because everyone likes it.
visual_association: A crowd gathered around one stall at a busy market.
difference_explained: Famous = known by many people. Popular = liked by many people.
mini_conversation:
A: Why is this cafe always full?
B: It's really popular — best coffee in town.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A student says, “She's the most popular girl in school — everyone wants to be her friend.”
news_style_line: News-style: “The app has become popular among students for organizing study groups.”
casual_conversation: Casual: “This show got really popular after the second season.”
mcq_options: A) Disliked by most  B) Liked by many  C) Expensive  D) Old-fashioned
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: This bakery is very ______ for its fresh bread. → popular
find_and_fix_to_correct: This is a very popular among youngsters. → This is very popular among youngsters.
translate: यह गाना बहुत लोकप्रिय है। → This song is very popular.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a place that is popular with tourists.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'liked or supported by many people'?
usage_tip: 'Popular' also means for ordinary people: 'popular culture'.

simple_explanation: Holding your attention; enjoyable to learn about or watch. When something makes you curious and you want to know more, it's interesting.
example_2: I found the documentary really interesting.
example_3: She has an interesting way of explaining things.
collocations: highly interesting, interesting fact, interesting to note, find something interesting
grammar_pattern: -ing adjective describes the thing (an interesting book) vs. -ed adjective describes the feeling (I was interested). Don't mix them up.
common_mistake: I am very interesting in history.
correct_version: I am very interested in history.
why_it_s_wrong: -ED describes how a person feels (interested). -ING describes what causes it (interesting).
pronunciation_tip: Native speakers usually drop the middle "er": "IN-tres-ting", not "in-ter-est-ing".
etymology: From "interest" (Latin "interesse" = to matter, to be of concern) + -ing.
mnemonic: Something INTERESTING makes you truly INTERESTED — the -ING just shows it's active, still holding your attention.
memory_trick: -ING gives the feeling; -ED gets the feeling. The book is interesting; I am interested.
visual_association: Someone leaning in closer, eyes wide with curiosity.
difference_explained: Interesting = causes interest (an interesting film). Interested = feels interest (I'm interested in films).
mini_conversation:
A: How was the lecture?
B: Surprisingly interesting, actually.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character leans forward and says, “Wait, tell me more — that's actually really interesting.”
news_style_line: News-style: “The study reveals an interesting link between sleep and memory.”
casual_conversation: Casual: “That's such an interesting point — I hadn't thought of it that way.”
mcq_options: A) Boring  B) Important  C) Interested  D) Intelligent
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The museum tour was surprisingly ______. → interesting
find_and_fix_to_correct: This book is interested. → This book is interesting.
translate: वह किताब बहुत दिलचस्प है। → That book is very interesting.
write_your_own_sentence: Write two sentences: one with 'interested' and one with 'interesting'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'holding your attention; enjoyable to learn about or watch'?
usage_tip: 'That's interesting' can also politely mean 'I'm not sure I agree'.

simple_explanation: Costing a lot of money. When the price of something is high compared to what people usually expect to pay, it's expensive.
example_2: Rent in the city center is very expensive.
example_3: This restaurant is a bit too expensive for us.
collocations: extremely expensive, expensive taste, too expensive, expensive to run
related_phrasal_verbs: cost a fortune, break the bank
grammar_pattern: expensive + for + person (expensive for students) / too + expensive + to-infinitive (too expensive to buy).
common_mistake: This bag is very much expensive.
correct_version: This bag is very expensive.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Very much' doesn't go before an adjective; use 'very' or 'much more'.
pronunciation_tip: The "x" makes a "ks" sound before the stressed "SPEN".
spelling_tip: "Expense" + "ive" — the S changes to no extra letter, just add -ive.
etymology: Latin "expensus" (past participle of "expendere", to weigh out/spend) + -ive.
prefix_root_suffix: ex- = out + pend(ere) = to weigh, pay + -ive
mnemonic: EXPENSIVE shares a root with EXPENSE — something expensive costs you a big EXPENSE.
memory_trick: EX-PENSIVE: money goes OUT ('ex') of your purse.
visual_association: A price tag with a surprisingly high number, and a raised eyebrow.
difference_explained: Expensive is everyday. Costly also means causing loss: 'a costly mistake'.
mini_conversation:
A: How much was the flight?
B: Honestly, way more expensive than I expected.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A shopper puts an item back and sighs, “That's way too expensive for me right now.”

simple_explanation: Having great value, meaning, or effect. When something matters a lot and deserves attention, it's important.
example_2: Sleep is important for your health.
example_3: It's important to double-check your work.
collocations: extremely important, important role, important decision, important to note
related_phrasal_verbs: matter a lot, count for a lot
grammar_pattern: it's important + to-infinitive (it's important to rest) / it's important + that-clause (it's important that you come).
common_mistake: It is important that you should come.
correct_version: It is important that you come.
why_it_s_wrong: After 'It is important that…', use the base verb (you come), not 'should'.
pronunciation_tip: The final "-tant" is quick and unstressed — don't over-pronounce it.
spelling_tip: "Import" + "ant" — the base word "import" (to bring in) is hidden inside.
etymology: Latin "importare" (to bring in, to matter) + -ant.
mnemonic: IMPORTANT things are the ones you IMPORT into your life first — they matter enough to bring in.
memory_trick: IM-PORT-ANT: things that are IMPORTed matter to the country.
visual_association: A document stamped with a bold red “URGENT” or star symbol.
difference_explained: Important = has great value. Necessary = must be done or needed.
mini_conversation:
A: Can this wait until tomorrow?
B: No, it's important — we need to handle it now.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character says solemnly, “Listen carefully — this is important, and I need you to remember it.”
news_style_line: News-style: “Experts say early diagnosis is important for successful treatment.”
casual_conversation: Casual: “Sorry to interrupt, but this is important — can we talk for a second?”
mcq_options: A) Unnecessary  B) Significant  C) Impossible  D) Impatient
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: It's ______ to drink enough water every day. → important
find_and_fix_to_correct: This is a important information. → This is important information.
translate: यह जानकारी बहुत महत्वपूर्ण है। → This information is very important.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about the most important thing in your life.

reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'having great value, meaning, or effect'?
usage_tip: 'The most important thing is…' is a clear way to give a main point.

simple_explanation: Feeling sure of yourself and your abilities. When you believe in yourself and don't doubt your ability to do something, you feel confident.
example_2: He felt confident going into the interview.
example_3: Practice makes you more confident on stage.
collocations: quietly confident, confident about, feel confident, growing confident
related_phrasal_verbs: believe in oneself, hold one's own
grammar_pattern: confident + about/in + noun (confident about the results) / confident + that-clause (confident that we'll win).
common_mistake: I am confident for passing the exam.
correct_version: I am confident about passing the exam.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'confident ABOUT' or 'confident OF', not 'for'.
pronunciation_tip: The middle syllable reduces almost to nothing: "KON-fi-dnt".
etymology: Latin "confidere" (con- = thoroughly + fidere = to trust) — to trust fully.
mnemonic: CONFIDENT comes from the same root as CONFIDE — a confident person fully trusts (confides in) their own ability.
memory_trick: CON-FIDENT: FIDE = faith (like 'fidelity'): faith in yourself.
visual_association: Someone walking into a room with their head held high.
difference_explained: Confident = sure of yourself. Confidential = secret (confidential documents).
mini_conversation:
A: Nervous about the presentation?
B: Actually, I feel pretty confident today.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A coach tells a nervous player, “Walk out there confident — you've trained for this.”
news_style_line: News-style: “The finance minister sounded confident about the economy's recovery.”
casual_conversation: Casual: “You seem really confident about this plan — what changed?”
mcq_options: A) Insecure  B) Calm  C) Curious  D) Careful
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: After weeks of practice, she felt truly ______ on stage. → confident
find_and_fix_to_correct: He is confident on his skills. → He is confident in his skills.
translate: वह अपने काम को लेकर बहुत आत्मविश्वासी है। → He is very confident about his work.

reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'feeling sure of yourself and your abilities'?
usage_tip: 'Confident' is a positive quality in interviews.

simple_explanation: Feeling annoyed or upset because you can't achieve something. When you keep trying but things don't work out, and it makes you upset, you feel frustrated.
example_2: I get frustrated when my internet keeps disconnecting.
example_3: She was frustrated after failing the test twice.
collocations: deeply frustrated, growing frustrated, frustrated with, visibly frustrated
related_phrasal_verbs: hit a wall, at wit's end
grammar_pattern: frustrated + with/about + noun (frustrated with the delay) / it's frustrating (the thing itself) vs. I'm frustrated (how you feel).
common_mistake: This traffic is so frustrated.
correct_version: This traffic is so frustrating.
why_it_s_wrong: The thing causing the feeling is 'frustrating'; the person feels 'frustrated'.
pronunciation_tip: Three clear syllables, with a crisp "str" cluster in the middle.
etymology: Latin "frustrare" (to disappoint, deceive) + -ed.
word_family: frustration (n.), frustrating (adj., describes the cause), frustrate (v.)
mnemonic: FRUSTRATED sounds like a train that's "STRAYED" off track — you feel stuck and can't reach your goal.
memory_trick: -ED = the person feels it. -ING = the thing causes it.
visual_association: Someone rubbing their temples in front of a frozen computer screen.
difference_explained: Frustrated = how you feel. Frustrating = what makes you feel it.
mini_conversation:
A: You look upset.
B: Yeah, I'm frustrated — this printer won't work.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character throws up their hands and says, “I'm so frustrated — nothing is going right today!”
news_style_line: News-style: “Commuters expressed frustration over repeated train delays this week.”
casual_conversation: Casual: “I'm getting really frustrated with this slow wifi.”
mcq_options: A) Delighted  B) Annoyed and stuck  C) Confused  D) Relaxed
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: He felt ______ after losing the match in the final minute. → frustrated
find_and_fix_to_correct: This app makes me so frustrating. → This app makes me so frustrated.
translate: बार-बार कोशिश करने के बाद भी वह निराश हो गया। → Even after trying repeatedly, he became frustrated.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something that makes you frustrated.

reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'feeling annoyed or upset because you can't achieve something'?
usage_tip: Common complaint: 'This is so frustrating!'

simple_explanation: Feeling thankful for something. When someone helps you or something good happens, and you appreciate it deeply, you feel grateful.
example_1: I am grateful for your help.
example_2: She was grateful for her friends' support during a hard time.
example_3: We're grateful to have a roof over our heads.
collocations: deeply grateful, grateful for, grateful to someone, forever grateful
grammar_pattern: grateful + for + thing (grateful for the opportunity) / grateful + to + person (grateful to my teacher).
common_mistake: I am grateful of your help.
correct_version: I am grateful for your help.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'grateful FOR' a thing and 'grateful TO' a person.
spelling_tip: "Grate" (sounds like "great") + "ful" — only one L at the end.
etymology: Latin "gratus" (pleasing, thankful) + -ful.
mnemonic: GRATEFUL sounds just like “GREAT-FULL” — when you're grateful, your heart feels full of great thanks.
memory_trick: GRATE-FUL: full of GRATitude.
visual_association: Two hands folded together in a gesture of thanks.
difference_explained: Same meaning. Grateful is slightly more formal.
mini_conversation:
A: Thank you so much for helping me move.
B: Of course! I'm just grateful I could be there.

news_style_line: News-style: “Survivors said they were grateful for the quick response of rescue teams.”
casual_conversation: Casual: “I'm really grateful you took the time to explain this.”

simple_explanation: Feeling worried or nervous about something that might happen. When you keep thinking about a possible problem and it makes you uneasy, you feel anxious.
example_1: She felt anxious before the exam.
example_2: He was anxious about the job interview.
example_3: I get anxious before flying.
collocations: increasingly anxious, anxious about, anxious to please, visibly anxious
grammar_pattern: anxious + about + noun (anxious about the results) / anxious + to-infinitive (anxious to leave — means eager, a special use).
common_mistake: I am anxious for the exam results tomorrow.
correct_version: I am anxious about the exam results tomorrow.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'anxious ABOUT' something that worries you. 'Anxious for' means eager for.
pronunciation_tip: The "xi" spelling makes a "ksh" sound, not "ks-ee".
spelling_tip: "Anxi" + "ous" — tricky because it doesn't sound like it's spelled.
etymology: Latin "anxius" (troubled in mind), from "angere" (to choke, distress).
mnemonic: ANXIOUS contains “ANX”, close to “ANKS” as in a tight knot — anxiety can feel like your stomach is tied in a knot.
memory_trick: ANXIOUS has 'X' — like crossed fingers when you're worried.
visual_association: Someone biting their nails while watching a clock.
difference_explained: Nervous = worried before a specific event. Anxious = worried, often for longer or about the unknown.
mini_conversation:
A: You seem quiet today.
B: Yeah, I'm a bit anxious about the results.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character paces the hallway, saying, “I'm so anxious, I can't sit still waiting for news.”
news_style_line: News-style: “Parents are anxious about the safety of the new school route.”
casual_conversation: Casual: “I've been feeling anxious about the presentation all week.”
mcq_options: A) Worried  B) Angry  C) Excited  D) Tired

find_and_fix_to_correct: He is anxious for his health problems. → He is anxious about his health problems.

write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something that makes you anxious.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'feeling worried or nervous about something that might happen'?
usage_tip: 'Anxious to' can also mean eager: 'She's anxious to start.'

simple_explanation: Feeling ashamed or awkward in front of others. When you do or say something and feel self-conscious about how it looks to others, you feel embarrassed.
example_2: He was embarrassed when he forgot her name.
example_3: Don't be embarrassed — everyone makes mistakes.
collocations: slightly embarrassed, embarrassed about, deeply embarrassed, publicly embarrassed
related_phrasal_verbs: want the ground to swallow you
grammar_pattern: embarrassed + about/by + noun (embarrassed by the mistake) / feel embarrassed + to-infinitive (embarrassed to admit it).
common_mistake: This situation is very embarrassed.
correct_version: This situation is very embarrassing.
why_it_s_wrong: The situation is 'embarrassing'; the person feels 'embarrassed'.
pronunciation_tip: Double R, but pronounced as one crisp "r" sound.
spelling_tip: Two R's, two S's: em-BARR-ASS-ed — the trickiest part of this word's spelling.
etymology: French "embarrasser" (to block, obstruct), from Italian "imbarrare" (to bar).
word_family: embarrassment (n.), embarrassing (adj., describes the cause), embarrass (v.)
mnemonic: EMBARRASSED has a “BAR” hidden in it — imagine wanting to hide BEHIND A BAR when you feel embarrassed.
memory_trick: EMBARRASSED: double R, double S — a doubly red face.
visual_association: Someone's face turning red, hand covering their eyes.
difference_explained: Embarrassed = awkward in front of others. Ashamed = feel guilty about something wrong you did.
mini_conversation:
A: Why are you so red?
B: I called my teacher ‘mom’ by accident — so embarrassed!
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character covers their face and mutters, “Oh no, I'm so embarrassed — please tell me no one saw that.”
news_style_line: News-style: “The company issued an apology after the embarrassing data leak.”
casual_conversation: Casual: “I was so embarrassed when my phone rang loudly in the meeting.”
mcq_options: A) Proud  B) Ashamed or self-conscious  C) Excited  D) Confident

find_and_fix_to_correct: I felt so embarrassing in front of everyone. → I felt so embarrassed in front of everyone.

reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'feeling ashamed or awkward in front of others'?
usage_tip: Very commonly misspelt: e-m-b-a-r-r-a-s-s-e-d.

simple_explanation: Feeling worried or uneasy, often before something important. When your body and mind feel tense and uneasy right before a challenge, you feel nervous.
example_1: He was nervous before the game.
example_2: I always get nervous before public speaking.
example_3: She felt nervous walking into the new office.
collocations: extremely nervous, nervous energy, nervous about, nervous laugh
grammar_pattern: nervous + about + noun (nervous about the trip) / nervous + to-infinitive (nervous to speak up).
common_mistake: I am nervous of the exam.
correct_version: I am nervous about the exam.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'nervous ABOUT' something, not 'of'.
spelling_tip: "Nerve" + "ous" — the E is dropped before adding -ous.
etymology: Latin "nervosus" (sinewy, vigorous), from "nervus" (sinew, nerve) — later came to mean "of the nerves."
mnemonic: NERVOUS comes straight from NERVE — when you're nervous, you can feel it in your nerves.
memory_trick: NERV-OUS: your NERVES are shaking.
visual_association: Someone's leg bouncing under a table while waiting.
difference_explained: Nervous = worried and uneasy. Scared = afraid of something that might hurt you.
mini_conversation:
A: You look pale — you okay?
B: Just nervous, my interview is in ten minutes.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character wipes their palms and says, “I'm so nervous, my hands won't stop shaking.”
news_style_line: News-style: “Investors grew nervous as markets swung sharply this week.”
casual_conversation: Casual: “Are you nervous about tomorrow's meeting?”
mcq_options: A) Uneasy  B) Angry  C) Bored  D) Proud
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: She was ______ before her first day at the new job. → nervous
find_and_fix_to_correct: I feel nervous for my speech tomorrow. → I feel nervous about my speech tomorrow.

reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'feeling worried or uneasy, often before something important'?
usage_tip: 'Nervous' is normal before exams and interviews.

simple_explanation: Feeling pleased about your own or someone else's achievement. When you or someone close to you does something well, and it makes you feel good about it, you feel proud.
example_2: Her parents were proud of her graduation.
example_3: He felt proud after finishing the marathon.
collocations: extremely proud, proud moment, make someone proud, proud of yourself
related_phrasal_verbs: stand tall, hold one's head high
grammar_pattern: proud + of + noun/-ing (proud of you / proud of finishing) / make someone + proud.
common_mistake: I am proud for my achievement.
correct_version: I am proud of my achievement.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'proud OF' something or someone, not 'for'.
pronunciation_tip: The "ou" makes the "ow" sound, as in "out".
spelling_tip: P-R-O-U-D — no silent letters, straightforward spelling.
etymology: Old French "prod/prud" (valiant, excellent), from Latin "prode" (advantageous).
mnemonic: PROUD rhymes with LOUD — when you're proud, you want to shout it out LOUD.
memory_trick: PROUD: your chest goes out, like the round letters O and U.
visual_association: Someone standing tall with a medal around their neck.
difference_explained: Proud = pleased about an achievement (good). Arrogant = thinks they're better than others (bad).
mini_conversation:
A: I finally passed my driving test!
B: That's amazing — I'm so proud of you!
everyday_scene: Everyday: A parent hugs their child and says, “I am so proud of you — you worked so hard for this.”
news_style_line: News-style: “The coach said he was proud of the team's effort despite the loss.”
casual_conversation: Casual: “You should be proud — that presentation went really well.”
mcq_options: A) Ashamed  B) Pleased about an achievement  C) Angry  D) Confused
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: My parents were so ______ when I got the job. → proud
find_and_fix_to_correct: She is proud about her work always. → She is always proud of her work.
translate: मुझे तुम पर गर्व है। → I am proud of you.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something you are proud of.

usage_tip: 'I'm proud of you' is a powerful thing to say to a child or friend.

simple_explanation: Having a greater than average height. "Tall" describes someone or something that reaches higher than usual, like a tall person, a tall building, or a tall tree.
example_2: She is the tallest girl in her class.
example_3: The skyscraper is one of the tallest buildings in the city.
collocations: tall building, tall tree, grow tall, tall and thin
related_phrasal_verbs: walk tall, stand tall, a tall order (idiom, meaning a difficult task)
where_it_s_used: Describing people, buildings, nature, sports (basketball players)
grammar_pattern: subject + be + tall (He is tall.) / tall + noun (a tall man)
common_mistake: He is more tall than his brother.
correct_version: He is taller than his brother.
why_it_s_wrong: One-syllable adjectives take -er, not 'more': taller.
pronunciation_tip: Rhymes with "ball" and "call" -- the "a" is a broad "aw" sound: /to:l/.
etymology: From Old English/Middle English "tal" (meaning quick, prompt, or seemly) -- its meaning shifted over time to describe height, becoming common in this sense by the 16th century.
mnemonic: TALL has two L's standing up straight, just like a tall person.
memory_trick: TALL: two tall Ls standing side by side.
visual_association: A giraffe standing tall above the surrounding trees.
difference_explained: Tall = height of people, trees, buildings. High = distance above the ground (a high shelf, a high mountain).
mini_conversation:
A: Wow, your son has grown so much!
B: I know, he's already taller than me.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character looks up in awe and says, "This building is even taller than I imagined."
news_style_line: News-style: "The city just approved plans for the tallest skyscraper in its history."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Wow, you've gotten so tall since I last saw you!"
mcq_options: A) Having little height  B) Having greater than average height  C) Being very heavy  D) Being very thin

find_and_fix_to_correct: She is the most tall person in the room. → She is the tallest person in the room. (use the superlative "tallest," not "most tall")
translate: वह अपनी कक्षा का सबसे लंबा लड़का है। → He is the tallest boy in his class.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence comparing your height with a family member's.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'having a greater than average height'?
usage_tip: 'Tall' is for people, buildings and trees. 'High' is for mountains and walls.

simple_explanation: Having less than average height or length. "Short" describes someone or something that doesn't extend very far -- in height, length, or even time.
example_2: He is shorter than his older brother.
example_3: The line at the store was surprisingly short today.
collocations: short person, short hair, short distance, fall short
related_phrasal_verbs: fall short, cut short, run short of, in short (idiom for summarizing)
grammar_pattern: subject + be + short (She is short.) / short + noun (a short man)
common_mistake: He is more short than me.
correct_version: He is shorter than me.
why_it_s_wrong: One-syllable adjectives take -er, not 'more': shorter.
pronunciation_tip: A short, crisp vowel sound: /Sh-ort/, rhymes with "sport" (without the p).
spelling_tip: Note the "sh" sound at the start -- s-h-o-r-t.
etymology: From Old English "sceort," meaning "cut off" or "brief" -- related to the idea of something not extending far.
mnemonic: SHORT things don't stretch far -- picture a SHORT stick cut off quickly.
memory_trick: SHORT: the opposite of TALL and of LONG.
visual_association: A small, stubby pencil next to a much longer, unused one.
difference_explained: Short = little height or length. Brief = short in time (a brief meeting).

reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'having less than average height or length'?
usage_tip: 'Short of money' = not having enough money.

simple_explanation: Having little width or not much flesh on the body. "Thin" describes something narrow or not thick -- it can describe a person's body, or objects like paper, wire, or slices of food.
example_1: He looks very thin after being sick.
example_2: She sliced the bread into thin pieces.
example_3: The wire was too thin to hold the weight.
collocations: thin slice, thin layer, thin person, wafer-thin
related_phrasal_verbs: thin out, wear thin, thin on the ground (idiom for scarce)
grammar_pattern: subject + be + thin (He is thin.) / thin + noun (a thin book)
common_mistake: She became more thin after the diet.
correct_version: She became thinner after the diet.
why_it_s_wrong: One-syllable adjectives take -er, and 'thin' doubles the n: thinner.
pronunciation_tip: The "th" is a soft, unvoiced sound: /thin/, like blowing air between your teeth and tongue.
spelling_tip: Only three sounds -- easy to remember: t-h-i-n.
etymology: From Old English "thynne," meaning "narrow, slender, not thick" -- a very old Germanic root shared across many European languages.
word_family: thin (adj./v.), thinness (n.), thinly (adv.), thinner (n., a solvent)
mnemonic: THIN things take up little space -- think of a THIN sheet of paper.
memory_trick: THIN → THINNER: double N.
visual_association: A single thin slice of bread compared to a thick loaf.
difference_explained: Thin = little flesh or width (can sound unhealthy). Slim = thin in an attractive way.
tone: Neutral, sometimes sensitive when describing people
mini_conversation:
A: You look really thin lately -- are you eating okay?
B: Yeah, I've just been really busy and forgetting meals.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A doctor examines a patient and says gently, "You've lost a lot of weight -- you're much thinner than last visit."
news_style_line: News-style: "Nutritionists warn that being too thin can be just as unhealthy as being overweight."
casual_conversation: Casual: "This blanket is way too thin for winter -- I need a thicker one."
mcq_options: A) Having a lot of width or flesh  B) Having little width or not much flesh  C) Being extremely tall  D) Being very colorful
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The ice on the lake was too ______ to walk on safely. → thin
find_and_fix_to_correct: Cut the cheese into more thin slices. → Cut the cheese into thinner slices. (use "thinner," not "more thin")
translate: बीमारी के बाद वह बहुत पतला हो गया। → He became very thin after the illness.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a book or object that is very thin.
