usage_tip: 'Curious' can also mean strange: 'a curious smell'.

simple_explanation: Unwilling to work or make an effort; preferring to rest. A lazy person avoids work or effort, often choosing to relax instead of doing what needs to be done.
example_1: Don't be lazy -- finish your homework first.
example_2: He's too lazy to clean his own room.
example_3: It was a lazy Sunday afternoon with nothing planned.
collocations: lazy afternoon, feel lazy, lazy habit, purely lazy
grammar_pattern: lazy + to (too lazy to cook / a lazy day)
common_mistake: Don't be lazy for work.
correct_version: Don't be lazy about work.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'lazy ABOUT' something, not 'for'.
pronunciation_tip: Two syllables: LAY-zee, stress on the first syllable.
etymology: Origin uncertain; first recorded in the 16th century, possibly related to Low German "lasich" (weary, sluggish).
mnemonic: A LAZY cat just LAYS around all day, never wanting to move.
memory_trick: LAZY: the Z looks like sleeping 'Zzz'.
visual_association: Someone lying on the couch, remote in hand, ignoring a pile of laundry.
difference_explained: Tired = needs rest. Lazy = doesn't want to make an effort.
mini_conversation:
A: Are you going to the gym today?
B: Nah, I'm feeling too lazy today.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character stretches out on the couch and mumbles, "I'm too lazy to move, order takeout instead."
news_style_line: News-style: "The report criticized the agency for lazy oversight of safety regulations."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I've been so lazy this weekend, I haven't left the house."
mcq_options: A) Hardworking and energetic  B) Unwilling to work or make an effort  C) Extremely careful  D) Very generous
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: I've been feeling ______ all weekend and haven't done any chores. → lazy
find_and_fix_to_correct: She always act lazily about her chores. → She always acts lazy about her chores.
translate: होमवर्क खत्म किए बिना आलसी मत बनो। → Don't be lazy -- finish your homework first.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a lazy habit you want to stop.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'unwilling to work or make an effort; preferring to rest'?
usage_tip: 'Lazy Sunday' = a relaxed day.

simple_explanation: Putting a lot of effort into work; not lazy. A hardworking person makes a strong effort in their job, studies, or tasks, often working long hours to do well.
example_1: My mother is the most hardworking person I know.
example_2: She's hardworking and always meets her deadlines.
example_3: The hardworking farmer was in the fields before sunrise.
collocations: hardworking employee, hardworking student, incredibly hardworking
related_phrasal_verbs: put in the hours, burn the midnight oil (idioms related to hard work)
grammar_pattern: hardworking + noun (a hardworking student / hardworking staff)
common_mistake: He works hardly.
correct_version: He works hard.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Hardly' means almost not. Someone hardworking 'works hard'.
pronunciation_tip: Three syllables: HAHRD-wurk-ing, stress on the first syllable.
spelling_tip: One word in modern usage -- hardworking, though "hard-working" with a hyphen is also accepted.
etymology: From "hard" + "working" -- a straightforward compound describing someone who works with great effort.
mnemonic: A HARDWORKING person WORKS HARD, no shortcuts.
memory_trick: HARD + WORKING: someone who works HARD.
visual_association: Someone still at their desk with the lights on long after everyone else has left.
difference_explained: Works hard = puts in a lot of effort. Hardly works = almost doesn't work.
mini_conversation:
A: How did she get promoted so fast?
B: She's incredibly hardworking -- always the first one in the office.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A mentor pats a young employee on the back and says, "Keep being this hardworking, and you'll go far."
news_style_line: News-style: "The award recognized hardworking volunteers who rebuilt homes after the storm."
casual_conversation: Casual: "You're so hardworking, when do you even rest?"
mcq_options: A) Lazy and unmotivated  B) Putting in a lot of effort  C) Extremely shy  D) Very careless
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The ______ students stayed late to finish their project. → hardworking
find_and_fix_to_correct: He always working hard for his family. → He always works hard for his family.
translate: मेरी माँ सबसे मेहनती इंसान हैं जिन्हें मैं जानता हूँ। → My mother is the most hardworking person I know.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about the most hardworking person you know.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'putting a lot of effort into work; not lazy'?
usage_tip: Spelt 'hardworking' or 'hard-working'. Both are fine.

simple_explanation: Having a strong desire to succeed or achieve something. An ambitious person sets big goals for themselves and works hard to reach them, whether in career, study, or life.
example_1: She is very ambitious about her career.
example_2: He's an ambitious young lawyer with big plans.
example_3: Their ambitious project aims to plant a million trees.
collocations: highly ambitious, ambitious plan, ambitious goal, too ambitious
related_phrasal_verbs: aim high, go for it, reach for the stars
where_it_s_used: Career talk, job interviews, goal-setting, school
grammar_pattern: ambitious + about/to + verb (ambitious about her goals / ambitious to succeed)
common_mistake: He is ambitious for become a manager.
correct_version: He is ambitious to become a manager.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'ambitious to + verb', not 'for + verb'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: am-BISH-us.
spelling_tip: Note the "-tious" ending, pronounced "shus" -- easy to misspell as "ambitous."
etymology: From Latin "ambitio" (a going around, canvassing for votes) via French "ambitieux" -- originally about seeking favor/office, later general drive for success.
prefix_root_suffix: ambit- = root (from Latin "to go around") + -ious = adjective suffix (full of)
mnemonic: AMBITIOUS people are always "on a mission" to climb higher.
memory_trick: AMBITIOUS: AIM high.
visual_association: A person climbing a mountain toward a distant flag at the peak.
emotion_feel: Drive and determination, sometimes mixed with pressure
difference_explained: Ambitious = wants to succeed (positive). Greedy = wants more than they need (negative).
mini_conversation:
A: What are your plans after graduation?
B: I'm quite ambitious -- I want to start my own company.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A mentor tells a young intern, "You're ambitious, and that's exactly what this company needs."
news_style_line: News-style: "Analysts called the company's ambitious expansion plan a bold gamble."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I love that you're so ambitious about your studies."
mcq_options: A) Has no goals  B) Strongly wants to achieve success  C) Gives up easily  D) Avoids challenges
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: He's very ______ and hopes to become CEO one day. → ambitious
find_and_fix_to_correct: She is ambitious for becoming a doctor. → She is ambitious about becoming a doctor.
translate: वह एक बहुत महत्वाकांक्षी छात्र है। → He is a very ambitious student.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about your ambition.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'having a strong desire to succeed or achieve something'?
usage_tip: 'An ambitious plan' = a big, hard plan.

simple_explanation: Not boasting or showing off about your abilities or achievements. A modest person plays down their own success and doesn't like to be praised too much in public.
example_1: He stayed modest even after winning the award.
example_2: She's very modest about her achievements.
example_3: Despite being famous, he lives a modest life.
collocations: stay modest, modest about, modest lifestyle, modest income
related_phrasal_verbs: play down, keep a low profile
where_it_s_used: Praise, success stories, personality descriptions, interviews
grammar_pattern: modest + about + noun (modest about his success)
common_mistake: She is modest about she won the prize.
correct_version: She is modest about winning the prize.
why_it_s_wrong: After 'about', use -ing: 'about winning'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the first syllable: MOD-ist.
etymology: From Latin "modestus" (keeping due measure), from "modus" (measure) -- someone who doesn't overstate their abilities.
prefix_root_suffix: modest = root (from Latin "modus," measure) + -y = noun form (modesty)
mnemonic: A MODEST person keeps their "mode" of talking about themselves low-key.
memory_trick: MODEST: MODE of quiet — doesn't show off.
visual_association: Someone quietly stepping back from a spotlight.
difference_explained: Almost the same. Modest can also mean small (a modest house).
mini_conversation:
A: You must be proud of winning first place!
B: Thanks, but it was a team effort -- I try to stay modest.
everyday_scene: Everyday: An award winner says quietly, "I don't deserve all the credit -- so many people helped."
news_style_line: News-style: "Despite record profits, the founder remains famously modest about his success."
casual_conversation: Casual: "He's so modest, he never talks about his awards."
mcq_options: A) Brags about achievements  B) Doesn't show off about success  C) Is always angry  D) Never works hard
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Even after winning, she stayed ______ about her success. → modest
find_and_fix_to_correct: He is very modest of his success. → He is very modest about his success.
translate: वह अपनी सफलता के बारे में बहुत विनम्र है। → He is very modest about his success.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about someone modest about their success.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'not boasting or showing off about your abilities or achievements'?
usage_tip: 'A modest salary' = not very high.

simple_explanation: Happy and positive in a way that others can notice. A cheerful person or place feels bright and full of good energy, often smiling and easy to be around.
example_1: She always has a cheerful smile.
example_2: The cheerful waiter greeted every customer warmly.
example_3: His cheerful attitude made the long meeting bearable.
collocations: cheerful mood, stay cheerful, cheerful smile, cheerful personality
where_it_s_used: Greetings, workplaces, morning routines, personality descriptions
grammar_pattern: cheerful + noun (cheerful smile) or subject + be + cheerful
common_mistake: He is cheerful with the news.
correct_version: He is cheerful about the news.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'cheerful ABOUT' the reason, not 'with'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the first syllable: CHEER-ful.
spelling_tip: Remember "-ful" has only one "l" at the end.
etymology: From "cheer" (Old French "chere," face/expression) + "-ful" (full of) -- literally "full of good spirits."
prefix_root_suffix: cheer = root (good spirits) + -ful = adjective suffix (full of)
word_family: cheer (n./v.), cheerfully (adv.), cheerfulness (n.), cheery (adj., informal synonym)
mnemonic: A CHEERFUL person always gives you a "cheer" -- like a happy shout of encouragement.
memory_trick: CHEER-FUL: FULL of CHEER.
visual_association: Sunshine streaming through a window onto a smiling face.
difference_explained: Happy = feeling good inside. Cheerful = showing happiness to others.
mini_conversation:
A: You seem really cheerful today.
B: Yeah, I got great news this morning!
everyday_scene: Everyday: A neighbor waves and calls out, "Good morning! Isn't it a cheerful day?"
news_style_line: News-style: "Volunteers stayed cheerful despite the long hours at the shelter."
casual_conversation: Casual: "She's always so cheerful, even on Monday mornings."
mcq_options: A) Sad and quiet  B) Happy and positive  C) Angry and loud  D) Tired and bored
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The children were ______ on the first day of school. → cheerful
find_and_fix_to_correct: She is cheerful for her promotion. → She is cheerful about her promotion.
translate: वह हमेशा खुशमिजाज़ रहती है। → She is always cheerful.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about the most cheerful person in your family.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'happy and positive in a way that others can notice'?
usage_tip: A 'cheerful room' = bright and pleasant.

simple_explanation: Not joking or playful; thoughtful and important. "Serious" can describe a person who doesn't joke much, or a situation that is important and needs careful attention.
example_2: He's quite serious and rarely laughs at work.
example_3: The doctor said it's a serious illness.
collocations: serious problem, take something seriously, serious about, dead serious
related_phrasal_verbs: get down to business, mean business
where_it_s_used: Health, work discussions, personality descriptions, warnings
grammar_pattern: serious + about + noun (serious about his studies) or take + something + seriously
common_mistake: Please take it more serious.
correct_version: Please take it more seriously.
why_it_s_wrong: After 'take it', use the adverb 'seriously'.
pronunciation_tip: Three syllables: SEER-ee-us, stress on the first.
spelling_tip: Just one "r," but two "s"s at the end: se-r-i-ous.
etymology: From Latin "seriosus"/"serius" (earnest, weighty) via French "serieux."
prefix_root_suffix: seri- = root (Latin "serius," earnest) + -ous = adjective suffix (full of)
mnemonic: A SERIOUS face rarely smiles -- think of a strict teacher's stern look through a "series" of lessons.
memory_trick: SERIOUS: no smile — a straight face.
visual_association: A furrowed brow and a firm, unsmiling expression.
difference_explained: Serious = adjective (a serious man). Seriously = adverb (take it seriously).
mini_conversation:
A: Are you joking about quitting?
B: No, I'm being completely serious.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A doctor sits down and says gently, "I need to be serious with you for a moment."
news_style_line: News-style: "Officials described the situation as a serious threat to public safety."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Wait, are you being serious right now?"
mcq_options: A) Funny and light  B) Important and not joking  C) Careless  D) Loud and excited
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: This is a ______ matter, so please listen carefully. → serious
find_and_fix_to_correct: He never take anything serious. → He never takes anything seriously.
translate: यह एक गंभीर समस्या है। → This is a serious problem.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a serious problem in your city.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'not joking or playful; thoughtful and important'?
usage_tip: 'Are you serious?' = are you joking?

simple_explanation: Full of fun and enjoying games or jokes. A playful person or animal likes to have fun, joke around, and not take things too seriously.
example_1: The kitten was very playful today.
example_2: Their playful banter made everyone laugh.
example_3: The dog gave her a playful nudge.
collocations: playful mood, playful smile, playful banter, playful teasing
related_phrasal_verbs: goof around, mess around, joke around
where_it_s_used: Pets, children, friendly teasing, casual relationships
grammar_pattern: playful + noun (playful smile) or subject + be + playful
common_mistake: She was playful with me for the exam.
correct_version: She was playful with me during the exam.
why_it_s_wrong: To say when something happened, use 'during', not 'for'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the first syllable: PLAY-ful.
spelling_tip: "Play" + "ful" -- keep the "y," don't change it to "i" before "-ful."
etymology: From "play" (Old English "plegan," to move briskly/exercise) + "-ful" (full of).
mnemonic: A PLAYFUL puppy always wants to PLAY.
memory_trick: PLAY-FUL: FULL of PLAY.
visual_association: A puppy chasing its own tail in circles.
difference_explained: Playful = full of fun. Naughty = behaving badly (for children).
mini_conversation:
A: Your puppy is adorable!
B: Thanks, she's so playful -- always chasing her tail.
everyday_scene: Everyday: Two friends nudge each other, one laughing, "Stop being so playful, we're late!"
news_style_line: News-style: "The zoo's newest otters have delighted visitors with their playful antics."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I love how playful he is with the kids."
mcq_options: A) Full of fun and teasing  B) Very strict  C) Extremely tired  D) Angry and upset
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The children were being ______ in the pool. → playful
find_and_fix_to_correct: He gave me a playful looks. → He gave me a playful look.
translate: बिल्ली का बच्चा बहुत चंचल है। → The kitten is very playful.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a playful animal you know.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'full of fun and enjoying games or jokes'?
usage_tip: 'A playful puppy' is very common.

simple_explanation: Not nervous, upset, or excited; peaceful. A calm person stays relaxed and doesn't panic, even in a stressful situation.
example_2: She remained calm during the emergency.
example_3: The sea was calm this morning.
collocations: stay calm, keep calm, calm down, calm voice
related_phrasal_verbs: calm down, cool off, settle down
grammar_pattern: calm + down (phrasal use) or subject + be/stay/remain + calm
common_mistake: Please calm, everything is fine.
correct_version: Please calm down, everything is fine.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Calm' as an adjective needs 'be': 'Please be calm.' As a verb, use 'calm down'.
pronunciation_tip: The "l" is silent -- pronounce it "kahm," not "kalm."
spelling_tip: Remember the silent "l" -- easy to forget when spelling by sound.
etymology: From Old French "calme," ultimately from Greek "kauma" (heat of the day) -- originally the stillness after midday heat, at sea.
word_family: calmness (n.), calmly (adv.), calm (v., as in "calm down")
mnemonic: Picture a CALM lake -- no waves, no noise, just "kahm" quiet.
memory_trick: CALM has a silent L: say 'kaam'.
visual_association: A completely still lake reflecting a clear sky.
difference_explained: Quiet = little noise. Calm = peaceful, not worried or excited.
mini_conversation:
A: I'm so nervous about the interview!
B: Just stay calm -- you've prepared well.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A pilot's steady voice comes over the speaker, "Please remain calm, everything is under control."
news_style_line: News-style: "Officials urged residents to stay calm as evacuation routes opened."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Just breathe and stay calm, we'll figure this out."
mcq_options: A) Nervous and shaky  B) Peaceful and relaxed  C) Angry and loud  D) Confused
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: He stayed ______ even when everyone else panicked. → calm
find_and_fix_to_correct: She is very calmly person. → She is a very calm person.
translate: परीक्षा के दौरान शांत रहो। → Stay calm during the exam.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about how you stay calm in an exam.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'not nervous, upset, or excited; peaceful'?
usage_tip: 'Keep calm' = don't panic.

simple_explanation: Having moods that change often and unpredictably, sometimes becoming irritable. A moody person's feelings can shift suddenly -- happy one moment, upset or quiet the next -- often without a clear reason.
example_1: My brother is really moody in the mornings.
example_2: Teenagers can be moody sometimes.
example_3: He's been moody all week because of stress at work.
collocations: moody teenager, moody mornings, get moody
related_phrasal_verbs: snap at, blow hot and cold
grammar_pattern: subject + be/get + moody (+ time expression)
common_mistake: She is moody about the weather.
correct_version: She gets moody in bad weather.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Moody' describes a person's changing moods, not a reaction 'about' something.
pronunciation_tip: Two syllables: MOO-dee, stress on the first.
etymology: From "mood" (Old English "mod," mind/spirit) + "-y" (having the quality of) -- someone whose mood changes often.
prefix_root_suffix: mood = root + -y = adjective suffix (having the quality of)
mnemonic: A MOODY person's MOOD can flip in a minute -- sunny one moment, stormy the next.
memory_trick: MOOD-Y: many MOODs.
visual_association: A weather vane spinning quickly between sun and storm clouds.
difference_explained: Angry = feels anger now. Moody = moods change often and unexpectedly.
mini_conversation:
A: Why is he so quiet today?
B: He's just moody -- he'll be fine by tomorrow.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A parent sighs and says, "He's been so moody since he turned fifteen."
news_style_line: News-style: "Analysts described the moody, unpredictable market as difficult to forecast."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Sorry I was moody earlier, I didn't sleep well."
mcq_options: A) Mood stays the same all the time  B) Mood changes often and unpredictably  C) Mood is always cheerful  D) Mood never affects others
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: He's a bit ______ today, so give him some space. → moody
find_and_fix_to_correct: She is moody with her exam results. → She is moody about her exam results.
translate: वह आजकल बहुत चिड़चिड़ा हो गया है। → He has become very moody these days.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about when you get moody.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'having moods that change often and unpredictably, sometimes becoming irritable'?
usage_tip: 'Moody lighting' = dim, emotional light.

simple_explanation: Able to be trusted to do what is expected, again and again. A reliable person or thing always does what it's supposed to do -- you never have to worry whether it will let you down.
example_2: This car has proven very reliable over the years.
example_3: She's a reliable employee who never misses deadlines.
collocations: reliable source, reliable friend, highly reliable, prove reliable
related_phrasal_verbs: count on, depend on, come through
where_it_s_used: Work references, friendships, product reviews, transportation
grammar_pattern: reliable + noun (reliable source) or subject + be + reliable
common_mistake: He is reliable in his friends.
correct_version: He is reliable to his friends. / He is a reliable friend.
why_it_s_wrong: Avoid 'reliable in'. Say 'a reliable friend' or 'reliable to his friends'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: ri-LY-uh-bul.
spelling_tip: Remember "rely" hides inside "reliable" -- re + ly + able.
etymology: From "rely" (Old French "relier," to bind again) + "-able" -- someone you can "bind" your trust to.
mnemonic: You can always RELY on someone RELIABLE.
memory_trick: RELY-ABLE: ABLE to be RELIED on.
visual_association: A sturdy bridge that never wobbles, no matter how many times you cross it.
difference_explained: Reliable = does what's expected every time. Trustworthy = honest and can be trusted.
mini_conversation:
A: Can we trust him to finish the report on time?
B: Definitely, he's always been reliable.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A manager tells the team, "She's the most reliable person on this project -- give it to her."
news_style_line: News-style: "The new bus route has proven reliable, with on-time rates above ninety percent."
casual_conversation: Casual: "You can always count on him, he's super reliable."
mcq_options: A) Can be trusted to do what's expected  B) Always late  C) Easily broken  D) Unpredictable
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: She's the most ______ person I know -- always on time. → reliable
find_and_fix_to_correct: This car is very reliable to drive it every day. → This car is very reliable to drive every day.
translate: वह एक बहुत भरोसेमंद दोस्त है। → He is a very reliable friend.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a reliable friend or device.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'able to be trusted to do what is expected, again and again'?
usage_tip: 'A reliable source' = information you can trust.

simple_explanation: Not able to be trusted or depended on. If someone or something is unreliable, you can't count on it to work or behave the same way every time -- it often lets you down.
example_1: This old phone is really unreliable.
example_2: The bus service here is unreliable, especially in winter.
example_3: He's too unreliable to be given more responsibility.
collocations: unreliable source, unreliable narrator, prove unreliable, notoriously unreliable
related_phrasal_verbs: let down, flake out, back out
where_it_s_used: Work complaints, technology reviews, transportation, relationships
grammar_pattern: unreliable + noun (unreliable source) or subject + be + unreliable
common_mistake: This information is unreliable for trust.
correct_version: This information is unreliable, so don't trust it.
why_it_s_wrong: Don't follow 'unreliable' with 'for + verb'. Split into two clauses.
pronunciation_tip: Four syllables with stress on the third: un-ri-LY-uh-bul.
spelling_tip: Just "un" + "reliable" -- no extra letters, no hyphen.
etymology: "Un-" (not) + "reliable" -- the negative form, in use since the 19th century as "reliable" became common.
mnemonic: An UNRELIABLE friend is never there when you rely on them -- the "un" cancels the trust.
memory_trick: UN-RELIABLE: NOT reliable.
visual_association: A wobbly ladder that might collapse under your weight.
difference_explained: Unreliable = can't be depended on. Untrue = false.
mini_conversation:
A: Did the courier deliver on time again?
B: No, that company is so unreliable lately.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character throws up their hands, "I can't work with someone this unreliable anymore."
news_style_line: News-style: "Residents complained the water supply had become dangerously unreliable."
casual_conversation: Casual: "My old laptop is so unreliable, it shuts down randomly."
mcq_options: A) Trustworthy and steady  B) Cannot be trusted or depended on  C) Extremely fast  D) Very expensive
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: He's known for being ______, so people stopped counting on him. → unreliable
find_and_fix_to_correct: This source is unreliable for read. → This source is unreliable to read from.
translate: यह जानकारी अविश्वसनीय है। → This information is unreliable.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something unreliable in your daily life.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'not able to be trusted or depended on'?
usage_tip: 'An unreliable bus service' = buses don't come on time.

simple_explanation: Having good judgment, often from experience and knowledge. A wise person makes good decisions because they understand life well, often from years of experience, not just book knowledge.
example_2: It was wise of you to save some money.
example_3: The wise old teacher always gave good advice.
collocations: wise decision, wise choice, wise advice, wise old
grammar_pattern: it is wise + to + verb (It's wise to save money.) or wise + noun
common_mistake: He is wise for choosing that job.
correct_version: He was wise to choose that job.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'wise to + verb', not 'for + -ing'.
pronunciation_tip: Rhymes with "eyes" -- the "s" sounds like "z": wyz.
etymology: From Old English "wis" (learned, sagacious), Germanic root related to "wit" (to know).
mnemonic: A WISE owl makes decisions with open EYES (wise rhymes with eyes) and years of experience.
memory_trick: WISE: like a WISE old OWL.
visual_association: An elderly figure with kind eyes, nodding slowly in thought.
difference_explained: Clever = quick to learn. Wise = makes good judgments, often from experience.
mini_conversation:
A: Should I take the job or keep saving money first?
B: It might be wise to save a little more first.
everyday_scene: Everyday: An old mentor places a hand on the hero's shoulder, "A wise person listens more than they speak."
news_style_line: News-style: "Economists called the early investment a wise move that paid off years later."
casual_conversation: Casual: "That was a wise decision, saving money before the trip."
mcq_options: A) Careless and hasty  B) Having good judgment from experience  C) Loud and confident  D) Young and inexperienced
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: It would be ______ to check the weather before you leave. → wise
find_and_fix_to_correct: It was very wise for him to save money. → It was very wise of him to save money.

usage_tip: 'It would be wise to…' is polite advice.

simple_explanation: Feeling pleased or joyful. When good things happen or you feel good about your life, you are happy.
example_2: She looked happy when she saw her old friend.
example_3: We were happy with the results of the test.
collocations: happy birthday, happy to hear, extremely happy, make someone happy
where_it_s_used: Celebrations, greetings, good news, daily conversation
grammar_pattern: happy + about/with/for + noun (happy about the news / happy with the results)
common_mistake: I am happy for see you.
correct_version: I am happy to see you.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'happy to + verb', not 'for + verb'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the first syllable: HAP-ee.
etymology: From Middle English "hap" (chance, luck) + "-y" -- originally meant "lucky," evolved to mean feeling joy.
prefix_root_suffix: hap = root (chance/luck) + -y = adjective suffix (having the quality of)
mnemonic: HAPPY starts with "HAP," like the "hap" in "happen" -- good things happening make you happy.
memory_trick: HAPPY → HAPPIER: Y becomes IER.
visual_association: A wide, genuine smile with bright, sparkling eyes.
difference_explained: Happy FOR a person (their good news). Happy ABOUT a thing.
mini_conversation:
A: You look really happy today!
B: Yeah, I just got some great news.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A child jumps up and down shouting, "This is the happiest day of my life!"
news_style_line: News-style: "Surveys show people in the region report feeling happier than the national average."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I'm so happy you could make it to the party!"
mcq_options: A) Feeling pleased or joyful  B) Feeling tired  C) Feeling angry  D) Feeling confused
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: I felt so ______ when I heard the good news. → happy
find_and_fix_to_correct: I am happy of the good news. → I am happy about the good news.
translate: मैं आज बहुत खुश हूँ। → I am very happy today.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about what makes you happy every day.

reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'feeling pleased or joyful'?
usage_tip: 'Happy to help' is a polite reply at work.

simple_explanation: Feeling unhappy, often because of a loss or disappointment. You feel sad when something bad happens, like losing something or someone, or when things don't go the way you hoped.
example_1: I feel sad when it rains all day.
example_2: She was sad when her friend moved away.
example_3: The ending of the movie made everyone sad.
collocations: feel sad, sad news, sad story, look sad
grammar_pattern: sad + about/that-clause (sad about the news / sad that she left)
common_mistake: I am sad for the news.
correct_version: I am sad about the news.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'sad ABOUT' the reason, not 'for'.
pronunciation_tip: One short syllable, short "a" sound: sad, rhymes with "bad."
spelling_tip: Just three letters -- "sad," easy to spell but easy to confuse with "sat" or "sand" for beginners.
etymology: From Old English "sæd" (sated, weary), which shifted over centuries from "full/tired" to today's "unhappy."
mnemonic: SAD rhymes with "bad" -- bad news makes you sad.
memory_trick: SAD → SADDER: double D.
visual_association: A single tear rolling down a lowered face.
difference_explained: Sad = unhappy. Upset = unhappy and disturbed, often suddenly.
mini_conversation:
A: Why do you look so sad?
B: I just said goodbye to my best friend at the airport.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character stares out a rainy window, whispering, "I've never felt this sad before."
news_style_line: News-style: "The whole town felt sad after hearing the beloved shop was closing."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I feel a bit sad today, I'm not sure why."
mcq_options: A) Feeling joyful  B) Feeling unhappy  C) Feeling excited  D) Feeling proud

find_and_fix_to_correct: He is sad from the exam result. → He is sad about the exam result.
translate: वह अपने दोस्त के जाने से दुखी है। → He is sad about his friend leaving.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something that made you sad recently.

usage_tip: 'Sad but true' = unfortunately true.

simple_explanation: Feeling strong displeasure or annoyance. You feel angry when someone treats you unfairly, or when something frustrating or upsetting happens.
example_1: He was angry at the driver.
example_2: She got angry when he was late again.
example_3: The customer was angry about the broken product.
collocations: get angry, angry with someone, angry about something, angry outburst
related_phrasal_verbs: blow up, lash out, fly off the handle
grammar_pattern: angry + with + person / about + situation (angry with him / angry about the delay)
common_mistake: I am angry of you.
correct_version: I am angry with you.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'angry WITH' (or 'at') a person and 'angry ABOUT' a thing.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the first syllable: ANG-gree.
spelling_tip: Watch the double "g" sound spelled with "ng" -- "angry," not "angery."
etymology: From Old Norse "angr" (grief, distress) via Middle English -- originally about sorrow, later narrowed to anger.
prefix_root_suffix: angr- = root (Old Norse, grief/distress) + -y = adjective suffix
mnemonic: ANGRY sounds like "hangry" -- when you're really hungry, you often get angry too!
memory_trick: ANGRY → ANGRIER: Y becomes IER.
visual_association: Steam rising from a boiling kettle.
emotion_feel: Heat, tension, and a strong urge to react
difference_explained: Annoyed = a little angry. Angry = strongly displeased.
mini_conversation:
A: Why is your face so red?
B: I'm angry -- someone just cut in line in front of me.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character slams a door, shouting, "I have never been this angry in my life!"
news_style_line: News-style: "Residents grew angry after learning about the delayed repairs."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I was so angry when they cancelled the flight last minute."
mcq_options: A) Calm and peaceful  B) Feeling strong displeasure  C) Feeling sleepy  D) Feeling proud

write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about what makes you angry on the road.

reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'feeling strong displeasure or annoyance'?
usage_tip: 'Don't make me angry' is a common warning.

simple_explanation: Feeling very happy and full of energy about something. You feel excited when you're looking forward to something great, and you can barely wait for it to happen.
example_1: I'm so excited for the trip!
example_2: The kids were excited about the birthday party.
example_3: She got excited when she heard the good news.
collocations: get excited, excited about, really excited, excited to hear
related_phrasal_verbs: psych up, hype up, look forward to
where_it_s_used: Trips, events, good news, celebrations, anticipation
grammar_pattern: excited + about + noun / to + verb (excited about the trip / excited to see you)
common_mistake: I am exciting to go on vacation.
correct_version: I am excited to go on vacation.
why_it_s_wrong: The person feels 'excited'; the thing is 'exciting'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: ik-SY-tid.
etymology: From Latin "excitare" (to call forth, rouse), via "excite" + "-ed."
prefix_root_suffix: ex- (out) + cit(e) (from Latin "citare," to set in motion) + -ed (adjective suffix)
mnemonic: When you're EXCITED, your energy "exits" your body -- you can't sit still!
memory_trick: -ED = I feel it. -ING = it causes it.
visual_association: A child bouncing on their toes, eyes wide, waiting to open a gift.
difference_explained: Excited = how you feel. Exciting = what makes you feel it.
mini_conversation:
A: Guess what -- we're going to Japan next month!
B: Wow, I'm so excited for you!
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character bursts through the door shouting, "You won't believe it -- I'm so excited I can't even breathe!"
news_style_line: News-style: "Fans expressed excitement ahead of the stadium's grand reopening."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I'm really excited about the new season starting."

simple_explanation: Feeling uninterested because there's nothing fun or interesting to do. You feel bored when a situation is dull or repetitive and you have nothing engaging to occupy your mind.
example_2: The students got bored during the long lecture.
example_3: He felt bored waiting at the airport for hours.
collocations: get bored, bored of, bored stiff, easily bored
where_it_s_used: Waiting rooms, long meetings, rainy days, repetitive tasks
grammar_pattern: bored + with/of + noun (bored with the routine / bored of waiting)
common_mistake: This class is very bored.
correct_version: This class is very boring.
why_it_s_wrong: The class causes the feeling (boring); the students feel it (bored).
etymology: Origin of "bore" (to weary) uncertain, first recorded in 18th-century English; possibly linked to the earlier sense of "bore" (to drill a hole).
mnemonic: When you're BORED, time feels like it's "boring" a hole through your patience.
memory_trick: -ED = I feel it. -ING = it causes it. 'I'm boring' means you make others bored!
visual_association: A clock's hands barely moving while someone stares blankly at the wall.
difference_explained: Bored = how you feel. Boring = what makes you feel it.
mini_conversation:
A: What are you doing?
B: Nothing, I'm just so bored right now.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A teenager slumps on the couch, sighing, "There's nothing to do, I'm dying of boredom."
news_style_line: News-style: "Surveys show many workers feel bored during long virtual meetings."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I'm so bored, do you want to do something?"
mcq_options: A) Excited and thrilled  B) Uninterested because nothing is fun  C) Angry and upset  D) Proud and confident

find_and_fix_to_correct: This movie makes me boring. → This movie makes me bored.

reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'feeling uninterested because there's nothing fun or interesting to do'?
usage_tip: 'Bored to death' = extremely bored.

simple_explanation: Feeling afraid of something. You feel scared when something makes you fear that you or someone else might get hurt, or when something unfamiliar frightens you.
example_1: The child was scared of the dark.
example_2: She was scared when she heard the loud noise.
example_3: He's scared of spiders.
collocations: scared of, scared stiff, get scared, look scared
related_phrasal_verbs: freak out, jump out of one's skin
where_it_s_used: Horror movies, storms, animals, dark places, danger
grammar_pattern: scared + of + noun/gerund (scared of dogs / scared of flying)
common_mistake: I am scared for spiders.
correct_version: I am scared of spiders.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'scared OF' something, not 'for'.
spelling_tip: "Scare" + "d" -- keep the silent "e" dropped, just add "d": "scared."
etymology: From Old French "escarer" (to frighten), rooted in Latin "excordare" (to deprive of heart).
prefix_root_suffix: scare = root (from Old French "escarer") + -d = adjective suffix (feeling)
mnemonic: When you're SCARED, you look like you just saw a SCARY movie.
memory_trick: SCARED: the SCAR of fear.
visual_association: Wide eyes and a racing heartbeat in a dark room.
difference_explained: Same meaning. Afraid is slightly more formal and isn't used before a noun ('a scared child', not 'an afraid child').

A: Why did you scream?
B: I got scared -- I thought I saw a snake!

news_style_line: News-style: "Residents said they felt scared during the sudden power outage last night."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I'm a little scared of the dentist, honestly."
mcq_options: A) Feeling brave  B) Feeling afraid  C) Feeling bored  D) Feeling proud

find_and_fix_to_correct: He is scared from dogs. → He is scared of dogs.

usage_tip: 'Scared stiff' = very frightened.

simple_explanation: Feeling anxious or concerned about something that might go wrong. You feel worried when you keep thinking about a possible problem and can't stop feeling uneasy about it.
example_2: She was worried about her son's health.
example_3: He looked worried before the interview.
collocations: worried about, deeply worried, don't worry, worried sick
grammar_pattern: worried + about + noun/gerund (worried about the test / worried about losing)
common_mistake: I am worrying about the exam tomorrow.
correct_version: I am worried about the exam tomorrow.
why_it_s_wrong: The person feels 'worried'. 'Worrying' describes a situation: 'a worrying trend'.
pronunciation_tip: Two syllables: WUH-reed, stress on the first.
etymology: From Old English "wyrgan" (to strangle), which shifted in meaning to "to harass," then to today's sense of mental unease.
word_family: worry (n./v.), worrying (adj., describes the situation), worriedly (adv.)
mnemonic: When you're WORRIED, your mind keeps "worrying" the same problem over and over, like a dog with a bone.
memory_trick: WORRY → WORRIED: Y becomes I.
visual_association: Someone pacing back and forth, checking their phone every few seconds.
difference_explained: Worried = how you feel. Worrying = causing worry (worrying news).
mini_conversation:

B: Yeah, I'm worried about my presentation tomorrow.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A parent paces by the phone, muttering, "I'm so worried, why hasn't she called yet?"
news_style_line: News-style: "Experts say they are worried about the rising cost of basic goods."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I'm worried about my exam results, honestly."
mcq_options: A) Feeling relaxed  B) Feeling anxious about something  C) Feeling proud  D) Feeling bored

simple_explanation: Feeling calm, free of stress or tension. You feel relaxed when your body and mind are calm, with no worries or tension pulling at you.
example_2: She felt relaxed after the massage.
example_3: The atmosphere at the beach house was very relaxed.
collocations: feel relaxed, stay relaxed, relaxed atmosphere, completely relaxed
where_it_s_used: Weekends, vacations, spa days, casual settings
grammar_pattern: subject + feel/look/be + relaxed
common_mistake: This place makes me relaxing.
correct_version: This place makes me relaxed.
why_it_s_wrong: The person feels 'relaxed'; the place is 'relaxing'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: ri-LAKST.
etymology: From Latin "relaxare" (to loosen, ease) via "relax" + "-ed."
mnemonic: When you're RELAXED, your muscles go LAX (loose) -- no tension at all.
memory_trick: -ED = I feel it. -ING = it causes it.
visual_association: Someone lying in a hammock with their eyes closed, completely at peace.
difference_explained: Relaxed = how you feel. Relaxing = what makes you feel it.
mini_conversation:

B: Amazing -- I feel so relaxed now.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character sinks into a beach chair, sighing, "I haven't felt this relaxed in years."
news_style_line: News-style: "Health experts say a relaxed daily routine can lower stress levels significantly."
casual_conversation: Casual: "You seem so relaxed today, what's your secret?"
mcq_options: A) Feeling tense and stressed  B) Feeling calm and at ease  C) Feeling angry  D) Feeling scared

simple_explanation: Feeling unhappy or resentful because someone else has something you want. You feel jealous when you want what another person has -- their success, relationship, or belongings -- and it bothers you.
example_1: He was jealous of his brother's new car.
example_2: She felt jealous when her friend got the promotion.
example_3: He gets jealous whenever she talks to other people.
collocations: jealous of, get jealous, jealous boyfriend, extremely jealous
related_phrasal_verbs: green with envy, keep up with
grammar_pattern: jealous + of + noun (jealous of her success)
common_mistake: I am jealous with your new phone.
correct_version: I am jealous of your new phone.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'jealous OF', not 'with'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the first syllable: JEL-us.
spelling_tip: Remember the "eal" in the middle -- "jealous," not "jelous."
etymology: From Old French "jalous," ultimately from Greek "zelos" (zeal, ardent feeling) -- originally about intense devotion, narrowed to envy.
prefix_root_suffix: jeal- = root (from Greek "zelos," zeal) + -ous = adjective suffix (full of)
mnemonic: A JEALOUS person feels like their "jelly" wobbles when they see what someone else has.
memory_trick: JEALOUS: the green-eyed monster — J for 'Just want what you have'.
visual_association: A green-tinted glare aimed at someone else's shiny new possession.
difference_explained: Envious = want what someone has. Jealous = the same, or afraid of losing someone to another person.
mini_conversation:

B: That's amazing -- I'm a little jealous, honestly!

reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'feeling unhappy or resentful because someone else has something you want'?
usage_tip: 'Jealous' can be light and joking: 'I'm so jealous of your holiday!'

simple_explanation: Feeling sad because you are alone or have no one to talk to. You feel lonely when you wish you had company but don't -- it's the sad feeling of being on your own.
example_1: She felt lonely in the new city.
example_2: He felt lonely after his roommate moved out.
example_3: Moving to a new country can make you feel lonely at first.
collocations: feel lonely, lonely nights, get lonely, lonely life
where_it_s_used: Moving away, old age, being new somewhere, holidays
grammar_pattern: subject + feel/get + lonely (+ time/place expression)
common_mistake: I am lonely of my friends.
correct_version: I am lonely without my friends.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'lonely without' someone, not 'of'.
pronunciation_tip: Two syllables: LOHN-lee, stress on the first.
etymology: From "lone" (alone, shortened from "all one") + "-ly."
prefix_root_suffix: lone = root (shortened from "all one") + -ly = adjective suffix
mnemonic: LONELY = "LONE" (alone) + feeling sad about it.
memory_trick: LONELY has 'LONE' (alone) inside.
visual_association: A single empty chair at a long dinner table.
difference_explained: Alone = no one with you (neutral). Lonely = sad because you're alone.
mini_conversation:

B: Honestly, I get pretty lonely sometimes.

find_and_fix_to_correct: She is lonely from her family. → She is lonely without her family.

reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'feeling sad because you are alone or have no one to talk to'?
usage_tip: 'Lonely' is a feeling; 'alone' is just being by yourself.

simple_explanation: Feeling shocked or amazed by something unexpected. You feel surprised when something happens that you didn't expect, whether it's good or bad.
example_1: I was surprised by the news.
example_2: She was surprised to see her old classmate at the store.
example_3: We were surprised by how quickly the project finished.
collocations: totally surprised, surprised to hear, pleasantly surprised, surprised look
where_it_s_used: Parties, unexpected news, gifts, plot twists
grammar_pattern: surprised + by/at + noun / to + verb (surprised by the news / surprised to see you)
common_mistake: I am surprising about the results.
correct_version: I am surprised about the results.
why_it_s_wrong: The person is 'surprised'; the result is 'surprising'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: sur-PRYZD.
spelling_tip: Watch the silent "e" -- "surprise" + "d" = "surprised," and don't forget the "r" after "su."
etymology: From Old French "surprendre" (to overtake, catch unawares) -- "sur-" (over) + "prendre" (to take).
prefix_root_suffix: sur- (over) + pris(e) (from French "prendre," to take) + -ed (adjective suffix)
mnemonic: When you're SURPRISED, something "sur-prizes" you -- takes you over before you expect it.
memory_trick: -ED = I feel it. -ING = it causes it.
visual_association: Wide eyes and raised eyebrows, mouth slightly open.
difference_explained: Surprised = how you feel. Surprising = what makes you feel it.
mini_conversation:
A: Guess who I ran into today -- your old teacher!
B: Wow, I'm surprised, I haven't thought about her in years.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character opens the door to a room full of friends shouting, "Surprise!" and gasps, "I'm completely surprised!"
news_style_line: News-style: "Economists were surprised by the sudden drop in unemployment figures."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I was so surprised when he showed up at my door."
mcq_options: A) Feeling bored  B) Feeling shocked by something unexpected  C) Feeling calm  D) Feeling tired
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: We were all ______ when she announced her engagement. → surprised
find_and_fix_to_correct: The news was very surprised. → The news was very surprising.
translate: मैं यह खबर सुनकर हैरान रह गया। → I was surprised to hear this news.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something that surprised you this year.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'feeling shocked or amazed by something unexpected'?
usage_tip: 'Surprised at/by' is more common than 'surprised about'.

simple_explanation: Not able to think clearly or understand something. You feel confused when information doesn't make sense to you, or when you don't know what to do or believe.
example_2: She looked confused after the teacher's explanation.
example_3: He was confused about which bus to take.
collocations: totally confused, confused about, get confused, confused look
grammar_pattern: confused + about/by + noun (confused about the rules / confused by the map)
common_mistake: This explanation makes me confusing.
correct_version: This explanation makes me confused.
why_it_s_wrong: The person is 'confused'; the explanation is 'confusing'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: kun-FYOOZD.
etymology: From Latin "confundere" (to pour together, mix up) via Old French "confus."
prefix_root_suffix: con- (together) + fus(e) (from Latin "fundere," to pour) + -ed (adjective suffix)
mnemonic: When you're CONFUSED, everything is "con-fused" together in your mind, like two things melted into one messy blob.
memory_trick: -ED = I feel it. -ING = it causes it.
visual_association: A tangled ball of string with no visible end.
difference_explained: Confused = how you feel. Confusing = what makes you feel it.
mini_conversation:
A: Do you understand the new schedule?
B: Honestly, I'm still a bit confused about it.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character scratches their head at a whiteboard full of arrows, muttering, "I'm so confused right now."
news_style_line: News-style: "Many residents said they were confused by the sudden change in traffic rules."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Wait, I'm confused -- can you explain that again?"
mcq_options: A) Understanding clearly  B) Not able to think clearly  C) Feeling excited  D) Feeling calm
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The students were ______ by the complicated math problem. → confused
find_and_fix_to_correct: The instructions were very confused. → The instructions were very confusing.
translate: मैं इन निर्देशों से भ्रमित हूँ। → I am confused by these instructions.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a topic that confuses you.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'not able to think clearly or understand something'?
usage_tip: 'I'm a bit confused' is a polite way to ask for more explanation.

simple_explanation: Feeling sad because something didn't happen the way you hoped. You feel disappointed when your expectations aren't met -- something you hoped for turns out worse than you wanted.
example_1: She was disappointed with her grade.
example_2: He was disappointed when the concert was cancelled.
example_3: Her parents were disappointed by her decision.
collocations: deeply disappointed, disappointed with, disappointed in, bitterly disappointed
where_it_s_used: Exam results, sports, relationships, cancelled plans
grammar_pattern: disappointed + with/in/by + noun (disappointed with the result / disappointed in him)
common_mistake: This movie is very disappointed.
correct_version: This movie is very disappointing.
why_it_s_wrong: The movie is 'disappointing'; the viewer is 'disappointed'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the third syllable: dis-uh-POYN-tid.
etymology: From French "desappointer" (to remove from office/undo an appointment), later meaning to fail to fulfill someone's hopes.
prefix_root_suffix: dis- (not/opposite) + appoint(ed) (assigned/expected) = not turning out as expected
mnemonic: DISAPPOINTED = "dis" (not) + "appointed" (as hoped) -- things didn't turn out as you had "appointed" (planned) in your mind.
memory_trick: DISAPPOINTED: one S, two Ps.
visual_association: A deflated balloon slowly sinking to the floor.
emotion_feel: A quiet sadness mixed with unmet hope
difference_explained: Disappointed = how you feel. Disappointing = what makes you feel it.
mini_conversation:
A: How did the interview go?
B: Not great -- I'm honestly a bit disappointed with myself.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A coach shakes his head slowly and says, "I'm not angry, I'm just disappointed."
news_style_line: News-style: "Fans expressed disappointment after the match was postponed for the third time."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I was really disappointed when the trip got cancelled."
mcq_options: A) Sad because expectations weren't met  B) Excited about the future  C) Angry without reason  D) Confident and proud
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: He felt ______ when he didn't make the team. → disappointed
find_and_fix_to_correct: The results were very disappointed. → The results were very disappointing.
translate: वह अपने अंकों से निराश था। → He was disappointed with his grades.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a disappointing experience.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'feeling sad because something didn't happen the way you hoped'?
usage_tip: 'I'm disappointed in you' is strong criticism from parents or teachers.

simple_explanation: Feeling pleased because something met your expectations or needs. You feel satisfied when you get what you wanted or needed, and you don't feel like anything is missing.
example_1: I am satisfied with my job.
example_2: The customers were satisfied with the quick service.
example_3: She felt satisfied after finishing the marathon.
collocations: fully satisfied, satisfied customer, satisfied with, feel satisfied
related_phrasal_verbs: measure up, live up to expectations
where_it_s_used: Customer service, work reviews, meals, achievements
grammar_pattern: satisfied + with + noun (satisfied with the service)
common_mistake: I am satisfied of the meal.
correct_version: I am satisfied with the meal.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'satisfied WITH', not 'of'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: SAT-is-fyd.
etymology: From Latin "satisfacere" (to do enough) -- "satis" (enough) + "facere" (to do/make).
mnemonic: SATISFIED contains "satis" (Latin for "enough") -- when you have enough, you're satisfied.
memory_trick: SATIS-FIED: SATIS = enough (Latin). You've had enough.
visual_association: Someone leaning back after a good meal, hands folded, smiling gently.
difference_explained: Satisfied = your need or expectation was met. Happy is a stronger, general good feeling.
mini_conversation:
A: How was the hotel?
B: Really good -- we were very satisfied with the room.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A chef watches a diner finish their plate and smiles, "You look satisfied -- that's all I need to see."
news_style_line: News-style: "A new survey shows most employees feel satisfied with remote work options."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I'm really satisfied with how the renovation turned out."
mcq_options: A) Feeling that needs were met  B) Feeling angry  C) Feeling confused  D) Feeling bored
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: She was ______ with the quality of the product. → satisfied
find_and_fix_to_correct: He is satisfied for his new job. → He is satisfied with his new job.
translate: मैं अपनी नौकरी से संतुष्ट हूँ। → I am satisfied with my job.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something you're satisfied with.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'feeling pleased because something met your expectations or needs'?
usage_tip: 'Customer satisfaction' surveys ask if you're satisfied.

simple_explanation: Feeling calmly happy and satisfied with what you have. Being content means you're at peace with your life or situation -- you don't feel like you need more to be happy.
example_1: He is content with a simple life.
example_2: She seemed content just sitting by the lake.
example_3: They are content with their small apartment.
collocations: content with, perfectly content, feel content, content life
related_phrasal_verbs: settle for, be at peace with
where_it_s_used: Simple living, retirement, minimalism, quiet moments
grammar_pattern: content + with + noun (content with what he has)
common_mistake: I am content about my life.
correct_version: I am content with my life.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'content WITH', not 'about'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable for the adjective: kun-TENT (different from the noun CON-tent).
spelling_tip: Same spelling as the noun "content" -- context and stress tell them apart.
etymology: From Latin "contentus" (contained, satisfied), past participle of "continere" (to hold together).
prefix_root_suffix: con- (together) + ten(t) (from Latin "tenere," to hold) = holding together peacefully
mnemonic: When you're CONTENT, you're happy to stay "in" your "tent" -- no need to go anywhere else.
memory_trick: The adjective is con-TENT (stress 2nd). The noun is CON-tent (what's inside).
visual_association: Someone sitting peacefully by a window, watching the rain with a small smile.
difference_explained: con-TENT = satisfied. CON-tent = what's inside a book, video or website.
mini_conversation:
A: Don't you want a bigger house someday?
B: Not really -- I'm content with what we have.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character sits on a porch at sunset, sighing happily, "Right now, in this moment, I'm completely content."
news_style_line: News-style: "The report found that people with strong friendships tend to feel more content overall."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I'm just content spending the evening at home tonight."
mcq_options: A) Angry and restless  B) Calmly satisfied  C) Extremely excited  D) Deeply confused
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: She felt completely ______ with her quiet life in the countryside. → content
find_and_fix_to_correct: He is content for his simple life. → He is content with his simple life.
translate: वह अपनी सादी ज़िंदगी से संतुष्ट है। → He is content with his simple life.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about what makes you feel content.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'feeling calmly happy and satisfied with what you have'?
usage_tip: 'Content with little' = happy with a simple life.

simple_explanation: Feeling that good things will happen. You feel hopeful when you believe things will turn out well, even if you're not completely sure yet.
example_2: She remained hopeful despite the setback.
example_3: We're hopeful that the surgery will go well.
collocations: cautiously hopeful, remain hopeful, hopeful sign, hopeful about
related_phrasal_verbs: look on the bright side, keep the faith
where_it_s_used: Medical news, job searches, difficult times, new beginnings
grammar_pattern: hopeful + about + noun / that-clause (hopeful about the results / hopeful that it will work)
common_mistake: I am hopeful for the results will be good.
correct_version: I am hopeful that the results will be good.
why_it_s_wrong: Before a full clause, use 'that', not 'for'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the first syllable: HOHP-ful.
etymology: From "hope" (Old English "hopa") + "-ful" (full of).
mnemonic: When you're HOPEFUL, you're "full" of "hope" for good things ahead.
memory_trick: HOPE-FUL: FULL of HOPE.
visual_association: The first light of sunrise breaking over dark clouds.
difference_explained: Hopeful = hopes for one thing. Optimistic = generally expects good things.
mini_conversation:
A: Do you think you'll get the job?
B: I'm hopeful -- the interview went really well.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character looks toward the horizon and says quietly, "Whatever happens, I'm staying hopeful."
news_style_line: News-style: "Scientists remain hopeful that the new treatment will show promising results."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I'm hopeful things will get better soon."
mcq_options: A) Feeling that good things will happen  B) Feeling certain of failure  C) Feeling angry  D) Feeling bored
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Doctors are ______ that she will make a full recovery. → hopeful
find_and_fix_to_correct: He is hopeful of pass the exam. → He is hopeful of passing the exam.
translate: मुझे भविष्य को लेकर आशा है। → I am hopeful about the future.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something you're hopeful about.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'feeling that good things will happen'?
usage_tip: 'A hopeful candidate' = someone hoping to win or be chosen.

simple_explanation: Feeling that there is no hope or chance of improvement. You feel hopeless when a situation seems so bad that you believe nothing will get better, no matter what you do.
example_1: He felt hopeless about finding a solution.
example_2: She felt hopeless after failing the exam again.
example_3: The situation seemed hopeless during the storm.
collocations: feel hopeless, completely hopeless, hopeless situation, hopeless case
related_phrasal_verbs: give up on, throw in the towel
grammar_pattern: hopeless + about + noun (hopeless about the situation)
common_mistake: I am hopeless for this problem.
correct_version: I am hopeless about this problem.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'hopeless ABOUT' something. 'Hopeless AT' = very bad at a skill.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the first syllable: HOHP-lis.
etymology: "Hope" + "-less" (without) -- literally "without hope."
mnemonic: HOPELESS = HOPE + LESS -- literally, less hope than before.
memory_trick: HOPE-LESS: LESS hope — none at all.
visual_association: A single candle flickering out in total darkness.
difference_explained: Hopeless = no hope. Helpless = unable to help yourself.
mini_conversation:
A: Should we keep trying to fix the car?
B: I don't know, it feels kind of hopeless at this point.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character slumps against the wall, whispering, "It's hopeless, we're never getting out of here."
news_style_line: News-style: "Aid workers said the situation looked hopeless before international support arrived."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I felt so hopeless before I finally found a solution."
mcq_options: A) Full of hope  B) Feeling there's no chance of improvement  C) Feeling excited  D) Feeling calm
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: She felt ______ after months of searching for a job. → hopeless
find_and_fix_to_correct: This situation is hopeless of improve. → This situation is hopeless -- it won't improve.
translate: समाधान न मिलने पर वह निराश महसूस कर रहा था। → He felt hopeless about finding a solution.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something you're hopeless at.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'feeling that there is no hope or chance of improvement'?
usage_tip: 'I'm hopeless at maths' = I'm very bad at it (often joking).

simple_explanation: Feeling embarrassed or guilty because of something bad you did. You feel ashamed when you've done something wrong or embarrassing and you feel bad that others might know about it.
example_1: He was ashamed of his mistake.
example_2: She felt ashamed after lying to her parents.
example_3: He was ashamed of losing his temper in public.
collocations: ashamed of, feel ashamed, deeply ashamed, nothing to be ashamed of
related_phrasal_verbs: hang one's head, hide one's face
grammar_pattern: ashamed + of + noun/gerund (ashamed of his behavior / ashamed of lying)
common_mistake: I am ashamed for what I did.
correct_version: I am ashamed of what I did.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'ashamed OF', not 'for'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: uh-SHAYMD.
etymology: From Old English "ascamian" (to feel shame), "a-" (intensive prefix) + "sceamian" (to shame).
prefix_root_suffix: a- (intensifying prefix) + shame(d) (root: feeling of guilt/embarrassment)
mnemonic: When you're ASHAMED, you wish you could hide -- "a-shame-d" that others might see.
memory_trick: A-SHAMED: full of SHAME.
visual_association: Someone lowering their head, unable to make eye contact.
emotion_feel: Guilt mixed with a wish to hide
difference_explained: Ashamed = guilty about doing wrong. Embarrassed = awkward in front of others.
mini_conversation:
A: Why won't you look at me?
B: I'm ashamed of what I said to you yesterday.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character lowers their head and admits quietly, "I'm ashamed I let everyone down."
news_style_line: News-style: "The official said he felt ashamed after the investigation revealed the mistake."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I was so ashamed when I forgot her birthday."
mcq_options: A) Proud of an achievement  B) Feeling guilty or embarrassed  C) Feeling excited  D) Feeling calm
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: He was ______ of how he had treated his friend. → ashamed
find_and_fix_to_correct: She is ashamed about her behavior yesterday for. → She is ashamed of her behavior yesterday.
translate: वह अपनी गलती पर शर्मिंदा था। → He was ashamed of his mistake.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a time you felt ashamed of a mistake.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'feeling embarrassed or guilty because of something bad you did'?
usage_tip: 'You should be ashamed of yourself' is strong criticism.

simple_explanation: Feeling responsible for doing something wrong. You feel guilty when you know you did something wrong and it bothers your conscience.
example_2: She felt guilty for forgetting her friend's birthday.
example_3: He looked guilty when the teacher asked who broke the window.
collocations: feel guilty, guilty conscience, plead guilty, guilty about
where_it_s_used: Apologies, courtrooms, personal conscience, small mistakes
grammar_pattern: guilty + about/of + noun (guilty about lying / guilty of the crime)
common_mistake: I am guilty for eat the last cookie.
correct_version: I am guilty of eating the last cookie.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'guilty OF + -ing', not 'for + verb'.
pronunciation_tip: Two syllables: GIL-tee, stress on the first.
etymology: From Old English "gylt" (crime, sin, offense) + "-y."
mnemonic: If you feel GUILTY, it's like a heavy "guilt" sitting on your chest.
memory_trick: GUILTY: the court says 'Guilty!' — you did it.
visual_association: A small dark cloud following someone around all day.
difference_explained: Guilty = responsible for doing wrong (can be legal). Ashamed = the painful feeling about it.
mini_conversation:
A: You seem quiet -- is something wrong?
B: I feel guilty about missing your call yesterday.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character avoids eye contact, muttering, "I feel so guilty, I have to tell her the truth."
news_style_line: News-style: "The jury found the defendant guilty after a three-week trial."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I feel guilty for eating the last slice of cake."
mcq_options: A) Feeling proud  B) Feeling responsible for wrongdoing  C) Feeling calm  D) Feeling excited
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: He felt ______ after breaking his sister's toy. → guilty
find_and_fix_to_correct: She feels guilty about forget the meeting. → She feels guilty about forgetting the meeting.
translate: झूठ बोलने पर मुझे अपराधबोध महसूस हुआ। → I felt guilty about lying.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something small you feel guilty about.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'feeling responsible for doing something wrong'?
usage_tip: 'Feel guilty' = feel bad about something you did.

simple_explanation: Feeling glad that a worry or problem has ended. You feel relieved when something you were worried about turns out okay, and the stress or fear suddenly goes away.
example_1: I was relieved to pass the test.
example_2: She felt relieved when the doctor said everything was fine.
example_3: He was relieved that the flight wasn't cancelled.
collocations: greatly relieved, relieved to hear, feel relieved, relieved that
related_phrasal_verbs: breathe a sigh of relief, weight off one's shoulders
where_it_s_used: Test results, health news, safe arrivals, resolved problems
grammar_pattern: relieved + that-clause / to + verb (relieved that it's over / relieved to see you)
common_mistake: I am relieving that the exam is over.
correct_version: I am relieved that the exam is over.
why_it_s_wrong: The person feels 'relieved'. 'Relieving' is rarely used.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: ri-LEEVD.
etymology: From Old French "relever" (to raise up again) via "relieve" + "-ed" -- the sense of a burden being lifted.
prefix_root_suffix: re- (again) + liev(e) (from Latin "levare," to raise/lighten) + -ed (adjective suffix)
mnemonic: When you're RELIEVED, a heavy weight is LIFTED (relieved) off your shoulders.
memory_trick: RELIEVED: a weight is lifted — you breathe out.
visual_association: A tightly held breath finally let out in a long exhale.
difference_explained: Relaxed = calm. Relieved = happy because a worry has ended.
mini_conversation:
A: How did the surgery go?
B: It went well -- we're all so relieved.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character exhales deeply after a phone call, "Thank goodness, I'm so relieved she's safe."
news_style_line: News-style: "Families were relieved after all the miners were brought up safely."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I'm so relieved the interview is finally over."
mcq_options: A) Anxious about the future  B) Glad that a worry has ended  C) Confused about a topic  D) Proud of an achievement
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: She was ______ when she found her lost keys. → relieved
find_and_fix_to_correct: I am relieved for the test is over. → I am relieved that the test is over.
translate: परीक्षा पास करने पर मुझे राहत महसूस हुई। → I was relieved to pass the exam.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a moment you felt relieved.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'feeling glad that a worry or problem has ended'?
usage_tip: 'What a relief!' is the common exclamation.

simple_explanation: Feeling unhappy, hurt, or troubled about something. You feel upset when something has hurt your feelings or disturbed your peace of mind, whether it's big or small.
example_1: She was upset about the bad news.
example_2: He got upset when his friend cancelled last minute.
example_3: She was upset after the argument with her sister.
collocations: get upset, really upset, upset about, upset stomach
where_it_s_used: Arguments, disappointments, bad news, hurt feelings
grammar_pattern: upset + about + noun (upset about the news)
common_mistake: I am upset with the bad news.
correct_version: I am upset about the bad news.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'upset ABOUT' events and 'upset WITH' people.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable as an adjective: up-SET.
spelling_tip: One word, double "t" not needed -- "upset," not "upsett."
etymology: From "up" + "set" -- originally a nautical/mechanical term meaning to overturn, later applied to emotional disturbance.
prefix_root_suffix: up + set = compound word (no traditional prefix/root/suffix breakdown)
mnemonic: When you're UPSET, your feelings are "set up" the wrong way -- everything feels off-balance.
memory_trick: UP-SET: your feelings are SET UPside down.
visual_association: A cup knocked over, its contents spilling everywhere.
difference_explained: Angry = strong displeasure. Upset = unhappy and disturbed, often with hurt.
mini_conversation:
A: Why are you so quiet?
B: I'm just upset about what happened this morning.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character wipes their eyes and says, "I'm not mad, I'm just really upset right now."
news_style_line: News-style: "Parents were upset after the school announced sudden changes to the schedule."
casual_conversation: Casual: "She got really upset when her flight was delayed again."
mcq_options: A) Feeling calm and settled  B) Feeling unhappy or troubled  C) Feeling proud  D) Feeling bored
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: He was ______ when he lost his favorite watch. → upset
find_and_fix_to_correct: She is upset for the argument. → She is upset about the argument.
translate: बुरी खबर सुनकर वह परेशान हो गई। → She was upset about the bad news.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something that made you upset.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'feeling unhappy, hurt, or troubled about something'?
usage_tip: 'Upset stomach' = a stomach ache.

simple_explanation: Feeling slightly angry or irritated by something. You feel annoyed when something small keeps bothering you, like a repeated noise or someone's habit.
example_2: She was annoyed when her brother kept interrupting her.
example_3: He got annoyed at the slow internet connection.
collocations: get annoyed, really annoyed, annoyed at/with, mildly annoyed
related_phrasal_verbs: get on one's nerves, wind up
grammar_pattern: annoyed + at/with + person / by + thing (annoyed at him / annoyed by the noise)
common_mistake: I am annoying by the loud music.
correct_version: I am annoyed by the loud music.
why_it_s_wrong: The person feels 'annoyed'; the music is 'annoying'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: uh-NOYD.
etymology: From Old French "enoier" (to harm, weary), ultimately from Latin "in odio" (in hatred).
prefix_root_suffix: annoy = root (from Latin "in odio," in hatred) + -ed = adjective suffix (feeling)
mnemonic: When you're ANNOYED, it feels like something's constantly "on-you," bugging you.
memory_trick: -ED = I feel it. -ING = it causes it.
visual_association: A buzzing fly that won't stop circling your head.
difference_explained: Annoyed = how you feel. Annoying = what makes you feel it.
mini_conversation:
A: Why do you keep sighing?
B: I'm just annoyed -- my neighbor's dog won't stop barking.

simple_explanation: Feeling sad because you miss your home while you're away. You feel homesick when you're far from home -- studying abroad, traveling, or living elsewhere -- and you miss your family, friends, or familiar places.
example_1: She felt homesick during her first week abroad.
example_2: He got homesick after moving to a new country for college.

pronunciation_tip: Stress on the first syllable: HOHM-sik.

example_1: She was heartbroken after the breakup.

simple_explanation: Not difficult; simple to do or understand. Something is easy when it takes little effort or skill to do or understand.

simple_explanation: Not complicated; easy to understand or do. Something simple has few parts or steps, so it's easy to understand or explain, without being complicated.

simple_explanation: Made up of many connected parts; not simple. Something complex has many parts that relate to each other, which can make it hard to fully understand at once.
example_1: The human brain is very complex.
example_2: The plot of the novel is quite complex.
example_3: This is a complex issue with no easy answer.
collocations: complex system, highly complex, complex issue, complex relationship
grammar_pattern: complex + noun (complex issue) or subject + be + complex
common_mistake: This problem is too complex for solve.
correct_version: This problem is too complex to solve.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'too complex to + verb', not 'for + verb'.
pronunciation_tip: As an adjective, stress on the second syllable: kum-PLEKS.
etymology: From Latin "complexus" (embraced, entwined), past participle of "complecti" (to entwine, encompass).

mnemonic: A COMPLEX system is like many things woven or "entwined" together (from Latin "complecti").

usage_tip: A 'complex' is also a group of buildings: 'a shopping complex'.

simple_explanation: Difficult to understand or deal with because of many connected details. When something is complicated, it has so many details or steps mixed together that it becomes confusing or hard to handle.
example_2: The tax form was too complicated for beginners.
example_3: Their relationship has become complicated recently.
collocations: overly complicated, complicated process, unnecessarily complicated, get complicated
where_it_s_used: Paperwork, relationships, technical instructions, legal matters
grammar_pattern: complicated + noun (complicated process) or subject + be/get + complicated
common_mistake: This is very complicated for me understand.
correct_version: This is very complicated for me to understand.
why_it_s_wrong: 'For me to understand': 'to' is needed before the verb.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the third syllable: kom-PLIK-ay-tid.
spelling_tip: "Complicate" + "-ed" -- watch the double "c" at the start: "complicated."
etymology: From Latin "complicare" (to fold together), past participle "complicatus."
prefix_root_suffix: com- (together) + plicat(e) (from Latin "plicare," to fold) + -ed (adjective suffix)
mnemonic: Something COMPLICATED has too many things "folded" together (from Latin "complicare") -- hard to unfold and understand.
memory_trick: COMPLI-CATED: like a tangled cat's wool.
visual_association: A knot of tangled wires impossible to trace from end to end.
difference_explained: Difficult = hard to do. Complicated = hard because of many connected details.
mini_conversation:
A: How's it going with your visa application?
B: It's really complicated -- so many documents to submit.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character throws up their hands over a contract, muttering, "This is way too complicated, I need a lawyer."
news_style_line: News-style: "Analysts called the new regulations unnecessarily complicated for small businesses."
casual_conversation: Casual: "It's complicated -- can we talk about it later?"
mcq_options: A) Very easy  B) Difficult to understand because of many details  C) Extremely fun  D) Very cheap

find_and_fix_to_correct: The process is complicated to understanding. → The process is complicated to understand.
translate: यह स्थिति बहुत जटिल है। → This situation is very complicated.
