example_2: The company made a huge profit this year.
example_3: There was a huge crowd at the concert.
collocations: huge success, huge difference, huge amount, absolutely huge
related_phrasal_verbs: n/a (used mainly as a standalone adjective)

common_mistake: This is a very huge house.
correct_version: This is a huge house.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Huge' is already extreme; say 'really huge' or 'absolutely huge', not 'very huge'.
spelling_tip: "Hu" + "ge" -- the "g" is soft (like "j") because of the following "e."
etymology: From Old French "ahuge"/"ahoge," of uncertain further origin -- in English since the Middle Ages, meaning "very large."
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- "huge" is a single-morpheme root word

simple_explanation: Extremely small. "Tiny" describes something very, very small -- much smaller than what you'd normally expect.
example_2: There's a tiny chance she'll say yes.
example_3: He lives in a tiny studio apartment.
collocations: tiny bit, tiny amount, absolutely tiny, tiny piece

simple_explanation: Extremely large in size, amount, or degree. "Enormous" describes something so large it goes beyond what's normal or expected.
example_1: They live in an enormous mansion.
example_2: The company faced enormous losses this year.
example_3: There was an enormous turnout at the rally.
collocations: enormous amount, enormous pressure, absolutely enormous, enormous success
related_phrasal_verbs: n/a (used mainly as a standalone adjective)
where_it_s_used: Descriptions of size, business results, emotions, crowds
grammar_pattern: enormous + noun (enormous pressure) / an enormous amount of + noun
common_mistake: The building is very enormous.
correct_version: The building is enormous.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Enormous' is already extreme, so 'very' is not used.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: ih-NOR-muhs.
spelling_tip: "E-normous" -- single "n" after the "e," then "-mous" at the end.
etymology: From Latin "enormis" (e- "out of" + norma "rule/pattern") -- literally "out of the normal pattern," i.e., irregularly huge.
prefix_root_suffix: e- (out of) + norm (a rule/pattern) + -ous (adjective suffix, "full of") = out of the normal pattern
word_family: enormously (adv.), enormity (n., often means the "seriousness/scale" of something bad)
mnemonic: Something ENORMOUS is so big it seems out of the NORMal range -- e- (out) + norm.
memory_trick: ENORMOUS: E-NORM-OUS — out of the NORM in size.
visual_association: A single ship dwarfed beside a massive iceberg.
emotion_feel: Awe, sometimes slight fear or being overwhelmed
difference_explained: Same meaning. Enormous sounds slightly more formal.
mini_conversation:
A: How was the turnout at the event?
B: Enormous -- way more people came than we expected.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A sailor stares at the wave and shouts, "It's enormous -- brace yourselves!"
news_style_line: News-style: "The charity raised an enormous amount of money for flood victims this month."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I felt enormous relief when the results finally came in."
mcq_options: A) Extremely small  B) Extremely large  C) Somewhat unusual  D) Perfectly average
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Losing his job put ______ pressure on the family's finances. → enormous
find_and_fix_to_correct: It's a very enormous house. → It's an enormous house. (avoid "very" with "enormous" since it's already an extreme adjective)
translate: उस इमारत का आकार बहुत विशाल है। → The size of that building is enormous.

simple_explanation: Very large and heavy or powerful. "Massive" describes something impressively big, whether it's a physical object, an amount, or an impact.
example_1: They built a massive bridge across the river.
example_2: The company suffered a massive financial loss.
example_3: There was a massive earthquake in the region last year.
collocations: massive impact, massive amount, absolutely massive, massive scale
related_phrasal_verbs: n/a (used mainly as a standalone adjective)
grammar_pattern: massive + noun (a massive building) / on a massive scale
common_mistake: There was a massive traffic.
correct_version: There was massive traffic.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Traffic' is uncountable, so no 'a'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the first syllable: MASS-iv.
etymology: From French "massif" (Latin "massa," a lump/mass) -- literally "having great mass," i.e., very large and heavy.
prefix_root_suffix: mass (root, a lump/large quantity) + -ive (adjective suffix, "having the quality of") = having great mass
mnemonic: Something MASSIVE has a huge MASS (weight and size).
memory_trick: MASSIVE: full of MASS.
visual_association: A boulder so large it blocks an entire road.
difference_explained: Heavy = weighs a lot. Massive = very large and heavy, or very big in amount.
mini_conversation:
A: How big was the crowd at the stadium?
B: Massive -- probably the biggest I've ever seen.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A general studies the map and mutters, "We're facing a massive force -- we need reinforcements."
news_style_line: News-style: "The storm caused massive damage across the coastal towns."
casual_conversation: Casual: "That was a massive mistake on my part, honestly."

usage_tip: Informal: 'massive' = very big or important ('a massive win').

simple_explanation: Extremely large, like a giant from a story. "Giant" describes something so large it reminds you of the mythical giants from folk tales -- much bigger than normal.
example_1: They planted a giant pumpkin this year.
example_2: The tech giant announced a new product launch.
example_3: A giant wave crashed over the boat.
collocations: giant screen, giant leap, industry giant, giant panda
related_phrasal_verbs: n/a (used mainly as a standalone adjective/noun)
grammar_pattern: giant + noun (a giant screen) / noun + giant (industry giant, compound-noun use)
common_mistake: This company is a very giant.
correct_version: This company is a giant.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Giant' is already extreme; 'very' isn't used with it.
etymology: From Greek "gigas" (a mythical giant), via Latin "gigas" and Old French "geant" -- originally a mythological huge being, now a general word for very large.
prefix_root_suffix: gi(g)ant = root (Greek "gigas," a mythical huge being) -- no separable prefix/suffix
mnemonic: A GIANT is a mythical huge creature -- use the word for anything that seems that big.
memory_trick: GIANT: like the giant in stories.
visual_association: A skyscraper next to a tiny bicycle parked outside.
difference_explained: Large = big. Giant = extremely big.

simple_explanation: Very great in degree; far beyond what is usual. "Extreme" describes something at the very highest or most intense level -- much more than what's normal or moderate.
example_1: They experienced extreme heat during the trip.
example_2: He took extreme measures to protect his family.
example_3: The region suffers from extreme poverty.
collocations: extreme weather, extreme measures, extreme caution, in extreme cases
related_phrasal_verbs: n/a (used mainly as a standalone adjective)
grammar_pattern: extreme + noun (extreme weather) / to the extreme (as a phrase)
common_mistake: The weather was very extreme yesterday.
correct_version: The weather was extreme yesterday.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Extreme' is already at the top of the scale, so 'very' isn't needed.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: ik-STREEM.
etymology: From Latin "extremus" (superlative of "exter," outer) -- literally "outermost," extended to mean "to the highest degree."
prefix_root_suffix: extrem(e) = root (Latin "extremus," outermost) -- no separable prefix/suffix
mnemonic: EXTREME comes from "EXTRA" -- extreme weather is EXTRA intense.
memory_trick: EXTREME: at the EXTREME end of the line.
visual_association: A thermometer with its needle pushed all the way to the red zone.
difference_explained: Extreme = at the very end of a scale. Severe = very serious or harsh.
tone: Neutral to Negative (often used for danger/difficulty)

B: Because of the extreme weather warning this morning.

simple_explanation: Average in amount, degree, or intensity; neither too much nor too little. "Moderate" describes something balanced and reasonable -- not extreme in either direction.
example_1: They expect moderate rainfall this week.
example_2: Moderate exercise is good for your heart.
example_3: There was moderate traffic on the way home.
collocations: moderate exercise, moderate amount, moderate temperatures, in moderate quantities
related_phrasal_verbs: n/a (used mainly as a standalone adjective)
where_it_s_used: Weather, exercise, politics, food, lifestyle advice
grammar_pattern: moderate + noun (moderate exercise) / in moderate amounts
common_mistake: The weather is very moderate today.
correct_version: The weather is moderate today.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Moderate' already means a middle level, so 'very' sounds odd.
pronunciation_tip: As an adjective, stress the first syllable: MOD-er-it (the verb "to moderate" ends differently: MOD-er-ayt).
etymology: From Latin "moderatus" (moderare -- to control/regulate) -- kept within reasonable limits, not extreme.
prefix_root_suffix: moder(ate) = root (Latin "moderare," to control/regulate) -- no separable prefix/suffix
mnemonic: MODERATE things stay in the MIDDLE -- not too hot, not too cold.
memory_trick: MODERATE: in the MODE of balance — not too much, not too little.
visual_association: A dial set exactly in the middle, not at either extreme.
difference_explained: Medium = middle size. Moderate = middle amount or degree.

B: Just a moderate amount, maybe one cup a day.

casual_conversation: Casual: "I try to keep my spending moderate, especially during the holidays."

simple_explanation: Gentle or not very strong or severe. "Mild" describes something soft, gentle, or weak in intensity -- not extreme in any way.
example_1: The curry has a mild flavor.
example_2: We had mild weather all week.
example_3: She has a mild case of the flu.
collocations: mild weather, mild flavor, mild case, relatively mild
related_phrasal_verbs: n/a (used mainly as a standalone adjective)
grammar_pattern: mild + noun (mild weather) / a mild case of + noun
common_mistake: The winter was very mild than usual.
correct_version: The winter was milder than usual.
why_it_s_wrong: For comparison, use 'milder than', not 'very mild than'.
spelling_tip: "Mild" -- just four letters; don't confuse with "mold" or "milled."
etymology: From Old English "milde" -- gentle, not harsh; a Germanic root shared with other Germanic languages' words for "gentle."
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- "mild" is a single-morpheme root word
mnemonic: MILD rhymes with CHILD -- think of a gentle, MILD voice you'd use with a child.
memory_trick: MILD: soft and gentle, like mild soap.
visual_association: A gentle breeze on a warm, sunny afternoon.
difference_explained: Soft = easy to press, or quiet. Mild = gentle, not strong or severe.
mini_conversation:

B: No, it's actually pretty mild -- perfect for kids.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A chef reassures the guest, "Don't worry, this dish is quite mild -- it won't be too spicy."
news_style_line: News-style: "Meteorologists say the region can expect a mild winter this year."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I only have a mild headache, nothing serious."

simple_explanation: Very serious, harsh, or intense. "Severe" describes something extreme in a bad way -- very serious, painful, strict, or damaging.
example_1: He suffered a severe injury in the accident.
example_2: The region experienced a severe drought last summer.
example_3: She received a severe punishment for the mistake.
collocations: severe weather, severe pain, severe shortage, severe consequences
related_phrasal_verbs: n/a (used mainly as a standalone adjective)
grammar_pattern: severe + noun (severe damage) / suffer severe + noun
common_mistake: The pain was very severe than before.
correct_version: The pain was more severe than before.
why_it_s_wrong: For comparison, use 'more severe than'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: suh-VEER.
etymology: From Latin "severus" (strict, serious), via Old French "severe" -- describing something harsh or strict.
prefix_root_suffix: sever(e) = root (Latin "severus," strict/harsh) -- no separable prefix/suffix
mnemonic: SEVERE sounds like "so severe" -- a SEVERE storm is SO serious.
memory_trick: SEVERE: like a SEVERE storm that cuts everything.

casual_conversation: Casual: "My allergies have been severe this spring, honestly."

simple_explanation: Very strong or extreme in feeling, degree, or effect. "Intense" describes something felt or experienced very strongly -- emotions, heat, effort, or focus at a high level.
example_1: The match ended with an intense final round.
example_2: She felt an intense wave of relief after the exam.
example_3: The training program is physically intense.
collocations: intense heat, intense pressure, intense competition, absolutely intense
related_phrasal_verbs: n/a (used mainly as a standalone adjective)
grammar_pattern: intense + noun (intense heat) / feel intense + emotion
common_mistake: The feeling was very intense than before.
correct_version: The feeling was more intense than before.
why_it_s_wrong: For comparison, use 'more intense than'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: in-TENS.
spelling_tip: "In-" + "tense" -- note the single "s" before the final "e."
etymology: From Latin "intensus" (past participle of "intendere," to stretch out/strain), via French "intense" -- stretched to a high degree.
prefix_root_suffix: in- (into) + tens(e) (from Latin "tendere," to stretch) = stretched to a high degree
mnemonic: An INTENSE moment feels so TENSE you can barely breathe.
memory_trick: INTENSE: IN TENSion — strong and tight.
visual_association: A pot of water boiling rapidly over high heat.
difference_explained: Intense = very strong (intense heat). Intensive = concentrated effort (an intensive course).
mini_conversation:
A: How was the interview?
B: Honestly, pretty intense -- they asked some tough questions.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A coach warns the team, "Get ready -- the next five minutes are going to be intense."
news_style_line: News-style: "Firefighters battled intense flames throughout the night."
casual_conversation: Casual: "That workout was intense -- I can barely walk today."
mcq_options: A) Very weak  B) Very strong in feeling or degree  C) Completely boring  D) Slightly unusual
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The final scene of the movie was incredibly ______. → intense

simple_explanation: Small in amount or degree; barely noticeable. "Slight" describes something so small it's almost not worth mentioning -- a tiny amount or a minor difference.
example_1: There's a slight chance of rain today.
example_2: She has a slight accent when she speaks English.
example_3: There was a slight delay on the flight.
collocations: slight chance, slight delay, slight increase, slight difference
related_phrasal_verbs: n/a (used mainly as a standalone adjective)
where_it_s_used: Weather forecasts, health, description of change, apologies
grammar_pattern: slight + noun (a slight problem) / a slight + comparative noun (a slight increase)
common_mistake: There is a slightly problem.
correct_version: There is a slight problem.
why_it_s_wrong: Before a noun, use the adjective 'slight'. 'Slightly' is the adverb.
etymology: From Old Norse "slettr" (smooth/slender), via Middle English -- originally meant "slim," now used more for "small in degree."
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- "slight" is a single-morpheme root word
mnemonic: A SLIGHT change is so small it's barely in SIGHT.
memory_trick: SLIGHT: a LIGHT amount.
visual_association: A thermometer needle moving just one small notch.
difference_explained: Slight = adjective (a slight problem). Slightly = adverb (slightly late).
mini_conversation:
A: Is there any change in his condition?
B: Just a slight improvement so far.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A pilot announces calmly, "We're expecting a slight delay due to weather -- nothing serious."
news_style_line: News-style: "Economists reported a slight increase in consumer spending last month."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I have a slight headache, but I'll be fine."
mcq_options: A) Very large  B) Small in amount or degree  C) Completely absent  D) Extremely serious
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: There's been a ______ change in the schedule. → slight
find_and_fix_to_correct: He has a slightly headache. → He has a slight headache. (use the adjective "slight" before a noun, not the adverb "slightly")
translate: उसके बोलने में हल्का सा विदेशी लहजा है। → He has a slight foreign accent when he speaks.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a slight change in your routine.

simple_explanation: Large enough to be important or noticed; fairly large. "Considerable" describes an amount, effort, or effect that's significant -- big enough that people have to take it seriously.
example_1: They spent a considerable amount of time on the project.
example_2: The company made considerable progress this year.
example_3: There was considerable interest in the new product.
collocations: considerable amount, considerable effort, considerable success, considerable time
related_phrasal_verbs: n/a (used mainly as a standalone adjective)
where_it_s_used: Business reports, academic writing, achievements, statistics
grammar_pattern: a considerable amount of + noun / considerable + noun (considerable effort)
common_mistake: He has considerable of experience in this field.
correct_version: He has considerable experience in this field.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Considerable' goes straight before the noun, with no 'of'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: kuhn-SID-er-uh-buhl.
etymology: From Latin "considerare" (to examine closely, con- "together" + sider- relating to "sidus," star) + "-able" -- originally "worth considering," now "fairly large in amount."
prefix_root_suffix: consider (root, to think about carefully) + -able (suffix, "worthy of") = worth considering (i.e., significant)
mnemonic: A CONSIDERABLE amount is big enough that you have to CONSIDER it seriously.
memory_trick: CONSIDER-ABLE: big enough to CONSIDER.
visual_association: A stack of papers growing noticeably taller and taller.
difference_explained: Considerable = large. Considerate = kind and thoughtful.
mini_conversation:
A: How much did the renovation cost?
B: A considerable amount, actually -- more than we expected.
everyday_scene: Everyday: An advisor reports to the board, "We've made considerable progress, but there's still work to do."
news_style_line: News-style: "The city invested a considerable sum in upgrading public parks this year."
casual_conversation: Casual: "It took considerable effort to finish the marathon."
mcq_options: A) Very small and unimportant  B) Large enough to be significant  C) Completely free  D) Extremely rare
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The new policy caused ______ debate among lawmakers. → considerable
find_and_fix_to_correct: She is very considerable in her field. → She has considerable experience in her field. ("considerable" describes amounts/qualities, not a person directly)
translate: इस काम में उन्होंने काफ़ी मेहनत की। → They put in considerable effort on this work.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about someone with considerable experience.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'large enough to be important or noticed; fairly large'?
usage_tip: 'At considerable cost' = at a high cost.

simple_explanation: Large in amount, size, or importance. "Substantial" describes something big enough or important enough to have a real, noticeable effect.
example_1: They made substantial changes to the design.
example_2: The company reported substantial growth this quarter.
example_3: She received a substantial raise after the promotion.
collocations: substantial amount, substantial evidence, substantial increase, substantial progress
related_phrasal_verbs: n/a (used mainly as a standalone adjective)
where_it_s_used: Business, academic writing, finance, legal contexts
grammar_pattern: a substantial amount of + noun / substantial + noun (substantial evidence)
common_mistake: He earns substantial money than before.
correct_version: He earns substantially more money than before.
why_it_s_wrong: Before 'more', use the adverb 'substantially'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: suhb-STAN-shuhl.
etymology: From Latin "substantia" (that which stands beneath, sub- "under" + stare "to stand") -- originally philosophical ("of real substance"), now used for "large in amount."
prefix_root_suffix: sub- (under) + stant (from Latin "stare," to stand) + -ial (adjective suffix) = standing as real substance
word_family: substance (n.), substantially (adv.), substantiate (v., to prove/support with evidence)
mnemonic: Something SUBSTANTIAL has real SUBSTANCE behind it -- it's not just a small amount.
memory_trick: SUBSTANTIAL: has real SUBSTANCE.
visual_association: A thick stack of solid evidence files on a desk.
difference_explained: Substantial = adjective (a substantial increase). Substantially = adverb (increased substantially).
mini_conversation:
A: Did the new policy make a difference?
B: Yes, actually -- a substantial one.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A lawyer tells the jury, "The evidence presented here is substantial and cannot be ignored."
news_style_line: News-style: "The report showed substantial improvements in air quality this year."
casual_conversation: Casual: "We'd need a substantial budget increase to make that happen."
mcq_options: A) Very small or minor  B) Large in amount or importance  C) Completely free  D) Very rare
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Fixing the roof will require a ______ amount of money. → substantial
find_and_fix_to_correct: This is a substantial for our team. → This is substantial for our team. (drop the article "a" before the predicate adjective "substantial")
translate: कंपनी को इस साल पर्याप्त लाभ हुआ। → The company made substantial profit this year.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a substantial change in your city.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'large in amount, size, or importance'?
usage_tip: 'A substantial meal' = a large, filling meal.

simple_explanation: The smallest amount or level possible. "Minimal" describes something reduced to the least amount necessary -- very little, often on purpose.
example_1: The design has a minimal style.
example_2: We hope to keep costs to a minimal level.
example_3: The damage from the storm was minimal.
collocations: minimal effort, minimal impact, minimal risk, keep to a minimal
related_phrasal_verbs: n/a (used mainly as a standalone adjective)
where_it_s_used: Design, business risk, health, environmental impact
grammar_pattern: minimal + noun (minimal effort) / with minimal + noun (with minimal risk)
common_mistake: The effect was very minimal.
correct_version: The effect was minimal.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Minimal' already means the smallest, so 'very' is avoided.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the first syllable: MIH-nuh-muhl.
spelling_tip: "Minim" + "-al" -- related to "minimum," keep the same root spelling.
etymology: From Latin "minimus" (smallest, superlative of "parvus," small) -- the least possible amount.
prefix_root_suffix: minim (root, Latin "minimus," smallest) + -al (adjective suffix, "relating to") = relating to the smallest amount
mnemonic: MINIMAL is the MINIMUM amount -- as little as possible.
memory_trick: MINIMAL: MINIMUM.
visual_association: A nearly empty glass with just a single drop of water inside.
difference_explained: Little = small amount. Minimal = the smallest possible amount.
mini_conversation:
A: How much did the flood damage the store?
B: Luckily, the damage was minimal.
everyday_scene: Everyday: An engineer reports, "With this design, the risk of failure is minimal."
news_style_line: News-style: "City officials confirmed the power outage caused only minimal disruption."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I'm trying to keep my phone use minimal this week."
mcq_options: A) The largest possible amount  B) The smallest possible amount  C) An average amount  D) An unknown amount
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The team achieved great results with ______ resources. → minimal
find_and_fix_to_correct: We need minimal of effort for this. → We need minimal effort for this. (no "of" needed -- "minimal" directly modifies "effort")
translate: तूफ़ान से नुकसान बहुत कम हुआ। → The damage from the storm was minimal.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a job that needs minimal effort.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'the smallest amount or level possible'?
usage_tip: 'Minimal design' = simple, with little decoration.

simple_explanation: Important enough to be noticed or to matter. "Significant" describes something big or important enough to have a real effect or meaning.
example_1: There was a significant improvement in her grades.
example_2: The discovery had a significant impact on medicine.
example_3: There's a significant difference between the two plans.
collocations: significant impact, significant progress, significant difference, statistically significant
related_phrasal_verbs: n/a (used mainly as a standalone adjective)
where_it_s_used: Science, business, academic research, personal achievements
grammar_pattern: significant + noun (a significant change) / play a significant role in + noun
common_mistake: This is a significant to our success.
correct_version: This is significant to our success.
why_it_s_wrong: As an adjective after 'is', 'significant' takes no 'a'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: sig-NIF-ih-kuhnt.
spelling_tip: "Sign" + "-ificant" -- notice the word "sign" hidden at the start.
etymology: From Latin "significare" (to signify/indicate, signum "sign" + facere "to make") -- literally "making a sign," i.e., meaningful.
prefix_root_suffix: sign (root, a mark/indicator) + -ificant (adjective-forming ending, from Latin "facere," to make) = making a meaningful mark
mnemonic: A SIGNIFICANT event leaves a SIGN (mark) that matters.
memory_trick: SIGN-IFICANT: a SIGN that something matters.
visual_association: A graph line jumping sharply upward at one clear point.
emotion_feel: Seriousness, sometimes excitement or concern depending on context
difference_explained: Important = matters. Significant = large or important enough to notice.
mini_conversation:
A: Did the new medicine help?
B: Yes, there was a significant improvement in just a week.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A researcher tells her team, "These results are significant -- this could change everything."
news_style_line: News-style: "Scientists reported a significant breakthrough in renewable energy research."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Losing that client was a significant setback for us."
mcq_options: A) Completely unimportant  B) Important enough to matter  C) Extremely small  D) Very cheap
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: There has been a ______ rise in online shopping this year. → significant
find_and_fix_to_correct: This news is significantly for us. → This news is significant for us. (use the adjective "significant," not the adverb "significantly," after "is")
translate: उसके काम में एक महत्वपूर्ण बदलाव आया। → There was a significant change in his work.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a significant day in your life.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'important enough to be noticed or to matter'?
usage_tip: 'Significant other' = a partner.

simple_explanation: Too small or unimportant to matter. "Insignificant" describes something so small or minor that it doesn't really affect anything.
example_1: The mistake was insignificant compared to the overall success.
example_2: His contribution seemed insignificant at first, but it mattered later.
example_3: The price difference is insignificant.
collocations: relatively insignificant, seem insignificant, insignificant amount, insignificant detail
related_phrasal_verbs: n/a (used mainly as a standalone adjective)
grammar_pattern: insignificant + noun (an insignificant detail) / seem insignificant
common_mistake: This amount is insignificant for change anything.
correct_version: This amount is too insignificant to change anything.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'too insignificant to + verb', not 'for + verb'.
pronunciation_tip: Five syllables, stress on the fourth: in-sig-NIF-ih-kuhnt.
spelling_tip: "In-" + "significant" -- keep the "sign" root inside the negative form.
etymology: "In-" (not) + "significant" -- a straightforward negative prefix on the Latin-derived "significant."
mnemonic: Something INSIGNIFICANT leaves no meaningful SIGN behind -- it just doesn't matter.
memory_trick: IN-SIGNIFICANT: NOT significant.
visual_association: A single grain of sand on a huge beach.
difference_explained: Same meaning. Insignificant is more formal.
mini_conversation:
A: Should we worry about that small error?
B: No, it's completely insignificant.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character stares at the stars and murmurs, "Out here, our problems feel so insignificant."
news_style_line: News-style: "Analysts said the price change was statistically insignificant."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Don't worry about the typo, it's insignificant."
mcq_options: A) Extremely important  B) Too small to matter  C) Very expensive  D) Well organized
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Compared to last year's loss, this year's dip in sales feels ______. → insignificant
find_and_fix_to_correct: It is insignificant thing. → It is an insignificant thing. (don't forget the article "an" before a singular countable noun)
translate: उसकी गलती इतनी बड़ी सफलता के सामने महत्वहीन लगी। → His mistake seemed insignificant next to such a big success.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a problem that seemed big but was insignificant.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'too small or unimportant to matter'?
usage_tip: Used to say something is too small to worry about.

simple_explanation: Extremely large in area, amount, or extent. "Vast" describes something huge in scale, often used for wide open spaces, big amounts, or large ranges of knowledge.
example_1: The desert stretched out over a vast area.
example_2: She has a vast knowledge of history.
example_3: The company controls a vast network of stores.
collocations: vast amount, vast area, vast majority, vast knowledge
related_phrasal_verbs: n/a (used mainly as a standalone adjective)
grammar_pattern: vast + noun (a vast area) / the vast majority of + noun
common_mistake: India is a vast country with vast population.
correct_version: India is a vast country with a huge population.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Vast' is for areas and amounts. For population, 'huge' or 'large' is more natural.
spelling_tip: "V" + "ast" -- just four letters, don't add an extra "s."
etymology: From Latin "vastus" (empty, immense) -- describing huge, often open, expanses.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- "vast" is a single-morpheme root word (from Latin "vastus")
mnemonic: VAST rhymes with FAST -- picture flying FAST across a VAST desert that never seems to end.
memory_trick: VAST: a VAST desert — endless.
visual_association: An open ocean stretching to the horizon with no land in sight.
difference_explained: Wide = large from side to side. Vast = extremely large in area or amount.
mini_conversation:
A: How big is the Sahara?
B: It's absolutely vast -- it covers most of North Africa.
everyday_scene: Everyday: An explorer looks out and says, "The jungle stretches on, vast and endless, as far as I can see."
news_style_line: News-style: "The company has built a vast network of suppliers across the region."
casual_conversation: Casual: "The library here has a vast collection of old manuscripts."
mcq_options: A) Extremely small  B) Extremely large in area or amount  C) Somewhat unusual  D) Very expensive
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The ______ majority of students passed the final exam. → vast
find_and_fix_to_correct: This land is a vast of area. → This is a vast area of land. (rearrange -- "vast" directly modifies "area," no "of" needed here)
translate: उसे इतिहास का अपार ज्ञान है। → He has a vast knowledge of history.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a vast place you have visited.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'extremely large in area, amount, or extent'?
usage_tip: 'The vast majority' = almost all.

simple_explanation: Extremely large; huge beyond normal measure. "Immense" describes something so big that it's hard to fully measure or grasp -- often used for size, effort, or feelings.
example_1: She felt immense pride in her son's achievement.
example_2: The project required an immense amount of effort.
example_3: There was immense pressure to finish the report on time.
collocations: immense pressure, immense pride, immense amount, immense relief
related_phrasal_verbs: n/a (used mainly as a standalone adjective)
grammar_pattern: immense + noun (immense pride) / feel immense + emotion
common_mistake: It gave me immense of pleasure.
correct_version: It gave me immense pleasure.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Immense' goes straight before the noun, with no 'of'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: ih-MENS.
etymology: From Latin "immensus" (in- "not" + mensus, past participle of "metiri," to measure) -- literally "immeasurable," i.e., too big to measure.
prefix_root_suffix: im- (not) + mens(e) (from Latin "metiri," to measure) = not able to be measured
mnemonic: IMMENSE literally means "not able to be MEASURED" -- too big to measure!
memory_trick: IM-MENSE: can't be MEASURED.
visual_association: A single small boat crossing an immense, endless ocean.
emotion_feel: Overwhelming emotion, whether positive or negative depending on context
difference_explained: Same meaning. Immense is more formal and often used for feelings.
mini_conversation:
A: How did you feel when you finished the marathon?
B: Honestly, immense relief and pride.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A father hugs his daughter and says, "I feel immense pride watching you graduate today."
news_style_line: News-style: "The disaster caused immense suffering for thousands of families."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I owe you an immense thank-you for helping me move."
mcq_options: A) Extremely small  B) Extremely large or great  C) Slightly annoying  D) Perfectly average
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Winning the award brought her ______ joy. → immense
find_and_fix_to_correct: It's a very immense challenge. → It's an immense challenge. (avoid "very" with "immense" since it's already an extreme adjective)
translate: उसे अपने बेटे की सफलता पर अपार गर्व हुआ। → She felt immense pride in her son's success.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a person you feel immense respect for.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'extremely large; huge beyond normal measure'?
usage_tip: 'Immense pleasure', 'immense gratitude' — formal and strong.

simple_explanation: More than enough; plenty. "Ample" describes an amount that's generously sufficient -- there's plenty, with room to spare.
example_1: There's ample parking near the venue.
example_2: We have ample time to finish the project.
example_3: The kitchen has ample storage space.
collocations: ample time, ample opportunity, ample space, ample evidence
related_phrasal_verbs: n/a (used mainly as a standalone adjective)
grammar_pattern: ample + noun (ample time) / have ample + noun + to + verb
common_mistake: We have very ample food for the party.
correct_version: We have ample food for the party.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Ample' already means more than enough, so 'very' isn't needed.
spelling_tip: "Am-" + "-ple" -- just five letters, don't confuse with "apple."
etymology: From Latin "amplus" (large, spacious), via French "ample" -- more than enough, generously sized.
prefix_root_suffix: ampl(e) = root (Latin "amplus," large/spacious) -- no separable prefix/suffix
mnemonic: AMPLE sounds like "AMPLE apple pie" -- so much pie there's plenty for everyone!
memory_trick: AMPLE: AMPLE room, like an AMPlifier makes sound more than enough.
visual_association: A table overflowing with more food than the guests could possibly eat.
difference_explained: Enough = as much as needed. Ample = more than enough.
mini_conversation:
A: Will we have enough time to pack?
B: Yes, we have ample time before the flight.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A host welcomes the guests, saying, "Please, help yourselves -- there's ample food for everyone."
news_style_line: News-style: "Officials confirmed there is ample water supply for the summer season."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Don't rush, we have ample time before the meeting."
mcq_options: A) Barely enough  B) More than enough; plenty  C) Completely absent  D) Extremely rare
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The new office has ______ space for the whole team. → ample
find_and_fix_to_correct: There is ample of room in the car. → There is ample room in the car. (no "of" needed -- "ample" directly modifies "room")
translate: हमारे पास तैयारी के लिए पर्याप्त समय है। → We have ample time to prepare.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a place with ample space.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'more than enough; plenty'?
usage_tip: 'Ample parking' = plenty of parking.

simple_explanation: Not enough of something; hard to find. "Scarce" describes something that's in short supply -- there isn't much of it available.
example_1: Clean water was scarce during the drought.
example_2: Jobs are scarce in this small town.
example_3: Fresh vegetables became scarce during the winter storm.
collocations: scarce resources, increasingly scarce, become scarce, scarce supply
related_phrasal_verbs: n/a (used mainly as a standalone adjective)
grammar_pattern: scarce + noun (scarce resources) / become scarce
common_mistake: Water is very scarce than before in this area.
correct_version: Water is scarcer than before in this area.
why_it_s_wrong: For comparison, use 'scarcer', not 'very scarce than'.
etymology: From Old French "escars" (scanty), via Vulgar Latin "excarpsus" (picked out, limited) -- describing something in short supply.
prefix_root_suffix: scarc(e) = root (Old French "escars," scanty) -- no separable prefix/suffix
mnemonic: SCARCE rhymes with "stairs are bare" -- when resources are SCARCE, the shelves are BARE.
memory_trick: SCARCE: so few that it's SCARY.
visual_association: An empty shelf in a store with just a few items left.
difference_explained: Rare = not common. Scarce = not enough of something needed.
mini_conversation:
A: Why are prices so high right now?
B: Because supplies have become really scarce lately.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A survivor rations the last of the food and says, "Supplies are scarce -- we have to make this last."
news_style_line: News-style: "Farmers reported that rainfall has become increasingly scarce this decade."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Good apartments are scarce in this neighborhood right now."
mcq_options: A) Available in large amounts  B) Not enough; hard to find  C) Extremely cheap  D) Perfectly balanced
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Affordable housing has become ______ in the city center. → scarce
find_and_fix_to_correct: Food is scarce for people to find. → Food is scarce, so it's hard for people to find. ("scarce" describes availability itself -- don't follow it directly with "for people to find")

write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something scarce in summer.

reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'not enough of something; hard to find'?
usage_tip: 'Make yourself scarce' = go away quickly.

simple_explanation: Existing in large quantities; plentiful. "Abundant" describes something that's available in great supply -- there's more than enough.
example_1: The region has abundant natural resources.
example_2: Fresh fruit is abundant during the summer months.
example_3: The forest is home to abundant wildlife.
collocations: abundant supply, abundant wildlife, abundant resources, abundantly clear
related_phrasal_verbs: n/a (used mainly as a standalone adjective)
grammar_pattern: abundant + noun (abundant rainfall) / be abundant in + noun (abundant in minerals)
common_mistake: This place is very abundant of fish.
correct_version: This place is abundant in fish.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'abundant IN', not 'of'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: uh-BUHN-duhnt.
spelling_tip: "Abund" + "-ant" -- related to "abundance," keep the same root spelling.
etymology: From Latin "abundare" (to overflow, ab- "away" + undare "to rise in waves," from "unda," a wave) -- literally "overflowing," i.e., plentiful.
prefix_root_suffix: ab- (away/from) + und(ant) (from Latin "unda," a wave -- to overflow) = overflowing with plenty
mnemonic: ABUNDANT resources make everything ABOUND -- overflowing with plenty.
memory_trick: ABUNDANT: a BUNch of it, plenty.
visual_association: A basket overflowing with ripe fruit at a farmers' market.
difference_explained: Abundant = adjective (abundant water). Plenty = pronoun or noun (plenty of water).
mini_conversation:
A: Is fishing good around here?
B: Yes, the lake has abundant fish this time of year.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A farmer surveys the field and smiles, "This has been our most abundant harvest in years."
news_style_line: News-style: "Researchers found abundant evidence linking the two events."
casual_conversation: Casual: "The market has abundant fresh produce this week."
mcq_options: A) Very rare and hard to find  B) Existing in large quantities  C) Extremely expensive  D) Completely missing

find_and_fix_to_correct: There are abundant of opportunities here. → There are abundant opportunities here. (no "of" needed -- "abundant" directly modifies "opportunities")
translate: इस क्षेत्र में प्राकृतिक संसाधन प्रचुर मात्रा में हैं। → This region has abundant natural resources.

simple_explanation: Having a lot of room; large and open. A spacious place gives you plenty of room to move, store things, or relax without feeling squeezed in.
example_1: Their new house is very spacious.
example_2: The hotel room was surprisingly spacious for the price.
example_3: We looked for a spacious apartment with a big kitchen.
collocations: spacious room, spacious garden, feel spacious, light and spacious
related_phrasal_verbs: n/a (no strong phrasal-verb link, compare "open up, " "stretch out")
where_it_s_used: Real estate, hotel reviews, interior design, travel
grammar_pattern: spacious + noun / be + spacious (a spacious kitchen / The hall is spacious.)
common_mistake: This car has a spacious for five people.
correct_version: This car is spacious enough for five people.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'is spacious', not 'has a spacious'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress the first syllable: SPAY-shus, and note the "ci" makes a "sh" sound.
spelling_tip: Remember the "ci" spelling for the "sh" sound, like in "gracious" and "precious."
etymology: From Latin "spatiosus" (roomy), from "spatium" (space), via Old French "spacieux."
prefix_root_suffix: spac(e) = root (Latin spatium) + -ious = adjective suffix meaning "full of"
mnemonic: SPACIOUS has "SPACE" hidden right at the start -- lots of space to move around.
memory_trick: SPACIOUS: full of SPACE.
visual_association: A big, sunlit living room with wide-open floor space.
difference_explained: Big = large. Spacious = has a lot of room inside.
mini_conversation:
A: How's the new flat?
B: Really spacious -- we finally have room for a proper dining table.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A realtor swings the door open and announces, "As you can see, the living room is wonderfully spacious."
news_style_line: News-style: "The new community center features a spacious hall that can host over three hundred guests."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I love how spacious your balcony is -- you could fit a whole garden out here."
mcq_options: A) Narrow and tight  B) Having plenty of room  C) Expensive  D) Dark and gloomy
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The museum's ______ lobby can hold hundreds of visitors at once. → spacious
find_and_fix_to_correct: The garden is more spacious than the old one house. → The garden is more spacious than the old house.
translate: उनका नया फ्लैट बहुत विशाल है। → Their new flat is very spacious.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about the most spacious room in your home.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'having a lot of room; large and open'?
usage_tip: Property ads: 'spacious 2BHK flat'.

simple_explanation: Too small and tightly packed to move comfortably. A cramped space makes you feel squeezed in -- there isn't enough room for people or things to move freely.
example_1: The office felt cramped with five desks.
example_2: Six of us shared a cramped tent during the trip.
example_3: The old kitchen was cramped and hard to cook in.
collocations: cramped space, feel cramped, cramped conditions, cramped quarters
related_phrasal_verbs: n/a (no strong phrasal-verb link, compare "squeeze in, " "pack in")
grammar_pattern: cramped + noun / be + cramped (a cramped room / The bus felt cramped.)
common_mistake: The room is very cramped of furniture.
correct_version: The room is very cramped with furniture.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'cramped WITH', not 'of'.
pronunciation_tip: One syllable: KRAMPT -- the "-ed" is pronounced as a hard "t," not a separate syllable.
spelling_tip: Don't forget the "m" before "p" -- cra-M-ped, like the muscle cramp.
etymology: From "cramp" (Middle English, related to Middle Dutch "crampe" -- a metal clamp), extended to mean tightly restricted or squeezed.
prefix_root_suffix: cramp = root (clamp/squeeze) + -ed = adjective suffix (describing a state)
mnemonic: When space is CRAMPED, your legs practically get a CRAMP from having no room to stretch.
memory_trick: CRAMPED: like a leg CRAMP when there's no room to move.
visual_association: Four people trying to sit around a tiny table meant for two.
difference_explained: Crowded = too many people. Cramped = too little space.
mini_conversation:
A: How was the train ride?
B: Awful -- the carriage was so cramped I couldn't even open my bag.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character squeezes past boxes muttering, "This apartment is so cramped I can barely turn around."
news_style_line: News-style: "Families in the flooded district are living in cramped shelters while repairs continue."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Sorry the car's a bit cramped back there -- just push the seat forward."
mcq_options: A) Wide and open  B) Tightly packed with little space  C) Freshly cleaned  D) Brightly lit
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The three of them shared a ______ dorm room in college. → cramped
find_and_fix_to_correct: It was too cramped for do any exercise. → It was too cramped to do any exercise.
translate: छोटे से कमरे में इतना सामान भरा था कि चलना मुश्किल था। → The small room was so cramped with belongings that it was hard to walk.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a cramped bus or room.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'too small and tightly packed to move comfortably'?
usage_tip: 'Cramped conditions' = too little space for people.

simple_explanation: Small and neatly arranged, using space efficiently. Something compact takes up little space but still contains everything needed -- like a compact car or a compact kitchen design.
example_1: She bought a compact camera for travel.
example_2: The compact design of the apartment made great use of every corner.
example_3: He prefers a compact laptop that fits easily in his bag.
collocations: compact car, compact design, compact and efficient, compact size
related_phrasal_verbs: n/a (no strong phrasal-verb link, compare "pack down, " "fit in")
grammar_pattern: compact + noun / be + compact (a compact car / The device is compact.)
common_mistake: This phone is more compact than the another one.
correct_version: This phone is more compact than the other one.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'the other', not 'the another'.
pronunciation_tip: As an adjective, stress the first syllable: COM-pakt (the verb form stresses the second: com-PAKT).
spelling_tip: One word, double "c" sound but single letters -- com-pact, not com-packed.
etymology: From Latin "compactus," past participle of "compingere" (com- together + pangere to fasten) -- literally "packed firmly together."
prefix_root_suffix: com- (together) + pact = root (from Latin pangere, to fasten)
word_family: compact (n./v. - a compact agreement or to compact soil), compactness (n.), compactly (adv.)
mnemonic: A COMPACT car PACKS everything you need into a small, efficient space.
memory_trick: COMPACT: PACKED tight.
visual_association: A folding bicycle collapsing neatly into a small bag.
emotion_feel: Approval and satisfaction with efficient design
difference_explained: Small = little. Compact = small and well-designed to save space.
mini_conversation:
A: Which suitcase should I take?
B: The compact one -- it's easier to carry through the airport.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A salesperson demonstrates a gadget, saying, "It's fully compact -- folds down to fit right in your pocket."
news_style_line: News-style: "The city introduced a fleet of compact electric cars for its downtown car-sharing program."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I need something compact for my dorm room -- there's barely any space."
mcq_options: A) Broken and unusable  B) Small but well organized  C) Extremely expensive  D) Old-fashioned
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: We chose a ______ washing machine because our kitchen is small. → compact
find_and_fix_to_correct: The design are very compact and modern. → The design is very compact and modern.
translate: यह कैमरा यात्रा के लिए बहुत कॉम्पैक्ट है। → This camera is very compact for travel.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a compact device you use.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'small and neatly arranged, using space efficiently'?
usage_tip: 'Compact car' = a small car.

simple_explanation: Large, heavy, and difficult to carry or handle. Something bulky takes up a lot of space and often feels awkward to move around, like a big winter coat or a large parcel.
example_1: The package was too bulky to carry alone.
example_2: He struggled to fit the bulky sofa through the door.
example_3: Winter jackets can feel bulky under a coat.
collocations: bulky item, bulky furniture, too bulky, bulky package
related_phrasal_verbs: n/a (no strong phrasal-verb link, compare "weigh down, " "take up")
grammar_pattern: bulky + noun / be + bulky (a bulky suitcase / The parcel is bulky.)
common_mistake: This bag is very bulky to carrying.
correct_version: This bag is very bulky to carry.
why_it_s_wrong: After 'to', use the base verb: 'to carry'.
pronunciation_tip: Two syllables: BUL-kee, with a short "u" sound like in "bull."
etymology: From "bulk" (via Old Norse "búlki," meaning a heap or cargo) + "-y" -- describing something large and heavy in shape.
prefix_root_suffix: bulk = root (Old Norse búlki, heap) + -y = adjective suffix
mnemonic: A BULKY box has so much BULK inside that it's hard to carry.
memory_trick: BULKY: has a lot of BULK.
visual_association: Someone struggling to squeeze a huge box through a narrow doorway.
difference_explained: Heavy = weighs a lot. Bulky = large and awkward, not always heavy.
mini_conversation:
A: Can we fit the printer in the car too?
B: It's pretty bulky -- let's see if there's room after the boxes.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A mover grumbles while carrying a wardrobe, "This thing is way too bulky for one person."
news_style_line: News-style: "The postal service now charges extra for bulky parcels that don't fit standard sorting machines."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Don't bring the big bulky backpack -- take the small one instead."
mcq_options: A) Light and thin  B) Large and awkward to handle  C) Fast-moving  D) Transparent
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The ______ generator took four men to move it. → bulky
find_and_fix_to_correct: These boxes are too bulky for fit in the trunk. → These boxes are too bulky to fit in the trunk.
translate: यह पैकेट अकेले उठाने के लिए बहुत भारी-भरकम है। → This package is too bulky to carry alone.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a bulky item you had to carry.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'large, heavy, and difficult to carry or handle'?
usage_tip: 'Bulky items' are hard to post or carry.

simple_explanation: Having a lot to do; not free. When you're busy, your time is full of tasks or activities, so you don't have free time right now.
example_1: I'm busy right now, call later.
example_2: She's too busy to join us for lunch today.
example_3: The restaurant gets busy every Friday night.
collocations: busy schedule, busy street, keep busy, busy with work
related_phrasal_verbs: tied up, snowed under, caught up in
where_it_s_used: Work, daily schedules, phone calls, city life
grammar_pattern: busy + with/doing something (busy with work / busy doing homework)
common_mistake: I am busy for finish this report.
correct_version: I am busy finishing this report.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'busy + -ing' or 'busy with + noun', not 'busy for + verb'.
pronunciation_tip: Pronounced BIZ-ee -- the "u" sounds like a short "i," not like in "bus."
spelling_tip: The "u" is silent in sound but must be written -- b-u-s-y, easy to misspell as "bizy."
etymology: From Old English "bysig," meaning occupied or active -- a very old native English word.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- "busy" is a simple native English word
word_family: busy (v. - to busy oneself), busily (adv.), business (n., related concept)
mnemonic: BUSY sounds like "BIZ-ee," and BIZ is short for business -- busy people are full of business.
memory_trick: BUSY: sounds like 'bizzy' — the U sounds like I.
visual_association: A calendar completely filled with appointments, no empty slots.
emotion_feel: Mild stress mixed with a sense of purpose
difference_explained: Busy = have a lot to do. Occupied = in use (a seat), or kept busy (formal).
mini_conversation:
A: Are you free this weekend?
B: Sorry, I'll be busy moving into my new place.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character rushes past, calling over their shoulder, "Can't talk now, crazy busy today!"
news_style_line: News-style: "Shopping streets were unusually busy this weekend ahead of the holiday season."
casual_conversation: Casual: "How's work been?" "Busy, honestly -- I've barely had a lunch break all week."
mcq_options: A) Having free time  B) Having a lot to do  C) Feeling sleepy  D) Being outdoors
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Mornings at the bakery are always the ______ time of day. → busy
find_and_fix_to_correct: She is busy to cook dinner. → She is busy cooking dinner.
translate: मैं अभी बहुत व्यस्त हूँ, बाद में बात करते हैं। → I'm very busy right now, let's talk later.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about what keeps you busy on weekdays.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'having a lot to do; not free'?
usage_tip: 'The line is busy' = someone is already on the phone.

simple_explanation: Not costing money, or not busy/available. "Free" can mean something costs nothing, or it can mean a person has no plans and is available.
example_2: The museum is free on the first Sunday of the month.
example_3: I'm free after five, so let's meet then.
collocations: free time, free of charge, set someone free, free Wi-Fi
related_phrasal_verbs: free up, break free, set free
grammar_pattern: free + to + verb / free from + noun (free to leave / free from stress)
common_mistake: This ticket is free of cost money.
correct_version: This ticket is free of cost.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Free of cost' already means no money, so 'money' is extra.
pronunciation_tip: One syllable, long "ee" sound: FREE, rhymes with "tree" and "see."
spelling_tip: Double "e" at the end -- f-r-e-e, not "free" with one "e."
etymology: From Old English "freo," related to words meaning "beloved" -- originally distinguishing free family members from slaves in a household, later broadened to mean "not bound."
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- "free" is a simple native English word
word_family: freedom (n.), freely (adv.), free (v. - to free someone), freeing (adj./gerund)
mnemonic: When you're FREE, you're like a bird set loose -- no cage, no cost, no chains.
memory_trick: FREE: no price tag.
visual_association: A bird flying out of an open cage into the sky.
difference_explained: Free = not busy, or no cost. Available = can be used or contacted.
mini_conversation:
A: Are you free for coffee tomorrow?
B: Yes, I'm completely free after ten.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A prisoner steps outside and breathes deeply, murmuring, "I'm finally free."
news_style_line: News-style: "The city council announced free public transport for students starting next month."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Are you free this weekend? Let's catch up."
mcq_options: A) Expensive  B) Costing nothing / available  C) Broken  D) Crowded
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Entry to the park is completely ______ on weekdays. → free
find_and_fix_to_correct: Are you free for talk right now? → Are you free to talk right now?
translate: क्या तुम आज शाम को खाली हो? → Are you free this evening?
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something you got free of cost.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'not costing money, or not busy/available'?
usage_tip: 'Free' has two meanings: no cost, or not busy ('Are you free tonight?').

simple_explanation: Prepared and able to do something right away. When you're ready, everything is in place for you to start or go -- there's nothing left to prepare.
example_1: Are you ready to leave now?
example_2: Dinner is ready, so come to the table.
example_3: She wasn't ready for the sudden exam.
collocations: ready to go, get ready, ready for action, ready-made
related_phrasal_verbs: gear up, get set, all set
where_it_s_used: Departures, exams, cooking, sports, daily routines
grammar_pattern: ready + to + verb / ready for + noun (ready to start / ready for the trip)
common_mistake: I am ready for leaving now.
correct_version: I am ready to leave now.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'ready to + verb' or 'ready for + noun', not 'ready for + -ing'.
pronunciation_tip: Two syllables: RED-ee -- the first syllable rhymes with "red," not "read."
spelling_tip: R-E-A-D-Y -- looks like "read" plus "y," but it's pronounced differently.
etymology: From Old English "ræde" / "geræde," meaning prepared for riding or a journey -- later broadened to mean prepared for anything.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- "ready" is a simple native English word
mnemonic: Think "READY, set, go!" -- when you're READY, you're all set to start.
memory_trick: READY: READ the plan, then you're READY.
visual_association: A runner crouched at the starting line, waiting for the signal.
difference_explained: Ready to + verb (ready to go). Ready for + noun (ready for the exam).
mini_conversation:
A: Is the food ready yet?
B: Almost -- give it five more minutes.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A coach claps and shouts, "Everyone ready? Let's go, on my count!"
news_style_line: News-style: "Emergency teams say they are fully ready to respond as the storm approaches the coast."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Ready to head out? The bus leaves in ten minutes."
mcq_options: A) Confused  B) Prepared to do something  C) Tired  D) Late
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Let me know when you're ______ to start the meeting. → ready
find_and_fix_to_correct: We are ready for start the project. → We are ready to start the project.
translate: क्या तुम अब जाने के लिए तैयार हो? → Are you ready to leave now?
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about how long it takes you to get ready.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'prepared and able to do something right away'?
usage_tip: 'Ready, steady, go!' starts a race.

simple_explanation: Able to be used, obtained, or reached. When something or someone is available, you can get, use, or contact them right now -- nothing is stopping you.
example_2: This model is available in three different colors.
example_3: The doctor isn't available until next Tuesday.
collocations: readily available, available online, make available, currently available
related_phrasal_verbs: free up, open up, come through
grammar_pattern: available + for/to + noun/verb (available for a call / available to help)
common_mistake: He is not available for talk right now.
correct_version: He is not available to talk right now.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'available to + verb', not 'for + verb'.
pronunciation_tip: Four syllables, stress on the second: uh-VAY-luh-buhl.
spelling_tip: Watch the ending: "-able," not "-ible" -- avail + able.
etymology: From Old French "availler" (to be of use), built on "value" (from Latin "valere," to be strong/worth) + "-able."
prefix_root_suffix: avail = root (from Latin valere, to be worth) + -able = suffix meaning "capable of"
mnemonic: If something is AVAILABLE, it's ABLE to be used right AWAY.
memory_trick: AVAIL-ABLE: ABLE to be used.
visual_association: A green "in stock" light glowing next to a product on a shelf.
difference_explained: Available = can be used or reached. Free = not busy, or costs nothing.
mini_conversation:
A: Is this jacket available in a medium?
B: Let me check -- yes, we have one left.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A receptionist picks up the phone and says, "I'm sorry, he's not available at the moment."
news_style_line: News-style: "Tickets for the festival will be available for purchase starting Monday morning."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Are you available for a quick call later today?"
mcq_options: A) Broken or unusable  B) Able to be obtained or reached  C) Extremely popular  D) Forbidden
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The apartment is ______ starting from next month. → available
find_and_fix_to_correct: This size is not available in this colour anymore. → This size is not available in this color anymore.
translate: क्या मैनेजर अभी उपलब्ध हैं? → Is the manager available now?
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about when you're usually available to talk.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'able to be used, obtained, or reached'?
usage_tip: 'Not available' is common on phone messages and shop signs.

simple_explanation: Not present in a place where you're expected to be. When you're absent, you're missing from somewhere you're supposed to be, like school, work, or a meeting.
example_1: He was absent from class today.
example_2: Three students were absent because of the flu.
example_3: She has been absent from work all week.
collocations: absent from, frequently absent, mark someone absent, absent without leave
related_phrasal_verbs: call in sick, take off, stay away
grammar_pattern: absent + from + noun (absent from school / absent from the meeting)
common_mistake: She was absent of school yesterday.
correct_version: She was absent from school yesterday.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'absent FROM', not 'of'.
pronunciation_tip: As an adjective, stress the first syllable: AB-suhnt.
spelling_tip: Watch the ending: "-ent," not "-ant" -- absent, like "present."
etymology: From Latin "absens/absentem," present participle of "abesse" (ab- away + esse to be) -- literally "being away."
prefix_root_suffix: ab- (away from) + sent = root (from Latin esse, to be, via absens)
mnemonic: If you're ABSENT, you've been SENT away -- you're simply not there.
memory_trick: AB-SENT: SENT AWAY ('ab' = away).
visual_association: An empty chair with a name tag but no one sitting in it.
emotion_feel: Neutral, sometimes worry or concern about the reason
difference_explained: Absent = not present where expected (a person). Missing = lost or can't be found.
mini_conversation:
A: Why wasn't Raj in class today?
B: He's been absent all week -- I heard he's sick.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A teacher scans the room and asks, "Does anyone know why Maria is absent today?"
news_style_line: News-style: "Attendance records show a spike in absent employees during the flu season."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I was absent yesterday -- can you send me the notes?"
mcq_options: A) Present and on time  B) Not there when expected  C) Very talented  D) Extremely busy
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: He was ______ from the meeting due to a doctor's appointment. → absent
find_and_fix_to_correct: He is absent since two days. → He has been absent for two days.
translate: वह आज क्लास से अनुपस्थित था। → He was absent from class today.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about why a student might be absent from class.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'not present in a place where you're expected to be'?
usage_tip: 'Absent-minded' = often forgets things.

simple_explanation: Not sleeping; conscious and alert. When you're awake, your eyes are open and your mind is active -- you're not asleep.
example_2: I was awake all night worrying about the exam.
example_3: She stayed awake to finish her assignment.
collocations: wide awake, stay awake, keep someone awake, barely awake
related_phrasal_verbs: wake up, stay up, keep up
where_it_s_used: Sleep routines, night shifts, mornings, babies
grammar_pattern: be/stay/keep + awake (I stayed awake all night.)
common_mistake: I am an awake person since 5 AM.
correct_version: I have been awake since 5 AM.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Awake' comes after a verb like 'be'; it doesn't go before a noun.
pronunciation_tip: Two syllables, stress on the second: uh-WAYK.
etymology: From Old English "awacan" / "awæcnan" (to wake up), formed from "a-" (intensifying prefix) + "wacan" (to wake).
prefix_root_suffix: a- (intensifying prefix) + wake = root (to become conscious)
word_family: wake (v.), waken (v.), awaken (v., more formal), wakeful (adj.)
mnemonic: AWAKE = A + WAKE -- you just WOKE up and now you're wide AWAKE.
memory_trick: A-WAKE: a person who is 'a-wake' (in the state of waking).
visual_association: Wide-open eyes staring at the ceiling in the middle of the night.
emotion_feel: Alertness, sometimes restlessness at odd hours
difference_explained: Awake = adjective (I'm awake). Wake = verb (I wake up at 6).
mini_conversation:
A: Are you awake?
B: Barely -- I only slept three hours.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character bolts upright in bed, wide awake, whispering, "Did you hear that?"
news_style_line: News-style: "Experts recommend staying awake at consistent hours to maintain a healthy sleep cycle."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Are you still awake? It's almost 2 a.m."
mcq_options: A) Sleeping deeply  B) Not sleeping; conscious  C) Feeling sick  D) Very hungry
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: I lay ______ for hours, unable to fall asleep. → awake
find_and_fix_to_correct: She kept me awaked all night with her music. → She kept me awake all night with her music.

simple_explanation: Sleeping; not awake. When you're asleep, you're resting with your eyes closed and your mind not active -- the opposite of awake.
example_2: He fell asleep during the movie.
example_3: She was fast asleep by nine o'clock.
collocations: fast asleep, fall asleep, sound asleep, half asleep
related_phrasal_verbs: doze off, drop off, nod off
grammar_pattern: be/fall + asleep (I fell asleep on the couch.)
common_mistake: He is an asleep baby right now.
correct_version: The baby is asleep right now.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Asleep' comes after a verb like 'is'; it doesn't go before a noun.
pronunciation_tip: Two syllables, stress on the second: uh-SLEEP.
spelling_tip: "A" + "sleep" -- one word, no hyphen, don't double the "s."
etymology: From Old English "on slæpe" ("in sleep"), which merged over time into the single word "asleep."
prefix_root_suffix: a- (in/on, from "on") + sleep = root (state of rest)
mnemonic: ASLEEP = A + SLEEP -- you are in A state of SLEEP.
memory_trick: A-SLEEP: in the state of sleep.
visual_association: A cat curled up in a sunny spot, eyes closed and breathing slowly.
difference_explained: Asleep comes after a verb (the baby is asleep). Sleeping can go before a noun (a sleeping baby).
mini_conversation:
A: Is Leo still asleep?
B: Yes, fast asleep -- let's keep the volume down.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A parent tiptoes out of the nursery, whispering, "Shh, she's finally asleep."
news_style_line: News-style: "Doctors warn that using phones in bed can make it harder to fall asleep quickly."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Don't call after ten -- I'm usually asleep by then."
mcq_options: A) Wide awake  B) In a state of sleep  C) Feeling hungry  D) Standing up
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: By the time we got home, the children were already ______. → asleep
find_and_fix_to_correct: She falled asleep on the train. → She fell asleep on the train.

write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about when you usually fall asleep.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'sleeping; not awake'?
usage_tip: 'Fall asleep' = start sleeping. 'My leg is asleep' = it's numb.

simple_explanation: Feeling like you need to eat. When you're hungry, your body is telling you it needs food -- you might feel it in your stomach.
example_2: The children were hungry after playing all afternoon.
example_3: Don't go grocery shopping when you're hungry.
collocations: very hungry, starving hungry, hungry for, get hungry
grammar_pattern: be + hungry (+ for + noun) (I'm hungry for pizza.)
common_mistake: I have hungry, let's eat something.
correct_version: I am hungry, let's eat something.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'be hungry', not 'have hungry' (Hindi: 'bhook lagi hai').
pronunciation_tip: Two syllables: HUNG-gree, with a hard "g" sound.
spelling_tip: "Hunger" drops the "e" before adding "-y": hung(e)r + y = hungry.
etymology: From Old English "hungrig," formed from "hunger" (the need for food) + "-ig" (adjective ending, now "-y").
prefix_root_suffix: hunger = root (need for food) + -y = adjective suffix
mnemonic: When you're HUNGRY, your stomach makes an ANGRY-sounding growl -- hungry rhymes with angry.
memory_trick: HUNGRY: your stomach GROWLS in the middle of the word.
visual_association: An empty plate with a fork tapping impatiently beside it.
difference_explained: Hungry = want food. Starving = extremely hungry (informal), or dying from lack of food.
mini_conversation:
A: I'm so hungry, what's for lunch?
B: There's leftover pasta in the fridge.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character opens an empty fridge and sighs, "I'm starving -- there's nothing to eat."
news_style_line: News-style: "The charity distributed meals to hungry families across the flood-affected region."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Are you hungry yet? We could order something."
mcq_options: A) Needing to sleep  B) Needing to eat  C) Feeling cold  D) Feeling proud
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: By noon, everyone in the office was ______ for lunch. → hungry
find_and_fix_to_correct: She is very hungry for eat a sandwich. → She is very hungry, so she wants to eat a sandwich.
translate: मुझे भूख लगी है, चलो कुछ खाते हैं। → I'm hungry, let's eat something.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about the food you want when you're very hungry.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'feeling like you need to eat'?
usage_tip: 'Hungry for success' = strongly wanting success.

simple_explanation: Feeling like you need to drink something. When you're thirsty, your body needs liquid -- usually you feel dryness in your mouth or throat.
example_2: He was thirsty after playing football in the heat.
example_3: She always feels thirsty during long flights.
collocations: really thirsty, thirsty for water, get thirsty, thirsty work
related_phrasal_verbs: n/a (no strong phrasal-verb link, compare "parched, " "dry out")
grammar_pattern: be + thirsty (+ for + noun) (I'm thirsty for something cold.)
common_mistake: I have very thirsty after the walk.
correct_version: I am very thirsty after the walk.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'be thirsty', not 'have thirsty'.
pronunciation_tip: Two syllables: THUR-stee, with the "th" as in "think."
spelling_tip: "Thirst" + "y" -- keep both letters, don't drop the "t."
etymology: From Old English "þurstig," formed from "þurst" (thirst, the need for liquid) + "-ig" (adjective ending).
prefix_root_suffix: thirst = root (need for liquid) + -y = adjective suffix
mnemonic: THIRSTY has THIRST inside it -- your throat is dry and you're bursting for water.
memory_trick: THIRSTY: THIRST + Y.
visual_association: A cracked, dry desert landscape under a blazing sun.
difference_explained: Thirsty = want to drink (people, animals). Dry = no water (land, a throat).
mini_conversation:
A: Are you thirsty? There's juice in the fridge.
B: Yes, please -- I'm so thirsty after that jog.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A hiker collapses onto a rock, gasping, "I'm so thirsty, I'd give anything for water."
news_style_line: News-style: "Health officials remind residents to stay hydrated as thirsty crowds gather for the outdoor festival."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I'm really thirsty -- can we stop for a drink?"
mcq_options: A) Needing to eat  B) Needing to drink  C) Feeling tired  D) Feeling cold

find_and_fix_to_correct: She feel thirsty after the gym class. → She feels thirsty after the gym class.

write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about what you drink when you're thirsty.
