reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'feeling like you need to drink something'?
usage_tip: 'Thirsty for knowledge' = eager to learn.

simple_explanation: Feeling like you need rest or sleep. When you're tired, your body or mind has used up its energy and wants to rest.
example_2: She felt tired after the long flight.
example_3: He's always tired on Monday mornings.
collocations: really tired, tired of, get tired, tired out
related_phrasal_verbs: wear out, burn out, run down
grammar_pattern: tired + of + noun/gerund (tired of waiting / tired of this noise)
common_mistake: I am tired for this long meeting.
correct_version: I am tired of this long meeting.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'tired OF' when annoyed and 'tired FROM' when you need rest.
pronunciation_tip: Two syllables: TY-uhrd, stress on the first.
spelling_tip: "Tire" + "d" -- drop nothing, just add "d" since "tire" already ends in "e."
etymology: From "tire" (Old English "teorian," to become weary or fail) + "-ed" (adjective ending describing a state).
prefix_root_suffix: tire = root (to become weary) + -ed = adjective suffix (describing a state)
mnemonic: When your TIRES (car wheels) are worn out, they're TIRED too -- both need rest.
memory_trick: TIRED: like a TYRE that has lost air.
visual_association: Someone yawning widely while rubbing their heavy eyelids.
emotion_feel: Fatigue, low energy, need for rest
difference_explained: Tired OF = bored or annoyed by. Tired FROM = need rest because of.
related_words: exhausted, weary, sleepy, drained, worn out
mini_conversation:
A: You look tired today.
B: Yeah, I barely slept -- the baby was up all night.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character slumps into a chair and mutters, "I am absolutely tired -- today never seemed to end."
news_style_line: News-style: "Studies show tired drivers are just as dangerous on the road as intoxicated ones."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I'm so tired -- I think I'll go to bed early tonight."
mcq_options: A) Full of energy  B) Needing rest or sleep  C) Feeling angry  D) Feeling proud
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: After the double shift, the nurse was completely ______. → tired
find_and_fix_to_correct: This is very tired for me today. → This is very tiring for me today.
translate: काम के बाद मैं थक गया हूँ। → I'm tired after work.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about what makes you tired every day.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'feeling like you need rest or sleep'?
usage_tip: 'Sick and tired of' = very annoyed by something.

hindi_meaning: बुरी तरह थका हुआ, थककर चूर
simple_explanation: Extremely tired, with no energy left. When you're exhausted, you're not just a little tired -- you're completely drained, physically or mentally.
example_2: The nurses were exhausted after the double shift.
example_3: She felt exhausted from studying all night.
collocations: totally exhausted, exhausted from, feel exhausted, physically exhausted
related_phrasal_verbs: wear out, burn out, run out of steam
where_it_s_used: Work, sports, parenting, travel, illness recovery
grammar_pattern: exhausted + from/by + noun (exhausted from the trip / exhausted by the heat)
common_mistake: I am exhausted for run more.
correct_version: I am too exhausted to run more.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'too exhausted to + verb', not 'exhausted for + verb'.
pronunciation_tip: Three syllables: eg-ZAWS-tid, with the "x" sounding like "gz."
spelling_tip: "Exhaust" + "ed" -- watch the "h" after the "x," easy to forget.
etymology: From Latin "exhaurire" (ex- out + haurire to draw, as water from a well), via "exhaustus" -- literally "completely drawn out."
prefix_root_suffix: ex- (out) + haust = root (from Latin haurire, to draw/drain) + -ed = adjective suffix
word_family: exhaust (v./n.), exhaustion (n.), exhausting (adj.), exhaustive (adj., meaning thorough)
mnemonic: A car's EXHAUST pipe lets out everything it has -- when you're EXHAUSTED, you've let out all your energy too.
memory_trick: EX-HAUSTED: all energy has gone OUT.
visual_association: Someone collapsing onto a sofa the moment they get home, coat still on.
difference_explained: Tired = need rest. Exhausted = extremely tired, no energy left.
related_words: drained, worn out, weary, burned out, spent
mini_conversation:
A: How was the hiking trip?
B: Amazing, but I'm completely exhausted now.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A runner crosses the finish line and collapses, gasping, "I'm completely exhausted."
news_style_line: News-style: "Relief workers described feeling exhausted after days of continuous rescue efforts."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I'm exhausted -- three back-to-back meetings today."
mcq_options: A) Slightly sleepy  B) Extremely tired with no energy left  C) Very excited  D) Well rested
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: After the twelve-hour flight, they arrived ______ but happy. → exhausted
find_and_fix_to_correct: This project is very exhausted to complete. → This project is very exhausting to complete.
translate: मैराथन के बाद मैं बुरी तरह थक गया हूँ। → I'm exhausted after the marathon.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a day that left you exhausted.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'extremely tired, with no energy left'?
usage_tip: 'Exhausted' also means used up: 'exhausted supplies'.

simple_explanation: Not feeling well; ill. When you're sick, your body isn't working normally -- you might have a fever, cold, or stomach trouble.
example_2: He stayed home because he was sick with a cold.
example_3: I felt sick after eating too much cake.
collocations: feel sick, call in sick, sick leave, sick and tired
related_phrasal_verbs: throw up, come down with, feel under the weather
where_it_s_used: Health, work absences, school, family life
grammar_pattern: be/feel + sick (+ with + noun) (feel sick with worry / sick with a cold)
common_mistake: I am sick since yesterday from a cold.
correct_version: I have been sick with a cold since yesterday.
why_it_s_wrong: For a duration up to now, use the present perfect: 'have been sick since'.
pronunciation_tip: One syllable: SIK, short "i" sound like in "pick."
spelling_tip: S-I-C-K -- short and simple, don't confuse with "sic" (a different, rare word).
etymology: From Old English "seoc," meaning ill or diseased -- a very old native English word.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- "sick" is a simple native English word
mnemonic: SICK rhymes with "click" -- like something clicked wrong inside your body.
memory_trick: SICK: a short, weak word for a weak body.
visual_association: Someone lying in bed with a thermometer and a box of tissues nearby.
difference_explained: Same meaning. Ill is slightly more formal (UK). 'Sick' in UK English can also mean vomiting.
mini_conversation:
A: You don't look well.
B: Yeah, I think I'm coming down with something -- I feel sick.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character calls their boss and says weakly, "I won't make it in today, I'm really sick."
news_style_line: News-style: "Health officials urge sick employees to stay home to prevent the virus from spreading."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I feel a bit sick -- maybe I ate something bad."
mcq_options: A) Full of energy  B) Not feeling well  C) Very happy  D) Extremely busy
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: He couldn't come to work because he felt ______. → sick
find_and_fix_to_correct: She is sick since three days. → She has been sick for three days.
translate: आज उसकी तबीयत ठीक नहीं है। → She feels sick today.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about what you do when you're sick.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'not feeling well; ill'?
usage_tip: 'Sick leave' = time off work because of illness.

simple_explanation: In good physical condition; not sick. Being healthy means your body works well and you generally feel good, often because of good habits like eating well and exercising.
example_2: He stays healthy by exercising every morning.
example_3: A healthy diet includes plenty of fruits and vegetables.
collocations: healthy diet, healthy lifestyle, stay healthy, healthy habits
related_phrasal_verbs: keep fit, work out, look after yourself
where_it_s_used: Diet, exercise, medical checkups, lifestyle advice
grammar_pattern: healthy + noun / be + healthy (a healthy meal / She is healthy.)
common_mistake: He eat healthy foods for stay strong.
correct_version: He eats healthy foods to stay strong.
why_it_s_wrong: He/she needs -s (eats), and use 'to + verb' for purpose.
pronunciation_tip: Two syllables: HEL-thee, with a soft "th" sound as in "think."
spelling_tip: "Health" + "y" -- keep the "th," a common misspelling drops it.
etymology: From "health" (Old English "hælþ," from "hal" meaning "whole") + "-y" -- literally, being "whole" or sound in body.
mnemonic: HEALTHY people have good HEALTH -- the word is built right into it.
memory_trick: HEALTHY: HEALTH + Y.
visual_association: A colorful plate of fresh fruits and vegetables next to running shoes.
difference_explained: Healthy = not sick, good for the body. Fit = in good physical shape from exercise.
mini_conversation:
A: What's your secret to staying healthy?
B: Mostly just sleeping well and eating fresh food.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A doctor smiles at the results and says, "Everything looks great -- you're perfectly healthy."
news_style_line: News-style: "Nutritionists recommend a healthy balance of protein, grains, and vegetables in daily meals."
casual_conversation: Casual: "You look great -- have you been eating healthy lately?"
mcq_options: A) Sick and weak  B) In good physical condition  C) Expensive  D) Very tired
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Drinking plenty of water is part of a ______ routine. → healthy
find_and_fix_to_correct: She always eating healthy food. → She always eats healthy food.
translate: सब्ज़ियाँ खाने से आप स्वस्थ रहते हैं। → Eating vegetables keeps you healthy.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a healthy habit you follow.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'in good physical condition; not sick'?
usage_tip: 'Healthy' is for people and food; 'healthful' is rare.

simple_explanation: Protected from danger or harm. When something or someone is safe, there's no danger nearby -- you don't need to worry about getting hurt.
example_2: Wear a helmet to stay safe while cycling.
example_3: The children are safe at home with their grandmother.
collocations: safe and sound, keep safe, safe distance, feel safe
related_phrasal_verbs: watch out for, look after, keep an eye on
grammar_pattern: safe + from + noun (safe from danger / safe from the storm)
common_mistake: This place is safe of thieves.
correct_version: This place is safe from thieves.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'safe FROM' danger, not 'of'.
spelling_tip: S-A-F-E -- one "f," not two, unlike some similar-sounding words.
etymology: From Old French "sauf," from Latin "salvus" (uninjured, in good health) -- the same root as "salvation" and "save."
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- "safe" comes directly from Latin "salvus" as a whole word
mnemonic: SAFE sounds like "SAVE" -- if you're SAFE, you've been SAVEd from danger.
memory_trick: SAFE: a SAFE (locker) keeps things safe.
visual_association: A child holding a parent's hand while crossing a busy street.
difference_explained: Safe = protected from danger. Secure = firmly fixed, or protected from threats (secure password).
mini_conversation:
A: Did everyone make it out okay?
B: Yes, everyone's safe -- no injuries at all.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A rescuer pulls someone from the water and says, "You're safe now, it's over."
news_style_line: News-style: "Officials confirmed all passengers were safe after the emergency landing."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Text me when you get home safe, okay?"
mcq_options: A) In danger  B) Protected from harm  C) Very expensive  D) Broken
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Always keep your passport in a ______ place while traveling. → safe
find_and_fix_to_correct: Drive careful so you stay safe. → Drive carefully so you stay safe.
translate: तुम यहाँ सुरक्षित हो। → You are safe here.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about the safest place in your home.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'protected from danger or harm'?
usage_tip: 'Better safe than sorry' = take care even if it seems too much.

simple_explanation: Damaged, in pieces, or not working. When something is broken, it's damaged and can't be used normally until it's fixed.
example_2: My phone screen is broken after I dropped it.
example_3: The elevator has been broken since Monday.
collocations: broken glass, broken promise, broken heart, badly broken
related_phrasal_verbs: fall apart, break down, come apart
grammar_pattern: be + broken (+ noun after "a broken") (a broken bone / The lock is broken.)
common_mistake: The lamp is break since last week.
correct_version: The lamp has been broken since last week.
why_it_s_wrong: With 'has been', use the past participle 'broken'.
pronunciation_tip: Two syllables: BROH-kuhn, stress on the first.
spelling_tip: Irregular past participle of "break" -- not "breaked" or "breaken."
etymology: Past participle of "break" (Old English "brecan"), now also used as a standalone adjective describing something damaged or not working.
prefix_root_suffix: break = root (to separate by force) + -en = irregular past-participle ending
mnemonic: BROKEN comes from BREAK -- once something BREAKS, it becomes BROKEN.
memory_trick: BREAK → BROKE → BROKEN.
visual_association: A cracked phone screen with jagged lines spreading across it.
difference_explained: Damaged = harmed. Broken = in pieces or not working at all.
related_words: damaged, faulty, cracked, shattered, out of order
mini_conversation:
A: Why isn't the printer working?
B: It's broken -- we need to call someone to fix it.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A mechanic wipes his hands and says, "The engine's broken -- you'll need a new part."
news_style_line: News-style: "City officials say the broken traffic signals will be repaired by the end of the week."
casual_conversation: Casual: "My headphones are broken again -- the left side stopped working."
mcq_options: A) Working perfectly  B) Damaged or not working  C) Brand new  D) Very expensive
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: We couldn't use the washing machine because it was ______. → broken
find_and_fix_to_correct: This chair is broke, don't sit on it. → This chair is broken, don't sit on it.
translate: खिड़की टूटी हुई है। → The window is broken.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something broken you need to fix.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'damaged, in pieces, or not working'?
usage_tip: 'Broken English' = English with many mistakes.

simple_explanation: Repaired, or set and unchanging. "Fixed" can mean something was repaired after breaking, or that something stays the same and doesn't change, like a fixed price.
example_2: The mechanic said the car is fixed and ready to drive.
example_3: We agreed on a fixed monthly rent.
collocations: fixed price, fixed schedule, get fixed, firmly fixed
related_phrasal_verbs: sort out, patch up, set right
grammar_pattern: be + fixed / a fixed + noun (The tap is fixed. / a fixed rate)
common_mistake: The price is fix and cannot change.
correct_version: The price is fixed and cannot change.
why_it_s_wrong: As an adjective, use the past participle 'fixed'.
pronunciation_tip: One syllable: FIKST -- the "-ed" is pronounced as a hard "t."
etymology: From Latin "fixus," past participle of "figere" (to fasten firmly) -- meaning something settled firmly in place, or repaired.
prefix_root_suffix: fix = root (from Latin figere, to fasten) + -ed = adjective suffix
mnemonic: Once something is FIXED, it's FIXed firmly in place -- either repaired or unmoving.
memory_trick: FIX → FIXED: set in place.
visual_association: A wrench tightening the last bolt on a repaired machine.
difference_explained: Fixed = repaired, or unchanging (a fixed rate). Repaired only means mended.
mini_conversation:
A: Did you get the washing machine fixed?
B: Yes, it's fixed now -- works like new.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A technician closes the laptop lid and announces, "All fixed -- should run smoothly now."
news_style_line: News-style: "The bridge, closed for months, has finally been fixed and reopened to traffic."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Is the Wi-Fi fixed yet, or is it still down?"
mcq_options: A) Still broken  B) Repaired or unchanging  C) Very old  D) Missing
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The plumber came yesterday and now the leak is ______. → fixed
find_and_fix_to_correct: We have a fix appointment at 3 PM. → We have a fixed appointment at 3 PM.
translate: मेरी साइकिल आखिरकार ठीक हो गई है। → My bike is finally fixed.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something with a fixed price.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'repaired, or set and unchanging'?
usage_tip: 'Fixed price' = no bargaining. 'Fixed deposit' = an Indian bank saving scheme.

simple_explanation: Not closed; allowing entry or access. When something is open, you can go in, use it, or see inside -- there's nothing blocking access.
example_2: Leave the window open for some fresh air.
example_3: The library stays open until nine on weekdays.
collocations: wide open, open door, stay open, open all day
related_phrasal_verbs: open up, open out, throw open
grammar_pattern: be + open (+ to + noun) (open to suggestions / The store is open.)
common_mistake: The museum is open in Monday to Friday.
correct_version: The museum is open from Monday to Friday.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'open FROM Monday TO Friday', not 'in'.
pronunciation_tip: Two syllables: OH-puhn, stress on the first.
spelling_tip: O-P-E-N -- short and simple, no tricky letters.
etymology: From Old English "open," a native Germanic word meaning "not shut, accessible."
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- "open" is a simple native English word
mnemonic: OPEN starts with "O," shaped like a wide-OPEN mouth or doorway.
memory_trick: OPEN: the O is an open door.
visual_association: A wide-open door with sunlight streaming through it.
difference_explained: Open = adjective (the shop is open). Opened = verb (she opened the door).
mini_conversation:
A: Is the bakery open yet?
B: Yes, it opens at seven every morning.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A shopkeeper flips the sign and says cheerfully, "We're open -- come on in!"
news_style_line: News-style: "The new bridge is now open to traffic after two years of construction."

example_3: He left the dishes dirty in the sink overnight.
collocations: get dirty, dirty dishes, dirty clothes, filthy dirty

simple_explanation: Covered or soaked with liquid, especially water. When something is wet, water or another liquid has touched it and it hasn't dried yet.
example_1: The floor is wet -- be careful.
example_2: My hair is still wet from the shower.
example_3: Don't sit on the wet bench.
collocations: wet floor, wet weather, soaking wet, get wet
related_phrasal_verbs: soak through, dry off, get drenched
grammar_pattern: be/get + wet (My shoes got wet. / The ground is wet.)
common_mistake: The paint is wet, don't touching it.
correct_version: The paint is wet, don't touch it.
why_it_s_wrong: After 'don't', use the base verb: 'don't touch'.
spelling_tip: W-E-T -- only three letters, simple to spell, but double the "t" when adding "-er/-est": wetter, wettest.
etymology: From Old English "wæt," meaning covered or soaked with liquid -- a native English word.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- "wet" is a simple native English word
mnemonic: WET rhymes with "GET" -- you GET WET when it rains without an umbrella.
memory_trick: WET → WETTER: double T.

simple_explanation: Free from water or moisture. When something is dry, there's no water or liquid on it or in it -- the opposite of wet.
example_2: Make sure the paint is completely dry before touching it.
example_3: It's been a dry summer with almost no rain.
collocations: bone dry, dry season, dry skin, dry weather
related_phrasal_verbs: dry out, dry up, air out
grammar_pattern: be/go + dry (The riverbed went dry. / The clothes are dry.)
common_mistake: The well is dried.
correct_version: The well is dry.
why_it_s_wrong: For the state, use the adjective 'dry' (or 'has dried up'), not 'is dried'.
spelling_tip: D-R-Y -- when adding endings, the "y" often changes to "i": dried, drier, driest.
etymology: From Old English "dryge," meaning free from moisture -- a native English word, the opposite of "wet."
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- "dry" is a simple native English word

simple_explanation: Having a high temperature. When something is hot, its temperature is high -- it might burn you if you touch it, or make you sweat if it's the weather.

example_3: It gets extremely hot here in July.
collocations: piping hot, hot weather, get hot, red hot
related_phrasal_verbs: heat up, warm up, cool down (opposite)
grammar_pattern: be/get + hot (It's getting hot outside. / The oven is hot.)

correct_version: The soup is too hot to drink now.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'too hot to + verb', not 'for + verb'.
spelling_tip: Double the "t" when adding endings: hotter, hottest.
etymology: From Old English "hat," meaning having a high temperature -- a native English word.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- "hot" is a simple native English word

simple_explanation: Having a low temperature. When something is cold, its temperature is low -- you might shiver in cold weather or need a jacket.
example_2: The water in the lake was freezing cold.
example_3: It gets very cold here in winter.
collocations: ice cold, cold weather, feel cold, stone cold
related_phrasal_verbs: warm up, cool down, catch a cold (idiom, for illness)

why_it_s_wrong: 'A cold' is an illness; you 'have a cold', not 'am having cold'.
pronunciation_tip: One syllable: KOHLD, with a long "o" sound.
spelling_tip: C-O-L-D -- don't forget the silent "l" isn't silent here; pronounce it clearly.
etymology: From Old English "cald" / "ceald," meaning having a low temperature -- a native English word.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- "cold" is a simple native English word
word_family: cold (n. - an illness), coldly (adv.), coldness (n.), colder/coldest (comparative/superlative)
mnemonic: COLD has "OLD" inside it -- imagine an OLD, empty house with no heating, freezing COLD.
memory_trick: COLD: the O is a round ice cube.

emotion_feel: Discomfort, sometimes coziness when paired with warm drinks/blankets

simple_explanation: Pleasantly hot; not cold or too hot. When something is warm, it has a comfortable, moderate heat -- not freezing, but not burning hot either. It can also describe a kind, friendly personality.

simple_explanation: Slightly cold, in a pleasant way; also, impressive or fashionable (informal). "Cool" means mildly cold and refreshing, like a cool breeze. In everyday casual talk, it also means something is great or impressive.

simple_explanation: Making a lot of noise; not quiet. When something is loud, the sound is strong and easy to hear, sometimes too much so, like loud music or a loud voice.

related_phrasal_verbs: turn up, turn down, speak up
where_it_s_used: Music, noise complaints, parties, public spaces

simple_explanation: Making little or no noise; calm. When it's quiet, there's very little sound around -- it feels calm and peaceful.
example_1: Please be quiet in the library.
example_2: The village is very quiet at night.
example_3: She's a quiet person who rarely speaks in meetings.
collocations: stay quiet, quiet neighborhood, dead quiet, quiet voice
related_phrasal_verbs: keep down, hush up, calm down
grammar_pattern: be/keep + quiet (Keep quiet, please. / The street is quiet.)
common_mistake: Please be quite, the baby is sleeping.
correct_version: Please be quiet, the baby is sleeping.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Quite' (fairly) and 'quiet' (silent) are different words.
pronunciation_tip: Two syllables: KWY-uht, not "kwyet" as one syllable.
spelling_tip: Q-U-I-E-T -- easy to confuse with "quite" (meaning "very"); quiet has an extra "e."

difference_explained: Quiet (KWY-it) = silent. Quite (KWYTE) = fairly or very.

simple_explanation: Living; not dead. When something is alive, it's living -- it breathes, grows, or functions as a living thing, unlike something dead or lifeless.
example_2: Doctors confirmed the patient was alive after the accident.
example_3: Her grandmother is still alive at ninety-five.
collocations: stay alive, keep alive, still alive, alive and well
related_phrasal_verbs: keep going, hang on, pull through
where_it_s_used: Health, survival stories, nature, city descriptions
grammar_pattern: be/stay/keep + alive (He stayed alive. / The fish is still alive.)
common_mistake: Is your grandfather alive person still?
correct_version: Is your grandfather still alive?
why_it_s_wrong: 'Alive' comes after a verb like 'be'; it doesn't go before a noun.
pronunciation_tip: Two syllables, stress on the second: uh-LYVE.
spelling_tip: "A" + "live" -- one word, no hyphen; don't confuse with "live" (rhymes with "give") meaning "to reside."
etymology: From Old English "on life" ("in life"), which merged over time into the single word "alive."
word_family: life (n.), live (v./adj.), living (adj.), lively (adj., meaning energetic)
mnemonic: ALIVE = A + LIVE -- you are living, full of life.
memory_trick: A-LIVE: in the state of LIVING.
visual_association: A small green sprout pushing up through cracked, dry soil.
difference_explained: Alive comes after a verb (he is alive). Living can go before a noun (a living thing).

B: Yes, believe it or not -- it's five years old now.

simple_explanation: No longer alive. When something is dead, it has stopped living -- it no longer breathes, grows, or functions as a living thing.
example_2: The battery in my phone is dead again.
example_3: They found the tree was dead after the drought.
collocations: stone dead, dead battery, drop dead, dead silence
related_phrasal_verbs: die out, pass away, wear out (for objects)
where_it_s_used: Nature, technology (dead battery), news, mood descriptions
grammar_pattern: be + dead (The plant is dead. / My phone battery is dead.)
common_mistake: This flower is dead since three days.
correct_version: This flower has been dead for three days.
why_it_s_wrong: For how long a state has lasted, use 'has been … for'.
pronunciation_tip: One syllable: DED, short "e" sound, like "bed."
spelling_tip: D-E-A-D -- the "ea" here makes a short "e" sound, unlike in "bead" or "read" (present tense).
etymology: From Old English "dead," meaning having ceased to live -- a native English word, the opposite of "alive."
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- "dead" is a simple native English word
word_family: death (n.), die (v.), deadly (adj., meaning dangerous), deaden (v.)
mnemonic: DEAD rhymes with "BED" -- like lying still and silent, with no life left.
memory_trick: DEAD: a final, heavy word.
visual_association: A wilted, brown plant drooping over the edge of a pot.
emotion_feel: Sadness or neutral acceptance, depending on context
difference_explained: Dead = adjective (the plant is dead). Died = past verb (the plant died).

simple_explanation: Doing things regularly; full of energy or movement. When someone or something is active, they're doing things, moving around, or working -- not sitting still or inactive.
example_2: My grandmother is still very active for her age.
example_3: She's active on social media, posting almost daily.
collocations: physically active, stay active, active member, active lifestyle
related_phrasal_verbs: keep moving, work out, get involved
grammar_pattern: be/stay + active (+ in + noun) (active in sports / She stays active.)
common_mistake: He is very active in play football.
correct_version: He is very active in playing football.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'active in + -ing', not the base verb.
pronunciation_tip: Two syllables: AK-tiv, stress on the first.
spelling_tip: "Act" + "ive" -- keep the "c," don't write "activ" without the final "e."
etymology: From Latin "activus," from "agere" (to do or act) -- describing something that does things or moves.
prefix_root_suffix: act = root (from Latin agere, to do) + -ive = adjective suffix meaning "tending to"
mnemonic: ACTIVE has "ACT" inside it -- an active person is always ready to ACT and move.
memory_trick: ACTIVE: full of ACTION.
visual_association: A person jogging briskly through a park at sunrise.
difference_explained: Busy = have a lot to do. Active = moving or taking part a lot.
mini_conversation:

B: I try to walk or cycle every single day.

simple_explanation: Not doing anything; not active. When someone or something is inactive, they've stopped moving, working, or being used -- like an old account or a person who doesn't exercise.
example_2: The gym membership becomes inactive after three missed payments.
example_3: He's been fairly inactive since he hurt his knee.
collocations: remain inactive, become inactive, physically inactive, inactive account
related_phrasal_verbs: shut down, wind down, slow down
grammar_pattern: be/become + inactive (The account became inactive. / He is inactive.)
common_mistake: This user is inactive since two months.
correct_version: This user has been inactive for two months.
why_it_s_wrong: For how long a state has lasted, use 'has been … for'.
pronunciation_tip: Three syllables: in-AK-tiv, stress on the second.
spelling_tip: "In-" + "active" -- one word, no hyphen, don't double the "n."
etymology: From "in-" (not) + "active" (Latin "activus," from "agere," to do) -- literally "not doing."
mnemonic: INACTIVE = IN (not) + ACTIVE -- the opposite of doing things.
memory_trick: IN-ACTIVE: NOT active.
visual_association: A dusty treadmill sitting unused in the corner of a room.
difference_explained: Inactive = not doing anything (neutral). Lazy = unwilling to make an effort (negative).
mini_conversation:

simple_explanation: Unable to move or make progress. When you're stuck, you can't move forward -- either physically (like a car stuck in mud) or mentally (like being stuck on a difficult question).
example_1: The car got stuck in the mud.
example_2: I've been stuck on this math problem for an hour.
example_3: We got stuck in traffic for two hours yesterday.
collocations: get stuck, stuck in traffic, stuck on a problem, badly stuck
related_phrasal_verbs: get stuck in, stuck with, hold up
grammar_pattern: be/get + stuck (+ in/on + noun) (stuck in traffic / stuck on a question)
common_mistake: I am stuck for answer this question.
correct_version: I am stuck on this question.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'stuck ON' a problem, or 'stuck IN' a place.
etymology: Past participle of "stick" (Old English "stician," to pierce or fix in place) -- now also used as a standalone adjective.
prefix_root_suffix: stick = root (to fix in place) + irregular past-participle form "stuck"
word_family: stick (v.), sticky (adj.), stuck-up (informal adj., meaning arrogant)
mnemonic: STUCK comes from STICK -- imagine gum STICKing to your shoe, and now you're STUCK.
memory_trick: STUCK: like a car STUCK in mud.
visual_association: A car's tires spinning uselessly in thick mud.
difference_explained: Stuck = can't move. Struck = hit (past of strike).

reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'unable to move or make progress'?
usage_tip: 'Stuck in traffic' is a daily Indian experience.

simple_explanation: Firm, stable, or moving at a constant, reliable pace. Something steady doesn't shake, wobble, or change suddenly -- it stays firm, constant, or reliable over time.
example_2: He has a steady job at the local hospital.
example_3: The runner kept a steady pace throughout the race.
collocations: steady pace, steady income, hold steady, steady hand
related_phrasal_verbs: hold on, keep going, level off
grammar_pattern: be/keep/stay + steady (Keep the camera steady. / The pace stayed steady.)
common_mistake: Please hold the camera more steady.
correct_version: Please hold the camera steadier.
why_it_s_wrong: For comparison, 'steadier' is natural; 'more steady' is also used.
pronunciation_tip: Two syllables: STED-ee, stress on the first.
spelling_tip: "Stead" + "y" -- watch the "ea" spelling, pronounced like a short "e" here.
etymology: From "stead" (Old English "stede," meaning place or position) + "-y" -- literally "firmly in place."
word_family: steadily (adv.), steadiness (n.), steady (v. - to steady oneself), unsteady (adj.)
mnemonic: STEADY sounds like "READY" -- when you're STEADY, you're firmly balanced and READY for anything.
memory_trick: STEADY: like a STEADY table with four legs.
visual_association: A tightrope walker balancing perfectly still, arms outstretched.
difference_explained: Steady = firm and not shaking, or at a constant pace. Stable = unlikely to change or fall.
mini_conversation:

simple_explanation: Firmly fixed or unlikely to change or fail. Something stable stays firm and secure -- it doesn't collapse, change suddenly, or become unpredictable.
example_2: They finally found a stable place to live after years of moving.
example_3: The company's finances have remained stable this year.
collocations: financially stable, remain stable, stable condition, emotionally stable
related_phrasal_verbs: settle down, hold steady, level out
grammar_pattern: be/remain + stable (The economy remains stable. / His condition is stable.)
common_mistake: The table is not very stable, it shake.
correct_version: The table is not very stable, it shakes.
why_it_s_wrong: He/she/it in the simple present needs -s: shakes.
pronunciation_tip: Two syllables: STAY-buhl, stress on the first.
spelling_tip: S-T-A-B-L-E -- don't confuse with "stabile" or add an extra vowel.
etymology: From Latin "stabilis" (firm, steadfast), from "stare" (to stand) -- the same root as "stand" and "establish."
prefix_root_suffix: stab(le) = root (from Latin stabilis, firm) + -le = adjective ending
mnemonic: STABLE sounds like "TABLE" -- a sturdy TABLE with four legs is STABLE and doesn't wobble.
memory_trick: STABLE: a STABLE for horses is a solid, safe place.
visual_association: A sturdy four-legged table that doesn't wobble no matter how it's pushed.
difference_explained: Stable = firmly fixed, unlikely to change. Steady = moving at a constant pace, or not shaking.
mini_conversation:
A: How's your dad doing after the surgery?
B: He's stable now, the doctors say he's recovering well.

reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'firmly fixed or unlikely to change or fail'?
usage_tip: 'His condition is stable' = not getting worse (hospital).

simple_explanation: Very pleasing to look at. When something is beautiful, it looks wonderful to the eyes -- it could be a person, a sunset, a song, or a piece of art.
example_2: She wore a beautiful dress to the wedding.
example_3: The mountains looked beautiful covered in snow.
collocations: truly beautiful, beautiful scenery, absolutely beautiful, beautiful smile
related_phrasal_verbs: n/a (no strong phrasal-verb link, compare "stand out, " "catch the eye")
grammar_pattern: beautiful + noun / be + beautiful (a beautiful garden / The view is beautiful.)
common_mistake: She is very beautiful girl.
correct_version: She is a very beautiful girl.
why_it_s_wrong: A singular countable noun needs 'a': 'a very beautiful girl'.
pronunciation_tip: Three syllables: BYOO-tuh-fuhl, stress on the first.
spelling_tip: "Beauty" changes "y" to "i" before adding "-ful": beaut(y) -> beauti + ful.
etymology: From "beauty" (Old French "beaute," from Latin "bellus," meaning pretty/fine) + "-ful" (full of).
prefix_root_suffix: beaut(y) = root (from Latin bellus, pretty) + -i- (linking vowel) + -ful = suffix meaning "full of"
mnemonic: BEAUTIFUL is FULL of BEAUTY -- the word literally tells you what it means.
memory_trick: BEAUTIFUL: Big Elephants Are Ugly — the first letters spell BEAU.
visual_association: A field of wildflowers stretching toward a colorful sunset.
difference_explained: Pretty = attractive in a delicate way. Beautiful = very attractive, deeper and stronger.

simple_explanation: Not pleasant to look at. When something is ugly, it's unattractive or unpleasant to look at -- the opposite of beautiful.
example_2: He thought the new logo design was ugly.
example_3: The old sofa was so ugly they threw it away.
collocations: really ugly, ugly duckling (idiom), ugly truth, look ugly
related_phrasal_verbs: n/a (no strong phrasal-verb link, compare "put off, " "turn off")
grammar_pattern: ugly + noun / be + ugly (an ugly color / The scar looked ugly.)
common_mistake: This shoes are so ugly, I no like it.
correct_version: These shoes are so ugly, I don't like them.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Shoes' is plural: 'these shoes are', 'I don't like them'.
pronunciation_tip: Two syllables: UHG-lee, stress on the first.
spelling_tip: U-G-L-Y -- no silent letters, straightforward spelling.
etymology: From Old Norse "uggligr" (dreadful, to be dreaded), from "uggr" (fear or dread) -- entered English through Middle English.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- "ugly" comes as a whole word from Old Norse
mnemonic: UGLY sounds a bit UGH -- something that makes you go "ugh" when you see it.
memory_trick: UGLY: the letters look lumpy.
visual_association: A rusty, dented old car parked awkwardly on a clean street.
difference_explained: Plain = simple, not especially attractive. Ugly = unpleasant to look at.

simple_explanation: Good-looking, especially used for men. "Handsome" describes an attractive appearance, traditionally used for men, though it can also describe a generous or impressive amount, like a handsome salary.
example_2: The groom looked handsome in his new suit.
example_3: Her grandfather was known as a handsome young man.
collocations: tall and handsome, handsome man, handsome reward, ruggedly handsome
related_phrasal_verbs: n/a (no strong phrasal-verb link, compare "dress up, " "clean up")
grammar_pattern: handsome + noun / be + handsome (a handsome actor / He is handsome.)
common_mistake: She is a very handsome woman.
correct_version: She is a very attractive woman.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Handsome' is traditionally used for men. For women, 'beautiful' or 'attractive' fits better.
pronunciation_tip: Two syllables: HAN-suhm -- the "d" is silent.
spelling_tip: H-A-N-D-S-O-M-E -- keep the silent "d" even though you don't pronounce it.
etymology: From Middle English "hand" + "-some," originally meaning "easy to handle," which shifted over centuries to mean "good-looking" (especially for men).
prefix_root_suffix: hand = root (originally "easy to handle") + -some = suffix meaning "tending to be"
mnemonic: HANDSOME has "HAND" in it -- imagine a well-dressed man extending his HAND to greet you, looking sharp.
memory_trick: HAND-SOME: HANDs of a strong, good-looking man.
visual_association: A well-groomed man in a tailored suit walking confidently down the street.
difference_explained: Handsome = good-looking (usually men). Beautiful = very attractive (usually women, places).

simple_explanation: Attractive in a pleasant, delicate way. "Pretty" describes something nice-looking, often in a soft or delicate way -- commonly used for girls, flowers, dresses, or scenery.
example_2: She has a pretty smile that lights up the room.
example_3: The town has some pretty little cafes along the river.
collocations: pretty dress, pretty face, quite pretty, pretty little
related_phrasal_verbs: n/a (no strong phrasal-verb link, compare "dress up, " "stand out")
grammar_pattern: pretty + noun / be + pretty (a pretty garden / She looks pretty.)
common_mistake: This is a pretty of dress.
correct_version: This is a pretty dress.
why_it_s_wrong: An adjective goes directly before its noun, with no 'of'.
pronunciation_tip: Two syllables: PRIT-ee, stress on the first.
spelling_tip: P-R-E-T-T-Y -- double "t" in the middle, easy to forget.
etymology: From Old English "prættig," originally meaning cunning or clever, which shifted over time to mean attractive or pleasing.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- "pretty" comes as a whole word from Old English
mnemonic: PRETTY things make you say "pretty please" -- something so nice you want more of it.
memory_trick: PRETTY: a PRETTY flower in the PETTY garden.
visual_association: A small bouquet of pastel-colored flowers tied with ribbon.
difference_explained: Pretty dress = attractive dress. Pretty good = quite good.

simple_explanation: Pleasing or appealing to look at. Something attractive draws your attention because it looks good -- this applies to people, places, and even deals or offers.
example_2: The job offer included an attractive salary package.
example_3: He found the city's old streets quite attractive.
collocations: physically attractive, attractive offer, find someone attractive, visually attractive
related_phrasal_verbs: n/a (no strong phrasal-verb link, compare "stand out, " "catch the eye")
where_it_s_used: Dating, marketing, real estate, job offers
grammar_pattern: attractive + noun / find + someone/something + attractive (I find her attractive.)
common_mistake: I find him very attractive man.
correct_version: I find him very attractive.
why_it_s_wrong: After 'find him', the adjective alone is enough.
pronunciation_tip: Four syllables, stress on the second: uh-TRAK-tiv.
etymology: From "attract" (Latin "attrahere," ad- toward + trahere to draw/pull) + "-ive" -- literally "having the power to draw people in."
prefix_root_suffix: at- (variant of ad-, toward) + tract = root (from Latin trahere, to pull) + -ive = adjective suffix
mnemonic: ATTRACTIVE things ATTRACT attention -- they pull your eyes toward them.
memory_trick: ATTRACT-IVE: it ATTRACTS attention, like a magnet.
visual_association: A shop window display so eye-catching that people stop to look.
difference_explained: Beautiful = very pleasing to see. Attractive = pleasing, or appealing (an attractive salary).
mini_conversation:
A: What do you think of the new apartment listing?
B: It looks attractive, and the price seems fair too.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character glances across the room and murmurs, "He's rather attractive, don't you think?"
news_style_line: News-style: "Analysts say the country remains an attractive destination for foreign investment."
casual_conversation: Casual: "That's a really attractive design for the new logo."
mcq_options: A) Repulsive or unpleasant  B) Pleasing or appealing to look at  C) Extremely cheap  D) Very slow
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The company's new offer looks quite ______ compared to the old one. → attractive
find_and_fix_to_correct: This deal is more attractive than the another one. → This deal is more attractive than the other one.
translate: उसकी मुस्कान बहुत आकर्षक है। → She has an attractive smile.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about an attractive offer you saw.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'pleasing or appealing to look at'?
usage_tip: 'An attractive offer' = a good deal.

simple_explanation: Graceful and stylish in a refined way. Something elegant looks polished, graceful, and tasteful -- not flashy, but carefully and beautifully put together.
example_1: She looked elegant at the party.
example_2: The hotel lobby had an elegant, old-fashioned design.
example_3: He wore an elegant black suit to the gala.
collocations: elegant dress, elegant solution, simple and elegant, elegant design
related_phrasal_verbs: n/a (no strong phrasal-verb link, compare "dress up, " "carry oneself well")
where_it_s_used: Fashion, interior design, formal events, writing
grammar_pattern: elegant + noun / be + elegant (an elegant gown / The design is elegant.)
common_mistake: She dress very elegant for the wedding.
correct_version: She dressed very elegantly for the wedding.
why_it_s_wrong: To describe how she dressed, use the adverb 'elegantly'.
pronunciation_tip: Three syllables: EL-uh-guhnt, stress on the first.
etymology: From Latin "elegans/elegantem" (tasteful, choice), related to "eligere" (to select carefully) -- the same root as "elect."
prefix_root_suffix: e- (variant of ex-, out) + leg = root (from Latin legere, to choose) + -ant = adjective suffix
mnemonic: ELEGANT people are carefully SELECTED in their style -- nothing looks accidental, everything is chosen with taste.
memory_trick: ELEGANT: E-LEG-ANT — long, graceful legs of a dancer.
visual_association: A crystal chandelier casting soft light over a perfectly set dinner table.
difference_explained: Stylish = fashionable now. Elegant = graceful and refined, timeless.
mini_conversation:
A: I love your outfit tonight.
B: Thank you, I wanted something elegant for the dinner.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character glides into the ballroom in a flowing gown, and someone whispers, "She looks absolutely elegant."
news_style_line: News-style: "Critics praised the museum's new wing for its elegant, minimalist architecture."
casual_conversation: Casual: "That's such an elegant way to solve the problem -- so simple."
mcq_options: A) Clumsy and messy  B) Graceful and refined  C) Extremely loud  D) Very cheap
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The bride chose a simple but ______ white gown. → elegant
find_and_fix_to_correct: This is the most elegant solution than others. → This is the most elegant solution of all.
translate: वह पार्टी में बहुत सुरुचिपूर्ण लग रही थी। → She looked elegant at the party.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about an elegant outfit or place.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'graceful and stylish in a refined way'?
usage_tip: 'An elegant solution' = simple and clever.

simple_explanation: Fashionable and attractive in a modern way. Something stylish looks fashionable and well put-together, following current trends of taste.
example_2: Her new haircut looks really stylish.
example_3: The cafe has a stylish, modern interior.
collocations: stylish outfit, stylish and modern, effortlessly stylish, stylish haircut
related_phrasal_verbs: n/a (no strong phrasal-verb link, compare "dress up, " "keep up with trends")
where_it_s_used: Fashion, interior design, hairstyles, social media
grammar_pattern: stylish + noun / be + stylish (a stylish bag / Her outfit is stylish.)
common_mistake: This bag looks very stylish and modernly.
correct_version: This bag looks very stylish and modern.
why_it_s_wrong: After 'looks', use adjectives: 'stylish and modern'.
pronunciation_tip: Two syllables: STY-lish, stress on the first.
spelling_tip: "Style" + "ish" -- drop nothing, just add "ish" since "style" ends in "e": styl(e) + ish.
etymology: From "style" (Latin "stilus," a writing tool, later extended to mean "manner" or "fashion") + "-ish" (having the quality of).
prefix_root_suffix: style = root (from Latin stilus, manner) + -ish = adjective suffix meaning "having the quality of"
mnemonic: STYLISH people have great STYLE -- the word wears its meaning right on its sleeve.
memory_trick: STYLE-ISH: with STYLE.
visual_association: A well-curated boutique window with a single eye-catching outfit on display.
difference_explained: Same idea. Fashionable = popular right now. Stylish = good-looking with style.
mini_conversation:
A: I really like your new glasses.
B: Thanks, I wanted something stylish but still practical.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character admires a shop window and says, "Now that is stylish -- I need that coat."
news_style_line: News-style: "The brand's stylish new collection quickly sold out within hours of launch."
casual_conversation: Casual: "You always dress so stylish -- any tips for me?"
mcq_options: A) Outdated and dull  B) Fashionable and attractive  C) Extremely cheap  D) Very heavy
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The new cafe downtown has a really ______ interior. → stylish
find_and_fix_to_correct: She always dresses stylish than everyone. → She always dresses more stylishly than everyone.
translate: उसने एक स्टाइलिश जैकेट पहनी थी। → He wore a stylish jacket.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a stylish item you own.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'fashionable and attractive in a modern way'?
usage_tip: 'Stylish' is common in fashion and product ads.

simple_explanation: Popular and in style at the moment. Something fashionable follows the current trends -- it's what's considered stylish or popular right now.
example_1: Skinny jeans were once very fashionable.
example_2: It's fashionable to wear bright colors this season.
example_3: The neighborhood has become a fashionable place to live.
collocations: fashionable trend, become fashionable, highly fashionable, fashionable clothes
related_phrasal_verbs: n/a (no strong phrasal-verb link, compare "catch on, " "keep up with")
grammar_pattern: fashionable + noun / be/become + fashionable (a fashionable cafe / It became fashionable.)
common_mistake: This style is fashionable since last year.
correct_version: This style has been fashionable since last year.
why_it_s_wrong: For something continuing from a past time, use 'has been … since'.
pronunciation_tip: Four syllables: FASH-uh-nuh-buhl, stress on the first.
spelling_tip: "Fashion" + "able" -- keep the full spelling of "fashion" before adding the suffix.
etymology: From "fashion" (Old French "façon," from Latin "factio," a making or doing) + "-able" -- literally "in keeping with current fashion."
prefix_root_suffix: fashion = root (from Latin factio, a making) + -able = suffix meaning "capable of/characterized by"
mnemonic: FASHIONABLE things are ABLE to follow the latest FASHION trends.
memory_trick: FASHION-ABLE: ABLE to follow FASHION.
visual_association: A crowded street where everyone seems to be wearing the same trending jacket.
difference_explained: Same meaning. Trendy is more informal and can suggest it won't last.
related_words: trendy, chic, in vogue, popular, hip
mini_conversation:
A: Is this cafe actually good, or just fashionable?
B: Both, honestly -- the coffee is great too.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character flips through a magazine and remarks, "Apparently oversized blazers are fashionable again."
news_style_line: News-style: "The seaside town has quietly become one of the most fashionable getaways this summer."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Are wide-leg trousers still fashionable, or has that trend passed?"
mcq_options: A) Outdated and unpopular  B) Popular and in style currently  C) Extremely expensive  D) Very uncomfortable
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Wearing sneakers with formal wear has become surprisingly ______. → fashionable
find_and_fix_to_correct: This area is more fashionable that it used to be. → This area is more fashionable than it used to be.
translate: स्किनी जींस कभी बहुत फैशनेबल हुआ करती थी। → Skinny jeans were once very fashionable.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a fashionable trend among students.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'popular and in style at the moment'?
usage_tip: 'Fashionably late' = arriving a little late on purpose.

simple_explanation: Simple, without decoration or extra features. Something plain is simple and basic -- no patterns, no extra flavor, no decoration. It's not fancy, but not necessarily bad.
example_1: She wore a plain white shirt.
example_2: He prefers plain rice without any spices.
example_3: The walls were left plain, without any paintings.
collocations: plain and simple, plain white, plain rice, keep it plain
related_phrasal_verbs: n/a (no strong phrasal-verb link, compare "tone down, " "strip back")
where_it_s_used: Food, clothing, interior decor, communication style
grammar_pattern: plain + noun / be + plain (a plain dress / The room looks plain.)
common_mistake: I like plain food without of spices.
correct_version: I like plain food without spices.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Without' is followed directly by a noun, with no 'of'.
pronunciation_tip: One syllable: PLAYN, rhymes with "rain" and "train."
spelling_tip: P-L-A-I-N -- don't confuse with "plane" (an aircraft or a flat surface).
etymology: From Old French "plain," from Latin "planus" (flat, level) -- the same root as "plane" and "planet" (indirectly, through "flat surface").
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- "plain" comes as a whole word from Latin "planus"
mnemonic: PLAIN sounds like "PLANE" -- flat and simple, with nothing sticking out.
memory_trick: PLAIN: a PLAIN field — flat, simple, nothing extra.
visual_association: A single white wall with no pictures or decorations.
difference_explained: Plain = simple. Plane = aeroplane, or a flat surface. Same sound.
mini_conversation:
A: How do you take your toast?
B: Just plain, thanks -- no butter or jam.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character glances at the menu and says, "I'll just have something plain -- maybe toast."
news_style_line: News-style: "The designer's new collection surprised critics with its plain, minimalist approach."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I like my walls plain -- no posters, no clutter."
mcq_options: A) Highly decorated  B) Simple, without decoration  C) Extremely expensive  D) Very colorful
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: He ordered a ______ sandwich with nothing extra on it. → plain
find_and_fix_to_correct: This dress is too plain for a party, no? → This dress is too plain for a party, isn't it?
translate: उसने एक सादी सफ़ेद शर्ट पहनी थी। → She wore a plain white shirt.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a plain food you like.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'simple, without decoration or extra features'?
usage_tip: 'Plain' also means clear: 'plain English'.

simple_explanation: Full of bright colors. Something colorful has lots of bright colors -- it stands out and looks lively, not dull or gray.
example_1: The market was full of colorful fruits.
example_2: The children painted a colorful mural on the school wall.
example_3: She loves wearing colorful scarves in winter.
collocations: colorful lights, bright and colorful, colorful design, colorful character (idiom)
related_phrasal_verbs: n/a (no strong phrasal-verb link, compare "light up, " "stand out")
grammar_pattern: colorful + noun / be + colorful (colorful balloons / The garden is colorful.)
common_mistake: This picture has too much colorful.
correct_version: This picture is too colorful.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Colourful' is an adjective, so use 'is too colourful'.
pronunciation_tip: Three syllables: KUHL-er-fuhl, stress on the first.
etymology: From "color" (Latin "color") + "-ful" (full of) -- literally "full of color." (British English spells it "colourful.")
prefix_root_suffix: color = root (from Latin color) + -ful = suffix meaning "full of"
mnemonic: COLORFUL is FULL of COLOR -- bright reds, blues, and yellows all packed in.
memory_trick: COLOUR-FUL: FULL of COLOURS.
visual_association: A rainbow-colored kite fluttering high against a clear blue sky.
difference_explained: Bright = strong light or colour. Colourful = many different colours.
mini_conversation:
A: I love the decorations for the festival!
B: Me too, everything looks so colorful this year.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character steps into the market and gasps, "Look at all these colorful stalls -- it's beautiful!"
news_style_line: News-style: "Thousands gathered downtown for the colorful parade celebrating the city's founding."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Your new curtains are so colorful -- they really brighten up the room."
mcq_options: A) Dull and gray  B) Full of bright colors  C) Extremely small  D) Very quiet
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The parade featured ______ costumes and dancing. → colorful
find_and_fix_to_correct: This design is more colorful than the another one. → This design is more colorful than the other one.

write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a colourful festival.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'full of bright colors'?
usage_tip: UK: colourful. US: colorful. Indian English usually uses UK spelling.

simple_explanation: Extremely beautiful or attractive. "Gorgeous" describes someone or something so beautiful that it really stands out -- stronger than just "nice" or "pretty."
example_1: The bride looked gorgeous in her white dress.
example_2: The view from the hilltop was absolutely gorgeous.
example_3: You look gorgeous in that blue dress.
collocations: gorgeous view, gorgeous dress, absolutely gorgeous, look gorgeous
related_phrasal_verbs: a sight for sore eyes, dressed to the nines
grammar_pattern: gorgeous + noun / look + gorgeous (a gorgeous sunset / She looks gorgeous.)
common_mistake: She is very gorgeous.
correct_version: She is gorgeous.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Gorgeous' is already extreme, so 'very' isn't added.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the first syllable: GOR-juhs; the "ge" makes a soft "j" sound, not a hard "g."
spelling_tip: Remember the "-eous" ending, not "-ious" -- GORGE + OUS.
etymology: From Old French "gorgias" (elegant, fashionable), possibly related to "gorge" (throat/ruff collar) -- originally described fancy dress, later stunning beauty in general.
prefix_root_suffix: gorge (root, from French for throat/collar) + -ous = adjective suffix ("full of")
mnemonic: A GORGEOUS sunset makes you gasp "gosh!" -- both start with that same breathy sound.
memory_trick: GORGEOUS: say it slowly — it sounds rich.
visual_association: A perfect golden-orange sunset reflected on calm ocean water.
difference_explained: Beautiful = very attractive. Gorgeous = extremely beautiful (informal).
mini_conversation:
A: Have you seen the sunset tonight?
B: Yes, it's absolutely gorgeous!
everyday_scene: Everyday: A guest gasps at the entrance, "Wow, this garden is gorgeous!"
news_style_line: News-style: "Tourists flocked to the coast to photograph the gorgeous autumn colors."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Check out her new haircut -- she looks gorgeous!"
mcq_options: A) Very beautiful  B) Slightly untidy  C) Somewhat boring  D) Extremely large
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The mountains looked ______ covered in fresh snow. → gorgeous
find_and_fix_to_correct: This is a very gorgeous painting. → This is a gorgeous painting. (drop "very" -- gorgeous already means extremely beautiful)
translate: उस पहाड़ी इलाके का नज़ारा बहुत ही मनोहर था। → The view of that hilly area was absolutely gorgeous.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a gorgeous view.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'extremely beautiful or attractive'?
usage_tip: Informal: 'Gorgeous!' = beautiful, lovely.

simple_explanation: Attractive in a small, pleasant, or charming way. We call something "cute" when it's small, young, or sweet-looking in a way that makes people smile -- like a baby or a puppy.
example_2: My little cousin has the cutest laugh.
example_3: They bought a cute little cottage by the lake.
collocations: so cute, cute baby, cute smile, look cute
where_it_s_used: Babies, pets, compliments, casual conversation, social media
grammar_pattern: cute + noun / look + cute (a cute puppy / She looks cute today.)
common_mistake: He is cute boy.
correct_version: He is a cute boy.
why_it_s_wrong: A singular countable noun needs 'a': 'a cute boy'.
pronunciation_tip: One syllable with a long "u" sound: KYOOT, rhymes with "flute."
spelling_tip: The silent "e" at the end makes the "u" say its own name -- CUT + E = "kyoot," not "kut."
etymology: A shortened, informal form of "acute" (sharp, clever) that arose in 18th-century English; the meaning drifted from "clever" to "charmingly attractive," especially for small or young things.
prefix_root_suffix: shortened from "acute" with the first syllable dropped -- no clear prefix/root/suffix in modern use
mnemonic: A CUTE puppy makes everyone say "awww" -- a short word for a small, sweet thing.
memory_trick: CUTE: a CUTE puppy.
visual_association: A small kitten with big round eyes.
difference_explained: Pretty = attractive, delicate. Cute = attractive in a small, sweet way.
mini_conversation:
A: Look at this photo of my new kitten!
B: Aww, it's so cute!
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character coos over a photo, "Oh my gosh, look how cute this is!"
news_style_line: News-style: "The zoo's newest baby panda has quickly become a cute local attraction."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Your dog is so cute -- what breed is he?"
mcq_options: A) Attractive in a small, charming way  B) Extremely tall  C) Very expensive  D) Old and worn out
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The baby giggled and looked absolutely ______. → cute
find_and_fix_to_correct: She has a cute dogs. → She has cute dogs. (drop "a" before a plural noun)
translate: उसकी छोटी बेटी बहुत प्यारी है। → Her little daughter is very cute.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a cute animal you saw.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'attractive in a small, pleasant, or charming way'?
usage_tip: 'Cute' is used for babies, animals and small things.

simple_explanation: Tidy, clean, and well-arranged. When something is "neat," it's arranged in an organized, clean way with nothing out of place.
example_1: Keep your room neat and tidy.
example_2: He always keeps his desk neat.
example_3: She wrote her notes in neat handwriting.
collocations: neat and tidy, keep neat, neat handwriting, neat appearance
where_it_s_used: Housekeeping, handwriting, appearance, organization, informal praise
grammar_pattern: neat + noun / keep + object + neat (a neat room / Keep your desk neat.)
common_mistake: Her room is very neat and organize.
correct_version: Her room is very neat and organized.
why_it_s_wrong: After 'very neat and', use the adjective 'organized', not the verb.
spelling_tip: The two vowels together -- "ea" -- spell the long "e" sound in "neat."
etymology: From French "net" (clean, pure), from Latin "nitidus" (shining) -- originally meant "clean/pure," later extended to "tidy and well-arranged."
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- a simple base adjective
mnemonic: A NEAT desk has everything in its place -- nothing extra, nothing out of order.
memory_trick: NEAT: short and tidy word.
visual_association: A perfectly organized bookshelf with everything lined up straight.
difference_explained: Clean = no dirt. Neat = tidy and well-arranged.
mini_conversation:
A: Wow, your handwriting is so neat!
B: Thanks, I practice it every day.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character glances around a spotless room and remarks, "Everything here is so neat."
news_style_line: News-style: "Volunteers left the park neat and clean after the weekend cleanup drive."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Wow, that's a neat trick -- can you teach me?"
mcq_options: A) Tidy and well-arranged  B) Loud and noisy  C) Extremely expensive  D) Broken or damaged

find_and_fix_to_correct: Please write more neatly, your handwriting is very messily. → Please write more neatly, your handwriting is very messy. (use the adjective "messy," not the adverb "messily," after "is")
translate: उसका कमरा हमेशा साफ़-सुथरा रहता है। → His room is always neat.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about someone with neat handwriting.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'tidy, clean, and well-arranged'?
usage_tip: Informal American 'Neat!' = great.

simple_explanation: Untidy, disorganized, or dirty. Something "messy" is not arranged properly -- it looks disorganized, dirty, or all over the place.
example_2: The kids left the kitchen messy after baking cookies.
example_3: Her hair looked messy after the windy walk.
collocations: messy room, messy hair, messy situation, get messy
related_phrasal_verbs: leave behind a mess, clean up
grammar_pattern: messy + noun / be + messy (a messy room / The room is messy.)
common_mistake: The room is too much messy.
correct_version: The room is too messy.
why_it_s_wrong: Before an adjective, use 'too', not 'too much'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the first syllable: MESS-ee.
spelling_tip: Keep the double "s" from "mess" before adding "-y" -- MESS + Y.
etymology: From "mess" (a disordered mixture, originally a portion of food from Old French "mes") + adjective suffix "-y."
mnemonic: A MESSY room looks like someone made a "mess" and never cleaned it up.
memory_trick: MESSY: MESS + Y.
visual_association: Clothes and papers scattered across an unmade bed.
difference_explained: Dirty = has dirt. Messy = untidy.
mini_conversation:
A: Sorry the apartment is so messy today.
B: Don't worry, mine looks the same after exams!
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character opens the door and sighs, "Ugh, this place is a total mess."
news_style_line: News-style: "City officials called the storm's aftermath a messy cleanup that could take weeks."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Can you help me clean up? The kitchen is so messy."
mcq_options: A) Untidy and disorganized  B) Very expensive  C) Extremely quiet  D) Well-organized
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: My little brother's room is always ______. → messy
find_and_fix_to_correct: Her handwriting is more messier than mine. → Her handwriting is messier than mine. (don't use "more" together with the "-er" comparative form)

write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about the messiest place in your house.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'untidy, disorganized, or dirty'?
usage_tip: 'A messy divorce' = a difficult, unpleasant one.

simple_explanation: Following official rules, or suitable for serious or official occasions. "Formal" describes clothes, language, or events that are proper and follow polite, official conventions -- like a business meeting or a wedding.
example_1: He wore a formal suit to the interview.
example_2: The invitation asked guests to wear formal attire.
example_3: She used formal language in her business email.
collocations: formal attire, formal language, formal invitation, formal meeting
where_it_s_used: Business, weddings, official letters, interviews, ceremonies
grammar_pattern: formal + noun (a formal letter / formal wear)
common_mistake: Please wear formals for the interview.
correct_version: Please wear formal clothes for the interview.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Formal' is an adjective. 'Formals' as a noun for clothes is Indian English.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the first syllable: FOR-muhl.
spelling_tip: Just one "r" and one "m" -- FOR + MAL, not "forrmal."
etymology: From Latin "formalis," from "forma" (shape/form) -- relating to established form, structure, or convention.
mnemonic: FORMAL events follow a strict FORM -- a suit, a set order, polite speech.
memory_trick: FORMAL: follows the FORM (the rules).
visual_association: A neatly pressed black-tie suit laid out for an evening event.
difference_explained: Official = from an authority. Formal = following strict rules of style.
mini_conversation:
A: What should I wear to the gala?
B: It's formal, so a suit or evening dress.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A butler announces at the door, "The formal dinner will begin shortly, sir."
news_style_line: News-style: "The two leaders signed the agreement at a formal ceremony this afternoon."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Is the wedding formal, or can I wear jeans?"
mcq_options: A) Following official or polite conventions  B) Extremely funny  C) Cheap and simple  D) Loud and colorful
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The office requires ______ dress on client visit days. → formal
find_and_fix_to_correct: She talk very formal in the meeting. → She talks very formally in the meeting. (use the adverb "formally" to describe how she talks, and add -s for third person)
translate: शादी में सभी मेहमानों को औपचारिक कपड़े पहनने थे। → All the guests had to wear formal clothes at the wedding.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a formal first line for an email to a company.
