usage_tip: Formal emails begin 'Dear Sir/Madam'.

simple_explanation: Relaxed and informal, without strict rules. "Casual" describes clothes, events, or behavior that are relaxed and easygoing, not strict or fancy.
example_1: He wore casual jeans and a T-shirt to the party.
example_2: It's a casual get-together, so no need to dress up.
example_3: She has a casual attitude toward deadlines.
collocations: casual clothes, casual conversation, casual Friday, dress casually
where_it_s_used: Weekend outings, workplace dress codes, friendly conversation, dating
grammar_pattern: casual + noun (a casual outfit / a casual chat)
common_mistake: The meeting was so much casual, everyone just talked freely.
correct_version: The meeting was so casual, everyone just talked freely.
why_it_s_wrong: Before an adjective, use 'so', not 'so much'.
pronunciation_tip: Three syllables: KAZH-oo-uhl, with a soft "zh" sound in the middle.
spelling_tip: Watch the "-ual" ending, not "-ul" -- CASU + AL.
etymology: From Latin "casualis," from "casus" (chance/occurrence) -- originally meant "happening by chance," later came to describe relaxed, unplanned style or behavior.
mnemonic: CASUAL clothes are for a CASUAL day -- jeans and a T-shirt, nothing fancy.
memory_trick: CASUAL: easy, like CASUAL Fridays at the office.
visual_association: A pair of comfortable sneakers and a plain T-shirt tossed on a chair.
difference_explained: Same idea. Informal is used for language; casual is common for clothes and behaviour.
mini_conversation:
A: What's the dress code for the barbecue?
B: Totally casual -- shorts and sandals are fine.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character shrugs and says, "It's just a casual get-together, don't overdress."
news_style_line: News-style: "More offices are adopting casual dress codes to boost employee comfort."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Is this a casual dinner, or should I dress up a bit?"
mcq_options: A) Relaxed and informal  B) Strict and official  C) Expensive and luxurious  D) Loud and aggressive
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The office allows ______ clothing every Friday. → casual
find_and_fix_to_correct: He speak very casual with his boss, which is disrespectful. → He speaks very casually with his boss, which is disrespectful. (use the adverb "casually" and add -s for third person)
translate: आज की पार्टी बिल्कुल अनौपचारिक है, तुम कुछ भी पहन सकते हो। → Today's party is completely casual, you can wear anything.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about casual clothes you like.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'relaxed and informal, without strict rules'?
usage_tip: 'Casual wear' = everyday clothes.

simple_explanation: Relating to the present time; new and up to date. "Modern" describes things that belong to today's world -- new designs, current technology, or recent ways of living, unlike older or traditional styles.
example_1: They live in a modern apartment downtown.
example_2: The museum has an impressive modern art collection.
example_3: Modern technology has changed how we communicate.
collocations: modern technology, modern art, modern lifestyle, modern design
related_phrasal_verbs: up to date, state of the art
grammar_pattern: modern + noun (modern art / modern life)
common_mistake: She has very modern thinkings.
correct_version: She has very modern ideas.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Thinking' as a noun is uncountable. Use 'ideas' for countable thoughts.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the first syllable: MOD-ern.
etymology: From Latin "modernus," from "modo" (just now) -- describing what belongs to the present time, as opposed to the past.
prefix_root_suffix: modern- (root, from Latin "just now") -- no separate prefix/suffix in the base form
mnemonic: MODERN things are made for the MOMENT -- new, current, up to date.
memory_trick: MODERN: MODE of today.
visual_association: A sleek glass skyscraper next to older brick buildings.
difference_explained: New = recently made. Modern = belonging to the present style.
mini_conversation:
A: I love the design of this new building.
B: Yeah, it has such a modern look.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A tour guide gestures at the skyline and says, "This city blends history with modern design."
news_style_line: News-style: "The city unveiled a modern transit system aimed at cutting commute times."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I really like your modern kitchen -- did you renovate recently?"
mcq_options: A) Relating to the present time  B) Very old and traditional  C) Extremely cheap  D) Difficult to understand
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The city built a ______ library with free Wi-Fi and study pods. → modern
find_and_fix_to_correct: This is most modern phone in the store. → This is the most modern phone in the store. (add the article "the" before a superlative)
translate: उनका घर बहुत आधुनिक ढंग से सजाया गया है। → Their house is decorated in a very modern way.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a modern building in your city.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'relating to the present time; new and up to date'?
usage_tip: 'Modern-day' = present time.

simple_explanation: Belonging to or typical of an earlier time; not modern. "Old-fashioned" describes styles, objects, or opinions that come from an earlier time and aren't up to date with current trends.
example_1: My grandfather has some old-fashioned ideas about work.
example_2: She collects old-fashioned typewriters as a hobby.
example_3: His manners seem old-fashioned but charming.
collocations: old-fashioned way, old-fashioned values, old-fashioned charm, seem old-fashioned
related_phrasal_verbs: out of date, behind the times
where_it_s_used: Family traditions, design, manners, nostalgia, technology comparisons
grammar_pattern: old-fashioned + noun (an old-fashioned recipe / old-fashioned manners)
common_mistake: This phone is very old-fashion.
correct_version: This phone is very old-fashioned.
why_it_s_wrong: Keep the -ed ending: old-fashioned.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on "old" and "fash": OLD-FASH-uhnd, said smoothly as one compound word.
spelling_tip: Don't forget the hyphen between "old" and "fashioned" -- it's one compound adjective.
etymology: A compound of "old" + "fashioned" (shaped/styled), used since the 16th century to describe styles or attitudes belonging to an earlier era.
prefix_root_suffix: old (root) + fashioned (root, past participle of "fashion") = compound adjective
mnemonic: An OLD-FASHIONED clock has hands, not a digital screen -- a style stuck in the past.
memory_trick: OLD + FASHIONED: made in the OLD fashion.
visual_association: A vintage rotary telephone sitting on a wooden desk.
difference_explained: Old = has existed a long time. Old-fashioned = in the style of the past.
mini_conversation:
A: Why do you still write letters by hand?
B: I guess I'm a bit old-fashioned that way.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A grandmother smiles and says, "Call me old-fashioned, but I still prefer letters to texts."
news_style_line: News-style: "Sales of old-fashioned vinyl records have risen again among younger listeners."
casual_conversation: Casual: "My dad's a bit old-fashioned -- he doesn't trust online banking."
mcq_options: A) Belonging to an earlier, less modern time  B) Extremely fast and efficient  C) Brand new and untested  D) Expensive and rare
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Grandma still uses an ______ recipe passed down for generations. → old-fashioned
find_and_fix_to_correct: He has old-fashion opinion about marriage. → He has an old-fashioned opinion about marriage. (add the article "an" and keep the "-ed" ending)
translate: मेरे दादाजी के विचार थोड़े पुराने ज़माने के हैं। → My grandfather's ideas are a bit old-fashioned.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about an old-fashioned habit your grandparents have.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'belonging to or typical of an earlier time; not modern'?
usage_tip: 'Old-fashioned' can be warm: 'old-fashioned values'.

simple_explanation: Following old customs or ways passed down for a long time. "Traditional" describes something that follows customs, beliefs, or styles that have existed for a long time and are passed from one generation to the next.
example_1: They cooked a traditional meal for the festival.
example_2: She wore a traditional dress at the wedding.
example_3: It's a traditional custom to remove your shoes indoors.
collocations: traditional dress, traditional food, traditional values, traditional custom
where_it_s_used: Festivals, food, clothing, ceremonies, family customs
grammar_pattern: traditional + noun (a traditional dance / traditional beliefs)
common_mistake: This is a traditional from my country.
correct_version: This is a tradition from my country.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Traditional' is an adjective. The noun is 'tradition'.
pronunciation_tip: Four syllables, stress on the third: truh-DISH-uh-nuhl.
spelling_tip: Remember "-tion" makes the "sh" sound -- TRADI + TION + AL.
etymology: From Latin "traditio" (a handing over/down), from "tradere" (to hand over) -- describing customs passed down through generations.
prefix_root_suffix: tradit(ion) (root, a handing down) + -al = adjective suffix ("relating to")
mnemonic: TRADITIONAL things TRAVEL down through generations, like a family recipe.
memory_trick: TRADITION-AL: from TRADITION.
visual_association: A grandmother teaching a child to fold traditional clothing.
difference_explained: Traditional = adjective. Tradition = noun.
mini_conversation:
A: What's this dish called?
B: It's a traditional soup my grandmother taught me to make.
everyday_scene: Everyday: An elder explains to a child, "This dance is traditional -- my grandmother taught it to me."
news_style_line: News-style: "The festival celebrated traditional music and dance from across the region."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Are you cooking anything traditional for the holiday dinner?"
mcq_options: A) Following long-established customs  B) Brand new and untested  C) Extremely expensive  D) Scientific and technical
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Every year, the town holds a ______ festival with music and dance. → traditional
find_and_fix_to_correct: We eat traditional foods on tradition festivals. → We eat traditional foods on traditional festivals. (use the adjective "traditional" before the noun "festivals")
translate: दिवाली पर हम पारंपरिक मिठाइयाँ बनाते हैं। → We make traditional sweets on Diwali.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a traditional food in your family.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'following old customs or ways passed down for a long time'?
usage_tip: 'Traditional dress' = clothes worn in the old way, like a saree or dhoti.

simple_explanation: Of the highest quality and remaining popular over a long time. "Classic" describes something -- a book, movie, style, or example -- that is excellent, well-known, and remains admired long after it was made.
example_1: This is a classic example of good design.
example_2: That movie is a classic everyone should watch.
example_3: He drives a classic car from the 1960s.
collocations: classic car, classic novel, classic mistake, classic example
where_it_s_used: Movies, books, cars, fashion, typical situations
grammar_pattern: classic + noun (a classic film / a classic case)
common_mistake: This is a classical film.
correct_version: This is a classic film.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Classic' = excellent and lasting. 'Classical' = ancient, or classical music.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the first syllable: KLAS-ik.
etymology: From Latin "classicus" (of the highest class), originally describing top-ranking Roman citizens, later extended to works of the highest, most enduring quality.
word_family: classics (n., academic subject), classical (adj., a related but distinct meaning), classically (adv.)
mnemonic: A CLASSIC movie is one people still watch, in style, years later.
memory_trick: CLASSIC = a CLASS above others, always.
visual_association: A polished vintage car parked outside an old cinema.
difference_explained: Classic = excellent and lasting (a classic film). Classical = traditional or ancient (classical music).
mini_conversation:
A: Have you seen that old film everyone talks about?
B: Yes, it's an absolute classic.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A film critic remarks, "Twenty years later, this is still a classic worth watching."
news_style_line: News-style: "The auction featured several classic cars from the mid-twentieth century."
casual_conversation: Casual: "That's such a classic dad joke -- I love it."
mcq_options: A) Excellent and remaining popular over time  B) Brand new and untested  C) Cheap and low quality  D) Difficult to find
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: My father still drives a ______ car from the 1970s. → classic
find_and_fix_to_correct: She like classical rock music from the 80s. → She likes classic rock music from the 80s. ("classic rock" is the correct term, not "classical rock," and add -s for third person)
translate: यह फ़िल्म एक कालजयी क्लासिक मानी जाती है। → This film is considered a timeless classic.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a classic film everyone should watch.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'of the highest quality and remaining popular over a long time'?
usage_tip: 'A classic mistake' = a very typical mistake.

simple_explanation: Very fashionable and currently popular. Something "trendy" is popular right now because it follows the latest style or fashion -- though it might go out of style quickly.
example_2: That trendy cafe is always full on weekends.
example_3: He bought a trendy pair of sneakers.
collocations: trendy restaurant, trendy clothes, trendy neighborhood, trendy style
where_it_s_used: Fashion, restaurants, social media, youth culture
grammar_pattern: trendy + noun (a trendy bar / trendy shoes)
common_mistake: This shop sells very much trendy clothes.
correct_version: This shop sells very trendy clothes.
why_it_s_wrong: Before an adjective, use 'very', not 'very much'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the first syllable: TREN-dee.
etymology: From "trend" (a general direction of change), from Old English "trendan" (to turn/roll) + adjective suffix "-y," describing what follows the current fashion.
mnemonic: A TRENDY cafe follows the latest TREND everyone's talking about.
memory_trick: TRENDY: follows the TREND.
visual_association: A crowded, brightly lit cafe full of people taking photos of their food.
difference_explained: Popular = liked by many. Trendy = fashionable right now.
mini_conversation:
A: Where should we eat tonight?
B: There's a new trendy place downtown everyone's raving about.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character glances around a busy cafe and says, "This place is so trendy right now."
news_style_line: News-style: "The neighborhood has become trendy, with new cafes opening every month."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I love your jacket -- is that the trendy brand everyone's wearing?"
mcq_options: A) Currently fashionable and popular  B) Old and worn out  C) Extremely quiet  D) Boring and plain
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: That new coffee shop downtown is really ______ right now. → trendy
find_and_fix_to_correct: This is more trendier than the other design. → This is trendier than the other design. (don't use "more" with the "-er" comparative form)
translate: आजकल छोटे बाल फिर से फ़ैशन में हैं। → Short hair is trendy again these days.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a trendy café or shop.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'very fashionable and currently popular'?
usage_tip: 'Trendy' can sound slightly negative, like 'just for show'.

simple_explanation: Attractive in an exciting, glossy, or luxurious way. Something "glamorous" looks exciting and impressive, often connected to fame, fashion, or a luxurious lifestyle.
example_1: She leads a glamorous life as a fashion designer.
example_2: The awards show was full of glamorous celebrities.
example_3: He imagined a glamorous career in the film industry.
collocations: glamorous lifestyle, glamorous career, glamorous event, glamorous look
related_phrasal_verbs: dress to impress, live it up
where_it_s_used: Fashion, celebrities, film industry, luxury travel
grammar_pattern: glamorous + noun (a glamorous party / a glamorous actress)
common_mistake: She has a glamour job in fashion.
correct_version: She has a glamorous job in fashion.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Glamour' is the noun. The adjective is 'glamorous' (no U before R).
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the first syllable: GLAM-uh-ruhs; don't over-stress the middle syllable.
spelling_tip: American spelling drops the "u" before "-ous" -- GLAMOR + OUS (British English keeps it: glamourous).
etymology: From "glamour," originally a Scots variant of "grammar" once linked with magic and enchantment, later meaning attractive, exciting charm; "-ous" makes it an adjective.
mnemonic: A GLAMOROUS star walks the red carpet in full GLAM style.
memory_trick: GLAMOUR → GLAMOROUS: the U disappears.
visual_association: A red carpet lined with flashing cameras and elegant gowns.
emotion_feel: Admiration mixed with a touch of envy
difference_explained: Luxurious = very comfortable and expensive. Glamorous = exciting and attractive.
mini_conversation:
A: Did you see the photos from the film premiere?
B: Yes, everyone looked so glamorous!
everyday_scene: Everyday: A photographer calls out, "Give me that glamorous smile for the cover!"
news_style_line: News-style: "The film festival drew glamorous crowds to the red carpet this weekend."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Your holiday photos look so glamorous -- where was that resort?"
mcq_options: A) Exciting and luxurious in appearance  B) Plain and simple  C) Cheap and basic  D) Quiet and shy
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The actress arrived at the premiere looking absolutely ______. → glamorous
find_and_fix_to_correct: The party was very glamour last night. → The party was very glamorous last night. (use the adjective "glamorous," not the noun "glamour")
translate: फ़िल्मी दुनिया की ज़िंदगी बहुत चमकदार लगती है। → Life in the film industry looks very glamorous.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a glamorous job.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'attractive in an exciting, glossy, or luxurious way'?
usage_tip: 'Glamorous lifestyle' = exciting and luxurious.

simple_explanation: Old, worn-out, and in poor condition. Something "shabby" looks old and worn from a lot of use -- clothes that are faded and torn, or a building that needs repair.
example_1: He wore a shabby old jacket.
example_2: The hotel looked shabby compared to the photos online.
example_3: She felt embarrassed by her shabby shoes.
collocations: shabby clothes, shabby building, look shabby, shabby condition
where_it_s_used: Clothing, buildings, furniture, describing poverty or neglect
grammar_pattern: shabby + noun (a shabby coat / a shabby apartment)
common_mistake: He was wearing shabby dress.
correct_version: He was wearing shabby clothes.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Dress' is a women's garment. For someone's outfit, say 'clothes'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the first syllable: SHAB-ee.
etymology: From "shab" (Old English "sceabb," a scab or skin disease), later meaning worn-out or in poor condition, and figuratively "unfair/mean" (shabby treatment).
prefix_root_suffix: shab(by) (root, from "scab/skin disease") + -y = adjective suffix ("full of/characterized by")
mnemonic: SHABBY clothes look like they've been sitting in a dusty old attic for years.
memory_trick: SHABBY: sounds like 'scabby' — worn and old.
visual_association: A faded, torn armchair with stuffing peeking out of the seams.
difference_explained: Dirty = has dirt. Shabby = old, worn and in poor condition.
mini_conversation:
A: This old sofa looks so shabby.
B: I know, we really need to replace it.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character eyes a rundown motel and mutters, "This place looks pretty shabby."
news_style_line: News-style: "Residents complained that the once-grand theater had grown shabby from years of neglect."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Sorry about my shabby old bike -- it's seen better days."
mcq_options: A) Old and worn-out  B) Brand new and shiny  C) Extremely expensive  D) Bright and colorful
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The old building looked ______ and needed urgent repairs. → shabby
find_and_fix_to_correct: Don't treat me so shabbily, it isn't fair, I deserve better than this shabbily. → Don't treat me so shabbily -- it isn't fair; I deserve better than this. (avoid repeating "shabbily" awkwardly at the end)
translate: उसने एक पुराना, जर्जर कोट पहना हुआ था। → He was wearing an old, shabby coat.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a shabby old building.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'old, worn-out, and in poor condition'?
usage_tip: 'Not too shabby' = quite good (informal).

simple_explanation: Elaborate, decorative, or expensive-looking. "Fancy" describes something more decorated, elegant, or expensive than the ordinary version -- like a fancy restaurant compared to a simple cafe.
example_1: We went to a fancy restaurant for our anniversary.
example_2: She wore a fancy dress to the gala.
example_3: He has a fancy new phone with lots of features.
collocations: fancy restaurant, fancy dress, fancy hotel, get fancy
grammar_pattern: fancy + noun (a fancy car / fancy clothes)
common_mistake: This restaurant is too much fancy for me.
correct_version: This restaurant is too fancy for me.
why_it_s_wrong: Before an adjective, use 'too', not 'too much'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the first syllable: FAN-see.
etymology: Shortened form of "fantasy" (Middle English "fantasie"), from Greek "phantasia" (imagination) -- came to mean elaborate or decorative due to imaginative design.
prefix_root_suffix: shortened from "fantasy" -- no clear modern prefix/root/suffix breakdown
mnemonic: FANCY restaurants make you feel like you're living out a FANTASY of luxury.
memory_trick: FANCY: full of decoration, like a FANCY dress.
visual_association: A table set with polished silverware and a folded cloth napkin.
emotion_feel: Excitement mixed with a bit of pressure to impress
difference_explained: Expensive = costs a lot. Fancy = elaborate and decorated (usually expensive too).
mini_conversation:
A: Where are we celebrating your birthday?
B: Somewhere fancy -- I already made a reservation.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A waiter pulls out a chair and says, "Right this way to our fanciest table."
news_style_line: News-style: "The hotel unveiled a fancy new rooftop restaurant overlooking the harbor."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Wow, this place is fancy -- are you sure we can afford it?"
mcq_options: A) Elaborate or high quality  B) Very plain and simple  C) Broken or damaged  D) Extremely cheap
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: They booked a ______ hotel for their honeymoon. → fancy
find_and_fix_to_correct: She always dress fancy for parties. → She always dresses fancily for parties. (use the adverb "fancily" and add -es for third person, since "dress" is a verb here)
translate: उसने पार्टी के लिए एक भड़कीला गाउन पहना। → She wore a fancy gown for the party.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a fancy restaurant.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'elaborate, decorative, or expensive-looking'?
usage_tip: 'Fancy dress' (UK) = a costume party.

simple_explanation: Good enough; acceptable in quality or behavior. "Decent" describes something that meets a reasonable standard -- not amazing, but good enough, or behavior that is polite and proper.
example_1: He got a decent score on the test.
example_2: We had a decent meal at the local diner.
example_3: She earns a decent salary at her new job.
collocations: decent salary, decent meal, decent person, pretty decent
where_it_s_used: Jobs, food, behavior, general quality assessments
grammar_pattern: decent + noun (a decent job / a decent price)
common_mistake: The food was decent enough, I very liked it.
correct_version: The food was decent enough -- I liked it.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Very' doesn't go before a verb like 'liked'. Use 'really liked'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the first syllable: DEE-suhnt.
spelling_tip: Note the "c" makes an "s" sound before "e" -- DE + CENT.
etymology: From Latin "decens" (fitting, proper), from "decere" (to be fitting) -- describing what is socially acceptable or of an acceptable standard.
prefix_root_suffix: decen(t) (root, from Latin "fitting") -- no separate suffix in the base adjective form
mnemonic: A DECENT job pays enough for you to live DECENTLY -- fair and acceptable.
memory_trick: DECENT: good enough to be ACCEPTED.
visual_association: A simple, clean plate of home-cooked food -- nothing fancy, but satisfying.
emotion_feel: Mild satisfaction, neither excited nor disappointed
difference_explained: Decent = good enough. Descent = going down. Different stress.
mini_conversation:
A: How was the new restaurant?
B: It was decent, nothing special but good value.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character shrugs after tasting the soup and says, "It's decent, not bad at all."

example_1: The dancer moved in a graceful way across the stage.
example_2: The swan glided gracefully across the lake.

pronunciation_tip: Stress on the first syllable: GRAYS-fuhl.
spelling_tip: Keep the "e" from "grace" before adding "-ful" -- GRACE + FUL.
etymology: From "grace" (Latin "gratia," favor/charm) + "-ful" -- describing movement or manner full of elegance and smoothness.
mnemonic: A GRACEFUL dancer moves with GRACE -- smooth, elegant, never clumsy.
memory_trick: GRACE-FUL: FULL of GRACE.

simple_explanation: Moving or acting in an awkward way, often dropping or bumping into things. Someone "clumsy" doesn't move smoothly -- they might trip, drop things, or knock objects over by accident.
example_1: He is quite clumsy and often drops his phone.
example_2: She felt clumsy trying to dance in high heels.
example_3: He made a clumsy attempt to fix the shelf.
collocations: clumsy attempt, clumsy movement, feel clumsy, clumsy mistake
grammar_pattern: clumsy + noun / be + clumsy (a clumsy mistake / He is clumsy.)
common_mistake: I am so clumsy, I drop things always.
correct_version: I am so clumsy, I always drop things.
why_it_s_wrong: Frequency adverbs like 'always' go before the main verb.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the first syllable: KLUHM-zee.
spelling_tip: The "l" is silent-ish but still written -- CLUM + SY.
etymology: From Middle English "clumsen" (to be stiff/numb with cold), related to "clumse" -- originally described stiff movement, later extended to awkward, uncoordinated movement generally.
prefix_root_suffix: clums(y) (root, from Middle English "numb with cold") -- no separate suffix, a base adjective
mnemonic: A CLUMSY person often bumps into furniture -- think "clumsy crashes messily."
memory_trick: CLUMSY: sounds like a CLUNK when something falls.
visual_association: Someone tripping over their own shoelaces while carrying a stack of plates.
difference_explained: Careless = not paying attention. Clumsy = moves awkwardly and drops things.

A: Oops, I knocked over my coffee again.
B: Ha, you're so clumsy today!

simple_explanation: Causing embarrassment or discomfort; not smooth or graceful. "Awkward" describes a situation that feels uncomfortable and embarrassing, or a movement that isn't smooth -- like an awkward silence or an awkward handshake.
example_1: There was an awkward silence after his joke.
example_2: It felt awkward when both of us reached for the same seat.
example_3: He gave an awkward smile during the photo.
collocations: awkward silence, awkward moment, feel awkward, awkward situation
where_it_s_used: Social situations, first meetings, misunderstandings, public speaking
grammar_pattern: awkward + noun / feel + awkward (an awkward moment / I felt awkward.)
common_mistake: I felt very awkward for meet my ex at the party.
correct_version: I felt very awkward meeting my ex at the party.
why_it_s_wrong: After 'felt awkward', use -ing, not 'for + verb'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the first syllable: AWK-werd.
spelling_tip: Remember the "-ward" ending, common in direction words like "forward" and "backward."
etymology: From Middle English "awke" (turned the wrong way, from Old Norse "öfugr," backward) + "-ward" -- literally "in a backward direction," later meaning clumsy or uncomfortable.
prefix_root_suffix: awk- (root, "wrong direction") + -ward = suffix meaning "in the direction of"
mnemonic: An AWKWARD silence feels like everyone is facing the WRONG WAY, unsure what to say.
memory_trick: AWKWARD: the W's bump into each other.
visual_association: Two people accidentally saying the same word at the same time and freezing.
difference_explained: Embarrassing = makes you feel ashamed. Awkward = uncomfortable or difficult.
mini_conversation:
A: Did you see how awkward that introduction was?
B: Yeah, nobody knew what to say.

usage_tip: 'Awkward silence' = a silence where no one knows what to say.

simple_explanation: Pleasant and attractive in a way that makes people like you. "Charming" describes someone or something so pleasant and likable that people are naturally drawn to it -- a charming smile, a charming village.
example_2: The old town had a charming, quiet atmosphere.
example_3: She won everyone over with her charming personality.
collocations: charming smile, charming personality, charming village, utterly charming
related_phrasal_verbs: win over, sweep off one's feet
where_it_s_used: Travel, personality descriptions, romance, small towns
grammar_pattern: charming + noun (a charming host / a charming little cafe)
common_mistake: He is charm man, everyone likes him.
correct_version: He is a charming man; everyone likes him.
why_it_s_wrong: Use the adjective 'charming' before a noun, and add 'a'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the first syllable: CHAR-ming.
spelling_tip: Drop the silent "e" in "charm" before adding "-ing" -- CHARM + ING.
etymology: From "charm" (Old French "charme," from Latin "carmen," song/incantation) + "-ing" -- originally magical enchantment, now pleasing personal appeal.
prefix_root_suffix: charm (root) + -ing = adjective suffix (describing an ongoing quality)
mnemonic: A CHARMING person seems to cast a CHARM (spell) that makes everyone like them.
memory_trick: CHARM-ING: has CHARM.

simple_explanation: Very bright, clear, and detailed. "Vivid" describes colors that are strong and bright, or memories, dreams, and descriptions that feel extremely clear and lifelike.
example_1: She has a vivid memory of her childhood home.
example_2: The painting used vivid shades of red and orange.
example_3: He gave a vivid description of the accident.
collocations: vivid memory, vivid imagination, vivid colors, vivid description
related_phrasal_verbs: come to life, stick in one's mind
grammar_pattern: vivid + noun (a vivid memory / vivid colors)
common_mistake: I have a very vivid memories of that day.
correct_version: I have very vivid memories of that day.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Memories' is plural, so no 'a'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the first syllable: VIV-id.
spelling_tip: Just one "v" in the middle -- VIV + ID.

mnemonic: A VIVID memory feels so ALIVE, like it's happening again right now.
memory_trick: VIVID: VIV = life — full of life.

difference_explained: Clear = easy to see or understand. Vivid = very bright and detailed.

simple_explanation: Refined and cultured, or highly advanced and complex. "Sophisticated" describes people with elegant, cultured tastes, or things -- like machines or ideas -- that are advanced and complex rather than simple.
example_1: She has very sophisticated taste in art.
example_2: The new software uses a sophisticated algorithm.
example_3: He wore a sophisticated navy suit to the conference.
collocations: sophisticated technology, sophisticated taste, sophisticated system, highly sophisticated
related_phrasal_verbs: know the ropes, well versed in
where_it_s_used: Technology, fashion, art, business, intellectual conversation
grammar_pattern: sophisticated + noun (a sophisticated design / sophisticated equipment)
common_mistake: This machine is very sophisticate.
correct_version: This machine is very sophisticated.
why_it_s_wrong: Use the adjective 'sophisticated', not the verb 'sophisticate'.
pronunciation_tip: Five syllables, stress on the fourth: suh-FIS-ti-kay-tid.
spelling_tip: Remember "-phist-" in the middle -- SO + PHIS + TI + CATED.
etymology: From Latin "sophisticare" (to tamper with/make artificial), from Greek "sophistes" (a wise or skilled person) -- meaning shifted to describe refined, cultured, or advanced and complex.
prefix_root_suffix: sophist- (root, from Greek "wise person") + -icated = adjective ending (describing a refined/complex state)
mnemonic: A SOPHISTICATED person seems worldly and refined -- think "SO fancy, SO advanced."
memory_trick: SOPHISTICATED: SOPHIA = wisdom — refined and clever.
visual_association: A sleek control panel covered in advanced dials and screens.
difference_explained: Complicated = hard to understand. Sophisticated = advanced and refined.

usage_tip: 'Sophisticated technology' = advanced technology.

simple_explanation: At all times; every time. When something happens 100% of the time, without exception, you use "always."
example_2: I always drink coffee in the morning.
example_3: He's always ready to help.
collocations: almost always, always ready, always remember, not always
grammar_pattern: Placed before the main verb but after "be": "I always eat breakfast" / "She is always late."
common_mistake: I eat always breakfast at seven.
correct_version: I always eat breakfast at seven.
why_it_s_wrong: Frequency adverbs go before the main verb: 'I always eat…'.
spelling_tip: "All" + "ways" — but written as one word, with only one L.
etymology: Old English "ealne weg" (literally "all the way") — came to mean "at all times."
word_family: (no separate noun/adjective forms — "always" is a standalone adverb of frequency)
mnemonic: ALWAYS = ALL the WAYS, at ALL times — it happens every single time, no exceptions.
memory_trick: ALWAYS = ALL WAYS, all times.
visual_association: A clock with hands that never stop moving in the same pattern.
emotion_feel: Neutral (can carry warmth in promises, or frustration in complaints)
difference_explained: Always = at all times. All ways = every method (rare).

B: I always try to leave early, just in case.

simple_explanation: Not often; almost never. When something happens very few times, much less than usual, you use "rarely."
example_2: We rarely eat out during the week.
example_3: She's rarely late for meetings.
collocations: rarely if ever, rarely seen, rarely used, rarely happens
grammar_pattern: Placed before the main verb but after "be", like other frequency adverbs: "I rarely go out" / "He is rarely wrong." Note: "rarely" at the start of a sentence needs inverted word order in formal writing: "Rarely have I seen such talent."
common_mistake: I go rarely to the gym.
correct_version: I rarely go to the gym.
why_it_s_wrong: Frequency adverbs go before the main verb: 'I rarely go…'.
spelling_tip: "Rare" + "ly" — drop the silent E before adding -ly.
etymology: "Rare" (Latin "rarus", thin, scattered) + -ly.
mnemonic: RARELY comes from RARE — something RARE doesn't happen often, so it happens RARELY.
memory_trick: RARELY: RARE things happen RARELY.
visual_association: A single four-leaf clover in a large field of ordinary ones.
difference_explained: Rarely = almost never. Never = not at all.

simple_explanation: Happening or done every day. When something is repeated once per day, on a regular routine, it happens daily.
example_2: The medicine should be taken daily, after meals.
example_3: We update the website daily with new content.
collocations: daily routine, daily basis, twice daily, daily habit
grammar_pattern: Can be an adverb (I exercise daily) or adjective (a daily routine) — same spelling, different function.
common_mistake: I am doing yoga in daily.
correct_version: I do yoga daily.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Daily' works alone as an adverb; don't add 'in'. A habit also uses the simple present.
spelling_tip: "Day" + "ly" — the Y changes to I before adding -ly.
etymology: Old English "dæg" (day) + -ly.
prefix_root_suffix: day + -ly = in a ___ manner / occurring every ___
mnemonic: DAILY = DAY + -LY — something daily happens once every DAY.
memory_trick: DAILY = DAY + LY: every day.
visual_association: A calendar with the same box checked off every single day.
difference_explained: Same meaning. 'Everyday' (one word) is an adjective: 'everyday clothes'.

B: Daily, usually for ten minutes each morning.

usage_tip: 'Daily' is also an adjective: 'a daily newspaper'.

simple_explanation: In a short time from now. When something will happen in the near future, not right now but not too far away either, it will happen soon.
example_2: The bus should arrive soon.
example_3: I'll finish this report soon.
collocations: as soon as possible, soon after, come soon, too soon
grammar_pattern: Usually placed at the end of a sentence: "I'll call you soon." "As soon as" introduces a clause: "Call me as soon as you arrive."
common_mistake: I will soon call you.
correct_version: I will call you soon.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Soon' usually goes at the end: 'I will call you soon.'
spelling_tip: S-O-O-N — double O, no silent letters.
etymology: Old English "sona" — immediately, at once (the meaning has softened slightly over time).
word_family: (no separate noun/adjective form — "soon" is a standalone time adverb)
mnemonic: SOON rhymes with MOON — just as the moon rises SOON after sunset, something happening SOON isn't far off.
memory_trick: SOON has two O's — two short moments.
visual_association: A sunrise just beginning to peek over the horizon.
difference_explained: Soon = in a short time from now. Early = before the usual time.

example_2: Sometimes she walks to work instead of driving.
example_3: He sometimes forgets to reply to messages.

related_phrasal_verbs: now and then, once in a while

simple_explanation: Not at any time; not ever. "Never" means something does not happen at all, at any point in time -- it's already negative, so it doesn't need "not" with it.
example_1: I never eat breakfast before 8 a.m.

example_3: He has never been to Japan.
collocations: never mind, never again, almost never, never ever
where_it_s_used: Habits, promises, describing experiences, strong statements
grammar_pattern: subject + never + verb (I never smoke. / She has never seen snow.)
common_mistake: I don't never eat meat.

why_it_s_wrong: 'Never' is already negative, so 'don't never' is a double negative.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the first syllable: NEV-er.
spelling_tip: Remember it's built from "ne" + "ever" -- NEV + ER.

word_family: ever (adv., its positive counterpart), nevermore (adv., poetic/archaic)
mnemonic: NEVER = NOT + EVER -- not ever, not one single time.
memory_trick: NEVER = NOT EVER.

simple_explanation: Sometimes, but not often; from time to time. "Occasionally" describes something that happens once in a while, less often than "sometimes" or "often."
example_1: I occasionally treat myself to ice cream.
example_2: She occasionally visits her grandparents on weekends.
example_3: He occasionally works late if there's a deadline.
collocations: occasionally happens, only occasionally, occasionally visit
related_phrasal_verbs: once in a blue moon, every now and then
where_it_s_used: Habits, hobbies, treats, exceptions to a routine
grammar_pattern: subject + occasionally + verb (I occasionally travel for work.)

why_it_s_wrong: With 'be', the adverb goes after the verb: 'I am occasionally late'.

memory_trick: FINAL-LY: at the FINAL point.

difference_explained: Same meaning. At last shows more relief or impatience.
mini_conversation:
A: Did you hear back about the job?
B: Yes! I finally got the offer letter today.

casual_conversation: Casual: "I finally cleaned out my closet -- it took all weekend."

simple_explanation: Not long ago; a short time before now. "Recently" describes something that happened a short time ago, close to the present moment.
example_1: I recently moved to a new city.
example_2: She recently started a new job.
example_3: We recently watched a great documentary.
collocations: recently moved, recently opened, until recently, recently discovered
where_it_s_used: News, updates, personal changes, describing new experiences
grammar_pattern: subject + have/has + recently + past participle (She has recently finished the project.) / subject + recently + past verb (He recently visited Paris.)
common_mistake: I recently am going to visit my parents.
correct_version: I recently visited my parents.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Recently' refers to the past, so use a past tense.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the first syllable: REE-suhnt-lee.
spelling_tip: Remember "recent" + "ly" -- RECENT + LY, no extra letters.
etymology: From "recent" (Latin "recens," fresh/new) + "-ly" -- describing something that happened not long ago.
mnemonic: RECENTLY = it just happened -- REcent times, not long ago.
memory_trick: RECENT-LY: in RECENT days.
visual_association: A calendar page from last week, still fresh in memory.
synonyms: lately, not long ago, of late
difference_explained: Recently = a short time ago (one event). Lately = during recent times (repeated).
mini_conversation:
A: Have you tried the new cafe downtown?
B: Yes, I recently went there with some friends.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character mentions, "I recently moved to this town -- still getting used to it."
news_style_line: News-style: "The company recently announced plans to expand into new markets."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I recently started going to the gym -- feeling much better already."
mcq_options: A) Not long ago  B) A very long time ago  C) In the distant future  D) Never
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: They ______ opened a new branch in the city center. → recently
find_and_fix_to_correct: She recently is working at a new company. → She recently started working at a new company. (use the past tense "started," not the present "is," with "recently")
translate: उसने हाल ही में एक नई नौकरी शुरू की है। → She has recently started a new job.

reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'not long ago; a short time before now'?
usage_tip: 'Recently' works with present perfect too: 'I've recently started…'.

simple_explanation: At the present time; right now. "Currently" describes something that is happening at this exact moment, or is true right now.
example_1: She is currently studying for her exams.
example_2: He is currently working from home.
example_3: They are currently renovating their kitchen.
collocations: currently working, currently available, currently living, currently studying
where_it_s_used: Job status, ongoing projects, official updates, reports
grammar_pattern: subject + be + currently + verb-ing (She is currently studying.)
common_mistake: Currently I am study in college.
correct_version: I am currently studying in college.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Currently' goes after 'am', and the continuous form needs -ing.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the first syllable: KUR-uhnt-lee.
etymology: From "current" (Latin "currens," running, from "currere," to run) + "-ly" -- describing what is happening right now, in the present flow of time.
word_family: current (adj./n.), currency (n., a related but distinct meaning)
mnemonic: CURRENTLY is like a river's CURRENT -- flowing right now, in the present moment.
memory_trick: CURRENT-LY: like a CURRENT flowing now.
visual_association: A "now playing" sign lit up on a screen.
synonyms: presently, at the moment, right now
difference_explained: Currently = at present. Actually = in fact. In some languages they look similar — a trap.
related_words: presently, nowadays, at the moment, now
mini_conversation:
A: What are you up to these days?
B: I'm currently working on a new project at the office.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A reporter states, "The suspect is currently believed to be in the area."
news_style_line: News-style: "The bridge is currently closed for emergency repairs."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I'm currently looking for a new apartment near downtown."
mcq_options: A) At the present time  B) A long time ago  C) Never  D) Occasionally in the past
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The team is ______ working on a new update for the app. → currently
find_and_fix_to_correct: She currently working as a nurse. → She is currently working as a nurse. (don't forget the auxiliary verb "is" before "working")
translate: वह फ़िलहाल एक अस्पताल में काम कर रही है। → She is currently working at a hospital.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about what you are currently learning.

simple_explanation: At this present moment; right now. "Now" refers to the current moment in time -- what's happening or true at this exact point.
example_2: Can you help me now?
example_3: She lives in London now.
collocations: right now, just now, from now on, now and then
where_it_s_used: Instructions, urgent requests, storytelling transitions, present situations
grammar_pattern: subject + verb + now (I'm leaving now.) / Now, + sentence (Now, let's begin the lesson.)
common_mistake: Now I am liking this song.
correct_version: I like this song now.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Like' is a state verb, so it doesn't take -ing here.
spelling_tip: Just three letters -- N + O + W, easy to remember.
etymology: From Old English "nu," a very old Germanic word for the present moment, related to Latin "nunc" and Sanskrit "nu."
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- one of the oldest, simplest words in English
word_family: nowadays (adv.), now (conjunction, e.g. "now that you're here...")
mnemonic: NOW is right NOW -- this very second, no delay.
memory_trick: NOW: short and immediate.
visual_association: A clock hand pointing exactly at the current second.
emotion_feel: Urgency or simple presence in the moment
difference_explained: Now = this moment. Nowadays = in the present period, compared with the past.
mini_conversation:
A: When should we start the meeting?
B: Let's start now, everyone's already here.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A pilot announces calmly, "We need to move now -- there's no time to waste."
news_style_line: News-style: "Officials say the situation is developing, and details are limited for now."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I have to go now, but let's talk later tonight."
mcq_options: A) At this present moment  B) A long time ago  C) At an unknown future time  D) Never
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: We need to make a decision right ______. → now
find_and_fix_to_correct: She is living in Paris since now. → She is living in Paris now. (drop "since" -- it doesn't fit with "now" in this context)
translate: मुझे अभी घर जाना है। → I need to go home now.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about what you are doing now.

usage_tip: 'Right now' = at this exact moment.

simple_explanation: At a time after the present moment or another event. "Later" refers to a point in time that comes after now, or after something else has happened.
example_2: We can finish this later today.
example_3: She arrived later than the rest of the guests.
collocations: later on, see you later, sooner or later, a bit later
related_phrasal_verbs: down the road, at a later date
grammar_pattern: subject + verb + later (I'll do it later.) / later + than + noun (later than expected)
common_mistake: I will call you more later.
correct_version: I will call you later.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Later' is already comparative, so 'more' is extra.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the first syllable: LAY-ter.
spelling_tip: Comparative of "late" -- LATE + R, just add "r."
etymology: Comparative form of "late" (Old English "læt," slow) -- meaning "at a further, more delayed point in time."
word_family: late (adj./adv.), latest (adj., superlative), lately (adv., a different meaning: "recently")
mnemonic: LATER means it comes LATE-r than now -- further down the timeline.
memory_trick: LATE → LATER: the -R pushes it further.
visual_association: A clock hand moving forward past the current hour.
difference_explained: Later = after some time. Latter = the second of two things mentioned.
mini_conversation:
A: Can we talk about this now?
B: Can we do it later? I'm in a meeting.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character waves and says, "Gotta run -- I'll explain everything later!"
news_style_line: News-style: "Officials said further details would be released later this week."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Let's grab coffee later, once I'm done with work."
mcq_options: A) At a time after now  B) Before this moment  C) Right now  D) Never
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: We can discuss the budget ______ this afternoon. → later
find_and_fix_to_correct: I will explain you later about this. → I will explain this to you later. (use "explain something to someone," not "explain you something")
translate: मैं तुम्हें बाद में सारी बात बताऊँगा। → I will tell you everything later.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something you'll do later today.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'at a time after the present moment or another event'?
usage_tip: 'See you later' is a casual goodbye.

simple_explanation: At a time before now or before another event. "Earlier" refers to a point in time that came before now, or before something else happened.
example_2: He left earlier than usual this morning.
example_3: We finished the project earlier than expected.
collocations: earlier today, earlier than expected, much earlier, as mentioned earlier
where_it_s_used: Schedules, daily routines, describing past events, meetings
grammar_pattern: subject + verb + earlier (I woke up earlier.) / earlier + than + noun (earlier than planned)
common_mistake: I woke up more earlier than usual.
correct_version: I woke up earlier than usual.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Earlier' is already comparative, so 'more' is extra.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the first syllable: UR-lee-er.
spelling_tip: Comparative of "early" -- change "y" to "i" and add "-er": EARLY -> EARLIER.
etymology: Comparative form of "early" (Old English "ærlice," from "ær," before) -- meaning "at a point before another time."
mnemonic: EARLIER means it happened EARLY-er than something else -- before, not after.
memory_trick: EARLY → EARLIER: Y becomes IER.
visual_association: A clock hand pointing to an hour that has already passed.
difference_explained: Earlier = at a time before now. Before + noun or clause: 'before lunch'.
related_words: before, previously, ahead of time, sooner
mini_conversation:
A: Did you see the announcement?
B: Yes, I read it earlier this morning.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A detective recalls, "As I mentioned earlier, the witness saw nothing unusual."
news_style_line: News-style: "The mayor addressed the issue earlier today at a press conference."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I tried calling you earlier, but you didn't pick up."
mcq_options: A) At a time before now  B) At a time after now  C) Right at this moment  D) Never

find_and_fix_to_correct: The train earlier arrived than we expected. → The train arrived earlier than we expected. (place "earlier" after the verb "arrived," not before it)
