fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: ______ of the dresses looked great on her. → Both
find_and_fix_to_correct: Both my three brothers live abroad. → All three of my brothers live abroad.
translate: मेरे दोनों माता-पिता शिक्षक हैं। → Both of my parents are teachers.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence using 'both … and …'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'the two of them; the one and the other together'?
usage_tip: 'Both … and …' joins two things: 'both tea and coffee'.

simple_explanation: Not one; zero of something in a group. "None" means that out of a group, not even a single one applies -- the total is zero.
example_1: None of the students knew the answer.
example_2: None of my friends could come to the party.
example_3: There's none of the cake left.
collocations: none of, none at all, none whatsoever, none the wiser
related_phrasal_verbs: none the wiser (idiom meaning "still not understanding")
where_it_s_used: Describing absence, empty groups, negative answers
grammar_pattern: none of + noun (none of the food) / none + verb (none is left / none are left)
common_mistake: None of the students didn't come.
correct_version: None of the students came.
why_it_s_wrong: 'None' is already negative, so don't add 'didn't'.
spelling_tip: Don't confuse with "nun" (a religious woman) -- same pronunciation, different spelling and meaning.
etymology: From Old English "nān," a combination of "ne" (not) and "ān" (one) -- literally "not one."
prefix_root_suffix: ne- (not) + one (from Old English "ān") -- literally "not one"
mnemonic: NONE = NOT ONE -- zero, nothing at all.
memory_trick: NONE = NOT ONE.
visual_association: An empty plate where cookies used to be, with only crumbs left.
emotion_feel: Neutral, sometimes disappointment when expected results don't appear
difference_explained: None = not any (of things or people). No one = not any person.
mini_conversation:
A: How many cookies are left?
B: None -- we finished them all last night.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character checks their phone and says quietly, "None of my messages went through."
news_style_line: News-style: "None of the passengers were injured in the incident, officials confirmed."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I asked around, but none of my coworkers wanted to go."
mcq_options: A) All of them  B) Not one; zero  C) Some of them  D) Most of them
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: ______ of the answers on the quiz were correct. → None
find_and_fix_to_correct: None of the shops was open on the holiday. → None of the shops were open on the holiday.
translate: पार्टी में मेरा कोई भी दोस्त नहीं आ सका। → None of my friends could come to the party.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence using 'none of'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'not one; zero of something in a group'?
usage_tip: In everyday English, 'none of the + plural' can take a plural verb.

simple_explanation: An unspecified amount or number of something; not all, not none. "Some" is used when there's a certain quantity, but you don't need to say exactly how much or how many.
example_2: She bought some fruit at the market.
example_3: Would you like some help with that?
collocations: some of, some time, some people, get some rest
related_phrasal_verbs: n/a (no common phrasal verb pairs with this word)
where_it_s_used: Offers, requests, describing unspecified quantities, polite speech
grammar_pattern: some + noun (some water, some ideas) -- typically in positive sentences and offers
common_mistake: Do you have some questions?
correct_version: Do you have any questions?
why_it_s_wrong: In most questions, use 'any'. 'Some' is used in offers and requests.
spelling_tip: "Some" has a silent "e" at the end -- don't drop it.
etymology: From Old English "sum," meaning "a certain amount or number of."
prefix_root_suffix: some- = base quantifier (root word, no further breakdown)
mnemonic: SOME sounds like "sum," as in "a small sum" -- a certain, unspecified amount.
memory_trick: SOME in positives and offers ('Would you like some tea?'). ANY in questions and negatives.
visual_association: A hand pouring a small, unmeasured amount of sugar into a cup.
emotion_feel: Neutral, often polite or generous in tone (offering something)
difference_explained: Some = positive, offers (I have some). Any = questions, negatives (Do you have any?).
mini_conversation:
A: Would you like some tea?
B: Yes, please, just some milk, no sugar.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character offers a plate and says, "Here, take some -- there's plenty for everyone."
news_style_line: News-style: "Some residents have already begun preparing for the upcoming storm."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Can I get some advice about this job offer?"
mcq_options: A) Negative sentences only  B) Positive statements and offers  C) Only formal writing  D) Only questions about numbers
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Would you like ______ coffee before we start the meeting? → some
find_and_fix_to_correct: There isn't some milk left in the fridge. → There isn't any milk left in the fridge.
translate: मुझे थोड़ा पानी चाहिए। → I would like some water.
write_your_own_sentence: Write an offer using 'some' and a question using 'any'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'an unspecified amount or number of something; not all, not none'?
usage_tip: 'Some' in a question sounds like you expect 'yes'.

simple_explanation: One or some, no matter which; used especially in questions and negatives. "Any" is used to ask if there's some amount of something, or to say there isn't any at all -- it doesn't specify which one.
example_2: I don't have any money left.
example_3: Is there any milk in the fridge?
collocations: any time, any questions, any longer, hardly any
related_phrasal_verbs: any longer (idiom meaning "not anymore" in negatives)
where_it_s_used: Questions, negative statements, offering choices, conditionals
grammar_pattern: any + noun (any book) -- typically in questions, negatives, and conditionals
common_mistake: I have any friends coming over tonight.
correct_version: I have some friends coming over tonight.
why_it_s_wrong: In a positive statement, use 'some', not 'any'.
spelling_tip: "Any" is spelled a-n-y -- don't confuse it with "many," though they rhyme.
etymology: From Old English "ænig," related to "ān" (one) -- originally meaning "any one at all."
prefix_root_suffix: any- = base quantifier (root word, no further breakdown)
mnemonic: ANY = it doesn't matter which specific one -- any will do.
memory_trick: ANY for questions and 'not' sentences.
visual_association: An open hand gesturing toward a row of identical boxes -- pick any one.
emotion_feel: Neutral, often curious in questions or firm in negatives
difference_explained: Any = questions and negatives. Some = positives.
mini_conversation:
A: Is there any coffee left?
B: No, there isn't any -- we finished it this morning.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A detective asks the witness, "Do you remember any details about the car?"
news_style_line: News-style: "Officials said any updates would be shared as soon as possible."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Do you have any plans for the weekend?"
mcq_options: A) Positive statements only  B) Questions and negative sentences  C) Only with numbers  D) Only in formal writing
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: I don't have ______ time to help you today. → any
find_and_fix_to_correct: She doesn't have some experience in teaching. → She doesn't have any experience in teaching.
translate: क्या फ्रिज में कोई दूध है? → Is there any milk in the fridge?
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence with 'not … any'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'one or some, no matter which; used especially in questions and negatives'?
usage_tip: 'Any' in a positive sentence = it doesn't matter which: 'Take any seat.'

simple_explanation: Every individual one in a group, considered separately. "Each" focuses on individual members of a group, one by one, rather than the group as a whole.
example_2: Each of the players has a different role.
example_3: She gave each child a small gift.
collocations: each other, each time, each one, each of us
related_phrasal_verbs: each other (reciprocal phrase, e.g. "they helped each other")
where_it_s_used: Distribution, individual assessment, classroom instructions, gift-giving
grammar_pattern: each + singular noun (each student) / each of + plural noun (each of the students)
common_mistake: Each students have their own desk.
correct_version: Each student has their own desk.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Each' takes a singular noun and singular verb: 'Each student has…'.
spelling_tip: "Each" is spelled e-a-c-h -- don't confuse it with "ache."
etymology: From Old English "ælc," a contraction of "a" (ever) plus "gelic" (alike) -- literally "ever alike."
word_family: no related derived forms (each is a closed-class quantifier)
mnemonic: EACH looks at every item one at a time, like reaching out to touch them one by one.
memory_trick: EACH = one by one.
visual_association: A row of gift boxes, one placed carefully in front of each person.
emotion_feel: Neutral -- highlights fairness and individual attention
difference_explained: Each = one by one, often a small group. Every = all together as a group. Both take singular nouns.
related_words: every, individually, separately, one by one
mini_conversation:
A: How many cookies do we get?
B: Each of us gets two.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A general addresses the troops, "Each of you has a role to play in this mission."
news_style_line: News-style: "Each household will receive a rebate check next month."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Each of us should bring something different to the potluck."
mcq_options: A) A group as a whole  B) Every individual member separately  C) None of the members  D) Only two members
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: ______ team member received a copy of the report. → Each
find_and_fix_to_correct: Each of the boys were given a prize. → Each of the boys was given a prize. (use a singular verb "was" with "each," even when followed by a plural noun)
translate: प्रत्येक छात्र को एक प्रमाणपत्र मिला। → Each student received a certificate.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something each person in your family does.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'every individual one in a group, considered separately'?
usage_tip: 'Each other' = two people doing the same to one another.

simple_explanation: All the members of a group, with no exceptions. "Every" describes something true for all members of a group, one hundred percent of the time, and it always takes a singular noun.
example_1: Every morning, I drink a cup of tea.
example_2: Every student must submit the form by Friday.
example_3: She checks her email every hour.
collocations: every day, every time, every single one, every other
related_phrasal_verbs: every other (idiom meaning "alternating, " e.g. "every other day")
grammar_pattern: every + singular noun (every student, every day)
common_mistake: Every students must bring their book.
correct_version: Every student must bring their book.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Every' takes a singular noun, even though it means all.
pronunciation_tip: Three syllables: EV-ree, sometimes shortened in fast speech.
spelling_tip: "Every" is spelled e-v-e-r-y -- don't drop the middle "e."
etymology: From Old English "æfre ælc," a combination of "ever" and "each" -- literally "ever each," meaning "all without exception."
prefix_root_suffix: every- = ever + each combined historically (no modern prefix/suffix breakdown)
mnemonic: EVERY = EVER + EACH -- always, without exception, for the whole group.
memory_trick: EVERY + ONE = EVERYONE: always singular.
visual_association: A calendar with every single box checked off, no days missed.
emotion_feel: Neutral, sometimes emphasizing routine or importance
difference_explained: Every = all of a group together. Each = one by one.
mini_conversation:
A: Do you exercise regularly?
B: Yes, every morning before work.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A coach tells the team, "Every single one of you matters -- give it your all."
news_style_line: News-style: "Every school in the district will follow the new safety guidelines."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I water my plants every other day."
mcq_options: A) A plural noun  B) A singular noun  C) A verb only  D) No noun at all
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: She reads a book ______ week without fail. → every
find_and_fix_to_correct: Every employees must attend the meeting. → Every employee must attend the meeting.
translate: हर सुबह मैं एक कप चाय पीता हूं। → Every morning, I drink a cup of tea.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence using 'every day'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'all the members of a group, with no exceptions'?
usage_tip: 'Every day' (two words) = daily. 'Everyday' (one word) = ordinary.

simple_explanation: A large amount; more than enough. "Plenty of" is used to say there's a generous, comfortable amount of something -- you don't need to worry about running out.
example_1: There's plenty of food for everyone.
example_2: We have plenty of time before the flight.
example_3: There's plenty of space in this room.
collocations: plenty of time, plenty of room, plenty of money, plenty more
related_phrasal_verbs: n/a (no common phrasal verb pairs with this word)
grammar_pattern: plenty of + noun (plenty of time / plenty of chairs)
common_mistake: We have plenty time to finish this.
correct_version: We have plenty of time to finish this.
why_it_s_wrong: Always add 'of' after 'plenty' before a noun.
pronunciation_tip: Two syllables: PLEN-tee, stress on the first.
etymology: From Latin "plenus" (full), via Old French "plente" -- meaning "an abundance, a full amount."
mnemonic: PLENTY sounds like "full plenty" -- picture a plate piled full of food.
memory_trick: PLENTY OF = more than enough.
visual_association: A table overflowing with food, more than anyone could possibly eat.
confusing_word: plenty of vs a lot of
difference_explained: Plenty of = more than enough. A lot of = a large amount.
mini_conversation:
A: Are we going to run out of snacks?
B: No way, we have plenty left.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A host gestures at the table and says, "Eat up -- there's plenty more where that came from."
news_style_line: News-style: "Officials assured residents there's plenty of supply to meet demand."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Take your time, we have plenty of it before the movie starts."
mcq_options: A) Not enough  B) A large, generous amount  C) Exactly zero  D) A tiny bit
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Don't rush -- we have ______ of time before the train leaves. → plenty
find_and_fix_to_correct: There is plenty chairs in the hall. → There are plenty of chairs in the hall.
translate: सबके लिए पर्याप्त से ज़्यादा खाना है। → There is plenty of food for everyone.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence using 'plenty of time'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'a large amount; more than enough'?
usage_tip: 'Plenty' alone: 'Don't worry, we have plenty.'

simple_explanation: As much as is needed; a sufficient amount. "Enough" describes the exact amount needed for something -- not extra, and not lacking.
example_1: We have enough chairs for everyone.
example_2: Is there enough time to finish this?
example_3: She doesn't have enough experience for the job.
collocations: enough time, enough money, more than enough, not enough
related_phrasal_verbs: had enough (idiom meaning "reached one's limit of patience")
grammar_pattern: enough + noun (enough money) / adjective + enough (good enough)
common_mistake: This coffee is enough hot for me.
correct_version: This coffee is hot enough for me.
why_it_s_wrong: With adjectives, 'enough' comes after: 'hot enough'. With nouns, before: 'enough money'.
pronunciation_tip: The "-ough" ending is pronounced "uff" -- ee-NUHF, not "ee-NOW."
spelling_tip: One of English's tricky "-ough" spellings -- memorize it as a whole: e-n-o-u-g-h.
etymology: From Old English "genog," meaning "sufficient, as much as needed."
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown (irregular spelling from Old English)
word_family: no related derived forms (enough functions as its own word)
mnemonic: ENOUGH rhymes with "tough" and "stuff" -- just the right, sufficient amount.
memory_trick: ENOUGH: after adjectives (big enough), before nouns (enough time).
visual_association: A measuring cup filled exactly to the line, no more, no less.
emotion_feel: Neutral, sometimes frustration in the idiom "had enough"
difference_explained: Enough = the right amount. Too = more than needed.
mini_conversation:
A: Do we have enough snacks for the trip?
B: I think so -- let's just double-check.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character throws up their hands and says, "I've had enough of this nonsense!"
news_style_line: News-style: "Officials say there isn't enough funding to complete the project this year."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Is there enough milk left for breakfast tomorrow?"
mcq_options: A) Too much  B) A sufficient amount  C) Not any  D) Far too little
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: We don't have ______ time to finish the whole tour. → enough
find_and_fix_to_correct: This box is enough big to hold all the books. → This box is big enough to hold all the books.
translate: क्या हमारे पास सबके लिए पर्याप्त कुर्सियां हैं? → Do we have enough chairs for everyone?
write_your_own_sentence: Write one sentence with 'enough + noun' and one with 'adjective + enough'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'as much as is needed; a sufficient amount'?
usage_tip: 'Enough!' alone = stop now.

simple_explanation: More than what is usual, needed, or expected. "Extra" describes something additional -- more than the normal amount, often as a bonus or backup.
example_1: Can I get extra cheese on my pizza?
example_2: She always packs extra snacks for the trip.
example_3: We need an extra chair for the guest.
collocations: extra time, extra money, extra effort, extra charge
related_phrasal_verbs: n/a (no common phrasal verb pairs with this word)
where_it_s_used: Shopping, food orders, work, packing for trips
grammar_pattern: extra + noun (extra time / extra help)
common_mistake: I need a extra blanket for tonight.
correct_version: I need an extra blanket for tonight.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Extra' starts with a vowel sound, so use 'an'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the first syllable: EK-struh.
spelling_tip: "Extra" is spelled e-x-t-r-a -- don't add an unnecessary letter at the end.
etymology: From Latin "extra" (outside, beyond) -- originally indicating something additional or beyond the normal.
prefix_root_suffix: extra- (from Latin, meaning "outside/beyond") functions as its own root here
word_family: extraordinary (adj., related in origin, not directly derived)
mnemonic: EXTRA sounds like "EXTRA-ordinary" -- something beyond the normal amount.
memory_trick: EXTRA: EXTRA = more than usual.
visual_association: A pizza box with a little extra cheese spilling over the edge.
emotion_feel: Neutral, sometimes a small sense of indulgence or generosity
difference_explained: More = a larger amount. Extra = more than the usual or needed amount.
mini_conversation:
A: Do you want extra sauce with that?
B: Yes, please, as much extra as possible!
everyday_scene: Everyday: A chef calls out to the kitchen, "Add some extra spice to that dish!"
news_style_line: News-style: "The airline is offering extra legroom seats for an additional fee."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Could I get an extra napkin, please?"
mcq_options: A) Less than needed  B) Additional; more than usual  C) Exactly enough  D) None at all
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Bring an ______ jacket in case it gets cold tonight. → extra
find_and_fix_to_correct: We need extra two chairs for the guests. → We need two extra chairs for the guests. (place the number before "extra," not after)
translate: क्या मुझे पिज़्ज़ा पर अतिरिक्त पनीर मिल सकता है? → Can I get extra cheese on my pizza?
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something extra you packed for a trip.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'more than what is usual, needed, or expected'?
usage_tip: 'Extra' also means very (informal): 'extra careful'.

simple_explanation: What is left after part of something has been used, removed, or completed. "Remaining" describes the part of something that's still there after the rest has already gone, been used, or finished.
example_1: Please finish the remaining homework by tonight.
example_2: The remaining tickets sold out within minutes.
example_3: We spent the remaining time reviewing notes.
collocations: remaining time, remaining balance, remaining tickets, the remaining few
related_phrasal_verbs: n/a (no common phrasal verb pairs with this word)
where_it_s_used: Finance (remaining balance), exams, event planning, time management
grammar_pattern: remaining + noun (the remaining students / the remaining balance)
common_mistake: The remain students left early.
correct_version: The remaining students left early.
why_it_s_wrong: Use the adjective 'remaining', not the verb 'remain'.
pronunciation_tip: Four syllables: ri-MAY-ning, stress on the second.
etymology: From Latin "remanere" (to stay behind), via Old French "remain" -- describing what is left after part is used or removed.
prefix_root_suffix: re- (again/behind) + main (from Latin "manere," to stay) + -ing (adjective/gerund suffix)
mnemonic: REMAINING = RE- (again/behind) + MAIN (stay) -- what stays behind after the rest is gone.
memory_trick: REMAIN-ING: what REMAINS.
visual_association: A pie with just one slice left after everyone has eaten.
emotion_feel: Neutral, sometimes urgency when tied to limited remaining time or resources
difference_explained: The remaining students = the rest of the students. Same meaning.
mini_conversation:
A: How much time do we have left?
B: Only the remaining ten minutes of class.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A narrator says, "With the remaining daylight fading fast, they pushed on toward the summit."
news_style_line: News-style: "Officials say the remaining survivors have been safely rescued."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Let's use the remaining budget wisely before the month ends."
mcq_options: A) Completely gone  B) Still left after some has been used  C) Brand new  D) Doubled in amount
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Please submit the ______ forms by Friday. → remaining
find_and_fix_to_correct: The remain balance on my account is low. → The remaining balance on my account is low.
translate: कृपया आज रात बचा हुआ होमवर्क पूरा करें। → Please finish the remaining homework tonight.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about the remaining days of the month.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'what is left after part of something has been used, removed, or completed'?
usage_tip: 'The remaining amount' is common in bills and payments.

simple_explanation: The largest amount, number, or level that is possible or allowed. "Maximum" describes the absolute upper limit -- the biggest amount something can be, with nothing allowed to go higher.
example_1: The maximum speed limit here is 60.
example_2: The elevator has a maximum capacity of ten people.
example_3: She scored the maximum marks on the test.
collocations: maximum capacity, maximum speed, maximum limit, maximum effort
related_phrasal_verbs: n/a (no common phrasal verb pairs with this word)
where_it_s_used: Safety limits, exams, sports records, capacity rules
grammar_pattern: maximum + noun (maximum speed / maximum effort)
common_mistake: This is the most maximum score possible.
correct_version: This is the maximum score possible.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Maximum' already means the most, so 'most maximum' repeats it.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the first syllable: MAK-suh-muhm.
spelling_tip: Remember the double "m" pattern in the middle and at the end: m-a-x-i-m-u-m.
etymology: From Latin "maximus," the superlative form of "magnus" (great) -- meaning "the greatest."
mnemonic: MAXIMUM sounds like "MAX" -- the max, the top, the highest possible limit.
memory_trick: MAXIMUM: MAX = the top.
visual_association: A speedometer needle pushed all the way to the highest number.
emotion_feel: Neutral -- describes a technical or measurable limit
difference_explained: Most = the largest amount. Maximum = the highest possible limit.
mini_conversation:
A: How many people can this elevator hold?
B: The maximum is eight people.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A pilot announces, "We're cruising at maximum altitude for this route."
news_style_line: News-style: "The factory is now operating at maximum capacity to meet demand."
casual_conversation: Casual: "What's the maximum weight this bag can hold?"
mcq_options: A) The smallest possible amount  B) The largest possible amount  C) An average amount  D) Zero
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The gym allows a ______ of thirty people at one time. → maximum
find_and_fix_to_correct: The maximum amount you can withdraw are $500. → The maximum amount you can withdraw is $500.
translate: यहां अधिकतम गति सीमा 60 है। → The maximum speed limit here is 60.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about the maximum speed on a road you know.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'the largest amount, number, or level that is possible or allowed'?
usage_tip: Short form: 'max' ('max 5 people').

simple_explanation: The smallest amount, number, or level that is possible or required. "Minimum" describes the lowest acceptable limit -- the least amount something can be, with nothing allowed to go lower.
example_1: You must be 18 at a minimum to apply.
example_2: The minimum wage increased this year.
example_3: There's a minimum order of two items.
collocations: minimum wage, minimum requirement, minimum age, minimum effort
related_phrasal_verbs: n/a (no common phrasal verb pairs with this word)
where_it_s_used: Employment, legal requirements, exams, age restrictions
grammar_pattern: minimum + noun (minimum wage / minimum age)
common_mistake: This job pays the minimum's wage.
correct_version: This job pays the minimum wage.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Minimum wage' is a compound noun; no apostrophe.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the first syllable: MIN-uh-muhm.
spelling_tip: Note the double "m" pattern, mirroring "maximum" -- m-i-n-i-m-u-m.
etymology: From Latin "minimus," the superlative form of "parvus" (small) -- meaning "the smallest."
mnemonic: MINIMUM sounds like "MINI" -- think tiny, the smallest amount allowed.
memory_trick: MINIMUM: MIN = the bottom.

emotion_feel: Neutral -- describes a technical or required limit

simple_explanation: Complete; entire; all of something, not divided into parts. "Whole" describes something in its complete, undivided form -- the entire thing, not just a piece of it.
example_1: I ate the whole pizza by myself.
example_2: She spent the whole day at the library.
example_3: The whole class passed the test.
collocations: the whole time, the whole world, whole grain, on the whole
where_it_s_used: Describing completeness, food, time spent, general summaries
grammar_pattern: the whole + noun (the whole story / the whole team)
common_mistake: She ate whole cake by herself.
correct_version: She ate the whole cake by herself.
why_it_s_wrong: Add 'the' before 'whole' for a specific complete thing.
spelling_tip: Don't confuse with "hole" (a gap or opening) -- same pronunciation, very different meaning.
etymology: From Old English "hal," meaning "healthy, complete, entire" -- related to "health" and "heal."
prefix_root_suffix: whole = root word (from Old English "hal," meaning "complete/healthy")
word_family: wholly (adv.), wholesome (adj., related but distinct meaning)
mnemonic: WHOLE sounds like "HOLE," but picture a WHOLE pie -- nothing missing, no pieces cut out.
memory_trick: WHOLE has a silent W: same sound as 'hole'.
visual_association: An entire, uncut pie sitting untouched on the table.
emotion_feel: Neutral, sometimes emphasis or exasperation, as in "the whole thing"
difference_explained: Whole = complete. Hole = an empty space. Same sound.
mini_conversation:
A: Did you finish the whole assignment?
B: Yes, the whole thing, start to finish.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character looks around the room and says, "The whole place feels different since they left."
news_style_line: News-style: "The whole community came together to rebuild after the flood."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I spent the whole weekend cleaning my apartment."
mcq_options: A) Half of something  B) Complete; entire  C) A small piece  D) Nothing at all

find_and_fix_to_correct: I cleaned whole house yesterday. → I cleaned the whole house yesterday.
translate: मैंने पूरा पिज़्ज़ा अकेले खा लिया। → I ate the whole pizza by myself.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something you finished the whole of.

reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'complete; entire; all of something, not divided into parts'?
usage_tip: 'On the whole' = in general.

simple_explanation: The number 0; none at all; nothing. "Zero" represents nothing or none of something -- the complete absence of a quantity.
example_1: The temperature dropped to zero degrees last night.
example_2: He has zero interest in sports.
example_3: The score was zero to zero at halftime.
collocations: zero tolerance, zero chance, below zero, zero interest
related_phrasal_verbs: zero in on (idiom meaning "to focus closely on something")
where_it_s_used: Temperature, sports scores, math, describing complete absence
grammar_pattern: zero + noun (zero degrees / zero chance)
common_mistake: I have a zero interest in politics.
correct_version: I have zero interest in politics.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Zero' meaning 'none' takes no 'a'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the first syllable: ZEE-roh.
spelling_tip: "Zero" is spelled z-e-r-o -- one word, no hyphen.
etymology: From Arabic "sifr" (empty, cipher), via Italian "zero" -- ultimately tied to the mathematical concept of "nothing."
prefix_root_suffix: zero = whole root word (from Arabic "sifr," meaning "empty")
mnemonic: ZERO looks like the number "0" -- an empty circle, nothing inside.
memory_trick: ZERO: the round O.
visual_association: A thermometer with the red line resting exactly on the '0' mark.
emotion_feel: Neutral, sometimes relief (zero cases) or disappointment (zero progress)
difference_explained: Same meaning. Nil is used in sports scores (UK) and formal forms.
mini_conversation:
A: What's the score so far?
B: Still zero to zero -- no goals yet.

news_style_line: News-style: "The city recorded zero new cases for the third day in a row."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Honestly, I have zero idea what happened last night."

write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence using 'zero' to mean 'none'.

reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'the number 0; none at all; nothing'?
usage_tip: 'Zero tolerance' = no acceptance at all.

simple_explanation: The word a speaker uses to refer to themselves. "I" is the subject pronoun you use when you're talking about yourself as the one doing the action.
example_2: I live in a small town.
example_3: I don't like spicy food.
collocations: I think, I believe, I guess, as I said
related_phrasal_verbs: n/a (no common phrasal verb pairs with this word)
grammar_pattern: I + verb (I go, I eat, I understand) -- always used as the subject of a sentence
common_mistake: Me and my brother went to the park.
correct_version: My brother and I went to the park.
why_it_s_wrong: As a subject, use 'I'. Politely, put yourself last: 'My brother and I'.
pronunciation_tip: A single long vowel sound: /aɪ/, like the word "eye."
spelling_tip: Always capital "I," even in casual texting -- lowercase "i" is considered incorrect in standard writing.
etymology: From Old English "ic," a Germanic first-person pronoun, gradually shortened and eventually capitalized in Middle English for clarity in handwriting.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown (a basic personal pronoun)
word_family: me (object form), my (possessive adjective), mine (possessive pronoun), myself (reflexive)
mnemonic: "I" stands tall and alone -- always capital, just like standing up straight to talk about yourself.
memory_trick: I is always a capital letter.
visual_association: A person pointing to their own chest while speaking.
emotion_feel: Neutral -- simply marks the speaker as the subject
difference_explained: I = subject (I went). Me = object (He saw me).
mini_conversation:
A: Where are you from?
B: I'm from a small village near the coast.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character looks into the camera and says, "I never thought this day would come."
news_style_line: News-style: "I am confident we can rebuild stronger," said the local mayor at the press briefing.
casual_conversation: Casual: "I really think we should leave earlier tomorrow."

usage_tip: Polite order: 'you and I', 'my friend and I'.

simple_explanation: The person or people someone is speaking to. "You" refers to whoever the speaker is talking to, whether that's one person or a group, and it works as both subject and object.
example_1: You did a great job today.
example_2: You should try this restaurant.
example_3: Can I help you with something?
collocations: thank you, how are you, you know, see you later
related_phrasal_verbs: n/a (no common phrasal verb pairs with this word)
grammar_pattern: you + verb (you go, you like) -- same form for subject and object, singular and plural
common_mistake: You are coming with me, isn't it?
correct_version: You are coming with me, aren't you?
why_it_s_wrong: A question tag must match the verb: 'You are…, aren't you?' 'Isn't it' doesn't fit every sentence.
spelling_tip: Just three letters -- y-o-u, no silent letters to worry about.
etymology: From Old English "eow" (originally the plural/object form), which eventually replaced both "thou" and "ye" in modern English.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown (a basic personal pronoun)
mnemonic: YOU always points at the other person -- picture pointing a finger toward someone else.
memory_trick: YOU: same word for one person or many.
visual_association: A finger pointing directly at another person across the table.
emotion_feel: Neutral, often warm when used in compliments or encouragement
synonyms: thou (archaic singular form, still used in some dialects and older texts)
difference_explained: Standard English uses 'you' for one or many. 'You all' / 'you guys' are informal plurals.
mini_conversation:
A: Are you free this weekend?
B: Yes, I am -- what did you have in mind?
everyday_scene: Everyday: A mentor places a hand on the hero's shoulder and says, "You were always ready for this."
news_style_line: News-style: "You deserve to know the full details," the spokesperson told reporters.
casual_conversation: Casual: "You look really happy today -- what's going on?"
mcq_options: A) Only a subject  B) Only an object  C) Both subject and object  D) Only a possessive form
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: ______ have done an amazing job on this project. → You
find_and_fix_to_correct: Is this book belongs to you? → Does this book belong to you?
translate: आपने आज बहुत अच्छा काम किया। → You did a great job today.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence with 'you are … aren't you?'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'the person or people someone is speaking to'?
usage_tip: 'Isn't it?' as a general tag is very common in Indian English but not standard.

simple_explanation: Used to refer to a male person already mentioned. "He" replaces a male person's name once it's clear who you're talking about, so you don't have to repeat the name.
example_2: He works at a hospital downtown.
example_3: She asked if he was coming to the party.
collocations: he said, he thinks, he believes, as he mentioned
related_phrasal_verbs: n/a (no common phrasal verb pairs with this word)
where_it_s_used: Storytelling, describing people, conversations about a third person
grammar_pattern: he + verb (he works, he likes) -- used as the subject of a sentence for a male person
common_mistake: Him is my teacher.
correct_version: He is my teacher.
why_it_s_wrong: As a subject, use 'he', not 'him'.
spelling_tip: Just two letters -- h-e, simple and short.
etymology: From Old English "he," a Germanic third-person masculine pronoun.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown (a basic personal pronoun)
mnemonic: HE refers to a male -- think of "HE" as a short label pointing at "Him."
memory_trick: HE starts sentences; HIM ends them.
visual_association: An arrow pointing toward a man standing across the room.
emotion_feel: Neutral -- simply identifies a male subject
difference_explained: He = subject (He is here). Him = object (I saw him).

simple_explanation: Used to refer to a female person already mentioned. "She" replaces a female person's name once it's clear who you're talking about, so you don't have to repeat the name.
example_2: She teaches math at the local school.
example_3: He asked if she was ready to leave.
collocations: she said, she thinks, she believes, as she explained
related_phrasal_verbs: n/a (no common phrasal verb pairs with this word)
where_it_s_used: Storytelling, describing people, conversations about a third person
grammar_pattern: she + verb (she works, she likes) -- used as the subject of a sentence for a female person
common_mistake: Her is my sister.
correct_version: She is my sister.
why_it_s_wrong: As a subject, use 'she', not 'her'.
spelling_tip: Just three letters -- s-h-e, easy to remember alongside "he."
etymology: From Middle English "sche/scho," likely developed from Old English "seo" (the feminine demonstrative) -- eventually replacing an earlier feminine pronoun form.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown (a basic personal pronoun)

memory_trick: SHE starts sentences; HER ends them.
visual_association: An arrow pointing toward a woman standing near the doorway.
emotion_feel: Neutral -- simply identifies a female subject
difference_explained: She = subject (She is my sister). Her = object (I met her).

simple_explanation: Used to refer to a thing, animal, or idea already mentioned. "It" replaces the name of an object, animal, or situation once it's already clear what you mean, so you don't need to repeat it.
example_2: I found my phone -- it was under the couch.
example_3: The movie was long, but it was worth watching.
collocations: it seems, it looks like, it's time, take it easy
related_phrasal_verbs: n/a (no common phrasal verb pairs with this word)
where_it_s_used: Weather, describing objects, time expressions, general statements
grammar_pattern: it + verb (it rains, it works) -- also used as a dummy subject (it is important that...)
common_mistake: It's dog is very friendly.
correct_version: Its dog is very friendly.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Its' (no apostrophe) shows possession. 'It's' always means 'it is' or 'it has'.
pronunciation_tip: Short and simple -- /ɪt/, rhymes with "bit" and "sit."
spelling_tip: Just two letters -- i-t, no apostrophe unless forming the contraction "it's" (it is).
etymology: From Old English "hit," the neuter form of the third-person pronoun, later losing the initial "h" in most uses.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown (a basic personal pronoun)
word_family: its (possessive, no apostrophe), it's (contraction of "it is"), itself (reflexive)
mnemonic: IT points at a THING, not a person -- picture pointing at an object on the table.
memory_trick: IT'S = IT IS. If you can't say 'it is', write ITS.
visual_association: A finger pointing at a mysterious box sitting on a table.
emotion_feel: Neutral -- refers to things, not people, so carries no inherent emotion
synonyms: that (a substitute demonstrative in some contexts)
difference_explained: Its = belonging to it. It's = it is / it has.
mini_conversation:

B: It's great -- much faster than my old one.

usage_tip: 'It's raining' / 'The dog wagged its tail.'

simple_explanation: Used by a speaker to refer to themselves and at least one other person. "We" is used when the speaker is part of a group -- it always includes "I" plus other people.
example_1: We are going to the beach this weekend.
example_2: We watched a movie together last night.
example_3: We should leave before it gets dark.
collocations: we think, we believe, as we discussed, we should
related_phrasal_verbs: n/a (no common phrasal verb pairs with this word)
where_it_s_used: Group activities, plans, shared opinions, teamwork
grammar_pattern: we + verb (we go, we like) -- always used as the subject, always plural
common_mistake: Us went to the market together.
correct_version: We went to the market together.
why_it_s_wrong: As a subject, use 'we', not 'us'.
spelling_tip: Just two letters -- w-e, simple and short.
etymology: From Old English "we," a Germanic first-person plural pronoun.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown (a basic personal pronoun)
word_family: us (object form), our (possessive adjective), ours (possessive pronoun), ourselves (reflexive)

memory_trick: WE starts sentences; US ends them.

simple_explanation: Used to refer to two or more people or things, or to one person of unspecified gender. "They" replaces the names of multiple people or things once it's clear who or what you mean, and it's also commonly used for a single person when the gender isn't stated.

why_it_s_wrong: As a subject, use 'they', not 'them'.

simple_explanation: Used to refer to a male person as the object of a sentence. "Him" is used when a male person is receiving the action rather than performing it -- like "call him" or "give it to him."
example_1: I saw him at the store yesterday.
example_2: Can you give him this message?
example_3: She invited him to the party.
collocations: tell him, give him, call him, between him and me
related_phrasal_verbs: n/a (no common phrasal verb pairs with this word)
where_it_s_used: Describing a male person, requests, storytelling
grammar_pattern: verb + him (call him, help him) -- used as the object of a verb or preposition, for a male person
common_mistake: I saw he at the market yesterday.
correct_version: I saw him at the market yesterday.
why_it_s_wrong: After a verb like 'saw', use the object form 'him'.
spelling_tip: Just three letters -- h-i-m, related closely to "he" and "his."
etymology: From Old English "him," the dative form of the third-person masculine pronoun "he."
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown (a basic personal pronoun)
mnemonic: HIM comes after the action, just like "give it to HIM" -- he's on the receiving end.
memory_trick: HIM after verbs: saw HIM, told HIM.
visual_association: A hand pointing toward a man while handing him an object.
emotion_feel: Neutral -- marks a male person as the receiver of an action
difference_explained: Him = object. He = subject.
mini_conversation:
A: Did you talk to your brother?
B: Yeah, I called him this morning.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character glances across the room and whispers, "I haven't seen him look this happy in years."
news_style_line: News-style: "Officers escorted him safely from the building," the report noted.
casual_conversation: Casual: "Did you tell him about the change in plans?"
mcq_options: A) The subject of a sentence  B) The object of a sentence, for a male  C) A possessive form  D) A plural pronoun
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Please give ______ a call when you arrive. → him
find_and_fix_to_correct: She gave the tickets to he. → She gave the tickets to him.
translate: मैंने उसे कल बाज़ार में देखा। → I saw him at the market yesterday.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something you told him.

simple_explanation: Used to refer to a female person as the object of a sentence, or to show something belongs to her. "Her" can mean the female person receiving an action, as in "I saw her," or it can show possession, as in "her book."
example_1: I gave her the good news.
example_2: Can you help her with the boxes?
example_3: This is her favorite restaurant.
collocations: tell her, give her, her own, ask her
related_phrasal_verbs: n/a (no common phrasal verb pairs with this word)
where_it_s_used: Describing a female person, showing possession, requests
grammar_pattern: verb + her (call her) -- object form; or her + noun (her house) -- possessive form
common_mistake: I saw she at the mall yesterday.
correct_version: I saw her at the mall yesterday.
why_it_s_wrong: After a verb like 'saw', use the object form 'her'.
spelling_tip: Just three letters -- h-e-r, related closely to "she" and "hers."
etymology: From Old English "hire," the dative/genitive form of the third-person feminine pronoun "heo" (she).
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown (a basic personal pronoun)
mnemonic: HER can mean "give it to HER" (object) or "HER book" (possession) -- two jobs, one word.
memory_trick: HER after verbs: saw HER, called HER.
visual_association: A hand placing a bouquet gently into a woman's open hands.
emotion_feel: Neutral -- refers to a female person as object or shows possession
difference_explained: Her = object or possessive. She = subject.
mini_conversation:
A: Have you met her new roommate?
B: Not yet, but I'd like to.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character hands over a photograph and says, "This one always reminds me of her."
news_style_line: News-style: "Neighbors described her as kind and always willing to help," the article stated.
casual_conversation: Casual: "I borrowed her umbrella since it started raining."
mcq_options: A) Only a subject pronoun  B) An object pronoun or a possessive adjective  C) Only a plural pronoun  D) Only a verb
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Please give ______ my regards when you see her. → her
find_and_fix_to_correct: That bag is she's, not mine. → That bag is hers, not mine.
translate: मैंने उसे अच्छी खबर दी। → I gave her the good news.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something you gave her.

usage_tip: 'Her' is also possessive: 'her book'.

simple_explanation: The object form of "we," used for the speaker plus at least one other person. You use "us" when the speaker and others are receiving an action, not performing it -- like in "call us" instead of "call we."
example_1: She invited us to the party.
example_2: Can you help us carry these bags?
example_3: The manager thanked us for our hard work.
collocations: help us, give us, between us, all of us
where_it_s_used: Requests, invitations, group activities, workplace communication
grammar_pattern: verb/preposition + us (Give us a call. / Sit with us.)
common_mistake: Us went to the market together.
correct_version: We went to the market together.
why_it_s_wrong: Before a verb as the subject, use 'we', not 'us'.
spelling_tip: Just two letters -- don't confuse it with "US" (capitalized), the abbreviation for the United States.
etymology: From Old English "ūs," the object form of "we" -- a core Germanic pronoun that has stayed almost unchanged for over a thousand years.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- "us" is a single unbroken Old English pronoun
word_family: we (subject form), our (possessive), ours (possessive pronoun), ourselves (reflexive)
mnemonic: US is the object -- picture "we" tossing the ball to US, and we catch it.
memory_trick: US after verbs and prepositions: with US, for US.
visual_association: A group of people standing closely together, arms linked.
emotion_feel: Neutral -- often carries a sense of togetherness or inclusion
synonyms: ourselves (in informal reciprocal phrases, e.g. "just between us/ourselves")
difference_explained: Us = object. We = subject.
related_words: we, our, ours, ourselves, group, team
mini_conversation:
A: Are you two coming to dinner?
B: Yes, save two seats for us!
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character turns to the group and says, 'They can't stop all of us.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Officials told us the repairs would be finished by next week.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Why don't you join us for coffee later?'
mcq_options: A) The subject of a sentence  B) The object of a verb or preposition  C) A possessive form  D) A question word
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Please send the documents to ______ by Friday. → us
find_and_fix_to_correct: Us are ready to start the meeting. → We are ready to start the meeting.
translate: उन्होंने हमें एक अच्छा तोहफ़ा दिया। → They gave us a nice gift.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence ending with 'for us'.

reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'the object form of "we," used for the speaker plus at least one other person'?
usage_tip: 'Let us / let's go' is a common suggestion.

simple_explanation: The object form of "they," used for two or more people or things. When "they" is doing the receiving instead of the doing, it becomes "them" -- like "I saw them" instead of "I saw they."
example_2: Please give them my regards.
example_3: The kids left their toys, so I put them away.
collocations: tell them, ask them, give them, between them
where_it_s_used: Storytelling, group references, instructions, workplace emails
grammar_pattern: verb/preposition + them (I met them. / He sat next to them.)
common_mistake: I gave the books to they.
correct_version: I gave the books to them.
why_it_s_wrong: After a preposition, use the object form 'them'.
pronunciation_tip: The "th" is voiced (like in "this"), not the soft "th" in "think": /ðem/.
spelling_tip: Don't drop letters in casual speech ("dem") when writing -- the correct spelling is always "them."
etymology: From Old Norse "þeim" (dative plural), which gradually replaced the native Old English form to become the modern object pronoun "them."
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- borrowed whole from Old Norse
word_family: they (subject form), their (possessive), theirs (possessive pronoun), themselves (reflexive)
mnemonic: THEM = THE + M(any) -- it points to more than one person or thing.
memory_trick: THEM after verbs and prepositions: to THEM, saw THEM.
visual_association: An arrow pointing away from the speaker toward a group of people in the distance.
emotion_feel: Neutral -- tone depends entirely on context
difference_explained: Them = object. They = subject.
related_words: they, their, theirs, themselves, group, others
mini_conversation:
A: What happened to the extra chairs?
B: I moved them into the storage room.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A detective points at the security footage and mutters, 'It's them -- I'd recognize that car anywhere.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Investigators say they identified the group and are questioning them today.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Did you text them about the change in plans?'
mcq_options: A) A possessive form  B) The subject of a sentence  C) The object of a verb or preposition  D) A reflexive pronoun
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The teacher handed the papers back to ______ after grading. → them
find_and_fix_to_correct: Me and them went to the concert. → They and I went to the concert.
translate: मैंने उन्हें कल फोन किया था। → I called them yesterday.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence ending with 'to them'.

reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'the object form of "they," used for two or more people or things'?
usage_tip: 'Them' is never used for 'those' in standard English ('them books' is wrong).

simple_explanation: Belonging to the speaker, used directly before a noun. "My" shows that something belongs to "I" -- you always put it right before the thing you own or are talking about.
example_2: My sister is studying in Canada.
example_3: I forgot my umbrella at home.
collocations: my own, my life, my job, my opinion
related_phrasal_verbs: in my opinion, on my own
where_it_s_used: Introductions, describing belongings, personal opinions, family talk
grammar_pattern: my + noun (my house, my friend, my idea)
common_mistake: This is book of my.
correct_version: This is my book.
why_it_s_wrong: Put 'my' directly before the noun.
spelling_tip: Just two letters -- don't confuse with "mine," which is used without a following noun.
etymology: From Old English "mīn," shortened over time before consonant sounds to "my," while "mine" was kept before vowels and at the end of a sentence.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- a shortened Old English possessive form
mnemonic: MY always sits right next to the noun it owns -- "my" never travels alone.
memory_trick: MY + noun: MY book, MY phone.
visual_association: A hand resting firmly on top of a bag, holding it close.
emotion_feel: Neutral -- often personal or sentimental depending on context
synonyms: mine (older, poetic form used before a vowel sound, e.g. "mine eyes")
difference_explained: My + noun (my book). Mine alone (the book is mine).
mini_conversation:
A: Whose jacket is this?
B: Oh, that's my jacket -- thanks!
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character clutches a photo and whispers, 'This was my mother's -- I can't lose it.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'The witness said, "In my opinion, the new policy will help small businesses."'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Have you seen my keys anywhere?'
mcq_options: A) Someone else's ownership  B) The speaker's ownership, before a noun  C) A question  D) A place
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: I left ______ phone charger at the office. → my
find_and_fix_to_correct: Is this pen your or my? → Is this pen yours or mine?
translate: यह मेरी किताब है। → This is my book.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about my favourite thing, using 'my'.

reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'belonging to the speaker, used directly before a noun'?
usage_tip: 'Oh my God!' / 'My goodness!' express surprise.

simple_explanation: Belonging to the person you're speaking to, used directly before a noun. "Your" tells the listener that something belongs to them -- it always comes right before the noun it describes.
example_2: Please bring your ID card to the exam.
example_3: Your presentation was excellent today.
collocations: your own, your name, your turn, your choice
related_phrasal_verbs: at your service, in your shoes
where_it_s_used: Instructions, forms, compliments, requests for information
grammar_pattern: your + noun (your name, your idea, your family)
common_mistake: Your welcome to join us.
correct_version: You're welcome to join us.
why_it_s_wrong: 'You're' = you are. 'Your' = belonging to you.
pronunciation_tip: Often a quick, unstressed "yer" sound in fast speech, or a fuller /jɔːr/ when stressed.
spelling_tip: "Your" (possession) has no apostrophe; "you're" (you + are) always does -- one of English's most common spelling errors.
etymology: From Old English "eower," the possessive form of "ye/you," which evolved through Middle English into modern "your."
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- evolved from an Old English possessive ending
mnemonic: YOUR has no apostrophe because it OWNS something outright -- no missing letters, no apostrophe needed.
memory_trick: If you can say 'you are', write YOU'RE.
visual_association: A hand pointing toward the listener while holding out an object.
emotion_feel: Neutral -- can feel warm in compliments or firm in instructions
synonyms: thy (archaic singular form, used in old or poetic English)
difference_explained: Your = belonging to you. You're = you are.
mini_conversation:
A: What's your favorite hobby?
B: Honestly, your guess is as good as mine -- I have too many!
everyday_scene: Everyday: A mentor places a hand on the hero's shoulder and says, 'Trust your instincts -- they've never failed you.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Officials reminded residents to keep your windows shut during the storm.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Can I borrow your charger for a minute?'
mcq_options: A) The speaker's ownership  B) A question about time  C) The listener's ownership, before a noun  D) A location
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Don't forget to bring ______ notebook to class. → your
find_and_fix_to_correct: Their going to your house or their's? → Are they going to your house or theirs?
translate: क्या यह तुम्हारा बैग है? → Is this your bag?
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence using both 'your' and 'you're'.

reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'belonging to the person you're speaking to, used directly before a noun'?
usage_tip: 'You're welcome' is the reply to 'thank you'.

simple_explanation: Belonging to a male person already mentioned. "His" shows that something belongs to a man or boy -- it can go before a noun or replace the noun entirely.
example_2: His flight landed an hour late.
example_3: The trophy is finally his after years of trying.
collocations: his own, his idea, his job, in his opinion
related_phrasal_verbs: on his own, in his shoes
where_it_s_used: Describing belongings, storytelling, sports, family conversations
grammar_pattern: his + noun, or noun/subject + is + his (his phone / The phone is his.)
common_mistake: This is he car.
correct_version: This is his car.
why_it_s_wrong: Before a noun, use the possessive 'his', not 'he'.
pronunciation_tip: Rhymes with "fizz": /hɪz/, with a voiced "z" sound, not a hissing "s."
spelling_tip: Just three letters, ending in "-is" -- don't add an apostrophe; "his" is already possessive.
etymology: From Old English "his," originally the possessive form of both "he" and "it"; it later narrowed to refer only to males.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- an original Old English possessive form
mnemonic: HIS = "H(e) IS the owner" -- picture "he" standing next to his own belongings.
memory_trick: HIS + noun: HIS car.
visual_association: A name tag reading 'His' stuck onto a jacket on a coat hook.
emotion_feel: Neutral -- pride or admiration in achievement contexts
synonyms: their (increasingly used as a gender-neutral singular alternative in modern English)
difference_explained: His = belonging to him. He's = he is / he has.
mini_conversation:
A: Whose turn is it to present?
B: I think it's his turn next.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A coach hands over the trophy and announces, 'This win is entirely his.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'The athlete said his recovery has been slower than expected.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Is that his car parked outside?'
mcq_question: "His" is used to show ownership by:
mcq_options: A) A female person  B) A male person  C) A group  D) An object
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: That backpack over there is ______. → his
find_and_fix_to_correct: He's car broke down this morning. → His car broke down this morning.
translate: वह लैपटॉप उसका है। → That laptop is his.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about his favourite food.

reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'belonging to a male person already mentioned'?
usage_tip: 'His' is both before a noun (his book) and alone (it's his).

simple_explanation: Belonging to a thing, animal, or idea already mentioned. "Its" shows ownership by something that isn't a person -- like a company, an animal, or an object -- and never takes an apostrophe.
example_2: The company announced its new product yesterday.
example_3: The tree lost most of its leaves in the storm.
collocations: its own, its purpose, its effect, its origin
where_it_s_used: Describing objects, nature, companies, animals, science writing
grammar_pattern: its + noun (its color, its size, its history)
common_mistake: The cat licked it's paw.
correct_version: The cat licked its paw.
why_it_s_wrong: Possessive 'its' has no apostrophe; 'it's' means 'it is'.
pronunciation_tip: One quick syllable: /ɪts/ -- it sounds identical to "it's"; only the spelling differs.
spelling_tip: One of the most misspelled words in English -- if you can replace it with "it is," you need the apostrophe; if not, leave it out.
etymology: A relatively young form in English -- Old English used "his" for "it" too; "its" emerged in the late 1500s to give non-living things their own possessive.
prefix_root_suffix: "it" + possessive "-s," a relatively late addition to English
mnemonic: ITS with no apostrophe is like HIS with no apostrophe -- both are already possessive, no extra letters needed.
memory_trick: HIS, HERS, ITS — possessives never take an apostrophe.
visual_association: A tree with an arrow curving out from its trunk and back to its own leaves.
emotion_feel: Neutral -- purely descriptive, no emotional charge
synonyms: of it (a periphrastic alternative, e.g. "the color of it" = "its color")
difference_explained: Its = belonging to it. It's = it is.
mini_conversation:
A: Why did the plant die?
B: I think it lost its roots when we moved it.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A narrator describes the old house: 'Its windows had been dark for thirty years.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'The company raised its prices for the third time this year.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'The phone finally died -- its battery just wouldn't hold a charge anymore.'
mcq_question: "Its" (no apostrophe) is used to show possession by:
mcq_options: A) A person speaking  B) A thing, animal, or idea  C) A group of people  D) The listener
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The museum is proud of ______ new exhibit. → its
find_and_fix_to_correct: The company changed it's logo last month. → The company changed its logo last month.
translate: कुत्ते ने अपनी पूंछ हिलाई। → The dog wagged its tail.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about an animal and its home.

reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'belonging to a thing, animal, or idea already mentioned'?
usage_tip: Used for animals and things: 'The company changed its logo.'

simple_explanation: Belonging to the speaker and one or more other people, used before a noun. "Our" shows that something belongs to a group that includes the speaker -- like "our team" or "our house."
example_2: Our flight leaves at six in the morning.
example_3: We finally finished our project on time.
collocations: our own, our team, our goal, our family
related_phrasal_verbs: in our favor, on our own terms
where_it_s_used: Family talk, teamwork, shared plans, community events
grammar_pattern: our + noun (our house, our plan, our friends)
common_mistake: This is house of our.
correct_version: This is our house.
why_it_s_wrong: Put 'our' directly before the noun.
pronunciation_tip: Rhymes with "hour" and "flower": /aʊər/ (or a shorter /ɑːr/ in fast speech).
spelling_tip: Don't confuse with "are" -- they can sound similar in fast speech, but "our" always shows possession, while "are" is a verb.
etymology: From Old English "ūre," the possessive form of "wē" (we) -- a core Germanic pronoun little changed over the centuries.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- an original Old English possessive form
mnemonic: OUR = "O(wned) U(nited) R(ight here)" -- it always shows things a group shares.
memory_trick: OUR + noun: OUR house.
visual_association: Several hands stacked together on top of one shared object.
emotion_feel: Neutral to warm -- often signals belonging or teamwork
synonyms: belonging to us (a descriptive equivalent used when no single word fits)
difference_explained: Our = belonging to us. Are = verb (we are). Different words.
mini_conversation:
A: Whose idea was this trip?
B: It was our idea -- we planned it together.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A captain rallies the crew: 'This ship is our home now -- let's take care of her.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Local leaders said, "Our community will rebuild stronger than before."'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Let's invite them over to see our new apartment.'
mcq_options: A) One other person only  B) The speaker and one or more others  C) The listener alone  D) A stranger
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: We spent the weekend cleaning ______ garage. → our
find_and_fix_to_correct: This car belongs to we. → This car belongs to us.
translate: यह हमारी कक्षा है। → This is our classroom.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about our country, using 'our'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'belonging to the speaker and one or more other people, used before a noun'?
usage_tip: 'Our' sounds like 'hour' in many accents.

simple_explanation: Belonging to more than one person or thing already mentioned. "Their" shows that something belongs to a group of people or things -- always placed right before the noun.
example_2: The students packed their bags for the trip.
example_3: Their new office is downtown.
collocations: their own, their turn, in their opinion, their behavior
related_phrasal_verbs: on their own, in their favor
where_it_s_used: Group descriptions, workplace talk, storytelling, family conversations
grammar_pattern: their + noun (their house, their decision, their names)
common_mistake: They forgot there books at school.
correct_version: They forgot their books at school.
why_it_s_wrong: Possessive 'their' shows belonging; 'there' is a place.
pronunciation_tip: Sounds exactly like "there" and "they're": /ðer/ -- only spelling and meaning differ.
spelling_tip: One of English's trickiest homophone sets: "their" (possession), "there" (place), "they're" (they are) -- learn all three together.
etymology: Borrowed from Old Norse "þeirra" during the medieval period, gradually replacing the native Old English possessive form for "they."
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- borrowed whole from Old Norse
mnemonic: THEIR has "HEIR" hidden inside it -- an heir inherits things that become THEIR own.
memory_trick: THEIR has HEIR (a person) inside — belongs to people.
visual_association: A group of houses, each with a small flag showing it belongs to a different family.
emotion_feel: Neutral -- context determines warmth or tension
synonyms: his or her (a traditional, more formal alternative in older or careful writing)
difference_explained: Their = belonging to them. There = place. They're = they are.
mini_conversation:
A: Do the twins share a room?
B: No, their parents gave them separate rooms.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A general studies the map and says, 'We need to know their next move before sunrise.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Residents said their power was restored by early afternoon.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Have you met their new puppy yet?'
mcq_options: A) The speaker  B) The listener  C) Two or more people or things  D) A place
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The players celebrated ______ victory on the field. → their
find_and_fix_to_correct: Their going to be late for the meeting. → They're going to be late for the meeting.
translate: मुझे उनकी टीमवर्क पसंद है। → I admire their teamwork.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence using 'their' correctly.

reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'belonging to more than one person or thing already mentioned'?
usage_tip: 'Their' is also used for one person: 'Someone left their bag.'

simple_explanation: Belonging to the speaker, used without a noun right after it. "Mine" replaces "my + noun" when the noun has already been mentioned -- like saying "that's mine" instead of "that's my book."
example_2: Is this pen yours or mine?
example_3: That idea was originally mine.
collocations: all mine, entirely mine, still mine
related_phrasal_verbs: make it mine (idiom: to fully claim or personalize something)
where_it_s_used: Claiming ownership, disputes, sharing, classroom activities
grammar_pattern: subject + verb + mine (This book is mine.)
common_mistake: This is mine book.
correct_version: This book is mine. / This is my book.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Mine' stands alone. Before a noun, use 'my'.

usage_tip: 'Let's enjoy ourselves' = let's have fun.

simple_explanation: Used when speaking to two or more people whose action comes back to them. "Yourselves" is the plural form of "yourself" -- use it when you're talking to a group about something they did to or for themselves.
example_2: Did you all enjoy yourselves at the concert?
example_3: Please introduce yourselves to the new team.
collocations: help yourselves, enjoy yourselves, introduce yourselves, by yourselves
related_phrasal_verbs: by yourselves (idiom: alone, without outside help)
grammar_pattern: subject "you" (plural) + verb + yourselves (You should treat yourselves well.)
common_mistake: Please help yourself, everyone.
correct_version: Please help yourselves, everyone.
why_it_s_wrong: For more than one person, use 'yourselves'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the third syllable: your-SELVES: /jɔːrˈselvz/.
spelling_tip: Plural ending is "-selves," never "-selfs" -- and it's one word.
etymology: From Middle English "your selves," combining "your" with the plural "selves"; fused into one word for reflexive/emphatic use when addressing more than one person.
mnemonic: YOUR + SELVES -- more than one listener, more than one "self."
memory_trick: YOUR + SELVES: plural, with -VES.
visual_association: A host opening the door wide and waving a group inside.
synonyms: personally (in emphatic plural use, e.g. "you built it yourselves")
difference_explained: Yourself = one person. Yourselves = two or more.
mini_conversation:
A: Can we start eating?
B: Of course -- help yourselves!
everyday_scene: Everyday: A host gestures toward the table and says warmly, 'Please, make yourselves at home.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Organizers told volunteers, "Take care of yourselves during the long shifts."'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'You two should really be proud of yourselves for finishing the race.'
mcq_options: A) One person  B) Two or more people  C) A third party  D) An object
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Please seat ______ anywhere you like. → yourselves
find_and_fix_to_correct: You guys should enjoy yourself tonight. → You guys should enjoy yourselves tonight.
translate: कृपया खुद नाश्ता ले लीजिए। → Please help yourselves to some breakfast.

simple_explanation: Used when a group of people or things do something to or for themselves. "Themselves" shows that the people or things doing the action are also the ones affected by it -- like children looking after themselves.
example_2: The workers organized themselves into small teams.
example_3: The animals protected themselves from the storm.
collocations: by themselves, proud of themselves, blame themselves, organize themselves
related_phrasal_verbs: by themselves (idiom: alone, without outside help)
grammar_pattern: subject "they" + verb + themselves (They taught themselves a new language.)
common_mistake: They finished the project by theirselves.
correct_version: They finished the project by themselves.
why_it_s_wrong: The reflexive is 'themselves'; 'theirselves' is non-standard.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the third syllable: them-SELVES: /ðəmˈselvz/.
spelling_tip: One word, plural ending "-selves" -- not "theirselves" or "themself" (a newer, informal singular form).
etymology: From Middle English "them selves," combining the object pronoun "them" with plural "selves"; fused into one word for reflexive/emphatic plural third-person use.
prefix_root_suffix: them + selves = object pronoun + plural of "self"
mnemonic: THEM + SELVES -- the group's action loops back onto that same group.
memory_trick: THEM + SELVES.
visual_association: A group of children building a fort together without any adult help.
synonyms: personally (in emphatic use, e.g. "they fixed it themselves")
difference_explained: They hurt themselves = each one hurt himself/herself. They hurt each other = A hurt B and B hurt A.
mini_conversation:
A: Did the students plan the whole event?
B: Yes, they organized everything themselves.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A narrator explains, 'The villagers had learned to fend for themselves long before help arrived.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Officials praised the volunteers, who organized themselves within hours of the emergency.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'The kids really surprised themselves with how well the performance went.'
mcq_options: A) One person acts alone  B) A group's action comes back to that same group  C) Speaking to the listener  D) Describing an object
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The team pushed ______ to finish before the deadline. → themselves
find_and_fix_to_correct: They hurt theirselves during the game. → They hurt themselves during the game.
translate: बच्चों ने खुद नाश्ता बनाया। → The kids made themselves breakfast.

usage_tip: 'By themselves' = alone, without help.

simple_explanation: Used to point to one specific thing that is near or being talked about right now. "This" points to something close to you physically, or something you're currently talking about or introducing.
example_2: This restaurant serves amazing pasta.
example_3: Can you explain this part of the lesson again?
collocations: this way, this time, this morning, this is why
related_phrasal_verbs: this and that (idiom: various small things)
where_it_s_used: Pointing things out, introductions, presentations, describing nearby objects
grammar_pattern: this + singular noun, or this + is/was (This idea is great. / This is my house.)
common_mistake: This shoes are too small.
correct_version: These shoes are too small.
why_it_s_wrong: With a plural noun, use 'these', not 'this'.
pronunciation_tip: /ðɪs/, rhymes with "kiss" but starts with the voiced "th" of "this," not "think."
spelling_tip: Just four letters -- don't confuse with "these" (plural) or "that" (far away).
etymology: From Old English "þis," a demonstrative pronoun from the same Germanic root family as "that," used to point to something near the speaker.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- an original Old English demonstrative
mnemonic: THIS is close -- like something right in front of you that you can almost touch.
memory_trick: THIS = one, near. THESE = many, near.
visual_association: A hand pointing directly at an object sitting right next to it.
emotion_feel: Neutral -- tone shifts entirely with context, from excitement to concern
synonyms: this one (used when replacing a noun already mentioned, e.g. "I'll take this one")
difference_explained: This + singular (this shoe). These + plural (these shoes).
mini_conversation:
A: What's this button for?
B: This one turns on the printer.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A detective slams a folder on the table and says, 'This changes everything.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Experts warned, "This trend could affect the entire industry within a year."'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'This is exactly the kind of weather I love.'
mcq_question: "This" is used to point to something that is:
mcq_options: A) Far away and plural  B) Near and singular  C) Far away and singular  D) Near and plural
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: ______ is the best coffee I've had in years. → This
find_and_fix_to_correct: I like this ideas a lot. → I like this idea a lot.
translate: यह मेरी पसंदीदा किताब है। → This is my favorite book.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence using 'this' and one using 'these'.

reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'used to point to one specific thing that is near or being talked about right now'?
usage_tip: 'This one' is used when pointing: 'I'll take this one.'

simple_explanation: Used to point to one specific thing that is farther away or already mentioned. "That" points to something farther from you physically, or refers back to an idea already mentioned in the conversation.
example_1: That house belongs to my uncle.
example_2: That was an incredible performance.
example_3: I didn't expect that from him.
collocations: that way, that time, that being said, now that
related_phrasal_verbs: that's it (idiom: expressing completion or agreement)
where_it_s_used: Referring back to ideas, pointing at distant objects, reactions, storytelling
grammar_pattern: that + singular noun, or that + is/was (That plan worked well. / That is surprising.)
common_mistake: That informations was very helpful.
correct_version: That information was very helpful.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Information' is uncountable, so it has no plural 'informations'.
pronunciation_tip: /ðæt/ -- the "th" is voiced, like in "this" and "there."
spelling_tip: Don't confuse with "than" (used in comparisons) -- similar spelling, very different meaning.
etymology: From Old English "þæt," a demonstrative pronoun from the same Germanic root as "this," used to point to something farther from the speaker.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- an original Old English demonstrative
mnemonic: THAT is far -- picture pointing across the room and saying "THAT one, over there."
memory_trick: THAT = one, far. THOSE = many, far.
visual_association: A finger pointing toward something far across a room or field.
emotion_feel: Neutral -- can carry surprise, admiration, or concern depending on context
synonyms: that one (used when replacing a noun already mentioned, e.g. "I'll take that one")
difference_explained: That + singular or uncountable (that information). Those + plural (those books).
mini_conversation:
A: Did you hear about the new policy?
B: Yes, that surprised me a lot.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A pilot glances at the storm clouds and says grimly, 'That doesn't look good.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Analysts said that decision could reshape the market for years.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'That was such a relaxing weekend.'
mcq_question: "That" is used to point to something that is:
mcq_options: A) Near and plural  B) Far away and singular  C) Near and singular  D) Far away and plural
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: I still can't believe ______ happened yesterday. → that
find_and_fix_to_correct: Those book on the table is mine. → That book on the table is mine.
translate: वह घर मेरे चाचा का है। → That house belongs to my uncle.
