reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'used to point to one specific thing that is farther away or already mentioned'?
usage_tip: 'That's it' = that's all.

simple_explanation: Used to point to more than one thing that is near or being talked about now. "These" points to two or more things close to you physically, or things you're currently discussing.
example_2: These are the best photos from the trip.
example_3: Can you carry these bags for me?
collocations: these days, these things, one of these, all of these
related_phrasal_verbs: these and those (informal way of referring to various items)
where_it_s_used: Describing nearby groups of items, current trends, instructions
grammar_pattern: these + plural noun (these books, these ideas, these people)
common_mistake: These book is mine.
correct_version: These books are mine.
why_it_s_wrong: 'These' needs a plural noun and verb: 'These books are…'.
spelling_tip: Don't confuse with "this" (singular) -- "these" always pairs with plural nouns.
etymology: From Old English "þās," the plural form of "this," retained in Middle English to point to multiple nearby things.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- the plural form of "this" since Old English
mnemonic: THESE has an extra E, just like it points to more than one thing near you.
memory_trick: THESE has an E-S-E: plural, many.
visual_association: A hand gesturing toward a small pile of objects sitting close by.
emotion_feel: Neutral -- often enthusiastic when describing something good nearby
synonyms: these ones (informal, used when replacing plural nouns already mentioned)
difference_explained: These + plural (these books). This + singular (this book).
mini_conversation:
A: Whose bags are these?
B: These are mine -- thanks for grabbing them.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A general looks over the troops and says, 'These are the soldiers who will lead the charge.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Officials said these measures should reduce traffic congestion significantly.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'These cookies are amazing -- did you bake them yourself?'
mcq_question: "These" is used to point to things that are:
mcq_options: A) Far away and singular  B) Near and plural  C) Far away and plural  D) Near and singular
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: ______ documents need to be signed before noon. → These
find_and_fix_to_correct: This shoes are too tight for me. → These shoes are too tight for me.
translate: ये जूते नए हैं। → These shoes are new.

reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'used to point to more than one thing that is near or being talked about now'?
usage_tip: 'These days' = nowadays.

simple_explanation: Used to point to more than one thing that is farther away or already mentioned. "Those" points to two or more things farther from you physically, or things already mentioned earlier in the conversation.
example_2: Those were the best years of my life.
example_3: Can you hand me those scissors on the desk?
collocations: those days, in those cases, one of those, those kinds of
related_phrasal_verbs: one of those days (idiom: a difficult or unlucky day)
where_it_s_used: Nostalgia, referring to distant objects, comparisons, storytelling
grammar_pattern: those + plural noun (those cars, those years, those people)
common_mistake: Those days, we lived in Delhi.
correct_version: In those days, we lived in Delhi.
why_it_s_wrong: To talk about a past period, say 'in those days'.
spelling_tip: Don't confuse with "these" (near) -- "those" always points to things farther from the speaker.
etymology: From Old English "þā," which developed into the plural form of "that" by Middle English, pointing to multiple things farther away.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- the plural form of "that" since Old English
mnemonic: THOSE things are over there, far from us -- the long "o" sound stretches out like the distance.
memory_trick: THOSE has an S: plural, many, far.
visual_association: An old photo album showing faded pictures of far-off memories.
synonyms: those ones (informal, used when replacing plural nouns already mentioned)
difference_explained: Those = far away or in the past. These = near or now.
mini_conversation:
A: Do you remember our college days?
B: Those were some of the best years ever.
everyday_scene: Everyday: An old man looks at a faded photograph and sighs, 'Those were simpler times.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Historians say those events shaped the region for generations.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'I still think about those summer trips we used to take.'

mcq_options: A) Near and singular  B) Far away and plural  C) Near and plural  D) Far away and singular

find_and_fix_to_correct: That shoes over there are mine. → Those shoes over there are mine.

usage_tip: 'In those days' = in that past period.

simple_explanation: A question or connecting word used to ask about or refer to a person. "Who" is used to ask which person did something, or to connect a clause describing a person, especially when that person is the subject.
example_2: Who wrote this book?
example_3: The man who called earlier left a message.
collocations: who knows, who cares, guess who, who else
related_phrasal_verbs: who's who (idiom: a list or description of important people)
grammar_pattern: who + verb, as subject (Who called you? / The woman who teaches us is kind.)
common_mistake: Who did you gave the letter to?
correct_version: Whom did you give the letter to?
why_it_s_wrong: For the object of a verb, formal English uses 'whom'; everyday English often uses 'who'. After 'did', use the base verb 'give'.
pronunciation_tip: The "wh" is pronounced like a plain "h": /huː/, rhyming with "zoo," not "why."
spelling_tip: Don't confuse with "how" -- both start with "wh/h" sounds but ask about completely different things.
etymology: From Old English "hwā," an interrogative/relative pronoun asking about or referring to a person; part of the "wh-" question word family.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- an original Old English question word
word_family: whom (object form), whose (possessive form), whoever (extended form)
mnemonic: WHO asks "which human?" -- both point to a person.
memory_trick: WHO = HE (subject). WHOM = HIM (object). Both end in M: HIM/WHOM.
visual_association: A magnifying glass hovering over a crowd of faces.
emotion_feel: Neutral -- often carries curiosity or suspicion
synonyms: that (informal relative pronoun for people, e.g. "the man that called")
difference_explained: Who = subject (Who called?). Whom = object, formal (To whom did you write?).
mini_conversation:
A: Who left this umbrella here?
B: I think it was the guy who sat near the window.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A detective looks around the room and asks sharply, 'Who was the last person to see her?'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Investigators are still trying to determine who was responsible for the incident.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Who's coming to the party this weekend?'
mcq_question: "Who" is mainly used to ask about or refer to:
mcq_options: A) A place  B) A person  C) A time  D) A reason
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: ______ is going to lead the meeting today? → Who
find_and_fix_to_correct: Who's book is this on the table? → Whose book is this on the table?
translate: दरवाज़े पर कौन है? → Who is at the door?
write_your_own_sentence: Write a question starting with 'Who…?'.

reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'a question or connecting word used to ask about or refer to a person'?
usage_tip: 'Who' is fine in speech for objects: 'Who did you meet?'

simple_explanation: The formal object form of "who," used for the person receiving an action. "Whom" is the formal way to ask about or refer to a person who is receiving the action, often after a preposition, like "to whom" or "for whom."
example_2: To whom should I address this letter?
example_3: She is a woman whom everyone respects.
collocations: to whom, for whom, whom it may concern
related_phrasal_verbs: to whom it may concern (a formal opening for letters)
where_it_s_used: Formal letters, academic writing, careful spoken English, legal language
grammar_pattern: preposition + whom, or whom + subject + verb (To whom it may concern... / The person whom I met.)
common_mistake: Whom is calling, please?
correct_version: Who is calling, please?
why_it_s_wrong: For the subject of a sentence, use 'who', not 'whom'.
spelling_tip: Ends in "-m," like "him" and "them" -- all three are object pronouns.
etymology: From Old English "hwām," the dative/object case of "hwā" (who); preserved in formal English as the object form of "who."
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- an original Old English case form
mnemonic: If you can answer with "him," use WHOM -- both end in "M."
memory_trick: WHOM only after verbs or prepositions: 'to whom', 'for whom'.
visual_association: A sealed envelope addressed 'To Whom It May Concern.'
emotion_feel: Neutral -- tends to sound formal or careful
synonyms: who (used informally as a substitute in modern spoken English)
difference_explained: Whom = object only. Who = subject (and informal object).
mini_conversation:
A: Whom should I contact about the visa application?
B: You should speak to the officer at the front desk.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A lawyer addresses the room formally: 'The question remains -- to whom does this property truly belong?'
news_style_line: News-style: 'The report did not specify to whom the funds were transferred.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'I honestly don't know whom to ask for help with this form.'
mcq_options: A) The subject of a verb  B) The object of a verb or preposition  C) A possessive form  D) A place word
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: ______ did you speak to about the refund? → Whom
find_and_fix_to_correct: Whom is your favorite teacher? → Who is your favorite teacher?
translate: आपने किसे आमंत्रित किया? → Whom did you invite?
write_your_own_sentence: Write a formal sentence with 'to whom'.

reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'the formal object form of "who," used for the person receiving an action'?
usage_tip: 'To whom it may concern' is a formal letter opening.

simple_explanation: A question or connecting word used to ask or state who owns something. "Whose" asks about ownership, or connects a clause showing who something belongs to -- always followed directly by a noun.
example_2: Whose idea was it to cancel the trip?
example_3: I met a man whose dog looks just like mine.
collocations: whose fault, whose turn, whose idea, whose responsibility
related_phrasal_verbs: whose side are you on (idiom: asking about loyalty in a dispute)
where_it_s_used: Questions about ownership, blame, responsibility, storytelling
grammar_pattern: whose + noun (whose phone, whose decision, whose turn)
common_mistake: Who's phone is ringing?
correct_version: Whose phone is ringing?
why_it_s_wrong: 'Whose' shows possession; 'who's' means 'who is' or 'who has'.
pronunciation_tip: Rhymes with "shoes": /huːz/ -- sounds exactly like "who's," but means something different.
spelling_tip: "Whose" (possession) has no apostrophe; "who's" (who is/has) always does.
etymology: From Old English "hwæs," the possessive case of "hwā" (who); it has always marked ownership by a person (or occasionally a thing).
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- an original Old English possessive case form
mnemonic: WHOSE shoes are those? -- it rhymes with "shoes" and asks about ownership.
memory_trick: WHO'S = WHO IS. If you can't say 'who is', write WHOSE.
visual_association: A single glove lying on the ground with a question mark above it.
emotion_feel: Neutral -- can carry curiosity or slight tension in blame situations
synonyms: of which (a formal alternative for things, e.g. "the book, the pages of which...")
difference_explained: Whose = belonging to whom. Who's = who is / who has.
mini_conversation:
A: Whose turn is it to do the dishes?
B: I think it's yours tonight.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A detective picks up a glove and asks the room, 'Whose is this?'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Investigators are trying to determine whose signature appears on the document.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Whose turn is it to pick the movie tonight?'
mcq_options: A) Time  B) Ownership  C) Location  D) Reason
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: ______ backpack is this on the chair? → Whose
find_and_fix_to_correct: Whose going to the concert tonight? → Who's going to the concert tonight?
translate: यह बैग किसका है? → Whose bag is this?
write_your_own_sentence: Write a question starting with 'Whose…?'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'a question or connecting word used to ask or state who owns something'?
usage_tip: 'Whose turn is it?' is common in games.

hindi_meaning: कौन सा, कौन सी, कौन से
simple_explanation: A question or connecting word used to ask about or refer to one option from a specific group. "Which" is used when there's a limited set of choices, or to add extra information about something already mentioned.
example_2: Which of these two shirts looks better?
example_3: The restaurant, which just opened last week, is already popular.
collocations: which one, which way, which is why, no matter which
related_phrasal_verbs: which is which (idiom: telling two similar things apart)
where_it_s_used: Choices, comparisons, multiple-choice questions, added descriptions
grammar_pattern: which + noun, or which + of + noun (Which book do you want? / Which of these is yours?)
common_mistake: What of these two shirts do you like better?
correct_version: Which of these two shirts do you like better?
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'which' when choosing from a small, known set.
pronunciation_tip: /wɪtʃ/ -- rhymes with "witch," starting with a soft "wh" sound.
spelling_tip: Don't confuse with "witch" (a person who practices magic) -- they sound identical but mean something completely different.
etymology: From Old English "hwilc" ("of what kind"), combining the "wh-" question root with a form meaning "like/kind"; used to ask about or select from a specific set.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- an original Old English question word
mnemonic: WHICH sounds like WITCH pointing her finger -- "which one do you choose?"
memory_trick: WHICH = choose from these few.
visual_association: Two paths splitting apart with a signpost in the middle.
emotion_feel: Neutral -- often signals a decision point
synonyms: that (used in restrictive clauses, e.g. "the book that I bought")
difference_explained: Which = choose from a known set. What = open question, any answer.
mini_conversation:
A: We have tea or coffee -- which would you like?
B: I'll have the coffee, please.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A guide points to two doors and says, 'Which one you choose determines everything that happens next.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'The committee has not yet decided which proposal to approve.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Which movie should we watch tonight?'
mcq_options: A) There are unlimited possible answers  B) Choosing from a specific, limited set of options  C) Asking about a person  D) Asking about a reason
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: ______ of these two routes is faster? → Which
find_and_fix_to_correct: What of these three colors matches the wall best? → Which of these three colors matches the wall best?
translate: आपको कौन सा रंग पसंद है? → Which color do you prefer?
write_your_own_sentence: Write a question with 'Which … do you prefer?'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'a question or connecting word used to ask about or refer to one option from a specific group'?
usage_tip: 'Which one?' = which of these?

simple_explanation: A question word used to ask for information about a thing, idea, or action, with no limited set of choices. "What" is the most general question word in English -- you use it to ask about almost anything when the answer isn't already narrowed down.
example_2: What time does the movie start?
example_3: I don't know what to say.
collocations: what time, what if, what's more, so what
related_phrasal_verbs: what's up (informal greeting), what if (idiom introducing a hypothetical)
where_it_s_used: Questions, requests for information, surprise, clarification
grammar_pattern: what + verb/noun (What happened? / What time is it?)
common_mistake: Which is your name?
correct_version: What is your name?
why_it_s_wrong: For open questions like a name, use 'what', not 'which'.
pronunciation_tip: /wʌt/ or /wɒt/ depending on accent -- the "wh" softens to a plain "w" sound for most speakers.
spelling_tip: Don't confuse with "watt" (a unit of power) -- same sound, completely different meaning.
etymology: From Old English "hwæt," the neuter form of the "wh-" interrogative root, historically the most general and open-ended question word in English.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- an original Old English question word
word_family: which (limited choices), who (for people), whatever (extended form)
mnemonic: WHAT opens the door wide to any answer -- unlike "which," it doesn't limit the choices.
memory_trick: WHAT = anything, open.
visual_association: A large question mark floating above someone's head.
emotion_feel: Neutral -- can carry curiosity, shock, or confusion depending on tone
synonyms: that which (formal/archaic equivalent, e.g. "what I need" = "that which I need")
difference_explained: What = open, unlimited choice. Which = limited choice.

A: What are you working on?
B: Just finishing up a report for tomorrow.

simple_explanation: An unspecified or unknown person. You use "someone" when you mean a person exists but you don't know or don't say who.
example_2: Someone left their umbrella here.
example_3: I need someone to help me carry this.
collocations: someone else, someone special, someone new, ask someone
grammar_pattern: someone + singular verb (Someone is calling you.)
common_mistake: Someone are knocking at the door.
correct_version: Someone is knocking at the door.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Someone' always takes a singular verb.
pronunciation_tip: Stress is on the first syllable: SUM-wun.
spelling_tip: One word, no hyphen -- not "some one."
etymology: From "some" + "one" -- an unspecified single person.
prefix_root_suffix: some- = unspecified quantity + -one = a single person
mnemonic: SOME + ONE = one unspecified person out there.
memory_trick: SOME + ONE: one person, so singular.
visual_association: A silhouette of an unknown person in a doorway.
emotion_feel: Neutral, sometimes curious or cautious depending on context
difference_explained: Someone = positive (someone called). Anyone = questions, negatives (did anyone call?).
mini_conversation:
A: Did someone call earlier?
B: Yes, someone from the bank.

simple_explanation: Any person at all, usually used in questions or negative sentences. You use "anyone" when it doesn't matter which specific person -- often in questions ("Is anyone home?") or negatives ("I didn't see anyone").
example_2: I didn't see anyone at the park.
example_3: Can anyone help me lift this box?
collocations: anyone else, hardly anyone, anyone can, if anyone
where_it_s_used: Questions, negative statements, conditionals, offers of help
grammar_pattern: anyone + singular verb, often in questions/negatives (Does anyone know the answer? / I don't know anyone here.)
common_mistake: Anyone are welcome to join the club.
correct_version: Anyone is welcome to join the club.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Anyone' always takes a singular verb.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the first syllable: EN-ee-wun: /ˈeniwʌn/.
spelling_tip: One word, no hyphen -- not "any one" (a separate phrase meaning "any single one of a group").
etymology: Formed by combining "any" + "one" in Middle English, meaning an unspecified person, typically used in questions, negatives, and conditionals.
prefix_root_suffix: any- = unspecified/every possible + -one = a single person
mnemonic: ANY + ONE = any single person at all, out of everyone possible.
memory_trick: ANY + ONE: one person, so singular.
visual_association: An open door with a voice echoing into an empty room.
emotion_feel: Neutral, sometimes hopeful (asking for help) or uneasy (in suspenseful situations)
difference_explained: Anyone = any person. Any one = any single item (any one of these books).

A: Does anyone want the last slice of pizza?
B: I'll take it if no one else wants it!

simple_explanation: All the people in a group, considered one by one. "Everyone" refers to all the people in a group -- even though it means "all," it's grammatically treated as singular.
example_2: Everyone was surprised by the news.
example_3: Please make sure everyone has a seat.
collocations: everyone else, almost everyone, everyone knows, everyone agrees
where_it_s_used: Group announcements, celebrations, general statements, instructions
grammar_pattern: everyone + singular verb (Everyone is here. / Everyone loves this song.)
common_mistake: Everyone are invited to the wedding.
correct_version: Everyone is invited to the wedding.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Everyone' always takes a singular verb.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the first syllable: EV-ree-wun: /ˈevriwʌn/.
spelling_tip: One word -- not "every one," which is a separate phrase meaning "each single one" (e.g., "every one of the plates broke").
etymology: Formed by combining "every" + "one" in Middle English, meaning all people within a group, considered individually.
prefix_root_suffix: every- = each without exception + -one = a single person
mnemonic: EVERY + ONE = each and every single person, all together.
memory_trick: EVERY + ONE: each person, singular verb.
visual_association: A large group of people raising their hands together at once.
difference_explained: Everyone = all people. Every one = each single item.
mini_conversation:
A: Did everyone get a copy of the schedule?
B: Yes, everyone has one now.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A host raises a glass and announces, 'Everyone, let's give a warm welcome to our guest of honor.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Officials reminded everyone to stay indoors during the storm warning.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Everyone's talking about the new café downtown.'

usage_tip: 'Everyone' can use 'their': 'Everyone has their own opinion.'

simple_explanation: Not a single person; nobody at all. "No one" means there isn't even one person -- it already contains the negative, so you don't need "not" or "n't" in the same clause.
example_2: No one knew the answer to the question.
example_3: No one wants to work on weekends.
collocations: no one else, no one knows, no one cares, no one wants
where_it_s_used: Describing absence, disappointment, mystery, empty places
grammar_pattern: no one + singular verb, no additional negative (No one is home. NOT "No one isn't home.")
common_mistake: No one doesn't like ice cream.
correct_version: No one likes ice cream.
why_it_s_wrong: 'No one' is already negative, so don't add 'doesn't'.
spelling_tip: Two separate words with a space -- not "noone" (the hyphenated "no-one" appears mainly in British English).
etymology: Formed from "no" + "one," meaning not a single person; written as two words (unlike "nobody," "someone," "anyone").
prefix_root_suffix: no + one = negative quantifier + a single person
mnemonic: NO + ONE = not even a single person is there.
memory_trick: NO + ONE: two words. 'Noone' is wrong.
visual_association: An empty chair at a table set for a dinner party.
emotion_feel: Often carries loneliness, disappointment, or relief (in the case of no injuries)
difference_explained: No one = no person. None = not any (of things or people).
mini_conversation:

B: No one came -- I think it got cancelled.

simple_explanation: An unspecified or unknown thing, idea, or matter. "Something" refers to a thing that exists but isn't named specifically -- you use it when you don't know or don't need to say exactly what it is.
example_1: I need to tell you something.
example_2: Something smells delicious in the kitchen.
example_3: There's something wrong with the printer.
collocations: something else, something wrong, something special, or something
related_phrasal_verbs: something's up (idiom: something unusual is happening)
where_it_s_used: Everyday conversation, requests, describing problems, surprises
grammar_pattern: something + singular verb (Something is bothering her.)
common_mistake: Something are wrong with my computer.
correct_version: Something is wrong with my computer.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Something' always takes a singular verb.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the first syllable: SUM-thing: /ˈsʌmθɪŋ/.
spelling_tip: One word, no hyphen -- not "some thing," which would emphasize a single, countable item more literally.
etymology: Formed from "some" + "thing" in Middle English, meaning an unspecified object, idea, or matter.
word_family: anything, everything, nothing (related indefinite pronouns for things)
mnemonic: SOME + THING = an unspecified thing exists, even if you don't know exactly what.
memory_trick: SOME + THING: one thing.
visual_association: A wrapped box with an unknown object inside.
emotion_feel: Neutral, often carries curiosity, unease, or anticipation
synonyms: a certain thing (descriptive equivalent, e.g. "I need a certain thing from you")
difference_explained: Something = positive (I want something). Anything = questions, negatives (I don't want anything).
mini_conversation:
A: You look worried -- is something wrong?
B: Yeah, something's been bothering me all day.

casual_conversation: Casual: 'I feel like I'm forgetting something important.'

find_and_fix_to_correct: I need to tell you anything important. → I need to tell you something important.

usage_tip: 'Something like that' = approximately that.

simple_explanation: Any thing at all, usually used in questions or negative sentences. "Anything" is used when it doesn't matter which specific thing -- often in questions ("Do you need anything?") or negatives ("I didn't buy anything").
example_2: I didn't find anything interesting at the store.
example_3: You can ask me anything.
collocations: anything else, hardly anything, anything but, or anything
related_phrasal_verbs: if anything (idiom: used to suggest the opposite might be true)
grammar_pattern: anything + singular verb, often in questions/negatives (Is anything wrong? / I don't want anything.)
common_mistake: I don't want something to eat right now.
correct_version: I don't want anything to eat right now.
why_it_s_wrong: In negative sentences, use 'anything', not 'something'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the first syllable: EN-ee-thing: /ˈeniθɪŋ/.
etymology: Formed from "any" + "thing" in Middle English, meaning an unspecified object or matter, used in questions, negatives, and conditionals.
word_family: something, everything, nothing (related indefinite pronouns for things)
mnemonic: ANY + THING = any object at all, no matter which.
memory_trick: ANY + THING: any thing at all.
visual_association: An open hand offering to help with an unspecified task.
emotion_feel: Neutral, often helpful or open-minded in tone
synonyms: whatever (in some uses, e.g. "you can have anything" = "you can have whatever you want")
difference_explained: Anything = questions and negatives. Something = positives and offers.

simple_explanation: Concerning a topic, or close to an amount. "About" is used to say what something concerns (a book about history), or to show an approximate number or time (about ten minutes).
example_1: This book is about space travel.
example_2: I called to ask about the job opening.
example_3: We waited for about an hour.
collocations: about time, talk about, worry about, think about
related_phrasal_verbs: bring about (idiom: to cause something to happen), how about (idiom: making a suggestion)
grammar_pattern: about + noun/gerund (a story about dragons / worried about losing)
common_mistake: This book talks for the environment.
correct_version: This book talks about the environment.
why_it_s_wrong: To show the topic, use 'about', not 'for'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: uh-BOWT: /əˈbaʊt/.
spelling_tip: Don't confuse with "above" -- both start with "ab-" but mean very different things.
etymology: From Old English "onbūtan" (on + be + ūtan, "on the outside of"), which narrowed over time to mean "concerning" or "approximately."
word_family: n/a -- "about" doesn't have common noun/verb/adjective forms
mnemonic: A-BOUT a topic means you're going ABOUT (around) the subject, covering it from different angles.
memory_trick: ABOUT = the topic around which the talk goes.
visual_association: A speech bubble with one small object floating at its centre.
emotion_feel: Neutral -- tone depends fully on the topic discussed
difference_explained: About = general topic (a talk about India). On = specific or academic topic (a lecture on economics).
mini_conversation:
A: What's this documentary about?
B: It's about climate change and its effects.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character flips through an old journal and says, 'This whole thing is about more than just revenge.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'The senator spoke about the need for new infrastructure funding.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Can we talk about the weekend plans later?'
mcq_options: A) Underneath something  B) Concerning a topic, or approximately  C) Exactly precise  D) Opposite of something
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The lecture was ______ the history of ancient Rome. → about
find_and_fix_to_correct: I'm worried for the exam results. → I'm worried about the exam results.
translate: यह किताब अंतरिक्ष यात्रा के बारे में है। → This book is about space travel.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a book and what it is about.

usage_tip: 'About' also means 'approximately': 'about ₹500'.

simple_explanation: At a higher position than something else. "Above" shows that something is higher than another thing, often with space between them, like a picture above a sofa.
example_1: The clock is above the door.
example_2: The plane flew above the clouds.
example_3: Her score was above average.
collocations: above average, above all, from above, mentioned above
grammar_pattern: above + noun (above the table, above sea level)
common_mistake: The picture is above from the fireplace.
correct_version: The picture is above the fireplace.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Above' takes its object directly; 'from' is not needed.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: uh-BUV: /əˈbʌv/.
spelling_tip: Ends in "-ove," rhyming with "love" and "glove," not "-oof."
etymology: From Old English "abufan" (on + be + ufan, "on/from above"), a compound describing a higher position.
prefix_root_suffix: a- (on) + bufan (above) -- from Old English, meaning "on high"
word_family: n/a -- "above" doesn't have common noun/verb/adjective forms
mnemonic: A-BOVE means higher up -- picture a bird flying ABOVE the clouds.
memory_trick: ABOVE = higher than, not touching.
visual_association: A bird soaring high above a mountain peak.
difference_explained: Above = higher than (not touching). Over = higher than, covering, or moving across.
mini_conversation:
A: Where's the fire extinguisher?
B: It's on the shelf above the door.

news_style_line: News-style: 'Temperatures rose to well above average for this time of year.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Can you check what's making that noise above us?'
mcq_options: A) Lower than something else  B) Higher than something else  C) Beside something else  D) Inside something else

find_and_fix_to_correct: The temperature rose above from normal levels. → The temperature rose above normal levels.

usage_tip: 'Above all' = most importantly.

simple_explanation: From one side of something to the other side. "Across" describes moving or being positioned from one side of a space to the opposite side, like walking across a street.
example_2: The store is just across the street.
example_3: She swam across the lake in twenty minutes.
collocations: across the street, across the world, spread across, straight across
related_phrasal_verbs: come across (idiom: to find by chance, or to seem a certain way)
where_it_s_used: Directions, travel, spreading news or trends, comparisons
grammar_pattern: across + noun (across the room, across the ocean)
common_mistake: He walked across of the street carefully.
correct_version: He walked across the street carefully.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Across' takes its object directly; 'of' is not needed.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: uh-CROSS: /əˈkrɔːs/.
spelling_tip: Contains "cross" -- think of crossing from one side to the other.
etymology: From Old French "a croix" ("in the shape of a cross"), reshaped in Middle English into "on cross" and then "across," meaning "from one side to the other."
prefix_root_suffix: a- (on) + cross -- from the idea of forming or following a cross-shaped path
mnemonic: A-CROSS has "CROSS" inside it -- picture walking across, forming a cross-like path.
memory_trick: ACROSS = from one side to the other, like a cross.
visual_association: A dotted line stretching from one riverbank straight to the other.
emotion_feel: Neutral -- purely describes movement or spread
synonyms: over (in the sense of crossing, e.g. "walk over the bridge")
difference_explained: Across = over a surface, side to side. Through = inside something, end to end.
mini_conversation:
A: How do we get to the bakery?
B: Just walk across the park, and it's right there.

news_style_line: News-style: 'The bridge across the river will remain closed for repairs until next month.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'I saw an old friend across the street yesterday.'
mcq_options: A) Underneath something  B) From one side to the other  C) Behind something  D) Inside something
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: They built a new bridge ______ the river. → across
find_and_fix_to_correct: The cat jumped across of the fence. → The cat jumped across the fence.

usage_tip: 'Come across' = find by chance.

simple_explanation: Opposed to something, or physically touching/leaning on it. "Against" shows opposition to an idea or team, or physical contact, like leaning against a wall.
example_2: Many people voted against the new law.
example_3: The ladder was resting against the fence.
collocations: against the law, against the odds, lean against, vote against
related_phrasal_verbs: up against (idiom: facing a difficult challenge)
grammar_pattern: against + noun (against the rules, against the wall)
common_mistake: I am against of this decision.
correct_version: I am against this decision.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Against' takes its object directly; 'of' is not needed.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: uh-GENST: /əˈɡenst/.
spelling_tip: Ends in "-nst," not "-nced" -- easy to misspell if written quickly.
etymology: From Old English "ongēan" ("opposite, in return"), with the "-st" ending added in Middle English by analogy with words like "amongst"; means opposed to or in contact with.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- from Old English "ongēan" with a later added "-st"
word_family: n/a -- "against" doesn't have common noun/verb/adjective forms
mnemonic: A-GAINST feels like pushing back -- imagine leaning AGAINST a wall, resisting gravity.
memory_trick: AGAINST: A GAINST — opposed.
visual_association: Two arm-wrestlers pushing against each other's hands.
emotion_feel: Often carries tension, opposition, or determination
difference_explained: Against = opposed to, or touching for support. Opposite = facing, on the other side.
mini_conversation:

B: Honestly, I'm against it -- it seems unfair.

news_style_line: News-style: 'Protesters gathered outside city hall to speak out against the proposed changes.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'I'm not against the idea, but I do have some concerns.'

find_and_fix_to_correct: He is against with the plan. → He is against the plan.

usage_tip: 'Lean against the wall' = rest your body on it.

simple_explanation: Following the length of something, like a road, river, or path. "Along" describes movement or position that follows the length of a line, road, or edge, from one point toward another.
example_2: There are cafes all along this street.
example_3: She jogged along the river every morning.
collocations: along the way, come along, get along, along with
related_phrasal_verbs: come along (idiom: to join someone, or to make progress), get along (idiom: to have a good relationship)
where_it_s_used: Directions, walks, travel, describing a row of things
grammar_pattern: along + noun (along the coast, along the corridor)
common_mistake: We drove along of the highway for hours.
correct_version: We drove along the highway for hours.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Along' takes its object directly; 'of' is not needed.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: uh-LONG: /əˈlɔːŋ/.
spelling_tip: Contains "long" -- think of following the long stretch of something.
etymology: From Old English "andlang" (and- "opposite" + lang "long"), originally meaning "extending the whole length of," which became "along."
prefix_root_suffix: a- (opposite/along) + long -- from Old English "andlang," meaning the full length of something
mnemonic: A-LONG has "LONG" inside it -- you move ALONG the long length of a path.
memory_trick: ALONG = following the length of something.
visual_association: A long, winding path following the edge of a river.
emotion_feel: Neutral -- often calm, associated with walking or travel
difference_explained: Along = following the length. Across = from one side to the other.
mini_conversation:
A: Is there anywhere good to eat near here?
B: Yeah, there are lots of restaurants along Main Street.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A traveler gazes at the horizon and says, 'The road ahead stretches on for miles along the coastline.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Officials are adding new bike lanes along several major streets downtown.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Let's walk along the river before it gets dark.'

simple_explanation: Surrounded by, or included as part of, a group of three or more. "Among" shows that something is within or part of a larger group, unlike "between," which is specifically for two.
example_2: The prize was shared among the five winners.
example_3: There was disagreement among the committee members.
collocations: among friends, among other things, choose among, among the best
related_phrasal_verbs: among other things (idiom: as one item in a larger, unlisted set)
grammar_pattern: among + plural noun (among the students, among the trees)
common_mistake: The gift was divided between the four children.
correct_version: The gift was divided among the four children.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'among' for three or more; 'between' is for two.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: uh-MUNG: /əˈmʌŋ/.
spelling_tip: Ends in "-mong," not "-mongst" (that spelling, "amongst," is an older British variant with the same meaning).
etymology: From Old English "on gemang" ("in a crowd/mixture"), gradually contracted into "among," used for position within a group of three or more.
prefix_root_suffix: a- (in) + mong (mixture/crowd) -- from Old English "gemang," meaning a mixed group
word_family: n/a -- "among" doesn't have common noun/verb/adjective forms
mnemonic: A-MONG sounds like "a-MANY" -- among is for a group of many, not just two.
memory_trick: AMONG = in a group of many.
visual_association: A single red flower standing out among a field of white ones.
emotion_feel: Neutral -- often signals belonging within a group
difference_explained: Between = two (between you and me). Among = three or more (among friends).
mini_conversation:
A: How did you choose the winner from so many entries?
B: It was tough picking just one among so many great ideas.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A narrator says, 'Somewhere among the thousands of stars, one story was about to change everything.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'The award was one of many shared among the winning research team.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'There's a lot of excitement among the students about the trip.'
mcq_options: A) Exactly two things  B) Three or more things  C) A single thing  D) No things at all
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The responsibilities were split ______ the team members. → among
find_and_fix_to_correct: Choose one between these five options. → Choose one among these five options.
translate: वह भीड़ के बीच खड़ी थी। → She stood among the crowd.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something shared among friends.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'surrounded by, or included as part of, a group of three or more'?
usage_tip: 'Among other things' = as well as other things.

simple_explanation: Surrounding something, or close to an amount, or moving from place to place. "Around" shows that something surrounds another thing, or gives an approximate number, or describes moving without a fixed direction.
example_2: There's a fence around the garden.
example_3: It costs around fifty dollars.
collocations: around the corner, around the world, come around, turn around
related_phrasal_verbs: come around (idiom: to change one's opinion, or to visit), turn around (idiom: to improve after a bad situation)
grammar_pattern: around + noun (around the table, around noon)
common_mistake: The book cost around of twenty dollars.
correct_version: The book cost around twenty dollars.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Around' takes its object directly; 'of' is not needed.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: uh-ROWND: /əˈraʊnd/.
spelling_tip: Contains "round" -- think of circling round something.
etymology: From Middle English "a-" + "round," meaning "in a circle" or "on all sides of" something.
prefix_root_suffix: a- (on) + round -- from Middle English, describing a circular position or movement
word_family: n/a -- "around" doesn't have common noun/verb/adjective forms
mnemonic: A-ROUND has "ROUND" inside it -- picture going in a circle, all the way round.
memory_trick: AROUND = in a circle, or approximately.
visual_association: A circle of friends sitting together around a table.
emotion_feel: Neutral -- often relaxed or social in tone
difference_explained: Both mean approximately (around/about ₹500). Around also means in a circle.
mini_conversation:
A: What time should we meet?
B: Let's say around seven o'clock.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A group of friends gather around a fire and one says, 'Let's just enjoy tonight -- everything else can wait.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Around two hundred volunteers showed up to help with the cleanup effort.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Do you want to walk around the market for a bit?'
mcq_options: A) Exactly, with no approximation  B) Surrounding something, or approximately  C) Underneath something  D) Opposite to something
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: There's a low wall built ______ the old castle. → around
find_and_fix_to_correct: We walked around of the whole park. → We walked around the whole park.
translate: हम अलाव के चारों ओर बैठे। → We sat around the campfire.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence using 'around' to mean 'approximately'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'surrounding something, or close to an amount, or moving from place to place'?
usage_tip: 'Around ₹500' = approximately ₹500.

simple_explanation: Used to show an exact place, time, or point. "At" points to a specific spot, moment, or activity -- like "at the door," "at 5 PM," or "at school."
example_1: I'll meet you at the station.
example_2: The meeting starts at nine o'clock.
example_3: She's waiting for you at the entrance.
collocations: at home, at work, at least, at first
related_phrasal_verbs: look at, arrive at, laugh at, good at
grammar_pattern: at + specific place/time (at the corner, at midnight, at noon)
common_mistake: I will meet you in the station.
correct_version: I will meet you at the station.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'at' for a specific meeting point.
pronunciation_tip: A short, quick vowel: /æt/, rhyming with "cat" and "hat."
spelling_tip: Just two letters -- among the shortest and most frequently used words in English.
etymology: From Old English "æt," a core Germanic preposition marking a specific point in space or time; one of the oldest and most basic words in English.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- one of the oldest and most basic Old English prepositions
word_family: n/a -- "at" doesn't have common noun/verb/adjective forms
mnemonic: AT marks an exact spot -- like a pin dropped AT a precise location on a map.
memory_trick: AT = a point on a map. IN = inside an area.
visual_association: A pin marking an exact point on a map.
emotion_feel: Neutral -- purely functional, showing precise place or time
difference_explained: At = a specific point (at the station). In = inside an area (in the station, in Delhi).
mini_conversation:
A: Where should we meet tonight?
B: Let's meet at the usual café, at seven.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A voice crackles over the radio: 'Rendezvous point is set -- we meet at the old bridge at midnight.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'The ceremony will be held at the city hall this Friday.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Are you still at the office, or have you left already?'
mcq_options: A) A general area  B) A specific point in place or time  C) A direction of movement  D) A comparison
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Please arrive ______ the venue by six o'clock. → at
find_and_fix_to_correct: She arrived to the airport early. → She arrived at the airport early.
translate: मैं तुमसे स्टेशन पर मिलूंगा। → I'll meet you at the station.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about where you will meet a friend.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'used to show an exact place, time, or point'?
usage_tip: 'At home', 'at work', 'at school' — no 'the'.

simple_explanation: At or toward the back of something, or not as advanced as expected. "Behind" shows something is positioned at the back of another thing, or that someone is falling short of a schedule or expected progress.
example_1: The keys are behind the couch.
example_2: He hid behind the tree.
example_3: We're a bit behind schedule today.
collocations: behind schedule, fall behind, leave behind, behind the scenes
related_phrasal_verbs: fall behind (idiom: to make less progress than others), leave behind (idiom: to not take something/someone along)
where_it_s_used: Directions, schedules, hiding, progress and delays
grammar_pattern: behind + noun (behind the door, behind schedule)
common_mistake: The dog is hiding behind of the tree.
correct_version: The dog is hiding behind the tree.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Behind' takes its object directly; 'of' is not needed.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: bee-HIND: /bɪˈhaɪnd/.
spelling_tip: Contains "hind," as in "hind legs" (back legs) -- both relate to the back or rear.
etymology: From Old English "behindan" (be- + hindan, "at the back"), meaning at or toward the back of something.
prefix_root_suffix: be- (at) + hind (back/rear) -- from Old English, meaning positioned at the rear
word_family: n/a -- "behind" doesn't have common noun/verb/adjective forms
mnemonic: BE-HIND has "HIND" in it, like the HIND (rear) legs of an animal -- both point to the back.
memory_trick: BEHIND = at the BACK.
visual_association: A shadow hiding just behind a half-open door.
emotion_feel: Neutral, sometimes tense (in suspenseful contexts) or stressed (about deadlines)
difference_explained: Behind = place (behind the house). After = time or order (after lunch).
mini_conversation:
A: Where did the cat go?
B: I think it's hiding behind the curtains.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character glances nervously over their shoulder and whispers, 'Something's behind us.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Construction on the new bridge has fallen behind schedule due to weather delays.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Sorry I'm behind on replying to your messages this week.'
mcq_options: A) In front of something  B) At the back of something  C) Above something  D) Beside something
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The remote control fell ______ the sofa. → behind
find_and_fix_to_correct: We are falling behind of our competitors. → We are falling behind our competitors.
translate: चाबियाँ सोफे के पीछे हैं। → The keys are behind the couch.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something behind your house.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'at or toward the back of something, or not as advanced as expected'?
usage_tip: 'Behind schedule' = late.

simple_explanation: At a lower position than something else. "Below" shows that something is positioned lower than another thing, often without touching it, like a lamp below a shelf.
example_1: The basement is below the kitchen.
example_2: Temperatures dropped below freezing last night.
example_3: Please sign your name below the line.
collocations: below average, below zero, below the surface, mentioned below
related_phrasal_verbs: below the belt (idiom: unfair or overly harsh, especially in an argument)
grammar_pattern: below + noun (below the line, below sea level)
common_mistake: Her grades are below from the class average.
correct_version: Her grades are below the class average.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Below' takes its object directly; 'from' is not needed.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: bee-LOH: /bɪˈloʊ/.
spelling_tip: Contains "low" -- think of something positioned low down.
etymology: From Middle English "bi-" (by) + "low" (low), literally meaning "by/at a low position"; the counterpart to "above."
prefix_root_suffix: be- (by/at) + low -- describing a position at a lower level
word_family: n/a -- "below" doesn't have common noun/verb/adjective forms
mnemonic: BE-LOW has "LOW" inside it -- picture something sitting down LOW, below everything else.
memory_trick: BELOW = lower than.
visual_association: A submarine gliding quietly below the surface of the ocean.
difference_explained: Below = lower than (a level). Under = directly beneath, often covered.
mini_conversation:
A: Where should I sign this form?
B: Just below the highlighted line.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A diver points downward and signals, 'There's something below us -- keep your light steady.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Forecasters expect temperatures to fall well below freezing this weekend.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Check the note below for more details on the schedule.'

find_and_fix_to_correct: The temperature fell bellow zero last night. → The temperature fell below zero last night.

write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something below zero.

usage_tip: 'Below average' = worse than average.

simple_explanation: Next to or at the side of someone or something. "Beside" tells you the exact position -- right next to a person or thing, usually very close.
example_1: She sat beside her best friend.
example_2: He parked the car beside the garage.
example_3: Come and sit beside me.
collocations: sit beside, stand beside, right beside, walk beside someone
where_it_s_used: Directions, seating arrangements, physical closeness, comfort/support
grammar_pattern: beside + noun/pronoun (beside the river / beside her)
common_mistake: He was so angry he was besides himself.
correct_version: He was so angry he was beside himself.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Beside himself' (very emotional) is a fixed idiom, with no -s.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: bih-SYD.
spelling_tip: One word -- "be" + "side," no extra "s" (that spelling is "besides").
etymology: Old English "be sidan" ("by the side") -- be + side.
prefix_root_suffix: be- (by) + side = positioned at the side
word_family: besides (different meaning: "in addition to") -- no verb/noun forms
mnemonic: BE-SIDE = be at the SIDE of something -- right next to it.
memory_trick: BESIDE = by the SIDE.
visual_association: Two chairs pushed close together, side by side.
emotion_feel: Neutral, often comforting or supportive in context
difference_explained: Beside = next to. Besides = in addition to, also.
mini_conversation:
A: Is this seat taken?
B: No, go ahead and sit beside me.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A friend places a hand on someone's shoulder and says, "I'll be right beside you, no matter what."
news_style_line: News-style: "A new bike lane was built beside the main road to improve safety."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Can you stand beside me for this photo?"
mcq_options: A) Far from  B) Next to  C) Above  D) Instead of

usage_tip: 'Beside the point' = not relevant.

simple_explanation: In addition to; apart from. You use "besides" to add another point or reason on top of what you already said.
example_1: Besides being smart, she's also very kind.
example_2: Besides English, he speaks French and German.
example_3: I don't want to go out; besides, it's raining.
collocations: besides that, besides which, besides being
related_phrasal_verbs: in addition to, apart from, on top of that
where_it_s_used: Giving extra reasons, adding information, casual arguments
grammar_pattern: besides + noun/gerund/clause (Besides studying, he works part-time.)
common_mistake: Besides he is tired, he still finished the race.
correct_version: Although he is tired, he still finished the race.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Besides' adds information; it doesn't show contrast. Use 'although' for contrast.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: bih-SYDZ, with a clear "z" sound at the end.
spelling_tip: Don't drop the final "-s" -- without it, the word becomes "beside" (a different meaning).
etymology: From "beside" plus an adverbial "-s" ending -- originally a variant of "beside" that split off to mean "in addition to."
word_family: beside (different meaning: next to) -- no verb/noun forms
mnemonic: BESIDES has an extra "S" -- think of it as adding one EXTRA thing on top.
memory_trick: BESIDES = plus, also.
visual_association: A shopping cart with one extra item added on top of the pile.
emotion_feel: Neutral, sometimes used to justify a decision casually
synonyms: also, apart from, in addition to
difference_explained: Besides = in addition to. Beside = next to.
tone: Neutral, common in speech and writing
mini_conversation:
A: Why don't you want the extra job?
B: I'm too busy already; besides, it doesn't pay well.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character shrugs and says, "Besides, we've come too far to turn back now."
news_style_line: News-style: "Besides the new policy, officials announced additional funding for schools."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I don't feel like cooking tonight -- besides, we still have leftovers."

translate: पढ़ाई के अलावा, वह खेलकूद में भी अच्छा है। → Besides studying, he is also good at sports.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence starting 'Besides English, I speak…'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'in addition to; apart from'?
usage_tip: 'Besides, …' at the start = another reason is…

simple_explanation: In the space or time separating two things. "Between" shows something is positioned in the middle of two points, people, or events.
example_1: The cat is sitting between the two chairs.
example_2: There's a small gap between the door and the wall.
example_3: The meeting is scheduled between 2 and 3 PM.
collocations: between you and me, between meals, choose between, difference between
grammar_pattern: between + noun/pronoun (between the trees / between us)
common_mistake: The ball fell between the three players.
correct_version: The ball fell among the three players.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'among' for three or more; 'between' is for two.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: be-TWEEN.
spelling_tip: Contains "tween" -- helps remember there are TWO things involved.
etymology: From Old English "betweonum," related to "twain" (two) -- originally meaning "by twos."
prefix_root_suffix: be- (by/near) + tween (two) = positioned by two points
mnemonic: BETWEEN has TWEEN in it, and TWEEN sounds like TWO -- between is for two things.
memory_trick: BETWEEN = two (Be-TWO-een).
visual_association: An arrow pointing to the exact midpoint of two objects.
emotion_feel: Neutral -- a spatial/relational word, not emotional on its own
difference_explained: Between = two. Among = three or more.
mini_conversation:
A: Where should I put this shelf?
B: Right between the window and the door.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A narrator says, "Somewhere between hope and fear, she made her choice."
news_style_line: News-style: "Talks between the two companies resumed on Monday."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Can you sit between us so we can all talk?"
mcq_options: A) Three or more things  B) Exactly two things  C) An unknown number  D) Only time, never place
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The store is located ______ the bank and the pharmacy. → between
find_and_fix_to_correct: Divide the candy among the two kids. → Divide the candy between the two kids.

write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence using 'between … and …'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'in the space or time separating two things'?
usage_tip: 'Between you and me' = this is a secret.

simple_explanation: On the far side of, or further than, a point or limit. "Beyond" shows that something is past a certain place, time, or limit -- further than expected or possible.
example_1: The village lies beyond the mountains.
example_2: His talent is beyond doubt.
example_3: The project went beyond our budget.
collocations: beyond doubt, beyond belief, beyond repair, go beyond expectations
related_phrasal_verbs: further than, past the point of
where_it_s_used: Limits, distances, abstract limits (understanding, doubt, repair), future time
grammar_pattern: beyond + noun (beyond the river / beyond expectations)
common_mistake: This problem is beyond of my understanding.
correct_version: This problem is beyond my understanding.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Beyond' takes its object directly; 'of' is not needed.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: bee-YOND.
spelling_tip: Remember "yond" (like "yonder," an old word for "over there") inside "beyond."
etymology: Old English "begeondan" (be- + geondan "further off, yonder") -- beyond a certain point.
prefix_root_suffix: be- (intensifying) + yond (from Old English "further off") = further off than
word_family: no related verb/noun/adjective forms -- used only as a preposition/adverb
mnemonic: BE-YOND = be far, YONDER -- past the point you can easily see.
memory_trick: BEYOND = farther than.
visual_association: A hiker standing at the edge of a cliff, looking toward distant mountains.
emotion_feel: Neutral, sometimes awe or hopelessness depending on context
difference_explained: Beyond = further than a limit. Above = higher than.
mini_conversation:
A: Do you think he can fix the old radio?
B: No, it's beyond repair -- we need a new one.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A captain looks at the horizon and says, "What lies beyond that ridge, no one has ever seen."
news_style_line: News-style: "The damage from the storm was beyond what officials had initially expected."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Honestly, fixing this laptop is beyond my skills -- let's call a technician."
mcq_options: A) Before  B) Further than a point or limit  C) Next to  D) During
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The old bridge is ______ repair; we need to build a new one. → beyond
find_and_fix_to_correct: Her kindness is beyond from words. → Her kindness is beyond words. (remove "from" -- beyond directly precedes the noun)
translate: यह समस्या मेरी समझ से परे है। → This problem is beyond my understanding.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something beyond your control.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'on the far side of, or further than, a point or limit'?
usage_tip: 'Beyond my control' = I can't change it.

simple_explanation: Near something, or showing who/what did an action, or a method or deadline. "By" is a small but flexible word -- it can mean "next to" (stand by the window), show who did something (written by her), describe a method (by bus), or mark a deadline (by Friday).
example_2: The lamp is standing by the window.
example_3: This novel was written by a famous author.
collocations: by chance, by mistake, by hand, by the way, by far
related_phrasal_verbs: by and large, stand by, drop by
where_it_s_used: Deadlines, passive voice, transport, location, methods
grammar_pattern: by + noun (by the agent, by the deadline, by the method -- e.g., "made by hand")
common_mistake: I will finish the report until Monday.
correct_version: I will finish the report by Monday.
why_it_s_wrong: 'By' = a deadline. 'Until' = something continues up to a time.
pronunciation_tip: A short, simple diphthong: rhymes with "my" and "sky" -- /baɪ/.
spelling_tip: Just two letters -- don't confuse with "buy" (to purchase) or "bye" (goodbye), which sound identical.
etymology: Old English "bi/be" meaning "near, in the vicinity of" -- one of the oldest prepositions in English.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- one of English's oldest, most basic prepositions
word_family: bye (unrelated homophone), buy (unrelated homophone) -- no related forms
mnemonic: BY the door = right near it; a small word for a word that stands close by everything.
memory_trick: BY Monday = on or before Monday.
visual_association: A calendar with a circle drawn around a due date.
emotion_feel: Neutral, sometimes urgency when tied to a deadline
difference_explained: By = deadline (finish by 5). Until = continuing up to (work until 5).
mini_conversation:
A: How did you get here so fast?
B: I came by taxi instead of walking.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A detective mutters, "This letter was written by someone who knew the victim well."
news_style_line: News-style: "The bridge is expected to reopen by the end of next month."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Can you send me the file by tonight?"
mcq_question: "By" in "This song was written by her" shows:
mcq_options: A) Location  B) The person who did the action  C) A deadline  D) A method of transport
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Please submit your application ______ Friday afternoon. → by
find_and_fix_to_correct: This cake was made from my grandmother. → This cake was made by my grandmother. (use "by" to show who performed the action)
translate: कृपया यह काम शुक्रवार तक पूरा कर लें। → Please finish this work by Friday.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something you must finish by Friday.
