reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'belonging to, made from, or a part of something'?
usage_tip: 'Made of' (material stays: wood table). 'Made from' (material changes: paper from wood).

simple_explanation: Away from a place, surface, or state of being on. "Off" shows that something has separated from a surface, stopped working, or moved away -- like taking a lid off a jar or turning off a light.
example_2: The picture fell off the wall.
example_3: Turn off the lights before you leave.
collocations: turn off, take off, get off, day off, off the record
related_phrasal_verbs: take off, turn off, get off, go off
where_it_s_used: Electronics, transport, clothing, schedules (a day off)
grammar_pattern: verb + off + noun (get off the train / take off your jacket)
common_mistake: Please close off the television.
correct_version: Please turn off the television.
why_it_s_wrong: For electronics, the phrase is 'turn off' or 'switch off', not 'close'.
pronunciation_tip: A short vowel with a firm "f" sound: /ɒf/ -- different from "of," which uses a "v" sound.
spelling_tip: Double "f" at the end -- don't write it with just one "f" (that would look like "of").
etymology: Old English "of," originally the same word as "of" -- split apart over time into two words with different stress and meaning (off = away/separated).
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- originally the same word as "of," now a separate function word
word_family: off-day (n.) -- "off" itself has no direct verb/noun forms beyond phrasal uses
mnemonic: OFF has a double F, like something falling FAR OFF, away and separated.
memory_trick: OFF = not ON.
visual_association: A light switch flipped down to the "off" position.
difference_explained: Off = away, not on (turn off). Of = belonging (a cup of tea). Different sound: off (short, F) / of (V sound).
mini_conversation:
A: Is the AC still running?
B: No, I turned it off an hour ago.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A pilot announces calmly, "We're cleared for takeoff -- please turn off all electronic devices."
news_style_line: News-style: "The factory was cut off from the power grid during the storm."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Can you turn the music off for a second?"
mcq_options: A) Connected to  B) Away from or separated from  C) Inside of  D) Toward
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Don't forget to switch ______ the stove before leaving. → off
find_and_fix_to_correct: She got off from the taxi near the mall. → She got off the taxi near the mall. (no "from" needed after "off" in this phrase)
translate: कृपया जाने से पहले पंखा बंद कर दें। → Please turn off the fan before you leave.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence asking someone to turn off a device.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'away from a place, surface, or state of being on'?
usage_tip: Indian English 'close the fan/TV' — standard: 'turn off / switch off'.

simple_explanation: Touching or resting on top of a surface, or on a specific day/date. "On" shows contact -- something resting on a surface -- or marks a specific day, date, or fixed occasion.
example_1: The book is on the table.
example_2: We're meeting on Friday.
example_3: There's a poster on the wall.
collocations: on time, on the phone, on purpose, on sale, depend on
related_phrasal_verbs: rely on, depend on, count on, go on
grammar_pattern: on + noun (on the table / on Monday)
common_mistake: The meeting is in Monday morning.
correct_version: The meeting is on Monday morning.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'on' for specific days, not 'in'.
pronunciation_tip: A short, open vowel: /ɒn/ -- keep it brief.
spelling_tip: Just two letters -- don't confuse with "own," a completely different word.
etymology: Old English "on," an ancient Germanic preposition showing contact with a surface or a point in time.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- an ancient basic preposition
mnemonic: ON = sitting ON top of a surface -- picture a cup ON a table.
memory_trick: ON + day. Think 'ON Monday' like a calendar page.
visual_association: A cup sitting on top of a saucer.
difference_explained: On + day/date. In + month/year/season.
mini_conversation:
A: What day is the party?
B: It's on Saturday evening.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A voice on the radio announces, "Stay tuned, more news right after this, only on this station."
news_style_line: News-style: "The new policy will take effect on the first of next month."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I left my keys on the kitchen counter again."
mcq_options: A) Months and years  B) Specific days and dates  C) Enclosed spaces only  D) Exact clock times only
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Her birthday party is ______ Saturday this year. → on
find_and_fix_to_correct: I will call you in Monday morning. → I will call you on Monday morning. (use "on" with specific days)
translate: किताब मेज़ पर रखी है। → The book is on the table.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about what you do on Sundays.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'touching or resting on top of a surface, or on a specific day/date'?
usage_tip: 'On time' = at the planned time.

simple_explanation: Moving to a position on top of a surface. "Onto" shows movement toward and onto a surface, unlike "on," which just shows the resting position.
example_1: The cat jumped onto the table.
example_2: He climbed onto the roof.
example_3: She stepped onto the stage nervously.
collocations: jump onto, climb onto, step onto, hold onto
grammar_pattern: verb of movement + onto + noun (jump onto the bed / climb onto the wall)
common_mistake: The ball rolled on the road from the sidewalk.
correct_version: The ball rolled onto the road from the sidewalk.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Onto' shows movement toward a surface.
pronunciation_tip: Two syllables: ON-too, with slightly heavier stress on the first.
spelling_tip: One word for the directional meaning ("jump onto the bed"); "on to" as two words appears in other structures ("hold on to your bag").
etymology: A combination of "on" + "to," first used together as one word to specifically show movement toward a surface.
prefix_root_suffix: on + to = movement toward a surface
word_family: on (related, position) -- "onto" has no direct verb/noun forms
mnemonic: ON-TO = moving ON, TO a surface -- like a cat jumping ON TO a shelf.
memory_trick: ONTO = ON + TO: movement onto a surface.
visual_association: A ball bouncing up and landing squarely onto a table.
emotion_feel: Neutral, sometimes tense in accident or action contexts
difference_explained: Onto = movement (jumped onto the bed). On = position (is on the bed).
mini_conversation:
A: How did the cat get onto the roof?
B: It must have climbed up the tree first.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A stuntman climbs onto the moving truck as the crowd gasps below.
news_style_line: News-style: "A tree fell onto the road during last night's storm, blocking traffic."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Careful, don't spill that onto the carpet!"
mcq_options: A) A fixed position on a surface  B) Movement to a position on a surface  C) A time period  D) A method
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The frog jumped ______ the lily pad. → onto
find_and_fix_to_correct: He climbed on the roof to fix the antenna. → He climbed onto the roof to fix the antenna. (use "onto" for the movement of climbing up onto a surface)
translate: बिल्ली मेज़ पर कूद गई। → The cat jumped onto the table.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something that jumped onto a table.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'moving to a position on top of a surface'?
usage_tip: 'Onto' can be one word (movement) or two: 'Hold on to this' (keep holding).

simple_explanation: Away from the inside of a place; not in. "Out" describes movement or position away from an enclosed space, or something no longer working or available.
example_2: He took the trash out.
example_3: She's out of town this week.
collocations: go out, find out, run out, out of order, hang out
related_phrasal_verbs: go out, find out, run out of, hang out
grammar_pattern: verb + out (of) + noun (go out of the room / find out the truth)
common_mistake: She went out from the room quickly.
correct_version: She went out of the room quickly.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'out of' before a noun, not 'out from'.
pronunciation_tip: A clear diphthong: /aʊt/ -- rhymes with "shout" and "about."
spelling_tip: Just three letters -- watch the vowel sound, it's not "oat" (a completely different word).
etymology: Old English "ut," a very old Germanic word meaning "away from the inside" -- the opposite of "in."
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- an ancient, basic directional word
mnemonic: OUT rhymes with SHOUT -- imagine shouting as you run OUT the door.
memory_trick: OUT OF: moving from inside to outside.
visual_association: An open door with someone stepping through it, leaving a room.
emotion_feel: Neutral, sometimes urgency (get out!) or relief (finding out the truth)
difference_explained: Out of = movement from inside (walk out of the room). Outside = position (wait outside the room).
mini_conversation:
A: Where's Sam?
B: He stepped out for a few minutes.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character bursts through the door yelling, "Everyone out, now! There's no time to waste!"
news_style_line: News-style: "Officials warned that supplies were running out faster than expected."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Do you want to hang out this weekend?"
mcq_options: A) Inside a place  B) Away from the inside  C) On top of  D) Beside something
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: We ran ______ of milk this morning. → out
find_and_fix_to_correct: Please get out from the pool now. → Please get out of the pool now. (use "out of," not "out from")
translate: कृपया कमरे से बाहर जाओ। → Please go out of the room.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about getting out of a bus or car.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'away from the inside of a place; not in'?
usage_tip: 'Out of order' = not working. 'Out of stock' = none left.

simple_explanation: Not inside a building or enclosed space; in the open air. "Outside" refers to the area beyond the walls of a building or enclosure -- literally not inside.
example_2: Wait for me outside the office.
example_3: It's freezing outside today.
collocations: outside the box, outside temperature, wait outside, go outside
related_phrasal_verbs: out of doors, out in the open
grammar_pattern: outside + noun (outside the house / outside the meeting room)
common_mistake: The children are playing outside of the garden.
correct_version: The children are playing outside the garden.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Outside' is enough; 'of' is usually dropped in standard English.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: owt-SYD.
spelling_tip: One word -- "out" + "side," no hyphen or space.
etymology: From "out" + "side," combined in Middle English to describe the outer part or area beyond an enclosed space.
mnemonic: OUT-SIDE = the SIDE that is OUT -- the exterior of a place.
memory_trick: OUTSIDE = OUT + SIDE.
visual_association: A person standing just beyond a closed front door.
emotion_feel: Neutral, sometimes refreshing or uncomfortable depending on weather
difference_explained: Outside + noun (outside the house). Out alone or 'out of' (go out, out of the house).
mini_conversation:
A: Is it raining outside?
B: Not yet, but the sky looks dark.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character peers through the curtains and whispers, "There's someone standing outside the gate."
news_style_line: News-style: "Protesters gathered outside the government building this morning."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Let's eat outside, the weather's really nice today."
mcq_options: A) Inside a building  B) Beyond or not inside a building  C) Underneath something  D) Between two places
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Please leave your muddy boots ______ the door. → outside
find_and_fix_to_correct: We had lunch outside of the restaurant patio. → We had lunch outside on the restaurant patio. (rephrase -- "outside of" the patio would mean not on it at all)
translate: बच्चे घर के बाहर खेल रहे हैं। → The children are playing outside the house.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about what is outside your window.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'not inside a building or enclosed space; in the open air'?
usage_tip: 'Outside of work' (US, informal) = apart from work.

simple_explanation: Above something, across something, more than an amount, or finished. "Over" is flexible -- it can show position above something, movement across it, a quantity greater than a number, or that something has ended.
example_1: The plane flew over the mountains.
example_2: The game is over now.
example_3: There were over fifty guests at the party.
collocations: over time, all over, get over, take over, game over
related_phrasal_verbs: get over, take over, look over, hand over
grammar_pattern: over + noun (over the bridge / over 100 people)
common_mistake: There were more than over ten people at the meeting.
correct_version: There were over ten people at the meeting.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Over' already means 'more than', so 'more than over' repeats it.
pronunciation_tip: Two syllables, stress on the first: OH-ver.
spelling_tip: Don't confuse with "ever" -- same ending, completely different meaning and beginning sound.
etymology: Old English "ofer," a Germanic word meaning "above, across" -- related to "up" and "above."
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown as a standalone word, though it forms many prefixed words (overcook, overreact)
mnemonic: OVER = arching OVER the top, like a rainbow going OVER a hill.
memory_trick: OVER = above, or more than.
visual_association: A bridge arching over a wide river.
emotion_feel: Neutral, sometimes relief when something difficult is "over"
difference_explained: Over = higher, covering, or across. Above = higher than, not touching.
mini_conversation:
A: Is the exam over yet?
B: Yes, thank goodness -- it finished an hour ago.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A commander shouts across the radio, "It's not over until I say it's over!"
news_style_line: News-style: "Officials confirmed over a hundred flights were delayed due to the storm."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Can you throw the blanket over the couch for me?"
mcq_options: A) Exactly fifty  B) More than fifty  C) Less than fifty  D) Around fifty, unclear
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The bird flew ______ the tall trees. → over
find_and_fix_to_correct: The movie is finish now. → The movie is over now. (use "over" to describe something that has ended)
translate: पचास से अधिक लोग पार्टी में आए। → Over fifty people came to the party.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence using 'over' to mean 'more than'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'above something, across something, more than an amount, or finished'?
usage_tip: 'Over the phone' = by phone. 'It's over' = finished.

simple_explanation: Beyond a point in space, or after a certain clock time. "Past" describes going beyond a place (walk past the shop) or shows time just after the hour (twenty past four).
example_1: We drove past the old church.
example_2: It's ten past nine already.
example_3: She walked past me without saying hello.
collocations: half past, ten past, drive past, walk past
grammar_pattern: past + noun (past the school / half past six)
common_mistake: It's six and half.
correct_version: It's half past six.
why_it_s_wrong: To tell time, use 'half past' + hour: 'half past six'.
pronunciation_tip: A short vowel: /pæst/ or /pɑːst/ depending on accent -- rhymes with "fast" and "last."
spelling_tip: Don't confuse with "passed" (the verb "pass" in past tense) -- they sound identical but are spelled differently.
etymology: Originally the past participle of "pass" (Middle English "passed"), it came to be used as a preposition/noun meaning "beyond" or "the time before now."
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- originally the past participle of "pass"
word_family: pass (v.), passed (past tense of "pass, " a homophone of "past")
mnemonic: PAST = you've already PASSED that point -- it's behind you now.
memory_trick: PAST = after the hour.
visual_association: A clock hand ticking just beyond the twelve.
emotion_feel: Neutral, sometimes nostalgic when referring to earlier times
difference_explained: Past = preposition/time (half past six). Passed = verb (I passed the exam).
mini_conversation:
A: What time is it?
B: It's just past noon.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A narrator says, "Long past midnight, the old house was still wide awake with secrets."
news_style_line: News-style: "The marathon route goes past several historic landmarks downtown."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Just walk past the bakery and turn left at the corner."
mcq_question: "Past" in "It's half past three" refers to:
mcq_options: A) A location  B) A point in clock time  C) A method  D) A quantity
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The library is just ______ the post office. → past
find_and_fix_to_correct: She past the store without stopping. → She passed the store without stopping. (need the verb "passed," not the preposition "past")
translate: वह बिना रुके दुकान के पास से गुज़र गई। → She walked past the shop without stopping.
write_your_own_sentence: Write the time 7:30 and 8:15 in words.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'beyond a point in space, or after a certain clock time'?
usage_tip: Indian English 'six and a half' is understood, but 'half past six' is standard.

simple_explanation: From one side of something to the other; by means of. "Through" describes movement that enters one side of something and exits the other, or a means by which something happens.
example_2: Light came through the window.
example_3: She got the job through a friend.
collocations: go through, look through, through and through, halfway through
related_phrasal_verbs: go through, get through, come through, see through
where_it_s_used: Physical movement, communication methods, difficult experiences, processes
grammar_pattern: through + noun (through the door / through hard work)
common_mistake: The dog ran across the tunnel and out the other side.
correct_version: The dog ran through the tunnel and out the other side.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'through' for going in one side and out the other.
pronunciation_tip: A tricky spelling but simple sound: /θruː/, rhymes with "true" and "blue."
spelling_tip: Notice the silent letters -- "th-r-ou-gh" -- often confused with "though," "thorough," and "throw."
etymology: Old English "þurh," a Germanic word meaning "from one side to the other" -- related to "thorough."
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- an old Germanic word for "from side to side"
mnemonic: THROUGH = going all the way THROUGH a tunnel, in one side and out the other.
memory_trick: THROUGH = in one side, out the other, like a tunnel.
visual_association: A beam of light passing through a narrow window.
emotion_feel: Neutral, sometimes triumphant when describing overcoming difficulty
difference_explained: Through = inside something (through a tunnel). Across = over a surface (across a road).
mini_conversation:
A: How did you hear about the job?
B: I found out through a former colleague.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A survivor says quietly, "We made it through the storm, together, somehow."
news_style_line: News-style: "Sunlight finally broke through the clouds after days of heavy rain."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Can you walk me through how this app works?"
mcq_options: A) Around the outside of something  B) From one side of something to the other  C) On top of something  D) Before something starts
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: We drove ______ the tunnel to reach the coast. → through
find_and_fix_to_correct: She walked across the door into the room. → She walked through the door into the room. (use "through" for passing from one side of an opening to the other)
translate: हम पार्क के बीच से होकर गुज़रे। → We walked through the park.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about walking through a market.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'from one side of something to the other; by means of'?
usage_tip: 'Through' is often misspelt: 'thru' is only informal American.

simple_explanation: During the whole of a period, or in every part of a place. "Throughout" emphasizes that something happens the entire time or exists in every part of a place -- not just at one moment or spot.
example_2: The theme is repeated throughout the novel.
example_3: Schools throughout the country closed early.
collocations: throughout the year, throughout history, throughout the world
related_phrasal_verbs: all through, from start to finish
where_it_s_used: Formal writing, history, weather, describing patterns
grammar_pattern: throughout + noun (throughout the day / throughout the building)
common_mistake: It rained throughout the whole day.
correct_version: It rained throughout the day.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Throughout' already means 'the whole', so 'the whole' repeats it.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: throo-OWT.
spelling_tip: Combines "through" and "out" -- remember both parts to spell it correctly.
etymology: From "through" + "out," combined in Middle English to intensify the meaning "all the way through, from start to finish."
prefix_root_suffix: through- (entire duration) + out (completeness) = all the way through
mnemonic: THROUGH-OUT = THROUGH the whole thing, from start to end, leaving nothing OUT.
memory_trick: THROUGH + OUT = from start to end.
visual_association: A single thread running unbroken through an entire piece of fabric.
difference_explained: Through = from one side to the other. Throughout = in every part, or for the whole time.
mini_conversation:
A: Did the noise stop at some point?
B: No, it continued throughout the whole concert.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A narrator intones, "Throughout the ages, this story has been told again and again."
news_style_line: News-style: "Heavy snow is expected throughout the region this weekend."
casual_conversation: Casual: "The kids were surprisingly quiet throughout the whole car ride."
mcq_options: A) At one specific moment  B) During the entire period or in every part  C) Before something begins  D) Only at the end
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The museum played soft music ______ the exhibition. → throughout
find_and_fix_to_correct: She smiled throughout of the entire ceremony. → She smiled throughout the entire ceremony. (remove "of" -- "throughout" doesn't need it)
translate: पूरे साल भारत में त्योहार मनाए जाते हैं। → Festivals are celebrated throughout India all year.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something that happens throughout the year.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'during the whole of a period, or in every part of a place'?
usage_tip: 'Throughout the year' = all year.

simple_explanation: Showing direction, destination, or the receiver of an action. "To" points toward a destination, a person receiving something, or introduces the base form of a verb (to run, to sleep).
example_2: She gave the book to her brother.
example_3: We drove to the coast for the weekend.
collocations: go to, listen to, talk to, according to, up to
related_phrasal_verbs: look forward to, get used to, up to
grammar_pattern: to + noun/verb (to school / to run)
common_mistake: She went to home after work.
correct_version: She went home after work.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Home' doesn't take 'to' when it means your own home.
pronunciation_tip: Often reduced to a quick "tuh" in fast speech, but pronounced clearly as /tuː/ when stressed.
spelling_tip: Don't confuse with "too" (also/excessively) or "two" (the number) -- all three sound identical.
etymology: Old English "to," one of the oldest and most frequent prepositions in English, showing direction or destination.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- one of English's oldest, most basic prepositions
word_family: too (unrelated homophone), two (unrelated homophone) -- "to" itself has no direct verb/noun forms
mnemonic: TO points forward -- like an arrow TO a destination.
memory_trick: GO HOME, COME HOME — no 'to'.
visual_association: A signpost with an arrow pointing toward a distant destination.
emotion_feel: Neutral -- a directional, purely functional word
confusing_word: go home vs go to home
difference_explained: Go home (correct). 'Go to home' is wrong. But 'go to my friend's home' is fine.
mini_conversation:
A: Where are you headed?
B: I'm heading to the gym before work.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character studies a map and declares, "There's only one road left, and it leads straight to the border."
news_style_line: News-style: "Officials announced a new bridge connecting the two towns will open to traffic next spring."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Can you pass this note to your sister?"
mcq_question: "To" in "She gave the pen to him" shows:
mcq_options: A) The giver  B) The receiver of an action  C) A method  D) A location only
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: We're driving ______ the airport early tomorrow morning. → to
find_and_fix_to_correct: I want going to the beach this weekend. → I want to go to the beach this weekend. (use "want to" + base verb, not "want going")
translate: मैं आज बाज़ार जा रहा हूँ। → I am going to the market today.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about when you go home.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'showing direction, destination, or the receiver of an action'?
usage_tip: Also: 'go abroad', 'go upstairs', 'go there' — no 'to'.

simple_explanation: In the direction of someone or something. "Towards" shows the direction something is heading or facing -- identical in meaning to "toward," just a different regional spelling.
example_2: The bus is heading towards the city center.
example_3: He showed great kindness towards strangers.
collocations: move towards, attitude towards, contribute towards, walk towards
where_it_s_used: British English writing/speech, direction, attitudes, progress, contributions
grammar_pattern: towards + noun (towards the beach / towards success)
common_mistake: He donated money towards to the charity.
correct_version: He donated money towards the charity.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Towards' takes its object directly; an extra 'to' is not needed.
pronunciation_tip: Two syllables, stress on the second: tuh-WORDZ.
spelling_tip: Add an "-s" to "toward" to get the British spelling "towards."
etymology: Same root as "toward" (Old English "toweard") with an added adverbial "-s" -- the standard British English spelling.
word_family: toward (American spelling variant) -- no direct verb/noun forms
mnemonic: TOWARDS has an extra "S," just like British spelling often adds extra letters (colour vs. color).
memory_trick: TOWARDS = in the direction of, or for.
visual_association: A flock of birds all flying towards the same distant point.
emotion_feel: Neutral, often warm when describing kindness or generosity towards someone
difference_explained: To = the destination (go to Delhi). Towards = in the direction of (walk towards Delhi).
mini_conversation:
A: Are we close to the station?
B: Yes, just keep walking towards that clock tower.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character points at the skyline and says, "Everything we've worked for is right there, towards the light."
news_style_line: News-style: "The charity raised thousands of pounds towards rebuilding the flood-damaged school."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Could you scoot a little towards the window, please?"
mcq_options: A) Away from  B) In the direction of  C) Underneath  D) Except for
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Every small donation helps ______ a good cause. → towards
find_and_fix_to_correct: They walked toward's the exit in a hurry. → They walked towards the exit in a hurry. (no apostrophe in "towards" -- it isn't possessive)
translate: वह अजनबियों के प्रति बहुत दयालु है। → He is very kind towards strangers.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about money you save towards something.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'in the direction of someone or something'?
usage_tip: 'Save towards a car' = save money for a car.

simple_explanation: In a lower position than something else, or less than a number. "Under" shows something is physically below another thing, describes an amount less than a stated number, or a condition someone is experiencing (under pressure).
example_1: The ball rolled under the sofa.
example_2: Children under twelve need a ticket.
example_3: She works well under pressure.
collocations: under pressure, under control, under construction, under twenty
related_phrasal_verbs: under way, under control, come under fire
grammar_pattern: under + noun (under the table / under review)
common_mistake: This bridge is under of construction.
correct_version: This bridge is under construction.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Under' takes its object directly; 'of' is not needed.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the first syllable: UHN-der.
spelling_tip: Don't confuse with "underneath," a longer, more emphatic synonym.
etymology: Old English "under," an ancient Germanic word meaning "beneath, below" -- one of English's core spatial prepositions.
prefix_root_suffix: under- (below) -- itself a base preposition, no further breakdown
mnemonic: UNDER = always at a lower position, below the surface.
memory_trick: UNDER = below, often covered.
visual_association: A small dog curled up under a large wooden table.
emotion_feel: Neutral, sometimes stressful (under pressure) or cautious (hiding under something)
difference_explained: Under = directly beneath, often covered. Below = at a lower level.
mini_conversation:
A: How's the new building coming along?
B: It's still under construction, but almost done.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character hides behind a car and whispers, "Get under cover, now!"
news_style_line: News-style: "The new policy is currently under review by a government committee."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I think my glasses fell under the couch."
mcq_options: A) Above something  B) In a lower position or less than an amount  C) Beside something  D) Through something
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Please keep this information ______ wraps for now. → under
find_and_fix_to_correct: He is under twenty years old age. → He is under twenty years old. (remove the extra word "age")
translate: बिल्ली बिस्तर के नीचे छिपी है। → The cat is hiding under the bed.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something under your bed.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'in a lower position than something else, or less than a number'?
usage_tip: 'Under construction', 'under pressure', 'under 18'.

simple_explanation: Toward a higher place or position. "Up" describes movement or position from a lower point to a higher one, or an increase -- like climbing up stairs or prices going up.
example_2: Prices have gone up this year.
example_3: He looked up at the stars.
collocations: stand up, wake up, up to date, look up
related_phrasal_verbs: wake up, give up, stand up, look up
grammar_pattern: up + noun/particle (up the stairs / stand up)
common_mistake: She climbed up of the tree quickly.
correct_version: She climbed up the tree quickly.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Up' takes its object directly; 'of' is not needed.
pronunciation_tip: A short, simple vowel: /ʌp/ -- rhymes with "cup."
spelling_tip: Just two letters -- very easy to spell, but combines with many verbs to form phrasal verbs (wake up, give up).
etymology: Old English "up/upp," an ancient Germanic word for "in a higher position or direction" -- the opposite of "down."
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- a simple, ancient directional word
mnemonic: UP points to the sky -- imagine an arrow shooting straight UP.
memory_trick: UP = to a higher place.
visual_association: A rocket launching straight up into the sky.
emotion_feel: Neutral, often energetic or hopeful when describing rising mood
difference_explained: Up = movement to a higher place. Above = position higher than.
mini_conversation:
A: What time did you wake up?
B: I got up really early today, around 6 AM.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A coach shouts encouragingly, "Get up! You're not done yet -- get back up!"
news_style_line: News-style: "Fuel prices went up sharply again this week, according to new figures."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Can you turn the volume up a little?"
mcq_options: A) Toward a lower place  B) Toward a higher place  C) Around something  D) Away from a place
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Please pick ______ your toys before dinner. → up
find_and_fix_to_correct: He picked up of the phone quickly. → He picked up the phone quickly. (remove "of" -- not needed in this phrasal verb)
translate: वह जल्दी से सीढ़ियाँ चढ़ गया। → He quickly went up the stairs.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about climbing up a hill.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'toward a higher place or position'?
usage_tip: 'Up to you' = your decision.

simple_explanation: On, but in a more formal or literary way. "Upon" is used the same way as "on," but it sounds more formal, and it's common in fixed expressions and storytelling.
example_1: Once upon a time, there lived a king.
example_2: The decision depends upon your answer.
example_3: He placed the crown upon her head.
collocations: once upon a time, depend upon, upon arrival, upon request
related_phrasal_verbs: depend upon, rely upon, call upon
where_it_s_used: Fairy tales, formal writing, legal/business language, set expressions
grammar_pattern: upon + noun/gerund (upon arrival / upon hearing the news)
common_mistake: The book is upon table.
correct_version: The book is on the table.
why_it_s_wrong: In everyday speech, 'on' is far more natural than 'upon', and 'the' is needed.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: uh-PON.
spelling_tip: One word -- "up" + "on" combined, no space or hyphen.
etymology: From "up" + "on," combined in Middle English as a more formal, literary synonym for "on."
prefix_root_suffix: up + on = combined into one formal preposition
word_family: on (everyday synonym) -- "upon" itself has no direct verb/noun forms
mnemonic: UP-ON = UP and ON top of something -- a fancier way to say "on."
memory_trick: UPON = ON, but old and formal.
visual_association: An old storybook opening to its very first line.
emotion_feel: Neutral, often formal or storytelling in tone
difference_explained: Same meaning. Upon is formal or literary.
mini_conversation:
A: When does the offer start?
B: It takes effect upon signing the contract.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A narrator begins solemnly, "Upon these very hills, a great battle once took place."
news_style_line: News-style: "The new law will take effect immediately upon approval by the senate."
casual_conversation: Casual: "You'll receive your ID card upon registration."
mcq_options: A) Under  B) On  C) Beyond  D) Without
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: ______ arrival, please check in at the front desk. → Upon
find_and_fix_to_correct: Upon the table there was of a lamp. → Upon the table there was a lamp. (remove "of" -- not needed here)
translate: एक बार की बात है, एक राजा रहता था। → Once upon a time, there lived a king.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence using 'once upon a time'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'on, but in a more formal or literary way'?
usage_tip: 'Once upon a time' starts fairy tales.

simple_explanation: Together with, or by using something. "With" shows that two things or people are together, or that a tool or method is being used to do something.
example_1: I went to the park with my friend.
example_2: She cut the paper with scissors.
example_3: He lives with his parents.
collocations: agree with, deal with, along with, together with
related_phrasal_verbs: deal with, agree with, come up with
grammar_pattern: with + noun (with a knife / with her sister)
common_mistake: I cut the bread with a knife's help.
correct_version: I cut the bread with a knife.
why_it_s_wrong: 'With' already shows the tool, so 'help' is extra.
pronunciation_tip: A soft "th" sound at the end: /wɪð/ -- don't replace it with a hard "t" or "d" sound.
spelling_tip: Just four letters -- ends in "th," a sound some learners drop by mistake.
etymology: Old English "wið," originally meaning "against," which gradually shifted to mean "accompanying" or "using."
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- one of English's most basic, frequent prepositions
word_family: within (related preposition), without (opposite) -- "with" itself has no direct verb/noun forms
mnemonic: WITH = things that go together WITH each other, side by side.
memory_trick: WITH = together, or using.
visual_association: Two puzzle pieces fitting together side by side.
emotion_feel: Neutral, often warm when showing companionship
difference_explained: With + a tool (with a knife). By + a method (by hand, by car).
mini_conversation:
A: How did you open the jar?
B: I opened it with a spoon, believe it or not.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character extends a hand and says, "Come with me if you want to see how this ends."
news_style_line: News-style: "The company signed a new agreement with an international partner this week."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Do you want to come with us to the movies tonight?"
mcq_question: "With" in "He wrote it with a pencil" shows:
mcq_options: A) Location  B) The tool used  C) A time period  D) A reason
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: She always drinks her coffee ______ a little sugar. → with
find_and_fix_to_correct: I agree to your opinion completely. → I agree with your opinion completely. (the fixed expression is "agree with," not "agree to")
translate: मैं अपने दोस्त के साथ पार्क गया। → I went to the park with my friend.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something you do with your hands.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'together with, or by using something'?
usage_tip: 'With' + tool: 'cut with a knife', 'write with a pen'.

simple_explanation: Inside the limits of a space, time, or amount. "Within" shows that something happens inside a certain boundary -- a place, a period of time, or an amount that isn't exceeded.
example_2: The office is within walking distance.
example_3: We must stay within our budget.
collocations: within reach, within limits, within a week, within reason
where_it_s_used: Deadlines, budgets, distances, formal writing, emotions/self
grammar_pattern: within + noun (within an hour / within the rules)
common_mistake: Please finish the task in within an hour.
correct_version: Please finish the task within an hour.
why_it_s_wrong: Don't combine 'in' and 'within'; choose one.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: wih-THIN.
spelling_tip: Combines "with" + "in" -- remember both parts to spell it correctly.
etymology: From "with" + "in," combined in Middle English to mean "inside the limits of" -- a more formal alternative to "in."
prefix_root_suffix: with- (together) + in (inside) = inside the boundary of
word_family: with (root word), in (root word) -- "within" itself has no direct verb/noun forms
mnemonic: WITH-IN = WITH something, IN its limits -- inside the boundary.
memory_trick: WITH + IN: inside a limit.
visual_association: A circle drawn around a smaller shape, showing it stays inside the boundary.
emotion_feel: Neutral, sometimes reflective when referring to inner feelings
difference_explained: In an hour = after an hour. Within an hour = before an hour is over.
mini_conversation:
A: How soon can you finish this?
B: I can have it done within two days.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A mentor tells the hero, "The strength you need has always been within you."
news_style_line: News-style: "Officials say the repairs should be completed within the next two weeks."
casual_conversation: Casual: "The pharmacy is within walking distance of my apartment."
mcq_options: A) Beyond a limit  B) Inside a limit or boundary  C) Next to something  D) Because of something
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Please submit the form ______ five business days. → within
find_and_fix_to_correct: The mall is within of ten minutes from here. → The mall is within ten minutes from here. (remove "of" -- "within" doesn't need it)
translate: कृपया चौबीस घंटों के भीतर जवाब दें। → Please reply within 24 hours.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something you must do within a week.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'inside the limits of a space, time, or amount'?
usage_tip: 'Within 24 hours' = before 24 hours pass.

simple_explanation: Not having, not using, or not accompanied by something. "Without" shows that something or someone is missing, absent, or not included.
example_2: She left without saying goodbye.
example_3: He passed the test without studying much.
collocations: without doubt, without fail, without a trace, go without
grammar_pattern: without + noun/gerund (without money / without asking)
common_mistake: She left without to say goodbye.
correct_version: She left without saying goodbye.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Without' is followed by -ing, not 'to + verb'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: wih-THOWT.
spelling_tip: Combines "with" + "out" -- remember both parts, unlike "with" alone.
etymology: From "with" + "out," combined in Old English to mean "on the outside of," later shifting to "not having" -- the opposite of "with."
word_family: with (opposite) -- "without" itself has no direct verb/noun forms
mnemonic: WITH-OUT = WITH something taken OUT -- missing, absent, not there.
memory_trick: WITH + OUT: not having.
visual_association: An empty chair at a table where someone used to sit.
emotion_feel: Neutral, sometimes lonely or resilient depending on context
difference_explained: Without + noun/-ing (without help). Unless + clause (unless you help).
mini_conversation:
A: How did you finish the puzzle so fast?
B: Honestly, without any help at all!
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character stands alone in the rain and says, "I never thought I'd make it this far without you."
news_style_line: News-style: "Thousands of homes remained without power for a second day after the storm."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I can't imagine getting through finals without coffee."
mcq_options: A) Together with  B) Not having or not using  C) Because of  D) In addition to
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: He left the house ______ locking the door. → without
find_and_fix_to_correct: I can't sleep without to listen to music. → I can't sleep without listening to music. (use "without" + verb-ing)
translate: मैं बिना कॉफी के नहीं रह सकता। → I can't live without coffee.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something you can't live without.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'not having, not using, or not accompanied by something'?
usage_tip: 'Without doubt' = certainly.

simple_explanation: As stated or reported by a particular source. "According to" is used to show where information comes from -- a person, a book, a report, or another source.
example_1: According to the weather report, it will rain tomorrow.
example_2: According to the manager, the store closes at 9.
example_3: According to this article, coffee has many health benefits.
collocations: according to plan, according to reports, according to the rules
related_phrasal_verbs: as stated by, based on, in line with
where_it_s_used: News, reports, citing sources, giving evidence
grammar_pattern: according to + noun (according to the doctor / according to the survey)
common_mistake: According with the report, sales increased.
correct_version: According to the report, sales increased.
why_it_s_wrong: The fixed phrase uses 'to', not 'with'.
pronunciation_tip: Four syllables in "according": uh-KOR-ding, then "to" said quickly after.
spelling_tip: Two words -- "according" + "to" -- never written as one word.
etymology: From "accord" (Old French "acorder," to agree) + "-ing" + "to" -- literally "in agreement with" a source.
prefix_root_suffix: ac- (toward, from Latin) + cord (root, "heart/agreement") + -ing + to = "in agreement with"
mnemonic: AC-CORD-ING TO = matching the reCORD, TO what the source says.
memory_trick: ACCORDING TO = as said by.
visual_association: A finger pointing at a printed report as the source of information.
confusing_word: according to vs in my opinion
difference_explained: According to = someone else's view (according to the report). For yourself, use 'in my opinion'.
related_words: based on, as reported, in accordance with, per
mini_conversation:
A: Is the flight still on time?
B: According to the app, yes, it's on schedule.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A detective reviews a file and says, "According to this report, the suspect was seen leaving at midnight."
news_style_line: News-style: "According to officials, the new bridge will open ahead of schedule."
casual_conversation: Casual: "According to my mom, dinner will be ready in ten minutes."
mcq_options: A) Give an opinion  B) Cite a source of information  C) Show a contrast  D) Give a reason
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: ______ the instructions, we need to press this button first. → According to
find_and_fix_to_correct: According the news, the roads are closed today. → According to the news, the roads are closed today. (add "to" -- the phrase is always "according to")
translate: मौसम विभाग के अनुसार, आज बारिश होगी। → According to the weather department, it will rain today.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence starting 'According to the news,…'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'as stated or reported by a particular source'?
usage_tip: Don't use 'according to me'; say 'in my opinion'.

simple_explanation: As a result of; for the reason of. "Because of" introduces the reason for something, but unlike "because," it must be followed by a noun or noun phrase, not a full sentence.
example_1: The game was cancelled because of rain.
example_2: We were late because of the traffic.
example_3: She missed school because of a fever.
collocations: because of you, because of this, because of the weather
related_phrasal_verbs: due to, owing to, on account of
where_it_s_used: Giving reasons, excuses, explanations, weather/traffic delays
grammar_pattern: because of + noun/gerund (because of the rain / because of being late)
common_mistake: We were late because of we missed the bus.
correct_version: We were late because we missed the bus.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Because of' + noun; 'because' + clause.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable of "because": bih-KUZ uv.
spelling_tip: Two words -- "because" + "of" -- don't merge them into one word.
etymology: From "because" (by + cause) + "of" -- combined to introduce a noun cause rather than a full clause.
word_family: because (related conjunction, + clause), cause (n./v., shared root)
mnemonic: BECAUSE OF = the CAUSE OF something -- directly points to the reason.
memory_trick: BECAUSE OF + thing. BECAUSE + sentence.
visual_association: A row of dominoes -- one falling because of the one before it.
emotion_feel: Neutral, sometimes apologetic or explanatory in tone
difference_explained: Because + subject + verb (because it rained). Because of + noun (because of the rain).
related_words: due to, owing to, as a result of, thanks to
mini_conversation:
A: Why was the meeting postponed?
B: Because of a scheduling conflict, apparently.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character shrugs and admits, "I only made it this far because of the people who believed in me."
news_style_line: News-style: "The event was postponed because of unexpected security concerns."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I couldn't sleep last night because of the noise outside."
mcq_options: A) A full clause with a subject and verb  B) A noun or noun phrase  C) An adjective only  D) Nothing at all
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The trip was cancelled ______ the storm warning. → because of
find_and_fix_to_correct: She was upset because of she failed the test. → She was upset because she failed the test. (use "because" + clause, not "because of" + clause)
translate: भारी बारिश के कारण मैच रद्द कर दिया गया। → The match was cancelled because of heavy rain.
write_your_own_sentence: Write one sentence with 'because' and one with 'because of'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'as a result of; for the reason of'?
usage_tip: 'Thanks to' = because of (for good results).

simple_explanation: Directly before or facing something. "In front of" describes a position facing something or someone, or standing before it -- the opposite of "behind."
example_1: The car is parked in front of the house.
example_2: She stood in front of the mirror.
example_3: There's a long line in front of the ticket counter.
collocations: stand in front of, park in front of, right in front of
grammar_pattern: in front of + noun (in front of the house / in front of everyone)
common_mistake: The dog is sitting in the front of the door.
correct_version: The dog is sitting in front of the door.
why_it_s_wrong: There's no 'the' between 'in' and 'front'.
pronunciation_tip: Four words spoken smoothly together: in-FRUNT-uv.
etymology: From "in" + "front" (Old French "front," from Latin "frons," forehead/face) + "of" -- literally "in the facing part of."
prefix_root_suffix: in (position) + front (root, from Latin "frons" = forehead/face) + of = facing position
word_family: front (n./adj.), frontal (adj.) -- "in front of" itself has no direct verb form
mnemonic: IN FRONT OF = standing IN the FRONT part, facing something directly.
memory_trick: IN FRONT OF: three words, no 'the'.
visual_association: A person standing directly facing a closed door.
emotion_feel: Neutral, sometimes nervous in public-speaking contexts
difference_explained: In front of = before, facing the same way. Opposite = facing, on the other side.
mini_conversation:
A: Where should we take the photo?
B: Let's stand in front of the fountain.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A performer takes a deep breath backstage and says, "I still get nervous in front of a crowd."
news_style_line: News-style: "Protesters gathered in front of the city hall to voice their concerns."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Can you wait for me in front of the cinema?"
mcq_options: A) Behind  B) Facing or before something  C) Underneath  D) Beside only
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: A big tree grows ______ our house. → in front of
find_and_fix_to_correct: He was standing in front the classroom. → He was standing in front of the classroom. (add "of" -- the full phrase is "in front of")
translate: गाड़ी घर के सामने खड़ी है। → The car is parked in front of the house.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about what is in front of your house.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'directly before or facing something'?
usage_tip: 'In the front of' = inside the front part: 'in the front of the car'.

simple_explanation: In place of; as a substitute for. "Instead of" shows that one thing replaces another -- you choose one option and skip the other.
example_1: I'll have tea instead of coffee.
example_2: She walked instead of taking the bus.
example_3: Let's meet on Friday instead of Thursday.
collocations: instead of that, instead of doing, go instead of
grammar_pattern: instead of + noun/gerund (instead of sugar / instead of waiting)
common_mistake: Instead of go by car, we walked.
correct_version: Instead of going by car, we walked.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Instead of' is followed by -ing, not the base verb.
spelling_tip: "Instead" is one word; "of" stays separate -- so "instead of," not "insteadof."
etymology: From "in" + "stead" (Old English "stede," place) + "of" -- literally "in the place of."
prefix_root_suffix: in (position) + stead (root, "place") + of = in the place of
word_family: stead (archaic root word, "place") -- "instead of" itself has no direct verb/noun forms
mnemonic: IN-STEAD-OF = taking the STEAD (place) OF something else -- a substitute.
memory_trick: INSTEAD OF = in the place of.
visual_association: A hand swapping one puzzle piece for another.
emotion_feel: Neutral, sometimes decisive when choosing between options
difference_explained: Similar. Instead of = replacing one thing. Rather than = preferring one thing.
related_words: rather than, in place of, alternatively, substitute
mini_conversation:
A: Do you want rice or noodles?
B: I'll have noodles instead of rice today.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character pauses and says, "Maybe it's time we tried kindness instead of anger."
news_style_line: News-style: "The city plans to build a park instead of a parking lot on that empty lot."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Can we order pizza instead of cooking tonight?"
mcq_options: A) Add extra information  B) Show a substitution or alternative  C) Give a reason  D) Show a time period
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Let's take the stairs ______ the elevator. → instead of
find_and_fix_to_correct: Instead to studying, he watched TV all night. → Instead of studying, he watched TV all night. (use "of," not "to," after "instead")
translate: आज मैं चाय की जगह कॉफी पिऊंगा। → Today I'll have coffee instead of tea.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something you did instead of watching TV.

usage_tip: 'Instead' alone ends a sentence: 'We walked instead.'

simple_explanation: Directly beside; in the closest position to. "Next to" shows the closest possible position beside a person or thing -- very similar to "beside," but slightly more common in everyday speech.
example_1: She sat next to the window.
example_2: The bakery is right next to the bank.
example_3: He placed his bag next to the door.
collocations: right next to, sit next to, live next to
grammar_pattern: next to + noun (next to the table / next to her)
common_mistake: My house is next of the park.
correct_version: My house is next to the park.
why_it_s_wrong: The fixed phrase uses 'to', not 'of'.
etymology: From "next" (Old English "niehsta," nearest) + "to" -- literally "nearest to" a place.
word_family: next (adj./adv., root word) -- "next to" itself has no direct verb/noun forms
mnemonic: NEXT TO = the spot right NEXT (nearest) TO something else.
memory_trick: NEXT TO = beside.
visual_association: Two houses built right beside each other on the same street.
emotion_feel: Neutral, often friendly when describing closeness to someone
difference_explained: Next to = right beside. Near = close, but maybe not touching.
mini_conversation:
A: Which seat is yours?
B: The one next to the aisle.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character slides into the booth and says, "Mind if I sit next to you?"
news_style_line: News-style: "A new coffee shop just opened next to the old cinema downtown."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Can you park next to my car?"
mcq_options: A) Far away from  B) Directly beside  C) Underneath  D) Instead of
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The pharmacy is ______ the grocery store. → next to
find_and_fix_to_correct: She lives next the hospital. → She lives next to the hospital. (add "to" -- the full phrase is "next to")
translate: मेरा स्कूल पार्क के बगल में है। → My school is next to the park.

reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'directly beside; in the closest position to'?
usage_tip: 'Next to nothing' = almost nothing.

simple_explanation: Moving from the inside to the outside, or not having something left. "Out of" describes leaving an enclosed space, running out of a supply, or the material something is made from.
example_1: He walked out of the office.
example_2: We're out of milk again.
example_3: She jumped out of the car.
collocations: out of stock, out of order, out of breath, made out of
related_phrasal_verbs: run out of, get out of, made out of
where_it_s_used: Movement, shortages, materials, exhaustion (out of breath)
grammar_pattern: out of + noun (out of the house / out of time)
common_mistake: She got out from the car quickly.
correct_version: She got out of the car quickly.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'out of', not 'out from'.
pronunciation_tip: Two words spoken quickly together: OWT-uv.
spelling_tip: Two separate words -- "out" + "of" -- never merged into one.
etymology: A combination of "out" + "of," used together since Middle English to show movement away from the inside of something, or a source/material.
prefix_root_suffix: out (exit, direction) + of (source/relation) = moving away from the inside
word_family: out (root word), outside (related) -- "out of" itself has no direct verb/noun forms
mnemonic: OUT OF = moving OUT, away OF the inside -- leaving a place completely.
memory_trick: OUT OF: always two words together.
visual_association: A genie escaping out of a bottle.
emotion_feel: Neutral, sometimes urgent (escaping) or frustrated (running out of something)
difference_explained: Out of = from inside (get out of the car). From = starting point (from Delhi).
mini_conversation:
A: Do we have any eggs left?
B: No, we're completely out of eggs.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character bursts out of a burning building, gasping for air.
news_style_line: News-style: "Officials say the region has run out of emergency supplies twice this month."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Can you grab my jacket out of the car?"
mcq_options: A) Into the inside of  B) From the inside to the outside, or lacking  C) Above something  D) Because of something
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: We ran ______ gas on the highway. → out of
find_and_fix_to_correct: The chair is made from of wood. → The chair is made out of wood. (use "out of" or simply "of," not both "from" and "of")
translate: हमारा दूध खत्म हो गया है। → We are out of milk.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence using 'out of the blue'.

reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'moving from the inside to the outside, or not having something left'?
usage_tip: 'Out of the blue' = unexpectedly.

simple_explanation: Caused by; because of. "Due to" introduces the reason or cause of something, working much like "because of," and is followed by a noun or noun phrase.
example_1: The trip was cancelled due to bad weather.
example_2: The delay was due to a technical problem.
example_3: Due to high demand, tickets sold out fast.
collocations: due to popular demand, due to circumstances, due to an error
related_phrasal_verbs: because of, owing to, on account of
where_it_s_used: Formal writing, news reports, explanations, delays
grammar_pattern: due to + noun/gerund (due to rain / due to being late)
common_mistake: The match was postponed due to it was raining.
correct_version: The match was postponed due to the rain.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Due to' + noun, not a full clause.
spelling_tip: Two words -- "due" + "to" -- and don't confuse with the non-standard "do to."
etymology: From "due" (Old French "deu," owed) + "to" -- literally "owed to," now meaning "caused by."
mnemonic: DUE TO = the result is DUE (owed) TO this specific cause.
memory_trick: DUE TO + noun (due to the rain).
visual_association: A signboard reading "Delayed" with a small note explaining the cause.
difference_explained: Similar. Due to often follows 'be': 'The delay was due to rain.'
related_words: because of, owing to, thanks to, as a result of
mini_conversation:
A: Why was the flight delayed?
B: Due to a mechanical issue, apparently.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A pilot announces over the intercom, "Due to weather conditions, we'll be experiencing a short delay."
news_style_line: News-style: "Due to rising costs, the company announced a small price increase."
casual_conversation: Casual: "The picnic got cancelled due to the sudden rain."
mcq_question: "Due to" is most similar in meaning to:
mcq_options: A) In spite of  B) Because of  C) Instead of  D) Regardless of
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The event was rescheduled ______ low ticket sales. → due to
find_and_fix_to_correct: Due to she was sick, she missed the exam. → Due to her illness, she missed the exam. (use "due to" + noun phrase, not a clause with "she was")
translate: खराब मौसम के कारण यात्रा रद्द कर दी गई। → The trip was cancelled due to bad weather.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something delayed due to weather.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'caused by; because of'?
usage_tip: 'Due to' is common in formal notices: 'due to technical reasons'.

simple_explanation: Without being affected or stopped by something. "In spite of" introduces something that could have caused a problem, but the result happened anyway -- exactly like "despite," just with "of" required.
example_1: In spite of the heat, they kept working.
example_2: In spite of his fear, he climbed to the top.
example_3: She smiled in spite of the pain.
collocations: in spite of everything, in spite of this, in spite of himself
where_it_s_used: Formal writing, overcoming obstacles, contrast statements
grammar_pattern: in spite of + noun/gerund (in spite of the cost / in spite of losing)
common_mistake: In spite the rain, we went for a walk.
correct_version: In spite of the rain, we went for a walk.
why_it_s_wrong: Never drop 'of' in 'in spite of'.
pronunciation_tip: Three words, light stress on "spite": in-SPYT-uv.
spelling_tip: Three separate words -- "in," "spite," "of" -- unlike "despite," which is one word with no "of."
etymology: From "spite" (Old French "despit," contempt), preceded by "in" -- literally "in contempt/defiance of," now simply "without being affected by."
prefix_root_suffix: in (state) + spite (root, from Latin "despectus," contempt) + of = "in defiance of"
mnemonic: IN SPITE OF = even IN the SPITE (bad feeling) OF a problem, the result still happens.
memory_trick: IN SPITE OF = three words, always.
visual_association: A single candle staying lit in spite of a strong wind blowing around it.
difference_explained: Same meaning. In spite of (with 'of'). Despite (without 'of').
mini_conversation:
A: How did she finish the race with an injured leg?
B: Pure willpower, in spite of the pain.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A mentor tells a student, "In spite of everyone doubting you, you proved them wrong."
news_style_line: News-style: "In spite of the economic challenges, the region saw record tourism this year."
casual_conversation: Casual: "In spite of being exhausted, she still helped clean up after the party."
mcq_question: "In spite of" must always be followed by:
mcq_options: A) A verb in past tense  B) The word "of"  C) Nothing  D) A question
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: ______ the traffic, we arrived right on time. → In spite of
find_and_fix_to_correct: In spite the difficulties, she never gave up. → In spite of the difficulties, she never gave up. (add "of" -- required after "in spite")
translate: थकान के बावजूद, उसने काम पूरा किया। → In spite of being tired, he finished the work.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence starting 'In spite of the…'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'without being affected or stopped by something'?
usage_tip: 'Despite' needs no 'of'; 'in spite of' always does.

hindi_meaning: की ओर से, के प्रतिनिधि के रूप में
simple_explanation: Acting or speaking for another person or group. "On behalf of" is used when someone does or says something as a representative of another person, group, or organization.
example_1: I'm speaking on behalf of the whole team.
example_2: She accepted the award on behalf of her colleagues.
example_3: On behalf of the company, he apologized for the delay.
collocations: speak on behalf of, act on behalf of, sign on behalf of
related_phrasal_verbs: for, representing, in the name of
where_it_s_used: Speeches, business letters, official statements, ceremonies
grammar_pattern: on behalf of + noun (on behalf of the team / on behalf of my father)
common_mistake: I am speaking in behalf of the students.
correct_version: I am speaking on behalf of the students.
why_it_s_wrong: The fixed phrase uses 'on', not 'in'.
spelling_tip: "Behalf" is one word, spelled with "-alf," not "-alve" -- watch that tricky ending.
etymology: From "on" + "behalf" (Middle English "bihalve," by the side of/on the part of) + "of" -- literally "on the side/part of" someone, meaning "representing them."
prefix_root_suffix: on + behalf (root, "by the side of") + of = representing someone's side
word_family: behalf (root word, used mainly in this fixed phrase)
mnemonic: ON BEHALF OF = standing ON the HALF (side) OF someone -- speaking for them.
memory_trick: ON BEHALF OF = in place of, representing.
visual_association: One person standing at a podium, speaking for a whole group behind them.
emotion_feel: Neutral, often respectful or formal in tone
difference_explained: On behalf of = representing someone. For = for someone's benefit.
related_words: representing, for, in the name of, delegate
mini_conversation:
A: Who's accepting the award tonight?
B: The director, on behalf of the entire cast and crew.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A spokesperson steps up to the microphone and says, "On behalf of the entire team, thank you all for your support."
news_style_line: News-style: "The mayor issued a statement on behalf of the city council this morning."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Can you sign this form on behalf of your parents?"
mcq_question: "On behalf of" is used when someone:
mcq_options: A) Argues against someone  B) Acts or speaks for someone else  C) Ignores a request  D) Competes with someone
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: He accepted the trophy ______ his entire team. → on behalf of
find_and_fix_to_correct: She spoke for behalf of her students. → She spoke on behalf of her students. (the fixed phrase is "on behalf of," not "for behalf of")
translate: मैं अपनी टीम की ओर से धन्यवाद कहना चाहता हूँ। → I would like to say thank you on behalf of my team.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence speaking on behalf of your class.

usage_tip: 'On behalf of the team, thank you' is common in speeches.

simple_explanation: Before a particular time or event. "Prior to" is a more formal way of saying "before," often used in official, written, or business contexts.
example_1: Please arrive prior to the scheduled time.
example_2: Prior to joining this company, she worked abroad.
example_3: Please read the instructions prior to using the device.
collocations: prior to arrival, prior to departure, prior to signing
related_phrasal_verbs: before, ahead of, in advance of
where_it_s_used: Business writing, legal documents, instructions, official notices
grammar_pattern: prior to + noun/gerund (prior to the meeting / prior to leaving)
common_mistake: Prior to eat, please wash your hands.
correct_version: Prior to eating, please wash your hands.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Prior to' is followed by -ing or a noun.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the first syllable of "prior": PRY-or too.
spelling_tip: "Prior" comes from Latin -- remember it's spelled with "-or," not "-er."
etymology: From Latin "prior" (former, earlier) + "to" -- a formal way of saying "before."
prefix_root_suffix: prior (root, from Latin "prior" = former) + to = before, earlier than
mnemonic: PRIOR TO = the PRIOR (earlier) point, TO which something happened first.
memory_trick: PRIOR = before (like PRIORity comes first).
visual_association: A calendar page turned back to an earlier date.
difference_explained: Same meaning. Prior to is formal.
mini_conversation:
A: When should we submit the documents?
B: Prior to the end of the month, ideally.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A lawyer states firmly, "Prior to signing this agreement, please review every clause carefully."
news_style_line: News-style: "Prior to the announcement, company shares had already begun to rise."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I had no idea about the change prior to today, honestly."
mcq_options: A) After  B) Before  C) During  D) Instead of
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: ______ the exam, students must switch off their phones. → Prior to
find_and_fix_to_correct: Prior the meeting, please review the agenda. → Prior to the meeting, please review the agenda. (add "to" -- the phrase is always "prior to")
translate: बैठक से पहले, कृपया रिपोर्ट पढ़ लें। → Prior to the meeting, please read the report.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a formal sentence using 'prior to'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'before a particular time or event'?
usage_tip: 'Prior to' is formal; 'before' is everyday.

simple_explanation: A short distance from, or emotionally near to. "Close to" shows that something is near in distance, time, or feeling -- like a place nearby or a person you feel connected to.
example_1: The hotel is close to the beach.
example_2: She's very close to her grandmother.
example_3: We're close to finishing the project.
collocations: close to home, close to tears, close to perfect, stay close to
where_it_s_used: Distances, relationships, emotions, progress toward a goal
grammar_pattern: close to + noun (close to the station / close to her heart)
common_mistake: My house is close the market.
correct_version: My house is close to the market.
why_it_s_wrong: The fixed phrase is 'close to'.
pronunciation_tip: "Close" here rhymes with "gross": /kloʊs/ -- the adjective and verb "close" sound different.
spelling_tip: Watch the pronunciation trap -- "close" (adjective, near) sounds different from "close" (verb, to shut).
etymology: From "close" (Old French "clos," shut/near) + "to" -- describing nearness in distance or relationship.
mnemonic: CLOSE TO = standing so CLOSE you're almost TOuching.
memory_trick: CLOSE TO = near.
visual_association: Two friends standing shoulder to shoulder, almost touching.
emotion_feel: Neutral, often warm when describing emotional closeness
difference_explained: Same meaning. Close to can also mean emotionally close.
mini_conversation:
A: How's the project going?
B: We're close to finishing, just a few details left.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character grips a friend's hand and says, "We're so close to the end -- don't give up now."
news_style_line: News-style: "The new stadium is being built close to the city's main train station."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Are we close to the restaurant yet? I'm starving."
mcq_options: A) Far away from  B) A short distance from  C) Instead of  D) Because of
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: We finally live ______ our favorite park. → close to
find_and_fix_to_correct: They are close of each other. → They are close to each other. (use "to," not "of," after "close")
translate: होटल समुद्र तट के करीब है। → The hotel is close to the beach.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something close to your home.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'a short distance from, or emotionally near to'?
usage_tip: 'Close to' also means almost: 'close to ₹1,000'.

simple_explanation: A long distance from, or not at all (in figurative use). "Far from" describes a big distance between two places, or figuratively means "definitely not" -- like saying something is far from perfect.
example_1: The airport is far from the city center.
example_2: Her hometown is far from here.
example_3: The results are far from satisfactory.
collocations: far from home, far from perfect, far from over, far from easy
grammar_pattern: far from + noun/adjective/gerund (far from home / far from perfect / far from finishing)
common_mistake: The hospital is far of my house.
correct_version: The hospital is far from my house.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'far from', not 'far of'.
etymology: From "far" (Old English "feor," distant) + "from" -- showing a large distance or strong contrast from something.
mnemonic: FAR FROM = so FAR away FROM something, it's almost out of reach.
memory_trick: FAR FROM = a long distance from.
visual_association: Two pins on a map placed at opposite ends, very far apart.
emotion_feel: Neutral, sometimes discouraging when used figuratively (far from ready)
difference_explained: Far from = a long distance. Away from = not at, any distance.
mini_conversation:
A: Is the situation improving?
B: Honestly, we're still far from a solution.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A traveler looks back at the road and sighs, "We're still far from where we need to be."
news_style_line: News-style: "Experts say a full economic recovery is still far from certain."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Don't worry, the store isn't far from here."
mcq_question: "Far from" in "The plan is far from perfect" means:
mcq_options: A) Exactly perfect  B) Definitely not perfect  C) Almost perfect  D) Perfect in every way
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The truth is ______ what the rumors suggested. → far from
find_and_fix_to_correct: My office is far from of downtown. → My office is far from downtown. (remove "of" -- not needed after "far from")
translate: हवाई अड्डा शहर के केंद्र से दूर है। → The airport is far from the city center.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a place far from your city.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'a long distance from, or not at all (in figurative use)'?
usage_tip: 'Far from perfect' = not perfect at all.

simple_explanation: Together with; in addition to. "Along with" shows that one thing or person accompanies another, or is included in addition to it.
example_1: She came along with her sister.
example_2: Send the report along with the invoice.
example_3: Along with rice, they also served fresh vegetables.
collocations: along with that, come along with, along with others
grammar_pattern: along with + noun (along with the letter / along with his friends)
common_mistake: He arrived along of his brother.
correct_version: He arrived along with his brother.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'along with', not 'along of'.
spelling_tip: Two separate words -- "along" + "with" -- never merged into one.
etymology: From "along" (Old English "andlang," the whole length of) + "with" -- literally "the whole way together with."
prefix_root_suffix: along (root, "the length of") + with = accompanying, the whole way together
word_family: along (adv./prep., root word) -- "along with" itself has no direct verb/noun forms
mnemonic: ALONG WITH = walking ALONG the same path, WITH someone else beside you.
memory_trick: ALONG WITH = together with.
visual_association: A line of ducklings walking along with their mother.
emotion_feel: Neutral, often friendly when describing group inclusion
difference_explained: Same meaning. Along with stresses 'in addition'.
mini_conversation:
A: Is anyone else coming to the trip?
B: Yes, my cousin is coming along with us.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A captain looks at the crew and says, "We sail together, along with everyone who trusted us with this journey."
news_style_line: News-style: "The proposal was approved along with several amendments to the original plan."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Can you bring your notes along with your laptop tomorrow?"
mcq_options: A) Instead of  B) Together with  C) Because of  D) Without
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Please bring your ID card ______ the application form. → along with
find_and_fix_to_correct: She traveled along her friends to Paris. → She traveled along with her friends to Paris. (add "with" -- the phrase is "along with," not "along" alone)
translate: कृपया आवेदन पत्र के साथ अपनी तस्वीर भी भेजें। → Please send your photo along with the application form.

spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'together with; in addition to'?
usage_tip: 'Along with' adds something: 'The phone comes along with a charger.'

simple_explanation: Except for something, or in addition to something. You use "apart from" to pull one item out of a group -- either to exclude it or to add it as an extra point.
example_1: Apart from the rain, the trip was perfect.
example_2: Apart from one typo, the report looks great.
example_3: Apart from Maria, everyone showed up on time.
collocations: apart from that, apart from a few, quite apart from
related_phrasal_verbs: aside from, except for, other than
where_it_s_used: Giving exceptions, adding extra points, describing lists
grammar_pattern: apart from + noun/pronoun/gerund (Apart from him, nobody knew.)
common_mistake: Apart of the noise, I slept well.
correct_version: Apart from the noise, I slept well.
why_it_s_wrong: The phrase is 'apart from', not 'apart of'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress the first syllable of "apart": uh-PART from.
spelling_tip: Two separate words -- don't write "appart" with a double p.
etymology: From "apart" (Old French "a part," to the side) + "from" -- literally "to the side, away from," extended to mean "except for" or "in addition to."
prefix_root_suffix: apart (a- + part, "to the side") + from (source/separation) -- a two-word compound preposition
mnemonic: Picture two puzzle pieces pulled APART -- everything FROM that pile is set aside as an exception.
memory_trick: APART FROM = except for, or in addition to.
visual_association: One item lifted out of a row of boxes and set to the side.
emotion_feel: Neutral -- often softens a complaint or adds a small exception
difference_explained: Apart from = except for, OR in addition to. Except = only 'not including'.
related_words: except, besides, excluding, in addition to

B: Apart from Sam, yes -- he had one concern.
