hindi_meaning: की परवाह किए बिना, चाहे कुछ भी हो
simple_explanation: Without being affected or influenced by something; no matter what. "Regardless of" tells us that one thing stays true no matter what another factor is -- the result doesn't change.
example_1: Regardless of the weather, the match will go ahead.
example_2: Regardless of your experience, you're welcome to apply.
example_3: She stays calm regardless of the pressure.
collocations: regardless of the outcome, regardless of age, regardless of consequences
related_phrasal_verbs: no matter, irrespective of, in spite of
grammar_pattern: regardless of + noun/gerund/wh-clause (regardless of what happens)
common_mistake: Regardless the price, I'm buying it.
correct_version: Regardless of the price, I'm buying it.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Regardless' needs 'of' before the noun.
pronunciation_tip: Four syllables: ri-GARD-less-uhv, with the main stress on "gard."
spelling_tip: A common error is writing "irregardless" -- that word is nonstandard; stick to "regardless."
etymology: From "regard" (Old French "regarder," to look at) + "-less" (without) + "of" -- literally "without regard to," i.e. not influenced by something.
mnemonic: RE-GARD-LESS: you pay LESS regard to the details -- the outcome stays the same either way.
memory_trick: REGARDLESS OF = without caring about.
visual_association: A door staying open in a storm, unaffected by the wind outside.
difference_explained: Similar. Regardless of = not affected by. Despite = even though something is true.
mini_conversation:
A: Will the event be cancelled if it rains?
B: No, it's happening regardless of the weather.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A general declares, "We hold this position, regardless of what comes next."
news_style_line: News-style: "The policy applies to all employees, regardless of their length of service."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I'm going for a run today, regardless of the cold."
mcq_options: A) Because of  B) No matter what / unaffected by  C) On behalf of  D) In comparison with
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Everyone must wear a helmet, ______ their age. → regardless of
find_and_fix_to_correct: Regardless of what you say, but I will go. → Regardless of what you say, I will go.
translate: मौसम की परवाह किए बिना, हम पिकनिक पर जाएँगे। → Regardless of the weather, we will go on the picnic.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence starting 'Regardless of the price,…'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'without being affected or influenced by something; no matter what'?
usage_tip: 'Irregardless' is not standard English.

simple_explanation: As well as something; besides something already mentioned. You use "in addition to" to add one more item, person, or fact to something you already mentioned.
example_1: In addition to English, she speaks French.
example_2: In addition to his salary, he receives a travel allowance.
example_3: In addition to studying, remember to rest.
collocations: in addition to that, in addition to this, in addition to being
related_phrasal_verbs: as well as, on top of, along with
where_it_s_used: Formal writing, listing extra points, job descriptions
grammar_pattern: in addition to + noun/gerund (In addition to cooking, she bakes.)
common_mistake: In addition to that, but I also cleaned the house.
correct_version: In addition to that, I also cleaned the house.
why_it_s_wrong: After 'In addition to that', don't add 'but'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress the third syllable of "addition": in uh-DISH-uhn too.
spelling_tip: Double "d" in "addition" -- easy to accidentally write with just one.
etymology: From Latin "additio" (an adding to), via French -- literally "in the state of adding to."
prefix_root_suffix: ad- (toward) + dit (from Latin "dare," to give) + -ion (noun suffix) -- "a giving toward"
mnemonic: IN ADDITION TO is like doing extra ADDITION in math -- you're adding one more thing to the list.
memory_trick: IN ADDITION TO = plus.
visual_association: A plus sign connecting two boxes on a list.
emotion_feel: Neutral -- signals a bonus or extra detail
difference_explained: Same meaning. Besides is more informal.
mini_conversation:
A: Does the job need any other skills?
B: In addition to English, you'll need basic Excel.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A mentor tells the recruit, "In addition to strength, you'll need patience for this job."
news_style_line: News-style: "In addition to the new bridge, the city plans to widen two main roads."
casual_conversation: Casual: "In addition to my job, I'm taking evening classes."
mcq_options: A) Instead of  B) As well as  C) Because of  D) Except for
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: ______ playing football, he enjoys swimming. → In addition to
find_and_fix_to_correct: In addition to work, she study at night. → In addition to work, she studies at night.
translate: अंग्रेज़ी के अलावा, वह स्पेनिश भी बोलती है। → In addition to English, she also speaks Spanish.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence starting 'In addition to my job,…'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'as well as something; besides something already mentioned'?
usage_tip: 'In addition to' + noun or -ing.

hindi_meaning: की स्थिति में, अगर हो तो
simple_explanation: If a particular situation happens. "In case of" warns you what to do if a specific event happens -- it's common in instructions and safety signs.
example_1: In case of emergency, call this number.
example_2: In case of rain, the picnic will move indoors.
example_3: Keep a spare key in case of a lockout.
collocations: in case of emergency, in case of fire, in case of doubt
related_phrasal_verbs: in the event of, just in case, should there be
where_it_s_used: Safety instructions, warnings, planning for problems
grammar_pattern: in case of + noun (In case of delay, we'll wait.)
common_mistake: In case of you need help, call me.
correct_version: In case you need help, call me.
why_it_s_wrong: 'In case of' takes a noun; 'in case' takes a clause.
pronunciation_tip: Even stress across the phrase, with a slight lift on "case": in-CASE-uhv.
spelling_tip: Don't confuse with "in case" alone (no "of") -- "in case of" is always followed directly by a noun.
etymology: From Latin "casus" (a falling, an event) via French "cas" -- "in case of" literally means "in the event/occurrence of."
prefix_root_suffix: case (root, from Latin "casus," an event) + of (linking preposition)
mnemonic: IN CASE OF fire, break glass -- picture the red emergency box with these exact words.
memory_trick: IN CASE OF + noun (in case of fire). IN CASE + clause (in case it rains).
visual_association: A red "break glass in case of fire" box mounted on a wall.
confusing_word: in case of vs in case
difference_explained: In case of + noun. In case + subject + verb.
mini_conversation:
A: What should we do in case of a power cut?
B: There are candles in the kitchen drawer.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A pilot's calm voice announces, "In case of turbulence, please remain seated."
news_style_line: News-style: "In case of severe weather, residents are advised to stay indoors."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I keep a torch in the car in case of a breakdown."
mcq_options: A) After  B) If this situation happens  C) Despite  D) Because
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: ______ fire, use the stairs, not the lift. → In case of
find_and_fix_to_correct: In case of you are late, text me. → In case you are late, text me.
translate: आग लगने की स्थिति में, लिफ़्ट का उपयोग न करें। → In case of fire, do not use the lift.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence using 'in case of'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'if a particular situation happens'?
usage_tip: 'In case of emergency' is a common sign.

simple_explanation: On the upper surface of something, or in addition to something else. "On top of" describes something resting above another thing, or -- figuratively -- one more problem or task added to an existing pile.
example_1: The books are stacked on top of the table.
example_2: On top of losing his job, his car broke down.
example_3: She keeps her glasses on top of her head.
collocations: on top of that, stay on top of, right on top of
related_phrasal_verbs: in addition to, pile up, keep up with
where_it_s_used: Describing position, piling problems, staying organized
grammar_pattern: on top of + noun (on top of the fridge / on top of everything else)
common_mistake: The cat is sitting on the top of the roof.
correct_version: The cat is sitting on top of the roof.
why_it_s_wrong: In everyday speech, use 'on top of', not 'on the top of'.
pronunciation_tip: Natural rhythm: on-TOP-uhv, with the main stress on "top."
spelling_tip: Three separate words -- never combined as "ontopof."
etymology: From "on" + "top" (Old English "top," the highest point) + "of" -- literally describing position above something, extended figuratively to mean "in addition to" or "in control of."
prefix_root_suffix: on (position) + top (root, highest point) + of (linking preposition)
mnemonic: Picture a cherry sitting ON TOP OF a cake -- it's literally above, or it's the "extra" thing added.
memory_trick: ON TOP OF = on the highest part.
visual_association: A pile of boxes with one more box balanced right on top.
emotion_feel: Neutral for position; overwhelmed or stressed for the figurative sense
difference_explained: On top of = touching the top. Above = higher, not touching.
mini_conversation:
A: Where did you put the remote?
B: It's on top of the bookshelf.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A tired manager sighs, "And on top of everything, the printer just broke."
news_style_line: News-style: "On top of the heavy rain, strong winds are expected to hit the coast tonight."
casual_conversation: Casual: "On top of studying for exams, I'm also working weekends."
mcq_question: "On top of" most nearly means (figurative use):
mcq_options: A) Instead of  B) In addition to  C) Because of  D) Far from
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: She placed her bag ______ the chair. → on top of
find_and_fix_to_correct: The lamp is on top the desk. → The lamp is on top of the desk.
translate: किताबें मेज़ के ऊपर रखी हैं। → The books are placed on top of the table.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence starting 'On top of that,…'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'on the upper surface of something, or in addition to something else'?
usage_tip: 'On top of that' = also, in addition (often bad things).

simple_explanation: In order to help or benefit someone or something. "For the sake of" explains the motive behind an action -- you do something because it benefits a person, value, or goal.
example_1: Please stop arguing, for the sake of peace.
example_2: She quit smoking for the sake of her children.
example_3: Let's compromise for the sake of the team.
collocations: for the sake of argument, for the sake of simplicity, for the sake of peace
related_phrasal_verbs: for the good of, for the benefit of, in the interest of
grammar_pattern: for the sake of + noun/gerund (for the sake of honesty / for the sake of saving time)
common_mistake: For the sake of he is happy, I agreed.
correct_version: For the sake of his happiness, I agreed.
why_it_s_wrong: 'For the sake of' takes a noun, not a clause.
spelling_tip: "Sake" (benefit) looks identical to the Japanese drink "sake" -- same spelling, unrelated word; context always makes it clear.
etymology: From Old English "sacu" (a cause, a legal case) -- "for the sake of" originally meant "for the cause of," now meaning "for the benefit/purpose of."
prefix_root_suffix: for (purpose) + the + sake (root, cause/benefit) + of (linking preposition)
mnemonic: FOR THE SAKE OF someone is like saying "just FOR THEM" -- picture doing a favor purely to help that person.
memory_trick: FOR THE SAKE OF = for the benefit of.
visual_association: Two hands shaking, with a small heart symbol between them.
synonyms: for the benefit of, for the good of
confusing_word: for the sake of vs for
difference_explained: For the sake of = to help or protect. For is more general.
mini_conversation:
A: Why did you apologize first?
B: For the sake of keeping the peace between us.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A leader pleads, "For the sake of this town, let's put our differences aside."
news_style_line: News-style: "Officials urged calm, for the sake of public safety."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Let's just agree to disagree, for the sake of the evening."
mcq_question: "For the sake of" most nearly means:
mcq_options: A) In order to benefit/help  B) Regardless of  C) Instead of  D) In comparison to
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: He agreed to compromise ______ the friendship. → for the sake of
find_and_fix_to_correct: For the sake of save money, she cooks at home. → For the sake of saving money, she cooks at home.
translate: बच्चों की खातिर, उसने सिगरेट पीना छोड़ दिया। → For the sake of the children, she gave up smoking.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something you did for the sake of your family.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'in order to help or benefit someone or something'?
usage_tip: 'For heaven's sake!' expresses annoyance.

simple_explanation: Used to join two words, phrases, or ideas together. "And" is the simplest way to add one thing to another -- two nouns, two actions, or two full sentences.
example_2: She bought apples, bananas, and oranges.
example_3: He studied hard and passed the exam.
collocations: black and white, here and there, now and then
related_phrasal_verbs: as well as, plus, along with
where_it_s_used: Everywhere -- lists, instructions, storytelling, everyday speech
grammar_pattern: X and Y (noun and noun / clause and clause)
common_mistake: I like pizza, and, I like pasta.
correct_version: I like pizza and pasta.
why_it_s_wrong: With just two items joined by 'and', no commas are needed.
pronunciation_tip: In fast speech, "and" often reduces to "uhn" or "n'" (e.g., "bread and butter" becomes "bread-n-butter").
spelling_tip: Just three letters -- a, n, d -- one of the first words learners memorize.
etymology: From Old English "and," a basic coordinating word present since the earliest records of English, joining equal elements.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- a short, ancient connecting word
word_family: no related word forms -- "and" is a basic function word
mnemonic: AND connects like a chain link -- item AND item AND item, all joined together.
memory_trick: AND = plus.
visual_association: Two puzzle pieces clicking together into one.
emotion_feel: Neutral -- purely connective, no emotional weight
difference_explained: And joins words or clauses. Also adds information inside a clause: 'I also like tea.'
mini_conversation:
A: What do you want for breakfast?
B: Toast and eggs, please.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A narrator opens the story: "It was a dark and stormy night when everything changed."
news_style_line: News-style: "The mayor and the governor met today to discuss the new budget."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Can you grab some milk and bread on your way home?"
mcq_options: A) Show contrast  B) Join similar ideas together  C) Give a reason  D) Offer a choice
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: She washed the dishes ______ dried them. → and
find_and_fix_to_correct: He like tea and she like coffee. → He likes tea and she likes coffee.
translate: मुझे चाय और कॉफी दोनों पसंद हैं। → I like both tea and coffee.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence joining three things with 'and'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'used to join two words, phrases, or ideas together'?
usage_tip: 'And' at the start of a sentence is fine in speech and informal writing.

simple_explanation: Used to introduce something that contrasts with what came before. "But" shows that the second part of a sentence goes against or limits the first part.
example_1: I'm tired, but I'll finish this task.
example_2: She wanted to go, but she had no money.
example_3: The movie was long but enjoyable.
collocations: but then, but still, but rather
related_phrasal_verbs: however, yet, on the other hand
grammar_pattern: clause + but + clause (I wanted to stay, but I had to leave.)
common_mistake: Although it was raining, but we went out.
correct_version: Although it was raining, we went out.
why_it_s_wrong: Don't use 'although' and 'but' in one sentence. Pick one.
pronunciation_tip: A short, quick vowel sound -- rhymes with "cut" and "hut": /bʌt/.
spelling_tip: Three letters, one "t" -- don't double it as "butt" (a completely different word).
etymology: From Old English "butan" (without, outside of), which narrowed over time to mean "except" and then "however/on the contrary."
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- a short, ancient connecting word
word_family: no related word forms -- "but" is a basic function word
mnemonic: BUT is a stop sign in a sentence -- it says, "wait, here's the opposite side."
memory_trick: BUT = contrast. Hindi 'haalaanki… lekin' uses both, but English uses only one.
visual_association: A road sign showing an arrow suddenly turning the opposite way.
emotion_feel: Neutral -- signals hesitation, contrast, or a gentle correction
difference_explained: But joins two clauses (It rained, but we went). Although starts a clause (Although it rained, we went).

A: Do you want to come to the party?
B: I'd love to, but I have to work late.

news_style_line: News-style: "The team played well, but a late goal cost them the match."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I like the plan, but can we change the date?"
mcq_options: A) Add a similar idea  B) Introduce a contrast  C) Give a result  D) Show a condition
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The food was cheap ______ delicious. → but
find_and_fix_to_correct: She is smart but she don't study. → She is smart, but she doesn't study.
translate: वह थका हुआ था, लेकिन उसने काम पूरा किया। → He was tired, but he finished the work.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence using 'but' to show contrast.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'used to introduce something that contrasts with what came before'?
usage_tip: 'But' is the most common contrast word in English.

simple_explanation: Used to show a choice between two or more things. "Or" connects options -- it tells you that only one of the things mentioned needs to be true or chosen.
example_1: Would you like tea or coffee?
example_2: You can pay by card or cash.
example_3: Call me tonight, or send a text.
collocations: either...or, sooner or later, now or never
where_it_s_used: Questions, choices, lists of options, warnings
grammar_pattern: X or Y (noun or noun / clause or clause)
common_mistake: Do you want tea and coffee? (when only one choice is meant)
correct_version: Do you want tea or coffee?
why_it_s_wrong: For a choice between options, use 'or', not 'and'.
pronunciation_tip: A single, clear vowel sound: /ɔːr/, rhyming with "door" and "more."
spelling_tip: Just two letters -- don't confuse with "are" (a verb), which beginners sometimes mistype.
etymology: From Middle English "other," gradually shortened to "or" -- originally meaning "the other (option)."
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- a short, ancient connecting word
word_family: no related word forms -- "or" is a basic function word
mnemonic: OR is like a fork in the road -- go this way OR that way, you must pick one.
memory_trick: OR = choose one.
visual_association: A signpost pointing two directions at a fork in the road.
emotion_feel: Neutral -- can add tension when used as a warning ("or else")
difference_explained: Or = one of the options. And = both together.

A: Should we drive or take the train?
B: Let's take the train, it's faster.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A voice on the radio warns, "Turn back now, or there's no going back."
news_style_line: News-style: "Residents must evacuate today or risk being trapped by the flood."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Should we order pizza or cook something at home?"
mcq_options: A) Add two things together  B) Offer a choice between options  C) Show contrast  D) Give a reason

find_and_fix_to_correct: You can have cake or ice cream, both if you want just one. → You can have cake or ice cream, whichever you prefer.

write_your_own_sentence: Write a question offering a choice with 'or'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'used to show a choice between two or more things'?
usage_tip: 'Or else' = otherwise (a warning).

simple_explanation: Used after a negative statement to add another negative one. "Nor" links two negative ideas together, usually paired with "neither" -- both things are true in their negative form.
example_1: I don't like coffee, nor do I like tea.
example_2: She neither called nor texted.
example_3: He can't sing, nor can he dance.
collocations: neither...nor, nor do I, nor does he
where_it_s_used: Formal writing, paired negatives, emphatic denial
grammar_pattern: neither X nor Y / nor + auxiliary + subject (Nor did she apologize.)
common_mistake: She doesn't drink, nor she smokes.
correct_version: She doesn't drink, nor does she smoke.
why_it_s_wrong: After 'nor', put the auxiliary before the subject: 'nor does she smoke'.
spelling_tip: Three letters -- don't confuse with "or" (a positive choice).
etymology: From Old English "ne" (not) + "or," contracted through Middle English into "nor" -- used to continue a negative statement.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- a short, ancient connecting word
word_family: no related word forms -- "nor" is a basic function word, paired with "neither"
mnemonic: NEITHER...NOR is a matching pair -- like salt and pepper, they always come together.
memory_trick: NOR = and not. NEITHER…NOR.
visual_association: Two closed doors side by side, both marked "no."
emotion_feel: Neutral to firm -- adds emphasis to a denial
difference_explained: Nor = and not (negative). Or = choice (positive).

A: Did anyone bring snacks?
B: Neither Tom nor Priya remembered.

news_style_line: News-style: "Officials confirmed the cause is neither mechanical nor weather-related."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I haven't seen the file, nor have I heard from him today."

find_and_fix_to_correct: She can't cook, nor she can bake. → She can't cook, nor can she bake.

write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence with 'neither … nor'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'used after a negative statement to add another negative one'?
usage_tip: 'Nor' is formal; 'and doesn't … either' is everyday.

simple_explanation: Used to introduce a result or consequence. "So" tells you what happened as a direct result of something mentioned just before it.
example_1: It was raining, so I took an umbrella.
example_2: He was hungry, so he made a sandwich.
example_3: The shop was closed, so we went home.
collocations: so far, so much, so that, so what
related_phrasal_verbs: therefore, as a result, that's why
where_it_s_used: Everyday storytelling, explaining results, casual speech
grammar_pattern: cause, so + result (It was late, so we left.)
common_mistake: Because it was late, so we left.
correct_version: It was late, so we left.
why_it_s_wrong: Don't use 'because' and 'so' together. Pick one.
pronunciation_tip: A pure, long "o" sound: /soʊ/, like "go" or "no."
spelling_tip: Just two letters -- don't confuse with "sew" (to stitch) or "sow" (to plant), which sound identical.
etymology: From Old English "swa" (in this way, thus) -- one of English's oldest words, used both as an adverb and, here, as a linking conjunction.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- a short, ancient connecting word
word_family: no related word forms -- "so" is a basic function word
mnemonic: SO connects cause and effect: this happened, SO that happened.
memory_trick: SO = result. BECAUSE = reason. One per sentence.
visual_association: One domino falling into the next.
difference_explained: Because = reason (I left because it was late). So = result (It was late, so I left).
mini_conversation:
A: The bus never came.
B: So we walked instead?
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character shrugs, "The plan failed, so we made a new one."
news_style_line: News-style: "Demand rose sharply, so the factory added a second shift."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I forgot my wallet, so can you cover lunch today?"
mcq_question: "So" (as a conjunction) is mainly used to:
mcq_options: A) Introduce a reason  B) Introduce a result  C) Show contrast  D) Offer a choice
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The lights went out, ______ we lit some candles. → so
find_and_fix_to_correct: I was tired so, I went to bed early. → I was tired, so I went to bed early.
translate: बारिश हो रही थी, इसलिए हम घर पर रुके। → It was raining, so we stayed home.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence using 'so' to show a result.

reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'used to introduce a result or consequence'?
usage_tip: 'So' is also used to start a story: 'So, yesterday…'.

simple_explanation: Used to introduce a surprising or unexpected contrast, similar to "but." "Yet" connects two ideas where the second one is surprising given the first -- it adds a note of contrast, often stronger than "but."
example_1: It looks simple, yet it's very hard.
example_2: He is rich, yet he lives very simply.
example_3: The test was long, yet she finished early.
collocations: and yet, yet again, yet still
where_it_s_used: Storytelling, descriptions, formal writing, surprising facts
grammar_pattern: clause, yet + clause (He tried hard, yet he failed.)
common_mistake: He has not come till now.
correct_version: He has not come yet.
why_it_s_wrong: With the present perfect in negatives, use 'yet', not 'till now'.
pronunciation_tip: Short, crisp vowel: /jɛt/, rhymes with "get" and "set."
spelling_tip: Three letters -- don't confuse with "get" (a different starting sound and meaning).
etymology: From Old English "gieta," originally meaning "up to now"; as a conjunction it developed to mean "but still," showing an unexpected contrast.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- a short, ancient connecting word
word_family: no related word forms in this sense -- "yet" is also a common time adverb (as in "not yet")
mnemonic: YET is a twist ending -- just when you expect one thing, YET flips it.
memory_trick: YET = up to now (not yet). Also: 'but' (young, yet talented).
visual_association: A small seed growing into a surprisingly tall tree.
emotion_feel: Neutral to thoughtful -- signals a meaningful contrast
difference_explained: Yet = in negatives and questions (not yet). Still = continuing (still waiting).
mini_conversation:
A: The house looks tiny from outside.
B: Yet it's actually huge once you're inside.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A narrator says, "The city slept, yet somewhere, one light stayed on."
news_style_line: News-style: "The bridge is old, yet engineers say it remains completely safe."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I'm nervous about the interview, yet somehow I feel ready."
mcq_question: "Yet" (as a conjunction) is closest in meaning to:
mcq_options: A) Because  B) But / however  C) So  D) Or
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The room was small, ______ it felt cozy. → yet
find_and_fix_to_correct: She is quiet, yet she is not shy, however. → She is quiet, yet she is not shy.
translate: वह थका हुआ था, फिर भी उसने दौड़ पूरी की। → He was tired, yet he finished the race.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence using 'not … yet'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'used to introduce a surprising or unexpected contrast, similar to "but."'?
usage_tip: 'Not yet' = not so far, but expected.

simple_explanation: Used to introduce a fact that contrasts with the main statement. "Although" joins two parts of a sentence that seem to disagree with each other, showing that one fact doesn't stop the other from being true.
example_1: Although he was late, he still got the job.
example_2: Although the shop was crowded, we found what we needed.
example_3: Although she is young, she manages the whole team.
collocations: although it may seem, although generally, although technically
related_phrasal_verbs: even though, despite, in spite of
where_it_s_used: Essays, formal speech, describing surprising contrasts
grammar_pattern: although + subject + verb, main clause (Although it rained, we went out.)
common_mistake: Although he studied hard, but he failed.
correct_version: Although he studied hard, he failed.
why_it_s_wrong: Never use 'but' with 'although'.
pronunciation_tip: Two syllables: awl-THOH, with the stress on the second syllable.
spelling_tip: "Al" + "though" -- remember it's one word, not "all though."
etymology: From Middle English "al" (wholly) + "though" -- literally "even though wholly true."
mnemonic: ALTHOUGH = "ALL of that is true, THOUGH something else surprises us."
memory_trick: ALTHOUGH… (no BUT). One contrast word only.
visual_association: A small crack in a wall that the whole structure still stands strong despite.
emotion_feel: Neutral -- signals contrast without strong emotion
difference_explained: Same meaning. Though is more informal and can end a sentence: 'It was good, though.'
mini_conversation:
A: How was the hike?
B: Although my legs were sore, it was totally worth it.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A coach tells the team, "Although we're behind, we still have time to turn this around."
news_style_line: News-style: "Although the numbers dipped slightly, analysts remain confident in the market."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Although I'm on a diet, I'm having one slice of cake today."
mcq_options: A) Add a similar idea  B) Introduce a contrasting idea  C) Give a reason  D) State a result
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: ______ it was expensive, she bought the dress anyway. → Although
find_and_fix_to_correct: Although it was dark, but he found his way home. → Although it was dark, he found his way home.
translate: हालांकि वह बीमार था, फिर भी वह काम पर गया। → Although he was sick, he went to work.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence starting 'Although…'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'used to introduce a fact that contrasts with the main statement'?
usage_tip: 'Although' can start or be in the middle of a sentence.

simple_explanation: Used to introduce a contrast, in a more casual way than "although." "Though" links two contrasting ideas, just like "although," but it feels more relaxed and can even be dropped in at the end of a sentence.
example_1: I'm tired, I'll finish this though.
example_2: Though it was late, she kept working.
example_3: The movie was long. It was good, though.
collocations: even though, as though, though not
grammar_pattern: though + clause, main clause / main clause...though. (informal, sentence-final use)
common_mistake: Though he is rich, but he is humble.
correct_version: Though he is rich, he is humble.
why_it_s_wrong: Don't use 'though' and 'but' together.
pronunciation_tip: Rhymes with "go" and "so": /ðoʊ/ -- don't confuse with "through" or "tough," which look similar but sound very different.
spelling_tip: T-H-O-U-G-H -- one of English's trickiest spellings; say it out loud to remember it rhymes with "go."
etymology: From Old English "þeah," a shortened, more informal relative of "although" -- both share the same Germanic root meaning "even if."
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- a short, ancient concession word
mnemonic: THOUGH is ALTHOUGH's short, casual twin -- same job, fewer letters.
memory_trick: THOUGH = although, informal.
visual_association: A friendly nudge added at the end of a sentence, like an afterthought.
difference_explained: Though (/ðəʊ/) = although. Through (/θruː/) = from one side to the other.
mini_conversation:
A: That test was so hard.
B: I passed, though, so it's fine.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character shrugs and adds, "It won't be easy, though."
news_style_line: News-style: "The storm has passed. Cleanup will take weeks, though, officials say."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I'm not hungry. I'll have dessert, though."
mcq_options: A) Because  B) Although  C) So  D) Unless
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: It's expensive. I might buy it, ______. → though
find_and_fix_to_correct: Though I'm busy, but I'll help you. → Though I'm busy, I'll help you.
translate: मौसम खराब था, फिर भी हम बाहर गए। → The weather was bad, though we went outside.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence ending with ', though.'
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'used to introduce a contrast, in a more casual way than "although."'?
usage_tip: At the end of a sentence, 'though' = however: 'It's expensive. Good, though.'

simple_explanation: Used to strongly emphasize a surprising contrast. "Even though" works like "although" but sounds stronger -- it highlights just how surprising or unexpected the contrast is.
example_1: Even though it was freezing, they went swimming.
example_2: Even though he apologized, she didn't forgive him.
example_3: Even though she's new, she already knows the job well.
collocations: even though it seems, even though technically, even though clearly
where_it_s_used: Emphasizing surprise, describing struggles, personal stories
grammar_pattern: even though + subject + verb, main clause (Even though he tried, he lost.)
common_mistake: Even though it was raining, but the game continued.
correct_version: Even though it was raining, the game continued.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Even though' already shows contrast, so drop 'but'.
pronunciation_tip: Two stressed words: EE-vuhn thoh -- both parts get more weight than in plain "though."
spelling_tip: Two separate words -- never write it as "eventhough."
etymology: Combines "even" (Old English "efne," used for emphasis) with "though" -- together they intensify the contrast beyond plain "although."
mnemonic: EVEN THOUGH adds "even" for extra emphasis -- it's ALTHOUGH turned up a notch.
memory_trick: EVEN THOUGH = stronger ALTHOUGH.
visual_association: A small plant pushing up through a crack in solid concrete.
emotion_feel: Admiration, determination -- highlights effort against odds
difference_explained: Even though = it's true (even though it's raining). Even if = it might be true (even if it rains).
mini_conversation:
A: Did you finish the marathon?
B: Yes, even though I twisted my ankle halfway through.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A soldier says quietly, "Even though we're outnumbered, we hold the line."
news_style_line: News-style: "Even though the economy slowed, unemployment stayed at a record low."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Even though I was scared, I asked the question anyway."
mcq_options: A) Give a mild reason  B) Emphasize a strong contrast  C) Add a similar fact  D) Show a result
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: ______ she was exhausted, she stayed up to help him. → Even though
find_and_fix_to_correct: Even though he is rich, but he is generous. → Even though he is rich, he is generous.
translate: भले ही वह थका हुआ था, उसने काम पूरा किया। → Even though he was tired, he finished the work.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence starting 'Even though…'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'used to strongly emphasize a surprising contrast'?
usage_tip: Use 'even though' for real facts; 'even if' for possible situations.

simple_explanation: Used to give the reason for something. "Because" answers the question "why?" -- it connects a result to its cause.
example_1: I stayed home because I was sick.
example_2: She was late because her car broke down.
example_3: Because it was raining, the game was cancelled.
collocations: because of, just because, simply because
where_it_s_used: Explaining reasons, answering "why" questions, everyday speech
grammar_pattern: result + because + reason (I'm happy because I passed.)
common_mistake: Because it was cold, so I wore a coat.
correct_version: Because it was cold, I wore a coat.
why_it_s_wrong: Don't use 'because' and 'so' together.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: bi-KUZ.
spelling_tip: Watch the ending -- "-cause," not "-cuz" or "-cos" (those are informal spellings only used in texting).
etymology: From Middle English "by cause" -- literally "by the cause of," later fused into a single word.
mnemonic: BE + CAUSE = literally "the CAUSE" behind something -- it answers the question "why?"
memory_trick: BECAUSE = the reason why.
visual_association: An arrow pointing from a cause straight to its effect.
difference_explained: Same for reasons. Since is more formal and also means 'from a time'.
mini_conversation:
A: Why are you smiling?
B: Because I just got some great news!
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character explains, "I came back because I couldn't leave things unfinished."
news_style_line: News-style: "The flight was cancelled because of a technical fault."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I'm calling because I need your advice."
mcq_options: A) Show a result  B) Give a reason  C) Show contrast  D) Offer a choice
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: She missed the bus ______ she woke up late. → because
find_and_fix_to_correct: I am tired because I didn't slept well. → I am tired because I didn't sleep well.
translate: मैं देर से आया क्योंकि ट्रैफिक बहुत था। → I came late because there was a lot of traffic.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence starting 'Because…'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'used to give the reason for something'?
usage_tip: 'Because' alone as an answer is informal: 'Why? — Because.'

simple_explanation: From a particular time until now, or used to give a reason. "Since" can point to a moment in the past that something has continued from, or it can quietly explain why something is true, similar to "because."
example_2: Since it's your birthday, dinner is on me.
example_3: She's been studying since morning.
collocations: since then, ever since, since when
where_it_s_used: Talking about duration, giving casual reasons, life updates
grammar_pattern: since + point in time (I've worked here since 2020.) or since + reason clause
common_mistake: I know him since five years.
correct_version: I have known him for five years.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Since' + a starting point; 'for' + a length of time. Use the present perfect.
pronunciation_tip: One syllable: /sɪns/ -- the "s" at the end is soft, not a "z" sound.
spelling_tip: Five letters -- don't drop the final "e."
etymology: From Old English "siððan" (after that), which developed both a time meaning ("from then until now") and a reason meaning ("given that").
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- from Old English "siððan"
word_family: no direct related forms -- functions as both a time and a reason conjunction
mnemonic: SINCE marks a starting point in time -- like a clock that started ticking and hasn't stopped SINCE.
memory_trick: SINCE 2020 (a point). FOR 5 years (a length).
visual_association: A timeline with a pin marking the exact starting point.
emotion_feel: Neutral -- can carry nostalgia in the time sense
difference_explained: Since + start point (since Monday). For + length (for three days).
mini_conversation:
A: How long have you two been friends?
B: Since we were in school together.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character reflects, "Nothing's felt the same since that summer."
news_style_line: News-style: "Since the new law passed, applications have tripled."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Since you're free tonight, want to grab dinner?"
mcq_options: A) A choice  B) A starting point in time or a reason  C) A contrast  D) A result only
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: He's been waiting ______ nine o'clock. → since
find_and_fix_to_correct: I haven't seen her since two weeks. → I haven't seen her for two weeks.
translate: जब से वह यहाँ आया है, वह बहुत खुश है। → Since he came here, he has been very happy.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence with 'since' + a year.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'from a particular time until now, or used to give a reason'?
usage_tip: 'Since' also means 'because': 'Since it's late, let's go.'

simple_explanation: Except if; only if something does not happen. "Unless" sets up one exception -- the main thing will happen, EXCEPT if the condition after "unless" comes true.
example_1: We'll go hiking unless it rains.
example_2: You won't pass unless you study.
example_3: Unless something changes, the meeting is at 5 PM.
collocations: unless otherwise stated, unless absolutely necessary, unless told
related_phrasal_verbs: except if, only if, if not
grammar_pattern: main clause + unless + condition (I'll wait unless you tell me not to.)
common_mistake: Unless you don't hurry, you'll miss the bus.
correct_version: Unless you hurry, you'll miss the bus.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Unless' already means 'if not', so don't add another negative.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second syllable: uhn-LESS.
spelling_tip: "Un" + "less" -- two familiar pieces joined into one word.
etymology: From Middle English "on lesse (than)" -- literally "on a lesser condition than," which narrowed to mean "except if."
prefix_root_suffix: un- (not, historically) + less (root, to a smaller degree) -- together meaning "except on a lesser condition"
word_family: less (adj./adv.) -- no other close related forms
mnemonic: UNLESS = "un-" (not) + "less" -- think "this happens, UNLESS one thing makes it LESS likely."
memory_trick: UNLESS = IF NOT.
visual_association: A locked gate that opens only for one specific key.
difference_explained: Unless you hurry = if you don't hurry. Same meaning; 'unless' is shorter.
mini_conversation:
A: Should I bring an umbrella?
B: Not unless the forecast changes.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A guard warns, "Nobody gets past this gate, unless they have the code."
news_style_line: News-style: "The factory will close unless new investment arrives by June."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I'm not going unless you come with me."
mcq_options: A) Because  B) Except if / if not  C) Although  D) So that
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: You can't enter ______ you have a ticket. → unless
find_and_fix_to_correct: Unless it's not raining, we'll go to the beach. → Unless it rains, we'll go to the beach.
translate: जब तक तुम मेहनत नहीं करोगे, तुम सफल नहीं होगे। → You won't succeed unless you work hard.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a warning using 'unless'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'except if; only if something does not happen'?
usage_tip: 'Unless' is common in warnings: 'Unless you study, you'll fail.'

simple_explanation: During the same time as something else, or to show a contrast. "While" links two actions happening at once, or it points out how two things differ from each other.
example_1: She read while he cooked dinner.
example_2: While I was studying, my phone kept buzzing.
example_3: He likes tea, while she prefers coffee.
collocations: while waiting, while doing, meanwhile
related_phrasal_verbs: whereas, during, at the same time as
grammar_pattern: while + clause, main clause (While he slept, she worked.)
common_mistake: While I am cooking dinner yesterday, he called.
correct_version: While I was cooking dinner yesterday, he called.
why_it_s_wrong: For a past action in progress, use the past continuous with 'while'.
etymology: From Old English "hwil" (a period of time) -- originally a noun meaning "a while," later grammaticalized into a time/contrast conjunction.
prefix_root_suffix: while (root, from Old English "hwil," a span of time)
word_family: meanwhile (adv.), a while (noun phrase, "a short time")
mnemonic: WHILE = a slice of time -- picture two clocks ticking together during the same "while."
memory_trick: WHILE = during the time that.
visual_association: Two clock hands moving together, side by side.
difference_explained: While + clause (while I was cooking). During + noun (during dinner).
mini_conversation:
A: What were you doing while I was out?
B: I was cleaning the kitchen, mostly.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A voiceover says, "While the city slept, one detective never stopped working."
news_style_line: News-style: "While inflation eased slightly, food prices remained high."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Can you watch the kids while I run to the store?"
mcq_options: A) A reason  B) Two things happening at the same time (or a contrast)  C) A result  D) A choice
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: ______ she was driving, she listened to a podcast. → While
find_and_fix_to_correct: While he was young, but he was very wise. → While he was young, he was very wise.
translate: जब वह खाना बना रही थी, मैं टीवी देख रहा था। → While she was cooking, I was watching TV.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence using 'while I was…'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'during the same time as something else, or to show a contrast'?
usage_tip: 'While' can also show contrast: 'While I like tea, I prefer coffee.'

simple_explanation: Used to compare two facts that are different from each other. "Whereas" points out a clear difference between two things, usually placing them right next to each other for comparison.
example_1: He is tall, whereas his brother is short.
example_2: Sales rose in the north, whereas they fell in the south.
example_3: Whereas I prefer mornings, my sister loves late nights.
collocations: whereas in fact, whereas previously, whereas normally
related_phrasal_verbs: while, on the other hand, in contrast
where_it_s_used: Formal writing, legal documents, statistical comparisons
grammar_pattern: clause A, whereas clause B (Prices rose here, whereas they fell there.)
common_mistake: Whereas he is rich, but he lives simply.
correct_version: Whereas he is rich, he lives simply.
why_it_s_wrong: Don't add 'but' after 'whereas'.
spelling_tip: "Where" + "as" -- both familiar words joined into one.
etymology: From Middle English "where" + "as" -- originally a legal term meaning "considering that," now used to highlight contrast between two facts.
word_family: where (adv./conj.), as (conj.) -- combined into a formal fixed form
mnemonic: WHEREAS puts two facts on a scale -- WHERE one side goes up, AS the other goes down.
memory_trick: WHEREAS = while on the other hand.
visual_association: A balanced scale with two clearly different weights on each side.
difference_explained: Same meaning for contrast. Whereas is more formal.
mini_conversation:
A: How do the two teams compare?
B: Our team focuses on defense, whereas theirs focuses on speed.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A narrator compares two characters: "He chased fame, whereas she chased peace of mind."
news_style_line: News-style: "Urban areas saw growth, whereas rural regions reported a decline."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I like spicy food, whereas my roommate can't handle any heat at all."
mcq_options: A) Add a similar point  B) Contrast two facts  C) Give a reason  D) State a condition
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The first design was expensive, ______ the second one was affordable. → whereas
find_and_fix_to_correct: Whereas she works hard, but she rarely gets recognized. → Whereas she works hard, she rarely gets recognized.
translate: मुझे चाय पसंद है, जबकि उसे कॉफी पसंद है। → I like tea, whereas she likes coffee.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence comparing two people using 'whereas'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'used to compare two facts that are different from each other'?
usage_tip: 'Whereas' is formal and common in comparisons and legal writing.

simple_explanation: Used to introduce a condition or possibility. "If" sets up a condition -- it tells you what needs to happen first before the rest of the sentence becomes true.
example_1: If it rains, we'll stay inside.
example_2: If you need help, just ask.
example_3: She would travel more if she had the money.
collocations: if possible, if necessary, if so, even if
related_phrasal_verbs: provided that, as long as, on condition that
grammar_pattern: if + condition, result (If you study, you'll pass.)
common_mistake: If it will rain, we will stay home.
correct_version: If it rains, we will stay home.
why_it_s_wrong: After 'if', use the present tense for a future meaning.
pronunciation_tip: Short and simple: /ɪf/, rhymes with "stiff" minus the "st."
spelling_tip: Just two letters -- one of the shortest and most useful words in English.
etymology: From Old English "gif," a core conditional word present since the earliest English texts, introducing possible or hypothetical situations.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- a short, ancient conditional word
word_family: no direct related word forms -- "if" is a basic function word
mnemonic: IF opens a door to a possibility -- IF this happens, then that follows.
memory_trick: IF + present, WILL + verb: 'If it rains, we will stay.'
visual_association: A branching path splitting into two possible directions.
emotion_feel: Neutral -- can carry hope, doubt, or caution depending on context
difference_explained: If = condition. Whether = choice between two ('I don't know whether to go').
mini_conversation:
A: What will you do if you win the prize?
B: If I win, I'll donate half of it.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A mentor advises, "If you truly want this, prove it tomorrow."
news_style_line: News-style: "If approved, the new bridge could open by next spring."
casual_conversation: Casual: "If you're free later, let's catch up over coffee."
mcq_options: A) A contrast  B) A condition or possibility  C) A result  D) A reason
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: ______ you finish early, call me. → If
find_and_fix_to_correct: If I will see him, I will tell him. → If I see him, I will tell him.
translate: अगर तुम मेहनत करोगे, तो तुम सफल होगे। → If you work hard, you will succeed.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence starting 'If it rains tomorrow,…'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'used to introduce a condition or possibility'?
usage_tip: First conditional: real future possibility.

simple_explanation: Up to the time when something happens; before a specific point. "Until" tells you how long something continues -- it marks the moment things change or stop.
example_2: She worked until midnight.
example_3: Don't eat until everyone is seated.
collocations: until now, until then, wait until
grammar_pattern: action + until + point in time (Stay until the rain stops.)
common_mistake: I will stay here until when you come.
correct_version: I will stay here until you come.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Until' already means 'up to the time when', so 'when' is extra.
etymology: From Old Norse "und" (as far as) + "til" (to) -- both parts meaning "up to a point," combined in Middle English.
prefix_root_suffix: un- (as far as) + til (to) -- together meaning "up to"
mnemonic: UNTIL is a countdown -- the action continues UNTIL the clock hits that moment.
memory_trick: UNTIL = up to that time.
visual_association: A finish-line tape stretched across a track, marking the stopping point.
emotion_feel: Neutral -- can add tension or patience depending on the wait
difference_explained: Until = continuing up to (wait until 5). By = deadline (finish by 5).
mini_conversation:
A: How long should I keep the oven on?
B: Until the top turns golden brown.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character vows, "I won't rest until I find the truth."
news_style_line: News-style: "The road will remain closed until repairs are complete."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I'm free until about six, then I have plans."
mcq_options: A) A reason  B) A point up to which something continues  C) A contrast  D) A choice
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Please stay quiet ______ the meeting ends. → until
find_and_fix_to_correct: I lived there until 2018 since two years. → I lived there until 2018.
translate: जब तक बारिश नहीं रुकती, हम यहीं रुकेंगे। → We will wait here until the rain stops.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence using 'until' with a future event.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'up to the time when something happens; before a specific point'?
usage_tip: 'Until further notice' = until you are told otherwise.

simple_explanation: Used to say at what time or under what circumstances something happens. "When" connects an action to the specific moment or situation it happens in.
example_2: When the bell rings, class starts.
example_3: I was cooking when the phone rang.
collocations: when possible, when necessary, since when
related_phrasal_verbs: as soon as, at the time, the moment that
grammar_pattern: when + clause, main clause (When it rains, I stay in.)
common_mistake: When I will finish, I will call you.
correct_version: When I finish, I will call you.
why_it_s_wrong: After 'when', use the present tense for the future, not 'will'.
pronunciation_tip: Rhymes with "ten" and "pen": /wɛn/, with a light "wh" sound.
spelling_tip: "Wh" + "en" -- don't confuse with "went" (the past tense of go).
etymology: From Old English "hwænne," a core question/time word present since the earliest English, used both as a question word and a conjunction.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- a core "wh-" time word
mnemonic: WHEN is a clock hand pointing to the exact moment something happens.
memory_trick: WHEN + present, WILL + verb.
visual_association: A clock hand landing exactly on a marked hour.
emotion_feel: Neutral -- can build anticipation depending on context
difference_explained: When = it will happen. If = it may happen.
mini_conversation:
A: When does the movie start?
B: When the ads finish, I think.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character whispers, "I knew, the moment I saw you, when everything would change."
news_style_line: News-style: "Officials will announce the results when the count is complete."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Text me when you're on your way."
mcq_options: A) A reason  B) A specific time or circumstance  C) A contrast  D) A choice
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: ______ the sun sets, the sky turns orange. → When
find_and_fix_to_correct: When I was young, I lived in a big house since then. → When I was young, I lived in a big house.
translate: जब बारिश होती है, मुझे चाय पीना पसंद है। → When it rains, I like to drink tea.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence starting 'When I finish…'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'used to say at what time or under what circumstances something happens'?
usage_tip: 'When' introduces time; 'if' introduces a condition that may not happen.

simple_explanation: At any time that; every time that. "Whenever" says something happens every single time a certain condition is true, not just once.
example_1: Whenever I'm stressed, I go for a walk.
example_2: Call me whenever you need help.
example_3: Whenever it rains, the road floods.
collocations: whenever possible, whenever needed, whenever you like
related_phrasal_verbs: every time, each time, no matter when
where_it_s_used: Habits, routines, offers of help, recurring events
grammar_pattern: whenever + clause, main clause (Whenever he calls, I answer.)
common_mistake: Whenever I will be free, I will visit you.
correct_version: Whenever I am free, I will visit you.
why_it_s_wrong: After 'whenever', use the present tense even for future meaning.
pronunciation_tip: Three syllables: wen-EV-er, stress on the middle syllable.
spelling_tip: "When" + "ever" joined into one word -- not two separate words.
etymology: From "when" + "ever" (Old English "æfre," always) -- literally "at any time when," emphasizing every occasion.
mnemonic: WHENEVER = WHEN + EVER -- "at any time, ever, that this happens."
memory_trick: WHENEVER = every time that.
visual_association: A door that's always unlocked, ready to open at any moment.
emotion_feel: Neutral -- can feel reassuring or open-ended
difference_explained: When = one time. Whenever = every time, or any time.
mini_conversation:
A: When should I come over?
B: Whenever suits you, honestly.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A mentor says, "Whenever you doubt yourself, remember why you started."
news_style_line: News-style: "Whenever demand spikes, prices tend to rise quickly."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Whenever you're ready, just let me know."
mcq_options: A) One specific time  B) At any/every time that  C) Never  D) Before
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: ______ I hear that song, I think of summer. → Whenever
find_and_fix_to_correct: Whenever you wants, we can start. → Whenever you want, we can start.
translate: जब भी मुझे समय मिलता है, मैं किताबें पढ़ता हूँ। → Whenever I get time, I read books.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence starting 'Whenever I feel tired,…'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'at any time that; every time that'?
usage_tip: 'Whenever you're ready' = no rush.

simple_explanation: Earlier than a particular time or event. "Before" tells you which action or event comes first -- it happens earlier than the other one mentioned.
example_1: Wash your hands before you eat.
example_2: Before I leave, I need to lock the door.
example_3: She checked her email before the meeting.
collocations: before long, the day before, just before
related_phrasal_verbs: prior to, earlier than, in advance of
grammar_pattern: before + clause/noun, main clause (Before you go, take an umbrella.)
common_mistake: Before you will leave, call me.
correct_version: Before you leave, call me.
why_it_s_wrong: After 'before', use the present tense for the future.
etymology: From Old English "beforan" (be- + foran, "in front") -- originally spatial, extended to mean earlier in time.
prefix_root_suffix: be- (near/by) + fore (root, front) -- "in front of, earlier"
mnemonic: BEFORE = "be" in "FRONT" (fore) of something in time.
memory_trick: BEFORE + present: 'Before you leave, call me.'
visual_association: A calendar page flipped back to an earlier date.
difference_explained: Before = earlier than something. Ago = back from now (two days ago).
mini_conversation:
A: Should I book the tickets now?
B: Yes, before prices go up.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A mentor warns, "Think twice before you make that promise."
news_style_line: News-style: "Inspectors checked the bridge before it reopened to traffic."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Let's grab coffee before the meeting starts."
mcq_options: A) A later time  B) An earlier time  C) A reason  D) A result
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Please knock ______ entering the room. → before
find_and_fix_to_correct: Before I leaving, I said goodbye. → Before I left, I said goodbye.
translate: खाना खाने से पहले अपने हाथ धो लो। → Wash your hands before you eat.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence starting 'Before you leave,…'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'earlier than a particular time or event'?
usage_tip: 'Before' is also a preposition: 'before lunch'.

simple_explanation: Later than a particular time or event. "After" tells you which action or event comes second -- it happens once the first one is finished.
example_2: After she finished her homework, she watched TV.
example_3: Call me after you land.
collocations: after all, shortly after, right after
grammar_pattern: after + clause/noun, main clause (After the storm passed, we went outside.)
common_mistake: After I will finish work, I will call you.
correct_version: After I finish work, I will call you.
why_it_s_wrong: After 'after', use the present tense for the future.
etymology: From Old English "æfter" (behind, later) -- related to "aft," the back part of a ship, extended to mean later in time.
prefix_root_suffix: af- (intensifying variant) + ter (root, related to "aft," behind) -- "coming behind in time"
mnemonic: AFTER comes AFT (behind) in the timeline -- it's what follows.
memory_trick: AFTER + present: 'After I finish, I'll call.'
visual_association: A finish line crossed, with the next event starting just beyond it.
difference_explained: After + clause or noun (after lunch). Afterwards alone (we ate afterwards).
mini_conversation:
A: When can we talk?
B: After lunch works for me.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A narrator says, "After the war ended, nothing looked quite the same."
news_style_line: News-style: "After months of delay, construction finally began this week."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Let's catch up after work today."
mcq_options: A) An earlier time  B) A later time  C) A reason  D) A condition
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: She felt relieved ______ the exam was over. → after
find_and_fix_to_correct: After I will eat, I will sleep. → After I eat, I will sleep.
translate: खाना खाने के बाद, हम टहलने गए। → After eating, we went for a walk.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence starting 'After I finish work,…'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'later than a particular time or event'?
usage_tip: 'Afterwards' = later, at the end of a sentence.

simple_explanation: Used to show time, reason, or comparison, depending on context. "As" can describe two things happening together in time, explain a reason, or compare how something is done.
example_2: As I was leaving, it started to rain.
example_3: As you know, the meeting is tomorrow.
collocations: as well, as usual, as soon as, as long as
where_it_s_used: Comparisons, simultaneous actions, giving known reasons
grammar_pattern: as + clause, main clause (As the sun rose, the birds sang.)
common_mistake: As I was busy, so I didn't call.
correct_version: As I was busy, I didn't call.
why_it_s_wrong: Don't use 'as' (reason) and 'so' together.
pronunciation_tip: A short, relaxed vowel: /æz/, like "has" without the h.
spelling_tip: Just two letters -- don't confuse with "has" (a verb).
etymology: From Old English "eallswa" (all so, just so), shortened over time to "as" -- one of English's most flexible small words, used for time, reason, and comparison.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- a short, ancient comparison/time word
word_family: no direct related word forms -- "as" is a basic, multi-purpose function word
mnemonic: AS is a Swiss Army knife word -- it can mean "while," "because," or "like," depending on the sentence.
memory_trick: AS = because (formal).
visual_association: Two paths running perfectly parallel, side by side.
difference_explained: As + clause or role (as a teacher). Like + noun for similarity (like a teacher).
mini_conversation:
A: Why didn't you call?
B: As you were busy, I didn't want to bother you.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A narrator intones, "As the clock struck midnight, everything began to change."
news_style_line: News-style: "As expected, the central bank raised interest rates today."
casual_conversation: Casual: "As I mentioned earlier, the flight got delayed."
mcq_options: A) Only contrast  B) Time, reason, or comparison  C) Only a condition  D) Only a choice
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: ______ the years passed, the town grew larger. → As
find_and_fix_to_correct: As I was young, I loved music, but I still do now, however. → As I was young, I loved music, and I still do now.
translate: जैसे ही मैं घर पहुँचा, फोन बजने लगा। → As soon as I reached home, the phone started ringing.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence starting 'As it was late,…'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'used to show time, reason, or comparison, depending on context'?
usage_tip: 'As' also means 'like' or 'when': 'as a child', 'as I walked in'.

simple_explanation: Used to describe something that seems true but probably isn't. "As if" compares a real situation to an imagined or unlikely one -- it describes how something appears or feels, not necessarily how it truly is.
example_1: She looked as if she had seen a ghost.
example_2: He talks as if he knows everything.
example_3: It feels as if summer will never end.
collocations: as if by magic, act as if, look as if
grammar_pattern: as if + past tense (unreal comparison) (She spoke as if she knew the answer.)
common_mistake: He talks as if he is the boss, but he isn't.
correct_version: He talks as if he were the boss.
why_it_s_wrong: For an unreal comparison in formal English, use 'were': 'as if he were the boss'.
spelling_tip: Two separate words -- never combined as "asif."
etymology: From "as" + "if," combined in Middle English to introduce an imagined or unreal comparison.
prefix_root_suffix: as (comparison marker) + if (conditional marker) -- combined for a hypothetical comparison
mnemonic: AS IF = "AS" it would be, "IF" it were true (but it probably isn't).
memory_trick: AS IF = pretending or imagining.
visual_association: A mirror reflecting an image slightly different from reality.
difference_explained: As if + clause (as if he were the boss). 'Like' + clause is informal.
mini_conversation:
A: Why is he smiling like that?
B: He looks as if he just won something.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character stares blankly, as if the words hadn't reached her yet.
news_style_line: News-style: "Markets reacted as if the announcement had already been made."
casual_conversation: Casual: "You're acting as if nothing happened -- are you okay?"
mcq_options: A) Something certainly true  B) A comparison to something imagined or unlikely  C) A simple reason  D) A time sequence
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: He speaks ______ he were the expert in the room. → as if
find_and_fix_to_correct: She looked as if she is tired. → She looked as if she were tired.
translate: वह ऐसे बात कर रहा था मानो उसे सब कुछ पता हो। → He was talking as if he knew everything.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence using 'as if' about someone's behaviour.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'used to describe something that seems true but probably isn't'?
usage_tip: In speech, 'as if he was' is also common.

simple_explanation: Used to explain the purpose or goal of an action. "So that" tells you WHY someone did something -- what result they were hoping to achieve.
example_1: I saved money so that I could travel.
example_2: She studied hard so that she could pass the exam.
example_3: He whispered so that no one would hear.
collocations: so that everyone can, so that we could, so that it works
related_phrasal_verbs: in order that, in order to, with the aim of
grammar_pattern: action + so that + purpose clause (I called so that she would know.)
common_mistake: I study hard so that to pass the exam.
correct_version: I study hard so that I can pass the exam.
why_it_s_wrong: 'So that' needs a full clause with a subject and verb.
pronunciation_tip: Two clear words: so that, with a slight stress on "that."
spelling_tip: Two separate words -- don't confuse with "so" alone, which shows result, not purpose.
etymology: From "so" (in such a way) + "that," combined to introduce a purpose or intended result.
prefix_root_suffix: so (root, in such a way) + that (linking conjunction)
mnemonic: SO THAT tells you the GOAL -- "I did this SO THAT [goal] could happen."
memory_trick: SO THAT + subject + can/could.
visual_association: An arrow drawn from an action straight to its intended goal.
difference_explained: So that = purpose (study so that I can pass). So = result (I studied, so I passed).
related_words: purpose, goal, intention, in order to
mini_conversation:
A: Why did you leave a note?
B: So that you'd know where I went.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A spy whispers, "I did it so that you'd never have to."
news_style_line: News-style: "The bridge was widened so that traffic could flow more smoothly."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I'm writing this down so that I don't forget."
mcq_options: A) A result  B) A purpose or goal  C) A contrast  D) A condition
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: She spoke slowly ______ everyone could understand. → so that
find_and_fix_to_correct: He locked the door so that to keep it safe. → He locked the door so that it would be safe.
translate: उसने जल्दी खाना खाया ताकि वह समय पर पहुँच सके। → He ate quickly so that he could arrive on time.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence using 'so that I can…'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'used to explain the purpose or goal of an action'?
usage_tip: 'In order to' + verb is a shorter option: 'in order to pass'.

simple_explanation: Used to introduce a contrast with the previous sentence. "However" signals that what follows goes against or qualifies what was just said, usually starting a new sentence.
example_1: I was tired. However, I kept working.
example_2: The plan sounded good. However, it had one major flaw.
example_3: She agreed to help; however, she had conditions.
collocations: however, however hard, however much
related_phrasal_verbs: but, nevertheless, on the other hand
where_it_s_used: Essays, reports, formal speech, presenting two sides
grammar_pattern: Sentence one. However, sentence two. (contrast between two independent sentences)
common_mistake: I like the plan, however I have one concern.
correct_version: I like the plan. However, I have one concern.
why_it_s_wrong: Use a full stop or semicolon before 'however', and a comma after it.
etymology: From "how" + "ever" -- originally meaning "in whatever way," later narrowed to introduce a contrast between sentences.
prefix_root_suffix: how (root, manner/question word) + -ever (suffix, emphasizing "in any way")
mnemonic: HOWEVER is a formal "but" that needs its own sentence -- picture it standing alone, followed by a comma.
memory_trick: HOWEVER: . However, … (full stop, capital, comma).
visual_association: A pause button pressed right before the sentence changes direction.
difference_explained: But joins two clauses in one sentence. However starts a new sentence (formal).
mini_conversation:
A: So the trip is confirmed?
B: Mostly, yes. However, the dates might still change.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A narrator concludes, "He seemed calm. However, something in his eyes said otherwise."
news_style_line: News-style: "The economy grew this quarter. However, analysts warn the pace may slow."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I really want to go. However, I'm not sure I can afford it."
mcq_options: A) Add a similar point  B) Introduce a contrast between sentences  C) Give a reason  D) State a result
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The food was expensive. ______, it was absolutely delicious. → However
find_and_fix_to_correct: She was nervous, however she gave a great speech. → She was nervous; however, she gave a great speech.
translate: मौसम खराब था। हालांकि, हमने यात्रा रद्द नहीं की। → The weather was bad. However, we didn't cancel the trip.
write_your_own_sentence: Write two sentences linked with 'However,'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'used to introduce a contrast with the previous sentence'?
usage_tip: 'However' can also mean 'in whatever way': 'However you do it, be careful.'

simple_explanation: Used to introduce a logical result or conclusion. "Therefore" shows that what comes next is the logical outcome of what was just stated -- like a formal "so."
example_1: It was late. Therefore, we went home.
example_2: The data was incomplete; therefore, the results are uncertain.
example_3: He missed the deadline. Therefore, his application was rejected.
collocations: and therefore, therefore concluded, therefore necessary
grammar_pattern: Statement. Therefore, conclusion. (formal cause-and-effect link)
common_mistake: Because it rained, therefore we stayed inside.
correct_version: It rained. Therefore, we stayed inside.
why_it_s_wrong: Don't use 'because' and 'therefore' together.
etymology: From Middle English "ther(e)fore" ("there" + "for," meaning "for that reason") -- literally pointing back to a cause already mentioned.
prefix_root_suffix: there (pointing back) + fore (variant of "for," reason) -- "for that (reason)"
mnemonic: THERE-FORE points back "there" (to the reason) and gives you the result "for" it.
memory_trick: THEREFORE = for that reason.
visual_association: An equals sign at the end of a math equation, pointing to the answer.
difference_explained: Same meaning. Therefore is formal; so is everyday.
mini_conversation:
A: The numbers don't add up.
B: Therefore, we need to recheck the entire report.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A scientist announces, "The results are conclusive. Therefore, our theory holds."
news_style_line: News-style: "Inflation remains high; therefore, interest rates are unlikely to fall soon."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I didn't study. Therefore, I'm a bit worried about the test."
mcq_options: A) A contrast  B) A logical result or conclusion  C) An exception  D) A choice
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The bridge was unsafe. ______, it was closed to traffic. → Therefore
find_and_fix_to_correct: He was late, therefore he missed but the bus. → He was late; therefore, he missed the bus.
translate: उसने बहुत मेहनत की, इसलिए वह सफल हुआ। → He worked very hard; therefore, he succeeded.
write_your_own_sentence: Write two sentences linked with 'Therefore,'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'used to introduce a logical result or conclusion'?
usage_tip: Common in maths and logic: 'Therefore, x = 5.'

simple_explanation: Used to add an additional, often important, point. "Moreover" introduces one more piece of evidence or information that strengthens the point already made.
example_1: The plan is risky. Moreover, it's expensive.
example_2: The product is well made. Moreover, it comes with a warranty.
example_3: She is talented; moreover, she works incredibly hard.
collocations: moreover, it should be noted, moreover, this suggests
where_it_s_used: Academic writing, essays, formal arguments, reports
grammar_pattern: Statement. Moreover, additional statement. (formal addition of supporting information)
common_mistake: Moreover than this, the house is old.
correct_version: Moreover, the house is old.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Moreover' stands alone, followed by a comma.
etymology: From "more" + "over" -- literally "further, in addition," combined in Middle English to add extra supporting information.
mnemonic: MORE-OVER = there's MORE to say, OVER and above what was already mentioned.
memory_trick: MOREOVER = MORE + OVER: adding more.
visual_association: A second brick placed firmly on top of the first, strengthening the wall.
difference_explained: Same idea. Moreover is formal and adds a stronger point.
mini_conversation:
A: Is this candidate a good fit?
B: Definitely. Moreover, she has exactly the experience we need.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A lawyer states, "The evidence is clear. Moreover, the witness confirms it."
news_style_line: News-style: "The bridge is structurally sound. Moreover, repairs were completed ahead of schedule."
casual_conversation: Casual: "This apartment is affordable. Moreover, it's close to my office."
mcq_options: A) Show a contrast  B) Add a further supporting point  C) Give a result  D) State an exception
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The hotel was clean and quiet. ______, the staff were very friendly. → Moreover
find_and_fix_to_correct: She is kind, moreover she is generous, but. → She is kind. Moreover, she is generous.
translate: यह घर सुंदर है। इसके अलावा, यह बाज़ार के पास भी है। → This house is beautiful. Moreover, it is also close to the market.
write_your_own_sentence: Write two sentences linked with 'Moreover,'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'used to add an additional, often important, point'?
usage_tip: Formal writing: essays, reports.

simple_explanation: Used to say something is still true despite what was just said. "Nevertheless" shows that, despite an obstacle or problem just mentioned, the result stays the same -- similar to "but still."
example_1: It was raining. Nevertheless, we went for a run.
example_2: The odds were against them; nevertheless, they won.
example_3: He was exhausted. Nevertheless, he finished the marathon.
collocations: nevertheless, it remains true, nevertheless important
where_it_s_used: Formal writing, speeches, persistence stories, reports
grammar_pattern: Statement (obstacle). Nevertheless, statement (result unaffected). (formal contrast)
common_mistake: Although it was hard, nevertheless he gave up.
correct_version: Although it was hard, he nevertheless didn't give up.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Nevertheless' shows the opposite of what you'd expect: he did NOT give up.
pronunciation_tip: Four syllables: nev-er-the-LESS, stress on the last syllable.
spelling_tip: "Never" + "the" + "less" -- three familiar words joined into one.
etymology: From "never" + "the" + "less" -- literally "not the less for it," meaning something remains true despite an obstacle.
prefix_root_suffix: never (root) + the + less (root, to a smaller degree) -- "not any less true for it"
mnemonic: NEVERTHELESS = "never the less" -- the outcome is NEVER any LESS true, despite the obstacle.
memory_trick: NEVER-THE-LESS: not any less because of it.
visual_association: A small boat sailing steadily through a storm.
difference_explained: Similar. Nevertheless stresses 'in spite of that'.
mini_conversation:
A: The weather looks terrible for the hike.
B: Nevertheless, I think we should still go.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A general states, "The odds are grim. Nevertheless, we fight on."
