simple_explanation: Used to say what will happen if something doesn't happen. "Otherwise" warns of a different, usually less desirable, result if the first thing doesn't happen.
example_1: Hurry up, otherwise we'll be late.
example_2: Take an umbrella; otherwise, you'll get wet.
example_3: Study tonight, otherwise you won't be ready for the test.
collocations: or otherwise, otherwise known as, otherwise busy
related_phrasal_verbs: or else, if not, if that doesn't happen
grammar_pattern: Instruction/condition, otherwise + consequence (Leave now, otherwise you'll miss it.)
common_mistake: Hurry up, otherwise if you'll miss the bus.
correct_version: Hurry up, otherwise you'll miss the bus.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Otherwise' already carries the condition, so 'if' is extra.
etymology: From "other" + "wise" (Old English "wise," manner/way) -- literally "in another manner," used to show an alternative outcome.
prefix_root_suffix: other (root, different) + wise (root, in a manner)
mnemonic: OTHERWISE = "the OTHER way" things could go if you don't act now.
memory_trick: OTHERWISE = if not.
visual_association: A fork in the road with a warning sign pointing to the riskier path.
difference_explained: Otherwise follows the action (Hurry, otherwise…). Unless comes before the condition (Unless you hurry…).
related_words: or else, if not, unless, warning

simple_explanation: In the same way; similarly. "Likewise" points out that the same thing is true for someone or something else, or is used to politely echo a greeting.
example_1: She works hard, and her brother does likewise.
example_2: He trained daily, and his teammates did likewise.
example_3: Nice to meet you. -- Likewise!
collocations: and likewise, do likewise, likewise impressed
related_phrasal_verbs: similarly, in the same way, the same goes for
grammar_pattern: Statement. Person/thing, likewise, verb. (or as a short standalone reply, e.g. "Likewise!")
common_mistake: Likewise my brother, I like cricket.
correct_version: Like my brother, I like cricket.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Likewise' is an adverb meaning 'in the same way'. To compare with a person, use 'like'.
etymology: From "like" + "wise" (Old English "wise," manner) -- literally "in a like manner," meaning "in the same way."
prefix_root_suffix: like (root, similar) + wise (root, manner) -- "in a similar manner"
mnemonic: LIKEWISE = in a LIKE (similar) manner/WISE.
memory_trick: LIKEWISE = in a LIKE WAY.
visual_association: Two mirrors reflecting the exact same image back and forth.
difference_explained: Like + noun (like my brother). Likewise alone (She did likewise).
mini_conversation:
A: It was great meeting you.
B: Likewise -- I really enjoyed our chat.

simple_explanation: In a way that is similar to what was just described. "Similarly" is used to introduce a fact, example, or situation that closely matches the one just mentioned.
example_1: He studies every evening. Similarly, his sister studies at night too.
example_2: Sales grew in Europe. Similarly, Asian markets showed strong growth.
example_3: The first test was hard; similarly, the second one required a lot of preparation.
collocations: similarly, in other regions, similarly structured, similarly affected
related_phrasal_verbs: likewise, in the same way, equally
grammar_pattern: Statement one. Similarly, statement two. (formal comparison between two facts)
common_mistake: Similarly like his father, he is tall.
correct_version: Like his father, he is tall.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Similarly' and 'like' together repeat the idea.
etymology: From "similar" (Latin "similis," like) + "-ly" (adverb suffix) -- literally "in a like manner."
mnemonic: SIMILARLY signals a SIMILAR point coming right up.
memory_trick: SIMILAR-LY: in a SIMILAR way.
visual_association: Two identical shapes placed side by side on a page.
difference_explained: Same meaning. Similarly is more common in writing.
related_words: likewise, equally, comparably, in the same way
mini_conversation:
A: How did the two teams perform?
B: The first team improved steadily. Similarly, the second team made great progress.

news_style_line: News-style: "House prices rose sharply downtown. Similarly, suburban prices climbed at a steady pace."

mcq_options: A) Show a contrast  B) Introduce a comparable point  C) Give a reason  D) State a condition

write_your_own_sentence: Write two sentences linked with 'Similarly,'.

usage_tip: 'Similarly' links two sentences with the same idea.

simple_explanation: As a direct result of something. "Consequently" links a cause to its effect -- it tells you what happened because of the situation described before it.
example_1: He missed the bus. Consequently, he was late for work.
example_2: The factory closed; consequently, hundreds lost their jobs.
example_3: Demand fell sharply. Consequently, prices dropped.
collocations: and consequently, consequently resulted in, consequently affected
grammar_pattern: Cause. Consequently, effect. (formal cause-and-effect link)
common_mistake: Because he was late, consequently he missed the meeting.
correct_version: He was late. Consequently, he missed the meeting.
why_it_s_wrong: Don't use 'because' and 'consequently' together.
etymology: From "consequent" (Latin "consequi," to follow closely) + "-ly" -- literally "following as a result."
prefix_root_suffix: con- (together) + sequ (root, from Latin "sequi," to follow) + -ent/-ly (suffixes)
mnemonic: CONSEQUENTLY = the CONSEQUENCE that followed, stated plainly.
memory_trick: CONSEQUENCE-LY: as a CONSEQUENCE.
visual_association: One domino toppling a whole line of others in sequence.
difference_explained: Same meaning. Consequently is formal.
related_words: therefore, thus, hence, as a result

A: Why was the flight cancelled?
B: The storm hit the runway. Consequently, all flights were grounded.

mcq_options: A) A contrast  B) A direct result  C) An example  D) A condition

usage_tip: Formal: reports and essays.

simple_explanation: In this way; as a result of what was just said. "Thus" shows a conclusion or result, or describes the manner in which something was done -- a short, formal connector.
example_1: The bridge was closed; thus, traffic was diverted.
example_2: The data was flawed. Thus, the study was redone.
example_3: She practiced daily, thus improving quickly.
collocations: thus far, thus proving, thus concluding
where_it_s_used: Academic writing, scientific reports, formal conclusions
grammar_pattern: Statement. Thus, conclusion. / verb + thus + gerund (proving the point, thus confirming the theory)
common_mistake: Thus, so the results were accepted.
correct_version: Thus, the results were accepted.
why_it_s_wrong: Don't combine 'thus' and 'so'.
spelling_tip: Just four letters -- don't confuse with "this" (a completely different word).
etymology: From Old English "þus" (in this way) -- one of English's oldest formal connecting words, still used to introduce a result or method.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- from Old English "þus," "in this way"
word_family: no direct related word forms -- "thus" is a basic formal connector
mnemonic: THUS is a short, punchy "therefore" -- one syllable doing the job of a whole phrase.
memory_trick: THUS = so, in this way.
visual_association: A neat conclusion drawn at the bottom of a formal document.
difference_explained: Thus = so / in this way. This = a pronoun.
mini_conversation:
A: How did they solve the puzzle?
B: They worked backward from the answer, thus finding the pattern.

casual_conversation: Casual: "I double-checked every step, thus avoiding any mistakes."

usage_tip: 'Thus' is formal and old-fashioned in speech.

simple_explanation: For this reason; therefore. "Hence" is a short, formal way of saying "therefore" -- it points from a fact or reason straight to its result.
example_1: The bridge is closed; hence the detour.
example_2: Costs rose sharply; hence, the price increase.
example_3: He trained for months, hence his excellent performance.
collocations: hence the name, hence the delay, henceforth
where_it_s_used: Formal writing, business reports, explanations of results
grammar_pattern: Reason; hence, result. (often followed by a short noun phrase, not a full clause)
common_mistake: Hence, therefore, we cancelled the trip.
correct_version: Hence, we cancelled the trip.
why_it_s_wrong: Don't combine 'hence' and 'therefore'.
etymology: From Middle English "hennes" (from here) -- originally meaning "from this place," now meaning "from this fact" or "for this reason."
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- from Middle English "hennes," "from here"
word_family: no direct related word forms -- "hence" is a basic formal connector
mnemonic: HENCE points "from HERE" (this fact) to the conclusion that follows.
memory_trick: HENCE = for this reason (formal).
visual_association: A signpost reading "FROM HERE" pointing straight to a conclusion.
difference_explained: Same meaning. Hence is more formal and can go before a noun: 'hence the delay'.
mini_conversation:
A: Why is the store called 'Old Mill Bakery'?
B: It used to be an old mill -- hence the name.

casual_conversation: Casual: "I was up all night studying, hence the tired eyes."

find_and_fix_to_correct: Hence why, the meeting was postponed. → Hence, the meeting was postponed.

simple_explanation: In a way that matches or fits the situation just described. "Accordingly" shows that an action was adjusted or taken to properly match the facts or instructions just given.
example_1: The rules changed; accordingly, we updated our plans.
example_2: Prices went up, so we adjusted our budget accordingly.
example_3: The weather turned bad; accordingly, the event was moved indoors.
collocations: act accordingly, plan accordingly, adjust accordingly
related_phrasal_verbs: therefore, in response, as a result
grammar_pattern: Fact/instruction. Accordingly, adjusted action. (formal result matching a situation)
common_mistake: Accordingly, therefore, we changed the schedule.
correct_version: Accordingly, we changed the schedule.
why_it_s_wrong: Don't combine 'accordingly' and 'therefore'.
etymology: From "accord" (Old French "acorder," to agree) + "-ing" + "-ly" -- literally "in agreement with" something, now meaning "as a fitting result."
mnemonic: ACCORDINGLY = act "in ACCORD" (agreement) with what was just said.
memory_trick: ACCORDING-LY: ACCORDING to what was said.
visual_association: A compass needle turning to match a new direction.
difference_explained: Accordingly = as a result / suitably. According to = as said by.

simple_explanation: Used to introduce a second idea that is different or opposite from the first. You use "on the other hand" when you've just said one thing and now want to show the opposite side or a different point of view.
example_1: The house is cheap; on the other hand, it needs a lot of repairs.
example_2: I love the city's energy; on the other hand, it's very noisy at night.
example_3: He's talented, but on the other hand, he doesn't work hard enough.
collocations: on the one hand ... on the other hand, but on the other hand
related_phrasal_verbs: on the flip side, then again, having said that
where_it_s_used: Essays, debates, comparing options, weighing pros and cons
grammar_pattern: [Statement 1], on the other hand, [contrasting statement 2].
common_mistake: On other hand, I think we should wait.
correct_version: On the other hand, I think we should wait.
why_it_s_wrong: Don't drop 'the': 'on the other hand'.
pronunciation_tip: Six words said in one smooth breath group, with stress on "OTH-er" and "HAND": on the OTHer HAND.
spelling_tip: Four separate words -- "on," "the," "other," "hand" -- never combined or hyphenated.
etymology: A literal phrase built from "hand" (Old English "hand"), long used to mean "side" or "position" -- "on the other hand" became a standard way in English to introduce a contrasting point.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- a fixed phrase built from ordinary words
word_family: hand (n.), handy (adj.), hands-on (idiom) -- closest related forms only
mnemonic: Picture holding up one hand for your first idea, then the OTHER HAND for the opposite idea.
memory_trick: ON THE OTHER HAND: think of your two hands — two sides.
visual_association: Two open palms held up like a scale, one on each side.
emotion_feel: Neutral -- signals balanced, thoughtful weighing of two sides
confusing_word: on the other hand vs on the contrary
difference_explained: On the other hand = another side (both true). On the contrary = the opposite is true.
mini_conversation:
A: Should we take the night bus or the flight?
B: The bus is cheaper. On the other hand, the flight saves a whole day.

simple_explanation: Used to show a clear difference between two things being compared. You use "in contrast" when you want to point out that something is very different from what was just mentioned.
example_1: The north is cold and dry; in contrast, the south is warm and humid.
example_2: Sales rose sharply in the city stores; in contrast, rural branches saw a decline.
example_3: My brother loves sports; in contrast, I prefer reading.
collocations: in contrast to, in sharp contrast, stand in contrast
related_phrasal_verbs: as opposed to, unlike, by comparison
where_it_s_used: Essays, reports, comparing data, describing differences
grammar_pattern: [Statement 1]; in contrast, [contrasting statement 2]. Also: "in contrast to + noun"
common_mistake: In contrast, she is very similar to her mother.
correct_version: In contrast, she is very different from her mother.
why_it_s_wrong: 'In contrast' must introduce a difference.
pronunciation_tip: Stress the first syllable of "contrast" here: in KON-trast (not con-TRAST, which is the verb form).
spelling_tip: One word "contrast" after "in" -- don't split it into "con trast."
etymology: From Latin "contrastare" (to stand against), via Old French "contraster" -- "contrast" entered English meaning a clear difference, and "in contrast" became a common linking phrase for comparisons.
prefix_root_suffix: in- (part of the fixed phrase) + contrast (root, from Latin "against" + "stand")
mnemonic: IN CONTRAST = you step IN to see the difference, like putting two photos side by side.
memory_trick: CONTRAST = difference.
visual_association: A black-and-white photo placed next to a bright, colorful one.
confusing_word: in contrast vs on the contrary
difference_explained: In contrast = comparing two different things. On the contrary = correcting a wrong idea.
mini_conversation:
A: How was the weather on your trip?
B: The coast was sunny. In contrast, the mountains were freezing.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A detective studies two photographs and mutters, "In contrast, this one was taken years later."
news_style_line: News-style: "In contrast to last year's figures, this quarter shows a steady rise in exports."
casual_conversation: Casual: "My old phone was slow. In contrast, this new one is lightning fast."
mcq_options: A) A similar idea  B) A reason  C) A clear difference  D) A conclusion
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The first chapter is slow; ______, the second is full of action. → in contrast
find_and_fix_to_correct: In contrast his sister works hard. → In contrast, his sister works hard. (add a comma after the introductory phrase)
translate: शहर में जीवन तेज़ है; इसके विपरीत, गाँव में जीवन शांत है। → Life in the city is fast; in contrast, life in the village is peaceful.
write_your_own_sentence: Write two sentences comparing cities with 'In contrast,'.

reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'used to show a clear difference between two things being compared'?
usage_tip: Used in comparisons and essays.

simple_explanation: Used to introduce a specific case that shows what you mean. When you say "for example," you're about to give one clear instance to help explain or support your idea.
example_1: Many fruits are healthy; for example, apples and oranges are full of vitamins.
example_2: Some countries have strict traffic laws; Japan, for example, fines drivers heavily for speeding.
example_3: You can save money in small ways -- for example, by cooking at home more often.
collocations: for example, such as, take ... for example
grammar_pattern: [general statement], for example, [specific case]. Also can start a sentence: "For example, ..."
common_mistake: For example the coffee here is very strong.
correct_version: For example, the coffee here is very strong.
why_it_s_wrong: Always add a comma after 'for example' at the start of a sentence.
pronunciation_tip: Stress falls on "ZAM" in example: for ig-ZAM-pul, with "for" said quickly and unstressed.
spelling_tip: "Example" has one "x," not "exemple" -- remember it comes from Latin "exemplum."
etymology: "Example" comes from Latin "exemplum" (a sample, something taken out to show) via Old French -- "for example" has long been used in English to introduce a specific illustrative case.
prefix_root_suffix: ex- (out) + empl(um) (take/sample) -- literally "something taken out to show"
mnemonic: FOR EXAMPLE = here's an EXAMPLE to prove my point.
memory_trick: FOR EXAMPLE = e.g.
visual_association: A magnifying glass zooming in on one item from a larger group.
difference_explained: For example + full sentence. Such as + list of nouns (fruits such as mangoes).
mini_conversation:
A: What kind of music do you like?
B: Upbeat stuff -- for example, pop and Latin music.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A teacher taps the whiteboard and says, "For example, look at how this character changes here."
news_style_line: News-style: "Several cities, London for example, have introduced new cycling lanes this year."
casual_conversation: Casual: "You should try new hobbies -- for example, painting or hiking."
mcq_options: A) Give a specific case that supports an idea  B) Show disagreement  C) End a story  D) Ask a question
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Some vegetables grow well in winter; ______, carrots and spinach. → for example
find_and_fix_to_correct: For example, tigers, lions and elephants are wild animal. → For example, tigers, lions, and elephants are wild animals. (plural noun "animals," not "animal")
translate: कुछ खेल टीम वर्क सिखाते हैं; उदाहरण के लिए, फुटबॉल। → Some sports teach teamwork; for example, football.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence using 'for example' to give one example.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'used to introduce a specific case that shows what you mean'?
usage_tip: 'For example' can go at the start, middle or end.

simple_explanation: Used to emphasize that something is true, often adding a stronger or surprising detail. You say "in fact" when you want to confirm or strengthen a point, sometimes by adding a detail that's even more surprising than what you already said.
example_1: I like tea; in fact, I drink it every single day.
example_2: The test wasn't hard; in fact, I finished it in half the time.
example_3: She wasn't just late -- in fact, she missed the meeting completely.
collocations: in fact, in point of fact, the fact is
related_phrasal_verbs: as a matter of fact, indeed, actually
where_it_s_used: Conversation, essays, clarifying or strengthening a point, correcting a misunderstanding
grammar_pattern: [statement], in fact, [stronger/surprising statement]. Also: "In fact, ..." at the start of a sentence.
common_mistake: In fact, I am agree with you.
correct_version: In fact, I agree with you.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Agree' is a verb by itself, so no 'am'.
pronunciation_tip: Both words get stress, with a slightly stronger hit on "FACT": in FAKT.
spelling_tip: Two separate words -- never write "infact" as one word.
etymology: "Fact" comes from Latin "factum" (a thing done) via French -- "in fact" developed in English to mean "in reality," emphasizing the truth behind a statement.
prefix_root_suffix: in- (within/in a state of) + fact (a thing done, from Latin "facere," to do)
mnemonic: IN FACT = here's the real FACT behind what I just said.
memory_trick: IN FACT = actually.
visual_association: A stamp marked "TRUE" pressing down firmly on a document.
emotion_feel: Neutral to mildly emphatic -- signals confidence in what's being said
difference_explained: Same meaning. Actually is more common in speech.
mini_conversation:
A: Was the flight delayed?
B: In fact, it left ten minutes early.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A witness leans forward and says, "In fact, I saw the whole thing happen."
news_style_line: News-style: "In fact, the new policy has already reduced waiting times by half."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I thought the movie would be boring, but in fact, I loved it."
mcq_options: A) Introduce a question  B) Emphasize or confirm a point  C) Show a contrast  D) End a topic
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The soup wasn't just warm; ______, it was still boiling. → in fact
find_and_fix_to_correct: In fact, she don't like the plan. → In fact, she doesn't like the plan. (third-person singular needs "doesn't," not "don't")
translate: मुझे लगा कि यह मुश्किल होगा; वास्तव में, यह बहुत आसान था। → I thought it would be difficult; in fact, it was very easy.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence starting 'In fact,…'.

usage_tip: 'In fact' adds a stronger or surprising point.

simple_explanation: Used to explain the same idea again, usually more simply. You use "in other words" to restate something you just said, often to make it clearer or easier to understand.
example_1: He's a workaholic -- in other words, he never takes a break.
example_2: The project is behind schedule; in other words, we won't finish by Friday.
example_3: She's a picky eater -- in other words, she only likes a few specific foods.
collocations: in other words, or in other words, put in other words
related_phrasal_verbs: that is to say, put simply, to put it another way
where_it_s_used: Explanations, clarifying complicated ideas, teaching, summaries
grammar_pattern: [complex/technical statement], in other words, [simpler restatement].
common_mistake: In other word, he means he's tired.
correct_version: In other words, he means he's tired.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Words' must be plural: 'in other words'.
pronunciation_tip: Four smooth words with the main stress on "OTH-er" and "WORDS": in UH-ther WURDZ.
etymology: A transparent English phrase built from "other" (Old English "oþer") and "words" -- used to signal that an idea is being restated in different terms.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- a fixed phrase built from ordinary words
mnemonic: IN OTHER WORDS = you're saying it again with OTHER (different) WORDS.
memory_trick: IN OTHER WORDS = to say it differently.
visual_association: The same sentence rewritten in simpler handwriting underneath the original.
synonyms: that is to say, put simply
confusing_word: in other words vs that is
difference_explained: Same meaning. 'That is' (i.e.) is more formal.
mini_conversation:
A: The contract says the deadline is flexible but penalties apply after 30 days.
B: In other words, we really do need to finish on time.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A lawyer summarizes, "In other words, my client is innocent."
news_style_line: News-style: "The report shows costs rising faster than wages -- in other words, workers have less spending power."
casual_conversation: Casual: "He said he's 'reconsidering' the plan -- in other words, he's probably cancelling it."
mcq_options: A) Introduce a new topic  B) Restate an idea more simply  C) Ask for permission  D) Show surprise
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The device is 'temporarily unavailable' -- ______, it's broken. → in other words
find_and_fix_to_correct: In other words, she is means she agrees. → In other words, she means she agrees. (remove the extra "is" before "means")
translate: वह हमेशा देर से आता है; दूसरे शब्दों में, वह भरोसेमंद नहीं है। → He always arrives late; in other words, he's not reliable.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence using 'In other words,'.

reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'used to explain the same idea again, usually more simply'?
usage_tip: Useful for explaining something again more simply.

simple_explanation: Used to show that something happened because of a previous event or action. "As a result" connects a cause to its effect -- it tells you what happened because of what came before.
example_1: It rained heavily all night; as a result, the streets were flooded.
example_2: He didn't study for the exam; as a result, he failed.
example_3: The factory upgraded its machines; as a result, production increased by 20 percent.
collocations: as a result of, as a direct result, and as a result
where_it_s_used: Essays, reports, explaining cause and effect, science and business writing
grammar_pattern: [cause], as a result, [effect]. Also: "as a result of + noun"
common_mistake: As a result of he was sick, he missed the class.
correct_version: He missed the class as a result of being sick.
why_it_s_wrong: 'As a result of' is followed by a noun or -ing; 'as a result' alone starts a new sentence.
pronunciation_tip: Light stress on "as" and "a," stronger stress on "ZULT": az uh ri-ZULT.
spelling_tip: Three words -- "as," "a," "result" -- with "result" spelled with one "s" and a double "l."
etymology: "Result" comes from Latin "resultare" (to spring back) via French, coming to mean "outcome" -- "as a result" became a standard English phrase linking a cause to its effect.
prefix_root_suffix: re- (back) + sult (to jump/spring, from Latin "saltare") -- literally "to spring back" as an outcome
mnemonic: AS A RESULT = something happened, and AS A RESULT, something else followed.
memory_trick: AS A RESULT (, sentence). AS A RESULT OF (+ noun).
visual_association: One domino falling and knocking over the next one in line.
confusing_word: as a result vs as a result of
difference_explained: As a result, … (alone). As a result of + noun.
mini_conversation:
A: Why is the store closed today?
B: The power went out. As a result, they had to shut down for the day.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A general reports, "The bridge collapsed. As a result, we've lost our only supply route."
news_style_line: News-style: "Fuel prices rose sharply; as a result, transport costs have gone up across the board."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I forgot my umbrella, and as a result, I got completely soaked."
mcq_question: "As a result" is used to show:
mcq_options: A) A similarity  B) A cause leading to an effect  C) A list of examples  D) A question
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The bridge was closed for repairs; ______, traffic was diverted for weeks. → as a result
find_and_fix_to_correct: As a result the team win the championship. → As a result, the team won the championship. (add a comma, and use the past tense "won")
translate: उसने बहुत मेहनत की; परिणामस्वरूप, उसे पदोन्नति मिली। → He worked very hard; as a result, he got a promotion.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence using 'as a result of'.

usage_tip: Common in reports and news.

hindi_meaning: इसके विपरीत, बल्कि (सच तो यह है कि)
simple_explanation: Used to say the opposite of what someone just said is actually true. You use "on the contrary" to directly disagree with or correct a previous statement, showing the real situation is the opposite.
example_1: "You seem upset." "On the contrary, I'm having a great day."
example_2: "Isn't this project boring?" "On the contrary, I find it fascinating."
example_3: He isn't lazy -- on the contrary, he's one of the hardest workers here.
collocations: on the contrary, quite the contrary
related_phrasal_verbs: quite the opposite, far from it, actually
where_it_s_used: Debates, correcting assumptions, formal writing, disagreements
grammar_pattern: [Statement/assumption], on the contrary, [opposite truth].
common_mistake: On the contrary, I also think the plan is good.
correct_version: I also think the plan is good.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'on the contrary' only to disagree or correct, not to agree.
pronunciation_tip: Stress the first syllable of "contrary": on thuh KON-trer-ee.
spelling_tip: "Contrary" ends in "-ary," not "-arry" -- one "r" in the middle.
etymology: "Contrary" comes from Latin "contrarius" (opposite) via Old French -- "on the contrary" has long been used in English to flatly oppose or correct a previous statement.
word_family: contrary (adj./n.), contrarian (n., someone who often disagrees)
mnemonic: ON THE CONTRARY = the CONTRARY (opposite) is actually true, so let me correct you.
memory_trick: CONTRARY = the opposite.
visual_association: A hand raised flat, firmly stopping and reversing an incorrect idea.
emotion_feel: Assertive, sometimes a little defensive or corrective
confusing_word: on the contrary vs on the other hand
difference_explained: On the contrary = the opposite is true. On the other hand = another side, both true.
tone: Neutral, can sound assertive or formal
mini_conversation:
A: I guess you didn't enjoy the concert.
B: On the contrary, it was the best show I've been to all year.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A suspect looks the detective in the eye and says, "On the contrary, I was nowhere near the building that night."
news_style_line: News-style: "Officials deny the project failed; on the contrary, they call it their biggest success this year."
casual_conversation: Casual: "You must be tired after the trip." "On the contrary, I feel really energized."
mcq_options: A) Agree strongly with a statement  B) Give an example  C) Say the opposite of a statement is true  D) Ask for clarification
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: "This job must be stressful." "______, I find it quite relaxing." → On the contrary
find_and_fix_to_correct: On the contrary I completely disagree with that. → On the contrary, I completely disagree with that. (add a comma after the introductory phrase "on the contrary")
translate: "क्या तुम थके हुए हो?" "बिल्कुल विपरीत, मैं बहुत तरोताज़ा महसूस कर रहा हूँ।" → "Are you tired?" "On the contrary, I feel very fresh."
write_your_own_sentence: Write a two-line dialogue using 'On the contrary'.

reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'used to say the opposite of what someone just said is actually true'?
usage_tip: 'On the contrary' corrects a wrong belief: 'Not boring? On the contrary, it's exciting!'

simple_explanation: Used to show a choice between two possibilities. "Either...or" connects two options and tells you that one of them (but not both) is true or must be chosen.
example_1: You can either call me or send a text.
example_2: Either you apologize, or the friendship is over.
example_3: We can eat either at home or at a restaurant tonight.
collocations: either...or, either way, either one
related_phrasal_verbs: neither...nor, one or the other, whether...or
where_it_s_used: Giving choices, decisions, everyday conversation, instructions
grammar_pattern: either + [option A] + or + [option B] (Either you come with us or you stay home.)
common_mistake: Either you or I is responsible.
correct_version: Either you or I am responsible.
why_it_s_wrong: With 'either…or', the verb agrees with the nearer subject.
pronunciation_tip: "Either" can be pronounced EE-ther or EYE-ther (both are correct) -- "or" is always unstressed and quick.
spelling_tip: "Either" has an "-ei-" spelling -- remember "either" and "neither" are spelled the same way at the start.
etymology: Both "either" and "or" come from Old English ("ǣgther" and "oþþe") -- paired together, they have presented a choice between two options since Old English.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- a paired conjunction from Old English
word_family: either (also stands alone as a pronoun/determiner: "either way, " "I don't like either")
mnemonic: EITHER...OR = pick ONE of TWO doors, not both.
memory_trick: EITHER … OR: pick one of two.
visual_association: Two doors side by side, with a sign pointing to only one.
emotion_feel: Neutral -- can carry tension when the choice is difficult
difference_explained: Either = one of two (positive). Neither = not one and not the other (negative).
mini_conversation:
A: What do you want for dinner?
B: Either pizza or pasta -- I can't decide!
everyday_scene: Everyday: A villain smirks and says, "You have two choices: either you help me, or you watch everything fall apart."
news_style_line: News-style: "Officials say the region will either receive new funding or face further budget cuts next year."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I'll either finish the report tonight or wake up early tomorrow to do it."
mcq_options: A) Two things happening together  B) A choice between two options  C) A reason for something  D) A comparison
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: You can ______ stay here ______ come with us -- it's your choice. → either...or
find_and_fix_to_correct: Either you finish now or later you will regret. → Either finish it now, or you will regret it later. (keep both options parallel and add a comma before "or")
translate: या तो तुम मुझे फोन करो या मुझे मैसेज भेज दो। → Either you call me or you send me a message.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence using 'either … or'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'used to show a choice between two possibilities'?
usage_tip: 'Either' alone: 'You can take either.'

simple_explanation: Used to say that two things are both not true or don't happen. "Neither...nor" rejects two things at once -- it means "not this one, and not that one either."
example_1: She neither called nor texted me back.
example_2: Neither the manager nor the staff knew about the change.
example_3: I have neither the time nor the money for a vacation this year.
collocations: neither...nor, neither one, neither way
where_it_s_used: Formal writing, describing absence of two things, negative comparisons
grammar_pattern: neither + [option A] + nor + [option B] (Neither the cat nor the dog made a sound.)
common_mistake: She neither like tea nor coffee.
correct_version: She likes neither tea nor coffee.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Neither' goes right before the first item: 'likes neither tea nor coffee'.
pronunciation_tip: "Neither" can be NEE-ther or NYE-ther -- both are correct; "nor" rhymes with "or."
spelling_tip: "Neither" has the same "-ei-" spelling as "either" -- learn them together.
etymology: "Neither" and "nor" both come from Old English negative forms related to "either" and "or" -- paired together, they reject two options at once.
word_family: neither (also stands alone as a pronoun/determiner: "neither of us, " "neither option")
mnemonic: NEITHER...NOR = not the first one, NOR the second one -- both are out.
memory_trick: NEITHER … NOR: not this, not that.
visual_association: Two empty boxes, both crossed out with an X.
emotion_feel: Neutral, sometimes emphasizing disappointment or lack
difference_explained: Neither…nor = not both (negative). Either…or = one of two (choice).
mini_conversation:
A: Did anyone bring snacks or drinks?
B: Neither -- neither Sam nor I remembered.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A judge declares, "Neither the evidence nor the testimony supports that claim."
news_style_line: News-style: "Neither the company nor its investors have commented on the reported merger."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I've had neither breakfast nor lunch today -- I'm starving."
mcq_options: A) Confirm two things are true  B) Say both things are not true  C) Give a choice between two things  D) Compare two things
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: ______ the teacher ______ the students noticed the mistake. → neither...nor
find_and_fix_to_correct: Neither John neither Mary came to the party. → Neither John nor Mary came to the party. (the second word must be "nor," not "neither" again)
translate: न तो उसने फोन किया न ही संदेश भेजा। → He neither called nor sent a message.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence using 'neither … nor'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'used to say that two things are both not true or don't happen'?
usage_tip: 'Neither do I' = I don't either.

simple_explanation: Used to emphasize that two things are true or included at the same time. "Both...and" links two items to show that they're equally true or equally included -- not just one of them.
example_1: Both my parents and my grandparents live nearby.
example_2: The hotel is both affordable and comfortable.
example_3: She speaks both English and French fluently.
collocations: both...and, both of us, both sides
related_phrasal_verbs: not only...but also, as well as, along with
where_it_s_used: Descriptions, emphasizing inclusion, formal and everyday writing
grammar_pattern: both + [item A] + and + [item B] (Both the coffee and the tea were too hot.)
common_mistake: Both my sister and my brother is coming.
correct_version: Both my sister and my brother are coming.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Both…and' takes a plural verb.
pronunciation_tip: Stress "BOTH" clearly; "and" is usually said quickly and lightly: BOHTH ... and.
spelling_tip: "Both" -- just four letters; don't confuse it with "bother" when typing quickly.
etymology: "Both" comes from Old Norse "báðir," adopted into English in the early medieval period -- paired with "and," it emphasizes that two things are true together.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- a paired conjunction from Old Norse "báðir"
word_family: both (also stands alone as a pronoun/determiner: "both of them, " "both options")
mnemonic: BOTH...AND = not one or the other -- BOTH count, AND that's final.
memory_trick: BOTH … AND: two together, plural.
visual_association: Two hands linked together, holding up one shared object.
emotion_feel: Neutral -- often carries a positive, inclusive tone
synonyms: as well as, not only...but also
difference_explained: Both…and = two together. Either…or = only one.
mini_conversation:
A: Do you want the salad or the soup?
B: Can I have both the salad and the soup, please?
everyday_scene: Everyday: A mentor says, "You'll need both courage and patience to finish this journey."
news_style_line: News-style: "Both local businesses and residents welcomed the new transport link."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I want both the blue shirt and the grey one -- I can't choose just one!"
mcq_options: A) Choose between two options  B) Reject two options  C) Include two things together  D) Compare prices
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: ______ the students ______ the teachers enjoyed the field trip. → both...and
find_and_fix_to_correct: Both my parents and also my grandparents were there. → Both my parents and my grandparents were there. (don't add "also" -- "both...and" already links the two items)
translate: वह दोनों गिटार और पियानो बजा सकती है। → She can play both the guitar and the piano.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence using 'both … and'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'used to emphasize that two things are true or included at the same time'?
usage_tip: 'Both' shows you mean the two together.

simple_explanation: Used to add a second surprising or important fact to a first one. "Not only...but also" emphasizes that two things are both true, with the second one often being extra or unexpected.
example_1: She is not only talented but also hardworking.
example_2: The app is not only free but also ad-free.
example_3: He not only apologized but also fixed the mistake himself.
collocations: not only...but also, not only that
related_phrasal_verbs: both...and, as well as, in addition to
where_it_s_used: Essays, presentations, praising or criticizing, emphasizing extra facts
grammar_pattern: not only + [fact A] + but also + [fact B] (with inversion when it starts the sentence: "Not only did she win, but she also broke the record.")
common_mistake: Not only he is smart but also kind.
correct_version: Not only is he smart, but he is also kind.
why_it_s_wrong: When 'not only' starts the sentence, invert: 'Not only is he…'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress falls on "ON-ly" and "AL-so": not OHN-lee but AWL-soh.
etymology: Built from the everyday English words "not," "only," "but," and "also" -- this paired structure has long been used to add emphasis to a second, connected fact.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- a fixed emphatic conjunction pair
word_family: only (adv./adj.), also (adv.) -- both used independently outside this paired structure
mnemonic: NOT ONLY...BUT ALSO = one fact isn't enough -- here's ANOTHER one too!
memory_trick: NOT ONLY … BUT ALSO: this AND that too.
visual_association: One gift box opened to reveal a second, bigger surprise inside.
emotion_feel: Positive or emphatic -- often used to build up praise or surprise
difference_explained: Similar. Not only…but also stresses the second item more.
mini_conversation:
A: How was the new restaurant?
B: Great -- not only was the food amazing, but also the service was fast.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A coach announces, "She's not only the fastest runner here, but also the most determined."
news_style_line: News-style: "The new law will not only reduce emissions but also create thousands of jobs."
casual_conversation: Casual: "This laptop is not only lightweight but also really affordable."
mcq_options: A) Show a contrast  B) Add emphasis to two connected facts  C) Give a reason  D) Express a condition
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The trip was ______ relaxing ______ educational. → not only...but also
find_and_fix_to_correct: Not only she cooked but also cleaned the house. → Not only did she cook, but she also cleaned the house. (use "did" for inversion after "not only" at the start of a sentence)
translate: वह न केवल स्मार्ट है बल्कि मेहनती भी है। → She is not only smart but also hardworking.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence using 'not only … but also'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'used to add a second surprising or important fact to a first one'?
usage_tip: Common in formal speech and essays.

simple_explanation: Used to show two possibilities when the choice doesn't change the result, or to report a yes/no question. "Whether...or" is used when something will happen no matter which of two options occurs, or to talk about an unresolved choice between two things.
example_1: I'll go for a run whether it rains or not.
example_2: She wasn't sure whether to call him or wait for a text.
example_3: Whether you agree or disagree, the decision has already been made.
collocations: whether or not, whether...or not, whether to
related_phrasal_verbs: either...or, regardless of, no matter whether
where_it_s_used: Decisions, uncertainty, reported questions, formal writing
grammar_pattern: whether + [option A] + or + [option B] (Whether we win or lose, we tried our best.)
common_mistake: I don't know if I should go whether stay.
correct_version: I don't know whether to go or stay.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'whether…or', not a mix of 'if' and 'whether'.
pronunciation_tip: "Whether" starts with a soft "wh" sound: WEH-ther (many speakers pronounce it just like "weather").
spelling_tip: Don't confuse "whether" (a choice/condition word) with "weather" (rain, sun, etc.) -- they sound identical but mean very different things.
etymology: "Whether" comes from Old English "hwæther" (which of two) -- originally a question word for choosing between two things, now often paired with "or."
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- from Old English "hwæther," an old comparative question word
word_family: whether (also used alone in indirect questions: "I wonder whether it's true")
mnemonic: WHETHER...OR = it doesn't matter WHETHER it's this OR that, the result is the same.
memory_trick: WHETHER … OR: two choices.
visual_association: A coin spinning in the air, not yet landed on either side.
emotion_feel: Neutral -- often reflects uncertainty or indecision
difference_explained: Whether = choice. Weather = rain, sun, etc. Same sound.
mini_conversation:
A: Are you coming to the party?
B: I haven't decided whether to go or stay home and rest.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A captain declares, "Whether we make it or not, we sail at dawn."
news_style_line: News-style: "Officials have not confirmed whether the event will proceed or be postponed."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I still can't decide whether to order pizza or cook something at home."
mcq_options: A) Confirm a fact  B) Present two possibilities or an uncertain choice  C) Give a command  D) Express thanks
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: He asked ______ I wanted tea ______ coffee. → whether...or
find_and_fix_to_correct: I'm not sure whether she is coming or she will come. → I'm not sure whether she is coming or not. (keep the two options short and parallel, instead of repeating a full clause)
translate: मुझे नहीं पता कि वह आएगा या नहीं। → I don't know whether he will come or not.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence using 'whether … or'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'used to show two possibilities when the choice doesn't change the result, or to report a yes/no question'?
usage_tip: 'Whether or not' = in either case.

hindi_meaning: बशर्ते कि, इस शर्त पर कि
simple_explanation: Used to state a necessary condition -- "only if this is true." "Provided that" introduces a strict condition -- the main statement is true only when that condition is met.
example_1: You can borrow the car, provided that you return it by evening.
example_2: The picnic will go ahead, provided that the weather stays dry.
example_3: Employees can work from home, provided that they finish their tasks on time.
collocations: provided that, provided (without "that"), provided always
related_phrasal_verbs: as long as, on condition that, so long as
where_it_s_used: Contracts, formal agreements, rules, academic writing
grammar_pattern: [main clause] + provided that + [condition] (You can go, provided that you finish your homework.)
common_mistake: Provided that you will finish early, we can leave.
correct_version: Provided that you finish early, we can leave.
why_it_s_wrong: Use the present tense after 'provided that', even for the future.
spelling_tip: "Provided" has one "d" before "-ed" -- don't double it ("providded" is wrong).
etymology: From the past participle of "provide" (Latin "providere," to foresee or prepare) -- "provided that" developed in formal and legal English to mean "on the condition that."
prefix_root_suffix: pro- (forward/before) + vide (to see, from Latin "videre") + -d/that -- literally "seen to in advance"
mnemonic: PROVIDED THAT = I'll PROVIDE my help, but only THAT this condition is met.
memory_trick: PROVIDED THAT = only if.
visual_association: A contract with one key clause underlined in red.
emotion_feel: Neutral, formal -- a careful, rule-setting tone
synonyms: as long as, on condition that
difference_explained: Similar. Provided that = only if (a strict condition).
mini_conversation:
A: Can I take Friday off?
B: Sure, provided that you finish the report by Thursday.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A wealthy benefactor states, "You'll inherit everything, provided that you finish your studies."
news_style_line: News-style: "The loan will be approved provided that the applicant meets all income requirements."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I'll help you move, provided that you buy the pizza afterward."
mcq_options: A) Even though  B) Only if / on condition that  C) Because  D) In addition to
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: You can join the trip, ______ you pay the deposit by Friday. → provided that
find_and_fix_to_correct: Provided that if you pay now, you get a discount. → Provided that you pay now, you get a discount. (don't use "if" together with "provided that" -- they mean the same thing)
translate: आप छुट्टी ले सकते हैं, बशर्ते कि आप अपना काम समय पर पूरा करें। → You can take leave, provided that you finish your work on time.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a condition using 'provided that'.

usage_tip: Formal; 'as long as' is more common in speech.

simple_explanation: Used to mean "on the condition that" or "if." "As long as" introduces a condition in an everyday, informal way -- it means the main thing is true only if the condition keeps being true.
example_1: You can stay out late, as long as you call me first.
example_2: As long as you try your best, I'll be proud of you.
example_3: We can sit outside as long as it doesn't rain.
collocations: as long as, for as long as
related_phrasal_verbs: provided that, so long as, on condition that
grammar_pattern: [main clause] + as long as + [condition] (You can drive my car, as long as you're careful.)
common_mistake: As long as it will be sunny, we'll go to the beach.
correct_version: As long as it's sunny, we'll go to the beach.
why_it_s_wrong: Use the present tense after 'as long as' for the future.
pronunciation_tip: All three words are said smoothly and quickly, with slightly more stress on "LONG": az long az.
spelling_tip: Three separate words -- "as," "long," "as" -- the same word "as" appears twice.
etymology: A comparative phrase ("as...as") built from Old English roots, comparing duration -- it later developed a figurative conditional sense of "on condition that."
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- a fixed comparative phrase ("as...as")
word_family: long (adj./adv.), length (n.), lengthen (v.) -- related to the literal sense of "long"
mnemonic: AS LONG AS = the condition stays true for AS LONG AS the situation lasts.
memory_trick: AS LONG AS = only if, or during the time that.
visual_association: A rope stretched between two points, holding steady as long as both ends stay fixed.
emotion_feel: Neutral -- often reassuring or setting a friendly condition
difference_explained: Similar. As long as = only if (a condition that must stay true).
mini_conversation:
A: Can I borrow your bike?
B: Sure, as long as you bring it back before dark.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A pilot reassures the passengers, "We'll be fine, as long as everyone stays calm."
news_style_line: News-style: "The mayor said the festival can continue as long as safety rules are followed."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I don't mind cooking tonight, as long as you do the dishes after."
mcq_question: "As long as" (in this conditional sense) most nearly means:
mcq_options: A) Because  B) On condition that  C) Even though  D) Instead of
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: You can watch TV ______ you finish your homework first. → as long as
find_and_fix_to_correct: As long as you don't tell anyone, I tell you a secret. → As long as you don't tell anyone, I'll tell you a secret. (use "will" in the main clause -- "I'll tell," not "I tell")
translate: जब तक तुम मेहनत करते रहोगे, तुम सफल होगे। → As long as you keep working hard, you will succeed.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence using 'as long as'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'used to mean "on the condition that" or "if."'?
usage_tip: 'As long as you're happy' = only that matters.

simple_explanation: Used to say something is true or will happen no matter what. "Even if" shows that a certain condition wouldn't change the result -- the main statement stays true regardless of that possibility.
example_1: I'll go for a walk even if it's cold outside.
example_2: Even if you apologize, it won't fix the damage.
example_3: She'll finish the marathon, even if it takes her six hours.
collocations: even if, even so, even then
related_phrasal_verbs: no matter if, regardless of whether, whether or not
where_it_s_used: Promises, determination, hypothetical situations, everyday conversation
grammar_pattern: [main clause] + even if + [hypothetical condition] (I won't give up, even if it gets hard.)
common_mistake: Even if it was raining, but we went out.
correct_version: Even if it was raining, we went out.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Even if' already introduces the contrast, so drop 'but'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress "E-ven," with "if" said quickly right after: EE-vuhn if.
spelling_tip: Two separate words -- "even" and "if" -- never combined.
etymology: "Even" comes from Old English "efne" (exactly, just) -- combined with "if," it emphasizes that a condition doesn't change the outcome.
word_family: even (adv./adj., as in "even so, " "even more"), if (conjunction, no separate related forms)
mnemonic: EVEN IF = EVEN in the worst case, IF that happens, nothing changes.
memory_trick: EVEN IF = whether or not.
visual_association: A candle flame that stays lit even as wind blows against it.
emotion_feel: Determined, resolute -- signals commitment despite obstacles
synonyms: no matter if, regardless of whether
difference_explained: Even if = possible (even if it rains). Even though = true fact (even though it's raining).
mini_conversation:
A: What if the shop is closed?
B: Even if it's closed, we can still order online.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A soldier vows, "We hold this position, even if we're the last ones standing."
news_style_line: News-style: "The team said the project will move forward even if funding is reduced next year."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I'm going to the gym even if I'm tired today."
mcq_question: "Even if" is used to show that a result:
mcq_options: A) Only happens under one condition  B) Stays the same no matter what  C) Never happens  D) Depends on the weather
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: I'll support you ______ everyone else disagrees. → even if
find_and_fix_to_correct: Even if he is tired, he was still finish the race. → Even if he is tired, he will still finish the race. (use "will" for the future outcome, not the past tense "was")
translate: भले ही बारिश हो, हम मैच खेलेंगे। → Even if it rains, we will play the match.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence starting 'Even if it rains,…'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'used to say something is true or will happen no matter what'?
usage_tip: Used for possible situations, not facts.

simple_explanation: Used to explain a precaution taken for something that might happen. "In case" means you're doing something now to be prepared for a possible situation in the future, even if it might not happen.
example_1: Take an umbrella in case it rains.
example_2: I saved a copy of the file in case my laptop crashes.
example_3: Keep some cash with you, in case the card machine doesn't work.
collocations: in case of, just in case, in case something happens
related_phrasal_verbs: just in case, to be safe, as a precaution
grammar_pattern: [precaution] + in case + [possible future event] (I'm bringing a jacket in case it gets cold.)
common_mistake: I'll call you in case if you need help.
correct_version: I'll call you in case you need help.
why_it_s_wrong: 'In case' already carries the condition, so 'if' is extra.
pronunciation_tip: Stress "CASE," with "in" said quickly before it: in KAYS.
spelling_tip: Two words -- "in" and "case" -- never written as one word "incase."
etymology: "Case" comes from Latin "casus" (a falling, an occurrence) via French -- "in case" developed in English to mean "as a precaution against a possible event."
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- "in" + "case" (from Latin "casus," a falling/happening)
word_family: case (n., as in "suitcase, " "in that case, " "a legal case")
mnemonic: IN CASE = "in the case that" something happens, I'm ready for it.
memory_trick: IN CASE = to be ready if.
visual_association: A spare key hidden under a doormat, just in case the main one is lost.
emotion_feel: Cautious, prepared -- a careful, forward-thinking tone
synonyms: as a precaution, just in case
difference_explained: In case = prepare before (take an umbrella in case it rains). If = only then (if it rains, take one).
related_words: precaution, backup, just in case, prepared
mini_conversation:
A: Why are you bringing extra batteries?
B: Just in case the flashlight dies during the hike.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A survivor packs a bag and mutters, "I'm bringing extra supplies, in case we're stuck here longer than planned."
news_style_line: News-style: "Authorities urged residents to stock emergency supplies in case the storm worsens."
casual_conversation: Casual: "I texted you the address in case you forget it later."
mcq_question: "In case" is used to talk about:
mcq_options: A) Something that already happened  B) A precaution for a possible future event  C) A strong command  D) A direct question
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Bring your ID card ______ they ask for it at the entrance. → in case
find_and_fix_to_correct: In case you will be late, please call me. → In case you're late, please call me. (use the present tense after "in case," even when talking about the future)
translate: छाता साथ ले लो, कहीं बारिश हो जाए। → Take an umbrella, in case it rains.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence using 'just in case'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'used to explain a precaution taken for something that might happen'?
usage_tip: 'Just in case' = as a precaution.

simple_explanation: Used to introduce a known fact that explains or supports the next statement. "Given that" means "since we accept this fact is true" -- you use it to build a conclusion on top of something already known.
example_1: Given that it's already 9 PM, we should leave now.
example_2: Given that the roads are icy, drivers should slow down.
example_3: Given that she has ten years of experience, she's a strong candidate for the role.
collocations: given that, given the circumstances, given the fact that
related_phrasal_verbs: considering that, since, in light of the fact that
where_it_s_used: Reports, arguments, academic writing, formal reasoning
grammar_pattern: given that + [known fact], [conclusion] (Given that it's raining, the match may be cancelled.)
common_mistake: Given that he is tired, but he kept working.
correct_version: Given that he was tired, he kept working.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Given that' already sets up the reason; drop 'but'. Keep both clauses in the same tense.
pronunciation_tip: Stress "GIV-en," with "that" said lightly: GIV-uhn that.
spelling_tip: "Given" has one "v" and ends in "-en" (the past participle of "give"), not "givven."
etymology: From the past participle of "give" (Old English "giefan") combined with "that" -- "given that" developed in formal English to mean "considering the fact that."
prefix_root_suffix: give (root, from Old English "giefan") + -en (past participle ending) + that
mnemonic: GIVEN THAT = I'm GIVING you this fact as true, so THAT is our starting point.
memory_trick: GIVEN THAT = considering that.
visual_association: A fact placed on one side of a scale, tipping the decision on the other side.
difference_explained: Similar. Given that = considering this fact (formal).
mini_conversation:
A: Should we reschedule the meeting?
B: Given that half the team is sick, yes, let's push it back.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A commander states, "Given that reinforcements aren't coming, we adjust the plan now."
news_style_line: News-style: "Given that inflation remains high, analysts expect interest rates to stay unchanged."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Given that it's your birthday, dinner is on me tonight."
mcq_options: A) Introduce an accepted fact as a basis for a conclusion  B) Ask a question  C) Show surprise  D) Give a command
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: ______ the store closes at 8, we should hurry. → Given that
find_and_fix_to_correct: Given that if the exam is hard, few students will pass. → Given that the exam is hard, few students will pass. (don't use "if" together with "given that" -- choose one)
translate: यह देखते हुए कि मौसम खराब है, हमें यात्रा टाल देनी चाहिए। → Given that the weather is bad, we should postpone the trip.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence starting 'Given that…'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'used to introduce a known fact that explains or supports the next statement'?
usage_tip: Formal and common in arguments.

hindi_meaning: सराहना करना, आभारी होना, कद्र करना
simple_explanation: To feel thankful for something, or to understand how good or important something is.
example_2: She doesn't appreciate how hard her mother works.
example_3: I would appreciate it if you could reply soon.
collocations: really appreciate, deeply appreciate, appreciate your help, appreciate the effort, appreciate it if
related_phrasal_verbs: —  (no common phrasal verb; use 'be grateful for', 'thank someone for')
where_it_s_used: Thanking people, emails, office, customer service, interviews
action_sequence: Before: someone helps you → During: notice the value of their help → After: say 'I really appreciate it'
grammar_pattern: appreciate + noun / appreciate + -ing / would appreciate it if + clause
common_mistake: I appreciate for your help.
correct_version: I appreciate your help.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Appreciate' takes a direct object — no 'for'. Also say 'I'd appreciate IT if…', not 'I'd appreciate if…'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on PREE. The 'ci' sounds like 'shee' (not 'see').
spelling_tip: Double P, and 'ci' in the middle: ap-PRE-ci-ate.
etymology: From Late Latin appretiare, 'to set a price on' (ad- 'to' + pretium 'price') — you put a value on something.
mnemonic: apPRECIate → PRICE: you see the real PRICE (value) of something.
memory_trick: When someone helps you, say 'I appreciate it' instead of only 'thank you' — sounds more mature.
visual_association: A person holding a small gift with both hands, smiling warmly at the giver.
synonyms: value, be grateful for, be thankful for, recognise
difference_explained: Thank = you say it to a person. Appreciate = you value the thing they did: 'Thank you' / 'I appreciate your help'.
mini_conversation:
A: I've sent you the notes from today's class.
B: Thanks a lot, I really appreciate it.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A student tells the shopkeeper, 'I appreciate you keeping this book for me.'
news_style_line: News-style: The team said it appreciated the support of local volunteers.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Bro, you drove me to the station at 5 a.m.? Really appreciate it.'
mcq_options: A) I appreciate for your time.  B) I appreciate your time.  C) I am appreciate your time.  D) I appreciating your time.
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: I'd ______ it if you could call me back. → appreciate
find_and_fix_to_correct: I would appreciate if you help me. → I would appreciate it if you helped / could help me.
translate: मैं आपकी मेहनत की कद्र करता हूँ। → I appreciate your hard work.
write_your_own_sentence: Write one sentence thanking a teacher or friend using 'appreciate'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to be thankful for something and value it'?
usage_tip: In emails, 'I'd appreciate it if…' is a polite way to make a request.

simple_explanation: To stop or wait for a moment before doing or saying something because you are unsure or nervous.
example_2: She hesitated before answering.
example_3: If you need anything, please don't hesitate to call me.
collocations: don't hesitate to, hesitate before, hesitate for a moment, without hesitating
where_it_s_used: Speaking practice, emails ('don't hesitate to contact'), interviews, decisions
action_sequence: Before: want to say something → During: pause, unsure → After: finally speak — or stay quiet
grammar_pattern: hesitate + to + verb / hesitate + before/about + noun or -ing
common_mistake: Please don't hesitate for asking.
correct_version: Please don't hesitate to ask.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Hesitate' is followed by 'to + verb', not 'for + -ing'.
pronunciation_tip: Say HEZ with a 'z' sound, not 'hes' with an 's'.
spelling_tip: One S between two vowels: he-SI-tate, not 'hessitate'.
etymology: From Latin haesitare, 'to stick fast, be undecided', from haerere 'to stick'.
mnemonic: HESITATE → 'He's-it? Wait!' — you pause because you aren't sure.
memory_trick: Every time you pause before speaking English, tell yourself: 'Don't hesitate — just start.'
visual_association: A boy with one foot lifted over a puddle, frozen mid-step, unsure whether to jump.
synonyms: pause, waver, hold back, think twice
difference_explained: Hesitate = you pause before acting. Doubt = you don't believe something is true.
mini_conversation:
A: Can I ask you something about the homework?
B: Of course — never hesitate to ask me.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A new employee hesitates before speaking in her first meeting.
news_style_line: News-style: Officials said they would not hesitate to act if prices rose further.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'I hesitated to call you — thought you'd be sleeping.'
mcq_question: Fill the gap: 'Feel free to message me. Don't ___ .'
mcq_options: A) hesitate  B) hesitating  C) hesitation  D) hesitated
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: He ______ for a second, then said yes. → hesitated
find_and_fix_to_correct: I hesitated to talk him. → I hesitated to talk to him.
translate: बोलने से पहले मत हिचकिचाओ। → Don't hesitate before speaking.
write_your_own_sentence: Write about a time you hesitated to speak English, using 'hesitate' or 'hesitated'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to pause because you feel unsure'?
usage_tip: End emails with: 'Please don't hesitate to contact me if you have any questions.'

hindi_meaning: स्थगित करना, टालना, आगे बढ़ाना (बाद के लिए)
simple_explanation: To move an event or action to a later time.
example_1: The match was postponed because of rain.
example_2: Can we postpone the meeting until Friday?
example_3: Don't postpone your studies till the last week.
collocations: postpone a meeting, postpone an exam, postpone until, postponed indefinitely
where_it_s_used: Office, school, events, sports, travel plans
action_sequence: Before: a meeting is fixed for Monday → During: something comes up → After: the meeting moves to Friday
grammar_pattern: postpone + noun / postpone + -ing / postpone + until/to + time
common_mistake: The exam is postponed for next week.
correct_version: The exam is postponed until (or to) next week.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'until' or 'to' for the new time; 'for' is used for a length of time ('postponed for two weeks').
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the second part: pohst-POHN.
spelling_tip: POST + PONE: 'post' (after) + 'pone' (put). Silent-looking T is spoken: pohst-POHN.
etymology: From Latin postponere, 'to put after' (post 'after' + ponere 'to put').
mnemonic: POST = after (like post-lunch). POSTpone = put it AFTER.
memory_trick: Remember the Indian-English pair: postpone (later) ↔ 'prepone' (earlier). In international English, say 'bring forward' for earlier.
visual_association: A calendar with a meeting note being lifted off Monday and stuck onto Friday.
synonyms: put off, delay, push back, reschedule (later)
difference_explained: Postpone = it will still happen, but later. Cancel = it will not happen at all.
mini_conversation:
A: I'm not ready for tomorrow's presentation.
B: Let's ask the manager to postpone it to Thursday.
everyday_scene: Everyday: The family postponed their trip because grandmother was unwell.
news_style_line: News-style: The board exams were postponed by a week due to heavy flooding.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Movie tonight? Can we postpone it? I'm too tired.'
mcq_question: The wedding is not cancelled; it has only been ___ .
mcq_options: A) postponed  B) posted  C) proposed  D) preponed
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: We had to ______ the picnic because of the storm. → postpone
find_and_fix_to_correct: He postponed to pay the bill. → He postponed paying the bill.
translate: मीटिंग सोमवार तक टाल दी गई है। → The meeting has been postponed until Monday.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a short message to a friend postponing a plan and giving a new day.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to move something to a later time'?
usage_tip: Postpone + -ing: 'I postponed calling him' (not 'postponed to call').

simple_explanation: Easy, useful, or suitable for your needs, time or plans.
example_2: Online shopping is very convenient.
example_3: The hotel is in a convenient location near the station.
collocations: convenient time, convenient location, convenient for you, very convenient, a convenient way to
grammar_pattern: be convenient FOR + person / convenient + noun / convenient + to + verb
common_mistake: Are you convenient tomorrow?
correct_version: Is tomorrow convenient for you? / Are you free tomorrow?
why_it_s_wrong: Times, places and things are convenient; a person is 'free' or 'available'. So the TIME is convenient FOR you.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on VEE: kun-VEE-nee-unt. Four syllables, don't drop 'nee'.
etymology: From Latin convenire, 'to come together, be suitable' (con- 'together' + venire 'to come').
mnemonic: A CONVENIENCE store is open late — it's CONVENIENT for everyone.
memory_trick: Replace the Indian-English 'Are you convenient?' with 'Does this time suit you?' or 'Is this time convenient for you?'
visual_association: A small shop right next to a bus stop, with a person grabbing milk without crossing the road.
difference_explained: Convenient = easy and suits your needs (time/place). Comfortable = physically or emotionally relaxed.
mini_conversation:
A: When should we meet to discuss the project?
B: Any time after 3 is convenient for me.
everyday_scene: Everyday: She chose the flat because it was convenient for her office.
news_style_line: News-style: The new metro line makes travel more convenient for thousands of commuters.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'UPI is so convenient — I don't even carry cash anymore.'
mcq_options: A) Are you convenient at 6?  B) Is 6 convenient for you?  C) Do you convenient at 6?  D) Is 6 convenience for you?
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Let me know a ______ time for the call. → convenient
find_and_fix_to_correct: I am not convenient on Sunday. → Sunday is not convenient for me.
translate: क्या कल सुबह आपके लिए सुविधाजनक है? → Is tomorrow morning convenient for you?
write_your_own_sentence: Write a message asking your teacher what time is convenient for a meeting.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which adjective means 'easy and suitable for your time or needs'?
usage_tip: In formal emails: 'at your earliest convenience' = as soon as you can.

hindi_meaning: सच में, वास्तव में, दिल से
simple_explanation: Really and truly; in an honest and sincere way.
example_2: She genuinely cares about her students.
example_3: Was he genuinely sorry, or just pretending?
collocations: genuinely happy, genuinely interested, genuinely sorry, genuinely believe, genuinely care
grammar_pattern: genuinely + adjective ('genuinely happy') / genuinely + verb ('genuinely care')
common_mistake: He is genuinely person.
correct_version: He is a genuine person. / He is genuinely kind.
why_it_s_wrong: Before a noun use the adjective 'genuine'. 'Genuinely' describes an adjective or verb.
spelling_tip: GENUINE + LY: keep the E — genuinELY.
etymology: From 'genuine', from Latin genuinus, 'native, natural'.
mnemonic: GENUINE = not fake. GENUINELY = in a not-fake way.
memory_trick: Use it to sound sincere: 'I'm genuinely grateful' is stronger than 'I'm very grateful'.
visual_association: A friend giving a real, wide smile (not a forced one) while hugging someone who just got good news.
difference_explained: Genuinely = truly/sincerely. Generally = usually, in most cases. They sound similar — don't mix them.
mini_conversation:
A: Did you like my speech, or are you just being nice?
B: No, I genuinely liked it — it was clear and confident.
everyday_scene: Everyday: The shopkeeper was genuinely surprised when the boy returned the extra change.
news_style_line: News-style: Residents said they were genuinely worried about the water shortage.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'I genuinely forgot your birthday — I'm so sorry!'
mcq_question: 'I'm ___ interested in your idea — tell me more.'
mcq_options: A) genuine  B) genuinely  C) generally  D) genius
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: She was ______ sorry for her mistake. → genuinely
find_and_fix_to_correct: He genuine wants to help. → He genuinely wants to help.

write_your_own_sentence: Write a compliment to a friend using 'genuinely'.
