hindi_meaning: (पैसे/समय) का खर्च उठा पाना, वहन कर पाना
simple_explanation: To have enough money or time to do or buy something.
example_1: I can't afford a new phone right now.
example_2: We can afford to eat out once a week.
example_3: You can't afford to waste time before exams.
collocations: can't afford, can afford to, afford a car, afford the time, can't afford to lose
action_sequence: Before: check your wallet → During: compare the price with your money → After: buy it, or decide you can't afford it
grammar_pattern: can/can't/could afford + noun / afford + to + verb (almost always with can/could/be able to)
common_mistake: I can't afford buying this car.
correct_version: I can't afford to buy this car.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Afford' is followed by 'to + verb', not '-ing'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on FORD; first 'a' is a soft 'uh'.
etymology: From Old English geforthian, 'to carry out, accomplish'.
mnemonic: AFFORD → 'a FORD car': can I afford a Ford?
memory_trick: Almost always used with can/can't: 'Can you afford it?'
visual_association: A student looking at a price tag in a shop window and checking his wallet.
synonyms: pay for, manage, have enough for
difference_explained: Afford = HAVE enough money. Pay = GIVE the money.
mini_conversation:
A: Are you going on the school trip?
B: I'd love to, but I can't afford it this month.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A family saves for months so they can afford a small car.
news_style_line: News-style: Many young people say they cannot afford to live in big cities.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Pizza again? Sorry yaar, I can't afford it till salary day.'
mcq_options: A) afford  B) affording  C) afforded  D) affordable
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Students often can't ______ expensive coaching. → afford
find_and_fix_to_correct: I can't afford for going abroad. → I can't afford to go abroad.
translate: मैं इतना महँगा फ़ोन नहीं ले सकता (पैसे नहीं हैं)। → I can't afford such an expensive phone.
write_your_own_sentence: Write about something you want to buy but can't afford yet.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which verb means 'to have enough money or time for something'?
usage_tip: 'Can't afford to + verb' also means it's too risky: 'We can't afford to lose this client.'

simple_explanation: To say that someone or something is good, or advise someone to do something.
example_1: Can you recommend a good dentist?
example_2: I recommend this book to all learners.
example_3: The doctor recommended that I rest for a week.
collocations: highly recommend, strongly recommend, recommend a book, recommended by, would you recommend
action_sequence: Before: try a good restaurant → During: tell a friend it's good → After: the friend goes there
grammar_pattern: recommend + noun / recommend + -ing / recommend + that + person + (should) + verb
common_mistake: I recommend you to read this book.
correct_version: I recommend reading this book. / I recommend that you read this book.
why_it_s_wrong: In standard English, 'recommend' is not usually followed by person + 'to' + verb.
pronunciation_tip: One 'c', double 'm': re-co-MM-end. Stress on MEND.
etymology: From Medieval Latin recommendare, re- + commendare 'to entrust, praise'.
mnemonic: reCOMMEND = you COMMEND (praise) it again to others.
memory_trick: Spelling trick: 1 C, 2 Ms — 'reCoMMend'.
visual_association: A friend holding up a phone showing a five-star restaurant, giving a thumbs-up.
difference_explained: Both give advice. Recommend often means you have tried it and think it is good.
mini_conversation:
A: Which course should I join for spoken English?
B: I'd recommend starting with daily speaking practice.
everyday_scene: Everyday: The waiter recommended the paneer tikka.
news_style_line: News-style: Experts recommend drinking more water in summer.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Bro, I highly recommend this movie — watch it this weekend.'
mcq_options: A) recommended  B) recommended to  C) recommend for  D) recommendation
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Would you ______ this hotel to a friend? → recommend
find_and_fix_to_correct: She recommended me to buy it. → She recommended that I buy it. / She recommended buying it.
translate: मैं आपको यह ऐप इस्तेमाल करने की सलाह दूँगा। → I'd recommend using this app.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence recommending a place to visit in your city.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which verb means 'to say something is good and advise others to try it'?
usage_tip: 'Letter of recommendation' is a common phrase for jobs and admissions.

hindi_meaning: संघर्ष करना, जूझना, मुश्किल से कर पाना
simple_explanation: To try very hard to do something that is difficult.
example_1: I struggle to speak English in front of people.
example_2: She struggled with maths at school.
example_3: Many families are struggling to pay their bills.
collocations: struggle to, struggle with, struggle for, struggle hard, still struggling
action_sequence: Before: face a hard task → During: try again and again → After: slowly manage it
grammar_pattern: struggle + to + verb / struggle + with + noun / struggle + for + noun
common_mistake: I am struggling in speaking English.
correct_version: I am struggling to speak English. / I struggle with speaking English.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'struggle to + verb' or 'struggle with + noun/-ing'.
pronunciation_tip: Two syllables: STRUG-ul; don't add an extra vowel ('sa-truggle').
spelling_tip: STRUG-GLE: double G, like two hands gripping hard.
etymology: Middle English strugle; the origin before that is uncertain.
mnemonic: STRUGGLE = STRong effort + wiGGLE to get free.
memory_trick: Normalise it for learners: 'Everyone struggles at first.'
visual_association: A person pushing a heavy cart up a steep hill.
synonyms: strive, battle, fight, find it hard
antonyms: find it easy, cope easily, breeze through
difference_explained: Try = make an attempt. Struggle = try with a lot of difficulty.
mini_conversation:
A: How's your new job?
B: Honestly, I'm struggling with the long hours.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A new student struggles to find his classroom on the first day.
news_style_line: News-style: Small shop owners are struggling because of rising rents.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'I struggled to wake up today — too many late nights.'
mcq_options: A) struggling with  B) struggling on  C) struggle to  D) struggles for with
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Many learners ______ with English pronunciation. → struggle
find_and_fix_to_correct: He struggled for finding a job. → He struggled to find a job.
translate: मुझे सुबह जल्दी उठने में दिक्कत होती है। → I struggle to wake up early.
write_your_own_sentence: Write about one thing you struggle with and how you are improving.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which verb means 'to try hard at something difficult'?
usage_tip: 'Struggle' is also a noun: 'Learning English was a struggle, but I did it.'

hindi_meaning: आख़िर में (बिना प्लान किए) किसी स्थिति में पहुँच जाना
simple_explanation: To finally be in a place or situation, usually without planning it.
example_1: We ended up eating at home.
example_2: If you don't study, you'll end up failing.
example_3: He ended up in Mumbai after many jobs.
collocations: end up doing, end up in, end up with, end up being, always end up
where_it_s_used: Stories, results of choices, travel, plans that change
action_sequence: Before: start with one plan → During: things change on the way → After: finally land somewhere unexpected
grammar_pattern: end up + -ing / end up + in/at + place / end up + with + noun / end up + adjective
word_forms: end up – ended up – ended up – ending up
common_mistake: We ended up to eat pizza.
correct_version: We ended up eating pizza.
why_it_s_wrong: 'End up' is followed by -ing, not 'to + verb'.
spelling_tip: Two words: END UP. No hyphen as a verb.
etymology: 'End' comes from Old English ende.
mnemonic: END UP = where you are at the END of the story.
memory_trick: Great for storytelling: 'We planned X, but we ended up doing Y.'
visual_association: A road map with a planned route, and a pin dropped somewhere totally different.
synonyms: finish up, wind up, land up (Indian English), turn out
difference_explained: Finally = at last, after waiting. End up = the unplanned final result.
mini_conversation:
A: Did you go to the mall?
B: No, it was raining, so we ended up watching a movie at home.
everyday_scene: Everyday: She went for a coffee and ended up talking for three hours.
news_style_line: News-style: Much of the plastic ends up in the ocean.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'I only went to buy milk and ended up buying chocolates too.'
mcq_question: 'We got lost and ___ in the wrong village.'
mcq_options: A) ended up  B) ended to  C) ended up to  D) end upping
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: If you keep skipping class, you'll ______ repeating the year. → end up
find_and_fix_to_correct: He ended up to become a teacher. → He ended up becoming a teacher.
translate: हम आख़िर में घर पर ही खाना खाने लगे। → We ended up eating at home.
write_your_own_sentence: Write about a plan that ended up differently than you expected.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which phrasal verb means 'to finally be in an unplanned situation'?
usage_tip: Indian English often says 'land up'; 'end up' is the international choice.

simple_explanation: Feeling admiration for someone or something because they are very good.
example_1: I was impressed by her English.
example_2: The judges were impressed with his performance.
example_3: I'm not easily impressed.
collocations: impressed by, impressed with, very impressed, deeply impressed, not impressed
grammar_pattern: be/feel + impressed + by/with
common_mistake: I was very impressing by the show.
correct_version: I was very impressed by the show.
why_it_s_wrong: -ed = your feeling; -ive = the thing ('an impressive show').
pronunciation_tip: One syllable at the end: im-PREST (not im-press-ED).
etymology: From Latin imprimere, 'to press into'.
mnemonic: imPRESSed = the good work PRESSED a mark into your mind.
memory_trick: Pair it: 'I was impressed by…' + 'It was impressive.'
visual_association: An audience standing and clapping after a child's dance.
difference_explained: Impressed = how YOU feel. Impressive = the THING that makes you feel it.
mini_conversation:
A: I finished the whole book in two days.
B: Wow, I'm impressed!
everyday_scene: Everyday: The customer was impressed by the quick delivery.
news_style_line: News-style: Visitors were impressed with the clean new railway station.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Not gonna lie, I'm impressed with your cooking.'
mcq_options: A) impressed  B) impressive  C) impress  D) impression
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Everyone was ______ by his confidence. → impressed
find_and_fix_to_correct: It was an impressed speech. → It was an impressive speech.
translate: मैं उसकी मेहनत से प्रभावित हूँ। → I am impressed by his hard work.
write_your_own_sentence: Write about something that impressed you recently.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which adjective describes how you feel when something is very good?
usage_tip: 'Make a good impression' (noun) is a key interview phrase.

hindi_meaning: सुनने में आया है कि, ऐसा लगता है कि
simple_explanation: Used to say that you heard something but are not sure it is true; or that something seems true.
example_1: Apparently, the exam has been postponed.
example_2: He's apparently moving to Canada.
example_3: Apparently it's going to rain tomorrow.
collocations: apparently not, apparently so, apparently true
grammar_pattern: Apparently + clause (start) / subject + is + apparently + ...
common_mistake: Apparently he is surely coming.
correct_version: Apparently he is coming.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Apparently' already shows you are not sure — don't add 'surely/definitely'.
spelling_tip: APPARENT + LY: double P, one R, -ENT not -ANT.
etymology: From 'apparent', from Latin apparere, 'to appear'.
mnemonic: APPARENTly = it APPEARS so (I heard it).
memory_trick: Use it to pass on news you haven't checked: 'Apparently, the shop is closed today.'
visual_association: A girl whispering news into a friend's ear with a shrug.
synonyms: reportedly, seemingly, it seems, I heard
difference_explained: Apparently = I heard / it seems (not sure). Obviously = clearly true, everyone can see it.
mini_conversation:
A: Is Priya coming to the party?
B: Apparently not — she has an exam.
everyday_scene: Everyday: Apparently the new café serves the best chai in town.
news_style_line: News-style: The minister is apparently planning to visit the flood area.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Apparently, Monday is a holiday. Can anyone confirm?'
mcq_question: Which word shows you heard something but aren't sure?
mcq_options: A) apparently  B) definitely  C) certainly  D) surely
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: ______, the train is running two hours late. → Apparently
find_and_fix_to_correct: Apparent he left early. → Apparently he left early.
translate: सुनने में आया है कि कल छुट्टी है। → Apparently, tomorrow is a holiday.
write_your_own_sentence: Write one piece of news you heard, starting with 'Apparently'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which adverb means 'I heard that / it seems that'?
usage_tip: Great for polite gossip — it shows you're only passing on information.

hindi_meaning: मूल रूप से, कुल मिलाकर, सीधी बात यह कि
simple_explanation: Used to give the main or simplest idea of something.
example_2: The two phones are basically the same.
example_3: He's basically a good person.
collocations: basically the same, basically true, basically means, so basically
grammar_pattern: Basically + clause / be + basically + adjective/noun
common_mistake: Basically, basically, I want to say that basically…
correct_version: Basically, I want to say that…
why_it_s_wrong: Use it once to simplify; overusing it as a filler sounds unprepared.
etymology: From 'basic', from 'base', ultimately Greek basis 'step, foundation'.
mnemonic: BASICally = go back to the BASIC point.
memory_trick: Spelling: basic + ALLY → basically.
visual_association: A person drawing one big simple circle over a messy diagram.
difference_explained: Basically = the main idea, simply put. Actually = in fact, often correcting something.
mini_conversation:
A: So what's the problem with the car?
B: Basically, the battery is dead.
everyday_scene: Everyday: Basically, the recipe is just rice, lentils and spices.
news_style_line: News-style: The two plans are basically the same, experts say.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Basically, I overslept and missed the bus.'
mcq_options: A) basically  B) basic  C) base  D) basicly
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: ______, you just need to press this one button. → Basically
find_and_fix_to_correct: He is basicly honest. → He is basically honest.
translate: सीधी बात यह है कि हमें और पैसे चाहिए। → Basically, we need more money.
write_your_own_sentence: Explain your daily routine in one sentence starting with 'Basically'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which adverb introduces the main, simple idea?
usage_tip: Common spelling mistake: 'basicly'. Correct: basically.

simple_explanation: Without any doubt; certainly.
example_2: This is definitely the best mango I've eaten.
example_3: 'Are you coming?' 'Definitely!'
collocations: definitely not, definitely will, definitely worth it, most definitely
grammar_pattern: before main verb: 'I'll definitely go' / after 'be': 'It's definitely true' / alone as an answer
common_mistake: I will go definitely tomorrow.
correct_version: I will definitely go tomorrow.
why_it_s_wrong: Put 'definitely' before the main verb (after will/be).
spelling_tip: DEFINITE + LY: keep the E; it's -ITE, not -ATE ('definately' is wrong).
etymology: From 'definite', from Latin definire, 'to set limits, fix'.
mnemonic: deFINITEly — it has 'finite' inside: FIXED, no doubt.
memory_trick: Spelling trap: it's defInItEly (not 'definately').
visual_association: A big green tick stamped firmly on a paper.
difference_explained: Definitely = 100% sure. Probably = about 70–80% sure.
mini_conversation:
A: Will you help me with the project?
B: Definitely — send me the details.
everyday_scene: Everyday: After tasting it, he definitely wanted a second plate.
news_style_line: News-style: The new bridge will definitely reduce traffic, officials said.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Definitely coming to your party — save me some cake!'
mcq_options: A) definitely  B) definite  C) definately  D) define
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: This book is ______ worth reading. → definitely
find_and_fix_to_correct: I definately agree. → I definitely agree.
translate: मैं ज़रूर आऊँगा। → I'll definitely come.
write_your_own_sentence: Write two things you will definitely do this week.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which adverb means 'without any doubt'?
usage_tip: As a one-word reply, 'Definitely!' sounds natural and friendly.

simple_explanation: To have earned something (good or bad) because of what you did or who you are.
example_2: She deserves the award.
example_3: He didn't deserve such rude treatment.
collocations: deserve a chance, deserve respect, deserve better, well-deserved, deserve to win
action_sequence: Before: work hard for months → During: your effort is noticed → After: you receive the reward you earned
grammar_pattern: deserve + noun / deserve + to + verb
word_forms: deserve – deserved – deserved – deserving (not used in continuous for this meaning)
common_mistake: You are deserving a holiday.
correct_version: You deserve a holiday.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Deserve' is a state verb — use simple, not continuous forms.
spelling_tip: DE-SERVE: the S sounds like Z.
etymology: From Latin deservire, 'to serve well, serve zealously'.
mnemonic: DESERVE = you SERVEd well, so you get the reward.
memory_trick: Kind phrase for friends: 'You deserve it!' after good news.
visual_association: A student receiving a trophy, her notebooks piled behind her.
difference_explained: Earn = get something by working. Deserve = should get it because it's fair (you might not get it yet).
mini_conversation:
A: I finally got the promotion!
B: Congratulations — you really deserve it.
everyday_scene: Everyday: After ten hours of work, the cook deserves a rest.
news_style_line: News-style: Experts say teachers deserve better pay.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'You deserve a pizza after that exam, bro.'
mcq_question: 'After all your hard work, you ___ this success.'
mcq_options: A) deserve  B) are deserving  C) deserving  D) deserved to
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Every child ______ a good education. → deserves
find_and_fix_to_correct: He is deserving punishment. → He deserves punishment.
translate: तुम इस इनाम के हक़दार हो। → You deserve this prize.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about someone who deserves more respect.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which verb means 'to have earned something because of your actions'?
usage_tip: 'Well-deserved' is a natural compliment: 'a well-deserved win'.

simple_explanation: To interrupt someone or make them feel worried or uncomfortable.
example_2: Please don't disturb me while I'm studying.
example_3: The news disturbed her a lot.
collocations: sorry to disturb you, do not disturb, disturb someone's sleep, deeply disturbed
action_sequence: Before: someone is studying → During: you make noise → After: they lose focus
grammar_pattern: disturb + person / be disturbed by + noun
common_mistake: Don't disturb to me.
correct_version: Don't disturb me.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Disturb' takes the person directly — no 'to'.
etymology: From Latin disturbare, dis- + turbare 'to throw into disorder'.
mnemonic: disTURB → TURBulence: shaking things up.
memory_trick: Polite opener before interrupting: 'Sorry to disturb you, but…'
visual_association: A hotel door with a 'Do Not Disturb' sign.
difference_explained: Very similar. Disturb often = interrupt someone's work/rest. Bother is more informal and general.
mini_conversation:
A: Sorry to disturb you, sir. Do you have a minute?
B: Sure, come in.
everyday_scene: Everyday: The children tiptoed so they wouldn't disturb their sleeping grandfather.
news_style_line: News-style: Residents said loud construction was disturbing their sleep.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Don't disturb me for the next two hours, I'm in exam mode.'
mcq_options: A) disturb  B) disturb to  C) disturbing to  D) disturbance
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: I'm sorry to ______ you so late. → disturb
find_and_fix_to_correct: Don't disturb to your father. → Don't disturb your father.
translate: माफ़ कीजिए, आपको परेशान किया। → Sorry to disturb you.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a polite message you'd send before disturbing your teacher.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which verb means 'to interrupt or bother someone'?
usage_tip: 'Disturbing' (adj) can mean shocking: 'disturbing news'.

simple_explanation: To help someone remember something, or make them think of something.
example_1: Please remind me to call Mum.
example_2: Can you remind him about the meeting?
example_3: You remind me of my brother.
collocations: remind someone to, remind someone about, remind someone of, gentle reminder
action_sequence: Before: a friend may forget → During: send them a message → After: they remember the task
grammar_pattern: remind + person + to + verb / remind + person + about + event / remind + person + of + similar thing
common_mistake: Please remember me to bring the book.
correct_version: Please remind me to bring the book.
why_it_s_wrong: You REMEMBER yourself; you REMIND another person.
spelling_tip: RE-MIND: put something back in someone's MIND.
etymology: Formed in English from re- ('again') + mind.
mnemonic: RE-MIND = put it in someone's MIND again.
memory_trick: 'Of' for similarity: 'This song reminds me OF college.'
visual_association: A sticky note on a fridge saying 'Call Mum!'
difference_explained: Remember = you keep it in your mind. Remind = you make SOMEONE ELSE remember.
mini_conversation:
A: Don't forget the bill tomorrow.
B: Thanks for reminding me!
everyday_scene: Everyday: The smell of rain reminds her of her village.
news_style_line: News-style: The bank sent a message reminding customers to update their details.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Remind me to buy chargers after class, okay?'
mcq_question: 'Can you ___ me to take my medicine?'
mcq_options: A) remind  B) remember  C) reminder  D) remind to
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: This photo ______ me of our school trip. → reminds
find_and_fix_to_correct: Remember me to call him. → Remind me to call him.
translate: मुझे कल की मीटिंग याद दिला देना। → Please remind me about tomorrow's meeting.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something that reminds you of your childhood.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which verb means 'to make someone remember'?
usage_tip: 'Just a gentle reminder…' is a polite email phrase.

simple_explanation: To answer or react to something.
example_1: She didn't respond to my message.
example_2: How did he respond to the news?
example_3: The patient is responding well to treatment.
collocations: respond to, respond quickly, respond positively, respond well to treatment
action_sequence: Before: receive a message → During: think of a reply → After: send your answer
grammar_pattern: respond + to + noun / respond + by + -ing / respond + that clause
common_mistake: He didn't respond my email.
correct_version: He didn't respond to my email.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Respond' needs 'to' before the thing you answer.
spelling_tip: RE-SPOND → RESPONSE: the D becomes SE in the noun.
etymology: From Latin respondere, 'to answer, promise in return'.
mnemonic: RESPOND = send your answer back (RE-).
memory_trick: Formal of 'reply': use 'respond' in emails and reports.
visual_association: A hand raised in class right after a teacher's question.
difference_explained: Respond = answer, often thoughtfully. React = act immediately, often with emotion.
mini_conversation:
A: Has the company responded to your application?
B: Not yet. I'll wait till Monday.
everyday_scene: Everyday: The dog responds to its name immediately.
news_style_line: News-style: The government has responded to the complaints with a new plan.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'He saw my message but didn't respond. Rude!'
mcq_options: A) respond  B) respond to  C) response  D) responding
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The team ______ quickly to the problem. → responded
find_and_fix_to_correct: She didn't respond my call. → She didn't respond to my call.
translate: उसने मेरे सवाल का जवाब नहीं दिया। → He didn't respond to my question.
write_your_own_sentence: Write how you respond when someone criticises you.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which verb means 'to answer or react'?
usage_tip: Noun: response — 'Thanks for your quick response.'

hindi_meaning: (किसी कार्यक्रम/कक्षा में) उपस्थित होना, शामिल होना
simple_explanation: To go to an event, class, meeting or place.
example_1: I attend English classes every evening.
example_2: Over 200 people attended the wedding.
example_3: Did you attend the meeting?
collocations: attend a meeting, attend classes, attend school, attend a wedding, well attended
action_sequence: Before: get an invitation → During: go to the event → After: take part and leave
grammar_pattern: attend + event (no preposition) / attend to + task (= deal with)
common_mistake: I attended to the meeting.
correct_version: I attended the meeting.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Attend' (go to) takes no preposition. 'Attend to' means 'deal with'.
spelling_tip: Double T: a-TT-end. The noun is 'attendance' (-ANCE).
etymology: From Latin attendere, 'to stretch toward, give heed to'.
mnemonic: ATTEND = be AT the event.
memory_trick: 'Attendance' = how often you are present: 'Your attendance is low.'
visual_association: A classroom with a teacher marking the attendance register.
synonyms: go to, be present at, take part in
difference_explained: Attend = be present at an event. Join = become a member or start being part of something.
mini_conversation:
A: Will you attend the parent-teacher meeting?
B: Yes, I'll be there at 10.
everyday_scene: Everyday: The whole village attended the festival.
news_style_line: News-style: Several ministers attended the opening ceremony.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'I can't attend the party — exam tomorrow.'
mcq_options: A) attended  B) attended to  C) attended at  D) attend on
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: All staff must ______ the training. → attend
find_and_fix_to_correct: He attended in the class. → He attended the class.
translate: मैं कल शादी में शामिल हुआ। → I attended the wedding yesterday.
write_your_own_sentence: Write about an event you attended recently.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which verb means 'to go to or be present at an event'?
usage_tip: In a CV: 'Attended a 3-day workshop on communication skills.'

simple_explanation: To plan or organise something; also to put things in order.
example_1: I'll arrange a meeting for Monday.
example_2: She arranged the books by colour.
example_3: Can you arrange a taxi for us?
collocations: arrange a meeting, arrange for someone to, arranged marriage, neatly arranged
action_sequence: Before: have a plan → During: book tickets and set a time → After: everything is ready
grammar_pattern: arrange + noun / arrange + to + verb / arrange for + person + to + verb
common_mistake: I arranged him to come.
correct_version: I arranged for him to come.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'arrange FOR someone TO do'.
etymology: From Old French arangier, a- + rang 'rank, row'.
mnemonic: arRANGE = put things in a nice RANGE (row).
memory_trick: 'Arranged marriage' is standard English — you can use it confidently.
visual_association: A table with plates, flowers and candles being neatly set for guests.
difference_explained: Arrange = plan it in advance. Manage = control it, or succeed in doing it.
mini_conversation:
A: Who's picking us up from the airport?
B: Don't worry, I've arranged a cab.
everyday_scene: Everyday: The mother arranges fruits on the plate for the guests.
news_style_line: News-style: The school arranged free buses for students.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'I'll arrange everything — you just come on time.'
mcq_question: 'I've ___ for the plumber to come at 5.'
mcq_options: A) arranged  B) arranged to  C) arranging  D) arrange
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: We ______ a small party for her birthday. → arranged
find_and_fix_to_correct: He arranged me a ticket to come. → He arranged a ticket for me.
translate: मैंने कल के लिए गाड़ी का इंतज़ाम कर दिया है। → I've arranged a car for tomorrow.
write_your_own_sentence: Write how you would arrange a surprise for a friend.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which verb means 'to plan or organise'?
usage_tip: 'Make arrangements' = plan: 'We've made all the arrangements.'

simple_explanation: To look at two or more things to see how they are similar or different.
example_2: Let's compare the prices before buying.
example_3: Compared to last year, sales are higher.
collocations: compare with, compare to, compared to/with, compare prices, compare notes
action_sequence: Before: see two phones → During: check price and features side by side → After: decide which is better
grammar_pattern: compare + A + with/to + B / compared with/to + noun (at start of a sentence)
common_mistake: Don't compare yourself from others.
correct_version: Don't compare yourself with (or to) others.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'with' or 'to', never 'from'.
etymology: From Latin comparare, from compar 'equal, alike'.
mnemonic: comPARE = put a PAIR side by side.
memory_trick: Kind advice for learners: 'Compare yourself only with who you were yesterday.'
visual_association: Two mangoes on a weighing scale, a hand pointing at both.
difference_explained: Compare = look at similarities AND differences. Contrast = focus on differences.
mini_conversation:
A: Which phone should I buy?
B: Let's compare the cameras and battery first.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A shopper compares two brands of rice before choosing.
news_style_line: News-style: Researchers compared results from five states.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Stop comparing your marks with Rahul's, yaar.'
mcq_options: A) Compared  B) Compare  C) Comparing to  D) Comparison
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Please ______ your answers with the key. → compare
find_and_fix_to_correct: He compared his life from mine. → He compared his life with mine.
translate: अपनी तुलना दूसरों से मत करो। → Don't compare yourself with others.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence comparing your city with another city.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which verb means 'to look at how things are similar or different'?
usage_tip: 'Compare notes' = share experiences: 'Let's compare notes after the interview.'

simple_explanation: To guess a number, size, cost or time using the information you have.
example_1: I estimate it will take two hours.
example_2: They estimated the cost at ₹5,000.
example_3: It's hard to estimate how many people came.
collocations: roughly estimate, estimate the cost, it is estimated that, underestimate, overestimate
action_sequence: Before: look at the job → During: guess the cost roughly → After: give a number
grammar_pattern: estimate + noun / estimate + that clause / It is estimated that…
common_mistake: I estimate that it will cost around about ₹500.
correct_version: I estimate that it will cost about ₹500.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Around' and 'about' mean the same — use only one.
etymology: From Latin aestimare, 'to value, appraise'.
mnemonic: ESTIMATE = your BEST guess (Est = best).
memory_trick: Verb ends '-mayt', noun ends '-mut' — listen for it.
visual_association: A painter holding up a thumb to measure a wall and writing a rough number.
difference_explained: Guess = without much information. Estimate = a careful guess using facts.
mini_conversation:
A: How long will the repair take?
B: I'd estimate about three days.
everyday_scene: Everyday: The mechanic estimated the repair at around ₹2,000.
news_style_line: News-style: Officials estimate that 50,000 people attended the fair.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'I estimate I've watched this movie ten times.'
mcq_question: 'Can you ___ how long the trip will take?'
mcq_options: A) estimate  B) estimation  C) estimated to  D) esteem
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The builder ______ the cost of the new room. → estimated
find_and_fix_to_correct: It is estimate that the population is growing. → It is estimated that the population is growing.
translate: मेरा अंदाज़ा है कि इसमें एक हफ़्ता लगेगा। → I estimate it will take a week.
write_your_own_sentence: Estimate how many hours a week you spend on your phone, in one sentence.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which verb means 'to make a careful guess about a number or cost'?
usage_tip: 'Underestimate' = think something is smaller/weaker than it is: 'Never underestimate a learner.'

simple_explanation: To need something, or to make something necessary (formal).
example_1: This job requires good communication skills.
example_2: Passengers are required to wear seat belts.
example_3: The recipe requires two eggs.
collocations: require skills, be required to, required documents, if required, as required
action_sequence: Before: read the rules → During: see what is needed → After: prepare it
grammar_pattern: require + noun / require + person + to + verb / be required to + verb
common_mistake: This form is requiring your signature.
correct_version: This form requires your signature.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Require' is a state verb — use simple tenses.
spelling_tip: RE-QUIRE: -QUIRE like 'choir' sound. The noun is 'requirement'.
etymology: From Latin requirere, 'to seek again, need'.
mnemonic: reQUIRE = you QUest (seek) again because you need it.
memory_trick: Formal twin of 'need': see it in forms and job ads, use 'need' when chatting.
visual_association: A form with a red star next to 'Signature (required)'.
difference_explained: Require = need (it must happen). Request = ask for politely (it may or may not happen).
mini_conversation:
A: What documents do I need?
B: The office requires your ID and two photos.
everyday_scene: Everyday: The plant requires water only once a week.
news_style_line: News-style: All visitors are required to show an ID at the gate.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Does this job require a degree?'
mcq_options: A) required  B) require  C) requiring  D) requirement
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Learning a language ______ daily practice. → requires
find_and_fix_to_correct: This post require experience. → This post requires experience.
translate: इस नौकरी के लिए अंग्रेज़ी ज़रूरी है। → This job requires English.
write_your_own_sentence: Write two things your dream job requires.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which formal verb means 'to need'?
usage_tip: 'Requirement' (noun) is key in job listings: 'Minimum requirement: graduation.'

hindi_meaning: (वादे/योजना से) पीछे हट जाना, मुकर जाना
simple_explanation: To decide not to do something you had agreed or promised to do.
example_1: He backed out of the deal at the last minute.
example_2: Don't back out now — we need you!
example_3: Two players backed out of the tournament.
collocations: back out of a deal, back out at the last minute, back out of a promise
action_sequence: Before: agree to join → During: feel unsure → After: say you won't do it after all
grammar_pattern: back out (alone) / back out + of + noun/-ing
word_forms: back out – backed out – backed out – backing out
common_mistake: She backed out from the plan.
correct_version: She backed out of the plan.
why_it_s_wrong: The preposition is 'of', not 'from'.
spelling_tip: Two words: BACK OUT. 'Backout' as one word is rare.
etymology: 'Back' comes from Old English bæc.
mnemonic: BACK OUT = walk BACKwards OUT of the room.
memory_trick: Often with 'last minute': 'Please don't back out at the last minute.'
visual_association: A person stepping backwards away from a signed paper on a table.
synonyms: pull out, withdraw, drop out, go back on
difference_explained: Cancel = stop a plan (anyone can). Back out = YOU leave a plan you agreed to.
mini_conversation:
A: Is Aman still coming on the trip?
B: No, he backed out yesterday.
everyday_scene: Everyday: The buyer backed out after seeing the house again.
news_style_line: News-style: A major sponsor has backed out of the event.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'You promised! You can't back out now.'
mcq_options: A) backed out  B) backed off out  C) backed from  D) back outed
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: It's not fair to ______ after saying yes. → back out
find_and_fix_to_correct: He backed out from the promise. → He backed out of the promise.
translate: वह आख़िरी समय पर पीछे हट गया। → He backed out at the last minute.
write_your_own_sentence: Write about a time someone backed out of a plan.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which phrasal verb means 'to leave something you had agreed to do'?
usage_tip: Business English: 'The investor backed out of the deal.'

simple_explanation: Demanding that rules are obeyed; not allowing people to break rules.
example_1: My maths teacher was very strict.
example_2: The school has strict rules about phones.
example_3: She follows a strict diet.
collocations: strict rules, strict teacher, strict parents, strict about, strictly speaking
grammar_pattern: be strict + with + person / be strict + about + thing
common_mistake: My father is very strict on me.
correct_version: My father is very strict with me.
why_it_s_wrong: Strict WITH a person, ABOUT a thing.
pronunciation_tip: Don't add a vowel: STRIKT, not 'sa-trict'.
spelling_tip: STRICT: one syllable, two Ts — S-T-R-I-C-T.
etymology: From Latin strictus, 'drawn tight'.
mnemonic: STRICT = rules pulled TIGHT like a rope.
memory_trick: 'Strictly speaking' = if we are very exact.
visual_association: A teacher with folded arms beside a clock, as a late student enters.
difference_explained: Strict = firm about rules (can be fair). Harsh = unkind or too severe.
mini_conversation:
A: Can you come out tonight?
B: No, my parents are strict about coming home late.
everyday_scene: Everyday: The hostel warden is strict about lights-out time.
news_style_line: News-style: The city has introduced strict rules on plastic bags.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'My coach is so strict — no sweets during training.'
mcq_options: A) strict  B) strictly  C) strictness  D) stricter than
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The exam hall had ______ security. → strict
find_and_fix_to_correct: The teacher is strict on students. → The teacher is strict with students.
translate: हमारे शिक्षक समय को लेकर बहुत सख़्त हैं। → Our teacher is very strict about time.
write_your_own_sentence: Write about a strict person in your life.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which adjective means 'firm about rules'?
usage_tip: 'Strictly prohibited' is common on notices.

simple_explanation: Easy to see or understand; clear to everyone.
example_2: The answer is obvious.
example_3: For obvious reasons, I can't tell you.
collocations: it's obvious that, obvious reason, obvious choice, painfully obvious, state the obvious
grammar_pattern: It's obvious (that) + clause / obvious + noun
common_mistake: It's obvious that he is obviously late.
correct_version: It's obvious that he is late.
why_it_s_wrong: Don't repeat the idea with 'obviously' in the same sentence.
etymology: From Latin obvius, 'in the way, meeting' (ob viam, 'in the way').
mnemonic: OBVIOUS = it's right in front of you, OB (in front) of the VIA (road).
memory_trick: 'State the obvious' = say something everyone already knows.
visual_association: A big red door with a huge arrow pointing at it and the word 'EXIT'.
difference_explained: Obvious = very clear, no doubt. Apparent = seems true (maybe not certain).
mini_conversation:
A: Why is everyone wearing jackets?
B: Isn't it obvious? It's freezing outside!
everyday_scene: Everyday: It was obvious from her smile that she had passed.
news_style_line: News-style: The problem with the old bridge is obvious to engineers.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Obvious answer: chai, not coffee.'
mcq_question: 'The mistake was so ___ that everyone saw it.'
mcq_options: A) obvious  B) obviously  C) obviousness  D) oblivious
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The reason for his silence was ______. → obvious
find_and_fix_to_correct: It is obviously that he lied. → It is obvious that he lied.
translate: साफ़ है कि वह नाराज़ है। → It's obvious that he's angry.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something obvious in your classroom or office.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which adjective means 'easy to see or understand'?
usage_tip: Don't confuse with 'oblivious' (= not aware).

simple_explanation: Lasting for only a short time; not permanent.
example_1: This is only a temporary job.
example_2: The road closure is temporary.
example_3: We're staying in a temporary flat.
collocations: temporary job, temporary solution, temporary problem, temporary address, only temporary
grammar_pattern: temporary + noun / be temporary
common_mistake: It is a temporarily problem.
correct_version: It is a temporary problem.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Temporary' is the adjective; 'temporarily' is the adverb.
spelling_tip: TEM-PO-RA-RY: four syllables — don't drop the -RA- ('tempory' is wrong).
etymology: From Latin temporarius, from tempus 'time'.
mnemonic: TEMPORARY = TEMPO (time) + only for a while.
memory_trick: Encouraging phrase: 'This failure is temporary.'
visual_association: A tent standing next to a half-built house.
difference_explained: Temporary = for a short time. Permanent = for always.
mini_conversation:
A: Is this your new office?
B: Only a temporary one until the building is ready.
everyday_scene: Everyday: The family moved into a temporary shelter after the flood.
news_style_line: News-style: The government announced a temporary ban on firecrackers.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Bad days are temporary, yaar. Keep going.'
mcq_question: 'This is a ___ arrangement until next month.'
mcq_options: A) temporary  B) temporarily  C) temper  D) tempo
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: He got a ______ job during the holidays. → temporary
find_and_fix_to_correct: The shop is temporary closed. → The shop is temporarily closed.
translate: यह एक अस्थायी समाधान है। → This is a temporary solution.
write_your_own_sentence: Write about a temporary problem you faced and solved.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which adjective means 'lasting only a short time'?
usage_tip: Sign language: 'Temporarily closed' = shut for now, will reopen.

hindi_meaning: दुर्भाग्य से, अफ़सोस की बात है कि
simple_explanation: Used to say that something is sad, disappointing or bad luck.
example_1: Unfortunately, I can't come to the party.
example_2: Unfortunately, the shop was closed.
example_3: He unfortunately missed the train.
collocations: unfortunately not, sadly and unfortunately, unfortunately for
where_it_s_used: Bad news, polite refusals, emails, stories
grammar_pattern: Unfortunately, + clause (start is most common) / subject + unfortunately + verb
common_mistake: Unfortunately, I can come.
correct_version: Unfortunately, I can't come.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Unfortunately' introduces bad news — the sentence should match.
spelling_tip: UN + FORTUNATE + LY: keep the E — unfortunatELY.
etymology: un- + 'fortunate', from Latin fortuna, 'chance, luck'.
mnemonic: UN-FORTUNE-ately = no good FORTUNE (luck).
memory_trick: Softens bad news in emails: 'Unfortunately, we are unable to…'
visual_association: A broken umbrella in heavy rain, its owner sighing.
difference_explained: Very close. Unfortunately is common for inconvenient news; sadly is more emotional.
mini_conversation:
A: Is the doctor available today?
B: Unfortunately, she's on leave until Monday.
everyday_scene: Everyday: Unfortunately, the rain ruined the picnic.
news_style_line: News-style: Unfortunately, the flight was cancelled due to fog.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Unfortunately, my data pack is over. Talk later!'
mcq_question: 'I'd love to help, but ___ I'm busy today.'
mcq_options: A) unfortunately  B) fortunately  C) unfortunate  D) fortune
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: ______, we lost the match by one run. → Unfortunately
find_and_fix_to_correct: Unfortunate, the bus was late. → Unfortunately, the bus was late.
translate: दुर्भाग्य से मैं समय पर नहीं पहुँच सका। → Unfortunately, I couldn't reach on time.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a polite refusal to an invitation using 'unfortunately'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which adverb introduces bad or sad news?
usage_tip: Pair with a positive next step: 'Unfortunately…, but I can…'.

hindi_meaning: के बारे में, के संबंध में
simple_explanation: About; concerning (formal).
example_2: Do you have any questions regarding the course?
example_3: Regarding the fees, please contact the office.
collocations: regarding your query, regarding the above, questions regarding, with regard to
grammar_pattern: regarding + noun (no 'about' after it)
common_mistake: I want to talk regarding about the salary.
correct_version: I want to talk about the salary. / I'm writing regarding the salary.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Regarding' already means 'about' — don't add 'about'.
etymology: From 'regard', from Old French regarder, 'to look at'.
word_family: regard (v/n), regards (n: 'Best regards'), with regard to
mnemonic: REGARDING = you LOOK AT (regard) this topic.
memory_trick: Email subject formula: 'Regarding: leave request for 5th May.'
visual_association: An email subject line: 'Regarding: Fee payment'.
synonyms: about, concerning, with regard to, as for, related to
difference_explained: Regarding = about (preposition). 'Regards' = good wishes at the end of an email: 'Best regards'.
mini_conversation:
A: I'm calling regarding my order.
B: Sure, may I have the order number?
everyday_scene: Everyday: The principal sent a notice regarding the new school timings.
news_style_line: News-style: The ministry issued guidelines regarding online safety.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Any update regarding tomorrow's plan, guys?'
mcq_options: A) regarding  B) regarding about  C) regard  D) regards
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Please contact us ______ any changes. → regarding
find_and_fix_to_correct: I am writing regarding about my leave. → I am writing regarding my leave.
translate: मैं अपनी छुट्टी के संबंध में लिख रहा हूँ। → I am writing regarding my leave.
write_your_own_sentence: Write an email subject line and first sentence using 'regarding'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which formal preposition means 'about'?
usage_tip: In casual talk, just say 'about'; save 'regarding' for emails and letters.

simple_explanation: To respect and like someone for what they do; to look at something with pleasure.
example_2: We stopped to admire the view.
example_3: She is admired by all her students.
collocations: admire someone for, deeply admire, admire the view, greatly admired
action_sequence: Before: see someone's good work → During: feel respect → After: want to be like them
grammar_pattern: admire + person + for + noun/-ing / admire + thing
common_mistake: I admire on him.
correct_version: I admire him.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Admire' takes the person directly — no preposition.
spelling_tip: AD-MIRE → ADMIRATION: the E drops in the noun.
etymology: From Latin admirari, 'to wonder at' (ad- + mirari 'to wonder').
mnemonic: adMIRE → MIRror: you look at them and wish to be like them.
memory_trick: Pattern: admire someone FOR something.
visual_association: A young boy watching a firefighter with wide, shining eyes.
synonyms: respect, look up to, praise, appreciate
difference_explained: Like = enjoy. Admire = respect because of a quality or skill.
mini_conversation:
A: Who is your role model?
B: My mother. I admire her patience.
everyday_scene: Everyday: Tourists stood silently, admiring the Taj Mahal at sunrise.
news_style_line: News-style: The scientist is widely admired for her work on clean water.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'I really admire how you balance job and studies.'
mcq_options: A) admire  B) admire on  C) admire to  D) admiration
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: People ______ him for his honesty. → admire
find_and_fix_to_correct: We admired at the paintings. → We admired the paintings.
translate: मैं उनकी मेहनत का आदर करता हूँ। → I admire their hard work.
write_your_own_sentence: Write about a person you admire and why.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which verb means 'to respect someone for their qualities'?
usage_tip: 'Admirable' (adj) = deserving respect.

simple_explanation: To pay no attention to someone or something, on purpose.
example_2: She ignored my messages all day.
example_3: Don't ignore the warning signs.
collocations: ignore someone, ignore advice, ignore a message, completely ignore, can't ignore
action_sequence: Before: someone calls your name → During: you hear but don't answer → After: they feel ignored
grammar_pattern: ignore + noun/person (no preposition)
common_mistake: Don't ignore to me.
correct_version: Don't ignore me.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Ignore' takes the person/thing directly.
etymology: From Latin ignorare, 'not to know, disregard'.
mnemonic: IGNORE → 'I-G-No-Reply': seen but no reply.
memory_trick: Ignore (choose not to notice) ≠ ignorant (not knowing).
visual_association: A phone lighting up with messages while its owner turns away.
antonyms: notice, pay attention to, respond to
difference_explained: Ignore = choose not to pay attention (verb). Ignorant = not knowing (adjective).
mini_conversation:
A: Some people laughed at my accent.
B: Ignore them. Keep speaking.
everyday_scene: Everyday: The dog ignored the ball and chased a butterfly.
news_style_line: News-style: Residents say their complaints were ignored for months.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'He ignored my call, then texted 'what?' lol.'
mcq_options: A) ignore  B) ignore to  C) ignorant  D) ignorance
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: She ______ my advice and failed. → ignored
find_and_fix_to_correct: He ignored to his teacher. → He ignored his teacher.
translate: उसने मेरी बात को अनदेखा कर दिया। → He ignored what I said.
write_your_own_sentence: Write about something negative you choose to ignore.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which verb means 'to pay no attention on purpose'?
usage_tip: Advice for learners: ignore laughter, not feedback.

simple_explanation: To stop someone while they are speaking or doing something.
example_1: Sorry to interrupt, but you have a call.
example_2: Please don't interrupt me.
example_3: The match was interrupted by rain.
collocations: sorry to interrupt, interrupt someone, constantly interrupt, be interrupted by
action_sequence: Before: someone is speaking → During: you start talking → After: they stop mid-sentence
grammar_pattern: interrupt + person/thing (no preposition)
common_mistake: Don't interrupt in between.
correct_version: Don't interrupt.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Interrupt' already means 'in between' — 'in between' is extra.
etymology: From Latin interrumpere, 'to break between' (inter- + rumpere 'to break').
mnemonic: interRUPT → eRUPT: you break into someone's sentence.
memory_trick: Polite way: 'Sorry to interrupt, but…'
visual_association: A person raising a finger in a meeting while someone else is mid-sentence.
synonyms: cut in, break in, disturb, butt in
difference_explained: Interrupt = stop someone mid-speech or mid-action. Disturb = bother someone (who may be resting or working).
mini_conversation:
A: So I was saying that the plan—
B: Sorry to interrupt, but the bus is here!
everyday_scene: Everyday: The baby's crying interrupted the phone call.
news_style_line: News-style: Power cuts interrupted the live broadcast twice.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Stop interrupting me, I'm telling the best part!'
mcq_options: A) interrupt  B) interrupt to  C) interruption  D) interrupt in
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: I'm sorry to ______ your meeting. → interrupt
find_and_fix_to_correct: He interrupted in between my talk. → He interrupted my talk.
translate: बीच में मत टोको। → Don't interrupt.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a polite sentence to interrupt your boss in a meeting.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which verb means 'to stop someone while they are speaking'?
usage_tip: Spelling: double R — inteRRupt.

simple_explanation: To act as if something is true when it is not.
example_2: Don't pretend you didn't see me!
example_3: Let's pretend we are in London and speak only English.
collocations: pretend to be, pretend that, pretend not to, just pretending
action_sequence: Before: know the truth → During: act as if it's different → After: others may believe you
grammar_pattern: pretend + to + verb / pretend + that clause
common_mistake: He pretended as if he was sick.
correct_version: He pretended to be sick. / He pretended (that) he was sick.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Pretend' doesn't need 'as if'.
etymology: From Latin praetendere, 'to stretch in front, put forward (as an excuse)'.
mnemonic: PRE-TEND = put a fake face IN FRONT of the real one.
memory_trick: Practice trick: 'Pretend you're a tour guide' — role-play builds speaking confidence.
visual_association: A child with closed eyes and a big smile, clearly not asleep.
synonyms: fake, act, make believe, put on
difference_explained: Lie = say something false. Pretend = act as if something is true (with or without words).
mini_conversation:
A: Why didn't you answer the teacher?
B: I pretended I hadn't heard the question.
everyday_scene: Everyday: The kids pretended the sofa was a boat.
news_style_line: News-style: The fraudster pretended to be a bank officer on the phone.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'I'm pretending to work, but I'm actually watching cricket.'
mcq_options: A) pretended  B) pretended as  C) pretend like to  D) pretending that to
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Don't ______ you know if you don't. → pretend
find_and_fix_to_correct: He pretended as if he knew me. → He pretended to know me.
translate: वह सोने का नाटक कर रहा था। → He was pretending to be asleep.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a fun role-play idea using 'Let's pretend…'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which verb means 'to act as if something is true when it isn't'?
usage_tip: Warning: bank or officer 'pretending' on calls is a common fraud — never share OTPs.

simple_explanation: To show that something is true by giving facts or evidence.
example_2: She proved everyone wrong.
example_3: The test proved that he was innocent.
collocations: prove something, prove someone wrong, prove yourself, prove that, prove useful
action_sequence: Before: make a claim → During: show facts and evidence → After: others accept it's true
grammar_pattern: prove + noun / prove + that clause / prove + adjective (= turn out)
common_mistake: He proved his innocent.
correct_version: He proved his innocence. / He proved (that) he was innocent.
why_it_s_wrong: After 'prove' use a noun or a that-clause, not a bare adjective.
spelling_tip: PROVE → PROOF: the verb has V, the noun has F.
etymology: From Latin probare, 'to test, show to be good'.
mnemonic: PROVE → PROOF: the verb and the noun share a root.
memory_trick: 'Prove yourself' = show people what you can do.
visual_association: A student holding up a solved sum on the board with a big smile.
difference_explained: Show = let someone see. Prove = show with evidence so there is no doubt.
mini_conversation:
A: Everyone said I couldn't speak in public.
B: And you proved them wrong!
everyday_scene: Everyday: The photo proved that she was at the event.
news_style_line: News-style: Scientists have proved that the new seed needs less water.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Watch me — I'll prove I can cook better than you.'
mcq_question: 'You have to ___ that you were there.'
mcq_options: A) prove  B) proof  C) proving to  D) proved to
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: His hard work ______ that he deserves the job. → proves
find_and_fix_to_correct: She proved her honest. → She proved her honesty. / She proved she was honest.
translate: उसने अपनी काबिलियत साबित कर दी। → She proved her ability.
write_your_own_sentence: Write about a time you proved someone wrong.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which verb means 'to show that something is true with evidence'?
usage_tip: Noun is 'proof': 'Do you have proof?'

simple_explanation: To say you will not do or accept something.
example_2: She refused the job offer.
example_3: The bank refused my loan application.
collocations: refuse to, refuse an offer, flatly refuse, refuse permission
action_sequence: Before: receive a request → During: think it over → After: say no
grammar_pattern: refuse + to + verb / refuse + noun
common_mistake: He refused for going.
correct_version: He refused to go.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Refuse' is followed by 'to + verb'.
pronunciation_tip: Verb: rih-FYOOZ (z sound). Noun 'refuse' (= rubbish) is REF-yooss.
spelling_tip: RE-FUSE: stress on FUSE (verb). REF-use (noun) = rubbish.
etymology: From Old French refuser, probably from Latin refusus, 'poured back'.
mnemonic: reFUSE: the FUSE blows — 'No power, no way!'
memory_trick: Opposite of 'agree to'.
visual_association: A child with folded arms and shut lips, pushing away a plate of karela.
synonyms: decline, turn down, reject, say no
difference_explained: Refuse = say you will not DO something. Deny = say something is NOT TRUE.
mini_conversation:
A: Did they give you leave?
B: No, my manager refused.
everyday_scene: Everyday: The toddler refused to wear his shoes.
news_style_line: News-style: The court refused to stop the construction.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'She refused to share her fries. Rude!'
mcq_options: A) refused  B) refused for  C) denied to  D) refusal
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: I ______ to give up on my dream. → refuse
find_and_fix_to_correct: They refused for helping us. → They refused to help us.
translate: उसने मदद करने से मना कर दिया। → He refused to help.
write_your_own_sentence: Write about something you refuse to do, and why.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which verb means 'to say you will not do something'?
usage_tip: Polite version: 'decline' — 'I'm afraid I must decline.'

simple_explanation: To achieve what you tried to do.
example_1: She succeeded in passing the exam.
example_2: If you practise, you will succeed.
example_3: He finally succeeded in finding a job.
collocations: succeed in, succeed in life, finally succeed, succeed at
action_sequence: Before: set a goal → During: work hard → After: reach it
grammar_pattern: succeed + in + -ing / succeed (alone)
common_mistake: He succeeded to pass the exam.
correct_version: He succeeded in passing the exam.
why_it_s_wrong: The pattern is 'succeed IN + -ing'.
spelling_tip: Double C and double E: su-CC-EE-d.
etymology: From Latin succedere, 'to come after, go near'.
mnemonic: SUCCEED: double C, double E — Success Comes, Effort Earns.
memory_trick: Family: succeed (v) → success (n) → successful (adj).
visual_association: A seedling growing into a tall tree over time.
difference_explained: Succeed = do what you tried to do (no object needed). Achieve = reach a specific goal (needs an object).
mini_conversation:
A: Did you get the visa?
B: Yes! We finally succeeded after three tries.
everyday_scene: Everyday: The village girl succeeded in becoming the first doctor in her family.
news_style_line: News-style: The mission succeeded in landing near the moon's south pole.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Tried to make rotis round… did not succeed.'
mcq_options: A) succeeded  B) succeed to  C) success  D) successful
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: If at first you don't ______, try again. → succeed
find_and_fix_to_correct: She succeeded to win. → She succeeded in winning.
translate: वह नौकरी पाने में सफल हो गया। → He succeeded in getting the job.
write_your_own_sentence: Write one thing you succeeded in doing this year.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which verb means 'to achieve what you tried to do'?
usage_tip: Formal meaning too: 'The prince succeeded his father' = came after him as king.

hindi_meaning: शक होना (कि कुछ सच है), संदेह करना
simple_explanation: To think something is probably true, usually something bad; to think someone may be guilty.
example_2: Police suspect a man in the theft.
example_3: I suspect it will rain later.
collocations: suspect someone of, suspect that, strongly suspect, I suspect so
action_sequence: Before: notice something odd → During: think someone may be guilty → After: watch them carefully
grammar_pattern: suspect + that clause / suspect + person + of + -ing
common_mistake: I suspect on him.
correct_version: I suspect him.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Suspect' takes the person directly — no 'on'.
etymology: From Latin suspicere, 'to look up at, mistrust'.
mnemonic: SUS-PECT → you insPECT someone because you feel something is wrong.
memory_trick: Stress changes meaning: verb su-SPECT, noun SUS-pect.
visual_association: A detective with a magnifying glass looking at footprints.
difference_explained: Suspect = think something IS probably true. Doubt = think something is probably NOT true.
mini_conversation:
A: Why is the dog so quiet?
B: I suspect he ate the cake.
everyday_scene: Everyday: The shopkeeper suspected the note was fake.
news_style_line: News-style: Doctors suspect the illness was caused by dirty water.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'I suspect my brother used my phone again.'
mcq_question: 'I ___ that she already knows the secret.'
mcq_options: A) suspect  B) suspect on  C) suspicion  D) suspicious
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The police ______ him of stealing the bike. → suspected
find_and_fix_to_correct: We suspect on the new guard. → We suspect the new guard.
translate: मुझे शक है कि वह झूठ बोल रहा है। → I suspect he is lying.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence starting 'I suspect…' about today's weather or plans.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which verb means 'to think something bad is probably true'?
usage_tip: 'I suspect so' is a natural, softer way to say 'probably yes'.

simple_explanation: To try to impress people by showing your skills or things; to proudly show something.
example_2: He loves showing off his new bike.
example_3: She wore the dress to show off her tailoring skills.
collocations: show off (alone), show off something, a show-off (n)
action_sequence: Before: get a new phone → During: show it to everyone again and again → After: people feel annoyed
grammar_pattern: show off (alone) / show off + thing / show + it/pronoun + off
word_forms: show off – showed off – shown off – showing off
common_mistake: He showed off with his car.
correct_version: He showed off his car.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Show off' takes the thing directly — no 'with'.
spelling_tip: Two words as a verb: SHOW OFF. The noun is 'show-off' (with a hyphen).
etymology: 'Show' comes from Old English sceawian, 'to look at'.
mnemonic: SHOW OFF → like switching the show-lights ON for yourself.
memory_trick: Noun with hyphen: 'Don't be a show-off.'
visual_association: A boy riding a bike with no hands, looking around to see who is watching.
difference_explained: Show = let someone see (neutral). Show off = show in a proud way to impress.
mini_conversation:
A: Did you see Raj's new watch?
B: Yes, he's been showing it off all day.
everyday_scene: Everyday: The kitten showed off by jumping onto the tallest shelf.
news_style_line: News-style: The city showed off its new riverfront at the festival.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Not showing off, but I got 95 in English!'
mcq_options: A) showing off  B) showing up  C) showing on  D) show offing
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: She practised hard, not to ______, but to improve. → show off
find_and_fix_to_correct: He showed off with his marks. → He showed off his marks.
translate: वह अपनी नई गाड़ी का दिखावा कर रहा था। → He was showing off his new car.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about someone who shows off on social media.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which phrasal verb means 'to try to impress people'?
usage_tip: 'Show up' is different: it means 'arrive'.

simple_explanation: To look or behave like an older family member.
example_2: Who do you take after?
example_3: He takes after his grandfather — very funny.
collocations: take after your father/mother, really take after
action_sequence: Before: a child grows up → During: looks and acts like a parent → After: people say 'she takes after her mother'
grammar_pattern: take after + older family member (not used in continuous)
word_forms: take after – took after – taken after – (not used in -ing for this meaning)
common_mistake: She is taking after her mother.
correct_version: She takes after her mother.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Take after' is a state — use simple tense.
spelling_tip: Two words: TAKE AFTER. Past: took after.
etymology: 'Take' comes from Old Norse taka.
mnemonic: TAKE AFTER = you come AFTER your parents and TAKE their looks.
memory_trick: Only for OLDER family members — not friends or younger siblings.
visual_association: A grandfather and grandson with the same big smile and glasses.
difference_explained: Look like = appearance only. Take after = appearance OR character, and only older family.
mini_conversation:
A: You're so good at cooking!
B: I take after my dad — he's a great cook.
everyday_scene: Everyday: The little girl takes after her father — she loves cricket.
news_style_line: News-style: The young leader is said to take after his late grandfather.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'I take after my mom — we both talk too much.'
mcq_question: 'He ___ his uncle — both are very tall.'
mcq_options: A) takes after  B) is taking after  C) takes over  D) took on
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Which parent do you ______? → take after
find_and_fix_to_correct: My son is taking after me. → My son takes after me.
translate: वह अपने पिता पर गया है। → He takes after his father.
write_your_own_sentence: Write about who you take after in your family and how.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which phrasal verb means 'to be similar to an older family member'?
usage_tip: 'Take over' is different: it means 'take control'.

simple_explanation: Known to you; or knowing something well.
example_2: Are you familiar with this software?
example_3: The song sounds familiar.
collocations: look familiar, sound familiar, familiar with, familiar face, become familiar with
grammar_pattern: be familiar + with + thing (you know it) / thing + be familiar + to + person (it is known to you)
common_mistake: I am familiar to this area.
correct_version: I am familiar with this area. / This area is familiar to me.
why_it_s_wrong: YOU are familiar WITH something; something is familiar TO you.
etymology: From Latin familiaris, 'of a household', from familia 'family'.
mnemonic: FAMILiar → like FAMILY: well known to you.
memory_trick: CV phrase: 'Familiar with MS Excel and Canva'.
visual_association: A person at a crowded station spotting an old classmate's face.
difference_explained: Familiar = known to YOU. Famous = known to MANY people.
mini_conversation:
A: Have we met before? You look familiar.
B: Maybe at Sunita's wedding?
everyday_scene: Everyday: The smell of the old school corridor felt familiar.
news_style_line: News-style: Voters are familiar with the candidate's promises.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'This street looks familiar… wait, did we pass it already?'
mcq_question: 'Are you ___ with the rules of chess?'
mcq_options: A) familiar  B) family  C) familiarity  D) famous
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The tune sounds ______ but I can't remember the name. → familiar
find_and_fix_to_correct: I am not familiar to this app. → I am not familiar with this app.
translate: क्या आप इस इलाक़े से परिचित हैं? → Are you familiar with this area?
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a skill you are familiar with.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which adjective means 'known to you'?
usage_tip: 'Familiarise yourself with…' = learn about something new.

simple_explanation: Right or acceptable for a particular person, purpose or situation.
example_1: This film isn't suitable for children.
example_2: Is this a suitable time to call?
example_3: We're looking for a suitable candidate.
collocations: suitable for, suitable time, suitable candidate, most suitable, not suitable
grammar_pattern: be suitable + for + person/purpose / suitable + noun
common_mistake: This course is suitable to beginners.
correct_version: This course is suitable for beginners.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'suitable FOR'.
etymology: From 'suit' + -able; 'suit' ultimately from Latin sequi, 'to follow'.
mnemonic: SUITable = it SUITS you, like a well-fitting suit.
memory_trick: Job ad word: 'Suitable candidates will be called.'
visual_association: A pair of shoes that fit perfectly next to ones that are too big.
difference_explained: Suitable = right for the purpose. Comfortable = feels physically good.
mini_conversation:
A: Can I wear jeans to the interview?
B: Formal clothes would be more suitable.
everyday_scene: Everyday: Sandy soil is suitable for growing groundnuts.
news_style_line: News-style: The land was found suitable for a new hospital.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Is 7 a suitable time for the Zoom call?'
mcq_question: 'This game is not ___ for young kids.'
mcq_options: A) suitable  B) suit  C) suitably  D) suited to for
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Please choose a ______ password. → suitable
find_and_fix_to_correct: This dress is suitable to the party. → This dress is suitable for the party.
translate: यह नौकरी मेरे लिए उपयुक्त है। → This job is suitable for me.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a suitable time to study.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which adjective means 'right for a purpose or person'?
usage_tip: Indian matrimonial ads often say 'suitable match' — standard English too.

simple_explanation: Able to speak a language easily, smoothly and well.
example_1: She is fluent in English and Hindi.
example_2: He speaks fluent French.
example_3: I want to become fluent in six months.
collocations: fluent in English, fluent speaker, speak fluent English, become fluent, fairly fluent
grammar_pattern: be fluent + in + language / speak + fluent + language
common_mistake: He is fluent English.
correct_version: He is fluent in English. / He speaks fluent English.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'fluent IN + language' or 'speak fluent + language'.
etymology: From Latin fluere, 'to flow'.
mnemonic: FLUENT → FLOW: words flow like water.
memory_trick: Fluency ≠ perfection. Fluent speakers still make small mistakes — they just keep going.
visual_association: A river flowing smoothly over stones.
difference_explained: Fluent = speaks smoothly without long pauses. Accurate = speaks without mistakes. Aim for both.
mini_conversation:
A: How long did it take you to become fluent?
B: About a year of speaking every single day.
everyday_scene: Everyday: The tour guide is fluent in four languages.
news_style_line: News-style: Candidates must be fluent in English and one regional language.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Six months of daily practice and I'm almost fluent!'
mcq_options: A) fluent  B) fluently  C) fluency  D) flow
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: My goal is to speak ______ English. → fluent
find_and_fix_to_correct: He speaks English fluent. → He speaks English fluently.
translate: वह धाराप्रवाह अंग्रेज़ी बोलता है। → He speaks fluent English.
write_your_own_sentence: Write your plan to become fluent in English.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which adjective means 'able to speak a language smoothly'?
usage_tip: CV line: 'Fluent in English, Hindi and Urdu.'

simple_explanation: Full of people.
example_2: I don't like crowded buses.
example_3: The beach gets crowded on Sundays.
collocations: crowded place, crowded train, very crowded, get crowded, overcrowded
grammar_pattern: be/get crowded / crowded + with + people
common_mistake: The station was very crowd.
correct_version: The station was very crowded.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Crowd' is the noun; 'crowded' is the adjective.
spelling_tip: CROWD + ED: the -ed is a full syllable — KROW-did.
etymology: 'Crowd' comes from Old English crudan, 'to press, hurry'.
mnemonic: CROWDED = full of a CROWD.
memory_trick: 'Packed' is a very natural informal alternative.
visual_association: A local train door with people hanging on the handle.
difference_explained: Busy = lots of activity (a busy road, a busy person). Crowded = full of PEOPLE, little space.
mini_conversation:
A: Shall we go to the mall today?
B: On a Sunday? It'll be too crowded.
everyday_scene: Everyday: The temple was crowded with devotees during the festival.
news_style_line: News-style: Crowded trains are a daily problem for city commuters.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Metro was so crowded I couldn't even move my hand.'
mcq_question: 'The shop was ___ because of the sale.'
mcq_options: A) crowded  B) crowd  C) crowding  D) crowdy
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Delhi Metro is ______ in the evening. → crowded
find_and_fix_to_correct: The bus was full crowd. → The bus was very crowded.
translate: बाज़ार में बहुत भीड़ थी। → The market was very crowded.
write_your_own_sentence: Write about the most crowded place you have been to.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which adjective means 'full of people'?
usage_tip: 'Overcrowded' = too many people for the space.

simple_explanation: Almost the same, but not exactly.
example_1: My phone is similar to yours.
example_2: The two sisters look very similar.
example_3: We have similar ideas.
collocations: similar to, very similar, similar in, look similar, something similar
grammar_pattern: be similar + to + noun / similar + in + quality
common_mistake: Your bag is similar like mine.
correct_version: Your bag is similar to mine.
why_it_s_wrong: Never say 'similar like' — use 'similar to'.
etymology: From Latin similis, 'like, resembling'.
mnemonic: SIMILAR → SIMILe: 'as brave AS a lion' — comparing things that are alike.
memory_trick: 'Similar to' is fixed — like 'different from'.
visual_association: Two nearly identical cups, one with a tiny chip.
difference_explained: Same = exactly one or identical. Similar = alike but with small differences.
mini_conversation:
A: Is Kannada like Tamil?
B: They're similar in some ways, but different languages.
everyday_scene: Everyday: The twins wear similar clothes but have different hobbies.
news_style_line: News-style: Similar problems have been reported in other cities.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Your laugh is so similar to your dad's!'
mcq_options: A) similar to  B) similar like  C) same like  D) similar with
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Our answers were very ______. → similar
find_and_fix_to_correct: His idea is similar like mine. → His idea is similar to mine.
translate: मेरी राय तुम्हारी राय से मिलती-जुलती है। → My opinion is similar to yours.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence comparing two things that are similar.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which adjective means 'almost the same'?
usage_tip: Adverb 'similarly' links ideas: 'Similarly, the second plan…'.

simple_explanation: Honestly and directly, even if it's not what someone wants to hear.
example_1: Frankly, I don't like the plan.
example_2: Can I speak frankly?
example_3: Frankly speaking, the food was cold.
collocations: frankly speaking, to be frank, speak frankly, quite frankly
grammar_pattern: Frankly, + clause / speak + frankly / 'Frankly speaking' / 'To be frank'
common_mistake: Frankly to say, I'm tired.
correct_version: Frankly speaking, I'm tired. / To be frank, I'm tired.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'frankly speaking', 'to be frank', or just 'frankly' — not 'frankly to say'.
etymology: From 'frank', via Old French franc, 'free' — the Franks were the free people.
mnemonic: FRANKly = FREE speech, no filter.
memory_trick: 'Frankly speaking' is common in India — fine, but 'Honestly' or 'To be honest' sound more natural internationally.
visual_association: A person looking straight at the camera, calm and serious.
synonyms: honestly, openly, bluntly, to be honest
difference_explained: Frankly = honestly and directly (can be polite). Rudely = without respect.
mini_conversation:
A: How was my presentation?
B: Frankly, the slides were too long.
everyday_scene: Everyday: Frankly, the old fan makes more noise than wind.
news_style_line: News-style: The minister spoke frankly about the problems in the health system.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Frankly, I'd rather sleep than go to that party.'
mcq_question: '___ speaking, I didn't enjoy the film.'
mcq_options: A) Frankly  B) Frank  C) Frankness  D) Freely
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: ______, I think we need a new plan. → Frankly
find_and_fix_to_correct: Frankly to say, he is right. → Frankly speaking, he is right.
