simple_explanation: Slowly, over a period of time; little by little.
example_2: The pain gradually went away.
example_3: Gradually, the city grew bigger.
collocations: gradually improve, gradually increase, gradually become, gradually change
grammar_pattern: subject + gradually + verb / Gradually, + clause / verb + gradually
common_mistake: Gradually gradually I improved.
correct_version: Gradually, I improved. / I improved little by little.
why_it_s_wrong: Hindi 'dheere-dheere' is doubled, but English 'gradually' is used once.
etymology: From 'gradual', from Latin gradus, 'step'.
mnemonic: GRADually → GRADES: step-by-step, one grade at a time.
memory_trick: Motivation line: 'Gradually is still progress.'
visual_association: A staircase with a person on the fourth step, looking up.
synonyms: slowly, steadily, little by little, step by step
difference_explained: Slowly = low speed. Gradually = changing little by little over time.
mini_conversation:
A: Are you speaking more confidently now?
B: Yes, gradually — every week feels easier.
everyday_scene: Everyday: The baby gradually learned to walk.
news_style_line: News-style: Temperatures will gradually rise over the week.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Gradually getting used to waking up at 6.'
mcq_options: A) gradually  B) gradual  C) grade  D) gradually gradually
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Prices have ______ increased this year. → gradually
find_and_fix_to_correct: Gradually gradually he learned. → Gradually, he learned.

write_your_own_sentence: Write about something that has gradually changed in your life.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review

simple_explanation: Correctly, in the right way.
example_2: I didn't sleep properly last night.
example_3: Hold the pen properly.
collocations: work properly, do it properly, eat properly, properly dressed, not properly
grammar_pattern: verb + properly / not + verb + properly
common_mistake: Do it proper.
correct_version: Do it properly.
why_it_s_wrong: After a verb, use the adverb 'properly', not the adjective 'proper'.
etymology: From 'proper', via Old French propre, from Latin proprius, 'one's own, particular'.
mnemonic: PROPERly → a PROPER job, done right.
memory_trick: Instruction word: 'Wash your hands properly.'
visual_association: A neatly made bed with folded corners.
difference_explained: Carefully = with attention to avoid mistakes. Properly = in the correct, expected way.
mini_conversation:
A: My phone isn't charging.
B: Is the cable plugged in properly?
everyday_scene: Everyday: The mechanic checked that the brakes were working properly.
news_style_line: News-style: Officials said the machines were not properly maintained.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'I haven't eaten properly all day — just chai.'
mcq_options: A) properly  B) proper  C) property  D) properness
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Chew your food ______. → properly
find_and_fix_to_correct: He didn't do the work proper. → He didn't do the work properly.
translate: ठीक से पढ़ाई करो। → Study properly.
write_your_own_sentence: Write an instruction for a friend using 'properly'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which adverb means 'in the correct way'?
usage_tip: Don't confuse with 'property' (land, belongings).

simple_explanation: More than usual; above all.
example_2: It's hot, especially in the afternoon.
example_3: This is especially important for beginners.
collocations: especially for, especially when, especially in, especially important
grammar_pattern: especially + noun/phrase / especially + adjective / especially when/if + clause
common_mistake: I like sports, specially cricket.
correct_version: I like sports, especially cricket.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Especially' = above all (emphasis). 'Specially' = for a special purpose ('made specially for you').
spelling_tip: ESPECIAL + LY: double L — especiaLLy. Starts with E, not 'specially'.
etymology: From Old French especial, from Latin specialis, 'particular'.
mnemonic: ESPECIALLY = Extra SPECIAL: this one stands out.
memory_trick: Rule of thumb: especially = 'particularly'; specially = 'for one purpose'.
visual_association: A basket of fruits with one golden mango glowing.
difference_explained: Especially = above all, particularly. Specially = for a particular purpose: 'specially made'.
mini_conversation:
A: Do you like Agra?
B: Yes, especially the food near the old city.
everyday_scene: Everyday: Grandma loves winter, especially sitting in the sun with peanuts.
news_style_line: News-style: The heatwave is dangerous, especially for elderly people.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Loved the trip — especially the boat ride.'
mcq_options: A) especially  B) specially  C) special  D) specialty
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Drink water, ______ in summer. → especially
find_and_fix_to_correct: I like sweets, specially jalebi. → I like sweets, especially jalebi.
translate: मुझे ख़ासकर सुबह पढ़ना पसंद है। → I like studying, especially in the morning.
write_your_own_sentence: Write about a food you like, especially one dish.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which adverb means 'above all, particularly'?
usage_tip: Spelling: e + special + ly → especially.

simple_explanation: In a serious way; also used to show surprise or ask 'really?'.
example_2: He was seriously injured.
example_3: Seriously? You finished the whole book?
collocations: take something seriously, seriously injured, seriously consider, seriously?
grammar_pattern: take + noun + seriously / seriously + adjective / 'Seriously?' (alone)
common_mistake: Take it serious.
correct_version: Take it seriously.
why_it_s_wrong: After a verb, use the adverb 'seriously'.
etymology: From 'serious', from Latin serius, 'grave, earnest'.
mnemonic: SERIOUSly = with a SERIOUS face.
memory_trick: As a one-word reply, 'Seriously?' = 'Really? Are you joking?'
visual_association: A student with a determined face, books open, phone face-down.
difference_explained: 'Seriously?' shows stronger surprise or disbelief than 'Really?'
mini_conversation:
A: I'm quitting sugar for a month.
B: Seriously? Even at Diwali?
everyday_scene: Everyday: The coach told the team to take practice seriously.
news_style_line: News-style: Two people were seriously injured in the accident.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Seriously, this is the best chai in Agra.'
mcq_options: A) seriously  B) serious  C) seriousness  D) seriously of
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: She is ______ thinking about changing jobs. → seriously
find_and_fix_to_correct: Don't take it serious. → Don't take it seriously.

write_your_own_sentence: Write one thing you will take seriously this month.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which adverb means 'in a serious way' or 'really?'
usage_tip: 'Seriously ill' = very ill; good for medical contexts.

simple_explanation: To give something to someone for a short time, expecting it back.
example_1: Can you lend me your pen?
example_2: The bank lent him ₹2 lakh.
example_3: I lent my bike to my cousin.
collocations: lend money, lend a hand (= help), lend someone something, lend to
action_sequence: Before: a friend needs money → During: give it for a short time → After: they pay it back later
grammar_pattern: lend + person + thing / lend + thing + to + person
common_mistake: Can you borrow me your pen?
correct_version: Can you lend me your pen?
why_it_s_wrong: LEND = give. BORROW = take. You borrow FROM someone; you lend TO someone.
spelling_tip: LEND → LENT: the past ends in T.
etymology: From Old English lænan; the final -d was added in Middle English.
mnemonic: LEND → LEAVE it with them (for a while). BORROW → BRING it to you.
memory_trick: 'Lend a hand' = help: 'Can you lend me a hand with these bags?'
visual_association: One hand passing an umbrella to another hand, with a small 'return' arrow.
difference_explained: Lend = give for a while (I lend TO you). Borrow = take for a while (I borrow FROM you).
mini_conversation:
A: Can you lend me ₹200 till Friday?
B: Sure, here you go.
everyday_scene: Everyday: The neighbour lent us her ladder to fix the fan.
news_style_line: News-style: Banks are lending more to small businesses this year.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Lend me your charger? Mine's dead.'
mcq_options: A) lend  B) borrow  C) lent to  D) loaned me to
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: I ______ him my book last week. → lent
find_and_fix_to_correct: Can I lend your car? → Can I borrow your car?
translate: क्या तुम मुझे अपनी किताब उधार दे सकते हो? → Can you lend me your book?
write_your_own_sentence: Write a request to lend something, and a request to borrow something.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which verb means 'to give something for a short time'?
usage_tip: Past tense is 'lent', not 'lended'.

simple_explanation: To have to pay back money, or to feel you should do something for someone because they helped you.
example_2: How much do I owe you?
example_3: I owe my success to my teachers.
collocations: owe money, owe someone a favour, owe an apology, owe something to someone, I owe you one
action_sequence: Before: borrow money → During: you still have to pay it back → After: you owe it until you pay
grammar_pattern: owe + person + amount/thing / owe + thing + to + person
word_forms: owe – owed – owed – owing (continuous rarely used for this meaning)
common_mistake: I am owing you ₹500.
correct_version: I owe you ₹500.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Owe' is a state verb — use simple tense.
spelling_tip: OWE: silent W, rhymes with 'go'. The phrase is 'owing to' (= because of).
etymology: From Old English agan, 'to have, own'.
word_family: owing to (prep: because of), IOU ('I owe you')
mnemonic: OWE = 'Oh!' — you remember the money you haven't paid.
memory_trick: 'I owe you one' = thanks, I'll return the favour.
visual_association: A small notebook page with 'Rahul — ₹500' written in it.
synonyms: be in debt, be indebted, be obliged
difference_explained: Borrow = the action of taking. Owe = the situation after — you still have to pay back.
mini_conversation:
A: Thanks for the lift!
B: No problem. But you owe me a samosa!
everyday_scene: Everyday: The shopkeeper reminded him that he owed ₹300 from last month.
news_style_line: News-style: Many farmers owe money to local lenders, the report says.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'I owe you one for covering my shift.'
mcq_question: 'How much do I ___ you for the tickets?'
mcq_options: A) owe  B) own  C) owing  D) owed to
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: I think I ______ you an apology. → owe
find_and_fix_to_correct: He is owing me money. → He owes me money.
write_your_own_sentence: Write about someone you owe your success to.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which verb means 'to have to pay someone back'?
usage_tip: 'Owe an apology' = you should say sorry.

simple_explanation: To become healthy again; to get back something lost.
example_1: He is recovering from the flu.
example_2: She recovered quickly after the operation.
example_3: Police recovered the stolen bike.
collocations: recover from, fully recover, recover quickly, recover the money, recover lost data
action_sequence: Before: fall ill → During: rest and take medicine → After: feel healthy again
grammar_pattern: recover + from + illness/event / recover + thing (get back)
common_mistake: I recovered my illness.
correct_version: I recovered from my illness.
why_it_s_wrong: You recover FROM an illness, but you recover a THING you lost.
etymology: From Old French recoverer, from Latin recuperare, 'to get again'.
mnemonic: RE-COVER = COVER your health AGAIN after losing it.
memory_trick: 'Get well soon' pairs with 'Hope you recover quickly.'
visual_association: A person on a hospital bed smiling as they sit up, a plant blooming by the window.
synonyms: get better, heal, get over; get back, regain
difference_explained: Recover = formal, for health and things. Get over = informal, also for emotions.
mini_conversation:
A: How is your father now?
B: Much better. He's recovering well.
everyday_scene: Everyday: The old tree recovered after the storm and grew new leaves.
news_style_line: News-style: The economy is slowly recovering after the slowdown.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Recovered from Friday's party only by Sunday lol.'
mcq_question: 'It took her two weeks to ___ from the fever.'
mcq_options: A) recover  B) recover of  C) recovery  D) cover
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The police ______ the stolen jewellery. → recovered
find_and_fix_to_correct: He recovered his cold. → He recovered from his cold.
translate: वह बीमारी से ठीक हो रहा है। → He is recovering from the illness.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a get-well message using 'recover'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which verb means 'to become healthy again'?
usage_tip: Noun: 'recovery' — 'Wishing you a speedy recovery.'

simple_explanation: To make something smaller in size, amount or price.
example_2: We need to reduce plastic use.
example_3: Prices were reduced by 20%.
collocations: reduce the price, reduce stress, reduce waste, reduce by 20%, reduce to
action_sequence: Before: spend too much → During: cut some costs → After: spend less
grammar_pattern: reduce + noun / reduce + by + amount / reduce + to + final amount
common_mistake: Please reduce down the price.
correct_version: Please reduce the price.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Reduce' already means 'make less' — 'down' is extra.
etymology: From Latin reducere, 'to lead back, bring back'.
mnemonic: RE-DUCE → REDUCE, REUSE, RECYCLE — make less waste.
memory_trick: 'By' = the change; 'to' = the result: reduced BY ₹100, TO ₹400.
visual_association: A price tag with ₹500 crossed out and ₹400 written in red.
difference_explained: Very close. Reduce = someone makes it less. Decrease can also be natural: 'Sales decreased.'
mini_conversation:
A: Can you reduce the price a little?
B: Okay, final price — ₹450.
everyday_scene: Everyday: Walking daily helped my uncle reduce his weight.
news_style_line: News-style: The city plans to reduce air pollution by 30%.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Trying to reduce screen time. Failing.'
mcq_options: A) reduced  B) reduced down  C) reduction  D) reducing to by
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Exercise can ______ stress. → reduce
find_and_fix_to_correct: Please reduce down the sugar. → Please reduce the sugar.
translate: हमें पानी की बर्बादी कम करनी चाहिए। → We should reduce water wastage.
write_your_own_sentence: Write one habit you want to reduce.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which verb means 'to make something less'?
usage_tip: Shop sign: 'Reduced prices' = on sale.

simple_explanation: To officially leave your job or position.
example_1: He resigned from his job last month.
example_2: The captain resigned after the defeat.
example_3: She resigned as manager.
collocations: resign from a job, resign as manager, forced to resign, resignation letter
action_sequence: Before: decide to leave the job → During: write a letter to the boss → After: leave the company
grammar_pattern: resign (alone) / resign + from + job / resign + as + role
common_mistake: He gave resign yesterday.
correct_version: He resigned yesterday. / He gave his resignation yesterday.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Resign' is a verb; the noun is 'resignation'.
spelling_tip: RE-SIGN: silent G, like 'sign'. Noun: resignation (G is spoken).
etymology: From Latin resignare, 'to unseal, give up'.
mnemonic: The G in resiGn is silent — like leaving quietly.
memory_trick: 'Put in your papers' is Indian English; internationally say 'resign' or 'hand in my resignation'.
visual_association: A person placing an envelope marked 'Resignation' on a desk.
difference_explained: Resign = leave a job by choice (any age). Retire = stop working at the end of your career.
mini_conversation:
A: Why is Ravi leaving?
B: He resigned to start his own business.
everyday_scene: Everyday: The shop manager resigned after twenty years.
news_style_line: News-style: The minister resigned after the scandal.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Resigned today! Two months' notice period though.'
mcq_options: A) resigned  B) gave resign  C) resignation  D) resign to
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: He decided to ______ and study abroad. → resign
find_and_fix_to_correct: I gave my resign. → I resigned. / I gave my resignation.
translate: उसने नौकरी से इस्तीफ़ा दे दिया। → He resigned from his job.
write_your_own_sentence: Write the first line of a polite resignation email.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which verb means 'to officially leave your job'?
usage_tip: 'Notice period' = time you work after resigning.

simple_explanation: To stay alive or continue after a danger or difficulty.
example_2: Plants can't survive without water.
example_3: I survived my first week at the new job!
collocations: survive an accident, survive a storm, struggle to survive, barely survive
where_it_s_used: Accidents, nature, business, jokes about hard days
action_sequence: Before: face danger → During: hold on and stay strong → After: come out alive
grammar_pattern: survive + event (no preposition) / survive (alone) / survive on + food/money
common_mistake: He survived in the accident.
correct_version: He survived the accident.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Survive' takes the event directly — no 'in'.
etymology: From Latin supervivere, 'to live beyond'.
mnemonic: SUR-VIVE = VIVA (life) goes on SURely.
memory_trick: Casual use for hard things: 'I survived exam week!'
visual_association: A small green plant growing through a crack in dry ground.
synonyms: live through, get through, endure, outlast
difference_explained: Live = be alive. Survive = stay alive or keep going through danger.
mini_conversation:
A: How was your first day teaching?
B: Tiring, but I survived!
everyday_scene: Everyday: The old banyan tree has survived many storms.
news_style_line: News-style: All passengers survived the emergency landing.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Survived a 6-hour train delay with just one packet of chips.'
mcq_options: A) survived  B) survived in  C) survival  D) survivor
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Camels can ______ many days without water. → survive
find_and_fix_to_correct: She survived from the flood. → She survived the flood.
translate: सभी लोग दुर्घटना में बच गए। → Everyone survived the accident.
write_your_own_sentence: Write about a difficult day you survived.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which verb means 'to stay alive through danger'?
usage_tip: 'Survive on' = manage with little: 'survive on ₹100 a day'.

hindi_meaning: स्वेच्छा से (बिना पैसे) काम करना, आगे आकर पेशकश करना
simple_explanation: To offer to do something without being asked or paid.

example_2: He volunteered to clean the classroom.
example_3: Who will volunteer to go first?
collocations: volunteer to, volunteer at, volunteer for, volunteer work

grammar_pattern: volunteer + to + verb / volunteer + at + place / volunteer + for + task
common_mistake: He volunteered for helping us.
correct_version: He volunteered to help us.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'volunteer to + verb' (or 'for + noun': 'volunteer for the event').

memory_trick: Speaking tip: volunteer to answer first in class — it builds confidence fast.
visual_association: A hand shooting up first in a classroom.
difference_explained: Offer = say you are willing. Volunteer = offer, often for unpaid or group work.
mini_conversation:
A: We need someone to host the event.
B: I'll volunteer!
everyday_scene: Everyday: College students volunteer at the village school on Sundays.
news_style_line: News-style: Hundreds volunteered to clean the riverbank.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Volunteered to make chai for the whole office. Regret.'
mcq_question: 'She ___ to help at the blood donation camp.'
mcq_options: A) volunteered  B) volunteered for helping  C) voluntary  D) volunteer to

find_and_fix_to_correct: He volunteered in teaching kids. → He volunteered to teach kids.

write_your_own_sentence: Write about a cause you would like to volunteer for.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which verb means 'to offer to do something without being asked'?
usage_tip: CV section: 'Volunteer experience' impresses employers.

simple_explanation: 1) To write information in the spaces of a form. 2) To do someone's job for a short time.

example_3: Can you fill in for me tomorrow?
collocations: fill in a form, fill in the blanks, fill in your details, fill in for someone
action_sequence: Before: get a blank form → During: write details in the boxes → After: the form is complete
grammar_pattern: fill in + form/blank / fill + it + in / fill in + for + person
word_forms: fill in – filled in – filled in – filling in
common_mistake: Please fill up this form.
correct_version: Please fill in (or fill out) this form.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Fill up' = fill a container completely ('fill up the tank'). Forms are 'filled in/out'.
etymology: 'Fill' comes from Old English fyllan.
mnemonic: FILL IN = put words IN the empty boxes.
memory_trick: British: fill in. American: fill out. Both correct for forms.
visual_association: A pen writing a name into a bank form's empty boxes.
difference_explained: Fill in = complete a form. Fill up = make a container full.
mini_conversation:
A: What do I need for the library card?
B: Just fill in this form and give one photo.
everyday_scene: Everyday: The farmer filled in the loan form with the clerk's help.
news_style_line: News-style: Applicants must fill in the form online by 30 June.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Can someone fill in for me at the meeting? I'm stuck in traffic.'
mcq_options: A) fill in  B) fill up  C) fill on  D) full in
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: ______ the blanks with 'a' or 'an'. → Fill in
find_and_fix_to_correct: Fill up the admission form. → Fill in the admission form.
translate: कृपया यह फ़ॉर्म भरें। → Please fill in this form.
write_your_own_sentence: Write an instruction for filling in a form.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review

usage_tip: 'Fill up the form' is common in India — international English uses 'fill in/out'.

simple_explanation: Knowing about something or noticing it.
example_1: Are you aware of the new rules?
example_2: I wasn't aware that the shop was closed.
example_3: We should be aware of our spending.
collocations: aware of, aware that, well aware, fully aware, become aware
grammar_pattern: be aware + of + noun / be aware + that clause
common_mistake: Are you aware about this?
correct_version: Are you aware of this?
why_it_s_wrong: The preposition is 'of', not 'about'.
etymology: From Old English gewær, 'watchful, cautious'.
mnemonic: AWARE → BEWARE: both about watching carefully.
memory_trick: 'Awareness campaign' = an effort to inform people.
visual_association: A pedestrian looking left and right before crossing.
difference_explained: Very close. Conscious can also mean 'awake' (medical).
mini_conversation:
A: Did you know the exam date changed?
B: No, I wasn't aware of that!
everyday_scene: Everyday: The villagers were aware of the snake near the well.
news_style_line: News-style: A campaign is making people aware of cyber fraud.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Just so you're aware — the Wi-Fi password changed.'
mcq_options: A) aware  B) awareness  C) awake  D) aware about
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: I am ______ that I need to practise more. → aware

simple_explanation: Having the ability or skill to do something.
example_1: You are capable of great things.
example_2: She's a very capable manager.
example_3: Is this phone capable of 5G?
collocations: capable of, highly capable, capable hands, fully capable
grammar_pattern: be capable + of + noun/-ing / capable + noun
common_mistake: He is capable to do this job.
correct_version: He is capable of doing this job.
why_it_s_wrong: Pattern: capable OF + -ing (compare: able TO + verb).
etymology: From Late Latin capabilis, from capere, 'to take, hold'.
mnemonic: CAPable → CAPtain: a captain is capable of leading.
memory_trick: Capable OF + -ing / Able TO + verb — learn them as a pair.
visual_association: A young girl confidently fixing a bicycle chain.
difference_explained: Able to + verb ('able to swim'). Capable of + -ing ('capable of swimming'). Capable often means 'skilled'.

mcq_options: A) capable  B) able  C) capability  D) capable to

find_and_fix_to_correct: I am capable to speak English. → I am capable of speaking English. / I am able to speak English.

write_your_own_sentence: Write about something you are capable of doing well.

reverse_quick_recall: Which adjective means 'having the ability to do something'?
usage_tip: 'In capable hands' = someone skilled is in charge.

simple_explanation: Not needing others; free from control.
example_2: India became independent in 1947.
example_3: I want to be financially independent.
collocations: financially independent, independent of, independent thinker, become independent
grammar_pattern: be independent + of + person/thing / independent + noun
common_mistake: She is independent person.
correct_version: She is an independent person.
why_it_s_wrong: Singular noun needs 'a/an' — and 'an' before the vowel sound 'in-'.
etymology: From in- ('not') + 'dependent', from Latin dependere, 'to hang from'.
mnemonic: IN-DEPENDENT = NOT hanging on anyone.
memory_trick: Independence Day = 15 August.
visual_association: A young woman carrying her own suitcase into a new city flat.
difference_explained: Alone = without people around. Independent = can manage without help.

spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review

simple_explanation: Behaving in a sensible, adult way; fully grown.
example_1: He is very mature for his age.
example_2: That was a mature decision.
example_3: Mango trees take years to become mature.
collocations: mature for your age, mature decision, emotionally mature, mature enough to
grammar_pattern: be mature / mature + noun / mature enough + to + verb
common_mistake: He is very matured.
correct_version: He is very mature.
why_it_s_wrong: The adjective is 'mature' (no -d). 'Matured' is the verb's past form.
etymology: From Latin maturus, 'ripe, timely'.
mnemonic: MATURE fruit = RIPE. A mature person = 'ripe' in thinking.
memory_trick: Opposite 'immature' = childish.
visual_association: A green mango and a ripe yellow one side by side.
difference_explained: Old = many years. Mature = sensible (can be young!).
mini_conversation:

write_your_own_sentence: Write about a mature decision you made.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review

simple_explanation: Arriving or doing things at the right time; not late.
example_2: Please be punctual for the interview.
example_3: Japanese trains are famous for being punctual.
collocations: always punctual, be punctual, punctual payment
grammar_pattern: be punctual / punctual + noun
common_mistake: He is punctual on time.
correct_version: He is punctual.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Punctual' already means 'on time' — don't repeat it.
etymology: From Medieval Latin punctualis, from punctum, 'point'.
mnemonic: PUNCTual = arrives at the exact POINT of time (like a punctuation dot).
memory_trick: Great CV/interview word: 'punctual and disciplined'.
visual_association: A man walking into an office as the clock strikes exactly 9.
difference_explained: Early = before the time. Punctual = exactly on time.
mini_conversation:

B: Very. He's punctual every single day.
everyday_scene: Everyday: The milkman is so punctual you can set your clock by him.
news_style_line: News-style: Airlines were ranked on how punctual their flights were.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'For once in my life I was punctual — and nobody else came!'

write_your_own_sentence: Write why being punctual matters.

simple_explanation: Easily hurt or upset; also understanding others' feelings; or needing care (a topic).
example_2: She is sensitive to other people's feelings.
example_3: Religion is a sensitive topic.
collocations: sensitive about, sensitive to, sensitive skin, sensitive topic, sensitive information
grammar_pattern: be sensitive + about + thing (easily hurt) / sensitive + to + thing (reacts to)
common_mistake: He is a sensitive person, he makes good decisions.
correct_version: He is a sensible person; he makes good decisions.
why_it_s_wrong: Sensitive = feels deeply. Sensible = practical and wise.
spelling_tip: SEN-SI-TIVE: -SITIVE, with an I after S.
etymology: From Latin sentire, 'to feel'.
mnemonic: SENSITIVE = SENSES on high alert: feels everything.
memory_trick: 'Sensible' ≠ 'sensitive' — a very common mix-up.
visual_association: A delicate plant closing its leaves when touched.
difference_explained: Sensitive = feels deeply / easily hurt. Sensible = practical, reasonable.
mini_conversation:
A: Why did she get upset?
B: She's sensitive about her marks — don't joke about them.
everyday_scene: Everyday: The child is sensitive to loud noises.
news_style_line: News-style: Officials said the files contained sensitive information.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'My teeth are so sensitive — can't eat ice cream.'
mcq_options: A) sensitive  B) sensible  C) sense  D) sensation

find_and_fix_to_correct: He took a sensitive decision to save money. → He took a sensible decision to save money.

write_your_own_sentence: Write about a topic you think is sensitive.

simple_explanation: Connected to what is being discussed or needed.
example_2: Is this question relevant to the topic?
example_3: Your experience is very relevant to this job.
collocations: relevant to, relevant information, highly relevant, relevant experience, still relevant
grammar_pattern: be relevant + to + noun / relevant + noun
common_mistake: This is relevant with my job.
correct_version: This is relevant to my job.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'relevant TO'.
etymology: From Medieval Latin relevans, from relevare, 'to raise up, lighten'.
mnemonic: RELEVANT → it's RELATED to the topic.
memory_trick: Exam tip: write only relevant points — examiners reward focus.
visual_association: A student highlighting only a few key lines in a textbook.
difference_explained: Related = connected in any way. Relevant = connected AND useful for the current purpose.
mini_conversation:
A: Should I add my cooking skills to my CV?
B: Only if it's relevant to the job.
everyday_scene: Everyday: The teacher asked us to bring only relevant books to the exam hall.
news_style_line: News-style: Officials were asked to submit relevant documents by Friday.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Is that meme relevant to the group topic? No. Is it funny? Yes.'

write_your_own_sentence: Write one skill that is relevant to your dream job.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review

usage_tip: Opposite 'irrelevant' = has nothing to do with it.

simple_explanation: Used to change topic or end a conversation; also 'despite that'.
example_1: Anyway, let's get back to work.
example_2: It was raining, but we went anyway.
example_3: Anyway, I have to go now — bye!
collocations: anyway, so anyway, but anyway, thanks anyway
grammar_pattern: Anyway, + clause (topic change) / clause + anyway (despite that)
common_mistake: Any way, let's start the class.
correct_version: Anyway, let's start the class.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Anyway' (one word) = topic change/despite. 'Any way' (two words) = any method: 'Is there any way to fix it?'
spelling_tip: ANY + WAY: one word, no S ('anyways' is informal).
etymology: Formed in English from any + way.
mnemonic: ANYWAY = whatever happened, we go ANY WAY forward.
memory_trick: 'Anyways' is very informal — 'anyway' is safer.
visual_association: A person in a conversation making a 'moving on' hand gesture.
synonyms: anyhow, in any case, still, nevertheless
difference_explained: Anyway = 'moving on' or 'despite that'. Any way = 'any method'.

B: No problem, thanks anyway!

news_style_line: News-style: Anyway, officials say the new bridge will open soon.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Anyway, enough about me — how's your job?'

simple_explanation: Mainly; most of the time; almost all.
example_1: I mostly study in the morning.
example_2: The class is mostly girls.
example_3: It's mostly sunny today.
collocations: mostly because, mostly true, mostly at home, mostly sunny
grammar_pattern: mostly + verb/adjective/noun phrase
common_mistake: Mostly people like cricket.
correct_version: Most people like cricket.
why_it_s_wrong: Before a noun, use 'most' (determiner), not 'mostly'.
etymology: From 'most' + -ly; 'most' from Old English mæst.
mnemonic: MOSTLY = MOST of the time.
memory_trick: Rule: 'most + noun' ('most students'); 'mostly' + verb/adjective ('mostly happy').
visual_association: A pie chart with a big 80% slice highlighted.
difference_explained: Most = determiner before nouns ('most people'). Mostly = adverb ('people mostly like…').
mini_conversation:

B: Mostly I sleep and watch movies.
everyday_scene: Everyday: The village is mostly farmland.
news_style_line: News-style: The crowd was mostly young people, officials said.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'My phone gallery is mostly food photos.'

find_and_fix_to_correct: Mostly girls like this song. → Most girls like this song. / This song is mostly liked by girls.

write_your_own_sentence: Write about what you mostly do in the evenings.

simple_explanation: Without doubt; also a polite way to say 'yes'.
example_2: 'Can you help me?' 'Certainly!'
example_3: She's certainly the best player on the team.
collocations: certainly not, most certainly, almost certainly, certainly worth
grammar_pattern: subject + will + certainly + verb / 'Certainly.' (reply)
common_mistake: Certainly I will come surely.
correct_version: I will certainly come.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Certainly' and 'surely' mean the same — use one.
etymology: From 'certain', from Latin certus, 'sure, settled'.
mnemonic: CERTAINly → a CERTIFICATE: officially sure.
memory_trick: Service English: 'Certainly, sir' is a polite 'yes'.
visual_association: A waiter nodding politely as a customer asks for water.
difference_explained: Very close. 'Certainly' sounds more polite/formal as a reply.
mini_conversation:

everyday_scene: Everyday: The shopkeeper said, 'Certainly, madam,' and packed the sweets.
news_style_line: News-style: The new rules will certainly affect small businesses.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Certainly not waking up at 5 for a jog.'

simple_explanation: Because something has just happened or is now true.
example_1: Now that you're here, we can start.
example_2: Now that I have a job, I can help my parents.
example_3: Now that the exams are over, let's relax.
collocations: now that you're here, now that it's over, now that I think about it
grammar_pattern: Now that + clause, + main clause
common_mistake: Now when you are here, let's begin.
correct_version: Now that you are here, let's begin.
why_it_s_wrong: The fixed phrase is 'now that', not 'now when'.
etymology: 'Now' comes from Old English nu.
mnemonic: NOW THAT = because NOW things have changed.
memory_trick: Great for reflecting: 'Now that I think about it…'
visual_association: A door opening as a friend arrives, others standing up to begin.
difference_explained: Since = because (any time). Now that = because of a NEW change.
mini_conversation:
A: I finally passed my driving test!
B: Great — now that you can drive, take me to Mathura!
everyday_scene: Everyday: Now that the rain has stopped, the kids can play outside.
news_style_line: News-style: Now that the bridge is open, travel time has halved.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Now that I think about it, I never returned your pen.'
mcq_options: A) Now that  B) Now when  C) Now so  D) Nowadays

find_and_fix_to_correct: Now when the class is over, we can go. → Now that the class is over, we can go.

write_your_own_sentence: Write about something you can do now that a situation has changed.

simple_explanation: As soon as; after something happens.

example_3: Once the rain stops, we'll leave.
collocations: once you, once it's done, once and for all (adv)

related_words: as soon as, after, when, then

simple_explanation: To say that someone has done something wrong.
example_2: She was accused of stealing the money.
example_3: Don't accuse people without proof.
collocations: accuse someone of, falsely accused, be accused of, accuse without proof
action_sequence: Before: suspect someone → During: say they did wrong → After: they must defend themselves
grammar_pattern: accuse + person + of + noun/-ing / be accused of
common_mistake: He accused him for stealing.
correct_version: He accused him of stealing.
why_it_s_wrong: The pattern is 'accuse someone OF'.

memory_trick: 'The accused' = the person charged in court.
visual_association: A finger pointing at a nervous boy next to a broken window.
difference_explained: Blame = say someone is responsible. Accuse = directly say someone DID something wrong (often a crime).

simple_explanation: To annoy or worry someone; to make the effort to do something.

collocations: sorry to bother you, don't bother, can't be bothered, bother someone, it bothers me

grammar_pattern: bother + person / bother + to + verb or + -ing / It bothers me that…

memory_trick: Also for problems: 'get rid of stress', 'get rid of mosquitoes'.
visual_association: A person dropping a bag of old things into a donation box.
synonyms: remove, throw away, eliminate, dispose of
confusing_word: get rid of vs throw away
difference_explained: Throw away = put in the bin. Get rid of = remove in any way (bin, sell, give, cure).
mini_conversation:
A: Why is the cupboard so empty?
B: I got rid of everything I don't use.
everyday_scene: Everyday: Grandma uses neem leaves to get rid of insects.
news_style_line: News-style: The city wants to get rid of single-use plastic.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Trying to get rid of my 3 a.m. snack habit.'
mcq_options: A) get rid of  B) get rid from  C) get off  D) rid of
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: We should ______ things we never use. → get rid of
find_and_fix_to_correct: How to get rid from mosquitoes? → How to get rid of mosquitoes?

write_your_own_sentence: Write about one thing you want to get rid of.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which phrase means 'to remove something unwanted'?
usage_tip: 'Good riddance!' = I'm glad it's gone.

hindi_meaning: अलग दिखना, सबसे अलग नज़र आना
simple_explanation: To be easy to see or notice because you are different or better.
example_1: Her red dress stood out in the crowd.
example_2: Your CV needs to stand out.
example_3: He always stands out in class.
collocations: stand out from the crowd, stand out in, make something stand out
action_sequence: Before: join a crowd → During: wear bright colours → After: everyone notices you
grammar_pattern: stand out (alone) / stand out + from/among + group
word_forms: stand out – stood out – stood out – standing out
common_mistake: He stands out of the crowd.
correct_version: He stands out from the crowd.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'stand out FROM' (or 'among').
spelling_tip: Two words as a verb: STAND OUT. 'Standout' as an adjective.
etymology: 'Stand' comes from Old English standan.
mnemonic: STAND OUT = STAND a step OUT of the line — everyone sees you.
memory_trick: Interview tip: 'What makes you stand out?'
visual_association: One orange balloon among many blue ones.
synonyms: be noticeable, shine, catch the eye
antonyms: blend in, fade into the background
difference_explained: Stand out = be noticed naturally. Show off = try hard to be noticed.
mini_conversation:
A: Why did they pick her for the job?
B: Her communication skills really stood out.
everyday_scene: Everyday: The yellow house stands out on the grey street.
news_style_line: News-style: One student's project stood out for its creativity, judges said.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'My handwriting stands out — for the wrong reasons.'
mcq_options: A) stand out  B) stand up  C) stand off  D) stand by
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: A good title makes your video ______. → stand out
find_and_fix_to_correct: She stood out of all the students. → She stood out from all the students.
translate: उसकी आवाज़ सबसे अलग सुनाई देती है। → Her voice stands out.
write_your_own_sentence: Write about what makes you stand out.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which phrasal verb means 'to be easy to notice'?
usage_tip: 'Outstanding' (adj) comes from the same idea: excellent.

simple_explanation: 1) To start a new hobby or activity. 2) To use space or time.
example_2: This sofa takes up too much space.
example_3: The meeting took up the whole morning.
collocations: take up a hobby, take up yoga, take up space, take up time, take up an offer
action_sequence: Before: feel bored → During: start a new hobby → After: enjoy it regularly
grammar_pattern: take up + noun/-ing / take + it + up
word_forms: take up – took up – taken up – taking up
common_mistake: I took up to singing.
correct_version: I took up singing.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Take up' takes the activity directly — no 'to'.
spelling_tip: Two words: TAKE UP. Past: took up.
etymology: 'Take' comes from Old Norse taka.
mnemonic: TAKE UP = pick UP a new hobby from the shelf.
memory_trick: Two meanings: a new hobby, or using space/time.
visual_association: A woman unrolling a yoga mat for the first time.
synonyms: start, begin, get into; occupy, fill
difference_explained: Start = begin anything. Take up = start a hobby/activity regularly.
mini_conversation:
A: What do you do in your free time?
B: I recently took up painting.
everyday_scene: Everyday: After retiring, Grandpa took up gardening.
news_style_line: News-style: New regulations take up a lot of teachers' time, a survey found.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Took up running. Ran once. Took down running.'
mcq_options: A) took up  B) took on up  C) took off  D) took up to
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: This old cupboard ______ too much space. → takes up
find_and_fix_to_correct: He took up to swimming. → He took up swimming.
translate: मैंने योग करना शुरू किया है। → I've taken up yoga.
write_your_own_sentence: Write about a hobby you want to take up.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which phrasal verb means 'to start a new hobby'?
usage_tip: 'Take up an offer' = accept it.

simple_explanation: To investigate or examine a problem or situation.
example_2: The police are looking into the case.
example_3: Can you look into why the app is slow?
collocations: look into the matter, look into a complaint, look into the problem, look into options
action_sequence: Before: hear a complaint → During: check the facts → After: find the cause
grammar_pattern: look into + noun/wh-clause (inseparable)
word_forms: look into – looked into – looked into – looking into
common_mistake: I'll look in to the matter.
correct_version: I'll look into the matter.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Into' is one word.
etymology: 'Look' comes from Old English locian.
mnemonic: LOOK INTO = LOOK deep INTO the box to find the problem.
memory_trick: Customer care classic: 'We'll look into it and get back to you.'
visual_association: A person shining a torch into a dark cupboard.
difference_explained: Look at = see with your eyes. Look into = investigate a problem.
mini_conversation:
A: My refund hasn't come yet.
B: I'm sorry. I'll look into it right away.
everyday_scene: Everyday: Mom looked into why the milk kept going sour.
news_style_line: News-style: The committee will look into complaints about the new roads.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Looking into cheap flights for Diwali. Crying.'
mcq_options: A) look into  B) look at into  C) look in to  D) look over into
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: We are ______ the problem and will reply soon. → looking into
find_and_fix_to_correct: I will look in to it. → I will look into it.
translate: पुलिस मामले की जाँच कर रही है। → The police are looking into the case.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a reply to a customer using 'look into'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which phrasal verb means 'to investigate'?
usage_tip: 'Look up' is different: search for information.

simple_explanation: Careful to avoid danger or problems.
example_1: Be cautious when you share personal information.
example_2: He's a cautious driver.
example_3: Doctors are cautious about new treatments.
collocations: cautious about, cautious approach, cautious driver, remain cautious
grammar_pattern: be cautious + about/of + noun / cautious + noun
common_mistake: Be cautious from online fraud.
correct_version: Be cautious about (or of) online fraud.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'cautious about/of', not 'from'.
etymology: From Latin cautio, from cavere, 'to beware'.
mnemonic: CAUTIOUS → a CAUTION sign.
memory_trick: Safety line: 'Be cautious with unknown links.'
visual_association: A person testing the ice with a stick before stepping on it.
difference_explained: Afraid = feeling fear. Cautious = acting carefully because of possible risk.
mini_conversation:
A: Should I invest all my savings in one share?
B: Be cautious — spread your money.
everyday_scene: Everyday: The mother was cautious and held the child's hand at the crossing.
news_style_line: News-style: Officials urged a cautious approach during the monsoon.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Cautious about new food places. Then I eat everything.'
mcq_question: 'Be ___ when you walk on wet floors.'
mcq_options: A) cautious  B) caution  C) cautiously  D) causeous
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: She was ______ about lending money. → cautious
find_and_fix_to_correct: Be cautious from strangers. → Be cautious of strangers.
translate: ऑनलाइन धोखाधड़ी से सावधान रहें। → Be cautious about online fraud.
write_your_own_sentence: Write one cautious habit that keeps you safe.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which adjective means 'careful to avoid danger'?
usage_tip: 'Caution' on signs = warning.

simple_explanation: Hopeful and expecting good things to happen.
example_2: She's always optimistic, even in hard times.
example_3: Doctors are optimistic about his recovery.
collocations: optimistic about, cautiously optimistic, stay optimistic, optimistic outlook
grammar_pattern: be optimistic + about + noun / optimistic + that clause
common_mistake: I am optimistic for the future.
correct_version: I am optimistic about the future.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'optimistic about'.
etymology: From 'optimism', from Latin optimum, 'the best'.
mnemonic: OPTIMISTIC → OPTIMUM: expecting the best.
memory_trick: Opposite: 'pessimistic' — expecting the worst.
visual_association: A glass of water being described as 'half full'.
difference_explained: Happy = feeling good now. Optimistic = expecting good in the future.
mini_conversation:
A: Do you think you'll get the job?
B: I'm optimistic — the interview went well.
everyday_scene: Everyday: The farmer was optimistic after the first rains.
news_style_line: News-style: Experts are cautiously optimistic about the economy.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Optimistic that I'll wake up early tomorrow. Very optimistic.'
mcq_options: A) optimistic  B) optimism  C) optimist  D) optimistically
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Stay ______ — things will get better. → optimistic
find_and_fix_to_correct: He is optimistic for the match. → He is optimistic about the match.
translate: मैं भविष्य को लेकर आशावादी हूँ। → I'm optimistic about the future.
write_your_own_sentence: Write about something you are optimistic about.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which adjective means 'expecting good things'?
usage_tip: 'Cautiously optimistic' = hopeful but careful.

hindi_meaning: व्यावहारिक, असल ज़िंदगी में काम का
simple_explanation: Useful and sensible in real situations; dealing with real things, not ideas.
example_2: We need a practical solution.
example_3: Heels are not practical for hiking.
collocations: practical solution, practical advice, practical skills, practical experience, be practical
grammar_pattern: be practical / practical + noun / practical + for + purpose
common_mistake: He is very practical man.
correct_version: He is a very practical man.
why_it_s_wrong: A singular noun needs 'a'.
etymology: From Greek praktikos, 'fit for action'.
word_family: practically (adv: almost; in a practical way), practice (n), impractical (adj)
mnemonic: PRACTICAL → PRACTICE: it works in real life.
memory_trick: 'Practically' also means 'almost': 'practically finished'.
visual_association: A person using a steel tiffin instead of a glass box on a trip.
difference_explained: Theoretical = about ideas. Practical = about doing, real use.
mini_conversation:
A: Should I buy a big car?
B: Be practical — parking is hard in your area.
everyday_scene: Everyday: Grandma gave practical advice: 'Keep a torch near the bed.'
news_style_line: News-style: The course focuses on practical skills for jobs.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Most practical gift ever: a power bank.'
mcq_question: 'We need a ___ plan, not a dream.'
mcq_options: A) practical  B) practically  C) practice  D) practise
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: English learning should be ______ and daily. → practical
find_and_fix_to_correct: She is very practical girl. → She is a very practical girl.
translate: हमें एक व्यावहारिक हल चाहिए। → We need a practical solution.
write_your_own_sentence: Write one practical tip for learning English.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which adjective means 'useful in real life'?

simple_explanation: Fair and sensible; (of prices) not too expensive.
example_2: That's a reasonable request.
example_3: Please be reasonable — I can't finish it in an hour.
collocations: reasonable price, reasonable request, be reasonable, reasonable doubt, fairly reasonable
grammar_pattern: be reasonable / reasonable + noun
common_mistake: This shop is very reasonable.
correct_version: The prices in this shop are very reasonable.
why_it_s_wrong: A price or request is reasonable; a shop's prices are reasonable.
etymology: From 'reason', via Old French, from Latin ratio, 'reckoning, reason'.
mnemonic: REASON-ABLE = ABLE to follow REASON (fair).
memory_trick: Shopping phrase: 'Is that your most reasonable price?'
visual_association: A vegetable stall with a fair price board and happy customers.
difference_explained: Cheap = low price (can mean poor quality). Reasonable = fair price for what you get.
mini_conversation:
A: How was the hotel?
B: Clean, and the price was very reasonable.
everyday_scene: Everyday: The tailor charges reasonable rates and finishes on time.
news_style_line: News-style: Parents say school fees should be kept reasonable.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Reasonable price, great food — rare combo.'
mcq_options: A) reasonable  B) reason  C) reasonably  D) reasoning
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Your demand is ______; I'll agree. → reasonable
find_and_fix_to_correct: This dhaba is reasonable. → The prices at this dhaba are reasonable.

write_your_own_sentence: Write about a shop with reasonable prices.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which adjective means 'fair and sensible'?
usage_tip: 'Reasonably' (adv) = fairly: 'reasonably good'.

simple_explanation: Honest and meaning what you say or feel.
example_2: He's a sincere and hardworking student.
example_3: Her smile was sincere.
collocations: sincere apology, sincere thanks, sincere student, sincere wishes, Yours sincerely
grammar_pattern: be sincere / sincere + noun
common_mistake: Yours sincerly,
correct_version: Yours sincerely,
why_it_s_wrong: Spelling: sincere + ly → sincerely (keep the 'e').
etymology: From Latin sincerus, 'pure, clean, genuine'.
mnemonic: SINCERE = SINgle, clear heart — nothing hidden.
memory_trick: Letter ending: 'Yours sincerely' when you know the person's name.
visual_association: A person looking straight into someone's eyes while apologising.
difference_explained: Serious = not joking. Sincere = honest in feelings. In Indian English 'sincere student' means hardworking — fine in India.
mini_conversation:
A: I'm really sorry about yesterday.
B: Thank you — I can see you're sincere.

news_style_line: News-style: The minister offered sincere condolences to the families.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Sincere apologies for replying 3 days late.'
mcq_options: A) sincere  B) sincerely  C) sincerity  D) since
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: I end formal letters with 'Yours ______'. → sincerely
find_and_fix_to_correct: Yours sincerly, Rahul → Yours sincerely, Rahul
translate: मेरी दिल से माफ़ी स्वीकार करें। → Please accept my sincere apologies.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sincere thank-you note to a teacher.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which adjective means 'honest and meaning what you say'?
usage_tip: 'Sincerely' = truly: 'I sincerely hope you get well.'

simple_explanation: Causing damage or hurt.

example_3: Too much screen time can be harmful for children.
collocations: harmful to, harmful effects, harmful chemicals, potentially harmful
grammar_pattern: be harmful + to + person/thing (most standard) / harmful + noun
common_mistake: Smoking is harmful for the health.
correct_version: Smoking is harmful to health.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Harmful to' is the most standard; drop 'the' before 'health'.
etymology: From Old English hearm, 'hurt, injury', + -ful.
mnemonic: HARM-FULL = FULL of harm.
memory_trick: Opposite 'harmless' = safe, no harm.
visual_association: A 'Danger — Poison' label on a bottle.
difference_explained: Dangerous = likely to cause harm soon. Harmful = causes damage (often slowly).
mini_conversation:
A: Is it okay to eat junk food daily?
B: No, it's harmful to your health in the long run.
everyday_scene: Everyday: Plastic is harmful to cows that eat it by mistake.
news_style_line: News-style: The report lists harmful chemicals found in some toys.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Harmful habit: checking the phone 100 times a day.'
mcq_options: A) harmful  B) harm  C) harmless  D) harmfully
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Loud music can be ______ to your ears. → harmful
find_and_fix_to_correct: Pollution is very harm for us. → Pollution is very harmful to us.

write_your_own_sentence: Write about a harmful habit and a healthy alternative.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which adjective means 'causing damage'?
usage_tip: Cigarette packets say: 'Tobacco is injurious to health' — same idea, more formal.

simple_explanation: Several different kinds of.

example_2: He has lived in various cities.
example_3: There are various ways to learn English.
collocations: various types, various reasons, various ways, various places, for various reasons
grammar_pattern: various + plural noun
common_mistake: Various type of books are available.
correct_version: Various types of books are available.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Various' is always followed by a PLURAL noun.

mnemonic: VARIOUS → VARIETY: many different kinds.
memory_trick: Always plural after it: various + nouns-with-s.
visual_association: A market stall with many kinds of spices in small heaps.
difference_explained: Different = not the same. Various = several different kinds (always plural).

A: Why did you leave the job?
B: For various reasons — mainly the long commute.
everyday_scene: Everyday: The fair had various stalls selling toys and food.
news_style_line: News-style: Various groups have raised concerns about the new law.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Tried various diets. Still love samosas.'
mcq_options: A) various  B) variety  C) vary  D) various of
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: I've tried ______ methods to improve my English. → various
find_and_fix_to_correct: Various student came late. → Various students came late.

write_your_own_sentence: Write about various things you do on weekends.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which adjective means 'several different kinds of'?
usage_tip: Noun: 'variety' — 'a variety of dishes'.

simple_explanation: Recently; in the last few days or weeks.

difference_explained: Similar. 'Recently' also works with one past event ('I recently moved'); 'lately' is for an ongoing period.

B: Yes, too many late-night shifts.

news_style_line: News-style: Prices of vegetables have gone up lately.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Lately my only exercise is scrolling.'
mcq_options: A) lately  B) late  C) later  D) latest
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Have you read any good books ______? → lately
find_and_fix_to_correct: The train arrived lately. → The train arrived late.

write_your_own_sentence: Write about something you've been doing lately.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which adverb means 'recently'?
usage_tip: Common trap: 'He came lately' is wrong for 'not on time' — use 'late'.

hindi_meaning: आसानी से, सरल ढंग से; बस, सिर्फ़

example_3: The view was simply amazing.

common_mistake: He explained it very simple.
correct_version: He explained it very simply.
why_it_s_wrong: After a verb, use the adverb 'simply'.

mnemonic: SIMPLY = in a SIMPLE way.
memory_trick: 'Simply put…' = in simple words.
visual_association: A teacher drawing one clear diagram on the board.
synonyms: easily, plainly, clearly; just, merely; truly
difference_explained: Just = only. Simply can mean 'just' but also 'in an easy way' and 'truly'.

news_style_line: News-style: The minister said the new app is simply designed for easy use.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'This mango is simply the best thing I've eaten today.'

find_and_fix_to_correct: She explained very simple. → She explained very simply.

write_your_own_sentence: Explain your job simply in one sentence.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review

simple_explanation: Used to say that something good or lucky happened.

correct_version: Fortunately, the bus waited for me.
why_it_s_wrong: At the start of a sentence, use the adverb 'Fortunately'.

mnemonic: FORTUNE-ately = good FORTUNE (luck) happened.
memory_trick: Pair with 'unfortunately' to tell stories: 'Unfortunately… but fortunately…'
visual_association: A cat landing safely on its feet.
difference_explained: Same meaning; 'luckily' is a little more informal.

news_style_line: News-style: Fortunately, the fire was controlled before it spread.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Forgot my lunch. Fortunately, mom sent it with dad.'

find_and_fix_to_correct: Fortunate, I passed. → Fortunately, I passed.

write_your_own_sentence: Write a short story using 'unfortunately' and 'fortunately'.

simple_explanation: Used to say something is true whatever the situation is.

example_3: Call me, no matter how late it is.

common_mistake: No matter what will happen, I'll be there.
correct_version: No matter what happens, I'll be there.
why_it_s_wrong: Use present simple after 'no matter what' for the future.
etymology: 'Matter' comes from Latin materia, 'substance, material'.

simple_explanation: To take goods to a place; to give a speech; to do what you promised.

memory_trick: Work phrase: 'deliver results' = achieve what's expected.

etymology: From Latin demandare, 'to entrust'; via French demander, 'to ask'.
mnemonic: deMAND → a strong MANDate: 'Give it now!'
memory_trick: 'In demand' = wanted by many: 'English teachers are in demand.'
visual_association: Protesters holding up placards outside an office.
synonyms: insist on, call for, require, claim
difference_explained: Request = ask politely. Demand = ask firmly, not accepting no.

news_style_line: News-style: Parents demanded better safety at the school gate.

grammar_pattern: disappoint + person / be disappointed + with/by + thing / in + person

memory_trick: 'Make money' is a common informal synonym.
visual_association: A person receiving a salary slip with a proud smile.
difference_explained: Earn = get by working. Win = get by being best or lucky.

simple_explanation: Needing or wanting something very much; feeling there's little hope.
example_1: I'm desperate for a cup of tea.
example_2: He was desperate to find a job.
example_3: The situation is desperate.

grammar_pattern: be desperate + for + noun / desperate + to + verb

correct_version: He is desperate for money.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'desperate FOR + noun' or 'desperate TO + verb'.
etymology: From Latin desperare, 'to lose hope' (de- + sperare 'to hope').
mnemonic: DESPERATE = DE (no) + SPERARE (hope): out of hope, needing help.
memory_trick: Casual humour: 'I'm desperate for sleep.'
visual_association: A thirsty traveller reaching for a water bottle in the desert.
synonyms: anxious, eager, in great need; hopeless
difference_explained: Eager = excited to do. Desperate = strongly needing, often with worry.

simple_explanation: Able to control your behaviour and follow rules or a routine.
example_1: He's very disciplined about his studies.
example_2: Soldiers are highly disciplined.
example_3: A disciplined routine helps you learn faster.
collocations: disciplined approach, highly disciplined, self-disciplined, disciplined routine
grammar_pattern: be disciplined + about + thing / disciplined + noun
common_mistake: He is very discipline.
correct_version: He is very disciplined.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Discipline' is the noun; the adjective is 'disciplined'.
etymology: From Latin disciplina, 'teaching, learning', from discipulus, 'learner'.

memory_trick: Motivation fades; discipline stays.
visual_association: A student at a desk at 6 a.m. with a timetable on the wall.
difference_explained: Strict = demands rules from OTHERS. Disciplined = follows rules or routines YOURSELF.

correct_version: He is an emotional person.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Emotion' is the noun; use 'emotional' before a person.

mnemonic: EMOTIONAL → your feelings MOVE you (motion).
memory_trick: 'Emotional support' = help with feelings.
visual_association: A bride's mother wiping tears at a vidaai.
difference_explained: Sensitive = easily hurt or aware of feelings. Emotional = showing strong feelings (in the moment).

simple_explanation: Mostly; used to show the most important part.
example_1: I come here mainly for the food.
example_2: The students are mainly from Bihar.
example_3: It's mainly a problem of time.
collocations: mainly because, mainly due to, mainly for, consist mainly of
grammar_pattern: mainly + phrase/noun/adjective / verb + mainly
common_mistake: The main reason is mainly money.
correct_version: The main reason is money. / It's mainly because of money.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Main' and 'mainly' say the same thing — use one.
etymology: From 'main' (Old English mægen, 'strength') + -ly.
mnemonic: MAINLY = the MAIN part.
memory_trick: Explaining tip: 'mainly because…' + one clear reason.
visual_association: A pie chart with one big slice highlighted.
difference_explained: Very close. 'Mostly' also means 'most of the time'.
mini_conversation:
A: Why do you want to learn English?
B: Mainly for my job.
everyday_scene: Everyday: The village mainly grows sugarcane.
news_style_line: News-style: The illness mainly affects older people, doctors say.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'My diet is mainly chai.'
mcq_options: A) mainly  B) main  C) mainly of  D) mains
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: I watch TV ______ for news. → mainly
find_and_fix_to_correct: The main problem is mainly traffic. → The main problem is traffic.
translate: मैं मुख्य रूप से नौकरी के लिए अंग्रेज़ी सीख रहा हूँ। → I'm learning English mainly for my job.
write_your_own_sentence: Write why you study, starting with 'mainly because'.
