usage_tip: Don't confuse with 'aboard' (on a ship/plane).

simple_explanation: Immediately; at once.
example_2: The pain stopped instantly.
example_3: The message was sent instantly.
collocations: instantly recognise, instantly feel, instantly available, work instantly
grammar_pattern: subject + instantly + verb / verb + instantly
common_mistake: The coffee is ready instant.
correct_version: The coffee is ready instantly.
why_it_s_wrong: After a verb, use the adverb 'instantly'.
etymology: From 'instant', from Latin instare, 'to be present, press upon'.
mnemonic: INSTANTLY → INSTANT noodles: ready at once.
memory_trick: 'Instant' (adj): 'instant coffee', 'instant reply'.
visual_association: A light switching on the moment a button is pressed.
difference_explained: Quickly = fast. Instantly = with no time gap at all.
mini_conversation:
A: Did the medicine work?
B: Almost instantly!
everyday_scene: Everyday: The puppy instantly recognised its owner's voice.
news_style_line: News-style: UPI payments are credited instantly, the bank said.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Opened the fridge. Instantly forgot why.'
mcq_options: A) instantly  B) instant  C) instance  D) instantly to
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The app updates your balance ______. → instantly
find_and_fix_to_correct: The problem was solved instant. → The problem was solved instantly.
translate: मैंने उसे तुरंत पहचान लिया। → I recognised her instantly.
write_your_own_sentence: Write about something you liked instantly.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which adverb means 'immediately'?
usage_tip: Don't confuse with 'instance' (example).

simple_explanation: In a way that is easy to see or understand; of course.
example_2: He was obviously tired.
example_3: 'Are you coming?' 'Obviously!'
collocations: obviously not, obviously true, obviously upset
grammar_pattern: Obviously, + clause / be + obviously + adjective
common_mistake: Obvious, he was late.
correct_version: Obviously, he was late.
why_it_s_wrong: At the start, use the adverb 'Obviously'.
etymology: From 'obvious', from Latin obvius, 'in the way'.
mnemonic: OBVIOUSLY → clear as daylight.
memory_trick: Tone warning: 'Obviously!' can sound rude, as if the question was silly.
visual_association: A person pointing to a huge 'EXIT' sign.
difference_explained: Apparently = it seems (not sure). Obviously = clearly true.
mini_conversation:
A: Why is he smiling so much?
B: He obviously passed the exam!
everyday_scene: Everyday: The dog was obviously hungry — it kept looking at the kitchen.
news_style_line: News-style: The plan obviously needs more money, experts said.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Obviously I'll eat dessert. Why would you even ask?'
mcq_options: A) obviously  B) obvious  C) obviousness  D) oblivious
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: ______, we can't finish the work in one day. → Obviously
find_and_fix_to_correct: Obvious, she was tired. → Obviously, she was tired.
translate: ज़ाहिर है, हमें और समय चाहिए। → Obviously, we need more time.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence using 'obviously' politely.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which adverb means 'clearly, of course'?
usage_tip: Use it softly to avoid sounding impatient.

simple_explanation: In a way that surprises you because you did not expect it.
example_2: The price dropped unexpectedly.
example_3: Not unexpectedly, the team won.
collocations: arrive unexpectedly, die unexpectedly, not unexpectedly, change unexpectedly
grammar_pattern: verb + unexpectedly / Unexpectedly, + clause
common_mistake: He came unexpectly.
correct_version: He came unexpectedly.
why_it_s_wrong: Spelling: un-expect-ED-ly.
etymology: From un- + 'expect' (Latin exspectare, 'to look out for') + -ed + -ly.
mnemonic: UN-EXPECTED-LY → it came WITHOUT being EXPECTED.
memory_trick: 'Not unexpectedly' = as expected.
visual_association: A surprise knock on the door at midnight.
synonyms: suddenly, surprisingly, out of the blue
difference_explained: Suddenly = very quickly. Unexpectedly = not predicted (can be slow too).
mini_conversation:
A: Why are there so many shoes at the door?
B: Relatives arrived unexpectedly!
everyday_scene: Everyday: The rain came unexpectedly and soaked the laundry.
news_style_line: News-style: Petrol prices fell unexpectedly this week.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Unexpectedly woke up early. Went back to sleep.'
mcq_options: A) unexpectedly  B) unexpectly  C) unexpected  D) expectedly
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: He passed away ______ last night. → unexpectedly
find_and_fix_to_correct: She came unexpectly. → She came unexpectedly.
translate: मेरा चचेरा भाई अचानक आ गया। → My cousin arrived unexpectedly.
write_your_own_sentence: Write about something that happened unexpectedly.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which adverb means 'in a surprising, not predicted way'?
usage_tip: 'Out of the blue' = informal twin.

simple_explanation: Used to show what will happen if something isn't done.
example_1: Hurry up, or else you'll miss the bus.
example_2: Wear a jacket, or else you'll catch a cold.
example_3: Give it back — or else!
collocations: or else you'll, or else!
grammar_pattern: instruction + or else + result clause
common_mistake: Study hard or else will fail.
correct_version: Study hard, or else you'll fail.
why_it_s_wrong: The result clause needs a subject: 'or else YOU will…'.
etymology: 'Else' comes from Old English elles.
mnemonic: OR ELSE = do it, OR something ELSE (bad) happens.
memory_trick: Alone, 'Or else!' sounds like a warning/threat — use it jokingly.
visual_association: A mother pointing at a clock: 'Sleep now, or else…'
difference_explained: Same meaning. 'Or else' is more informal and spoken.
mini_conversation:
A: I'll leave in ten minutes.
B: Leave now, or else you'll be stuck in traffic.
everyday_scene: Everyday: The shepherd shut the gate, or else the goats would run away.
news_style_line: News-style: Farmers must sow soon, or else the crop will fail, experts warn.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Return my charger, or else. (Please.)'
mcq_options: A) or else  B) or also  C) else or  D) if else
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Save your work, ______ you might lose it. → or else
find_and_fix_to_correct: Come fast or else will be late. → Come fast, or else you'll be late.
translate: जल्दी करो, वरना बस छूट जाएगी। → Hurry, or else you'll miss the bus.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a friendly warning using 'or else'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which conjunction means 'otherwise'?
usage_tip: Formal writing: prefer 'otherwise'.

simple_explanation: Travelling through a place; by means of.
example_1: We went to Goa via Mumbai.
example_2: I'll send it via email.
example_3: The train goes via Kanpur.
collocations: via email, via WhatsApp, via Delhi, via the internet
grammar_pattern: via + place/method
common_mistake: I sent it via by email.
correct_version: I sent it via email. / I sent it by email.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Via' already means 'by way of' — don't add 'by'.
etymology: From Latin via, 'road' (meaning 'by way of').
mnemonic: VIA → a road (via) through that place.
memory_trick: Ticket boards: 'Delhi to Agra via Mathura'.
visual_association: A route map with a dot marked 'via'.
synonyms: through, by way of, by means of
difference_explained: Through = in one side, out the other. Via = passing through a place, or using a method.
related_words: through, route, by, by way of
mini_conversation:
A: Is this a direct flight?
B: No, it goes via Hyderabad.
everyday_scene: Everyday: The pilgrims travelled to Kedarnath via Rishikesh.
news_style_line: News-style: Results will be shared via SMS, officials said.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Sent love via memes. Standard family communication.'
mcq_options: A) via  B) via by  C) by via  D) vias
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: We flew to London ______ Dubai. → via
find_and_fix_to_correct: I'll share it via through email. → I'll share it via email.
translate: हम मुंबई होकर गोवा गए। → We went to Goa via Mumbai.
write_your_own_sentence: Write about a journey you made via another city.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which preposition means 'through a place' or 'by means of'?
usage_tip: Common on bus and train boards.

simple_explanation: For each; in each.
example_2: The speed limit is 60 km per hour.
example_3: It costs ₹500 per person.
collocations: per kg, per person, per day, per hour, per cent (%)
grammar_pattern: number + per + unit (no 'one')
common_mistake: ₹40 per one kg.
correct_version: ₹40 per kg.
why_it_s_wrong: Don't add 'one' after 'per'.
etymology: From Latin per, 'through, by, for each'.
mnemonic: PER → for EACH one.
memory_trick: Indian 'as per my knowledge' → say 'As far as I know'. 'As per' is fine in formal letters ('as per the rules').
visual_association: A price tag reading '₹40 per kg'.
difference_explained: Same meaning: '₹40 per kg' = '₹40 a kg'. 'Per' is more formal.
mini_conversation:
A: How much is the room?
B: ₹1,500 per night.
everyday_scene: Everyday: The farmer sold milk at ₹60 per litre.
news_style_line: News-style: The scheme gives ₹6,000 per year to farmers.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Chai consumption: 5 cups per day. Minimum.'
mcq_options: A) per  B) per one  C) for per  D) each per
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The car was going at 80 km ______ hour. → per
find_and_fix_to_correct: As per my knowledge, he is right. → As far as I know, he is right.
translate: टमाटर ₹40 प्रति किलो हैं। → Tomatoes are ₹40 per kg.
write_your_own_sentence: Write three prices using 'per'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which preposition means 'for each'?
usage_tip: 'Per cent' / 'percent' = out of 100.

simple_explanation: To go somewhere with someone; to play music along with a singer.
example_1: Can you accompany me to the hospital?
example_2: Children must be accompanied by an adult.
example_3: He accompanied the singer on the tabla.
collocations: accompany someone to, be accompanied by, accompany on (music)
action_sequence: Before: a friend goes to hospital → During: you go with them → After: they feel supported
grammar_pattern: accompany + person (+ to + place) / be accompanied by
common_mistake: Please accompany with me.
correct_version: Please accompany me.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Accompany' takes the person directly — no 'with'.
etymology: From Old French acompaignier, from compaignon, 'companion'.
mnemonic: ACCOMPANY → be COMPANY for someone.
memory_trick: Formal twin of 'go with'.
visual_association: A son walking his old mother to the doctor.
synonyms: go with, escort, come along with
difference_explained: Follow = go behind. Accompany = go together with.
mini_conversation:
A: I'm nervous about the interview.
B: Don't worry, I'll accompany you there.
everyday_scene: Everyday: The younger brother accompanied his sister to the exam centre.
news_style_line: News-style: Minors must be accompanied by a parent on flights.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'My hunger accompanies me everywhere.'
mcq_options: A) accompany  B) accompany with  C) company  D) accompanying to
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The singer was ______ by a harmonium player. → accompanied
find_and_fix_to_correct: I will accompany with you. → I will accompany you.
translate: क्या तुम मेरे साथ अस्पताल चलोगे? → Can you accompany me to the hospital?
write_your_own_sentence: Write about a time you accompanied someone somewhere.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which verb means 'to go somewhere with someone'?
usage_tip: Informal: 'go with' / 'come along'.

hindi_meaning: स्वीकार करना; (पत्र/मेल) मिलने की सूचना देना
simple_explanation: To accept that something is true; to show you received something.
example_2: Please acknowledge this email.
example_3: She acknowledged me with a smile.
collocations: acknowledge a mistake, acknowledge receipt, acknowledge someone's help, widely acknowledged
action_sequence: Before: receive an email → During: reply 'Received, thanks' → After: the sender knows
grammar_pattern: acknowledge + noun / acknowledge + that clause
common_mistake: Please acknowledge about my email.
correct_version: Please acknowledge my email.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Acknowledge' takes the object directly — no 'about'.
spelling_tip: AC-KNOW-LEDGE: the K and W are silent: 'ak-NOL-ij'.
etymology: Formed in Middle English from an old verb 'aknow' ('recognise') + 'knowledge'.
mnemonic: ACKNOWLEDGE → show you have KNOWLEDGE of it.
memory_trick: Office line: 'Kindly acknowledge receipt of this letter.'
visual_association: A person nodding and replying 'Received, thanks!'
difference_explained: Admit = agree something (often bad) is true. Acknowledge = accept or recognise (more formal, neutral).
mini_conversation:
A: Did the office get my application?
B: Yes, they acknowledged it by email.
everyday_scene: Everyday: The principal acknowledged the students' hard work.
news_style_line: News-style: The minister acknowledged that the roads needed repair.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Acknowledging my mistake: I ate your fries.'
mcq_options: A) acknowledged  B) acknowledged about  C) knowledge  D) acknowledge to
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Please ______ receipt of the documents. → acknowledge
find_and_fix_to_correct: He acknowledged about the error. → He acknowledged the error.
translate: उसने अपनी ग़लती स्वीकार की। → He acknowledged his mistake.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence acknowledging someone's help.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which verb means 'to accept or recognise'?
usage_tip: Books have an 'Acknowledgements' page to thank people.

simple_explanation: To fasten or join; to add a file to an email; to feel close to (be attached to).
example_1: I've attached my CV to this email.
example_2: Attach the label to the bag.
example_3: She's very attached to her grandmother.
collocations: attach a file, attach to, attached file, be attached to (feelings)
action_sequence: Before: write an email → During: add a file → After: send both together
grammar_pattern: attach + thing + to + thing / be attached to + person
common_mistake: Please find the attach file.
correct_version: Please find the attached file.
why_it_s_wrong: Before a noun, use the adjective 'attached'.
etymology: From Old French atachier, 'to fasten'.
mnemonic: ATTACH → an email ATTACHMENT (the paper clip icon).
memory_trick: Email line: 'Please find my CV attached.'
visual_association: A paper-clip icon next to an email subject.
difference_explained: Add = put in more. Attach = fasten something to something else.
mini_conversation:
A: Did you send the photos?
B: Yes, I attached them to the email.
everyday_scene: Everyday: The farmer attached a bell to the cow's neck.
news_style_line: News-style: Applicants must attach a copy of their ID.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Attached the file. Forgot to attach the file. Classic.'
mcq_options: A) attach  B) attached to  C) attachment  D) attach with to
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: She is very ______ to her pet dog. → attached
find_and_fix_to_correct: Please find the attach document. → Please find the attached document.
translate: मैंने अपना सीवी ईमेल में अटैच किया है। → I've attached my CV to the email.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a short email line attaching a document.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which verb means 'to fasten' or 'to add a file'?
usage_tip: 'Attachment' (noun) = file or emotional bond.

simple_explanation: To ask for money or food; to ask very strongly or emotionally.
example_1: An old man was begging at the station.
example_2: I begged my parents to let me go.
example_3: I beg your pardon?
collocations: beg for, beg someone to, I beg your pardon, beg for mercy
action_sequence: Before: need help badly → During: ask again and again → After: hope they agree
grammar_pattern: beg + (for) + thing / beg + person + to + verb
common_mistake: He begged me for to stay.
correct_version: He begged me to stay.
why_it_s_wrong: Pattern: beg SOMEONE TO + verb.
etymology: Middle English beggen; origin uncertain.
mnemonic: BEG → a BEGGAR asks.
memory_trick: 'I beg your pardon?' = polite 'Sorry, what did you say?'
visual_association: A child with folded hands asking for one more ice cream.
difference_explained: Request = polite ask. Beg = ask very strongly, emotionally.
mini_conversation:
A: Did your dad agree to the trip?
B: Only after I begged him for a week!
everyday_scene: Everyday: The puppy begged for food at the table.
news_style_line: News-style: The families begged officials to repair the dam.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Begged my alarm for 5 more minutes. It agreed 3 times.'
mcq_options: A) begged  B) begged for to  C) begging to  D) beg for
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: I ______ your pardon — could you repeat that? → beg
find_and_fix_to_correct: He begged me for helping. → He begged me to help.
translate: मैंने माता-पिता से जाने देने की विनती की। → I begged my parents to let me go.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a funny sentence about begging for something.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which verb means 'to ask strongly or for money'?
usage_tip: Past: begged (double g).

simple_explanation: To do something wrong (a crime); to promise to do something.
example_2: I'm committed to learning English.
example_3: Don't commit to something you can't do.
collocations: commit a crime, commit to, be committed to, fully committed, commit suicide (sensitive)
action_sequence: Before: make a promise → During: decide firmly → After: stick to it
grammar_pattern: commit + crime / commit + to + noun/-ing / be committed + to + noun/-ing
common_mistake: I committed a mistake.
correct_version: I made a mistake.
why_it_s_wrong: You MAKE a mistake; you COMMIT a crime.
spelling_tip: COM-MIT → COMMITTED: double M, double T.
etymology: From Latin committere, 'to join, entrust'.
mnemonic: COMMIT → a COMMITMENT is a promise you keep.
memory_trick: Positive use: 'committed to my goals'.
visual_association: A person signing a promise card and pinning it to a wall.
difference_explained: Promise = say you will. Commit = promise AND dedicate yourself.
mini_conversation:
A: Can you join the course for six months?
B: Yes, I'm fully committed.
everyday_scene: Everyday: The teacher is committed to helping every student.
news_style_line: News-style: Police arrested the man who committed the robbery.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Committed to my diet. Until 6 p.m.'
mcq_options: A) committed  B) commit  C) commitment  D) committing to
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Teaching needs time and ______. → commitment
find_and_fix_to_correct: I committed a spelling mistake. → I made a spelling mistake.
translate: मैं अंग्रेज़ी सीखने के लिए प्रतिबद्ध हूँ। → I'm committed to learning English.
write_your_own_sentence: Write about a goal you are committed to.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which verb means 'to do (a crime)' or 'to promise yourself'?
usage_tip: 'Committed to + -ing': 'committed to improving'.

hindi_meaning: ठीक करना, इलाज करके रोग मिटाना
simple_explanation: To make an ill person healthy again; to end a disease or problem.
example_2: Can this disease be cured?
example_3: Laughter cures stress.
collocations: cure a disease, cure someone of, a cure for (n), completely cured
action_sequence: Before: a patient is ill → During: the doctor treats them → After: the illness is gone
grammar_pattern: cure + disease / cure + person + of + disease / a cure for + disease (noun)
common_mistake: They found a cure of cancer.
correct_version: They found a cure for cancer.
why_it_s_wrong: The noun takes 'for': 'a cure FOR'.
etymology: From Latin cura, 'care'.
mnemonic: CURE → CARE that makes you well.
memory_trick: Proverb: 'Prevention is better than cure.'
visual_association: A doctor handing medicine to a smiling patient.
difference_explained: Treat = give medical care. Cure = make the disease go away completely.
mini_conversation:
A: Is his cough better?
B: Yes, the syrup cured it in three days.
everyday_scene: Everyday: Grandma believes haldi milk cures every cold.
news_style_line: News-style: Scientists are searching for a cure for the rare disease.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Nothing cures a bad day like hot jalebis.'
mcq_options: A) cure  B) cure of  C) cured of  D) care
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: There is no ______ for the common cold. → cure
find_and_fix_to_correct: This is a cure of headache. → This is a cure for headache.
translate: दवा ने उसका बुख़ार ठीक कर दिया। → The medicine cured his fever.
write_your_own_sentence: Write your favourite home cure for a cold.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which verb means 'to make an ill person healthy'?
usage_tip: Always see a doctor for serious illness.

simple_explanation: To damage something so badly that it no longer exists or works.
example_2: The flood destroyed crops.
example_3: Don't let one mistake destroy your confidence.
collocations: destroy completely, destroy evidence, destroyed by fire, destroy confidence
action_sequence: Before: a storm comes → During: it breaks houses → After: nothing is left
grammar_pattern: destroy + noun / be destroyed by + cause
common_mistake: The rain destroyed our picnic.
correct_version: The rain spoilt our picnic.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Destroy' = damage completely. For plans or moods, 'spoil' or 'ruin' is more natural.
etymology: From Latin destruere, 'to pull down'.
mnemonic: DESTROY → DE-STRUCTURE: nothing left standing.
memory_trick: Match the strength: spoil (small) < ruin < destroy (total).
visual_association: A house after a storm, only the walls left.
difference_explained: Damage = harm (can be fixed). Destroy = harm so badly it can't be fixed.
mini_conversation:
A: What happened to the old bridge?
B: The flood destroyed it last year.
everyday_scene: Everyday: Termites destroyed the farmer's wooden cart.
news_style_line: News-style: The earthquake destroyed hundreds of homes.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'My younger brother destroyed my homework. Literally ate it.'
mcq_options: A) destroyed  B) destroy of  C) destruction  D) destroying to
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Plastic is ______ our oceans. → destroying
find_and_fix_to_correct: He destroyed my mood with that joke. → He spoilt my mood with that joke.
translate: आग ने दुकान नष्ट कर दी। → The fire destroyed the shop.
write_your_own_sentence: Write about how we can stop destroying forests.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which verb means 'to damage completely'?
usage_tip: Noun: 'destruction'.

simple_explanation: To give something and get something else in return.
example_1: Can I exchange this shirt for a bigger size?
example_2: We exchanged phone numbers.
example_3: They exchanged gifts at Diwali.
collocations: exchange A for B, exchange numbers, exchange gifts, exchange ideas, exchange rate (n)
action_sequence: Before: buy the wrong size → During: return it to the shop → After: get the right size
grammar_pattern: exchange + thing + for + other thing / exchange + things (with + person)
common_mistake: Can I exchange this from another?
correct_version: Can I exchange this for another?
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'exchange A FOR B'.
etymology: From Old French eschangier (ex- + change).
mnemonic: EX-CHANGE → CHANGE one thing for another.
memory_trick: 'Exchange offer' = give old item, get discount on new.
visual_association: Two people swapping gift boxes.
difference_explained: Change = make different. Exchange = give one, get another.
mini_conversation:
A: These shoes are too tight.
B: Keep the bill — you can exchange them.
everyday_scene: Everyday: The two friends exchanged letters for years.
news_style_line: News-style: The shop has an exchange offer on old phones.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Exchanged my salad for a samosa. Good trade.'
mcq_options: A) exchanged  B) exchanged from  C) exchange to  D) change for
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: What's today's ______ rate for dollars? → exchange
find_and_fix_to_correct: Exchange this bag from a new one. → Exchange this bag for a new one.
translate: क्या मैं यह कमीज़ बड़े साइज़ से बदल सकता हूँ? → Can I exchange this shirt for a bigger size?
write_your_own_sentence: Write about something you once exchanged.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which verb means 'to give and get in return'?

simple_explanation: To go and get something or someone and bring them back.
example_1: Can you fetch me a glass of water?
example_2: The dog fetched the ball.
example_3: I'll fetch the kids from school.

simple_explanation: Covered with something that sticks; hot and humid; difficult.

example_3: We're in a sticky situation.

why_it_s_wrong: 'Stick' is a verb/noun; 'sticky' is the adjective.

mnemonic: STICKY → things STICK to it.
memory_trick: 'Sticky note' = small paper you stick on things.
visual_association: A child's hands covered in honey.
difference_explained: Humid = wet air (weather). Sticky = humid and uncomfortable, or covered in glue/sugar.
mini_conversation:

write_your_own_sentence: Write about a sticky situation you handled.

example_2: She said 'No' firmly.
example_3: I firmly believe in hard work.

grammar_pattern: verb + firmly / firmly + believe
common_mistake: He believes firm in God.

why_it_s_wrong: After a verb, use the adverb 'firmly'.

why_it_s_wrong: After a verb, use the adverb 'gladly', usually before the main verb.

visual_association: A shopkeeper happily wrapping a gift for a customer.
difference_explained: Very close. 'Gladly' often = willingly (ready to help).

hindi_meaning: मुख्य रूप से, काफ़ी हद तक
simple_explanation: Mostly; mainly.
example_1: The success was largely due to teamwork.
example_2: The audience was largely students.
example_3: It's largely a matter of practice.
collocations: largely due to, largely because, largely responsible, largely ignored
grammar_pattern: largely + phrase/adjective
common_mistake: He spent largely on the wedding.
correct_version: He spent a lot on the wedding.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Largely' means 'mostly', NOT 'a lot' or 'in a big way'.
etymology: From 'large', from Latin largus, 'abundant'.
mnemonic: LARGELY → the LARGE part = most of it.
memory_trick: Trap: 'largely' ≠ 'a lot'.
visual_association: A pie chart with one big slice highlighted.
synonyms: mainly, mostly, chiefly, to a great extent
difference_explained: Same meaning. 'Largely' is more formal.

simple_explanation: And also; in addition to.

example_2: He sings as well as dances.

grammar_pattern: noun + as well as + noun / verb + as well as + verb/-ing
common_mistake: My brother as well as my sisters are coming.
correct_version: My brother, as well as my sisters, is coming.
why_it_s_wrong: The verb agrees with the FIRST subject ('my brother'), not the part after 'as well as'.
etymology: 'Well' comes from Old English wel.
mnemonic: AS WELL AS = AND ALSO.
memory_trick: CV line: 'fluent in English as well as Hindi'.

synonyms: and, in addition to, besides, along with

difference_explained: Cook = prepare food in any way. Boil = heat in bubbling water.

simple_explanation: To bite food many times in your mouth before swallowing.

example_3: Don't chew gum in class.
collocations: chew food, chew gum, chew slowly, chew on (think about)
action_sequence: Before: put food in your mouth → During: bite it again and again → After: swallow it
grammar_pattern: chew + food/thing / chew on + idea
common_mistake: Chew the food nicely nicely.
correct_version: Chew your food well.
why_it_s_wrong: Hindi repetition ('achhe se achhe se') isn't needed in English — just 'well' or 'properly'.

mnemonic: CHEW → sounds like the chewing: 'choo-choo'.
memory_trick: 'Chew on an idea' = think about it slowly.
visual_association: A child chewing a big piece of roti.
difference_explained: Bite = cut with teeth once. Chew = bite many times to break down food.
mini_conversation:

why_it_s_wrong: Use 'feel itchy' or 'be itching'.

mnemonic: ITCHY → you want to scratch-scratch.
memory_trick: 'Itchy feet' = wanting to travel.
visual_association: A child scratching a mosquito bite on the arm.
difference_explained: Painful = hurts. Itchy = makes you want to scratch.
mini_conversation:
A: Why are you scratching?
B: The mosquitoes bit me — it's so itchy!
everyday_scene: Everyday: The new school uniform was itchy in the heat.
news_style_line: News-style: Doctors say itchy eyes are common during pollen season.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Itchy feet. Want to travel. Wallet says no.'
mcq_options: A) itchy  B) itching me  C) itch  D) itchily
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: After the trip, he got ______ feet again. → itchy
find_and_fix_to_correct: I am feeling itching on my hand. → My hand feels itchy.

write_your_own_sentence: Write advice for someone with itchy skin.

reverse_quick_recall: Which adjective means 'making you want to scratch'?
usage_tip: Itching for days? See a doctor.

simple_explanation: (Of a face) having less colour than usual, often from illness or fear; (of colours) light.
example_1: You look pale — are you okay?
example_2: She turned pale when she heard the news.
example_3: I like pale blue.
collocations: look pale, turn pale, pale face, pale blue, pale yellow
grammar_pattern: be/look/turn pale / pale + colour
common_mistake: You look very paled.
correct_version: You look very pale.
why_it_s_wrong: The adjective is 'pale' (no -d).
etymology: From Latin pallidus.
mnemonic: PALE → colour draining away like a PAIL of water.
memory_trick: Colour use: pale pink, pale green = light shades.
visual_association: A person with a white face after a shock.
difference_explained: Light = not dark (colours). Pale = light colour, or a face without healthy colour.
mini_conversation:
A: You look pale today.
B: I skipped breakfast and feel weak.
everyday_scene: Everyday: The boy turned pale when he saw the snake.
news_style_line: News-style: Doctors say a pale face can be a sign of low iron.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Went pale seeing the restaurant bill.'
mcq_options: A) pale  B) paled  C) pail  D) palely
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: He went ______ with fear. → pale
find_and_fix_to_correct: You are looking very paled. → You look very pale.
translate: तुम पीले दिख रहे हो। → You look pale.
write_your_own_sentence: Write what you'd do if a friend suddenly looked pale.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which adjective means 'without much colour' (face) or 'light' (colour)?
usage_tip: Homophone: pail (bucket).

simple_explanation: Tired and ready to sleep; (of a place) quiet.
example_2: The warm room made me sleepy.
example_3: It's a sleepy little village.
collocations: feel sleepy, sleepy eyes, sleepy town, get sleepy
grammar_pattern: be/feel/get sleepy / sleepy + noun
common_mistake: Don't wake him, he is sleepy.
correct_version: Don't wake him, he is asleep.
why_it_s_wrong: SLEEPY = wanting to sleep. ASLEEP = already sleeping.
etymology: From 'sleep' (Old English) + -y.
mnemonic: SLEEPY → heavy eyes, ready for SLEEP.
memory_trick: 'Sleepy town' = quiet place, not much happening.
visual_association: A puppy with droopy eyes after a meal.
difference_explained: Sleepy = feel like sleeping. Asleep = sleeping now.
mini_conversation:
A: Why are you yawning?
B: This lecture makes me sleepy!
everyday_scene: Everyday: The heavy lunch made everyone sleepy.
news_style_line: News-style: The sleepy hill town becomes busy in summer.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Sleepy after lunch. Every. Single. Day.'
mcq_options: A) asleep  B) sleepy  C) sleeping to  D) slept
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Warm milk makes me ______. → sleepy
find_and_fix_to_correct: Be quiet, Grandpa is sleepy (already sleeping). → Be quiet, Grandpa is asleep.
translate: मुझे नींद आ रही है। → I'm feeling sleepy.
write_your_own_sentence: Write about a sleepy afternoon.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which adjective means 'wanting to sleep'?
usage_tip: 'Asleep' = sleeping; 'awake' = not sleeping.

simple_explanation: Bigger than normal, usually because of injury or illness; (of a river) higher than usual.
example_2: Her eyes were swollen from crying.
example_3: The river is swollen after the rain.
collocations: swollen ankle, swollen eyes, swollen face, swollen river
grammar_pattern: be swollen / swollen + noun
common_mistake: My leg is swelled.
correct_version: My leg is swollen.
why_it_s_wrong: As an adjective, use 'swollen'.
etymology: From 'swell' (Old English swellan).
mnemonic: SWOLLEN → it SWELLED up like a balloon.
memory_trick: First aid: ice + rest for a swollen ankle.
visual_association: A bandaged, puffy ankle with an ice pack.
difference_explained: Fat = large body. Swollen = part became bigger from injury or illness.
mini_conversation:
A: Why are you limping?
B: I twisted my ankle and now it's swollen.
everyday_scene: Everyday: The boy's cheek was swollen after the bee sting.
news_style_line: News-style: Swollen rivers flooded several villages.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Eyes swollen after watching a sad movie. Twice.'
mcq_options: A) swollen  B) swelled  C) swelling to  D) swallowed
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Put ice on the ______ area. → swollen
find_and_fix_to_correct: My knee is swelled. → My knee is swollen.
translate: मेरा टखना सूज गया है। → My ankle is swollen.
write_your_own_sentence: Write first-aid advice for a swollen ankle.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which adjective means 'bigger than normal from injury'?
usage_tip: Swelling that doesn't reduce? See a doctor.

simple_explanation: Very much; strongly (feelings); far down.
example_2: Breathe deeply.
example_3: She was deeply moved by the film.
collocations: deeply sorry, deeply grateful, deeply moved, breathe deeply, deeply rooted
grammar_pattern: deeply + adjective (feelings) / verb + deeply
common_mistake: I love my country very deep.
correct_version: I love my country deeply.
why_it_s_wrong: After a verb or before a feeling adjective, use 'deeply'.
etymology: From 'deep' (Old English deop) + -ly.
mnemonic: DEEPLY → feelings that go DEEP inside.
memory_trick: Strong apology: 'I'm deeply sorry.'
visual_association: A person with hand on heart, eyes closed.
difference_explained: 'Deep' works after some verbs ('dig deep'). For feelings, use 'deeply'.
mini_conversation:
A: I'm deeply sorry for my rude comment.
B: It's okay. Thank you for apologising.
everyday_scene: Everyday: The villagers were deeply grateful to the doctor.
news_style_line: News-style: The community was deeply affected by the floods.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Deeply in love with my bed.'
mcq_options: A) deeply  B) deep-ly  C) depth  D) deeper to
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: We are ______ thankful for your help. → deeply
find_and_fix_to_correct: I care about you very deep. → I care about you deeply.
translate: मुझे गहरा अफ़सोस है। → I'm deeply sorry.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sincere apology using 'deeply'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which adverb means 'very much, strongly'?
usage_tip: 'Deeply rooted' = firmly established.

simple_explanation: In large amounts; with great force or weight.
example_2: He depends heavily on his parents.
example_3: She breathed heavily after climbing.
collocations: rain heavily, heavily depend, heavily damaged, heavily loaded, smoke heavily
grammar_pattern: verb + heavily / heavily + past participle
common_mistake: It is raining very heavy.
correct_version: It is raining very heavily.
why_it_s_wrong: After a verb, use the adverb 'heavily'.
etymology: From 'heavy' (Old English hefig) + -ly.
mnemonic: HEAVILY → like a HEAVY rainstorm.
memory_trick: News phrase: 'heavily damaged', 'heavily guarded'.
visual_association: Rain pouring down on tin roofs.
difference_explained: 'It's raining hard' also works. 'Heavily' is a little more formal.
mini_conversation:
A: Should we go out?
B: No — it's raining heavily.
everyday_scene: Everyday: The farmer's cart was heavily loaded with sugarcane.
news_style_line: News-style: The old bridge was heavily damaged in the flood.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Relying heavily on coffee today.'
mcq_options: A) heavily  B) heavy  C) heaviness  D) heaved
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Many farmers depend ______ on the monsoon. → heavily
find_and_fix_to_correct: It snowed very heavy in Shimla. → It snowed very heavily in Shimla.
translate: बहुत तेज़ बारिश हो रही है। → It's raining heavily.
write_your_own_sentence: Write about a day when it rained heavily.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which adverb means 'in large amounts or with force'?
usage_tip: 'Heavily' + 'rely/depend' = depend a lot.

simple_explanation: Quietly or gently.
example_1: She spoke softly to the baby.
example_2: He closed the door softly.
example_3: The rain fell softly.
collocations: speak softly, smile softly, knock softly, softly spoken
grammar_pattern: verb + softly
common_mistake: Speak soft, the baby is sleeping.
correct_version: Speak softly, the baby is sleeping.
why_it_s_wrong: After a verb, use the adverb 'softly'.
etymology: From 'soft' (Old English softe) + -ly.
mnemonic: SOFTLY → as SOFT as a pillow.
memory_trick: 'Softly spoken' = has a quiet, gentle voice.
visual_association: A mother singing softly to a sleeping child.
difference_explained: Quietly = with little noise. Softly = quietly AND gently.
mini_conversation:
A: Why are you whispering?
B: I'm speaking softly — Grandpa is sleeping.
everyday_scene: Everyday: The breeze moved softly through the wheat.
news_style_line: News-style: The nurse spoke softly to calm the patient.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Opened the fridge softly at midnight. Mission successful.'
mcq_options: A) softly  B) soft to  C) softness  D) softer to
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: He knocked ______ on the door. → softly
find_and_fix_to_correct: Talk soft in the hospital. → Talk softly in the hospital.
translate: वह बच्चे से धीरे से बोली। → She spoke softly to the baby.
write_your_own_sentence: Write where you should speak softly.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which adverb means 'quietly and gently'?
usage_tip: Opposite: loudly.

simple_explanation: In a powerful or firm way; very much (opinions).
example_1: I strongly believe in hard work.
example_2: We strongly recommend booking early.
example_3: She strongly disagreed.
collocations: strongly believe, strongly recommend, strongly agree/disagree, strongly advise
grammar_pattern: strongly + verb (believe, feel, agree)
common_mistake: I strong believe it.
correct_version: I strongly believe it.
why_it_s_wrong: Before a verb, use the adverb 'strongly'.
etymology: From 'strong' (Old English strang) + -ly.
mnemonic: STRONGLY → a STRONG opinion.
memory_trick: Survey scale: strongly agree / agree / disagree / strongly disagree.
visual_association: A person pounding a table while making a point.
difference_explained: Firmly = steady, not changing. Strongly = with force or deep feeling.
mini_conversation:
A: Should I apply for the scholarship?
B: I strongly recommend it!
everyday_scene: Everyday: The villagers strongly opposed the new factory.
news_style_line: News-style: Doctors strongly advise wearing helmets.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'I strongly believe Sunday should be two days long.'
mcq_options: A) strongly  B) strong  C) strength  D) stronger
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: We ______ recommend carrying water on the trek. → strongly
find_and_fix_to_correct: I strong feel this is wrong. → I strongly feel this is wrong.
translate: मैं मेहनत में दृढ़ विश्वास रखता हूँ। → I strongly believe in hard work.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence starting 'I strongly believe…'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which adverb means 'in a powerful or firm way'?
usage_tip: Opinion builder for debates.

hindi_meaning: व्यापक रूप से, बड़े पैमाने पर
simple_explanation: By a lot of people or in many places.
example_1: Hindi is widely spoken in India.
example_2: It's widely believed that exercise helps memory.
example_3: The news spread widely.
collocations: widely spoken, widely used, widely known, widely believed, widely available
grammar_pattern: widely + past participle (spoken, used, known)
common_mistake: English is wide spoken.
correct_version: English is widely spoken.
why_it_s_wrong: Before a past participle, use 'widely'.
etymology: From 'wide' (Old English wid) + -ly.
mnemonic: WIDELY → spread WIDE, all over.
memory_trick: Essay phrase: 'It is widely believed that…'
visual_association: A map with dots spread across a whole country.
difference_explained: 'Wide' describes size ('a wide road'). 'Widely' describes how common something is.
mini_conversation:
A: Is UPI used in villages too?
B: Yes, it's widely used now.
everyday_scene: Everyday: Neem is widely used in Indian homes as a natural medicine.
news_style_line: News-style: The news was widely reported across the country.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'It is widely known that I love chai.'
mcq_options: A) widely  B) wide  C) width  D) widen
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The new app is ______ available in India. → widely
find_and_fix_to_correct: Tamil is wide spoken in Chennai. → Tamil is widely spoken in Chennai.
translate: हिंदी भारत में व्यापक रूप से बोली जाती है। → Hindi is widely spoken in India.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence using 'It is widely believed that…'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which adverb means 'by many people or in many places'?
usage_tip: 'Widely read' = has read many books.

simple_explanation: To the extent that; up to a place.
example_1: As far as I know, the shop opens at 9.
example_2: As far as I'm concerned, it's fine.
example_3: We walked as far as the river.
collocations: as far as I know, as far as I'm concerned, as far as I remember, as far as possible
grammar_pattern: as far as + I know/remember / as far as + subject + be concerned / as far as + place
common_mistake: As far as I concerned, it's okay.
correct_version: As far as I'm concerned, it's okay.
why_it_s_wrong: You need 'am/is/are' before 'concerned'.
etymology: 'Far' comes from Old English feorr.
mnemonic: AS FAR AS I KNOW = my knowledge goes only this FAR.
memory_trick: Replaces Indian 'as per my knowledge' → 'as far as I know'.
visual_association: A person pointing to the edge of a map.
synonyms: to my knowledge, I believe; up to
confusing_word: as far as vs as per
difference_explained: As per = according to (rules, formal). As far as I know = I think, but I'm not sure.
related_words: to my knowledge, according to, extent, distance
mini_conversation:
A: Is the bank open on Saturday?
B: As far as I know, yes — till 1 p.m.
everyday_scene: Everyday: The boy cycled as far as the next village.
news_style_line: News-style: As far as officials know, no one was hurt.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'As far as I'm concerned, weekends are for sleeping.'
mcq_question: '___ I remember, the exam is on Monday.'
mcq_options: A) As far as  B) As per  C) So far as to  D) As long
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: We can go ______ Agra by train, then take a bus. → as far as
find_and_fix_to_correct: As per my knowledge, he is married. → As far as I know, he is married.
translate: जहाँ तक मुझे पता है, दुकान 9 बजे खुलती है। → As far as I know, the shop opens at 9.
write_your_own_sentence: Write two sentences using 'as far as I know'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which expression means 'to the extent that' (I know)?
usage_tip: Great for polite uncertainty.

simple_explanation: On the other side of something, facing it.
example_1: The bank is opposite the post office.
example_2: She sat opposite me.
example_3: There's a temple opposite our house.
collocations: opposite the station, sit opposite, directly opposite, just opposite
grammar_pattern: opposite + place/person (usually no 'to')
common_mistake: He lives opposite to my house.
correct_version: He lives opposite my house.
why_it_s_wrong: For position, use 'opposite' without 'to'.
etymology: From Latin oppositus, 'set against'.
word_family: opposite (n: 'the opposite of hot is cold'), oppose (v)
mnemonic: OPPOSITE → face-to-face across the road.
memory_trick: Two uses: position ('opposite the bank') and meaning ('the opposite of big').
visual_association: Two shops facing each other across a street.
synonyms: facing, across from, in front of
difference_explained: In front of = directly before you (same side). Opposite = on the other side, facing.
related_words: facing, across, in front of, beside
mini_conversation:
A: Where's the chemist?
B: Just opposite the bus stop.
everyday_scene: Everyday: The tea stall is opposite the school gate.
news_style_line: News-style: The new hospital will be built opposite the railway station.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Sat opposite my crush. Forgot how to eat.'
mcq_options: A) opposite  B) opposite to of  C) opposit  D) in opposite
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: 'Hot' is the ______ of 'cold'. → opposite
find_and_fix_to_correct: The ATM is opposite to the temple. → The ATM is opposite the temple.
translate: बैंक डाकघर के सामने है। → The bank is opposite the post office.
write_your_own_sentence: Give directions to your house using 'opposite'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which preposition means 'facing, on the other side'?
usage_tip: 'Opposite number' = person in the same role elsewhere.

simple_explanation: To study something carefully to understand it.
example_2: The doctor analysed the test results.
example_3: Analyse your mistakes and learn from them.
collocations: analyse data, analyse results, analyse a problem, carefully analyse
action_sequence: Before: collect data → During: study it closely → After: find what it means
grammar_pattern: analyse + noun (no 'about')
common_mistake: We analysed about the problem.
correct_version: We analysed the problem.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Analyse' takes the object directly — no 'about'.

mnemonic: ANALYSE → break it into small parts to see inside.
memory_trick: UK: analyse / US: analyze. Noun plural: analyses.
visual_association: A person studying a chart with a magnifying glass.
difference_explained: Examine = look at carefully. Analyse = examine and break into parts to understand why.
mini_conversation:
A: Why did sales fall this month?
B: Let me analyse the numbers first.
everyday_scene: Everyday: The farmer analysed the soil before choosing a crop.
news_style_line: News-style: Experts analysed the causes of the accident.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Analysed my spending. Chai is 40% of it.'
mcq_options: A) analysed  B) analysed about  C) analysis  D) analyst
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Data ______ is a useful job skill. → analysis
find_and_fix_to_correct: He analysed about the report. → He analysed the report.
translate: चलो बिक्री के आँकड़ों का विश्लेषण करते हैं। → Let's analyse the sales data.
write_your_own_sentence: Write how you would analyse your weekly study time.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which verb means 'to study carefully in parts'?
usage_tip: CV word: 'analytical skills'.

simple_explanation: To give someone a task or a job.
example_1: The teacher assigned us an essay.
example_2: She was assigned to the sales team.
example_3: Each group was assigned a topic.
collocations: assign a task, assign homework, be assigned to, assign someone to
action_sequence: Before: have many tasks → During: give one to each person → After: everyone knows their job
grammar_pattern: assign + person + task / assign + task + to + person / be assigned to + team
common_mistake: He assigned to me a project.
correct_version: He assigned me a project. / He assigned a project to me.
why_it_s_wrong: Two patterns: assign PERSON TASK, or assign TASK TO PERSON.

mnemonic: ASSIGN → put a SIGN with your name on the task.
memory_trick: 'Assignment' = a piece of work given in college or office.

difference_explained: Give = general. Assign = officially give a task or role.

A: What's your role in the project?
B: I've been assigned the design part.
everyday_scene: Everyday: The sarpanch assigned each family a day to clean the well.
news_style_line: News-style: New officers were assigned to rural areas.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Assigned myself one task today: sleep.'
mcq_options: A) assigned  B) assigned to me  C) assignment  D) assign on
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Please submit your ______ by Monday. → assignment
find_and_fix_to_correct: She assigned to me the work. → She assigned me the work.
translate: शिक्षक ने हमें निबंध दिया। → The teacher assigned us an essay.
write_your_own_sentence: Write about a task you were assigned recently.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which verb means 'to give someone a task'?
usage_tip: Silent g: assi(g)n.

simple_explanation: To organise people or things so they work well together.

news_style_line: News-style: Several agencies coordinated the rescue operation.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Coordinating lunch plans takes longer than lunch.'
mcq_question: 'She ___ all the volunteers at the camp.'
mcq_options: A) coordinated  B) coordinated to  C) coordination  D) cooperate
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Good ______ saves time. → coordination
find_and_fix_to_correct: Please coordinate to the vendor. → Please coordinate with the vendor.

write_your_own_sentence: Write about an event you helped coordinate.

reverse_quick_recall: Which verb means 'to organise people to work well together'?
usage_tip: Job ads: 'coordination skills'.

simple_explanation: To copy files or apps from the internet to your device.

example_2: I downloaded the admit card.
example_3: The file is still downloading.

grammar_pattern: download + thing + from + source + to/onto + device

simple_explanation: Instead of; in preference to.

why_it_s_wrong: No 'to' after 'rather than'.

simple_explanation: In total; completely.

example_3: Altogether, it was a good trip.

correct_version: We sang the song all together.
why_it_s_wrong: ALTOGETHER = in total / completely. ALL TOGETHER = everyone at the same time.
spelling_tip: ALTOGETHER: one word, one L. Not 'all together' (everyone at once).

mnemonic: ALTOGETHER (one word) = total. ALL TOGETHER (two words) = everyone together.
memory_trick: Shop line: 'How much is it altogether?'
visual_association: A cashier adding up items to show one total.
synonyms: in total, in all; completely, entirely
difference_explained: Altogether = in total / completely. All together = all at the same time or place.
mini_conversation:

B: ₹80 altogether.
everyday_scene: Everyday: The farmer has twelve cows altogether.
news_style_line: News-style: The minister said the project was altogether a success.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Stopped eating sugar altogether. For one day.'
mcq_options: A) altogether  B) all together  C) altogeather  D) all-together
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The family sat ______ for dinner. → all together
find_and_fix_to_correct: We played altogether as a team. → We played all together as a team.
translate: कुल मिलाकर ₹500 हुए। → That's ₹500 altogether.

usage_tip: Tricky pair: altogether vs all together.

simple_explanation: Considering everything; in general.
example_2: The results were good overall.
example_3: What's the overall cost?
collocations: overall, it was, overall cost (adj), overall result, overall winner
grammar_pattern: Overall, + clause / overall + noun (adj)
common_mistake: Over all, the movie was nice.
correct_version: Overall, the movie was nice.
why_it_s_wrong: One word: overall.
etymology: Formed in English from over + all.
mnemonic: OVERALL → looking OVER ALL the parts.
memory_trick: Review tip: end with 'Overall, …'.
visual_association: A person giving a thumbs-up after looking at a report.
synonyms: in general, on the whole, generally
difference_explained: Both summarise. 'Altogether' is more for totals; 'overall' for general judgement.
related_words: generally, on the whole, total, summary
mini_conversation:

B: Some problems, but overall, good!

news_style_line: News-style: Overall, the state's literacy rate has improved.

mcq_options: A) Overall  B) Over all  C) Overally  D) All over
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: What is the ______ cost of the trip? → overall
find_and_fix_to_correct: Over all, it was fine. → Overall, it was fine.
translate: कुल मिलाकर यात्रा अच्छी थी। → Overall, the trip was great.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a short review ending with 'Overall, …'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which adverb means 'considering everything'?
usage_tip: 'Overalls' = one-piece work clothes.

simple_explanation: Used to say that something will happen in one condition and no other.
example_1: You can go out only if you finish your homework.
example_2: I'll come only if you come too.
example_3: Only if it rains will the match be cancelled.
collocations: only if you, only if necessary, only if it's true
grammar_pattern: main clause + only if + present simple / Only if + clause + inverted clause (formal)
common_mistake: Only if you will study, you will pass.
correct_version: You will pass only if you study.
why_it_s_wrong: Use present simple after 'only if' for the future.
etymology: 'Only' comes from Old English anlic.
mnemonic: ONLY IF = this ONE condition, nothing else.
memory_trick: Formal start: 'Only if…, will…' (verb comes before the subject).
visual_association: A gate that opens only when the correct key is used.
synonyms: provided that, as long as, on condition that
difference_explained: If = a condition. Only if = the ONLY condition.
related_words: if, unless, provided, as long as
mini_conversation:
A: Can I use your laptop?
B: Only if you're careful with it.
everyday_scene: Everyday: The farmer sells his mangoes only if the price is fair.
news_style_line: News-style: Refunds will be given only if the receipt is shown.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'I'll wake up early only if there's free breakfast.'
mcq_question: 'You'll get the bonus ___ you meet the target.'
mcq_options: A) only if  B) if only  C) even if  D) only when will
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: I'll help you ______ you promise to try. → only if
find_and_fix_to_correct: Only if you will pay, I'll give it. → I'll give it only if you pay.
translate: तुम तभी बाहर जा सकते हो जब होमवर्क पूरा करोगे। → You can go out only if you finish your homework.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a rule using 'only if'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which conjunction means 'in this one condition only'?
usage_tip: Don't confuse with 'if only' (a wish).

simple_explanation: Used to express a strong wish or regret.
example_1: If only I had more money!
example_2: If only I'd studied harder.
example_3: If only it would stop raining.
collocations: if only I had, if only I could, if only it were
grammar_pattern: If only + past simple (present wish) / If only + past perfect (past regret)
common_mistake: If only I have more time.
correct_version: If only I had more time.
why_it_s_wrong: For a present wish, use the past simple after 'if only'.
etymology: 'If' from Old English gif; 'only' from Old English anlic.
mnemonic: IF ONLY → 'Kaash!' in English.
memory_trick: Pattern: If only + past (now), had + past participle (past).
visual_association: A student looking at a result card, sighing.
difference_explained: If only = a wish (kaash). Only if = the only condition.
mini_conversation:
A: The train left two minutes ago.
B: If only we'd left home earlier!
everyday_scene: Everyday: If only the rain had come a week earlier, the crop would be saved.
news_style_line: News-style: 'If only we had acted sooner,' the minister said.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'If only chai had zero calories.'
mcq_options: A) If only  B) Only if  C) Even if  D) As if
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: ______ I had listened to my mother! → If only
find_and_fix_to_correct: If only I have a car. → If only I had a car.
translate: काश मेरे पास और पैसे होते! → If only I had more money!
write_your_own_sentence: Write two 'If only…' sentences — one wish, one regret.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which expression means 'kaash' (a strong wish)?
usage_tip: 'I wish' is the everyday twin.

simple_explanation: Not including.
example_2: The shop is open daily, excluding Sundays.
example_3: Everyone came, excluding my uncle.
collocations: excluding tax, excluding GST, excluding weekends, excluding delivery
grammar_pattern: excluding + noun (no 'of')

correct_version: ₹500 excluding GST. (or 'exclusive of GST')
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'excluding GST' or 'exclusive OF GST' — not 'excluding of'.

memory_trick: Opposite: including.
visual_association: A bill with one line crossed out and marked 'extra'.
difference_explained: Except = not including (general). Excluding = not included in a total or list (common with prices).

casual_conversation: Casual: 'Diet going well — excluding weekends.'

find_and_fix_to_correct: It costs ₹200 excluding of tax. → It costs ₹200 excluding tax.

write_your_own_sentence: Write a price quote using 'excluding'.

simple_explanation: Having a certain value; good or useful enough to do.

example_3: Is it worth the money?
collocations: worth + price, worth + -ing, worth it, worth the wait, worth a try
grammar_pattern: be worth + amount/noun / be worth + -ing / be worth it
common_mistake: This film is worth to watch.
correct_version: This film is worth watching.
why_it_s_wrong: After 'worth', use -ing, not 'to + verb'.
etymology: From Old English weorþ, 'value'.
mnemonic: WORTH → it has WORTH (value).
memory_trick: 'Worth it!' = the effort or money was justified.
visual_association: A shiny gold coin with a price label.
difference_explained: Worth + -ing / amount ('worth ₹500'). Worthy of + noun ('worthy of respect').

news_style_line: News-style: The new bridge is worth ₹200 crore, officials said.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Waited an hour for jalebis. Totally worth it.'

find_and_fix_to_correct: The trip is worth to visit. → The place is worth visiting.

write_your_own_sentence: Write about something that was worth the wait.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'having a value' or 'good enough to do'?
usage_tip: 'For what it's worth' = even if it's not important.

simple_explanation: To get on a train, bus, plane or ship.

grammar_pattern: board + vehicle (no 'in/on') / board + at + place

difference_explained: Same meaning. 'Board' is formal (announcements); 'get on' is everyday.

find_and_fix_to_correct: She boarded on the flight to Pune. → She boarded the flight to Pune.

write_your_own_sentence: Write an announcement for passengers to board a train.

why_it_s_wrong: 'Freeze' is irregular: freeze – froze – frozen.

memory_trick: Tech: 'My screen froze' = it stopped responding.
visual_association: A lake with a sheet of ice on top.
synonyms: ice over, solidify; stand still; hang

simple_explanation: (Of a plane) to come down to the ground; to arrive.

example_3: He landed a great job.

grammar_pattern: plane + land + in/at + place / land + a job
common_mistake: The flight landed on Delhi.

memory_trick: 'Land a job' = get a job (informal).
visual_association: A plane touching down on a runway.
difference_explained: Arrive = reach any place. Land = (plane) come down to the ground.

example_3: Her smile melted my heart.

write_your_own_sentence: Write about something that melts your heart.

pronunciation_tip: Short and quick; in speech it often becomes 'I'm'.

mnemonic: 'I am' — I and am always stand together.
memory_trick: 'Am' only ever follows 'I'.
visual_association: A person pointing at their own chest.
difference_explained: 'Am' goes only with 'I'. 'Is' goes with he/she/it.

simple_explanation: Used with he/she/it to talk about now.
example_2: It is very hot today.
example_3: Is this your phone?
collocations: is not, there is, it is
grammar_pattern: he/she/it + is + adjective/noun
common_mistake: She is having a car.
correct_version: She has a car.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Is' + '-ing' is for actions; 'have' (possess) is a state, so use 'has', not 'is having'.
etymology: Old English 'is', unchanged for over 1,000 years.
prefix_root_suffix: Form of 'be' for one person or thing.
mnemonic: 'Is' is for ONE: he, she, it.
memory_trick: 'Is' goes with just one thing — he, she, or it.
visual_association: A single finger held up.
difference_explained: 'Is' for one (she is). 'Are' for more than one and for 'you' (they are, you are).

news_style_line: News-style: 'The situation is under control,' police said.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'This movie is so good!'

simple_explanation: Used with you/we/they to talk about now.
example_2: You are right.
example_3: Are they coming today?

grammar_pattern: you/we/they + are + adjective/noun

why_it_s_wrong: 'They' is plural, so it needs 'are'.

prefix_root_suffix: Form of 'be' for you, we, they.
mnemonic: 'Are' is for 'ALL of you'.
memory_trick: 'Are' is for more than one — we, you, they.

difference_explained: 'Are' is a verb (we are). 'Our' shows belonging (our house). They sound almost the same.

write_your_own_sentence: Write what you are wearing today.
