usage_tip: English uses 'wear' for glasses, watches and perfume too.

simple_explanation: Divide with something sharp.
example_2: Cut the paper in half.
example_3: I cut my finger.
collocations: cut off, cut down, cut in half
related_phrasal_verbs: cut down, cut off, cut out
action_sequence: Before: pick up the knife → During: cut carefully → After: two pieces
grammar_pattern: cut + object
common_mistake: I cutted the bread.
correct_version: I cut the bread.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Cut' is the same in all forms: cut – cut – cut.
etymology: Middle English 'cutten'.
mnemonic: CUT never changes — like PUT and SHUT.
memory_trick: 'Cut' never changes: cut–cut–cut in every tense.
visual_association: Scissors cutting paper.
difference_explained: Cut = divide with a blade. Cut off = stop a supply (the power was cut off).
mini_conversation: A: Did you get a haircut? / B: Yes, I cut it short.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Cut the onions into small pieces.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'The bank cut interest rates.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Cut it out! Stop joking.'
mcq_question: Choose: He ___ the cake last night.
mcq_options: A) cutted  B) cut  C) cuts  D) cutting
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Please ___ the bread. → cut
find_and_fix_to_correct: I am cutting my hair every month. → I get my hair cut every month.
translate: केक काटो। → Cut the cake.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence with 'cut down on'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'divide with something sharp'?
usage_tip: If someone else cuts your hair, say 'I got my hair cut'.

simple_explanation: Move toward the speaker.
example_2: Can you come tomorrow?
example_3: She came home late.
collocations: come back, come on, come from
related_phrasal_verbs: come back, come in, come on
action_sequence: Before: get the invitation → During: travel here → After: arrive
grammar_pattern: come + to/from + place
common_mistake: I comed here.
correct_version: I came here.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Come' is irregular: come – came – come.
spelling_tip: C-O-M-E. Silent E. -ing form: COMING (drop the E).
etymology: Old English 'cuman'.
mnemonic: COME → CAME → COME (back where it started).
memory_trick: 'Come' is irregular: come–came–come, never 'comed'.
visual_association: A person walking toward you.
difference_explained: Come = toward the speaker. Go = away from the speaker.
mini_conversation: A: Are you coming to the party? / B: Yes, I'll come at eight.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Come here, look at this!'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Thousands came to see the parade.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Come on, hurry!'
mcq_question: Choose: He ___ to my house yesterday.
mcq_options: A) come  B) came  C) comed  D) coming
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: ___ here, please. → Come
find_and_fix_to_correct: I am coming from Delhi. (meaning your hometown) → I come from Delhi. / I am from Delhi.
translate: कल आना। → Come tomorrow.
write_your_own_sentence: Write an invitation using 'come'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'move toward the speaker'?
usage_tip: 'I'm coming' = I am on my way right now.

simple_explanation: Go away from a place.
example_2: The train leaves at six.
example_3: Don't leave your bag here.
collocations: leave home, leave for, leave behind
action_sequence: Before: pack your things → During: walk out → After: you are gone
grammar_pattern: leave + place / leave + object
common_mistake: I leaved home.
correct_version: I left home.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Leave' is irregular: the past is 'left', not 'leaved'.
etymology: Old English 'lǣfan'.
mnemonic: LEAVE → LEFT: when you leave, you have left.
memory_trick: 'Leave' is irregular: leave–left–left, never 'leaved'.
visual_association: A person walking out of a door.
difference_explained: Leave (long ee) = go away. Live (short i) = stay in a home.
mini_conversation: A: When do you leave for office? / B: Around nine.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'I left my umbrella in the bus.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'The flight left an hour late.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Leave me alone, I'm tired.'
mcq_options: A) leaved  B) left  C) leave  D) lefted
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: I ___ home at eight. → leave
find_and_fix_to_correct: I will leave from Mumbai tomorrow. → I will leave Mumbai tomorrow.
translate: मैं आठ बजे घर से निकलता हूँ। → I leave home at eight.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about when you leave for work or college.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'go away from a place'?
usage_tip: 'Leave' can also mean holiday from work: 'I'm on leave today.'

simple_explanation: Move down suddenly.
example_2: Leaves fall in autumn.
example_3: He fell off his bike.
collocations: fall down, fall over, fall asleep
related_phrasal_verbs: fall down, fall apart, fall for
action_sequence: Before: lose balance → During: drop down → After: hit the ground
grammar_pattern: fall + adverb (down/over)
common_mistake: I falled down.
correct_version: I fell down.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Fall' is irregular: fall – fell – fallen.
etymology: Old English 'feallan'.
mnemonic: FALL → FELL → FALLEN.
memory_trick: 'Fall' is irregular: fall–fell–fallen, never 'falled'.
visual_association: A leaf dropping from a tree.
difference_explained: Fall = go down by itself. Drop = let something fall.
mini_conversation: A: What happened to your knee? / B: I fell on the stairs.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Be careful, the floor is wet — don't fall.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Petrol prices fell for the third day.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'I almost fell asleep in class!'
mcq_question: Choose: The glass ___ off the table.
mcq_options: A) falled  B) fell  C) fall  D) fallen
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Be careful, don't ___. → fall
find_and_fix_to_correct: My phone fell down from my hand. → My phone fell out of my hand.
translate: वह सीढ़ियों से गिर गया। → He fell down the stairs.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something that fell.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'move down suddenly'?
usage_tip: 'Fall asleep' = start sleeping. 'Fall in love' = start loving.

simple_explanation: Use your mind to form ideas.
example_2: What do you think?
example_3: I'm thinking about the exam.
collocations: think about, think of, think over
related_phrasal_verbs: think over, think about, think of
action_sequence: Before: have a question → During: use your mind → After: get an idea
grammar_pattern: think + about/of + noun
common_mistake: I am thinking you are right.
correct_version: I think you are right.
why_it_s_wrong: For an opinion, 'think' is a state verb, so it doesn't take -ing.
pronunciation_tip: 'TH' with the tongue between the teeth — not 'tink'.
etymology: Old English 'thencan'.
mnemonic: THINK → THOUGHT, like BUY → BOUGHT.
memory_trick: 'Think' opinions usually skip 'am/is/are' — just 'I think...'.
visual_association: A person with a finger on their chin.
difference_explained: I think (= opinion). I'm thinking about (= considering).
mini_conversation: A: Do you think it will rain? / B: I think so.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'I think the shop is closed today.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Experts think prices will rise.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'I don't think so, yaar.'
mcq_options: A) am thinking  B) think  C) thinks  D) thought of
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: I ___ you are right. → think
find_and_fix_to_correct: I thinked about it. → I thought about it.
translate: मुझे लगता है तुम सही हो। → I think you are right.
write_your_own_sentence: Write your opinion about something with 'I think'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'use your mind to form ideas'?
usage_tip: 'I don't think he's coming' sounds more natural than 'I think he isn't coming'.

simple_explanation: Have information in your mind.
example_2: Do you know him?
example_3: I don't know the answer.
collocations: know about, know how to, get to know
action_sequence: Before: learn something → During: keep it in your mind → After: use it
grammar_pattern: know + noun / know + how to + verb
common_mistake: I am knowing the answer.
correct_version: I know the answer.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Know' is a state verb, so it doesn't take -ing: 'I know', not 'I am knowing'.
etymology: Old English 'cnāwan'.
mnemonic: KNOW has a silent K — you just have to KNOW it!
memory_trick: 'Know' is a state, not an action — never use '-ing' with it.
visual_association: A light bulb over a head.
difference_explained: Know = have information. No = the negative word. Same sound.
mini_conversation: A: Do you know where the bank is? / B: Yes, next to the post office.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'I know a good doctor near here.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Little is known about the new virus.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'You know what? Let's just go.'
mcq_options: A) know  B) have known  C) am knowing  D) knew
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: I ___ the answer. → know
find_and_fix_to_correct: I am knowing him for five years. → I have known him for five years.
translate: मैं उसे जानता हूँ। → I know him.
write_your_own_sentence: Write about someone you have known for a long time.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'have information in your mind'?
usage_tip: 'You know' is a common filler in speech — don't overuse it in interviews.

simple_explanation: Wish for something good to happen.
example_2: Hope to see you soon.
example_3: We hope it doesn't rain.
collocations: hope so, hope for, hope to
action_sequence: Before: want something good → During: wait and wish → After: see what happens
grammar_pattern: hope + (that) + clause / hope + to + verb
common_mistake: I hope that you will to feel better.
correct_version: I hope you feel better.
why_it_s_wrong: After 'hope', use a normal clause (I hope you feel better) — 'will to' is wrong.
spelling_tip: H-O-P-E. -ing: HOPING (one P). HOPPING (two Ps) = jumping.
etymology: Old English 'hopian'.
mnemonic: HOPE for good things; HOP like a frog.
memory_trick: 'Hope' + present tense clause, no extra 'to' inside it.
visual_association: A person looking at a sunrise.
difference_explained: Hope = possible future (I hope you pass). Wish = unreal or impossible (I wish I were taller).
mini_conversation: A: Is your mother better now? / B: Yes, thanks. I hope she's home soon.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'I hope the train is on time.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Officials hope to finish the road by March.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Hope you had fun!'
mcq_options: A) will be to  B) are  C) being  D) to be
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: I ___ you feel better. → hope
find_and_fix_to_correct: I wish you pass the exam. → I hope you pass the exam.
translate: उम्मीद है तुम जल्दी ठीक हो जाओगे। → I hope you get well soon.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence hoping something good for a friend.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'wish for something good to happen'?
usage_tip: 'I hope so' / 'I hope not' are short, natural replies.

simple_explanation: Speak words.
example_2: What did she say?
example_3: He said he was tired.
collocations: say hello, say so, that is to say
action_sequence: Before: hear someone → During: repeat their words → After: others know
grammar_pattern: say + object (no person directly after)
common_mistake: Say me the truth.
correct_version: Tell me the truth.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Say' doesn't take a person directly. You say something; you tell someone.
etymology: Old English 'secgan'.
mnemonic: SAY words. TELL people.
memory_trick: 'Say' the words; 'tell' a person — they're not interchangeable.
visual_association: A speech bubble.
difference_explained: Say + words (say hello). Tell + person (tell me).
mini_conversation: A: What did the doctor say? / B: She said I need rest.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Say thank you to Aunty.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'The police said the road is closed.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Say what? No way!'
mcq_question: Choose: She ___ that she was busy.
mcq_options: A) told  B) said  C) say to  D) said me
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: She ___ hello. → said
find_and_fix_to_correct: He said me to come. → He told me to come.
translate: उसने कहा कि वह थका हुआ है। → He said he was tired.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence reporting what a friend said.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'speak words'?
usage_tip: Use 'say something TO someone' if you need the person: 'She said sorry to me.'

simple_explanation: Give information to someone.
example_2: Tell me about your trip.
example_3: She told me a story.
collocations: tell the truth, tell a story, tell me
action_sequence: Before: know something → During: tell the person → After: now they know
grammar_pattern: tell + person + object
common_mistake: Tell to me the truth.
correct_version: Tell me the truth.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Tell' takes the person directly — no 'to' before the person.
etymology: Old English 'tellan'.
mnemonic: TELL → TOLD, like SELL → SOLD.
memory_trick: 'Tell' always needs a listener right after it — 'tell me'.
visual_association: A grandmother telling a bedtime story.
difference_explained: Tell + person (tell me). Say + words (say yes).
mini_conversation: A: Can you tell me the way to the station? / B: Go straight and turn left.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Tell your brother to call me.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Witnesses told police what they saw.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Don't tell anyone, okay?'
mcq_options: A) say  B) tell  C) speak  D) talk
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: ___ me the truth. → Tell
find_and_fix_to_correct: Tell to him to wait. → Tell him to wait.
translate: मुझे सच बताओ। → Tell me the truth.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence using 'tell someone to…'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'give information to someone'?
usage_tip: 'Tell the truth', 'tell a lie', 'tell a story', 'tell the time' — fixed pairs.

simple_explanation: Use your voice to talk.
example_2: Can I speak to the manager?
example_3: She speaks three languages.
collocations: speak up, speak to, speak English
action_sequence: Before: take a breath → During: speak clearly → After: people listen
grammar_pattern: speak + language / speak + to + person
common_mistake: Speak me in English.
correct_version: Speak to me in English.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Speak' needs 'to' before the person: speak to me.
spelling_tip: S-P-E-A-K. Past: SPOKE. Past participle: SPOKEN.
etymology: Old English 'specan'.
mnemonic: SPEAK → SPOKE → SPOKEN.
memory_trick: 'Speak to/with' a person, but 'speak' a language directly.
visual_association: A person talking into a mic.
difference_explained: Speak = more formal, languages, one person to many. Talk = conversation between people.
mini_conversation: A: Do you speak Hindi? / B: Yes, and a little Tamil.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Please speak slowly.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'The PM spoke to reporters.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Speak up, I can't hear you!'
mcq_question: Choose: Can I ___ to Mr Sharma, please?
mcq_options: A) say  B) tell  C) speak  D) talk to
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Do you ___ English? → speak
find_and_fix_to_correct: He speaks English very good. → He speaks English very well.
translate: क्या आप अंग्रेज़ी बोलते हैं? → Do you speak English?
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about the languages you speak.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'use your voice to talk'?
usage_tip: On the phone: 'Can I speak to…?' is polite; 'Who's speaking?' asks who is calling.

simple_explanation: Have a conversation.
example_2: We need to talk.
example_3: They talked for hours.
collocations: talk about, talk to, small talk
related_phrasal_verbs: talk over, talk back, talk into
action_sequence: Before: meet someone → During: talk together → After: understand each other
grammar_pattern: talk + about + noun / talk + to + person
common_mistake: Talk me about your day.
correct_version: Talk to me about your day.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Talk' needs 'to' or 'with' before the person: talk to me.
etymology: Middle English 'talken'.
mnemonic: TALK has a silent L — just like WALK.
memory_trick: 'Talk to/with' someone 'about' a topic — two prepositions needed.
visual_association: Two friends chatting over chai.
difference_explained: Talk = conversation. Speak = more formal or one-way.
mini_conversation: A: Can we talk after class? / B: Sure, I'll wait outside.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Let's talk about it at home.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'The two leaders talked for an hour.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Stop talking, the movie's starting!'
mcq_question: Choose: I want to talk ___ you.
mcq_options: A) —  B) to  C) at  D) of
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Let's ___ later. → talk
find_and_fix_to_correct: We discussed about the plan. → We talked about the plan. / We discussed the plan.
translate: मुझे तुमसे बात करनी है। → I need to talk to you.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about who you talk to every day.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'have a conversation'?
usage_tip: 'Talk about' + topic; 'discuss' + topic (no 'about').

simple_explanation: Get pleasure from something.
example_2: Enjoy your meal!
example_3: Did you enjoy the party?
collocations: enjoy yourself, enjoy doing, thoroughly enjoy
action_sequence: Before: do something fun → During: feel happy → After: remember it later
grammar_pattern: enjoy + verb-ing (never 'to')
common_mistake: I enjoy to read.
correct_version: I enjoy reading.
why_it_s_wrong: After 'enjoy', use the -ing form, not 'to' + verb.
etymology: Old French 'enjoir'.
mnemonic: ENJOY has JOY inside it.
memory_trick: 'Enjoy' ALWAYS takes '-ing', never 'to + verb'.
visual_association: People laughing at a party.
difference_explained: 'Enjoy' needs an object: 'I enjoyed the party' or 'I enjoyed myself' — not just 'I enjoyed'.
mini_conversation: A: How was the wedding? / B: Great — we really enjoyed it.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Enjoy your holiday!'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Visitors enjoyed the light show.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Enjoy the weekend, guys!'
mcq_question: Choose: I enjoy ___ in the rain.
mcq_options: A) walk  B) to walk  C) walking  D) walked
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: I ___ reading. → enjoy
find_and_fix_to_correct: We enjoyed a lot at the party. → We enjoyed ourselves at the party. / We had a lot of fun at the party.
translate: मुझे गाना पसंद है। → I enjoy singing.
write_your_own_sentence: Write two things you enjoy doing.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'get pleasure from something'?
usage_tip: 'We enjoyed a lot' is a common Indian-English slip — say 'We had a lot of fun'.

simple_explanation: Feel sad because someone is not there.
example_2: I missed the bus.
example_3: We miss you.
collocations: miss you, miss out, miss the bus
action_sequence: Before: someone is far away → During: think of them → After: feel sad
grammar_pattern: miss + object
common_mistake: I miss to you.
correct_version: I miss you.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Miss' takes the person directly — 'miss you', not 'miss to you'.
etymology: Old English 'missan'.
mnemonic: MISS = feel the gap, or be too late.
memory_trick: 'Miss' a person directly — no preposition needed.
visual_association: A bus leaving as someone runs.
difference_explained: Miss = not catch (a bus) or feel sad someone is away. Lose = no longer have something.
mini_conversation: A: Why are you late? / B: I missed the metro.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Hurry, or we'll miss the train.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'The team missed a penalty in the last minute.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Miss you, yaar! Come back soon.'
mcq_question: Choose: I ___ my family when I travel.
mcq_options: A) miss  B) lose  C) am missing to  D) forget
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: I ___ my family. → miss
find_and_fix_to_correct: I am missing my home. → I miss my home.
translate: मुझे तुम्हारी याद आती है। → I miss you.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about someone you miss.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'feel sad because someone is not there'?
usage_tip: 'Don't miss it!' = it's too good to skip.

simple_explanation: Continue to be in a place or state.

example_3: Stay calm.
collocations: stay here, stay with, stay calm
related_phrasal_verbs: stay up, stay in, stay away
action_sequence: Before: arrive at a place → During: remain there → After: leave later
grammar_pattern: stay + place/adjective
common_mistake: Stay here with I.
correct_version: Stay here with me.
why_it_s_wrong: After a verb or preposition, use the object pronoun 'me', not 'I'.
etymology: Old French 'ester' (to stand).
mnemonic: STAY = don't go away.
memory_trick: 'Stay' is simple: stay + a place, or stay + how you feel.
visual_association: A person relaxing in a hotel room.
difference_explained: Stay = for a short time (hotel, holiday). Live = your permanent home.
mini_conversation: A: How long are you staying in Goa? / B: Just three days.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Stay here, I'll be back.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Schools will stay closed until Monday.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Let's stay in tonight and watch a movie.'
mcq_question: Choose: We ___ at my uncle's house last summer.
mcq_options: A) lived  B) stayed  C) stay  D) staying
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: ___ here with me. → Stay
find_and_fix_to_correct: I am staying in Pune since 2019. → I have been living in Pune since 2019.
translate: मेरे साथ रुको। → Stay with me.
write_your_own_sentence: Write where you stayed on your last trip.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'continue to be in a place or state'?
usage_tip: In Indian English 'Where do you stay?' means 'Where do you live?' — abroad, 'live' is clearer.

simple_explanation: Need a certain amount of money.
example_2: How much does it cost?
example_3: The trip cost a lot.
collocations: cost a lot, at all costs, cost of living
action_sequence: Before: check the price → During: pay the money → After: feel it was worth it (or not)
grammar_pattern: subject + cost(s) + amount
common_mistake: This costed me ten dollars.
correct_version: This cost me ten dollars.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Cost' is the same in all forms: cost – cost – cost.
etymology: Latin 'constare' (to stand at).
mnemonic: COST never changes, just like CUT and PUT.
memory_trick: 'Cost' never changes: cost–cost–cost, unlike most verbs.
visual_association: A price tag.
difference_explained: Cost = verb or noun (it costs ₹50). Price = noun only (the price is ₹50).
mini_conversation: A: How much did your phone cost? / B: About fifteen thousand.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Tomatoes cost more this month.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'The flood cost the state crores.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'It cost me a fortune!'
mcq_options: A) costed  B) cost  C) costs  D) costing
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: This ___ me ten dollars. → cost
find_and_fix_to_correct: How much it costs? → How much does it cost?
translate: यह कितने का है? → How much does it cost?
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about how much your bag or phone cost.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'need a certain amount of money'?
usage_tip: 'It costs an arm and a leg' = it is very expensive (idiom).

simple_explanation: Use money to pay for things.
example_2: How do you spend your weekends?
example_3: I spent ₹2,000 on books.
collocations: spend on, spend time, well-spent
action_sequence: Before: have money or time → During: use it → After: it's gone
grammar_pattern: spend + amount + on + noun
common_mistake: I spended too much money.
correct_version: I spent too much money.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Spend' is irregular: the past is 'spent', not 'spended'.
etymology: Latin 'expendere' (to pay out).
mnemonic: SPEND → SPENT, like SEND → SENT.
memory_trick: 'Spend' is irregular: spend–spent–spent, never 'spended'.
visual_association: A wallet getting thin.
difference_explained: Spend = use (neutral). Waste = use badly.
mini_conversation: A: How was the weekend? / B: I spent it with my cousins.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Don't spend all your pocket money.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'The city will spend ₹50 crore on roads.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'I spent the whole day sleeping!'
mcq_question: Choose: She ___ two hours on homework.
mcq_options: A) spended  B) spent  C) spend  D) spends on
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: I ___ too much money. → spent
find_and_fix_to_correct: I spent two hours for studying. → I spent two hours studying.
translate: मैंने किताबों पर पैसे खर्च किए। → I spent money on books.
write_your_own_sentence: Write how you spent last Sunday.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'use money to pay for things'?
usage_tip: Spend money ON something; spend time + -ing (spend time reading).

simple_explanation: Keep money instead of spending it.
example_2: Save your work often.
example_3: He saved a child from drowning.
collocations: save up, save for, save money
action_sequence: Before: see a risk → During: act quickly → After: everything is safe
grammar_pattern: save + object / save + up + for + noun
common_mistake: I am saving of a trip.
correct_version: I'm saving for a trip.
why_it_s_wrong: You save FOR a goal: saving for a trip. 'Saving of' is wrong.
etymology: Latin 'salvare' (to make safe).
mnemonic: SAVE money FOR later.
memory_trick: 'Save' can mean keep money, or rescue someone.
visual_association: A piggy bank.
difference_explained: Save = collect money, or rescue. Keep = hold on to something.
mini_conversation: A: Are you saving for anything? / B: Yes, a new laptop.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Save the file before you close it.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Firefighters saved ten people.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'You saved my life, thank you!'
mcq_options: A) of  B) for  C) to  D) at
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: I'm ___ing for a trip. → saving
find_and_fix_to_correct: I am saving money from buying a bike. → I am saving money to buy a bike.
translate: मैं पैसे बचा रहा हूँ। → I am saving money.
write_your_own_sentence: Write what you would like to save money for.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'keep money instead of spending it'?
usage_tip: 'Save' also means 'avoid wasting': 'Walking saves time in traffic.'

simple_explanation: Reach the final point.
example_2: The film ended at ten.
example_3: How does the story end?
collocations: end up, in the end, dead end
action_sequence: Before: start something → During: reach the last part → After: it's over
grammar_pattern: subject + end(s)
common_mistake: The movie end at nine.
correct_version: The movie ends at nine.
why_it_s_wrong: With he/she/it in the present, the verb needs -s: 'the movie ends'.
spelling_tip: E-N-D. Noun ENDING, e.g. a happy ending.
etymology: Old English 'ende'.
mnemonic: END = THE END on a film screen.
memory_trick: 'End' is the simple, everyday word for reaching the finish.
visual_association: 'The End' written on a cinema screen.
difference_explained: Very close. 'Finish' is for completing a task (finish homework). 'End' is for events stopping (the war ended).
mini_conversation: A: When does the exam end? / B: At one o'clock.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'The meeting ended early.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'The strike ended after three days.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'We ended up eating pizza again!'
mcq_question: Choose: The class ___ at four every day.
mcq_options: A) end  B) ends  C) ending  D) is end
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The movie ___s at nine. → ends
find_and_fix_to_correct: The party finished at midnight and we ended up home. → The party ended at midnight and we went home.
translate: फ़िल्म दस बजे खत्म हुई। → The film ended at ten.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence using 'end up'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'reach the final point'?
usage_tip: 'End up' = finally be somewhere you didn't plan.

simple_explanation: Get first place or victory.
example_2: Who won the match?
example_3: She won first prize.
collocations: win a, win over, win-win
action_sequence: Before: play hard → During: beat the others → After: get the prize
grammar_pattern: win + object
common_mistake: Our team winned the game.
correct_version: Our team won the game.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Win' is irregular: the past is 'won', not 'winned'.
etymology: Old English 'winnan'.
mnemonic: WIN → WON (sounds like ONE — number one!).
memory_trick: 'Win' is irregular: win–won–won, never 'winned'.
visual_association: A trophy held up.
difference_explained: You win a match or prize. You beat a person or team.
mini_conversation: A: Did your team win? / B: Yes, by two wickets!
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'She won a scholarship.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'India won the series 3–1.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'You win, I give up!'
mcq_options: A) won  B) beat  C) win  D) winned
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Our team ___ the game. → won
find_and_fix_to_correct: We won them easily. → We beat them easily.
translate: हमने मैच जीत लिया। → We won the match.
write_your_own_sentence: Write about a time you won something.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'get first place or victory'?
usage_tip: Win the game; beat the opponent.

simple_explanation: Not win; fail to keep something.
example_2: Don't lose your ticket.
example_3: We lost the final.
collocations: lose to, lose weight, lose track
action_sequence: Before: have something → During: drop or forget it → After: it's gone
grammar_pattern: lose + object

correct_version: We lost the match.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Lose' is irregular: the past is 'lost', not 'losed'.
spelling_tip: L-O-S-E: one O. LOOSE (two Os) = not tight.

mnemonic: LOSE has lost an O (loose has two).
memory_trick: 'Lose' is irregular: lose–lost–lost, never 'losed'.
visual_association: An empty pocket.
difference_explained: Lose (one O, verb) = not have any more. Loose (two Os, adjective) = not tight.
mini_conversation: A: Why are you upset? / B: I lost my wallet.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'I always lose my pens.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'The company lost ₹10 crore last year.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Don't lose hope, you'll get it next time.'

mcq_options: A) loose  B) lose  C) lost  D) losing
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: We ___ the match. → lost

translate: मेरा फ़ोन खो गया। → I lost my phone.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something you once lost.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'not win; fail to keep something'?

simple_explanation: Put your clothes on.
example_2: Get dressed, we're leaving in ten minutes.
example_3: She got dressed for the party.
collocations: get dressed quickly, get dressed up
action_sequence: Before: wake up → During: put on your clothes → After: ready to go out
grammar_pattern: get dressed + (adverb)
word_forms: get dressed – got dressed – got/gotten dressed – getting dressed
common_mistake: I get dress quickly.
correct_version: I get dressed quickly.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Dressed' is an adjective here, so it keeps the -ed.
etymology: get + dress (Old French 'dresser', to arrange).
mnemonic: GET DRESSED = GET READY in clothes.
memory_trick: 'Get dressed' always keeps the '-ed' — think 'become dressed'.
visual_association: Someone buttoning a shirt in front of a mirror.
difference_explained: Get dressed = put on normal clothes. Dress up = wear special or fancy clothes.
mini_conversation: A: Are you ready? / B: Almost — just getting dressed.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'I get dressed after my bath.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Firefighters get dressed in under a minute.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Get dressed, lazy, we're late!'
mcq_options: A) dress  B) dressed  C) dressing  D) dresses
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: I ___ ___ quickly. → get dressed
find_and_fix_to_correct: She is dressing herself up for work every day. → She gets dressed for work every day.
translate: जल्दी से कपड़े पहनो। → Get dressed quickly.
write_your_own_sentence: Write your morning routine using 'get dressed'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'put your clothes on'?
usage_tip: 'Get changed' = take off one set of clothes and put on another.

simple_explanation: Try to find something.
example_2: What are you looking for?
example_3: She's looking for a new job.
collocations: look for a job, look for trouble, looking for
related_phrasal_verbs: look after, look up, look into
action_sequence: Before: notice something is missing → During: search everywhere → After: find it (or not)
grammar_pattern: look for + object
word_forms: look for – looked for – looked for – looking for
common_mistake: I'm looking my keys.
correct_version: I'm looking for my keys.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Look' alone means 'see'. To mean 'search', it needs 'for'.
etymology: look (Old English 'lōcian') + for.
mnemonic: LOOK FOR = search. FIND = the result.
memory_trick: 'Look for' something — the 'for' is easy to forget but essential.
visual_association: A torch shining under a bed.
difference_explained: Look for = the search. Find = the success.
mini_conversation: A: Can I help you? / B: Yes, I'm looking for the shoe section.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'I'm looking for my charger.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Police are looking for the driver.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'What are you looking for, yaar?'
mcq_question: Choose: I've been ___ my keys for an hour.
mcq_options: A) looking  B) looking for  C) finding  D) seeing
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: I'm ___ ___ my keys. → looking for
find_and_fix_to_correct: I looked for my keys and looked for them under the sofa. → I looked for my keys and found them under the sofa.
translate: मैं अपना फ़ोन ढूँढ रहा हूँ। → I'm looking for my phone.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something you are looking for.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'try to find something'?
usage_tip: In shops, 'I'm looking for…' is the natural way to ask for help.

simple_explanation: Return to a place.
example_2: I want to go back to my village.
example_3: Let's go back, it's getting dark.
collocations: go back home, go back to sleep, go back in time
action_sequence: Before: reach a place → During: turn around → After: return where you started
grammar_pattern: go back + (to place)
word_forms: go back – went back – gone back – going back
common_mistake: Let's go back at home.
correct_version: Let's go back home.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Home' already means 'to home', so no 'at' or 'to'.
etymology: go + back.
word_family: went back, gone back, going back
mnemonic: GO BACK = return, same road.
memory_trick: 'Go back' to a place you already left.
visual_association: A U-turn road sign.
difference_explained: Go back = return from here to there. Come back = return to here.
mini_conversation: A: When are you going back to Delhi? / B: Next Monday.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'I forgot my wallet — I have to go back.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Students will go back to school in June.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Let's go back to that café.'
mcq_question: Choose: After the holiday, we ___ to work.
mcq_options: A) went back  B) go backed  C) gone back  D) going back
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Let's ___ ___ home. → go back
find_and_fix_to_correct: I want to go back to home. → I want to go back home.
translate: मैं वापस घर जाना चाहता हूँ। → I want to go back home.
write_your_own_sentence: Write about a place you want to go back to.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'return to a place'?
usage_tip: 'Go back on your word' = break a promise.

simple_explanation: Move into a sitting position.
example_2: Please sit down.
example_3: He sat down next to me.
collocations: sit down please, sit down and relax
action_sequence: Before: walk to the chair → During: sit down → After: relax
grammar_pattern: sit down + (place)
word_forms: sit down – sat down – sat down – sitting down
common_mistake: Sit down please on chair.
correct_version: Please sit down on the chair.
why_it_s_wrong: Chairs and seats need an article: 'the chair', 'a seat'.
spelling_tip: SIT → SITTING: double T. Past: SAT.

mnemonic: SIT DOWN, STAND UP — opposites.
memory_trick: 'Sit down' needs no extra pronoun — it's already complete.
visual_association: A guest sitting on a sofa.
difference_explained: Sit down = the movement. Sit = be seated (sit still).
related_words: take a seat, be seated, stand up
mini_conversation: A: Please sit down. / B: Thank you.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Sit down and have some water.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Protesters sat down on the road.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Sit down, sit down, I'll make tea!'
mcq_question: Choose: She ___ down on the bench.
mcq_options: A) sit  B) sat  C) seat  D) seated
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Please ___ ___. → sit down
find_and_fix_to_correct: Please seat down. → Please sit down. / Please be seated.
translate: कृपया बैठ जाइए। → Please sit down.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a polite sentence asking a guest to sit.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review

simple_explanation: Move into a standing position.

example_3: Everyone stood up when the teacher came in.
collocations: stand up straight, stand up for, please stand up
action_sequence: Before: sit on a chair → During: rise to your feet → After: stand straight

word_forms: stand up – stood up – stood up – standing up
common_mistake: Everyone stand up for national anthem.
correct_version: Everyone, stand up for the national anthem.
why_it_s_wrong: Anthems, songs and events that everyone knows need 'the'.
etymology: stand (Old English 'standan') + up.
mnemonic: STAND UP = move UP from the chair.
memory_trick: 'Stand up' also means to defend someone (stand up FOR them).
visual_association: A class standing when a teacher enters.
confusing_word: stand up vs stand up for
difference_explained: Stand up = rise. Stand up for = defend someone.
mini_conversation: A: Why is everyone standing? / B: Stand up, it's the national anthem.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'I stand up and stretch every hour.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'The audience stood up to clap.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Stand up, you've been sitting all day!'

fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Everyone ___ ___, please. → stand up
find_and_fix_to_correct: Stand up for your seat. → Stand up from your seat.

write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about when people stand up at an event.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'move into a standing position'?
usage_tip: 'Stand up for yourself' = defend yourself — a very useful phrase.

simple_explanation: Enter a place.

example_3: May I come in?

action_sequence: Before: knock on the door → During: hear 'come in' → After: walk inside
grammar_pattern: come in + (place)
word_forms: come in – came in – come in – coming in

news_style_line: News-style: 'New rules come in from April.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Come in, come in, it's cold outside!'

fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Please ___ ___. → come in
find_and_fix_to_correct: Can I come inside of the room? → Can I come into the room?

write_your_own_sentence: Write what you say when a guest arrives.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'enter a place'?
usage_tip: 'May I come in?' is the polite school and office phrase.

news_style_line: News-style: 'People were told not to go out during the storm.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Let's go out, I'm bored.'

simple_explanation: Of low quality; unpleasant.
example_2: The weather is bad today.
example_3: Smoking is bad for you.
collocations: bad at, bad for, not bad
grammar_pattern: bad + noun / bad at + noun
common_mistake: I am bad in cooking.
correct_version: I am bad at cooking.
why_it_s_wrong: You are bad AT a skill, not 'in'.
etymology: Middle English 'badde'.
mnemonic: BAD → WORSE → WORST.
memory_trick: 'Bad at' + skill, just like 'good at' — same pattern, opposite meaning.
visual_association: A thumbs down.
difference_explained: Bad = adjective (a bad day). Badly = adverb (he played badly).
mini_conversation: A: How was your day? / B: Bad. Everything went wrong.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Junk food is bad for your health.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Bad weather delayed flights.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'My bad, I forgot!' (= my mistake)
mcq_question: Choose: Too much sugar is bad ___ you.
mcq_options: A) to  B) for  C) at  D) with
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: That was a ___ idea. → bad
find_and_fix_to_correct: I feel very badly today. → I feel very bad today.
translate: आज मेरा दिन बुरा था। → I had a bad day.
write_your_own_sentence: Write about a bad habit you want to stop.

reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'of low quality; unpleasant'?
usage_tip: 'Not bad' often means 'quite good'.

simple_explanation: Not old; recently made.
example_2: Is this a new phone?
example_3: We have a new teacher.
collocations: brand new, new to, what's new
grammar_pattern: new + noun
common_mistake: I have new a phone.
correct_version: I have a new phone.
why_it_s_wrong: Adjectives come before the noun, after 'a': 'a new phone'.
pronunciation_tip: 'Nyoo' in British English; 'noo' in American English.
etymology: Old English 'nīwe'.
mnemonic: NEW and KNEW sound the same — new has no K.
memory_trick: In English, the article always comes before the adjective: 'a new phone'.
visual_association: A box being unwrapped.
difference_explained: New = not old. Knew = past of 'know'. Same sound.
mini_conversation: A: Is that a new bag? / B: Yes, a birthday gift!
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'I'm new here — where is the office?'
news_style_line: News-style: 'The new rules start next month.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'What's new?' (= what's happening in your life?)
mcq_options: A) new a  B) a new  C) new  D) newly
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: I bought a ___ phone. → new
find_and_fix_to_correct: She is new comer in our class. → She is a newcomer in our class.
translate: यह नया घर है। → This is a new house.
write_your_own_sentence: Write about something new you learned this week.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'not old; recently made'?
usage_tip: 'Happy New Year' — New and Year both capital.

simple_explanation: Not new; having existed a long time.
example_2: My grandfather is very old.
example_3: I sold my old bike.
collocations: old friend, grow old, how old
grammar_pattern: old + noun / how old...?
word_forms: old – older – oldest (elder, eldest for family)
common_mistake: How many years do you have?
correct_version: How old are you?
why_it_s_wrong: English asks age with 'How old…?' and 'be', not 'have … years'.
etymology: Old English 'ald'.
mnemonic: 'How OLD are you?' — never 'how many years do you have'.
memory_trick: English asks 'how old ARE you', not 'how many years do you have'.
visual_association: A wrinkled hand.
difference_explained: Older = general comparison. Elder = older person in a family (my elder sister).
mini_conversation: A: How old is your sister? / B: She's twelve.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'This is my old school.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'The bridge is over 100 years old.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Hey, old friend!'
mcq_options: A) many years  B) old  C) age  D) much
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: This is an ___ building. → old
find_and_fix_to_correct: My elder brother is more old than me. → My elder brother is older than me.
translate: तुम्हारी उम्र क्या है? → How old are you?
write_your_own_sentence: Write your age and a family member's age.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'not new; having existed a long time'?
usage_tip: 'Elderly' is a polite word for old people.

simple_explanation: Great in length or time.
example_2: She has long hair.
example_3: The meeting was very long.
collocations: long time, long way, all day long
grammar_pattern: long + noun / how long...?
common_mistake: How much time you take?
correct_version: How long does it take?
why_it_s_wrong: For time, English asks 'How long does it take?'
etymology: Old English 'lang'.
mnemonic: LONG → LENGTH (the G stays).
memory_trick: 'How long' asks about duration — a very common English question form.
visual_association: A long road going to the horizon.
difference_explained: Long = length (long hair, a long road). Tall = height of people or buildings.
mini_conversation: A: How long is the flight? / B: About two hours.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'It's a long walk to the station.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'There were long queues at petrol pumps.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Long time no see!'
mcq_question: Choose: How ___ does it take to reach Delhi?
mcq_options: A) much  B) long  C) many  D) time
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: It was a ___ journey. → long
find_and_fix_to_correct: He is a long boy. → He is a tall boy.
translate: यह एक लंबा दिन था। → It was a long day.
write_your_own_sentence: Write how long it takes you to reach work or college.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'great in length or time'?
usage_tip: 'As long as' = only if: 'You can go as long as you're back by nine.'

simple_explanation: Far from the ground; a large amount.
example_2: The price is too high.
example_3: The wall is very high.
collocations: high school, high five, high quality
grammar_pattern: high + noun
common_mistake: The plane flies height.
correct_version: The plane flies high.
why_it_s_wrong: 'High' is also an adverb, so 'flies high' is correct. 'Height' is a noun.
etymology: Old English 'hēah'.
mnemonic: HIGH has a silent GH — it's hiding up high.
memory_trick: 'High' describes position; 'height' (noun) is the measurement itself.
visual_association: An airplane in the sky.
difference_explained: High = far from the ground, or a big number. Tall = people, trees, buildings.
mini_conversation: A: Is the fee high? / B: Yes, very high.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Keep medicines on a high shelf.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Temperatures hit a high of 45°C.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'High five!'
mcq_options: A) tall  B) high  C) height  D) highly
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The plane flies ___. → high
find_and_fix_to_correct: Petrol prices are very costly. → Petrol prices are very high.
translate: कीमत बहुत ज़्यादा है। → The price is very high.
write_your_own_sentence: Write about something with a high price.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'far from the ground; a large amount'?
usage_tip: Prices are 'high' or 'low' — not 'costly' or 'cheap'.

simple_explanation: Close to the ground; a small amount.
example_2: The price is low this week.
example_3: Speak in a low voice.
collocations: low cost, low key, feeling low
grammar_pattern: low + noun
common_mistake: The price is very less.
correct_version: The price is very low.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Less' compares amounts. For prices and levels, use 'low'.
etymology: Old Norse 'lágr'.
mnemonic: LOW is the opposite of HIGH.
memory_trick: 'Low' describes height/level; 'down' describes direction of movement.
visual_association: A short table near the floor.
difference_explained: Low = describes a level (low price). Less = a smaller amount (less money).
mini_conversation: A: Why are you buying so many? / B: The price is very low today.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'My phone battery is low.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Unemployment fell to a five-year low.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'I'm feeling a bit low today.' (= sad)
mcq_question: Choose: The battery is ___. Charge it.
mcq_options: A) less  B) low  C) little  D) lower than
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The shelf is ___. → low
find_and_fix_to_correct: The ceiling is very down. → The ceiling is very low.
translate: कीमत कम है। → The price is low.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something low in your house.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'close to the ground; a small amount'?
usage_tip: 'Feeling low' = feeling sad.

simple_explanation: Correct; also 'right?' at the end of a sentence to check that someone agrees.
example_2: You are right.
example_3: Turn right at the signal.
collocations: that's right, the right answer, turn right, right now
grammar_pattern: be + right / the right + noun / clause + right?
common_mistake: It's cold today, is right?
correct_version: It's cold today, right?
why_it_s_wrong: In a question tag, 'right?' stands alone — no 'is'.
etymology: Old English 'riht'.
mnemonic: RIGHT = correct. Also the side of your right hand.
memory_trick: RIGHT = correct. At the end of a sentence, 'right?' asks 'isn't it?'
visual_association: A green tick mark.
difference_explained: Right = correct or a direction. Write = put words on paper.
mini_conversation: A: The exam is on Monday, right? / B: Right.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Is this the right bus for Andheri?'
news_style_line: News-style: 'The court said the decision was right.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Right, let's start!'
mcq_question: Choose: Your answer is ___. Well done!
mcq_options: A) write  B) right  C) rite  D) rightly
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: It's cold today, ___? → right
find_and_fix_to_correct: You are absolutely correct right. → You are absolutely right.
translate: तुम सही हो। → You are right.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a question ending in 'right?'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'correct; also 'right?' at the end of a sentence to check that someone agrees'?
usage_tip: 'Right now' = immediately.

simple_explanation: Not correct.
example_2: That answer is wrong.
example_3: Something is wrong with my phone.
collocations: wrong number, go wrong, what's wrong
grammar_pattern: wrong + noun / what's wrong
common_mistake: You have wrong.
correct_version: You are wrong.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Wrong' describes the person with 'be': 'You are wrong'.
etymology: Old Norse 'rangr' (crooked).
mnemonic: WRONG has a silent W — the W is in the wrong place!
memory_trick: 'You are wrong' follows the same pattern as 'you are right'.
visual_association: A red cross mark.
difference_explained: Wrong = adjective (the wrong answer). Mistake = noun (I made a mistake).
mini_conversation: A: What's wrong? / B: I lost my keys.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Sorry, wrong number.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Officials admitted they were wrong.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Don't get me wrong, I like him!'
mcq_options: A) wrongly  B) wrong  C) mistake  D) wrongs
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: You have the ___ number. → wrong
find_and_fix_to_correct: I did a wrong. → I made a mistake. / I did something wrong.
translate: तुम गलत हो। → You are wrong.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence using 'What's wrong?'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'not correct'?
usage_tip: 'What's wrong?' is a kind way to ask if someone is okay.

simple_explanation: Moving quickly.
example_2: This train is very fast.
example_3: He drives too fast.
collocations: fast food, fast forward, pretty fast
grammar_pattern: fast + noun (adjective) / run fast (adverb)
common_mistake: He is a fastly runner.
correct_version: He is a fast runner.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Fast' is both adjective and adverb — 'fastly' is not a word.
etymology: Old English 'fæst'.
mnemonic: FAST is FAST — no -ly needed.
memory_trick: 'Fast' has NO '-ly' form — it works as both adjective and adverb already.
visual_association: A cheetah running.
difference_explained: Fast = speed of moving. Quick = short time (a quick call).
mini_conversation: A: Is the internet fast here? / B: Very fast.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Don't eat so fast!'
news_style_line: News-style: 'India is one of the fastest-growing economies.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'That was fast!'
mcq_options: A) fastly  B) fast  C) faster than  D) fasting
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: He is a ___ runner. → fast
find_and_fix_to_correct: She types very fastly. → She types very fast.
translate: वह तेज़ दौड़ता है। → He runs fast.
write_your_own_sentence: Write about something that is fast.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'moving quickly'?
usage_tip: 'Fast' also means not eating: 'I'm fasting today.'

simple_explanation: Moving without speed.
example_2: The internet is slow today.
example_3: Please speak slowly.
collocations: slow down, go slow, slow motion
grammar_pattern: slow + noun
common_mistake: The traffic is slowly.
correct_version: The traffic is slow.
why_it_s_wrong: After 'is', describe the noun with an adjective (slow), not an adverb (slowly).
etymology: Old English 'slāw'.
mnemonic: SLOW = snail. SLOWLY = how the snail moves.
memory_trick: 'Slow' describes a thing; 'slowly' describes how an action happens.
visual_association: A snail on a leaf.
difference_explained: Slow = adjective (a slow car). Slowly = adverb (drive slowly).
mini_conversation: A: Why are you late? / B: The traffic was so slow.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'My laptop is very slow.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Growth was slow this quarter.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Slow down, I can't keep up!'
mcq_options: A) slow  B) slowly  C) slowing  D) slower
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The traffic is ___. → slow
find_and_fix_to_correct: My phone is very slowly. → My phone is very slow.
translate: ट्रैफ़िक धीमा है। → The traffic is slow.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence with 'slow' and one with 'slowly'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'moving without speed'?
usage_tip: 'Slow down' = reduce speed — also 'relax, don't rush'.

simple_explanation: Before the usual time.
example_2: I get up early.
example_3: We had an early lunch.
collocations: early bird, early morning, arrive early
grammar_pattern: early + noun / arrive early
common_mistake: I woke up in early.
correct_version: I woke up early.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Early' is also an adverb, so it needs no 'in': woke up early.

mnemonic: EARLY bird gets the worm.
memory_trick: 'Early' works alone, no preposition needed before it.
visual_association: A sunrise and an alarm clock.
difference_explained: Early = before the usual time. Soon = in a short time from now.
mini_conversation: A: Why are you so early? / B: No traffic today!

news_style_line: News-style: 'Early results show a close contest.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'I'm an early riser.'

mcq_options: A) earlier than  B) early  C) earliest  D) in early

write_your_own_sentence: Write about your morning using 'early'.

reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'before the usual time'?
usage_tip: 'Early morning', 'early 2000s', 'early childhood' — common pairs.

simple_explanation: After the usual time.

example_3: We stayed up late.

grammar_pattern: late + for + noun

usage_tip: 'Better late than never.'

simple_explanation: Not old; early in life.
example_2: He is too young to drive.
example_3: She looks young for her age.
collocations: young at heart, look young, too young
grammar_pattern: young + noun
common_mistake: She has young.
correct_version: She is young.

mnemonic: YOUNG → YOUTH.
memory_trick: 'Be young' — describes a state, so it always uses 'be'.
visual_association: A baby smiling.

usage_tip: 'Younger than', never 'younger to' — Indian English often says 'to'.

simple_explanation: Pleasant; kind.
example_2: What a nice day!
example_3: She's really nice.

grammar_pattern: nice + noun / nice to + verb

difference_explained: Nice = pleasant, kind. Good = quality or skill.

news_style_line: News-style: 'Visitors enjoyed the nice weather.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Nice one!' (= well done)

write_your_own_sentence: Write a compliment using 'nice'.

simple_explanation: Very good.

example_3: We had a great time.

simple_explanation: Not the same.
example_2: We are very different.
example_3: Try a different colour.
collocations: different from, quite different, different types
grammar_pattern: different + from + noun
common_mistake: It is different with mine.
correct_version: It is different from mine.

memory_trick: 'Different from' is the classic, safe choice — 'than' is common but less formal.
visual_association: Two different coloured shoes.

simple_explanation: Perhaps; possibly.

difference_explained: Also = in the middle (I also like it). Too = at the end (I like it too).

memory_trick: Don't confuse 'than' (comparison) with 'then' (time) — different spelling, different job!
visual_association: A scale weighing two things.
difference_explained: Than = comparison (taller than). Then = time (and then).

memory_trick: 'Wow' shows real amazement — a short burst of excitement.
visual_association: Fireworks in the sky.
difference_explained: Wow = strong amazement. Oh = milder surprise.

memory_trick: 'Sorry' can start a full apology, or stand alone as a quick one.

difference_explained: Sorry = after a mistake. Excuse me = before interrupting.

write_your_own_sentence: Write an apology to a friend for missing their call.

reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'a way to apologize'?
usage_tip: 'Sorry?' with a rising tone = please repeat that.

simple_explanation: A polite way to get attention or apologize.
example_1: Excuse me, where is the station?
example_2: Excuse me, is this seat free?
example_3: Excuse me, I need to get past.
collocations: excuse me, sir, excuse me for
grammar_pattern: Excuse me, + question/clause
common_mistake: Excuse, where is the station?
correct_version: Excuse me, where is the station?
why_it_s_wrong: 'Excuse' alone is incomplete — the phrase is always 'Excuse me'.
pronunciation_tip: The S in 'excuse' (verb) sounds like Z: 'ik-SKYOOZ'.
etymology: Latin 'excusare' (free from blame).
mnemonic: EXCUSE ME = please let me…
memory_trick: 'Excuse me' politely gets attention, or apologizes for a small thing.
visual_association: A person raising a hand politely.
difference_explained: Excuse me = before disturbing. Sorry = after a mistake.
mini_conversation: A: Excuse me, where is platform 4? / B: Up the stairs, on the left.

news_style_line: News-style: (not used in formal news)
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Excuse me? What did you just say?' (annoyed)

usage_tip: 'Excuse me?' with a sharp tone means 'What did you say?!' — you're offended.

why_it_s_wrong: Put the person straight after 'show', or use 'to' after the thing — not 'show to me'.

mnemonic: SHOW-room — जहाँ चीज़ें दिखाई जाती हैं।
memory_trick: SHOW = let them SEE.

spelling_tip: B-R-I-N-G. Past: B-R-O-U-G-H-T (with R). BOUGHT (no R) is from 'buy'.

memory_trick: BRING → BROUGHT: the R stays.

casual_conversation: Casual: 'Bring some chips when you come!'

difference_explained: Sit = verb. Seat = noun (a seat), or a formal verb 'be seated'.

common_mistake: I am not able to stand this noise.

memory_trick: STAND → STOOD, like UNDERSTAND → UNDERSTOOD.

difference_explained: Stand = be on your feet. Stay = remain in a place.

memory_trick: SERVE → SERVICE.

simple_explanation: To stop living.

spelling_tip: D-I-E → DYING (IE becomes Y). DYEING = colouring cloth.

mnemonic: DIE rhymes with 'bye' — a final goodbye.

visual_association: A wilted flower.
difference_explained: Die = verb (he died). Dead = adjective (he is dead). Death = noun.

memory_trick: TIE → TYING, like DIE → DYING, LIE → LYING.

news_style_line: News-style: 'The match ended in a 2–2 tie.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Wear a tie — it's a formal party.'

reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to join things with string or rope and make a knot'?

simple_explanation: To close something, like a door, window or your eyes.

example_3: The shop shuts at nine.
collocations: shut the door, shut your eyes, shut down
related_phrasal_verbs: shut down, shut up, shut off
action_sequence: Before: see the open door → During: push it → After: it's closed
grammar_pattern: shut + thing
common_mistake: Shut the light.
correct_version: Switch off the light. / Turn off the light.
why_it_s_wrong: You shut doors, windows and boxes. Lights and fans are switched or turned off.
etymology: Old English 'scyttan'.
mnemonic: SHUTTER — the metal door of a shop that shuts.
memory_trick: SHUT never changes — like CUT and PUT.
visual_association: A shop shutter coming down.
difference_explained: Same meaning. 'Close' is a little softer and more common in polite speech.
mini_conversation: A: It's cold in here. / B: Let me shut the window.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Shut the fridge door properly.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'The factory was shut after the fire.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Shut up, no way!' (= I can't believe it)
mcq_question: Choose: Yesterday he ___ the door loudly.
mcq_options: A) shutted  B) shut  C) shuts  D) shutting
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Please ___ the window, it's raining. → shut
find_and_fix_to_correct: Shut the fan before you go. → Switch off the fan before you go.
translate: दरवाज़ा बंद करो। → Shut the door.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something you shut every night.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to close something, like a door, window or your eyes'?
usage_tip: 'Shut up' is rude; 'Please be quiet' is polite.

simple_explanation: To cut into something with your teeth.
example_2: Don't bite your nails.
example_3: Take a bite of this.
collocations: bite your nails, dog bite, a quick bite
action_sequence: Before: open your mouth → During: bite → After: chew
grammar_pattern: bite + thing/person
common_mistake: A mosquito bited me.
correct_version: A mosquito bit me.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Bite' is irregular: bite – bit – bitten.
etymology: Old English 'bītan'.
mnemonic: Sound-bite — खबर का छोटा सा 'टुकड़ा'।
memory_trick: BITE → BIT → BITTEN.
visual_association: A dog with a bone in its mouth.
difference_explained: Bite = with teeth (dog, mosquito). Sting = with a sharp end (bee, scorpion).
mini_conversation: A: What's that red spot? / B: A mosquito bite.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Take small bites and chew well.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Dog bites rose by 20% this year.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Let's grab a bite.' (= eat something small)
mcq_question: Choose: The dog ___ the postman yesterday.
mcq_options: A) bited  B) bit  C) bitten  D) bites
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: I got ___ by mosquitoes all night. → bitten
find_and_fix_to_correct: He has bit his lip. → He has bitten his lip.
translate: मुझे कुत्ते ने काटा। → A dog bit me.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence using 'bite'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to cut into something with your teeth'?
usage_tip: 'Bite your tongue' = stop yourself from saying something.

simple_explanation: To be on fire, or to hurt or destroy with fire or heat.
example_1: I burned my hand on the pan.
example_2: The candle burned all night.
example_3: Don't burn the rice!
collocations: burn your hand, burn calories, burn down
action_sequence: Before: touch something hot → During: feel pain → After: it turns red
grammar_pattern: burn + thing / burn + down
common_mistake: The milk got burnt fully.
correct_version: The milk burned. / The milk got completely burnt.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Fully' is odd here; use 'completely' or just 'burned'.
spelling_tip: B-U-R-N. Past: BURNED or BURNT (both correct).
etymology: Old English 'byrnan'.
mnemonic: BURN-OL — जलने पर लगाने वाली क्रीम।
memory_trick: Sun + BURN = SUNBURN.
visual_association: A candle flame.
difference_explained: Burn = verb. Fire = noun (the fire).
mini_conversation: A: What's that smell? / B: Oh no, the toast is burning!
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'I burnt my tongue on hot tea.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Fire burned 50 acres of forest.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Walking burns calories, you know.'
mcq_question: Choose: Careful, the stove will ___ your hand.
mcq_options: A) burn  B) burns  C) burnt  D) burning
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The house ___ down in the fire. → burned
find_and_fix_to_correct: My hand got burning. → My hand got burnt.
translate: मेरा हाथ जल गया। → I burned my hand.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about burning food.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to be on fire, or to hurt or destroy with fire or heat'?
usage_tip: 'Burn out' = become very tired from too much work.

simple_explanation: To hit your hands together to show you liked something.
example_2: Clap your hands!
example_3: The audience clapped for five minutes.
collocations: clap your hands, clap loudly, clap along
action_sequence: Before: see a great show → During: clap your hands → After: the performer smiles
grammar_pattern: clap / clap + for + person
common_mistake: Everyone claped for him.
correct_version: Everyone clapped for him.
why_it_s_wrong: Short vowel + one consonant → double it: clapped.
etymology: Old English 'clæppan'.
mnemonic: CLAP = 'क्लैप' — the sound itself!
memory_trick: CLAP → CLAPPED (double P).
visual_association: People clapping in a hall.
difference_explained: Clap = hit your hands together. Applaud = formal: show praise (usually by clapping).
mini_conversation: A: How was your speech? / B: Everyone clapped at the end!
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'The kids clapped for the magician.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Lawmakers clapped as the bill passed.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Give him a clap, guys!'
mcq_question: Choose: The crowd ___ after the song.
mcq_options: A) claped  B) clapped  C) clap  D) claps
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Let's ___ for the winner! → clap
find_and_fix_to_correct: Everyone did clap for her. → Everyone clapped for her.
translate: सबने ताली बजाई। → Everyone clapped.
write_your_own_sentence: Write about a time people clapped for you.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to hit your hands together to show you liked something'?
usage_tip: 'A round of applause' = a clap from everyone.

simple_explanation: To give out or reflect bright light.
example_2: Her eyes shone with joy.
example_3: Polish the shoes till they shine.
collocations: the sun shines, shine bright, shine a torch
action_sequence: Before: the clouds move → During: the sun comes out → After: everything is bright
grammar_pattern: shine / shine + light + on
common_mistake: The sun is shinning.
correct_version: The sun is shining.
why_it_s_wrong: Drop the E before -ing (shining); don't double the N.
etymology: Old English 'scīnan'.
mnemonic: Shoe SHINE — जूते चमकाने वाला।
memory_trick: SHINE → SHINING (one N) — the E leaves, no extra N comes.
visual_association: Sunlight on water.
difference_explained: Shine = bright light. Glow = soft, steady light.
mini_conversation: A: Great weather today! / B: Yes, the sun is shining.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Shine the torch here, I can't see.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Young players shone in the final.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Rise and shine!' (= wake up)
mcq_options: A) shine  B) shines  C) shining  D) shone to
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The sun is ___ brightly today. → shining
find_and_fix_to_correct: The floor is shinning. → The floor is shining.
translate: सूरज चमक रहा है। → The sun is shining.
write_your_own_sentence: Write about something that shines.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to give out or reflect bright light'?
usage_tip: 'Shine' also means do very well: 'She shone in the exam.'

simple_explanation: To make a bell sound; (UK) to phone someone.
example_2: Ring the bell twice.
example_3: I'll ring you later.
collocations: ring the bell, phone rings, ring back
action_sequence: Before: the phone rings → During: pick it up → After: talk
grammar_pattern: ring / ring + person (UK)
common_mistake: The bell has rang.
correct_version: The bell has rung.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Ring' is irregular: ring – rang – rung.
spelling_tip: R-I-N-G. Past: RANG. Past participle: RUNG.
etymology: Old English 'hringan'.
mnemonic: RING-tone — फ़ोन के बजने की आवाज़।
memory_trick: RING → RANG → RUNG, like SING → SANG → SUNG.
visual_association: A school bell.
difference_explained: Ring (UK) = phone someone. Call = more common everywhere.
mini_conversation: A: Is that your phone? / B: Yes, it's been ringing all morning.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Ring the bell, someone will open.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Temple bells rang at midnight.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Give me a ring tomorrow.'
mcq_question: Choose: The phone ___ three times and stopped.
mcq_options: A) ringed  B) rang  C) rung  D) rings
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The school bell ___ at 8 a.m. → rings
find_and_fix_to_correct: The bell was rang. → The bell was rung. / The bell rang.
translate: घंटी बज रही है। → The bell is ringing.
write_your_own_sentence: Write about a sound that rings every day near you.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to make a bell sound; (UK) to phone someone'?
usage_tip: 'That rings a bell' = it sounds familiar.

simple_explanation: To pull paper or cloth apart so it breaks into pieces.

example_3: My jeans are torn.
collocations: tear paper, tear apart, tear up
related_phrasal_verbs: tear up, tear down, tear off
action_sequence: Before: hold the paper → During: pull hard → After: it rips
grammar_pattern: tear + thing (+ up/in half)
common_mistake: I teared the paper.
correct_version: I tore the paper.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Tear' is irregular: tear – tore – torn.
spelling_tip: T-E-A-R. Past: TORE. Past participle: TORN.
etymology: Old English 'teran'.
mnemonic: TEAR (फाड़ना) rhymes with BEAR; TEAR (आँसू) rhymes with EAR.
memory_trick: TEAR → TORE → TORN, like WEAR → WORE → WORN.
visual_association: A page ripped in two.
difference_explained: Tear 'tair' = rip. Tear 'teer' = a drop from the eye. Same spelling!
mini_conversation: A: What happened to your shirt? / B: It tore on a nail.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Tear along the dotted line.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'The old bridge will be torn down.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Ugh, my bag is torn!'
mcq_options: A) teared  B) tore  C) torn  D) tears
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Don't ___ the pages of the book. → tear
find_and_fix_to_correct: My shirt got teared. → My shirt got torn.
translate: उसने कागज़ फाड़ दिया। → He tore the paper.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence using 'torn'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to pull paper or cloth apart so it breaks into pieces'?
usage_tip: 'Wear and tear' = normal damage from use.

simple_explanation: To check if something works, or check what someone knows.
example_1: Test the mic before the show.
example_2: The teacher tested us on verbs.
example_3: I tested positive.
collocations: test a product, test someone on, test drive
action_sequence: Before: prepare it → During: try it out → After: see the result
grammar_pattern: test + thing / test + person + on
common_mistake: I gave my test yesterday.
correct_version: I took my test yesterday. / I wrote my test yesterday.
why_it_s_wrong: You take (or write) a test; the teacher gives or sets it.
pronunciation_tip: Short 'e': 'test'. The -ed is a full syllable: 'TES-tid'.
etymology: Latin 'testum' (a pot for checking metals).
mnemonic: TEST match — क्रिकेट का सबसे लंबा 'परीक्षण'।
memory_trick: TEST = TRY + see the result.
visual_association: A student writing an exam.
difference_explained: Test = short check. Exam = big, formal test.
mini_conversation: A: Did you test the app? / B: Yes, it works fine.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Test the water before bathing the baby.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'The new vaccine was tested on 10,000 people.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Don't test my patience!'
mcq_question: Choose: They ___ the car before selling it.
mcq_options: A) tested  B) testing  C) tests  D) test
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Always ___ the brakes before a long drive. → test
find_and_fix_to_correct: We will give our exam tomorrow. → We will take our exam tomorrow.
translate: माइक को जाँच लो। → Test the mic.
write_your_own_sentence: Write about a test you took recently.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to check if something works, or check what someone knows'?
usage_tip: 'Test drive' = drive a car before buying it.

simple_explanation: To take money or things from a person or place by force or crime.
example_2: He was robbed on the train.
example_3: Someone robbed the shop at night.
collocations: rob a bank, rob someone of, get robbed
action_sequence: Before: plan the crime → During: take the money → After: run away
grammar_pattern: rob + person/place (of + thing)
common_mistake: Someone robbed my phone.
correct_version: Someone stole my phone. / Someone robbed me.
why_it_s_wrong: You rob a PERSON or PLACE. You steal a THING.
spelling_tip: R-O-B → ROBBED: double B. Noun: ROBBERY.
etymology: Old French 'rober'.
mnemonic: ROBBER-y = डकैती।
memory_trick: ROB a person, STEAL a thing.
visual_association: A thief running with a bag.
difference_explained: Rob + person/place (rob a bank). Steal + thing (steal money).
mini_conversation: A: Why is there a police van outside? / B: The jewellery shop got robbed.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Keep your bag close, people get robbed here.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Two men robbed a petrol pump last night.'
casual_conversation: Casual: '₹500 for a coffee? That's robbery!'
mcq_question: Choose: Thieves ___ the bank last week.
mcq_options: A) stole  B) robbed  C) robbing  D) robs
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Someone ___ my wallet on the bus. → stole
find_and_fix_to_correct: They robbed my bag. → They stole my bag. / They robbed me.
translate: उसे ट्रेन में लूट लिया गया। → He was robbed on the train.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence using 'rob' and one using 'steal'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to take money or things from a person or place by force or crime'?
usage_tip: 'Daylight robbery' = a price that is far too high.

simple_explanation: To look good together, or to be the same as something.

example_3: Match the words with the pictures.

action_sequence: Before: choose two things → During: put them side by side → After: they fit together
grammar_pattern: match + thing / match + with
common_mistake: Your shirt is matching with your pant.
correct_version: Your shirt matches your trousers.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Match' is a state here: simple present, and no 'with' after it.

memory_trick: MATCH ends in TCH, like CATCH and WATCH.
visual_association: Two matching socks.
difference_explained: Match = two things go together. Suit = something looks good on a person.
mini_conversation: A: Does this tie match my shirt? / B: Yes, perfectly.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Match the column A with column B.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'DNA samples matched the suspect.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'We're wearing matching T-shirts!'
mcq_options: A) match  B) matches with  C) matching  D) matched with
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Her earrings ___ her dress. → match
find_and_fix_to_correct: These colours are not matching. → These colours don't match.

write_your_own_sentence: Write about two things in your home that match.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to look good together, or to be the same as something'?
usage_tip: 'A perfect match' = two people or things that go very well together.

news_style_line: News-style: 'The event marked 75 years of independence.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'On your mark, get set, go!'

fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The teacher ___ our tests over the weekend. → marked
find_and_fix_to_correct: I got good marks in maths subject. → I got good marks in maths.

write_your_own_sentence: Write about the best marks you ever got.

reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to put a sign on something, or to check and score written work'?
usage_tip: 'Mark' also means celebrate an event: 'to mark the anniversary'.

reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'used in 'be born' — to come into the world as a baby'?

casual_conversation: Casual: 'My feet are killing me!' (= they hurt a lot)

find_and_fix_to_correct: He was died in a crash. → He was killed in a crash. / He died in a crash.

write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence using 'kill time'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to make someone or something die'?

common_mistake: I sliped on the stairs.
correct_version: I slipped on the stairs.
why_it_s_wrong: Short vowel + one consonant → double it: slipped.

news_style_line: News-style: 'Several bikers slipped on the oily road.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Sorry, it slipped my mind.' (= I forgot)

write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence using 'copy and paste'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to make something the same as another thing, or cheat by using someone else's work'?
usage_tip: 'Copy' as a noun = one item of a book or file: 'two copies of the form'.

correct_version: Mix the flour well.

memory_trick: MIX → MIXTURE.

difference_explained: Mix = combine. Mix up = confuse two things.

write_your_own_sentence: Write a recipe step using 'mix'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to put things together so they become one'?
usage_tip: 'Mixed feelings' = happy and sad at the same time.

simple_explanation: To write your name on a document to show you agree or it's yours.

example_3: They signed the contract.

why_it_s_wrong: 'Sign' is the verb. The written name is a 'signature'.
