mnemonic: Sign-BOARD — सड़क पर दिशा बताने वाला बोर्ड।
memory_trick: SIGN has a silent G — but SIGNATURE says it.
visual_association: A pen signing a paper.
difference_explained: Sign = verb (sign here). Signature = noun (your signature).
mini_conversation: A: Is the form complete? / B: Just sign at the bottom.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Sign the register when you enter.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'The two countries signed a trade deal.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Can you sign my T-shirt?'
mcq_question: Choose: Please ___ on the dotted line.

write_your_own_sentence: Write about a document you have signed.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to write your name on a document to show you agree or it's yours'?
usage_tip: 'Sign up' = register for something: 'sign up for a class'.

simple_explanation: To look good on someone, or to be convenient for someone.

grammar_pattern: suit + person
common_mistake: This dress is suiting on you.

why_it_s_wrong: 'Suit' is a state verb: no -ing, and no 'on'.

mnemonic: SUIT-case — जिसमें कपड़े रखते हैं।
memory_trick: SUIT + ABLE = SUITABLE.

difference_explained: Suit = looks good on you. Fit = the right size.
mini_conversation: A: Does this kurta suit me? / B: Yes, the colour is perfect on you.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Choose a time that suits everyone.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'The new rules suit small businesses.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Suit yourself!' (= do what you like)

spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to look good on someone, or to be convenient for someone'?
usage_tip: 'Suit yourself' can sound a little annoyed.

memory_trick: IT + RAIN — always 'it'.
visual_association: Rain on a window.

simple_explanation: To make a very loud, high sound because of fear, pain or excitement.

grammar_pattern: scream / scream + at/for
common_mistake: He screamed on me.
correct_version: He screamed at me.
why_it_s_wrong: You scream AT a person, not 'on'.
etymology: Middle English 'scremen'.
word_family: scream, screaming, ice cream (sounds like 'I scream'!)
mnemonic: I SCREAM, you SCREAM, we all scream for ICE CREAM!
memory_trick: SCREAM = SC + REAM, the 'ee' is loud and long.
visual_association: A person screaming on a roller coaster.
difference_explained: Scream = high sound, from fear or excitement. Shout = loud words.
mini_conversation: A: Why did you scream? / B: A lizard fell on my arm!
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'The kids screamed on the water slide.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Neighbours heard screams and called police.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'I screamed when I saw my results!'

fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Don't ___ at your little brother. → scream
find_and_fix_to_correct: She was screaming on the children. → She was screaming at the children.

write_your_own_sentence: Write about a time you screamed.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to make a very loud, high sound because of fear, pain or excitement'?

grammar_pattern: dig + hole/ground
common_mistake: They digged a hole.

spelling_tip: D-I-G → DIGGING: double G. Past: DUG.

common_mistake: They attacked on the village.

why_it_s_wrong: As a verb, 'attack' takes the object directly. 'Attack on' is only for the noun ('an attack on the village').

mnemonic: Heart ATTACK — दिल का दौरा, अचानक हमला।

difference_explained: Verb: attack the city. Noun: an attack on the city.

news_style_line: News-style: 'Hackers attacked the bank's website.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'I had a panic attack before the exam.'

fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The virus ___ the body's cells. → attacks

collocations: come from a family, come from a village, where it comes from
action_sequence: Before: be born in a place → During: grow up there → After: say where you're from
grammar_pattern: come from + place
word_forms: come from – came from – come from – coming from
common_mistake: I am coming from Kerala. (meaning your home state)
correct_version: I come from Kerala. / I am from Kerala.
why_it_s_wrong: For where you were born or grew up, use simple present: 'I come from'.
etymology: come + from.
mnemonic: 'Kahan se ho?' = 'Where do you come from?'
memory_trick: COME FROM = home place — simple present, always.
visual_association: A map with a pin on a hometown.
difference_explained: Same meaning: 'I come from Goa' = 'I am from Goa'.
mini_conversation: A: Where do you come from? / B: I come from Assam.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Where does this mango come from?'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Most of the players come from small towns.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Where's that noise coming from?'
mcq_options: A) is coming  B) comes  C) come  D) coming
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Most of our tea ___ from Assam. → comes
find_and_fix_to_correct: I am belonging to Rajasthan. → I come from Rajasthan. / I am from Rajasthan.
translate: मैं उत्तर प्रदेश से हूँ। → I come from Uttar Pradesh.
write_your_own_sentence: Write where you come from.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to be born in or live in a place; to start somewhere'?
usage_tip: 'I belong to Delhi' is Indian English — abroad, say 'I'm from Delhi'.

simple_explanation: To leave a place or person quickly and secretly, or to escape.
example_2: Don't run away from your problems.
example_3: The dog ran away from home.
collocations: run away from, run away with, run away home
action_sequence: Before: feel scared → During: run fast → After: hide somewhere
grammar_pattern: run away (+ from + person/place)
word_forms: run away – ran away – run away – running away
common_mistake: The thief runned away.
correct_version: The thief ran away.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Run' is irregular: run – ran – run.
spelling_tip: Two words as a verb. The adjective is RUNAWAY (one word): 'a runaway train'.
etymology: run + away.
mnemonic: 'Bhaag gaya' = ran away.
memory_trick: RUN → RAN → RUN.
visual_association: A cat running out of a door.
difference_explained: Run away = leave quickly. Escape = get free from danger or a closed place.
mini_conversation: A: Where's your cat? / B: She ran away last week.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'The children ran away when the dog barked.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'The accused ran away from police custody.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'I wanted to run away from that boring meeting!'
mcq_question: Choose: The boy ___ when he saw the teacher.
mcq_options: A) runned away  B) ran away  C) run away  D) running away
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: You can't ___ ___ from your fears. → run away
find_and_fix_to_correct: He runaway from home. → He ran away from home.
translate: चोर भाग गया। → The thief ran away.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence using 'run away from'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to leave a place or person quickly and secretly, or to escape'?
usage_tip: 'Running away' from a problem = avoiding it.

simple_explanation: To be one of the people doing an activity or event.
example_1: I took part in the race.
example_2: Everyone should take part in class.
example_3: Ten schools took part.
collocations: take part in a competition, take part in a debate
action_sequence: Before: register → During: join the event → After: finish it
grammar_pattern: take part + in + event
word_forms: take part – took part – taken part – taking part
common_mistake: I participated in the competition and took part on it.
correct_version: I took part in the competition.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Take part' takes 'in', not 'on' or 'at'.
spelling_tip: Three words in use: TAKE PART IN.
etymology: take + part.
mnemonic: 'Hissa lena' = take part.
memory_trick: TAKE PART IN — the 'in' is always there.
visual_association: Children running in a school race.
difference_explained: Same meaning. 'Participate' is more formal.
mini_conversation: A: Are you taking part in the quiz? / B: Yes, with Riya as my partner.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'All students must take part in sports day.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Over 5,000 runners took part in the marathon.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'I'm not taking part, just watching!'
mcq_question: Choose: She took part ___ the dance competition.
mcq_options: A) on  B) in  C) at  D) for
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Twenty teams will ___ ___ in the tournament. → take part
find_and_fix_to_correct: I took part at the debate. → I took part in the debate.
translate: मैंने दौड़ में भाग लिया। → I took part in the race.
write_your_own_sentence: Write about an event you took part in.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to be one of the people doing an activity or event'?
usage_tip: On a CV, 'participated in' sounds formal; in speech, 'took part in' is natural.

simple_explanation: To happen, especially as planned.
example_1: The wedding will take place in May.
example_2: Where did the accident take place?
example_3: The meeting takes place every Monday.
collocations: take place in, take place on, take place at
action_sequence: Before: plan the event → During: the day comes → After: it happens
grammar_pattern: event + take place + time/place
word_forms: take place – took place – taken place – taking place
common_mistake: The meeting will be taken place tomorrow.
correct_version: The meeting will take place tomorrow.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Take place' has no passive — the event itself 'takes place'.
etymology: take + place.
mnemonic: 'Aayojit hona' = take place (formal).
memory_trick: TAKE PLACE is never passive.
visual_association: A calendar with an event marked.
difference_explained: Take place = planned events (formal). Happen = anything, often unplanned.
mini_conversation: A: When does the exam take place? / B: On the 15th.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'The class takes place in Room 4.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'The summit will take place in Delhi next week.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Where's the party taking place?'
mcq_question: Choose: The match ___ at the city stadium.
mcq_options: A) took place  B) was taken place  C) taken place  D) take placed
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The final will ___ ___ on Sunday. → take place
find_and_fix_to_correct: The function was took place yesterday. → The function took place yesterday.
translate: शादी मई में होगी। → The wedding will take place in May.
write_your_own_sentence: Write about an event that took place in your town.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to happen, especially as planned'?
usage_tip: Formal notices often say 'The meeting will be held…' — that's also correct.

simple_explanation: To check or do something so that you are certain it happens.
example_1: Make sure the door is locked.
example_2: Make sure you eat something.
example_3: I made sure everyone got home.
collocations: make sure that, make sure of, just to make sure
action_sequence: Before: worry something is wrong → During: check it → After: feel sure
grammar_pattern: make sure (that) + clause / make sure of + noun
word_forms: make sure – made sure – made sure – making sure
common_mistake: Make sure to lock the door properly surely.
correct_version: Make sure you lock the door.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Make sure' already means 'be certain' — don't add 'surely'.
etymology: make + sure.
mnemonic: 'Pakka kar lena' = make sure.
memory_trick: MAKE SURE = MAKE it SURE.
visual_association: A hand checking a lock.
difference_explained: Same meaning; 'ensure' is more formal.
mini_conversation: A: Did you make sure the gas is off? / B: Yes, I checked twice.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Make sure you carry your ID.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Police will make sure the roads stay open.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Just making sure you're okay!'
mcq_options: A) Make sure  B) Make surely  C) Sure make  D) Making sure to
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Please ___ ___ the windows are closed. → make sure
find_and_fix_to_correct: Make sure that you will come. → Make sure that you come.
translate: पक्का कर लो कि दरवाज़ा बंद है। → Make sure the door is closed.
write_your_own_sentence: Write two things you always make sure of before leaving home.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to check or do something so that you are certain it happens'?
usage_tip: After 'make sure', use the present tense for the future: 'Make sure you come', not 'will come'.

simple_explanation: To become husband and wife.
example_2: When are you getting married?
example_3: She got married to a doctor.
collocations: get married to someone, get married in
action_sequence: Before: get engaged → During: have the wedding → After: start married life
grammar_pattern: get married (to + person)
word_forms: get married – got married – got married – getting married
common_mistake: She got married with him.
correct_version: She got married to him. / She married him.
why_it_s_wrong: You get married TO someone, not 'with'.
etymology: get + married (Latin 'maritare').
mnemonic: 'Shaadi ho gayi' = got married.
memory_trick: Married TO — like 'engaged TO'.
visual_association: A wedding mandap.
difference_explained: Marry + person directly (She married him). Get married + to (She got married to him).
mini_conversation: A: Did you hear? Priya is getting married! / B: Wow, when?
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'My cousin is getting married in December.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'The actor got married in a private ceremony.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Stop asking me when I'm getting married!'
mcq_question: Choose: My sister got married ___ an engineer.
mcq_options: A) with  B) to  C) by  D) for
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: They ___ ___ in 2019. → got married
find_and_fix_to_correct: He married with a teacher. → He married a teacher. / He got married to a teacher.
translate: उनकी पिछले साल शादी हुई। → They got married last year.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a wedding you attended.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to become husband and wife'?
usage_tip: 'Married' also works as an adjective: 'Are you married?'

simple_explanation: To have something in your mind; to consider it.
example_2: Think about it and tell me.
example_3: What are you thinking about?
collocations: think about the future, think about it, think about doing
action_sequence: Before: get an offer → During: think about it → After: decide
grammar_pattern: think about + noun/-ing
word_forms: think about – thought about – thought about – thinking about
common_mistake: I am thinking to buy a car.
correct_version: I am thinking about buying a car. / I am thinking of buying a car.
why_it_s_wrong: After 'think about/of', use -ing — not 'to' + verb.
etymology: think + about.
mnemonic: 'Soch raha hoon' = I'm thinking about it.
memory_trick: THINK ABOUT + -ING.
visual_association: A person looking at the sky, thinking.
difference_explained: Think about = consider in detail. Think of = have an idea, or remember.
mini_conversation: A: Will you take the job? / B: I'm still thinking about it.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Think about your answer before you speak.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'The government is thinking about new tax rules.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Don't even think about it!'
mcq_question: Choose: I'm thinking about ___ a new course.
mcq_options: A) join  B) to join  C) joining  D) joined
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: What are you ___ ___? You look worried. → thinking about
find_and_fix_to_correct: I am thinking to change my job. → I am thinking about changing my job.
translate: मैं तुम्हारे बारे में सोच रहा था। → I was thinking about you.
write_your_own_sentence: Write about something you are thinking about doing.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to have something in your mind; to consider it'?
usage_tip: 'Think about it' = take your time to decide.

simple_explanation: A polite greeting used before 12 noon.
example_2: Good morning, sir.
example_3: She said good morning with a smile.
collocations: say good morning, good morning everyone
grammar_pattern: Good morning (+ name/sir/madam)
common_mistake: Good morning! Very good morning to you.
correct_version: Good morning! / A very good morning to you.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'A very good morning to you' as a whole phrase, or just 'Good morning'.
etymology: good + morning.
mnemonic: 'Suprabhaat' = good morning.
memory_trick: Good MORNING — only before noon.
visual_association: A sun rising with a cup of tea.
difference_explained: Good morning = hello (before noon). Good night = goodbye before sleep.
mini_conversation: A: Good morning, Ma'am! / B: Good morning, class. Sit down.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Good morning! Did you sleep well?'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Good morning, here are today's top stories.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Morning!' (short form)
mcq_question: Choose: It's 9 a.m. What do you say?
mcq_options: A) Good night  B) Good morning  C) Good evening  D) Goodbye
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Say ___ ___ to your teacher. → good morning
find_and_fix_to_correct: Good night, sir! (arriving at 7 p.m.) → Good evening, sir!
translate: सुप्रभात, सब लोग! → Good morning, everyone!
write_your_own_sentence: Write how you greet people at school or work in the morning.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'a polite greeting used before 12 noon'?
usage_tip: After 12 noon say 'Good afternoon'; after about 5 p.m. say 'Good evening'.

simple_explanation: Said when leaving at night or going to bed.
example_2: She said good night and left.
example_3: Good night, see you tomorrow.
collocations: say good night, good night and sweet dreams
grammar_pattern: Good night (+ name)
common_mistake: Good night! (arriving at a party at 9 p.m.)
correct_version: Good evening!
why_it_s_wrong: 'Good night' is only for leaving or sleeping — to greet someone at night, say 'Good evening'.
etymology: good + night.
word_family: goodnight (one word also used), good evening
mnemonic: 'Shubh ratri' = good night.
memory_trick: NIGHT = bye. EVENING = hello.
visual_association: A moon and a pillow.
difference_explained: Good night = goodbye at night. Good evening = hello in the evening.
mini_conversation: A: I'm going to sleep. / B: Okay, good night!
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Good night, Mummy!'
news_style_line: News-style: 'That's all for tonight, good night.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Night night!' (to children)
mcq_question: Choose: You arrive at a dinner at 8 p.m. You say:
mcq_options: A) Good night  B) Good evening  C) Good morning  D) Goodbye
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Before bed, say ___ ___ to your parents. → good night
find_and_fix_to_correct: Good night, how are you? (meeting someone) → Good evening, how are you?
translate: शुभ रात्रि, अच्छे से सोना। → Good night, sleep well.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a good-night message to a friend.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'said when leaving at night or going to bed'?
usage_tip: 'Sweet dreams' often follows 'Good night'.

simple_explanation: A friendly way to say goodbye.
example_2: See you later.
example_3: See you soon, take care.
collocations: see you later, see you soon, see you tomorrow
grammar_pattern: See you + time
common_mistake: See you at tomorrow.
correct_version: See you tomorrow.
why_it_s_wrong: Time words like tomorrow, soon and later take no preposition.
etymology: see + you.
mnemonic: 'Phir milte hain' = see you.
memory_trick: SEE YOU + time, no 'at'.
visual_association: Friends waving goodbye.
difference_explained: See you = casual, you'll meet again. Goodbye = more formal or final.
mini_conversation: A: I have to go now. / B: Okay, see you tomorrow!
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'See you at lunch!'
news_style_line: News-style: (not used in formal news)
casual_conversation: Casual: 'See ya!'
mcq_options: A) see you tomorrow  B) see you at tomorrow  C) seeing you  D) see tomorrow
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Bye! ___ ___ next week! → See you
find_and_fix_to_correct: See you on tomorrow. → See you tomorrow.
translate: कल मिलते हैं! → See you tomorrow!
write_your_own_sentence: Write how you say bye to a friend after class.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'a friendly way to say goodbye'?
usage_tip: 'See you around' = maybe we'll meet again, no fixed plan.

simple_explanation: A kind way to say goodbye, or to tell someone to be careful.
example_2: Take care of yourself.
example_3: Take care on the road.
collocations: take care of, take care of yourself, take good care
grammar_pattern: Take care (+ of + person/thing)
word_forms: take care – took care – taken care – taking care
common_mistake: Take care of your health properly nicely.
correct_version: Take good care of your health.
why_it_s_wrong: Use one describing word: 'take good care'.
etymology: take + care.
mnemonic: 'Apna khayal rakhna' = take care.
memory_trick: TAKE CARE = keep yourself safe.
visual_association: A mother waving from a doorway.
confusing_word: take care vs take care of
difference_explained: Take care = goodbye, be careful. Take care of = look after someone or something.
mini_conversation: A: I'm leaving for the airport now. / B: Take care, message me when you land!
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Take care of your little sister.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Doctors urged people to take care in the heat.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Take care, yaar!'
mcq_question: Choose: Please take care ___ my plants while I'm away.
mcq_options: A) for  B) of  C) about  D) with
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Bye, ___ ___! → take care
find_and_fix_to_correct: Take care about your health. → Take care of your health.
translate: अपना ख्याल रखना। → Take care of yourself.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a goodbye message to someone who is travelling.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'a kind way to say goodbye, or to tell someone to be careful'?
usage_tip: 'I'll take care of it' = I'll handle it, don't worry.

simple_explanation: A friendly way to say 'it's okay' or to reply to 'thank you' or 'sorry'.
example_2: 'Sorry I'm late.' 'No problem.'
example_3: Can you help me? — No problem!
collocations: no problem at all, not a problem
grammar_pattern: No problem (+ at all)
common_mistake: No problem, it's my duty only.
correct_version: No problem, happy to help.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Only' at the end is Indian English; say 'happy to help'.
etymology: no + problem.
mnemonic: 'Koi baat nahi' = no problem.
memory_trick: NO PROBLEM = all okay.
visual_association: A thumbs-up.
synonyms: no worries, it's fine, you're welcome
difference_explained: Both reply to 'thank you'. 'You're welcome' is a bit more polite.
mini_conversation: A: Thanks for the notes! / B: No problem.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'No problem, I'll drop you home.'
news_style_line: News-style: (not used in formal news)
casual_conversation: Casual: 'No problem, bro!'
mcq_options: A) No problem  B) No thanks  C) Sorry  D) Not at all problem
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: 'Sorry I'm late.' — '___ ___, we just started.' → No problem
find_and_fix_to_correct: Not problem, I will do. → No problem, I'll do it.
translate: कोई बात नहीं। → No problem.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a reply to a friend who says sorry.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'a friendly way to say 'it's okay' or to reply to 'thank you' or 'sorry''?
usage_tip: In formal emails, 'You're welcome' or 'Happy to help' sounds better than 'No problem'.

hindi_meaning: आपका स्वागत है / कोई बात नहीं
simple_explanation: The polite reply when someone thanks you.
example_2: You're welcome to stay for dinner.
example_3: You're always welcome here.
collocations: you're welcome, you're welcome to + verb
grammar_pattern: You're welcome (+ to + verb)
common_mistake: Welcome! (as a reply to 'thank you')
correct_version: You're welcome.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Welcome' alone means 'come in'. As a reply to 'thank you', say 'You're welcome'.
etymology: you are + welcome.
mnemonic: 'Aapka swagat hai' — but after 'thank you' it means 'koi baat nahi'.
memory_trick: YOU'RE = YOU ARE welcome.
visual_association: A smiling host at a door.
synonyms: no problem, my pleasure, not at all
difference_explained: You're (you are) welcome = correct. 'Your welcome' = spelling mistake.
related_words: my pleasure, no problem, not at all
mini_conversation: A: Thank you so much for your help. / B: You're welcome.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'You're welcome to join us.'
news_style_line: News-style: (not used in formal news)
casual_conversation: Casual: 'You're welcome, anytime!'
mcq_options: A) Your welcome  B) You're welcome  C) Welcome to you  D) Thank you
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: 'Thank you, sir.' — 'You're ___.' → welcome
find_and_fix_to_correct: Your welcome! → You're welcome!
translate: 'धन्यवाद!' 'आपका स्वागत है।' → 'Thank you!' 'You're welcome.'
write_your_own_sentence: Write a short dialogue with 'thank you' and 'you're welcome'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'the polite reply when someone thanks you'?
usage_tip: 'My pleasure' is a warmer, more formal reply.

simple_explanation: The short form of 'cannot' — shows something is not possible or not allowed.
example_2: You can't park here.
example_3: I can't find my keys.
collocations: can't wait, can't stand, can't help
where_it_s_used: Every negative about ability or permission
grammar_pattern: can't + base verb
common_mistake: I can't to come today.
correct_version: I can't come today.
why_it_s_wrong: After 'can't', use the base verb without 'to'.
etymology: can + not.
mnemonic: 'Nahi kar sakta' = can't.
memory_trick: CANNOT is one word; CAN'T drops the 'no'.
visual_association: A 'No Parking' sign.
difference_explained: Same meaning. 'Can't' in speech; 'cannot' in formal writing.
mini_conversation: A: Can you come to the party? / B: Sorry, I can't — I have an exam.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'I can't hear you, speak louder.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Officials said the bridge can't take heavy trucks.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'I can't even!' (= I'm too shocked)
mcq_question: Choose: I can't ___ this box. It's too heavy.
mcq_options: A) to lift  B) lift  C) lifting  D) lifted
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Sorry, I ___ help you right now. → can't
find_and_fix_to_correct: He can't able to walk. → He can't walk. / He isn't able to walk.
translate: मैं तैर नहीं सकता। → I can't swim.
write_your_own_sentence: Write three things you can't do yet.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'the short form of 'cannot' — shows something is not possible or not allowed'?
usage_tip: 'Can't be' shows you're sure it's not true: 'That can't be right!'

simple_explanation: Most important or biggest.
example_2: What's the main idea of the story?
example_3: Rice is our main food.
collocations: main reason, main road, main course
grammar_pattern: the/my + main + noun
common_mistake: This is the most main reason.
correct_version: This is the main reason.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Main' already means 'most important', so it has no 'more' or 'most'.
etymology: Old English 'mægen' (strength).
mnemonic: 'Main road' = मुख्य सड़क।
memory_trick: MAIN = No. 1 — nothing is 'more main'.
visual_association: A big road with small lanes branching off.
difference_explained: Main = adjective (main reason). Mainly = adverb (mainly because).
mini_conversation: A: Where's the shop? / B: On the main road, near the bank.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'The main door is locked at ten.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Traffic was the main problem during the festival.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'That's the main thing — you're safe!'
mcq_question: Choose: Health is the ___ reason I walk daily.
mcq_options: A) mainly  B) main  C) most main  D) mains
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: What is the ___ point of the lesson? → main
find_and_fix_to_correct: The very main problem is money. → The main problem is money.
translate: मुख्य समस्या पैसा है। → The main problem is money.
write_your_own_sentence: Write about the main reason you are learning English.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'most important or biggest'?
usage_tip: 'Main course' = the biggest dish of a meal.

simple_explanation: Loved; also used to start a letter.
example_2: She is a dear friend.
example_3: Oh dear, I forgot!
collocations: dear friend, Dear Sir, oh dear
grammar_pattern: Dear + name (letters) / a dear + noun
common_mistake: Dear Sir, I want to say you that…
correct_version: Dear Sir, I would like to tell you that…
why_it_s_wrong: 'Say' doesn't take a person — use 'tell you'.
etymology: Old English 'dēore' (precious).
mnemonic: 'Dear' = प्रिय — letter की शुरुआत में।
memory_trick: DEAR has EAR — you listen to people dear to you.
visual_association: An envelope that starts 'Dear…'.
difference_explained: Dear = loved. Deer = an animal. Same sound.
mini_conversation: A: How do I start a formal email? / B: 'Dear Mr Sharma,' is fine.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'She's a very dear friend of mine.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Onions are dearer this month.' (UK = more expensive)
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Oh dear, look at the time!'
mcq_question: Choose: How do you start a formal letter?
mcq_options: A) Hi Sir  B) Dear Sir  C) Respected Sir, hi  D) Hey Sir
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: ___ Madam, I am writing to apply for the job. → Dear
find_and_fix_to_correct: Dear friend, how are you? I am fine here and hope same there. → Dear friend, how are you? I hope you are well.
translate: प्रिय मित्र, → Dear friend,
write_your_own_sentence: Write the first line of an email to your teacher.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'loved; also used to start a letter'?
usage_tip: 'Oh dear' = a mild 'oh no'.

simple_explanation: Treating people equally and honestly; reasonable.
example_2: The teacher is fair to everyone.
example_3: We need a fair price.
collocations: fair price, fair game, fair chance
grammar_pattern: be + fair + to + person
common_mistake: This is not fare!
correct_version: This is not fair!
why_it_s_wrong: 'Fare' is a ticket price. The word for 'just and equal' is 'fair'.
pronunciation_tip: 'Fair', rhymes with 'hair'. Same sound as 'fare' (ticket price).
etymology: Old English 'fæger' (beautiful).
mnemonic: Fair play — खेल में ईमानदारी।
memory_trick: FAIR is for everyone; FARE is for the bus.
visual_association: Scales that are balanced.
difference_explained: Fair = honest/equal. Fare = ticket price. Same sound.
mini_conversation: A: He got two sweets and I got one! / B: That's not fair.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Take turns, be fair.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Voters demand a free and fair election.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Fair enough!' (= okay, I accept that)
mcq_question: Choose: The judge was ___ to both sides.
mcq_options: A) fare  B) fair  C) fairy  D) fairly to
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: It's not ___ to blame him for everything. → fair
find_and_fix_to_correct: The bus fair is ₹20. → The bus fare is ₹20.
translate: यह ठीक नहीं है! → That's not fair!
write_your_own_sentence: Write about a time something was not fair.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'treating people equally and honestly; reasonable'?
usage_tip: Using 'fair' to mean light skin can hurt people — use 'light-skinned' only if needed.

simple_explanation: Last; coming at the end.
example_2: The final match is on Sunday.
example_3: Final exams start in March.
collocations: final exam, final decision, final match
grammar_pattern: the + final + noun
common_mistake: This is the last and final warning.
correct_version: This is the final warning.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Last' and 'final' mean the same; using both is repetition.
etymology: Latin 'finalis' (of the end).
mnemonic: FINAL = FINISH — both start with FIN.
memory_trick: FINALLY = FINAL + LY (double L).
visual_association: A trophy at the end of a tournament.
difference_explained: Final = adjective (final answer). Finally = adverb (at last).
mini_conversation: A: Is this your final decision? / B: Yes, I've thought it through.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'The final bus leaves at eleven.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'India reached the final after a thrilling win.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Final answer: pizza!'
mcq_options: A) finally  B) final  C) finale  D) finish
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The ___ exam is next week. → final
find_and_fix_to_correct: Finally, the final result came. → The final result finally came.
translate: यह मेरा अंतिम जवाब है। → This is my final answer.
write_your_own_sentence: Write about a final match you watched.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'last; coming at the end'?
usage_tip: 'The finals' = the last stage of a competition or exams.

simple_explanation: From or in another country.
example_2: Have you been to a foreign country?
example_3: foreign tourists came to the fort.
collocations: foreign country, foreign language, foreign trip
grammar_pattern: foreign + noun
common_mistake: He went to foreign.
correct_version: He went abroad.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Foreign' is an adjective and needs a noun. For the place, use 'abroad'.
spelling_tip: F-O-R-E-I-G-N: silent G, E before I.
etymology: Old French 'forain' (outside).
mnemonic: 'Foreign' = विदेशी; the place is 'abroad' (विदेश में)।
memory_trick: FOREIGN: 'E-I' breaks the 'I before E' rule — it's foreign to it!
visual_association: A passport with stamps.
difference_explained: Foreign = adjective (a foreign country). Abroad = adverb (go abroad).
mini_conversation: A: Have you ever travelled abroad? / B: Yes, my first foreign trip was to Nepal.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Learning a foreign language opens doors.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Foreign investment rose by 10%.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'This word is totally foreign to me.' (= unknown)
mcq_options: A) foreign  B) abroad  C) in foreign  D) foreigner
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: English is a ___ language for many people. → foreign
find_and_fix_to_correct: My uncle is settled in foreign. → My uncle is settled abroad.
translate: वह विदेश जा रहा है। → He is going abroad.
write_your_own_sentence: Write about a foreign country you want to visit.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'from or in another country'?
usage_tip: 'Foreigner' can sound unfriendly; 'visitor' or 'tourist' is kinder.

simple_explanation: The newest or most recent.
example_1: Have you seen his latest film?
example_2: Here is the latest news.
example_3: This is the latest model.
collocations: latest news, latest version, at the latest
grammar_pattern: the + latest + noun / at the latest
common_mistake: This is the last news.
correct_version: This is the latest news.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Last' = final (nothing comes after). 'Latest' = newest (more may come).
etymology: late + -est.
mnemonic: LATEST phone model — सबसे नया।
memory_trick: LATEST = newest; LAST = the end.
visual_association: A phone with 'New!' sticker.
difference_explained: Latest = most recent, more may come. Last = final.
mini_conversation: A: Did you update the app? / B: Yes, I have the latest version.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Send it by Friday at the latest.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'The latest figures show a fall in prices.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'What's the latest?' (= any news?)
mcq_question: Choose: Have you heard her ___ song?
mcq_options: A) last  B) latest  C) lately  D) late
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Download the ___ version of the app. → latest
find_and_fix_to_correct: This is the last fashion. → This is the latest fashion.
translate: यह सबसे नया मॉडल है। → This is the latest model.
write_your_own_sentence: Write about the latest thing you bought.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'the newest or most recent'?
usage_tip: 'At the latest' = no later than: 'by 6 p.m. at the latest'.

simple_explanation: Very important, serious or large.
example_2: Delhi is a major city.
example_3: She had major surgery.
collocations: major problem, major change, major city
grammar_pattern: a + major + noun
common_mistake: It was a very major accident.
correct_version: It was a major accident.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Major' already means very big or serious — 'very major' sounds wrong.
etymology: Latin 'major' (greater).
mnemonic: Army MAJOR — बड़ा अफ़सर।
memory_trick: MAJOR = BIG, MINOR = small.
visual_association: A big red warning sign.
difference_explained: Major = one of the important ones. Main = the most important one.
mini_conversation: A: Is the damage bad? / B: No major damage, just a scratch.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Traffic is a major problem in our area.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'A major fire broke out in the market.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'That's a major win, congrats!'
mcq_question: Choose: Pollution is a ___ problem in big cities.
mcq_options: A) majority  B) major  C) majorly  D) mayor
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: There were no ___ changes in the rules. → major
find_and_fix_to_correct: It is a very major issue. → It is a major issue.
translate: यह एक बड़ी समस्या है। → It's a major problem.
write_your_own_sentence: Write about a major change in your life.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'very important, serious or large'?
usage_tip: Don't confuse 'major' (important) with 'mayor' (city head).

simple_explanation: Small and not very important or serious.
example_2: We made a few minor changes.
example_3: There's a minor problem with the car.
collocations: minor injury, minor change, minor mistake
grammar_pattern: a + minor + noun
common_mistake: It is a very minor small issue.
correct_version: It is a minor issue.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Minor' already means small — don't add 'small'.
etymology: Latin 'minor' (smaller).
mnemonic: MINOR = MINI.
memory_trick: MINOR vs MAJOR — small vs big.
visual_association: A small bandage on a finger.
difference_explained: Minor = small. Miner = a person who works in a mine. Same sound.
mini_conversation: A: Was anyone hurt? / B: Only minor injuries.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'It's a minor cut, just wash it.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'The accident caused minor damage.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Minor detail — I forgot my wallet!'
mcq_question: Choose: He had a ___ accident but is fine now.
mcq_options: A) minor  B) miner  C) minority  D) minus
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The report has a few ___ errors. → minor
find_and_fix_to_correct: It is a small minor mistake. → It is a minor mistake.
translate: यह मामूली चोट है। → It's a minor injury.
write_your_own_sentence: Write about a minor problem you had this week.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'small and not very important or serious'?
usage_tip: A 'minor' (noun) is a person under 18.

simple_explanation: Right, correct or suitable.
example_1: Wear proper shoes for the trek.
example_2: Eat a proper meal.
example_3: Put things in their proper place.
collocations: proper food, proper way, proper place
grammar_pattern: proper + noun
common_mistake: Do it properly way.
correct_version: Do it the proper way. / Do it properly.
why_it_s_wrong: Use the adjective with a noun (the proper way) or the adverb alone (properly).
etymology: Latin 'proprius' (one's own).
mnemonic: 'Proper' = ठीक-ठाक, सही तरीके का।
memory_trick: PROPER + LY = PROPERLY.
visual_association: A neatly set dinner table.
difference_explained: Proper = adjective (a proper meal). Properly = adverb (eat properly).
mini_conversation: A: Did you have lunch? / B: Just biscuits — no proper meal.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Sit in the proper position while studying.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Patients did not get proper care, the report said.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'This is proper Hyderabadi biryani!'
mcq_options: A) properly  B) proper  C) property  D) propers
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: You need ___ rest after the fever. → proper
find_and_fix_to_correct: He didn't explain proper. → He didn't explain properly.
translate: ठीक से खाना खाओ। → Eat a proper meal.
write_your_own_sentence: Write about the proper way to do something you know well.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'right, correct or suitable'?
usage_tip: 'Proper' also means 'real': 'a proper cup of tea'.

simple_explanation: Tasting of sugar; also, kind and lovely.
example_2: That's so sweet of you!
example_3: She has a sweet voice.
collocations: sweet tooth, sweet dreams, sweet of you
grammar_pattern: sweet + noun / be + sweet (of someone)
common_mistake: It's very sweet from you.
correct_version: It's very sweet of you.
why_it_s_wrong: The fixed phrase is 'sweet OF you' (like 'kind of you').
etymology: Old English 'swēte'.
mnemonic: 'Sweet' = मिठाई — मीठी और प्यारी।
memory_trick: Double E = double sweet!
visual_association: A plate of jalebis.
difference_explained: Sweet = adjective (a sweet mango). Sweets = noun (Indian mithai).
mini_conversation: A: I brought you flowers. / B: Oh, that's so sweet of you!
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'The tea is too sweet for me.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Sweet shops saw huge crowds before Diwali.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Sweet! We got the tickets!' (= great)
mcq_question: Choose: That was very sweet ___ you.
mcq_options: A) from  B) of  C) to  D) by
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: I have a ___ tooth — I love desserts. → sweet
find_and_fix_to_correct: Thank you, it's very sweet from you. → Thank you, it's very sweet of you.
translate: यह आम बहुत मीठा है। → This mango is very sweet.
write_your_own_sentence: Write about the sweetest thing someone did for you.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'tasting of sugar; also, kind and lovely'?
usage_tip: 'Sweet dreams' = a kind way to say good night.

simple_explanation: Complete; the whole amount.
example_2: It was a total failure.
example_3: Total silence filled the room.
collocations: total cost, total number, in total
grammar_pattern: the + total + noun / in total
common_mistake: Total how much?
correct_version: How much is it in total? / What's the total?
why_it_s_wrong: A question needs a question word and verb: 'How much is it in total?'
etymology: Latin 'totus' (whole).
mnemonic: 'Total' = कुल जोड़।
memory_trick: TOTAL + LY = TOTALLY (double L).
visual_association: A bill with the total circled.
difference_explained: Total = adjective (a total failure). Totally = adverb (totally wrong).
mini_conversation: A: What's the total? / B: ₹1,250, including tax.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'The total bill was higher than we thought.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'A total of 300 people were rescued.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'He's a total genius!'
mcq_question: Choose: The ___ number of students is 45.
mcq_options: A) totally  B) total  C) totals  D) totalling
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: What is the ___ amount? → total
find_and_fix_to_correct: Total we are five people. → There are five of us in total.
translate: कुल कीमत कितनी है? → What is the total cost?
write_your_own_sentence: Write the total cost of something you bought, with two items.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'complete; the whole amount'?
usage_tip: 'In total' = all together.

simple_explanation: Living or growing in nature, not controlled by people.
example_2: Wild flowers grow on the hills.
example_3: The party got a bit wild.
collocations: wild animals, wild flowers, go wild
grammar_pattern: wild + noun / go wild
common_mistake: Lion is a wild animal and dangerous also.
correct_version: The lion is a wild animal, and it's also dangerous.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'the' for a whole species, and put 'also' before the adjective or verb.
etymology: Old English 'wilde'.
mnemonic: Jungle ka 'wild' — जंगली।
memory_trick: WILD + LIFE = WILDLIFE.
visual_association: A tiger in a forest.
difference_explained: Wild = lives freely in nature. Tame = trained and calm near people.
mini_conversation: A: Did you see any wild animals on the safari? / B: Yes, two elephants!
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Don't feed wild monkeys.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'A wild elephant entered the village.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'The crowd went wild after the six!'
mcq_question: Choose: Dogs are pets, but wolves are ___.
mcq_options: A) tame  B) wild  C) wildly  D) wilder
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The fans went ___ when the team won. → wild
find_and_fix_to_correct: Tiger is a wild animal. → The tiger is a wild animal. / Tigers are wild animals.
translate: बाघ जंगली जानवर है। → The tiger is a wild animal.
write_your_own_sentence: Write about a wild animal you have seen.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'living or growing in nature, not controlled by people'?
usage_tip: 'Go wild' = become very excited.

simple_explanation: Not able to do something.
example_2: He was unable to sleep.
example_3: We are unable to process your request.
collocations: unable to + verb
grammar_pattern: be + unable + to + verb
common_mistake: I am unable for coming.
correct_version: I am unable to come.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Unable' is always followed by 'to' + base verb.
etymology: un (not) + able.
mnemonic: UN-ABLE = not able — 'असमर्थ'।
memory_trick: UNABLE TO + verb.
visual_association: A locked door with no key.
difference_explained: Unable = adjective (not able). Disable = verb (turn off, or make unable).
mini_conversation: A: Can Mr Rao take the meeting? / B: I'm afraid he's unable to attend today.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Sorry, I'm unable to pick up the call.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Rescuers were unable to reach the village.'
casual_conversation: Casual: (too formal — say 'I can't')
mcq_question: Choose: She was unable ___ the exam due to illness.
mcq_options: A) to take  B) taking  C) for taking  D) take
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: We are ___ to accept late forms. → unable
find_and_fix_to_correct: I am unable in joining the meeting. → I am unable to join the meeting.
translate: मैं आज आने में असमर्थ हूँ। → I am unable to come today.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a polite email line using 'unable to'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'not able to do something'?
usage_tip: In speech 'can't' is more natural; 'unable to' suits emails and notices.

simple_explanation: Having a good flavour.
example_2: She cooks tasty dishes.
example_3: These chips are too tasty to stop.
collocations: tasty food, tasty snack
grammar_pattern: tasty + food / be + tasty
common_mistake: The food is very taste.
correct_version: The food is very tasty.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Taste' is a noun or verb. The adjective is 'tasty'.
spelling_tip: T-A-S-T-Y: drop the E from 'taste' and add Y.
etymology: taste + -y.
mnemonic: 'Tasty' = स्वादिष्ट।
memory_trick: TASTE – E + Y = TASTY.
visual_association: A plate of hot samosas.
difference_explained: Tasty = has good flavour (casual). Delicious = very tasty (stronger).
mini_conversation: A: How's the biryani? / B: Super tasty!
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Street food is cheap and tasty.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Chefs shared tasty millet recipes.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Mom, this is so tasty!'
mcq_options: A) taste  B) tasty  C) tasted  D) tasting
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: This dosa is so ___! → tasty
find_and_fix_to_correct: The dal is very taste. → The dal is very tasty.
translate: खाना बहुत स्वादिष्ट है। → The food is very tasty.
write_your_own_sentence: Write about the tastiest food you ate this week.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'having a good flavour'?
usage_tip: 'Tasty' is casual; in a restaurant review, 'delicious' sounds better.

simple_explanation: Very tasty.
example_2: Thank you for the delicious dinner.
example_3: The smell was delicious.
collocations: delicious food, smells delicious
grammar_pattern: be + delicious / delicious + food
common_mistake: This food is very delicious.
correct_version: This food is delicious. / This food is really delicious.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Delicious' is already strong; 'very delicious' sounds weak — use 'really' or 'absolutely'.
etymology: Latin 'deliciae' (delight).
mnemonic: 'Delicious' = उँगलियाँ चाटते रह जाओ!
memory_trick: DE-LI-CIOUS: the CI sounds like SH.
visual_association: A chef kissing their fingers.
difference_explained: Delicious = stronger and more polite. Tasty = casual.
mini_conversation: A: How was dinner? / B: Absolutely delicious, thank you!
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Mom makes delicious kheer.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Visitors enjoyed delicious local food at the fair.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Yum, that smells delicious!'
mcq_options: A) delicious  B) delicate  C) delight  D) deliciously
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Thank you for the ___ meal. → delicious
find_and_fix_to_correct: The paneer is very much delicious. → The paneer is absolutely delicious.
translate: खाना बहुत स्वादिष्ट था। → The food was delicious.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a thank-you line to someone who cooked for you.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'very tasty'?
usage_tip: Strong adjectives like 'delicious' take 'absolutely' or 'really', not 'very'.

simple_explanation: Very silly or strange; also, very excited about something.
example_2: He's crazy about cricket.
example_3: The traffic today is crazy.
collocations: crazy about, go crazy, drive someone crazy
grammar_pattern: be + crazy + about + thing
common_mistake: She is crazy for music.
correct_version: She is crazy about music.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Crazy' (= loves a lot) takes 'about'.
etymology: craze + -y.
mnemonic: 'Crazy fan' = दीवाना।
memory_trick: CRAZY ABOUT = दीवाना।
visual_association: Fans screaming at a concert.
difference_explained: Crazy = silly or very excited. Mad (UK) = angry or crazy.
mini_conversation: A: I'm going to run 10 km every day! / B: Are you crazy?
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'My brother is crazy about cars.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'The 'crazy' price rise has hit families.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'This week has been crazy!'
mcq_options: A) for  B) about  C) on  D) with
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The noise is driving me ___! → crazy
find_and_fix_to_correct: I am very crazy for this song. → I am crazy about this song.
translate: वह क्रिकेट का दीवाना है। → He is crazy about cricket.
write_your_own_sentence: Write about something you are crazy about.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'very silly or strange; also, very excited about something'?
usage_tip: Calling a person 'crazy' can hurt — use it for ideas and situations.

simple_explanation: Having good things happen by chance.
example_2: Seven is my lucky number.
example_3: We were lucky to get tickets.
collocations: lucky number, lucky day, lucky to have
grammar_pattern: be + lucky + to + verb / lucky + noun
common_mistake: I am lucky that I got the job luckily.
correct_version: I was lucky to get the job.
why_it_s_wrong: Don't repeat the idea: 'lucky' already says it.
etymology: luck + -y.
mnemonic: 'Lucky' = किस्मत वाला।
memory_trick: LUCK + Y = LUCKY.
visual_association: A four-leaf clover.
difference_explained: Lucky = adjective (a lucky man). Luckily = adverb (Luckily, it stopped raining).
mini_conversation: A: I found ₹500 on the road! / B: Lucky you!
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'We were lucky — the bus was late too.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Lucky survivors walked out of the building.'

simple_explanation: Happy or satisfied.

example_3: She was pleased to hear the news.
collocations: pleased with, pleased to meet you, very pleased
grammar_pattern: be + pleased + with + thing / pleased + to + verb
common_mistake: I am pleased from your work.

simple_explanation: Happy about something.

grammar_pattern: be + glad + (that) + clause / glad + to + verb

news_style_line: News-style: 'The old market is gone forever.'

write_your_own_sentence: Write about something you want to keep forever.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'for all time; always'?
usage_tip: 'Take forever' = take a very long time (informal exaggeration).

simple_explanation: Separated by a distance or time; into pieces.

example_3: The toy fell apart.

grammar_pattern: be/stand/live + apart / apart from + noun
common_mistake: Apart this, everything is fine.
correct_version: Apart from this, everything is fine.

spelling_tip: A-P-A-R-T: one word. 'A part' (two words) = a piece.

mnemonic: 'Alag' = apart.
memory_trick: APART FROM = except.

difference_explained: Apart (one word) = separated. A part (two words) = a piece.
mini_conversation: A: Do you see your brother often? / B: No, we live far apart.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Keep the plants two feet apart.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Apart from minor delays, the event went smoothly.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'My old phone is falling apart!'

fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The twins can't be kept ___. → apart
find_and_fix_to_correct: Apart of Sunday, I work every day. → Apart from Sunday, I work every day.

write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence using 'apart from'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'separated by a distance or time; into pieces'?
usage_tip: 'Fall apart' = break into pieces, or stop working.

grammar_pattern: verb + aside / aside from + noun
common_mistake: Aside that, all good.
correct_version: Aside from that, all good.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Aside' needs 'from' before the thing you leave out.
etymology: a- + side.
mnemonic: 'Ek taraf' = aside.
memory_trick: ASIDE = to A SIDE.
visual_association: A person stepping to the side of a path.
difference_explained: Aside = to one side. Beside = next to.
mini_conversation: A: Can I pass? / B: Sorry, let me step aside.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Set aside ten minutes to revise.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'The court set aside the earlier order.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Jokes aside, are you okay?'

reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to one side; out of the way'?
usage_tip: 'Jokes aside' = now let's be serious.

simple_explanation: Of this kind; to a great degree (before a noun).
example_1: It was such a nice day!
example_2: I've never seen such a crowd.
example_3: Don't say such things.
collocations: such a, such as, such a lot
grammar_pattern: such + a/an + adjective + noun / such as
common_mistake: It was so a good film.
correct_version: It was such a good film.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Such' goes before 'a' + noun. 'So' goes before an adjective alone (so good).
etymology: Old English 'swylc'.
mnemonic: 'Aisa' = such.
memory_trick: SUCH A + noun. SO + adjective.
visual_association: Big eyes looking at a huge crowd.
difference_explained: Such + (a) noun (such a nice day). So + adjective (so nice).
mini_conversation: A: How was the concert? / B: It was such a great night!
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Fruits such as mango and papaya are good for you.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Such incidents will not be tolerated, police said.'

find_and_fix_to_correct: He is so nice person. → He is such a nice person. / He is so nice.

write_your_own_sentence: Write two sentences with 'such a'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review

simple_explanation: To move from one place to another, away from where you are.
example_1: I go to school by bus.
example_2: Where did you go yesterday?
example_3: Let's go!
collocations: go home, go shopping, go to bed
related_phrasal_verbs: go on, go out, go back, go through
action_sequence: Before: get ready → During: travel there → After: arrive
grammar_pattern: go + to + place / go + -ing (go shopping) / go + home
common_mistake: I goed to the market.
correct_version: I went to the market.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Go' is irregular: go – went – gone.
spelling_tip: G-O. Past: WENT (a completely different word!).
etymology: Old English 'gān'.
mnemonic: 'Go' = जाओ — 'Let's go' = चलो!
memory_trick: GO → WENT → GONE: 'went' doesn't look like 'go' at all.
visual_association: A person walking out of a door with a bag.
difference_explained: Go = away from the speaker. Come = toward the speaker.
mini_conversation: A: Where are you going? / B: To the bank, back in ten minutes.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'I go for a walk every evening.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Prices of vegetables have gone up.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Go, go, go! We're late!'
mcq_question: Choose: She ___ to Delhi last week.
mcq_options: A) goed  B) went  C) gone  D) go
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: We ___ shopping every Saturday. → go
find_and_fix_to_correct: I am going to home. → I am going home.

write_your_own_sentence: Write three places you go every week.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to move from one place to another, away from where you are'?
usage_tip: 'Home' needs no 'to': go home, not 'go to home'.

simple_explanation: To get and carry something; to need (time); to use (transport).

example_3: I take the metro to work.
collocations: take a bus, take time, take a photo, take medicine
related_phrasal_verbs: take off, take care of, take part, take after
action_sequence: Before: pick it up → During: hold it → After: carry it with you
grammar_pattern: take + thing / it takes + time / take + transport
common_mistake: I taked the bus.
correct_version: I took the bus.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Take' is irregular: take – took – taken.
spelling_tip: T-A-K-E. Past: TOOK. Past participle: TAKEN.
etymology: Old Norse 'taka'.
mnemonic: 'Take' = लो — 'Take this' = यह लो।
memory_trick: TAKE → TOOK → TAKEN.
visual_association: A hand picking up a bag.
difference_explained: Take = from here to there. Bring = from there to here.
mini_conversation: A: How long does it take to reach Pune? / B: About three hours.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Take your medicine after food.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'The new PM took charge on Monday.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Take it easy, relax!'

mcq_options: A) taked  B) took  C) taken  D) take

find_and_fix_to_correct: He has took my pen. → He has taken my pen.
translate: छाता ले लो। → Take an umbrella.
write_your_own_sentence: Write about how long it takes you to get ready.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to get and carry something; to need (time); to use (transport)'?
usage_tip: 'Take a photo', 'take a bath', 'take a break' — English uses 'take' where Hindi uses many verbs.

simple_explanation: To make an effort to do something; to test something to see if you like it.
example_2: I'll try to come.
example_3: Try this sweet, it's homemade.
collocations: try hard, try again, try on, give it a try
action_sequence: Before: have a goal → During: make an effort → After: succeed or learn
grammar_pattern: try + to + verb / try + -ing / try + thing
common_mistake: I will try that I come.
correct_version: I will try to come.
why_it_s_wrong: After 'try', use 'to' + verb (or -ing), not a 'that' clause.
spelling_tip: T-R-Y → TRIED, TRIES (Y → I), but TRYING.
etymology: Old French 'trier' (to sift).
mnemonic: 'Try' = कोशिश — 'Try karo' हम रोज़ बोलते हैं।
memory_trick: TRY → TRIED, but TRYING keeps the Y.
visual_association: A child trying to ride a cycle.
difference_explained: Try to do = make an effort. Try doing = test a method (Try restarting the phone).
mini_conversation: A: I can't open this jar. / B: Try hot water on the lid.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Try the new dosa place near the station.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Firefighters tried for hours to control the fire.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Nice try!'
mcq_question: Choose: I'll ___ to finish it tonight.
mcq_options: A) tried  B) try  C) trying  D) tries
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: She ___ three times before she passed. → tried
find_and_fix_to_correct: He tryed his best. → He tried his best.
translate: मैं कोशिश करूँगा। → I will try.
write_your_own_sentence: Write about something you tried for the first time.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to make an effort to do something; to test something to see if you like it'?
usage_tip: 'Try on' = wear clothes in a shop to check them.

simple_explanation: To have something and not give it back; to stay or make something stay the same; to continue.

example_3: Keep walking straight.
collocations: keep quiet, keep calm, keep a secret, keep in touch
related_phrasal_verbs: keep up, keep on, keep away
action_sequence: Before: get something → During: put it safely → After: still have it later
grammar_pattern: keep + thing / keep + adjective / keep + -ing
common_mistake: Keep patience.
correct_version: Be patient. / Have patience.
why_it_s_wrong: English doesn't say 'keep patience'. Use 'be patient'.
etymology: Old English 'cēpan'.
mnemonic: Goal-KEEPER — जो गोल को 'रखता' (बचाता) है।
memory_trick: KEEP → KEPT, like SLEEP → SLEPT.
visual_association: A person locking something in a drawer.
difference_explained: Keep = have it for a long time. Put = place it somewhere once.
mini_conversation: A: Can I keep this book for a week? / B: Sure, no hurry.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Keep your phone away while studying.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Prices kept rising all year.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Keep going, you're almost there!'

mcq_options: A) keeped  B) kept  C) keeps on  D) keep
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Please ___ the door closed. → keep
find_and_fix_to_correct: Keep quite in the library. → Keep quiet in the library.

write_your_own_sentence: Write about something you keep safely.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to have something and not give it back; to stay or make something stay the same; to continue'?
usage_tip: 'Keep in touch' = stay in contact.

simple_explanation: To move to face a different direction; to change; to make something go round.

example_3: Turn the key slowly.
collocations: turn left, turn around, turn red
related_phrasal_verbs: turn on, turn off, turn up, turn down, turn into

common_mistake: Take a turn from left.
correct_version: Turn left. / Take a left turn.
why_it_s_wrong: The natural direction is 'turn left' or 'take a left'.

memory_trick: TURN + adjective = become: turn red, turn cold.

difference_explained: Turn + colour/age (turn red, turn 18). Become = general.

news_style_line: News-style: 'The protest turned violent.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'It's your turn!'

mcq_options: A) turn  B) turns  C) turning  D) turned to
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The milk ___ sour. → turned
find_and_fix_to_correct: He turned 18 years. → He turned 18.

write_your_own_sentence: Write directions from your gate to the main road.

reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to move to face a different direction; to change; to make something go round'?
usage_tip: 'Your turn' = it's time for you to play or speak.

simple_explanation: To change position or place; to go to live somewhere new.

related_phrasal_verbs: move in, move out, move on

casual_conversation: Casual: 'That film really moved me.' (= touched emotionally)

casual_conversation: Casual: 'Hold on, I'm coming!'

example_3: Time passes quickly.
