simple_explanation: To say numbers in order; to find the total; to matter.
example_2: Count the money carefully.
example_3: Every vote counts.
collocations: count money, count on, count down
action_sequence: Before: see the pile → During: count one by one → After: know the total
grammar_pattern: count + things / count + on + person
common_mistake: You can believe on me.
correct_version: You can count on me.
why_it_s_wrong: For 'trust someone to help', the phrase is 'count on'.
etymology: Latin 'computare'.
mnemonic: Shop COUNTER — जहाँ पैसे गिने जाते हैं।
memory_trick: COUNT → COUNTER → COUNTLESS.
visual_association: Fingers counting notes.
difference_explained: Count = one by one. Calculate = work out with maths.
mini_conversation: A: How many chairs do we need? / B: Let me count the guests.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Count your change before you leave the counter.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Vote counting will start at 8 a.m.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Count me in!' (= I'll join)
mcq_question: Choose: You can always count ___ me.
mcq_options: A) at  B) on  C) for  D) to
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Let's ___ down: 10, 9, 8… → count
find_and_fix_to_correct: Believe on me, I will help. → Count on me, I will help.
translate: पैसे गिनो। → Count the money.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence using 'count on'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'to say numbers in order; to find the total; to matter'?
usage_tip: 'Count me in' = I'll join; 'count me out' = I won't.

simple_explanation: Not intelligent or not sensible.
example_2: Don't be stupid!
example_3: I feel so stupid.
collocations: stupid mistake, stupid question, feel stupid
grammar_pattern: stupid + noun / be + stupid
common_mistake: It was very much stupid.
correct_version: It was really stupid.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Very much' doesn't go before an adjective — use 'very' or 'really'.
etymology: Latin 'stupidus' (stunned).
mnemonic: 'Stupid' = बेवकूफ़ — careful, it can hurt.
memory_trick: Call MISTAKES stupid, not PEOPLE.
visual_association: A person hitting their own forehead.
difference_explained: Stupid = strong, can be rude. Silly = softer, playful.
mini_conversation: A: I left my keys inside again! / B: Don't worry, it's not stupid, it happens.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'I made a stupid mistake in the exam.'
news_style_line: News-style: (usually avoided in formal news)
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Stupid phone, it froze again!'
mcq_question: Choose: I feel ___ — I forgot her name.
mcq_options: A) stupidity  B) stupid  C) stupidly  D) stupids
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: That was a ___ idea, sorry. → stupid
find_and_fix_to_correct: He is having stupid ideas always. → He always has stupid ideas.
translate: यह एक बेवकूफ़ी भरी गलती थी। → It was a stupid mistake.
write_your_own_sentence: Write about a stupid mistake you once made.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'not intelligent or not sensible'?
usage_tip: Calling someone 'stupid' is rude; 'That wasn't a good idea' is kinder.

simple_explanation: Liked more than all the others.
example_2: Who is your favourite actor?
example_3: This is my favourite song.
collocations: favourite food, favourite colour, all-time favourite
grammar_pattern: my/your + favourite + noun
common_mistake: This is my most favourite song.
correct_version: This is my favourite song.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Favourite' already means 'liked most' — no 'most'.
pronunciation_tip: 'FAY-vrit' — three letters in the middle go quiet.
etymology: favour + -ite.
mnemonic: 'Favourite' = सबसे पसंदीदा।
memory_trick: FAVOURITE = No. 1 already — never 'most favourite'.
visual_association: A heart icon next to a song.
difference_explained: Favourite = liked most. Favour = help or kindness (do me a favour).
mini_conversation: A: What's your favourite food? / B: Rajma chawal, always!
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Sunday is my favourite day.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'India start as favourites for the final.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'You're my favourite cousin!'
mcq_options: A) most favourite  B) favourite  C) favour  D) favoured
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: What is your ___ subject? → favourite
find_and_fix_to_correct: She is my most favourite teacher. → She is my favourite teacher.
translate: मेरा पसंदीदा रंग नीला है। → My favourite colour is blue.
write_your_own_sentence: Write about your three favourite things.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'liked more than all the others'?
usage_tip: 'The favourites' in sport = the team expected to win.

simple_explanation: A polite request.
example_2: I could swim when I was five.
example_3: It could rain later.
collocations: could you, could be, I could
grammar_pattern: could + base verb
common_mistake: I could to go.
correct_version: I could go.
why_it_s_wrong: After 'could', use the base verb — no 'to'.
spelling_tip: C-O-U-L-D: silent L, like WOULD and SHOULD.
etymology: Old English 'cūthe'.
mnemonic: 'Could you…?' = क्या आप… कर सकते हैं? (polite)
memory_trick: 'Could' is 'can' in the past — or 'can' being extra polite.
visual_association: A person politely asking at a counter.
difference_explained: 'Could you…?' is more polite than 'Can you…?'. Could is also the past of can.
mini_conversation: A: Could you help me with this bag? / B: Of course.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Could I have the bill, please?'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Officials said the bridge could collapse.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'I could eat a whole pizza right now!'
mcq_options: A) Give me water.  B) Can I get water?  C) Could I have some water, please?  D) Water!
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Fill in (polite): '___ you pass the salt?' → Could
find_and_fix_to_correct: Could you to help me? → Could you help me?
translate: क्या आप दरवाज़ा बंद कर सकते हैं? → Could you close the door?
write_your_own_sentence: Write two polite requests with 'Could you…?'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'a polite request'?
usage_tip: 'Could' makes any request softer — use it with teachers and strangers.

simple_explanation: It is possible.
example_2: May I come in?
example_3: She may be late today.
collocations: may I, it may, may or may not
grammar_pattern: may + base verb
common_mistake: May I to leave?
correct_version: May I leave?
why_it_s_wrong: After 'may', use the base verb — no 'to'.
spelling_tip: M-A-Y. Capital M = the month May.
etymology: Old English 'mæg'.
mnemonic: 'May I come in?' — school का सबसे पहला अंग्रेज़ी वाक्य।
memory_trick: 'May' is the polite cousin of 'can'.
visual_association: A student at a classroom door.
difference_explained: 'May I…?' = formal permission. 'Can I…?' = everyday.
mini_conversation: A: May I use your pen? / B: Sure, go ahead.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'May I have your name, please?'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Heavy rain may hit the coast tomorrow.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'I may or may not have eaten your chocolate!'
mcq_question: Choose: ___ I leave early today, sir?
mcq_options: A) May  B) Must  C) Should  D) Would
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Fill in (polite): '___ I ask a question?' → May
find_and_fix_to_correct: May I to sit here? → May I sit here?
translate: क्या मैं अंदर आ सकता हूँ? → May I come in?
write_your_own_sentence: Write two formal permission questions with 'May I…?'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'it is possible'?
usage_tip: 'Maybe' (one word) = perhaps. 'May be' (two words) = might be.

simple_explanation: Have permission to do something.
example_1: You are allowed to leave early today.
example_2: Are we allowed to use phones?
example_3: Visitors are not allowed to take photos.
collocations: be allowed to leave, not allowed to
grammar_pattern: subject + be + allowed to + verb
word_forms: am/is/are allowed to – was/were allowed to – will be allowed to
common_mistake: I am allow to go.
correct_version: I am allowed to go.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Allowed' is the past participle: 'be allowed', never 'be allow'.
spelling_tip: A-L-L-O-W-E-D: double L. Not 'aloud' (in a voice).
etymology: allow (Old French 'alouer').
mnemonic: ALLOWED = permission मिली हुई।
memory_trick: 'Allowed' has '-ed' because permission was given TO you.
visual_association: A 'No photos' sign with a cross.
difference_explained: Allowed = permitted. Aloud = out loud (read aloud). Same sound.
mini_conversation: A: Are we allowed to bring food? / B: Only water, sorry.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Students are not allowed to leave during the exam.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Trucks will not be allowed to enter the city by day.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Am I allowed to eat this last piece?'
mcq_options: A) allow  B) allowed  C) aloud  D) allowing
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: You are ___ ___ leave early today. → allowed to
find_and_fix_to_correct: We are not allow to talk in class. → We are not allowed to talk in class.
translate: यहाँ फ़ोटो लेने की अनुमति नहीं है। → You are not allowed to take photos here.
write_your_own_sentence: Write three rules at your school or office with 'allowed to'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'have permission to do something'?
usage_tip: 'Allowed to' is for rules; 'can' is often used for the same thing in speech.

simple_explanation: It is necessary (a strong rule), or I am almost sure this is true.
example_1: You must be tired after that trip.
example_2: You must wear a helmet.
example_3: She must be tired after the trip.
collocations: must wear, must be, you must
where_it_s_used: Rules, strong duty, being almost sure
grammar_pattern: must + base verb
common_mistake: I must to go.
correct_version: I must go.
why_it_s_wrong: After 'must', use the base verb — no 'to'.
pronunciation_tip: Short 'u'. In fast speech, the T is often dropped: 'mus'.
etymology: Old English 'mōste'.
mnemonic: MUST = ज़रूरी है।
memory_trick: 'Must' is a strong order — no 'to', no arguing.
visual_association: A 'Helmet compulsory' road sign.
difference_explained: Must = the speaker's own rule. Have to = a rule from outside. 'Mustn't' = don't do it; 'don't have to' = not necessary.
mini_conversation: A: The door is locked. / B: They must be out.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'You must switch off your phone in the hall.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'All passengers must wear masks, the airline said.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'You must try this biryani!'
mcq_question: Choose: You ___ stop at a red light.
mcq_options: A) must  B) must to  C) musts  D) musting
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Fill in (strong rule): 'You ___ wear a seatbelt.' → must
find_and_fix_to_correct: You must to wear a seat belt. → You must wear a seat belt.
translate: तुम्हें समय पर आना ही होगा। → You must come on time.
write_your_own_sentence: Write three rules using 'must'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'it is necessary (a strong rule), or I am almost sure this is true'?
usage_tip: 'You must try this!' = a strong, friendly recommendation.

simple_explanation: It is necessary to do this.
example_2: I need to sleep early today.
example_3: You don't need to come.
collocations: need to leave, don't need to
grammar_pattern: subject + need to + base verb
word_forms: need to – needed to – needing to
common_mistake: I need go.
correct_version: I need to go.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Need' + another verb needs 'to': need to go.
etymology: need (Old English 'nēodian').
mnemonic: 'Mujhe jaana hai' = I need to go.
memory_trick: 'Need' always wants a 'to' before the next verb.
visual_association: A clock and a person rushing.
difference_explained: Need to = necessary for you. Have to = a rule or duty. 'Don't need to' = not necessary.
mini_conversation: A: Why are you leaving? / B: I need to catch the 6 o'clock train.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'We need to buy milk.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'The city needs to improve its roads, experts say.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'You need to chill, yaar!'
mcq_options: A) need  B) need to  C) needs to  D) needed
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: We ___ ___ leave soon. → need to
find_and_fix_to_correct: I need go now. → I need to go now.
translate: मुझे आराम करने की ज़रूरत है। → I need to rest.
write_your_own_sentence: Write three things you need to do this week.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'it is necessary to do this'?
usage_tip: 'You don't need to' = it's not necessary (a kind way to say 'no need').

simple_explanation: This is good advice.
example_2: You should drink more water.
example_3: Should I call her?
collocations: you should, should have, shouldn't
grammar_pattern: should + base verb
common_mistake: You should to rest.
correct_version: You should rest.
why_it_s_wrong: After 'should', use the base verb — no 'to'.
etymology: Old English 'sceolde'.
mnemonic: 'Should' = चाहिए।
memory_trick: 'Should' gives advice — no 'to' needed.
visual_association: A doctor giving advice.
difference_explained: Should = advice (it's a good idea). Must = strong rule (no choice).
mini_conversation: A: I have a headache. / B: You should rest for a while.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'You should sleep before midnight.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Experts say children should play outside daily.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'You should totally come to the party!'
mcq_question: Choose: You look tired. You ___ go to bed.
mcq_options: A) should  B) should to  C) shoulds  D) shouldn't to
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Fill in (advice): 'You ___ drink more water.' → should
find_and_fix_to_correct: You should to ask the teacher. → You should ask the teacher.
translate: तुम्हें डॉक्टर को दिखाना चाहिए। → You should see a doctor.
write_your_own_sentence: Write three pieces of advice for a new student using 'should'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'this is good advice'?
usage_tip: 'Should I…?' asks for advice: 'Should I take the job?'

simple_explanation: This is the right thing to do.
example_2: You ought to say sorry.
example_3: We ought to leave now.
collocations: ought to apologize, ought to leave
grammar_pattern: ought to + base verb
word_forms: ought to (no other forms); negative: ought not to
common_mistake: You ought apologize.
correct_version: You ought to apologize.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Ought' is always followed by 'to'.
etymology: Old English 'āhte' (past of 'own').
mnemonic: 'Ought to' = should (थोड़ा formal)।
memory_trick: 'Ought' is the one modal that always keeps its 'to'.
visual_association: Scales with 'right' written on one side.
difference_explained: Same meaning. 'Should' is much more common in speech.
mini_conversation: A: I forgot her birthday. / B: You ought to call her today.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'We ought to thank our teachers more often.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'The government ought to act quickly, experts said.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'You ought to see this — it's amazing!'
mcq_options: A) ought  B) ought to  C) ought for  D) oughts to
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: You ___ ___ apologize. → ought to
find_and_fix_to_correct: You ought apologise. → You ought to apologise.
translate: तुम्हें माफ़ी माँगनी चाहिए। → You ought to apologise.
write_your_own_sentence: Write one sentence with 'ought to' and the same idea with 'should'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'this is the right thing to do'?
usage_tip: In everyday speech, 'should' sounds more natural than 'ought to'.

simple_explanation: It is possible, a bit less sure than "may.".
example_2: I might go to the party.
example_3: Take an umbrella, it might rain.
collocations: might be, might rain, might not
grammar_pattern: might + base verb
common_mistake: She might to be late.
correct_version: She might be late.
why_it_s_wrong: After 'might', use the base verb — no 'to'.
etymology: Old English 'meahte'.
mnemonic: 'Might' = शायद।
memory_trick: 'Might' is 'may' with even less certainty — a soft maybe.
visual_association: A sky with half sun, half clouds.
difference_explained: Very close. 'Might' is a little less sure and more common in speech.
mini_conversation: A: Are you coming tomorrow? / B: I might, I'm not sure yet.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Call first — the shop might be closed.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Petrol prices might go up next month.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'I might be a bit late, sorry!'
mcq_question: Choose: Take a jacket. It ___ get cold.
mcq_options: A) might  B) might to  C) mights  D) might getting
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: It ___ rain later. → might
find_and_fix_to_correct: She might to be busy. → She might be busy.
translate: शायद आज बारिश हो। → It might rain today.
write_your_own_sentence: Write two things you might do this weekend.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'it is possible, a bit less sure than "may."'?
usage_tip: 'Might' is a soft way to say 'maybe I will'.

simple_explanation: Strong advice; something bad may happen if not.
example_2: You had better hurry.
example_3: We'd better leave now.
collocations: had better hurry, better not
grammar_pattern: had better + base verb
word_forms: had better (fixed — used for present and future); negative: had better not
common_mistake: You had better to go.
correct_version: You had better go.
why_it_s_wrong: After 'had better', use the base verb — no 'to'.
etymology: had + better.
mnemonic: 'Had better' = वरना मुसीबत होगी!
memory_trick: 'Had better' warns you: something bad happens if you don't!
visual_association: A clock about to strike, and a running person.
difference_explained: Had better = stronger, with a warning (or something bad will happen). Should = general advice.
mini_conversation: A: The train leaves in ten minutes! / B: Then we'd better run.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'You'd better take an umbrella.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Fans had better book early, organisers warned.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'You'd better not tell Mom!'
mcq_question: Choose: You ___ better finish your homework before Dad comes.
mcq_options: A) have  B) had  C) has  D) having
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: You ___ ___ hurry, the train is leaving. → had better
find_and_fix_to_correct: You had better to study. → You had better study.
translate: तुम्हें जल्दी करनी चाहिए, वरना देर हो जाएगी। → You had better hurry.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a warning to a friend using 'You'd better…'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'strong advice; something bad may happen if not'?
usage_tip: 'Had better' is about now or the future, even though 'had' looks past.

simple_explanation: Used for imagined situations, polite offers and requests, and past habits.
example_1: Every summer, we would visit our grandparents.
example_2: I would help you if I could.
example_3: Would you like some tea?
collocations: would like, would you, wouldn't
where_it_s_used: Imagined situations, polite offers, past habits
grammar_pattern: would + base verb
common_mistake: If I would have money, I would buy it.
correct_version: If I had money, I would buy it.
why_it_s_wrong: In an 'if' clause about something unreal, use the past (If I had…), not 'would'.
etymology: Old English 'wolde'.
mnemonic: 'Would' = होता / करता (imagined)।
memory_trick: 'Would' is 'will' wearing a polite, softer mask.
visual_association: A person day-dreaming about a big house.
difference_explained: Will = real future (I will go). Would = imagined or polite (I would go if…).
mini_conversation: A: What would you do with a crore? / B: I would travel the world.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Would you like to sit here?'
news_style_line: News-style: 'The minister said he would resign if found guilty.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'I would never do that!'
mcq_question: Choose: If I ___ rich, I would buy a house.
mcq_options: A) would be  B) was / were  C) will be  D) am
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: If I had time, I ___ come. → would
find_and_fix_to_correct: If it would rain, we would stay home. → If it rained, we would stay home.
translate: अगर मेरे पास समय होता, तो मैं आता। → If I had time, I would come.
write_your_own_sentence: Write what you would do if you had a free day.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'used for imagined situations, polite offers and requests, and past habits'?
usage_tip: 'Would you…?' is a polite way to ask: 'Would you close the window, please?'

simple_explanation: Used to make a suggestion.
example_2: Shall we start?
example_3: Shall I open the window?
collocations: shall we, shall I
grammar_pattern: shall + base verb (with I/we)
common_mistake: Shall we to go?
correct_version: Shall we go?
why_it_s_wrong: After 'shall', use the base verb — no 'to'.
etymology: Old English 'sceal'.
mnemonic: 'Shall we?' = चलें?
memory_trick: 'Shall we...?' is a friendly way to suggest doing something together.
visual_association: A host offering a guest a seat.
difference_explained: 'Shall I/we…?' = offer or suggestion. 'Will' = future.
mini_conversation: A: Shall we order food? / B: Yes, let's.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Shall I help you with that?'
news_style_line: News-style: 'The rules shall apply from April 1.' (legal style)
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Shall we go? I'm starving.'
mcq_question: Choose: It's hot. ___ I turn on the fan?
mcq_options: A) Shall  B) Must  C) Would  D) Do
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Fill in (suggestion): '___ we go now?' → Shall
find_and_fix_to_correct: Shall we to go now? → Shall we go now?
translate: क्या मैं खिड़की खोल दूँ? → Shall I open the window?
write_your_own_sentence: Write two offers starting with 'Shall I…?'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'used to make a suggestion'?
usage_tip: 'Shall' is mostly used only with I and we in questions.

simple_explanation: Was a habit or fact in the past, not now.
example_1: I used to play football every day.
example_2: I used to live in Patna.
example_3: Did you use to play cricket?
collocations: used to play, didn't use to, get used to
grammar_pattern: subject + used to + base verb
word_forms: used to (past only); question/negative: did … use to
common_mistake: I am used to play football.
correct_version: I used to play football.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Used to' (past habit) + base verb. 'Be used to' (be comfortable with) + -ing.
pronunciation_tip: 'YOOST-tuh' — the D is silent in speech.
spelling_tip: U-S-E-D T-O. After 'did': USE TO (no D).
etymology: use + -d + to.
mnemonic: 'Pehle … karta tha' = used to.
memory_trick: 'Used to' + verb = an old habit that has now stopped.
visual_association: An old black-and-white photo.
confusing_word: used to vs be used to
difference_explained: Used to play = did it often in the past. Be used to playing = it's normal for me now.
mini_conversation: A: Do you play the guitar? / B: I used to, but I stopped.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'There used to be a cinema here.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'The town used to be famous for its silk.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'We used to be best friends in school!'
mcq_question: Choose: I ___ walk to school when I was small.
mcq_options: A) use to  B) used to  C) am used to  D) was use to
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: I ___ ___ play football every day. → used to
find_and_fix_to_correct: I am used to play cricket every day. → I used to play cricket every day.
translate: मैं पहले चाय नहीं पीता था। → I didn't use to drink tea.
write_your_own_sentence: Write three things you used to do as a child.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'was a habit or fact in the past, not now'?
usage_tip: 'Used to' is only for the past; for present habits say 'usually'.

simple_explanation: Necessary, often from outside rules.
example_2: I have to go now.
example_3: Do you have to work on Sunday?
collocations: have to go, don't have to
grammar_pattern: subject + have to + base verb
word_forms: have to – has to – had to – will have to
common_mistake: I have to going.
correct_version: I have to go.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Have to' is followed by the base verb, not -ing.
pronunciation_tip: Often 'haf-tuh' in speech (the V sounds like F).
spelling_tip: H-A-V-E T-O. He/she: HAS TO. Past: HAD TO.
etymology: have + to.
mnemonic: 'Mujhe jaana padega' = I have to go.
memory_trick: 'Have to' = an outside rule is pushing you to act.
visual_association: An office ID card and a clock.
difference_explained: Have to = rule from outside (my boss says). Must = my own strong feeling. 'Don't have to' = not necessary.
mini_conversation: A: Are you coming out? / B: Sorry, I have to finish this report.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'I have to wake up at five tomorrow.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Drivers will have to pay a new toll.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Do I have to? I'm so tired!'
mcq_question: Choose: She ___ wear a uniform at work.
mcq_options: A) have to  B) has to  C) having to  D) has
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: I ___ ___ leave now. → have to
find_and_fix_to_correct: He have to go. → He has to go.
translate: मुझे कल काम पर जाना है। → I have to go to work tomorrow.
write_your_own_sentence: Write three things you have to do every day.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'necessary, often from outside rules'?
usage_tip: 'You don't have to' = it's not necessary. 'You mustn't' = it's not allowed.

simple_explanation: One to the other (two people).
example_2: We help each other with homework.
example_3: They haven't seen each other for years.
collocations: love each other, help each other, know each other
grammar_pattern: subject (2 people) + verb + each other
common_mistake: They love themselves.
correct_version: They love each other.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Themselves' means each person does it to himself or herself; for two people doing it to one another, use 'each other'.
spelling_tip: Two words: EACH OTHER. Possessive: EACH OTHER'S.
etymology: each + other.
mnemonic: 'Ek doosre ko' = each other.
memory_trick: Two people doing the same thing back to one another.
visual_association: Two friends giving each other a high five.
difference_explained: Each other = A to B and B to A. Themselves = A to A, B to B.
mini_conversation: A: Do you and your sister get along? / B: Yes, we talk to each other every day.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'The neighbours help each other.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'The two leaders praised each other.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'We don't even like each other!'
mcq_options: A) themselves  B) each other  C) itself  D) ourselves
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: They love ___ ___. → each other
find_and_fix_to_correct: They are talking with themselves. → They are talking to each other.
translate: हम एक-दूसरे की मदद करते हैं। → We help each other.
write_your_own_sentence: Write about a friend and you using 'each other'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'one to the other (two people)'?
usage_tip: 'One another' means the same and is slightly more formal.

simple_explanation: A big amount or number (either type).
example_1: She has a lot of friends.
example_2: I have a lot of work today.
example_3: There were a lot of people at the fair.
collocations: a lot of friends, a lot of money, a lot of fun
grammar_pattern: a lot of + noun (countable or uncountable)
word_forms: a lot of / lots of (both countable and uncountable)
common_mistake: A lot of people is here.
correct_version: A lot of people are here.
why_it_s_wrong: The verb agrees with the noun after 'of': a lot of people ARE.
spelling_tip: Three words: A LOT OF. 'Alot' is always wrong.
etymology: a + lot + of.
mnemonic: 'Bahut saara' = a lot of.
memory_trick: 'A lot of' works for both countable and uncountable nouns.
visual_association: A big pile of books.
difference_explained: A lot of = both, and natural in positive sentences. Many/much = more formal, common in negatives and questions.
mini_conversation: A: Do you have any friends in Delhi? / B: Yes, a lot of them.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Drink a lot of water in summer.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'A lot of students applied this year.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Thanks a lot!'
mcq_question: Choose: There ___ a lot of cars on the road.
mcq_options: A) is  B) are  C) was being  D) be
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: She has ___ ___ ___ friends. → a lot of
find_and_fix_to_correct: I have alot of homework. → I have a lot of homework.
translate: मेरे पास बहुत काम है। → I have a lot of work.
write_your_own_sentence: Write three sentences with 'a lot of'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'a big amount or number (either type)'?
usage_tip: 'A lot' (without 'of') is used at the end: 'I like it a lot.'

simple_explanation: A small number, seen as enough (countable).
example_2: I have a few questions.
example_3: Wait a few minutes.
collocations: a few days, a few friends, a few times
grammar_pattern: a few + plural countable noun
common_mistake: A few money.
correct_version: A little money.
why_it_s_wrong: 'A few' is for countable nouns (a few friends). For uncountable nouns, use 'a little'.
etymology: a + few.
mnemonic: 'Kuch' (गिनने वाली चीज़ें) = a few.
memory_trick: 'A few' has a positive feel — a small, useful number.
visual_association: Three or four coins on a table.
difference_explained: A few = some, enough (positive). Few = almost none (negative): 'Few people came.'
mini_conversation: A: How many people are coming? / B: Just a few friends.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'I'll be back in a few minutes.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'A few shops were damaged in the storm.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Give me a few seconds!'
mcq_question: Choose: I need ___ eggs for the cake.
mcq_options: A) a little  B) a few  C) much  D) a lot
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: I have ___ ___ questions. → a few
find_and_fix_to_correct: I have a few money. → I have a little money.
translate: मेरे कुछ दोस्त दिल्ली में हैं। → I have a few friends in Delhi.
write_your_own_sentence: Write about a few things you bought this week.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'a small number, seen as enough (countable)'?
usage_tip: 'Quite a few' = a fairly large number.

simple_explanation: A small amount, seen as enough (uncountable).
example_2: Add a little sugar.
example_3: I speak a little French.
collocations: a little time, a little salt, a little help
grammar_pattern: a little + uncountable noun
common_mistake: A little people.
correct_version: A few people.
why_it_s_wrong: 'A little' is for uncountable nouns (a little milk). For countable nouns, use 'a few'.
pronunciation_tip: 'uh LIT-ul' — the T is soft in fast speech.
etymology: a + little.
mnemonic: 'Thoda sa' = a little.
memory_trick: 'A little' has a positive feel — a small, useful amount.
visual_association: A spoon with a little salt.
difference_explained: A little = some, enough (positive). Little = almost none: 'There's little hope.'
mini_conversation: A: Do you want milk in your tea? / B: Just a little, please.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'I'm a little tired today.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Prices fell a little last month.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Can you move a little? I can't see!'
mcq_options: A) a few  B) a little  C) many  D) few
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Add ___ ___ salt. → a little
find_and_fix_to_correct: There are a little people here. → There are a few people here.
translate: थोड़ा पानी दो। → Give me a little water.
write_your_own_sentence: Write three sentences with 'a little'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'a small amount, seen as enough (uncountable)'?
usage_tip: 'A little' also means 'slightly' before adjectives: 'a little late'.

simple_explanation: Go into a place.
example_2: Enter your password.
example_3: Nobody entered the room.
collocations: enter a room, enter a contest, enter data
action_sequence: Before: reach the door → During: walk in → After: you are inside
grammar_pattern: enter + object (no preposition needed)
common_mistake: Enter to the room.
correct_version: Enter the room.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Enter' already means 'go into', so no 'to' or 'in' after it.
etymology: Latin 'intrare'.
mnemonic: ENTER key — कंप्यूटर में 'अंदर' भेजने वाला बटन।
memory_trick: 'Enter' already means 'go into' — don't add another preposition.
visual_association: A door with an 'Entry' sign above it.
difference_explained: Enter = more formal. 'Go in' / 'come in' = everyday speech.
mini_conversation: A: How do I log in? / B: Enter your email and password.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Enter through the side gate.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Thieves entered the shop through the roof.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Did you enter the contest?'
mcq_options: A) enter into  B) enter  C) enter to  D) entering in
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Please ___ the room. → Enter
find_and_fix_to_correct: He entered in the classroom late. → He entered the classroom late.
translate: कमरे में चुपचाप दाखिल हो। → Enter the room quietly.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about entering a building.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'go into a place'?
usage_tip: For typing data, 'enter' is the right verb: 'Enter your PIN.'

simple_explanation: Go out of a place.
example_2: Exit the app and open it again.
example_3: Please exit by the rear door.
collocations: exit here, emergency exit, exit a program
action_sequence: Before: find the exit sign → During: walk out → After: you are outside
grammar_pattern: exit + (through) + place
common_mistake: Exit from the door.
correct_version: Exit through the back door.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Exit' already means 'go out', so 'from' before the door is wrong; you exit THROUGH or BY a door.
etymology: Latin 'exire' (go out).
mnemonic: EXIT = बाहर जाने का रास्ता।
memory_trick: 'Exit' can be a verb (to leave) or a noun (the way out).
visual_association: A green 'EXIT' sign.
difference_explained: Exit = formal, signs and apps. Leave = everyday.
mini_conversation: A: How do I close this program? / B: Just click 'Exit'.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Exit the metro at gate 3.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Fans exited the stadium calmly.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'I'm exiting this group chat!'
mcq_question: Choose: In case of fire, ___ by the stairs.
mcq_options: A) exit  B) exit from  C) exiting to  D) exits
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: ___ through the back door. → Exit
find_and_fix_to_correct: Exit from the building from the back. → Exit the building by the back door.
translate: पिछले दरवाज़े से बाहर निकलें। → Exit through the back door.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence using 'exit' for an app or a building.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'go out of a place'?
usage_tip: In everyday talk, 'leave' is more natural: 'Let's leave.'

simple_explanation: Go from one side to another.
example_2: Look both ways before you cross.
example_3: We crossed the river by boat.
collocations: cross the road, cross over, cross out
action_sequence: Before: look left and right → During: walk across → After: reach the other side
grammar_pattern: cross + object (road/river)
common_mistake: Cross of the street.
correct_version: Cross the street.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Cross' takes the road directly — no 'of'.
etymology: Old English 'cros'.
mnemonic: Zebra CROSSING — सड़क पार करने की जगह।
memory_trick: 'Cross' the street directly — no extra preposition.
visual_association: A zebra crossing.
difference_explained: Cross = verb (cross the road). Across = preposition (walk across the road).
mini_conversation: A: How do I get to the bank? / B: Cross the road and turn left.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Cross at the zebra crossing.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Thousands crossed the border last month.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Fingers crossed for tomorrow!'
mcq_question: Choose: Be careful when you ___ the road.
mcq_options: A) cross  B) across  C) crossing of  D) crosses
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: ___ the street carefully. → Cross
find_and_fix_to_correct: He crossed the road from the zebra crossing. → He crossed the road at the zebra crossing.
translate: सड़क ध्यान से पार करो। → Cross the road carefully.
write_your_own_sentence: Write directions using 'cross'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'go from one side to another'?
usage_tip: 'Keep your fingers crossed' = hope for good luck.

simple_explanation: Move very quickly.
example_1: We rushed to catch the bus.
example_2: Don't rush, we have time.
example_3: She rushed to the hospital.
collocations: rush hour, rush to, in a rush
action_sequence: Before: see you're late → During: move very fast → After: arrive out of breath
grammar_pattern: rush + to + place
common_mistake: Rush for catch the bus.
correct_version: Rush to catch the bus.
why_it_s_wrong: To give the purpose, 'rush' takes 'to' + verb, not 'for' + verb.
etymology: Old French 'ruser'.
mnemonic: RUSH hour — भीड़ और जल्दबाज़ी का समय।
memory_trick: 'Rush' + 'to' shows the urgent direction you're headed.
visual_association: People running for a train.
difference_explained: Very close. Rush = move fast, often too fast. Hurry = be quick.
mini_conversation: A: Why are you so late? / B: Rush-hour traffic!
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Don't rush your food, eat slowly.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Ambulances rushed the injured to hospital.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'No rush, take your time.'
mcq_options: A) for catch  B) to catch  C) catching  D) catch
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: We ___ed to catch the bus. → rushed
find_and_fix_to_correct: Don't do rush, drive slowly. → Don't rush, drive slowly.
translate: वह जल्दी से अस्पताल गई। → She rushed to the hospital.
write_your_own_sentence: Write about a time you had to rush.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'move very quickly'?
usage_tip: 'No rush' = take your time.

simple_explanation: Move by lifting and putting down your foot.
example_2: Step inside, please.
example_3: Mind the step.
collocations: step back, step by step, step forward
related_phrasal_verbs: step back, step in, step down
action_sequence: Before: lift your foot → During: put it forward → After: move one step
grammar_pattern: step + adverb (back/forward)
common_mistake: Step to back.
correct_version: Step back.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Back' is already a direction — no 'to'.
etymology: Old English 'steppan'.
mnemonic: STEP by step = कदम-दर-कदम।
memory_trick: Picture lifting one foot and setting it down — that's a 'step'.
visual_association: Feet on a staircase.
difference_explained: Step = one movement of the foot. Walk = many steps.
mini_conversation: A: Can I come in? / B: Sure, step inside.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Step back from the edge.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'The CEO stepped down after the scandal.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Watch your step, it's slippery!'
mcq_question: Choose: Please ___ aside and let her pass.
mcq_options: A) step  B) stepped  C) stepping to  D) steps to
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: ___ back, please. → Step
find_and_fix_to_correct: He steped on my foot. → He stepped on my foot.
translate: एक कदम पीछे हटो। → Step back.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence using 'step' and 'step by step'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'move by lifting and putting down your foot'?
usage_tip: 'Step down' = leave an important job.

simple_explanation: Move closer to something.
example_2: Winter is approaching.
example_3: Approach the problem calmly.
collocations: approach the topic, close approach, new approach
action_sequence: Before: see the target → During: move closer → After: now you're near
grammar_pattern: approach + object (no preposition)
common_mistake: Approach to the door.
correct_version: Approach the door.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Approach' takes the place directly — no 'to'.
etymology: Old French 'aprochier' (come near).
mnemonic: 'Approach road' — मुख्य सड़क तक पहुँचने वाली सड़क।
memory_trick: 'Approach' already means 'move toward' — no extra 'to' needed.
visual_association: A car moving toward a gate.
difference_explained: Approach = come nearer. Reach = arrive.
mini_conversation: A: Is the exam close? / B: Yes, it's approaching fast.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Slow down as you approach the school.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'A cyclone is approaching the coast.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'I approached her and said hi.'
mcq_question: Choose: The train is ___ the platform.
mcq_options: A) approaching to  B) approaching  C) approached to  D) approach at
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The storm is ___ing. → approaching
find_and_fix_to_correct: He approached to me for help. → He approached me for help.
translate: तूफ़ान पास आ रहा है। → The storm is approaching.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something that is approaching.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'move closer to something'?
usage_tip: As a noun, 'approach' = a way of doing: 'a new approach to teaching'.

simple_explanation: Arrive at, or stretch to touch.
example_1: We reached the top of the hill.
example_2: Call me when you reach home.
example_3: I can't reach the top shelf.
collocations: reach out, reach for, within reach
action_sequence: Before: travel for hours → During: arrive → After: call home
grammar_pattern: reach + object (no preposition)
common_mistake: Reach to the top.
correct_version: Reach the top.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Reach' takes the place directly — no 'to' or 'at'.
etymology: Old English 'rǣcan'.
mnemonic: 'Pahunch gaya' = reached.
memory_trick: 'Reach' already means 'arrive at' — skip the extra 'to'.
visual_association: A hand stretching to a high shelf.
difference_explained: Reach + place (reach home). Arrive + at/in (arrive at the station).
mini_conversation: A: Did you reach safely? / B: Yes, just now.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'I'll reach the office by ten.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Petrol prices reached a new high.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Reach home and text me!'
mcq_options: A) reached to  B) reached  C) arrived  D) reached at
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: We ___ed the top of the hill. → reached
find_and_fix_to_correct: I reached to home late. → I reached home late.
translate: मैं घर पहुँच गया। → I reached home.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about when you reach home every day.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'arrive at, or stretch to touch'?
usage_tip: 'Reach out' = contact someone to offer or ask for help.

simple_explanation: Think something will happen.
example_2: I expect it will rain.
example_3: We are expecting guests tonight.
collocations: expect to, expect a baby, as expected
action_sequence: Before: think it will happen → During: wait for it → After: it happens (or not)
grammar_pattern: expect + to + verb / expect + object
common_mistake: I expect you come early.
correct_version: I expect you to come early.
why_it_s_wrong: After 'expect' + person, use 'to' + verb: expect you to come.
etymology: Latin 'exspectare' (look out for).
mnemonic: 'Umeed karna' = expect.
memory_trick: 'Expect' + object + 'to + verb' is a very common pattern.
visual_association: A person looking at the door, waiting.
difference_explained: Expect = think something will happen. Wait = stay until it happens.
mini_conversation: A: When is the parcel coming? / B: I expect it today.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'I didn't expect so much traffic.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Prices are expected to rise.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'I knew it — as expected!'
mcq_question: Choose: My parents expect me ___ well.
mcq_options: A) do  B) to do  C) doing  D) did
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: I ___ it will rain. → expect
find_and_fix_to_correct: I am not expecting this from you. → I didn't expect this from you.
translate: मुझे उम्मीद है कि वह आएगा। → I expect him to come.
write_your_own_sentence: Write what you expect to happen tomorrow.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'think something will happen'?
usage_tip: 'She's expecting' = she is pregnant.

simple_explanation: Think something is probably true.
example_2: I suppose you're right.
example_3: You're supposed to be home by ten.
collocations: suppose so, I suppose, supposed to
action_sequence: Before: think it's probably true → During: say 'I suppose' → After: wait and see
grammar_pattern: suppose + (that) + clause
common_mistake: I am supposing you're right.
correct_version: I suppose you're right.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Suppose' (= think) is a state verb, so no -ing.
etymology: Latin 'supponere'.
mnemonic: 'Suppose karo' = maan lo।
memory_trick: 'Suppose' is a state verb — avoid the '-ing' form.
visual_association: A person shrugging.
difference_explained: I suppose = I think so. Be supposed to = it's the rule or plan.
mini_conversation: A: Is he coming? / B: I suppose so.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'We're supposed to wear formals on Monday.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'The road was supposed to open in May.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Suppose you win — what will you do?'
mcq_question: Choose: You ___ to be at school by eight.
mcq_options: A) suppose  B) are supposed  C) supposing  D) supposed
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: I ___ you're right. → suppose
find_and_fix_to_correct: I am supposing he is busy. → I suppose he is busy.
translate: मुझे लगता है तुम सही हो। → I suppose you're right.
write_your_own_sentence: Write one sentence with 'I suppose' and one with 'supposed to'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'think something is probably true'?
usage_tip: 'I suppose so' = a mild, unsure 'yes'.

simple_explanation: Have thoughts or pictures while sleeping.
example_2: Last night I dreamed about my school.
example_3: She dreams of becoming a pilot.
collocations: dream about, dream of, dream big
action_sequence: Before: fall asleep → During: see pictures in your mind → After: wake up
grammar_pattern: dream + about/of + noun
common_mistake: I dreamed about to fly.
correct_version: I dreamed about flying.
why_it_s_wrong: After 'about' or 'of', use the -ing form, not 'to' + verb.
etymology: Old English 'drēam' (joy).
mnemonic: 'Sapna' = dream.
memory_trick: 'Dream about/of' + '-ing' — night visions or big hopes.
visual_association: A cloud with pictures above a sleeping head.
difference_explained: Dream of = hope for (dream of success). Dream about = things you see while sleeping (and hopes too).
mini_conversation: A: What's your dream? / B: To open my own café.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'I dreamt I was flying!'
news_style_line: News-style: 'The village girl dreamed of the Olympics — and made it.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Keep dreaming!' (= that won't happen)

mnemonic: 'Achha lagta hai' = sounds good.
memory_trick: 'Sound' + adjective directly — how something seems by ear.
visual_association: A phone with sound waves.
difference_explained: Sound = your impression from hearing. Seem = from anything.
mini_conversation: A: Let's go for pizza. / B: Sounds good!

news_style_line: News-style: 'Experts say the idea sounds good on paper.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'You sound like my mom!'
mcq_options: A) sound  B) sounds  C) sounding  D) is sounding
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: That ___s fun. → sounds
find_and_fix_to_correct: It sounds like fun activity. → It sounds like a fun activity. / It sounds fun.

reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'seem a certain way, based on hearing'?
usage_tip: 'Sound like' + noun (sounds like a plan); 'sound' + adjective (sounds good).

simple_explanation: Have something that belongs to you.
example_2: Do you own a car?
example_3: She owns a small shop.
collocations: own a, on your own, own up
action_sequence: Before: save money → During: buy it → After: now it's yours
grammar_pattern: own + object
common_mistake: I own of a car.
correct_version: I own a car.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Own' takes the thing directly — no 'of'.

mnemonic: OWNER — मालिक।
memory_trick: 'Own' something directly — it belongs completely to you.
visual_association: A person holding house keys.
difference_explained: Own = it legally belongs to you. Have = general.
mini_conversation: A: Is this your flat? / B: Yes, we own it.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'I don't own a TV.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'The family owns three hotels.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'You act like you own the place!'
mcq_options: A) own  B) owns  C) owning  D) owns of
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: I ___ a small car. → own
find_and_fix_to_correct: Whose owner is this bag? → Who is the owner of this bag? / Whose bag is this?

write_your_own_sentence: Write about something you own that you love.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'have something that belongs to you'?
usage_tip: As an adjective: 'my own room' = a room only for me.

simple_explanation: Get something that was given or sent.
example_2: Did you receive my email?
example_3: She received an award.
collocations: receive from, receive a gift, well-received
action_sequence: Before: someone sends it → During: it arrives → After: you receive it
grammar_pattern: receive + object + from + person
common_mistake: I have received your letter yesterday.
correct_version: I received your letter yesterday.
why_it_s_wrong: With 'yesterday' (a finished time), use the simple past, not 'have received'.
spelling_tip: R-E-C-E-I-V-E: E before I after C.

mnemonic: 'Prapt karna' = receive.
memory_trick: 'Receive' = something arrives to you from someone else.
visual_association: A parcel at a door.
difference_explained: Receive = formal. Get = everyday.
mini_conversation: A: Did you receive the parcel? / B: Yes, this morning.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'I received your message, thanks.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'The hospital received 200 patients.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'I got your text!' (casual form of 'received')
mcq_options: A) have received  B) received  C) receive  D) receiving
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: I ___d your letter. → received
find_and_fix_to_correct: Please receive me at the station. → Please pick me up at the station.
translate: मुझे तुम्हारा पत्र मिला। → I received your letter.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a formal email line using 'receive'.

usage_tip: 'Receive someone at the airport' is Indian English; 'pick someone up' is common abroad.

simple_explanation: Say you are willing to give or do something.
example_2: Can I offer you some tea?
example_3: He offered to help.
collocations: offer to, offer a, kind offer
action_sequence: Before: see someone needs help → During: say you'll help → After: they accept or refuse
grammar_pattern: offer + person + object / offer + to + verb
common_mistake: She offered to me a job.
correct_version: She offered me a job.

mnemonic: Diwali OFFER — ख़ास छूट।
memory_trick: 'Offer' someone something directly — no extra 'to'.
visual_association: A host holding a tray.
difference_explained: Offer = say you'll give (they can say no). Give = hand over.
mini_conversation: A: Can I offer you a lift? / B: Oh, that's kind, thanks.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'She offered me a seat on the bus.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'The company offered jobs to 500 graduates.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Thanks for the offer!'

mcq_options: A) offered  B) offering  C) offered me to  D) offer to
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: She ___ed me a job. → offered
find_and_fix_to_correct: They gave me an offer letter to join. → They gave me an offer letter. / They offered me the job.

usage_tip: 'Offer to' + verb: 'He offered to drive.'

simple_explanation: Agree to take something.
example_2: I accept your offer.
example_3: Please accept my apology.
collocations: accept an, widely accepted, accept defeat
action_sequence: Before: get an offer → During: think about it → After: say yes
grammar_pattern: accept + object
common_mistake: I accept of your invitation.
correct_version: I accept your invitation.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Accept' takes the thing directly — no 'of'.
etymology: Latin 'acceptare'.
mnemonic: 'Sweekar karna' = accept.
memory_trick: 'Accept' something directly — you're saying yes to it.
visual_association: A hand taking a gift.
difference_explained: Accept = say yes / take. Except = but not (everyone except me).
mini_conversation: A: Will you accept the job? / B: Yes, I already said yes.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'We accept UPI and cards.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'The minister accepted the report.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Just accept it, yaar, and move on.'
mcq_options: A) except  B) accept  C) accept of  D) accepting
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: I ___ your invitation. → accept
find_and_fix_to_correct: Everyone came accept Rahul. → Everyone came except Rahul.

write_your_own_sentence: Write about an invitation you accepted.

reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'agree to take something'?

simple_explanation: Give something and get something else back.
example_2: India trades with many countries.
example_3: Do you want to trade seats?
collocations: trade with, trade for, fair trade
action_sequence: Before: have something → During: swap it → After: get something else
grammar_pattern: trade + object + for + object
common_mistake: They traded of toys.
correct_version: They traded toys.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Trade' takes the things directly — no 'of'.
etymology: Middle Low German 'trade' (track).
mnemonic: TRADER — व्यापारी।
memory_trick: 'Trade' items directly — swapping one thing for another.
visual_association: Two hands swapping cards.
difference_explained: Trade = buy and sell, or swap. Exchange = give and receive, often formal.
mini_conversation: A: I'll trade my samosa for your sandwich. / B: Deal!
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Kids trade cricket cards at school.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'The two countries will trade in local currencies.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Trade places with me, I want the window!'

mcq_options: A) traded  B) trade of  C) trading of  D) trades of
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: They ___d toys. → traded
find_and_fix_to_correct: I did trading of shares. → I traded shares.

simple_explanation: Give something someone needs.
example_2: The hotel provides free Wi-Fi.
example_3: Please provide your ID.
collocations: provide with, provide for, provider
action_sequence: Before: see a need → During: give what's needed → After: the need is met
grammar_pattern: provide + object + for + person
common_mistake: The hotel provides of towels.
correct_version: The hotel provides towels.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Provide' takes the thing directly — no 'of'. Provide someone WITH something.
etymology: Latin 'providere' (foresee).
mnemonic: Service PROVIDER — सुविधा देने वाला।
memory_trick: 'Provide' something needed — no extra preposition before the object.
visual_association: A hotel desk with towels.
difference_explained: Provide = supply what's needed (formal). Give = everyday.
mini_conversation: A: Do you provide lunch? / B: Yes, it's included.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Please provide a phone number.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'The government will provide free rations.'
casual_conversation: Casual: (too formal — say 'give')
mcq_question: Choose: The school provides students ___ books.
mcq_options: A) of  B) with  C) to  D) for
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The hotel ___s towels. → provides
find_and_fix_to_correct: They provided us of food. → They provided us with food. / They provided food for us.
translate: होटल तौलिए देता है। → The hotel provides towels.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a formal sentence with 'provide … with'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'give something someone needs'?
usage_tip: Two patterns: 'provide something to/for someone' or 'provide someone with something'.

simple_explanation: Give a needed amount of something.
example_2: The dairy supplies milk to the city.
example_3: Who supplies your vegetables?
collocations: supply with, supply and demand, in short supply
action_sequence: Before: have goods → During: send them regularly → After: shops receive them
grammar_pattern: supply + object + to + noun
common_mistake: They supplyed food.
correct_version: They supplied food.
why_it_s_wrong: After a consonant, Y becomes I before -ed: supplied.
etymology: Latin 'supplere' (fill up).
mnemonic: Water SUPPLY — पानी की आपूर्ति।
memory_trick: 'Supply' changes 'y' to 'ied' — like a larger, ongoing 'provide'.
visual_association: A truck unloading boxes.
difference_explained: Supply = regular delivery of goods. Provide = give what someone needs.
mini_conversation: A: Where does this shop get its bread? / B: A local bakery supplies it.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Who supplies water to our building?'
news_style_line: News-style: 'The factory supplies parts to car makers.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'We're running out of supplies!'
mcq_question: Choose: Farmers ___ vegetables to the market.
mcq_options: A) supplys  B) supply  C) supplies of  D) supplying of
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: They ___ food to schools. → supply
find_and_fix_to_correct: They supplyed food to the school. → They supplied food to the school.
translate: वे स्कूलों को खाना देते हैं। → They supply food to schools.
write_your_own_sentence: Write about who supplies milk or water to your home.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'give a needed amount of something'?
usage_tip: 'Supplies' (noun) = things you need: 'office supplies'.

simple_explanation: Move forward or improve.
example_2: Work on the bridge is progressing slowly.
example_3: How is your project progressing?
collocations: progress well, make progress, work in progress
action_sequence: Before: start the task → During: work step by step → After: get closer to the end
grammar_pattern: subject + progress(es)
common_mistake: Her health is progress well.
correct_version: Her health is progressing well.
why_it_s_wrong: After 'is', use the -ing form for a continuing action: 'is progressing'.
pronunciation_tip: Verb: stress on GRESS (pruh-GRES). Noun: stress on PRO (PROH-gres).
etymology: Latin 'progressus'.
mnemonic: PROGRESS report — आगे बढ़ने की रिपोर्ट।
memory_trick: 'Progress' as a verb needs '-ing' after 'is/are'.
visual_association: A chart line going up.
difference_explained: Progress = move forward. Improve = get better.
mini_conversation: A: How's your English? / B: It's progressing well, thanks.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'My fitness is progressing slowly.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Talks are progressing, officials said.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Any progress on the job hunt?'
mcq_options: A) progress  B) progressing  C) progressed to  D) progresses to
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Her health is ___ing well. → progressing
find_and_fix_to_correct: I made a lot of progresses. → I made a lot of progress.
translate: मेरी पढ़ाई अच्छी चल रही है। → My studies are progressing well.
write_your_own_sentence: Write about something that is progressing in your life.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'move forward or improve'?
usage_tip: As a noun, 'progress' is uncountable — no 'a' and no -s.

simple_explanation: Become worse or smaller.

example_3: She politely declined the offer.
collocations: decline in, sharp decline, politely decline
action_sequence: Before: numbers were high → During: they go down → After: the graph drops
grammar_pattern: subject + decline(s)
common_mistake: His health decline last year.
correct_version: His health declined last year.

mnemonic: 'Decline' = घटना / मना करना।
memory_trick: 'Decline' means getting worse, or politely saying 'no thanks'.
visual_association: A graph going down.
difference_explained: Decline = politely say no (formal). Refuse = say no firmly.
mini_conversation: A: Did he take the job? / B: No, he declined.

news_style_line: News-style: 'Car sales declined for the third month.'

fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: His health ___d. → declined
find_and_fix_to_correct: His health declined of years passed. → His health declined over the years.

spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'become worse or smaller'?

simple_explanation: Harm or hurt something.

example_3: Don't damage the book.
collocations: damage to, badly damaged, damage control
action_sequence: Before: something hits hard → During: parts break → After: it needs repair
grammar_pattern: damage + object
common_mistake: The storm damaged of the roof.
correct_version: The storm damaged the roof.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Damage' takes the thing directly — no 'of'.

memory_trick: 'Damage' harms something, but doesn't always destroy it completely.
visual_association: A car with a dent.
difference_explained: Damage = things. Hurt = people and feelings.
mini_conversation: A: What happened to your phone? / B: I dropped it and damaged the screen.

news_style_line: News-style: 'The flood damaged 200 houses.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Ugh, the damage is done now.'
mcq_question: Choose: The storm badly ___ the roof.
mcq_options: A) damaged  B) damaged of  C) damaging to  D) damages of
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The storm ___d the roof. → damaged
find_and_fix_to_correct: There was a lot of damages. → There was a lot of damage.

write_your_own_sentence: Write about something that got damaged at home.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'harm or hurt something'?
usage_tip: As a noun, 'damage' is uncountable: 'a lot of damage' (no -s).

simple_explanation: Spoil something completely.

example_3: Don't ruin the surprise!

action_sequence: Before: have a plan → During: something goes wrong → After: the plan is spoiled
grammar_pattern: ruin + object
common_mistake: The rain ruined of our picnic.
correct_version: The rain ruined our picnic.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Ruin' takes the thing directly — no 'of'.

memory_trick: 'Ruin' spoils something completely — a picnic, a surprise, a plan.

difference_explained: Ruin = destroy completely. Spoil = make worse (food spoils).
mini_conversation: A: How was the trip? / B: The rain ruined it.

news_style_line: News-style: 'The fire ruined the old market.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'You ruined the ending — no spoilers!'

mcq_options: A) ruined  B) ruined of  C) ruins of  D) ruining of

find_and_fix_to_correct: Stop to ruin my mood. → Stop ruining my mood.

write_your_own_sentence: Write about a time something ruined your plan.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'spoil something completely'?
usage_tip: 'Ruins' (plural noun) = remains of old buildings.

news_style_line: News-style: 'Five parties formed a new alliance.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Ice formed on the window overnight.'

fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Clouds ___ in the sky. → form
find_and_fix_to_correct: The friends forms a group. → The friends form a group.

simple_explanation: Let something happen.

example_3: Phones are not allowed in the exam.

mnemonic: 'Anumati dena' = allow.

casual_conversation: Casual: 'Am I allowed to sit here?'

find_and_fix_to_correct: They don't allow me go out. → They don't allow me to go out.

write_your_own_sentence: Write two things your school or office doesn't allow.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'let something happen'?

simple_explanation: Make someone do something against their will.

example_3: They forced the door open.
collocations: force to, by force, workforce
action_sequence: Before: say no → During: they push you → After: you do it unwillingly
grammar_pattern: force + object + to + verb
common_mistake: Don't force him eat.
correct_version: Don't force him to eat.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Force' + person + 'to' + verb: force him to eat.
etymology: Latin 'fortis' (strong).
mnemonic: Air FORCE — ताकत वाली सेना।
memory_trick: 'Force' someone 'to' do something they don't want to do.
visual_association: A hand pushing a stuck door.
difference_explained: Force = strong, often unfair. Make = everyday (make him eat — no 'to').
mini_conversation: A: Why did you quit? / B: They forced me to work weekends.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Don't force the zip, it'll break.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Floods forced 5,000 people to leave their homes.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Nobody's forcing you, relax!'

fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Don't ___ him to eat. → force
find_and_fix_to_correct: They forced us for signing. → They forced us to sign.

write_your_own_sentence: Write about a time you were forced to change plans.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'make someone do something against their will'?
usage_tip: 'Make' needs no 'to': 'They made me wait.' 'Force' does: 'They forced me to wait.'

simple_explanation: Try to do something.

example_3: Attempt all questions.

grammar_pattern: attempt + to + verb

why_it_s_wrong: 'Attempt' + another verb needs 'to': attempt to fix.

mnemonic: 'Koshish' = attempt.
memory_trick: 'Attempt' is a more formal word for 'try'.
visual_association: A high-jumper mid-jump.
difference_explained: Attempt = formal 'try'.
mini_conversation: A: Did you finish the paper? / B: I attempted all the questions.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Attempt the easy questions first.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Police stopped an attempt to rob the bank.'

simple_explanation: Mostly true, in general.
example_2: Generally, I agree with you.
example_3: The weather is generally good in March.
collocations: generally speaking, generally agree, generally true
grammar_pattern: subject + generally + verb
common_mistake: Generally I am agree with you.
correct_version: Generally, I agree with you.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Agree' is a verb — 'am' before it is wrong.

mnemonic: 'Aam taur par' = generally.
memory_trick: 'Generally speaking' is a great phrase to introduce a broad opinion.
visual_association: A big umbrella over many people.
difference_explained: Generally = mostly true for most people. Usually = what happens most times.

fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: ___, I agree with you. → Generally

write_your_own_sentence: Write something that is generally true about your city.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'mostly true, in general'?
usage_tip: 'Generally speaking' = talking about most cases.

simple_explanation: In front, further forward.
example_2: Go straight ahead.
example_3: Plan ahead for the exam.
collocations: go ahead, straight ahead, plan ahead
grammar_pattern: verb + ahead
common_mistake: Look to ahead.
correct_version: Look straight ahead.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Ahead' already shows direction — no 'to' before it.
etymology: a- + head.
mnemonic: 'Aage' = ahead.
memory_trick: 'Ahead' means further forward — no extra preposition needed.
visual_association: A road going straight forward.
difference_explained: Ahead = in front, or in the future. Forward = toward the front.
mini_conversation: A: Where's the station? / B: Keep walking — it's just ahead.

news_style_line: News-style: 'India is ahead in the series 2–1.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Go ahead, start eating!'

write_your_own_sentence: Write directions using 'straight ahead'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'in front, further forward'?
usage_tip: 'Go ahead' = yes, you can start.

simple_explanation: Very likely.
example_2: I'll probably be late.
example_3: It's probably going to rain.
collocations: probably not, will probably, probably right
grammar_pattern: subject + will + probably + verb
common_mistake: It will rain probably.
correct_version: It will probably rain.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Probably' usually goes after 'will' and before the main verb: 'will probably rain'.
etymology: probable + -ly.
mnemonic: 'Shayad' = probably.
memory_trick: 'Probably' usually sits right before the main verb.
visual_association: A 70% weather sign.
difference_explained: Probably = more sure (about 70–80%). Maybe = 50–50.
mini_conversation: A: Are you coming tonight? / B: Probably, if I finish work.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'He's probably stuck in traffic.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Prices will probably rise next month.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Probably not, sorry!'

write_your_own_sentence: Write two things you will probably do tomorrow.

reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'very likely'?
usage_tip: 'Probably not' = a soft no.

simple_explanation: Possibly; maybe.
example_2: Perhaps we should wait.
example_3: Perhaps she didn't hear you.
collocations: perhaps not, perhaps so, perhaps later
grammar_pattern: Perhaps + clause
common_mistake: Perhaps she forget.
correct_version: Perhaps she forgot.
why_it_s_wrong: The action finished in the past, so use the past tense 'forgot'.
etymology: per + hap (luck).
mnemonic: 'Shayad' = perhaps.
memory_trick: 'Perhaps' is a slightly more formal cousin of 'maybe'.
visual_association: A person thinking with a hand on the chin.
difference_explained: Same meaning. 'Perhaps' is a little more formal.
mini_conversation: A: Where is Anil? / B: Perhaps he's still at lunch.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Perhaps we can meet on Friday.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'This is perhaps the best film of the year.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Perhaps, perhaps not!'

mcq_options: A) Perhaps  B) Perhap  C) Perhaps to  D) May

find_and_fix_to_correct: Perhaps he will comes. → Perhaps he will come.

simple_explanation: In addition; too.

example_3: She plays the guitar, and sings as well.

common_mistake: As well I want to come.

memory_trick: 'As well' sits at the END of the sentence, unlike 'also' or 'too'.
visual_association: A plus sign at the end of a line.
difference_explained: As well = at the end. Also = in the middle (I also want).
mini_conversation: A: I'm getting pizza. / B: I'll have one as well.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Bring your ID and a photo as well.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'The minister visited the hospital as well.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Me as well!'

simple_explanation: Used to add emphasis to something surprising.
example_2: Even my dad likes this song.
example_3: It's even hotter today.
collocations: even so, even if, even though
grammar_pattern: even + subject/noun (emphasis)
common_mistake: Even my dad like it.
correct_version: Even my dad likes it.
why_it_s_wrong: 'My dad' is one person, so the verb takes -s: 'likes'.
etymology: Old English 'efne'.
mnemonic: 'Even' = तक / भी (surprise)।
memory_trick: 'Even' adds surprise: this is unexpected, but true anyway.
visual_association: A surprised face.
difference_explained: Even = surprising addition (even the teacher laughed). Also = normal addition.
mini_conversation: A: Did everyone like the film? / B: Yes, even my grandma!
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Even a small donation helps.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Even experts were surprised by the result.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'I didn't even know!'
mcq_options: A) even  B) also  C) too  D) ever
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: ___ my dad likes it. → Even
find_and_fix_to_correct: He didn't even not call me. → He didn't even call me.
translate: मेरी दादी को भी यह पसंद है। → Even my grandmother likes it.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence with 'even' to show surprise.

reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'used to add emphasis to something surprising'?
usage_tip: 'Even if' = whatever happens: 'I'll come even if it rains.'

simple_explanation: Right after this.
example_2: What should I do next?
example_3: See you next week.
collocations: what's next, next time, right next
grammar_pattern: next + noun / What's next?
common_mistake: What is next on list?
correct_version: What's next on the list?
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'the' before 'list', and 'next' with no 'the' for time: 'next week'.
etymology: Old English 'nēhst' (nearest).
mnemonic: 'Agla' = next.
memory_trick: 'Next' can be an adjective (next time) or adverb (do this next).
visual_association: A 'Next ▶' button.
difference_explained: Next = the one after this. Last = the one before this (last week).
mini_conversation: A: When is the next bus? / B: In ten minutes.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Who's next in line?'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Elections will be held next year.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'What's next — pizza or a movie?'

fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: What's ___ on the list? → next

spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review

simple_explanation: Used to correct or add surprising information.
example_2: Actually, I'm from Delhi, not Mumbai.
example_3: Did he actually say that?
collocations: actually, I, quite actually (unusual, just 'actually')
grammar_pattern: Actually, + clause (correction/emphasis)
common_mistake: Actually, I am agree with you.
correct_version: Actually, I agree with you.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Agree' is a verb, so it doesn't need 'am'.
etymology: actual + -ly.
mnemonic: 'Asal mein' = actually.
memory_trick: 'Actually' politely corrects, or adds a surprising true detail.
visual_association: A person raising a finger to correct.
difference_explained: Actually = in fact. It does NOT mean 'now' — use 'currently' for that.
mini_conversation: A: You're a teacher, right? / B: Actually, I'm a nurse.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Actually, I've changed my mind.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'The report shows prices actually fell.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'I actually liked the film!'
mcq_question: Choose: 'Is it far?' '___, it's just five minutes away.'
mcq_options: A) Actually  B) Actual  C) Currently  D) Really to
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: ___, I think you're right. → Actually
find_and_fix_to_correct: Actually what happened is that actually I missed the bus. → Actually, I missed the bus.
translate: असल में मैं दिल्ली से हूँ। → Actually, I'm from Delhi.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence correcting someone politely with 'actually'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review

usage_tip: Don't overuse 'actually' — many Indian speakers start every sentence with it.

simple_explanation: Moving in the opposite direction.

example_3: She lives away from her family.
collocations: stay away from, run away from, far away from
grammar_pattern: verb + away from + noun
common_mistake: Stay away the edge.
correct_version: Stay away from the edge.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Away' needs 'from' before the place or thing.
etymology: away + from.
mnemonic: 'Se door' = away from.
memory_trick: 'Away from' shows movement to a distance, in the opposite direction.
visual_association: A 'Keep away' warning sign.
difference_explained: Away from = in the opposite direction, separated. Far from = a long distance.
mini_conversation: A: Where do you study? / B: Away from home, in Pune.

usage_tip: 'Away from home' = not living with your family.

simple_explanation: Added to; in addition to.

example_3: The price is ₹500, plus tax.

grammar_pattern: number + plus + number

correct_version: Two plus two is four.
why_it_s_wrong: In maths, English says 'plus', not 'add'.

mnemonic: '+' = plus.
memory_trick: 'Plus' is the everyday math word for 'added to'.

difference_explained: Plus = maths or 'also, in addition'. And = general joining.

grammar_pattern: number + minus + number
common_mistake: Five less two is three.
correct_version: Five minus two is three.
why_it_s_wrong: In maths, English says 'minus', not 'less' or 'subtract'.
etymology: Latin 'minus' (less).
mnemonic: '−' = minus.
memory_trick: 'Minus' is the everyday math word for 'subtract'.
visual_association: A minus sign on a thermometer.
difference_explained: Minus = maths and temperature. Less = a smaller amount (less sugar).

simple_explanation: For that reason (informal).
example_1: It was raining, that's why I was late.
example_2: I missed the bus. That's why I'm late.
example_3: He was ill — that's why he didn't come.
collocations: and that's why, that's why I
grammar_pattern: clause. That's why + clause
common_mistake: That's why I was late because it was raining.
correct_version: It was raining. That's why I was late.
why_it_s_wrong: 'That's why' and 'because' both give the reason — use one, not both.
etymology: that is + why.
mnemonic: 'Isliye' = that's why.
memory_trick: 'That's why' informally links a cause to its obvious result.
visual_association: An arrow from 'cause' to 'result'.
difference_explained: That's why = reason first, then result. Because = result first, then reason.
mini_conversation: A: Why are you so happy? / B: I got the job — that's why!
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'It's raining. That's why I'm taking the car.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Costs went up; that's why fares rose, the company said.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Ohh, that's why you called!'

mcq_options: A) Because  B) That's why  C) So that  D) Why
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: It was raining, ___ ___ I was late. → That's why
find_and_fix_to_correct: Because it was raining, that's why I stayed home. → It was raining. That's why I stayed home.

write_your_own_sentence: Write a reason and result with 'That's why'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'for that reason (informal)'?
usage_tip: 'So' works the same way and is shorter: 'It was raining, so I stayed home.'

simple_explanation: On each occasion that.

example_2: Every time I call, he's busy.
example_3: She smiles every time she sees him.

why_it_s_wrong: After 'every time' + it/he/she, the present verb takes -s: 'every time it rains'.

mnemonic: 'Jab bhi' = every time.
memory_trick: 'Every time' introduces a pattern that repeats, again and again.

difference_explained: Same meaning. 'Whenever' is one word and a bit more general.
mini_conversation: A: Why do you carry an umbrella? / B: Every time I don't, it rains!

news_style_line: News-style: 'Every time it rains, the underpass floods.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Every time, yaar! Every single time!'

find_and_fix_to_correct: Everytime I call, he doesn't pick up. → Every time I call, he doesn't pick up.
