usage_tip: Pair: physically / mentally.

simple_explanation: In a way related to the mind.
example_2: I'm mentally tired after exams.
example_3: Prepare yourself mentally for the interview.
collocations: mentally strong, mentally tired, mentally prepared, mentally healthy
grammar_pattern: mentally + adjective / verb + mentally
common_mistake: I am mental tired.
correct_version: I am mentally tired.
why_it_s_wrong: Before an adjective, use the adverb 'mentally'.
etymology: From 'mental', from Latin mens, 'mind', + -ly.
mnemonic: MENTALLY → about the MIND (mens).
memory_trick: Kind language: never use 'mental' as an insult.
visual_association: A person meditating calmly on a mat.
difference_explained: Emotionally = about feelings. Mentally = about the mind and thinking.
mini_conversation:
A: You look exhausted.
B: Not physically — mentally. Too many deadlines.
everyday_scene: Everyday: The shepherd is mentally sharp even at ninety.
news_style_line: News-style: Experts say sports keep children mentally healthy.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Mentally, I'm already on my weekend.'
mcq_options: A) mentally  B) mental  C) mentality  D) mentaly
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Meditation helps me stay ______ calm. → mentally
find_and_fix_to_correct: He is mental strong. → He is mentally strong.
translate: वह मानसिक रूप से मज़बूत है। → She's mentally strong.
write_your_own_sentence: Write two habits that keep you mentally healthy.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which adverb means 'related to the mind'?
usage_tip: Feeling low for long? Talk to someone you trust.

hindi_meaning: बुरी तरह से, गंभीर रूप से
simple_explanation: Very badly or seriously; very strictly.
example_2: The crops were severely damaged.
example_3: She was severely punished.
collocations: severely injured, severely damaged, severely affected, severely punished
grammar_pattern: severely + past participle/adjective
common_mistake: He was severe injured.
correct_version: He was severely injured.
why_it_s_wrong: Before a past participle, use the adverb 'severely'.
spelling_tip: SEVERE + LY: keep the E — severELY.
etymology: From 'severe', from Latin severus, + -ly.
mnemonic: SEVERELY → in a SEVERE way.
memory_trick: News phrase: 'severely affected areas'.
visual_association: A tree split in half after a storm.
difference_explained: Very close. 'Severely' stresses damage or strictness.
mini_conversation:
A: How bad was the flood?
B: Our village was severely affected.
everyday_scene: Everyday: The hailstorm severely damaged the farmer's wheat.
news_style_line: News-style: Several districts were severely affected by the cyclone.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Severely addicted to chai. No treatment needed.'
mcq_options: A) severely  B) severe  C) severity  D) severly
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The ______ of the storm surprised everyone. → severity
find_and_fix_to_correct: The house was severe damaged. → The house was severely damaged.
translate: वह बुरी तरह घायल हो गया। → He was severely injured.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a news-style sentence using 'severely'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review

usage_tip: Opposite: mildly.

simple_explanation: In a bad way; seriously; very much.
example_2: She sings badly.
example_3: I need a holiday badly.
collocations: badly hurt, badly damaged, play badly, need something badly, go badly
grammar_pattern: verb + badly / badly + past participle
common_mistake: I feel badly about it.
correct_version: I feel bad about it.
why_it_s_wrong: After 'feel' (a linking verb), use the adjective 'bad'.
etymology: From 'bad' + -ly.
mnemonic: BADLY → in a BAD way.
memory_trick: Comparatives: badly – worse – worst.
visual_association: A cracked phone screen after a fall.
difference_explained: Bad = adjective (after 'feel', 'look'). Badly = adverb (after action verbs).
mini_conversation:
A: How did the interview go?
B: Badly — I forgot my own CV details!
everyday_scene: Everyday: The farmer's cart was badly damaged in the storm.
news_style_line: News-style: The team played badly and lost by 50 runs.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Badly need a nap. Urgently.'
mcq_question: 'I feel ___ that I missed your birthday.'
mcq_options: A) bad  B) badly  C) worse  D) baddly
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The old bridge is ______ in need of repair. → badly
find_and_fix_to_correct: He feels badly about his mistake. → He feels bad about his mistake.
translate: वह बुरी तरह घायल हुआ। → He was badly hurt.
write_your_own_sentence: Write about a time something went badly and what you learned.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which adverb means 'in a bad way' or 'very much'?
usage_tip: Remember: feel BAD, do something BADLY.

simple_explanation: Completely.
example_2: The hotel is fully booked.
example_3: I fully agree with you.
collocations: fully recovered, fully booked, fully aware, fully understand, fully vaccinated
grammar_pattern: fully + past participle/adjective / verb + fully
common_mistake: He is full recovered now.
correct_version: He is fully recovered now.
why_it_s_wrong: Before a past participle, use 'fully'.
spelling_tip: FULL + Y = FULLY: keep the double L.
etymology: From 'full' + -ly.
mnemonic: FULLY → FULL, 100%.
memory_trick: Common: 'fully charged', 'fully booked'.
visual_association: A battery icon showing 100%.
difference_explained: Same meaning. 'Fully' is common with 'recovered', 'booked', 'aware'.
mini_conversation:
A: Is your father well now?
B: Yes, he's fully recovered after the surgery.
everyday_scene: Everyday: The farmer waited until the wheat was fully ripe.
news_style_line: News-style: All trains to Patna are fully booked before Chhath.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Fully charged phone. Half-charged me.'
mcq_question: 'Please make sure your phone is ___ charged.'
mcq_options: A) fully  B) full  C) fullly  D) fulled
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: I ______ understand your problem. → fully
find_and_fix_to_correct: She is full aware of the rules. → She is fully aware of the rules.
translate: वह पूरी तरह ठीक हो गया है। → He has fully recovered.
write_your_own_sentence: Write about something you fully believe in.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which adverb means 'completely'?
usage_tip: Spelling: fully (double l).

simple_explanation: Because of (formal).
example_1: Owing to heavy rain, the match was cancelled.
example_2: The flight was delayed owing to fog.
example_3: Owing to illness, he missed the exam.
collocations: owing to bad weather, owing to a shortage, owing to technical problems
grammar_pattern: owing to + noun
common_mistake: Owing to he was ill, he stayed home.
correct_version: Owing to his illness, he stayed home. / Because he was ill, he stayed home.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Owing to' + noun, not a full clause.
spelling_tip: OWING TO: 'owing' from 'owe' (drop the E). Two words.
etymology: From 'owe' — as if the result is 'owed' to a cause.
mnemonic: OWING TO → the result is OWED TO this cause.
memory_trick: Formal twin of 'because of' — perfect for notices.
visual_association: A notice board: 'Owing to repairs, the office is closed'.
synonyms: because of, due to, on account of
difference_explained: Very close. 'Owing to' usually starts a phrase; 'due to' often follows 'be'.
related_words: because of, due to, reason, cause
mini_conversation:
A: Why is the train late?
B: Owing to a technical fault near Kanpur.
everyday_scene: Everyday: Owing to the drought, the farmer sold two cows.
news_style_line: News-style: Owing to low demand, the factory cut production.
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Owing to extreme laziness, the gym plan is postponed.'
mcq_options: A) Owing to  B) Owing  C) Owing to that  D) Owning to
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: The meeting was postponed ______ the minister's absence. → owing to
find_and_fix_to_correct: Owing to it rained, we stayed in. → Owing to the rain, we stayed in.
translate: भारी बारिश के कारण मैच रद्द हो गया। → Owing to heavy rain, the match was cancelled.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a formal notice using 'owing to'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review

usage_tip: Don't confuse with 'owning' (possessing).

simple_explanation: The everyday spoken form of 'yes'.

example_3: Oh yeah, I forgot!
collocations: yeah right, oh yeah, yeah sure
grammar_pattern: Yeah, + clause
common_mistake: Yeah sir, I'll send the file.
correct_version: Yes, sir, I'll send the file.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Yeah' is casual — with teachers, bosses and customers, say 'yes'.
etymology: Casual form of 'yes', 1900s.
mnemonic: 'Haan' (casual) = yeah.
memory_trick: YEAH for friends, YES for formal.
visual_association: Two friends nodding.
difference_explained: Yeah = casual. Yes = all situations.
mini_conversation: A: Want to get chai? / B: Yeah, let's go.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Yeah, I saw the message.'
news_style_line: News-style: (not used in formal news)
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Yeah right!' (= I don't believe you)

mcq_options: A) Yeah  B) Yep  C) Yes, I can.  D) Ya ya

find_and_fix_to_correct: Yeah yeah yeah, I know. → Yes, I know.

simple_explanation: A sound you make while you think of what to say.
example_2: It's, uh, about ten kilometres.
example_3: Uh, can I ask something?
collocations: uh-huh, uh-oh
grammar_pattern: Uh, + clause
common_mistake: Aaa… I think… aaa…
correct_version: Uh… I think…
why_it_s_wrong: English speakers pause with 'uh' or 'um', not a long 'aaa'.
etymology: Imitation of a sound.
mnemonic: 'Uh' = सोचने की छोटी आवाज़।
memory_trick: UH / UM = thinking sounds. Use a few, not in every sentence.
visual_association: A person scratching their head.
difference_explained: Uh = thinking pause. Uh-oh = 'there's a problem'.
mini_conversation: A: What's the capital of Australia? / B: Uh… Canberra?
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Uh, excuse me, is this seat free?'
news_style_line: News-style: (not used in formal news)
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Uh-oh, I dropped my phone.'
mcq_question: Choose: Which sound shows 'something went wrong'?
mcq_options: A) uh  B) um  C) uh-oh  D) hmm
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: 'It's, ___, around the corner.' → uh
find_and_fix_to_correct: Uh uh uh uh I don't know. → Uh, I don't know.

write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence with one natural 'uh' pause.

simple_explanation: A sound you make while you think, or when you feel unsure.
example_2: I think it's, um, Tuesday.
example_3: Um, sorry, what?
collocations: um, uh
grammar_pattern: Um, + clause
common_mistake: Hmm hmm, I think… (while thinking of words)
correct_version: Um, I think…
why_it_s_wrong: 'Hmm' is for thinking about an idea; 'um' fills a pause while you find words.
etymology: Imitation of a sound.
mnemonic: 'Um' = रुककर सोचने की आवाज़।
memory_trick: UM = a polite pause.
visual_association: A person looking up, thinking.
difference_explained: Um = pause for words. Hmm = thinking about an idea.
mini_conversation: A: Where's the report? / B: Um, I'll send it in five minutes.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Um, is this the right bus?'
news_style_line: News-style: (not used in formal news)
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Um, no thanks!'
mcq_question: Choose: A pause while you look for a word:
mcq_options: A) Wow  B) Um  C) Ouch  D) Yay
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: 'It's, ___, hard to explain.' → um
find_and_fix_to_correct: Um um um, the answer is five. → Um, the answer is five.
translate: अम… मैं कुछ कहूँ? → Um, can I say something?
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence with one 'um'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'a sound you make while you think, or when you feel unsure'?
usage_tip: Too many 'um's sound nervous — practise short pauses instead.

simple_explanation: A sound that shows surprise, or asks someone to repeat.

example_3: Nice, huh?

difference_explained: Huh? = what?/surprise. Uh-huh = yes.

news_style_line: News-style: (not used in formal news)
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Cool, huh?'

write_your_own_sentence: Write a casual sentence ending in '…, huh?'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'a sound that shows surprise, or asks someone to repeat'?
usage_tip: '…, huh?' at the end asks for agreement: 'Hot today, huh?'

simple_explanation: A sound that shows you understand, or feel relief or pleasure.

casual_conversation: Casual: 'Ah well, never mind.'

simple_explanation: An unspecified or unknown person -- the same meaning as "someone." "Somebody" refers to an unspecified person, just like "someone" -- the two words are interchangeable, with "somebody" sounding a bit more casual.
example_2: Somebody needs to fix this printer.
example_3: I heard somebody knocking on the door.
collocations: somebody else, somebody important, somebody said
grammar_pattern: somebody + singular verb (Somebody is at the gate.)
common_mistake: Somebody are waiting outside for you.
correct_version: Somebody is waiting outside for you.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Somebody' always takes a singular verb.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the first syllable: SUM-buh-dee: /ˈsʌmbədi/.
spelling_tip: One word -- "somebody," not "some body" (which would literally mean "some physical body").
etymology: Formed from "some" + "body" in Middle English, where "body" originally meant "person" (as still seen in "anybody," "everybody").
mnemonic: SOME + BODY = some (unspecified) person's "body," i.e., a person.
memory_trick: SOME + BODY: one person.
visual_association: A shadow moving just out of sight around a corner.
emotion_feel: Neutral, sometimes uneasy or urgent depending on context
difference_explained: Same meaning. Somebody is slightly more informal.
mini_conversation:
A: I think somebody's at the door.
B: I'll go check who it is.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character glances over their shoulder and mutters, 'Somebody's watching us.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Somebody reported seeing smoke near the old warehouse this morning.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Can somebody grab me a glass of water?'
mcq_options: A) No person  B) An unspecified person  C) Every person  D) A specific named person
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: ______ needs to answer that phone call. → Somebody
find_and_fix_to_correct: Somebody forgot his umbrella, don't they? → Somebody forgot his umbrella, didn't they?
translate: किसी ने लाइट जलती छोड़ दी। → Somebody left the lights on.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about somebody you met today.

usage_tip: 'Somebody' is slightly more informal than 'someone'.

simple_explanation: All the people in a group -- the same meaning as "everyone." "Everybody" is the more casual twin of "everyone" -- both mean "all the people," but "everybody" is grammatically singular.
example_2: Everybody clapped when the show ended.
example_3: Not everybody agrees with the new rule.
collocations: everybody else, everybody knows, everybody agrees
grammar_pattern: everybody + singular verb (Everybody wants to succeed.)
common_mistake: Everybody were happy with the results.
correct_version: Everybody was happy with the results.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Everybody' takes a singular verb: 'Everybody was happy'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the first syllable: EV-ree-buh-dee: /ˈevribədi/.
spelling_tip: One word -- "everybody," not "every body," which would literally mean "each physical body."
etymology: Formed from "every" + "body" in Middle English, using "body" in its older sense of "person"; means all people in a group.
mnemonic: EVERY + BODY = every single person, all together.
memory_trick: EVERY + BODY: each person.
visual_association: A crowded stadium with everyone cheering together.
difference_explained: Same meaning. Everybody is slightly more informal.
mini_conversation:
A: Did everybody enjoy the concert?
B: Yes, everybody had a great time.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A performer bows to the crowd and shouts, 'Thank you, everybody -- you were amazing tonight!'
news_style_line: News-style: 'The mayor said everybody should stay informed about the upcoming changes.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Everybody's excited about the long weekend.'
mcq_options: A) One specific person  B) All the people in a group  C) No people  D) Only the speaker
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: ______ enjoyed the fireworks display last night. → Everybody
find_and_fix_to_correct: Everybody are welcome to the barbecue. → Everybody is welcome to the barbecue.
translate: हर किसी को एक अच्छी कहानी पसंद है। → Everybody loves a good story.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about something everybody likes.

reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'all the people in a group -- the same meaning as "everyone."'?
usage_tip: 'Everybody knows that…' introduces common knowledge.

simple_explanation: Not a single person; the same meaning as "no one." "Nobody" means there isn't even one person present or willing -- like "no one," it's already negative on its own.
example_2: Nobody believed his excuse.
example_3: There was nobody in the office when I called.
collocations: nobody else, nobody knows, nobody cares, nobody's perfect
related_phrasal_verbs: no one, not a single soul
where_it_s_used: Describing absence, disappointment, blame, empty spaces
grammar_pattern: nobody + singular verb, no additional negative (Nobody is here. NOT "Nobody isn't here.")
common_mistake: Nobody doesn't want to help.
correct_version: Nobody wants to help.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Nobody' is already negative, so don't add 'doesn't'.
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the first syllable: NO-buh-dee: /ˈnoʊbədi/.
spelling_tip: One word -- "nobody," not "no body," which would literally mean "no physical body."
etymology: Formed from "no" + "body" in Middle English, using "body" in its older sense of "person"; means not a single person.
mnemonic: NO + BODY = not even a single person.
memory_trick: NO + BODY: no person.
visual_association: A single empty chair in the middle of a large, silent room.
emotion_feel: Often carries disappointment, loneliness, or frustration
difference_explained: Same meaning. Nobody is slightly more informal.
mini_conversation:
A: Who's going to volunteer for this task?
B: Looks like nobody wants to.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character stares at the empty stage and says quietly, 'Nobody's coming to save us -- we have to do this ourselves.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Officials said nobody has claimed responsibility for the damage yet.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Nobody told me the store closes early on Sundays.'
mcq_options: A) Everyone  B) Not a single person  C) A group of people  D) A specific person
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: ______ wanted to admit the mistake. → Nobody
find_and_fix_to_correct: Nobody don't like being ignored. → Nobody likes being ignored.
translate: मीटिंग में कोई नहीं आया। → Nobody came to the meeting.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence using 'nobody'.

reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'not a single person; the same meaning as "no one."'?
usage_tip: 'Nobody's perfect' = everyone makes mistakes.

simple_explanation: Any person at all, usually used in questions or negative sentences -- the same meaning as "anyone." "Anybody" is the more casual twin of "anyone" -- use it in questions ("Is anybody there?") or negatives ("I don't know anybody here").
example_2: I don't think anybody heard the announcement.
example_3: Can anybody explain this rule to me?
collocations: anybody else, hardly anybody, anybody home
where_it_s_used: Casual questions, negative statements, offers, phone calls
grammar_pattern: anybody + singular verb, often in questions/negatives (Does anybody want coffee? / I can't see anybody.)
common_mistake: Anybody are home right now?
correct_version: Is anybody home right now?
why_it_s_wrong: 'Anybody' takes a singular verb: 'Is anybody home?'
pronunciation_tip: Stress on the first syllable: EN-ee-buh-dee: /ˈenibədi/.
etymology: Formed from "any" + "body" in Middle English, using "body" in its older sense of "person"; used in questions, negatives, and conditionals.
mnemonic: ANY + BODY = any (unspecified) person at all.
memory_trick: ANY + BODY: one person.
visual_association: A hand knocking on a closed door with no answer.
emotion_feel: Neutral, sometimes urgent or worried in emergency contexts
difference_explained: Same meaning. Anybody is slightly more informal.
mini_conversation:
A: Is anybody home?
B: Just me -- everyone else is out.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character knocks loudly and shouts, 'Is anybody in there?'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Rescue workers called out to see if anybody was still trapped inside.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Does anybody have a charger I could borrow?'
mcq_options: A) Positive statements only  B) Questions and negative sentences  C) Formal writing only  D) Past tense only
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: I didn't recognize ______ at the reunion. → anybody
find_and_fix_to_correct: I didn't tell somebody about the surprise. → I didn't tell anybody about the surprise.
translate: क्या वहाँ कोई है? → Is anybody there?

usage_tip: 'Anybody there?' is a common call into an empty room.

simple_explanation: Up to a particular time; until. "Till" shows that something continues up to a certain point in time, then stops -- it's an informal way of saying "until."
example_2: The shop stays open till 9 PM.
example_3: She won't leave till the work is finished.
collocations: till now, till then, till late, wait till
where_it_s_used: Casual conversation, informal writing, everyday schedules
grammar_pattern: till + noun/clause (till Monday / till she arrives)
common_mistake: I will stay here till from Monday.
correct_version: I will stay here till Monday.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Till' takes its object directly; 'from' is not needed.
spelling_tip: Double "l" at the end -- don't confuse with "tilt," a different word.
etymology: From Old Norse "til," meaning "to" -- an older, informal variant of "until," commonly used in speech.
prefix_root_suffix: no clear prefix/root/suffix breakdown -- a short, ancient function word
word_family: until (formal synonym) -- "till" itself has no direct verb/noun forms
mnemonic: TILL sounds like a shorter "UNTIL" -- think of it as UNTIL with its front cut off.
memory_trick: TILL = until, informal.
visual_association: A countdown timer ticking down toward zero.
emotion_feel: Neutral, sometimes anticipation while waiting for something
difference_explained: Same meaning. Until is slightly more formal.
related_words: until, before, up to, so far
mini_conversation:
A: How long is the sale on?
B: It runs till the end of the month.
everyday_scene: Everyday: A character glances at a clock and says, "We've got till sunrise to figure this out."
news_style_line: News-style: "The exhibit will remain open till the end of next month, organizers confirmed."
casual_conversation: Casual: "Can you wait till I finish this call?"
mcq_options: A) Since  B) Until  C) Beyond  D) Because of
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: Let's stay at the party ______ ten o'clock. → till
find_and_fix_to_correct: She studied since midnight last night. → She studied till midnight last night. (use "till/until" for an endpoint, "since" for a starting point)
translate: हम आधी रात तक इंतज़ार करते रहे। → We waited till midnight.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence using 'till'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'up to a particular time; until'?
usage_tip: 'Till' is not short for 'until'; it's an old word. ''Til' is informal.

simple_explanation: Coins and notes, or the value you use to buy things.

simple_explanation: A unit of distance (about 1.6 km).

example_3: Miles away from home.
collocations: miles away, for miles, a mile long
grammar_pattern: a mile · plural miles
common_mistake: It is two mile far.
correct_version: It is two miles away.
why_it_s_wrong: More than one needs 'miles'; 'away' is more natural than 'far' here.
etymology: Latin 'mille' (thousand paces).
mnemonic: 'Meel' = mile.
memory_trick: MILE + STONE = MILESTONE (an important point).
visual_association: A road sign showing miles.
difference_explained: Mile = about 1.6 km. India uses kilometres; UK/US use miles.
mini_conversation: A: How far is the beach? / B: About a mile.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'I ran three miles today.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Traffic jams stretched for miles.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'You're miles better than me!' (= much better)
mcq_question: Choose: The village is five ___ away.
mcq_options: A) mile  B) miles  C) mileses  D) milestones
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: 'We walked for ___ in the hills.' → miles
find_and_fix_to_correct: It is 3 mile far only. → It's only three miles away.
translate: यहाँ से दो मील है। → It's two miles from here.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about a distance you often travel.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'a unit of distance (about 1.6 km)'?
usage_tip: 'Milestone' = an important step: 'Her first job was a milestone.'

simple_explanation: A device or system for listening to sound broadcasts.
example_1: I heard it on the radio.
example_2: Turn on the radio.
example_3: My grandfather listens to the radio every morning.
collocations: on the radio, radio station, FM radio
grammar_pattern: the radio · on the radio
common_mistake: I heard it in radio.
correct_version: I heard it on the radio.
why_it_s_wrong: Programmes are 'on the radio'.
etymology: Latin 'radius' (ray).
mnemonic: 'Radio' — same in Hindi!
memory_trick: ON THE RADIO, ON TV.
visual_association: An old radio.
difference_explained: Radio = sound only. TV = sound and pictures.
mini_conversation: A: Did you hear the news? / B: Yes, on the radio.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Mann ki Baat is on the radio every month.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'The radio station reached remote villages.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Turn up the radio, I love this song!'
mcq_question: Choose: I heard the song ___ the radio.
mcq_options: A) in  B) on  C) at  D) by
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: 'My dad listens to the ___ in the car.' → radio
find_and_fix_to_correct: I listen radio daily. → I listen to the radio every day.
translate: मैंने रेडियो पर सुना। → I heard it on the radio.
write_your_own_sentence: Write about a radio show you know.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'a device or system for listening to sound broadcasts'?
usage_tip: 'Listen TO the radio' — don't drop 'to'.

simple_explanation: A very stupid person (rude).
example_2: I felt like an idiot.
example_3: Some idiot parked in front of my gate.
collocations: total idiot, feel like an idiot
grammar_pattern: an idiot · plural idiots
common_mistake: He is a idiot.
correct_version: He is an idiot.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Idiot' starts with a vowel sound — 'an'.
etymology: Greek 'idiōtēs' (ordinary person).
mnemonic: 'Bewakoof' = idiot.
memory_trick: '3 Idiots' — the famous film!
visual_association: A person hitting their forehead.
difference_explained: Both rude. 'Idiot' is stronger.
mini_conversation: A: I locked my keys in the car. / B: I feel like such an idiot.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'I felt like an idiot when I fell.'
news_style_line: News-style: (not used in news)
casual_conversation: Casual: 'You idiot, I was joking!' (between friends)
mcq_options: A) a  B) an  C) the one  D) one
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: 'Don't be an ___ — wear your helmet!' → idiot
find_and_fix_to_correct: He is a idiot fellow. → He is an idiot.
translate: मैं बेवकूफ़ जैसा महसूस कर रहा था। → I felt like an idiot.
write_your_own_sentence: Write about a time you felt silly.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'a very stupid person (rude)'?
usage_tip: Use it for yourself ('I felt like an idiot'); calling others 'idiot' is rude.

simple_explanation: A round object used in games.
example_2: The ball went over the wall.
example_3: The ball is in your court.
collocations: throw a ball, catch a ball, football
grammar_pattern: a ball · plural balls
common_mistake: Catch the ball fastly.
correct_version: Catch the ball quickly.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Fastly' is not a word.
etymology: Old Norse 'böllr'.
mnemonic: 'Gend' = ball.
memory_trick: FOOT + BALL = FOOTBALL.
visual_association: A cricket ball.
difference_explained: Ball = solid, for games. Balloon = filled with air, for parties.
mini_conversation: A: Throw the ball! / B: Catch!
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'The kids broke the window with a ball.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'He hit the ball for six.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'The ball is in your court.' (= your turn to decide)
mcq_question: Choose: He kicked the ___ into the goal.
mcq_options: A) bat  B) ball  C) balloon  D) bowl
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: 'Throw me the ___, please.' → ball
find_and_fix_to_correct: I threw the bowl. (meaning ball) → I threw the ball.
translate: गेंद मुझे फेंको। → Throw me the ball.
write_your_own_sentence: Write about a game you play with a ball.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'a round object used in games'?
usage_tip: 'Have a ball' = have a great time.

simple_explanation: Thin material for writing; also a newspaper or an exam.
example_1: Write it on a piece of paper.
example_2: Did you read the paper today?
example_3: The maths paper was easy.
collocations: a piece of paper, newspaper, exam paper
grammar_pattern: paper (uncountable = material) · a paper (newspaper/exam)
common_mistake: Give me one paper. (meaning one sheet)
correct_version: Give me a sheet of paper. / a piece of paper.
why_it_s_wrong: For one sheet, say 'a sheet/piece of paper'.
etymology: Latin 'papyrus'.
mnemonic: 'Kaagaz' = paper.
memory_trick: NEWS + PAPER = NEWSPAPER.
visual_association: A stack of paper.
difference_explained: Material = uncountable. An exam or newspaper = countable (a paper).
mini_conversation: A: How was the paper? / B: Easy, except question 5!
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Recycle old paper.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'The paper printed the story on page one.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Paperwork is so boring!'
mcq_question: Choose: Can I have a ___ of paper?
mcq_options: A) peace  B) piece  C) pieces  D) paper
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: 'Our science ___ is tomorrow.' → paper
find_and_fix_to_correct: Give me two papers to write. → Give me two sheets of paper.
translate: कागज़ पर लिखो। → Write it on a piece of paper.
write_your_own_sentence: Write about an exam paper you found hard.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'thin material for writing; also a newspaper or an exam'?
usage_tip: 'On paper' = in theory: 'On paper, it looks good.'

simple_explanation: A metal piece that opens a lock; the most important part.
example_2: Hard work is the key to success.
example_3: Press any key.
collocations: car keys, house keys, the key to
grammar_pattern: a key · the key to + noun
word_forms: key – keys (also an adjective: key point)
common_mistake: The key of success is hard work.
correct_version: The key to success is hard work.
why_it_s_wrong: 'The key TO success', not 'of'.
etymology: Old English 'cǣg'.
mnemonic: 'Chaabi' = key.
memory_trick: KEY + BOARD = KEYBOARD.
visual_association: A bunch of keys.
difference_explained: Noun = opens a lock. Adjective = very important (a key point).
mini_conversation: A: Have you seen my keys? / B: On the fridge.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Don't forget the house keys.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Education is key to development.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Low-key, I'm excited!' (= a little)
mcq_question: Choose: Practice is the key ___ fluency.
mcq_options: A) of  B) to  C) for  D) in
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: 'I lost my car ___.' → keys
find_and_fix_to_correct: Where is the key of the door? → Where is the door key?
translate: मेरी चाबियाँ कहाँ हैं? → Where are my keys?
write_your_own_sentence: Write about the key to your success.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'a metal piece that opens a lock; the most important part'?
usage_tip: 'Key' as an adjective = very important: 'a key player'.

simple_explanation: A small vessel for travelling on water.
example_1: We went on a boat ride.
example_2: The fishermen took their boats out.
example_3: We're all in the same boat.
collocations: boat ride, by boat, fishing boat
grammar_pattern: a boat · by boat
common_mistake: We went in the boat to island.
correct_version: We went to the island by boat.
why_it_s_wrong: For transport, 'by boat' with no article.
etymology: Old English 'bāt'.
mnemonic: 'Naav' = boat.
memory_trick: HOUSE + BOAT = HOUSEBOAT (Kashmir, Kerala).
visual_association: A boat on a lake.
difference_explained: Boat = small. Ship = large, for the sea.
mini_conversation: A: Did you enjoy Kerala? / B: Yes, especially the boat ride!
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'We took a boat to Elephanta.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Rescue boats reached the flooded villages.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'We're all in the same boat.' (= same problem)
mcq_question: Choose: We crossed the river ___ boat.
mcq_options: A) by  B) in the  C) with  D) on a
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: 'The fisherman rowed his ___ to the shore.' → boat
find_and_fix_to_correct: We sat in boat for ride. → We went for a boat ride.
translate: हम नाव की सवारी पर गए। → We went on a boat ride.
write_your_own_sentence: Write about a boat ride you took or want to take.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'a small vessel for travelling on water'?
usage_tip: 'In the same boat' = in the same difficult situation.

simple_explanation: A yellow precious metal; also the colour.
example_1: This ring is made of gold.
example_2: Gold prices went up.
example_3: She won gold at the Olympics.
collocations: gold ring, gold medal, gold price
grammar_pattern: gold (uncountable) · (adjective) a gold ring
common_mistake: I bought a golden chain of gold.
correct_version: I bought a gold chain.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Gold chain' already says the material; 'golden' means gold-coloured.
etymology: Old English 'gold'.
mnemonic: 'Sona' = gold.
memory_trick: GOLD = metal. GOLDEN = gold-coloured or very special.
visual_association: A gold medal.
difference_explained: Gold = made of gold. Golden = gold-coloured, or wonderful (a golden chance).
mini_conversation: A: Is that real gold? / B: Yes, 22 carat.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Gold is costly this Diwali.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'India won three gold medals.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'You're pure gold, yaar!'
mcq_question: Choose: This is a ___ opportunity — don't miss it.
mcq_options: A) gold  B) golden  C) goldy  D) golds
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: 'She won ___ in the 100 m race.' → gold
find_and_fix_to_correct: I bought golds. → I bought some gold. / I bought gold jewellery.
translate: यह अंगूठी सोने की है। → This ring is made of gold.
write_your_own_sentence: Write about gold in Indian festivals.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'a yellow precious metal; also the colour'?
usage_tip: 'Heart of gold' = a very kind person.

simple_explanation: A place that serves drinks; a long piece of something; a block (a bar of chocolate).
example_1: Can I have a chocolate bar?
example_2: They met at a bar.
example_3: Hold the bar tightly.
collocations: chocolate bar, bar of soap, signal bars
grammar_pattern: a bar of + noun
common_mistake: Give me one chocolate. (meaning a whole bar)
correct_version: Give me a bar of chocolate. / Give me a chocolate bar.
why_it_s_wrong: 'A bar of' is the natural unit for chocolate and soap.
etymology: Old French 'barre'.
mnemonic: 'Bar' = chocolate bar / signal bar.
memory_trick: A BAR of chocolate, a BAR of soap.
visual_association: A chocolate bar.
difference_explained: Bar = a place for drinks (general). Pub = a British-style bar, often with food.
mini_conversation: A: My phone has only one bar. / B: The signal is bad here.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Buy a bar of soap, please.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'The court raised the bar for approval.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'This sets the bar high!' (= a high standard)
mcq_question: Choose: I bought a ___ of soap.
mcq_options: A) piece  B) bar  C) bars  D) bit
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: 'Can I have a chocolate ___?' → bar
find_and_fix_to_correct: Give me one soap. → Give me a bar of soap.
translate: एक चॉकलेट बार दो। → Give me a chocolate bar.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence with 'a bar of'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'a place that serves drinks; a long piece of something; a block (a bar of chocolate)'?
usage_tip: 'Raise the bar' = set a higher standard.

simple_explanation: An animal that lives in water; its meat as food.
example_2: There are many fish in the river.
example_3: Let's go fishing.
collocations: fish curry, go fishing, fresh fish
grammar_pattern: a fish · plural fish (usually)
common_mistake: I saw many fishes in the pond.
correct_version: I saw a lot of fish in the pond.
why_it_s_wrong: The usual plural of 'fish' is 'fish'.
etymology: Old English 'fisc'.
mnemonic: 'Machhli' = fish.
memory_trick: ONE fish, TWO fish — same word.
visual_association: Fish swimming in a pond.
difference_explained: Fish = normal plural. Fishes = different types of fish (rare).
mini_conversation: A: Veg or non-veg? / B: Non-veg — fish curry, please.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Bengalis love fish.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Thousands of dead fish were found in the lake.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Like a fish out of water!' (= uncomfortable)
mcq_question: Choose: There are ten ___ in the tank.
mcq_options: A) fishes  B) fish  C) fishs  D) fish's
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: 'We go ___ on Sundays.' → fishing
find_and_fix_to_correct: He caught three fishes. → He caught three fish.
translate: मैं मछली नहीं खाता। → I don't eat fish.
write_your_own_sentence: Write about fish as food or a pet.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'an animal that lives in water; its meat as food'?
usage_tip: 'A fish out of water' = someone in an unfamiliar place.

simple_explanation: Something bad that happens by chance, like a crash.
example_1: There was an accident on the highway.
example_2: Sorry, it was an accident.
example_3: I met with an accident.
collocations: road accident, by accident, have an accident
grammar_pattern: an accident · by accident
common_mistake: I met an accident yesterday.
correct_version: I had an accident yesterday.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Met with an accident' is Indian English; 'had an accident' is common abroad.
etymology: Latin 'accidens'.
mnemonic: 'Durghatna' = accident.
memory_trick: BY ACCIDENT = not on purpose.
visual_association: A car with a dent.
difference_explained: Accident = unplanned, often with damage. Incident = any event (often unpleasant).
mini_conversation: A: Why is the road blocked? / B: There's been an accident.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Drive slowly to avoid accidents.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Three people were hurt in a road accident.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Sorry, total accident!'
mcq_question: Choose: He had ___ accident on the way home.
mcq_options: A) a  B) an  C) the one  D) one
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: 'I broke the glass by ___.' → accident
find_and_fix_to_correct: He met an accident. → He had an accident.
translate: हाईवे पर दुर्घटना हुई। → There was an accident on the highway.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a road-safety tip to avoid accidents.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'something bad that happens by chance, like a crash'?
usage_tip: 'By accident' = without meaning to.

simple_explanation: The group of people who run a country or state.
example_2: She has a government job.
example_3: Which party is in government?
collocations: central government, state government, government job
grammar_pattern: the government
common_mistake: Government has given holiday.
correct_version: The government has declared a holiday.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Government' needs 'the'.
etymology: Latin 'gubernare' (to steer).
mnemonic: 'Sarkaar' = government.
memory_trick: GOVERN + MENT = GOVERNMENT (don't drop the N).
visual_association: A parliament building.
difference_explained: Government = the whole group. Governor = the head of a state (in India).
mini_conversation: A: Why is the office closed? / B: The government declared a holiday.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'My father has a government job.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'The state government will build 500 schools.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Blame the government!'
mcq_question: Choose: ___ has raised the price of petrol.
mcq_options: A) Government  B) The government  C) A government  D) Governments
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: 'The ___ is building a new highway.' → government
find_and_fix_to_correct: Goverment gave us free books. → The government gave us free books.
translate: सरकार ने नए नियम घोषित किए। → The government announced new rules.
write_your_own_sentence: Write about one thing the government should do.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'the group of people who run a country or state'?
usage_tip: Common spelling mistake: 'goverment' (missing N).

simple_explanation: A bright point in the night sky; a famous person.
example_2: She's a film star.
example_3: The hotel has five stars.
collocations: film star, five-star, shooting star
grammar_pattern: a star · plural stars
word_forms: star – stars (also a verb: to star in a film)
common_mistake: He is hero star of the film.
correct_version: He is the star of the film.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Star' already means the main actor.
etymology: Old English 'steorra'.
mnemonic: 'Taara' = star.
memory_trick: SUPER + STAR = SUPERSTAR.
visual_association: A night sky full of stars.
difference_explained: Star = famous actor or player (also in the sky). Celebrity = any famous person.
mini_conversation: A: Who's in the film? / B: A big star from the South.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'We saw thousands of stars in Ladakh.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'The star player was injured.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'You're a star, thanks!' (= very helpful)
mcq_question: Choose: Shah Rukh Khan is a film ___.
mcq_options: A) stars  B) star  C) starry  D) starring
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: 'On a clear night you can see many ___.' → stars
find_and_fix_to_correct: She acted as star in the film. → She starred in the film.
translate: आसमान में तारे देखो! → Look at the stars!
write_your_own_sentence: Write about your favourite film star or a starry night.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'a bright point in the night sky; a famous person'?
usage_tip: 'You're a star!' = you're very kind or helpful.

simple_explanation: The large area of salt water that covers much of the Earth.
example_2: The sea is calm today.
example_3: They live by the sea.
collocations: by the sea, at sea, sea level
grammar_pattern: the sea
common_mistake: We went to sea beach.
correct_version: We went to the beach. / We went to the seaside.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Sea beach' is Indian English; 'beach' already means by the sea.
etymology: Old English 'sǣ'.
mnemonic: 'Samundar' = sea.
memory_trick: SEA + FOOD = SEAFOOD.
visual_association: Waves on a sea.
difference_explained: Sea = smaller, near land. Ocean = very large (Indian Ocean).
mini_conversation: A: Where's your hotel? / B: Right by the sea!
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'The sea is rough during monsoon.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Fishermen were told not to go to sea.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Sea breeze, bliss!'
mcq_question: Choose: We love holidays by the ___.
mcq_options: A) see  B) sea  C) seas  D) ocean's
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: 'The ship sailed across the ___.' → sea
find_and_fix_to_correct: We went to Juhu sea beach. → We went to Juhu Beach.
translate: हम समुद्र में तैरे। → We swam in the sea.
write_your_own_sentence: Write about a day at the sea.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'the large area of salt water that covers much of the Earth'?
usage_tip: 'At sea' = on a ship, or confused.

simple_explanation: Something difficult that needs to be fixed.
example_2: We have a small problem.
example_3: Solve this maths problem.
collocations: big problem, solve a problem, no problem
grammar_pattern: a problem · plural problems
common_mistake: I am having one problem.
correct_version: I have a problem.
why_it_s_wrong: Use 'a', and the simple present for 'have' (possession).

mnemonic: 'Samasya' = problem.
memory_trick: NO PROBLEM = it's okay.
visual_association: A person stuck with a puzzle.
difference_explained: Problem = countable (a problem). Trouble = usually uncountable.
mini_conversation: A: What's the problem? / B: My laptop won't start.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Traffic is a big problem here.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'The water problem will be fixed by May.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Not my problem!'
mcq_question: Choose: Can you help me solve this ___?
mcq_options: A) problems  B) problem  C) problematic  D) probe
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: 'We have a small ___ with the booking.' → problem
find_and_fix_to_correct: I am having many problems in this. → I have a lot of problems with this.
translate: समस्या क्या है? → What's the problem?
write_your_own_sentence: Write about a problem you solved.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'something difficult that needs to be fixed'?
usage_tip: 'No problem' is a friendly reply to 'thank you' (see INT-018).

simple_explanation: A person, often a police officer, who finds out who did a crime.
example_2: I love detective stories.
example_3: She hired a private detective.

grammar_pattern: a detective · plural detectives
common_mistake: Byomkesh is a famous jasoos detective.
correct_version: Byomkesh is a famous detective.
why_it_s_wrong: Use one word — 'detective'.

mnemonic: 'Jaasoos' = detective.
memory_trick: DETECT (find) → DETECTIVE (finder).
visual_association: A person with a magnifying glass.
difference_explained: Detective = investigates crimes. Police officer = any officer.
mini_conversation: A: What are you reading? / B: A Sherlock Holmes detective story.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'My son wants to be a detective.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Detectives are questioning two suspects.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Okay, detective, who ate my chocolate?'
mcq_question: Choose: Sherlock Holmes is a famous ___.
mcq_options: A) detect  B) detective  C) detection  D) detected
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: 'The ___ found the missing necklace.' → detective
find_and_fix_to_correct: He did detective of the case. → He investigated the case.
translate: जासूस ने केस सुलझा लिया। → The detective solved the case.
write_your_own_sentence: Write about a famous detective you know.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'a person, often a police officer, who finds out who did a crime'?
usage_tip: 'Private detective' = one you hire and pay yourself.

simple_explanation: A building where criminals are kept.
example_1: He went to prison for five years.
example_2: He escaped from prison.

simple_explanation: A small piece of stiff paper or plastic; a greeting card.
example_2: She sent me a birthday card.
example_3: Let's play cards.
collocations: credit card, birthday card, ID card, play cards
grammar_pattern: a card · pay by card
common_mistake: Can I pay from card?
correct_version: Can I pay by card?
why_it_s_wrong: 'Pay BY card'.
etymology: Latin 'charta' (paper).
mnemonic: 'Card' — same in Hindi!
memory_trick: PAY BY CARD, PAY IN CASH.
visual_association: A debit card.
difference_explained: Same word — plastic card for money, or paper card for wishes.
mini_conversation: A: Cash or card? / B: Card, please.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Show your ID card at the gate.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Card payments rose by 20%.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Let's play cards tonight!'
mcq_options: A) from  B) by  C) with the  D) through a
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: 'I got a lovely birthday ___.' → card
find_and_fix_to_correct: Swipe card from here. → Swipe your card here.
translate: क्या मैं कार्ड से पेमेंट कर सकता हूँ? → Can I pay by card?
write_your_own_sentence: Write about the cards in your wallet.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'a small piece of stiff paper or plastic; a greeting card'?
usage_tip: 'On the cards' = likely to happen.

simple_explanation: A girl or woman someone is in a romantic relationship with; (for women) a female friend.
example_2: This is my girlfriend, Priya.
example_3: She went out with her girlfriends.
collocations: my girlfriend, ex-girlfriend
grammar_pattern: a girlfriend · plural girlfriends
common_mistake: She is my girlfriend. (said by a boy, meaning just a friend)
correct_version: She is my friend.
why_it_s_wrong: For a boy, 'girlfriend' means romantic partner — use 'friend' for a friend.
etymology: girl + friend.
mnemonic: 'Premika' = girlfriend.
memory_trick: GIRL + FRIEND = GIRLFRIEND (one word).
visual_association: A couple holding hands.
difference_explained: Girlfriend (for a man) = romantic. Friend = no romance.
mini_conversation: A: Is that your girlfriend? / B: No, just a friend!
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'He's taking his girlfriend to dinner.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'The actor was seen with his girlfriend.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Girls' night out with my girlfriends!'
mcq_question: Choose: A romantic partner who is a girl is a ___.
mcq_options: A) girl friend  B) girlfriend  C) girls friend  D) friend girl
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: 'He introduced me to his ___.' → girlfriend
find_and_fix_to_correct: She is my girl friend from school. (meaning just a friend) → She is my friend from school.
translate: यह मेरी गर्लफ़्रेंड प्रिया है। → This is my girlfriend, Priya.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence using 'boyfriend' or 'girlfriend' correctly.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'a girl or woman someone is in a romantic relationship with; (for women) a female friend'?
usage_tip: Women often call their female friends 'girlfriends' — no romance meant.

simple_explanation: An opening in a wall with glass, to let in light and air.
example_2: I want a window seat.
example_3: Close all the windows on your screen.
collocations: open the window, window seat, shop window
grammar_pattern: a window · plural windows
common_mistake: Open the window glass.
correct_version: Open the window.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Window' already includes the glass.
etymology: Old Norse 'vindauga' (wind eye).
mnemonic: 'Khidki' = window.
memory_trick: WIND + OW = WINDOW (a hole for the wind!).
visual_association: A window with curtains.
difference_explained: Window = look through, let air in. Door = walk through.
mini_conversation: A: It's hot in here. / B: Let me open the window.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'I always ask for a window seat.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Windows broke in the storm.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'I'm just window shopping!' (= looking, not buying)
mcq_question: Choose: Can I have a ___ seat, please?
mcq_options: A) windows  B) window  C) widow  D) wind
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: 'Please close the ___, it's raining.' → window
find_and_fix_to_correct: Close the window's door. → Close the window.
translate: खिड़की खोलो। → Open the window.
write_your_own_sentence: Write about the view from your window.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'an opening in a wall with glass, to let in light and air'?
usage_tip: 'Window shopping' = looking in shops without buying.

simple_explanation: The way people or groups are connected; a romantic partnership.
example_2: Are you in a relationship?
example_3: The two countries have a strong relationship.
collocations: good relationship, in a relationship, relationship with
grammar_pattern: a relationship with + person
common_mistake: He is my relation. (meaning relative)
correct_version: He is my relative.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Relation' for a family member is old; 'relative' is common.
etymology: relation + -ship.
mnemonic: 'Rishta' = relationship.
memory_trick: RELATION + SHIP = RELATIONSHIP.
visual_association: Two linked hands.
difference_explained: Relationship = the connection. Relative = a family member.
mini_conversation: A: How's your relationship with your boss? / B: Pretty good, actually.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Trust is important in any relationship.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'India and Japan have a strong relationship.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Relationship status: it's complicated!'
mcq_question: Choose: I have a good ___ with my neighbours.
mcq_options: A) relative  B) relationship  C) relation's  D) related
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: 'Are you in a ___?' → relationship
find_and_fix_to_correct: He is my close relation. → He is my close relative.
translate: हमारा अच्छा रिश्ता है। → We have a good relationship.
write_your_own_sentence: Write about a good relationship in your life.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'the way people or groups are connected; a romantic partnership'?
usage_tip: 'Relationship with' + person: 'my relationship with my sister'.

simple_explanation: A side of a room or building; a structure around a place.
example_1: Hang the picture on the wall.
example_2: The wall needs painting.
example_3: There's a wall around the school.
collocations: on the wall, wall clock, brick wall
grammar_pattern: a wall · on the wall
common_mistake: Stick the poster in the wall.
correct_version: Stick the poster on the wall.
why_it_s_wrong: Things hang 'on' a wall.
etymology: Latin 'vallum'.
mnemonic: 'Deewar' = wall.
memory_trick: WALL + PAPER = WALLPAPER.
visual_association: A clock on a wall.
difference_explained: Wall = solid, brick or stone. Fence = wood or wire.
mini_conversation: A: Where should I put the clock? / B: On that wall.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Don't write on the walls!'
news_style_line: News-style: 'A wall collapsed after heavy rain.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'It's like talking to a wall!' (= nobody listens)
mcq_question: Choose: The painting is ___ the wall.
mcq_options: A) in  B) on  C) at  D) over to
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: 'The ___ of my room is blue.' → wall
find_and_fix_to_correct: Hang the photo in wall. → Hang the photo on the wall.
translate: तस्वीर दीवार पर टाँगो। → Hang the picture on the wall.
write_your_own_sentence: Describe the walls of your room.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'a side of a room or building; a structure around a place'?
usage_tip: 'Walls have ears' = be careful, someone may be listening.

simple_explanation: A place to sit.
example_2: Please take a seat.
example_3: I booked two seats.
collocations: take a seat, window seat, front seat
grammar_pattern: a seat · take a seat
common_mistake: Please seat.
correct_version: Please sit. / Please take a seat.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Seat' is a noun; the verb is 'sit' (or formal 'be seated').
etymology: Old Norse 'sæti'.
mnemonic: 'Seat' — same in Hindi!
memory_trick: TAKE A SEAT = sit down (polite).
visual_association: An empty cinema seat.
difference_explained: Seat = noun (a seat). Sit = verb (sit here).
mini_conversation: A: Is anyone sitting here? / B: No, the seat is free.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Wear your seatbelt.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'The party won 40 seats.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Grab a seat, I'll get the popcorn!'
mcq_options: A) the  B) a  C) an  D) one of
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: 'I booked a window ___ on the train.' → seat
find_and_fix_to_correct: Please seat here. → Please sit here. / Please take a seat.
translate: कृपया बैठ जाइए। → Please take a seat.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a polite sentence offering someone a seat.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'a place to sit'?
usage_tip: In elections, 'seats' = places won in Parliament.

simple_explanation: The place where something is; a job; a situation.
example_1: I applied for the position of manager.
example_2: Stay in this position.
example_3: I'm not in a position to help.
collocations: job position, first position, in a position to
grammar_pattern: a position · the position of
common_mistake: He got first rank position.
correct_version: He came first in class.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Came first' is more natural than 'got first position/rank'.
etymology: Latin 'positio'.
mnemonic: 'Pad / sthaan' = position.
memory_trick: IN A POSITION TO = able to.
visual_association: A chess piece on a board.
difference_explained: Both mean a job. 'Position' is more common in job ads.
mini_conversation: A: What job did you apply for? / B: The position of sales manager.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Sit in a comfortable position.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'India is in a strong position after day two.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'I'm in no position to lend money!'
mcq_question: Choose: I'm not ___ a position to decide.
mcq_options: A) on  B) in  C) at  D) by
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: 'She applied for the ___ of teacher.' → position
find_and_fix_to_correct: He got first rank position in exam. → He came first in the exam.
translate: मैंने मैनेजर के पद के लिए आवेदन किया। → I applied for the position of manager.
write_your_own_sentence: Write about a job position you'd like.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'the place where something is; a job; a situation'?
usage_tip: 'In a position to' = able to (often formal).

simple_explanation: An officer rank in the army, navy or police.
example_1: He's a lieutenant in the army.
example_2: Lieutenant Singh reported for duty.
example_3: The lieutenant gave the order.
collocations: army lieutenant, Lieutenant + name
grammar_pattern: a lieutenant · Lieutenant + name
common_mistake: He is left-tenant in army.
correct_version: He is a lieutenant in the army.
why_it_s_wrong: Spell it L-I-E-U: the sound 'lef' is not how it's written.
etymology: French 'lieu tenant' (place holder).
mnemonic: 'Lieutenant' — Hindi mein bhi yahi!
memory_trick: LIEU-TENANT = holds the place of a senior officer.
visual_association: An army officer with shoulder badges.
difference_explained: Lieutenant is a lower rank than captain in the army.
mini_conversation: A: What rank is your brother? / B: He's a lieutenant.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'My cousin became a lieutenant this year.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'Lt Sharma led the rescue team.'
casual_conversation: Casual: (usually not used casually)
mcq_question: Choose: The short form of 'lieutenant' is ___.
mcq_options: A) Lnt  B) Lt  C) Lieu  D) Ltn
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: 'He joined the army as a ___.' → lieutenant
find_and_fix_to_correct: He is lieutinant in navy. → He is a lieutenant in the navy.
translate: वह सेना में लेफ़्टिनेंट है। → He's a lieutenant in the army.
write_your_own_sentence: Write a sentence about an army rank.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'an officer rank in the army, navy or police'?
usage_tip: The spelling doesn't match the sound — learn it by sight.

simple_explanation: A device with moving parts that does work.
example_2: Put money in the machine.
example_3: This machine makes ice.
collocations: washing machine, coffee machine, ATM machine
grammar_pattern: a machine · plural machines
common_mistake: Withdraw money from ATM machine.
correct_version: Withdraw money from the ATM.
why_it_s_wrong: 'ATM' already contains 'machine' (Automated Teller Machine).
etymology: French 'machine'.
mnemonic: 'Mashin / yantra' = machine.
memory_trick: MACHINE — CH sounds SH, like 'chef'.
visual_association: A washing machine.
difference_explained: Machine = one (countable). Machinery = machines in general (uncountable).
mini_conversation: A: Why are the clothes still dirty? / B: The washing machine stopped.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'The ticket machine takes only coins.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'New machines will make the factory faster.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'He's a machine — works non-stop!'
mcq_question: Choose: We need to fix the washing ___.
mcq_options: A) machinery  B) machine  C) machines of  D) mashine
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: 'Put the clothes in the washing ___.' → machine
find_and_fix_to_correct: The ATM machine is not working. → The ATM is not working.
translate: वॉशिंग मशीन खराब है। → The washing machine is broken.
write_your_own_sentence: Write about a machine you use every day.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'a device with moving parts that does work'?
usage_tip: 'Machinery' (uncountable) = all the machines in a place.

simple_explanation: Painting, drawing, music and other creative work.
example_2: She's good at art.
example_3: The museum has modern art.
collocations: art class, work of art, modern art
grammar_pattern: art (uncountable) · the arts
common_mistake: I am studying in arts line.
correct_version: I am studying arts. / I'm an arts student.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Arts line/stream' is Indian English; 'studying arts' is enough.
etymology: Latin 'ars'.
mnemonic: 'Kala' = art.
memory_trick: ART → ARTIST (the person).
visual_association: A painter at an easel.
difference_explained: Art = creative expression. Craft = making useful or decorative things by hand.
mini_conversation: A: What's your favourite subject? / B: Art — I love painting.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'Our art teacher is very kind.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'The art show opens this weekend.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Cooking is an art!'
mcq_options: A) in  B) at  C) on  D) with
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: 'We saw beautiful ___ at the museum.' → art
find_and_fix_to_correct: He is in arts line. → He is studying arts.
translate: मुझे कला पसंद है। → I love art.
write_your_own_sentence: Write about a piece of art you like.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'painting, drawing, music and other creative work'?
usage_tip: 'The arts' = music, theatre, painting and so on.

simple_explanation: A feeling of happiness; used in polite replies.
example_1: It's a pleasure to meet you.
example_2: 'Thank you!' 'My pleasure.'
example_3: Reading is my greatest pleasure.
collocations: my pleasure, with pleasure, a pleasure
grammar_pattern: a pleasure · with pleasure
common_mistake: It is my pleasure to meet with you.
correct_version: It's a pleasure to meet you.
why_it_s_wrong: 'Meet' takes the person directly.
etymology: Old French 'plaisir'.
mnemonic: 'Khushi' = pleasure.
memory_trick: MY PLEASURE = warm 'you're welcome'.
visual_association: A person smiling while reading.
difference_explained: Pleasure = noun (a pleasure). Please = the polite word or verb.
mini_conversation: A: Thank you so much for dinner. / B: My pleasure!
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'It was a pleasure working with you.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'The minister said it was a pleasure to visit.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'With pleasure!' (= happily yes)
mcq_options: A) My pleasure  B) Pleased  C) Please  D) Pleasant
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: 'It's a ___ to meet you.' → pleasure
find_and_fix_to_correct: It was my pleasure meeting to you. → It was a pleasure meeting you.
translate: आपसे मिलकर ख़ुशी हुई। → It's a pleasure to meet you.
write_your_own_sentence: Write two polite replies using 'pleasure'.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'a feeling of happiness; used in polite replies'?
usage_tip: 'With pleasure' = yes, happily.

simple_explanation: The language of the UK, the US and many other countries.
example_2: My English is getting better.
example_3: English is a global language.
collocations: speak English, learn English, in English
grammar_pattern: English (no 'the') · (adjective) English food
common_mistake: My english is weak.
correct_version: My English is weak.
why_it_s_wrong: Language names always start with a capital letter.
etymology: Old English 'Englisc'.
mnemonic: 'Angrezi' = English.
memory_trick: ENGLISH — always a capital E, like HINDI.
visual_association: A person speaking with a speech bubble 'Hello!'.
difference_explained: English = the language, or from England. British = from the UK (England, Scotland, Wales, N. Ireland).
mini_conversation: A: How long have you been learning English? / B: About a year.
everyday_scene: Everyday: 'I watch English films with subtitles.'
news_style_line: News-style: 'More students are learning English online.'
casual_conversation: Casual: 'Say it in English, please!'
mcq_options: A) in  B) on  C) at  D) with
fill_in_the_blank_to_answer: 'I want to improve my ___.' → English
find_and_fix_to_correct: I am weak in english. → My English is weak. / I'm not good at English.
translate: क्या आप अंग्रेज़ी बोलते हैं? → Do you speak English?
write_your_own_sentence: Write about why you are learning English.
spaced_repetition_plan: Day 1 learn → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 14 → Day 30 review
reverse_quick_recall: Which word means 'the language of the UK, the US and many other countries'?
usage_tip: Say 'speak English' (no 'in') or 'say it in English'.
